approach_variants.name: Cold Springs, then west around onto the southwest flank
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cold Springs trailhead, work around onto the mountain's southwest flank using the Round the Mountain trail system, and approach the glacier from below.

The climb is a gently sloping glacier ascent of the Avalanche and White Salmon glaciers, mostly moderate to steep snow to about 40 degrees, simul-climbable, with occasional ice work where the White Salmon has broken up. A steeper headwall variation exists where the two glaciers merge and can be alpine ice late in the season.

Descent is south via the South Spur snowfields, or the snowfield beside the Avalanche and White Salmon glaciers, back toward the Morrison Creek and Cold Springs approach, glissading where conditions allow — so this is a loop off one trailhead rather than an out-and-back.

Forest roads to Cold Springs and Morrison Creek are gravel and open as snow clears.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul; crevasse hazard grows through the season as the glaciers open up
hazards: Crevasse hazard that increases through the season as the glacier opens up
Alpine ice at the merge headwall late in the season, on a route otherwise climbed with one axe
Genuine glacier travel on a flank that sees very little traffic, so no track and no other parties
A long contour off the standard route with route-finding on the way round
Seasonal gravel road access
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE SOUTH SPUR YOU ARE ON, AND IT IS A DECISION MADE LOW.

From Cold Springs the standard South Climb goes up the SOUTH SPUR to the Lunch Counter at about 9,300 ft. This route leaves that line and works WEST, round onto the southwest flank, to the Avalanche and White Salmon glaciers. IF THE LUNCH COUNTER IS STILL AHEAD OF YOU OR ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE NOT LEFT THE STANDARD ROUTE.

THE NEGATIVE HERE INVERTS THE USUAL INSTINCT AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE MARKER: YOU SHOULD MEET ALMOST NOBODY. The South Spur is the most-travelled route on this mountain and carries a trench and camps most of the season. This flank sees a fraction of that traffic. A boot pack underfoot is evidence you are still on the South Climb, not evidence you are on route.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A JUNCTION OF TWO GLACIERS: the Avalanche and the White Salmon MERGE, and the headwall at that merge is the steeper variation. A single unbroken snow slope with no second glacier joining it is not the base — keep contouring.

THE CONDITION TEST DECIDES WHICH CLIMB YOU GET: the merge headwall is snow early and can break out into alpine ice late, which is why a spare tool and a couple of screws are worth carrying even though most of the route is a walk. If it is bare ice and you brought one axe, that is a finding about the day, not about the route.

WHAT COMING BACK LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS WHY THIS DOES NOT NEED A SHUTTLE: you descend SOUTH off the summit onto the South Spur snowfields and back toward the same trailhead. Reversing the ascent line is not the plan.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek and High Camp, then the north-facing slope below the Adams Glacier terminus
approach_variants.notes:
Forest roads from the Takhlakh Lake area to the Killen Creek trailhead, then Killen Creek Trail #113 to the PCT junction and High Camp Trail #10 to the meadow camp at about 6,900 ft.

From camp, gain the north-facing slope that sits between the Adams Glacier and the crest of the Northwest Ridge. The line deliberately gains access BELOW the Adams Glacier terminus to avoid its crevasses and moats, then follows steepening 40 to 45 degree neve past a narrow rock-band pinch to the ridge crest near 10,000 ft and on to the summit.

The ridge crest itself is avoided on purpose: the rock on it is poor.

Descent is along the North Ridge back to the Adams Glacier basin high camp, or in ski conditions the route itself can be reversed, threading the same rock-band pinch.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul, on neve
hazards: A terrain trap between cliff bands with limited escape once committed mid-route
A narrow rock-band pinch that tightens to AI2-3 in low-snow years
Crevasse and moat hazard where the route gains ground below the Adams Glacier terminus
Poor rock on the adjacent ridge crest, which is why the line avoids it
Sustained 40-45 degree neve with a running belay the only practical protection
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS THE GROUND BETWEEN TWO THINGS, SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU HAVE ONE ON EACH SIDE.

AS YOU CLIMB, THE ADAMS GLACIER SHOULD BE ON YOUR LEFT AND THE CREST OF THE NORTHWEST RIDGE ON YOUR RIGHT. If both are on the same side of you, you are on one of them rather than between them, and you are not on this route.

THE ROCK IS THE NEGATIVE ON ONE SIDE, AND IT IS TACTILE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT AT NIGHT: this line stays OFF the crest because the crest's rock is poor. If you are pulling on loose blocky rock instead of kicking steps in neve, you have drifted right onto the ridge.

THE CREVASSES ARE THE NEGATIVE ON THE OTHER SIDE: the route gains its ground BELOW the Adams Glacier terminus specifically so it does not have to deal with the glacier's crevasses and moats. If you are stepping across crevasses, you are too far left and on the Adams Glacier route, which is a different and harder climb.

THE POSITIVE, AND IT IS COUNTABLE: ONE CONSTRICTION. A narrow pinch through a rock band, ski-width or body-width, is the crux and the only place the route squeezes. If you have climbed a couple of thousand feet of 40 to 45 degree neve and met no constriction, the pinch is still above you and you are on route. If you met a constriction in the first rope length, you are somewhere else.

WHAT THE PINCH MEANS FOR CONDITIONS: it gets tighter in a low-snow year, which is when it becomes the AI2-3 crux rather than a step. It is also a terrain trap — you are between cliff bands there with limited escape, so decide about it from below rather than at it.

TOP-OUT CHECK: the route joins the NORTHWEST RIDGE CREST near 10,000 ft. Gaining a crest at that height is correct; gaining one much lower means you climbed onto the ridge early instead of past it.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and lower Ptarmigan Ridge, then 1,000 ft down to the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Wonderland Trail from Mowich Lake about 4 miles to Spray Park, then the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge. At about 8,300 ft the route DESCENDS roughly 1,000 ft onto the North Mowich Glacier and crosses to the base of the face.

There are two lines from about 12,500 ft. The original variation cuts LEFT into an hourglass of snow, ice and rock, gaining a ledge that leads to a 40-50 degree ramp to the top. The harder variation cuts RIGHT through a couple of AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow to the same high point.

Mowich Lake has had no public road access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently in April 2025; reaching it now means a long walk in from another park entrance.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug
hazards: Ice steps and steep snow with rockfall exposure
A 1,000 ft descent onto the glacier on the approach, which must be reclimbed if you retreat
Remote approach with limited bailout options
Crevasses on the North Mowich crossing
No road access on this side of the park since the April 2025 Fairfax Bridge closure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST THING TO GET RIGHT IS THAT YOU LOSE A THOUSAND FEET ON THE WAY IN. At about 8,300 ft on lower Ptarmigan Ridge you stop climbing and drop onto the North Mowich Glacier. A party that keeps gaining height is on Ptarmigan Ridge, not on this face, and will not find out for hours.

FOUR CLIMBS COME OFF THIS WALL AND THEY ARE SEPARATED BY WHERE THE STEEP GROUND IS, NOT BY THE WALK IN.

THE POSITIVE TEST FOR THIS ROUTE IS AN ABSENCE, WHICH IS UNUSUAL BUT IT IS THE RELIABLE ONE HERE: THERE IS NO CONSTRICTION LOW DOWN. You cross the schrund and climb open face. The hourglass on this route is HIGH — around 12,500 ft — not at the bottom. So if your first 50 ft above the schrund is a steep pinch of mixed rock and ice, you are on the North Mowich Headwall and you crossed too far round.

THE ROCK BAND SETTLES IT DEFINITIVELY, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE THE TWO LINES BEHAVE OPPOSITELY. On this face, at the rock band you can TRAVERSE RIGHT SEVERAL HUNDRED FEET AND SKIRT THE BAND ENTIRELY. On the North Mowich Headwall you cannot: you have to clear the band, at 5th class in a lean year. If the band in front of you has to be climbed rather than walked around, you are one line over.

SCHRUND CHECK: the bergschrund under the central face has been passed by a bypass through a rock band on climber's LEFT. If the only way across in front of you is beside a pair of twin gendarmes, that is the Edmunds Headwall's schrund and you are further round the mountain than you meant to be.

CHOOSE YOUR VARIATION BEFORE 12,500 FT, NOT AT IT. Left is the original: an hourglass, a ledge, a 40-50 degree ramp. Right is harder: AI2-3 ice steps and four to six pitches of 50-60 degree snow. They rejoin, but you cannot swap once you are on one.

access.fees: $82 per person, per climb — Climbing Cost Recovery Fee (2026 rate). Each climb needs its own fee; it no longer covers a whole calendar year. Separate from the park entrance fee.
access.notes: $82 climbing fee per person, per climb (Pay.gov), $12 wilderness permit per person/night (May 1-Sept 15). Mount Rainier National Park requires backcountry permit. CRITICAL: Mowich Lake Road is CLOSED — WSDOT permanently closed the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge on April 22, 2025, and the park's road-status page (updated September 18, 2026) lists no public access to Mowich Lake from SR 165. When open: mid-July to mid-October. Helmet and rescue gear essential. Permit advance planning required via Recreation.gov.
access.rules: Blue bags required for human waste above high camp — pack out and deposit only in barrels marked "Human Waste" at Camp Muir or the trailhead; do not cache on-route. Check-out is required after every climb.
access.permit: Climbing permit (the permit itself is free, but each climber must pay the climbing cost recovery fee first)
access.closures: SR 165 Fairfax Bridge permanently closed (April 2025) — no vehicle access to the Mowich Lake trailhead until further notice
access.landManager: National Park Service - Mount Rainier National Park
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: Climbing Cost Recovery Fee ($82 per person, per climb) plus the park entrance pass

overnight_permit.what: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, plus climbing registration (fee) above 10,000 ft or on glaciers
overnight_permit.where: Reserve a wilderness permit in advance and pay the climbing fee online, then register at a park wilderness information center before the climb; about half of each camp is held for walk-ups.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the bivy between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Mowich Face approach and is shared with three other climbs: Mowich Lake, the Wonderland Trail through Spray Park, then cross-country southeast between Echo Rock and Observation Rock onto the climbers' path up lower Ptarmigan Ridge.

The bivouac for this route sits at roughly 9,600 to 10,000 ft on the divide BETWEEN the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers. Two days to reach it is the normal plan rather than a cautious one.

From the bivy the climbing starts almost at once. Above the hourglass, roughly 2,000 ft of about 45-degree snow leads to a rock band; the documented way through is to look for an arch in the rock on the right, traverse left, then work back right to gain the ice cap. In a low-snow year that band can demand unprotected loose 5th-class climbing, which is the part of this route that changes most from season to season.

Mowich Lake has had no public road access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently in April 2025; reaching it now means a long walk in from another park entrance.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, climbed early in the day for rockfall
hazards: A rock band crux that can require unprotected loose 5th-class climbing in low-snow years
Sustained steep ice with rockfall exposure — climb it early
Crevasses and avalanche debris on the glacier crossing out of camp
Remote position, two-day approach, and no quick retreat from high on the face
No road access on this side of the park since the April 2025 Fairfax Bridge closure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FOUR CLIMBS SHARE THIS WALL AND THIS CAMP. From the divide bivy the discriminator is WHICH GLACIER YOU CROSS AND WHERE THE HOURGLASS IS.

THE POSITIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE STRONG ONE: THIS ROUTE'S HOURGLASS IS LOW. Within 40 to 50 ft of leaving the bivy you should be in a STEEP CONSTRICTION OF MIXED ROCK AND ICE. First ground, immediately, right off the deck. That is the North Mowich Headwall's signature.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS MOST IS THE CENTRAL MOWICH FACE NEXT DOOR, AND IT ALSO HAS AN HOURGLASS — BUT AT 12,500 FT, NOT AT 10,000. So the question at the base is not 'is there an hourglass on this route' but 'is the hourglass HERE, NOW, in the first 50 ft'. If your first 2,000 ft is open snow with no constriction at all, you are on the Central Mowich Face and your hourglass is still two thousand feet above you.

THE OTHER NEGATIVE IS THE EDMUNDS HEADWALL, AND IT IS SETTLED BY THE SCHRUND: the Edmunds is entered by bypassing its bergschrund on climber's LEFT near a pair of TWIN GENDARMES. If you crossed the schrund beside two rock towers, you are on the Edmunds and you crossed the wrong glacier out of camp.

SEQUENCE CHECK ONCE COMMITTED, IN ORDER: 40-50 ft hourglass of rock and ice, then roughly 2,000 ft of sustained 45-degree snow, then a rock band that has to be cleared. If the rock band arrives early, you are not on this line. If it never arrives, you traversed off onto the Central Mowich, which skirts the band entirely by going right.

WHAT BEING TOO FAR ROUND LOOKS LIKE: if you left camp and CLIMBED rather than crossing a glacier, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the Freedom or Death ramp
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as Freedom or Death and Thin Red Line: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

This route was equipped largely rope-solo and first freed in August 2016 and originally documented under an earlier name. It climbs the first three pitches of Freedom or Death, then steps right onto Thin Red Line just below its third-pitch anchor before eight new pitches of its own.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: No independent start; a party that mislocates Freedom or Death mislocates this route
A fixed pin and wire as the first rappel anchor off M&M Ledge
Two ropes needed for the descent
Loose talus in the upper approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE DOES NOT HAVE A START OF ITS OWN. IT STARTS ON FREEDOM OR DEATH, AND THAT IS THE FACT TO CARRY UP THE TALUS. So the base finding is Freedom or Death's base finding: A SMALL LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP JUST TO THE RIGHT OF LIBERTY CRACK, WITH BOLTS VISIBLE ON THE FACE ABOVE IT.

WHY THAT IS ACTUALLY USEFUL RATHER THAN A DODGE: it means you are not hunting for a fifth start among the East Face cluster. There are three pitches of shared, well-bolted climbing before this route becomes its own thing, and the decision point is up on the wall where you can see it, not down in the talus where you cannot.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: LIBERTY CRACK IS 40 FT LEFT ALONG THIRD AND FOURTH CLASS LEDGES FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS. If you are scrambling left on ledges you are heading for Liberty Crack. If you have walked well right past a series of starts you are among the Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice and Independence lines.

COUNTABLE ON THE CLIMB: three pitches of 5.10, 5.11 and 5.11, then a step RIGHT. If you are still going straight up after three pitches you have missed the junction with Thin Red Line.

AND THE DESCENT FOLLOWS THIN RED LINE'S, NOT FREEDOM OR DEATH'S: rappel with two ropes off M&M Ledge from a fixed pin and wire, then move climber's-left to bolted anchors for four double-rope rappels back to the base. Five rappels, all on bolted stations after the first.

approach_variants.name: Gardner Meadows to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.
approach_variants.season: The upper slopes face south and are normally clear from about early July. Earlier in the season, firmer snow makes the loose upper talus easier to travel at the cost of carrying an axe and crampons.
hazards: The mapped trail is abandoned and largely invisible leaving the meadows
Heavy deadfall low down, with long stretches of climbing over and under log jams
No maintained tread and no reliable cairns; the boot path that does exist is short and intermittent
Loose class 2 and 3 boulders and scree on the crest, with route choice left entirely to the party
Water is limited to the stream near the tarn — nothing dependable above it
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE DRIED-UP TARN WITH CABIN REMNANTS IS THE PROOF, AND THE OLD MINE ON THE CREST CONFIRMS IT. Working west from the meadows, the tread becomes distinct only as you near a small dried-up tarn on the peak's northeast side, known to some as Nasty Pond. Beside it are the remnants of a small cabin and an old pot sitting on a fire pit. That wreckage is the marker — there is no sign, no cairn at the turn, and no maintained trail — and a good stream just below it is the last reliable water. From the tarn, climb the spur ridge rising directly to the main north ridge; expect a few class 3 moves on it. Once on the crest you pick up a short stretch of boot path running through old mining evidence, with metal cables and other equipment lying on the rocks, and that hardware is the confirmation you are on the historic line rather than a game trail. The path disappears past the mine and the rest is pick-your-own-line class 2 and 3 through boulders and scree to the top. Coming down, the scree slope back to the pond is generally preferred over reversing the spur ridge.

_raw.notes: Glacier Peak Wilderness, approached from the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road
_raw.permit_type: Self-issue wilderness permit (sign the trailhead register)
_raw.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
_raw.group_size_limit: Maximum 12 per party (people and stock combined)
_raw.parking_pass_required: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass
_raw.permit_pickup_location: Self-issue at the Downey Creek Trailhead register

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit: sign the register at the Downey Creek Trailhead
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Suiattle River Road (FR 26) is washed out and closed to vehicles at about milepost 4.5 after the December 2025 flood, under a closure order running to 1 January 2028 unless lifted sooner, so the Downey Creek Trailhead cannot be reached by car. The Downey Creek Trail itself is also closed through 31 December 2026 under a separate fire closure. Call the Darrington Ranger District, (360) 436-1155, before planning a trip.
access.seasonal: Suiattle River Road (FS 26) is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4.5 after flood washouts, under an order running to January 1, 2028 unless lifted sooner — check current conditions before a trip.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, jointly administered by Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass required at the Downey Creek Trailhead — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register
overnight_permit.where: Sign the register at the trailhead. Camping on the North Cascades National Park side of Cache Col needs a park wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or Recreation.gov.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
approach_variants.notes: The long way in from the west. Start at the Downey Creek trailhead off the Suiattle River Road and work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor — Itswoot Ridge, Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek — on rugged, largely off-trail ground with real bushwhacking and glacier travel. Budget a full day, often two, before you are anywhere near rock. This is an experienced-mountaineers approach and nothing about it is a walk-in.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the bushwhacking is out of snow and the glaciers are travellable.
hazards: Open moat between glacier ice and the foot of the face; it hangs free enough that a rappel to the glacier has come off the rock well above the snow
Loose, poor-quality rock from the first pitch upward
Glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the approach and directly below the climb
Multi-day committing approach with no realistic quick exit
approach_variants.baseFinding: The east face of this peak rises directly out of the glacier, so the base of the climb is the ice-to-rock junction and the MOAT is the marker. Traverse the glacier under the east side until you find the point where the face rears up clean out of the ice rather than sitting back behind broken ground. The start is a finger-and-hand crack system you can step into straight out of the moat and follow for about a rope length to a ledge — if you cannot enter the crack from the moat without first scrambling talus, you are not at it. Expect the moat to be open and to need gear or a bridge; a recorded rappel back onto this glacier from above hung free over it, so the gap at the bottom is a permanent feature of this side rather than a bad year. Negative markers: if the wall in front of you is catching afternoon sun, you have crossed the crest and are on the WEST side of the peak; if you are looking up at a pair of clean dihedrals side by side, you are around on the ridge south of the summit at the start of the ridge route.

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek from the east
approach_variants.notes: The other documented way into this range comes from the east, via the lake ferry and the long trail up Agnes Creek before leaving it for the brush. Parties using it camp on rock ridges above the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing on the same day. It is not a shortcut — the bushwhack off the trail takes most of a day on its own — but it puts you on the glacier side of the crest, which is the side this route starts from.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long approach with a full day of brush before any alpine ground
Crevasses and a persistent moat at the foot of the east faces
Loose rock throughout the climb
The peak is one of four closely spaced summits on one crest, easily confused from below
approach_variants.baseFinding: Camping on the ridges above the glacier puts you looking straight across at the east faces, which is the one view that makes this route findable: pick the line before you drop onto the ice, because from the glacier itself the faces foreshorten and the individual crack systems disappear. On the ice, work under the peak until the face rises clean from the moat and a finger-and-hand crack can be entered directly out of it. Negative marker: the peak is the southernmost of the four named summits on this short crest, so if you are still under a summit with more towers to the south of you, you are one peak too far north.

rappel_detail.pull: Keep both ends clear of the constriction above the wide crack before the last climber pulls - it is the documented rope trap on this descent.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel of the shared North Face descent line.
hazards: A single 60 m rope does NOT reach the bolts: you finish roughly 10 ft above them and downclimb easy 5th class to get there. A 70 m single is the length that reaches, and is what recent parties recommend
This is the rappel where a party got a rope end stuck in a constriction above a wide crack and had to lead 5.8 back up to free it
rappel_detail.station: The summit anchor - the heavily slung summit boulder - dropping down the upper north face to what is reported to be the only bolted anchor on the whole rappel route. Everything below it is slung natural gear, so this is the one station you can identify with certainty.

rappel_detail.notes: Traverses to reach the next anchor.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolts to a ledge near a rock arch
hazards: The line does not follow the route, so what you see going down is not what you climbed
rappel_detail.station: Down toward the main ledge system. Parties on two ropes report doubling up and rappelling climber's-LEFT of the climbing line to reach the next station rather than dropping straight down it.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to a slung horn.
hazards: Ledge-to-ledge rappelling on this face means loose material sitting on every stance above you
rappel_detail.station: A single rappel from the ledge system down to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: Down to scree ledges.
hazards: You have to walk under and past a large block to find this station, so it is not visible from where the previous rappel lands
Traversing a ledge with the ropes still out is where they snag on this descent
rappel_detail.station: From the ledge, cut climber's LEFT to the station, which sits just after you walk back underneath the large block. A station is also reported at the top of pitch 4, reached by a ledge traverse - the ledge is the feature to navigate by, not the fall line.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel back to Burgundy Col, 5-10 minutes from Action Potential's own start.
hazards: The notch is the aiming point; below the col the descent continues down loose gullies on foot
rappel_detail.station: The last rappels run down through the sandy terraces to Burgundy Col. From the final stance the rappel route is a straight shot through the obvious notch in the rock below to the ground.

wa_action_potential.rappel_count_note: The five stations are the DOUBLE-ROPE count. The same descent is not five rappels for everyone: a party taking many shorter rappels on a single rope logged 9-10 to reverse the route back to Burgundy Col, and a party on two 60 m ropes describes doubling up for the first, one single rappel to the ledge at the bottom of pitch 3, then three more double rappels to the col. Neither is wrong. Action Potential has no rappel line of its own - parties finish into North Face terrain near Burgundy Ledge and take that route's descent. On rope choice, experience differs in a way worth knowing: two ropes are faster, but one party found double ropes on this descent annoying and prone to getting stuck, and recommends a single 70 m instead - a single 60 m leaves you about 10 ft above the only bolted anchor on the route. Per-station distances are not known; the figures given are estimates, not measurements.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then 5-10 minutes around the north face to the splitter flake
approach_variants.notes: From the SR-20 pullout at about 4,310 ft near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 miles east of Washington Pass and opposite Silver Star, a boot path drops through talus into forest, passes a register box, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft. The trail climbs east, roughly 2,200 ft, to a flat bench and campsite at about 6,460 ft, the halfway point and a common high camp, then works up through loose scree gullies and a final cairned stretch of unstable scree-over-slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770-7,800 ft. Roughly 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Unstable cairned scree-over-slab on the final stretch to Burgundy Col, the approach's main hazard in both directions
Loose rock and sometimes steep snow on the walk around the base of the north face
Anchors on the descent are a mix of slung boulders and horns with fixed bolts; watch for old webbing
Ledges on the face that catch a pulled rope
Reliable water only at Early Winters Creek; seasonal water near the Bench and an unreliable trickle near the col
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ACTION POTENTIAL DOES NOT START AT THE COL. FROM BURGUNDY COL, SCRAMBLE DOWN AND AROUND THE BASE OF BURGUNDY'S NORTH FACE FOR ABOUT 5 TO 10 MINUTES UNTIL YOU ARE BELOW A CLEAN SPLITTER FLAKE. THAT FLAKE IS THE ROUTE START.

SO THE THREE THINGS TO CHECK ARE A DIRECTION, A DURATION AND A FEATURE: DOWN and AROUND the north face, FIVE TO TEN MINUTES, and a CLEAN SPLITTER FLAKE. Clean is the operative word on a peak where most of the rock is not.

THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS ONE PLACEABLE: THIS ROUTE SITS JUST BEYOND ULTRAMEGA OK'S START. Ultramega OK is only about 15 FT climber's-right of this route, at a TWIN-CRACK SYSTEM MARKED BY OBVIOUS LOOSE BLOCKS ABOUT 60 FT UP. So: IF YOU ARE LOOKING AT TWO CRACKS WITH LOOSE BLOCKS SIXTY FEET ABOVE YOU, KEEP GOING ABOUT 15 FT.

AND IF YOU HAVE NOT WALKED AT ALL, YOU ARE ON THE NORTH FACE: that line starts with 4th-class scrambling straight above the col, which is also where the last rappel of the standard descent lands. The North Face start at the near end, twin cracks with loose blocks five to ten minutes along, and the splitter flake about 15 ft beyond them.

EARLY IN THE SEASON THE WALK ALONG THE BASE MAY BE SNOW RATHER THAN SCREE, sometimes steep enough to want an axe into midsummer. That does not change the count; it changes the footing.

DESCENT IS THE NORTH FACE'S, WHICH RETURNS YOU TO BURGUNDY COL: five double-rope rappels from the summit area, ending with a final 60 m to the col, 5-10 minutes from this route's start.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: As for Orbit, to the Silver Tongue slab
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead; the trail two to two and a half miles until the wall is opposite; right off the trail, down to the log crossing, then boulders and talus and a bootpath gaining about 500 ft to the base.

From the base, take the Orbit approach — left along the foot of the wall until the ground starts dropping steeply, then scramble up over fourth-class terrain to a pedestal.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
hazards: Fourth-class approach scrambling to the pedestal
The log crossing at high water and loose talus below the wall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Afterburner sits RIGHT of Orbit and the Mary Jane Dihedral and LEFT of Hyperspace, so it is bracketed by three routes you can identify independently.

The staging point is the Silver Tongue slab, beneath a big pine tree — that tree is the landmark, and it gives shade to gear up in. From there go up and LEFT on class 3 ground to just before another large pine on the ledge, where the first belay is built.

The start itself is unambiguous once you are on the right feature: a slab with a single bolt on it. If you are on a pedestal with no bolt in sight, you have not reached it; if you are looking at a chimney, you have gone left onto Orbit.

approach_variants.name: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
approach_variants.notes: From the highway just past the rest area, turn north onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road (Forest Road 6910) — the turn is on a curve with fast traffic, so watch for it — and follow good gravel a few miles before turning onto the short spur that ends at the Round Mountain Trailhead. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about a mile and a half through forest and an older burn to its junction with Nason Ridge Trail #1583. Turn left and west and follow the ridge trail, which undulates along the crest for a few miles to the lookout spur. A longer alternative reaches the same ridge trail from the west via the Merritt Lake trail, used mainly for through-hikes or when this side is inaccessible.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through October once the ridge melts out; the lookout is one of the few in the range still staffed.
hazards: The turn off the highway is on a blind curve with fast traffic
The ridge trail narrows to a knife edge with steep rock-filled gullies dropping away on both sides
The crest is exposed to weather with no shelter along it
The lower trail climbs steeply through burn with little shade or water
approach_variants.baseFinding: A '9' NAILED TO A TREE IS THE MARKER, AND THE KNIFE EDGE IS THE CONFIRMATION. Walking west along Nason Ridge Trail #1583, the crest pinches down to a ten-foot-wide knife edge with steep, rock-filled gullies falling away to the highway on the south and into the river drainage on the north — that narrowing is Ninemile Saddle, and a sign carrying the numeral 9 is fixed to a tree there. It is the only labelled feature on this stretch of ridge. From the saddle the lookout spur breaks right and climbs the last short distance to the staffed lookout on the summit. The negative marker is simple: the ridge trail carries straight on west past the spur, so if the ground has stopped climbing, the crest has widened out again, and no building has come into view, you have walked through the junction and should turn back to the narrow section with the numbered tree.

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake, Rampart Ridge, and the cairned Alta turnoff on the Lila Lake trail
approach_variants.notes:
From the Rachel Lake trailhead at 2,800 ft, at the end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Road from I-90 exit 62, take Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first 2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek at a gentle grade with reliable water throughout.

At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses the creek and hits the section known locally as the mile from hell: a heavily rooted, rocky climb gaining roughly 1,300 ft in a mile with big step-ups and no switchbacks. It is the fitness crux of the day, not a technical one.

At Rachel Lake, 4,700 ft, a use trail branches right near the outhouse, skirts the lake's north side, and switchbacks steeply about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest at about 5,100 ft. At the ridge junction go RIGHT toward Lila Lake; the left branch leads to Rampart Lakes and is not this route. After about 0.3 mile a cairn marks a fork: Lila Lake is straight ahead, and the climbers' path up Alta's south ridge is the left branch.
approach_variants.season: July to October. The route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge
hazards: Sustained exposure along the ridge crest, including a section skirting a cliff edge
Three false summits and a class 3 downclimb crux near the top
Loose rock and large step-ups on the initial climbers' path
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long exposed crest
Lingering snow in the approach gully in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TAKEOFF IS A CAIRN ON THE LILA LAKE TRAIL, NOT ANYTHING IN THE RAMPART LAKES BASIN. At the ridge-top junction above Rachel Lake turn RIGHT (left goes to Rampart Lakes); about 0.3 mile along, a cairn marks a fork where Lila Lake is straight on and the unsigned climbers' path to Alta goes left. If you find yourself among the Rampart tarns, you took the wrong branch at the ridge.

WHERE IT PUTS YOU: the climbers' path climbs Alta's south ridge, steep, loose and shadeless at first, before easing onto the narrow crest that leads to the summit block.

WHAT THE RIDGE THEN DOES, SO YOU CAN COUNT YOUR WAY ALONG IT: THREE FALSE SUMMITS, class 2-3 rock steps, at least one near-vertical step of 6 to 8 ft with good holds and serious exposure, and a class 3 DOWNCLIMB crux near the top. A party that has crossed one bump and thinks it is at the summit is two bumps early.

AND THE ONE PLACE WHERE THE FINDING IS A WARNING RATHER THAN A DIRECTION: there is a section where the path skirts a cliff edge. Fall consequences there are serious. This route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge, and it is not a place for anyone uneasy with heights or for dogs.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT DESCRIPTION OF THE SAME TAKEOFF: an unsigned climbers' path marked by a CAIRN leaves the maintained trail near the Rachel Lake / Lila Lake junction and climbs the south ridge. Steep, loose, big steps and no shade at first, then it moderates onto the knife-edge crest.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot just before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left to the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This starts AS FOR Numbah Ten, in the obvious groove LEFT of Iron Horse, and only becomes its own line higher up.

So the thing to find on the ground is Numbah Ten's bolted dihedral and the groove at its base. Sharing a start with an easier neighbour is correct here.

If you are under a line that shares an anchor with Sagittarius you have stepped right onto Iron Horse.

approach_variants.name: High Pass and the Gargett Mine, then the long sidehill under Larrabee to the South AmBo Saddle
approach_variants.notes:
CONTAMINATION WARNING BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: this is AMERICAN Border Peak, 7,998 ft, in Washington. CANADIAN Border Peak is about a kilometre north across the international line and is a different mountain with its own routes, reached from British Columbia. Beta for the two is routinely mixed up because both are called 'Border Peak'. Everything here is the Washington approach from Twin Lakes.

From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft, take the High Pass Trail; at a quarter mile it splits from the short spur up Winchester Mountain — stay LEFT, north. The trail contours the west side of Winchester, dips across Low Pass, and climbs to High Pass near 5,960 ft, about two miles and 750 ft of gain, where Mount Baker comes into view south.

At High Pass leave the maintained tread and follow the climbers' path north and west DOWN to the old Gargett Mine workings around 5,400 ft. The mine creek is the last reliable water until lingering snow high on the peak.

From the mine, traverse north and contour onto Mount Larrabee's southwest and west flanks. This is a long, unmarked, exposed sidehill of well over a mile across steep talus, scree, heather and brush.

Most parties camp at Gargett Basin or in the moraine bowl and climb from there rather than pushing summit day from the car.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and never on wet grass or wet rock
hazards: Chronic rockfall — the defining hazard of this approach, helmets on from the Larrabee traverse
A long unmarked exposed sidehill on steep talus, scree, heather and brush
Wet grass or wet rock on the sidehill is a documented no-go condition
Two 60 m gullies of loose rock with climber-triggered rockfall onto the party below
Two to four rappels on descent off aged natural tat, with at least one recorded stuck and abandoned rope
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 6,200-6,300 FT NOTCH ON LARRABEE'S NORTHWEST RIB IS THE FIRST GATE, AND THE SOUTH AMBO SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,840 FT IS THE SECOND. Those two are the whole navigation of this approach and both are cols — places where the ridge is low and you can stand on the crest with ground falling away on the far side. In cloud you are counting cols, not looking at the peak.

BETWEEN THEM IS A RED TALUS AND MORAINE BOWL. From the notch you drop slightly into it and then climb north out of it, up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs, to the saddle. Red rock underfoot after the first col is the confirmation you are in the right bowl.

ARRIVAL AT THE SADDLE: it is on the ridge crest DIRECTLY SOUTH of the summit. Standing there, the peak is north of you and Larrabee is behind you to the south. That bearing is the check — this is not a saddle you reach with the mountain to one side.

WHERE THE CLIMBING ACTUALLY STARTS IS 200 YARDS ABOVE THE SADDLE, NOT AT IT. From the saddle, go up the ridge crest on a faint climbers' path for roughly 200 yards, THEN start traversing RIGHTWARD on slabby RED LEDGES. The rock scrambling begins where the angle steepens noticeably at a distinctive rock rib: the first real move is up a small Class 3.5 cleft CLOSELY LEFT OF THAT RIB.

DE GAULLE'S NOSE IS THE AIMING MARK ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE RED FACE, at about 7,300 ft. The rising traverse across the red slopes goes toward it and the crossing feels very exposed. Beyond it come two 60-metre gullies with a sand-covered ledge traverse between them, and a chimney at the top of the second reached by a very airy ledge. If your route has no red traverse and no pair of long gullies, it is not this one.

AND THE HARD CONDITION RULE: do not attempt the Larrabee sidehill on wet grass or wet rock. Parties flag that as a genuine no-go rather than a discomfort.

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Andrews Pass
bivy.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
bivy.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
bivy.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake, round the west side of the water to the Ka'aba Buttress
approach_variants.notes:
Get to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by whichever of the long trails suits — this is the same basin used for Cathedral Peak, one to two days in from any trailhead.

The climbing is directly above the water, which is why every published approach time is measured in minutes rather than hours: ten to thirty minutes from camp. If you are camped on the north side of the lake, walk around it on the WEST side and straight up to the buttress.

Amphitheater's crags rise above the lake on the far side, and the two named buttresses on that wall are visible from your first sight of the water: Ka'aba on the LEFT, Middle Finger on the RIGHT.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Note the wall is north-west facing and stays in shade until around three in the afternoon, so an early start here is a cold one
hazards: A snow moat on the left side of the entry block into early July
The north-side descent gully holding firm snow through July
A north-west aspect that stays cold and shaded until mid-afternoon
Very remote — the nearest trailhead is a multi-day walk
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COUNT IS THE TEST. Middle Finger Buttress is the BIGGEST feature on the wall, and Ka'aba — where this route is — sits TWO BUTTRESSES TO ITS LEFT. So find the biggest one first, then count two left. Ka'aba itself is blocky and stepped, described as looking like stepping stones, which is quite unlike the clean sweep of Middle Finger. Be aware that the two buttresses between them are unnamed, so the count is the only handle you have — there is no known left-to-right inventory of this wall. Arrival is a LARGE BLOCK at the base that you scramble onto for the first pitch, and getting onto it has a known seasonal trap. Approaching from the LEFT side of the block runs into a large snow moat that stopped one party in early July. The RIGHT side goes, though it needs some care on friction moves crossing the top of the block to reach the wall. Walk-off, and there are two. The short one is a gully on the north side about a thousand feet east of Ka'aba, roughly thirty-five to forty degrees, giving a half-mile return to the lake — but it can hold firm snow through July. The longer one circles south around Amphitheater's western arm on sand and then meadows with a decent trail, rejoining the Boundary Trail and returning to the lake in about two miles and fifty minutes of easy walking.

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Andrews Pass
bivy.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
bivy.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
bivy.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

bivy.name: Remmel Lake and the Spanish Camp meadows
bivy.notes: This sits a short way off the main line to Cathedral Pass and works well as a base if Remmel Mountain is on the list alongside Cathedral and Amphitheater. The meadow ground is soft and easily damaged, so pull back onto the timber edge rather than pitching in the open grass. There is a signed spur from near the guard station running up toward the Cathedral basin, which makes this a workable alternative if the lakes above are full or posted closed. Being lower and more sheltered, it is a considerably kinder camp in bad weather than anything at the pass.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake plus the creeks draining the meadows. Along with Upper Cathedral, the other place on the approach where you can count on filling.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit, no quota. The cabin at Spanish Camp is a Forest Service ADMINISTRATIVE structure, not a public shelter, and should not be treated as available lodging.
bivy.capacity: Broad grassy meadows with room for multiple parties, but the sites are dispersed rather than developed and horse parties use this area heavily

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind
