bivy.name: Amphitheater Mountain upper basin
bivy.notes: Reached by following the trail southeast around Amphitheater's west ridge from Upper Cathedral Lake and then a boot path up scree and grass into the basin. Worth considering only if you want to be on the ridge at first light, because the water problem is real and it gains you very little over camping at the lake. The ground is loose and sparsely vegetated, which makes it easy to occupy without leaving a mark if you are careful. Treat it as an emergency or tactical bivy rather than a planned camp. No elevation is recorded — none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early. Once the last patches go there is nothing up here, so plan on carrying everything up from the lake. This is the driest camp option in the zone.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue trailhead permit covers it; no quota, no reservation, and no designated-site system in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on scree and grass benches; informal ground, no established sites

approach_variants.name: Granite Sidewalk to Proxima Wall
approach_variants.notes:
FS 2060 south out of Darrington, LEFT fork at about 5 miles, then park at a small pullout on the west side of the road roughly 0.4 miles past the fork.

The approach follows the Granite Sidewalk — a long continuous low-angle granite ramp reached by walking up the creek bed east for about 10 minutes and then taking the gully on its left. Compared with a typical North Cascades approach this is close to schwack-free, and that is the confirmation you are on the sidewalk rather than in the timber beside it.

From the west slabs an approach gully leads to the base in roughly 20 minutes. Total from the car is about an hour to an hour and a half.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
hazards: Long unroped friction on the Granite Sidewalk
Approach gully above the west slabs
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Proxima Wall faces west. The start is a bolted prow, and the specific thing to look for is a large Metolius bolt at the bottom of it.

A prow with a bolt on it is the marker — not a crack, not the tree patch. The tree patch at the top of the sidewalk belongs to Blueberry Buttress, and the single bolt 100-150 feet left of the tree below it belongs to Dark Rhythm; both are on Blueberry Hill, the same west face, and both are easy to mistake for this if you stop at the first thing you reach.

bivy.name: Honeymoon Meadows
bivy.notes: Established camp on the West Fork Dosewallips trail about 8 miles past the old ranger station, below Anderson Pass. The usual base for the Anderson Glacier side of the massif.
bivy.water: West Fork Dosewallips River and side streams
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required
bivy.capacity: Several established tent sites

bivy.name: Enchanted Valley and Anderson Pass — the approach to Anderson's Thumb
bivy.notes: The East Fork Quinault runs about thirteen miles from Graves Creek to the Enchanted Valley chalet, with staged camps at Pony Bridge around three miles, O'Neil Creek around six and a half and Pyrites Creek around nine, all of which are useful for breaking the walk in. This is the approach to ANDERSON'S THUMB, the pinnacle on the Anderson massif, reached by continuing from the valley up to Anderson Pass at 4,480 ft and then onto the glacier remnant and the rock above. Camping at the pass rather than in the valley saves you several miles and roughly two thousand feet on climbing day and puts you in quiet country; camping in the valley gets you a flatter, warmer night and a spectacular setting at the cost of a very long summit day and a great deal of company. Bears are habituated and confident here, so the canister rule is enforced rather than advisory, and food left out is food lost. The same pass is reached from the Dosewallips on the east side, which is the shorter approach to the Anderson massif if that road is open — worth checking before committing to the Quinault side.
bivy.water: Reliable everywhere — the East Fork Quinault runs the length of the valley and small streams cross the trail up toward the pass
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and the EAST FORK QUINAULT RIVER IS A QUOTA AREA — reserve on the federal recreation site rather than turning up hopeful. Summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and reservations for it release on 15 April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for adults, six dollar booking fee. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY AND STRICTLY REQUIRED HERE: this valley was closed to camping over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Canisters are loaned free at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness information centres.
bivy.capacity: A large valley camping area at the chalet meadow that can hold well over a hundred people on a summer weekend, plus a much smaller and quieter camp up near Anderson Pass

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
approach_variants.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear LEFT onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up beside the southeast ridge. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep
hazards: Wrong-fork error onto Bean Creek Trail near the start
Ingalls Creek ford is a genuine obstacle in early season or after rain
Loose talus in the basin; hard snow in shoulder season warranting axe and crampons
Long, remote approach — a partial day just to reach the base, so plan a car-camp or bivy
Teanaway-side trail closures following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — verify before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climb follows the crest of the southeast ridge, which rises from the Ingalls Creek side to the southeast spire, the lowest of Argonaut's three summits. The lower pitches are blocky, lichen-covered and awkward, which is the sign you are on the ridge proper.

Low down, the ridge can be crossed at a notch near 6,750 ft between the south slope and Porcupine Basin; that crossing is a way between the two drainages, not a feature of the climb.

Above the southeast spire, two single-rope rappels or one double-rope rappel take you into the notch, and the route continues to the true summit on the west spire.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek off-trail to the basin under Argonaut's north face
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake split and then leave it, heading up toward Argonaut's north side. There is no maintained path for this and route choice through the lower ground is yours: the terrain is swampy in places, there is a log crossing of the creek, and there is a notorious slide-alder slope that is best avoided by taking nearby talus instead.

Consistent snow generally starts around 4,700 ft. Above that, follow the drainage up toward the north face; parties have used snowshoes for much of this section.

Nothing published gives a reliable trailhead-to-base time for this approach, and the accounts that do quote figures are quoting whole days that also include a traverse of Colchuck, so no figure is given here.

The couloir above runs a constant, sustained 35-50 degrees for about 1,200 ft with no significant steps, narrowing as it goes, and exits on mid-fifth-class or icy ground onto the summit ridge system.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow climb; consistent snow starts around 4,700 ft in a normal spring
hazards: A notorious slide-alder slope on the approach, best bypassed on talus
A log crossing of Mountaineer Creek and swampy ground below the snowline
1,200 ft of sustained 35-50 degree snow with avalanche and rockfall exposure as the day warms
A mid-fifth-class or icy exit pitch
A descent involving rappels down slabs and a traverse of a wet ledge into the east gully
No maintained trail on the approach and no reliable published timing for it
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COULOIR THAT NARROWS IS THE RIGHT ONE. This is the most useful in-fog property of the line: it holds a constant angle for its whole length and it TAPERS, from roughly fifty feet wide at the bottom to as little as ten feet near the top. A gully that stays the same width, or that has obvious steps and pitches in it, is not this feature.

ORIENTATION AGAINST THE ROCK: the couloir sits immediately EAST of the Northeast Buttress, so from inside the couloir the buttress rock is the bounding rib on its WEST side. Standing at the entrance with a defined rock rib to the west and open snow slopes to the east is the correct position; standing with rock on both sides in a short, steep slot means you are in one of the minor gullies rather than the main line.

AND THE EXIT AS A CONFIRMATION: this couloir does NOT run to the summit. It finishes with one mid-fifth-class or icy pitch onto the summit-ridge system, followed by third and fourth class scrambling to distinctive A-frame summit blocks. A line that appears to run straight to the top is a different feature.

HONEST LIMIT, STATED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: no landmark is known that distinguishes the base from neighbouring gullies at close range. The shape of the couloir and the buttress on its west are real, reliable tests; a specific arrival marker at the toe is not known and none is invented here. Scout the face from lower in the basin in good visibility before committing in the dark.

approach_variants.name: Nason Creek logging grade from US-2
approach_variants.notes: Park at the unmarked shoulder pullout on US-2 beside the highway maintenance and tunnel-entrance yard east of Stevens Pass — room for two or three cars, no sign, no trail number and no maintained tread anywhere on this route. Walk back west along the shoulder, cross to the north side just past the Nason Creek bridge, get across the creek, and then cross the active rail line that parallels the highway. On the far bank pick up the old logging grade running beside the creek, duck under a set of powerlines and skirt the standing runoff ponds in the first few minutes, and follow the level bed roughly east-southeast until the ground on the uphill side steepens into unbroken timber.
approach_variants.season: Almost always climbed with snow on the ground, roughly late autumn to spring. On bare ground the same slopes are brushy and log-choked and travel is far slower.
hazards: The route crosses an active main-line railway on foot, with no crossing and no signals — trains use this corridor frequently
Nason Creek runs high and cold during snowmelt and there is no bridge on the climbers' line
Short rock bands around 3,400 ft can cliff a party out inside the trees
Snow under the canopy above about 3,700 ft can be firm or icy while it is soft in the open
No trail, no signage and no tread the whole way; in flat light the line is easy to lose in both directions
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE LEVEL GRADE ENDING AT A CREEK-CUT BANK IS THE PROOF. The old logging bed is flat and wide enough to have carried a truck, and it stays beside Nason Creek. About a mile from the highway, near 2,700 ft, the creek has cut the uphill bank into a short steep step and the timber above that step runs unbroken toward the crest. That step is where you leave the road, and nothing marks it — no cairn, no blaze at the turn, no path breaking off. Once you are climbing, faded blue and yellow forestry paint on scattered trunks is the confirmation that other parties have used this line. If you are still walking level ground with water beside you, you have not reached it; if the grade has petered out or swung away from the creek, you have gone past. Higher, near 3,400 ft, short rock bands break the slope and force a little route-finding. Which side they are best turned on is unsettled, so read the ground rather than committing to a direction: work whichever way keeps a continuous walkable line, and if you find yourself under a continuous wall with no weakness in it, back off and try the other side rather than pressing straight up into it.

bivy.name: Tumwater Canyon campgrounds on US 2
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in camping to Arrowhead that is not already recorded in a neighbouring zone file, deliberately chosen over the Lake Wenatchee corridor camps for that reason. It is a drive of half an hour or so west along the highway to the pullout, which suits a party that wants a proper night with water and a table before a dawn start. The catch is the season: these canyon campgrounds run roughly late spring to early autumn, which is precisely the half of the year when Arrowhead is at its worst. FOR THE WINTER ASCENT, WHICH IS THE ONE MOST PARTIES WANT, THESE ARE CLOSED and the answer is a night in the vehicle at the pullout or a very early drive from town. Note also that the December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this district and a closure order covering them runs into 2027, and that a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026; neither touches the highway itself, but both change what is open either side of it, so check before relying on a specific campground.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed sites during the operating season, plus the river alongside. This is the one place where water is not a problem, and it is the sensible place to fill everything before driving up to the pullout.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee at the developed campgrounds, with some sites reservable in advance and the rest first come, first served. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply through the summer in the canyon and are commonly total bans by late season — this is one of the driest and most fire-prone stretches of highway in the state.
bivy.capacity: Small developed forest campgrounds strung along the highway in the canyon between Leavenworth and the Chiwaukum front, taking modest vehicles and a moderate number of parties. Sites are a mix of first come and reservable, and they fill on summer weekends with Leavenworth traffic that has nothing to do with the mountains.

bivy.name: The US 2 pullout by the maintenance yard
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead and, realistically, the accommodation. The pullout sits roughly seven miles east of Stevens Pass at the east tunnel end. The route walks west along the highway shoulder for a few hundred yards, crosses the Nason Creek bridge and drops onto an old logging spur that parallels the creek to the railway grade; parties then follow the tracks a short way before scrambling up the bank at about 2,700 ft and climbing steep timber to snowline around 3,700 ft. A variation stays on the spur, crosses Henry Creek, takes the right fork and then the left to the bottom of a clearcut at about 4,200 ft, climbs the clearcut directly south and traverses east into the trees to gain the north ridge. TWO CAUTIONS THAT ARE NOT ABOUT CLIMBING. The highway shoulder walk is on a fast, busy road with poor sightlines and is more dangerous than anything above it, and the railway line is active — treat both as hazards to be got off quickly rather than as part of the walk. Winter parking here is genuinely tight and the shoulder is where the ploughs put the snow, so an early arrival is worth more than an early start.
bivy.water: Nason Creek runs alongside and under the highway bridge the route crosses, and it needs treating. There is no potable supply. THERE IS NO WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN ITSELF once you leave the creek and the lower spur — the north ridge and the clearcut above carry nothing, so in summer everything is carried from here, and in winter the answer is melting snow.
bivy.permit: None. This is not designated wilderness, there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no lottery anywhere on this peak. Highway shoulder parking needs no forest pass, which is worth knowing because the trailheads a few miles either side of it do. There is no fee and no registration. Note that the WSDOT rest area further along the highway is a rest area and not a campground, and overnight camping there is not what it is for.
bivy.capacity: Shoulder parking and a pullout by the road turnoff for the maintenance station, with room for about three vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground, no fee site, no table and no toilet. In winter the plough berm decides how much of it exists on any given morning.

bivy.name: The lower spur and Henry Creek flat
bivy.notes: Recorded chiefly as the water point rather than as a camp, because knowing where Henry Creek is matters more on this mountain than knowing where you could pitch. The spur climbs east-southeast off the highway after the Nason Creek bridge, crosses the creek, and then forks twice — right at the first junction by an unnamed creek, left at the second — before reaching the bottom of the clearcut at about 4,200 ft. In winter the fork-finding is the navigational crux of the day and it is done under snow with the road cuts filled in, which is why parties who have been up before make much better time than parties who have not. As sleeping ground it is a poor substitute for the pullout, being no warmer, no flatter and a mile further from the car, and its one genuine use is for a party arriving in the small hours who would rather walk a mile and sleep than sit on the highway shoulder. Bring an axe for the steep timber above regardless of season; the slope from the railway grade to snowline is unrelenting.
bivy.water: Henry Creek at the crossing, and Nason Creek below — both need treating and both run all year. This is the last water on the route and the only water on it, and its position at the very bottom of the climb is the whole water story of this peak: everything above is dry, so this is where you fill.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness, no permit, no quota. The spur network crosses mixed ownership in places, including railway and utility corridors, so read the signage at junctions and do not assume a road is open ground just because it is drivable-looking. No fee, no registration.
bivy.capacity: Rough ground on the old logging road network in the first mile, where the spur crosses Henry Creek. Room for a tent or two on the road grade itself. Nothing established, nothing signed, and no reason to be here except timing.

bivy.name: The clearcut benches on the north ridge, around 4,200 feet
bivy.notes: Included as a contingency and as an honest negative. There is no reason to sleep on Arrowhead: the whole outing is six miles and three thousand feet and a fit party is up and down in seven or eight hours, so the only situation where this ground matters is a winter party that has broken trail through deep new snow, run out of daylight low down, and would rather bivouac than descend a steep wooded slope in the dark. Under those conditions the flat around the top of the clearcut at roughly 4,200 ft is the obvious place, being out of the timber and out of the terrain trap of the creek drainages. What you get is a snow camp with no shelter and no water; what you avoid is a night descent. In summer this same ground is slash and regrowth and there is nothing to recommend it. THE ROUTE IS CHOSEN FOR ITS AVALANCHE CHARACTER and is described as steep but safe by that measure, which is exactly the sort of judgement that changes with the year's snowpack — assess it rather than inheriting it.
bivy.water: None whatsoever. Henry Creek on the lower spur is the last water on the way up and it is a long way below. In winter this is a snow camp and you melt; in summer you carry, and the amount you would have to carry is the argument against being here at all.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness national forest and old logging ground, no permit, no quota, no fee. Fires are a poor idea in a clearcut full of dry slash and are prohibited under the summer restrictions that run most years on this side of the pass. Some of the lower spur network crosses a mix of ownership, so read the signs at the junctions rather than assuming everything is public.
bivy.capacity: No established site of any kind. Under deep snow the clearcut and the flat bench above it give as much room as a party wants; in bare conditions there is very little usable flat ground and it is all slash, stumps and brush. Recorded to say plainly that nobody camps on this mountain, rather than to invent a site for it.

wa_austera_peak.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From camp, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) climbing to the high camp on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier below Eldorado's east ridge. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. IMPORTANT — this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak itself, despite being filed under the same area: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.

approach_variants.name: Eldorado camp, Klawatti Col, and the 75-ft rappel onto the Klawatti Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is the same day out as the Southwest Ridge route on this peak and the two describe substantially the same ground. From the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,600 ft, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti Col. Tepeh Towers are passed along this same traverse. From the col, follow the ridge line along the McAllister Glacier to a break at about 7,900 ft, where the standard sequence is a rappel of about 75 ft onto the Klawatti Glacier, then a traverse high and left across it toward Austera. This is meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado, and it is worth saying plainly: this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak, despite the catalog filing several of these objectives out of the same area. Austera Peak is the high point of the Austera Towers arête, not a free-standing summit, and it is the most accessible top in that group — which is exactly why parties end up on the wrong one.
approach_variants.season: Aug is the usual window; the timing is set by the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glaciers being safely negotiable rather than by the rock
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration, McAllister and Klawatti glacier traverses
A moat at the rappel point that has to work in both directions
Loose rock on the final summit tower
Rime or verglas on the final chimney even in summer
Exposed climbing on the closing pitches above a remote glacier, with a long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A BREAK IN THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,900 FT THAT YOU RAPPEL INTO, NOT WALK THROUGH. That is the single most useful thing to know here: the correct notch takes about 75 ft of rope to get down onto the Klawatti Glacier, and on the way back it is roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 to climb out. A gap you strolled through is Klawatti Col, one col short, at about 7,800 ft.

GET THERE BY COUNTING, NOT BY SIGHTING AUSTERA. Cross the Inspiration to Klawatti Col; pass Klawatti Peak on your LEFT through that col; follow the ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 mile to the SECOND break. Austera is the high point of a whole arête of towers and picking it out from below is not a reliable way to navigate.

ABOVE THE GLACIER TRAVERSE THE CLIMBING IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: a few hundred feet of 4th class gains a SUB-SUMMIT, and a further short pitch — about 30 to 50 ft of low fifth, taken around to the RIGHT on the northeast face — reaches the true top.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS THE REAL HAZARD ON THIS PEAK, AND IT IS THE TEST THAT MATTERS. Parties top out a few feet short of the true summit again and again. THE TRUE SUMMIT IS REACHED ONLY AFTER CROSSING A NARROW, OFTEN SNOWY RIDGE BETWEEN TWO BLOCKS AND CLIMBING A SHORT CHIMNEY OR A FEW FEET OF LOW FIFTH BEYOND IT. If you got to where you are standing without a rope-worthy move and without crossing that ridge, you are on the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

THE MOAT BESIDE THE RAPPEL POINT is the thing most likely to change year to year; check it on the way in, because it has to work in the other direction at the end of the day.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

approach_variants.name: Three glaciers and two cols to the Klawatti-Austera notch, then the chockstone chimney
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near mile 20 (about 2,100 ft) and find the log crossing of the Cascade River near the Eldorado Creek confluence — it has been rebuilt repeatedly after flood damage and can be an awkward single log, so scout it before committing. On the far bank the unsigned climbers' path pushes through swampy brush and devil's club into open old growth, gains roughly 1,500 ft, then breaks onto two wide talus fields. Above them an alpine meadow leads to a slabby ramp onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and put crampons on there.

Camp at Eldorado Creek Basin around 5,600 ft, Roush Creek Basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, or push to a high camp near Eldorado's East Ridge at 7,200-7,600 ft.

From high camp the day is three miles of sustained glacier travel across three basins and two cols: the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier (crevasses worst near Eldorado's east ridge), the upper Inspiration at about 7,800 ft to KLAWATTI COL, then past Klawatti Peak on its left and along the upper McAllister Glacier beneath Klawatti's west face for about 0.4 mile to the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA notch at about 7,900 ft. Guide figures for that leg are roughly 1,280 ft of ascent and 592 ft of descent over 2.8 miles, about four hours one way.

Austera Peak is the HIGH POINT OF THE AUSTERA TOWERS ARÊTE rather than a separate peak, which is why the top of this climb needs as much care as the bottom.
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul to Aug, while the notch is still bridged and the three glacier crossings are consolidated
hazards: Crevasse fall on all three glaciers, worse as the season progresses and bridges soften
A moat gap at the Klawatti-Austera notch that often needs stemming or a rappel of about 75 ft to reach the upper Klawatti Glacier
Route-finding in flat light or whiteout on an open ice cap with no handrail
Loose rock on every exposed rock section of the tower — the false-summit approach is explicitly loose class 3
Rime and verglas icing the final chimney even in summer
A genuinely committing and remote position with long retreat times
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE KLAWATTI-AUSTERA NOTCH AT ABOUT 7,900 FT, AND YOU IDENTIFY IT BY COUNTING COLS, NOT BY LOOKING AT AUSTERA. From the Inspiration Glacier you cross Klawatti Col first at about 7,800 ft — that one is not it. Keep Klawatti Peak on your right, follow its west face along the McAllister Glacier for about 0.4 mile, and the SECOND break in the ridge is the one. It sits a hundred feet higher than the first.

THE NOTCH ANNOUNCES ITSELF BY BEING A PROBLEM. It is not a walk-through: a moat gap has to be stemmed or rappelled — about 75 ft — to get down onto the upper Klawatti Glacier. IF YOU STEPPED THROUGH A COL WITHOUT HAVING TO SOLVE ANYTHING, YOU ARE STILL AT KLAWATTI COL. Old anchors have been found at the right notch; treat them as aging tat and back them up rather than as proof of position.

ABOVE THE NOTCH, COUNT THREE THINGS IN ORDER: broken 4th-class rock off the notch, then a short cliff band that many parties bypass on scree and ledges to the RIGHT (east) rather than climbing direct, then the chockstone gully at the base of the summit tower.

THE HARDEST THING TO GET RIGHT ON THIS PEAK IS NOT THE BASE, IT IS THE TOP, AND THE CHIMNEY IS THE TEST. Parties routinely finish on a FALSE SUMMIT a few feet short of the true one. The true summit is reached only by crossing a narrow, exposed ridge between the two blocks and then climbing the CHOCKSTONE CHIMNEY — roughly THREE jammed chockstones in about 60 ft, stemming and face moves on the chimney's LEFT wall. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A NARROW RIDGE AND CLIMBED A CHIMNEY, THE POINT YOU ARE STANDING ON IS THE FALSE SUMMIT. A class 3+ ledge bypass on the peak's east side reaches the same notch without the chimney, so a party that took it has not gone wrong — but it has not confirmed its position either.

approach_variants.name: Azurite Pass, the 7,400 ft shoulder and the west-face traverse
approach_variants.notes: From Azurite Pass leave the trail and work northeast and east up krummholz, sand, scree and talus to a flat shoulder at about 7,400 ft — flat enough that parties cache overnight gear on it, and easy to relocate on the way down. Continue up the crest to roughly 7,600 ft, where a lower south summit obstructs the ridge and the well-cairned climbers' route drops off westward. From there a gently rising traverse crosses a series of ribs, gullies and sandy slopes, well marked with ducks and cairns, staying below the cliffs rather than in them, and crossing two or three short snow runnels that an ice axe handles. The traverse runs toward the peak's prominent west rib.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock on the traverse and in the final gully — stay off each other's fall line
The final gully often holds snow into midsummer; ice axe, and crampons if icy
Two or three short snow runnels to cross on the west-face traverse
Many ribs and gullies that all look like viable options when seen obliquely from a distance
approach_variants.baseFinding: TURN UP TOO LATE AND YOU MEET THE SOUTHWEST FACE — THAT IS THE ERROR TO WATCH FOR. The correct gully is narrow at its base and cannot be seen from the ridge, so parties keep traversing hoping for something obvious, run out onto the imposing southwest face, and find it goes Class 4 in a hurry. The stated fix from those who have made that mistake is to retreat to the LAST GULLY TO THE SOUTH and go up that. The right line stays loose and never harder than short steps of Class 3 for roughly the last 200 ft to the top: if you are climbing more than short sections of Class 4, you are off route, and if you have drifted onto cleaner, more solid rock high on the gully's climber's-left wall you have left the gully floor for steeper and more exposed ground. One gully on this line pinches to about three feet, tight enough to touch both walls with your arms out — that constriction is a confirmation you are in a real line, not a warning.

approach_variants.name: Anderson Lakes and the saddle chain to the northeast camp
approach_variants.notes: Take the Watson Lakes Trail from the road end and, at the saddle about 1.4 miles in, leave the maintained tread for a hiker's path running south along the ridge high above Lower Anderson Lake. The path opens into meadows and reaches Upper Anderson Lake — the last easy water. Leave the lake heading northeast up a short wooded gully and continue that way onto open moraine and heather slopes near 5,300 ft. Traverse under the Watson peaks and DROP to about 5,000 ft to get around a buttress on their east side, then climb to a saddle at 5,360 ft and cross to the SOUTH side of the ridge. Continue east, losing a little height toward the next low point in the ridge, a saddle near 4,900 ft, crossing a short buttress on easy ledges on the way. A good camp sits at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of Bacon Peak.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: No tread, no signage and no marked line above Upper Anderson Lake
Lingering snowfields on the traverse beneath the Watson peaks
Crevasse hazard on the icecap if the line drifts onto it
Featureless snow slopes near the top — navigation in whiteout is the real difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SADDLE SEQUENCE IS THE PROOF, AND THE HEIGHTS GO DOWN BEFORE THEY GO UP. From the open moraine and heather at about 5,300 ft this line LOSES height twice: first to roughly 5,000 ft to get round the buttress east of the Watson peaks, then again beyond the 5,360 ft saddle, dropping toward a 4,900 ft saddle reached over a short buttress on easy ledges. A party that keeps gaining height through this stretch has stayed on the wrong side of the ridge — at the 5,360 ft saddle you cross to the SOUTH side, and remaining on the north side is the mistake. The camp lies at 5,900 ft, half a mile northeast of the summit, and from it the peak is gained by climbing southeast. The last test is what is under your feet: this line reaches the summit without crossing a glacier at all, so if the ground ahead is crevassed ice rather than a snow-covered slope, you have drifted onto the icecap and should rope up or come back to the walking line.

bivy.name: Upper Diobsud Lakes
bivy.notes: The highest comfortable camp on the massif and the natural pivot for anyone crossing it, in the upper Diobsud Creek basin on the far side of Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road. It is the camp a party reaches at the end of a long traverse day, and the one they leave from for the summit, for the ground east toward Berdeen, or for the long line north over the divide toward Hagan and Blum. What sets it apart from every other high site here is that it has water at six thousand feet, which nothing on the connecting ridges does. It is alpine meadow, so the heather is the thing to protect and the tent goes on rock. Snow covers this basin well into July and the lakes can still be part frozen at the start of the season. There is no shelter, no cell coverage, and no quick way down from here in any direction.
bivy.water: The lakes, dependable and right at camp — the best water this high anywhere on the massif. Treat it.
bivy.permit: This basin lies on the North Cascades National Park side of the divide, so a park backcountry permit for the correct cross-country zone is required for an overnight, collected in person at the wilderness information center. No campfires. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste in a blue bag from snow and glacier ground. The party limit in a park cross-country zone is small — confirm the number when you collect the permit rather than assuming a Forest Service twelve.
bivy.capacity: Room for a small party or two on alpine meadow and heather benches beside the upper pair of lakes; established by use rather than designation, with no facilities

bivy.name: Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM: FS 1107 has been closed at a washout at milepost 3.8, well below the road end, since July 8, 2026, and the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert, still posted on September 26, 2026, gives no end date; the closure cuts off the trailhead and the Anderson Creek Sno-Park. While it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
bivy.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
bivy.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Northeast Bacon camp, above the glacier
bivy.notes: The high camp for Bacon Peak from the Anderson Creek road, and the reason the peak is a two-day trip rather than an epic. It is reached by leaving the Watson Lakes trail at the saddle, climbing the ridge above Lower Anderson Lake, and working east through meadows and moraine across the massif — a long undulating traverse rather than a climb, and the part of the day that eats the time. From camp the summit is a short ascent to the southeast, and it is possible to reach the top without crossing glaciers at all, which is what makes this a scramble for a competent party rather than a rope-up. Immediately north the ground falls away past post-glacial moraine to the saddle above the green lake below the glacier, and that is the line onward for anyone continuing east or north across the range. It is a fully exposed shelf with nothing to shelter behind and the weather here comes across from Baker with no warning. The season is roughly mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse is a long snow slope, later and the water is gone.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier melt near camp through most of the season, and tarns in the moraine below. Late in a dry summer expect to be melting snow. Treat anything you find, and do not count on liquid water in early season when the whole shelf is still covered.
bivy.permit: This camp sits on the boundary country between the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness and North Cascades National Park, and which one it falls in decides whether you need a permit at all. Ask specifically when you plan the trip: the Forest Service side needs no overnight permit, while the park side needs a backcountry permit written for the correct cross-country zone. No campfires on either side of the line. Camp on snow, rock or gravel and never on the heather, keep well back from water, and pack out all waste — on snow and glacier that means blue bags carried out.
bivy.capacity: Open ground for a couple of small parties on gravel, rock and heather about half a mile northeast of the summit; informal, with nothing built and no toilet

approach_variants.name: North ridge direct from the Foss River Road bridge
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail of any kind. Park on the road shoulder just past the concrete bridge over the East Fork Foss River, cross to the far side of the road, and go straight into the forest to pick up the toe of the north ridge around 1,600 ft. The first several hundred feet of gain are spent weaving over down timber rather than walking; near 2,600 ft the forest turns to older growth and the underbrush thins so the crest becomes easy to follow. Moderate going holds until about 4,500 ft, where the ridge narrows and steepens into the brushiest stretch of the day, then opens into rock and heather by 5,200 ft. Carry all your water from the river — nothing above the road is dependable.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: No trail and no marked start from the road
Down timber low down, then slide alder and small trees crowding a narrow crest between 4,500 and 5,200 ft
Hard snow and ice in the bypass gully and on the traverse into midsummer
Rockfall off the cliff band above the traverse
No water anywhere above the river
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts where the crest hits a wall. Once the brush releases near 5,200 ft the ridge opens into rock and heather and the summit block comes into view for the first time; a short stretch of open crest past that viewpoint runs straight into a cliff band standing square across the ridge at about 5,400 ft. That wall is the marker, not the route — parties who take it head-on are on the wrong ground. The way through breaks LEFT (east) off the crest into a small gully, and this is where helmets go on and where an axe and light traction earn their weight, since the shaded north-facing ground beyond holds hard snow and ice well into summer. From the gully the correct line is a rising traverse into the upper summit basin, regaining the crest near 6,100 ft. If you are still on a pointy, brush-crowded crest with drop-offs on both sides you have not reached the band yet; if the ground ahead is open rock with no wall in it, you are already above the bypass.

bivy.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
bivy.notes: The valley-bottom staging option for every Foss River objective, and worth a line of its own because of what the road has been doing. The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.
bivy.water: Piped or hand-pumped drinking water on site, with the South Fork Skykomish and the Miller River beside them. No treating required.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fees, and reservations for most sites. No wilderness permit needed at this elevation — pick that up at the trailhead the next morning. Campfires are allowed in the provided rings when there is no seasonal fire ban in force, which is the last time you will see one on any of these trips.
bivy.capacity: Money Creek has around twenty-five sites, a couple of them first-come; Miller River is a group camp of about fifteen sites with a gathering area. Both take vehicles and both fill on summer weekends, so reserve where you can.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trailhead, back down the road to the driveway
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Snow Creek trailhead on Icicle Road. Walk back down the road about 0.1 mile to a driveway signed that hikers and climbers enter at their own risk, follow it to a retaining wall, then take the trail rising RIGHT toward the crags. A public-land boundary sign appears shortly after the driveway. Roughly 30 minutes to the crag, past smaller outcrops on the way.

The lower ground is private — stay on the path and keep clear of the houses.
approach_variants.season: Early season — south-facing with little shade
hazards: Private land on the lower approach
South-facing with almost no shade
Ledgy, tiered terrain that confuses route counting
Descent by scrambling down climbers' right from the uppermost ledge system
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Bale/Kramar sits at the LEFT EDGE of the rock, immediately LEFT of Careno Corners — the two are adjacent and Careno Corners is described by its position relative to this route, so they are best identified as a pair.

The confirmation is which end of the crag you are at. The biggest face, in the middle, with prominent dihedrals running to a large lone tree, is Regular Route; if that is above you, you have walked too far right and need to come back to the left edge.

If you find yourself on a steep crack that runs right and then traverses back left to a shared belay beneath a large roof, you are on Careno Corners, one line to the right of this route.

The crag is tiered with several ledge systems, so check which level you are standing on before counting lines across the face.

wa_baring_mountain_east_face.descent: Undocumented. Assume you will either rappel the route or top out and descend the standard northwest-ridge / BASE-jumper trail to the west.
wa_baring_mountain_east_face.descent_text: No descent is published for this route. If the line tops out on or near the summit ridge, the standard walk-off applies: from the summit take the BASE-jumper boot track down and west, swing counterclockwise across talus into the notch between the north and south summits at roughly 5,550-5,600 ft, descend the gully west into the boulder basin at about 4,900 ft, drop through heather and boulders onto the west/northwest ridge near 4,000 ft, and follow the steep, eroded climbers' path about 1,500 ft through old-growth forest to the abandoned logging road above the Barclay Lake trailhead — roughly three hours from the summit. If the route ends below the ridge, plan on rappelling your own line, which on a 1992 route with no recorded repeats means building every anchor yourself and carrying plenty of tat.

approach_variants.name: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
approach_variants.notes:
Distance and gain are round trip to the true summit. Drive US-2 to milepost 42 in Baring — the turnoff is directly across from the store — and turn north onto Barclay Creek Road (FR 6024). Cross the railroad tracks immediately and bear LEFT at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Roughly 4.3 to 4.5 miles of gravel reach the Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft: parking for around 20 cars, a vault toilet, picnic tables, and no potable water.

Do NOT start on Barclay Creek Trail 1055. The climbers' path begins BEHIND THE OUTHOUSE, on the overgrown abandoned logging road that continues uphill from the parking area. Follow that road two or three tenths of a mile to the first creek. Look RIGHT for a cairn where a steep, heavily eroded path turns straight uphill toward the ridge. Orange, green or pink tape has been reported and may or may not be present.

You cross the creek twice — that double crossing is a useful confirmation you are on the correct path. From there the path climbs relentlessly and directly up the forested north/west side, with a short badly eroded class 3 step where hand lines have been reported, and several places where the tread braids. Trekking poles help on the loose lower section. There is no reliable water above the creek.
approach_variants.season: May-Oct; the notch gully holds snow into mid-summer
hazards: Very steep, loose, heavily eroded lower path — braided tread easy to lose
Cliffing out by staying high on the west ridge crest
Loose ash and obscured tread through the 2022 burn scar
Snow in the notch gully into mid-summer; the step at the notch varies year to year with snowpack
Loose rock in the summit basin — helmet
Creek crossings have been a ford when the log is out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The transition from approach to route is a change in the ground, not a landmark: the path tops out on the WEST RIDGE CREST at about 4,000-4,100 ft, where the angle suddenly eases and the tread visibly improves. If you are still fighting steep eroded dirt, you have not reached it.

Follow the crest east for roughly a mile. Where the cliff bands appear you must drop BELOW them — this is where parties go wrong. Staying high on the crest feels natural and cliffs you out, forcing steep and dangerous downclimbing to recover; hold a lower trajectory, cross the wooded gully, pick up the faint path on the far side and traverse into the talus basin at about 4,900 ft. From the basin the main gully to the notch at about 5,550 ft between South Baring and the true summit is obvious and navigation is straightforward. A 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope has left loose ash and dirt that can obscure the tread along the crest.

hazards: Loose and vegetated rock is the defining hazard of the Baring north face and is why the wall goes years between ascents.
Rockfall, both natural and climber-triggered, funnels into the couloirs and brush slopes between Barclay Lake and the base of the face.
Maritime weather can move in fast off Puget Sound with little warning and soaks the wall within minutes.
The descent forest on the west and northwest side is steep, eroded and cliff-banded, with route-finding consequences that have proved fatal.
BASE jumpers use this face and can dislodge rock or drop equipment onto climbers below.
wa_baring_mountain_oatmeal_man.rappels: No established rappel line is documented. Descent from the summit is on foot by reversing the standard northwest-ridge/BASE-jumper trail; retreat from the wall means rappelling the line itself off gear and whatever 1992-vintage fixed anchors remain, which should not be assumed to exist.
wa_baring_mountain_oatmeal_man.descent: Walk off via the summit ridge and the standard northwest-ridge / BASE-jumper trail down the west side to the old logging road at the Barclay Lake trailhead.
pro_tips: This route has no modern topo and effectively no repeat beta — the original first-ascent note is the only account, so plan it as an exploratory ascent rather than a route you follow.
Carry over the top. There is no sane way back down the north face, and the walk-off dumps you at the same trailhead, so leave nothing at a base camp you cannot afford to abandon.
Scout the northwest-ridge descent as a separate day trip first. Descending unfamiliar, cliff-banded forest at 4,000 ft in the dark after fourteen pitches is where this outing goes wrong.
Wait for a genuinely long dry spell. Cascade west-slope gneiss at this elevation stays greasy for days after rain, and the approach hillside is soaking wet vegetation.
Baring's north face is an active BASE-jumping site; if you hear or see activity above you, get out from under the fall line before continuing.
wa_baring_mountain_oatmeal_man.descent_text: There is no rappel descent of the north face. From the summit, follow the BASE-jumper boot track down and west for a few minutes, then swing counterclockwise toward the talus and drop into the notch between the north and south summits at roughly 5,550–5,600 ft. Descend west out of the notch through the gully and into the boulder-filled basin at about 4,900 ft — this is talus in late summer and fall but holds a steep snow headwall well into summer, and parties routinely want an axe here. From the basin, traverse and drop through meadows, heather and boulders (roughly 700 vertical feet) onto the west/northwest ridge crest near 4,000 ft, then pick up the steep game-trail-grade climbers' path through old-growth forest. The final section is a relentless, eroded 1,500-foot descent in the trees — steep, muddy when wet, with a short class-3 step where hand lines have been reported — that dumps out on the abandoned logging road just uphill of the Barclay Lake trail parking area. Reckon on about three hours from the summit to the car, longer if you are tired or the forest is wet, and do not attempt to shortcut into the wrong drainage: this is the slope where a climber died in 1952 and where the mountain's fatality history is concentrated.
wa_baring_mountain_oatmeal_man.itinerary: Realistically a full car-to-car day with a very early start, or a two-day outing. Day 1: drive to the Barclay Lake trailhead the night before, hike the 2.2 miles to Barclay Lake in the evening and bivy near the lake (established sites exist; Wild Sky Wilderness rules apply). Day 2: leave camp before first light, brush-bash to the base of the north face, climb the fourteen pitches, top out, and take the northwest-ridge/BASE-jumper trail all the way down to the trailhead — you will not be returning to a lakeside camp, so carry everything over the top or accept a retrieval walk back in.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek Trail 1055 to the lake, then straight up the north face hillside
approach_variants.notes:
From US-2 at milepost 42 in Baring, directly across from the store, turn north onto Barclay Creek Road (FR 6024), cross the BNSF tracks and bear left at the fork about 0.2 miles up. Follow about 4.3 to 4.5 miles of gravel to the Barclay Lake trailhead at roughly 2,280 ft — parking for about 20 cars, a vault toilet, picnic tables, no potable water.

Unlike the ridge and face routes, this one uses the maintained trail: Barclay Creek Trail 1055 runs gently east up the valley about 2.2 miles to Barclay Lake at around 2,420 ft, directly beneath the wall. The north face rises roughly 3,700 vertical feet from the lake in only half a mile of horizontal distance.

Leave the trail near the lake and climb the steep forested, brushy hillside beneath the wall. The 1961 first-ascent account of this face describes the first 1,000 ft as exactly that — a brush-and-forest struggle to reach a camp below the couloirs — and nothing about that terrain has improved. Allow several hours from the car to the base.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Pathless steep brush and blowdown for the first 1,000 ft
Wet vegetation and loose ground
No fixed protection or path — retreat is by the same brush
Easy to end up on the Dolomite Tower approach in the wrong drainage
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is NO maintained climbers' path to the main-peak wall, and that absence is itself the navigation aid. The fixed lines, hand lines and boot track that exist on this mountain belong to the DOLOMITE TOWER approach, which leaves the trail well BEFORE the lake and goes up a different drainage. If you find fixed rope, bolted slab or a worn boot track on your way to the base, you are in the wrong drainage entirely — turn around and go back to the lake. The correct ground is pathless: wet vegetation, blowdown and loose forest floor, gained by leaving the trail at the lake and going straight up.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Lake trailhead to Couloir Camp and the North Face
approach_variants.notes:
Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near Baring; Northwest Forest Pass at the self-issue kiosk.

Leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts BEHIND THE OUTHOUSE, not on the main trail. Follow the old abandoned logging road about a third of a mile to a cairn at roughly 2,450 ft where a rough unmaintained path splits off toward the base of the mountain. That split is easy to miss and carries no trail sign.

From the cairn the boot path climbs steep loose dirt and crosses the creek draining the face several times. STAY CLOSE TO THE WATER: the tread is faint and repeatedly lost in the brush, and the creek is the handrail. In total the lower approach fights through roughly 2,300 vertical feet of dense slide alder, vine maple and devil's club before any technical rock. Allow around seven hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear boots or sturdy approach shoes rather than carrying them.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; snow lingers in the couloir into August
hazards: Missing the unsigned cairn split at ~2,450 ft
About 2,300 ft of slide alder, vine maple and devil's club
Faint tread constantly lost in brush — losing the creek loses the line
Steep loose dirt slopes
Snow in the couloir between the ribs into August
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COULOIR CAMP at about 4,300 ft — around 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — is the landmark that tells you which approach you are on. It is a used bivy shelf directly beneath the wall, historically the base camp for the first-ascent siege, and it remains a reasonable first night for parties splitting the approach. Above it, the ground to follow runs BETWEEN TWO precipitous brush-and-cliff-covered rock RIBS that flank a large couloir; snow often lingers there into August, so an axe is worth having early season. Follow that ground to the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead.

Negative marker: if you have gained a ridge crest and the walking has suddenly got easier, you are on the northwest-ridge scramble line on the west side of the mountain, not on the face — the face approach never eases.

approach_variants.name: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
approach_variants.notes: Note that this route and the Northwest Ridge route describe the same physical climbers' path up the west side of the mountain; the naming differs by source, the ground does not. Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,200-2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road, shared parking with the Barclay Lake day hike. Go around the outhouse and pick up the old overgrown logging-road grade for a few hundred yards before it turns sharply uphill into a steep, muddy, eroded gully — that is the start of the unmaintained climbers' trail. Look for cairns and boot tread; this is not a maintained trail and is easy to lose. The tread is steep and often slick from the first steps, and there is no reliable water past the initial creek, so fill up at the car. After roughly a mile and 1,800 ft the path tops out on Baring's west ridge at about 4,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the basin and notch gully hold snow late
hazards: Steep, muddy, eroded unmaintained tread from the first steps
Cliffing out by holding the crest too long
Loose ash and obscured tread in the burn scar
Late snow in the basin and notch gully — axe and possibly crampons into mid-summer
Loose rock from the boulder field onward — helmet
No water above the trailhead creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The west ridge crest at about 4,000 ft is the handover point — the angle eases and the tread improves noticeably. Follow the crest generally east/southeast. Where the cliff bands appear, watch for the point where the path dips slightly BELOW them into a wooded gully before regaining the ridge; staying too long on the crest is the recorded error and forces a downclimb back to the correct line. The 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope adds loose ash and hides the tread here.

The route then drops into a talus and boulder basin, crosses it, and climbs the main gully up to the notch at about 5,550 ft between South Baring and the true summit. That gully and basin hold snow late; the step right at the notch is sometimes called the vertical snow wall and its difficulty varies year to year. From the notch scramble up and right a short way, break onto an open slope, then trend left/north over class 2-3 boulder and heather to the base of the summit block, which is climbed on its LEFT (west) side at class 3-4 to reach 6,127 ft.

wa_bear_mountain_chilliwack_north_buttre.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams from small (~0.4in) up to 3in max, DOUBLED on the 0.5in, 0.75in, 1in, and 2in sizes — this specific doubling comes directly from a route-focused trip report and gear list, not a generic guess. Bring a set of stoppers/nuts for thinner, more delicate placements on the 5.6-5.10a pitches. No pitons needed on modern ascents (historic 1960s FA account mentions pins, but current parties climb it clean).

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs nearly level for the first mile and then climbs at a steady grade to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. Drop off the east side and continue down into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail proper. The tread loses height past a backcountry camp to the Chilliwack River crossing - historically a hand-pulled cable car, and a serious ford if it is not running, so check its status before you plan around it - then runs down-valley past further camps to the Bear Creek confluence. The camp at that confluence has been closed since fire came through the drainage, so confirm it is open rather than assuming a bed there.

At Bear Creek the maintained trail ends. Ford the creek, which can be a genuinely committing crossing in snowmelt, and climb steep brushy timber eastward; higher the brush turns to huckleberry and slide alder before opening into meadows above Ruta Lake. Traverse the divide from there, skirting the loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points and crossing a rock rib, to a broad saddle at about 6,480 ft with running water and heather tent sites. Most parties split this over two days.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the Chilliwack crossing has dropped and the buttress is dry
hazards: a river crossing that depends on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber and slide alder with no tread
loose south-facing traverse slopes below the divide points
rockfall and icefall out of the shrinking glacier in the couloir
a moat between neve and slab that worsens through the season
a position days from any road, on either side of the border
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS BY LOSING HEIGHT, AND THAT IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW AT CAMP. From the 6,480 ft saddle you drop down steep scree, trending climber's right, and cross several minor gullies to reach the toe of the small glacier remnant spilling out of the couloir below the buttress. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS UPWARD FROM THE SADDLE TOWARD ROCK IS THE WRONG ONE.

IDENTIFY THE SADDLE FIRST: it is broad, it has running water on it and flat heather sites, and it sits on the north-west ridge with the wall around the corner rather than above you. A saddle with no water and no camping is not it.

AT THE ICE, THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE BUTTRESS YOU GO UP. This route climbs the glacier or neve on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress and then works into slabs that lead to a corner system - the corner is where the technical climbing starts. THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS ITSELF, WHERE THE ROCK MEETS THE ICE ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE, IS THE START OF THE DIRECT AND NOT OF THIS ROUTE. If you are roping up at the very bottom of the rock rather than walking past it on snow, you are on the harder line.

WATCH THE JOIN BETWEEN SNOW AND ROCK. A moat opens where the neve pulls away from the slabs and it deepens through the season; getting out of it onto the slabs is often the awkward move of the approach and it is worth an axe and crampons even in high summer.

A CROSS-CHECK ONCE COMMITTED: the climbing above the corner runs up to about 5.10 with the hardest move an offwidth part-way up, and it finishes on the buttress top, from where a scramble gains the true summit. If your first pitch off the ice is already at your limit, you have started too low and too far right.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
