approach_variants.notes: There is a far shorter line to the same camp from the road on the Canadian side of the border - a fraction of the distance the Hannegan approach covers. It crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, and this page cannot say that crossing is lawful, so confirm it with the border authorities before planning on it; and the tread turns unmaintained and badly overgrown after the first mile or two, so the miles it saves are not all easy ones. Most parties starting in the United States take the long way rather than deal with it; parties already north of the border have the opposite calculation.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with the documents and permissions that implies
unmaintained and heavily overgrown tread for most of the distance
the same loose divide traverse and the same glacier remnant beneath the buttress
a rescue that may involve two countries
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH VARIANT CHANGES ONLY HOW YOU ARRIVE AT THE 6,480 FT SADDLE. Once there, everything is as for the long approach: the camp is the broad saddle with running water and heather sites on the north-west ridge, and the route starts by DROPPING off it on steep scree, trending climber's right, across several minor gullies to the toe of the glacier remnant beneath the couloir.

THE SAME TWO TESTS APPLY AT THE ICE. Go up the snow on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of the buttress into the slabs and the corner system. If you are tying in at the very toe of the rock where it meets the ice on the right, you are under the Direct.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE MARKER: gaining height straight from the saddle toward rock means you have not gone far enough down. The wall is below and around the corner from camp, not above it.

approach_variants.name: FS-3160 road-end boot path to Church Lake, then the basin rim to the 6,066 ft knoll
approach_variants.notes:
From the FS-3160 road-end parking, reached via Canyon Creek Road (FS-31) then FS-3160, the route follows an unmaintained but heavily used boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail. It climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first stretch is the steepest sustained grade of the day.

Skirt the lake along its east (left) shore; the best flat campsites are on the far side.

Beyond the lake the tread fades into intermittent boot path and cairns through meadows and heather benches. Keep LEFT — east — up the basin rim toward a broad knoll around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block. That stretch accounts for most of the remaining 900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 miles one way.

Church Lake is the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow patches persist into July on shaded ground and in the summit gullies
hazards: An unmaintained boot path with no numbered trail and no maintained tread past the lake
Intermittent cairns through meadows and heather with nothing built to follow
Snow patches into July on shaded ground and in the summit gullies
A loose scree and dirt descent chute that parties use as a shortcut
Church Lake is the last water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CHURCH LAKE IS THE HANDRAIL AND IT IS UNMISSABLE — 0.6 TO 0.7 MILE UP, 400 FT OF GAIN, AND THE STEEPEST GROUND OF THE DAY IS BEHIND YOU WHEN YOU REACH IT. Everything about this route is oriented from the lake. Skirt it on its EAST, left-hand, shore.

ABOVE THE LAKE THE INSTRUCTION IS ONE WORD: LEFT. Keep left — east — up the basin rim. The tread is intermittent boot path and cairns through meadows and heather benches and there is nothing built to follow, so the bearing is what you navigate on.

THE 6,066 FT KNOLL IS THE TOP OF THE APPROACH: a broad high point on the ridge separating the Church Lake basin from the summit block, only a few tens of feet lower than the true summit. Arriving somewhere the ground falls away on every side is the confirmation.

FROM THE KNOLL, DROP SLIGHTLY AND TRAVERSE NORTH. The base of the summit block is across a rocky heather bowl to the north. That short descent is the step people skip; a party that keeps climbing straight off the knoll is on the ridge rather than under the block.

THE CLIMBING IS THE LAST 300 FT AND NOTHING BELOW IT. From the base of the block, roughly 300 ft of easy Class 2-3 on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure only in the last stretch, reaches the 6,091 ft summit. If you are scrambling for much more than 300 ft you are on the wrong feature.

DESCENT SHORTCUT WORTH KNOWING, because it changes what you should look for on the way up: many parties come down a scree and dirt chute that cuts straight from the ridge to the lake shore, shortcutting the traverse. It is loose. Noting where it tops out on the way up is what makes it usable on the way down.

bivy.name: Douglas Fir Campground
bivy.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.
bivy.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
bivy.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/year day-use fee (Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Pass, or Digital Day Pass accepted)
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead, in effect May 15-Oct 31
access.closures: Salmon la Sac Trailhead and Salmon La Sac Campground are CLOSED by Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-03-2026-44 (Three Queens Fire), effective 18 Sep 2026 through 31 Oct 2026 unless lifted sooner.
access.landManager: Alpine Lakes Wilderness — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Cle Elum Ranger District
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Interagency Pass / Digital Day Pass

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and the PCT, then the Shovel Creek fisherman's trail to the foot of the slab
approach_variants.notes:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, hike the Waptus River Trail about nine miles to Waptus Lake. The bridge has been out, so wade or rock-hop the river at the horse ford. Where the trail joins the PCT, head SOUTHBOUND (west).

Shortly before the PCT crosses the Waptus River, leave the trail and head northwest toward a faint shoulder and bench through flat, easy forest. Pick up a fisherman's trail on the southwest side of that bench and follow it toward Shovel Creek, then up and over the bench past an informal campsite with a GIANT CAIRN, where it starts to climb the shoulder on the EAST side of Shovel Creek.

Before long the trail leaves the forest straight onto talus. Easy talus walking brings you to Shovel Creek; cross where convenient.

Roughly 13 miles to the base, five to six hours. Most parties camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge.
approach_variants.season: July to September; documented ascents cluster in August
hazards: About 2,000 ft of unprotected friction slab, mostly climbed unroped
Rock quality deteriorating markedly on the final three summit-block pitches
No water on the slab — carry the whole climbing day's supply
A long, remote approach with no confirmed cell coverage
The Shovel Lake descent alternative involves loose dirt high, brush and cliff bands low, and heavy route-finding
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CROSSING SHOVEL CREEK OFF THE TALUS PUTS YOU AT THE FOOT OF THE MEGA SLAB — THAT IS THE ARRIVAL, AND IT IS A CREEK CROSSING RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT. The slab drops from the peak's southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft all the way to Shovel Creek at about 3,700 ft, so there is no ambiguity about which piece of rock it is: it is the enormous unbroken sheet above you, one of the longest continuous sandstone slabs in North America.

WHICH LINE ON THE SLAB IS THE REAL QUESTION HERE, AND FOR THIS ROUTE THE ANSWER IS A SINGLE WORD: LOWEST. Infinite Beauty begins at the LOWEST PART of the slab, on a SHALLOW RIB. Walk the base downhill until it stops going down, and start on the rib there.

HOW THAT DISTINGUISHES IT FROM ITS NEIGHBOUR: Timeless Treasure climbs the MIDDLE of the slab. So if you have walked out along the base looking for a nicer-looking start, you are on Timeless Treasure. The lowest point is the whole distinction and it is decidable by walking downhill rather than by looking.

WHAT THE ROCK SHOULD FEEL LIKE, AS CONFIRMATION: clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone with minimal breaks, and roughly 2,000 ft of sustained fourth class. Approach shoes or trail runners friction well on it and most of the slab is climbed unroped. If you are pulling into cracks or dodging vegetation, you are off the clean sheet.

AND WHERE THE ROUTE ENDS ITS OWN IDENTITY: after about 2,000 ft the line naturally angles RIGHT and joins Timeless Treasure for brief, unexposed low-fifth moves up overlaps trending up and right to the southeast shoulder. Easy scrambling then leads to the summit block, where the rock quality noticeably deteriorates over the final three pitches.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie and Williams Creek to Dutch Miller Gap, then a camp below the face
approach_variants.notes:
From North Bend, take I-90 to exit 34, follow 468th Ave SE north 0.6 mile, then right onto Middle Fork Road, FS Road 56. Continue twelve miles as the pavement gives out and roughens, then about five more rough miles — high clearance recommended — to the Dutch Miller Gap trailhead at the old roadbed terminus, about 2,850 ft.

Hike the Middle Fork Snoqualmie / Williams Creek corridor roughly fifteen miles to Dutch Miller Gap, then continue to a camp below the southwest face. The whole outing is about 30 miles of trail.

Camp to summit runs about six hours and summit to camp about four and three quarter, so budget a full day above camp.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Loose, broken rock throughout the gully and the lower pitches
Marginal protection near an old, deteriorating piton at the pitch 1 crux
Complex, slow route-finding through ledges on the descent
A long, remote multi-day approach on a rough forest road with limited rescue access
No walk-off once on the roped summit block: the three rappels are the only reasonable retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE COUNTING GULLIES, AND THERE ARE EXACTLY TWO. The southwest face carries TWO PARALLEL GULLIES. Take the LEFT-HAND one. That is the entire base finding and it works in cloud because two parallel features are countable from close range without seeing the summit.

WHAT THE LEFT GULLY SHOULD DELIVER: roughly 1,000 ft of class 3-4 ground ending at a RIDGE NOTCH NORTHWEST of the true summit. Notch on the ridge, summit up and to your southeast: that is the correct arrival at the technical climbing.

THE ROPED PART IS SHORT AND ITS SHAPE CONFIRMS THE LINE: three short pitches to 5.6 up the summit block from that notch. Not a long face climb — three pitches. If you are looking at hundreds of feet of steep rock above the notch, you are at the wrong notch.

AND THE DESCENT MIRRORS IT EXACTLY, which is worth knowing before you start up: three single-rope rappels down the WEST side of the summit block back to the notch, then downclimb the class 3-4 gully. A 50 m rope suffices; a 60 m or two 50 m ropes is better for a party of three. Route-finding through the ledges on the way down is reported as the crux of the descent and slower than the ascent.

HISTORICAL CONFIRMATION THAT THIS IS THE ORDINARY WAY UP THE PEAK: this face gave the mountain's first ascent, on 8 August 1939, by Fred Beckey at sixteen with Joe Barto and Wayne Swift.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/year day-use fee (Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Pass, or Digital Day Pass accepted)
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead, in effect May 15-Oct 31
access.closures: Salmon la Sac Trailhead and Salmon La Sac Campground are CLOSED by Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-03-2026-44 (Three Queens Fire), effective 18 Sep 2026 through 31 Oct 2026 unless lifted sooner. The order also closes the Pacific Crest Trail between Ridge Lake and Lake Vicente.
access.landManager: Alpine Lakes Wilderness — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Cle Elum Ranger District
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Interagency Pass / Digital Day Pass

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and the PCT, then the Shovel Creek track to the middle of the slab
approach_variants.notes:
From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, follow the Waptus River Trail and the PCT about nine miles to Waptus Lake and on to a camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge, roughly eleven to twelve flat miles in all. The Waptus River bridge has been out, so plan on a ford at the horse crossing.

From camp, an old, faint, unmaintained track parallels Shovel Creek through forest to a bench around 3,400 ft, then talus-hops to the base of the Mega Slab at roughly 3,700 ft.

About 19.3 km one way and 4,697 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: A long, remote approach with no confirmed reliable cell coverage
Loose rock and heavy route-finding on the Shovel Lake descent
No water on the slab itself
Deteriorating rock on the shared summit-block pitches
approach_variants.baseFinding:
SAME SLAB, DIFFERENT PLACE ON IT: THIS ROUTE TAKES THE MIDDLE. Once you have crossed Shovel Creek off the talus and are standing under the Mega Slab, walk along the base to its MIDDLE and start there. The slab runs from about 3,700 ft at the creek to the southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft, so the middle is a real and findable place along a very long base.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST ITS NEIGHBOUR IS A SINGLE STEP: Infinite Beauty starts at the LOWEST point of the slab, on a shallow rib. If you are at the bottom end of the base, you are on Infinite Beauty. Walk up along the base until you are in the middle of the sheet.

WHAT THE ROCK SHOULD FEEL LIKE: perfect stone, mostly fourth class with occasional low-fifth moves higher up. If it is broken or vegetated you have drifted off the clean centre of the slab.

WHERE THE TWO ROUTES MERGE, AND WHY THAT MATTERS TO THE FINDING: both finish on the SAME three-pitch 5.6+ summit block. So being on the correct route matters for the first 2,000 ft and stops mattering above the shoulder. If you are already on the summit block and unsure which line you climbed, the question no longer has a practical answer.

A PRACTICAL NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE FINDING HERE: most parties either reverse the slab, which is easy and secure, or descend toward Shovel Lake. Reversing is the recommended option precisely because you already know that ground.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the chimney left of the two Vs
approach_variants.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach, shared with every other line on this face: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, hazardous under lingering snow into early July because of a creek and moat hidden beneath it.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way.

If the standard trailhead or the pass is shut — wildfire closures have done this — the Snow Lakes trail reaches the same face by a longer and less direct line past Lake Viviane and a climbers' path onto the south side of the peak. One party clocked that version at about ten miles and 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country travel for the final approach
Six rappels down the north face on ageing natural anchors — carry extra tat
A possible extra rappel from the West Ridge notch to regain the south-face base
Snafflehounds at the base will eat gear left unattended
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LOOK FOR TWO LARGE Vs AND START IN THE CHIMNEY TO THEIR LEFT. That is the whole identification, it is published in exactly those terms, and the accompanying note is that you cannot miss it. Two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; the route's first pitch takes the chimney immediately LEFT of them.

CONFIRM WITH THE FIRST PITCH ITSELF: from the chimney you move LEFT and climb up on knobs to a belay, at about 5.7. Knobs after a leftward move out of a chimney is the signature. If you are pulling straight up out of the chimney with no traverse, look again.

POSITION RELATIVE TO ITS NEIGHBOUR, which is the check that catches the common error: this route is to the climber's RIGHT of the classic south-face line. So if you are at the middle of the base of the face, you are one route too far left. Walk RIGHT until the two Vs are on your right-hand side and you are at a chimney.

AND A DISTANCE CHECK ON THE ROUTE AS A WHOLE: seven pitches, about 650 ft, running 5.5 to 5.9, with a long chimney-gully crossing to a big ledge partway up and a forced rightward dihedral as the crux. A four- or five-pitch route ending on the West Ridge is one of the shorter lines on the left flank, not this.

IN CLOUD, when you cannot see the Vs from a distance, walk the foot of the face and count chimneys rather than guessing: the Vs are large features and they are visible from close under them even when the summit is not.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, staying WEST of the creek longer than the West Face line, then over the Half Moon col into the south basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20, follow the cairned climbers' trail south along the WEST side of Early Winters Creek toward Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, BUT STAY ON THE TRAIL, ON THE RIGHT OR WEST SIDE OF THE CREEK, LONGER THAN THE WEST FACE LINE DOES. Do not cross the creek where that route splits off.

Continue up-valley as the trail fades into open talus and boulder fields, then work toward the head of the basin. Roughly 2 miles and 2,440 ft one-way to the base, with 2.5-5 hours a reasonable estimate given the route-finding through boulder fields. Noticeably longer and more sustained than the standard West Face gully route.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Talus hopping and route-finding through boulder fields for 2 miles
A lot of large loose rock on the route, making rappelling it inadvisable
An exposed unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old bolt if tagging the true summit
A steep, loose upper gully on the shared descent
Snow lingering in the approach basin and the gullies near the top of the route in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CUT LEFT, EAST, TOWARD THE LOW POINT ON THE RIDGE BETWEEN BIG KANGAROO AND HALF MOON. That col drops and traverses you into the SOUTH-FACING BASIN DIRECTLY BELOW BIG KANGAROO'S SOUTH WALL.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROUTE ITSELF IS VISUAL AND UNAMBIGUOUS WHEN YOU CAN SEE THE WALL: THE BECKEY-TATE'S OBVIOUS CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITS THE FACE. A single ramp system running up the middle of a south wall, splitting it, is the line.

SO THE ORDER OF FINDS IS: stay west of the creek, reach the head of the basin, cut east to the Half Moon col, drop into the south basin, then look for the ramp splitting the middle of the wall.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE WEST FACE, WHICH IS THE COMMONEST ERROR FROM THIS CAR: THE WEST FACE ROUTE CROSSES EARLY WINTERS CREEK AFTER ONLY HALF A MILE, AT THE EDGE OF THE TALUS FIELD, AND TAKES A BROAD SHALLOW WEST-FACING GULLY WITH A CHOCKSTONE IN IT. If you crossed the creek early and are looking at a chockstone, you are on the west side of the mountain.

AND AGAINST THE OTHER SOUTH-FACE LINES, WHICH SHARE THIS BASIN: KEARNEY-THOMAS crosses the creek and ascends the prominent gully system TAKING THE LEFT FORK AT THE HIGH Y-JUNCTION. GOING DOWN UNDER starts at the Beckey-Tate base and then TRAVERSES RIGHT ACROSS OVERLAPS to its own start ledge. SKINNY START is ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT of the Kearney-Thomas start. So on this wall: the central ramp is Beckey-Tate, and everything else is measured from either it or Kearney-Thomas.

DESCENT IS NOT DOWN THIS ROUTE, AND THE REASON MATTERS: rappelling the Beckey-Tate is technically possible with two ropes, roughly five to six rappels off slings and trees, but the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, so rope-stuck and rockfall risk is high and most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead scramble about 20 ft up and LEFT to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which is a few hundred feet higher, and descend the gully from there.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

approach_variants.name: Merry Brook path and the key ramp
approach_variants.notes: Start from the unsigned boot path off the FR 4096 spur, marked only by a small cairn and rock pile in the roadside grass and notoriously easy to drive past — accounts disagree on the mileage and on which switchback it leaves from, so mark it on the way in rather than trusting a figure. The path drops into forest and follows Merry Brook upstream, the last reliable water, then swings north out of the drainage onto a forested ridge. It is aggressively steep with deadfall to climb under and over, and eases where it turns south above and just west of a small tarn. Pink and blue flagging is tied to branches, roots and sticks about every hundred yards; go more than about thirty yards without seeing any and backtrack rather than press on. Four boulder fields are crossed on the way up, the first near 3,500 ft and the second near 4,200 ft, which holds snow into summer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmaintained track with blowdown, brush and faint braids — parties regularly lose it, and it is far less obvious on descent
A moat where the snow meets the rock at the cliff band, which is what actually stops parties
Climbing back out of the wrong gully means steep dirt above a cliff edge — reported as the most dangerous move on the route
Devil's club on the short descending traverse near 5,200 ft
Many pinnacles on the summit ridge; in poor visibility it is hard to tell which is the last and correct one
approach_variants.baseFinding: A DISTINCTIVE CLUSTER OF BOULDERS, THEN A SHARP TURN EAST ONTO A RAMP YOU CANNOT SEE FROM BELOW. Somewhere between about 4,900 and 5,100 ft the boulder fields give way to meadows and a cliff band bars the way; you should be OUT of the trees by here. The marker is a unique, distinctive cluster of boulders. About fifty feet above it, turn sharply EAST, cross a V-notch and climb the far side on a mossy ramp that is invisible from underneath, then pass to the east of a large buttress. Flagging is thick at the correct start. The trap is the gully lying straight ahead: do not go straight up the basin. That gully cliffs out, and climbing back out of it over steep dirt with the cliff edge below is the most dangerous move on the route. If you are in a gully rather than crossing a notch onto a ramp, drop back and hunt for the boulder cluster and the flagging. The difficulty at the ramp is usually the moat where snow meets rock, not the ramp itself, which parties describe as straightforward once found.

bivy.name: Bedal Basin, below the north side of Bedal Peak
bivy.notes: The high camp for BEDAL PEAK, sitting directly under its steep north side and its cliffs, and the only sensible place to sleep for a party attempting the peak rather than just visiting the basin. Getting here is about two and a half miles from the road end at around 2,800 ft, climbing steadily through old forest and across avalanche tracks, and the trail deteriorates as it goes — it receives very little maintenance, is thickly overgrown in the avalanche chutes by midsummer, and effectively gives out about a mile and a half in, after which the way is up the rocky creek bed and through thin forest into the basin. Expect brush, wet feet and route-finding rather than a walk. The basin holds the remains of a pioneer cabin among the boulders, which makes a useful landmark for orienting the last of the approach. The peak above needs route-finding and, on most lines, real climbing rather than scrambling, so the short approach should not be read as a short day. The spur road itself is the other constraint: two steep, rough miles where high clearance is genuinely wanted rather than merely advised. Bedal Campground sits a mile down the main loop road from the junction and is the drive-in fallback for a party that arrives too late to start up the spur, and it is already recorded in the earlier upper-loop file. Snow lies in the basin into July.
bivy.water: Bedal Creek and its meltwater feeders run through the basin and are reliable through the climbing season, thinning late in a hot August. The creek is crossed twice on the way up and both crossings are straightforward by midsummer but pushy in snowmelt.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS, which begins about half a mile up the trail — free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the road end, no reservation and no quota, and a twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass to leave a vehicle. Fires are legal in principle at this elevation but inappropriate in a small meadow basin with limited dead wood, and summer restrictions usually prohibit them outright; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A meadow basin with room for several small parties on durable ground near the boulders, though flat spots are fewer than the open look of the place suggests. It is quiet — this trail sees very little traffic and you can have the basin to yourself on a summer weekend.

bivy.name: Berdeen Lake benches
bivy.notes: The camp for Berdeen Peak and the substance of the Bacon Creek side of this zone. The documented approach starts at the Bacon Creek road end at valley-bottom elevation, scrambles up Porkbelly Ridge, crosses the east side of the peak around 6,400 ft and drops to camp above the lake — a very big first day with four thousand feet of gain, much of it trackless. The lake sits in a deep cirque a little over a mile east of Hagan Mountain and drains east over an enormous waterfall into a tributary of Bacon Creek, which is the geography that settles the argument about which road it belongs to: it faces Bacon Creek, not Baker Lake. It can be reached from the Blum Lakes over the divide to the northwest, but that is a traverse variation for a party already committed to a long trip, not an approach. From camp Berdeen Peak's east ridge is the way up, and the ground south and west continues onto the Bacon massif. Season is roughly mid-July into September, held back at the front by snow on the ridge and at the back by short days on a route with no trail.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams, fed off the glaciers above and reliable all season. Treat it. This is the first dependable water since the valley bottom, over four thousand feet below.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required for any overnight and written for a cross-country zone rather than a designated camp — a different thing to ask for, and it must be collected in person at the wilderness information center, which is a long way round on the far side of the range from the Anderson Creek trailheads. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and never in the meadow, keep a hundred feet back from the water, and carry out human waste. A bear canister is the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from; they can usually be borrowed at the permit office.
bivy.capacity: A handful of tent-sized spots on benches above the lake shore; the basin is large but the flat, durable ground is limited, and this is a cross-country zone with a small party cap rather than an established campground

bivy.name: Bacon Creek road end and Porkbelly Ridge
bivy.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMPING ON THIS APPROACH and the honest answer is to start early and reach the lake basin in one push. The road leaves the highway a few miles east of Marblemount and runs up the valley to a road end around 850 ft, from which Porkbelly Ridge is climbed trackless — steep timber, deadfall and brush with better travel once the ridge crest establishes itself, and no benches, clearings or water worth the name in four thousand feet. THE ROAD IS THE FIRST PROBLEM: it carries very large potholes over long stretches, a bridge on the main road beyond one of the side creeks has been out, and the spurs off it are variously blocked by missing bridges, washouts and downed timber, so how far a vehicle gets is a live question that changes year to year and adds miles at the bottom when it goes against you. A party that runs out of daylight on the ridge flattens a spot among the trees and moves at first light; that is the realistic use of this camp, not a plan. The same road end is the start for the Diobsud Creek side of Bacon Peak, which is climbed on a longer line past Salvation Peak with a glacier saddle camp around 6,250 ft — a spring and early summer objective needing snow travel gear, and a different proposition entirely from the summer scramble off the Anderson Creek road.
bivy.water: The creek near the road end, treated. Above it there is nothing dependable until the lake basin high on the ridge, so fill everything before you start climbing.
bivy.permit: The road end and the lower part of the ridge are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, where a night in a pullout is generally tolerated and no permit is issued. The ground higher up crosses into North Cascades National Park, so if you sleep anywhere above the lower ridge you need a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone. The boundary is not marked on the ground on this ridge, so ask at the permit office where it falls before planning a bivy rather than deciding on the hill. No campfires above the road, and total burn bans are common on this side through a dry August.
bivy.capacity: Rough parking at the road end and whatever flat ground you can find in the timber; one party, found rather than chosen. There is no camp here, and that is worth saying plainly.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope end has jammed in a crack on the RIGHT side of this rappel, forcing the party to climb back up the other strand to free it - and the ground you would climb to reach it is loose. Watch where the ends land and pull away from the crack.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the shared summit down to the P7 anchor on Mile High Club's line; single 60m rope reaches comfortably.
rappel_detail.anchor: summit rap rings, station ~8ft south of summit bolts and ~4ft off the ground
hazards: The edge below this station has cut a rope badly enough that the party had to chop it in half and retire it. The route page says the edge has since been ground down; the Beyond Redlining page still tells you exactly where to lay the rope, so treat it as live

A hard pendulum. The first-ascent advice is to lower to the large flake and walk left to the belay rather than rappelling free; a 2025 party swung hard right into a separate rock face on this rappel, on both of their visits
The nuts on these rap rings have been found loose - check them before you weight the station

Rappelling Beyond Redlining's own line is what this station exists to avoid: its first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it needs angling rappels off single bolts, many of which only reach the next anchor on rope stretch
rappel_detail.station: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings are set BACK from the top of the route, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down to the lower anchor at the base of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's LEFT of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.

rappel_detail.notes: A face-descent rappel down to the P6 anchor.
hazards: Dropping to the dihedral-top anchor instead is a specific, named mistake - the station you want is above and left of it
The published reason for tossing left is that parties climb directly below: keep the rope and anything you knock loose off them
rappel_detail.station: Toss the rope slightly LEFT of the bolt line rather than straight down. Rappel the pitch-6 face, then move to a rap anchor about 10 ft skier's left and 10 ft ABOVE the anchor at the top of the dihedral pitch. Do not continue to the top of the dihedral pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: A short rappel down to a ledge at P5; source explicitly flags this one as short.
hazards: Free-hanging above a ledge, so you arrive spinning onto a stance rather than sliding onto it
rappel_detail.station: A short rappel from the pitch-5 station to an anchor on a ledge off to the side of the dihedral pitch. It is free-hanging above the ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to P4, where one of two available anchor options is used.
hazards: Most stations on this route have two anchors a few feet apart so ascending and descending parties do not share one - taking the wrong one puts you on top of climbers
Rope thrown from here lands on anyone on pitch 4 below
rappel_detail.station: Two anchors are available here; take the skier's-LEFT one where you can, which keeps you off the climbing line.

rappel_detail.pull: A rope has been stuck in a crack pulling from the pitch-3 rap anchors; pull away from the crack. Feed the rope through the cedar bushes rather than throwing it.
rappel_detail.notes: The most commonly botched rappel on the descent — aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line; a hidden intermediate anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the visible upper-P3 station.
hazards: The route page states it outright: do not rappel down the vertical face on a single rope, because you will not reach the next anchors. Parties who miss it end up either doing two double-rope rappels from the top of pitch 3 or, on an 80 m, nearly reaching the pitch-2 anchors and then having to scramble across exposed ground
One party that missed it could not retrieve their rope at all - the pull angle around the intervening features made it stick and recovering it was judged unsafe
The tree the beta says will be flagged has never been flagged; it is still described as 'we will flag this tree soon' years later
rappel_detail.station: The confusing one, and by a wide margin the most-reported problem on this descent. From the pitch-4 anchor, pass through cedar bushes directly below the station and rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3 - it is mostly walking. Aim for a tree about 10 ft tall standing roughly 15 ft skier's left of the climbing line; the intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree. Look for it right where the ground turns from slabby to vertical. You CANNOT see this anchor on the way up, so it cannot be scouted on the climb; parties have found chalk arrows pointing at it.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down to a lower-P3 anchor, landing on a large ledge.
hazards: This is the vertical face the station above exists to get you onto safely; it is the ground you would be stranded above having missed the nook
rappel_detail.station: From the nook anchor, rappel the vertical section at the start of pitch 3 down to a large ledge, and set up at either of the anchors at the top of pitch 2 - the skier's-left one if it is free.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to the P2 anchor.
hazards: Parties consistently record being surprised that the last anchor before the ground is a separate one, offset from the climbing anchor
rappel_detail.station: The station is NOT the pitch-1 climbing anchor, which is what people expect and head for. The rap anchor is about 10 ft down and 10-15 ft skier's left of the pitch-1 belay anchor.

rappel_detail.pull: Consider staying on rappel and walking back to the belay bolt at the start of the route, then pulling the rope from there.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel(s) via the P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base of the route.
hazards: Do not treat the base of the route as the ground - the ledge you land on is exposed and hundreds of feet up
The gully to climber's right throws natural rockfall onto the start of the scramble; keep helmets on until you are clear of it, especially with parties above
rappel_detail.station: Final rappel to the base of the route. The starting ledge is several hundred feet above the ground and quite exposed.

wa_beyond_redlining.rappel_count_note: Eight rappels down Mile High Club's line on a SINGLE 60 m rope. That configuration is newer than the route: a dedicated rappel line was added alongside Mile High Club in August 2019 specifically so the descent could be done on a single 60, and the eight-station descent dates from then. Before that, parties used a single 70 m or two 60 m ropes, and counts from that era differ honestly - eight single-rope rappels on a 70, or seven - so an older count disagreeing with this table describes the pre-2019 descent, not an error. The line stays about 10-15 ft skier's LEFT of the bolt line throughout, and you should prefer the skier's-left anchor wherever two exist, because most stations are doubled so that rappelling and climbing parties are not on the same anchor. Beyond Redlining is equipped for rappelling but its own line is explicitly not recommended: the first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it requires angling rappels off single bolts where many rappels only reach the next anchor on rope stretch. Beyond Redlining's own hardware - a mid-pitch-1 bail station, a missing maillon on pitch 3 - belongs to that line and not to this one. No per-station rappel distances are known for the Mile High Club descent, and the rappel line does not follow the climbing line, so the pitch lengths are not a substitute; the figures given are nominal rather than measured.

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail to the cairned talus traverse
approach_variants.notes: Sunrise Mine trailhead, then the trail for about two and a half miles through the two unbridged creek crossings and up through forest to the LAST MAJOR SWITCHBACK before the final zigzags toward the pass — leave the trail there, not at the pass. A cairned traverse then runs northeast across talus toward the tower, crossing two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees and passing just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees. The boot path is well established in season because three routes share it. Top up water at the seep by the red-rock outcrop in the gully; there is none higher.
approach_variants.season: June to September. This face is west-facing and stays shaded and cold until roughly midday; significant snow can lie at the base from December through May.
hazards: Two unbridged creek crossings in the first mile
Loose talus on the traverse and party-inflicted rockfall across several pitches
West-facing and shaded until around midday, so cold starts are the norm
Steep snow against the base into early summer, which makes the last stretch of talus and the step onto rock its own small crux
The fifty-five-metre opening pitch commits you before any real bail option
approach_variants.baseFinding: Stay on the talus at the foot of the tower's WEST face — do not go up into the red gully on the right. Find the TWO LARGEST BOULDERS at the base of the tower and look straight up: the start is on the DARK GREY FACE directly above them. The confirmation is the bolt count — the first pitch is a single fifty-five-metre rope length with sixteen bolts in it, so if what you are under is short, or has only a handful of bolts, it is not this. Negative markers: if you have scrambled up and left on loose ledges past a LONE FIR to a SINGLE bolt on a narrow ledge, you are on the arete route one line to your right, which shares this tower's summit but not its face; if you left the traverse into a gully on the RIGHT-HAND side of the tower and gained a notch on the skyline ridge through cedar and heather, you are on the next tower along.

approach_variants.name: South Fork log crossing to Dry Creek basin
approach_variants.notes:
Two starts reach the same ground: the Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves trailhead at about 1,640 ft, or the Mount Dickerman trailhead across the highway, which lands you nearer the drainage. Either way, walk to the South Fork Stillaguamish and hunt up and down the bank for a large sound log — there is no bridge, but several substantial logs are usually available.

On the south bank travel southeasterly through open forest, roughly a mile, with heavy log debris and tall vegetation obstructing the line. A dense band of slide alder guards the forest edge before the creek; turning west generally avoids most of it.

Follow the broad, smoother bed of Dry Creek upward. Water surfaces around 2,200 ft. The headwall ahead carries a visible waterfall. Above the headwall, the upper basin opens onto talus.
approach_variants.season: Late spring to summer — after the couloir snow consolidates, before it melts to bare loose rock
hazards: Unbridged log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish
Dense slide alder at the forest edge below Dry Creek
Steep, icy, committing main couloir with no escape once started
Exposed class 4 on the red slabs
Heavy blowdown and pathless forest travel — no trail of any kind
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is more than one gully in the headwall and the choice matters. The NORTHERNMOST gully is the winter line. In dry conditions take the one trending WEST toward the upper basin, gained by a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps rather than by a snow chute; in snow conditions the hidden chute goes instead.

From the upper basin, walk SOUTH across several gullies before you commit. The correct main couloir is the one that is noticeably NARROWER than the ones you crossed to get there, and it is the point where crampons go on. A gully you can stroll into without committing is not it — the right one is steep and offers no reprieve from the first steps. Higher, a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave, from where a rightward class 4 traverse on RED slabby rock gains the South Ridge of the Main Peak; red rock underfoot on that traverse is the confirmation.

bivy.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
bivy.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.
bivy.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
bivy.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
bivy.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is DAY USE ONLY and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.

approach_variants.name: Ice Caves nature trail to the north face basin
approach_variants.notes:
The shortest approach on this list. Walk the nearly wheelchair-accessible paved nature trail from the Big Four Picnic Area toward the ice caves, and continue to the open basin below the north face. The face rises about 4,000 ft directly above.

From the trail's end move RIGHT to find the break in the lower cliff band. With adequate snow cover this is straightforward walking; in a sparse-snow year the only way through is a bushwhack far out to the right.
approach_variants.season: Winter to early spring — deliberately an early-season line
hazards: Spindrift avalanches down the couloir — the route is named for them
Avalanche hazard on the whole north face in winter
Thin cliff-band break in low-snow years forcing exposed bushwhacking
No retreat once committed to the couloir
approach_variants.baseFinding: The lower cliff band is the gate, and whether it is open is the first thing to read. With the face in condition the break on the right goes as a snow walk and deposits you in the basin under the couloir; if you are forced into bushwhacking out on the far right to get through, the face is thin and the route is out of nick. The route was established in early March after a week of rain followed by a cold snap, which is the pattern that brings it in.

bivy.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
bivy.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. That same activity is why this is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.
