bivy.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is DAY USE ONLY and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully to the Beckey-Tate base, then traverse RIGHT across the overlaps
approach_variants.notes:
Same south-face approach as Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully taking the LEFT fork at the high Y-junction to the base of the Beckey-Tate start.

Five pitches, established in 2012.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: No independent ground start; the base is another route's base plus a traverse
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Several routes starting within a short distance on the same wall
Unreliable water late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
START AT THE BECKEY-TATE BASE AND THEN TRAVERSE RIGHT ACROSS OVERLAPS TO THIS ROUTE'S OWN START LEDGE. So the find is two-step and the first step is the easiest thing on the wall to identify: THE BECKEY-TATE'S OBVIOUS CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITS THE SOUTH FACE.

THE SECOND STEP IS A TEXTURE TEST: OVERLAPS. You traverse RIGHT across overlapping rock features to reach a ledge. If you are walking along flat ground at the foot of the wall rather than moving across overlaps, you are not on the traverse.

WHY STARTING AT BECKEY-TATE IS AN ADVANTAGE RATHER THAN A HANDICAP HERE: the central ramp is the one feature on this face that is described as obvious, and every other line is measured from it. Find the ramp, then move right.

THE OTHER TWO STARTS ON THIS WALL, SO YOU KNOW WHEN YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR: KEARNEY-THOMAS is the standard south-face start, and SKINNY START IS ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT OF IT. If your rightward traverse has run out of overlaps and you have arrived at a plainly separate ground start, you have gone past this route into that cluster.

DESCENT: from the top, join the standard descent, scrambling to the notch just north of the true summit and following the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout, south along Early Winters Creek about 2 miles, then cross and take the LEFT fork at the high Y-junction
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, roughly milepost 163, about a mile east of Washington Pass. Follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak climbers' path south along Early Winters Creek for roughly 2 miles, then leave the trail to cross the creek and ascend the prominent gully system to the base of the south face.

Expect 2.5 to 5 hours of approach time; water is unreliable late season. Seven pitches.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A Y-junction where the wrong fork puts you on different ground
2.5 to 5 hours of approach with unreliable water late season
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Three routes starting within about 30 metres on the same wall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGH Y-JUNCTION IN THE APPROACH GULLY IS THE DECISION POINT, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE LEFT FORK. That is a countable, binary choice on the ground, and every south-face route on this peak depends on it.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS: roughly TWO MILES south along the creek, then CROSS, then up a prominent gully to a Y, then LEFT. Crossing after half a mile instead of two puts you on the West Face approach, on the other side of the mountain, in a broad shallow gully with a chockstone in it.

ARRIVAL AT THE WALL: the base of the SOUTH FACE. The Beckey-Tate's obvious CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITTING THE FACE is the reference feature here, because two other routes are measured from this one and from that ramp.

HOW THE SOUTH FACE STARTS SORT OUT, IN ORDER, AND THE ONE MEASUREMENT THAT SEPARATES THEM: SKINNY START IS ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT OF THE STANDARD KEARNEY-THOMAS START. GOING DOWN UNDER starts from the Beckey-Tate base and traverses RIGHT ACROSS OVERLAPS to its own ledge. THE CENTRAL RAMP IS BECKEY-TATE. SO: IF YOU HAVE WALKED THIRTY METRES RIGHT OF WHERE YOU MEANT TO BE, YOU ARE ON SKINNY START.

WATER IS UNRELIABLE LATE SEASON. Carry it from the creek before crossing, since the crossing is the last of it.

DESCENT: as with the neighbouring Beckey-Tate line, scramble to the notch just north of the true summit and follow the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin pullout and the south-face gully, LEFT fork at the Y, then 30 metres right of Kearney-Thomas
approach_variants.notes:
Same south-face approach as Kearney-Thomas and Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully taking the LEFT fork at the high Y-junction to the base of the south face.

Three pitches, established in 2012.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A 30-metre offset from a neighbouring start as the only positional marker
A reported failure to find the expected rappel anchor on the standard descent
A loose scree-and-snow descent gully
Unreliable water late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS ABOUT 30 METRES RIGHT OF THE STANDARD KEARNEY-THOMAS START. THIRTY METRES IS THE WHOLE MARGIN, WHICH MEANS YOU MUST FIND KEARNEY-THOMAS FIRST AND THEN PACE IT OUT.

HOW TO ANCHOR YOURSELF ON THIS WALL: the BECKEY-TATE'S OBVIOUS CENTRAL RAMP-AND-LEDGE SYSTEM SPLITS THE FACE and is the feature everything else is described against. Kearney-Thomas is the standard south-face start; this route is thirty metres right of it; Going Down Under starts at the Beckey-Tate base and traverses right across overlaps to its own ledge.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS DIRECTIONAL AND SHORT: IF YOU ARE LEFT OF KEARNEY-THOMAS YOU ARE HEADING TOWARD THE CENTRAL RAMP AND BECKEY-TATE. THIRTY METRES IS ROUGHLY FORTY PACES ALONG THE BASE; IF YOU HAVE WALKED A HUNDRED, YOU HAVE OVERSHOT.

A WARNING ABOUT THE DESCENT THAT SHOULD CHANGE WHAT YOU CARRY, AND IT COMES FROM A PARTY WHO ACTUALLY HIT IT: the intended descent follows the Beckey-Tate line, scrambling to the notch north of the summit and then the loose gully back to the Hairpin. AT LEAST ONE PARTY WAS UNABLE TO FIND A RAPPEL ANCHOR ALONG THE TOP OF THAT SUGGESTED DESCENT and instead had to change into rock shoes and make a high traverse to a saddle before descending. BUDGET EXTRA TIME AND BE PREPARED TO BUILD YOUR OWN ANCHORS.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, cross Early Winters Creek at the talus edge, then the west gully with the chockstone
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 about a mile east of Washington Pass near milepost 163, pick up the cairned climbers' trail on the WEST side of Early Winters Creek, the same start used for Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak. Follow it roughly 0.5-0.7 mile through open timber to where it meets the edge of a talus and boulder field.

RATHER THAN CONTINUING SOUTH TOWARD KANGAROO PASS, WHICH IS THE KANGAROO TEMPLE LINE, LEAVE THE TRAIL HERE AND CROSS EARLY WINTERS CREEK. Normally an easy rock-hop, but treat it with respect during peak snowmelt or after rain; there is no bridge. Once across, the route becomes an open boot-track and light bushwhack through slide alder and slabs, trending east into the basin below Big Kangaroo.

One-way gain to the base of the roped climbing is roughly 2,700 ft over about 2 miles; budget 2.5-4 hours, longer early season. Car-to-car is commonly 6-plus hours.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: An unbridged crossing of Early Winters Creek that runs high in snowmelt
A loose gully that narrows onto downsloping slabs at mid-height
An exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old rusty quarter-inch bolt at the summit
The gully sheds loose rock readily; keep helmets on for the whole descent
Snow in the gully into July in some years
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AROUND 6,000 FT, AIM FOR THE BROAD, SHALLOW WEST-FACING GULLY THAT LEADS UP TOWARD THE NOTCH JUST NORTH OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK, IDENTIFIABLE BY A DISTINCT CHOCKSTONE PARTWAY UP. THE CHOCKSTONE IS THE MARKER. One block jammed in the gully, and you climb past or around it.

SO THE COUNT IS ONE: one chockstone, in one broad shallow gully on the west side. If you are passing several jammed blocks, or if your gully is narrow and steep rather than broad and shallow, you are in the wrong one.

FOOTING AS A CONFIRMATION, BECAUSE IT IS UNUSUALLY SPECIFIC HERE: the gully is loose underfoot and the advice is to STAY NEAR ITS EDGES OR ON THE THIN VEGETATION rather than the centre choss. It NARROWS WITH DOWNSLOPING SLABS ABOUT HALFWAY, and some parties bypass that by favouring the adjacent north-side gully. A gully that narrows onto downsloping slabs at mid-height is this one.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROPED CLIMBING: the rope goes on BELOW THE CHOCKSTONE. The first pitch passes it to the notch, the second traverses around the summit block, and the third is the summit slab.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE SOUTH-FACE ROUTES, AND IT IS A CREEK-CROSSING TEST: the south-face lines, Beckey-Tate, Kearney-Thomas and the rest, follow the climbers' trail MUCH FURTHER SOUTH along the west side of the creek before crossing, then take a prominent gully with a HIGH Y-JUNCTION. If you crossed the creek at the talus edge after half a mile, you are set up for the West Face. If you are still walking south after a mile and a half, you are heading for the south side.

THE LAST MOVE IS THE CRUX OF THE WHOLE OUTING AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING NOW: an exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old rusty quarter-inch bolt to a tiny summit, downclimbed or top-roped back rather than rappelled, because there is no real anchor up top and no room to stand.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

approach_variants.name: As for the East Ridge, but stopping at the LOWER Hardscrabble Lake
approach_variants.notes:
Approach exactly as for the East Ridge / Hardscrabble route: walk or bike the gated Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path — half a mile short of the old horse camp, across the road from a large fallen log — and follow the climbers' path east through forest.

The difference is that this route stops at the LOWER lake rather than continuing to the upper one.

This line sees very few repeat ascents, so beta is thin and any fixed anchors should be treated as unreliable.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: The east face and buttress drop directly into lower Hardscrabble Lake in steep walls
Very few repeat ascents, so beta and any fixed anchors may be sparse or unreliable
The original ascent used aid pitons on the class 5 sections; free beta is secondhand
A long, remote approach with a road walk or bike out
No documented descent line for the buttress itself
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LAKE TELLS YOU WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ON: this one belongs to the LOWER Hardscrabble Lake, and the East Ridge belongs to the upper one. If you have walked on to the upper lake, you have passed the buttress.

FROM THE LOWER LAKE THE SEQUENCE IS COUNTED, AND THE COUNT IS TWO: traverse the lake's LEFT — north — side, then scramble over TWO ROCK BANDS to reach the SOUTH side of the buttress at about 5,400 ft. Two bands and an altimeter reading of 5,400 ft is the arrival test. One band means you are not there yet.

THE FEATURE ITSELF IS UNMISTAKABLE ONCE YOU ARE UNDER IT: the east face and buttress drop directly into the lower lake in steep walls. A buttress rising straight out of the water below you and a south flank you have just scrambled onto is the correct position.

WHAT THE CLIMBING SHOULD BE: ten pitches close to the crest, working under overhangs, on generally SOLID GRANITE — originally four pitches of class 4 followed by class 5 with occasional aid pitons, later freed at about 5.10. Solid granite close to a crest, with overhangs to work beneath, is the confirmation. Loose scrambling means you are on the ridge route instead.

HONEST LIMIT, STATED BECAUSE IT MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL HERE: this is a thin record. The published position is the lake side, the two bands and the 5,400 ft elevation, and that is all. Nothing finer is documented, and the route sees so few ascents that no worn line will help you.

approach_variants.name: The gated Middle Fork road to the Hardscrabble Lakes boot path
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Dingford Creek trailhead gate and walk — or mountain-bike, which is the sensible choice — the closed Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road about seven miles.

The boot path for the Hardscrabble Lakes leaves roughly half a mile SHORT of the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, across the road from a LARGE FALLEN LOG. Follow the climbers' path east through forest to upper Hardscrabble Lake.

About 20 km and 5,300 ft, and very light foot traffic — do not expect a reliable boot path throughout.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: The east face and buttress above lower Hardscrabble Lake are steep and cliffy — stay on the inlet-side path
A long, remote approach with no maintained trail for the final stretch
Very light foot traffic, so no dependable boot path
Early-season snow in the gully to the col
A multi-mile road walk out at the end of a long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAIL DEPARTURE IS MARKED BY A FALLEN LOG ACROSS THE ROAD FROM IT, AND IT IS HALF A MILE SHORT OF THE HORSE CAMP. Those two facts together are what make it findable, because the boot path itself is unmarked. If you have reached the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, you have gone about half a mile too far.

THE RULE THAT KEEPS YOU ALIVE ON THE WAY TO THE LAKES: climbing past the lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, STAY CLOSE TO THE INLET. Straying LEFT leads into cliff bands, and the east face and buttress above the lower lake drop directly into the water in steep walls. Inlet on your side, cliffs away to the left.

FROM UPPER HARDSCRABBLE LAKE, THE SEQUENCE IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: climb a gully to a COL, drop onto the OPEN GRANITE SLAB of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit. Gully, col, granite slab, ridge. If you top the gully and are not looking at an open slab of granite, you are at the wrong col.

WHAT THIS ROUTE IS NOT: the East BUTTRESS is a ten-pitch technical line on the same side of the mountain, reached from the LOWER lake rather than the upper one. If you are roping up, you are on the buttress and not on this route.

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
bivy.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.
bivy.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

approach_variants.name: Dingford Creek Trail to Myrtle Lake, then off-trail past Big Snow and Snowflake Lakes
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Dingford Creek trailhead gate via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road / FSR 56, about eighteen miles from North Bend, with the last several miles rough gravel and high clearance recommended.

Hike the Dingford Creek Trail roughly 3.2 miles to the Hester Lake Trail junction, then continue LEFT (east) toward Myrtle Lake, about two miles more.

From Myrtle Lake the maintained trail ends. Serious route-finding and bushwhacking start here and failed attempts from losing the line are common.

About 9.7 km and 5,280 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to September, best once the gullies and couloir have melted out
hazards: No maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake, and any boot path stays faint
Steep gullies and chutes above Big Snow Lake holding snow or ice well into summer
Crumbly, mossy rock in the chutes
Remote, seldom-visited terrain with real self-rescue implications
Rough gravel road access with high clearance recommended
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THREE LAKES IN ORDER ARE THE WHOLE NAVIGATION, AND THEY ARE THE ONLY THINGS ON THIS ROUTE THAT CLOUD CANNOT TAKE AWAY: MYRTLE, then BIG SNOW, then SNOWFLAKE. Leave the maintained trail at Myrtle Lake. Climb steep, increasingly brushy ground to Big Snow Lake. Then traverse RIGHT around Snowflake Lake. If you have not passed a lake in the last while, you are off the line.

WHERE THE CLIMBING BEGINS: above Snowflake Lake, ascend gullies and chutes — a snow couloir early in the season — on the mountain's northwest flank to the upper rock fields. The transition from brush and heather to rock fields is the arrival at the climbing proper, and it is a change underfoot rather than a view.

WHAT THE FINAL GROUND IS: class 2-3 scrambling across the upper rock fields to the summit. If you find yourself needing a rope, you have wandered into steeper ground than this route takes.

THE HONEST WARNING, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE HERE: there is no maintained trail beyond Myrtle Lake and light foot traffic keeps any boot path faint. Parties fail on this peak by losing the line rather than by finding the climbing hard. Carry a track, and treat the lake sequence as the route.

approach_variants.name: As for the South Ridge to Wing Lake, then the hogsback moraine wide right to the low point in the Northeast Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the South Ridge: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20, the right fork at the signed junction toward Heather Pass, then the unmarked climbers' path north across two talus fields to Lewis Lake and up roughly 1,000 ft more to a camp at Wing Lake at about 6,900 ft.

Five pitches, first climbed in September 1973.
approach_variants.season: May-Oct, best Jun-Sep
hazards: A permanent snowfield or mini-glacier below the col persisting into September
Unstable ground on a direct line to the notch; the wide-right moraine line is the stable one
A descent by the South Ridge's loose cairned gully, found from above
The same unmarked off-trail approach stretch between Heather Pass and Lewis Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CAMP, ASCEND SNOW TOWARD THE LOW POINT IN THE NORTHEAST RIDGE. THE ROUTE-FINDING RULE IS THE USEFUL PART AND IT IS COUNTERINTUITIVE: FOLLOWING THE HOGSBACK MORAINE WIDE RIGHT AND THEN TRAVERSING BACK LEFT TO THE NOTCH IS REPORTED TO STAY ON MORE STABLE GROUND THAN A DIRECT LINE.

SO YOU DELIBERATELY GO WIDE AND THEN COME BACK, AND THE HANDRAIL IS A MORAINE, which is a ridge of rubble you can keep under your feet without seeing anything. If you are on snow with no moraine beside you, you have taken the direct line and you are on the looser ground.

A SMALL PERMANENT SNOWFIELD OR MINI-GLACIER CAN PERSIST BELOW THE COL INTO SEPTEMBER, so expect snow under the notch even late in the year. That persistence is itself a confirmation: this is the shaded side.

ARRIVAL: the LOW POINT of the ridge, a notch. Five pitches follow.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE SOUTH RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME CAMP AT WING LAKE: that route goes around the RIGHT, NORTH, SIDE OF THE LAKE and up an obvious talus and snow gully into THE COULOIR JUST SOUTH OF THE SUMMIT, exiting climber's-right to the SOUTH COL. South col and a couloir means the other route; northeast notch and a moraine means this one.

AND THE DESCENT IS THE SOUTH RIDGE'S, WHICH YOU WILL HAVE TO FIND FROM ABOVE: from the summit, work down and south toward the South Ridge route, using one rappel or a downclimb to get below the initial band of rock, then continue south to the south col. From there the descent follows the South Ridge's loose, cairned gully, described by multiple parties as tedious and choss-prone, back down to snow slopes and Wing Lake.

approach_variants.name: Alpental lot, boot path east along the base of the South Rib
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road off I-90 exit 52. Take the boot path and old ski track up from the lot and traverse EAST along the base of Guye Peak's South Rib. The crag is passed on that traverse; it is roughly half a mile of walking and about 15 minutes, not an approach in any real sense.

This is a single 50 ft pitch that does not top out, so it is a crag visit rather than a mountain day.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May to October. This south-facing crag low on the mountain dries early and stays dry late, but it bakes on a hot midsummer afternoon — mornings and shoulder seasons climb better
hazards: Rockfall from the South Rib and the loose slopes above the crag
Aging, seldom-inspected fixed hardware on a route with almost no recorded traffic
Poor rock quality typical of Guye Peak's fractured rhyolite even on a bolted line
South aspect low on the mountain bakes on hot afternoons
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU CAN SEE THE CRAG FROM THE CAR PARK, AND THAT IS THE ANSWER IN BAD WEATHER. The cliff is visible from the west-most parking lots at the Summit West base area. Look at it from the road before you walk in, fix which lump of rock it is, and the walk becomes trivial.

WHERE IT SITS RELATIVE TO THE PEAK: it is an isolated crag, separate from the rest of Guye, low down and near the base of the South Rib. If you are looking at the large WEST FACE, this cliff is just around the corner to the RIGHT of it and well below. So: west face on your left shoulder, corner, small isolated cliff low on the right.

THE MOVE OFF THE GROUND IS THE PROOF, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE. The pitch starts steeply off a LEFT-HAND SIDE-PULL, and the first piece is a #1 Camalot plugged into a POD, before you clip the first bolt. If there is no pod at head height taking a #1 and no bolt above it, you are at the wrong bit of rock.

AND THE SHAPE OF THE WHOLE THING, as a final check: 50 ft, a rest ledge partway up, then a pumpy sequence moving left to a TWO-BOLT CHAIN ANCHOR. It does not top out. Any line here that continues into the mountain above is not this route.

HONEST CAVEAT: this is a 2014 line with almost no recorded traffic, so the fixed gear is aging and seldom inspected.

approach_variants.name: Hairpin pullout to the Poster Peak drainage
approach_variants.notes: Park at the large hairpin-turn pullout on SR-20 about a mile east of Washington Pass — not the Blue Lake Trailhead, which serves the far side of the Liberty Bell group and puts you on the wrong mountain. Take the climbers' path south up the valley toward Kangaroo Pass. About half a mile along, before the path rears up for the pass, a drainage comes down off Poster Peak on the right; leave the path there and follow it up over talus and slab benches toward the two northeast-facing buttresses on the skyline. Reckon on a little over an hour from the car to the rock. Coming out, walk southeast off the summit to the col on the southeast ridge near 7,130 ft, drop the loose gully back to the foot of the buttresses, and pick the cairns back up to the hairpin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Considerable loose rock on the buttress crest — the ridge sheds onto anyone below
Talus and slab benches in the approach drainage are slick when wet
Lingering snow in the drainage and in the descent gully into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROOF IS THE PROOF. Poster Peak throws two buttresses down to the northeast and from underneath they look alike; the one you want is the southerly, left-hand one as you look up from the highway, and the feature that separates it is a large, obvious roof low on the buttress at its base. Walk up the drainage until that roof is directly overhead, then traverse around its left-hand (southeast) side to a system of easy ledges that lets you step onto the crest — the climbing starts just uphill from the roof, on ledgy ground rather than on a clean wall. If you are standing under a buttress with no roof over you, you are beneath House Buttress, the northern of the pair, and need to walk back south. If you are on steep clean granite from the very first move, you have started above and right of the ledges.

approach_variants.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as its neighbours and the same camp: drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then about eleven miles of trail and cross-country to a camp near 7,000 ft at the North Star-Bonanza col. It is a full day of travel and approach before anything else happens.

From camp the base is reached over talus. This route is on the WEST FACE proper rather than the north-west buttress its two neighbours share, and it tops out just right of the Southwest Summit.

It is sixteen pitches, just over 2,000 ft of net gain and about 2,800 ft of climbing, with a great deal of loose rock and several pitches where the protection is minimal and the holds are portable. Bail options near the summit roof systems are poor.

The descent from the Southwest Summit traverses to the Isella Glacier and follows an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then crosses a notch in the south ridge back to the col camp — two ropes.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the only ascent on record is late August, and its two neighbours were also climbed in late summer for the driest rock
hazards: Abundant loose rock over sixteen pitches, with several pitches on minimal protection and portable holds
Poor retreat options near the summit roof systems on a wall with no fixed gear
A descent that crosses the Isella Glacier and a notch in the south ridge, needing two ropes and daylight
Rock quality that varies pitch by pitch, including a choss band low on the route taken at 5.9R

Remoteness on the scale of a three-day weekend before the first pitch, on boat-and-bus access through Lucerne and Holden that has been closed since January 28, 2026 (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-05-26-04, through December 31, 2027)
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST PITCH BEGINS AT A SMALL CARET-SHAPED SNOWPATCH, AND YOU START JUST RIGHT OF IT. That patch is the marker the first-ascent party chose to record, and it is the only thing at the base of this wall that is a shape rather than a description. Walk the talus until you find it.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A COLOUR CHANGE, AND IT IS EXCELLENT IN BAD LIGHT: pitch one is a 220 ft scramble at about 5.4 up WHITE SLABS to a stance below a large, steeper band of DARKER rock. White below, dark above, easy climbing. If your first pitch is hard, or if the rock is uniform, you are somewhere else.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS ABOVE THE FIRST: from that stance you are aiming for an OBVIOUS, LARGE OPEN BOOK, which takes the second pitch at 5.8. A big open corner directly above easy white slabs is the pair of features that identifies this route. One without the other is not enough.

LEFT TO RIGHT ACROSS THIS WALL, FACING IT FROM THE WEST: OREGONIAN, SOVIET, CASCADIAN. This is the RIGHT-hand one — looker's right of both older routes, which are on the north-west buttress and are out of view at the far left margin of the wall from here. If you can see two other lines to your left and none to your right, you are in the correct place.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE STRONGEST ON THIS PAGE, AND IT IS ABOUT WHAT LIES FURTHER RIGHT: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the LONG SNOWFIELD, IS UNCLIMBED, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious. This route begins just right of a TINY snowpatch, not above a long one. If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.

WHERE IT EASES: difficulties relent only on reaching the ridge just south of the true summit, sixteen pitches up. There is no midway escape.

access.fees: Lady of the Lake ferry fare (Chelan or Field's Point Landing to Lucerne) plus the Holden Village bus; a Northwest Forest Pass covers the Railroad Creek trailhead at Holden Campground.
access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required ($5/day or $30/annual). No specific climbing permit.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; Glacier Peak Wilderness group-size limits apply; no motorized/mechanized travel. CURRENT CLOSURE: FR 8301 (Lucerne-Holden) and Holden Village are closed to hikers for the 2026 season following a Dec 2025 flood/landslide (Okanogan-Wenatchee NF order through Dec 31, 2027) — verify access is restored before planning this route.
access.permit: Self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead.

access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness

approach_variants.name: Holden Village via the Lake Chelan ferry, then Holden Lake and Holden Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Getting to the trailhead is part of the trip and it runs on someone else's timetable: drive to Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry up the lake to the Lucerne landing, then the roughly thirteen-mile bus up to Holden Village at about 3,300 ft. Reservations and a look at the ferry and bus schedules come before anything else in the planning.

From Holden, walk the gravel road and Railroad Creek Trail west about a mile to the signed Holden Lake Trail junction and bear right. That trail climbs steadily about four miles through forest and brush, with small side-creek crossings for water, to Holden Lake at 5,278 ft, in a cirque directly beneath Bonanza's east face — a natural camp and the last easy water.

Past the lake outlet the tread fades. Skirt the north shore through slide alder and talus, which is real bushwhacking and route-finding especially with high water early in the season, then climb a hillside traverse north-west to Holden Pass at 6,360 ft — the standard high camp and the last reliable water before the glacier. That is roughly five miles and three thousand feet from the village.

It is worth going in July in most years: later the glacier breaks up and the problem becomes getting off the ice and onto the rock at all.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct, best early to mid July
hazards: wet, slabby class 3 with a waterfall running through it below the glacier
loose, rockfall-prone gullies below the glacier's retreating margin — keep out of the fall line of parties above
icefall above the slabs
moat at the top of the glacier, which widens through the season
slide alder and vague route-finding past Holden Lake, worst with high water
black flies between about 3,000 and 4,000 ft, mosquitoes from the lake upward
the trip is gated by the ferry and bus schedule, so a delay is not recoverable on the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Holden Pass a use trail — which may be under snow — climbs north and west toward the ridge. After several hundred feet of gain you reach a large ledge at about 6,700 ft, often snow-covered. That ledge is the first checkpoint; if you are still on the pass or on undifferentiated slope, you have not gained it.

The unmistakable marker for the start of the climbing is water. Above the ledge is a set of low-angle slabs with a waterfall running down them, draining the Mary Green Glacier — the 'waterfall slabs'. Running water on slabby rock at around 7,000 to 7,300 ft is the confirmation you are in the right place; there is nothing else like it on this side of the peak.

The route up them is class 3 and the rule is to start HIGH and to the RIGHT, skirting the waterfall rather than climbing through it. That is the test that separates the right line from the wrong one: if water is running over the rock you are on, and the holds are wet and mossy, you are too far left and too low — traverse right and up before committing. Topping the slabs puts you on the northern edge of the glacier.

On the glacier itself, bear west along its north (climber's right) edge, then traverse south-west along the base of the north-east ridge to the glacier's upper corner, where the moat is usually a single step across onto rock.

bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
bivy.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

access.fees: Lady of the Lake ferry fare (Chelan or Field's Point Landing to Lucerne) plus the Holden Village bus; Northwest Forest Pass at the Railroad Creek trailhead.
access.rules: Glacier Peak Wilderness regulations: Leave No Trace, group size limits, no motorized/mechanized travel. approach_variants.name: Holden Village to Holden Lake and Holden Pass, then the Mary Green's north margin to the buttress toe
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this trailhead. Drive to Chelan or Field's Point Landing, take the passenger boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, and ride the village bus up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. The whole trip is gated by a boat and bus timetable rather than by the weather window, so build the itinerary around sailing days. Both the road and the boat shuttle have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide — verify access exists before planning anything.

From the village, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 runs about a mile up the valley on near-level grade to a signed fork. Turn RIGHT and climb roughly four miles and 1,700 ft of switchbacks to Holden Lake at about 5,280 ft, the usual first-night camp. Carry water up from the creek — there is none on the switchbacks.

From the head of the lake a climbers' path gains about 1,100 ft over heather benches and rocky terraces to Holden Pass near 6,400 ft. That is effectively the last water; everything above has to be carried.

What makes this route different from the standard line starts at the pass: instead of angling onto the glacier, it stays on benches and talus to climber's RIGHT of it. Expect about three more hours and a long climb above the pass to reach the buttress toe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun to mid-Jul for the easiest bergschrund and glacier margin; the buttress itself is dry rock and tolerates a later start into August
hazards: Rockfall the whole length of the glacier-margin traverse, because holding the margin puts you under rock rather than over crevasses
Loose, lichen-covered rock on the buttress with sustained 5.6-5.7 and wild exposure to the glacier below
A moat and steep snow crossing near the summit ridge that parties rope even when they scramble everything else
Route-finding through unmarked benches, talus and heather above Holden Pass, on loose footing, with no obvious line
Total dependence on a boat and bus timetable — and both have been closed since the December 2025 flood
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GLACIER IS THE HANDRAIL AND THE BUTTRESS TOE IS WHERE IT RUNS OUT. Once you have gained the Mary Green Glacier's northern edge around 7,800 ft, follow the glacier's climber's-RIGHT (north) margin west, then bend south-west along the foot of the north-east ridge to the glacier's upper south-west corner. The rock rib comes down into the ice there, around 8,350 ft. Walk the margin until the ice meets rock; that is the base, and you do not need to see the summit to find it.

HOLDING THE MARGIN IS A TRADE, AND IT IS DELIBERATE: staying on the edge keeps crevasse exposure low and puts you underneath rock the entire way. Helmets on from the moment you start the traverse, not from the moment you start climbing.

GETTING ONTO THE GLACIER IN THE FIRST PLACE — the step most parties get wrong: from Holden Pass make a RISING traverse west along the ridge over benches, talus and heather until a snowfield appears below a band of slabs, then scramble the slabs to the glacier's north edge. There is no single obvious line through the benches, the footing is loose, and it is real routefinding. If you are contouring flat rather than rising, you will end up under the slabs rather than on them.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE STANDARD ROUTE, WHICH LEAVES FROM THE SAME CAMP: the standard line goes UP THE GLACIER and it identifies itself by WATER — low-angle slabs with a waterfall running down them at roughly 7,000 to 7,300 ft. This route never touches those slabs and never crosses the glacier's middle. If you are climbing wet rock beside running water, you are on the standard route.

THE CONFIRMATION ONCE YOU ARE ON IT: the crest steepens and narrows IMMEDIATELY above the toe — several rope lengths of Class 4 and low fifth on and just right of the crest, running into sustained 5.6-5.7 with glacier falling away on both sides. If the ground above the toe stays broken and easy for a long way, you have started up the wrong rib.

WHAT TOO FAR ALONG LOOKS LIKE: the licheny mid-buttress at about 9,000 ft is the sustained section, and from the toe to the summit is roughly four hours on the ridge. Reaching easy fourth-class crest with gendarmes to turn means you are near the top, not near the start.

approach_variants.name: The North Star-Bonanza col, then past the Soviet buttress and across the pocket glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard one for this side of the peak and is shared with the route next door: Lake Chelan ferry to Lucerne, village bus to Holden, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 west up the valley to Hart Lake at about 3,956 ft, then leave the trail and climb the rock-and-heather terraces on the west side of the drainage to camp near the 7,100 ft col between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak.

The first-ascent party did not use it — ferry and road closures that year forced them into a roughly 32-mile one-way approach from the west up the Suiattle, including about ten miles of mountain biking, then the PCT to Suiattle Pass, Cloudy Pass and cross-country to the col. That was a workaround, not the route's approach, and it should not be copied unless the boat is out again.

From the top of the col to the first climbing is about an hour and a half of talus and scree.

The route is roughly 2,200 ft with about 1,600 ft of independent ground, sustained 5.6-5.8 with moves to 5.9+, and it joins the route next door for the last 600 ft to the summit block.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Sep; the first ascent was in early September
hazards: Loose, sparsely protected and often lichen-covered rock on a long sustained buttress
A near-vertical 600 ft wall with significant overhangs directly above the bivy ledge, passed only by a small left-trending ledge system
Very few bail options once above the lower ledge, on a wall with no fixed gear
A rising traverse up the toe of a pocket glacier just to reach the rock, in approach shoes for most parties
Total dependence on the Lake Chelan boat and the Holden bus, both closed since the December 2025 flood
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU REACH THIS ROUTE BY CROSSING SNOW, AND ITS NEIGHBOUR BY NOT CROSSING ANY. That is the cleanest test on this wall. From the col, traverse north-east PAST the Soviet Route's buttress — about an hour and a half, some of it excellent scree — and then make a rising traverse UP THE TOE OF A SMALL POCKET GLACIER. If you got to rock without touching snow or ice, you stopped one buttress short and you are at the Soviet.

THE EXACT POINT YOU GAIN ROCK: a FEW DOZEN YARDS UPHILL AND LEFT OF THE LOWEST POINT OF THE BUTTRESS, off the top of that pocket-glacier traverse. Not at the toe, and not on the right side.

THE CONFIRMATION IS INSTANT AND IT IS THE STRONGEST THING ON THIS PAGE: you are making NEAR-VERTICAL 5.8-5.9 MOVES IMMEDIATELY, from the first pitch. There is no easing-in. If the climbing above where you stepped onto rock is scrambly, or a chimney, or 5.7, you are on the Soviet buttress instead — that route starts with a narrow chimney 60 ft above its own toe and is a full grade easier out of the blocks.

LEFT TO RIGHT ACROSS THE WALL, FACING IT FROM THE WEST: OREGONIAN, SOVIET, CASCADIAN. This is the LEFT-hand (northern) one, which is why the instruction is always "keep walking".

THE MID-ROUTE CHECKPOINT, which matters because the first ascent bivied there: seven pitches of moderate ground with harder moves, often loose, sparsely protected and lichenous but on the crest of the buttress, lead to a LOWER LEDGE flat enough to sleep on. Above it a near-vertical wall with several significant overhangs rises for more than 600 ft, and the way through is a small ledge system traversing LEFT to regain the crest — that pitch has the best rock on the climb. A party staring up at overhangs and thinking about rappelling is in the right place and looking at the wrong feature.

WHERE IT STOPS BEING ITS OWN ROUTE: the last 600 ft are shared with the Soviet, and the two lines converge at a pinnacle around 8,700 ft before continuing to the Southwest Summit. Meeting another route's ground high up is expected here, not a sign you have wandered.

approach_variants.name: Head of Park Creek: easier cliffs to the small glacier, then right through the icefall
approach_variants.notes:
A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend LEFT up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse RIGHT through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.
approach_variants.season: Climbed historically in early-to-mid August; the window is narrow because it depends on a stable, well-bridged icefall and on residual snow and ice in the summit gully
hazards: An icefall traversed on the approach, with crevasse and serac fall the standing hazard and the crossing itself described as frightening
A crumbly red rock stratum crossing the whole face at mid-height, which is where the rockfall comes from
Extreme remoteness — an incident on a 3,000 ft face this rarely climbed would be very hard to get help for
Heavy packs on class 4-5 ground, which the first-ascent account flags as compounding the difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SEQUENCE IS COUNTABLE FROM BOTTOM TO TOP AND IT IS THE BEST THING THIS ROUTE HAS: EASIER CLIFFS, THEN A SMALL GLACIER, THEN LEFT UP IT TO AN ICEFALL, THEN RIGHT THROUGH THE ICEFALL TO THE ROCK. The direction reverses — left to reach the icefall, right to get through it — and that reversal is what tells you the crossing you are making is the intended one. THE ROPE-UP POINT IS A LEDGE SYSTEM NEAR THE SECOND PROMINENT TREE, where the ledge makes its first descent. An oddly specific marker, and a genuinely countable one if the trees are visible. THE MID-ROUTE CONFIRMATION IS A COLOUR AND IT CROSSES THE WHOLE FACE: a PROMINENT, CRUMBLY RED STRATUM at roughly half height. You cannot go round it — it spans the face — so meeting a red band of bad rock at mid-height is proof you are on the line and not beside it. It is also the crux and the rockfall source, so it is worth expecting. BETWEEN THOSE TWO, FOLLOW THE PROMINENT CENTRAL RIB essentially straight up. Near the top a 100-FT NOTCH is passed on steep snow or ice through a narrow gully angling across the rib, and then it is easier ground to the summit. AND THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE WHOLE PEAK: Booker's other two routes are walks. If the ground you are on is class 2-3 talus, you are on the Northwest Route or the South Ridge — this is the only technical line on the mountain, and the first ascent said so in as many words.

bivy.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
bivy.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
bivy.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
bivy.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

bivy.name: Skagit Queen Camp

bivy.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.

bivy.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass, the sandy gully and the rocky point, then up to the Booker-Buckner col
approach_variants.notes:
The usual approach is a multi-day backpack up the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground to Park Creek Pass — on the order of forty miles round trip with roughly 7,000 ft of cumulative gain — or as a leg of a Ptarmigan-style traverse linking Cascade Pass, Buckner and Park Creek Pass.

From a camp near Park Creek Pass, this is a short day. Hike about 0.4 mile north on the Thunder Creek trail, pick up the climber's track, and traverse northeast: cross a BROAD SANDY GULLY at about 6,900 ft, roughly a mile from the pass, continue toward a SHARP ROCKY POINT at about 7,760 ft, then turn RIGHT and uphill on talus and snow to the col and its small glacier.

The col is around 8,100 ft and the scramble above it is class 2-3 with no technical rock. Booker sees roughly one party a year, so expect no boot track and no cairns.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, when the snowbridges near the Booker-Buckner col are still intact but consolidated. Conditions change year to year and can degrade within days
hazards: Crevasses and a bergschrund at the Booker-Buckner col, bypassed only on snowbridges of variable reliability — one such bridge collapsed within a week of another party crossing it, with climbers on both sides
Loose blocks in the summit gully, with rockfall released by climbers above as the route's principal hazard
Slick meltwater-run rock slabs for parties coming in from the Horseshoe Basin side
A remote, multi-day position far from any road or quick rescue
No boot track and no cairns — the route is walked by about one party a year
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS NAVIGATED BY A CHAIN OF THREE POSITIONS RATHER THAN ONE LANDMARK, AND THE CHAIN IS COUNTABLE IN FOG: A BROAD SANDY GULLY AT ABOUT 6,900 FT, roughly a mile from Park Creek Pass. Then a SHARP, ROCKY POINT AT ABOUT 7,760 FT. Then TURN RIGHT AND UPHILL to the col. Miss the gully and you are too low; pass the rocky point without turning and you are traversing past the peak.

THE BASE IS THE BOOKER-BUCKNER COL AT ABOUT 8,100 FT, and it is the col rather than the summit that the whole day is about: the upper snow and the glacier margin below it hold the crevasses, and the same snowbridges have to work on the way back down. Sound them, cross early while frozen, and note where you crossed.

ABOVE THE COL, A NORTH-FACING GULLY LEADS TOWARD THE SUMMIT WITH ONE SHORT CLASS 3 STEP. Keep to one side of it rather than the gut, and do not stack the party one above another.

THE ROUTE-FINDING TRAP IS AT THE TOP AND IT IS SPECIFIC: LEAVING THE GULLY TOO EARLY PUTS YOU ABOVE A SHORT WALL ON THE WEST, and forces an awkward traverse back on small ledges. Cut RIGHT out of the gully onto low-angle talus and scree, and walk those to the summit. If you find yourself edging along small ledges above a wall, you exited one notch too soon.

TELL IT FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER WALK-UP BY HEIGHT: the South Ridge is gained across Horseshoe Basin at a permanent snowfield around 7,000-7,200 ft and trends to the ridge WEST of the summit. This route goes a thousand feet higher, to the col between Booker and Buckner. If you never got above 7,500 ft before starting to climb, you are on the South Ridge.

bivy.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
bivy.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.

bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.

approach_variants.name: Horseshoe Basin at 6,400-6,600 ft to the north-facing gully and the permanent snowfield
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft. Hike the Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and 1,700 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then continue up the Sahale Arm trail toward Sahale Glacier and Sahale Camp.

Leave the maintained trail near Sahale Camp and descend cross-country into Horseshoe Basin by a snow-free gully on Sahale's south side around 6,600 ft. Traverse the basin staying roughly between 6,400 and 6,600 ft, past the Buckner buttress.

Most parties combine Booker with Buckner on the same trip, since both share this approach and this traverse. Route-finding through Horseshoe Basin is the crux of the day; the climbing is not.
approach_variants.season: July through September, after Cascade River Road opens and once Horseshoe Basin's snowfields have consolidated; early attempts face more snow travel and less obvious route-finding, late ones find slopes melted to loose scree and slab
hazards: Loose scree and slabby terrain throughout Horseshoe Basin, easy to lose the line on in both directions
Cliff bands flanking the south ridge that have to be route-found around
Rockfall potential in the gullies flanking the ridge
A remote position with no cell coverage and very infrequent traffic if a rescue is needed
A cross-country traverse and an exposed summit gully that are far more hazardous to reverse in the dark or after a thunderstorm has softened the snowfields
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NORTH-FACING ROCK GULLY AND A PERMANENT SNOWFIELD AT ABOUT 7,000-7,200 FT, reached by crossing Horseshoe Basin rather than by climbing to any col. The snowfield is the marker: it is permanent, so it is there whatever the month, and the gully leads off it to the south-trending ridge WEST of Booker's summit.

THE HEIGHT IS THE TEST THAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM ITS NEIGHBOUR, AND IT IS A THOUSAND FEET WIDE. The Northwest Route starts at the BOOKER-BUCKNER COL at about 8,100 ft, reached from Park Creek Pass by way of a sandy gully at 6,900 ft and a sharp rocky point at 7,760 ft. THIS ROUTE STARTS A THOUSAND FEET LOWER AND ON THE OTHER SIDE. If you are standing at a col between two peaks, you are not on the South Ridge.

THE APPROACH TEST IS THAT YOU GO DOWN BEFORE YOU GO UP: from Sahale Camp you descend Sahale's south side through a snow-free gully near 6,600 ft into Horseshoe Basin and traverse at 6,400-6,600 ft. If your day has been a continuous climb from the trailhead, you have not reached the basin traverse yet.

THE FINISH IS SHORT AND EXPOSED AND IT IS THE ONE PIECE OF REAL CLIMBING: talus and slabs give way to a short, somewhat exposed 3rd-class gully or dike — locally described as taking a 4th-class step — to the summit.

WHAT IS HONESTLY THIN HERE: this ridge is barely documented. The only outside mention found is of a party who ABANDONED the South Ridge for loose terrain and moved to the Northwest Route, finding existing rappel slings on the ridge — which suggests it is sometimes retreated from rather than climbed. Treat the snowfield and the gully as the navigation and expect to do your own route-finding above them.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the west face basin, then the central line beneath the dagger
approach_variants.notes: From the Bedal Creek Trailhead at the end of FR-4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway near 2,800 ft, follow Bedal Creek Trail #705 up the drainage. FR-4096 is not plowed, so in winter the approach starts lower on the road and is normally skinned; travel eases considerably above about 3,700 ft. The valley beneath the west face is reached around 5,000 ft. From there this route boots directly up the central weakness of the face to a flat basin below the first ice step, and the first ascent party reached that base at first light after leaving the car in the dark. The climb is about 1,900 ft, six pitches, and the difficulty is front-loaded and then front-loaded again: WI5 out of the basin, WI4 in a corner, a WI3 gully beneath the dagger, then the M7 crux through overhanging rock on thin gear with three fixed pitons, a blue-ice traverse, and a long snow-and-ice headwall at 45 to 60 degrees to the summit ridge. THREE WINTER LINES SHARE THIS FACE.
approach_variants.season: Deep winter — the first ascent was 19 January. It needs the west face frozen and the ice formed, which on this aspect means cold, settled weather rather than a date
hazards: High-consequence, exposed belay stances the whole way up, with a crux led on thin gear
Solar warming of the west face bringing rockfall and debris onto the upper snow-and-ice headwall
A committing line — the escape is up, or a V-thread rappel descent of a different route
Winter approach on an unplowed road, so a benightment starts hours from the car
The route's condition cannot be judged from the valley; the dagger forms or it does not
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FACE HAS AN OBVIOUS LINE ON THE RIGHT AND THIS IS NOT IT. That single sentence sorts out most of the confusion here. The right-hand side of the west face carries the older, easier ice line; this route is the CENTRAL weakness, left of it. If you have walked to the most obvious continuous flow you can see and started up, you are on the wrong climb and on a much easier one.

THE ARRIVAL IS A FLAT BASIN, NOT A WALL. Boot straight up the central weakness of the face until the ground goes level: there is a flat basin immediately below the first ice step, and that flat is where the route starts. If you are still on a rising slope, you have not got there; if you are already swinging tools, you passed it.

THE FEATURE THAT NAMES THIS ROUTE IS A HANGING DAGGER, AND IT IS WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE LINE IT SHARES A START WITH. The lower pitches follow the older central route. That older route CUTS RIGHT to easier ground partway up the big rock band; the dagger hangs DIRECTLY ABOVE the point where it does. So the decision is not made at the base at all — it is made at the rock band, and the rule is: where the tracks go right, this route goes straight up under the dagger. A party that follows the rightward escape has climbed the other route.

THE GRADE IS THE CONFIRMATION. Above the schrund-free basin the first pitch is WI5 and steep. Pitch four is M7 through an overhang on thin gear with three fixed pitons in it — fixed pitons are the one hard physical confirmation on the route. If the hardest thing you have met is WI4 and there is no rock crux, you are on a neighbouring line.

WHAT THE DESCENT MEANS FOR THE START: there is no rappelling this route to get out. You either finish and descend the standard line off the summit with rappels and a lot of downclimbing on sustained 60-degree ground, or you rappel the neighbouring ice line on V-threads. Decide which before you leave the basin, because both cost daylight.

approach_variants.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to the Sahale-Boston col, then the connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft at about mile 21.7 of Cascade River Road, the unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and slide alder into Boston Basin, roughly 3.2 miles and 3,100 ft. Most parties camp at high camp near 6,400 ft; the low camp near 5,300 ft works for slower groups. Sahale Glacier Camp on the other side of the ridge serves the same objective for parties coming over Cascade Pass.

An alpine start is standard. Rope up the QUIEN SABE GLACIER — the big crevasses are low on the glacier and the direct line through them runs to about 45 degrees and is very exposed, so most parties take the left side and traverse in beneath Sharkfin Tower. Later in the season, end-run the bergschrund below the col by traversing climber's right, then cut back up-left above it to gain the SAHALE-BOSTON COL at about 8,200 ft.

From the col the route follows the connecting ridge toward Boston: flat at first, then widening onto loose rock, staying generally right and on the crest.

The difficulty here is the rock quality, not the grade. This peak has a real fatality history and the descent — three rappels off fixed slings down the southeast side — should not be treated casually.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Crevasses on the Quien Sabe, with a potentially poorly bridged bergschrund below the col that worsens through the season
Notoriously loose and rotten rock, with rockfall onto and within the party
Essentially unprotectable class 4 with real exposure on the knife-edge section
A short but exposed snow traverse on the col that wants axe and crampons
Aging natural rappel anchors on the descent — slung horns and blocks, not bolts
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SAHALE-BOSTON COL AT ABOUT 8,200 FT, AND THE COL IS THE ONE THING ON THIS ROUTE THAT IS HARD TO MISTAKE: it is the saddle shared with the Sahale trade route, so it carries traffic and it has ground falling away on both sides. If you gained a high point rather than a saddle, you are not there.

THE APPROACH TEST IS THE BERGSCHRUND. Later in the season the way onto the col is to traverse climber's RIGHT to end-run the schrund and then cut back up-LEFT above it. A party that walked onto the col without meeting a schrund has almost certainly come up in early-season conditions — fine, but it means the position cannot be confirmed that way and the ridge itself has to do it.

THE COUNTABLE SEQUENCE ON THE RIDGE, AND THE FALSE SUMMIT IS THE POINT OF IT: the crest steepens, widens, and then narrows to a KNIFE EDGE — that is where the route becomes genuinely exposed. At the high point of that ridge a FALSE SUMMIT stands in front of you. YOU DO NOT CLIMB IT. Make the class 4 downclimbing moves and follow the cairned line along the cliff edge to the RIGHT (east) around it. After about 100 ft of that bypass the Boston Glacier and the true summit pyramid come into view for the first time.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST IS THE LAST ONE, AND IT WORKS IN FOG: YOU CROSS ABOUT 200 FT OF GLACIER ABOVE A BERGSCHRUND IMMEDIATELY BEFORE THE FINAL SUMMIT BLOCK. If you are scrambling loose rock to a high point and you have NOT crossed snow above a schrund in the last few minutes, that high point is the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

THE LAST FEATURE BEFORE THE TOP is a small ledge on the LEFT just short of the summit block, sometimes with a moat at it; above that it is class 3 on loose rock to the true summit.

approach_variants.name: The Quien Sabe's northwest corner to the lower of the two gullies
approach_variants.notes:
In winter the recorded approach is Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead gate, then bike or ski up the Cascade Pass trail to the highest switchback near 6,400 ft, angling up and dropping into the Soldier Boy drainage, then a rising traverse to the QUIEN SABE GLACIER'S NORTHWEST CORNER. Rope up for the glacier crossing. In summer the standard Boston Basin approach reaches the same ground.

The face is used deliberately as the lower-consequence alternative to the Southeast Face when that side is too icy and too unprotected — which is worth knowing, because it means a party may arrive here having changed its mind rather than having planned it.

Five pitches: two of steep snow heading northeast, a large gully east on the third, a fourth to about 200 ft north of the summit, and a fifth across an exposed ridge with a short rock step to the true top.
approach_variants.season: Condition-dependent rather than calendar-dependent — documented ascents span a September first ascent on steep snow and a February first winter ascent
hazards: A bergschrund near the base of the face
Crevasses on the Quien Sabe Glacier approach
Rime ice needing removal before anything can be climbed or protected, on the winter ascent
Rock bands between the gullies that are poor rock and poor protection — the gullies themselves protect better than the face between them
Loose rock characteristic of this peak, especially on the summit rock step
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE GULLIES: THERE ARE TWO PROMINENT ONES ON THIS FACE AND THE ROUTE TAKES THE LOWER. That is the one countable fact published about the start and it is the one to carry. A party at the base of the other gully is on a different piece of the face, with the rock band between them as the divider.

THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS THE SCHRUND, AND ITS SOLUTION IS DIRECTIONAL: the bergschrund at the base is turned by climbing to CLIMBER'S RIGHT. If your way past the schrund went left, re-examine which gully you are under.

COUNT THE FIRST TWO BELAYS, WHICH ARE DESCRIBED BY WHAT THEY SIT UNDER RATHER THAN BY HEIGHT: two pitches of steep snow head NORTHEAST, the first belay UNDER A BULGE and the second WHERE A GULLY OPENS TO THE EAST. If your second stance is not at a place where a gully opens away east, the line is wrong.

AND YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN IF YOU CROSSED A COL. The Southeast Face — the standard route — is reached over the Sahale-Boston col at about 8,200 ft and shares that saddle with the Sahale trade route. This face is climbed straight off the northwest corner of the Quien Sabe with no col crossed at all. If you walked over a saddle to get where you are standing, you are under the standard route, not this one.

THE FINISH CONFIRMS IT: pitch four tops out about 200 ft NORTH of the summit and the last pitch crosses an exposed ridge with a short rock step to the true top. A route that deposits you on the summit directly has not been this one.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, then a hundred feet right of the left-flank classic
approach_variants.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, the crux of the walk in, dangerous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face — roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way, the last stretch unmarked over slabs and talus.

Four pitches, about 450 ft: a short crack and slab to a corner, a long exposed and somewhat dirty face-crack pitch, a corner with a bouldery move, and a finishing fingers-to-hands pitch to the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A long, exposed and dirty second pitch
Natural non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side, periodically rebuilt as old tat accumulates
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Afternoon thunderstorms with a long walk back over the pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PACE IT OFF FROM THE LEFT-FLANK CLASSIC: this route starts ABOUT 100 FEET TO THE RIGHT of it, on the west side of the south face. That is a measurable distance rather than a description, and it is what makes the start findable — everything else on this end of the face is identified relative to the same outside corner.

SO THE PROCEDURE IN POOR VISIBILITY IS TWO STEPS. First find the outside corner where the south face turns onto the west side. The classic left-flank line starts just right of that corner. Then walk right roughly a hundred feet along the base. That is where you are.

WHAT TELLS YOU YOU HAVE OVERSHOT: keep walking right along the base and the ground under the middle of the face is where the summit route starts, and beyond that the two large V-features of the next line along. Reaching either means you have gone several hundred feet too far.

WHAT TELLS YOU YOU ARE SHORT: a large roof at the base means you have crossed the corner onto the west face entirely and are two routes left.

FIRST-PITCH CONFIRMATION: a SHORT crack and slab leading to a corner. It is not a long lead and it is not hard. The long, exposed, somewhat dirty face crack is the SECOND pitch. If your first pitch is long and dirty you have started one pitch too high or on the wrong line.
