AND THE TOP-OUT CHECK: this route finishes on the West Ridge, not the summit — the same as its two neighbours on this flank. That shared finish is why they share one rappel descent on the north side.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch at the base of the Southwest Rib, then three pitches up before this route starts
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the Southwest Rib: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail about 1.25 miles to the northwest clearing, then the climber's path up into the basin.

Three pitches at 5.10b as counted here, but understand what the route is: it is pitch 5 of a combined line, about 100 ft of sustained climbing under and through a pair of roofs.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: No ground start; three pitches of another route must be climbed first
A loose block right at the start of the roof pitch
Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and undocumented, so bailing here means natural gear anchors
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE HAS NO GROUND START, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FACT ABOUT FINDING IT. You reach it by climbing THE FIRST THREE PITCHES OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and THEN GOING LEFT AT A LEDGE WHERE THE TWO ROOFS COME INTO VIEW.

SO THE BASE OF THE DAY IS THE BASE OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, AND THAT HAS A LANDMARK YOU CAN STAND UNDER: THE Y-SHAPED LARCH TREE AT THE BASE OF THE SOUTHWEST RIB, LEFT OF THE SOUTHWEST COULOIR. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

THE IN-ROUTE TEST IS VISUAL AND BINARY: GO LEFT AT THE LEDGE WHERE THE TWO ROOFS COME INTO VIEW. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A HAZARD RIGHT AT THE START OF THE PITCH, RECORDED BECAUSE IT IS EXACTLY WHERE A PARTY IS COMMITTING: THERE IS A LOOSE BLOCK RIGHT AT THE START OF THE ROOF PITCH.

WHAT NOBODY DOES HERE, WHICH ANSWERS THE OBVIOUS QUESTION: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the RABBIT EARS then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors down the gully.

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. From the LOWER, eastern end of the pullout walk about fifty yards downhill to pick up the climbers' trail, which climbs steeply to the Lower Wall.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished granite
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Trail check first: the path from the western, uphill end of the pullout traverses onto Logger's Ledge and serves Upper Castle, one wall higher than this.

Brass Balls sits on the Lower Wall with Mr. Clean and the west-to-east line of The Fault, Catapult, The Vertebrae and The Bone. Use The Fault as the fixed point — it is reached directly by the short trail from the right of the parking area.

The wall is identified by its many roofs and by Logger's Ledge above. Newer routes on the RIGHT-hand side of this wall are better bolted than the older gear lines.

approach_variants.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
approach_variants.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. The loop can also be picked up from the Grove of the Patriarchs end via the Eastside Trail, which is the alternative when work on the campground side has closed the near entrance — that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons, so check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late spring through fall, whenever the southeast corner of the park is open to vehicles
hazards: Nothing alpine — the real risks are trail closures and construction in this corner of the park
Landing on forest floor with roots and uneven ground
Seasonal road closure to the southeast entrance in winter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS THAT YOU NEVER LEAVE THE TRAIL. The boulder sits a few feet off the Silver Falls Loop, roughly a mile round from the Ohanapecosh day-use area. If you have stepped off maintained tread, started bushwhacking, or gained more than about a hundred feet, you have walked past it — go back rather than searching uphill.

THE SHAPE IS THE NAME: a low boulder with a loaf-shaped top hold, climbed on its left side. One problem, a couple of moves.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE IS ABOUT THE WHOLE OUTING RATHER THAN THE LAST HUNDRED YARDS, AND IT IS WORTH STATING BECAUSE THIS ROUTE IS FILED UNDER THE MOUNTAIN: if you are on snow, on a glacier, or anywhere above a few thousand feet, you are not near this boulder and never will be. It is in low forest in the southeast corner of the park, tens of miles and twelve thousand feet from the summit routes filed beside it.

WATER AND ESCAPE ARE NON-PROBLEMS HERE — the loop has running water nearby and you can walk out either way round it. That is the honest description; do not carry mountain planning onto it.

approach_variants.name: Denny Creek Trail to Hemlock Pass, then the ridge
approach_variants.notes: The standard summer approach. From the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft), reached from I-90 Exit 47 by Denny Creek Road and FR 5830, follow the Denny Creek Trail #1014 toward Melakwa Lake past waterfalls and up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft of gain. Leave the trail at the pass for the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September for a dry scramble; earlier the ridge and talus hold snow and an axe is needed
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall on the summit block
Lingering snow on the ridge and talus early in the season
Brush in the notch below the talus once the snow has gone
Exposure on the north side of the summit block
approach_variants.baseFinding: HEMLOCK PASS IS WHERE THE TRAIL STOPS CLIMBING. At its crest, before the trail drops toward Melakwa Lake, turn right onto the ridge and hold a bearing of about 33°, skirting the cliff bands mainly on their left. The check that you are on line is a plateau and meadow on the ridge, then a talus field wrapping most of the peak's base with the summit block above. Negative marker: if you are descending toward a lake, you stayed on the trail past the pass.

approach_variants.name: Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the Bryant-Chair gully
approach_variants.notes: A steeper alternative from the Alpental side, better known as a winter and spring snow climb than as a summer scramble. From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits LEFT (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
hazards: The gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring; avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm
Loose scree, with the centre and left of the gully markedly worse than the right
The gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow, requiring axe and crampons
Exposed and loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when the block is dry
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE THUMBTACK IS THE LANDMARK YOU WALK PAST, AND THE GULLY IS THE ONE IMMEDIATELY BEYOND IT. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

WHAT THE GULLY IS, IN OTHER WORDS: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

THE FOOTING TEST TELLS YOU WHERE TO BE WITHIN IT: climb favouring the FAR CLIMBERS' RIGHT side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

WHERE IT DELIVERS YOU: the gully tops out on the BRYANT-CHAIR CONNECTING RIDGE, not on a summit. From there you work SOUTH over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. A gully that finishes on a summit is not this one.

AND THE LAST STEP CHANGES CHARACTER WITH THE SNOW, which is worth knowing before you commit: with snow on the block the final scramble is easy class 3 with little real exposure. Dry, the only reasonable line goes round the NORTH — climbers' left — side on exposed and distinctly loose class 3. Test every hold.

approach_variants.name: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. FILL UP WITH WATER THERE — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse from the Berge saddle crosses steep heather that is nasty when wet, and holds snow into summer
hazards: No water for four miles beyond Buck Creek Pass on an exposed ridge
Steep heather ledges at the Berge saddle, very sketchy when wet
Waterfall slabs below the traverse line if you lose too much height
Hard snowfields at High Pass wanting crampons
Loose rubbly schist on the summit crest, with a fatal fall on record on this peak
Burn scar on the lower Buck Creek trail — hot, and blowdown
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical instruction on the traverse is about HEIGHT, and it comes with a stated consequence: from the saddle south of Berge, curving right around the bowl toward the mountain, STAY HIGH. Drop too low and you end up in steep waterfall slabs. If you are looking at running water over slabby ground, you have lost too much elevation and should climb back.

The arrival is unmistakable and it is not rock: you reach a beautiful forested bench with larches — good enough that parties note it as a campsite — and CROSS A RIVER. Once across that river you are at the base of Buck.

Above there the ground is broad pumice, talus and low-angle snowfield up to the south ridge around 7,400 ft, and then rubbly slabby schist along the crest with a short step up to Class 3-4 near a horn close to the top.

SUMMIT WARNING, and it is a genuine unresolved disagreement rather than a caution: parties do not agree how many summits Buck has or which is highest. One party climbed the middle of the long crest, found the register there, and judged it higher than both the north point and the south by twenty feet or more. Another says the south is the true one. A third found the register — dated 1967 — on the NORTH horn and reported the two tops as roughly equal. Only one of those parties actually measured anything. The summit crest holds several bumps within a few feet of each other, so expect to walk the crest rather than to arrive at an obvious high point, and do not treat a register as proof.

A useful sighting cue from a party approaching by a different line: the summit does not come into view until you reach the flat ground around 8,000 ft, in an upper cirque one climber described as looking like the flying bridge of a boat.

This mountain has killed someone — a climber fell fifty feet scrambling on a route on the east side, direct from Trinity, in 2018. The direct east line involves a river ford and a savage brushy bushwhack and is generally recommended as a descent rather than an ascent.

bivy.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.
bivy.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
bivy.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full

bivy.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.
bivy.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the BOSTON BASIN trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward SHARKFIN COL rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the BOSTON GLACIER. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse SOUTH toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.

A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.
approach_variants.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
hazards: A short rappel or a steep no-fall-zone downclimb off Sharkfin Col on crumbly mixed rock — the crux of the approach, and it has to be reversed
A viciously crevassed upper Boston Glacier with cracks scattered randomly across the ice
A bergschrund at the toe of the face that can run its full width, needing rock scrambling to bypass
Wind-scoured ice on some ascents and moderate powder on others — the face's character changes completely with conditions
Cornices on the summit ridge, and rockfall as the day warms
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BERGSCHRUND AT THE TOE OF THE FACE, ON THE BOSTON GLACIER, AND THE POSITION TEST IS DIRECTIONAL: from the col you traverse SOUTH across the glacier. If you turned north you are heading for Forbidden's north side.

THE ENTRY MOVE IS A ZIG-ZAG AND IT IS THE POSITIVE TEST: WORK CLIMBER'S LEFT OF THE BERGSCHRUND, THEN BACK RIGHT INTO THE CENTRE OF THE LOWER FACE, AND THEN STRAIGHT UP. Left, right, up. A party that crossed the schrund directly and started climbing where it stood has not found the line the face is climbed on.

WHAT YOU ARE CLIMBING CONFIRMS IT: about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, continuous, with no rock pitches. If you are on rock below the summit ridge, you have drifted off the face.

THE FINISH IS THE OTHER COUNTABLE POINT, AND GETTING IT WRONG COSTS TIME AT THE WORST MOMENT: continue straight up until UPPER ROCK CLIFFS force a rising traverse to the LEFT. Then, within about 200 ft of the summit, GO LEFT AROUND A CRAGGY ROCK OUTCROP at the end of those cliffs, and only then back right to the top. Both moves are left. A party that goes right at the cliff band has misread the finish.

AND THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THIS PEAK'S OTHER ROUTE: the Southwest Face is reached over Cascade Pass, Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin, on the opposite side of the mountain, and the two share no ground until the summit ridge. IF YOU WALKED PAST AN OLD MINE IN A BASIN AT 7,000 FT, YOU ARE ON THE SOUTHWEST ROUTE.

approach_variants.name: Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin to the cowskull snowfield
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road. The maintained Cascade Pass trail switchbacks through old growth and traverses subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass at 5,400 ft, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft. From the pass take the Sahale Arm trail north through heather meadows, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier and SAHALE GLACIER CAMP near 7,600 ft — 5.9 miles and about 3,940 ft from the trailhead, and the standard base. NPS permit and bear canister required; camp only in the designated sites. Sahale Arm above the meadows is dry, so carry water or a filter.

From camp the route goes off-trail and DOWNHILL first: descend Sahale Peak's south ridge on class 1-2 rock, then a short class 3 step into a notch near 6,800 ft, and traverse roughly two miles across HORSESHOE BASIN on talus, slabs and lingering snow, passing near the old DAVENPORT MINE around 7,000 ft, to reach the base of the southwest face.

Most parties take two to three days for the roughly 20-mile round trip and 7,400 ft of gain, though strong parties have done it in one very long day.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September
hazards: A steep, snow-filled cleft on Sahale's south ridge that must be downclimbed, exposed and fall-prone on firm early-season snow
Rockfall across the Horseshoe Basin traverse, which is loose and easy to lose the line on in both directions
Cliff bands below the basin ledge system — stay on the mid-elevation line rather than dropping
Steep snow on the cowskull with wet-slide potential in the afternoon; many parties run a picket belay
Loose scree and rubble above the snow, all the way to the summit ridge
An axe and crampons needed for steep snow patches into midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE HAS A LANDMARK YOU CANNOT MISTAKE FOR ANYTHING ELSE, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS FACE IS NAVIGABLE AT ALL: A DISTINCTIVE COWSKULL-SHAPED SNOWFIELD HIGH ON THE FACE. Climbers describe it as looking like a ghost early in the season. Steepening southwest-facing snowfields lead to a snow chute and then to the cowskull itself, and if you cannot pick a cowskull out of the snow above you, you are under the wrong part of the face.

THE MID-APPROACH CHECKPOINT IS THE DAVENPORT MINE, around 7,000 ft, roughly midway across the Horseshoe Basin traverse. The ruins are unambiguous. If you have crossed the basin without passing old mine workings, you are on the wrong ledge line — and the ones below cliff out.

AND THE APPROACH BEGINS BY LOSING HEIGHT, WHICH IS THE FIRST SANITY CHECK OF THE DAY: from Sahale Glacier Camp at 7,600 ft you descend Sahale's south ridge and a class 3 step into a notch near 6,800 ft before you traverse. If you have been climbing since camp, you have not started the route yet.

ABOVE THE COWSKULL, THE GROUND CHANGES CHARACTER AND THAT IS THE SIGNAL TO PUT THE CRAMPONS AWAY: step off the snow, then grovel up loose scree and rubble to the summit ridge, finishing with about 100 ft of class 2-3 rock. Snow the whole way to the top is not this route.

KNOW WHICH SUMMIT YOU ARE AIMING FOR: Buckner has two nearly equal tops, the southwest at about 9,114 ft and the northeast about two feet lower, separated by a few hundred feet of ridge. This route reaches the SOUTHWEST one, which is the accepted high point; the northeast top needs the connecting ridge.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE NORTH FACE IS THE WHOLE MOUNTAIN: that route comes from Boston Basin, over Sharkfin Col and across the Boston Glacier, on the opposite side. If you rappelled off a col onto a glacier this morning, you are on the north side.

approach_variants.name: Entiat River Trail #1400 to Entiat Meadows
approach_variants.notes: This is the long east-side valley approach, not a boat-access trip. From the road-end trailhead follow Entiat River Trail #1400 up-valley, staying on #1400 at each junction in turn — Anthem Creek, Cow Creek and Myrtle Lake, Larch Lakes, Emerald Park, and Ice Creek. Refill at the reliable creeks in the middle miles, because the long stretch above them crosses repeated burn scars with almost no shade and no water. The valley opens into Entiat Meadows and travel slows through downed timber; step over it where you can, since the detours around it are what lose the tread. Past the Cool Creek junction the trail grows faint and choked with brush and deadfall as it nears timberline; keep going to the open clearing, which is the last dependable water and the camp that keeps the summit day short.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September once the meadows melt out. In early season the south side holds firm snow and the final ridge can be corniced, turning this into a genuine mountaineering objective.
hazards: Heat and sun exposure through the long burn sections with no shade and no water
Heavy deadfall on the upper trail, where the detours around downed timber are what lose the tread
Loose, ball-bearing scree and slick wet heather on the open south face
Rockfall on the open slope — keep in close under the buttress
Cornices and minor gendarmes on the narrow blocky crest into early summer
The whole face is exposed with nowhere to shelter from afternoon storms
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE RIB CLOSEST TO CAMP IS THE ROUTE, AND GOING TOO FAR EAST IS HOW PARTIES GET IT WRONG. From the open clearing at the head of the meadows the whole south side rises as one broad old avalanche path split into several parallel ribs and gullies, and they look alike from below. No named feature distinguishes the right one: parties pick it as the rib directly above camp, because it carries the least brush and gives the straightest line, or aim for the one big open avalanche swath on an otherwise timbered face. The failure to guard against is drifting east, where cliffs over steeper ground stop you short and force a retreat — so if the way ahead closes out against rock, traverse back west onto the open rib rather than pressing on. Old maps show a boot path toward the east ridge; a party that looked for it never found it among the downed logs, so finding no path is expected and is not evidence you are off route. Climb scree and heather, hugging the buttress to stay out of the rockfall line, and gain the east ridge somewhere between about 7,200 and 7,900 ft — the higher you gain it, the less of the jagged, gendarmed crest you have to fight.

approach_variants.name: Stevens Pass crest trail to Chain Lakes and Bullseye Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the large lot on the south side of the highway at the pass, follow the crest trail south past Lake Susan Jane and into the Icicle Creek drainage, then take the signed Icicle Creek Trail down toward the head of the valley and turn up Chain Lakes Trail #1569. That trail climbs steeply and without switchbacks through forest, brush and talus benches into the Chain Lakes basin near 5,700 ft, which is the last reliable water and the standard camp. From camp the climb goes cross-country around Upper Chain Lake and up the couloir above it. Note that the trail pass between the Chain and Doelle basins is a separate feature reached by trail, and it is the jumping-off point for a different and much harder summit rather than for this one.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to early October, once the basin and the couloir have melted out.
hazards: Lower slopes are a deceptively complex mix of steep heather, mossy slabs, brush and short cliff bands
Loose footing in the couloir with a real rockfall risk onto parties below — group up rather than string out
The last hundred feet turns looser and sandier than the talus below it
No dependable water above the Chain Lakes
Entirely unmarked cross-country travel beyond the lakes, with no cairned or established line
The upper mountain is fully exposed to afternoon thunderstorms with no bail-out shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding: HUGE PALE TALUS IN A NORTHWEST-FACING COULOIR, THEN TWO POINTS AT A NOTCH — THE RIGHT-HAND ONE IS THE TOP. From the basin, hike around Upper Chain Lake and climb the couloir above it. Low down the slope is a deceptively complex mix of steep heather, mossy slabs, bushes and short cliffs; the clean, huge, whitish talus higher up is what tells you that you are into the correct couloir rather than picking your way up the general hillside. It tops out at a notch between two points on the crest, and from that notch it is genuinely not obvious which is higher — take the right-hand, southern one. That is the summit, and the last stretch to it turns looser and sandier. The negative marker is a different summit sharing this name: a lower, fang-shaped tower southeast of the trail pass between the Chain and Doelle basins, shaped like a giant cuspid, which takes Class 4 and 5 climbing and rappels to get off. If you are standing under a spire that plainly needs a rope, you are beneath that one. The high point described here is bulky, and nothing about it is tooth-like.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork ford and the north-side gully
approach_variants.notes: Do not follow the maintained trail out of the road-end lot. Walk roughly 300 ft upstream and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to its true-right bank; in early summer this runs thigh-deep and cold, so scout upstream for a braided section or a log rather than forcing the main channel. Everything above is trailless: a boulder field, a brushy gully, timber, and open talus, with nearly all the day's gain packed into the last two miles. There is no water once you leave the river apart from occasional snowmelt trickles near the pass.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Cold, pushy river ford at the very start
Sustained salmonberry and black currant bushwhack in the lower gully
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Firm, sustained snow ramp below the pass — genuine self-arrest terrain
Moat between snow and rock near the top of the ramp
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two things have to be identified, and both are easy to get wrong. The first is the gully entrance: from the far bank climb the boulder and talus field straight above the river for about 400 vertical feet until a rock band stops you. That band is the signal — do not try to force it, and do not drift right. Angle LEFT (west) off the boulders into the steep gully choked with salmonberry and black currant, follow it into timber near 3,900 ft, then traverse upward through the trees until they run out onto open talus. The second is the notch. Work up and climber's-left toward the low saddle beside Point 5,841 — the gap separating Burnt Boot's summit block from the peak immediately west — keeping to talus and boulders to stay off the steepest snow, with the heather and cedar benches giving the easiest going. The last couple of hundred vertical feet to that notch is the snow ramp itself, and near its top a moat often forces a short traverse beneath the snow edge to reach solid rock. From the notch a short class 3-4 step heading east begins the summit block. The neighbouring northwest gully holds harder, class 4 ground and is not the way up.

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

approach_variants.name: Glacier Basin: the mine-tailing streak across the creek
approach_variants.notes: Ride or walk the gated Monte Cristo road from Barlow Pass to the townsite, rack the bike under the trees, cross the footbridge and take the Glacier Basin Trail up alongside Glacier Creek past the falls. Roughly 1.8 miles above the townsite, at about 4,400 ft, the creek flattens out among house-sized boulders; this is where the scramble starts. Ford the creek here — a genuine wade during snowmelt — and climb the rib between the two gullies on Cadet's southwest flank, using cairns and occasional flagging once the maintained tread is gone. The rib gains the ridge crest near 5,400 to 5,500 ft, after which you stay on or close to the crest. Higher up there is a second trap worth knowing before you set out: at about 6,300 ft, look up at the wide dark cliff band that sits at exactly 6,500 ft. A good-looking notch straight above you is where most people go wrong, and enough have done it that a well-defined trail leads to it. The line is roughly a hundred yards left, marked by a blocky gendarme standing up on the band — more visible the higher you get — with a deep, scary-looking gully a further seventy-five yards left again; the route is the ridge just inches right of that big gully. Cross below the gendarme, then look up for a small, short, exposed ledge.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: The Glacier Basin creek ford is swift and cold during snowmelt
The tailings gully and the upper talus are loose and rockfall-prone with parties above
Avalanche-prone snow slopes on early-season attempts into July
The cliff band and the deep gully beside it are invisible from above — note how you got through before going higher
Three summits on this peak, and the maps have argued about which is highest
approach_variants.baseFinding: LOOK FOR THE ECRU-AND-RUST STREAK ACROSS THE CREEK. Where the Glacier Basin creek levels out among house-sized boulders at about 4,400 ft, the far bank carries an unmistakable pale-and-rusty stain running down the mountainside — old mine tailings, and there is nothing else like it in the basin. That streak marks the start. The gully it stains is dirty brown, roughly 200 yards long and only about ten yards wide, dropping straight off Cadet, and in June and often July it is full of snow. Climb it, or the rocks and rib to its right. WHERE YOU LEAVE IT IS DESCRIBED THREE DIFFERENT WAYS and they do not agree, so expect to judge it: one party takes the gully to its very end and traverses left about 200 ft to the foot of a grey rocky gully; one climbs to roughly 25 ft below a headwall with a small waterfall and exits climber's LEFT onto a band of red rock and ledges through scrub; the most recent crosses the erosion gully near its top and goes left up a ramp into a cedar-filled gully, explicitly warning against the first rocky gully above. Every one of them exits LEFT and none carries straight on up. If you are still in the gully at the waterfall you have gone too high.

bivy.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
bivy.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
bivy.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge, ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Serious exposure on the pitch-two traverse off Saber Ledge
Runout slab on the upper pitch
Polished rock and full southwest sun
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Canary starts from the RIGHT-HAND portion of Logger's Ledge and climbs to the top of Castle Rock in three pitches.

The reliable measure is Saber: Canary starts about 100 ft to the LEFT of it. Saber is identified by the large low roof with a left-angling ramp just to its right, so find the roof, then count back a hundred feet left.

The first pitch is the technical crux — face climbing into a dihedral system leading up to Saber Ledge. If you have arrived on Saber Ledge, you are where the route's famous second pitch begins: an airy step straight off the ledge into instant exposure and a traverse that people find far more unnerving than its grade. That step is the confirmation you are on Canary rather than continuing up Saber.

Upper ground gets slabbier with runouts on easier climbing.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile trailhead and the burned slopes to the northeast ridge crest
approach_variants.notes: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road about eight miles, then turn left onto the signed gravel Eightmile Road, cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large lot at the road end. A Northwest Forest Pass is required. This route starts from the Stuart Lake trailhead lot at the road end, the same lot used for Colchuck Lake. The route climbs steep, bushy, loose burned slopes to gain the ridge crest, then follows and traverses beneath the crest, and finishes with a talus gully and a short scramble to the summit block. It is described as an ascent route only. Most parties come down the other side of the mountain instead — Prusik Pass, the Upper Enchantment basin, down Aasgard Pass and out via Colchuck Lake to the Stuart Lake trailhead — which makes this a demanding roughly fifteen-mile loop with sustained Class 3 and bushwhacking, at least twelve hours car to car, and it finishes back at the same lot it started from, so no car shuttle is needed.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, once the snow is off the ridge and out of the ground around Coney Lake
hazards: Steep, bushy, loose burned slopes with no trail on the lower half
A third of a mile of loose traversing below a band of unclimbable towers — the crux of the route
Sustained Class 3 scrambling and bushwhacking over a roughly fifteen-mile day
Descent is over the summit and out via Aasgard Pass and Colchuck Lake, a long way round back to the same trailhead
At least twelve hours car to car, so an early start is not optional
Snow lingering around Coney Lake and on the ridge in early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOWERS ARE THE MARKER, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS TO GO UNDER THEM. The identifying feature of this ridge is a band of towers on the crest that CANNOT be climbed directly, and the route's answer to them is a loose traverse of about a third of a mile BELOW the crest. That traverse is the route's signature and its worst ground.

SO THE TEST WHEN YOU GAIN THE CREST IS: keep going until the crest stops being walkable. When rock towers block the ridge in front of you, do not look for a way over them — drop onto the flank and traverse beneath. A party that finds itself scrambling technical rock on the crest has missed the traverse.

AND THE ARRIVAL TEST AT THE OTHER END: the traverse ends at a TALUS GULLY. Talus, after loose sidehill traversing, is the cue that the towers are behind you. From the top of that gully it is a short scramble to the summit block.

WHAT GOING TOO LOW LOOKS LIKE: the traverse is beneath the crest, not down in the basin. If you have lost enough height that the towers are well above you and you are on continuous scree, you will have to regain it — this is the most common way the traverse costs more than the third of a mile it looks like on a map.

BEFORE ANY OF THAT — THE LOWER HALF IS THE REAL PROBLEM. Steep, bushy, loose burned slopes with no path, and this route is best done in mid to late summer once the snow is gone from around Coney Lake and off the ridge. Snow on the lower slopes turns an unpleasant ascent into a serious one.

AND THE DIRECTIONAL WARNING: this is an ascent-only line. Do not plan to reverse it. The descent is over the top and down the far side of the mountain, looping back to the same trailhead via Aasgard Pass.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes trail to Perfection Lake, Prusik Pass and the Druid Plateau
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lakes trailhead, about four miles up Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth. Follow Snow Lakes Trail #1553 through burn-scarred forest and switchbacks above Icicle Creek, past Nada and Snow Lakes at roughly six to seven miles, and on into the core basin — Lake Viviane, Leprechaun, Sprite, then Perfection Lake, by which point you have covered ten or eleven miles and about 6,000 ft.

At the north side of Perfection Lake, leave the main trail on the scramblers' path that switchbacks up to Prusik Pass at about 7,460-7,500 ft. That junction is easy to miss and the pass is the last reliable water.

From the pass everything is cross-country. Contour northwest across talus and heather benches at roughly 7,300-7,400 ft, keeping to the WEST side of the Lorelei Lakelets, then north to a broad rib at about 7,900-8,000 ft. From just below 8,000 ft turn northwest and climb steep talus and scree onto the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft.

There are no cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass. Round trip is 30-plus miles with 7,300-plus ft of gain, so essentially everyone camps.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the cross-country section above Prusik Pass frequently holds snow into July
hazards: No cairns and no tread above Prusik Pass — serious route-finding on talus and heather
Snow frequently lingering on the cross-country section into July
An exposed, holdless friction slab for the final fifteen feet, harder to downclimb than to climb
Verglas on shaded ground into July, adding real exposure to otherwise easy terrain
No bail-out shelter: sun, lightning and afternoon storms on open high ground
Core Zone overnight permits are competitive and effectively required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS A SEPARATE OBJECT AND THE PLATEAU IS NOT THE TOP. This is the failure mode on Cannon: parties gain the Druid Plateau at about 8,350 ft, find themselves on broad high ground, and treat arriving there as arriving. The actual climbing is a distinct BLOCK that only comes into view once you are on the plateau, across it to the west.

SO THE TEST IS: can you see a discrete block of rock standing above the plateau surface? If you are on flat or gently rolling ground with nothing obviously above you, you have not crossed the plateau yet. Cross it and take the WESTERN slopes to the foot of the block.

WHICH SIDE OF THE BLOCK, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS IN CLOUD: the way up is a RAMP on the block's SOUTH side. It is the last fifteen feet or so to the true summit, low-angle friction slab with almost no positive holds. If you have walked round the block and found only steep unfriendly rock, you are on the wrong aspect — keep going round to the south.

WHAT THE RIGHT GROUND FEELS LIKE: this is a friction problem, not a hold problem. Approach shoes with good rubber, or rock shoes, make a real difference, and the downclimb of the same ramp is the psychological crux of the day for most parties because low-angle slab is harder to read going down.

STAGING CHECK BELOW THE PLATEAU: from Prusik Pass you should pass the Lorelei Lakelets on their WEST side and reach a broad rib around 7,900-8,000 ft before turning northwest. If you passed the lakelets on their east, you are drifting toward the wrong drainage.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Cannon Creek basin — the shorter, rougher side
approach_variants.notes:
The documented alternative reaches the same staging ground near the Druid Plateau from the north instead, out of the Stuart Lake trailhead: up the Mountaineer Creek valley and then cross-country into the Cannon Creek basin.

This is much shorter than the Snow Lakes walk, and that is the whole of its appeal. It is also markedly rougher: the lower section is brushy and there are cliff bands to negotiate, and there is no trail for any of it.

Cannon has no maintained trail to its summit by any line, so both approaches end in the same cross-country problem. What differs is how much of the day is spent on tread before that starts — nearly all of it on the Snow Lakes side, very little on this one.

No reliable published time or distance exists for this variant and none is given. Treat it as a full day of navigation rather than a walk with a scramble at the end.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the lower cross-country section is brushy and holds snow later than the trail does
hazards: Brushy lower cross-country with cliff bands to negotiate and no trail
No cairns or tread anywhere on the upper mountain
An exposed holdless friction ramp on the summit block
Snow and verglas on shaded ground into July
No published timing for this variant — plan conservatively
No bail-out shelter on the high ground
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BOTH APPROACHES CONVERGE ON THE DRUID PLATEAU, SO THE BASE TEST IS IDENTICAL AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS NOT. Coming from the north you reach the plateau area from the Cannon Creek basin rather than from Prusik Pass, so the Lorelei Lakelets and the broad rib are NOT on your route and cannot be used to confirm position — do not try to apply the southern approach's landmarks here.

WHAT STILL HOLDS: the summit block is a distinct object standing above the plateau, reached across the plateau on its WESTERN slopes, and the way up it is a low-angle friction ramp on its SOUTH side, roughly the last fifteen feet to the true summit. Almost no positive holds. That is the base, and it is the same base for anyone who gets here.

THE NORTH-SIDE-SPECIFIC WARNING: the ground below the basin has CLIFF BANDS in it. Unlike the southern route, where the navigation problem is featureless open talus, here it is possible to be cliffed out and to have to lose height to get round. If you are on steepening ground with the basin still above you, come down and traverse rather than pushing on.

AND A ROUTE-CHOICE NOTE: the northeast ridge is a separate line on this mountain and is described as an ascent route only, with most parties descending the Prusik Pass side. If you have come up from the north expecting to reverse it, check which line you are actually on before committing to that plan.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/annual 'Digital Day Pass' at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (payable via the Recreation.gov app or on-site), or a Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful interagency pass.
access.rules: Standard National Forest rules apply (Leave No Trace). The North Fork Entiat Trailhead lot itself is day-use/no-camping, though parking there overnight while backpacking is fine.
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required. Cardinal Peak and the North Fork Entiat approach lie in general National Forest land outside designated wilderness — north of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness boundary (which runs close by, near Emerald/Saska Peaks) and well south of the Glacier Peak Wilderness, which is across the Entiat/White River divide.
access.closures: CLOSED since 3 September 2026: the Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect through 31 October 2026 unless lifted sooner, closes the Entiat River Road (FR 5100), FR 5606, the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 and the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433, which is this route's entire access. Separately, the Entiat River Road corridor (FR-51) sustained damage in the December 2025 storm event; the Forest Service's road-conditions table (as of June 3, 2026) reports a landslide near the upper end of the road (beyond the FR-5606 junction, near Cottonwood Campground/Entiat River Trailhead) requiring a high-clearance-only temporary bypass with trailers prohibited. That damage is past the FR-5606 turnoff used for Cardinal Peak, but check current Okanogan-Wenatchee NF alerts/current-conditions pages before driving.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Entiat Ranger District
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency (America the Beautiful) Pass, or the trailhead's $5/day Digital Day Pass — required specifically at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the North Fork Entiat, Entiat River or Phelps Creek trailhead kiosk.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the west-side basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the end of FR-5606 at the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,940 ft, take North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. The lower trail is OUTSIDE the wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal on the first several miles and many parties use one on a 20-mile round trip.

The first six miles follow the river on a gentle forested grade, straight through old burn. The river is the last reliable water — everything above is dry — so fill before leaving the valley. Expect to work over, under and around blowdown, and to lose the tread briefly among downed timber; Grouse Creek is crossed on a log inside one of the worst of those stretches.

A signed spur to Fern Lake splits off at about mile 6.1 — stay on #1437. Around mile 7 near 5,800 ft the trail bends sharply EAST and switchbacks about half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 junction near 6,600 ft. That junction is a useful timing landmark: the summit is roughly a mile from it.

Leave the trail there and head east through sparse forest and then talus toward the peak's west and south-west flank. A camp flat sits around 7,100 ft in the open basin.
approach_variants.season: Late May-Sep. In late May and June this is effectively a snow climb — the gully to the saddle holds 40-50 degree snow and wants an axe and crampons. By August it dries into loose Class 3 talus
hazards: A gully that is loose top to bottom in summer and 40-50 degree snow through June, with the whole party in the fall line
An exposed, sometimes-corniced summit ridge traverse of roughly 500 ft with genuine consequence
A short unrated technical step between the middle summit and the true south summit that many parties decline
Constant loose rock on the traverse below the summit ridge, so parties must not stack up
A dry, long approach through burn with heavy blowdown, and no water above the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A GULLY THAT LEADS TO A GAP BETWEEN TWO SUMMITS, AND THE GAP IS WHAT YOU NAVIGATE TO — NOT THE PEAK. From the basin camp, contour onto the peak's WESTERN slopes and work SOUTH below the summit ridge across steep talus and scree until you are underneath the broad gully leading to the NOTCH BETWEEN THE NORTH AND MIDDLE SUMMITS, at about 8,300 ft. Every party uses that same notch whichever flank they approached from, so it is the one landmark this mountain has.

THE GULLY IS BROAD, NOT A CLEFT, AND IT FACES NORTH-WEST. Early season it is moderately steep snow up to about 40 degrees; later it is loose Class 2 talus and scree the whole way. If the feature above you is a narrow slot, or if it is not the widest weakness on that stretch of face, you are under the wrong one.

THE CONFIRMATION IS WHAT HAPPENS AT THE TOP OF IT: you arrive on a SADDLE with summits on BOTH sides of you. From there the ground is a ridge scramble along or just east of the crest. If you top out of a gully onto a single continuous slope rather than a gap, you are not there.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT THE SUMMIT AND IT DECIDES WHETHER YOUR DAY IS OVER: the ridge from the saddle leads to the MIDDLE summit, which is non-technical and where most scramblers stop. The TRUE summit is the slightly higher SOUTH one, and reaching it takes a SHORT EXPOSED STEP — described historically as a vertical chimney onto a foot-wide summit ridge, unrated and treated by every account as the crux. If you have walked to a top without meeting a hard move, you are on the middle summit.

THE THING THAT SENDS PARTIES HERE FROM THE NORTH SIDE, worth knowing so you recognise it if you meet them: when the north ridge holds snow and verglas, parties abandon it and drop onto the east and south-east slopes below the summit ridge to finish — this route's ground. That is a documented retreat, not an error.

STOW CRAMPONS AT THE TOP OF THE GULLY if the rock above is dry. The exposure on the ridge is real and the moves near the top run Class 3 and arguably Class 4.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trailhead, back down the road to the driveway
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Snow Creek trailhead on Icicle Road. Careno Crag is the big formation a few hundred feet above the houses just downstream of the lot.

Walk back down the road roughly 0.1 mile and look for a driveway with a sign to the effect that hikers and climbers enter at their own risk — that driveway is the current access. Follow it to a retaining wall, then pick up a trail rising to the RIGHT toward the crags. A sign marking the boundary onto public land appears shortly after you leave the driveway.

The path keeps climbing past smaller outcrops. Around 30 minutes to the crag. A previously used approach appears to have been lost, so keep to this one, stay on the path, and give the residences a wide berth — the lower part is private ground.
approach_variants.season: Comes into condition early — it is south-facing with almost no shade and bakes in high summer
hazards: Private land on the lower approach — access depends on staying on the path and being respectful
South-facing with little shade; genuinely hot in summer
Ledgy terrain where it is easy to be on the wrong tier
Descent is a scramble down climbers' right from the uppermost ledge system; most routes have bolted rappel belays
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Careno Corners starts immediately to the RIGHT of Bale/Kramar, near the LEFT EDGE of the rock — so you are looking at the left-hand end of the formation, not the middle.

The first pitch identifies itself by what it does rather than what it looks like: a steep crack system that moves RIGHT, then traverses back LEFT to a shared belay underneath a large roof. If your first pitch runs straight up with no traverse and no roof above the belay, you are on a neighbouring line.

The route wanders. Pitch two skirts around that roof through an easy gully with some third-class ground, and the crux is pitch three — an imposing wide corner crack that narrows from offwidth down to hands and fists.

Context that helps rule the route in or out: the biggest face on the crag, in the middle, with prominent dihedrals running up it to a large lone tree, is Regular Route. If that is what is above you, you are too far right.

The crag is laid out on multiple ledge tiers, which makes linkups and unusual pitch combinations common — check which tier you are on before counting pitches.

road.name: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) to Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211)
road.status: CLOSED as of May 20, 2026 (USFS Forest Order #06-17-07-2026-11): FR 6200 is closed to vehicles at milepost 18.2, just past Atkinson Flat Campground, after a debris flow deposited roughly 150 cubic yards of material and cut ruts near the Dry Creek Bridge. No reopening estimate has been given; the order runs effective May 20, 2026 through December 31, 2027 unless rescinded sooner. Check the Okanogan-Wenatchee NF alerts page before driving — the Phelps Creek Trailhead is unreachable by vehicle beyond this closure. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes Phelps Creek Road and the Carne Mountain Trail.
road.driveNote: From Coles Corner on US-2 (about 15 miles west of Leavenworth), take WA-207 north ~4.4 miles, bear right onto Chiwawa Loop Road for 0.4 mile, then right onto County Hwy 22/Chiwawa River Road for 0.8 mile to Forest Road 6200. Continue north on FR 6200 about 22 miles (paved for roughly the first half, then rough gravel) to FR 6211, then turn right and drive the rough, potholed Phelps Creek Road 2.3 miles to the trailhead (3,500 ft). Low-clearance vehicles should go slowly on the upper roads.
road.seasonalGate: Not gated, but the upper road and trailhead are typically snow-covered and impractical until roughly June; check current USFS road/trail conditions.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek Trail to the Carne Mountain Trail #1508 fork
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end lot at the top of the Phelps Creek Road spur, the trail leaving the parking area is the wide, nearly level Phelps Creek Trail #1511 heading north up-valley through open forest — which is not what the rest of the day looks like. A quarter to four-tenths of a mile along it, a signed junction sends the narrower Carne Mountain Trail #1508 steeply uphill to the right. Fill water at the fork or at the small creeklet just past it, because everything above is dry apart from early-season snowmelt. The trail then switchbacks up through open forest, vine maple and beargrass with very little flat ground until it breaks out into a small cirque holding campsites and a stream, then climbs past a faint junction at a low pass to a broad saddle on the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through October. Snow lingers on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early or mid July, and the larch display peaks in late September and early October.
hazards: Sustained steep grade with essentially no water above the low fork
Snow lingering on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early or mid July, worth carrying an axe for
The saddle and summit ridge are exposed to wind
Loose talus and scree on the final switchbacks below the summit block
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE UNSIGNED JUNCTION AT THE BROAD SADDLE IS THE REFERENCE, AND WHICH TREAD LOSES HEIGHT IS THE TEST. Above the little basin the trail switchbacks up to a wide open saddle near 6,800 ft — the first place the whole panorama opens at once, with Mount Maude, Seven Fingered Jack, Clark Mountain and Glacier Peak in view together. Two treads leave it and neither is signed. The Rock Creek tread carries on east and immediately loses height down the far side of the ridge into the wilderness; the summit line bears left and switchbacks up open talus and scree. If you are descending, or the big peaks have swung behind you, you are on Rock Creek and should turn round. A lower junction earlier in the climb has the same shape, and there the tell is thickness of tread: the Old Gib path is noticeably fainter than the main one. A minor false high point sits beside the summit path — the tread continues past it rather than ending on it.

approach_variants.name: Bivy at the C-J col, then across the moat onto the peak's northwest side
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as the East Ridge: Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass trailhead, the Cascade Pass trail to the pass at 5,392 ft, then cross-country by way of Mixup Arm and the Cache Glacier to the CASCADE-JOHANNESBURG COL. The col sits directly between Cascade Peak and Johannesburg Mountain, and it is the staging point.

From a bivy at the col, cross the moat below Cascade Peak's northwest side to reach the base of the route. One documented party started up around 9 a.m. the morning after bivying at the col.

Three pitches. This route sees so few ascents that it should be treated as an unmaintained line rather than a climb with beta: the 2013 party found NO rappel anchors, NO pitons and NO summit register, and rated the crux first pitch nearer 5.10 than the published 5.8 because of the loose rock.

Budget for building every anchor from scratch on the way down. That party's descent from the summit to the col took about four and a half hours.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the moat below the northwest side is crossable — the one documented ascent is a July trip
hazards: Extreme rockfall and loose rock on all three pitches
No fixed protection and no fixed anchors anywhere on the route — natural placements are the norm and can be poor
A moat below the northwest side that is the gate on the whole climb
So few ascents that neither conditions nor anchors can be assumed to be in place
A first pitch that has been found two grades harder than its published rating
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ABSENCE OF FIXED GEAR IS THE CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS AN UNUSUALLY RELIABLE ONE HERE. A 2013 party climbing this route found no rappel anchors, no pitons and no summit register on the entire peak. IF YOU ARRIVE AT A BASE WITH TAT, BOLTS OR A WORN START, YOU ARE NOT ON THE NORTHWEST CHIMNEY — everything around Cascade Pass that sees traffic shows it, and this does not.

THE BASE IS ACROSS A MOAT FROM THE CASCADE-JOHANNESBURG COL. You do not walk to it: from the col you cross the gap where the snow has pulled back from the peak's northwest side, and the route starts on the rock beyond. The col itself is unmistakable — it is the notch between Cascade Peak and Johannesburg, and it is where the C-J couloir tops out.

COUNT THREE PITCHES AND EXPECT THE MIDDLE ONE TO BE THE SHAPE THE ROUTE IS NAMED FOR: a broken, loose crack pitch first; then the CHIMNEY — aesthetic, sparsely protected, and wanting a large offset or Big Bro-style cam; then very loose fifth-class ground simul-climbed from a FALSE SUMMIT to the true summit. If there is no chimney on your second pitch, the line is wrong.

AND THE FALSE SUMMIT IS PART OF THE ROUTE, NOT AN ERROR: the third pitch runs from it to the true top. Stopping at the first high point is stopping one pitch short.

WHAT IS HONESTLY THIN HERE: beyond the published entry and that single 2013 trip report there is essentially no published description of this line, and no elevation is recorded for its base. The col and the moat are what can be navigated to; everything above is the party's own route-finding.

approach_variants.name: North-side scree traverse to the ridge crest
approach_variants.notes:
Reached from the same Eightmile Lake / Lake Caroline / Windy Pass approach as the West Ridge — Eightmile Lake Trail #1552 for about 2.8 miles to the junction past Little Eightmile Lake, right onto Eightmile-Trout Creek #1554 to Lake Caroline, then on toward Windy Pass and cross-country east onto the west end of the mountain.

Rather than staying on the crest, cross over to the north side of the ridgeline below the summit pyramid and traverse the north-facing scree field eastward.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; in early season the north side holds steep snow
hazards: Steep north-facing snow with poor run-outs in early season
Loose scree on the traverse
Exposed class 3 if you stay on the crest instead of traversing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ridge is joined, not climbed to from a distinct base, so the question is whether you are on the right crest.

You are on the northeast ridge when you have finished crossing the north-facing scree field and are standing on a crest that runs directly up at the summit pyramid, with the north face dropping away steeply behind you. From there the line goes straight up.

If you are still weaving back and forth between notches on a crest studded with gendarmes, you are on the WEST ridge and have not crossed far enough. If you are traversing under the summit rather than up at it, keep going: the ridge is gained at its low point below the pyramid, not partway up the face.

In early season the north side changes the route's character entirely — parties report steep snowfields with poor run-outs, and the alternative of staying on the crest becomes exposed class 3 rather than a scree walk. An easy, dry scree traverse is the summer case only.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Trail, old logging road and the burn
approach_variants.notes:
Start up the Eightmile Lake Trail. Not far in, leave it and push through brush onto an old logging road — this is scrappy going and there is no sign.

From the road, head up the hillside into the burn. The next thousand feet of gain is booting up ashen slopes and stepping over deadfall in a fire scar young enough that little more than shrubs have come back.

Above the burn the angle eases. Go cross-country up and to the LEFT, aiming at the southeast gullies. A snowfield is normally crossed before the gullies proper; a cold night leaves it firm enough to want crampons even in June.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun; the southeast aspect and thinner snowpack clear earlier than the Windy Pass side
hazards: Bushwhacking and deadfall on the old logging road and through the burn
Loose ash, dirt and standing dead trees in the fire scar
A firm snowfield below the gullies early in the season
Thin ice on gully rock even in early summer
Gullies effectively indistinguishable in fog
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The route takes the gully between the south and southeast ridges, and above the snowfield more than one gully line is on offer.

The correct one is easy: class 2 to 3 on reasonably solid rock. That is the test — the scrambling should stay hands-on but casual the whole way. The recorded error is trending too far LEFT out of the gully, which drops you straight into harder ground; if the difficulty stiffens past easy class 3, you have drifted left and want to work back right into the floor of the gully.

Expect thin ice glazing the rock in the gully even on a June ascent, and note that access to the final scramble can itself be the problem early in the season — carry an axe and crampons if in any doubt.

One honest limitation: in fog there is nothing above the burn to navigate by, and a party who climbed this in cloud reported simply not being able to see enough to distinguish the gullies. This is a poor route to attempt in poor visibility.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Lake to Lake Caroline and Windy Pass
approach_variants.notes:
