Eightmile Lake Trailhead, reached off Icicle Creek Road and Eightmile Road. Start on the Eightmile Lake Trail (#1552). At about 2.8 miles, just past Little Eightmile Lake, a junction appears — go right onto the Eightmile-Trout Creek Trail (#1554), signed for Lake Caroline.

That trail switchbacks up through a recovering burn. At roughly 5.5 miles it crosses the ridgeline and drops to Lake Caroline, then continues past Little Lake Caroline. From Little Lake Caroline it is about another 0.8 mile toward Windy Pass; Mount Stuart, Dragontail and Colchuck Lake come into view as you gain the pass.

Leave the maintained trail at about 6,850 ft and walk cross-country to the east. Camp spots and the last reliable water appear a little further on, around 7,100 ft. From there climb north-northeast to the broad col on the peak's west side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep once the snowfield below Windy Pass has gone; Jun trips normally still find snow on the traverse
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the class 3-4 ground from the col upward
Rockfall onto your own party — the standard advice is to keep the group tight rather than strung out
A snowfield below Windy Pass that persists into mid-summer; an axe or microspikes are worth carrying
A summit block only about the size of a table, with gusts reported over 30 mph
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The scrambling starts at the broad col on the west side, but the col is not the part people get wrong — the gully is.

Working east from the col you pass a run of tooth-like gendarmes. Do NOT commit to a chimney or gully while you are still among them: stay low, on the SOUTH side while you pass the western spires, then cross onto the north face and keep traversing low rather than climbing.

The gully you want only presents itself once you are on the NORTH side and the END of the summit formation is in sight ahead of you. From there a class 3 gully opens directly above you and leads to a notch. Standing in that notch you can see down the far side of the mountain — that view through is the confirmation. From the notch it is easy scrambling straight up the crest with one short corkscrew move to a summit block no bigger than a dinner table.

Two errors are on record and they are opposite. If the ground is pushing you into fourth-class moves, or the summit formation still runs on ahead of you, you took a gully too early. If you find yourself climbing a cliffy step out of a notch, you walked past the correct gully and are forcing the first notch you came to.

what_to_bring: bear-resistant food storage (canister or hang; free canister loans available at the NPS Marblemount Wilderness Information Center)
satellite communicator (InReach/SPOT) - no cell coverage on route

emergency.notes: No cell coverage exists at Hozomeen or anywhere along the approach; carry a satellite messenger (InReach/SPOT) given the multi-day self-rescue distance. The peak's position just south of the border means straying north of the boundary swath, even accidentally, is a federal violation — carry GPS/map and know the border line. Call 911 for emergencies.
emergency.county: Okanogan / Whatcom (the summit sits on the county line)
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Winthrop, WA (Okanogan-Wenatchee NF) for the Pasayten Wilderness portion; North Cascades National Park Service Complex Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, WA (360-854-7245) for the Ross Lake NRA approach.
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster, WA and Mid-Valley Hospital, Omak, WA are the nearest general hospitals to the Methow Valley side (each roughly 30 mi from Winthrop); actual time-to-care from the peak itself is many hours given the multi-day hike/boat exit.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies; Okanogan County Sheriff non-emergency/SAR dispatch: 509-422-7232

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail
approach_variants.notes:
This is the way in that stays entirely inside the United States, and it is the reason the peak costs three or four days.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross the lake by water taxi, or paddle a private or inflatable boat portaged down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail starts at about 1,500 ft. Parties with their own boat commonly start walking around four in the morning to leave daylight for the day above; the water taxi runs only in the daytime, 8am to 5pm.

After a couple of hours watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek trail. The stretch immediately above that junction is the hardest navigation of the entire approach: steep rock and alder slopes that want a rising, diagonal line before you regain forest and real tread. Intermittent orange flagging marks it and is worth hunting for.

Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September in a normal year; the creek is hard to ford until the snowmelt drops
hazards: Several similar-looking gullies in the upper basin; the wrong one cliffs out above the creek
The steep rock-and-alder section above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the approach
Krummholz and vegetation-covered rock on the crux band
Teetering blocks near the summit
Days long enough that parties routinely finish the descent in the dark, with a boat pickup to make
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock start to find on this route. What you are finding is the right GULLY out of a basin that offers several, and getting that wrong is how parties get cliffed out.

Above where the tread dies, climb the Freezeout drainage and work up steep heather, talus and scree toward the NOTCH ON THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT. That notch is the target and it is the only feature in the upper basin worth navigating to. Cross to the east side of the creek at roughly 5,000 ft on the way up.

THE PHYSICAL TESTS ON THE CLIMB ITSELF ARE ROCK QUALITY AND TERRAIN GRADE, in that order. This is granite and the rock is genuinely good — clean, coarse and solid, the sort people compare to the best cragging ranges. It is mostly class 2 with short class 3 steps, and the crux is a steeper band with KRUMMHOLZ AND BLUFFS where you are pulling on vegetation-covered rock. If you are roping up, you are off route.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS ENORMOUS AND UNMISTAKABLE. This peak's north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs holding ice or the remains of it, with a glacier at its foot. If you are looking up at that, you are on the wrong side of the mountain entirely and you are under the technical routes. The scramble never sees the north face.

MARK YOUR EXACT ASCENT GULLY BEFORE YOU LEAVE IT, and this is the single most important sentence here. The upper basin holds several gullies and chutes that look alike from above, and dropping into the wrong one on descent risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek. Do not improvise a shortcut down. Reverse exactly what you came up.

Near the summit, watch teetering blocks, and expect the final ground to be exposed and windy.

approach_variants.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
hazards: A long unpaved mountain road with 17 percent grades, no passing room and an unguarded drop
The road opens late and closes with the first autumn storms
Very long approach on foot with exposed, windy high camps
The international boundary lies about a mile north of the summit and crossing it here is unlawful
Similar-looking descent gullies that cliff out above the creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Castle Pass the peak lies roughly four miles to the west-northwest, and what you are looking for is the head of the drainage on its southern flank rather than a base of rock.

Drop off the pass into the head of the creek basin on the peak's south side and work up it. The scramble ground is the same ground the eastern approach reaches from the other direction: heather, talus and scree leading to the NOTCH ON THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT, then class 2 granite with short class 3 steps to the summit.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THE ROCK. Once you are on it, the granite is clean, coarse and solid, and the difficulty stays at scrambling grade with one steeper krummholz-and-bluff band as the crux. Roped climbing means you are not on the standard route.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is the whole mountain: the north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot granite wall above a glacier. From anywhere on this approach you should be looking at broken scrambling ground, not at a wall. If a wall is above you, you have gone round the mountain.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is a legal one rather than a navigational one. The summit sits about a mile south of the international boundary and the boundary clearing is visible from high on the peak. Do not follow ground north from the summit or from the basin. Crossing on foot away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, the corridor is patrolled, and this is the one mistake here that ends with more than a long walk.

On descent, mark your ascent gully. The basin holds several that look alike from above and the wrong one cliffs out.

approach_variants.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass, then the head of Castle Creek
approach_variants.notes:
READ THIS FIRST. The line most often written up for this route walks in from the provincial park to the north and crosses the international boundary cross-country in the clearing south of the creek. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over.

The way that stays inside the United States is the crest trail. The high pass road climbs about twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama, single track with pullouts rather than passing room, a wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades near seventeen percent high up. Trailers are prohibited. It opens with the snowmelt, usually early to mid July.

From the pass the crest trail runs north for a long way over high, open country to Castle Pass, where the Boundary Trail crosses. Castle Creek heads right there, so the pass puts you at the top of the basin this route climbs from.

The other wholly-US option is the eastern one — a boat across the lake and the abandoned creek trail — but that lands you on the far side of the mountain and serves the standard scramble rather than this line.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through September, once the basin brush and wetlands are passable and the high road is open
hazards: The commonly published approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Alder, brush and wetland openings in the lower basin
Two gullies handed off to each other with a notch between; the transition at about 6,800 ft is the routefinding crux
Snow patches persist near the summit well into the season
Extremely remote from any US trailhead; the crest-trail approach is a multi-day walk each way
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route works from a camp in the basin at about 5,500 ft, so the first thing to find is the basin floor rather than any rock. From the pass, drop into the head of the creek and follow it down and out into the open basin below the peak's south side. The lower ground here is alder, brush and wetland openings; the walking improves as you gain the basin proper.

FROM CAMP THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF TWO GULLIES AND A NOTCH, and each hands off to the next. First, the WIDE GULLY ON THE SOUTH SIDE — the broad one, not a narrow chute. Take it to roughly 6,800 ft. Second, at about that height, move INTO THE NORTH-EAST GULLY and aim for a NOTCH at around 7,400 ft. Third, from the notch, cross granite slabs, boulders and lingering snow patches south of the top, and finish with a short scramble to the true summit.

THE PHYSICAL TEST THROUGHOUT IS THAT NOTHING IS STEEP. Granite slabs, boulders and snow patches are the correct texture. If a rope comes out of the pack for anything other than a snow patch, you are not on this line.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is the whole north half of the mountain: the north face is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier, carrying several hard routes. If that is above you, you have walked round the peak and you are under the technical climbing.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER, on the boundary. The summit sits about a mile south of the international line and the boundary clearing is a visible feature from up here. Do not use it as a route, and do not follow ground north out of the basin.

Descent reverses everything: back through the notch, down the north-east gully, then the wide south gully to camp.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
hazards: Several unmarked routes on one fourteen-hundred-foot wall; position under the summit is the only identifier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall; the first pitch exists mainly to escape the fall line
Dirt and moss-filled cracks through the middle section and teetering blocks near the top
Multi-day approach with no cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by POSITION AGAINST THE SUMMIT and nothing else.

THE TEST IS SIMPLE AND IT IS THE WHOLE IDENTIFICATION: this route takes the CENTRAL BUTTRESS, and that buttress sits DIRECTLY BELOW THE SUMMIT. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the ROCKFALL LINE rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

CONFIRM ON PITCH TWO, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the LEFT via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the LEFT EDGE of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE LEGAL POINT FIRST. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides with one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face
Retreat from anywhere on this trip is measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

FROM THAT VIEW, DROP A PLUMB LINE FROM THE SUMMIT. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the ROCKFALL LINE rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

NEGATIVE MARKER: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the LEFT EDGE of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage is unreliable within the park; NPS climbing rangers coordinate backcountry rescues via radio and helicopter.
emergency.county: Lewis County, WA (Mount Rainier NP spans both Lewis and Pierce Counties)
emergency.rangerStation: Longmire Wilderness Information Center / Ranger Station: (360) 569-6650; MORA park headquarters: (360) 569-2211
emergency.nearestHospital: Arbor Health - Morton Hospital (Morton General Hospital), Morton, WA — 24-hour ER, roughly 30-40 min drive from Longmire/Reflection Lakes
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Lewis County Sheriff's Office non-emergency: (360) 748-9286 (dial 911 for active emergencies)

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes and the Pinnacle traverse to the taller summit spire
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is shared with the standard Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes at about 4,859 ft, take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the saddle, then contour east across Pinnacle's south scree to the base of Castle's southeast side, and scramble up broken third-class ground to reach the base of the summit block.

The climbing itself is short: about two-thirds of the pitch is easier ground, there is one solid cam placement, then three slabby crux moves, a jug pull, and easier climbing to a large belay ledge about 10 ft left of the true summit.

From the belay ledge, traverse climber's right past the true summit to the heavily trafficked top-out shared with the Southeast Face, where slings are typically in place, and make a single short rappel back to the base of the technical section.

Stevens Canyon Road typically opens late May and closes with fall snowfall; Narada Falls is the winter and spring trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Exposed third-class scrambling with real fall potential just to reach the base of the pitch
A crux high on a short pitch, above ledges
Early-season snow and ice on the traverse from the saddle
Loose rock on the approach scramble and gully
Afternoon thunderstorms and exposure on the summit block and connecting ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
SAME COL AND SAME BROKEN GROUND AS THE STANDARD ROUTE — SO THE DISCRIMINATOR IS NOT THE WALK IN, IT IS WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU AT THE FOOT OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK.

THIS ROUTE IS A DIHEDRAL ON THE TALLER OF THE SUMMIT SPIRES. THE STANDARD ROUTE IS A CRACK-CHIMNEY. So: A CORNER YOU STEM IS THIS ROUTE. A SLOT YOU GET INSIDE IS THE SOUTHEAST FACE. That single distinction separates a 5.7 with an 5.8 crux from an easy-5th scramble, and it is decided at the ground.

THE ORDERING WITHIN THE PITCH IS THE SECOND CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS COUNTABLE: roughly two-thirds of the pitch is easier climbing, THEN one good cam placement, THEN three slabby crux moves, THEN a jug pull, then easy ground to the ledge. IF THE HARD MOVES COME AT THE VERY START, YOU ARE NOT ON THIS ROUTE. The crux here is high on a short pitch, which is also why a fall from it has consequence — there are ledges below.

THE TOP-OUT TEST IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES IT AFTERWARDS: this pitch finishes on a LARGE BELAY LEDGE ABOUT 10 FT LEFT OF THE TRUE SUMMIT. Topping out level with the summit rather than on it is correct here. You then traverse climber's RIGHT, past the true summit, to reach the shared rappel station.

SO THE NEGATIVE IS: IF YOU TOPPED OUT DIRECTLY AT A SLUNG HORN WITH OLD TAT ON IT, YOU CLIMBED THE STANDARD SOUTHEAST FACE. That horn is the shared descent anchor, not this route's finish.

ONE PRACTICAL FINDING FOR THE APPROACH SCRAMBLE ITSELF: the third-class ground below the block is exposed enough that a fall has real consequence. It is the part of this outing that is soloed by everyone and guarded by nobody.

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes, Pinnacle Saddle and the scree traverse east to the Castle-Pinnacle col
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road, or at the year-round Narada Falls lot when that road is snowed in. Take the signed Pinnacle Peak Trail from the south side of the road; it climbs steadily through forest and subalpine meadow for about 1.3 miles and 1,050 ft to the saddle at about 5,920 ft.

From the saddle, do not climb Pinnacle. Traverse east across Pinnacle's south-facing scree and boulder field, holding roughly 6,000-6,200 ft, about another half mile of cross-country travel to the col between Pinnacle and The Castle.

From the col, scramble onto Castle's south rib, make a short class-3 traverse onto the east flank, and follow the crack-chimney system up and right to a notch beside a natural rock horn. A brief exposed class 3-4 scramble along the summit crest reaches the true summit.

Stevens Canyon Road is gated and closed by snow roughly mid-October to late May or early June.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for dry rock; the line is scrambled into June and October with snow on the approach
hazards: Exposed, largely unprotected class 3-4 terrain along the summit ridge crest
A short 5th-class pitch with sparse natural protection
Loose volcanic rock on the approach scree traverse and off-route
Residual snow and ice on the shaded traverse into early summer
Rapid afternoon thunderstorm development typical of this range in summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO SADDLES, AND YOU WANT THE SECOND ONE. That is the whole approach problem and it is countable.

The maintained trail ends at PINNACLE SADDLE at about 5,920 ft — the notch between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak. THAT IS NOT YOUR OBJECTIVE. From there you leave the trail and contour EAST across Pinnacle's south scree at 6,000-6,200 ft to a SECOND col, the one between Pinnacle and The Castle. The Castle's base is there.

THREE WAYS TO BE WRONG, AND EACH IS A DIFFERENT PEAK. Start climbing at the first saddle and you are on PINNACLE. Go west from the first saddle and you are heading for PLUMMER. Stop short on the traverse and you are on Pinnacle's south face rather than at the col.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS ONE FEATURE AND IT IS A HOLE, NOT A FACE: an OBVIOUS CRACK-CHIMNEY SYSTEM on the southeast and east flank, gained after a short class-3 traverse off the south rib. If you are on open face with no continuous crack to follow, you are off it — the easy-5th line is in the chimney.

CONFIRMATION AT THE TOP OF THE PITCH, AND IT IS WORTH FINDING DELIBERATELY ON THE WAY UP BECAUSE YOU WILL WANT IT ON THE WAY DOWN: the chimney ends at a NOTCH BESIDE A NATURAL ROCK HORN. That horn is the rappel anchor. Carry your own webbing rather than trusting tat left there.

THE LAST NEGATIVE, AND IT COSTS PEOPLE THE SUMMIT: THE NOTCH IS NOT THE TOP. The true summit is the NORTHERNMOST block, reached by a short exposed scramble along the crest from the notch. If you have topped out of the chimney and stopped, you are one airy scramble short.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout, climbing east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: An awkward, committing move onto the ramp at the very start
Shared belay ground on Saber Ledge with several routes converging
Full southwest sun and polished rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Cat Burglar is one of the group of routes on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge, the same section that holds Canary, Saber and Century — so the large low roof marking Saber's ramp is the anchor landmark for this whole end of the bench.

The route identifies itself by an awkward first move: a weird step onto a ramp, which then leads into cracks running up to Saber Ledge. The second pitch goes up and to the right.

If your start is a straightforward walk onto easy cracks with no committing move onto a ramp, you are on a neighbouring line. And if you have finished on Saber Ledge, you are where several of these routes converge — the upper pitch is what separates them, and Cat Burglar's goes up and RIGHT rather than traversing left across the exposure like Canary.

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. From the LOWER, eastern end of the pullout walk about fifty yards downhill to the climbers' trail, which climbs steeply to the base of the Lower Wall.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and heavily polished rock
Roof features overhead at the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Wrong-trail test first: the path leaving the UPHILL, western end of the pullout traverses east onto Logger's Ledge and belongs to Upper Castle. If you are gaining a wide bench halfway up the formation, you are one wall too high.

On the Lower Wall the selected routes run west to east as The Fault, then Catapult, then The Vertebrae, then The Bone — so Catapult is the second along, immediately east of The Fault, which the short trail from the right of the parking area reaches directly.

The Lower Wall identifies itself by roofs and by sitting directly BELOW Logger's Ledge. Two pitches from the base put you on that ledge, and a trail leads from the ledge back down to the parking area — so if your route tops out onto a big walkable bench rather than the summit, that is correct here.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. This is the shortest drive of the three ways in and it is paved the whole way.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles cross an old burn, so there is almost no shade, the tread is overgrown and soaks you after rain, and blowdown is normal. Andrews Creek runs beside the trail for that whole stretch and is reliable water. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

From the pass continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Bear off near the old wilderness guard-station cabin. Strong parties walk it in one long day with heavy packs; others split it with a camp partway up the drainage.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking way in from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the penalties are severe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-July through September, once the trails and the face have shed snow
hazards: No climbers' trail and no marked start; the base is identified by landform and by what is above you
Rockfall from parties above and from loose blocks on the featured lower face
Afternoon storms on a summit that is the local high point
A walk-off descent whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap near the summit
Remote enough that any injury becomes a multi-day evacuation
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no climbers' trail to the base. Cross the parkland and talus from camp toward the deep gully that divides Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower leaning against the lower right side of the wall. Thirty to sixty minutes from camp.

THE FIRST TEST IS THE TOWER, AND IT IS A NEGATIVE ONE. This route is on the MAIN wall, not on the tower and not on the buttress behind it. If a separate tower stands between you and the rock you are about to climb, walk further left along the base — you are under the Southeast Buttress. If you are looking up at an open thousand-foot face with nothing standing in front of it, you are in the right place.

Now place yourself across that face. This line takes the RIGHT-HAND portion of the open wall, between the central line and the line further right. There is no start ledge, no cairn and no fixed gear to find; the ground low down is heavily featured and the first ascent treated it as choose-your-own, so the start is a zone rather than a point. Pick the most featured rock in that right-hand third and go up.

CONFIRM IT ABOVE YOU BEFORE YOU COMMIT, because the low ground will accept almost any line. Look for a long ramp slashing rightward across the middle of the face, and above the ramp a steep, clean crack splitting a headwall. Those two features in that order are this route. If the ramp is not there and instead you find a big curving chimney above you, you have drifted into the centre of the wall and you are on the original central line — several number grades easier, and a different day.

Second negative marker, at the top: this route joins the buttress route for its final hand crack to the summit. Arriving at that shared pitch is correct. Arriving at it early, without having crossed a rightward ramp and pulled a thin headwall, means you traversed off.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
This is a TRAIL, #510A, not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then the forest roads up to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print under three or four spellings, and one of those names also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not to the name.

The trail descends from its high trailhead to join the valley trail below, and from there it is the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. This is the shortest walk and the least climbing of the ways in.

The catch sits at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail drops to meet the valley, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way OUT, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-July through September
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip, on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
Beta headed South Face may describe the small tower rather than the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The way in changes; the base does not. From Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same walk toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, and the same question at the bottom: is there a tower standing between you and the rock? If yes you are under the buttress, not this face.

What this approach genuinely changes is your first sighting of the wall. Coming up the valley you arrive in the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side presents itself at once from across the water. Use that. Standing at the lake, pick out three things before you walk up: the tower at the lower right of the wall, the open thousand-foot face left of it, and the long ramp that slashes rightward across the middle of that face. This route is the right-hand third of the open face, working up to that ramp and to the steep crack in the headwall above it.

That identification is far easier from across the lake than from underneath, where the face foreshortens and the ramp disappears into the general featuring. Photograph it or draw it before you leave camp.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if from the lake you cannot see a ramp at all on the face you are looking at, you are looking at the wrong wall. The tower has its own south face with its own short routes on it, and beta written about that tower will also say South Face. The tower is small and stands clear of the mountain; the main face runs the full height of the peak behind it.

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,080 ft, roughly a five-hour drive from Seattle and the shortest drive of the three ways in.

Walk Andrews Creek trail #504 up the drainage. The lower miles pass through an old burn, so there is little shade and the tread can be overgrown and wet after rain, but the creek is beside you and reliable. The trail tops out at Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, where the burn gives way to open parkland.

Continue on the Boundary Trail #533 and drop on the Cathedral Lakes side trail to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. Published figures for the whole walk from this trailhead are about nineteen miles with 5,550 ft of gain, and everyone splits it over at least two days.

Of the three trailheads this one has the shortest drive and the most walking gain; the Thirtymile trailhead is only about five and a half miles further along the same road, which makes a car shuttle between them easy.

One thing to leave alone: there is a shorter-looking approach from the Canadian side. Crossing into the United States here is illegal, the border is patrolled, and the fines are severe.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow lingers at Andrews Pass into early July
hazards: No climbers' trail to the base; navigation is off the landform and photographs
Long approach through burn with little shade and overgrown tread
A no-fall step-across or hop on the walk-off descent
Remote enough that a two- to four-day trip is the norm, so a retreat is slow
approach_variants.baseFinding: THERE IS NO CLIMBERS' TRAIL TO THE BASE. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the FIRST SWITCHBACK after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go UP INTO the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 FEET UP the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the LEFT wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a TALL PEDESTAL there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. HOW TO TELL THIS FROM THE SOUTH FACE ROUTES, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
This is a TRAIL, #510A, and not a four-wheel-drive road, despite a persistent claim to the contrary — the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to the Iron Gate spur, a different road. Access is from Loomis by Toats Coulee Road, then a Y junction, then NF-39 and NF-300 to the trailhead at about 5,570 ft.

Be careful with the trailhead name. It appears in print as Cathedral Driveway, Chewuch, and Chewack Driveway, and the Chewuch name also belongs to a completely different trailhead near Winthrop. Navigate to the road, not the name.

The Cathedral Driveway descends from its trailhead to join the Chewuch trail #510 around mile 4.8 at about 4,300 ft, and from there it is the Chewuch valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. Total is about seventeen and a half miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain — the shortest walk and the least climbing of the three approaches.

The catch is at both ends. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead sits high and the trail drops to meet the Chewuch, you finish the trip with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way OUT, at the point when you least want it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead with four different published names
Same lack of any climbers' trail to the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The approach changes but the base does not. From camp at Upper Cathedral Lake it is the same thirty to sixty minutes: cross toward the deep gully dividing Cathedral Peak from The Monk, go about 150 feet up INTO the gully, and start on the LEFT wall from a tall pedestal.

What this approach does affect is your first sighting. Coming down the Chewuch you arrive in the basin from below rather than over Andrews Pass, so take the time at the lake to pick out The Monk as a separate tower leaning against the peak's flank before walking up. The tower in front of the wall is the whole discriminator between this route and the South Face, and it is far easier to identify from across the water than from underneath.

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Andrews Pass
bivy.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
bivy.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
bivy.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the trail toward Cathedral Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Drive north from Winthrop up the Chewuch River road to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft and walk trail #504 up the drainage to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft. The lower half is an old burn with no shade and brushy tread. From the pass, drop into the next drainage and take the Cathedral Lakes trail up to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft. That is the base camp and it is a full long day of walking, usually two.

One early-season bonus is worth planning around: the chasm that splits the summit rocks is often snow-filled early, which makes the first step-across easy or trivial. Late season means a bare hole and the pure version of the move. It can snow here in any month, so carry layers whatever the forecast says.

The alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, gentle but longer, and the Cathedral Driveway trail from the high trailhead above Loomis (not the longer Iron Gate route), which walks least but drives longest and leaves you 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: July to mid-September; the sunny south-west aspect melts out first
hazards: The step-across onto the chockstone is easy climbing over serious exposure and is harder in descent than in ascent
The second step-across never has snow in the hole, whatever the season
Ducks and cairns are the only route markers on the granite section
Loose blocks and sandy slopes that plunge-step well going down and slide going up
This is also the descent for every technical route here, so parties meet it tired and often late in the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route has no rock start to find. It begins where you LEAVE THE TRAIL, and that spot is defined by the pass, not by a cairn: walk about 0.6 mile of trail from Upper Cathedral Lake toward Cathedral Pass and step off just short of the pass at roughly 7,600 ft. If you have crested the pass and started descending the far side, you have gone too far — turn round.

Above that, the route confirms itself by TEXTURE, in a fixed order. First several hundred vertical feet of easy sandy slopes with no rock scrambling at all. Then ducks and cairns over coarse granite blocks and slabs, solid rock, class 2 to 3, with two minor steps that need a hand and one place where a friction push gets you over a block. If you are pulling on anything harder than that, you have wandered off the ducks.

The route then enters a HIDDEN CLEFT running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. That cleft is the strongest confirmation on the whole climb, because it cannot be seen from below and you either find yourself in it or you do not.

The last feature is the crux and it is unmistakable: a long chasm cleaving the summit rocks into a north and a south half, with a big chockstone jammed in the slot. Step onto the chockstone and mantle onto the bulge on the far side. The move is easy; the exposure is not, and most parties rig a handline with prusiks for the return. Lower down there is a cannonhole giving an easier alternative to one vertical step.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if at any point you are standing under a thousand-foot wall with a detached tower leaning against its lower right side, you have walked round to the south side of the mountain and you are below the technical routes, not on the walk-up.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Rock Trail to the pass, then a rising traverse under the east face
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 80 at Cle Elum, take SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald along Cle Elum Lake for about 14.8 miles, then gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 for 12.3 miles and the short NF-153 spur to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, Trail #1345, at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free self-issue wilderness permit.

The trail climbs through old growth to Nosh Nosh Wahtum, formerly Squaw Lake, at about 4,850 ft and 2.5 miles, then opens into meadow with Cathedral Rock ahead. At about 4 miles you reach Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft and the PCT junction.

Walk north on the PCT for a couple of minutes, then cut across the meadow to a stand of trees. Parties cache the gear they do not need on the climb there. From the trees, start a rising traverse under the east face, past the meadows, and then across a loose talus slope with the northeast buttress in sight.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to September. The northeast side is shaded and dries slowly, so give it time after rain and expect approach snow into July
hazards: Loose, fractured andesite throughout — poor and unpredictable protection on every technical route on this peak
A short steep snowfield with loose and sharp rock below it, crossed by parties in approach shoes
The moat at the top of the snow
Rockfall down the gully systems from parties, wind and thaw
Descent route-finding on the shattered south and southwest flanks, where many plausible gullies cliff out
Summer convection over the Cascade crest, on an exposed tower with no cell coverage and a remote trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE TOP OF A SHORT, STEEP SNOWFIELD, AND THAT SNOWFIELD IS THE ARRIVAL TEST. Crossing the loose talus under the east face you come to it; it is short but steep enough that parties in approach shoes have picked their way up it holding stones for security. Reaching the top of that snow patch is reaching the start of the climbing.

AND HERE IS THE MISTAKE PARTIES ACTUALLY MAKE AT THAT POINT, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING TO KNOW ABOUT THIS ROUTE: at the top of the snow it is natural to exit RIGHT onto ledges and start up from there. That is wrong. A party that does it finds the ground harder than the fourth class the description promises, wanders left, right and up, and comes back down. The correct start is to exit back LEFT into the MOAT at the top of the snow, where the terrain is much easier.

SO THE TEST IS A DIFFICULTY TEST: if your first moves off the snow feel harder than fourth class, you are on the wrong side of the snowfield. Go back and take the moat on the left.

WHAT SHOULD FOLLOW: easy ground you can simul-climb, then a LEDGE SYSTEM that traverses RIGHTWARD toward the crest of the buttress. Beckey gives the buttress seven pitches, about 900 ft, at 5.7 and grade III. A route that is sustained from the first pitch is not it.

AND ONE THING TO SETTLE BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE TREES: this peak is descended by the SOUTH side, not by reversing the buttress. Note where you came up.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass, the gear-cache trees, and the traverse to the original route's first pitch
approach_variants.notes:
Drive and hike as for the Northeast Buttress: Trail #1345 from the Cathedral Rock trailhead at about 3,350 ft, past Nosh Nosh Wahtum at 2.5 miles, to Cathedral Pass and the PCT junction at 5,550 ft and 4 miles. Sign the wilderness permit at the register.

Cut across the meadow to the stand of trees — the usual gear cache — and traverse under the east face across talus to the northeast side.

This variation does not have its own start on the ground: it begins where the ORIGINAL Northeast Ridge route finishes its first pitch.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September. Late August and September give the driest rock and the coldest, most stable air, which is worth waiting for where the protection is already marginal
hazards: Shattered, friable andesite giving loose holds and unreliable protection
An explicitly unstable class 4+ section low on the route that must be crossed to reach the good climbing
PG13 protection with significant fall consequences
Rockfall onto belayers from a ridge littered with loose blocks
Six pitches at 5.9 plus a route-finding descent make benightment a real risk on a short day
No cell coverage and a remote gravel-access trailhead: slow rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR: THIS ROUTE'S BASE IS THE TOP OF SOMEBODY ELSE'S FIRST PITCH. You find the original Northeast Ridge start — the short steep snowfield on the northeast side, exiting LEFT into the moat rather than right onto the harder ledges — climb its first pitch, and only then are you at the beginning of the 2003 line.

THE FEATURE THAT PROVES YOU ARE ON THE VARIATION AND NOT ON THE ORIGINAL, and this is the one to memorise, is YELLOW-SPECKLED ROCK. From the top of that first pitch, traverse LEFT and up over a short pitch of genuinely unstable class 4+ ground, aiming for a LEFT-HAND VERTICAL CRACK in a LEFT-FACING CORNER, identified by yellow-speckled rock with ROOFS ABOVE IT. Yellow speckles plus roofs above a left-facing corner is the target; nothing else on this side of the peak reads that way.

THE CONFIRMATION IS THE THIRD PITCH: it climbs that crack and exits over its LEFT side. It is the best pitch on the route, 5.7 to 5.8 and well protected — which is worth knowing precisely because everything below it is not. If pitch three is poorly protected choss, you are not in the corner you wanted.

A HIGHER CHECK: above, the rock eases, and a short difficult LEFT-LEANING CRACK at 5.9+ comes before moderate terrain to the summit.

AND THE HONEST WARNING THAT BELONGS IN A BASE FINDING HERE: the pitch you must cross to reach the good climbing is described by the first-ascent party as scary and unstable. It is rated PG13, and the route would carry more stars if not for that second pitch. Knowing that in advance is what stops a party assuming they are off route when the ground feels wrong.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass trail #1345 from the Cle Elum River road end
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are TWO trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads NORTH. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading WEST, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn LEFT, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the LEFT path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct. Early season, with the gullies still snow-filled, the rockfall hazard is lower — this is the rare Cascade route that is arguably safer under snow
hazards: Serious rockfall in the summit gully, the peak's named hazard, worst with parties above
Loose rock on the summit scramble as well as in the gully
Picking the Hyas Lake / Deception Pass trailhead by mistake at the road end
Vehicle break-ins at the trailhead
Braided use paths across the meadows near Cathedral Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The handrail is elevation plus one named feature. Follow the scramble gully on the RIGHT side of the rounded spur upward until the spur runs into the summit formation at about 6,400 ft. That contact point — where broken spur ground ends against continuous rock — is where the approach stops and the climb starts.

From there the line is the obvious gully on the upper LEFT, to the left of the South Buttress. If the buttress is on your left you have gone too far right; the buttress should be to your RIGHT as you enter the gully.

One recorded refinement inside that gully, which is around a hundred yards long: stay right at first and cross left higher up, scrambling on rock, rather than taking the centre — the middle holds the loose rock and the steeper steps.

One to two pitches of the southwest face above the gully reach the ridge crest, and most parties rope up for that even though it is graded fourth class. From the crest it is a short scramble to the top.

What is NOT here, and the absence is worth saying: there is no famous single wrong gully at Cathedral Rock. The published hazard is rockfall and loose rock, stated repeatedly and in plain terms. The genuinely wrong-start stories on this peak are all from the Northeast Buttress, a different route on the other side, so do not import them.

approach_variants.name: Peggy's Pond, gaining the summit gully from the ledge above the pond
approach_variants.notes:
Walk to Cathedral Pass as for the standard, then continue on Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond. The final half mile or so into the pond is primitive, crossing narrow ledges with real exposure, and it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail before it.

Peggy's Pond is the last reliable water and the last established camp, so this is the variant for parties splitting the day or combining the climb with Mount Daniel.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ledge traverse into the pond is nastier with a heavy pack or under snow
hazards: Exposed narrow ledge traverse on the way into Peggy's Pond
Rockfall in the summit gully
Snow lingering on the pond ledges into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the pond you gain the same summit gully, but from below and on the south side rather than by traversing in from the pass. Climb to the ledge above the pond and follow it to the foot of the gully system.

The identification is unchanged: you want the gully to the LEFT of the South Buttress, entered where the spur ground dies against the continuous summit rock near 6,400 ft. Coming from the pond you meet that rock from underneath, so the check is that the buttress stands to your right as you turn up into the gully.

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
bivy.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.
bivy.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
bivy.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs east onto Logger's Ledge, ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Full southwest sun on the upper wall
Polished granite typical of this crag
Descent is by climbers' trail off the back of the formation down to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Century is one of the classic trad lines on the southwest-facing upper wall and lies with Cat Burglar, Canary, Saber, Old Gray Mare and Crack of Doom on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge. The reliable anchor for this end of the bench is the large low roof with the left-angling ramp to its right — that is Saber, at the far right end. Canary is about 100 ft to Saber's left. Work from those two known points rather than trying to count lines. The general Upper Castle test still applies and catches most people: if you are at the foot of the rock at road level rather than standing on a wide bench halfway up the formation, you took the trail from the eastern end of the pullout and are at Lower Castle. No source consulted here gives Century's own start marker relative to its immediate neighbours; confirm it on the ground against a topo rather than assuming a position on the ledge.

approach_variants.name: Source Lake and the WNW gully into the east-face basin
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot (about 3,100 ft) via I-90 exit 52. A cat track leaves the end of the lot and runs up the valley just left of the stream; the Snow Lake trail forks at roughly 1.5 miles — take the left/west branch toward Source Lake. About half a mile along that branch, look for a fairly narrow rocky gully heading west-northwest starting around 4,200 ft. Depending on the season it holds snow, with water running down it. Climb the gully. Around 4,800 ft you reach a small cliff; work through the notch there, then cross the basin beyond on climbers' path or snow, heading southwest straight at Chair's east face.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; an axe is useful in shoulder-season snow
hazards: snow and running water in the approach gully around 4,200 ft
loose scree on the final stretch to the wall
rockfall in the basin below the face
the descent gully off the summit drops east to a notch in the southeast ridge - do not confuse it with the approach gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Go PAST the Thumb Tack. The Thumb Tack is a freestanding rock sitting in the middle of the basin and it is a waypoint, not the base — parties that stop and rack up there are several hundred feet low and one bench short of the wall. From the Thumb Tack, continue up the basin to the foot of the east face proper, around 5,500 ft.

The other confusion at that rock is directional: if you turned sharply right at the Thumb Tack and started scrambling heather and ledges toward a divide, you are on the Northeast Buttress approach, not the East Face. For the East Face you keep going straight up the basin with the wall filling the view ahead.

You are at the base when the basin runs out against a continuous face rising directly above you and the ground underfoot changes from basin talus to loose scree banked against rock.

approach_variants.name: Alpental valley to the Thumb Tack, then over the northeast ridge
approach_variants.notes: Park at the upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road. Head up the Alpental valley, on the old ski-area cat track for the first stretch and then on trail, toward Source Lake. The maintained tread effectively ends at Source Lake around 3,700-3,740 ft. If stability allows, climb the open slopes at the head of the valley and make a rising traverse into the cirque under Chair's east face, finishing at a freestanding rock called the Thumb Tack. That rock is the one unambiguous fix on the whole approach — use it as your reference, because everything above it is decided by aspect rather than by tread. From the Thumb Tack, go north up a gully to gain the Northeast Ridge. Take the gully rather than attacking the ridge directly from the northeast. This gully is a known avalanche path and has killed climbers. Once on the ridge, follow it to the buttress and round onto the north side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Dec-Mar, below-freezing conditions after a thaw
hazards: the gully from the Thumb Tack to the northeast ridge is an avalanche path with a fatal accident history (two deaths in 1996)
avalanche paths cross the approach the length of the Alpental valley
route is only in condition below freezing after a thaw
moat at the base of the face late in the season
creek crossing near Source Lake at high flow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most important thing: the north face is NOT reached by climbing straight up the head of the Alpental cirque. You get onto it by crossing the northeast ridge first and coming round. A party grinding up the snow at the back of the cirque with the east face above them is under the wrong aspect entirely.

Once on the north side, the route starts roughly halfway across the face at a prominent open book — a corner with a gully feeding into it. Pitch one takes that corner on thin alpine ground; pitch two goes up steep snow and ice to a TREE belay. The tree is your confirmation you picked the right corner.

If you are standing under a continuous, featureless snow apron with no corner system above it, you have stopped short — keep traversing across the face. If you are past the halfway point of the face with the summit block directly overhead, you have gone too far.

The route is only worth starting in below-freezing conditions, ideally after a thaw has consolidated the ice and snow; on the wrong day the corner is unprotectable slush over rock.

approach_variants.name: Source Lake basin to the divide (summer and fall rock)
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot, I-90 exit 52. Snow Lake Trail up the valley — the first stretch is the old ski-area cat track — to the fork at about 1.5 miles, then left/west toward Source Lake, where the maintained trail ends near 3,700-3,740 ft. Leave the tread and head northwest into the basin below Chair's east face on climbers' path, talus and heather. The Thumb Tack, a freestanding rock in the basin, is the landmark to aim for; parties commonly reach it in about two hours from the car. At the Thumb Tack there is a genuine fork in what you do next. Continuing up the basin takes you to the foot of the east face. For the Northeast Buttress, angle sharply RIGHT from the Thumb Tack and scramble rocky heather slopes and ledges to the top of the divide, then walk along the NORTH side of the divide to the base of the buttress. That line is less obvious than the gully but easier and less exposed.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct, snow-free
hazards: loose rock on the heather-and-ledge scramble up to the divide
the basin sits under avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain
rockfall onto the gully from parties above
no water above the Source Lake outlet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The start is unmistakable once you have it in view, and every route description carries a photo of it: a blocky S-shaped gully, sometimes described as an open book, beginning just down and RIGHT of the divide. It climbs, curves right, then straightens again and finishes in a clump of trees. Two pitches of gully and chimney.

The clump of trees at the top of the S is the confirmation. If the gully in front of you runs straight with no rightward curve, and nothing green at its top, it is not the route.

In poor visibility, take the Thumb Tack as your last certain position and navigate from there: sharply right and up to the divide, then everything else happens on the divide's north side. If you are on the south or east side of the divide looking at the east face, you have not crossed over yet.

Above the gully the buttress continues on blocky low-angle rock, angling left across exposed slabby ledges toward another cluster of trees near the prow.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, on snow
approach_variants.notes: Same line up the valley, but in snow the summer tread is abandoned and parties skin or boot the valley bottom to Source Lake, then up into the basin, commonly reaching the Thumb Tack shortly after first light. Skis are cached in the basin. In snow the approach gully from the basin up toward the buttress is itself the hazard: it is a classic early-season slide path, and trip reports from this basin describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity and wind loading. Rope, axe and crampons usually come out from the basin onward rather than at the base of the route, because the approach gully is exposed enough on its own.
approach_variants.season: Dec-Apr, ice and mixed
hazards: the approach gully to the buttress is a known early-season slide path
wind loading and wet-slab activity reported repeatedly in this basin
deep postholing on the basin approach
avalanche terrain the length of the Alpental valley below
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same S-shaped gully, curving right and finishing in trees. Under snow the curve is easier to read from a distance than close up, so pick the line out from the basin before you commit to the divide, and hold that picture.

The trees at the top of the S are what stay visible when the rock is plastered. If you are at the foot of a straight snow runnel with no trees above it, you are on a different feature.

If the ground you are on is exposed and you have not yet crossed to the north side of the divide, stop — the gully line direct to the ridge is steeper and more exposed than the walk along the divide's north side, and it is not the recommended way to the base.

approach_variants.name: East face approach to Thumbtack Rock, then the grassy gully over the divide
approach_variants.notes: Follow the Northeast Buttress and east face approach from the Alpental lot: Snow Lake trail, the Source Lake fork, then the climbers' path and snow up the broad basin running southwest toward Chair's east face. About two hours in, that basin brings you to Thumbtack Rock, the small pinnacle every route on this side uses as its landmark. At Thumbtack Rock the northwest ridge parts company with everything else. Turn RIGHT and climb a grassy gully that carries you over the ridge and around onto the northwest side, then head for the ridge itself. About 4.8 km and roughly 3,100 ft of gain from the car to the top.
approach_variants.season: Summer and autumn, once the ridge is free of snow
hazards: Poor, broken rock and runout ridge climbing — the route's own reputation is that the setting beats the climbing
A hard-to-protect move on a small vertical face of poor rock above the chockstone
Exposure on both sides of a narrow crest
A descent that goes SOUTH over false summits to find a rappel tree in the SECOND gully east — the first gully you meet is not it
Fixed rappel gear on the descent has been found set for snow conditions and out of reach on dry rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THUMBTACK ROCK IS THE DECISION POINT, AND THE TURN IS RIGHT AND UP A GRASSY GULLY. Everything else on this side of the mountain continues straight on up the basin to the foot of the east face. This route is the one that leaves at the Thumbtack and crosses the divide. A published fix for the Thumbtack is 10T 0616013E 5257415N. If you are still walking up the basin under a big east face, you have gone past the turn.

THE START ITSELF IS A SADDLE WITH TREES ON IT, and the first pitch goes up the gully to the LEFT of that saddle. Trees on a saddle, gully immediately left — that pairing is the arrival test, and both halves are visible from below in poor light.

CONFIRMATION ONE PITCH UP, which is the strongest signal on the route: pitch one runs about 200 ft to the crest and you belay off trees on the SOUTH side of the ridge. From those trees you scramble down and left to a chimney-shaped feature with a CHOCKSTONE jammed at its top. You cannot see that chockstone from the trees; it becomes obvious as soon as you scramble across. A chockstone-capped chimney at the end of a short downward scramble means you are on the northwest ridge and nothing else.

NEGATIVE TESTS: if your first pitch is bolted, you are on Voie de Chaise on the east face. If you are looking up at a big buttress from the head of the basin, you never made the Thumbtack turn.

approach_variants.name: Alpental and the Source Lake talus to the Chair snow patch, then the east face scree
approach_variants.notes: From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, take the summer trail toward Source Lake. Where the trail meets the talus field, do NOT drop down — dropping is the turn for The Tooth. Instead hold your height and gain 100 to 200 horizontal feet until you can pass small cliff bands on your right. Above them the tread improves and runs just below a waterfall. Leave the trail at a longer talus field, usually marked by a large cairn, and climb up and left on good paths between the talus to the permanent snow patch under the east face. Climb the snow patch to its top, then take the last 200 to 300 ft of loose scree, keeping hard against the base of the peak where the scree lies at a gentler angle. Reckon two to three hours from the car to the foot of the route.
approach_variants.season: Summer into autumn, once the snow patch below the face has shrunk and the rock is dry
hazards: The final 200-300 ft of approach scree is loose and sits directly under the face
A newer alpine line: loose pebbles and small rock still come off the upper pitches, and the last two pitches were left very dirty after cleaning
Several rappels leave under 5 ft of rope to spare on a 60m — knots in the ends are not optional
The eighth pitch must be belayed back down rather than rappelled, because rappelling it showers rock on anyone below
Parties stacked on the face: this and the East Face share the same descent gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
