THE LINE OF BOLTS IS THE TEST, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE YOU NEED IN CLOUD. This is a fully bolted alpine sport line. Every other route that starts on this side of Chair Peak is climbed on gear. If you cannot see a bolt from the ground, you are not at the start of this route, whatever the terrain looks like.

WHERE ALONG THE BASE: at the top of the scree there is a band of third and fourth class rock that guards the RIGHT-HAND side of Chair Peak. The route starts just past the LEFT edge of that band. So walk the base leftward until the guarding band ends, and the first bolted line past it is this one.

WHAT PITCH ONE FEELS LIKE, as confirmation: a few tricky moves straight off the ground at about 5.7, and then it eases into sustained, clean 5.6 slab for roughly 120 ft. Hard slab on clean rock with bolts is right. Broken blocky ground, or a chimney, is not.

HOW TO TELL IT FROM THE EAST FACE ROUTE, which is the mistake worth avoiding: the first-ascent party deliberately kept this line clear of the East Face, and the East Face both starts and finishes WELL TO THE RIGHT of it. So if you are at a gear start on broken rock, you have not walked far enough left along the base.

AND THE DESCENT GIVES YOU A BACK-BEARING: the ordinary Chair Peak gully descent lands you only about a hundred feet uphill of this route's base. A party coming down that gully that walks a hundred feet downhill is standing at the start.

approach_variants.name: Alpental and the Northeast Buttress approach, then round onto the slabs on the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Use the standard Chair Peak trailhead at Alpental, the same start the Northeast Buttress uses. From the basin, traverse slabby ground round onto the west side of the peak. Early in the season that slab traverse holds snow and can be cut by glide cracks, which is the part of this approach worth respecting rather than the walking.

Roughly two to two and a half hours from the parking area to the foot of the route.
approach_variants.season: Spring into mid-summer while the slabs still hold snow that can be crossed; a light axe and light crampons are the usual kit until midsummer, after which it goes on dry rock
hazards: Early-season snow on the slab traverse, with glide cracks opening in it
Loose rock along the ridge crest
Sections of the crest with little available protection
The descent couloir on the south side funnels into the same narrow rappel gully every other Chair Peak route uses, so expect traffic above you
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE LOOKING FOR THE BOTTOM OF A NARROW COULOIR, NOT FOR THE CREST. The route does not start on the ridge. It starts up a narrow couloir about 220 ft long that delivers you to the LOW POINT of the west ridge, and only then does the climbing follow the crest.

THE TOWER IS THE MARKER. That low point sits immediately EAST of a distinct tower on the ridge. So find the tower, look east of it for the lowest saddle in the skyline, and the couloir is the direct line beneath that saddle. Tower on your left as you look up the couloir, low point of the ridge at its top: that is the start.

WHAT THE FIRST TWO PITCHES SHOULD FEEL LIKE: two pitches of 5.7 in the gully to reach the top of it. If the couloir tops out on ground that is obviously not the lowest gap on the ridge, you are in the wrong gully and you will meet the tower rather than the ridge above it.

WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, since this is the commonest gross error here: the standard descent for Chair Peak runs down a couloir on the SOUTH side into a narrow rappel gully. That is a different feature and it is a way down, not this route's way up. If you are on the side you approached from and staring at the east face, you have not gone round far enough.

access.fees: No day-use fee charged at Little Giant Trailhead.
access.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead for entry into Glacier Peak Wilderness.
access.closures: CLOSED: the Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) has been closed to vehicles for storm damage since 20 May 2026 from Atkinson Flat Campground, about 2 miles short of the Little Giant Trailhead, north to Trinity, under Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11, which runs through 31 December 2027. On top of that, the Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect from 3 September through 31 October 2026 unless lifted sooner, closes the Chiwawa River Road and the Little Giant Trail #1518 itself.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (Glacier Peak Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead on the Chiwawa River road, ford the Chiwawa — there is no functional bridge, and it runs knee to thigh deep, colder and higher earlier in the season — and climb the Little Giant Pass trail through steep forest and meadows to the pass on the ridge above. Descend a long way into the Napeequa valley and follow the river, off-trail in its upper reaches, toward the Butterfly Butte area, where most parties camp. From camp the line climbs onto Butterfly Butte's west ridge and follows the ridgeline to a bench near 6,800 ft that looks straight out over the glacier, then continues through larch and pumice terrain, passing north of the crevassed glacier, over granite slabs and past tarns beneath the peak's north ridge.
approach_variants.season: Late summer into early autumn, once the Chiwawa ford drops and the upper valley is passable. The glacier is at its most broken late in the season.
hazards: Unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the start, deeper and colder early in the season
A long descent into the valley that all has to be regained on the way out
Off-trail travel through brush and windfall in the upper valley
The glacier below the route is crevassed — the line stays north of it rather than on it
An avalanche slope on the southeast face just below the summit
Loose rock on the final ridge, and no water high on the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: LARCH AND PUMICE TO THE BENCH, SLABS AND POOLS BELOW THE RIDGE, AND THEN THE NORTHEASTERN OF TWO NOTCHES. From camp, climbing west through vibrant larch and pumice reaches a bench near 6,800 ft from which the crevassed glacier appears through thinning trees — if you cannot see ice, you are not on the bench yet. A pool sits at the foot of the glacier; keep north of the ice rather than dropping onto it, and weave through massive granite slabs and pockets of standing water below the north ridge. That slab-and-tarn ground is the last confirmation. The error parties actually make here is not a wrong gully but aiming too high on the broken ridge and having to drop back into the upper basin, so hold your height rather than drifting up. Two notches present themselves, one northeast and one southwest; the line takes the northeastern of them by a scree gully around 8,000 ft, gaining about 250 ft to the crest, and the rest is a walk on loose rock. Climbing directly out of the col between this peak and its neighbour is loose fourth class or low fifth and is not the easier option it looks.

access.fees: $5/vehicle day-use fee (or $30 annual) at White River Trailhead.
access.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead for entry into Glacier Peak Wilderness.
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Recreation Pass, or Recreation.gov Digital Day Pass

approach_variants.name: North Exfo approach to lower Salami Slab
approach_variants.notes: As for Snagglepuss: FS 2060 south from Darrington, LEFT fork at about 5 miles, and then an unmarked climbers' path to the west-facing slabs below the north end of Exfoliation Dome. There is no maintained trail; the slab is visible from Three O'Clock Rock, which is the easiest way to identify the objective before walking in.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
hazards: Unmarked, unmaintained climbers' path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Chehalis is on the RIGHT side of lower Salami Slab — right of the point where the approach path lands, which is where Snagglepuss begins.

The character is the confirmation: this is a long clean slab pitch that is nearly all friction, with very few knobs to pull on. If you are linking slabby corridors toward a prominent overlap you have started on Snagglepuss instead.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then the snow traverse south beneath Burgundy's east face onto the Silver Star Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile west of the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, a steep faint climber's trail descends to Early Winters Creek. Cross the creek and follow the climber's path and talus benches switchbacking up the far side, gaining about 3,500 ft over just under 5 miles to Burgundy Col, roughly 3-4 hours car-to-col with an overnight pack. STAY CLIMBER'S-LEFT TOWARD THE OBVIOUS COL NOTCH where the boot-path braids through timber and boulders lower down.

A snow patch at or near the col is the last dependable water and is unreliable by late summer, so carry water up from the creek if climbing after midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A snow and glacier traverse that can be firm or icy in the morning; carry an axe through midsummer
The last dependable water is a snow patch at the col which is unreliable by late summer
Rope-snag hazard in the chimney and offwidth pitches on the rappel descent
Fixed anchors that should be visually checked at each station; this is not a bolted sport descent
A re-ascent of 200-300 ft back to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM BURGUNDY COL, DROP A SHORT SNOW AND ROCK STEP AND TRAVERSE SOUTH BENEATH BURGUNDY SPIRE'S EAST FACE, ACROSS A SMALL SNOWY RIB, ONTO THE UPPER SILVER STAR GLACIER, AND AROUND TO CHIANTI SPIRE'S OBVIOUS EAST SIDE AT ABOUT 7,900 FT. Under an hour from a col or bench camp.

SO THE SEQUENCE OF SURFACES IS THE HANDRAIL, AND YOU CAN FEEL EACH ONE UNDERFOOT: rock step down, snow traverse, a rib, then glacier. If you have not crossed onto glacier you have not gone far enough.

THE ROUTE ON THE FACE, AND THIS IS WHERE THE TWO EAST-FACE LINES ARE TOLD APART: REBEL YELL'S DIHEDRAL IS THE OBVIOUS FEATURE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE FACE. LICHEN BOUQUET'S RAMP STARTS DIRECTLY BELOW THE SUMMIT AND LEANS LEFT. SO: A BIG CORNER ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE WALL IS THIS ROUTE. A RAMP UNDER THE SUMMIT THAT LEANS LEFT IS NOT.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: seven pitches at III 5.10b, with chimney and offwidth pitches that readily snag ropes on the way down. Four double-rope rappels on two 60 m ropes get you back down the route itself, trending generally climber's-right, starting from the summit block and then anchors near the top of pitch 5.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE ON THE APPROACH: continuing south past Chianti along the glacier brings you under Pernod and toward the Pernod-Chablis notch, which serves different routes and involves loose fourth-class ground.

AN ICE AXE IS WANTED FOR THIS TRAVERSE THROUGH MIDSUMMER; the snow rib and glacier margin can be firm or icy in the morning, and that is exactly when you will be crossing them.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout, the bench camp and the main gully to Burgundy Col, then south on year-round snow to the ramp below the summit
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-20 to Washington Pass, then about 4 miles east to a wide pullout on the south side of the highway near milepost 166 at roughly 4,250 ft, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake road and about 2 miles east of the hairpin turn. No Northwest Forest Pass is required on the highway shoulder.

Descend a steep, faint scree path about 300 ft to Early Winters Creek, cross on logs, then follow the climbers' trail steeply uphill to a wooded bench at 6,400-6,600 ft, the standard low camp. THERE IS A YEAR-ROUND SPRING ABOUT 200 YARDS NORTH OF THE TRAIL AT THE BENCH, and a seasonal spring in the sandy gully above.

Above the bench the trail fades; follow cairns up loose gullies, trending right and up, into the main gully below Burgundy Col at 7,800-7,950 ft. The gully holds a roughly 40-degree snow finger into midsummer. Roughly 3.5 miles and about 3,700 ft of gain to the col in 3-4 hours.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A roughly 40-degree snow finger in the main gully below the col into midsummer
Year-round snow on the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face, with seasonal rock bands
Rope-snagging flake and offwidth features on the rappel descent
A 200-300 ft re-ascent to the col at the end of the day
Sand-over-slab above the bench, described by trip reports as the worst part of the outing
Rockfall from parties above in the gullies; keep helmets on
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LICHEN BOUQUET'S RAMP STARTS DIRECTLY BELOW THE SUMMIT AND LEANS LEFT. THAT IS THE TEST, AND IT IS BOTH POSITIONAL AND DIRECTIONAL: stand where the summit is straight above you, and look for a ramp that leans LEFT.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE OTHER LINE ON THE SAME FACE, AND THEY ARE GENUINELY EASY TO CONFUSE FROM BELOW: REBEL YELL'S DIHEDRAL IS THE OBVIOUS FEATURE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE FACE. IF YOU ARE UNDER A BIG CORNER ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE WALL RATHER THAN A LEFT-LEANING RAMP UNDER THE TOP, YOU ARE ON REBEL YELL.

GETTING THERE: from Burgundy Col, DESCEND 200-300 FT ON THE SOUTH SIDE AND TRAVERSE RIGHT BENEATH BURGUNDY SPIRE'S EAST FACE ON YEAR-ROUND SNOW, with seasonal rock bands, UNTIL CHIANTI'S EAST FACE IS IN VIEW. Under an hour from the col.

SO THE SNOW IS THE HANDRAIL AND IT IS THERE ALL YEAR, which is unusual and useful: if you are not walking on snow beneath a big east-facing wall, you have not started the traverse.

DESCENT, AND THE ROUTE'S OWN FINISH SUGGESTS THE ALTERNATIVE: most east-face parties descend as Rebel Yell parties do, scrambling from the summit pedestal to a TWO-BOLT ANCHOR AT THE SOUTHEAST BASE OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK and making four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes back to the snow, trending generally to the rappeller's right and pulling ropes carefully, since the flake and offwidth features snag readily. The alternative this route's finish naturally suggests is to reverse to the NOTCH BETWEEN BURGUNDY SPIRE AND CHIANTI and descend from there.

THE STING IN THE TAIL, WHICH IS A TIMING DECISION MADE AT THE BASE: whichever way you come down, you must regain the 200-300 ft to Burgundy Col, and that is MUCH EASIER ON FIRM MORNING SNOW THAN ON LATE-DAY SLUSH OR BARE SAND.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to Burgundy Col, then traverse in to the Burgundy-Chianti notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the boot path drops to Early Winters Creek, crosses on logs, and climbs the timbered rib to the bench camp at 6,400-6,600 ft and on up the loose main gully to Burgundy Col.

This is the 1952 first ascent of Chianti Spire itself. The original party approached from a camp at the head of Silver Star Creek, climbed 500 ft of difficult rock to the notch between Chianti and Pernod, made a 250 ft rappel on the west face, and followed a loose gully to the Chianti-Burgundy notch, where the north face was found to hold the only route.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A 200-300 ft re-ascent to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
Loose main gully below the col, with rockfall from parties above
Sand-over-slab descent above the bench, unanimously described as the worst part of the day
A short loose scramble on scree and boulders for the last 300 ft up from Early Winters Creek to the highway
A route with a single detailed historical account and little modern traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE NOTCH BETWEEN CHIANTI AND BURGUNDY SPIRES, AND THE MODERN WAY IN IS TO TRAVERSE TO IT FROM BURGUNDY COL RATHER THAN TO RAPPEL INTO IT FROM THE WEST AS THE FIRST ASCENT DID. From the notch, the north face is climbed directly to the summit.

SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE IN A GAP BETWEEN TWO NAMED SPIRES WITH A WALL RISING NORTH OF YOU. Burgundy on one side, Chianti on the other, and the face you are about to climb between them.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER LINES, AND IT IS A SIDE-OF-THE-SPIRE TEST: the two EAST FACE routes are reached by descending 200-300 ft SOUTH from Burgundy Col and traversing on snow beneath Burgundy's east face until Chianti's east face comes into view. This route stops short of that, at the notch. IF YOU ARE STANDING ON SNOW LOOKING AT A BIG EAST-FACING WALL WITH A DIHEDRAL ON ITS RIGHT SIDE, YOU HAVE GONE PAST THE NOTCH AND ARE UNDER REBEL YELL.

AND THE OTHER NOTCH ON THIS SPIRE IS THE ONE AT THE FAR END: the first ascent reached the CHIANTI-PERNOD notch first, on the other side of the peak, and had to rappel 250 ft off the west face and follow a loose gully to get to this one. Two notches, one at each end of Chianti. This route uses the BURGUNDY end.

WHAT COMING BACK LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS THE SAME STING THE EAST FACE ROUTES CARRY: downclimb or make a short rappel off the summit block onto the north face, reverse the line to the notch, traverse north on snow beneath Burgundy's east face and CLIMB THE 200-300 FT BACK UP TO BURGUNDY COL. Firm morning snow makes that far easier than afternoon slush or bare sandy rock.

approach_variants.name: PCT from Snoqualmie Pass, leaving the trail half a mile SHORT of Chikamin Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, Trail #2000, off I-90 exit 52, the trail switchbacks through timber and avalanche paths, crosses beneath Kendall Peak, and reaches the Kendall Katwalk around mile 5 at about 5,400 ft — a good checkpoint, though not reliable water late in the season.

Continue north past Ridge Lake at about mile 6.5, which has reliable camping and water, and the Alaska Lake and Joe Lake junctions, then along the rolling rocky PCT beneath Alaska and Huckleberry Mountains to the Huckleberry-Chikamin saddle around mile 10.25. The trail then contours below the Four Brothers and Chikamin's south face, passing the Park Lakes Trail junction.

About 13.5 miles one way to the base of the gullies with roughly 4,600 ft of gain, so most parties camp at Ridge Lake or the 5,200 ft pack camp and make it a two or three day trip.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: An unmarked gully turnoff near Chikamin Pass — overshooting puts you in the cliffy Four Brothers
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gully system
A steep, snow-filled and rubble-choked gully in early season
Short but exposed class 3 moves on the summit horn
A long trail approach with camps well short of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS TO LEAVE THE TRAIL BEFORE YOU REACH THE PASS, AND THAT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE ENOUGH THAT IT IS THE WHOLE FINDING. At roughly mile 13.5 — about HALF A MILE SHORT of Chikamin Pass, near an established pack camp at about 5,200 ft — leave the PCT and climb steep grassy and heather slopes into the gully systems on the south and southeast face.

THE NEGATIVE IS EXPLICIT AND EXPENSIVE: do NOT continue to Chikamin Pass before cutting uphill. Doing so puts you in the middle of the FOUR BROTHERS, a band of cliffy towers that force technical terrain on a route that is otherwise a scramble. If you are standing at Chikamin Pass, you have overshot the turn.

SO USE THE PACK CAMP AS THE MARKER: an established camp at about 5,200 ft on the trail, with the peak's south face above and the pass still ahead of you. Turn uphill there.

WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO, IN ORDER: class 2 hiking low on grass and heather, then loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 as you gain Chikamin Ridge with some exposure near the crest, and finally a short, well-protected class 3-4 CHIMNEY or slot of about 10 ft right below the summit block, with roughly 75 more feet of easy scrambling above it to the top. A 10 ft chimney immediately below the summit horn is the confirming feature.

SNOW CHANGES THE CHARACTER OF THE GULLY ENTIRELY: early in the season it is a steep, rubble-choked chute and an axe is needed.

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek and Park Lakes, then the gullies above Glacier Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at the end of FR-46 / Cooper Pass Road at about 2,400 ft, the trail is brushy low down but well trodden. It climbs steadily beside Mineral Creek to Park Lakes at 4.3 to 5.4 miles and about 2,570 ft of gain, and ties into the PCT.

From the PCT / Park Lakes junction, head north toward the Spectacle Point saddle overlooking Spectacle Lake, then drop about a mile to Glacier Lake, a common camp, before climbing the southeast-slope gullies above it.

This is the shortest line in — day-trip feasible for a strong party at roughly 14 to 16.5 miles round trip — but the tread is rougher and there are creek crossings low down.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Brushy lower trail and creek crossings on the Mineral Creek approach
Loose scree and rockfall in the upper gullies
Exposure near the final ridge crest
Snow-filled gullies in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THIS SIDE THE ARRIVAL IS A LAKE, NOT A TRAIL JUNCTION: you climb the gullies directly ABOVE GLACIER LAKE. Standing at the lake with the southeast slopes rising in front of you is the arrival, and the lake is a hard landmark that cloud does not remove.

WHAT THE GROUND BELOW THE GULLIES LOOKS LIKE, AS CONFIRMATION: brooks, waterfalls, tarns, heather benches, sandstone slabs and blocky breccia low down. Running water and heather benches are right for this side; if you are on bare scree from the lake upward, you have started too high.

THE TWO APPROACHES MEET ON THE SAME UPPER MOUNTAIN, so the finding from there is identical: loose scree and dirt-and-heather slots in the upper gully, sustained class 3 to the crest of Chikamin Ridge, and a short well-protected 10 ft class 3-4 chimney below the summit block with about 75 ft of easy scrambling above it.

AND THE SAME NEGATIVE APPLIES ONCE YOU ARE ON THE PCT: do not wander south toward Chikamin Pass looking for a way up. The Four Brothers sit between the pass and the route.

bivy.name: Pyrites Creek — where the Chimney Peak approach leaves the trail
bivy.notes: This is the camp for CHIMNEY PEAK, and the reason it rather than the chalet meadow is that the approach leaves the East Fork Quinault trail at about nine miles, which is where this camp sits. Push on to the chalet and you have walked four miles past your own turning and given yourself them back again in the morning. The peak stands immediately north above the valley with its southeast face rising something like 4,800 ft in less than a mile, streaming waterfalls into the valley below — spectacular from the trail and completely useless as a line of ascent. The climb goes round to the southwest ridge and is class 3 scrambling once you are on it, with the first ascent not made until 1941, which says something about how the ground below it behaves. Expect a long, steep, largely trackless day out of the valley floor. June through September is the workable window. The walk in from Graves Creek is thirteen miles to the chalet with staged camps at Pony Bridge and O'Neil Creek before this one, so most parties take two easy days in rather than one hard one.
bivy.water: Reliable — the East Fork Quinault and the creek the camp is named for both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and THE EAST FORK QUINAULT IS A QUOTA AREA. It has been run under a nightly cap of thirty permits or roughly two hundred people since 2024, so this is a booking to make the day reservations open rather than a fortnight out. The summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and releases in one drop in mid-April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over plus a six dollar booking fee, or an annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY REQUIRED IN THIS VALLEY and enforced rather than advised — the Enchanted Valley was closed over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Free loaners at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness offices.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested riverside camp with a handful of sites, quieter than the valley above it because most parties push the extra four miles to the chalet meadow

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the Chimney Creek climbers' path, then straight up the glacier under the summit
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is the same as for the East Face and is described in full there: Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to Pete Lake, on to the Pacific Crest Trail, then roughly a mile of PCT to the hairpin in the old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft. Look west from that hairpin for twin waterfalls; the climbers' path leaves the forest between the two rounded outcrops right of the falls and the cliff band right of those. Camp below the moraine at roughly 4,650 to 4,800 ft.

From camp, drop about two hundred feet to the lower Chimney Glacier, rope up, and cross it. Gain the upper glacier by the rock or snow gully in the cliff band just left of the icefall, by the snow finger out on the far left, or by the icefall itself if you are equipped for it.
approach_variants.season: Early summer. Late in the year the moat under the face is the problem rather than the climbing
hazards: The moat directly under the summit, whose passability is a seasonal accident
Icefall between the lower and upper Chimney Glacier
Crevasses on the glacier
Loose rock on the face
A long, poorly-tracked approach where the flagging is unreliable
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route and the ordinary East Face part company on the upper glacier, and the difference is where you aim.

The Direct does NOT go to the U-Gap. Once on the upper glacier, keep going up until you are on the east face of the MAIN peak, directly beneath the summit — you want the summit vertically above you, not a notch off to one side. That position is the whole identification.

The arrival test is the moat that forms there. It is the gate: you are looking for a place where fallen ice has bridged or filled it enough to step from snow onto rock. If you find yourself traversing sideways along the base looking for a way in, that is normal and expected here.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if you have climbed to a notch on the skyline and are now working across ledges on the SOUTH peak toward the main summit, you have taken the U-Gap and you are on the ordinary East Face, not the Direct. That is a perfectly good climb, but it is not this one.

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
bivy.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
bivy.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

approach_variants.name: Chimney Glacier to the East Gully
approach_variants.notes: Shares the whole trailhead-to-basin stretch with the East Face line: the Pete Lake Trail to the lake, on to the Pacific Crest Trail, north about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche path, then a flagged climbers' path on the east bank of Chimney Creek up through steep brush and several ravines to Sunrise Knob at about 4,650 ft and the bivy basin at the toe of the glacier. Budget four to five hours car to knob and treat the whole outing as two or three days. Above camp, climb the moraine and take the wet, grubby gully through the rock band onto the ice, then rope up and cross toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier
A moat at the base of the face that widens badly through late season
Rock that stays wet on this aspect, so short fourth-class steps feel harder than their grade
Rockfall out of the gullies above the glacier
Long, remote approach with no quick retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding: The target is the notch between the central (main) summit and the lower south peak, and the gully that drops from it to the Chimney Glacier. Do not climb in the gully itself: the line takes the face to its LEFT, about three pitches of wet, slippery fourth-class rock, then a system of ledges, some very wide, that leads to just below the notch. The way onto the rock is across the moat at the foot of the face, which widens as the season goes on; look for a place where collapsed snow blocks or a bridge let you step across. On the way up the glacier, avoid the icefall and keep away from the deep bergschrund. At the notch the main summit is the other way; the south peak is about 400 ft above you.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to Chiwawa Basin and the 6,300 ft benches
approach_variants.notes:
Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and BEAR RIGHT at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear LEFT into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the EAST side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 under storm-damage order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is not reachable by vehicle. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40) also closes the Chiwawa River Road and the trails from Trinity through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep. The road to Trinity is often not melted out until mid-June, and the upper mountain and col hold snow into July in heavy years
hazards: Misidentifying the gully near the col, which leads to an exposed low-fifth-class dead end
Loose, sandy rock flanking the col and loose talus on the upper mountain
Cornices and early-season snow at the Fortress-Chiwawa col
An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater, and fading braided tread that becomes a bushwhack if you drift into timber
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 (order 06-17-07-2026-11, through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is unreachable by vehicle
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NOTCH IN SOMEBODY ELSE'S RIDGE, AND SAYING IT THAT WAY IS WHAT MAKES IT FINDABLE: the Fortress-Chiwawa col at about 7,200 ft is the NOTCH IN FORTRESS MOUNTAIN'S EAST RIDGE. From the 6,300 ft benches, traverse steep heather and aim for that notch. You are walking toward a gap on the skyline of the mountain NEXT DOOR, not toward the peak you are climbing.

WHAT THE LAST STRETCH FEELS LIKE, so you know you are on it: the snow slope up to the col is moderate and then steepens noticeably in the final section below the notch, and the rock flanking it is loose and sandy. Stay on the snow or on the most solid line you can find rather than the flanking rock. A slope that stays uniformly moderate all the way to a gap is not this one.

FROM THE COL THE ROUTE HAS NO SINGLE LINE AND THAT IS THE CORRECT ANSWER, NOT A GAP IN THE BETA: work up the south-west side on slabs, gullies and talus taking the path of least resistance. Nothing here is cairned or named.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXPLICIT AND IT HAS A STATED CONSEQUENCE: misidentifying the correct gully near the col leads to an exposed low-fifth-class DEAD END. If the ground you are on has stopped offering an easy option and is committing you to fifth-class moves, reverse and pick a different line — this route never needs them.

THE CRUX IS SHORT AND IT IS AT THE TOP: the step gaining the SUMMIT RIDGE is loose and exposed Class 2-3 and is the hardest ground on the route. After it, an easy traverse of about 100 ft to the WEST — to your right — reaches the top. If you gain a ridge and the summit is to your left, you are on the wrong section of crest.

GOING BACK DOWN, USE A DIFFERENT LINE THAN YOU CAME UP FOR ONE STRETCH ONLY: below the benches, the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better descent, and the loose climber's-left skyline gully should be avoided.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek variant to the col west of the summit
approach_variants.notes:
A less-travelled alternative starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead rather than Trinity. It bushwhacks to about 5,500 ft and follows a gully to the right of Point 5971 up to the col WEST of the summit, then takes easy Class 2 ground along the west ridge to the top.

This is the shorter line on paper and the rougher one on the ground: there is no tread on the bushwhack and no camp equivalent to the Chiwawa Basin benches. It is genuinely used, but not recommended over the Trinity approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Sep, as for the main line
hazards: An unmaintained bushwhack with no tread from about 5,500 ft and no published landmarks below the gully
No established camp on this side, so it commits you to a long day
Early-season snow in the gully and at the col
Loose rock on the west ridge, as everywhere on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT'S BASE IS A DIFFERENT COL FROM THE MAIN ROUTE'S, AND CONFUSING THE TWO PUTS YOU ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. The standard line goes to the FORTRESS-CHIWAWA col, which is SOUTH-WEST of the summit and is a notch in Fortress's east ridge. This variant goes to the col WEST of the summit, gained from Phelps Creek by a gully to the RIGHT of Point 5971.

THE TEST IS WHAT LIES ABOVE THE COL YOU REACH. From this one, the WEST RIDGE runs to the summit on easy Class 2 ground — a walk, essentially. From the Fortress-Chiwawa col you face slabs, gullies and talus on the south-west FACE with a loose Class 2-3 step at the top. If you have reached a col and the way on is a broad easy crest, you are on this variant. If it is a face with no obvious line, you are on the standard one.

THE APPROACH MARKER IS A NUMBERED POINT AND THAT IS ALL THERE IS: the gully is to the RIGHT of Point 5971. Nothing else about the bushwhack below it is published, which is why this is the second variant and not the first. Carry a track.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the chasm between the two spires
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, walk the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction just past a small stream and a large cairn, then take the climbers' path up through slabs, talus and heather into the basin below the west faces.

The objective from here is the huge cleft that splits the two Early Winters Spires, seen from the WEST side. Head for its foot. Note this is the west-side gully — the couloir that splits the same two spires on the EAST side, reached from the highway hairpin, is a different feature and a different route.

Be ready to swap between rock shoes and boots if snow is still lying in the gully.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: snow lingering in the gully early season — axe and crampons
loose rock funnelled down the gully, including from parties above
wind in the gully; it channels weather
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is at the very foot of the enormous chasm dividing North from South Early Winters Spire — it is the biggest single feature on this side of the group and it is unambiguous even in poor visibility, because nothing else on the west faces is a full-height cleft between two summits. The route opens with a short step of low-fifth-class slab and layback moves, and then it is walking up the gully bed; if you are pulling on anything hard in the first rope length you are on one of the face routes to either side, not in the gully. Pitch one takes cracks and ramps along the LEFT edge of the gully rather than the middle. The house-sized chockstone that names the route sits much higher up the same gully, so do not expect to see it from the base as your confirmation.

road.name: Forest Road 38 (Mosquito Lake Road to Elbow Lake Trailhead)
road.status: CLOSED at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given, as listed on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026 — this blocks vehicle access to the Elbow Lake Trailhead, which is about 11 miles in. Good gravel and paved forest road when open; check the forest's alerts page before driving.
road.driveNote: From Mosquito Lake Road near Deming/Acme, turn east onto FS Road 38 and drive about 11 miles of forest road to the Elbow Lake Trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: Gated at Wallace Creek, about 1.3 miles before the trailhead, roughly Dec 1-Jun 15.

approach_variants.name: Elbow Lake Trail and the Green Creek path to the low notch on the Cinderella-Little Sister ridge
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Elbow Lake Trailhead (Trail #697) at the end of FS Road 38. The trail immediately meets the Middle Fork Nooksack — there is no bridge at the marked crossing, and fording can be dangerous or impassable at high water. Many parties use an unofficial log crossing roughly a quarter mile downstream of the official ford, made of logs lashed between two boulders. Once across, climb through forest about 1.5 miles to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where the unmaintained, blue-blazed Green Creek Climber's Trail splits LEFT into the Green Creek cirque. Look closely for the small blue markers; it is easy to walk past. Follow it up into the basin — Green Creek runs clear and is a reliable water source along this stretch. Above treeline the trail gives way to talus and boulder fields and then loose, unstable scree, with Class 3 rock steps to reach the toe of the Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier. Route-finding through that section is the crux of the approach. Cross the low-angle glacier to the low notch on the ridge between Cinderella and Little Sister. Fit parties often do it car-to-car in one long day; others camp in the Green Creek basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing, impassable at high water
An easy-to-miss blue-blazed junction near Hildebrand Creek
Loose unstable scree and Class 3 steps to reach the glacier — the crux of the approach
A moat at the glacier margin in both directions
A connecting ridge toward Little Sister that accounts describe as a missile zone
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LOW NOTCH ON THE CINDERELLA-LITTLE SISTER RIDGE IS THE BASE, AND IT IS WHERE YOU STOW GLACIER GEAR. Cross the low-angle Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier and step off ice onto rock at the notch. It is a col: a low point with a peak at each end of it, Cinderella one way and Little Sister the other.

THE MOAT AT THE GLACIER MARGIN IS THE LAST OBSTACLE AND IT IS SEASONAL, NOT STRUCTURAL — trivial in a heavy snow year, a real step late in the season, and exactly the same problem in reverse on the way down. Plan for it in both directions rather than being surprised at 4pm.

FROM THE NOTCH, GO EAST, NOT WEST. Cinderella's WEST RIDGE rises eastward from the notch and is the route — a long ridge, mostly straightforward walking on broken ground with a short section of enjoyable scrambling to the true summit. Turning the other way out of the notch heads for Little Sister.

DO NOT BE TEMPTED ALONG THE CREST TOWARD LITTLE SISTER. This is not mere caution: at least one party calls that connecting ridgeline a missile zone and recommends dropping back to the glacier from this notch instead of traversing it. The notch serves two peaks and connects neither.

ON THE WEST RIDGE, THE CREST DIRECT IS THE TRAP. Taking it absolutely direct runs into stretches of committing downclimbing; the standard escape is to DROP INTO A GULLY ON THE SOUTH SIDE and regain easier ground above. Committing downclimbing on a Class 3-4 scramble means you have stayed on the crest too long.

THE ROCK IS DUNITE AND IT BEHAVES TWO WAYS AT ONCE, which is the single most useful thing to know about holds here: notably grippy on WEATHERED surfaces, and greasy where a block has FRESHLY BROKEN. Judge each hold on its surface, not on the rock type.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes:
US 2 to the Index turnoff, into town, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the road runs beside the railway.

Cross the active railway tracks, bear left off the crossing to the trail, then take the RIGHT branch that runs along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
Traffic on the pitches above — this is the busiest part of the wall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
City Park is itself the landmark of the Lower Town Wall — the obvious crack that every neighbouring route is located from. If you are looking for something subtle you are looking at the wrong wall.

Stand directly beneath the obvious crack. If the feature in front of you is a shallow right-facing groove or corner system you have drifted RIGHT onto Godzilla, which is the line immediately right of this one.

The second pitch of this route is also the standard way parties reach Slow Children, so expect traffic moving through the line above you.

access.fees: $5 day-use Northwest Forest Pass or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass at the White River Trailhead lot
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, available at the White River trailhead kiosk
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass required for trailhead parking ($5 day-use ePass or $30 annual)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Creek and the sheepherder's trail to the south basin — the non-glacier line
approach_variants.notes: Start at the White River trailhead at the end of White River Road, FR 6400, at about 2,300 ft; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed. Walk the White River trail #1507 about four flat miles — one party gained all of three hundred feet in a little over an hour — to the Boulder Creek trail #1562 junction. Turn east up Boulder Creek. At about the 5,000 ft level, roughly four and a half miles up this trail, pick up an old sheepherder's trail heading west and follow it to around 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Note that published mileages on this stretch do not reconcile cleanly between sources, so navigate by elevation and by the basin rather than by a mile count. There is a faint path that contours, crosses the creek and climbs the west side of Boulder Creek, firming up into decent tread as it gains the slope. Leave the sheepherder's trail in the basin above Boulder Creek around 5,700 ft and climb open heather north-north-west to the southern ridge running off Clark's south-east peak, Point 8373. Car to summit is given as about eleven and a half miles one way with roughly 6,500 ft of gain, and essentially every party camps in the Boulder Creek basin rather than trying it in a day.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep
hazards: Getting cliffed out on the spur while looking for a gully that is really a ledge
Unbridged Boulder Creek crossing, cold and thigh-deep early season and sometimes braided
Losing the sheepherder's trail — it is notoriously hard to find from the White River trail
Heavy mosquitoes on the valley walk
No water above the Boulder Creek basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: EVERYTHING TURNS ON ONE FEATURE AND IT IS MISDESCRIBED BY ITS OWN NAME. Published descriptions call it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft. The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it FEELS MORE LIKE A SLOPING LEDGE THAN A GULLY. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two accounts both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half. The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting DOWN to it, which is what the ledge is for. Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top. A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the Walrus Glacier — the glacier line
approach_variants.notes:
Approach identically to Boulder Basin: White River trail #1507 four miles to the Boulder Creek trail #1562, then up into the open basin at roughly 5,300 ft, about five to six hours and three thousand feet from the car. That basin is the camp.

From camp, climb north-east to Boulder Pass at about 6,300 to 6,330 ft. Drop down steep snow on the far side, then climb to a bench at about 6,700 ft on Clark's eastern arm.

THE BENCH IS WHERE YOU ROPE UP. Do it there, before you go anywhere, because of what comes next.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jun-Sep, on the earlier side while the crevasses are still bridged
hazards: Crevasses and snowbridges on the lower Walrus Glacier
Steep snow on the far side of Boulder Pass
No view of the glacier until you have committed around the eastern arm
Unbridged Boulder Creek ford lower down
The 7,200 ft south-basin gully is a landmark for a different route and will mislead you here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU CANNOT SEE THE WALRUS GLACIER UNTIL YOU ARE COMMITTED TO IT. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the LEFT, SOUTHERN margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the SOUTH BASIN route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the middle line on the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Shared approach with the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, take the maintained Snow Lake Trail about a mile and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake, the last water. Skirt the west and north shore; the tread continues a short way over a tree-covered rise before petering out into talus.

Work up and right toward the obvious talus and dirt gully on the peak's northwest side; a climbers' path picks up again on a heather bench near the top of the gully. Follow it into the basin, then climb moraine along the left side of the small permanent snow patch to Unicorn Col just west of the summit. A climbers' path traverses below the cliffs — easier travel than the scree either side — and leads east around the south side to the base of the summit horn.

The climb itself is a single pitch of blocky low-fifth-class climbing, about 40-50 ft, on the south and southeast face, with one fixed piton mid-pitch.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and about 2,400 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose blocks on the approach scramble to the base of the horn
A short exposed pitch above broken ground where a fall has real consequence
A rappel that may not reach the ground on a 30 m rope, particularly with an open moat late season
An old bleached snag at the top that is no longer a sound anchor
Two different rappel lines off the same block landing in different places
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ALONG THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. All three start within about 70 ft of each other and all three finish at the same slung block, so the BOTTOM is the only place this can be got right.

THE CLASSIC ROUTE IS THE MIDDLE ONE, AND IT TAKES THE SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST FACE DIRECT — blocky low-fifth climbing straight up, one pitch of about 40-50 ft, with ONE FIXED PITON MID-PITCH. A piton at half height on open face is the positive confirmation.

THE DISTANCE TEST IS THE PRACTICAL ONE AND IT WORKS BY FEEL RATHER THAN BY SIGHT:
  — THE ROOF STARTS ABOUT 20 FT TO YOUR LEFT, at the point where the RIDGELINE MEETS THE BLOCK.
  — OPEN BOOK STARTS ABOUT 50 FT TO YOUR RIGHT, at TWO WIDE, LEFT-LEANING CRACKS.

SO THE TWO NEGATIVES ARE TACTILE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT WHEN THE HORN IS IN CLOUD: IF YOU ARE FIGHTING A WIDE AWKWARD CRACK THAT WANTS BIG CAMS, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THIS ROUTE TO THE RIGHT AND YOU ARE ON OPEN BOOK. IF THERE IS A ROOF OVER YOUR HEAD AND YOU ARE IN A GULLY OR CHIMNEY, YOU HAVE GONE LEFT PAST IT AND YOU ARE ON THE ROOF, at 5.6.

CHARACTER TEST: this is blocky face and crack climbing on the OPEN face. Not inside a chimney, not in a wide crack. If you are inside anything, you are on a neighbour.

WHY IT MATTERS: this is the middle grade of the three — 5.4, against Open Book's easy fifth and The Roof's 5.6. Being one line out changes the grade in whichever direction you drifted, on a short pitch above broken ground.

DESCENT DETAIL WORTH SETTLING AT THE TOP RATHER THAN OVER THE EDGE: there are effectively two rappel lines off the summit block, one dropping to the notch and the ground below the horn, the other landing on the snow patch side. A 30 m rope has been reported as just short depending on which one you use and on how open the moat is late season; 40 m removes the guesswork. Use the ROCK HORN — the old bleached snag some older reports mention is no longer sound.

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

approach_variants.name: Tatoosh Creek, the timber band and the Lane-Denman saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road, open roughly late May through mid-October, or from Narada Falls when the road is gated — from Narada Falls a short steep climb of about 200 ft through open timber gains the road.

Walk the road roughly half a mile to where it bends sharply and begins heading east. Leave the pavement there and drop south through sparse open forest to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft, losing a couple of hundred feet. Cross the creek — a rock-hop most of the season, more involved at peak snowmelt — and angle up a broad talus slope of about 250 vertical feet.

At the top of the talus, continue up through trees STAYING RIGHT of a short cliff band. Roughly 700 ft above the creek, near 5,200 ft, you break out of the trees onto open slopes and continue to the broad Lane-Denman saddle at about 5,440 ft.

From the saddle, turn right and climb moderate open ground to the gully weakness in the southeast face. Follow it up, trending left near the top for a final short scramble to the summit. Round trip is a bit over 3 miles with roughly 1,400-1,500 ft of gain, and no water past Tatoosh Creek.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Cliffing out in the brushy timber band if the line drifts left of the cliff band
Loose rock and rockfall in the narrow summit gully, especially with parties above
Exposed fourth-class moves just below the true summit
Tatoosh Creek can be difficult during high spring runoff
Afternoon thunderstorms are common over this range in summer
Inconsistent glissade conditions in the gully once it melts out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN FROM THE THREE COULOIRS, AND THE MISTAKE IT INVITES IS WALKING INTO THE NORTH-FACE BASIN WITH THE ICE CLIMBERS. The single clearest separator is Tatoosh Creek: THE COULOIR ROUTES STAY LOW IN THE BASIN. THIS ROUTE CROSSES THE CREEK AND CLIMBS THE OTHER SIDE.

THE SEQUENCE, EACH ITEM A CHECK, IN ORDER:
1. Off the road at the 90-degree bend, south, down to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. CROSS IT.
2. Up a talus slope of about 250 vertical feet.
3. Into trees, STAYING RIGHT OF A SHORT CLIFF BAND. This is the one place on the route where an error commits you to bad ground — the timber is brushy and drifting left cliffs you out. If you find yourself under rock in the trees, traverse back right before gaining more height.
4. Break out of the trees about 700 ft above the creek, near 5,200 ft.
5. Arrive at the broad LANE-DENMAN SADDLE at about 5,440 ft.

THE SADDLE TEST IS A COUNT OF PEAKS: you should have HIGH GROUND ON BOTH SIDES OF YOU — Lane on one hand, Denman on the other. A col with only one peak above it is not this saddle.

FROM THE SADDLE, TURN RIGHT — WEST. DENMAN IS THE OTHER WAY, and it is an easy mistake in cloud because both directions climb.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS THE OBVIOUS GULLY WEAKNESS IN THE SOUTHEAST FACE, and it is the feature the route is named for. THE CONFIRMATION INSIDE IT IS AN OBJECT: a STURDY TREE roughly 200 ft up the climbing, which is the main anchor and the rappel point. Reaching a good tree in the gully means you are in the right gully.

LAST: trend LEFT near the top for the final short scramble. Plentiful holds, minimal exposure — if it feels serious, you have drifted out of the gully onto the face.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

approach_variants.name: Silver Star Creek to the east prow of Juno Tower
approach_variants.notes: Clean Break faces east, and the direct line to it is the Silver Star Creek drainage rather than the Burgundy Creek path used for the Wine Spires. Park at the small pullout on SR-20 roughly eight and a half miles east of Washington Pass. A good climbers' trail follows the east side of the creek for a couple of miles, then crosses the creek and climbs talus and forest up the western edge of the valley toward the foot of Juno Tower. At about 5,000 ft, make a rising traverse leftward across the slope; taken at the right height this threads most of the slide alder and lands you under the tower's east prow. Parties reverse this on descent, or cross west and drop back to the highway on the standard Burgundy Col trail.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Slide alder on the rising traverse below the wall
Rockfall onto the lower pitches from parties above
Fifteen pitches with the crux in the first hundred feet — a committing day once started
Afternoon storms on an exposed east prow
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE FIXED PIN BESIDE A DEEP NARROW GULLY IS WHAT SETTLES IT. The rising traverse from about 5,000 ft ends on a ledge under the east prow of Juno Tower. Find the deep, narrow gully that splits the wall: the route starts on the ledge immediately to its LEFT, at a low anchor pin driven into the rock. Above that ledge is the feature the climb is named for — a single dead-vertical, clean-cut thin-hands splitter in white granite, roughly a hundred feet of it, with no alcove, chimney or vegetation anywhere in it. If the crack above you widens into a chimney, or you are standing in the gully bed rather than beside it, you are right of the start. If the rock above you is grey and broken rather than white and clean, you have wandered onto the flank of the prow instead of its nose.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

road.name: Chiwawa River Road (FSR 6200) to Phelps Creek Road (FSR 6211)/Phelps Creek Trailhead, or FSR 6200 to Trinity Trailhead; alternatively no road needed via the Lake Chelan ferry + Holden Village approach
road.status: CLOSED since May 20, 2026: FSR 6200 is closed from the Atkinson Flat Campground junction north to Trinity under Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through December 31, 2027), cutting off both Phelps Creek and Trinity trailheads from this side; the Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes FSR 6200 and the Phelps Creek Trail
road.driveNote: When open: from Leavenworth, US-2 W 15 mi to Coles Corner, WA-207 N 4.4 mi, Chiwawa Loop Rd, then FSR 6200 ~22 mi (gravel after mile 11) to Phelps Creek Rd/FSR 6211, then 2.3 mi to Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft). Rough, rutted road, not recommended for low-clearance vehicles even when fully open.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet, east-side talus to the col
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road). Colchuck Lake Trail #1599 runs 4 miles and 2,280 ft to the lake outlet in about two and a half to three hours; the lake is the last reliable water.

At the lake take the LEFT fork and stay high on the ridge, avoiding the spur trails that drop to the water's edge. Continue to the small dam near the lake's north end and cross the outlet creek at or just below it. Pick up the trail on the far side and follow it south roughly 100 yards to a slight clearing with boulders and talus on the LEFT.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Outlet creek crossing at the dam
Brief 3rd/4th class rock step gained on vegetation
Loose talus
No water above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: The clearing with boulders and talus on the left, about 100 yards south of the outlet crossing, is the turn — it is easy to walk past. Ascend the talus angling slightly left into the woods and negotiate a brief 3rd/4th class rock step, using roots and branches as holds; that step is the confirmation you are on the right line and not on a lakeside spur. From there the path climbs southward through open, cairned forest for about an hour to the col, which overlooks a boulder-strewn camp area with views of Dragontail and Colchuck peaks.

approach_variants.name: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles with a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek near the 1.5-mile mark, then left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, a second log crossing, and steep rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about four miles and 2,280 ft, an hour and three quarters to two hours for a fit party carrying a rack.

The shorter of the two ways into the west cirque starts at the lake OUTLET, at the north end below the small dam. Cross there and follow a well-cairned climbers' path across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and deposits you on the talus field under the west face. Reckon about an hour from the lake, plus twenty to twenty-five minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the wall itself.

This is the way parties who have been there recommend, and it is the one to take unless the outlet crossing is unreasonable.

Colchuck Lake is the last water. The cirque and the route are dry.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep, once the gully and cirque talus are snow-free
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges can be slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
The outlet crossing below the dam is a real crossing, not a step-across
Cirque talus is loose and the boulder-hop to the wall is ankle-breaking ground
Snow can linger in the approach terrain into early summer
No water above Colchuck Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are looking for the START OF THE WEST FACE ROUTE on a wall that carries half a dozen hard lines, so the useful information is what sits either side of it.

The West Face route's first pitch begins at a LEFT-FACING, LIGHTLY VEGETATED CORNER at the base of the wall. That corner is the thing to find. From the talus you scramble up to a ledge and the first pitch goes from there.

Orient yourself with the neighbours: The Tempest starts LOWER than the West Face and lies to its RIGHT, taking a system of cracks up a black-streaked headwall — the black streaking is visible from the talus and is a good negative marker. The Scoop is further RIGHT again, right of both the West Face and the Tempest. Scarface climbs the large, obvious pale rock SCAR on the formation, several hundred feet right of the old northwest buttress line. If you are under black streaks or under a conspicuous scar, you are right of where you want to be.

Rack up on the talus rather than at the wall — the base is boulders and the flat ground is below.

approach_variants.name: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative when you do not want to cross the outlet. Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, then cut north through a band of slide alder — look for cairns, because this is a genuine bushwhack — and climb the LEFTMOST gully about 1,000 ft to its top. From there contour east on easy ground into the cirque.

An hour and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line and a lot more brush, but no ford. A winter/spring variation on the same idea follows a steepening gully starting near the lake's southwest edge.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the gully holds snow into early summer
hazards: Slide alder band is a real bushwhack; cairns are the only guide
1,000 ft of loose gully
Lingering snow in the gully into early summer
More elevation gain than the outlet approach
No water above Colchuck Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Once you contour east into the cirque, the base identification is the same as the outlet approach: find the LEFT-FACING, LIGHTLY VEGETATED CORNER at the foot of the wall, and use the black-streaked headwall of The Tempest and the pale rock scar of Scarface, both to the RIGHT, to confirm you have not drifted along the base.

The difference this way in is that you arrive in the cirque from the south, higher up, so your first sight of the wall is from the side rather than head-on. Walk out into the talus and look at the face square-on before committing to a start; foreshortened from the flank, several corners look like the corner.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.
approach_variants.season: Jun-early Jul, while the glacier is well filled and crevasses stay bridged
hazards: Loose scree and talus if you do not gain the moraine crest early
Rockfall off the surrounding faces onto the glacier, worst during the morning warm-up
