Moats and thin bridging at the glacier margins
~100 ft of 40-degree snow below the col
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
Glissading the descent is normal here and is also how people get hurt — axe in hand, clear runout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route's 'base' is the toe of the glacier, at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft, and the way to know you are there is that the moraine crest you have been walking runs out against continuous snow that keeps rising ahead of you.

From the toe, take the LEFT (east) lobe of the glacier. That side passes directly beneath the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes — seeing that big northwest wall on your left is the confirmation you are on the correct lobe. You are climbing beside those routes, not on them.

The glacier is easy angle for most of its length and then steepens for the last stretch: about 100 ft of 40-degree snow immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col (Colchuck Col / Banshee Pass) at roughly 8,200 ft. If the angle has not kicked back, you are not at the col yet.

From the col the summit is northwest: 3rd-class sandy steps up to a summit plateau around 8,500 ft, then continue west and north over the plateau to the true summit at 8,705 ft. The plateau is the trap in cloud — it is broad and flat and the first high ground you reach on it is not the summit.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
approach_variants.notes:
The walk to Colchuck Lake and up the moraine is the same, and easier without snow. What changes is everything above the moraine.

By August the glacier typically melts out to hard, sun-cupped ice. It is not heavily crevassed, but crevasses and marginal moats that were bridged in June are open, and the surface no longer takes a boot step. Crampons and an axe stop being optional and a rope becomes a real consideration for the margins.

The scree and talus below the moraine is at its loosest now, and rockfall off the surrounding walls is more frequent with no snow holding things in place. The glissade descent is gone — plan on down-climbing everything you came up, which is the main reason the day gets longer.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the glacier has opened up and gone to bare, sun-cupped ice
hazards: Bare sun-cupped ice: crampons and axe required, self-arrest unreliable
Open crevasses and moats at the glacier margins
Increased rockfall from the surrounding faces with no snow cover
No glissade descent — the day is longer at both ends
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The same landmarks, read differently. The toe of the glacier is further up the basin than it was in June — glacial retreat and seasonal melt both push it back — so the moraine crest walk is longer before you meet ice.

Stay on the LEFT (east) lobe under the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes. Late in the season a thin crevasse zone has been reported opening on the descent side, and parties are advised to stay climber's left of it coming down.

The steepening to about 40 degrees immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col at roughly 8,200 ft is still the marker that you have arrived, and on bare ice it feels considerably more serious than the same slope in snow.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier to the col, then the ridge west to the summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction, fork right and switchback up to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft — roughly four miles and 2,200 ft.

Follow the boot path round the lake and across the boulder field at its south end into the basin, then climb the Colchuck Glacier toward the col between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail. Keep climber's right on the glacier to reduce exposure to rockfall coming off Dragontail's north face.

From the col the route is the ridge running WEST to Colchuck's summit — Class 2-3, hands needed in places, no protection, generally solid granite with good friction.

Navigate from the glacier and the col rather than from a compass bearing off the lake: the peak lies south-west of Colchuck Lake and the col lies south-east of the summit.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep as a scramble; earlier the glacier is a snow climb and wants an axe and crampons
hazards: Rockfall onto the Colchuck Glacier from Dragontail's north face — stay climber's right
Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the glacier
Exposure on the ridge crest despite the easy grade
Wandering off the crest onto steeper flanking ground in poor visibility
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge with no shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS THE BASE, AND YOU KNOW YOU ARE ON IT BECAUSE THE GROUND FALLS AWAY BEHIND YOU. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier you are in a closed basin; at the col the far side opens and drops south into the Ingalls Creek drainage. That change from enclosed to open is the arrival, and it happens whether or not you can see anything.

THEN TURN RIGHT. From the col, Colchuck Peak is WEST and Dragontail is EAST. The two peaks share this col, so a party that gains it in cloud and turns the wrong way is climbing a different mountain on a different route — and Dragontail's side of the col is not Class 2-3.

THE HANDS TEST: this ridge is Class 2-3. You will use your hands in places, and you should never need protection or a rope. If you find yourself on ground where you want gear, you have left the crest onto the north or south flank, and the correct answer is to come back to the crest rather than to press on.

CONFIRMATION UNDERFOOT: the granite here is solid with good friction, unlike the loose scree of the glacier basin below. Rambling on loose rubble means you are still below the ridge proper.

A WARNING WORTH CARRYING: this is also the standard DESCENT for the harder routes on the peak's north side, so parties will be coming down it. Meeting people descending is not evidence you are on the wrong line — it is evidence you are on the right one.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the glacier to the ice below the Hidden Couloir
approach_variants.notes:
As for the other north-side lines: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the signed fork, right for Colchuck Lake and up the switchbacks to the lake at 5,570 ft, then the east-shore path to the inlet and up the basin to the Colchuck Glacier and moraine below the peak's northeast face.

In the season this route is in, expect the road to be gated well below the trailhead and the approach to be a longer day than the summer figures suggest. No trailhead-to-base time is given here because the known times are winter ones and vary too much to average.

Above the base the route runs two 60 m pitches of ice, several hundred feet of 50-60 degree snow trending up and left, then unconsolidated snow over rock, a short leftward traverse into a chimney at about M6, and a final steep band to a notch on the north ridge crest.

A variation climbs the ice start and then continues up the Hidden Couloir itself and across the North Buttress — a more sustained moderate line and a genuinely different day.
approach_variants.season: Winter and early spring, when the two ice pitches at the base are formed; the first ascent was in January
hazards: A winter approach with the road gated, in avalanche terrain above Colchuck Lake
Two rope-lengths of AI3 ice off the deck with committing ground above
Unconsolidated snow over rock above the ice — poor protection
An M6 chimney reached by a short traverse, with retreat from it difficult
Short winter daylight on a Grade IV route
Topping out on the north ridge crest, still a long way from the ordinary descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIDDEN COULOIR IS THE MARKER AND THE ROUTE STARTS UNDERNEATH IT. This is the cleanest base identification on the whole face: find the Hidden Couloir, and the start is immediately BELOW it — two 60 m pitches of good ice leading up to its base.

POSITION ON THE GLACIER, which is how you find the couloir in the first place: this line sits BETWEEN the North Buttress Couloir and the Northeast Couloir. So walking up the glacier you pass the North Buttress Couloir first; the next thing is this. If you have already passed a second deep slot you have gone too high and are under the Northeast Couloir.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THE ICE ITSELF. This is the only line on the face that begins with two full rope-lengths of continuous ice off the deck. If the ground in front of you is snow, or mixed, or rock, it is not the start — whatever else it might be.

AND THE DIVERGENCE ABOVE, because it is decided a couple of pitches up and not at the bottom: from the top of the ice this route goes UP AND LEFT from the base of the Hidden Couloir onto difficult mixed ground. The variation instead climbs INTO the Hidden Couloir. Both start on the same ice. One is M6; the other is sustained moderate. Know which you have come for before you leave the second belay.

If you cannot find a couloir above your ice, you are not below the Hidden Couloir and should not assume the ice is the right ice.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 to Colchuck Lake — roughly four to four and a half miles and 2,200 ft, commonly two and a half hours. Before the road opens, add about four miles of Eightmile Road each way on foot or ski, which is the single biggest variable in the day.

When the lake is frozen (typically until around mid-May) parties ski or walk straight across it. Otherwise take the boot path around to the far, south side; the large flat boulder there is the usual gear-up and pack-stash spot.

From the south side, climb up and gain the lateral moraine. In spring there is often a boot pack this far and nothing beyond it. Follow the moraine crest RIGHT (west, toward the glacier) and then drop into the couloir. From the flat boulder to the couloir entrance is about an hour when trail-breaking is easy.

Overnight parties camp at the south end of the lake.
approach_variants.season: Mar-Jun, as soon as road access allows and while the couloir is continuously filled; by late summer it bares out
hazards: Moat at the couloir entrance opens as the season progresses and can force a higher traverse in
Avalanche hazard on the moraine and in the couloir in spring
Four extra road miles each way before FR 7601 opens
Descent is over the back onto the Colchuck Glacier — soft afternoon snow there has been reported as slow and exhausting
Do not confuse with the Northeast Couloir, a separate route east of the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The North Buttress Couloir rises directly out of the EDGE of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine — that relationship is the identification. From the far side of the lake you gain the moraine, follow it right, and the couloir is the first major gully the moraine runs you into. You do not traverse across the face looking for it; the moraine delivers you to its foot.

The route that gets confused with it is the NORTHEAST Couloir, which is the main north-side cleft and starts EAST of the summit. If you are working east along the base of the north side toward an obvious big cleft, you have walked past the NBC. The NBC is the one to the west, coming off the moraine.

The couloir runs about 2,000 ft from the base up to a notch. Once inside, you are in a defined gully with walls, not on an open snow slope — if the ground stays open and fanned out you are still on the moraine apron.

The moat at the entrance is the recurring problem and it changes the approach: when it has opened up, parties contour along the lateral moraine and traverse into the couloir higher rather than entering at its true base. If you cannot get from snow onto the couloir at the bottom, that traverse is the accepted workaround, not a sign you are in the wrong place.

wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.watch_out:
CRITICAL AVALANCHE TERRAIN: Slope angle of 35-45 degrees with extensive vertical relief and frequent terrain traps—couloir is prime avalanche slope with multiple fatal accidents (3 deaths in Feb 2023); only climb in ideal snow conditions with confirmed low/minimal avalanche hazard
Entry and exit of steep couloir can be technical with snow or ice up to 60 degrees—difficult down-climbing if route-finding error occurs; requires excellent snow/ice judgment
Rock and ice fall from walls above couloir—stay alert and compact party; position out of direct fall line; watch for ice/rock loosening due to solar warming
Bergschrund crossing at glacier base—may be significant obstacle early/mid-season with potential fall hazard; probe and belay crossing if uncertain
Late-season glacier becomes bare ice (July+)—surface becomes extremely difficult and icy; crampons and ice tools essential; increased rockfall risk from warming
Crevasses on the Colchuck Glacier approach are few, but they open as the season goes on—rope up and probe if any are showing
Limited escape options once committed to upper couloir—retreat can be hazardous in poor conditions; plan to turn back early if conditions deteriorate
Navigation difficulty in whiteout conditions—few visual landmarks; GPS/map essential; descending in low visibility is particularly risky

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the true-right margin of the Colchuck Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction and fork RIGHT for Colchuck Lake — straight on goes to Stuart Lake and a different valley. Switchback up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles and 2,200 ft in, and fill water: it is the last easy source. Take the boot path along the lake's EAST shore, which is faster than the west, to the inlet at the south end. Leave the trail there and climb talus, heather benches or snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Now the important part. Do NOT continue up-glacier toward the col — that is the Colchuck Glacier route. Traverse along the glacier's TRUE-RIGHT (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the fall line under the face. If Eightmile Road is gated in early season, add roughly four miles of road each way.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun as a snow and ice climb; by high summer the entry moat opens and the couloir sheds rock
hazards: Rockfall down the couloir once the sun reaches the face
An entry moat that can require an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer
Avalanche-prone slopes above Colchuck Lake in spring and early summer
Steep snow and ice to 60-plus degrees at the exit
Reversing the couloir is discouraged — plan on the Colchuck Glacier walk-off, which is long
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COULOIRS COME IN ORDER, AND COUNTING THEM IS THE TEST. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier along its true-right margin you pass features in a fixed sequence, and this one is the SECOND deep slot you meet, not the first.

Lowest on the glacier: the North Buttress Couloir. Above it, and starting with two rope-lengths of ice below a hidden couloir: the Holsten-Hilden. HIGHER UP THE GLACIER than either: the Northeast Couloir — the one you want. Above and south of it: the rock of the Northeast Buttress.

SO THE PAIRED CHECK IS SLOT-AND-RIB. You are correct when you are standing in an obvious narrow slot splitting the face, with the prominent rock buttress immediately to your SOUTH. If the buttress is not there, you are too low on the glacier. If you are scrambling onto the toe of that rock rather than into a slot, you are on the Northeast Buttress and on a fourteen-pitch rock route instead of a snow and ice one.

THE MOAT IS PART OF THE ARRIVAL, not an obstacle before it: gaining the couloir means crossing the moat at the glacier's edge, and it runs from a step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by late summer. If you reach rock with no moat to cross at all, you have probably reached it somewhere it is filled and should confirm the slot above you before committing.

WHAT IT DOES ABOVE, as confirmation: the couloir winds up, steepens, and runs into a steep WALL. The exit is along the base of that wall to the climber's LEFT, finishing on 60-plus degree snow or ice to the summit ridge. A couloir that simply keeps going without hitting a wall is not this one.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 and the Coleman Glacier to the bench beneath the north faces
approach_variants.notes: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR-39) near 3,700 ft, follow Trail #677 about two miles through forest, over a plank bridge on Grouse Creek and across one avalanche path below Hogsback that can hold debris and running water in warm conditions. The trail breaks out of trees near the Coleman icefall viewpoint around 4,900-5,000 ft — the last reliable running water before the moraine. Gain the lateral moraine and the well-worn Coleman-Deming boot track, staying on or near the moraine crest before dropping onto ice. Rope up here. Contour and ascend the Coleman climber's RIGHT — northeast — toward the bench beneath Colfax's north faces, staying low and left around the large crevasse that guards the direct line. Parties in good booting conditions commonly reach the bench in three to four and a half hours from the car. FOUR ROUTES SHARE THIS BENCH.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Oct-May. This is a cold-season route: it wants the north faces frozen, and it avalanches after new snow
hazards: An overhanging bergschrund that is the crux obstacle of the approach in lean years
Avalanche on this aspect after any new snow — do not climb it on a loaded slope
Crevasses on the Coleman, including one large one that guards the direct line to the bench
Sun-warming of the north faces later in the day, so the schrund must be crossed early
A glacier descent that multiple parties specifically warn against doing after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM LEFT TO RIGHT AS YOU STAND ON THE BENCH FACING THE FACE, THE FOUR LINES ARE: KIMCHI SUICIDE VOLCANO, POLISH ROUTE, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. Learn that order before you leave the car. It is the only thing that separates a WI4 from a WI6 in the dark, and all four start within a few hundred metres of each other above the same bergschrund.

COSLEY-HOUSTON IS THE SECOND FROM THE RIGHT AND THE EASIEST LINE ON THE FACE. Cross or tunnel the bergschrund and go UP AND RIGHT of the Polish Route. If you have gone left of the continuous ice line up the middle of the face, you are on the Polish Route and you are on a grade harder than you came for.

THE POSITIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE STRONG ONE: above the schrund this route opens with a LOW-ANGLE ICE RAMP leading up to the base of an obvious crux pillar. Low-angle first, pillar second. If your first ground above the schrund is steep — a continuous fat ice line that stands up immediately — you are on the Polish. If it is rock with face holds and mixed moves rather than ice, you are far left on Kimchi.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE CRUX OBSTACLE OF THE APPROACH, not a formality. It is frequently overhanging and in lean years it has needed a mixed traverse in from the right. Cross it early, before the north-facing slopes see any sun.

WHAT BEING TOO FAR RIGHT LOOKS LIKE: Ford's Theatre is hidden from the standard approach, tucked in a cleft around the right side of a buttress. If you have walked right until the face disappears behind a buttress, you have gone past Cosley-Houston entirely.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then right around the buttress into the cleft
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is shared with Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano: from Glacier, WA up Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail #677 onto the Coleman Glacier moraine and glacier travel climber's right to the bench beneath Colfax's north face.

What is different about this route begins at the bench rather than before it. Ford's Theatre is the RIGHTMOST of the four lines and it is about 500 ft long and graded AI4+: an ice step of three pitches (about one 70 m rope-length in good ice) before the angle relents into steep snow gullies. Belay options after the first pitch are scarce, and the first-ascent party recommended running pitches two and three together to avoid hanging ice-screw belays.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr — the first ascent was 20 April 2015 and this is a cold-season ice line
hazards: Sustained AI4+ with almost no belay options after the first pitch
Hanging ice-screw belays if the pitches are not run together
The route is hidden from the approach, so its condition cannot be assessed before committing
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow, and the same overhanging bergschrund problem as the neighbouring lines
Crevasses on the Coleman and a glacier descent that should not be left until after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IF YOU CAN SEE YOUR ROUTE FROM THE BENCH, IT IS NOT FORD'S THEATRE. That is the single most useful fact about this climb and it is the one the first-ascent party chose to record: most of the route is HIDDEN during the standard approach to the north face, because it sits in a cleft around the RIGHT side of a buttress. The other three lines are all visible from the approach. This one is not.

SO THE PROCEDURE IS: walk right along the base of the face, past the Cosley-Houston line, until a buttress cuts the face off from view — then go around the right side of that buttress. The route is in the cleft behind it. A climber who stops at the first steep ice they can see has stopped on Cosley-Houston.

LEFT TO RIGHT, THE FOUR LINES ARE: KIMCHI, POLISH, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. This is the far right end of that list, which is why the instruction is always 'keep going'.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: a steep ice step of three pitches, roughly one 70 m rope-length, then the angle eases into snow gullies; the whole line is roughly 500 ft. Belays are hard to find after the first pitch. If you get a comfortable stance every rope length, or if the route stays steep for far more than 500 ft, you are on something else.

WHAT BEING SHORT LOOKS LIKE: Cosley-Houston starts with a LOW-ANGLE ICE RAMP above the schrund leading to a crux pillar. If you are walking up a ramp, you are one line to the left of where you meant to be — which is a fine route and a different one.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then the leftmost line on the face
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as its three neighbours: Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, Trail #677 through forest to the Coleman Glacier moraine, the Coleman-Deming boot track onto the ice, and climber's right to the bench beneath Colfax's north face. Rope up on the glacier.

The route itself is about 300 m at AI4+ M5 R. Its first-ascent party described it as more of a mixed climb than a pure ice climb, on rock that is well featured with plenty of face holds — which is what the M5 and the R are about.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr — the first ascent was April 2015, in cold-season conditions
hazards: M5 R protection — a graded runout, not an incidental one
300 m of mixed ground with the schrund below it
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow
Crevasses on the Coleman approach and descent
A rarely repeated line, so conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE LEFTMOST LINE ON THE FACE, AND THE TEST IS WHETHER YOU ARE CLIMBING ROCK. Left to right the four lines are KIMCHI, POLISH, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. Kimchi takes an independent line to the LEFT of the Polish Route, so from the bench you walk left, past the obvious continuous ice line up the middle of the face, and keep going.

THE CHARACTER OF THE GROUND IS THE CONFIRMATION, and it discriminates cleanly against the route next door. The Polish Route is continuous ICE — that is its whole identity, and it is graded WI6 for it. This route is MIXED: the first-ascent account is explicit that it is more mixed than pure ice, and that the rock is well featured with plenty of face holds. So the question to ask at the schrund is not 'which line is this' but 'am I about to use my hands on rock'. If the answer is no, you are on the Polish and on a much harder ice grade than you came for.

THE R IN THE GRADE IS PART OF THE BASE FINDING. This is AI4+ M5 R, and R means the protection is poor enough that a fall has consequences beyond the fall. Being one line right of here — on continuous well-protected ice — is a materially different commitment. Confirm which you are on before the leader is 30 m up.

WHAT BEING TOO FAR RIGHT LOOKS LIKE, all the way across the face: a low-angle ice ramp to a crux pillar is Cosley-Houston, the easiest line here. A route you cannot see at all from the bench, tucked behind a buttress, is Ford's Theatre at the far right end.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman to the bench, then the schrund guarding the middle of the face
approach_variants.notes:
The trailhead and the lower approach are the same as Cosley-Houston: Heliotrope Ridge trailhead near 3,700 ft, Trail #677 for roughly two miles through forest, water at the moraine/treeline break, then the standard Coleman-Deming boot track onto the glacier and climber's right toward the bench under Colfax's north faces. Rope up for crevasse travel on the glacier.

Parties leaving the car around 3:30 am with a well-consolidated track have reported the bench in under three hours; that figure varies enormously with snowpack and traffic and should not be planned on.

Gear up on the bench. The bergschrund here guards the Polish Route directly, is frequently large and overhanging, and has required parties to traverse right and tunnel through overhanging snow and ice to gain the first ice pitch.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-May
hazards: A large, frequently overhanging bergschrund that has needed tunnelling
WI6 ice on a face that catches afternoon sun despite its northwest aspect
Avalanche on this aspect after new snow — do not do the schrund on a loaded slope
A retreat from partway up by short V-thread rappels on threads you build yourself; the normal way down is a walk-off
Crevasses on the Coleman on the way out, with the glacier descent flagged as hazardous after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ON THIS FACE: KIMCHI, POLISH, COSLEY-HOUSTON, FORD'S THEATRE. The Polish Route is the SECOND FROM THE LEFT and it takes the OBVIOUS CONTINUOUS ICE LINE UP THE MIDDLE OF THE FACE, just left of and parallel to the Cosley-Houston gully.

THE TEST IS THE ICE ITSELF, AND IT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING THE WHOLE FACE. This is a WI6 — the hardest line here by a wide margin — and above the schrund it stands up immediately. If the first ground above the schrund is a LOW-ANGLE RAMP you can walk up, you are on Cosley-Houston, which is the easiest line on the face and sits immediately to your right. That single difference, ramp versus steep ice off the deck, separates WI4 from WI6 at the moment of committing.

IF THE ROCK MATTERS MORE THAN THE ICE, YOU ARE TOO FAR LEFT. Kimchi Suicide Volcano takes an independent line to the LEFT of this route and is described by its first-ascent party as more of a mixed climb than a pure ice climb, on well-featured rock with plenty of face holds. Continuous ice with no rock moves is the Polish; face holds and mixed ground is Kimchi.

CONFIRM WITH THE SCHRUND: the schrund that guards this route specifically is frequently large and overhanging, and the documented workaround is to traverse RIGHT and tunnel through overhanging snow. If you crossed a schrund comfortably on a snow bridge and walked straight onto easy ground, you have probably crossed at the Cosley-Houston line.

WHY IT MATTERS TO CHECK THE PARALLEL GULLY: the two lines run parallel up the same face, so being one line out does not become obvious until you are committed on steep ice with the wrong rack.

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake, the 5,800 ft notch, and the traverse to the glacier toe
approach_variants.notes: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead the maintained trail ends at the lake around 2,600 ft; above that a climbers' path follows the ridgeline to the notch under Pyramid Peak at about 5,800 ft. Near the top of the now-open ridge, take the path that veers left down a cedar bench and forested ledge, using cedar pulls and low-grade rock scrambling to drop into the Colonial Creek basin. Two ways across: a high line holding roughly 5,800 ft, or a lower one that gives up some height but keeps a good boot path and regains it just before the Colonial Creek waterfall. Where the trail opens onto rock slabs below Pyramid Peak, head climber's left across the talus fields toward the ice. A large tarn sits at the northwest toe of the glacier and makes a good water source and camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: The talus traverse under Pyramid Peak's crumbly north face is loose and exposed to rockfall from above
Crevasses on the Colonial Glacier, usually bridged under seasonal snow but present
Cornices on the traverse toward the col that are invisible from camp below
Loose rock and real exposure on the upper ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE WIDE SNOW FINGER, CLIMBED FOR HALF ITS LENGTH AND NO FURTHER. Where the ice steepens, one broad snow finger runs up toward the summit ridge and it is the line. Go up it for about HALF its length, then make a short loose rock scramble to the LEFT and traverse talus and the high firnfield to the notch immediately west of the summit pyramid, gaining the top by the rock ridge above. Entering the glacier is easiest where dirt-and-rock slide fans stream out onto the ice — they give solid footing and put you far enough up to find safe lateral lines above the worst of the crevasses. Two errors are on record. Riding the snow finger to its top instead of stepping left commits you to steeper ground than the route intends. And higher up, from the open mossy rock field, going STRAIGHT up lands you on a false summit; bear left toward the true one. A documented variation stays north of and below the finger, crossing to the snowfield on talus just under a band of cliff.

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes saddle and the west spur
approach_variants.notes: From the Twin Lakes saddle around 5,000 ft, leave the trail and go cross-country up the east side and east crest of East Twin Peak. Most parties never reach the lakes: a distinct path forges off to the left somewhere between about 5,200 and 5,400 ft, roughly a hundred feet below the junction where the way trail drops into the lake basin, and taking it saves several hundred feet of regain. Traverse talus and heather toward a dip in the ridge, follow the bootpath up through boulders, rock, scree and heather, then stay close to the ridge crest across a meadow and a gravelly slope, keeping high. On the connecting ridge stay LOW rather than crossing its crest — climbing over the top has been tried and reported as a poor idea.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock in the gully above the buttress — keep the party close together and wear helmets
Snow lingering on the upper ledges into early summer makes the route significantly more hazardous
Route-finding through the boulder fields in cloud
A tiny ledge with a big runout just below the final summit scramble
approach_variants.baseFinding: TWO DIFFERENT HEIGHTS, AND THEY ARE EASILY CONFUSED. The snow patch at about 6,300 to 6,400 ft is where walking ends and scrambling starts — a short class 3 step, avoidable on the left up very steep dirt, with a boulder field above it. The buttress that holds the route's one hard move is HIGHER, at roughly 6,700 to 6,800 ft, and it arrives as an impasse. A use trail runs left around that buttress and it is the trap: taking it opens a view of the Columbia Glacier, so if the glacier comes into sight you have gone the wrong side. Instead climb straight up the buttress's left side for a five-foot fourth-class move, choosing either the chimney or the crack beside it; an alternative stays right and south on the boulder field and enters a roughly fifty-foot gully by an easier reach. Above that, cross the southwest face to the slabs, and where the headwall appears go ALL THE WAY to it before traversing climber's right — stopping short and staying right makes the ground harder. A stone-staircase formation near the top confirms the line.

bivy.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
bivy.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
bivy.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

bivy.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
bivy.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
bivy.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
bivy.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
bivy.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

approach_variants.name: State Creek approach, continuing low to the buttress toe
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the standard South Buttress approach: the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, the cairned climbers' track leaving from the east end of it, down through timber, across State Creek (last water), and up into the meadow and basin below the peak.

Where the standard route bears right in the boulder field for the leftmost entry gully, this route instead keeps going lower and further around, leaving the boot path to contour on talus and heather benches to the very bottom of the ridge. That extra contouring is off-trail and adds meaningful distance and gain over the standard walk-in — budget more than the roughly hour-and-a-half everyone quotes for the standard start.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: off-trail contouring on talus and heather with no path to follow
much longer day than the standard route for the same summit
dated fixed tat at the two half-rope rappels into notches on the lower ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: The distinguishing fact about this variation is that it starts BELOW where everyone else does. The correct start is the toe of the lower ridge, on easy ledgy third- and fourth-class slabs, well down and around from the leftmost gully that the standard South Buttress uses. If you are stood at the foot of a steep gully that forks near its top, you are at the standard start and have not gone low enough. The right ground here is unmistakably easy — many rope lengths of ambling slab before anything steepens — so if the first moves feel like real climbing you are too high on the buttress.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington go south on Madison Ave to a T, right onto Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and drive to the washout that gates it.

Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing and on toward the old trailhead. The South Face turn-off is a made object, not a natural feature: look for TWO CUT LOGS, one on either side of the road, with old logging cable visible. At those logs turn right onto a well-beaten boot track.

The boot track drops to the creek for a ford, then climbs steeply through old-growth forest. The upper part is steep and dirty before it breaks out into open grassland. Around three hours from the trailhead to the main bivy.

This is a different turn-off from Waterfall Basin, which is further along at the wide white-boulder streambed. Two cut logs with cable = South Face; 50-foot streambed of white boulders = Waterfall Basin.
approach_variants.season: Summer; the boot track is steep and dirty and the saddle bivy is snow-free only in high summer
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek on the boot track
Steep, dirty ground in the upper forest
Long approach with no maintained trail above the cut logs
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The reference point for the whole South Face is the grassy saddle bivy, and Concerto is the route that starts at it — the saddle sits near this route's start, which is why every other line here is described relative to it. A second, smaller saddle lies about ten minutes west along the wall; if you are at a small saddle with no route starting off it you are at the wrong one.

Standing at the main saddle, the granite apron of the South Face runs out in front of you. Concerto starts off that apron at the saddle itself. If you are crossing the apron away from the saddle you are heading for Nature's Way; if you are ascending class 4 ramps to a dihedral you are on the Primal Scream / Miracle Ramps side.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
bivy.permit: None
bivy.capacity: Small ledges, one party

hazards: ACCESS CLOSURE: Holden Village is closed to all guests, and Forest Service Road 8301 (Lucerne dock to Holden) and the Lucerne commercial dock have been closed since January 28, 2026 under Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-05-26-04 following December 2025 flood/landslide damage, through December 31, 2027 unless rescinded sooner - the standard boat-and-shuttle approach to this route is not usable; verify status with the Chelan Ranger District before planning a trip.
crevasses on the Southeast Glacier/snowfield remnant
loose class 3-4 rock in the ridge-notch gully
exposed, insecure class 4 move below the summit ridge
rockfall
remote, multi-day self-rescue terrain with no cell service
standing dead timber/deadfall in an old burn along the Copper Creek approach trail

approach_variants.name: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
approach_variants.notes:
There is no drivable trailhead. Ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, shuttle up to Holden Village near 3,300 ft. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood and landslide.

From the village, walk the old mine road and Railroad Creek Trail about half a mile east to a large TAILINGS PILE around 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off on the far side of the creek. A footbridge is the normal crossing; if it is out this becomes a ford and it runs highest in early season.

Above the tailings the boot trail turns steep at once, climbing about 0.7 mile of open burned hillside — loose footing in standing dead timber, unmaintained, slower than its half-mile suggests — before dropping into the Copper Creek drainage. It then parallels the creek south about three miles to an open bench at roughly 5,600 ft, which is the standard camp. Maps show maintained tread ending near 4,750 ft but the boot path continues; do not read the end of the mapped trail as the end of the path.

From camp, ford Copper Creek to its WEST side and climb into the upper basin on talus and slabs, following the outlet stream that drains the glacier remnant on the peak's east face.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, best in August; the snowfield below the ridge often still wants crampons and an axe into July
hazards: Several notches in the spur ridge, most of them Class 5 from below — picking the wrong one is the route's real crux
Crevasses and rock-margin moats on the diminished glacier remnant, worst late summer
A short exposed Class 4 step below the summit ridge with no fixed protection
Standing dead timber and loose footing in the burn above the tailings pile
Two creek crossings that both run high in early-season melt, one of them dependent on a footbridge that may be out
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A NOTCH, AND IT IS THE BEST NEGATIVE MARKER ON THIS PEAK: SEVERAL NOTCHES CUT THE SPUR RIDGE AND MOST OF THEM ARE CLASS 5 FROM BELOW. The one you want is THE HIGHEST NOTCH YOU CAN REACH EASILY, gained by a loose Class 3-4 gully on climber's RIGHT — the north side — near the top of the glacier. Picking it is the route. If the notch in front of you needs fifth-class moves to enter, it is the wrong notch and there is a better one further up and right. HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE UNDER IT: you have crossed the glacier remnant on the east face, roped, and you are near its top. The glacier is a fraction of its mapped size and crevasses are usually minor and walkable around, but the moats along the rock margins are what show themselves late in the summer. THE STREAM IS THE HANDRAIL FROM CAMP: leave the trail at the bench, ford to the west side, and follow the OUTLET STREAM that drains the glacier. It comes from the thing you are walking to, so in cloud it is a line you can follow uphill without seeing anything. WHAT HAPPENS IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE NOTCH, so you can confirm you took the right one: turn LEFT and traverse a short, steep snowfield — roughly a hundred feet of exposed side-hilling that usually wants crampons and is worth a belay if the surface has gone hard. Once on the crest, blocky Class 3 leads up the ridge to the summit. Notch, then a hundred feet of side-hill snow, then the crest. If there is no snow traverse beyond the notch, you are in a different one. THE LAST OBSTACLE IS ONE MOVE, NOT A PITCH. A single short, exposed Class 3+ or 4 step sits just below the top, and some parties carry a short handline for one airy notch there — a fixed handline, not a rappel. If you are looking for rappel anchors on this route you will not find any; nothing on it is rappelled. A NOTE ON THE ROUTE'S NAME: the south-east in this route's aspect is the glacier remnant itself, which faces south-east from under the spur ridge on the peak's east side; the finish is on the upper NORTH-EAST ridge. Navigate by the glacier and the notch, not by the compass point in the name.

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then Lewis Lake and the Lewis Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes: From the Rainy Pass trailhead (4,855 ft) on SR-20, 52 miles east of Marblemount where the PCT crosses the highway, take the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail. This is the Rainy Pass Lake Ann, not the one below Mount Shuksan. At roughly 1.25 miles stay right at the Lake Ann junction; the lake just below it is the last reliable on-trail water. Switchbacks through heather meadows lead to Heather Pass at about 6,080 ft, roughly 2 miles in, where the maintained trail ends and the off-trail travel to Lewis Lake and the glacier begins.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the off-trail travel beyond Heather Pass
Snow, bare ice and moats on the Lewis Glacier remnant; carry an axe and crampons early season
Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass well into July
Loose ground on the 400 ft downclimb into the west-face cirque; move one at a time
One distinctly steeper class 4 step on the descent, with no fixed anchor reported
Lake Ann is the last reliable on-trail water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS A CHAIN OF NOTCHES, AND THE FIRST ONE DECIDES THE DAY. From Heather Pass, head west across talus, passing south of Lewis Lake (about 5,700 ft), to the crest of the Lewis Glacier's east lateral moraine near 6,400 ft. Follow the moraine onto the glacier remnant and climb southeast, BEARING LEFT NEAR THE TOP, to a notch in the ridge at about 7,500 ft. Bearing right instead puts a party on narrow, sand-covered ledges and a steep, constricted snow gully — a much harder line.

FROM THE FIRST NOTCH, follow the ridge west to a second notch, then DOWNCLIMB ROUGHLY 400 FT of dirt or snow into the cirque under the west face. The ground is loose; space the party out.

FROM THE CIRQUE, an easy gully leads to a large notch on the Southwest Ridge, and the ridge crest — exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves — goes to the 8,107 ft summit.

SO THE SEQUENCE OF HEIGHTS IS 6,400, 7,500, THE CIRQUE BELOW IT, THE RIDGE NOTCH, 8,107: moraine, first notch, downclimb, ridge gained, summit.

THE DESCENT REVERSES THE SAME LINE, INCLUDING THE CLIMB BACK OUT OF THE CIRQUE TO THE 7,500 FT NOTCH. Fix the notches in your mind on the way up; they are easy to lose from above.

approach_variants.name: Cosho Camp to the 7,830 ft saddle and the north snowfield
approach_variants.notes: From Cosho Camp continue west down the Fisher Creek Trail about a mile and leave it at one of the gullies due south of the Cosho-Kimtah saddle, starting around 3,800 ft. The climb up is the crux of the day: sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush for the first thousand feet, then loose, tedious scree and steep grass with occasional solid rock, roughly 4,000 ft of gain to the saddle at about 7,830 ft. Parties combining Cosho with Kimtah come the other way instead, descending Kimtah's south gully and following cairns down the connecting traverse to the same saddle.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Four thousand feet of loose, brushy off-trail gain with no water above the creek
Firm snow on the north side of the saddle — carry an ice axe
Remote and rarely visited; navigating back to the correct gully in poor visibility is the real danger
The wrong gully on the way down leads into brush
approach_variants.baseFinding: AT THE SADDLE, CROSS TO THE NORTH SIDE AND CLIMB SNOW UNTIL IT RUNS OUT. From the 7,830 ft saddle the route does not follow the crest: step over onto the snowfield on the NORTH side and climb moderate snow northwest to roughly 8,100 ft. Where the snow ends is the base of the climbing — a couple of hundred feet of third-class rock on the upper east face, reported mostly solid, with cairns marking the stretches where the ground is ambiguous, finishing at the summit. That snow-to-rock transition at about 8,100 ft is the test. If you are still on talus and scree on the south side of the saddle with no snowfield below you, you have not crossed over. If you are working up a broad crest with no snow anywhere, you are on the wrong saddle: the correct one lies due north of the point at which you left the Fisher Creek Trail, between Cosho and Kimtah.

approach_variants.name: West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 to Fish Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the spur off East Buttermilk Creek Road, sign in at the wilderness register and follow Trail #411 up the West Fork valley through ponderosa and larch. The creek is crossed unbridged within the first half mile on unsecured, often wobbly downed logs, and several more crossings follow — all of them push hard with snowmelt through June. Maintenance is light and blowdown is common in the lower miles, so expect detours where the flagging and tread both thin out. The trail climbs steadily to Fish Creek Pass, where it tops out and meets the Fish Creek Trail; Star Lake sits just below the far side and is the last reliable water and the usual high camp.
approach_variants.season: Late June through early October; a popular early-October objective for larch colour along the crest. Snow lingers in the gullies off the crest into July.
hazards: Unbridged creek crossings on unsecured logs, worst during June snowmelt
Heavy blowdown in the lower miles where the tread and flagging both disappear
Lingering snow in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July
Loose class 2+ blocks in the last few hundred feet where the boot path breaks up
No water above Star Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: YOU ARRIVE AT FISH CREEK PASS THROUGH LARCH AND LOOK DOWN ON STAR LAKE — AND WHICH WAY YOU TURN IS THE WHOLE TEST. Trail #411 tops out on an open saddle reached through a beautiful larch forest, and from the crest you look down on Star Lake with a second larch forest around it on the far side. Do not descend. Star Peak, the higher neighbour less than a mile southeast, is the one you reach by dropping past that lake and climbing again; this peak goes the other way, straight up the ridge from the pass with no loss of height at all. So the test is simple: if you are giving back elevation, you are heading for the wrong summit. Leave the tread at the pass and take the boot path up the open ridge on tundra and small talus — a genuine worn path rather than a line you invent. A few hundred feet below the top the path breaks up and the ground turns into large class 2 blocks; that boulder ground is the top of the route and not a sign you have lost it. There is no false summit on this ridge to catch you out.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout, climbing east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Full southwest sun
Polished rock
Walk-off descent down the back of the formation to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Crack of Doom is on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge with the rest of the upper-wall classics — Canary, Saber, Cat Burglar, Century and Old Gray Mare. Use Saber as the anchor: far right end of the ledge, a large low roof with a left-angling ramp immediately right of it. Canary sits about 100 ft to Saber's left. Locate those, then place this route against a topo. The standing Upper Castle check: all of these begin from the bench halfway up the formation. If you are at the base of the rock beside the highway you are one wall too low, on Lower Castle, and took the trail from the eastern end of the pullout. No source consulted gives an independent start marker for this route; identify it against a topo on the ledge rather than by guessing from the crack width.

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Jackita Ridge #738 and the Crater Lake trail #746
approach_variants.notes: Park at the Canyon Creek trailhead at about 1,900 ft on Highway 20 near milepost 141, roughly fifty-five miles west of Winthrop or thirty-three east of Marblemount. Vault toilet, no drinking water. THERE IS NO BRIDGE OVER CANYON CREEK on Jackita Ridge trail #738, and the Forest Service describes the crossing as difficult and potentially hazardous in spring and early summer. How people get across changes from year to year — one season a shin-deep wade a hundred yards upstream, another a log fifty metres up — so do not plan on a fixed method. The first mile and a half is brushy. The trail then climbs steeply through timber on a long series of switchbacks to the junction with the Crater Lake trail #746. That junction is UNSIGNED, reported by two separate parties, and its elevation is published as either 5,000 or 5,260 ft. Turn onto #746 and climb toward Crater Lake. There is a second unmarked junction just before the lake, leading to the old east lookout site; stay with the main path, which runs along the SOUTH shore. Crater Lake is the last water — the ground above is dry, and the lake itself is shallow enough that water filtered at the outlet comes out warm. The whole peak is commonly given as fourteen to fifteen miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; the Canyon Creek ford is the constraint in spring and early summer
hazards: An unbridged Canyon Creek ford, hazardous in spring and early summer, with no fixed crossing point
Yellow paint marks that lead into a steep, loose gully rather than along the better line
Loose rock through the scramble section, reported by most parties
No water above Crater Lake
Broken glass and nails around the old lookout remains on the east peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are three markers above the lake and they come in order. FIRST, at about 6,800 ft the grade mellows and the trail turns north. Two parties record the same elevation for it. SECOND, at about 7,600 ft THE TRAIL ENDS — it does not fade, it disappears into a loose gully, and three accounts agree on the height. That is where the scrambling starts. THIRD, and this is the thing you can see: the gully is marked by a downscoping RIBBON OF WHITE ROCK and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it. NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is important because the marking itself is the trap: the paint tempts you straight UP that gully. It starts well and turns steep and loose with rolling pebbles higher up. A party who followed the paint up found on the way down that the better line TRAVERSES ACROSS the gully and around the corner, where cairns lead upward. Once you reach a yellow ARROW, the ground improves markedly for the rest of the way. HOW YOU KNOW YOU HAVE FINISHED THE HARD PART, corroborated four ways and genuinely reassuring: the scrambling ENDS well below the summit and real trail resumes. A mellow path runs the last quarter mile to the top, past the remnants of an old tramway at the top of the cliff section. If you are still scrambling within sight of the summit, you are off the line. There is one false top, a bump on the south ridge, and the trail bypasses it to the WEST — the real summit sits directly behind it and is not visible from below. Two things to have straight before you go, because both are commonly stated wrongly. The historic lookout stood on the HIGHEST summit, not a lower one; the second, lower lookout site is on a peak about a mile EAST. And the lookout tender here was Gary Snyder in 1952 — Jack Kerouac was on Desolation Peak, a different mountain some fifteen miles away, four years later. The summit register itself carries a card that conflates the two.

approach_variants.name: Devils Dome loop from the East Bank trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
A genuinely different approach with a specific purpose: it EXISTS TO AVOID THE CANYON CREEK FORD. The party who wrote it up said so directly, having judged a day trip from Canyon Creek to involve a difficult crossing at the time they were there.

It starts from the East Bank trailhead near Ruby Creek and runs roughly forty-eight miles with about 13,100 ft of gain over three days, taking in Devils Dome. That is a very different undertaking from the day-trip standard, and it is chosen for access rather than for the mountain.

Nothing is published on a Granite Creek or East Creek approach, so do not assume one exists.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, as a multi-day trip
hazards: A three-day committing loop with substantial cumulative gain
Same loose gully and misleading paint above
Long stretches with no bail-out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The summit end of the day is the same regardless of how you got into the basin: the trail dies around 7,600 ft into a loose gully marked by a ribbon of white rock and a yellow X, the paint leads you up rather than across, and the scrambling finishes well below the top where real trail resumes for the last quarter mile.

What differs is your bearing on arrival. Coming round by Devils Dome you meet the peak from the north-east rather than up from Crater Lake, so identify the south-ridge false top and the white ribbon from a distance before dropping into the basin, rather than expecting to walk into them off a known trail.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
bivy.notes: Narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the Crooked Thumb Glacier, reached from Perfect Pass across the Challenger Glacier and down through the notch west of Challenger. The base camp for Crooked Thumb and Phantom from the north. Fully exposed to weather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier melt only
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few tents on a narrow moraine

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. Whatcom Camp and both Graybeal camps have been closed because of fire damage from 2022, and the park's fire-closures page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists them closed until further notice, so there is no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier and through West Challenger Notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, the Hannegan Pass Trail runs about 4 miles and 2,500 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then drops off the north side into the Chilliwack River valley and loses most of the gain again.

The valley traverse passes Copper Creek Camp around mile 9 and U.S. Cabin Camp around mile 12; expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin and, in blowdown years, real timber. One party logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks beyond the cable-car crossing. The Chilliwack is crossed on a hand-pulled cable car, which is mandatory and somewhat exposed; the river is not reliably fordable.

Beyond it the Brush Creek Trail climbs to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, roughly 17 miles in. From Whatcom Camp, leave trail and traverse below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank on the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass, about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft. Perfect Pass has reliable running water and is a common high camp. From there rope up, climb the Challenger Glacier to a high bench near 8,100 ft, and descend through West Challenger Notch onto the Crooked Thumb Glacier. Round trip is on the order of 40 miles.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep. The Crooked Thumb Glacier itself can be severely crevassed with open moats late in the season
hazards: A mandatory, somewhat exposed hand-pulled cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack River; the river is not reliably fordable
Blowdown on the Chilliwack River Trail, measured at roughly two hours per 1.5 miles in bad years
Crevasses and open moats on the Whatcom, Challenger and Crooked Thumb Glaciers
Loose class 4-5 rock throughout the upper route, described in trip reports as horribly loose
Weathered fixed tat on the north-ridge horn that should not be trusted without backing up
A 40-45 degree snow couloir that wants pickets or flukes when firm
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE FOOT OF A SNOW COULOIR ON THE NORTHWEST SIDE, AND THE COULOIR IS THE ONLY THING ON THE PEAK YOU CAN IDENTIFY IN CLOUD. From the moraine camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier, the line goes up a 40-45 degree northwest-facing snow couloir to the saddle just north of the peak. In fog, do not navigate by the summit; navigate by the fact that you are in a confined snow gully with rock walls on both sides, steepening steadily to about 45 degrees. If the ground opens out and flattens, you are on the glacier, not in the couloir.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP, WHICH IS THE HARDER FIND: the camp is a LATERAL MORAINE, i.e. a ridge of rubble sitting on the ice, reached by descending through West Challenger Notch off the Challenger Glacier bench at about 8,100 ft. The notch is the crux of the navigation, not the couloir. You are through it when the ground stops dropping and you are standing on loose rock with ice on both sides.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: above the couloir the route works along loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles, and the crux is a single roughly 10 ft near-vertical crack, 5.8+ or 5.2 with a point of aid, taken at the top of a headwall. A rock horn draped with old slings sits below those pinnacles. If you have climbed the couloir and are on clean, moderate rock with good stances, you are not on this route; everything here is described as horribly loose.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the Challenger Glacier past the 8,100 ft bench instead of dropping through the notch takes you toward Challenger's own summit rocks, which is a different peak.

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. Fully exposed alpine ground with no shelter and long views out to the volcanoes. The moraine is loose and the glacier below it is heavily crevassed with big moats late in the season — rope up leaving camp, not after.
bivy.water: glacier meltwater
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: tight — a narrow strip, enough for a small party

bivy.name: Perfect Pass
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, and widely rated one of the finest bivy sites in the range — granite slabs, reliable running water, and the Challenger Glacier starting at the doorstep. It is the standard last camp before roping up. Open and high, so weather arrives without warning; parties have had to navigate back down to it in fog off the glacier, which is an argument for marking it before you leave in the morning.
bivy.water: running water at the pass
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: a few tents on slabs and heather

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, flat dry ground near Whatcom Pass at the end of the maintained trail and the last comfortable night of the trip — reports describe it as vastly more pleasant than anything above. This is where the route leaves trail for the Whatcom Glacier traverse, about four and a half hours and 1,750 ft of gain below Perfect Pass. Sheltered valley-head position. A knoll above the pass around 6,500 ft is also camped, with water a rock-hop away at the creek.
bivy.water: running water beside camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: a party of several

bivy.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth knowing this ledge is there and worth carrying enough to survive it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: three at a squeeze

bivy.name: West Challenger Notch / Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp

approach_variants.name: State Creek approach, then over the rib into the east basin
approach_variants.notes:
Same walk-in as the South Buttress rock routes: the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, the cairned climbers' track from its east end, down through timber, across State Creek, and up toward the basin south of the peak. Then cross the rib running south from the South Buttress and drop into the basin EAST of Cutthroat Peak.

The window is set by the highway. SR-20 over Washington Pass is closed each winter, usually from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, and this route is climbed as soon as practical after it reopens.
approach_variants.season: Soon after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr-May
hazards: east aspect in the sun most of the day — avalanche and wet-slide danger
unmarked crossing of the rib into the east basin
creek crossing in spring flow
very short season tied to the highway reopening
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route takes the big couloir on the East Face, so being in the correct basin is the whole navigation problem — from the east basin the couloir is the obvious dominant gully and cannot be confused with anything else. If the buttresses above you face south and you can see the entry gullies used by the rock routes, you are still on the wrong side of the rib. The climbing starts on snow or névé at the foot of the couloir and steepens gradually to the first ice pitch, so there is no distinct rock feature marking a start.

watch_out: HIGH HAZARD - Documented rappel failure incident (April 28, 2024: girth hitch failure, ~400 foot fall, broken leg)
Steep water ice sections requiring technical ice climbing
Avalanche hazard in upper couloir sections
Rappel setup critical - verify anchors and rappel setup redundancy
Verify all rappel hardware: girth hitches have known failure modes
wa_cutthroat_peak_cauthorn_wilson_couloi.approach:
This route is on the EAST face, so the approach is the South Buttress approach with one extra step. From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, take the cairned climbers' track from its east end, drop through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak.

From there, cross the rib that runs south from the South Buttress into the basin EAST of the peak.
