Once you are in the right basin there is no ambiguity about the line — the objective is the large couloir splitting the East Face, and it is the dominant gully on that aspect. The error to avoid here is a basin error, not a gully error.

Usually climbed soon after SR-20 reopens, typically April into May.

approach_variants.name: State Creek approach, then over the rib into the east basin
approach_variants.notes:
This route is on the EAST face of Cutthroat Peak, and the approach is the South Buttress approach with an extra step. Park in the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, find the cairned climbers' track leaving the east end of it, drop through timber and cross State Creek, then climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak.

From there, cross OVER the rib that extends south from the South Buttress and drop into the basin EAST of Cutthroat Peak. That crossing is what separates this approach from the rock-route approach, and it is the part with no boot path.

The route is in condition for a short window right after the highway opens each spring, usually April or May. SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated all winter — typically closing late November or early December and reopening mid-April to early May — so the season starts when the gate does.
approach_variants.season: Soon after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr-May
hazards: east-facing slopes take sun for most of the day — serious avalanche and wet-slide concern, and a strong argument for a very early start
no established path across the rib into the east basin
State Creek crossing in spring melt
short seasonal window tied to the SR-20 opening
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the east basin the objective is the large couloir splitting the East Face; it is the dominant gully feature on that aspect and there is no ambiguity about which one it is once you are in the correct basin. The navigational error to avoid is a basin error, not a gully error — if you are looking up at the south-facing buttresses and gullies that the rock routes use, you have not crossed the rib yet. The couloir begins as snow or névé and climbs several hundred feet before the first proper ice pitch, so the transition from approach to route is gradual; treat the base of the continuous snow in the couloir as the start.

wa_cutthroat_peak_northeast_face.approach:
From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' track from its east end down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak. Then traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin EAST of Cutthroat Peak, where the East Face routes begin.

Avoid the steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall on the way in.

approach_variants.name: The SR-20 pullout, over the rib south of the South Buttress into the basin EAST of the peak
approach_variants.notes: From the long pullout on the NORTH side of SR-20 about a mile and a half WEST of Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' track from its EAST end down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak. Six pitches, Grade III, first climbed in 1976. Note that this route is filed as northeast face while its name and aspect both say EAST.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall that must be avoided rather than climbed
A descent by a different route than the one climbed, with no route-specific beta
A creek crossing and brushy climbers' path low down
No published marker at the base of the route itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: TRAVERSE OVER THE RIB THAT EXTENDS SOUTH FROM THE SOUTH BUTTRESS INTO THE BASIN EAST OF CUTTHROAT PEAK. THAT SECOND BASIN IS WHERE THE EAST FACE ROUTES BEGIN. SO THE COUNT IS TWO BASINS, AND THE RIB BETWEEN THEM IS THE THING YOU CROSS: first the basin below the peak's south side, which is where the South Buttress and North Ridge parties go, then over a rib, then the east basin. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A RIB, YOU ARE STILL IN THE SOUTH BASIN AND YOU ARE UNDER THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE NORTH RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME BOULDER FIELD: that route bears RIGHT AND NORTH into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch, and gains it by a loose runout 5.7 pitch. If you are roping up for a single hard pitch to reach a notch, you are on the North Ridge, not on the East Face. A HAZARD THAT IS ALSO A ROUTE-FINDING INSTRUCTION, AND IT IS STATED IN BOTH ROUTES ON THIS SIDE: AVOID THE STEEP, LOOSE SCREE CHIMNEYS DIRECTLY BELOW THE WALL ON THE WAY IN. If your line into the base is up a confined chimney full of scree, you have picked the wrong way through and should back out and go round. THERE IS NO NAMED CRACK OR FLAKE AT THE START: no per-route detail beyond this shared approach is published for this line, and the peak's other east-side route carries no marker either. What is recorded is the basin, the rib and the chimneys to avoid, and those are all real ground features. DESCENT: no route-specific beta exists beyond the general east-face pattern. Parties commonly descend the South Buttress with multiple rappels, or the West Ridge on fixed-anchor rappels plus downclimbing, rather than reversing the technical face.

wa_cutthroat_peak_southeast_buttress.approach:
Drop to the State Creek crossing as for the South Buttress: the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, then the cairned track from its east end down through timber to the creek.

From the creek, climb the open slopes on the EAST side of the southeast-draining stream, which brings you into the basin immediately south of the peak. At the headwall, look for twin gullies running up to a notch — that notch is the base of the Southeast Buttress. Start up the right-hand gully and traverse into the left-hand one before you reach the notch; taking them in the other order is the common mistake here.

approach_variants.name: State Creek to the basin south of the peak, then the twin gullies
approach_variants.notes:
From the highway, drop to the State Creek crossing as for the South Buttress — the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, cairned track from its east end down through timber to the creek.

From the creek, climb the open slopes on the EAST side of the southeast-draining stream, which takes you into the basin immediately south of Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half to the foot of the gully system.

Continue up to the basin headwall.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in both gullies
State Creek crossing in high water
the West Ridge descent option is looser and more rockfall-prone than the ascent line
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the headwall look for TWIN gullies running up to a notch — that notch is the base of the Southeast Buttress and it is the target. The sequence that matters: start up the RIGHT-hand gully, and traverse across into the LEFT-hand gully BEFORE you reach the notch. Getting that order backwards is the classic error, because from the basin the left gully looks like the direct line. Scramble the lower part of the gully, then rope up and pitch out the upper section to the notch. Above the notch the ground eases to scrambling before a short steep face, and from there you stay near the buttress crest.

rappel_detail.notes: First bolted station reached after downclimbing/simul-climbing the upper West Ridge from the true summit; single 60m rope.
hazards: The traverse to reach it is the ultra-exposed ridge crest, with loose rock and gravel over the ledges
rappel_detail.station: Reached by downclimbing and simul-climbing the exposed upper West Ridge crest west from the true summit. The first bolted station is the obvious one just west of the summit - it is the one anchor on this descent nobody reports having trouble finding.

rappel_detail.notes: Second of three further rappels down the north/northwest side, interspersed with short downclimbs and a traverse back to the ridge crest.
hazards: Multiple abandoned tat anchors in the same gully make it easy to commit to the wrong descent line
Rappelling straight down from station 1 takes you past the correct station
rappel_detail.station: The station parties lose. It is not in the fall line below the first - look out to skier's left before committing to a rappel direction. Several old tat-marked stations are scattered through this gully and compete for attention; the correct continuation is the bolted pair, since the whole line was rebolted with chain anchors in 2010.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the north/northwest side of the upper ridge.
hazards: Two southwest-facing gullies below the flat section look like the way down and are not - parties are regularly drawn into them. Bypass both and stay with the crest and the south-side ledges
rappel_detail.station: Below the upper rappels the ridge flattens out. The continuation is down the crest and then onto third-class ledges on the SOUTH side of the ridge; the next bolted station sits above the large dihedral that dominates this part of the west side.

rappel_detail.notes: Final of the four rappels; below it, downclimb loose exposed 3rd-class terrain and cross a cairned scree bowl back to the boulder field and approach trail.
hazards: Off the ropes it is easy to drift too far skier's left and cliff out. Traverse right, pick up the cairn across the large scree bowl, then zig-zag down to the boulder field and the approach trail
rappel_detail.station: The last bolted station takes you down the dihedral itself and onto the upper scree slopes.

approach_variants.name: State Creek climbers' trail from the SR-20 pullout
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the long pullout on the NORTH side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass. The trail leaves from the EAST end of that pullout and drops straight into the woods; the climbers' track actually starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the pullout's eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past.

The path drops through timber, crosses State Creek — fill up, it is the last reliable water — and then climbs steadily up into the big meadow and basin below Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half from the car to the foot of the entry gully.

Above the meadow the trail steepens into a boulder field beneath the south buttress.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: climbers' trail from the pullout is genuinely hard to find in the dark
State Creek crossing can be awkward in high spring flow
loose rock in the entry gully with parties above
the standard West Ridge descent is looser than the ascent line and has cairned traverses where the direct-looking line cliffs out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Standing in the boulder field, several large gullies come down out of the south buttress. Bear RIGHT and take the LEFTMOST of those gullies — that specific choice is the crux of the navigation and it is where parties get it wrong, because from below the gullies look interchangeable.

Climb the gully as scrambling terrain. The place to rope up is not the bottom: continue up until you are about 100 feet from its top, where the gully FORKS and visibly steepens. That fork is the marker. Pitch one goes up the LEFT side of the gully from there to gain the ridge crest. If you rope up down at the base you burn time on ground everybody scrambles; if you find yourself topping out of a gully with no fork and no steepening, you are in the wrong one.

approach_variants.name: Roadside pullout west of the Blue Lake Trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
There is a broad shoulder with room to park on SR-20 roughly half a mile WEST of the Blue Lake Trailhead, with a view through the trees to the peak. Parties commonly meet at the Blue Lake lot and then drive the short distance west to this pullout.

From there head up into the basin below the peak. Reported round-trip times are on the order of six hours up and four hours down for the whole climb, so this is a long day even though the walk-in is short.

On the way out, the descent line drops skier's right onto a sandy rib with a faint climbers' track, then into another gully further skier's right for the lower part — going straight down instead puts you into loose ground.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock throughout the ridge and on the descent gullies
long day relative to the short approach
route-finding on the descent — the direct-looking line down cliffs out
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up into the basin, stay somewhat LEFT to arrive at the notch at the base of the west ridge — that notch, not the ridge crest above it, is the reference point. From the notch, traverse along ledges for about 100 feet to reach the foot of a shallow gully that runs up and LEFT to gain the ridge crest, and that gully is where the climbing begins. Three rope lengths or so above it you arrive at a sandy area at the top of the southwest gully, which is the natural regrouping spot and confirms you are on line. If you rope up at the notch itself without making the ledge traverse, you are starting one feature too early.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, then east along the ledge and up a long steep hillside — around 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge to the rock.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close annually for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep approach hillside
Steep, coarse granite with few moderates
Northwest aspect — shaded and cold in the morning
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up and right from Logger's Ledge, the LEFT side of Midnight Rock is what you meet first. Midnight is the tall wall — about 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging, coarse granite with parallel-sided cracks — and it faces northwest, so it is shaded through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime, alongside, has almost nothing on it. Before hunting along the ground for a start, note that several of Midnight's lines begin from the enormous ledge crossing the middle of the CENTRE of the wall, reached by first climbing Stevens Pass Motel, The Sting or Wasp — so a route you cannot find at deck level may not have a deck-level start at all. No source consulted for this pass records this route's own start position; confirm against a topo.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail on the WEST side of the parking area; it leads up to Upper Castle Rock and Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Runout chimney climbing above the crux
Strenuous wide crack from the ground with the crux in the first 30 ft
Full southwest sun and polished rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Damnation Crack is defined by Jello Tower, so find the tower first — it is the pillar standing off the main wall on the ledge.

The route takes the wide crack and chimney that SEPARATES the main wall from Jello Tower, on the tower's WEST side. Midway is on the tower's other side, the RIGHT, and is an easy corner and chimney; so the two routes bracket the same pillar and the side you are on decides which route you get.

The climbing identifies itself immediately: it starts hand-size, widens to offwidth and then to chimney, and the crux comes in the first thirty feet. If your first thirty feet is easy, you are on Midway, not Damnation. Above the crux the chimney stays runout, so the difficulty does not stay at the bottom.

approach_variants.name: Swamp Creek climbers' path to the col
approach_variants.notes: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.
approach_variants.season: Early to mid summer gives firm, well-bridged snow with least crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are open and the glacier is less stable.
hazards: About a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple on an officially abandoned path
A forested cut up the headwall to the right of the waterfall looks like the way and is not — taking it forces a Class 3/4 rock wall in the trees
The slab cut onto the glacier is easy snow early in the season and a gully with a stream running in it later, needing Class 2/3 slab work
The glacier is genuinely crevassed; roped travel with crevasse rescue capability is the expectation
Wet-loose runouts come off snow slabs perched on wet rock along the glacier margins
The moat crossing onto the summit rock varies through the season and can be the hardest move of the climb late in a dry year
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE HEADWALL HAS A TEMPTING WRONG LINE ON IT, AND THE GLACIER HAS A TEMPTING WRONG LINE ABOVE IT. Coming up the basin the headwall looks formidable; the way up is at its far left, through a brushy gully where the headwall corners, and there is an appetising forested cut up the wall to the right of the waterfall that must not be taken — cutting right early forces you onto the low end of the rock wall in the trees. Above, steep forest veers right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft, where a piece of orange flagging has marked the way. Beyond that, a third and higher basin near 5,500 ft sits below the slabs of the receding glacier, and a natural cut on that basin's southwest side leads through the slabs onto the ice: easy snow early in the season, later a gully with a stream in it. Once on the glacier, the second trap: a snow and talus slope under the north side of the summit looks enticing and leads to the northeast ridge, which is far more exposed and saves nothing. Do not take it.

approach_variants.name: Crest trail to Hemlock Camp and the northwest climb
approach_variants.notes: The newer variant continues farther south on the crest trail, roughly to the Hemlock camp, then leaves the trail and climbs northwest through open forest and slopes — about 3,500 ft of gain — to reach the glacier from the ridge above. It avoids nearly all of the Swamp Creek brush and is substantially easier ground, even though the Swamp Creek line is still the one usually called standard. It is the better choice for a party that wants to arrive with something left, and it is what the far side of the ridge separating this peak from its neighbour gives access to.
approach_variants.season: Early to mid summer for the best glacier conditions, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Trackless climbing through open forest and slopes with no established line
The drop-in onto the glacier off the ridge has needed a rappel
Crevasses, and the season-dependent moat crossing onto the summit rock
The gentle-looking snowfield on the north side of the summit ridge ends in a dead vertical rock face
Many unbalanced rocks on the final crest, and cornices along it early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding: OPEN FOREST AND SLOPES, NOT BRUSH, IS THE SIGN YOU ARE ON THIS VARIANT. Leaving the crest trail farther south, the climb northwest gains roughly 3,500 ft through timber and open slope that stays walkable; if you are fighting slide alder and vine maple you have started up the Swamp Creek drainage instead and are on the older, much harder line. Veer left near the top of the drainage to reach the drop-in point onto the glacier — parties have needed a rappel to get off the ridge here, so carry the means to do it. Once on the ice, ignore the snow and talus slope running up under the north side of the summit: it looks enticing from the glacier and leads to the northeast ridge, which is much more exposed and saves no time. Leave the glacier by crossing the moat onto the rock instead, then take the three step-ups — up and left, up and left, up and left — to gain the west spur around 8,200 ft, east of the actual saddle.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: Upper Swamp Creek basin
bivy.notes: Upper basin reached by the abandoned Swamp Creek trail and a Class 2-3 climb left of the waterfall. It puts the Dark Glacier in view and shortens the summit day. Brushy and slow to reach.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and streams in the basin
bivy.permit: Same overnight permit as the rest of the trip
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots on heather and rock

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

approach_variants.name: Granite Sidewalk to Blueberry Hill (west face)
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington head south and get onto FS 2060 (the Clear Creek road, also given as Frog Creek Road). Drive roughly 5 miles and take the LEFT fork — this is the opposite choice from the Three O'Clock Rock / Green Giant side of the same road, which is the right fork.

Carry on past the Witch Doctor pullout (about half a mile past the fork) and past the first washout. Park at the SECOND washout; that is the Blueberry Hill / Granite Sidewalk access.

Walk up a creek bed heading east for about 10 minutes until a continuous slab of granite of maybe 20 degrees runs uphill in front of you — this is the Granite Sidewalk. Go up the gully on the left to gain it, then climb the sidewalk for around 1,200 vertical feet to the base of the dome. It is walking and easy friction rather than a bushwhack, which is unusual for Darrington and is the sign you are on the right feature.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn; the sidewalk is friction the whole way and is not worth attempting damp
hazards: Long unroped friction on the Granite Sidewalk — a slip has a long slide
Washouts on FS 2060 dictate where you can park; the drive-in point changes with road damage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At the top of the sidewalk a patch of trees marks the start of the Blueberry route, with a largish tree just below the patch. That tree is your reference point, and it is NOT your route.

From the largish tree, walk about 100-150 feet LEFT along the base and look for a single bolt. That bolt is the start of Dark Rhythm.

Negative marker: if you have racked up in or right at the tree patch you are on Blueberry Buttress. Dark Rhythm is a rope-length or so further left, and the only thing confirming it is the lone bolt.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout, then contour off the East Face path onto the NORTHEAST aspect
approach_variants.notes:
The shortest approach of the major Liberty Bell technical lines. The first-ascent party describe the wall as about 20 minutes from the road. Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, the same general area as the East Face approach, and follow the cairned path from the pond toward the East Face.

Ten pitches, 1,100 ft, bolted ground-up by rappel over two seasons and completed in August 2019. Expect scrambling and scree underfoot near the base; carry a helmet through the loose sections.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Scree and scrambling near the base, with rockfall potential
A 5.13-plus grade over ten pitches with no easier escape
An 80 m rope needed to rappel the route as designed
A short approach that makes it tempting to start without a full weather margin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS A TIME AND A TURN: ABOUT TWENTY MINUTES FROM THE ROAD, AND YOU LEAVE THE EAST FACE PATH BEFORE IT REACHES THE MAIN EAST FACE TALUS. Contour toward the NORTHEAST aspect of the wall rather than continuing all the way in. If you have walked a full hour and are standing in the big talus field under the East Face, you have gone past this route and are under Liberty Crack's wall instead.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE STRONGEST ONE HERE, BECAUSE THE POSITIVE ONE IS SHORT: THE EAST FACE APPROACH TAKES ABOUT AN HOUR. THIS ONE TAKES ABOUT TWENTY MINUTES. A THREEFOLD DIFFERENCE IN WALKING TIME IS MEASURABLE IN ANY VISIBILITY.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: the wall is 1,100 ft on the northeast face, and it is the ground BEYOND the right-hand, north end of the East Face. The Independence Route marks that end, at the profusely overhanging northeast CORNER with a red roof, the Baer Ceiling, about 85 m up. Dark Side is round the corner from it.

CONFIRM BY THE HARDWARE, WHICH IS DISTINCTIVE ON THIS PEAK: the route was bolted with ANCHORS AT ROUGHLY 40 M INTERVALS ALONG GOOD STANCES, all fixed and bolted, so no natural gear is needed to descend it. Most parties rappel the route itself on a single 80 m rope, working out at eight or nine rappels of up to 40 m. A fully bolted rap line at even 40 m spacing is not what any other line on this mountain offers.

approach_variants.name: Railway tracks to The Country, then the Upper Town Wall trail
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Lower Town Wall lot (Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles) and cross the railway tracks as for the Lower Wall.

Rather than turning up to the Lower Wall, follow the tracks along to the far north end, past the Lower Wall, to the clearing at The Country. The landmark on the way is the huge tunnel door; you cut left by the Country area near it.

At the clearing, walk to the FAR RIGHT of it, near the start of the route GM, where there may be a notice board. From there an obvious path leads uphill.

Allow about 30 minutes; one party took 50 minutes through ferns and moss. It is short but very steep, with cliffy drop-offs beside the path — this is the part of Index where people get hurt walking.
approach_variants.season: Dry days; the Upper Wall trail is steep and slick when wet
hazards: Steep climbers' trail with cliffy drop-offs
Railway crossing and walking the tracks — active line, several trains daily
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Davis-Holland is IMMEDIATELY TO THE LEFT of the point where the standard approach trail arrives at the Upper Town Wall. It is the first thing you meet, not something you hunt for.

The start takes a corner that lies to the LEFT of a blank face — the blank face is the discriminator; the corner beside it is yours.

If you have kept walking uphill past the arrival point you are heading for the Sport Wall, which sits further up. The standard link-up continues into Lovin' Arms above, so the three pitches of Davis-Holland ending at a belay is correct, not the top.

approach_variants.name: Gorge Creek: straight up, and the 3,800 ft vine maples
approach_variants.notes: From the Gorge Creek Overlook parking area near 1,100 ft, cross the footbridge and start climbing essentially straight up the slope above; the bearing is unsubtle and the line is narrow. The first thousand feet is the slowest of the day — fallen timber stacked like pick-up-sticks, young trees and burnt charcoal from the fire that ran through here — and can take an hour on its own. Cliff bands come at about 2,400 ft and again at about 2,800 ft and are bypassed on the RIGHT. Above them a network of animal paths climbs a slight ridge feature through open timber, which is the sign you are past both. Fill up at Gorge Creek: there is no reliable water above the lower forest.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Dense blowdown and burnt deadfall in the lower forest; deviating even a short way off the line puts you in far worse brush
Two cliff bands below 3,000 ft
Avalanche-prone snow on the slopes around Point 5,872 in shoulder-season conditions
Wet, slime-coated slabs near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE LADDER OF FOUR MARKERS, THEN A HARD LEFT UNDER THE SLABS. From about 3,800 ft the route works LEFT through vine maples to a partially snow-filled gully at roughly 4,000 ft; that gully leads to a tiny talus draw at about 4,500 ft, then to alpine snowfields near 4,800 ft, and the ground first looks promising at granite slabs around 4,850 ft, where the angle eases onto the southwest ridge crest. Take those four in order — vine maple, snow gully, tiny talus draw, granite slabs — and you are on the line. Stay left and north of Point 5,872 rather than committing to its slopes; parties have found avalanche-prone snow there and turned back, and the bump beyond it on the east ridge is a false summit, not Davis. At the top the buttress that looks steep and loose is reasonable Class 2-3 except for slime-coated slabs near the summit: the instruction is a HARD LEFTWARD TRAVERSE, resisting the temptation to scramble the slabs. If you are on wet slab, you are off route.

bivy.name: Gorge Creek overlook, the trailhead you sleep at
bivy.notes: This is where the standard scramble starts, on Highway 20 between Newhalem and Diablo. You cross the creek on the bridge and go straight into steep forest with no trail of any kind. The peak is famous for the sheer drop off its far side, and the ground you climb reflects that: expect around ten miles and roughly seven and a half thousand feet of gain, with cliff bands to be turned in the timber around twenty-four hundred and twenty-eight hundred feet and a stretch of vine maple higher. Thirteen or fourteen hours car to car is a normal time for a fit party, and that is why so many sleep at the car rather than carry overnight gear up it. Being west of the seasonal highway gate, the pullout is reachable all year, but the route wants firm snow or dry ground rather than the rotten mix in between.
bivy.water: Gorge Creek itself, immediately below, and it is the last certain water for a long way up. Nothing is provided at the pullout.
bivy.permit: No permit and no fee to park or to sleep in a vehicle. A DAY climb from here needs no backcountry permit at all, which is the usual way this peak is done. The moment you sleep on the mountain you need a National Park Service backcountry permit for the Davis Peak cross-country zone.
bivy.capacity: A highway pullout and viewpoint parking area, not a campground. Parties routinely spend the night in a vehicle here to start at first light. There are no sites, no pitches, and nowhere to put a tent.

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, Newhalem
bivy.notes: About five minutes' drive west of the Gorge Creek overlook, this is the practical base for a party that wants a real campsite the night before rather than a night in the driver's seat. It is low, forested and close to the highway, with none of the character of the alpine above it, and that is fine for its purpose. It also stays open later in the year than the larger campgrounds nearby, which matters on a peak whose best conditions are often outside the busy season. THE OBVIOUS CLOSER OPTION IS GONE: the small tent campground at Gorge Lake, right beside the creek in Diablo, has been shut for an extended period over debris-flow and flooding hazard on ground burned in an earlier fire, and should not be planned around without confirming it has reopened.
bivy.water: Potable water while the campground is serviced; the river is the fallback and needs treating. Availability drops off outside the main season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No backcountry permit needed to sleep here. It has historically been the free, year-round, minimal-service option in the Newhalem cluster while the fee campgrounds close for winter — confirm the current fee and season, because the park has been adjusting both.
bivy.capacity: A modest road campground on the Skagit with a mix of standard sites and a couple of group sites, small enough that a busy summer weekend fills it.

bivy.name: Snowfield benches on the south side, around 4,800 feet
bivy.notes: The forest below is the whole difficulty of this mountain — steep, tangled and unrelenting, with the route picked out along animal paths and through weaknesses in the cliff bands. Getting up to this level and stopping turns a punishing single day into a manageable two, and this is the first ground on the route where a party can lie flat and see out. A partly snow-filled gully around four thousand feet is the usual way through the last of the trees onto these slopes; it is straightforward when it holds firm snow and considerably less pleasant when it is running wet or bare. Early summer is the moment for this camp, because the same snow that makes the gully work is what supplies the water.
bivy.water: Running snowmelt while there is snow, which is exactly what makes this level worth stopping at. Once the slopes bare out later in summer, water here becomes unreliable and the gully lower down is the last dependable source.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Davis Peak cross-country zone: six people maximum in a party, and a maximum of three parties in the zone on any night. Walk-up only, collected in person at the Marblemount wilderness office rather than reserved in advance. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and not in meadow or within a hundred feet of water. No fires anywhere in the zone. Pack waste out where the ground will not take a cathole.
bivy.capacity: Open ground rather than sites. Where the timber finally releases into alpine snow and slabs there is room for a small party to lie down, and no established platform to aim for.

bivy.name: The 5,720 ft saddle south of the summit
bivy.notes: A little over half a mile south of the summit, this notch in the ridge is the highest sensible sleeping ground on the peak and the launching point for the last of the climbing. From here the standard finish takes the rock buttress on the south ridge at easy scrambling, a couple of grades of hands-on ground rather than anything technical. Parties have also tried the broad snow slopes of the east ridge from the saddle and been stopped by a step a few hundred feet under the top, so the south side is the line to plan for. Being a saddle it is exposed to whatever the weather is doing and there is nothing to shelter behind, which argues for using it on a settled forecast and otherwise sleeping lower. NOTE THE OTHER APPROACH: the peak's steep north-east side is reached instead from the Stetattle Creek trail out of Diablo, leaving the path after a couple of miles and fording the creek — but that trail has been closed outright for falling dead trees on burned ground, so treat the Gorge Creek side as the only way in until it reopens.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only while snow is present at the notch. Late in a dry summer there is nothing here and everything has to be carried up from the snowfields below.
bivy.permit: Same National Park Service backcountry permit and Davis Peak cross-country zone as the ground below: party of six maximum, three parties per night, walk-up from Marblemount, no fires, durable surfaces only.
bivy.capacity: Room for about two small tents on a snow ledge by the saddle. That is the whole capacity, and it is not a place to plan on sharing.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Vanishing Point. Barclay Lake trailhead; walk the level main Barclay Creek trail about 20 minutes and a mile to the bridge over a large creek (often dry mid-to-late summer). Do NOT cross it — break RIGHT into forest around a large boulder just before it.

Bushwhack through open forest or up the creek bed to an open boulder field, cross it to large trees and an open wash, then climb around the RIGHT side of a steep chossy waterfall (exposed). Above, a ramp with hand lines, a 60-70 degree forested rib with fixed lines, and about 800 ft of mostly roped slab on bolts and natural features.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Exposed scrambling around the waterfall
Fixed lines of unknown age
Steep forested rib
Loose rock and brush
approach_variants.baseFinding: Reach the base of the tower as for Vanishing Point — unrope at the top of the roped slabs and scramble up and LEFT. If the ground is unprotected and feels sketchy, you have come off the approach line; the whole approach is protected. Deep Blue's first pitch starts about 100 ft LEFT of Vanishing Point's, so find Vanishing Point's start first and traverse from it rather than trying to identify Deep Blue in isolation.

approach_variants.name: Barlow Pass, Gothic Basin Trail #724, Foggy Lake
approach_variants.notes:
Distance and gain are round trip. Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead, about 2,360 ft, where the Mountain Loop Highway pavement ends. Walk the gated road roughly a mile to the signed junction for the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin Trail #724, which branches RIGHT off the old railroad grade.

The trail climbs steeply and steadily through timber, fording Weden Creek about a mile past the junction — a wet rock-hop in early season or after rain. Roughly 1.2 miles above the creek, and about three miles from the trailhead, the trail crosses a steep avalanche gully that runs as a cascading waterfall in summer but can hold a firm, consequential snow tongue well into July. That crossing is the main hazard on the walk in.

Above treeline the trail breaks into the meadows and rock slabs of Gothic Basin around 5,000 ft. The meadows are fragile — travel on rock and gravel where possible. From the basin a boot path runs past a small tarn and up boulder and talus slopes to Foggy Lake at about 5,200 ft, roughly 4.7 miles in. The lake is the last reliable water and the last flat staging or camping ground.

From Foggy Lake, cross the boulder field on the climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then work up Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward the permanent snowfield below the summit walls at roughly 6,200 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the trail's snow gully can need an axe into July
hazards: Steep snow tongue where the trail crosses the avalanche gully, into July
Weden Creek ford
Loose rock on the upper wall — helmet from Foggy Lake onward
Blind entry into the dead-end gully in cloud
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the top of the snowfield you face a rock wall with one obvious gully splitting it. THE OBVIOUS GULLY IS THE WRONG LINE: it looks like the natural way, and it steepens and ends against a vertical wall about a hundred vertical feet below the top. The correct start is the blocky, staircase-like class 3-4 ledge system immediately to climber's LEFT of that gully. It carries a boot path — if there is a bootpath under your feet you are on it, if you are on clean untracked rock in a narrowing groove you are not. The ledges lead to a notch on the southeast ridge at about 6,350 ft; from the notch turn LEFT (west) for the last short scramble to the true summit at 6,610 ft. If the ground you are on constricts into a chimney and turns class 4 near its top, you are in the gully — reverse and move left onto the ledges. Parties who scramble directly to the notch on 4th class have simply missed the class 3 ledges a little further left.

bivy.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
bivy.notes: The usual camp for Gothic Peak and Del Campo Peak, at the top of the Gothic Basin trail beneath both summits. The basin is fragile, so keep off the meadows and heather.
bivy.water: Lake and snowmelt tarns
bivy.permit: No permit required; no campfires; camp only on rock or established sites
bivy.capacity: A few established sites, mostly on rock and bare ground near the south shore; space is tight on summer weekends

bivy.name: Weden Creek trail junction, one mile up the Monte Cristo road
bivy.notes: This is for the party that runs long rather than the party that plans well. The walk out from Gothic Basin is a steep descent on greasy slab in fading light and it is where people get hurt on this approach, so a known flat spot at the bottom of the climbing — before the last mile of road back to Barlow Pass — is worth recording. It is also a legitimate soft start: a party arriving late can walk the flat mile up the old road, sleep beside the creek, and be climbing at first light with the whole basin ahead of them rather than the drive still in their legs. The first three quarters of a mile of the Weden Creek trail runs almost level along the creek before it turns uphill in earnest, and that stretch is where the usable ground is. Do not confuse this with the Monte Cristo townsite four miles further up the same road, which is a different place serving different peaks. The road from Barlow Pass is gated to vehicles and stays that way, so everything here is on foot. Being valley bottom, it is buggy in early summer and stays cold and damp long into the morning.
bivy.water: Weden Creek runs right there and is the easiest water on the whole approach, but it drains the same mineralised ground as the basin above and carries the same metals question. Treat it as washing and cooking-fire water at best, and carry drinking water in.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside wilderness, so dispersed camping is allowed and needs no permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Fires are a poor idea in a wooded valley bottom under summer restrictions and are usually banned outright from midsummer; assume a stove.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents at most, on flat forest ground near where the trail leaves the road and follows the creek. This is dispersed camping on undeveloped ground, not a site — no table, no ring, no toilet, nothing signed.

bivy.name: Lower Gothic Basin — the slab benches and tarns short of Foggy Lake
bivy.notes: The basin lip, where the climbers' trail finally stops climbing and opens out among tarns and slabs, sits about a mile below Foggy Lake and is the quieter alternative to it. For GOTHIC PEAK this costs almost nothing — Gothic's ordinary line goes up from the basin side and the extra mile to the lake buys no advantage — while for DEL CAMPO it does cost you, because Del Campo's southeast ridge is entered from the north side of Foggy Lake and camping short of it adds a mile and several hundred feet to summit day. Choose accordingly: this is the Gothic camp and the bad-weather camp, not the Del Campo one. Getting here means the Weden Creek trail, which is a mining-era path rather than a graded one — steep, direct, rocky, with slabby sections that are genuinely unpleasant when wet and a few spots where hands come out. It gains close to three thousand feet in under five miles after the flat mile of road walking. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to dig in, so waste comes out with you. Snow lies here well into July in an ordinary year and the timing moves by weeks between a heavy and a light winter. Old adits and workings are scattered through the basin and some are open holes in bad light; keep to the used ground.
bivy.water: Melt streams and the tarns run through the basin most of the season and thin out late in a hot August. TREAT THE PROVENANCE OF THIS WATER SERIOUSLY: the whole drainage is old mining ground and metals leached from tailings, arsenic in particular, are documented through this valley system. Filters, tablets and boiling deal with organisms and do nothing whatever about dissolved metals. Draw from snowmelt and small feeder runnels well above any workings rather than from anything draining a spoil heap, and if in doubt carry it in.
bivy.permit: National forest land OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no camping permit, no quota and no party-size limit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass to leave a vehicle. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED throughout the basin regardless of season, and there is nothing to burn anyway — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small parties spread wide. The ground is polished slab, boulder and thin heather with pockets of flat gravel rather than any built-up site, so it takes two or three tents comfortably and rewards walking another five minutes to find your own rather than crowding the first flat spot.

approach_variants.name: Alpental base area and the ski runs under the old Armstrong Express line
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the large Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road, about 3,100 ft. There is no signed trailhead and no maintained trail for Denny Mountain. Cross the base area and pick up boot tracks and climbers' paths on the north-facing slopes under the old Armstrong Express and Sessel chair lines.

On snow this is simple: walk the barren lower slopes a few hundred feet to snowline, put on crampons and axe, and follow the Lower International run into a small basin, then the steep Upper International run — a double-black pitch that holds firm snow late and is the crux in spring — to the top of the Edelweiss chairlift unloading station.

Dry, the same line is a rough boot path and scree scramble through slide alder, small hemlocks and huckleberry, with only intermittent flagging that does not reliably mark anything.

About 2.3 to 2.4 miles and 2,500 ft one way.
approach_variants.season: Late spring to mid-July, after the resort closes but before the snow gullies melt out and expose looser rock and scree
hazards: Loose footing on scree and dirt once the snow has gone
Neck-deep slide alder and bramble low on the mountain in summer, with unreliable flagging
Ski-area infrastructure on the route
A brief exposed class 2-3 step and narrow ledge at the true summit
Avalanche terrain on these slopes when snow-covered
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS PEAK GIVES YOU MAN-MADE LANDMARKS, WHICH IS UNUSUAL AND WORTH USING. Navigate by the ski runs and the lift, not by the mountain: Lower International, then the steep Upper International, then the TOP OF THE EDELWEISS CHAIRLIFT UNLOADING STATION. Standing at that lift station is the arrival test for the end of the approach, and it is a building — it does not disappear in cloud.

WHERE THE REAL CLIMBING BEGINS: above the lift station, angle up the WIDE OPEN RAMP toward the summit horn, which changes underfoot from scree and heather to broken rock.

THE UNMISTAKABLE MARKER IS A FIXED STEEL CABLE. A short via-ferrata-style handline protects an exposed, down-sloping and often slick ledge traverse just below the top. There is nothing else like it on this mountain. If you have reached steep ground and there is no cable, you are not on the correct line to the summit block.

AND THE TOP CONFIRMS ITSELF: past the cable, a short class 2-3 scramble through a NARROW ROCK CLEFT reaches a summit carrying an old radio-relay structure and a survey marker. Hardware on the summit is the final proof.

THE HARD PART, HONESTLY STATED: on dry ground the route-finding LOW on the mountain is the hazard, not the summit. The flagging is pink, white and blue, inconsistent, and does not reliably mark the line. In snow this problem disappears entirely, which is why the season here is spring rather than summer.

approach_variants.name: Devore Creek Trail and the Bird Creek basin
approach_variants.notes: There is no road to this side of the valley: come up the lake by passenger ferry, then reach the Devore Creek Trail either by shuttle to the Harlequin Bridge stop and three flat miles of river trail, or by water taxi to Weaver Point and join the same junction from the other direction. The trail then climbs hard — roughly thirty switchbacks through rock bluffs to the wilderness boundary, then a relentless grade alongside Devore Creek on lightly maintained, brushy tread. Above the established camp, leave the trail and follow use paths and animal trails up along Bird Creek, gaining a hundred feet or so of hillside before sidehilling rather than fighting up the creekbed. Heather benches and a talus staircase, then a looser gully of scree and dirt, open into the lake basin near 7,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers in the basin and on the col approach well into July.
hazards: Lightly maintained, brushy tread on the middle section of the trail
The gully out of the creek tops out in a false, larch-filled minor basin before the real lake basin
Snow on the north side of the Bottles into July, with a short stretch around forty degrees — crampons wanted
Later in the season that snow shrinks to a moat squeeze at its edge that parties have backed off
An exposed ledge traverse across the southeast face with mixed rock, some solid and some slab under loose gravel
A short vertical step below the summit with no cracks, only ledges and slabs, that most parties rappel on the way down
A false summit before the true one
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BOTTLES SIT ABOVE THE COL, NOT BELOW IT, AND YOU PASS THEM ON THEIR NORTH SIDE. From the Bird Lakes basin climb talus and scree southeast to a saddle around 7,500 ft, just west of the point marked 7657; that saddle is where you gain the ridge, and the two towers known locally as the Bottles are not there yet. An easy ridgewalk west along the crest brings you to them near 7,650 ft, and the way past is across the snow on their north side to the small notch immediately west of them — early season easy snow with one short stretch around forty degrees, later in the year a squeeze up the moat at the snow's edge that parties have backed off from. If you are hunting for towers before you have reached the crest, you are looking too low. Beyond the notch the route crosses the southeast face, and the line is marked by hardware rather than by rock features: a rappel anchor sits at the edge of the summit ridge, and cairns run from it along the left-hand side of the crest. The unavoidable step near the top has a second rappel station visible above it, which makes it look shorter than it climbs — there are no cracks in it, only ledges and slabs. Above the step, traverse left at the same height around an exposed corner until an obvious gully with a short boot path leading into it appears; if no such gully turns up, you are on the wrong ledge.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
approach_variants.notes:
Bedal Creek is the preferred trailhead for this side of the peak because it avoids the river fords. FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway, about 18.25 miles south of Darrington and roughly a mile south of Bedal Campground; the spur is rough and narrow. Trailhead about 2,790 ft.

Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth and along the creek's steep banks until the tread ends at a large washout, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in. Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path, which leaves LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft under pink flagging and switchbacks steeply up to about 4,900 ft. Talus and meadow then lead to the 5,300 ft Bedal-Sloan saddle — last reliable water before the wall.

The Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk alternative from FR 49 reaches the same basin from the north but requires fording the North Fork Sauk plus a cold Cougar Creek crossing, slide alder and devil's club. Either way this is a full day of walking before a long rock route.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Large washout with loose boulders and blowdown at the end of the maintained trail
Brush and real route-finding in the forest band
North Fork Sauk ford if approaching from FR 49
Long committing day — the base alone is most of a full day's walking
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the saddle, cross the low connecting ridge into the Southwest Face basin and its meadows rather than continuing onto the glacier. The base of the wall is gained from meadow and talus, dry-shod. Stepping onto glacier ice means you are on the Corkscrew approach, not this one.

bivy.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
bivy.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
bivy.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

bivy.name: Bivy at the base of Sloan's southwest face
bivy.notes: Reached from the Bedal Creek trailhead by the west-face approach, traversing over a notch to the southwest. Parties who do not climb in a single long day sleep here.
bivy.water: Running water near the base of the routes through midsummer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead
bivy.capacity: A few small tent or bivy sites

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and the Chilliwack River Trail to Bear Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the road end at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 climbs to Hannegan Pass near 5,100 ft, then drops off the east side into the Chilliwack valley, bearing right at the park boundary onto the Chilliwack River Trail. Past a backcountry camp the trail reaches the Chilliwack River crossing, historically a hand-pulled cable car and a serious ford without it, then continues down-valley to the Bear Creek confluence, where the maintained trail ends. The camp there has been closed since fire came through, so confirm rather than assume.

Ford Bear Creek, climb steep brushy timber east through huckleberry and slide alder into meadows above Ruta Lake, then traverse the divide - loose south-facing slopes below two unnamed points, and a rock rib - to the broad 6,480 ft saddle with running water and heather tent sites. Two days for most parties.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for dry rock and a river crossing that is passable
hazards: a river crossing dependent on a cable car being in service
the Bear Creek ford in snowmelt
steep brushy timber, slide alder, and a loose divide traverse
rockfall and icefall from the glacier remnant in the couloir
a deep moat at the toe of the buttress late in the season
sustained hard climbing days from the nearest road, with a descent onto the other side of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRECT STARTS AT THE VERY BOTTOM OF THE ROCK, AND THAT IS WHAT SEPARATES IT FROM THE ROUTE IT SHARES A CAMP WITH. From the saddle you first go DOWN: steep scree trending climber's right, across several minor gullies, to the small glacier remnant filling the couloir below the wall.

THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS LIES ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THAT ICE, WHERE THE ROCK RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW. THAT JUNCTION IS THE START. You should be tying in with the whole buttress rising above you and no snow left to climb.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND IT IS THE COMMON MISTAKE: THE REGULAR NORTH BUTTRESS WALKS PAST THIS TOE AND CONTINUES UP THE GLACIER ON THE BUTTRESS'S CLIMBER'S-LEFT SIDE, then moves onto slabs leading into a corner system well above the bottom of the rock. IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING ON SNOW WITH THE BUTTRESS RISING TO YOUR RIGHT, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE DIRECT AND ARE HEADING FOR THE REGULAR START. Turn round and go back to where rock meets ice.

A SECOND CHECK IS HOW SOON IT GETS HARD. The Direct gives sustained climbing from low down, with an offwidth, thin cracks and steep crest pitches; the regular line gives a snow climb and slabs first. A long easy start means you are not on the Direct.

WATCH THE MOAT AT THE JUNCTION. Where the neve has pulled away from the rock the gap deepens through the season and can be the hardest move of the day before any climbing has started.

approach_variants.name: From the Chilliwack Lake road on the Canadian side
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter walk to the same saddle camp exists from the road on the Canadian side, but it crosses the border on foot where there is no port of entry, which this page cannot say is lawful, and follows an unmaintained, heavily overgrown tread after the first stretch. It is the natural choice for parties already north of the border and the awkward one for parties starting south of it.
approach_variants.season: Same window, and only if the border crossing is confirmed lawful
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
overgrown unmaintained tread
the same glacier remnant, moat and rockfall beneath the buttress
a cross-border rescue picture
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL DIFFERS, THE START DOES NOT. From the 6,480 ft saddle drop down steep scree trending climber's right, cross the minor gullies, and reach the glacier remnant under the couloir.

TIE IN AT THE TOE OF THE ROCK ON THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE ICE, WHERE THE BUTTRESS RUNS DOWN INTO THE SNOW AND THERE IS NO MORE SNOW ABOVE YOU. If you find yourself climbing neve with the buttress on your right, you have passed the Direct's start and are on the regular route's line toward the slabs and corner.

Expect the moat where snow has pulled back from the rock to be the first real obstacle, and expect the climbing to be hard immediately rather than after a snow lead.

bivy.name: Basin below the Bear Mountain saddle
bivy.notes: The launching point for the north side of Bear Mountain, reached by leaving the Chilliwack valley trail and following a lightly marked line up the ridge toward treeline and then over into the basin. It is a long way in — most parties treat it as a second or third night rather than something reachable from the road — and the ground above the trail is faint enough that route-finding matters. accounts disagree on how usable the alternative approach from Chilliwack Lake in British Columbia is, with the cross-border stretch reported at times as heavy bushwhacking, so the length of the trail-based approach from Hannegan Pass is the price of certainty.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and tarns in the basin, reliable in early summer and can fail entirely by late season — carry water up if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a designated camp, arranged at Marblemount. Zones are quota-limited with their own siting rules, so ask for the zone by name rather than assuming a valley camp reservation covers you.
bivy.capacity: Informal boulder-and-heather sites for a small party; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
bivy.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2022 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
bivy.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. The 2021 and 2022 fires closed camps and trails on this side of the pass for long stretches, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was closed for a time after the 2021 and 2022 fires, so confirm its status before a trip is built around it.
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

approach_variants.name: Same gully as the standard buttress — the difference is one turn at its top
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Southwest Buttress's, without exception: from the Cascade River Road trailhead near 2,100 ft, cross the river, climb the climbers' path through forest and talus into Eldorado / Roush Creek Basin, and on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — about 5.8 miles and 5,500 ft from the car.

From camp, cross the Inspiration Glacier to the Inspiration-McAllister col, descend onto the McAllister Glacier (the best passage is on its skier's right side near the steeper crevassed sections), and ascend the prominent, often snow-filled gully that runs from about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass up to the base of the buttress. A rope may be wanted here: a moat guarding the base can present an exposed, deep gap.

Everything to this point is shared with the 1985 standard line. The two routes part company at the top of the gully, and after two pitches they rejoin.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, when the approach glaciers are consolidated and the buttress is snow-free
hazards: Crevasse and moat crossings on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
A long, remote approach with no easy bail once you are on the buttress
Sustained 5.10 low on the route, which is the wrong place to discover the crux pitch is wet
Loose rock on the upper pitches once the two routes have rejoined
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TWO ROUTES SHARE EVERY STEP OF THE APPROACH AND SEPARATE AT ONE POINT: THE TOP OF THE SNOW GULLY. THE STANDARD SOUTHWEST BUTTRESS TRAVERSES AROUND TO THE RIGHT THERE. THIS ROUTE GOES STRAIGHT UP.

AND THEN THE CONFIRMATION IS COUNTABLE, WHICH IS AS GOOD AS THIS GETS ON AN ALPINE ROUTE: two direct-start pitches of fourth and low-fifth scrambling lead to THREE VERTICAL CRACKS. YOU CLIMB THE RIGHTMOST OF THE THREE. Not the left, not the middle — the rightmost, which starts around 5.8, turns strenuous at 5.10, and finishes with a MANTEL ONTO A LARGE BENCH.

SO THE TEST IS: COUNT TO THREE, TAKE THE RIGHT-HAND ONE, AND EXPECT A MANTEL. If there are not three cracks in front of you, you have gone right at the top of the gully and you are on the standard line — a fine route, two grades easier, and the one you will end up on anyway.

THE SECOND PITCH IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER: awkward 5.8+ climbing rejoins the original 1985 route AT A LARGE WHITE SLABBY ROCK. That white slab is the merge point and it is named in the route's own description. Once you are past it, the two lines are one and the remaining pitches to the summit ridge are the standard route's.

SO THE DIRECT START IS TWO PITCHES LONG. IF YOU ARE THREE OR FOUR PITCHES IN AND STILL LOOKING FOR THE MERGE, YOU HAVE MISSED THE WHITE SLAB — the merge is early, not high.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
