bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and the bench camp, then up and right past two minor buttresses into the talus gully under the tallest wall
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff heading west from Winthrop and roughly 3.75 miles east of the Washington Pass hairpin. A climbers' boot path drops steeply off the highway shoulder through loose talus and duff and reaches Early Winters Creek at about 4,080 ft, where log crossings get you across; use caution in early-season high water.

From the creek the trail firms up for roughly a quarter mile through forest before angling steeply uphill BETWEEN TWO FEEDER GULLIES, gaining close to 2,400 ft to a flat bench at about 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard bivy and staging camp for the Wine Spires. Water there is unreliable late season; some parties find a small seasonal trickle in a dry sandy side-gully near the bench, but do not count on it.

Roughly 3,000-3,500 ft of gain over about 2-2.5 miles one-way from the car to the base.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: The only fixed rappel anchor on the route is on the summit ridge, where nuts have been left in place
Old aid bolts on the route, one reported missing a hanger and another loose in its hole
Ball-bearing scree over slab in the last few hundred feet of the approach gully
A descent onto the opposite side of the spire followed by a substantial re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Unreliable water at the bench camp late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PERNOD'S WEST FACE IS THE TALLEST WALL IN THE WINE SPIRES, AND THAT IS THE TEST. From the bench camp, continue up and RIGHT, east, passing A COUPLE OF MINOR BUTTRESSES, to gain a BROAD TALUS AND SCREE GULLY THAT RUNS DIRECTLY TO THE BASE OF THAT WALL.

SO THE COUNT IS: TWO MINOR BUTTRESSES PASSED, THEN ONE BROAD GULLY, THEN THE BIGGEST WALL IN THE GROUP. If the wall above you is not obviously the largest thing here, you have stopped at one of the buttresses you were supposed to pass.

THE CRITICAL DIFFERENCE FROM EVERY OTHER ROUTE IN THIS BASIN, AND IT IS THE THING THAT MAKES THIS APPROACH DISTINCT: THIS ROUTE DOES NOT GO TO BURGUNDY COL. It leaves the main Burgundy Col trail at the bench. IF YOU ARE GRINDING UP LOOSE SCREE TOWARD A NOTCH BETWEEN TWO SPIRES, YOU ARE ON THE BURGUNDY COL TRAIL AND HAVE MISSED THE TURN AT THE BENCH.

THE LAST FEW HUNDRED FEET OF THE GULLY ARE LOOSE BALL-BEARING SCREE OVER SLAB, WITH CAIRNS MARKING THE BETTER LINE. Helmets should go on well before entering the gully because of rockfall from any party above.

EIGHT PITCHES AT 5.10-PLUS R. Descent is NOT back down this face: rappel EAST down the gully to the PERNOD-CHABLIS NOTCH, then a couple more rappels down steep slabs to the neve below, three rappels total, on two 60 m ropes. From the neve, trend north around the base of Chianti Spire and climb back up to Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' path to the bench and the boot path to the highway.

SO YOU COME DOWN THE OTHER SIDE AND WALK OUT PAST A COL YOU NEVER VISITED ON THE WAY IN. Budget real time: the three rappels only reach the neve, after which there is a substantial re-ascent to the col before the walk-off begins.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: Tieton Road spring, climbers' trail, then left along the base
approach_variants.notes: Drive past the Rimrock Lake dam, turn south onto the reservoir road, and park in a pullout a short distance past the SPRING with the SPLIT-RAIL FENCE around it. Walk back to the spring and take the steep climbers' trail leaving its right-hand side. That trail does not go to this route — it goes to the neighbouring line — so plan on a traverse along the base once it runs out. Watch for rattlesnakes on the approach and at the cliff foot.
approach_variants.season: May to October.
hazards: Loose material on the slopes above the cliff, with rockfall from parties above
Rattlesnakes documented on the approach and at the cliff base
A past rockfall event closed part of this area for over a month — treat the exposure as recurring
Traversing the cliff base is on loose ground below the routes; a helmet from the spring onward is the sensible call
The upper pitches include an exposed knife-edge traverse with loose blocks and thin protection
approach_variants.baseFinding: Do NOT stop where the climbers' trail ends: that is the neighbouring route's base, on the right-hand end of the cliff. Continue LEFT along the foot of the wall. The start is on the SECOND OBVIOUS RIB you come to — count ribs, not steps or minutes. Confirm from the rock immediately above: the first pitch here is easy, on face holds and MOSS-COVERED SLAB, and it finishes at a TREE BELAY. That combination — mossy low-angle slab to a tree — is the test. Negative markers: if the wall above you is steep and relatively clean with a PROMINENT ROOF overhead and a bolted belay at the top of the very first pitch, you are back at the right-hand route where the trail ended; if you have counted only one rib, keep going.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Y-shaped larch, up two or three pitches, then LEFT to the dark chasm
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Blue Lake Trailhead on Highway 20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail roughly 1.25 miles, about an hour of easy hiking at modest gain, to the open meadow and clearing on the northwest side of the Liberty Bell massif, marked by a WOODEN TRAIL SIGN. Leave the maintained trail there and follow the well-worn climber's path up through talus and heather benches into the basin below South Early Winters Spire's west side.

A single spectacular pitch of about 75 ft at 5.9+ R, first climbed in 1967.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: No ground start; two or three pitches of another route come first
5.9+ R with sparse gear in an offwidth and chimney
Rope management on any rappel of the chimney itself deserves extra care
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
DOLPHIN CHIMNEY IS NOT STARTED FROM THE GROUND. It is gained by climbing the FIRST TWO OR THREE PITCHES of the Southwest Rib or the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, then TRAVERSING LEFT OVER EASY TERRAIN TO THE OBVIOUS DARK, UNMISTAKABLE CHASM ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF THE BOVING ROOF.

SO THE FEATURE ITSELF IS THE TEST AND IT IS AS GOOD AS THEY GET ON THIS WALL: A DARK CHASM. Not a crack, not a corner, and not something you could talk yourself into. If you are unsure whether you are looking at it, you are not looking at it.

THE MEASURED OFFSET GIVES A SECOND CHECK: ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF THE BOVING ROOF. The Boving Roofs pitch is the double-roof feature reached by going left at a ledge from the same rib. Two roofs stacked above you, then a hundred feet further left, is the chimney.

THE GROUND-LEVEL AIMING POINT FOR THE WHOLE DAY: THE Y-SHAPED LARCH TREE LEFT OF THE SOUTHWEST COULOIR, at the base of the Southwest Rib. That is the landmark most parties use to start up this wall, and it is the one thing here you can find at ground level.

HOW THIS ROUTE IS ACTUALLY DONE, WHICH SHOULD SHAPE THE PLAN: it is a one-pitch add-on within a Southwest Rib or Boving-Pollock day, not a climb with its own descent. Most parties continue past it on easier cracks to rejoin the Southwest Rib and finish to the summit, then take the standard South Arete descent to the RABBIT EARS, two boulder towers with fixed rappel slings, then a short traverse and downclimb into the descent gully and three single-rope 60 m rappels to the base. A party doing the Dolphin as an out-and-back lowers or makes a single rappel back to the ledge below.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Suiattle River Road, take the Downey Creek Trail on the east bank through old growth — about six and a half miles to the Six Mile campsite at roughly 2,440 ft. The maintained trail effectively ends there.

The Bachelor Creek route continues on the north side of the creek and crosses to the south at about 4,000 ft on a log; some parties cross higher, nearer 4,400. Between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft the tread is genuinely overgrown — parties describe swimming through brush without being able to see their feet — but the important point is that the trail IS still there under it, so do not abandon it and start making your own line. At about 4,500 ft an old avalanche swath from 2002 wiped out the trail and this is the hardest stretch to get through.

Above that, cross the pass at about 5,900 ft north-west of Cub Lake and descend to the lake at 5,338 ft, around fourteen miles in. Good camping. A well-established trail then crosses flats and climbs heather beside a cascade to Itswoot Ridge at about 6,200 ft, which is the better-placed camp for summit day. Reported car-to-camp times have been nine to eleven hours; this is a multi-day approach, not a hike-in.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: brush so dense between roughly 3,800 and 4,400 ft that the trail is invisible underfoot
the 2002 avalanche swath at about 4,500 ft where the trail is destroyed
Bachelor Creek crossing on a log
open avalanche paths below Spire Point in early-season snow
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
unmarked cross-country traverse if the cairns are lost
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Itswoot Ridge the traverse north-east toward the Dome Glacier goes through a basin that is well marked with CAIRNS and is followable even with reduced visibility — so in cloud, look for cairns rather than trying to hold a bearing. Losing the cairns is the sign you have drifted.

The climbing starts where you rope up at the glacier's edge. The upper Dome Glacier is mellow, so the arrival is undramatic; the feature you are climbing to is the notch or col at 8,560 ft immediately NORTH of the summit block. It is confirmed by what happens on the far side: from the col a snow slope of about three hundred feet and then a rock arete of about five hundred feet lead to the summit at 8,920 ft.

The useful cross-check in poor visibility is that the col also gives onto the Chickamin Glacier beyond — a much larger icefield than the one you came up. So a very big glacier appearing on the far side is CORRECT and not a sign you are in the wrong place; the thing to verify is that the summit block is immediately to your south. If the ground on the far side does not drop away onto a large icefield, you are at a different notch.

approach_variants.name: Ptarmigan Traverse from Cascade Pass
approach_variants.notes: Dome Peak is the far end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, so it is also reached from the Cascade Pass trailhead by travelling the whole traverse south. This is the long way in by a wide margin and is undertaken as part of the traverse rather than as an approach to the peak; parties heading only for Dome use the Downey Creek side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: multi-day committing traverse with several glacier crossings before Dome is reached
crevasses on the Dome Glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding: Arriving from the north along the traverse, the reference points are the same: the cairned basin traverse toward the Dome Glacier, and the 8,560 ft col north of the summit block with the Chickamin Glacier beyond it and the summit rock arete immediately to the south.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
bivy.permit: None
bivy.capacity: Small ledges, one party

approach_variants.name: Inspiration and McAllister to the col between Point 8386 and the Needle
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,100 ft — the first ten miles paved, the rest rough gravel and high-clearance recommended. Hike the Eldorado climbers' trail through forest, cross the creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft, roughly four miles and 6,000 ft of gain.

From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the COL BETWEEN POINT 8386 AND DORADO NEEDLE at about 7,600 ft. That col is the base.

Most parties take eight to twelve hours round trip from high camp, and descend by the Northwest Ridge rather than reversing this line — which means the day ends on unfamiliar ground with rappels and a moat, so scout the Northwest Ridge's top as you pass it.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once glacier bridges and moats have stabilised but before the early-season storms return
hazards: Crevasse-fall potential on the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers
Loose, thinly protectable rock on the first pitch off the col — test every placement
A bottomless moat on the glacier traverse partway up the route, where the line steps off the ridge and back on
A complex, easy-to-misroute Northwest Ridge descent with moat and rappel-anchor hazards at the end of a long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A NAMED COL: THE ONE BETWEEN POINT 8386 AND DORADO NEEDLE, AT ABOUT 7,600 FT. The climbing starts immediately off it — steep, exposed mid-fifth moves straight from the col, no walk-in. IF YOU HAD TO TRAVEL FURTHER ALONG THE GLACIER AFTER CROSSING A COL BEFORE YOU FOUND ROCK, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG COL.

THE FIRST PITCH IDENTIFIES ITSELF BY BEING NASTY AND BY CARRYING A MARKER: it is a loose, poorly protectable 5.5, and A HORN WITH AN EXISTING SLING SITS ABOUT 100 FT UP. Loose rock plus a slung horn a rope-length up is the confirmation.

THERE IS AN ALTERNATIVE START AND IT HAS ITS OWN LANDMARK: a line beneath the 'CANNONBALL HOLE' to the RIGHT avoids that first loose section, at the cost of a moat crossing. A hole in the rock you could name is not a feature you find by accident — if you can see it, you are in the right place and you have a choice to make.

TELL IT FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS BY LENGTH AND BY DIFFICULTY, BECAUSE ALL FOUR ROUTES ON THIS NEEDLE ARE DIFFERENT SIZES. This one is longer and a bit harder than the Northwest Ridge (three short pitches from a small col at the top of the McAllister apron) and easier than the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from a gully 700 ft below the Marble Creek-McAllister pass). It follows the CENTRE portion of the rock on an obvious ridge line.

THE ROUTE STEPS OFF THE RIDGE PARTWAY UP AND THAT IS EXPECTED, NOT AN ERROR: after several ropelengths of class 3-4 you descend into a notch, traverse the glacier, and regain the ridge at a LEDGE MARKED BY QUARTZITE BANDS. Watch for a bottomless moat there. Pale banded rock on a ledge is the marker to aim for.

AND THE FINISH IS COUNTABLE: two short rappels drop into the notch below the true summit, then TWO sustained 5.7 crack pitches to the top. If you have climbed one hard pitch and stood on a summit, you were on the sub-summit tower.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Serpentine approach as far as the moraine: Stuart Lake Trailhead, left at the junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, about four miles and 2,280 ft to Colchuck Lake — roughly an hour and a half of uphill from the trail junction. Fill water and use the toilet near the lake's south end; there is nothing above.

Past the campsites you drop out of the forest into large talus blocks and follow cairns, then pick up the climbers' path along the moraine, passing a small creek on your left, until the face opens up in front of you.

A perennial snow patch sits below the start; its size varies year to year and it is usually short enough that crampons and axe are a convenience rather than a necessity by midsummer. Above it, a loose gully and gravel ledges lead to the scrambling.

Parties report roughly four and a half to five and a half hours from car to the first roped pitch.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; light crampons and an axe are worth carrying earlier for the snow patch below the base and for the descent gully
hazards: Perennial snow patch below the base, size varies year to year
Loose gully and gravel ledges on the approach scramble
Serious rockfall exposure on the lower face; a rockfall accident has occurred here
Cliffing-out on the bushy ramps is normal but disorienting for a party expecting a clean line
The standard descent gully ices up late season, which changes it from a walk-off into a rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Backbone takes the rib immediately LEFT of Serpentine Arete as you face the northwest wall, and the two starts are close enough that people confuse them — about 200 ft apart, with Backbone's start roughly 200 ft LOWER on the face.

Tell them apart by what is under your feet. Serpentine starts on bare orange rock that is 5th class off the ground. Backbone starts on low-angle, LEFT-TRENDING RAMP SYSTEMS full of bushes. If you are pushing through vegetation on ramps, you are on Backbone; if you are pulling on clean orange rock immediately, you are on Serpentine.

The sequence from there is counter-intuitive and worth committing to memory before you are standing in cloud: scramble up and LEFT on the bushy ledges until you cliff out — being stopped is part of the route, not a mistake — then turn up and RIGHT and work back toward the ridge crest. Zigzagging left and right along ledges and ramps on 4th-class ground is normal here.

The end of the approach scrambling is marked unambiguously: a short 5.4 step finishing at a tree with slings on it, which lands you on a large flat terrace. That terrace is the belay for pitch 1 and is where the real climbing starts. If you have not reached a spacious platform with a slung tree just below it, you have not finished the approach.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and Aasgard Pass to the east saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft of gain.

From the lake's west side follow the cairned climbers' path up Aasgard Pass, gaining roughly 2,200 ft in about three quarters of a mile.

The pass itself is where people get hurt, and the rule is simple: stay LEFT. A few hundred feet above the lake the path crosses to the climber's left of the creek and stays there. At the first grove of larches keep well clear to the left of the rock, in any season. At about 6,400 ft stay left of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it and ignore every side path leading toward the waterfall — deaths are on record on that side, and the right-hand ground cliffs out.

From the top of the pass head right and south along a short ridge above a tarn to reach Dragontail's east saddle, then cross the Snow Creek Glacier basin — a mellow slope with little crevassing, snow-covered through most of the summer — to the saddle on the east ridge.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep for a scramble; the Snow Creek Glacier basin usually holds snow into late July
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose rock, rockfall onto parties below, and cliff-out terrain right of the trees near the waterfall band at ~6,400 ft
Snow in the Snow Creek Glacier basin into late July — firm early in the day
Airy sections of class 3 on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route has no rock base; what you are identifying is the saddle, and the confirmation is a change of medium.

You are at the right place when the snow or till of the Snow Creek Glacier basin ends against the crest of the east ridge at a saddle, with the ridge running west up toward the summit ahead of you and the ground on the far side dropping away. From there it is a class 3 scramble and ridge walk with a few airy sections, nothing harder.

If you are still on the pass looking at the tarn, you are short — the short ridge above the tarn only takes you to the east saddle, and the basin crossing comes after it. If the ground you have gained requires roped climbing, you are not on this route: Dragontail's technical lines are all on the north side, reached from Colchuck Lake, not from Aasgard.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, counter-clockwise to the north face talus
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail then Colchuck Lake Trail about four miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

From the lake go counter-clockwise around to the SOUTH side, then head uphill on talus and snow toward the base of Dragontail's north face, aiming a little EAST of the face's lowest point. The base of the couloir sits at roughly 6,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: Apr-Jul; the couloir holds snow and ice into mid-summer
hazards: Overhead rock and icefall on the apron below the north face
Talus and moraine travel around the lake, awkward under snow
Snow and ice at 40-50 degrees for the first 800 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The name is the base-finding instruction, and it is the most useful fact about this route: the first couloir of the Triple Couloirs system is called the HIDDEN Couloir precisely because you cannot see it from Colchuck Lake.

So the test runs backwards from the usual one. If you have picked out an obvious couloir line from lake level and walked at it, you are not looking at the Hidden Couloir — you are looking at something else on the face. It only opens up once you are close under the wall.

What you are aiming for from the talus is the prominent snow finger at the foot of the north face, a little east of the face's lowest point, at about 6,400 ft. The first couloir gives roughly 800 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice — sustained but not technical. The hard parts of the wider route are the transitions between couloirs, not the couloirs themselves, so easy climbing at the bottom is expected and is not a sign you are off line.

If you have ended up at the very lowest point of the wall rather than east of it, you are at the Gerber-Sink start, a different route.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake to the toe of the nordwand
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

In the winter and spring conditions most parties come for, this is a much bigger undertaking than the summer figure suggests: expect snowshoes or skis, real avalanche exposure, and most parties camping at the lake rather than trying it car-to-car. Allow three to five hours from the lake to the base depending on the snowpack.

From the lake, work up talus and snow along the moraine beneath the north face. Move as a rope team across the apron below the wall — the overhead rock and icefall hazard is the reason.
approach_variants.season: Summer as a rock route; late winter and spring for ice and mixed, which is how it is usually climbed now
hazards: Overhead rock and icefall on the apron below the face — move as a rope team
Avalanche exposure on the winter and spring approach
800 ft of simul-climbing before any belayed pitch
Long approach from the lake under snow (3-5 hours)
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Gerber-Sink takes the LOWEST point of Dragontail's north wall. That is the whole test, and it is a thing you can see rather than a distance you have to pace out.

Standing on the moraine, find the point where the talus and snow apron runs highest into the rock — the toe of the face. Triple Couloirs starts further LEFT (west) of it and Backbone Ridge with its Fin is further RIGHT (east); Gerber-Sink is the line between them, out of the toe. In winter conditions the easiest entry is just to the RIGHT of the toe of the face.

Higher up, the feature that confirms the line is the dome or tower sitting BETWEEN Backbone's Fin and the tower at the foot of the third of the Triple Couloirs — the route traverses across it. If the feature above you is one of those two towers rather than the dome between them, you are on the wrong side of the correct line.

One inverted marker worth knowing: the first 800 ft or so is low-angle simul-climbing before you reach the rock band where the technical climbing starts. Easy ground at the bottom is correct here and is not evidence that you are off route.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Glacier to Colchuck Col
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — roughly 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft.

This one does not use Aasgard Pass. Continue around the lake's west and south side toward the Colchuck Glacier under the Colchuck-Dragontail col. Ascend talus and then the glacier: mostly snow early in the season, turning to firmer neve and ice with talus showing through by late season. The east lobe is generally reported free of significant crevassing but gets hard enough to want crampons and an axe. Late in the season a band of blue ice can span most of the snowfield, and parties have found a continuous snow finger on the right to get past it.

Allow three to four hours from the lake.
approach_variants.season: May-Jul, best on a firm consolidated snowpack
hazards: Firm morning snow and ice on the glacier — crampons and axe
A blue-ice band across the snowfield late in the season
The couloir is a fall-line funnel for rockfall and icefall from above — start early, before sun-loosened debris and softening snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Climb the glacier to Colchuck Col. The couloir entrance is NOT at the col — it is a couple of hundred feet LEFT of it, meaning east, toward Dragontail.

The confirmation is what the gully ends in. Pandora's Box is a notch that goes right THROUGH the ridge: standing in it you look down the far side, into the Colchuck basin on one hand and the Dragontail side on the other. If the gully you are in simply fades out onto a summit slope rather than opening into a slot you can see through, you are in the wrong feature.

From the notch the summit is reached by descending a little and traversing left, north-east, toward the top; there is also an exit about thirty feet below the notch leading left onto twenty feet or so of class 4 rock and then the ridgeline.

If you have topped out at the col itself with Colchuck Peak on your right, you have simply reached the col and not yet started the route — walk left along the base of the ridge.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, spring — lake frozen or partly frozen
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Creek Road is plowed only as far as Bridge Creek Campground at about 9.2 miles from Leavenworth, which leaves roughly 3.5 miles of road to walk, snowshoe or ski to the Stuart Lake / Mountaineer Creek trailhead at 3,400 ft. Plan for that; it is a substantial part of the day and it is why so many parties do this route on skis.

The trail follows the creek about two miles, crosses to the west side, and continues another mile to the fork. Take the left fork, cross back, and continue southeast — about five miles from the trailhead in total — to the north end of Colchuck Lake. Campsites are on the western banks.

When the lake is frozen, cross it directly. That is the fast option and it puts you under the north face in minutes rather than an hour of shore boulders. It is also a judgement call about ice, and it stops being available once break-up starts.

Once FR 7601 opens for the season the road walk disappears and the approach shortens dramatically — but by then the couloirs are usually past their best.
approach_variants.season: Feb-Apr; the lake ice typically breaks up around mid-May
hazards: 3.5 miles of unplowed road each way in winter
Avalanche hazard on the approach and in the couloirs — this route needs a stable snowpack, not just cold
Crossing a frozen Colchuck Lake is an ice judgement, not a shortcut to take on faith
Steep, exposed snow with possible ice right at the couloir entrance, before any belay
5-9 hours one way from the lake means a benighting is a real outcome
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Triple Couloirs starts on the NORTH face, which is not where Serpentine and Backbone start. Do not follow the moraine southwest toward the Colchuck-Dragontail col — that is the northwest face and a different set of routes.

From the lake, go counter-clockwise to the SOUTH end, then head uphill aiming just a little EAST (climber's east) of the LOWEST POINT of Dragontail's north face. The face has a clear low point where it meets the basin; the entrance to the first couloir — the Hidden Couloir — sits slightly east of it, around 6,400 ft.

The visible marker is a prominent SNOW FINGER running down out of the face at that point. In poor visibility, work the base of the wall until the rock stops going down and starts going up — that low point is your reference — then move a short distance east and look for the snow tongue leading up into a cleft. The entrance itself is steep, exposed snow and sometimes ice; it is narrow enough that you will know when you are in it.

The couloir is called Hidden because it does not read as a continuous line from the lake. Do not expect to see the full route from below and pick it out; find the low point of the face first, then the snow finger, then commit.

Once in, you get roughly 800 vertical feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice before the route makes any decisions — if you have climbed several hundred feet of moderate snow inside a defined cleft, you are on it.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601) to Colchuck Lake: about four miles and 2,280 ft, taking a fit party with a rack roughly three hours, four if loaded. Stay left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and grind the rocky switchbacks to the lake at 5,574 ft. There is a pit toilet near the south end of the lake and this is the last easy water.

Work around the east and south shore, then boulder-hop up onto the crest of the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine as early as you reasonably can — staying low costs you time in loose scree. Once on the moraine, turn slightly left and follow it south/southeast toward the northwest face of Dragontail, roughly in the direction of the Colchuck-Dragontail col, gaining about another 1,000 ft above the lake.

Allow roughly an hour from the lake to the moraine crest and another stretch of boulder-hopping beyond that. Parties report about four hours car-to-base moving well.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep once the moat at the base has opened enough to step across; a snow patch can linger into early July
hazards: Moat between snow and rock at the base; axe and often crampons needed into early July
Loose scree and talus below the moraine crest
Rockfall on the lower route — a fatal-injury rockfall accident has occurred on the neighbouring Backbone Ridge, and parties above you are the main hazard
Afternoon thunderstorms are routine in summer on this face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The whole face is one grey wall except for one thing, and that one thing is the start: a band of ORANGE rock low on the northwest face. Trip reports call it the orange wall, the orange rock band, or the coloured pile of rocks — it is visible from the moraine well before you get there and it is the only strongly coloured rock at the base. Walk the moraine until you are directly under it.

Second confirmation, for when the base is in cloud and you cannot see colour: a distinct black tower stands roughly 500 ft up the wall above the start. If you can see a black tower above you, the ground beneath it is the right ground.

At the base you will normally have to deal with a moat between the snow and the rock — the transition off the snow finger onto granite is where an axe earns its keep, and parties who left crampons behind have regretted it into July. Above the moat, 4th-class ledges lead up through the orange band; the climbing turns 5th class almost immediately off the deck, so if you are still walking after several hundred feet you have started somewhere else.

Do not confuse this with Backbone Ridge, which starts about 200 ft away and roughly 200 ft LOWER on the same face, on low-angle bushy ramps. If the ground in front of you is vegetated ramp systems trending left, that is Backbone. Serpentine's start is bare orange rock that goes up.

approach_variants.name: Copper Creek roadbed, three waterfalls and the tunnel
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway southeast of Darrington take FR 2060 (Clear Creek) for five or six miles and bear RIGHT at the fork. Pass the Eightmile Creek trailhead parking and keep going as the road deteriorates; after roughly another 1.5 miles it becomes effectively undriveable and there is a turnaround. The last couple of miles of the Copper Creek road have gone unmaintained for well over a decade, so how far you drive depends on the year and your clearance.

On foot: follow the old road extension for about half a mile, where it drops onto an older mining road. Where that ends, cross a side fork of Copper Creek, bear slightly left and follow the main fork up to a series of three waterfalls.

At the waterfalls, take a sharp RIGHT into a brushy rocky tunnel. This is the single move people get wrong. Continuing upward alongside the waterfalls leads into trouble, and there can be flagging near the waterfalls that was not put there by climbers — do not follow tape uphill past the tunnel. Through the tunnel, a tiny gully heads up and right into the maples and opens into a larger gritty slab gully that is followed all the way to the rock.

About 3 miles and 1,500 feet from the end of the driveable road, roughly two hours in.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn; the gully and slab approach are miserable and slick when wet
hazards: Missing the tunnel at the waterfalls and continuing uphill — the recorded way parties get into trouble here
Non-climber flagging near the waterfalls
Creek crossings on Copper Creek
Long unmaintained road; no cell service in the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The staging area is a few hundred feet BELOW the steeper rock, and the honest answer is that there is no dramatic landmark. What distinguishes it is vegetation: a few small cedars standing straight up, where everything above that point looks bushier and scrappier. If the trees around you are upright cedars rather than bushes, you are at the staging area.

The routes start on the right-hand side of the buttress. From the staging area you scramble up and rightward; from there Dreamer and Safe Sex carry on past the dihedral to the right and up the apron below the buttress proper.

Easy scrambling and low-angle apron before anything that feels like climbing is CORRECT on this buttress — it is not evidence you are below the wrong feature.

access.rules: Leave No Trace; standard Glacier Peak Wilderness regulations apply (group size limits, no stock in the last half-mile to Phelps Basin).
access.permit: No fee and no wilderness permit purchase required; self-issue wilderness registration may be requested at the trailhead kiosk once inside Glacier Peak Wilderness (entered at 2.6 miles on the Phelps Creek Trail).
access.closures: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) has been CLOSED since May 20, 2026 under Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through Dec 31, 2027, no reopening estimate given) starting at the Atkinson Flat Campground junction and continuing north -- well before reaching Phelps Creek Road/FR 6211. The order lists Phelps Creek Trailhead among the affected sites, and the Forest Service's road-conditions table (as of September 3, 2026) says the road is unlikely to reopen in summer 2026. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes FR 6200, Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211) and the Phelps Creek Trail. This closes the standard vehicle approach to Dumbell Mountain entirely for the foreseeable future; confirm current status with the Ranger District (509-548-2550) before planning this route. The final 2.3 miles on Phelps Creek Road/FR 6211 are rough and not recommended for low-clearance vehicles even when the road is open.
access.landManager: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Glacier Peak Wilderness) — (509) 548-2550, closed Wednesdays.
access.passRequired: None required at Phelps Creek Trailhead — it is not a fee site, so no Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass is needed for parking.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk (Phelps Creek, Trinity, Entiat River, or the Holden trailheads). Holden Village and its access road are closed to hikers through at least summer 2026.

road.name: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) to Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211)
road.status: paved to Chiwawa Loop Road, then gravel/rough forest road; final 2.3 miles very rough -- CLOSED as of the 2026 season beyond Atkinson Flat Campground under an active USFS storm-damage closure order (in effect through at least Dec 31, 2027)
road.driveNote: From Coles Corner take WA-207 north, then Chiwawa Loop Road, then Chiwawa River Road/FR 6200 for about 22 miles, then right on Phelps Creek Road/FR 6211 for 2.3 miles to the trailhead (~3,500 ft). The Railroad Creek/Lyman Lake side is reached separately via boat or trail from Lake Chelan to Holden Village — a much longer alternate approach, not the standard route to Dumbell.
road.seasonalGate: Not gated in a normal year, but the road has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground since May 20, 2026 for storm/debris-flow damage, under Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11, which runs through December 31, 2027, and the Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect from September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211) and the Phelps Creek Trail — this blocks the standard drive to the Phelps Creek Trailhead. In normal open years it is also subject to lingering snow on the upper road/trail into June.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the EAST side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. THE FORK IS UNSIGNED: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the RIGHT-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village — used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep. Before that the approach gully and the upper basin are full snow, wanting an axe and often crampons; snow returns to the upper mountain by late September
hazards: Several parallel gullies and ledge systems on the south face that look identical and do not all go — the documented way to get cliffed out here
A reported truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully
Loose rock and rubble in the gully and on the summit ledges, with parties above you
Lookalike notches and false summits near the top
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the standard drive entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH TO THE CLIMBING IS A CREEK, AND IT IS THE ONLY WAY THROUGH AN OTHERWISE CLIFFY FACE. From camp in upper Phelps Basin, leave the last of the boot path and head EAST-NORTH-EAST beside a TUMBLING SIDE CREEK. That creek cuts the one weakness in the cliffs above the basin; the broad talus-and-scree gully on Dumbell's south side follows it. If you are working up an open face with no water beside you, you are not in the breach.

THE FIRST ARRIVAL IS A NOTCH ON THE SOUTH-EAST SHOULDER, around 7,900 ft, reached by climbing that gully out of the basin directly south of the summit. Grass and heather give way to talus and — through about mid-August — moderate snow.

THEN COMES THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDES THE DAY, AND IT IS COUNTED IN YARDS RATHER THAN LOOKED FOR: FROM THE NOTCH, GO 100 TO 200 YARDS LEFT — WEST — AND TAKE THE GULLY THERE. Not the gully at the notch. Aim for the right-hand side of the south face, where the easiest gully system starts. Several parallel gullies and ledge lines look alike here and they do not all go: the wrong one cliffs you out below the summit ridge.

WHAT CONFIRMS YOU CHOSE RIGHT: a little scrambling above that gully gains a SYSTEM OF LEDGES which then ZIG-ZAGS up onto the WEST RIDGE. Ledges that zig-zag rather than a continuous line, and a ridge crest at the top of them, is the confirmation. A gully that runs out against steeper rock with no ledge system is the wrong one — go back down and try further west.

THE SUMMIT WARNING IS REAL AND IT IS ABOUT LOOKALIKES: from the west ridge a few hundred feet of easy but exposed Class 3 leads to the top, and similar-looking notches and false summits near the top have sent parties astray. Keep track of which top you are on rather than assuming the first one is it.

ONE OBJECT TO KNOW ABOUT: a party has reported an unstable, truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully. Treat the direct line under it as loaded ground rather than a shortcut.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass, then east and southeast to the light-coloured rock below Dragontail's south ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, the Stuart Lake Trail to the signed fork at about 2.5 miles, left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and across Mountaineer Creek, then up through forest and a boulder field to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly 4.3 miles. Last reliable water.

Skirt the lake's east and south shore on climbers' trail through talus to the foot of Aasgard Pass, then up the eroded boot path — 2,200 to 2,500 ft in well under a mile of loose scree, boulders and lingering snow. This is the biggest hazard of the day and the place route-finding errors happen in cloud.

From the pass at roughly 7,750-7,800 ft, the split from the other Witches Tower routes happens immediately. Instead of contouring west toward the col used by the south face and southwest corner lines, work EAST and SOUTHEAST across talus and boulders below Dragontail's south ridge, staying high along the rim of the basin, to reach the tower's east-facing side.

No water above Colchuck Lake beyond snowmelt trickles.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the talus is clear; snow patches persist right up to the base into midsummer
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,200-2,500 ft of loose eroded scree, snow and ice into July, rockfall from parties above
Blocky talus and short snow patches right up to the base
Little or no protection on the climbing itself
A four-foot summit slot that must be jumped
The descent is normally down the south face or southwest corner, i.e. NOT the way you came — you finish on the other side of the tower
No water above Colchuck Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU NEVER GO TO A COL ON THIS ONE, AND THAT IS THE TEST. Every other route on the tower is reached by gaining a notch — the southwest col, or the col behind the tower. This line approaches the EAST side directly across talus, staying high along the rim of the basin under Dragontail's south ridge. If you find yourself climbing to a notch, you are on a different route.

WHICH DIRECTION FROM THE PASS: east to southeast. The col routes go west and southwest. That is a genuine fork at the top of Aasgard Pass and it is made within a few minutes of arriving there, so decide before you top out rather than after.

THE ROCK IS THE MARKER: aim for the light-coloured, white granite face on the tower's east side. From below it, the route works up a series of ZIG-ZAGGING LEDGES to the summit — that stepped, ledgy character is what identifies it. A face that is continuous and blank in front of you is not the line, and there is a well-known short hand crack on one of the standard variations through it.

GRADE CHECK: this is fourth class, one pitch, with little or no protection typically placed. If you are looking at sustained fifth-class climbing you have picked the wrong start on the face.

AND THE SUMMIT CHECK COMMON TO THE WHOLE TOWER: the true summit is guarded by a four-foot slot that has to be jumped. No slot means no summit.

HONEST LIMIT: the east side of the tower is less documented than the col routes, and published descriptions of the exact start line are thin. The direction from the pass, the white rock and the zig-zag ledges are solid; a precise first-move marker is not available and none is invented here.

approach_variants.name: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed beside Beverly Creek, and at the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the wrong valley for this peak. The Bean Creek tread climbs through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley, drops to a ford of Bean Creek, then keeps climbing until the forest breaks open into a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. That basin is the last dependable water. At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than left into the upper basin; tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking to a broad saddle on the divide.
approach_variants.season: Class 2 on dry ground from July into October, and a popular spring snow climb before that, when an axe and sometimes crampons are wanted on the steep south-facing summit slopes.
hazards: The Bean Creek ford runs cold and pushy in May and June and is the real decision point of the day
Old avalanche debris crosses the trail just above the ford
Sustained loose scree, sand and broken rock on the final ridge, easy to kick down onto a party below
No dependable water above the meadows
Steep, icy south-facing snow on a spring ascent
approach_variants.baseFinding: AT THE SADDLE, STRAIGHT ON GOES SOMEWHERE ELSE AND THE PEAK IS LEFT AND STRAIGHT UP. Above the flower basin the tread goes intermittent through upper meadows and switchbacks to a broad, largely treeless saddle on the divide between the two drainages, around 6,200 ft, with scattered flat tent sites on it. The climbers' track up the peak is obvious underfoot but carries no marker of any kind — no cairn, no post, no blazed tree — so the test is the fork rather than a landmark: carrying straight on to the east takes you toward the far creek and away from the mountain, while the summit line turns left, to the north, and goes straight up the ridge. If you are still among flower meadow and old-growth stands you are in the basin below and have not reached the saddle at all. The upper ridge is roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting loose scree, sand and broken rock with the track fading in and out. Accounts disagree about whether there is one false top or several undulating bumps below the summit, so treat any high point with more ridge rising beyond it as another bump rather than the end.

wa_early_winter_couloir.rappel_count_note: Four rappels plus downclimbing, on a single 60 m rope, using the standard summer bolted stations down the west side to the North/South Early Winters Spire notch, then the piton-and-nut anchor in the skier's-right wall to get past the West Couloir chockstone. The competing figure of about six belongs to a DIFFERENT line: a newer, fully bolted rappel route down the right side of the West Face, roughly six stations spaced about 100 ft (30 m) apart. That line does not include the chockstone rappel; a 60 m rope only just works on it, and on its third station you have to reach down to clip in before letting the rope run through, so knot the ends. Do not mix stations between the two lines.

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (snow)
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the hairpin curve on SR-20 roughly a mile southeast of Washington Pass, directly under the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. This is the east-side approach; the Blue Lake Trailhead serves the west side and is the wrong side of the mountain for this route.

From the pullout, go straight up Spire Gully on snow. Reports put it at around 1,500 feet of steep snow to the start of the technical ground, and in April that snow can be unconsolidated enough to posthole to the waist — one party described slogging in to the thigh and beyond, while a party on firmer May snow was at the base in under an hour from the car. Time it for a cold night and an early start.

The window is narrow and it is set by the highway. SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated all winter, usually closing late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May, and this route is only in condition for a few weeks after that gate opens.
approach_variants.season: A few weeks right after SR-20 reopens — typically Apr to early May
hazards: 1,500 ft of steep snow with avalanche and wet-slide potential on a sun-affected aspect
deep unconsolidated snow early in the window
no fixed anchors in the couloir — a party that retreats down it is improvising anchors on steep broken rock, and a fatal accident occurred this way in 2025
cornice at the top of the couloir
route only exists once SR-20 reopens, and closes out within weeks
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir is the obvious gash splitting the two spires as seen FROM THE HIGHWAY — you can pick it out from the hairpin before you start walking, which is the best moment to fix it in your mind if cloud is forecast. From the top of Spire Gully do not continue straight up into the cleft; traverse NORTH to gain a ramp of snow lying at about 40 degrees, and the technical climbing starts from the TOP of that ramp. The ramp is the handrail: a distinctly moderate-angled snow feature leading leftward into the base of the steeper couloir. Parties that push straight into the cleft from the gully below the ramp are starting too low.

road.name: Downey Creek Trailhead via Suiattle River Road (FR 26)
road.status: Suiattle River Road (FR 26) suffered major flood/washout damage and is CLOSED to vehicles at approximately milepost 4.5 under a closure order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028. The Downey Creek Trail itself is also closed August 15 through December 31, 2026 under the Forest Service's Miner's Fire closure order. Vehicle access to the historic trailhead is not possible while the road order stands.
road.driveNote: Normally about 2.5-3 hours from Seattle via Darrington and the Suiattle River Road when fully open; while the road closure order (April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028) stands, it requires walking or biking the closed road from the MP 4.5 closure gate, adding several miles to the approach.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col, then down and south under the east faces
approach_variants.notes: From the milepost 166 pullout, take the boot path down across Early Winters Creek and up the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the bench camp near 6,500 ft, then continue to Burgundy Col at about 7,720 ft. The east faces are on the far side of the col: drop roughly 200 to 300 ft down its east side — steep snow, loose rock, or moats depending on the season — then traverse south beneath the walls. Chablis is the southernmost of the spires, so you pass beneath the others on the way. In winter and early spring parties come up the Silver Star Creek drainage instead and reach the same ground on snow.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Moats and steep snow immediately below the east side of Burgundy Col
Rockfall while traversing under the line of east faces
25-30 ft of unprotectable climbing on a dyke on the second pitch
The final moves onto the horned summit take no protection
approach_variants.baseFinding: A LARGE HANGING SPLIT BLOCK WITH A PIN AT IT IS THE MARKER. Chablis is the southernmost of the Wine Spires, so keep walking south under the walls until the rock above you carries a big block hanging off the face, visibly split down its middle, with an ugly-looking chimney behind it. The first pitch climbs up to a handrail — often at snow level early in the season, and sometimes buried entirely — then traverses right along that handrail toward the block, where a fixed pin protects a slightly awkward step across onto it. From the block you can take the obvious finger crack straight up, or keep traversing right on much easier ground to the same ledge. If there is no split block hanging above you and no chimney behind it, you are still beneath one of the spires to the north; keep going south along the base. If deep snow has buried the handrail, the pin at the block is your only remaining confirmation — do not commit to a line without seeing it.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: Pond pullout east of Washington Pass to the east-side talus
approach_variants.notes: The east faces of the Liberty Bell group are reached from the highway side, not from Blue Lake. Drive to a few hundred yards east of Washington Pass, where a small pond sits beside SR-20, and park near it. Head up through the forest bearing south-southwest until the trees give out and you break into the talus field beneath the east walls of the group. Cross and climb the talus to the left-hand corner of Minuteman's base, at the foot of the gully separating Minuteman from Lexington Tower. This is the same walk-in used for the east faces of Lexington Tower and Liberty Bell, so a party ahead of you may not be going where you are.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose, blocky rock on the first three or four pitches
Rockfall in the talus and in the Minuteman-Lexington gully
Snow banked against the base into early summer
Route-finding dependent lower half — the line wanders up and right
approach_variants.baseFinding: MINUTEMAN IS THE SMALL ONE, AND YOU START AT ITS LEFT CORNER. Out of the trees and onto the talus, keep crossing until you are under the shortest tower in the group — Minuteman is markedly smaller than the walls either side of it, so a face that towers over its neighbours is not it. The start is the left-hand corner of the base, right where the gully dividing Minuteman from Lexington Tower runs out into the talus. The first pitch climbs a corner up that left edge, and the route stays on or near the left corner for two or three pitches before working diagonally up and right. If you are looking at clean, steep, solid granite from the first move you are under the wrong tower: the lower third of this face is loose and blocky, and the good rock and the hand cracks do not arrive until the top half. Early in the season snow banks against the base — boulder the first few feet to a dry ledge and change shoes there.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake trail and the PCT, then the Chimney Creek climbers' path to the moraine basin
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Pete Lake trailhead off Cooper Lake Road, FR 46 then FR 4616. Trailhead elevations are given from about 2,790 to 2,900 ft, so do not treat any one figure as exact. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Bikes are allowed on roughly the first two and a half miles of trail and no further. Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River, about four flat forested miles to Pete Lake, then on past the lake staying left at the forks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Follow the PCT roughly a mile to a mile and a half. The turn-off is a landmark, not a mileage, and parties consistently describe it the same way: the trail crosses an old avalanche swathe at about 3,360 ft and switchbacks sharply. Stop at that hairpin and look west across the valley. Twin waterfalls come down out of a hanging basin — that meltwater is coming off the Chimney Glacier and that basin is where you are going. To the right of the falls are two rounded rock outcrops and further right a cliff band; the climbers' path goes up the forest BETWEEN the rounded outcrops and the cliff band. One party puts its start at an obvious logjam giving creek access, only about twenty yards inside the forest rather than the two hundred sometimes given. Orange flagging appears in places and should not be relied on. One known wrong turn on that path: it climbs north-west and runs up to a rocky gully. Do not go up the rocky gully. The line continues LEFT through vine maple and bracken fern, where the tread is buried under a season's growth. The path crosses three ravines, the second being the awkward one, and reaches bivy ground below the moraine. A rock buttress above the waterfalls is known as Sunrise Knob at roughly 4,650 to 4,700 ft; another party camped in a meadow at about 4,800 ft. Times from the car to that camp are reported anywhere from four and a half to over six hours, and planning three days is a common recommendation for what many parties attempt in two.
approach_variants.season: Early summer is better than late here. As the season runs on the glacier opens up and the moat at the foot of the rock becomes the thing that turns parties around
hazards: The moat and bergschrund at the base of the east face, which can be impassable late season
Crevasses on the Chimney Glacier and an active icefall between the lower and upper sections
Very serious route-finding — a well-known serious fall on this peak happened off route
Loose rock throughout the summit ledges and gullies
Vine maple and bracken burying the climbers' path, and flagging that may lead nowhere
Mosquitoes heavy down at lake level
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bivy the thing to identify is the U-Gap, the notch that almost every party climbing this peak passes through. Chimney Rock is the second peak to the RIGHT of the U-Gap. Fix that relationship from camp, in daylight, before you are on the glacier. Getting onto the upper glacier is a three-way choice and it is always the same three: a rock or snow gully in the cliff band just left of the icefall (the usual, described as grungy and wet), a snow finger far to the left, or the icefall climbed directly if you have screws and the conditions for it. THE MOAT IS THE ARRIVAL, and whether you can get from snow onto rock at all is the crux of the day rather than a formality. Parties describe reaching the bergschrund at the foot of the face and finding it large, then getting across only because fallen ice blocks had tumbled in and built a ramp and platform to step off. If there is no such ramp there may be no way onto the rock, and that is a condition of the season, not a route-finding failure. Above the U-Gap the traverse across the South Peak toward the Main Peak is a sequence of ledges that one party fairly called improbable — the first of them begins about fifteen vertical feet BELOW the U-Gap on its east side, so a search at gap level finds nothing. NEGATIVE MARKER worth carrying: the blind chimney on the way to the broad ledge under the summit tower was found by one party to be a very loose, dangerous, grungy gully. They backed out of it and instead downclimbed about fifty feet from the Main Notch and picked up an obvious reddish third-to-fourth-class ramp leading to the small notch they wanted. If you are grovelling in rotten grunge you are probably in the feature they abandoned. A final sanity check on how rarely this is done: the summit register suggests roughly one party a year. Do not expect a boot track or fresh tat to confirm anything for you.

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
bivy.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork.
