From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.
bivy.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each

approach_variants.name: Alpental into the basin below the east face, avoiding the summer gully in winter
approach_variants.notes: From the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead at about 3,100 ft, hike or skin toward Source Lake, then turn south into the basin beneath The Tooth's east face. In winter, do not use the summer approach path and gully that run directly below the east face. That line is avalanche terrain and the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is the pre-trip read, not an optional one. Take the broader basin instead and come at the face from open ground. About 3.2 km and 2,500 ft to the top.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, and only when the upper mixed ground has built up enough snow and ice to climb and protect — first climbed in winter 1995 and genuinely condition-dependent
hazards: Avalanche danger in the Source Lake basin and specifically in the summer gully below the east face — take the broad basin in winter
PG13: sustained runout climbing on marginal protection with real injury potential
Rockfall from above onto the east face
Steep unconsolidated snow on the final pitch, prone to sloughing
The descent is the South Face rappel line, shared with other parties, on a short winter day
approach_variants.baseFinding: THIS ROUTE STARTS ON THE SUMMER EAST FACE, SO FINDING THE EAST FACE IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM, AND THE ANSWER IS TO GO PAST THE SOUTH FACE START. From the notch at the top of Pineapple Pass, where the South Face begins, walk RIGHT (north) along the base, underneath the east face. That is the published direction and it is a walk, not a climb. WHAT THE FIRST TWO PITCHES SHOULD FEEL LIKE: fourth class to about 5.5, on sub-par rock with tricky protection. Easy ground that is hard to protect is right for this face. If pitch one is clean and well protected you are somewhere else on the mountain. THE MOVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM THE SUMMER ROUTE, and the point at which you will know for certain: after roughly two pitches on the summer line, this variation TRAVERSES LEFT about 30 ft, with little protection on the traverse, into a corner sitting below a steep rock barrier. That corner is the crux — 5.8-ish with one aid move, or M5 when it is iced. A leftward traverse into a corner under a barrier means you are on the variation; carrying straight on up means you are on the summer East Face. AND THE FINISH CONFIRMS IT: the last pitch is steep SNOW, belayed off small trees, trending slightly right to finish near the summit. A rock finish is the summer route. HONEST LIMIT: accounts describe this line in these blocks rather than pitch by pitch. If the ice is not there, there is no route to find, and that is a real answer rather than a route-finding failure.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek to Terror Basin, then the Terror Glacier and the 40-degree snow gully to the West-East McMillan col
approach_variants.notes:
From SR-20 near Newhalem, park at the Goodell Creek Group Campground at about 600 ft just east of Goodell Creek. The climbers' path starts BEHIND A LARGE BOULDER at the back of the campground and follows the old Goodell Creek roadbed upvalley for roughly 3.5-4 miles of gentle but brushy going, with deadfall and a handful of washouts. Two creek crossings low on the path can run high and fast on hot afternoons from snowmelt.

An obvious cairn near 1,700 ft marks where the route leaves the roadbed and climbs steeply up a timbered spur ridge south of Terror Creek, passing about 3,200 ft on the way up. Benches of heather, slabs and rock lead into Terror Basin at about 5,800 ft, roughly 5,200 ft of gain and 6-7 miles in, the standard base camp with reliable water and flat tent sites.

From camp, a long ascending traverse across snow, slabs and heather, crossing a shallow snow-fed depression near 5,500 ft, gains the Terror Glacier below West McMillan Spire.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Two creek crossings low on the path that run high and fast on hot afternoons
Deadfall and washouts on an unmaintained boot path
Crevasses can open on the Terror Glacier despite firm late-season travel being common
A snow gully steepening to about 40 degrees for its final 200-300 ft
Exposure on the summit ridge, the route's main hazard on both ascent and descent
Loose, eroded tread on the steep upper section of the path on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A SADDLE BETWEEN TWO SPIRES AND THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO IT, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART: A STEEP SNOW GULLY, OR A REDDISH LEDGE. From the Terror Glacier, continue up glacier and snow toward the col between WEST AND EAST MCMILLAN SPIRES. The standard line follows a steep snow gully that STEEPENS TO ROUGHLY 40 DEGREES FOR THE FINAL 200-300 FT to the saddle. Parties who prefer rock over steep snow instead follow a REDDISH, RIGHTWARD-TRENDING LEDGE SYSTEM and a short 4th-class rib on the TRUE-LEFT side of the gully to reach the same saddle.

SO THE COLOUR IS THE MARKER FOR THE ROCK VARIANT AND THE ANGLE IS THE MARKER FOR THE SNOW ONE. A gully that stays at a walking angle to the top is not this gully; this one kicks back hard for its last 200-300 ft.

ARRIVAL: the saddle. From it, easy but exposed 3rd-class scrambling along the connecting ridge crest, which is the west ridge, leads directly to East McMillan Spire's 7,992 ft summit. That last stretch is the whole climb.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE NEIGHBOURING SPIRE, AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH GULLIES RISE OFF THE SAME GLACIER: the col between INSPIRATION AND WEST MCMILLAN is the one the West McMillan route uses, at about 7,200 ft. The col between WEST AND EAST MCMILLAN is this one. If the summit above your col on the right is the one you just walked under, check which two peaks the gap is actually between before committing to the ridge.

WHAT THE DESCENT SAYS ABOUT THE BASE, WHICH IS A USEFUL CROSS-CHECK: the crux of the way down is the short rock step just below the saddle, and most parties make ONE rappel there off a natural anchor. One rappel, not a sequence. There is no fixed or bolted hardware anywhere on this route.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

approach_variants.name: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles to the signed forest road 1570 junction and turn right. Cross the river on a concrete bridge and continue about half a mile to a Y-junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders; park there, at roughly 1,150 to 1,300 ft, because a long-standing washout keeps most parties from driving higher.

A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every fifty to a hundred and fifty feet leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth - about seventeen hundred vertical feet in its first mile, with few switchbacks - to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. From the saddle the route climbs roughly a thousand feet to Peak 5791, then traverses heather benches and meadows above the lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of the east ridge.
approach_variants.season: June through September
hazards: a rooty, eroded and very slick steep mile that is worse descending than ascending
an easy-to-miss junction at the saddle where the two routes on this peak diverge
no water on the steep climb from the roadbed
rolling ridge travel that takes longer than the distance suggests
an exposed camp and no bail-out once out on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE JUNCTION AT THE SADDLE IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THIS APPROACH AND IT IS EASY TO MISS. At the ridge saddle near Point 5116, GO LEFT and climb about a thousand feet to Peak 5791. IF YOU FIND YOURSELF DROPPING TOWARD A LAKE, OR CONTOURING THE WEST SIDE OF THE CREST ON A FAINT TREAD, YOU HAVE TAKEN THE OTHER BRANCH AND ARE ON THE KINDY RIDGE LINE THAT SERVES THE STANDARD ROUTE.

THE PINK RIBBON IS THE HANDRAIL ON THE STEEP MILE BELOW. It is spaced closely enough that losing sight of it for long means you have drifted; the tread is rooty and eroded and very slick when wet, so on the descent the ribbon matters more than the ground does.

ABOVE THE SADDLE THE MARKERS ARE TWO NAMED HIGH POINTS IN ORDER: Peak 5791 first, then heather benches and meadows above the lake, then Peak 5860 crossed or contoured. YOU SHOULD PASS TWO DISTINCT POINTS BEFORE THE RIDGE BEGINS - arriving at what you take for the base without having crossed them means you are short.

THE BASE ITSELF IS WHERE THE EAST RIDGE RISES OUT OF THE GROUND ABOVE THE LAKE BASIN AND RUNS WEST TOWARD THE SUMMIT. IF THE GROUND AHEAD OF YOU IS A GLACIER RATHER THAN A RIDGE, YOU HAVE CONTOURED PAST THE RIDGE'S FOOT AND JOINED THE STANDARD ROUTE'S APPROACH TO THE ICE. The east ridge is rock and heather with air on both sides; the standard route crosses snow.

Note that the two routes on this peak describe the ridge junctions differently and one says go left where the other says stay right at a fork. They are not the same fork. Follow the description belonging to the route you intend to climb and use the physical markers - a ribbon-marked steep mile, a saddle, then two high points - rather than reconciling the two.

approach_variants.name: Camping at the lake below the ridge
approach_variants.notes: The lake below the ridge is the common overnight for this route and turns it from a very long day into a comfortable two. The camping is in the meadows on the lake's east side and there is reliable water. Parties doing it in a day still pass through the same ground and should treat the lake as the last water before the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Same window
hazards: no water above the lake
a wind-exposed basin camp
loose blocks where the ridge rises out of the benches
committing ridge travel with no easy descent off either side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LAKE THE BASE OF THE EAST RIDGE IS GAINED BY CROSSING OR CONTOURING PEAK 5860 AND CONTINUING ON HEATHER BENCHES ABOVE THE BASIN. The ridge foot is where that benched ground runs out against the crest and the rock begins rising west toward the summit.

THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE ON A CREST, NOT ON A BENCH. Once established the ground should fall away on both sides. Heather benches with a wall above you and the basin below are still the approach.

AND THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS SNOW. IF YOU ARE STEPPING ONTO GLACIER ICE, YOU HAVE CONTOURED ROUND PAST THE FOOT OF THE RIDGE AND ARE ON THE STANDARD ROUTE'S GROUND. Turn back and gain the crest.

Carry water from the lake. There is none on the ridge.

bivy.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
bivy.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
bivy.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek Trailhead near Mazama, gaining the ridge at the Cedar and Early Winters Creek confluence
approach_variants.notes: THIS IS THE ROUTE'S DEFINING LOGISTICAL FACT: IT USES A DIFFERENT TRAILHEAD FROM EVERY OTHER ROUTE ON THE PEAK. Start from the Cedar Creek trailhead near Mazama, at the end of Sandy Butte-Cedar Creek Road #200 about 4.25 miles west of Mazama off SR-20, NOT the Silver Star Creek or Wine Spires pullouts on SR-20 that serve the Glacier and Northeast Ridge routes. Gain the ridge near the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters Creeks, then follow the crest north and west for roughly 3.5 miles to the summit. And note this is SILVER STAR MOUNTAIN IN OKANOGAN COUNTY at 8,876 ft above Washington Pass, not the Silver Star Mountain in Clark County near Vancouver, Washington, which is a different peak entirely.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A descent that finishes at a different trailhead several highway miles from the start
Real crevassed glacier terrain on the descent
A 3.5-mile ridge traverse with sustained route-finding
Two peaks in Washington named Silver Star Mountain; this is the Okanogan County one
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE TRAILHEAD IS THE TEST, AND IT IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL ONE HERE BECAUSE THE TWO OPTIONS ARE SEVERAL HIGHWAY MILES APART. IF YOU PARKED AT A PULLOUT ON SR-20 OPPOSITE THE WINE SPIRES, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG TRAILHEAD FOR THIS ROUTE. The East Ridge is entered from CEDAR CREEK, on the Mazama side. ARRIVAL AT THE RIDGE: gain the crest NEAR THE CONFLUENCE OF CEDAR AND EARLY WINTERS CREEKS. Two named creeks meeting is a feature you can identify by sound in fog, and the ridge rises directly above it. FROM THERE THE HANDRAIL IS THE CREST ITSELF, FOR ROUGHLY 3.5 MILES NORTH AND WEST TO THE SUMMIT. That is a long ridge, and the navigation rule is the same as on any long ridge: keep it under your feet. Sidehilling off either side of a 3.5-mile crest at 5.9-plus is how a day here goes wrong. AND THE DESCENT LANDS YOU AT THE OTHER TRAILHEAD, WHICH IS THE PLANNING PROBLEM THIS ROUTE SETS: from the summit, downclimb or rope down a short distance onto the SILVER STAR GLACIER, descend it west and northwest toward BURGUNDY COL, then over the col onto the Burgundy Col climbers' trail, which drops to Highway 20 near milepost 166 about 4 miles from Washington Pass. THAT IS SEVERAL MILES OF HIGHWAY FROM THE CEDAR CREEK TRAILHEAD YOU STARTED AT. Arrange a shuttle before you leave, not afterwards. CARRY GLACIER TRAVEL GEAR, and an axe and crampons in early season: the descent crosses real crevassed glacier terrain, not just snow slopes.

approach_variants.name: As for the West Ridge and South Face to the Terror Glacier, then across the glacier below the South Face to the moat under its eastern end
approach_variants.notes:
Shares the Goodell Creek trailhead and the same long approach as the West Ridge and South Face: about 4 easy miles along the creek to roughly 1,600 ft and the last reliable water, then a steep switchback-free climbers' boot path grinding up 3,400-4,000 ft of forested hillside with no water to timberline around 5,000-5,200 ft, then a rising traverse on meadow, slab and snow to the broad saddle at 6,000-6,200 ft with camp just below it in Terror Creek Basin.

From camp the ground to the base runs across glacier-scoured slabs and onto the Terror Glacier beneath Inspiration's South Face. This is consistently rated one of the longer, more strenuous approaches in the North Cascades, and reaching the base alone typically consumes most of a full day.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A low-angle but heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
Sustained exposure once the ridge crest is gained
Loose, dirty rock on the lower pitches before the ridge crest
No established descent; the way down is 12-14 rappels on other routes' ground
An approach that consumes most of a full day before the climb starts
Parties commonly finish the exit after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ROUTE YOU REACH BY KEEPING GOING, AND THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE STRONGEST THING ABOUT IT. Unlike the West Ridge and South Face lines, the East Ridge start is reached by CONTINUING ACROSS THE GLACIER BELOW THE SOUTH FACE, past the South Face start, and crossing the moat or bergschrund toward the face's eastern end.

SO, IN ORDER, WHAT YOU PASS AND MUST NOT STOP AT: first the BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END with a 300 ft gully above it, which is the West Ridge. Then the SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS AT THE LOWER-LEFT CORNER OF THE SOUTH FACE where rock meets ice, which is the South Face. If you have roped up at either, you have stopped one or two routes short of this one. Keep walking east along the foot of the face before crossing onto rock.

ARRIVAL: above the moat the route opens with a few hundred feet of broken gullies, vegetated ledges and blocky rock, usually simul-climbed, toward a notch that puts you on the ridge. The sustained, exposed climbing on better rock starts once the crest is gained.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN: nothing published names the notch or gives it a height, and this is a Grade IV 5.9 with very light traffic. What is recorded is its POSITION IN A SEQUENCE, which is why the base finding is written as a sequence rather than as a feature.

AND THE FACT THAT SHOULD BE READ BEFORE STARTING, NOT AFTER: there is NO established East Ridge descent. The way down combines the upper West Ridge and the South Face, the same descent West Ridge climbers use, because the East Ridge is reported as distinctly poorer, looser rock for descending and nobody downclimbs it. So you will have to find the other two routes' ground anyway, in the dark, tired, from above.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the south-face basin, then the heather-and-talus slope to the ESE notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead at I-90 exit 52, about 3,000 ft, follow the PCT north through Commonwealth Basin and up the Kendall Ridge switchbacks. At roughly 5.5 to 5.7 miles you cross the Kendall Katwalk, the exposed cut in the cliff band most parties use as a progress checkpoint.

Continue north past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, the last reliable water before the high basin, and on to the foot of Bumblebee Pass. A short, steep, unmaintained climbers' path with loose tread climbs to the 5,400 ft pass, then drops down the north side into the open basin directly below Mount Thomson's south face — the same basin West Ridge parties camp in.

Roughly eight miles one way with about 3,600 ft of cumulative gain, since the up-and-over at Bumblebee adds height beyond the net summit gain. Three to five hours car to basin, nine to eleven hours round trip is typical.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk when icy or windy
Loose tread on the unmaintained Bumblebee Pass path, awkward with a pack
Loose talus and minor route-finding on the slope to the notch
A short but exposed class 4 step at the summit, downclimbed or rappelled on the way back
A long day with an up-and-over on the return
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE BASIN, LOOK FOR THE STEEP HEATHER-AND-TALUS SLOPE THAT LEADS TO AN OBVIOUS NOTCH AT ABOUT 5,600 FT ON THE EAST-SOUTHEAST RIDGE. Heather and talus rather than clean rock is the signal you are on the correct slope; the West Ridge side is scree and gendarmes.

THE ALTITUDE IS THE DISCRIMINATOR BETWEEN THE PEAK'S TWO ROUTES, AND IT IS WORTH SETTING YOUR ALTIMETER FOR: this notch is at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side. The West Ridge notch is at about 5,960 ft on the other end of the mountain. Roughly 360 ft and a full traverse of the peak separate them.

WHAT FOLLOWS CONFIRMS IT: from the notch, scramble up and TRAVERSE LEFT along the ridge crest on mostly class 2-3 ground to the base of the final summit block. Easy scrambling with a leftward traverse is right for this route. Chimneys and fifth-class corners are the West Ridge.

AND THE ROUTE ENDS AT ONE SPECIFIC OBSTACLE, WHICH IS THE BEST CONFIRMATION OF ALL: a short, exposed 20 ft CLASS 4 STEP guarding the true summit. Most parties protect it with a rope or a handline. If you reached a summit without meeting that step, you are on a false one.

USEFUL CONTEXT: this is the easiest way up the peak and it is also the standard descent for West Ridge parties, so a party coming down at you is normal rather than a sign of a mistake.

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle, then east behind Pinnacle to the Castle-Pinnacle col
approach_variants.notes:
From the Reflection Lakes trailhead, follow the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail 1.3 miles and about 1,000-1,050 ft to the Pinnacle-Plummer saddle. From there, continue on unmaintained boot path east and behind Pinnacle toward Castle Peak to reach the Castle-Pinnacle col. That segment typically takes roughly 2 to 3 hours and about 1,500 ft of gain.

The east ridge rises directly from the col. Pitch 1 scrambles mostly fourth-class ground to a belay ledge at a large dead tree. Pitch 2 is the crux: blocky mid-fifth climbing with an exposed traverse to a sandy belay bench carrying a fixed rappel anchor down the south face. Pitch 3 is mellow ground to the true summit, often simul-climbed or soloed.

Loose rock and scree are a serious and repeatedly noted concern throughout.

Descent is either the rappel off the pitch-2 bench down the south face, or over the summit and down the standard south-side scramble to Pinnacle Saddle — the second is only sensible if the leader already knows that line.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock and scree throughout — a serious and repeatedly noted concern on this route
An old, unreliable piton at the pitch-2 crux traverse
Pitch 3 can run longer than a 60 m rope from the pitch-2 anchor to the true summit
Exposure on the pitch-2 traverse with sparse natural protection
Rockfall onto the col and onto anyone approaching The Castle from the same place
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE CASTLE-PINNACLE COL, NOT PINNACLE SADDLE, AND THE TWO ARE HALF A MILE AND ONE PEAK APART. The maintained trail ends at the saddle; you keep going EAST, on boot path, behind Pinnacle, toward The Castle.

WHEN YOU ARE AT THE COL YOU CANNOT MISS THE ROUTE: THE EAST RIDGE RISES DIRECTLY FROM IT. If you are at a col and no defined ridge crest goes up from it toward Pinnacle, you are at the wrong col.

THE CONFIRMATIONS ARE OBJECTS, IN ORDER, AND EACH IS ONE OF A KIND ON THIS ROUTE:
PITCH 1 — mostly fourth-class scrambling ending at a belay ledge AT A LARGE DEAD TREE. One tree, one ledge. If you have run out a full pitch and found no tree, you are not on the ridge.
PITCH 2 — blocky mid-fifth climbing with an exposed traverse, an OLD PITON partway up, ending on a SANDY BELAY BENCH with a FIXED RAPPEL ANCHOR dropping the south face. Piton, then sand, then an anchor, in that order. Treat the piton as a backup clip and not as protection.
PITCH 3 — mellow ground to the true summit.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS AT THE COL, BECAUSE TWO PEAKS SHARE IT: The Castle's own route also starts here. IF WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU IS A CRACK-CHIMNEY SYSTEM ON A ROCK FLANK RATHER THAN A DEFINED RIDGE CREST, YOU ARE FACING THE CASTLE AND YOU NEED TO TURN AROUND — Pinnacle is the other side of the col.

THE SECOND NEGATIVE, FOR PARTIES WHO CAME UP THE PEAK'S OTHER LINE BEFORE: this route does not start from Pinnacle Saddle and does not touch the south-face chute. If you are on scree below the south face you are on the scramble route.

ROPE PLANNING AS PART OF THE FINDING: from the pitch-2 bench, a 60 m rope may come up short of the true summit on pitch 3, depending on where the anchor sits; the ground above is easy, so this is rarely a problem. The rappel from that bench down the south face is the quicker of the two descents.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead to Lake Ingalls, then the north-east notch gully
approach_variants.notes:
Drive and walk exactly as for the South Ridge: Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of FR 9737, right at the low fork onto Ingalls Way #1390, left at the higher fork where Longs Pass branches off, over Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, and on to Lake Ingalls at roughly 6,400-6,480 ft, about 4 miles and the last water.

The two routes part company ABOVE the lake. Skirt the lake on its left (west and north) side and cross a band of slabs to reach a large talus gully. A boot path shows itself in patches through the talus. This gully runs more directly than the South Ridge slabs and is steeper and looser — expect Class 2-3 scree with real rockfall potential if anyone is above you.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the approach gully holds snow well into summer and is often climbed on snow
hazards: Steep loose talus in the approach gully, worse with parties above
Lingering snow in the gully into midsummer
No water above Lake Ingalls
A 60 m rope comes up short on the shared South Ridge rappel descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the east ridge of the NORTH peak, and the notch it starts from is the one on the far side of the summit from the South Ridge — between the North peak's eastern terminus and the separate East peak. Two obvious gullies rise off the ground above Lake Ingalls to two different notches on the same mountain, and choosing between them is the whole navigational problem here. The South Ridge's gully leads to the notch between North and South; this one leads round to the north-east side.

Going up, the arrival test is a change in the rock rather than a change in angle. Climb the obvious gully — usually snow early in the season — until you reach an odd, anomalous rock layer that does not match what you have been walking over. From there move about fifteen feet LEFT and you are at the base. An alternative published description of the same spot has you looking RIGHT for a smaller third-class gully and starting where it stiffens into easy fifth-class rock; either way the marker is the change in the rock underfoot, not the height on the ridge.

Confirmation once you are moving: there are slings with rap rings at the top of the first pitch, used as the belay for the second. If you climbed a rope length and found nothing fixed, doubt the start.

Touch test: the rock through here is serpentine — greenish, slick, and quite unlike granite friction. That slickness is normal for this peak and is not a sign you are on harder ground than intended.

POSITIVE MARKER that reads like a mistake: a couple of pitches up, after passing a mid-sized gendarme on its right, you are forced to downclimb about twenty feet of fourth class into a notch in the ridge. That downclimb is correct here and is evidence you are ON the East Ridge, not that you have gone wrong. The easy knife-edge traverse midway along is the same kind of confirmation.

The descent is the South Ridge rappels, ending at three bolts at the top of that route — so the 60 m rope warning from the South Ridge applies to this climb too even though you never touch its approach.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek and Lucky Ridge to the Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130, near 1,200 ft. Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly six miles to McAllister Camp, then continue past Tricouni Camp around mile eight.

A ford of Thunder Creek at a log jam is normally required and the bridge near McAllister Camp has been out in past years — check current NPS conditions rather than assuming a dry crossing.

Leave the maintained trail at Tricouni Camp and climb the climbers' path up LUCKY RIDGE, the ridge between McAllister and Thunder creeks: roughly 4,000 ft of gain over a couple of miles through brush and devil's club, with two short cliff-band scrambles. Camp near the northeast corner of the proglacial lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier around 6,000 ft, with the icefall in view above.

Rope up around 7,000 ft on the flat snow shelf and climb the glacier's EASTERN margin — the central icefall splits the lower and upper tiers and has caught parties who drifted climber's-left.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August, while enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses; by late September the glacier is largely bare and the pass can be bullet ice and loose rock
hazards: A mandatory Thunder Creek ford with a powerful current, worse later in the day as snowmelt rises
The central icefall on the Borealis Glacier — stay on the eastern margin
Hidden crevasses that open both vertically and horizontally, and moats where snow pulls off rock, worst late season
Cloud and fog that move in on this glacier routinely
A long, remote approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS LUCKY PASS AT ABOUT 7,200 FT, AND THE PASS IDENTIFIES ITSELF BY WHAT IT DIVIDES: it is the notch at the HEAD of the Borealis Glacier between Primus and Tricouni Peak, and the route to Tricouni splits off east from the same spot. If the ground only falls away on one side of you, you are not at the pass.

FROM THE PASS THE EAST SLOPE RISES DIRECTLY WEST — a bouldery class 3 slope, not a ridge crest and not a face. Parties describe the climbing above the pass as nothing more than a walk, which is the honest summary: the difficulty of this route is the creek, the brushy ridge and the glacier, all of which are behind you by the time you are at the pass.

THE COUNTING TEST IS THE FALSE SUMMIT, AND IT IS THE ONE THING ABOVE THE PASS THAT CAN GO WRONG. A false summit stands at about 8,270 ft. YOU TRAVERSE CLIMBER'S-LEFT AROUND IT — you do not go over it — and the true summit at 8,508 ft is beyond. If you reached a high point without having traversed around anything, you are 240 ft short.

NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER ROUTES, AND IT WORKS BEFORE YOU EVER LEAVE THE CAR: this route is the only one reached from the THUNDER CREEK side. The South Ridge is reached from the Eldorado ice cap across five glaciers, and the North Ridge from an unnamed glacier north of the peak. If you walked up a creek trail from a campground on Highway 20, you are on this one.

bivy.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
bivy.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
bivy.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

bivy.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
bivy.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
bivy.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

bivy.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

bivy.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
bivy.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether it is usable at all depends on snow: early season gives flat platforms, late season leaves broken rock. Treat it as an emergency or opportunistic bivy and carry the means to melt water.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
bivy.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared

bivy.name: Bivy at toe of Borealis Glacier

approach_variants.name: Crescent Creek Basin to the Eye Col
approach_variants.notes: From the basin camp below Mount Terror around 6,050 ft, head west and drop about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek. Traverse north through Crescent Creek Basin, keeping the party together through the scree to limit rockfall and hugging the cliffs, then make a rising traverse beneath the Eye Col gully that carries you past an adjacent buttress rather than straight up at it. The notch at about 7,400 ft is reached by continuing PAST a gully that would otherwise force a rappel — that decoy gully is the thing to walk by. The last stretch to the col is scree you walk up rather than rock you climb.
approach_variants.season: Mid Jul-early Sep
hazards: Constantly falling rock in the Eye Col gully
Steep, loose gully climbing with genuine route-finding uncertainty on this south side
Disorienting in cloud or low light — the south side carries comparatively sparse route information
A multi-day committing approach over The Barrier before any of this begins
approach_variants.baseFinding: CHOCKSTONES ARE THE GATE, AND THE VIEW THROUGH THE COL IS THE CONFIRMATION. Going up toward the Eye Col, the small chockstones low in the gully present no real problem and are scrambled past; higher, the LARGER chockstones put the ground into fifth class, and that size change is where the rope comes out. If you are still stepping over rubble you are low; if you are stemming past a jammed block you are at the transition. The Eye Col itself is the notch between East and West Twin Needle at about 7,400 ft, gained on scree from the south, and it announces itself: from it you get your first sight through the gap to the Northern Pickets, and East Twin Needle stands directly above it. Know which line you intend before you leave the col — the Eye Col sits on the WEST side of East Twin Needle, while the peak's hard, tremendously exposed east arete is on the opposite flank and is reached along the ridge from the east, not from here.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the south side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

approach_variants.name: Glacier Basin Trail to the east notch
approach_variants.notes: Reach the Monte Cristo townsite on foot or by bike from Barlow Pass, then take the Glacier Basin Trail less than a mile. The spire stands on your left above the trail, roughly 2,000 ft above the basin. When it makes sense, leave the trail and start up toward the base of the ridge — a snowfield early in the season, extremely loose talus once it has gone. Snow or talus leads up a narrowing gully to the lower col, steepening as it goes, commonly 35 to 45 degrees, with the final couloir steeper and more exposed than anything below it. Best done early in the year while the gully still holds snow: melted out it is loose scree badly exposed to rockfall and a poor outing in late summer. Fixed stations exist in the gully and parties have used them to bypass melted-out gaps on the way down.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul, on snow
hazards: Serious rockfall in the approach gully once the snow has melted out
Steep, exposed snow in the final couloir — crampons, and a second tool is worth having
Cornices and hanging snow slabs above the left-hand branch of the gully
Moats and a schrund where the gully snow melts back from the rock
Loose rock on the route itself, especially low on each pitch and on the east aspect
approach_variants.baseFinding: THERE ARE TWO COLS, AND YOU ROPE UP AT THE SECOND ONE. The snow gully out of Glacier Basin delivers you to the LOWER col, and that is not where the climbing starts. From it, scramble around the SOUTH face on very loose talus to the upper, east notch, and belay there: the first pitch climbs the east side of the spire a short way, then downclimbs a 5.5 crack about twenty feet to a ramp. Two things confirm you are in the right gully on the way up. Where it narrows, a branch heads LEFT and up — that one leads to the northwest ramp of Wilmans Peak, a different objective entirely, and it carries cornices and hanging snow slabs; the left branch at the narrowing is the documented wrong turn. And once the gully is melted out, an old mine shaft sits in it with yellow tailings all around, open enough to look down into. Confirm again at the top: this summit is a table-top barely larger than the three-piton anchor on it. A summit you can walk about on is one of the other spires.

bivy.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
bivy.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
bivy.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

approach_variants.name: Cutthroat Creek trail #483 from the Cutthroat Lake trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
THIS IS NOT THE APPROACH TO CUTTHROAT PEAK, and the confusion is the commonest way people waste a morning here. The peak is approached from an unmarked highway pullout west of the pass with no maintained trail at all. This wall is reached from the signed Cutthroat Lake trailhead at about 4,500 ft, a mile up a spur road off the highway east of the pass, with a kiosk and a large gravel lot.

Start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek trail. After a short distance — the first few minutes, still on the old roadbed running parallel to the main trail — leave it on the climbers' left and start uphill into the forest.

From there it is a climbers' path through light brush, trees and talus, trending climbers' right toward the buttress, until you reach a flat area beneath the cliff. Reckon on the better part of an hour to two depending on how well you read it.

A warning about the markers: there are cairns, and they are not all route markers. Trend right toward the wall and use the buttress itself rather than the rock piles.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September; the corners seep earliest in the season, and access is gone entirely while the highway is gated shut
hazards: Shares its name with a peak reached from a different trailhead with no trail at all
Two route starts about fifty feet apart on one slab platform
Cairns on the approach are not all route markers
The descent is the crux of the day; the obvious gully below the notch is the wrong one and is loose
Corners seep early in the season and stay wet after rain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark at the foot of the wall is a GRANITE PATIO — a flat slab platform under the cliff where two routes begin about fifty feet apart. Everything here is decided by that patio.

THIS ROUTE IS THE LEFT-HAND OF THE PAIR. From the patio, head UP AND LEFT into a corner. The route to the right of the patio, roughly fifty feet away, is a different line at 5.9 that wanders far more.

CONFIRMATION IS A STRIPED CORNER, and it is the landmark to hold in your head for the whole climb rather than only at the base. There is a distinctly banded corner feature used as the on-route check throughout this line; it seeps water early in the season, which is itself a useful sign that you are looking at the right thing. If you never pass it, you are not on this route.

The hardest and best pitch is high: a hundred-foot RIGHT-FACING CORNER that varies from hands to fingers, secure but sustained. Reaching a long right-facing corner near the top is the strongest confirmation the route offers.

NEGATIVE MARKERS, both of them real. If you have walked UPHILL from the patio and are standing at a small OUTCROP OF TREES with an open book just left of it, you are at the third route on this wall, a hundred and fifty feet climbers' left and above this one, and it is a full grade harder. And if you started to the RIGHT of the patio and your second pitch ends on a ledge with two big gnarled trees, you are on the 5.9.

The descent is where this wall actually hurts people, so study it before you leave the ground: from the topout, reach the notch between the westernmost and the higher central buttress, marked by a slung horn or tree, rappel one rope length over a chockstone tunnel to a dirty ramp with a small cave, then find the UPWARD-trending gully or ledge system on skier's LEFT. Do not descend the obvious loose gully directly below the notch.

wa_eldorado_peak_eldorado_glacier_nw.descent_text: From the summit, do not reverse the couloir — descend via the standard East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier route: downclimb the knife-edge summit ridge, drop through the gap in the lower East Ridge, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, then descend the Eldorado Glacier back toward Roush Basin and Eldorado Creek Basin, finishing on the timbered climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead (see the East Ridge route for full detail). This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappels required on the descent itself — one party even skied the knife-edge ridge and glacier on the way down. Rappelling comes up on this route only on the approach/entry into the couloir, not on the summit descent: one party used a 40-meter rappel off the Inspiration Glacier side to drop into the couloir's gully system, anchored on two pitons with some newish tat, and noted a full 60m rope would get a party through everything in one rappel rather than needing to downclimb the remainder — but again, this is describing getting INTO the route, not descending FROM the summit. Because the descent is the shared East Ridge walk-off, treat glacier crevasse hazard and knife-edge icing exactly as on that route, and carry a rope for the glacier crossings regardless of whether any rappelling was used higher on the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Rappel off the ice cap into the Marble Creek cirque, then the couloir splitting the northwest face
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 near 2,100 ft, the log crossing of the Cascade River about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield around 4,500 ft, and on into Eldorado Creek Basin.

From there this route diverges: rather than continuing over the ridge into Roush Basin for the standard camp, traverse the Roush Divide and ascend the Eldorado Glacier, trending toward the mountain's northwest side and the wild Marble Creek Cirque. High camp is either in Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek Basin or at the Eldorado-Inspiration site near 7,500-7,600 ft.

The usual way in is from above: follow the East Ridge glacier track to about 8,100 ft, traverse to the notch between the North Ridge and the first rock spire — the same notch sometimes called the Eldorado-Dean's Spire or Dean's Tower col — and RAPPEL from it into the cirque below. A full 60 m rope gets a party through in one; parties on shorter ropes have downclimbed the remainder. One party used a belayed downclimb of about 35 m plus two 30 m rappels to land within about 100 yards of the couloir. One single-push ascent took roughly five hours from the trailhead to the couloir's base.

The alternative is simply to continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft.
approach_variants.season: Highly conditions-dependent. Spring, roughly April to early May, can give steep thin ice and moderate mixed; mid-to-late summer the couloir is usually mostly snow with a few ice steps; a good cold snap in late October or November can bring in firm, well-bonded ice. Grade moves with it, roughly AI2-3 up to WI3 in lean conditions
hazards: An extreme funnel: the whole face feeds into a narrow confined couloir, so anything the leader dislodges lands on the belay
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers and a long featureless crossing that is disorienting in whiteout
A moat or bergschrund where the glacier meets the couloir, widening through the summer
Cornices and crevasses at the couloir's exit near the knife-edge ridge
Rappelling the couloir is the only retreat once you are high, and it is slow — the practical escape is over the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ONCE YOU ARE IN THE CIRQUE THE ROUTE IS OBVIOUS, AND TWO SEPARATE PARTIES SAY SO IN NEARLY THE SAME WORDS: on looking up from below the rappel, one recorded instantly seeing the line — steep, fat and unmistakable. THE COULOIR SPLITS THE NORTHWEST FACE and there is nothing else in the cirque it could be confused with. So the navigation problem is not identifying the couloir; it is getting into the cirque at all.

THE NOTCH IS THE THING TO FIND, AND IT IS SHARED WITH THE NORTH RIDGE. It is the obvious gap between the North Ridge and the FIRST ROCK SPIRE, at about 8,100 ft, reached by traversing north from the East Ridge glacier track. AT THAT NOTCH THE TWO ROUTES GO OPPOSITE WAYS: rappel down the far side into the cirque and you are on this route; climb steep snow up onto the rock crest and you are on the North Ridge.

THE BASE ITSELF IS THE TRANSITION AT ABOUT 7,800 FT where the couloir meets the glacier — which is the usual place to find the moat or bergschrund, and it widens as summer goes on. Rope up on the glacier BEFORE you reach it.

ONE BRANCH POINT WORTH KNOWING: at least one party climbed a steep line just to CLIMBER'S LEFT of the main gut of the couloir rather than the gut itself. Both go; the gut is the route as described.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMBING: the line runs from about 7,800 ft to about 8,800 ft, roughly 1,000 ft, commonly described as eight 60 m pitches, and the character is a succession of short ice steps broken by lower-angle snow rather than one continuous wall. Steps around 70-80 degrees with occasional near-vertical bulges for a body length is right; sustained vertical ice for a full pitch is not this route in any season.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer.
