Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

approach_variants.name: Down the Inspiration Glacier to the ice-couloir notch, then snow onto the crest
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Eldorado one to the high camp on the Inspiration Glacier: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the river crossing, the steep boot path, the boulder field, Eldorado Creek basin, and up the Eldorado Glacier to the East Ridge camp near 7,500-7,600 ft.

From camp, the route goes DOWN before it goes up. Descend the Inspiration Glacier toward the notch used as the rappel point for the Northwest Ice Couloir — an obvious gap between the North Ridge and the first rock spire, at about 8,100 ft — and climb steep snow from there onto the North Ridge proper.

The ridge follows generally solid rock on its EASTERN aspect with good friction and incut holds, so the exposure toward the glacier side stays modest while the drop to the west is dramatic. Near the top you can finish directly up steeper ice and rock or join the classic East Ridge finish.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ridge is largely snow-free
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier both on the way to the notch and on the way back
Loose rock in places along the crest
Wind exposure high on the ridge
Wet rock, which raises the difficulty of this route noticeably rather than marginally
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE NOTCH IS THE LANDMARK, AND IT IS SHARED WITH ANOTHER ROUTE — WHICH IS WHY THE TEST IS WHAT YOU DO THERE, NOT WHERE YOU STAND. The gap you are looking for is the obvious notch between the North Ridge and the FIRST ROCK SPIRE along the crest, at about 8,100 ft, reached by descending the Inspiration Glacier from the East Ridge camp. That same notch is the rappel station for the Northwest Ice Couloir. SO: AT THE NOTCH, IF YOU ARE PUTTING A ROPE THROUGH AN ANCHOR AND GOING DOWN INTO THE CIRQUE ON THE OTHER SIDE, YOU ARE ON THE NORTHWEST COULOIR. IF YOU ARE CLIMBING STEEP SNOW UP OUT OF THE NOTCH ONTO A ROCK CREST, YOU ARE ON THE NORTH RIDGE. Two routes, one notch, opposite directions. THE ROCK TELLS YOU WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST TO BE ON, AND THAT IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE ANSWER. This route stays on the ridge's EAST side — clean, solid rock with good friction and incut holds, snow on the northeast face below you keeping the exposure feeling manageable. IF THE DROP IS ON BOTH SIDES OR YOU HAVE DRIFTED WEST INTO SERIOUS AIR AND WORSE ROCK, COME BACK EAST. WHAT IS HONESTLY NOT PUBLISHED: no source names a single fixed starting point on this crest — one description says simply to climb the path of least resistance from your point of choice on the ridge. The notch is the findable thing; above it, the route is defined by staying east on the good rock rather than by a marked start. The crux moves are 5.7, so do not read a hard move as evidence you are off route.

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp

approach_variants.name: Over the ice cap to Dorado Needle Col, then down into Marble Creek Cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, and gain the Eldorado Glacier. Most parties treat this as three days: approach, climb, exit, with a base camp at the East Ridge site near 7,500 ft or on the western margin of the Eldorado Glacier.

The defining feature of the approach is that you must get DOWN to the base. The line runs from the ice cap across to the Dorado Needle Col area, then a loose fourth-class downclimb — accounts on the neighbouring line describe rappelling, steep névé downclimbing and moat work over roughly 1,000 ft of descent — into the MARBLE CREEK CIRQUE on Eldorado's west side, and the toe of the ridge is at the bottom of that.

This is a long day: parties have taken up to about 17 hours round trip from the East Ridge base camp, and an unplanned bivouac is a real possibility if the middle section goes slowly.

A warning from parties who have done it: published route descriptions for this arête have been called inaccurate and sandbagged, and at least one party went off route immediately as a result. Trust the terrain over the topo.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer once fully snow-free, with maximum daylight for a long climbing day; Cascade River Road is often not open until late June
hazards: A loose fourth-class downclimb into the cirque that has to be reversed or bypassed at the end of the day
Rockfall and loose rock over the full length of the arête, including the opening pitch
Large moats on both sides of the ridge at its foot, and a building-sized snow remnant to keep clear of
Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers that open through the summer
A confusing middle section where slow progress turns into a bivouac
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE AT THIS ROUTE BY GOING DOWN, NOT UP, AND THAT IS THE FIRST CHECK. The toe of the arête sits at roughly 6,000 ft in the Marble Creek Cirque, reached only by a loose fourth-class downclimb off the Dorado Needle Col area. If your approach has been a continuous ascent from camp, you have not reached this route.

THE SEQUENCE AT THE BOTTOM IS COUNTABLE AND IT IS THE POSITIVE TEST: from the snow at the base, spooky scrambling on GLACIER-POLISHED SLABS leads to a STEEP, OPEN CHIMNEY FEATURE. Slabs first, chimney second. The rock climbing proper begins a couple of hundred feet above the toe of the ridge on its NORTH side.

THE FIRST PITCH CONFIRMS IT BY BEING BAD. The opening pitch is unbelievably loose 5.6 on the ridge crest. If your first pitch is clean and solid, you are on the wrong feature.

THERE IS A HARDER LINE ON THE SAME WALL AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: the SOUTHWEST ARÊTE — climbed in full only in 2022, about 3,600 ft at grade V 5.10 — takes the same cirque approach and a different arête. This route is the shorter 1969 line at about 2,800 ft, sustained 5.6-5.7 with an old-school 5.8 crux. IF THE CLIMBING IS RELENTLESSLY HARDER THAN MID-FIFTH FROM LOW DOWN, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG ARÊTE.

CONFIRM AT THE CRUX: a set of rocky towers ends in a face traverse protected by a SINGLE IN-SITU PITON. One piton, one traverse. That is the hardest move on the route and it is the landmark for the upper half.
