approach_variants.name: Sourdough Mountain Trail to the Stetattle Ridge crest
approach_variants.notes: From the Diablo trailhead behind the pool building, climb the Sourdough Mountain Trail's switchbacks; take care at the Sourdough Creek crossing in spring, where the bridge can be no more than a thin snow bridge over high water. The turn-off is an UNMARKED junction somewhere around 4,300 to 4,400 ft — it is given variously between 4,000 and 4,400 ft, so treat the elevation as approximate and the feature as the thing to find. From it, a left turn takes you straight north up the ridge crest immediately WEST of Sourdough Creek rather than continuing toward the Sourdough Mountain lookout. You break out of the trees just before reaching the crest, at around 6,000 ft. On the ridge, keep on or southwest of the top: the northeast side is very steep.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Sourdough Creek can be a thin snow bridge over high water in spring
The northeast side of Stetattle Ridge drops away steeply the length of the walk
Brush, mossy micro-cliffs and steep impassable treed slopes on the ground around the summit obstacle
A long committing ridge walk with a large drop to Elephant Butte's base
approach_variants.baseFinding: TREE LINE AT ABOUT 6,000 FT CONFIRMS THE CREST; A CAIRN AND A DROP TO THE WEST CONFIRM THE HIGH POINT. Take the unmarked junction and go straight north up the ridge crest just west of Sourdough Creek — if the creek is on your left as you climb, you are on the wrong rib. You break out of the trees just below the crest around 6,000 ft. The high point of Stetattle Ridge, near 6,495 ft, is deceptive because several knobs crowd the area; a cairn should mark the true one and there is a noticeable drop to the west of it. Between there and Elephant Butte the ridge loses a great deal of height to a saddle, with cliffs and steep treed slopes on both flanks and one short class 3 step that is two high-step mantle moves. At the Butte itself the direct line over the top takes a short overhung fifth-class move, poor with an overnight pack; the alternative drops well off the crest and traverses through brush and mossy micro-cliffs. Which side that bypass takes is NOT reliably recorded anywhere — scout it rather than committing on a guess.

bivy.name: Sourdough Camp, Sourdough Creek
bivy.notes: A little over four miles up from Diablo, this is the only designated camp on the lower half of the approach and it exists mainly to break a brutal climb. The Sourdough Mountain trail gains close to five thousand feet in a bit over five miles and is routinely called the hardest maintained trail in the park; the first three and a half miles are relentless forest switchbacks with nothing to drink. Stopping here makes the second day the good one. Note that the climbers' line for Elephant Butte does not continue to the lookout at all — it leaves this trail at an unmarked junction somewhere around four thousand three hundred to four thousand four hundred feet and turns north up the ridge crest west of the creek. No elevation is recorded for the camp because no confident figure was found. Both this camp and the trail it sits on have been closed by fire for most of the last three years; confirm before planning around it.
bivy.water: Sourdough Creek runs at the camp and is the first water on the whole climb from Diablo — the lower trail has essentially none. Early in the season the crossing can be bridged by snow, which is worth treating with care rather than walking onto.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, collected at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing process. This is a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night rather than open ground, so a walk-up can be refused. A BEAR CANISTER IS REQUIRED here through the main season; the park lends them free at the permit desk. No fires. Pets are not allowed at the camp.
bivy.capacity: A few tent spots only, with a hard limit of FOUR people on the site. That is the smallest party cap of anything on this approach and it rules the camp out for a larger group entirely.

bivy.name: Sourdough Mountain summit ground
bivy.notes: The summit sits a little over six thousand feet directly above Diablo Lake, and parties heading out along the ridge in snow conditions have used it as a first night. It is included because the road to Diablo is west of the seasonal highway gate and therefore open all year, which makes this one of the few high camps in the corridor reachable in winter — a late-March overnight on continuous snow is a known way to do the ridge, with the caveat that spring sun softens the slopes badly by mid-morning. For a summer ascent of the butte it is a detour, since the climbers' line leaves the trail well below the lookout and never comes here. It also carries the same warning as everything else: the trail, both designated camps, and the Sourdough and Elephant Butte zones have all been closed by an active fire in the drainage, on top of an earlier fire that shut the trail for two and a half years before it briefly reopened. Check the closure status first; it is the single thing most likely to end this trip.
bivy.water: Melted snow in the cold months, which is when this site makes sense. In summer there is nothing at the summit and the tarns further along the ridge are the supply.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Sourdough cross-country zone: six people per party, six parties a night, walk-up only. The lookout building is closed and camping is not permitted at it, so the site is the open ground near the top rather than the structure. Same durable-surface, no-fire and no-meadow rules as the rest of the zone.
bivy.capacity: Open ground near the summit, a small party at a time. In winter and spring it is a snow camp with no defined pitch at all.

bivy.name: Stetattle Ridge tarn camps
bivy.notes: This is the camp for the peak. Once the climbers' line breaks out of the trees near six thousand feet the ridge runs north-west in a long open crest of heather, gravel and tarns, and parties simply pick a spot. The best-documented ascent camped beside a late-season tarn at about six and a half thousand feet and went for the summit from there. It is still a long way: from the ridge high point the ground drops something like fifteen hundred feet before you regain that and another thousand to the top, and a full trip is closer to twenty miles and ten thousand feet of gain and loss over two nights. Several strong parties have reached the ridge in a single push and turned round because the butte was still too far. The north-east side of the crest is very steep, so stay on it or just south-west of it. Snow-free is roughly late July into September, which is unhelpfully the same window in which the water disappears.
bivy.water: Small tarns and snowmelt ponds scattered over the ridge — plentiful in late June, and the single best reason to come early. THEY DO DRY. By August in a warm year parties report water on the ridge becoming a real problem, and which pools survive latest is not documented anywhere reliable. Late in the season carry enough to camp dry.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. There is NO Stetattle Ridge zone — the ridge falls between the Sourdough zone and the Elephant Butte zone, and your permit has to name the one you will actually sleep in. Both allow a party of six and six parties a night. Neither is reservable in advance: they are walk-up zones, issued in person, with a share of the allocation held for same-day and next-day pickup. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow pockets that make the ridge look inviting, and not within a hundred feet of a tarn. NO FIRES in a cross-country zone. Waste in a cathole, or carried out on snow and bare rock. A canister is not formally required in these two zones, but the ridge is open ground with nothing to hang from, so bring one anyway.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country ground rather than sites. Small grassy pockets and gravel benches recur the length of the ridge, easily enough for the zone's limit of six parties, and no two accounts stop in the same place.

bivy.name: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
bivy.notes: There is no camp at the base of this peak and inventing one would be dishonest — parties sleep where the daylight runs out, on whatever flat ground the shoulder offers. From the ridge the summit itself is not technical, more a broad lump on a crest than a spire, and the standard finish takes its gentle west side at walking-to-scrambling ground. The EAST ridge is a different proposition entirely and has been described by a party crossing it on a long Picket traverse as among the hardest ground of that whole trip, needing roped downclimbs and rappels — so do not read the easy summit as an easy mountain from every side. The named benches near the pass east of the butte belong to the traverse route rather than to this approach, and a party coming from Stetattle Ridge will not pass them. NO ELEVATION IS RECORDED: no account that slept on this shoulder coming from Stetattle Ridge stated one, and the figures published for the traverse-side benches describe different ground.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small pools, entirely seasonal. There is no dependable source and nothing to plan on. Fill on the ridge before committing to the descent toward the butte.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Elephant Butte cross-country zone: six people maximum, six parties a night, walk-up only from Marblemount. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail and out of sight of both, which up here is automatic. Durable surfaces only, no fires, waste packed out above treeline.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no name. Parties travelling the crest report finding flat ground on the shoulder and on the benches near the pass east of the peak, tight enough that three tents felt crowded. Treat it as somewhere you stop, not somewhere you book.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass Trail to the Ellation crag
approach_variants.notes: Drive SR-542 east about 46 miles from the interstate, then turn onto Forest Road 32 and follow it to the road end at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead. Mamie Peak is the large, complex mass of granite standing directly above the trailhead, and its tiered walls come into view from the trail within a few minutes of setting off. Walk the trail roughly four minutes to a clearing where a large white boulder is visible perched several hundred feet overhead, and leave the trail there. Reckon on about an hour and 1,200 ft of gain to the base. The descent is by rappelling the route, which goes with single-rope raps on a 70 m cord.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct
hazards: The approach is faint and easy to lose — parties have gone astray at the gully
Mossy slabs are slick when wet
Sustained 5.10 face and friction climbing; partially bolted, so a medium rack is still needed
Loose rock in the approach gully if another party is above you
approach_variants.baseFinding: A BOLT LOW ENOUGH TO CLIP FROM THE GROUND IS THE CONFIRMATION. From the white-boulder clearing, work up to a mossy slab and, standing literally at its base, cut left and up a slight hill on a reasonably well-defined trail running along the foot of the slab. About five minutes of that reaches a dry streambed under a gully. Scramble the gully thirty feet or so, then cut hard left through brush into open forest and a dry creekbed, and follow the creekbed up to a large white boulder. Switchback up the woods above it and cut out to the right once you are 50 to 100 ft from the base of the wall. Ellation starts up a series of shallow grooves ABOVE AND LEFT of the single-pitch crag, and the proof is that bolt near the ground with a couple more on the first pitch. If you are standing at the foot of a single-pitch crag, the route is above and left of you; if you cannot see a bolt near the ground, you are not at the start.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.notes: Park at the roadside pullout near milepost 166 and start straight uphill to the north — there is no trail and no sign. Head for the talus at the foot of the gully that splits the wall; the gully forces you briefly out to the left before you rejoin it higher. Two ledge systems break the wall. The lower one comes first; keep going past it to the upper ledge, where the long routes start. The wall faces due south and there is no shade below the cave, so on a hot day the approach is the hottest part of the route.
approach_variants.season: Late June to September, once the gully has melted out and the lower pitches have dried; the highway over the pass is gated shut all winter, so there is no cold-season access at all.
hazards: Loose talus and creek-bed footing in the approach gully, with rockfall from anyone above you in it
Full south-facing sun on the whole approach with no shade until the cave
Water and seepage on the lower pitches persists into early summer in wet years
The highway is gated closed through winter and well into spring, so the approach can be unreachable by car
approach_variants.baseFinding: Get onto the UPPER of the wall's two ledge systems — not the first ledge you meet coming up the gully. Then walk right. This is the right-hand line on the wall and the huge cave that gives the wall its name is directly above you, not off to one side. The check on the ground is the first pitch itself: a left-facing corner about forty metres long that runs to a stance directly beneath a pair of TWIN CRACKS SLANTING LEFT. Count the corner's length and look for the twin cracks above the first stance — that pair is unique on this section of wall. Negative markers: if the corner above you is short, slabby and only about twenty-five metres to its anchor, you have drifted left into the middle of the wall and are under the eleven-pitch line; if you are standing on a treed ledge that two separate lines leave from, you are further left again. And if the cave is high above you but you are on a narrow ledge with one lone bolt at ground level, you never left the lower ledge and are on the three-pitch apron route.

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
approach_variants.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead near 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, take Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over and around deadfall rather than walking clean tread. Grouse Creek has been crossed on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or on a deteriorating footbridge, depending on the year.

Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction. In early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. FILL AND TREAT WATER THERE — the valley bottom is the last easy water and there is little of it above.

From the clearing the travel is cross-country: angle west then south-west, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to GIVE BACK 200-300 ft to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor around 6,900 ft. A camp flat sits near 7,000-7,100 ft.
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul-Sep for snow-free scrambling; late May and June need an axe and crampons for neve in the summit gullies. October is popular for larch colour and brings short days
hazards: Loose rock and choss in the summit gullies, with several similar-looking gully and bench variations that do not all go
A small summit area with a steeply inclined south slab whose slip line runs down the east face
Lingering snow and possible cornices in the summit gullies through June
A dry approach above the valley bottom, with the last easy water a quarter mile past the trail's end
Unmaintained, log-choked trail sections from past wildfire damage on the lower six miles
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS THE UPPER BASIN WEDGED BETWEEN SASKA AND EMERALD, AND THE THING THAT LEADS YOU INTO IT IS RUNNING WATER. From the 6,900 ft basin, cross a shoulder near 7,100 ft and climb a gully system into that upper basin. THE SLABBY WATERCOURSE DRAINING IT GIVES THE MOST CONTINUOUS LINE and holds snow well into early summer — so in cloud, follow the drainage uphill rather than picking a gully by eye.

THE ARRIVAL IS A BENCH AT ABOUT 7,800 FT beneath the south-east side of the summit ridge. From there several scramble lines look much alike and NONE IS OBVIOUSLY BETTER THAN THE REST. That is the honest state of this route and it is why the rule below is a direction rather than a description.

THE RULE IS: WORK UP AND TO CLIMBERS' RIGHT TO STAY ON THE STANDARD LINE. Right, from the bench. If you have drifted left you are on one of the variations that this face is full of, and they do not all go.

WHAT THE CORRECT GULLY DOES AT ITS TOP, which is the confirmation: it TOPS OUT AT A NOTCH IN THE SUMMIT RIDGE, and from that notch it is only a SHORT Class 2-3 scramble to the top — one described account calls it a very short Class 3 scramble near the top. So the test is proportion: if you have topped out of a gully and there is a great deal of climbing still above you, you are in the wrong gully.

THE SUMMIT IS TWO POINTS ABOUT 100 FT APART and the NORTH one is the true, marginally higher top. The south point is a noticeably steeper inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the EAST FACE. The whole summit area is small and drops away within a few paces in most directions, and several nearby lower rock points can be mistaken for the summit — so the exposure, not the difficulty, is what deserves attention at the top.

WHAT THIS ROUTE IS NOT: it is not a ridge climb despite the name. The name describes the ridge and notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just to the south-east. The climbing is a gully and a short scramble.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Entiat River Road and then the switchbacking forest-road spur to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, and follow North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley. Almost all of the distance to the peak is on trail. The usual staging point is the trail camp in the meadow below the summit around 6,700 ft, and the climb starts from the tread a short way north of it. A boat-access alternative exists on the far side, reaching the peak from Emerald Park via Trail #1230 out of the lakeshore settlement; it is a genuine second way in, but where that line joins the climbing is unclear, so the base-finding below is written for the trail camp side.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July into early October. Snow can hold in the gullies well into the season, and an axe is worth carrying early and mid-season.
hazards: Deep loose scree with a boot path dug into it in places — kicked rock runs straight onto anyone below, so spread out and wear a helmet
Several gullies present themselves and the correct one is hidden until you round a buttress
The whole summit area is small and becomes exposed within a few paces of its centre
The south point is a steeply inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the East Face
Sub-summits nearby are convincing enough that parties have tagged them by mistake
No water once you leave the meadow
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SMALL BOGGY MEADOW WHERE THE TRAIL TURNS SHARPLY LEFT IS THE DEPARTURE. From the meadow camp, follow the tread north until it turns sharply left at a small boggy meadow around 6,900 ft — past that turn the trail carries on around the south shoulder of the neighbouring peak, which is not where you are going. Leave it there and climb north, or slightly east of due north, over open ground almost to the ridge crest between the two peaks. Just before the crest, look for a scree and talus slope leading up and to the right to a notch on the northwest ridge. Take that about halfway, then cut right and south into the adjacent gully, and climb it to the depression between the two summits. Expect to see several gullies on the way in and not the one you want: it stays hidden until you round a buttress, and cairns only start marking the way once you are past that corner. The true summit is the north point, to the left of the depression as you arrive. Do not use a register to settle which point you are on — parties have found none on either.

wa_enchantment_enchainment.beta: Peak order and exact lines are up to the party; the loop below runs west to east. STUART: from the Stuart Lake valley climb slopes toward Long Pass, then steep snow to a notch at about 7,950 ft on the northwest face; drop slightly, traverse snow to a gully that shortcuts onto the upper West Ridge (continuous snow early season, with 3rd class rock beside it), then follow the West Ridge to the summit. The West Ridge is a notorious route-finding trap that benights parties climbing it for the first time, so know the line before you go. SHERPA: descend the upper Cascadian Couloir and cut east to the Stuart-Sherpa col (a short 4th class downclimb on the way), then climb Sherpa's West Ridge, keeping left of the steeper cracks on easier ground. Leave Sherpa by the north side: a short 4th/5th class downclimb, then trend skier's left through a scrambly gully to a large vegetated ledge near 8,100 ft, and on down a broader gully to about 7,200 ft. SHERPA TO ARGONAUT: a long, time-consuming traverse across high granite slabs and goat paths to Argonaut's south-side gullies; the alternative is to drop to the valley trail and climb back up. ARGONAUT: ascend the southern gullies on easy ground to just below the east ridge, with a short easy-fifth-class step to the summit; descend by rappel down the east face. COLCHUCK AND DRAGONTAIL: gain the Colchuck-Dragontail col and tag each summit by its scramble from the col, then descend to Aasgard Pass. THE CORE: from Aasgard Pass continue into the upper Enchantment basin for Little Annapurna (a walk-up from the basin), McClellan Peak (loose scrambling), then Enchantment Peak via Prusik Pass (talus, with a 4th class summit pillar; it has two summits of similar height, so tag both if in doubt) and finally Cannon Mountain from the Enchantment side.

access.fees: Day use free. Overnight: $6 non-refundable lottery application fee plus $5 per person per day.
access.permit: Enchantment Permit Area. DAY USE: free, self-issued wilderness permit filled out at the trailhead. OVERNIGHT (May 15 to October 31): an Enchantment overnight permit for one zone (Core Enchantment, Colchuck Lake, Stuart Lake, Snow Lake or Eightmile/Caroline), allocated by an advance lottery with leftover dates released later; camping in the permit area without one is prohibited.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency (America the Beautiful) pass

approach_variants.name: Prusik Pass to the northeast summit
approach_variants.notes:
Prusik Pass is reached either from the west — Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake, Aasgard Pass, then across the core Enchantment basin — or from the north and east on the much longer Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail (#1553) into the upper basin.

From the pass the line heads west and up the peak's shoulder. Most of it is walking with occasional use of hands, class 2, along the eastern arm; there is a single steeper step at around 7,900 ft.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun to early Oct for snow-free ground; outside that the basin travel needs snowshoes or skis
hazards: A single steep step on the east arm around 7,900 ft
Snow lingering across the basin approach and the shoulder well into summer
Committing onto the crest toward the southwest summit turns the day into exposed 4th class
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock base to find here — you walk onto the ridge from the pass. What you have to get right is WHICH SUMMIT you finish on, and this is the trap on Enchantment Peak.

The climbing proper is the last fifteen feet or so: a short third-class pull onto a small flat block roughly six feet square. If your top-out was a short, fun scramble onto a table-sized block, you are on the northeast summit — and a 2023 survey put that summit six to seven feet HIGHER than the southwest one, so this is the true high point despite being the easy one.

The negative marker: if you have traversed a long way southwest along the crest and are being drawn into sustained, very exposed fourth-class ground, you have left the northeast summit behind. The southwest summit lies about 1,500 ft further along the crest and is a serious exposed fourth-class scramble, not a continuation of this route.

If you top out on something broad and walkable with no scramble at all, you are on one of the intermediate bumps between the two summits, which are noticeably lower than the northeast top.

wa_enchantment_peak_southwest_scramble.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line. This route tops out on the NORTHEAST summit, which a 2023 survey confirms is the true high point, and its descent is a walk-off: downclimb the short, loose 3rd-class gully off the summit plateau — the same step you came up — then reverse the cross-country traverse back through the Reginleif/Sigrun tarn basin to the top of Aasgard Pass. Downclimbing Aasgard Pass is the descent's main hazard: steep, loose talus that's arguably harder to descend than ascend — plunge-step or downclimb deliberately and stay off snow you can't see the run-out on. Do not glissade the snow-filled sections of Aasgard Pass; several serious and fatal accidents have occurred there from glissaders sliding into hidden moats and sub-snow meltwater channels, especially in early-to-mid season. From the base of the pass, follow the Colchuck Lake shoreline and the Colchuck Lake Trail / Stuart Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route overall — no established rappels on the standard line.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the core basin to the south side
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead on FS Road 7601. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 north through forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on footbridges, moderate for the first 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake junction — go left and uphill. Steeper and rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. That is the last easy water before the high basin.

Skirt the lake's south shore to the foot of Aasgard Pass and climb the pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles on faint tread, cairns, loose talus and boulders.

Aasgard has one route-finding rule that matters more than any other and it has killed people. A few hundred feet above the lake the path veers to the climber's LEFT of the creek. Keep left. At the first grove of larches, stay well clear to the left of the rock, whatever the season. At around 6,400 ft stay LEFT of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it, and do not follow any side path toward the waterfall. Drifting right of the trees, toward the waterfall ground, is how parties get cliffed out.

From the pass drop gently into the upper core basin past Isolation Lake and traverse cross-country on use-paths and cairns through the Tranquil / Perfection / Sigrun / Reginleif tarns toward the Enchantment Peak massif. This route leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus onto the peak's south side, toward the gully below the northeast summit.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun to early Oct snow-free; Apr-Jun normally needs an ice axe for Aasgard Pass and the upper basin
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose shifting rock and genuine rockfall risk onto parties below
Getting cliffed out right of the trees / near the waterfall band at ~6,400 ft — fatalities are on record there
Early-season snow and ice turning the pass into a steep exposed snow climb
Sustained exposure on the class 2-3 talus and slab above the basin, worse when snow lingers
Fragile alpine ground in the permit core zone — stay on rock or snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The scrambling starts where the basin talus steepens onto the peak's south flank — there is no cliff base, just a change of angle, so the useful test is about the summit rather than the start.

This route finishes on the northeast summit: class 2-3 ground and a short third-class finish onto a small flat block, which a 2023 survey found to be six or seven feet higher than the southwest summit. The southwest summit, roughly 1,500 ft away along the crest, is a very exposed fourth-class scramble and is not part of this route — if the crest ahead turns into sustained, exposed fourth-class ground, you have gone past your summit.

On the way in, the marker that you have left the basin at the right place is the pair of lakes: the line goes between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun onto the south side. If you are heading for Prusik Pass you have taken the longer, mellower option, which is a reasonable choice in spring conditions but does not lead to this scramble.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, round the corner onto the west face
approach_variants.notes:
The shared Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boulder field at the south end, and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, hazardous under snow into early July.

From the pass, cross-country north past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way from the trailhead.

Five pitches, about 450 ft: a burly and somewhat dirty roof pitch straight off the deck, an exposed corner to a good ledge, a short aid section through steep ground, a fingery crack between two features, and then the final corner crack shared with the neighbouring line to finish.

Because it joins that neighbour near the top, it shares its descent: a single full-length rappel on the north side and about thirty minutes of scrambling back round to the base.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This one faces west rather than south, so it comes into the sun later in the day and is a cold morning start
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow
A burly, dirty roof pitch immediately off the ground
A short aid section through steep terrain at mid-height
Shared natural rappel anchors on the north side that have been rebuilt and relocated over the years
A west aspect: late sun, cold mornings, and afternoon weather arriving unseen from behind the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROOF AT GROUND LEVEL IS THE MARKER, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE YOU NEED. This route starts underneath a large roof formation at the very base — climbing it is the first pitch, straight off the deck. No other line at this end of the peak starts under a roof. Standing under a big overhang means you are here.

WHICH SIDE OF THE CORNER YOU ARE ON DECIDES IT. The south face turns an outside corner onto the west side. This route is LEFT of that corner, i.e. on the WEST face; the left-flank south-face classic is just RIGHT of it. So: corner on your right, roof over your head, west face — correct. Corner on your left and no roof — you have stepped back onto the south face and are on a different climb.

ASPECT AS A SANITY CHECK: this one faces WEST. If you have been standing in the sun all morning, you are on the south face and not here.

MID-ROUTE CONFIRMATION: there is a pair of rock features partway up that the route is named for, with a steep fingery crack running between them. If you never pass between two distinct features, you are not on this line.

AND THE TOP: this route joins its neighbour's final corner crack, so the last pitch is shared and the summit is not reached directly — you finish on the West Ridge. That shared finish is also why the rappel descent is the same one.

approach_variants.name: Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 to the last switchback
approach_variants.notes: This is the standard approach. From the De Roux trailhead follow the Boulder-De Roux Trail west up the valley between the peaks and the mountain opposite; at the junction a mile or so in, the left branch is the signed De Roux spur and the way on is the right-hand trail signed for Gallagher Head Lake. That climbs steadily for another mile and a half, topping out at a creek crossing that takes some balance, and passes several waterfalls before making its final switchback across a talus ridge below an open scree field. The Esmeralda Basin trail on the far side of the massif connects to this one only as a long loop by way of the jeep road and the lake, so it is a different way round to the same departure rather than a separate climbing line.
approach_variants.season: July into October. The slope faces south and clears early, though the scree is at its worst fully dry.
hazards: A sustained scree and talus slope of roughly 1,100 ft with nothing to hold a slip
Navigation through the meadows, tree cover and upper boulder fields is genuinely tricky and many paths lead up with none of them obvious
The upper hundred to hundred and fifty feet is loose broken rock, easy to send down onto a party below
One short section of steeper scrambling has been used to reach the final summit block
Two summits within about ten feet of each other in height, with the maps and the register disagreeing about which is which
No water once you leave the valley trail
approach_variants.baseFinding: A HOUSE-SIZED BOULDER AT THE LAST SWITCHBACK IS THE MARKER, AND YOU LEAVE THE TRAIL ON ITS CLIMBER'S LEFT. Walking up the valley past the waterfalls, the trail makes its final switchback across a talus ridge somewhere around 5,500 to 5,600 ft, and a single boulder the size of a house sits at that turn. Leave the tread there, on the boulder's climber's-left side, and head straight up the hillside on a northeast bearing. The overshoot tell is unmistakable: past that last switchback the trail stops climbing altogether and begins a long traverse toward the lake at the head of the valley, so if you are contouring rather than gaining and no big rock has appeared, you have gone by it. The upper mountain comes into view around 6,200 ft. Nothing above is marked and many faint paths lead up — none is the route, and either the line under the southwest ridge or the talus further climber's right will go. At the top there are two knobs a couple of hundred yards apart: the western one is a walk-up and is very slightly the higher, while the eastern is the one the maps mark. Tag both.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass Road pullout
approach_variants.notes: Drive the highway east through Glacier and continue about thirteen miles to an unpaved turn on the LEFT — the Hannegan Pass forest road — just before the highway crosses the river near the milepost. Follow the forest road a fraction of a mile, a couple of minutes' driving, to a pullout. The crag is the obvious cliff on the left, a few feet off the road. The bolts on this wall are old and rusty: the accepted practice is to walk or scramble around to the TOP and rig a top-rope from the tree above, so factor the walk-around into the approach rather than treating this as a lead from the pullout.
approach_variants.season: Spring to autumn for the rock line while the road is open; the same line is used as a cold-season dry-tooling and mixed practice route.
hazards: Aging, unreplaced bolts throughout the crag — do not weight or lead on them
Loose and muddy sections mid-route, especially at and around the ledge
Roadside setting, so there is minimal but real traffic exposure while rigging
The fixed static line above the route is left gear of unknown age — inspect it rather than trusting it
approach_variants.baseFinding: The wall is only about fifty feet high and holds a small handful of lines, so this comes down to picking the right one off the road. This is THE CRACK — the wall's most obvious continuous crack system, the one feature you can jam from the ground. Three things confirm it. The start is MILDLY OVERHANGING and holds the pumpiest move on the climb low down. Partway up the crack is broken by a MUDDY LEDGE, which is what gave the route its name. Above that the crack thins and is well protected to the top. A STATIC ROPE is normally left rigged from a tree above this line, so a fixed line hanging down the crack is a positive marker. Negative marker: if the line you are under is blank and technical for its first ten feet with nothing to jam from the ground, you are on the harder route immediately to the RIGHT — that one's whole crux is packed into the first ten feet and it has no crack at ground level.

approach_variants.name: Summit road, down the grassy ledges under the powerlines
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the last parking area before the Mount Erie summit, at a sharp left-hand bend on the summit road; it takes about six cars, and the upper lot is a sub-five-minute walk away if it is full.

Contour down and west on grassy ledges and short rock steps, through a short belt of woods and under the powerlines, to the top of a cliff above Lake Erie. A low third-class ramp descends from there to the wall.
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
hazards: Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent to the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the bottom of the ramp, turn LEFT along the lower tier. False Impressions is one of the lower-tier lines, alongside Lethal Weapon, Intimidator and Terminator.

The fixed reference on this tier is Intimidator, which starts at the lowest point of the wall — locate that and work along the base from it.

If you find yourself scrambling two blocky fourth-class steps southward you have left the lower tier for the upper one (Tindall's Terror, Scarface) and gone too far.

approach_variants.name: Bench Lake and Snow Lake into the Unicorn Creek cirque, beneath the northwest face
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Stevens Canyon Road to the Bench Lake and Snow Lake trailhead, on the south side of the road about 1.5 miles east of the Reflection Lakes parking area. From the trailhead near 4,550 ft, follow the trail 0.75 mile to Bench Lake, then a further half mile to Snow Lake at 4,685 ft, which sits in a glacial cirque directly below the peak.

From the lake, continue up the Unicorn Creek drainage south and east into the upper cirque to the base of the northwest face. Roughly 1.5 to 2 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain from the car to the base of the ice.

In winter, when Stevens Canyon Road is gated, add about 3 miles of unplowed road from Narada Falls; one spring party on skis reported four hours from the car to the base of the climbing.

There are no fixed anchors on the face. Retreat means threads you build.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Mar, and only in a year when it forms at all
hazards: The route does not form every year, and there are no fixed anchors on the face — retreat means V-threads
Rime and choss on the upper pitch
A committing descent off the summit in winter, through avalanche terrain in the basin and gully, often in fading light
A corniced col on the descent between Unicorn and West Unicorn
A cold, exposed northwest aspect with a long unplowed road walk when the highway is gated
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS ON THE OPPOSITE SIDE OF THE PEAK FROM EVERY OTHER ROUTE HERE, AND THAT IS THE FIRST AND CLEAREST FINDING. The summit-block lines are approached round to the SOUTH side via Unicorn Col. THIS ONE CLIMBS THE NORTHWEST FACE DIRECTLY OUT OF THE SNOW LAKE CIRQUE — you never go to the col at all. If you are traversing under cliffs on the south side of the peak, you are on the wrong side of the mountain for this climb.

THE APPROACH IS COUNTABLE AND ENTIRELY ON KNOWN GROUND: Bench Lake at about 0.75 mile, Snow Lake at 4,685 ft at about 1.25 miles, then up the Unicorn Creek drainage south and east into the upper cirque. SNOW LAKE SITS DIRECTLY BELOW THE FACE — the wall you are looking at from the lake is the wall you climb. There is no second cirque to confuse it with.

THE STRONGEST TEST IS THE ICE ITSELF, AND IT IS A GO OR NO-GO RATHER THAN A NAVIGATION AID: PITCH ONE IS SUSTAINED VERTICAL ICE. IF WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU IS 50-DEGREE SNOW, EITHER YOU ARE NOT AT THE ROUTE OR IT HAS NOT FORMED THIS YEAR. This climb does not always form, and there is nothing fixed to rappel off if you go up and find that out at half height.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE CONFIRMS IT, IN ORDER: vertical ice, then about 50-degree ice, then steep rime and choss to the summit. If the climbing eases early and STAYS eased, you are on a snow line and not on this.

AND THE THING THAT MAKES THIS COMMITTING RATHER THAN MERELY HARD: IT FINISHES ON THE SUMMIT. There is no walk-off from the top of the face. You rappel the summit block — about 50 ft, off the slung block on the south side rather than the retired snag — then downclimb the class 3 south slope and ridge WEST to the col at about 6,605 ft between Unicorn and West Unicorn, drop north into the basin, and follow it back to Snow Lake. In winter that descent is a serious undertaking on its own: the basin and gully are avalanche terrain, the col can be corniced, and you will likely be doing it in fading light. Know that ground before you start up it in the dark.

approach_variants.name: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
approach_variants.notes: This is the shorter alternative to the Entiat River approach. From the Basalt Pass trailhead, climb to the pass — the small stream in the gully below it is the last water, and there is none at all beyond — then follow the ridge north. The trail bypasses the first high point about 300 ft below it, and beyond the trail fork the tread fades into slick pumice. Continue north past the neighbouring tower's saddle, then through a col around 7,480 ft on the next peak's southwest ridge, dropping through a scree gully into the basin west of it. Hop the massive boulders in that basin, cross a small larch meadow, and regain the ridge. The peak can also be reached from the Entiat River side by way of Myrtle Lake, the Larch Lakes and Cow Creek Pass — that is the line the main approach and waypoints describe; the marks below are written for this Basalt Ridge side.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through early October, and popular in early autumn for the larch.
hazards: No water at all beyond the stream in the gully below Basalt Pass
Slick pumice where the ridge trail fades out
A scree gully to descend off the col, and a 500 ft loss into the boulder basin that must be regained
Loose rock and tree debris on the south ridge
The ridge is long, open and fully exposed to afternoon weather
approach_variants.baseFinding: A LARCH FOREST AND THEN FIFTH OF JULY PASS IS THE GATEWAY TO THE SOUTH RIDGE. After the boulder basin and the small larch meadow put you back on the ridge, the ground drops gradually and you walk through a larch forest immediately before arriving at Fifth of July Pass — that named saddle is where the south ridge begins, and the larch immediately below it is the confirmation. From the pass the south ridge is straightforward, with tree debris to avoid, and a short traverse along a long, broken ridgetop reaches the high point. The negative marker is the neighbouring tower: Devils Smoke Stack is a separate and harder summit with a sheer north side, climbed by steep gullies on its south with two tall steps of choss, and it lies on the far side of the intervening peak. You cannot arrive at one thinking it is the other without crossing that peak in between — so if the ground ahead rears into a tower with sheer cliffs on its north and no walkable line, you are back at the Smoke Stack rather than on this mountain's long broken crest.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
approach_variants.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead, about 2,790-2,800 ft. Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth along the creek's steep banks; the maintained tread peters out roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in at a large brushy washout below the basin.

Scrambling the washout is the route-finding crux of the approach. Look for a cairn marking the exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves LEFT around 3,500 ft near 48.0560, -121.3631 and is often flagged with pink tape — and follow it in steep forest switchbacks to about 4,900 ft.

Above treeline the path crosses talus and a meadow bench between 4,900 and 5,300 ft, passing a stagnant tarn at the Bedal-Sloan saddle. Last reliable water is there or at the cascading streams just below. The ground beyond turns rocky and exposed toward the glacier toe at about 5,800 ft.

A fit party familiar with the line reaches the base in around three hours. The Cougar Creek / North Fork Sauk trailhead on FR 49 converges with this line between 5,000 and 5,500 ft but adds a ford of the North Fork Sauk.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the approach snow has cleared
hazards: Boulder- and blowdown-choked washout at the end of the maintained tread
Steep, exposed scrambling above the meadow bench
Firm snow near the glacier toe early in the season
Ford of the North Fork Sauk if using the FR 49 alternative
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Southwest Face and the standard Corkscrew part company at the saddle, and the discriminator is a low connecting ridge rather than a signpost. From the 5,300 ft saddle, CROSS the low ridge that divides the West Face basin from the Southwest Face basin and drop into the meadows on its far side. The Southwest Face wall rises straight out of meadow — you should reach its foot without touching snow or ice. If you find yourself roping up for glacier travel, you have followed the Corkscrew line and the face you want is behind and to your right.

bivy.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
bivy.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
bivy.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

bivy.name: Bivy at the base of Sloan's southwest face
bivy.notes: Reached from the Bedal Creek trailhead by the west-face approach, traversing over a notch to the southwest. Parties who do not climb in a single long day sleep here.
bivy.water: Running water near the base of the routes through midsummer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead
bivy.capacity: A few small tent or bivy sites

approach_variants.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, then a long ledge traverse across the face
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the highway turnout about two miles east of Washington Pass, near milepost 165, at roughly 4,900 ft. Nothing is signed.

The climbers' path drops steeply from the WEST end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked here and there by cairns, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs, and climbs into an open rocky drainage and talus below the formation. The old line finishes with two or three informal fixed ropes across an avalanche path; a newer variation bears RIGHT just before them and needs only a little scrambling.

This route sees very few ascents, so current conditions beta effectively does not exist and there will be no traffic to follow. Budget the extra time the traverse costs on top of the walk in.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the creek crossing and approach snow have gone
hazards: The base is a 250-yard third and fourth-class traverse away from the obvious start
Very few ascents, so no chalk, no traffic and no current conditions information
The crux comes off a belay high on the route in thin cracks with sparse protection; knifeblades and thin pins are useful
Dirty and vegetated cracks in places
Descent is by the neighbouring route's rappels or its loose gully, not by reversing this line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU DO NOT START WHERE THE PATH ENDS. Arrive first at the base of the formation's trade route — identified by TREE SNAGS on the left as the ground steepens, before the gully. From there, TRAVERSE ABOUT TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY YARDS ACROSS THE FACE on third and fourth-class ledges, finishing JUST RIGHT OF CENTRE on the north-west face. That traverse is the approach to this climb and it is the piece everyone underestimates.

The test that you have gone far enough is the first pitch itself. It is a HUNDRED-FOOT CHIMNEY AND HAND CRACK ending on a LARGE LEDGE, and it is easy — around 5.4. If the ground in front of you is steep or technical at the very start, you have stopped short. A hundred feet of easy chimney to a big ledge is the signature.

CONFIRM ON THE PITCHES ABOVE, because the low ground is not distinctive. Pitch two is a slightly vegetated hands-and-fists corner. Pitch three follows the same corner then breaks RIGHT on thin face climbing to a LEDGE WITH A CAVE. Pitch four is finger cracks to a large slabby ledge. Corner, then a cave ledge, then a slabby ledge: that sequence is the line.

NEGATIVE MARKERS, and both are easy to fall into. If you racked up at the snags and started climbing without traversing, you are on the trade route — much easier, and it will feel like it. If your first pitch is protected by BOLTS, you are on the partly bolted four-pitch line beside the gully; this route's first pitch has no bolts, and its only fixed hardware is higher up — two bolted belays and a single bolt at the crux.

Be warned that the line is not continuously natural and some cracks are dirty and vegetated. That is the character of the route rather than evidence you are off it. The crux comes late, right off a belay high on the climb, in very thin cracks with sparse protection.

At the top it joins the trade route for its final scrambly ridge pitches, and the descent is that route's line: rappel it, or take the third-class gully on climbers' right, which is faster and loose.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to True Grit and Ragged Edge. Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine trailhead: log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish, Wirtz Basin, cairned talus, Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles with loose rock and rockfall exposure in the narrow couloir, then down to Vesper Creek and Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft and 3.5 miles — last water.

Stay on the summit trail to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, leave it and swing north across the slabs to the saddle with the two large cairns at about 5,700 ft. The heather ledges start about 30 ft above the cairns; traverse east on the goat trail across the north face. Plan three hours or more to the base.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the ledge traverse holds snow into mid-summer
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Slick, exposed heather on the ledge traverse
Snow lingering on the traverse into mid-to-late summer
Runout friction climbing off the deck on pitch 1
approach_variants.baseFinding: Fish & Whistle is not a separate landmark on the traverse — it is found by reference to True Grit. Continue the same ledge traverse and the start is at a LARGE TREE about 50 ft LEFT (west) of True Grit's start, on the talus and boulder apron directly under the north face. The confirmation is the first pitch itself: a clean friction slab passing FIVE BOLTS in about 80 ft. Neither True Grit nor Ragged Edge begins on a bolt ladder up open slab, so five bolts in a row is the check. If you have walked past the tree and are on ground with no bolted slab above it, you have gone too far along the ledges.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

approach_variants.name: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
approach_variants.notes: Come up the lake by passenger ferry or floatplane, ride the shuttle up the valley road to the bridge, cross it and follow the road past the camp and the airstrip to pick up the river trail. Follow that mostly flat trail southeast to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, then climb steeply through rock bluffs and open forest into the wilderness and traverse brushy, dry hillside to Bird Creek Camp — the only designated camp in that stretch of trail, sitting about fifty yards before the creek crossing, with room for about three tents and a cook area. From camp the peak is a long day of its own; it does not combine with the neighbouring summit above the same camp, and every account allows a full day for each.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends.
hazards: Off-trail navigation with no tread and no user path through the woods
Two distinct ways to end up in the wrong basin, both described below
A 600 ft descent off the divide into the creek that must be reclimbed on the return
Talus that starts as large solid boulders and degrades into fist- to football-sized rock that moves underfoot
The rock throughout is loose rubbly gneiss on lower-angle slopes
The north side of the true summit is craggy enough to block a traverse to the lower north point
approach_variants.baseFinding: TWO ELEVATIONS TELL YOU YOU ARE IN THE WRONG PLACE, AND BOTH ARE WORTH MEMORISING. Leave the trail at about 5,000 ft, cross the creek and bear east-southeast; if you have climbed to 5,200 ft you have gone too far along the trail and risk dropping into the wrong basin when you turn off. Then, if you find yourself heading cross-country into a narrow basin as early as 6,200 ft, you are too far south — contour northward at once, round the corner below the steeper ground, and get into the next basin over. The correct basin leads to a divide at about 7,460 ft on the south ridge of the neighbouring peak, reached up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle on climber's left, the rock starting as large solid boulders and degrading into loose softball- and football-sized stuff. From the divide, descend about 600 ft off its east side toward the creek, contouring around at roughly 6,800 ft to avoid steeper ground, then aim for the high southwest basin, from which a simple talus scramble reaches the top. The true summit is the south end of the massif; the north point is about a hundred feet lower.

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp
bivy.notes: The only designated camp on the upper Devore Creek trail, just before the Bird Creek crossing. Parties base here and climb Flora in a long day, 4 to 5 hours up. Higher camps are possible in the larch basin around 6,500 to 6,900 ft.
bivy.water: Bird Creek, beside camp
bivy.permit: Same overnight permit as the rest of the trip
bivy.capacity: About three tents and a cook area

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pullout on the EAST side, staying RIGHT of the gully that divides the two spires
approach_variants.notes:
This route is approached from the hairpin turn pullout on SR-20 east of Washington Pass, not from the Blue Lake Trailhead that serves North Early Winters Spire's west-side routes. Approach as if heading for the Direct East Buttress on South Early Winters Spire.

Ten pitches, 5.10b, first climbed in 1965 and freed onsight solo in 1990.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A descent that requires crossing to the opposite side of the peak from the climb
Two trailheads on opposite sides of Washington Pass serving the same summit
A 70 m rope is needed for the bolted West Face rappel option
No water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAY RIGHT OF THE GULLY THAT DIVIDES THE TWO SPIRES, AND SCRAMBLE TO A FLAT LEDGE. Those are the two things to find: the DIVIDING GULLY, kept on your left, and a FLAT LEDGE where the route starts.

WHY THE GULLY IS THE RIGHT HANDRAIL TO USE HERE: North and South Early Winters Spires are separated by a single continuous cleft, a chockstone-filled chasm on the west side and a gully on the east. It runs the full height between the two peaks, so it is the one feature on this side you cannot lose. Keep it on your LEFT and you are on North Early Winters Spire's ground; cross it and you are on South Early Winters Spire, where the Direct East Buttress and Southern Man start.

ARRIVAL: a FLAT LEDGE, gained by scrambling. Flat ground on a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation.

THE TRAILHEAD TEST, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT COSTS AN HOUR IF YOU GET IT WRONG: this route is on the EAST side and is reached from the HAIRPIN PULLOUT. The other two North Early Winters Spire routes here, The West Face and Labor Pains, are on the WEST side and are reached from the BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, which is about 2.5 miles away by road on the far side of Washington Pass. Those are different cars.

AND THE DESCENT CROSSES BACK OVER THE MOUNTAIN, WHICH YOU SHOULD PLAN FOR BEFORE STARTING: from the summit, traverse to the WEST side of the peak and rappel either the Chockstone Route with a 60 m rope or the bolted West Face anchors with a 70 m rope. Both require crossing over from the east-side climbing line to the west-side descent infrastructure.

approach_variants.name: Glacier Basin Trail to the timbered ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Monte Cristo townsite take the Glacier Basin Trail — not the Poodle Dog Pass trail, which leaves the townsite southward toward Silvertip and Columbia and does not reach Foggy Peak at all. Follow it about a mile and a half, a short distance above the falls, and leave it near 4,200 ft at the point where Glacier Creek is easy and brush-free to reach; that is the last reliable water. There are TWO traverses on this route with a climb between them, and collapsing them into one is how parties get it wrong. First, cross the creek and traverse nearly level to the BASE of the timbered ridge. Then climb that ridge — start on its right where there is less brush and shift onto its left side after several hundred feet to avoid small cliff bands, where a game trail helps — carrying on up to anywhere between about 4,800 and 5,300 ft. Lower means more brush, higher means gain you give straight back, and 5,100 ft is the usual compromise. Only then turn left for the second, near-level traverse.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Brushy sidehill traversing, and small cliff bands on the timbered ridge
Conditions at the gully entrance vary enormously by month — one party met ice-hard snow with deep moats on the right and huge overhangs on the left
The summit gully is steep with abundant loose, downsloping rock — helmets, and do not climb directly beneath one another
Real exposure on the short final scramble off the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ONLY RIDGE IN THE AREA WITH LARGE TREES ON IT, THEN A CLIFFY NUISANCE RIDGE. Cross Glacier Creek above the falls and traverse nearly level to the base of a timbered ridge — unmistakable, because it is the only rib on this slope carrying big trees while everything either side of it is brush and talus. That ridge is the first landmark and it is CLIMBED, not skirted. The second comes at the end of the upper traverse near 5,100 ft: a cliffy ridge that has to be got around rather than crossed. Once past it, TURN RIGHT and go straight up the talus slopes toward the summit gully. At the gully entrance the season decides the day — in a good year the snowfield runs continuously into the gully, and where it has pulled back, the rock immediately to its LEFT has gone at short class 4. The gully above is mostly class 3 and finishes at a notch on the skyline just WEST of the true summit; aim for that notch, not for the summit block. A gully topping out at the summit, or east of it, is the wrong one.

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
bivy.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
bivy.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet.
