Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approach_variants.name: East around the basin and up the loose gullies to the notch below the Solitary Gendarme
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and Boston Basin climbers' trail as the West Ridge — the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about a mile, then a steep path with several creek crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft, then talus and heather to the usual high camp at 6,300-6,600 ft, roughly four to five miles and three to four hours from the car.

From camp, do NOT cross toward the south-face couloir. Traverse climber's-left and east around the basin and gain the ridges and gullies flanking the glacier on Forbidden's east side, sometimes loosely called the Unnamed Glacier. This leg is the honest part of the route's reputation: a few hours over choss-covered slabs, loose rock and seepage, several small stream crossings, and usually a snow gully at the end that wants crampons or microspikes to gain the upper benches. Parties describe holding a bearing of roughly 058 degrees up the east side of that glacier.

Reckon five to six hours and over 5,000 ft above the trailhead to the notch — noticeably longer and far more route-finding than reaching the West Ridge notch.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September; August is the most reliable for dry granite
hazards: Hours of loose, choss-covered slabs and seepage on the approach, with real route-finding in poor visibility
A snow gully at the top of the approach that wants crampons even in midsummer
Aging fixed rappel anchors in the gendarme notches
Sustained exposure and complex route-finding over multiple gendarmes once on the crest
Afternoon thunderstorms on a long crest with no quick way off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LANDMARK IS A SINGLE TOWER WITH A NAME: THE SOLITARY GENDARME. The high bivy sits at roughly 8,000 ft, about 300 ft BELOW it, and the notch where the technical climbing starts is just above that bivy. A lone tower standing up on the crest, with the ridge running away west toward the summit, is the confirmation you are at the right place on a ridge that offers many wrong ones.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE HERE THAN ELSEWHERE: this crest carries several gendarmes and the ridge can be joined almost anywhere along it. Joining it high — past the gendarmes, with an unobstructed view of the summit and nothing in the way — means you have missed the route rather than found a shortcut. IF THERE IS NOTHING BETWEEN YOU AND THE SUMMIT, YOU ARE TOO HIGH.

THE FIRST MOVE TEST: from the notch you go LEFT around the first gendarme, then simul-climb easy blocks at about 5.4 on clean granite to gain the crest proper. Easy ground first, hard ground later. If your opening pitch is hard, you are not on the East Ridge Direct.

THE DIRECT LINE IS DEFINED BY REFUSING THE BYPASSES. Every gendarme here can be walked around on the north or south flank. A day that never once required a move you would rope up for means you have been taking the bypasses and are on the easier variant, not the Direct.

CONFIRM AT THE CRUX, LATE: the 5.8 crux comes after climbing a steep pitch up the LAST gendarme and RAPPELLING DOWN ITS BACK SIDE into a narrow notch with a steep wall directly ahead. A notch you scrambled into rather than rappelled into is not that notch.

DO NOT CONFUSE THIS RIDGE WITH THE EAST LEDGES. The Ledges are the loose descent traverse that stays WELL BELOW the crest and rejoins the ridge near the Solitary Gendarme. If you are traversing ledges rather than climbing a crest, you are on the descent line — the one that carries a documented fatality.

approach_variants.name: Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier, then north to the foot of the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft on Cascade River Road, the old Diamond Mine roadbed runs about a mile to the mine site, then the climbers' path climbs hard through forest with four stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at about 6,400 ft. From high camp, follow the moraine and the west edge of the QUIEN SABE GLACIER up to about 7,500 ft and climb to SHARKFIN COL at 7,720 ft — roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and 200 ft of a class 3 gully to gain it, on loose scree underfoot. The col is the commitment. From it you rappel roughly 100-150 ft, in one or two stages depending on snow, down a loose gully onto the BOSTON GLACIER; retreat after that means re-climbing to the col. Traverse north through crevassed ground toward the north end of the glacier, then re-ascend to the ridge. Three Forbidden routes cross Sharkfin Col and use this rappel. Where you LEAVE the Boston Glacier is what separates them.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, for dry rock and a glacier that is still bridged where it matters
hazards: A rappel of roughly 100-150 ft (depending on snow) down a loose gully off the col, with rope-snag on loose rock, and no easy retreat once you are down it
A heavily crevassed traverse of the Boston Glacier where a fall would be serious
A distinct moat where the glacier meets the North Ridge rock, sometimes needing technical work to exit, and worse late season
Steep snow gully sections on the ridge itself where a slip runs uncontrolled onto the Boston Glacier
A long, exposed crest with the descent on a completely different side of the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FIRST, IDENTIFY SHARKFIN COL CORRECTLY, BECAUSE EVERYTHING AFTER IT IS COMMITTED. It is the LOW POINT ON THE RIDGE IMMEDIATELY LEFT OF SHARKFIN TOWER — a distinct rock tower stands beside it. A notch on that skyline with no tower beside it is not the col. You gain it by about 10 ft of 5.7 and a 200 ft class 3 gully; if you walked up to it, you are somewhere else.

SECOND, ON THE BOSTON GLACIER, GO NORTH AND KEEP GOING. The base of this route is at the FAR NORTH END of the glacier, where the ice meets the foot of the ridge, and the crossing point is itself a notch rather than an arbitrary spot on the crest. You should pass a rock buttress on the way; if you have turned uphill without passing it, you have turned too early.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS THE FIRST MOVE, AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: THE CLIMBING STARTS WITH A SHORT, STEEP LEFT-FACING CORNER AT 5.6, STRAIGHT OFF THE COL AT THE FOOT OF THE RIDGE. That corner is the route's crux and it is the first thing you climb. IF THE FIRST GROUND ABOVE THE GLACIER IS 300 FT OF LOW-ANGLE ROCK LEADING TOWARD AN ICE PATCH, YOU ARE ON THE NORTHEAST FACE and you turned west off the glacier far too soon.

AND YOU SHOULD BE AT A COL, NOT ON A FACE. The base is the gap between Boston and Forbidden: ground falls away on BOTH sides of you. If the mountain is above you and glacier below you and nothing behind, you are under a face, not at the col.

CONFIRM AS YOU CLIMB: above the corner the crest passes a wildly exposed bivy platform — two small snow-free spots just below the crest on the northeast side — and above roughly 8,400 ft the rock notably improves. Poor rock all the way to the top means you never got onto the upper ridge.

rappel_detail.notes: From near the summit/West Ridge notch, first of a series of rappels along the arete on climber's left of the Cat Scratch Gullies, chosen because it's largely out of the gully's rockfall line.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed sling/rap ring on the small arete beside the descent gully
hazards: Everything in this gully system funnels rockfall, and party-induced rockfall from groups above is the main objective danger of the descent. The rib line exists to keep you out of the channel - do not shortcut into the gully to save a rappel
rappel_detail.station: From the West Ridge notch - reached by downclimbing and short rappels along the ridge from the summit - the descent takes the rock rib bordering the snow couloir rather than the couloir's own fall line. The first station is on that rib. One rope works for these rappels.

rappel_detail.notes: Continuing down the arete rap line.
hazards: Abundant anchors of very mixed vintage; some are old slings with no hardware
rappel_detail.station: Successive stations continue down the rib. Anchors are plentiful here because this is the standard way off anything on Forbidden, so the problem is choosing among them rather than finding one.

rappel_detail.notes: Middle rappel; anchors are described as plentiful along this line, with some downclimbing/simul-downclimbing possible between stations depending on party and conditions.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed sling/rap ring or natural anchor
hazards: Carry spare webbing and rap rings - stations on this line routinely need backing up or rebuilding before use
rappel_detail.station: Mid-sequence on the rib. Downclimbing and simul-downclimbing between stations is normal and is how parties get the count down.

rappel_detail.notes: Lower arete rappel toward the base of the Cat Scratch Gully system.
hazards: The rock gully alongside can be wet and loose; a wet rope pulled across it picks up grit and jams
rappel_detail.station: Lower rib, approaching the base of the gully system.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel back into Boston Basin terrain; late-season/dry conditions can require additional short rappels (up to 6-7 total) not captured in this 5-rap average.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed sling/rap ring or natural anchor near gully base
hazards: The landing is at the moat/bergschrund between rock and snow, and crossing it can be the hardest move of the descent
The lowest anchor has been removed by other parties before now - carry enough gear and cord to leave a station behind
Dry late-season conditions add rappels here rather than removing them
rappel_detail.station: Before rappelling the last cliff band onto snow, look for the station off to the LEFT rather than continuing straight down. Parties have found the lowest slung-boulder anchor stripped by a descending group, so be prepared to build one.

approach_variants.name: Sharkfin Col, the schrund rappel and an ice wall, then west across the Boston Glacier to the ice patch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft. Continue along the moraine and the west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier to SHARKFIN COL at about 7,720 ft, gained by roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and a class 3 gully.

The first-ascent party rappelled from the col INTO the bergschrund and climbed a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the Boston Glacier. Expect the schrund to be the awkward part of the day before the climbing starts.

From the glacier, traverse WEST — a short traverse, not the long northward one the North Ridge makes — to the base of the face.

This line is climbed rarely enough that no fixed gear should be assumed and modern first-hand descriptions are scarce; treat any description of it, including this one, as an outline.
approach_variants.season: Late spring to early summer, when the face still holds the best ice and snow
hazards: A rappel into a bergschrund and a 15 ft vertical ice wall to get out of it onto the glacier
A north-facing ice feature that has thinned over recent decades — verify there is ice deep enough to take a screw rather than assuming it
Everything on the face funnels through the ice patch, so it is the exposed spot for anything released from above
A remote position with a long, complex retreat and a descent by the West Ridge on the far side of the peak
So few ascents that conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ICE PATCH IS THE LANDMARK AND YOUR POSITION RELATIVE TO IT IS THE WHOLE TEST. From the Boston Glacier a large, conspicuous patch of ice sits on the lower face — about 300 ft tall. YOU START ON ROCK BELOW AND TO THE LEFT (WEST) OF IT, NOT ON IT AND NOT TO ITS RIGHT.

SO THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS: ROCK FIRST, ICE SECOND. About 300 ft of rock, protected by a few pitons on the first ascent, comes before you reach the ice at all. IF YOU ARE SWINGING TOOLS WITHIN A ROPE-LENGTH OF LEAVING THE GLACIER, YOU HAVE STARTED TOO FAR RIGHT — you are on the patch itself rather than the rock beside it.

COUNT THE THREE SECTIONS IN ORDER: 300 ft of rock, then 300 ft of ice at about 50 degrees, then about 600 ft of steep-looking but upward-dipping slabs to the top. A route that stays on one medium the whole way is not this one.

TELL IT FROM THE NORTH RIDGE BY HOW FAR YOU WALKED. Both cross Sharkfin Col and use the same schrund rappel. The North Ridge then traverses a long way NORTH to the far end of the Boston Glacier and starts at a col with ground falling away on both sides. This route turns WEST after a short traverse and starts under a face. If you walked past a rock buttress and kept going, you have gone to the North Ridge.

A GENUINE NAMING TRAP, WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU LEAVE CAMP: Forbidden's 'northeast face route' is sometimes used loosely to mean a HIGH TRAVERSE BELOW THE EAST RIDGE that skirts the gendarmes — an easier, quite different line, and the one some descent descriptions mean. This route is the technical ice-patch face above the Boston Glacier. If the description you are following has you traversing under a ridge crest rather than climbing a face, you are reading about the other thing.

Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

wa_forbidden_peak_northwest_face.rappel_count_note: The 3 stations listed are the ridge portion only; the full descent is longer. A party on a single 60 m rope reports "a few key rappels high on the route before unroping to downclimb the remainder of the ridge... Another 7 rappels brought us down the Cat Scratch gullies to snow." Good early-season snow lets much of the couloir be downclimbed instead. The ~5-rappel / 400 ft East Ledges figure belongs to the EAST side descent, not this route.

approach_variants.name: All the way round to the Forbidden Glacier's north arm
approach_variants.notes: This is the hardest-to-reach established line on the peak and most parties treat it as three days. The recorded approach goes the long way round: from the Boston Basin trailhead, three to four miles by the old mine road and the climbers' path with four stream crossings to high camp near 6,400 ft, often pushing on to a bench near 7,500 ft beside the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Tower. Ascend the west side of the Quien Sabe to the notch above Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier below the bergschrund, traverse that heavily crevassed glacier, and continue around to the NORTH ARM OF THE FORBIDDEN GLACIER on the mountain's other side. Other parties reach the same basin without the Boston Glacier at all — by dropping west off the North Ridge line, by rappelling from the West Ridge notch over crevasses and moats, or over Torment Col. All of them end in the same place. From the north arm, about 900 ft of 30 to 40-plus degree snow and ice leads to the base of the rock.
approach_variants.season: Mid summer, for the best balance of firm ice and dry rock
hazards: Two crevassed glaciers before any climbing, with a large crevasse that opens around 7,600 ft in many seasons and can cost real time
A committing rappel off Sharkfin Col — retreat means re-climbing to the col
A moat or bergschrund where the snow pulls back from the foot of the rib
A shaded, cold aspect that holds hard ice late, and a face that tops out at a cornice near 8,375 ft
A descent on a completely different side of the mountain, by the West Ridge couloir
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECIDING FACT IS WHICH GLACIER YOU ARE STANDING ON, AND IT SETTLES THIS ROUTE AGAINST BOTH ITS NEIGHBOURS IN ONE LOOK. This route starts from the FORBIDDEN GLACIER'S NORTH ARM, on the mountain's WEST side. The North Ridge and the Northeast Face both start from the BOSTON GLACIER, on the east. If your approach ended on the Boston Glacier and you started climbing there, you are on one of those two, not this.

THE POSITIVE LANDMARK IS THE RIB. From the north arm an obvious rock rib runs roughly 1,800 ft up the face, with ICE ON BOTH SIDES OF IT — the face is two ice sections split by a narrow rock band. You should be able to see a continuous rib rising from where you stand. IF WHAT IS ABOVE YOU IS A BROAD, UNDIFFERENTIATED SNOW AND ICE SLOPE WITH NO RIB IN IT, YOU ARE NOT UNDER THIS ROUTE.

THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS SNOW, NOT ROCK. Above the moat comes roughly 900 ft of 30 to 40-plus degree snow and ice BEFORE any technical rock. If you stepped off the glacier straight onto rock, you are on the Northeast Face — which begins with 300 ft of rock and only then reaches its ice.

COUNT THE GROUND ABOVE THE ICE: about 500 ft of somewhat loose 4th to low-5th, soloed or simul-climbed, leads to a KNIFE-EDGE RIDGE crossed at 5.6, and the 5.8 crux follows immediately after it. A knife edge is the confirmation that you are on the rib and not on ground beside it.

AND THE LARGE CREVASSE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT IS A POSITION MARKER AS WELL AS A HAZARD — it opens on the approach in most seasons and is the thing most likely to make you detour; note where you crossed it, because you are not reversing this way.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.

rappel_detail.pull: Set the knot well clear of the lip and check the pull before committing.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the top of the crux tower. Plan on what a 60 m rope reaches doubled, as used throughout the descent.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural horn/block, top of the crux tower
hazards: The pull angles here are awkward and a rope that is not weighted cleanly off the horn can hang up. Watch the rope over the edge before the last person goes.
rappel_detail.station: On the tower at the top of the steep section, roughly 175 ft below the summit. Slings and cord are usually in place here; it is the first station most parties actually use rather than downclimb.

rappel_detail.notes: Second rappel, landing on snow on the north side of the couloir/'Cat Scratch Gullies' system.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural horn/block, dropping onto north-side snow
hazards: This one lands on snow, and the transition from rock to snow is where parties come off the rappel awkwardly. Have crampons and an axe accessible before you start down, not stowed.
rappel_detail.station: Below the crux tower, dropping toward the north-side snow. Anchors here are natural — slung horns and blocks with accumulated tat rather than a bolted station.

rappel_detail.pull: A 60m rope doubled covers the reported stations; a 45m has been reported as only just sufficient. Carry enough cord to build an extra station if you cannot find the next one.
rappel_detail.notes: Explicitly reported as a 30m rappel (60m rope doubled) through the steepest snow section to the top of the upper moat/bergschrund - the last of the representative 3-rappel sequence before reversing the glacier-remnant/talus traverse back to Boston Basin.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural anchor above the upper moat
hazards: The descent line follows fixed anchors on the small rib to the down-climber's LEFT of the gully. Parties that drift into the right-hand gully end up off route on loose ground with no stations — this is the single most commonly reported descent error on the route.
Stations are intentionally short in places and easy to rappel straight past. Do not skip an anchor because the next one is not yet visible.
The moat at the bottom of the couloir reappears on the way down and can require a step across or a short downclimb.
rappel_detail.station: Above the upper moat, at the top of the steepest remaining snow. This is the station most commonly reported as hard to find — if you cannot see the next anchor, stop and look on the rib to the down-climber's LEFT of the gully before continuing.

approach_variants.name: South face couloir to the West Ridge notch
approach_variants.notes: From the Boston Basin high camp, traverse up and east across talus and the remains of the Quien Sabe Glacier toward Forbidden's south face. Where the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is usually faster and drier than staying on snow; where it is snow-covered or crevassed, rope up. The couloir itself runs about 500 ft and steepens to 40–50° near the top, which is where crampons and an axe stop being optional. Reaching the notch is roughly 2,000 ft above camp.
approach_variants.season: Jun–early Aug, while it still holds snow
hazards: A moat where the snow pulls back from the rock guards the top of the couloir. Expect a short steep step or a band of loose rock to get over it, and expect it to be worse the later in the season you go.
Rockfall once the sun reaches the couloir — parties above are the usual source, so it pays to be off it early.
40–50° snow near the top, on ground where a slip does not stop on its own.
approach_variants.baseFinding: The notch is the low point on the skyline between Forbidden and Mount Torment, at 8,265 ft, and the couloir below it is the obvious continuous snow line splitting the left-hand edge of the south face. Navigate to the NOTCH, not to the first gully you reach — several lines start off the same snowfield and only this one tops out at the crest. You are at the base of the climbing when you step through the notch onto the ridge crest; from there the route to the summit runs to climber's right.

approach_variants.name: Cat Scratch gullies (late season, once the couloir has melted out)
approach_variants.notes: When the couloir has gone to loose talus and scree, the usual line moves off the snow onto the rock gully system immediately west — climber's left — of it. Roughly the first 200 ft is class 4, easing to grassy class 3 for the last 200 ft to the notch. It is loose the whole way, and it is slower than it looks on the approach.
approach_variants.season: Late Aug–Sep, dry conditions
hazards: Loose rock from bottom to top. Keep the party out of one another's fall line rather than spread across the gully.
The parallel gullies are easy to confuse, and committing to the wrong one puts you on the ridge away from the notch with loose ground to traverse back.
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cat Scratch is not the snow couloir, and that mix-up is the usual reason parties lose time here: it is the parallel ROCK gully system just west (climber's left) of the couloir, and it tops out at the same 8,265 ft notch. Several parallel gullies in that system look alike from below — the correct one finishes at the notch itself rather than on the ridge either side of it, so pick your line by where it ENDS on the skyline, not by which entrance looks easiest from the basin.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to the Chiwawa-Fortress col
approach_variants.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of FR-6200, follow the Buck Creek and Chiwawa River trails up-valley beneath Red Mountain to about 6,580 ft, then leave the trail and traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress. Some parties go over Chiwawa's summit first instead. Others approach by way of the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin, fording the Chiwawa River — the same basin the Chiwawa Mountain route uses, which puts you on the col from below rather than from along the ridge.

The col is a common high camp and this route is very often combined with Chiwawa Mountain from it, which is the practical reason to camp there rather than lower.

Rock quality is notably BETTER on the East Ridge itself than in the gully that gains it or on Fortress's south-west face — the opposite of what most parties expect.

FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat, adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct. Crampons and an axe are commonly used on the snow slopes crossing to the col even in late summer
hazards: Loose rock in the gully gaining the East Ridge from the col — the worst ground on the route, and reversed on the way down
An exposed, normally unroped fourth-class step on the final summit pitch
Cold thigh- to knee-deep fords of the Chiwawa River drainage on the Chiwawa Basin approach
Steep firm snow crossing to the col, wanting crampons and an axe even late in the season
About seven extra miles of road-walking each way while FR-6200 is closed beyond Atkinson Flat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS THE CAMP AND THE GULLY IS THE ROUTE, AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME PLACE. From the roughly 7,200 ft Chiwawa-Fortress col, the East Ridge is gained by a LOOSE CLASS 3-4 GULLY. Standing on the col is not standing at the base; you still have a gully to find and climb before the ridge starts.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS THE CONFIRMATION, AND IT WORKS BACKWARDS FROM WHAT YOU WOULD GUESS: the gully is the loose ground and the ridge above it is the SOLID ground. So the test that you have topped out of the correct gully onto the correct crest is that the rock gets BETTER. If you have gained a crest and it is still rubble, you are on a subsidiary rib rather than the East Ridge.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE ON THIS MOUNTAIN: the south-west face is reached from an entirely different valley — Buck Creek Trail and Pass No Pass at about 6,400 ft — and never comes near this col. If your approach involved a way-trail and a pass rather than a cross-country traverse off the Chiwawa River Trail, you are on the other side of the peak.

THE FINISH IS ONE MOVE AND IT IS UNPROTECTED IN PRACTICE: an exposed fourth-class step just below the summit, normally climbed unroped. That step is the route's crux and its arrival marker — reaching it means the ridge is behind you.

COMING BACK DOWN, THE HEAD OF THE GULLY IS THE THING TO FIND, and it is easier to walk past from above than from below. Follow the crest back until the ground drops away toward the col, and descend carefully; the gully is the loosest part of the day in both directions.

IF YOU CONTINUE TO CHIWAWA MOUNTAIN from the col — which many parties do — note that its route works up the SOUTH-WEST side on slabs and talus from that same col, so the two climbs share a base and diverge immediately.

access.fees: None — no climbing fee (National Forest wilderness, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) — same Glacier Peak Wilderness system that covers Glacier Peak itself (one contiguous wilderness spanning both Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forests).
access.permit: None required — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, no reservation.
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) is closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground after December 2025 storm damage, under closure order 06-17-07-2026-11 in effect through 31 December 2027 unless lifted sooner, so the Trinity Trailhead cannot be reached by car. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes FR 6200 and the Buck Creek and Chiwawa River trails. Check with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before planning a trip. In winter the road is unplowed in any case.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District) and Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at some trailheads (fee day-use sites) — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk (Phelps Creek, Trinity, Entiat River, or the Holden trailheads). Holden Village and its access road are closed to hikers through at least summer 2026.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail #1513 and the Pass No Pass way-trail
approach_variants.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead at 2,800 ft, follow Buck Creek Trail #1513 roughly nine to nine and a half miles, climbing through forest and an old avalanche debris field near 4,500 ft.

The turn is the thing to watch for and it is NOT MARKED: an unmarked junction with the Pass No Pass way-trail bears RIGHT at about 5,800 ft. Follow the way-trail to Pass No Pass near 6,400 ft and the alpine camping benches beyond it, from which the face and the south ridge come into view.

Since 2026 storm damage has closed FR-6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground around mile 16, adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way before you even reach the trailhead.

From a high camp in the Pass No Pass basin, parties report about three and a half to four hours up and two and a half to three back.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct, best Jul-Sep once the south-west face has melted out; an axe and sometimes crampons for early-season snow on the approach slopes below the pass
hazards: The direct south-west gully is the loosest ground on the mountain and is directly above anyone below
Steep snow on the approach slopes below Pass No Pass into early summer, needing self-arrest skills
An unmarked way-trail junction at about 5,800 ft that is easy to walk past on a nine-mile approach
Creek crossings and brushy, indistinct trail lower down
Roughly seven extra miles of road-walking each way while FR-6200 is closed beyond Atkinson Flat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE PASS IS WHERE THE MOUNTAIN BECOMES VISIBLE, AND THAT IS THE ARRIVAL TEST: from Pass No Pass and the benches beyond it, Fortress's SOUTH-WEST FACE AND SOUTH RIDGE COME INTO VIEW. Below the pass you cannot see the peak at all. If you are still walking with no mountain in front of you, you have not crossed it.

THE CLIMBING STARTS AT A CHANGE OF SURFACE, NOT AT A FEATURE. From the basin below the pass, green slopes and scree steepen into Class 2-3 talus and slab. There is no step, no toe and no notch to arrive at — grass gives way to rock and that is the base.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE ON THIS ROUTE: THE DIRECT GULLY UP THE FACE IS THE LOOSEST GROUND ON THE MOUNTAIN. If you are in a defined gully with rubble moving under every step, you are on the line to avoid, not the line to take. Angle RIGHT onto slabbier rock, or follow the south ridge crest instead. A party in 2015 found and cairned an alternate Class 3 line over more solid blocky terrain to skier's right of the gully, and later parties have followed it — so cairns on solid blocky ground here are a good sign, which is the reverse of the situation in the gully.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER SIDE OF THIS PEAK: the East Ridge is reached from the Chiwawa-Fortress col at about 7,200 ft, approached cross-country off the Chiwawa River Trail, and it starts with a loose Class 3-4 gully onto a crest of notably better rock. Nothing on that route involves a way-trail or a named pass. If you walked over a pass to get here, you are on the south-west side.

THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS TALUS. There is no technical finish on this route; if you are looking at a fourth-class step you have wandered onto the east side's ground.

approach_variants.name: Park Lakes basin to the Chikamin Ridge crest
approach_variants.notes: Mineral Creek Trail from the signed trailhead: the Kachess River on logs or a wade, past the old mill site, across Mineral Creek at the wilderness boundary, then a long traverse high above the creek through old-growth and a string of grown-in avalanche paths where brush and deadfall make for slow going. Ford the tributary creek near four miles — the last dependable water before the basin — and grind the steep pitch above it into the Park Lakes benches. Stay on the trail to the pack camp where it meets the Pacific Crest Trail, then leave it and climb heather benches and rock slabs cross-country.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September
hazards: Loosely stacked talus high on the route
Snow lingering in the gully well into July
Route-finding among four separate rock points that all look like summits from below
Steep heather and dirt near the ridge crest
Cliff bands and pinnacles that have to be threaded rather than climbed
approach_variants.baseFinding: Four Brothers is a cluster of four cliffy points strung along Chikamin Ridge, so the identification problem is which side of the group you are standing on rather than which summit you can see. Gain the crest at the saddle NORTHWEST of the group — the col between Chikamin Peak and the Four Brothers — and keep to the north side of the points on the way up. Do not try to climb directly from below on the crest side: that aspect throws up genuinely technical obstacles, and parties bound for Chikamin deliberately detour around it on steep grassy slopes and gully systems. From the col, traverse back southeast onto the southwest-facing aspect. The base of the climb is where the heather benches end and a gully-and-slope system of stacked talus begins beneath the points; that gully is the line, and picking a way through the pinnacles and cliff bands above it is the real crux of the peak, harder than any single move on it. The south peak is the objective. Leave enough daylight to find the same gully going down — improvising a line off the pinnacles late in the day is how parties end up on much steeper ground than they intended.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the basin below the west face, then 40 ft DOWN AND RIGHT of the chockstone chimney
approach_variants.notes:
Same basin approach as Mojo Rising and the Northwest Face: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail to the northwest-side clearing, then the climber's path up talus into the basin below the west face.

Six pitches, 5.11-.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start explicitly described as nondescript, confirmed only at the first belay
Three routes starting within about 60 ft of each other on one wall
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS ROUGHLY 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT OF THE LARGE CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY BETWEEN THE TWO SPIRE FORMATIONS, ON A NONDESCRIPT CRACK THAT LEADS TO A TWO-PIECE FIXED ANCHOR ON A PEDESTAL.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS AT THE TOP OF PITCH ONE, NOT AT THE BOTTOM, AND THAT IS THE HONEST WAY TO USE THIS ROUTE: the crack itself is described as NONDESCRIPT, which means you will not identify it by looking at it. What you can identify is where it ends. A ROPE LENGTH UP, THERE IS A TWO-PIECE FIXED ANCHOR ON A PEDESTAL. If you arrive at a stance with no fixed gear, come down and move along the wall.

PITCH TWO GIVES A SECOND CONFIRMATION: OBVIOUS DOUBLE INCIPIENT CRACKS leading up to a series of ledges. Two thin parallel cracks, not one.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE TWO NEIGHBOURS, AND THE MEASUREMENTS ARE THE POINT: MOJO RISING is ABOUT 20 FT DOWNHILL of the chimney on an OBVIOUS BOLTED FACE. The NORTHWEST FACE, Boving-Pollock, is entered by TRAVERSING INTO A STEEP CORNER. THIS ROUTE IS 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT ON A PLAIN CRACK. Bolts mean Mojo Rising; a corner means Boving-Pollock; a plain crack forty feet right of the chimney means Free Mojo.

RETREAT FROM LOW ON THE ROUTE IS STRAIGHTFORWARD, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING WHEN YOU ARE UNSURE OF THE START: a party retreating from the fixed anchor atop pitch 1 rappels to the ground; above it the belays are built from gear, so retreating higher means leaving gear. There is no penalty for starting, finding the ground wrong, and coming back down.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek path, past Terror Basin to a Crescent Creek Basin camp, then over the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft off Hwy 20 near Newhalem. Follow the old roadbed and climbers' path along Goodell Creek for about 4 miles, gaining only about 1,000 ft, to a junction around 1,700 ft marked by a stone arrow, a post and a large cairn. That junction is the standard jump-off for EVERY Southern Pickets objective and the last easy, reliable water before the climb steepens.

The unmaintained Terror Creek climbers' trail cuts uphill to the right and turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 4,000-4,700 ft in well under 3 horizontal miles through old-growth forest and brush, with head-high slide alder and devil's club depending on the season, before breaking out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft onto heather benches, slabs and snowfields.

From treeline, rather than stopping at Terror Basin, continue a rising traverse west-northwest staying near the 5,800-6,400 ft band into Crescent Creek Basin, reached via a steep initial drop into the basin on mixed snow and talus followed by roughly an hour of traversing.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Head-high slide alder and devil's club on a relentlessly steep unmaintained path
No dependable water for roughly 4,500 ft of climbing
Broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered ground on the 500 ft descent to the route's base
The north side of the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col is a rappel proposition with glacier and moat terrain below it
Glacier edges near the col have been described as unable to hold body weight late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS REACHED BY GOING OVER A COL AND THEN DOWN THE FAR SIDE, AND THE DOWNHILL IS THE TEST. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp, climb east or northeast onto the ridge to gain the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then DOWNCLIMB AND SCRAMBLE ROUGHLY 500 FT down broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered ground on the FRENZEL SPITZ side to reach the base of the South Route proper. If you are still on the col, or above it, you have not started.

WHICH SIDE OF THE COL IS WHICH, AND IT IS THE ONE FACT THAT KEEPS PARTIES OUT OF TROUBLE HERE: the SOUTH, Crescent Creek side of that col is the friendly side, loose but moderate 3rd and 4th class scrambling. The NORTH side is sustained loose 5th class and drops into a broken couloir and glacier and moat terrain, and parties commonly need a rappel to get down it. That north side is the way to Frenzel Spitz, which sits under Ottohorn's north face: the 500 ft descent to the route's base goes down it, and the friendly Crescent Creek side is only the way up to the col and back to camp.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP, WHICH IS THE OTHER PLACE THIS DAY GETS LOST: Crescent Creek Basin, not Terror Basin. Terror Basin is where the McMillan, Inspiration and Terror parties stop. The Frenzel Spitz, Himmelhorn, Ottohorn and Chopping Block camp is the NEXT basin west, reached by holding the 5,800-6,400 ft band and traversing about an hour further. Stopping at the first flat ground above treeline puts you a basin short.

NO DEPENDABLE WATER above the Terror Creek junction until snowmelt or tarns near camp; carry enough for 4,500-plus ft of climbing in between.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

approach_variants.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
A bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, with about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHITMAN NOTCH AT ABOUT 9,100 FT IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU KNOW IT BY WHAT BECOMES VISIBLE RATHER THAN BY THE ALTIMETER: IT IS THE FIRST PLACE THE WHITMAN GLACIER COMES INTO VIEW. Until you can see a SECOND glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING PROPER IS HIGHER STILL, AND IT IS A CHANGE OF SURFACE: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a SHORT step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

THE ROUTE-FINDING TRAP IS LOW, NOT HIGH, AND IT IS THE ONE THING ON THIS CLIMB THAT REGULARLY COMMITS PARTIES TO BAD GROUND: between Summerland and Meany Crest, IF YOU FIND YOURSELF CONTOURING CLIMBER'S RIGHT INTO A BOWL UNDER ROCK BANDS, YOU ARE CLIFFED OUT AND OFF THE LINE. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

THE SUMMIT-CREST TEST IS A NEGATIVE AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

TIMING AS A FINDING: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

approach_variants.name: Gardner Meadows: west bank of the stream to the scree
approach_variants.notes: From Gardner Meadows around 5,700 ft leave the maintained trail and get onto the WEST side — climber's left — of the small stream draining south off Gardner Mountain toward Wolf Creek, then climb the steep meadows paralleling it, staying west of the streambed the whole way. A small meadow basin arrives at about 6,200 ft. Keep working toward the ridgeline; at roughly 7,100 ft the meadows give out and the ground turns to loose, marble-sized scree over sand, which is the slog that defines this route — about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile. A faint bootpath exists in places and is easy to lose. Reckon on four to five hours from the meadows.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Standing dead snags and blackened deadfall the length of the burnt Wolf Creek corridor
1,400 ft of loose scree over sand — poor footing in both directions
Lingering snow patches in the cliff bands and gullies into early summer
Loose, exposed scrambling with gendarmes on the connecting ridge if you carry on to North Gardner
approach_variants.baseFinding: STAY WEST OF THE STREAM, AND DO NOT CLIMB THE GULLY IT COMES OUT OF. Three gullies drain this face and they are not equivalent. The EASTERN one is where the stream originates, and it is the one that can cliff-band you out — which is exactly why every description of this route tells you to stay west of the stream from the meadows upward. The CENTRAL open gully and slopes just west of the stream is the most direct line and tops out at the saddle southeast of the summit. A further large gully west of that reaches the saddle southwest of the true summit, between the mountain's two highpoints. The transition to watch for is at about 7,100 ft where meadow turns to rock and the scree begins; above it you climb directly up steep rocky slopes, picking over scree and rock buttresses. At the top the ground flattens onto a high plateau and the summit sits on the ridge crest, WIDE AND GENTLE. If you are standing on a pointed bump with higher ground to the north, you are on one of the sub-peaks southeast of the true top.

approach_variants.name: FR 5620 pulloff to the base of the west peak slab
approach_variants.notes:
I-90 Exit 34 east of North Bend, east on Edgewick Road, then right at the stop sign after 0.4 miles onto SE Middle Fork Road, which becomes FR 56. Drive about 12.3 miles to the Middle Fork / Taylor River junction just after the Taylor River bridge, turn right onto road 5620 and go about a mile to a small gravel pulloff — five cars at most — near 47.54604, -121.52151 at about 1,174 ft. Washouts on the Middle Fork road have periodically added a mile or more of walking.

The path leaves the road a hundred to two hundred yards further along, on the left, marked by a cairn. From there it climbs steeply through forest switchbacks for roughly 30 to 45 minutes. The tread is not signed but it is genuinely worn: if you have been walking more than a few minutes on ground that does not look like a trail, you are off it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Rockfall down the lower slab pitches — bent hangers record it
Steep, loose, unsigned approach tread
Road washouts on the Middle Fork road adding approach distance
No water on the approach or the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
About 50 yards below the start of the climbing there is a LARGE CAIRN BUILT OF FLAT WHITE ROCKS — by a clear margin the biggest cairn on the approach trail, and the marker to look for. The base itself sits near 47.549, -121.5137 at about 1,700 ft.

From there the confirmation is bolts. This is a continuous bolted line up the slab, so a slab with no bolts on it is not the route. Two supporting details: the lower pitches are easy, low-angle and somewhat runout on solid, sometimes water-polished slab; and several hangers down there are visibly BENT from rockfall coming down the route, which both identifies the ground and tells you why to keep moving through it. Parties simulclimbing the easy lower pitches have gone off-track precisely by not tracking the bolts.

approach_variants.name: Gravel wash pullout on FR 56, dry creekbed and dirt gully
approach_variants.notes:
Distance is one-way horizontal; almost all of the effort is vertical. From I-90 Exit 34 at North Bend, drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FR 56) east — paved, then good gravel — staying on FR 56 PAST the Taylor River Road (FR 5620) junction, about 2.6 miles further, to a wide gravel wash and old borrow-pit pullout on the north side of the road at roughly 1,150-1,200 ft.

There is no maintained or numbered Forest Service trail here. This is an unmaintained climbers' boot path with intermittent cairns and pink flagging.

From the wash, follow the dry creekbed uphill for roughly a mile. A boot path exits climber's LEFT into second-growth forest with light brush before the creek narrows. Several boot-path branches exist low down: AVOID the flat, early traverse that cuts across to the slab too low, and take the higher up-and-down traverse instead.

At about 2,200 ft the path enters a loose dirt-and-scree gully mixed with vegetation — unpleasant, roughly 400 ft of gain — then exits climber's LEFT onto a wooded ridge for another 400 ft of steep but relatively brush-free ground. There is no reliable water past the creek near the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, and only in bone-dry conditions
hazards: No water above the trailhead creek
About 40-degree loose duff above the slab; huckleberry stems are the handholds
Slabs and dirt gullies become treacherous when even slightly wet
Braided boot paths low down leading to the slab at the wrong height
Loose and mossy rock in #2 Gully
Serious route-finding above the slab — intermittent path, cairns and flagging only
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the FIRST MAJOR SLAB at about 2,900 ft, roughly an hour and 1,700 ft above the car. It is unmistakable by contrast: it is the first clean rock of the day after nothing but duff, dirt and scree. Two low-fifth pitches follow intersecting DIKES up it; parties either solo them or rope up.

The negative marker is the dirt gully. If you have arrived at slab WITHOUT first grovelling through the loose dirt-and-scree gully at about 2,200 ft, you took the low flat traverse and you are on the slab too far along — traverse up and left to regain the line. Above the slab the landmarks come in a fixed order and that order is how you confirm you are still on it: dirt and heather above the slab's upper-LEFT edge, a tiny notch, a knife-edge razorback, and then a flat bivy clearing known as the glade saddle. A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20 ft scramble step follows, then a rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse leading to the Y Notch, where the line joins the gully locally called #2 Gully — loose rock on one side, polished mossy rock on the other — for the last 600 ft or so to the summit ridge at 5,519 ft.

approach_variants.name: Gravel wash pullout on FR 56, dry creekbed and dirt gully
approach_variants.notes:
I-90 Exit 34 near North Bend, then Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) past the Taylor River bridge junction to a pullout roughly 2.6 miles further on, beside a gravel wash. From the car the whole route is only about 1.5 miles horizontally but 4,400 vertical feet.

Start up the dry creek bed and leave it partway up into the woods, following a mix of pink flagging tape and faint tread up steep pine-needle slopes — 'scrumbling', pulling on whatever vegetation is at hand. Low down the path braids: take the higher up-and-down traverse rather than the flat early one that cuts to the slab too low. About an hour in, at roughly 2,200 ft, you reach the dirt gully.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, bone dry only
hazards: Loose 40-degree duff above the slab
No water above the trailhead creek
Slabs lethal when damp
Braided boot path low down
Exposed ledge traverse below the Y Notch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The dirt gully at about 2,200 ft is the gate, and the first major SLAB at about 2,900 ft is the base. Clean rock after one to two hours of nothing but duff and scree is the confirmation. Reaching slab without having passed through the dirt gully means you took the low traverse and are too far along the base — go up and left.

Above the slab the pine-needle slopes run about 40 degrees on loose duff, and huckleberry stems make the best handholds. The sequence above is the tiny notch, the razorback, the glade saddle, the wooded ramp with a 20 ft step, the exposed ledge traverse, and then the Y Notch where the route joins the gully system. Reaching the Y is what confirms you are on the South Route rather than on one of the neighbouring gully lines.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the Infinite Bliss climber's path just before it turns left to the base and head straight up into steep forest for nearly 1,000 ft, with class 4 steps and thick brush, until you can drop into the gully on the left.
Descend the gully several hundred feet to a ledge and cross Infinite Bliss at the base of its pitch 8. This is a net elevation LOSS of roughly 300 ft.
Continue across to the forest on the left side of the wall, then climb the steep forest angling back right to gain the left end of the ledge that sits level with the base of Infinite Bliss pitch 11.
Before reaching the IB line, turn up and start the long exposed class 4 scramble — this section is assumed to be the Roach/Springgate/Wells February 1963 route. An old piton was found here in 2002.
Where the 1963 line begins angling left, follow the natural right-angling ramp that connects into the Infinite Bliss scramble section above the top of IB pitch 15.

Continue up the ramp past where IB turns toward the lone stunted cedar; when the ramp fades, head straight up (the 1979 Fryberger/Brown line) into a shallow gully that reaches the ridge crest at a slight saddle.
Hike the heather benches right of the crest to the 30-foot summit block; a couple of low 5th class moves gain the top of Infinite Peak (4,804 ft).

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col to the east side of Silver Star's ridge
approach_variants.notes: Whine Spire is a sub-peak on the east side of Silver Star Mountain's ridge, below and south of the line of Wine Spires, and its east face is reached from the far side of Burgundy Col. From the pullout on SR-20 a few miles east of Washington Pass, take the boot path down to Early Winters Creek, cross on the log near 4,080 ft, and climb the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the bench camp near 6,500 ft, then on to the col. Drop off the east side and traverse south beneath the east faces. Expect a patch of steep snow on that traverse and, later in the season, awkward scree-filled moats where the snow has pulled back from the rock.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Steep snow patch and scree-filled moats on the traverse in to the base
Runout 5.8 sections on loose granite
A 5.9+ offwidth chimney section high on the route
Twelve long pitches, most 180 ft or more — a full day for most parties
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE HAND CRACK, NOT THE CHIMNEY — THAT IS THE ONE DECISION AT THE BOTTOM. Standing under the east face of Whine Spire there are two plausible starts within a few metres of each other. Around the corner and to the RIGHT is a clean, blocky chimney that looks better than it is, and the route deliberately avoids it. The climb proper begins to its LEFT on a steep crack that gives finger locks and solid hand jams straight off the ground and never narrows into a chimney or a squeeze. Commit only when the feature above you is a crack you can jam, set in a face rather than tucked in a corner. Late in the season a scree-choked moat sits between the snow and the rock at the base: cross it and rack up on the rock, because there is nowhere flat to sort gear once you have stepped across.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier camp to the notch south of the peak
approach_variants.notes: Ghost is climbed from the high camp shared with Crooked Thumb and Phantom, all three being within a few tenths of a mile of each other. From that camp a roped glacier crossing reaches the foot of the peak. The original line gained the notch SOUTH of the peak, and gained it FROM THE WEST rather than by attacking the notch directly from the glacier below, then stayed on the south and west sides of the mountain following obvious weaknesses at easy-to-moderate fourth and low fifth class.
