Access from camp is described as obvious once you are established there; the difficulty is knowing which of the three summits you are under.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Crevasse risk on the Whatcom and Challenger Glaciers on the way in, and on the crossing from camp
Loose, exposed ground near the high camp that is easy to lose in cloud
Three summits crowding one skyline — route-finding is the crux in poor visibility
Early-season fords on the Chilliwack River on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROCK ITSELF TELLS YOU WHICH PEAK YOU ARE ON. Ghost is not a peak-shaped peak: it is a sheer, small rock horn of very little prominence wedged between its neighbours, about a fifth of a mile south of Crooked Thumb and about three tenths of a mile north-northeast of Phantom, with a huge steep east face. If the formation in front of you reads as an independent summit with real prominence, it is Crooked Thumb or Phantom, not this. The decisive test is rock quality, and it is unambiguous. Ghost gives steep, solid rock with incut holds, often compared to golden granite, and it is described as generally solid by Pickets standards. Crooked Thumb's own line goes up a horribly loose slot-gully and a narrow crumbly ledge; Phantom's descent is rotten rock and dirt. If you are on good rock you are on Ghost; if you are pulling on rubble you are on a neighbour. Aim for the notch on the peak's SOUTH side and reach it from the WEST, then keep to the south and west flanks — the east face is the steep one and is not the way.

bivy.name: Luna Cirque high camp (near Lousy Lake)
Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. Whatcom Camp and both Graybeal camps have been closed because of fire damage from 2022, and the park's fire-closures page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists them closed until further notice, so there is no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

approach_variants.name: Conrad Meadows to the north side, the Conrad Glacier and the 7,200 ft saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the South Tieton Creek and Conrad Meadows trailhead, approach the north side of the peak and ascend the EAST side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, traverse onto the Meade Glacier, then finish over boulders, scree and a summit snowfield.

The Conrad is the more active of the peak's two small glaciers, so this line wants a rope, a harness and a crevasse-rescue kit rather than just an axe and crampons.

Descent reverses the traverse: back over the saddle and down the Conrad to Conrad Meadows. It is normally done over two or more days given the long approach through the drainage and the talus.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; rated for summer and fall and not recommended in spring or winter conditions
hazards: Glacier travel on the Conrad, the more active of the peak's two glaciers
Loose rock, scree and boulder terrain below the summit
A long approach through the Conrad Creek drainage and talus
Not recommended in spring or winter conditions
A traverse between two glaciers with the same ground to reverse on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO GLACIERS WITH ONE SADDLE BETWEEN THEM. THAT SEQUENCE IS THE ROUTE AND IT IS THE TEST.

You climb the EAST side of the CONRAD GLACIER to a saddle at about 7,200 ft, and from that saddle you TRAVERSE ONTO A SECOND GLACIER — the Meade — before any of the summit ground. Glacier, saddle, glacier, then boulders, scree and a summit snowfield, in that order.

THE NEGATIVE AT THE SADDLE IS THE ONE WORTH CARRYING: IF YOU REACH A SADDLE AND THE GROUND BEYOND IT IS BOULDERS AND SCREE WITH NO SECOND GLACIER, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SADDLE. This route's saddle opens onto ice. A saddle that opens onto rock belongs to the ridge line, which is the peak's other route from the same trailhead.

THE ELEVATION IS A CROSS-CHECK RATHER THAN A MARKER: about 7,200 ft. Well above that and you have climbed the glacier past its col; well below and you are still on the apron.

WHICH SIDE OF THE GLACIER MATTERS AND IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG IN THE DARK: the EAST side of the Conrad. Drifting west takes you up the glacier's other flank and away from the saddle.

THE APPROACH-SIDE FINDING: this route comes at the peak from the NORTH. If you have climbed onto a long ridge with the peak in view along it, you are on the Klickton Divide line instead — a fine route, a different day, and it does not need a rope.

approach_variants.name: Conrad Meadows and the Surprise Lake loop to the Meade Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Conrad Meadows and South Fork Tieton trailhead at road's end, about 4,044 ft, reached by the Tieton Reservoir road and then the South Fork Tieton road off the highway west of Naches. The last several miles are gravel.

Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows, crossing Conrad Creek, into the Goat Rocks Wilderness and on to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin. Cross it left of some large mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

This is a long day: roughly 20 miles round trip with real gain, and limited water late in a dry season.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A steep snowfield below the summit requiring solid self-arrest
Loose rock on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk between parties climbing close together
A receding glacier that can still hide crevasses and moats
A long, remote round trip of roughly 20 miles with limited water in a dry year
Basin navigation that depends on visibility once off the trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEAVING THE TRAIL IN THE RIGHT PLACE AND FINDING THE FOOT OF THE MEADE IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM, AND EVERYTHING BEFORE IT IS TRAIL.

Take the RIGHT fork of the Surprise Lake loop and stay on it to its HIGH POINT. From there climb WEST into a basin, cross it keeping LEFT of the large mounds, and drop a short way to the foot of the glacier. If you are climbing onto a long ridge crest before you have reached any snow, you are on the ridge line to the south, not this route.

ON THE GLACIER, ONE ROCK BAND ORGANISES EVERYTHING. It splits the lower glacier from the upper; go up near the center of the cirque and pass it on its RIGHT. Above it, stay right of the snow dome and the ridge comes easily.

THE BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE IS A SMALL SADDLE, AND THE SUMMIT IS JUST WEST OF IT. From the ridge a rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to that saddle; the true summit is immediately to its west, a short, loose class 3 scramble. If the ground keeps rising well beyond a gap, you are at the wrong gap.

THE NEGATIVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM ITS SIBLING ON THE SAME PEAK: this line reaches the Meade from BELOW, out of the basin. The other route from this trailhead crosses the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle east of the summit and drops onto the Meade from above. If you are on the Conrad Glacier, you are on that one instead.

SELF-ARREST IS PART OF THE BASE FINDING HERE, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the snowfield below the summit is steep enough that the route assumes you can hold a slip on it. Arriving without an axe is a reason to turn round at the foot of the glacier.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flats and the Goat Ledges traverse to the black prow
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat trailhead in the Chambers Lake area on the west side of the Goat Rocks, at about 4,650 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Hike Snowgrass Trail #96 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft along Goat Creek to Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow; the flat itself is closed to camping, so camp at the established sites below it.

From camp, head cross-country and scramble east across the Goat Ledges and Goat Ribs — a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies — at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. This is often combined with Old Snowy and Ives in a single traverse day.

A lower variation holds a consistent traverse elevation of about 7,500 ft, which reduces exposure to rockfall knocked down by other parties.

The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous. Careful route-finding along the correct band and on goat paths is what makes it a reasonable class 4 passage rather than a bad one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the ledges are dry
hazards: Significant rockfall on the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse, worst with parties stacked at different elevations
Loose andesite, pyroclastic breccia and tuff throughout the upper mountain
Steep, insecure sections approaching the summit block even in dry late-season conditions
Route-finding failure — the whole route depends on correctly identifying the white aggregate band
A class 4 downclimb through the notch on the way back, on the same loose ground
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHITE BAND IS THE ROUTE. THAT IS THE ENTIRE FINDING AND IT IS A COLOUR TEST, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVES BAD LIGHT.

On the Goat Ribs and Goat Ledges traverse at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft there is a band of SOLID, ABRASIVE, WHITE PYROCLASTIC AGGREGATE. It points at a NOTCH BEHIND A PROMINENT DARK ROCK TOWER — the black prow. So there are two objects to find and they are opposite colours: a white band and a dark tower, with the notch behind the tower.

THE NEGATIVE IS TACTILE AND IT TELLS YOU IMMEDIATELY, WITHOUT A VIEW: THE WHITE BAND IS SOLID AND ABRASIVE. THE ROCK ABOVE IT AND BELOW IT IS LOOSE. If the holds are moving under your hands you are off the band — traverse back to the white rather than pressing on.

HOLD YOUR HEIGHT AT ABOUT 7,500 FT. Drifting HIGH is worse than drifting low: it puts you above the band and above other parties, in the position that generates the rockfall this traverse is notorious for. The low variation is a deliberate choice, not a mistake.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING IS THE NOTCH BEHIND THE BLACK PROW. Everything before it is traversing; the class 4 finish begins there. If you are scrambling steeply and you have not passed a dark tower, you have started up too early.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the traverse ends at the peak. If the ribs and gullies keep coming and you have not found a white band pointing anywhere, you are on the wrong tier of the mountain — go back to a rib you can identify and re-find the band, rather than gaining height to look.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the 7,200 ft camp
approach_variants.notes:
White Chuck River trailhead at about 2,300 ft — subject to the same long-running road access problems as the Sitkum approach, so confirm before relying on it. Follow the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about six miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail about a mile and three quarters to the PCT.

Head north on the PCT about three miles — roughly two thirds of a mile past the Kennedy Creek crossing, which is your water — to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the trail. That path climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: long-running road access problems on the White Chuck side
unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT
loose moraine and boulders low on the Kennedy Glacier
very loose rock around the Rabbit Ears, worst in warm dry conditions
crevasses on the Ptarmigan, Vista and Kennedy glaciers
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. THAT saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are NOT visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

approach_variants.name: Suiattle River Road and the PCT via Milk Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from Darrington to its end at Sulphur Creek Campground. Follow the Suiattle River trail about seven miles to the bridge over the river, then the PCT southbound about nine miles to a camp in the East Fork Milk Creek basin at about 5,600 ft. From there continue up the ridge on snow and pumice to the same standard high camp near 7,200 ft.

The Suiattle River Road has a long history of flood damage and multi-year closures, so its status is worth confirming rather than assuming.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: repeated flood damage and long closures on the Suiattle River Road
very long PCT approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the Kennedy Ridge variation
approach_variants.baseFinding: Identical above the 7,200 ft camp: traverse the upper south-west Ptarmigan slopes to about 8,000 ft, round Kennedy Peak to the 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy glaciers, up the Kennedy to the 8,800 ft saddle where the ridge begins. Remember that the Rabbit Ears stay hidden until you are directly beneath them slightly east of the crest.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk to White Pass, then north
approach_variants.notes: Some parties use the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass — about nine miles and 5,900 ft — and then make a long traverse north on or near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area. It is a twenty-mile-plus approach day and is chosen when the other two roads are out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: twenty-mile-plus approach day
same upper-mountain hazards as the other variations
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the other variations: the 8,800 ft saddle above the Kennedy Glacier is where the ridge starts, and the Rabbit Ears do not become visible until you are immediately below them.

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a couple of bivy-scale sites

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River and Kennedy Ridge to the Glacier Creek camps
approach_variants.notes:
The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, and it is one of the shorter windows on the mountain — the upper Kennedy is a small, steep glacier that opens into a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses as the season runs on
hazards: An upper glacier described by parties as a maze of 5-15 ft crevasses that needs deliberate, slow routefinding
Seracs on climber's left beneath the Kennedy Peak wall, where some parties have had to belay off bare glacier ice
Trading crevasse navigation for rockfall by hugging the left wall — the simplification is real and so is the cost
A bergschrund at the head of the glacier whose only crossing may be a single bridge found from the snow dome above it
8,200 ft of gain from a trailhead served by a road that has been closed at milepost 3.7, so the walk in may be far longer than the mileage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMB IS BELOW YOU, NOT ABOVE YOU, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE TEST. From the Glacier Creek camp the climbers' trail climbs a gully to the CREST of Kennedy Ridge — and then you go DOWN off the far side, to climber's right, to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. A party that tops the ridge and keeps climbing has left the route. If you have not lost height since the ridge crest, you have not reached the base.

ARRIVAL: the foot of the glacier, where ridge ground runs out into ice. Rope up there. On the lower glacier keep RIGHT; on the upper glacier take the CENTRE. That right-then-centre sequence is worth memorising before you leave camp, because the upper Kennedy is a maze and there is nothing to sight on inside it.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST FROSTBITE RIDGE, which shares this mountain flank and this camp: Frostbite rounds Kennedy Peak to the saddle between the VISTA and KENNEDY glaciers at about 8,000 ft, climbs the Kennedy to a saddle at about 8,800 ft, and then leaves the ice for the RIDGE. This route never leaves the ice. If you are standing on a saddle looking for a rock crest to follow, you are on Frostbite. If you are still roped on glacier at 9,500 ft heading for a bergschrund, you are on this one.

THE TOP END, AND IT IS A REAL DECISION POINT: the bergschrund sits at the head of the glacier. Reach it by climbing LEFT to the top of a snow dome and looking for a bridge from there — do not walk the schrund's length hunting for a gap at its lowest point. Above it the headwall runs about 40 degrees; stay LEFT of, but close to, the prominent rock outcrops, and that puts you on the crater rim.

WHAT HUGGING THE LEFT WALL COSTS: parties commonly move under the Kennedy Peak wall on climber's left to simplify the crevasse problem. It works, and it buys the simplification with rockfall and serac exposure. That is a trade to make deliberately, not one to drift into.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required for parking. No climbing permits or camping fees required. Trail status: The White Chuck River Trail was severely damaged by a 2003 flood; contact Darrington Ranger Station for current conditions.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.permit: Self-Issue Wilderness Permit
access.closures: CLOSED: White Chuck Road (FR 23) is closed to vehicles from milepost 3.7 to its end, and Rat Trap Pass Road (FR 27) from milepost 4, for flood damage, since 19 March 2025, with no end date given, as listed on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert last updated 30 June 2026. White Chuck River Trail #643 is listed as inaccessible, with no road or trail access, since the 2003 flood. Use the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead and the Pacific Crest Trail instead. Darrington Ranger District: (360) 436-1155.
access.seasonal: Mountain Loop Highway has a seasonal gate closure (Deer Creek–Bedal, ~14 mi), typically Nov–mid/late May. Suiattle River Road (FSR 26), the primary Glacier Peak access, has had storm-damage closures — check current conditions before a trip.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass
approach_variants.notes: The way in since the White Chuck side closed. North Fork Sauk Trail #649 runs up the valley through old growth to Mackinaw Shelter and then switchbacks steeply to the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly eight to nine miles from the trailhead. Turn north on the PCT, cross Red Pass a mile or two on, and descend into the upper White Chuck valley, following the PCT down it for roughly seven to nine miles past the old White Chuck River Trail junction to Sitkum Creek. It is much longer than the old approach, and the climb back over Red Pass comes on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: very long approach on the PCT with substantial gain and loss
no signed junction for the climbers' path
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route above is unchanged: the marker is Boulder Basin — trees giving way to heather and rock benches with running water at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft — and then snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum above it. Coming down the valley on the PCT the risk is walking past the start of the climbers' path, so mark the old White Chuck River Trail junction and Sitkum Creek on the map before you set out rather than expecting signage.

approach_variants.name: White Chuck River Trail #643 (closed since the 2003 flood)
approach_variants.notes:
This was the standard way up Glacier Peak until the October 2003 flood. The White Chuck Road (FR 23) is now closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and the trail has been listed as inaccessible since the flood, so this is kept as a record of the old line rather than as a way in.

From the trailhead at about 2,350 ft the trail runs upstream through old growth, crossing Pumice, Glacier and Kennedy Creeks — reliable water, but high with snowmelt in early summer. At about five and a half miles is the old Kennedy Hot Springs area at around 3,300 ft, still a popular campsite; the pool, lodge and guard station were destroyed by the 2003 flood and never rebuilt, so there is no usable hot pool there.

Another mile and a half brings you to Sitkum Creek and the PCT junction at about 3,850 ft. Turn north on the PCT for about half a mile to a forested camp near 4,100 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: road closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 and trail listed as inaccessible
creek fords running high with early-summer snowmelt
steep unmaintained climbers' path with no signage leaving the PCT
crevasses on the Sitkum
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The path that leaves the PCT for Boulder Basin is unsigned and steeper than anything before it — climbers describe it as more of a fisherman's track than a trail. The test is direction, not appearance: the correct path goes STRAIGHT UP the forested ridge. Anything that contours is the PCT or a game trail.

You know you have arrived at the top of it when the trees break: Boulder Basin at roughly 5,500 to 6,000 ft is heather and rock benches with running water, and it is the standard high camp. If you are still in continuous forest, you are below it, however long the climb has felt.

From camp the route ascends snowfields onto the toe of the Sitkum. Rope up at the point the snowfield stops being a slope you can see the bottom of and becomes continuous glacier — there is no rock landmark for this, so the transition is judged on the ground rather than found.

approach_variants.name: Goat Mountain Trail #673 to the viewpoint shoulder, then around the south side of the West Peak
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and the same first four miles as the standard scramble: from Glacier, SR-542 east 12.5 miles to FR-32, then FR-32 to the Goat Mountain Trailhead near 2,470 ft, and Goat Mountain Trail #673 up the switchbacks and ridge to the viewpoint shoulder around 5,400-5,700 ft.

The difference is what you do with the West Peak. This line leaves the maintained trail at the shoulder and traverses BELOW the West Peak on its SOUTH side to gain the ridge running toward the East Peak, rather than going over the West Peak's corniced top.

It is the line that avoids the cornice problem, at the cost of a sidehill traverse on 40-50 degree slopes.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, but the traverse slopes hold snow and an axe is wanted early season
hazards: A sidehill traverse on 40-50 degree slopes, wanting an axe and sometimes crampons
Cornices on the West Peak above the traverse
A 300 ft regain on the return that is easy to walk past in cloud
No maintained tread from the viewpoint shoulder onward
No reliable water past the forest creek crossings (about the first 2.5 miles of trail)
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAVERSE GOES UNDER THE WEST PEAK, NOT OVER IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING DECISION. From the viewpoint shoulder near 5,400-5,700 ft, leave the trail and traverse BELOW the West Peak on its SOUTH side. If you are gaining height toward a summit ahead of you, you are on the standard scramble over the false summit; if you are holding height and sidehilling with the peak above your left shoulder, you are on this one.

THE ANGLE IS THE CONFIRMATION. The traverse slopes run 40-50 degrees. That is steep enough that an axe and, early season, step-kicking or crampons are wanted, and it is steep enough to feel wrong if you have wandered onto easier ground. Easy walking on this traverse means you have dropped too low into the basin.

ARRIVAL: you have arrived at the climbing when the traverse delivers you onto the connecting RIDGE between the two peaks — ground with air on both sides, running east toward the higher summit. The scramble to the East Peak's top is the last short section above that ridge.

THE 300 FT REGAIN IS THE RETURN TEST, worth knowing before you commit: coming back, you descend to the saddle and then have to regain roughly 300 ft to reach the Goat Mountain Trail viewpoint shoulder. If you are heading home and only ever going downhill, you have missed the shoulder and are descending an unmaintained slope.

WHICH SUMMIT: the EAST peak is the true and higher one, near 6,890 ft. The West Peak at about 6,600 ft is the false summit that the standard route walks over the top of.

approach_variants.name: Goat Mountain Trail #673 to the end of maintained tread, then over the West Peak false summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goat Mountain Trailhead, day-use parking just off FS-32 (Hannegan Pass Road) about 2.1-2.5 miles up from the Glacier Public Service Center, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It is well built and relentlessly steep, gaining the ridge by dozens of switchbacks and crossing a small cascading creek repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock.

Around a mile in, near 3,200 ft, the grade eases and the trail traverses a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly two miles it crosses into the Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur — the Old Goat Trail — splits east toward an old lookout site. Stay on the main tread.

Meadows and big views open by 2.7 miles; the maintained trail tops out on the crest at a 5,200 ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft.

Beyond that it is an open ridge boot path, about 0.8 mile and 1,000 ft more to the West Peak false summit near 6,600 ft, and then on to the true East summit.

There is no reliable water beyond the creek crossings in the forest, roughly the first 2.5 miles of trail.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on this ridge and reports have found solid snow from 4,300-4,500 ft well into summer
hazards: Cornices on the West Peak false summit, invisible from above
Solid lingering snow from 4,300-4,500 ft upward well into summer
A knife-edge-ish exposed section near the true summit
No reliable water beyond the forest creek crossings (about the first 2.5 miles)
An unsigned spur trail near the wilderness boundary that leads to an old lookout site instead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL STOPS, NEAR 5,600 FT, AND THAT END IS ABRUPT. Below it, built tread and switchbacks. Above it, an open ridge boot path with nothing constructed. If you are still on graded trail you have not started the route.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS CORNICED — DO NOT GO OVER ITS TOP. This is the one hard rule on the ridge and it is a safety instruction rather than a route preference: the West Peak at about 6,600 ft is corniced and exposed, and the correct line bypasses it on the SOUTH or WEST slope. Cornices are invisible from above and this is precisely the terrain where cloud sits.

THE 300 FT DROP IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU HAVE PASSED THE FALSE SUMMIT, AND IT IS THE STRONGEST TEST ON THE ROUTE. Past the West Peak the ridge DROPS ROUGHLY 300 FT into a notch before climbing again. So: if you have not descended 300 ft, the high ground in front of you is not the true summit — it is the false one you were supposed to walk around. An altimeter settles this in zero visibility and eyesight does not.

AFTER THE NOTCH it is a final stretch of mixed snow, rock and short exposed steps to the true East summit at 6,892 ft. The crux is a narrow, moderately exposed knife-edge-ish section near the top — keep the axe in hand and self-arrest-ready on the steep snow.

CARRY THE AXE FROM 4,300-4,500 FT, not from where the snow looks serious. That is where reports put the solid snow, and it is well below the point where a party without an axe realises it wanted one.

bivy.name: Open benches on the broad ridge
bivy.notes: The best camping on the mountain if you are willing to haul water, and the natural base for the south ridge scramble. A series of level shelves on a broad, open ridge above treeline, past a viewpoint knob near 5,200 ft, with Baker, Shuksan and Sefrit filling the skyline and the Border Peaks and the Pickets beyond. From here the maintained trail continues to its end on the shoulder and the scramble to the summits goes on from there, so a camp at the benches leaves a short and pleasant summit morning. The slope faces south and melts early, so this is usually accessible from late June, sometimes earlier; the trade is that it bakes and stays dry all summer. It is fully exposed to wind and to weather rolling in from the west with nothing to duck behind. Excellent huckleberries in early autumn, and bears know it.
bivy.water: NONE. Everything must be carried up from the last crossing in the forest. Snow patches linger into July in shaded pockets and can be melted early in the season, but by August the whole crest is dry
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead. No campfires. Camp on bare ground, gravel or an existing flat rather than in the heather, and store food securely against bears
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents spread across the benches, kept apart so the heather is not trampled into one bare patch

bivy.name: Last stream crossing, top of the forest
bivy.notes: Listed for the water rather than for the camping, and the water is the point. The trail climbs steeply from the trailhead through about a dozen switchbacks in the first mile and stays in deep forest for two and a half, crossing several small creeks on the way; the highest of them sits right where the trees thin into heather and huckleberry. Above this line the mountain gives you nothing. Parties heading to the benches or the crest should stop here, top up, and accept carrying the weight for the last stretch. Late in a dry summer even these crossings run thin, so do not assume the lower ones are still flowing on the way down. Elevation is not stated because the exact crossing shifts with the season and the snowpack; navigate to it by the transition out of the timber, not by an altimeter reading.
bivy.water: THIS IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN, at roughly mile 2.7 where the final creeks cross the tread. Treat it. Everything on the ridge above is dry, so fill every container here whether or not you intend to camp
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary the trail crosses around mile 2. No overnight permit is required and none is issued. Twelve-person party limit. Campfires are not permitted on this trail, so carry a stove. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid here. Black bears work this slope in huckleberry season and food must be secured overnight
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on rough ground beside the trail where the timber gives out; there is no established site and the slope is steep, so flat spots are few

bivy.name: Ridge crest at the end of the maintained trail
bivy.notes: The highest ground with anything like a flat pitch, where the maintained trail ends on Goat Mountain's shoulder and the route becomes a steep boot path up grass and heather to the false summit and the west peak. The crest carries on upward from here toward 5,600 ft and above, and the east peak, which is the higher of the two, is a further meadow scramble along the ridge with no trail. Camping here shortens summit day to almost nothing, which is the only argument for it: it is stony, cramped and completely exposed, and it is the driest spot on a dry mountain. Snow can lie across the upper slope into July and the grass traverse above is genuinely slippery when wet, so this is a fair-weather choice. Sunrise and sunset from the crest are the reason people put up with all of it.
bivy.water: NONE, and the nearest is the forest crossings far below. In early season there are snow patches on the north side of the crest to melt; from midsummer there is nothing at all
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. This is national forest rather than national park — the park boundary lies well east beyond Hannegan Pass — so no park backcountry permit applies
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the shoulder where the tread runs out; small, stony and windy

bivy.name: Basin below the east peak
bivy.notes: The one camp on Goat Mountain that solves the water problem, in the basin lying east and below the higher east peak, seen from the overlook near the top of the maintained trail. It has ample flat terrain and running water, which nothing on the ridge does. The cost is that reaching it means leaving the trail entirely and dropping off the crest on trackless ground, which is more commitment than most parties want for a scramble that can be done in a day from the benches — so it is chosen mainly by people camping two nights, going for the east summit as well as the west, or arriving too late in the season for the crest to hold snow. Approach it from the end of the maintained trail rather than trying to contour in low. No elevation is given because the usable ground spreads across the basin floor rather than sitting at one identifiable spot.
bivy.water: Present, which makes this basin unique here — snowmelt streams and pools that last well into the season, unlike anything on the crest. Treat it, and check that it is still running before relying on it in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. Camp on durable ground away from the water and secure food overnight
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents with room to spread out; the most generous ground on the mountain

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes:
Index turnoff from US 2, into town, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right just before the road parallels the railway.

Cross the tracks — an active line with several trains a day. Bear a little left off the crossing to find the trail up toward the wall, then take the branch that turns RIGHT, which runs along the base of the Lower Wall past the Great Northern Slab and on to the Main Wall. Five minutes from the car.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day; full sun when the sun is out
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach — several trains daily
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking area
Busy wall — queues and parties above you dropping gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
City Park is the landmark for this whole section — the obvious, unmistakable crack splitting the Main Wall. Find it first; everything here is described from it.

Godzilla is the crack and corner system IMMEDIATELY RIGHT of City Park. Standing at the base, the start is a shallow right-facing groove/face, positioned just right of being directly beneath the City Park crack.

So if you are stood exactly under the obvious splitter you have gone one line too far left. Step right until you are under a right-facing corner system and that is it.

approach_variants.name: Via the centre route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: You can scramble on up the gully to this climb's own ledge, but many parties add pitches instead: do the usual gully approach from the pullout near milepost 166 to the wall's upper ledge, then climb the lower pitches of the centre eleven-pitch line to the shared midway ledge system and traverse left from there. Rack for the pitches you are climbing to get there as well as for this route.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried; the pitches used to reach it are the same ones that seep into early summer in wet years.
hazards: From the lower pitches, a retreat means reversing or rappelling somebody else's route
Loose and deteriorating rock on the lowest pitches and again high on the line
Belays are bolted but not all of them are rigged for rappel, so find the rappel stations before you need them
Everything below you is occupied ground; manage rockfall onto parties on the route you climbed in on
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are looking for a TWO-BOLT ANCHOR sitting on the midway ledge, and the trees are what place it: the anchor is on the ledge BELOW a stand of trees, not level with them and not above them. Traverse LEFT along the ledge until the trees are above you and the two bolts are at your feet. Confirm it from the rock: the first pitch off this anchor is a technical corner with loose chockstones at its hardest moves, so if what rises from your anchor is a clean face or a slab you are at the wrong station. Negative markers: if the anchor you have clipped is one of the bolted rappel stations belonging to the route you just climbed, you have not traversed at all; if the trees are still off to your left, you have not traversed far enough.

approach_variants.name: Via the right-hand cave route's lower pitches
approach_variants.notes: The same idea from the other side: climb the lower pitches of the right-hand cave line off the upper ledge to reach the shared midway ledge system, then traverse left. This is the longer leftward traverse of the two, so allow for it.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the wall has dried.
hazards: From the lower pitches, escape means rappelling a neighbouring line
Loose and deteriorating rock low and high on the route
Not all belays are rappel-rigged, so plan the descent before you leave the ledge
Long leftward traverse on a ledge with loose material on it
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the midway ledge, traverse LEFT — further than from the centre line — until you find the TWO-BOLT ANCHOR set on the ledge directly BELOW a stand of trees. The trees are the test: below them, not beside them. The first pitch above the anchor is a technical corner holding loose chockstones at the crux, which distinguishes it from the clean faces either side. Negative markers: if you are still passing bolted rappel stations that belong to the route you climbed up, keep traversing; if you have reached ground where the ledge system ends and the wall closes down, you have gone past it.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT over Cutthroat and Granite Passes to the Snowy Lakes spur
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-20 to Rainy Pass at 4,880 ft near milepost 158, about 35 miles west of Winthrop or 51 miles east of Marblemount, and park at the Rainy Pass North PCT trailhead.

Hike north on the Pacific Crest Trail through forest and switchbacks to Cutthroat Pass at about 6,800 ft, continue past Granite Pass at roughly 6.25 miles, where snowfields can linger into August, and along a cliff-cut trail toward Methow Pass. ABOUT A MILE BEFORE METHOW PASS, A SIGNED SPUR TRAIL SWITCHBACKS UP TO LOWER AND THEN UPPER SNOWY LAKE at about 6,700-7,000 ft. Roughly 10-11 miles and 2,700 ft of gain one-way. Good campsites sit in the meadow near the lakes.

Two pitches. This is also the peak's overall first ascent line, made in September 1946.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct, with late September and early October favoured for larch colour and stable weather
hazards: Snowfields lingering at Granite Pass into August
A cliff-cut section of trail beyond Granite Pass
Loose class 2-3 scree and talus on the upper mountain
A 10-11 mile approach before any climbing
Little reliable water between Cutthroat Pass and Snowy Lakes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SPUR TO THE LAKES IS SIGNED, AND THAT IS THE ONE PIECE OF SIGNAGE ON THE WHOLE DAY, SO USE IT: it leaves the PCT ABOUT A MILE BEFORE METHOW PASS. IF YOU HAVE REACHED METHOW PASS, YOU HAVE WALKED ABOUT A MILE TOO FAR.

CAMP IS AT THE LAKES, AND THE LAKES ARE THE BASE OF THE DAY. From there the route is a scramble on the southwest side of the peak with only two pitches of climbing at the top.

THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS WHAT MAKES THIS ROUTE FINDABLE, AND THE DESCENT DESCRIBES IT PRECISELY: parties make A SINGLE SHORT RAPPEL OF ROUGHLY 40 FT OFF THE SUMMIT BLOCK to regain the ridge, then downclimb and scramble class 2-3 scree and talus back toward Snowy Lakes. SO THE TECHNICAL PART OF THIS MOUNTAIN IS ABOUT FORTY FEET TALL AND IT IS AT THE VERY TOP. If you are roping up low on the peak you have found something harder than the Southwest Route.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER ASPECTS, AND IT IS A DIRECTION FROM CAMP: the NORTH side is reached by travelling NORTHWEST from Snowy Lakes into Golden Horn's basin. The EAST FACE is reached by scrambling the ridge, traversing a scree field on the SOUTHWEST side, and then DESCENDING to the base of the east face. THIS ROUTE NEVER DESCENDS. It stays on the southwest flank and goes up. If you are losing height to reach a wall, you are on the east face approach.

PLUNGE-STEPPING THE LOOSE SCREE SPEEDS THE DESCENT CONSIDERABLY, which is worth knowing because the scree is otherwise the slowest part of the day.

approach_variants.name: Off the Bridge Creek trail to the toe of the arete descending northeast off the main ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead near 4,800 ft, head south on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly nine to ten miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp, then up the increasingly brushy North Fork trail.

WHERE TO LEAVE THE TRAIL IS DISPUTED AND BOTH VERSIONS ARE GIVEN RATHER THAN AVERAGED. The first-ascent account describes leaving at an obvious CLEARING BEFORE GRIZZLY CREEK and climbing from there to the toe of the arete. The route's own catalog description instead has the party continue past Grizzly Creek to around trail-mile 14, ford the North Fork, work up scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the large waterfall, and then commit to a steep sustained bushwhack through slide alder and timber for roughly the last half mile.

Either way the objective is the same feature and the total approach is on the order of twelve or more miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing. Most parties bivy low on the ridge; water is reliable along Bridge Creek and scarce once you are on the rock, so tank up before you leave the creek.

The first ascent climbed its first fifth-class pitch at dusk and bivied on a bench, with the real difficulty starting the next morning.
approach_variants.season: Late summer, August into September, once the approach bushwhack and the glacier are most passable; a long committing route that wants a stable weather window
hazards: Hidden cliff bands inside the brush and loose footing on the slabs beside the waterfall
A very long sustained ridge — 2,800 to 3,000 ft of climbing with about 5,000 ft of exposure on one side and 4,000 on the other
Mostly simul-climbed with sparse belayed pitches, so long sections carry limited protection
Very few documented repeats, so beta and bail options are both thin
Benightment on the ridge is a real risk, and the standard descent drops into the Park Creek drainage on the far side of the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FEATURE IS A CLEAN-LOOKING ARETE THAT DESCENDS NORTHEAST OFF THE MAIN RIDGE, AND YOU AIM FOR ITS TOE. That is what both accounts of this route agree on. It sits close beneath the Goode Glacier's lower icefall — near it, not on it.

THE SINGLE STRONGEST TEST IS THAT YOU NEVER CROSS THE GLACIER. The Northeast Buttress, the peak's other big route on this side, is reached by stepping off the Goode Glacier across a moat at a band of red rock. THIS ROUTE IS GAINED FROM THE EAST, FROM BRUSH AND ROCK, WITH NO GLACIER CROSSING AT ALL. If you have crampons on to reach your base, you are on the Buttress.

THE ARETE ANNOUNCES ITSELF BY BEING CLEAN. It is described as a clean-looking arete precisely because the ground around it is not — the last half mile of approach is slide alder and timber. Emerging from brush onto a distinct clean crest running down to the northeast is the confirmation.

COUNT THE FIRST STAGE: simul-climbing up the lower arete to a TOWER AT ABOUT 8,200 FT, then ONE RAPPEL off it, and only then running-belay climbing along the crest toward the southeast peak. A rappel early on a ridge you are ascending is a strong positional marker and it is the first one this route gives you.

THE CRUX IS LATE AND IT IS ABOVE THE GLACIER: three long pitches of 5.9-5.10 on the southeast peak headwall, with easier options further left, and then an overhanging 5.10 headwall above the Goode Glacier near Black Tooth Notch with an icy moat to negotiate. If you have met your hardest climbing in the first half of the day, you are on something else.

bivy.name: Goode Glacier approach bivy, timbered knoll
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the North Fork trail after Grizzly Creek, fording the creek and grinding up timber and scree beside the drainage off the Goode Glacier, this is the classic first bivy under the buttress. Reports differ on whether it is the better choice: it sits noticeably west of the line of travel, so some parties consider the extra push to higher ground worth doing. Sparse timber gives a little shelter, which matters more here than the small elevation saving. Human waste goes in a cathole or is packed out above treeline, and there is no toilet.
bivy.water: Meltwater from the Goode Glacier drainage nearby, but flow is seasonal and can be a walk away or thin late in the year
bivy.permit: Inside the Goode CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE, not a designated camp — the permit is issued for the zone, party size is capped at six, no campfires, and camping is only allowed on durable ground such as snow, rock or bare earth.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small tents on a timbered knoll

bivy.name: Upper bivy in the rock bands east of the buttress toe
bivy.notes: Sitting in the rock bands just east of where the Northeast Buttress meets the ground, this puts you at the base with a few hundred feet already banked for summit day, which is the argument for grinding past the lower knoll. The exact elevation is reported inconsistently — figures in the 5,400 to 5,600 ft range all refer to broadly the same shelf system, so navigate to the terrain rather than to a number. It is exposed and rocky, so a poor choice in unsettled weather compared with the timbered ground lower down. Confirm you have water before committing to it late in the summer.
bivy.water: Running meltwater has been found at or near these sites, but it is snow-fed and not dependable once the drainage dries out later in the season
bivy.permit: Goode cross-country zone permit, six-person maximum, no fires, durable surfaces only; zone camping must also keep clear of designated camps and trails by the park's stated distances.
bivy.capacity: Tight — commonly described as just enough flat ground for a party of about four

bivy.name: Fireweed Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT
bivy.notes: A Bridge Creek corridor camp on the PCT well short of the North Fork junction, near the Twisp Pass trail area. It is only useful to a Goode party as an overflow choice when the North Fork camps are booked out, which happens in peak season because so few sites serve this valley. Camping here adds miles to an already long approach day. Treat it as a fallback rather than a plan.
bivy.water: Reliable — Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, same Recreation.gov / Marblemount walk-up system and the same per-person and reservation fees.
bivy.capacity: Designated camp with hiker and stock use

bivy.name: North Fork Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT junction
bivy.notes: This sits right at the junction where the PCT leaves Bridge Creek for the North Fork, roughly ten miles in from the SR 20 trailhead, so it is the natural first-night stop for a party that started late. It is a long way below the climb, which means a very big second day to reach the glacier bivies. Its value is logistical rather than tactical — it shortens the drive-day push without needing a cross-country zone permit. Being a valley-bottom camp in forest, expect bugs through midsummer.
bivy.water: Reliable year round — Bridge Creek and the North Fork run beside the camp
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round; reserve the specific camp on Recreation.gov or take a walk-up from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee applies.
bivy.capacity: Small designated hiker camp with a handful of numbered sites; the site is reserved by name on the permit

bivy.name: Walker Park Camp
bivy.notes: Roughly two miles up the North Fork trail from the junction, this is the first camp that meaningfully shortens the walk to the Goode Glacier drainage. The tread to here is still ordinary maintained trail, so it is an easy target even arriving in the dark. Parties usually treat it as a place to shed weight rather than a base, since the climb is still hours of rough ground above. No elevation is recorded — the valley section stays well under 4,000 ft, but no confident figure was sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — sits on the North Fork of Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, booked by camp name; same NPS fee structure as any Bridge Creek camp, and it must be carried for the night you actually sleep there.
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp, a couple of parties at most

bivy.name: Grizzly Creek Camp
bivy.notes: About four miles up the North Fork trail, this is the last designated camp before the country turns unpleasant, and the practical decision point for the whole approach. Beyond it the tread gets brushy and faint — stinging nettles are a recurring complaint and long trousers are worth carrying regardless of the heat — and the North Fork has to be forded or crossed on a log, with difficulty that swings hard with snowmelt. A party arriving late, or facing high water, is usually better off sleeping here than committing to the bushwhack and the crossing in poor light.
bivy.water: Reliable — Grizzly Creek and the North Fork are both at hand
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit reserved by name through Recreation.gov or issued walk-up at Marblemount; per-person and reservation fees apply.
bivy.capacity: Larger than the other North Fork camps and open to stock parties, so you may be sharing it

approach_variants.name: The cairned ledge into the gully, and the black stairs inside it
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159 (about 4,875 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound along Bridge Creek — losing roughly 2,000 ft over about 9.5 miles through forest — to the North Fork Camp junction, where the PCT crosses Bridge Creek. A footbridge there has been washed out in past years, so check NPS conditions rather than counting on it.

Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, roughly seven miles regaining about 1,700 ft, growing brushier as you go until it peters out in the big cirque below Goode, Storm King and Mount Logan. Around mile 13-14 ford the North Fork — easier a short way upstream near a cairn — and pick up an intermittent boot path and cairns through talus and alder, including tunnel sections through the brush, toward the toe of the Goode Glacier.

Some parties deliberately stay on moraine and talus rather than the glacier basin, because of icefall and audible rumbling from the seracs. Bivy near the glacier toe around 6,400-6,800 ft, or higher on ledges closer to the couloir. The whole approach is commonly 15-16 miles and 4,000-4,800 ft to high camp.

This is the peak's original route, first climbed in 1936, and it is also the descent for the Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge — so expect to meet parties coming down it.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September depending on snow and ice in the couloir; an axe and crampons are often wanted for the gully approach even in summer
hazards: A rockfall funnel: the couloir is loose and gets worse with multiple parties on it
Receding hidden-glacier snowbridges below 8,000 ft on the way to the gully
A demanding headwall of largely terrible rock near the top
Active rockfall and icefall noise from the Goode Glacier seracs beside the approach
A mouth that opens onto cliffy ground above a waterfall — the one real route-finding trap of the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ENTRY IS MARKED: A NARROW LEDGE WITH A CAIRN ON IT LEADS INTO THE SOUTHWEST GULLY. After skirting snow you scramble talus and loose scree to that ledge. A cairn on a narrow ledge is the confirmation; an unmarked scramble straight into a gully is not this route.

INSIDE THE GULLY THE TEST IS COLOUR, AND IT IS BOTH A ROUTE-FINDING AND A SAFETY INSTRUCTION: HUG THE LEFT SIDE, WHERE THE DARK ROCK IS SOLID. Parties call that band the black stairs and it offers cleaner scrambling than the middle of the gully. IF YOU ARE ON PALE, RUBBLY ROCK, YOU ARE IN THE GUT OF THE COULOIR AND ON THE LOOSE LINE.

EXPECT ONE SHORT LOW-FIFTH PITCH LOW DOWN, then class 3 and 4 in the main gully, steepening near the notch between the summit and the West Tower.

BLACK TOOTH NOTCH IS THE UPPER LANDMARK AND IT IS SHARED, SO IT IDENTIFIES THE MOUNTAIN RATHER THAN THE ROUTE: a foot-wide notch gained by an exposed class 4 traverse, with a fixed sling marking the crux step, and loose rock throughout. The Northeast Buttress and Megalodon Ridge both DESCEND through it; this is the only one of the three that climbs UP through it.

AND THE MOST USEFUL NEGATIVE FACT IS ABOUT GOING DOWN, BECAUSE THAT IS WHEN IT BITES: the couloir's mouth opens onto cliffs above a WATERFALL. EXIT LEFT ONTO EASIER HEATHER BENCHES rather than continuing straight down. A party that is still descending the fall line when it hears water below has gone too far.

bivy.name: 5,500 ft bivy below the slabs
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the most commonly used one on this side of the peak. Reached after the slide-alder section and a crossing of the creek, tucked just below the low-angle slabs with rock walls around it and running water on hand. Nothing above it is comfortable, and the slabs above lead straight onto the glacier in the morning.
bivy.water: the creek right at camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: about four people

bivy.name: Goode Glacier toe
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the moraine and rubble between roughly 6,400 and 6,800 ft. Flat ground is genuinely limited and the good spots are specific rather than general — expect to hunt for them, and expect glacier noise all night. It is the highest planned camp and the one that makes the couloir a reasonable day, but the water problem is real by late summer.
bivy.water: scarce near camp late season; fill at the last reliable stream below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: limited — a small number of usable flat spots, not a big-party site

bivy.name: 5,200 ft camp to the west
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the fallback if you run out of daylight in the brush below. Perfectly serviceable, but reports consistently say the extra three hundred feet up to the higher bivy is worth carrying, because summit day from here is long enough already.
bivy.water: creek nearby
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: West Tower ledge, upper mountain
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp. A narrow shelf on the north side of the crest between the West Tower and the main summit, where a solo climber spent a night wedged between rocks and still lost sleep to constant south wind. No water, no flat ground worth the name, and a serious place to be caught. It exists, and that is the only reason to know about it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: Lateral moraine camp above Goode Glacier

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then take the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge.

The wall these routes are on sits in the amphitheatre roughly MIDWAY BETWEEN STUART PASS AND GOAT PASS, rising about 1,000 ft out of the snow. It is known as the West Face Wall — worth saying plainly, because it faces west and some descriptions of the mountain's south side sweep it in with the south face, which sends parties looking on the wrong aspect.

Bivy sites are at Stuart Pass and at Goat Pass. Most parties camp at one of them and walk in to the wall in the morning.

The descent goes over the top: continue up the West Ridge to the summit, or take the main West Ridge gully down with scrambling and downclimbing, breaking right onto a large bench where a single-rope rappel gets you back toward the Stuart Pass bivies.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul-early Sep, once the snow below the wall has gone down enough to reach the start by a short scramble and before autumn storms
hazards: Snow at the foot of the wall early in the season, making the short scramble to the start awkward
Long runouts between placements and hidden loose chockstones
A west-facing wall that gets full afternoon sun and afternoon weather
Topping out high on the West Ridge with a long descent still to do
An unplanned bivy is a real outcome; parties carry for it
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WALK THE FOOT OF THE WALL UNTIL YOU FIND A SPLITTER YOU CAN PUT BOTH HANDS IN. The start is an obvious hand-and-finger splitter crack, and it does NOT begin at ground level — it starts on a small ledge about 15 to 25 feet above the snow or talus, reached by a short scramble. That gap between the ground and the first moves is the single best confirmation you are in the right place: a crack running all the way to the snow is not this one.

WHERE ON THE WALL: you are in the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, roughly halfway between them, under about 1,000 ft of rock. If you are still on either pass you have not arrived; if the wall has ended and you are back on open talus you have walked past it.

SHARED START, AND SAY IT OUT LOUD BEFORE YOU RACK UP: this route and the other two lines on this wall begin at the SAME crack and share the first four pitches. The differences are higher up, at the major ledge system splitting the wall — this route goes LEFT there where the original line continues right. So finding the base correctly does not settle which route you are on, and the choice has to be made deliberately at that ledge rather than followed.

WHAT TO EXPECT ABOVE, as confirmation you started right: two pitches of corners and arêtes to a bolted anchor, then a long horizontal traverse rightwards on the third pitch. If nothing on your third pitch traverses, you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Barlow Pass, Gothic Basin Trail #724, Foggy Lake outlet
approach_variants.notes:
Distance is round trip to Foggy Lake. Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway, about 19.3 miles east of the Verlot Public Service Center, on the Weden Creek / Gothic Basin trail (USFS #724).

The first two thirds of a mile follows an old closed mining road before singletrack begins climbing through forest. The trail fords Weden Creek at around 1.1 miles — no bridge, and the main reliable water low on the route. Above that it switchbacks up a steep root-and-rock staircase, gaining close to 1,000 ft per mile through a roughly two-mile band that is the physical crux of the walk. That section holds lingering snow patches and old avalanche debris across the tread well into early summer in heavy years.

At about 3.5 to 4 miles the trail breaks out of timber into the open slabs and tarns of Gothic Basin — the last dependable water and a sensible bail-out point in bad weather. Continue up talus and slab benches another half mile and roughly 600 ft to the saddle above Foggy Lake, then drop slightly and traverse three or four tenths of a mile along and above the shore to the lake's OUTLET.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; cairns can be buried by snow into early summer
hazards: Snow patches and avalanche debris across the tread in the steep timber band
Weden Creek ford
Buried cairns in early season, leading parties onto exposed class 4 left of the correct line
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scramble begins at the lake's OUTLET, not from a random point on the shore, and getting on it early or late is the usual error. From the outlet, look up at the obvious low point on Gothic's southeast ridge. The line is NOT the ridge crest: stay in the SCREE on the climber's RIGHT of the crest and follow the cairns, which are numerous and continuous, past a small tarn at the foot of a snowfield. Cairns underfoot and scree, not rock, is the confirmation. At the very top, where the summit block stops the scree, cut LEFT onto a narrow sidewalk of downsloping rock — slightly exposed easy friction — and switchback back up and right to the base of the block; the final scramble is about 30 ft of low-exposure class 3. Two negatives: if you are on the crest itself you have drifted right off the easy line, and if you find yourself on exposed class 4 to climber's LEFT just below the summit block you have gone too far left, which is where most parties who get into trouble end up. In early season the cairns can be buried and the correct line is genuinely hard to hold.

bivy.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
bivy.notes: The usual camp for Gothic Peak and Del Campo Peak, at the top of the Gothic Basin trail beneath both summits. The basin is fragile, so keep off the meadows and heather.
bivy.water: Lake and snowmelt tarns
bivy.permit: No permit required; no campfires; camp only on rock or established sites
bivy.capacity: A few established sites, mostly on rock and bare ground near the south shore; space is tight on summer weekends

bivy.name: Weden Creek trail junction, one mile up the Monte Cristo road
bivy.notes: This is for the party that runs long rather than the party that plans well. The walk out from Gothic Basin is a steep descent on greasy slab in fading light and it is where people get hurt on this approach, so a known flat spot at the bottom of the climbing — before the last mile of road back to Barlow Pass — is worth recording. It is also a legitimate soft start: a party arriving late can walk the flat mile up the old road, sleep beside the creek, and be climbing at first light with the whole basin ahead of them rather than the drive still in their legs. The first three quarters of a mile of the Weden Creek trail runs almost level along the creek before it turns uphill in earnest, and that stretch is where the usable ground is. Do not confuse this with the Monte Cristo townsite four miles further up the same road, which is a different place serving different peaks. The road from Barlow Pass is gated to vehicles and stays that way, so everything here is on foot. Being valley bottom, it is buggy in early summer and stays cold and damp long into the morning.
bivy.water: Weden Creek runs right there and is the easiest water on the whole approach, but it drains the same mineralised ground as the basin above and carries the same metals question. Treat it as washing and cooking-fire water at best, and carry drinking water in.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside wilderness, so dispersed camping is allowed and needs no permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Fires are a poor idea in a wooded valley bottom under summer restrictions and are usually banned outright from midsummer; assume a stove.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents at most, on flat forest ground near where the trail leaves the road and follows the creek. This is dispersed camping on undeveloped ground, not a site — no table, no ring, no toilet, nothing signed.

bivy.name: Lower Gothic Basin — the slab benches and tarns short of Foggy Lake
bivy.notes: The basin lip, where the climbers' trail finally stops climbing and opens out among tarns and slabs, sits about a mile below Foggy Lake and is the quieter alternative to it. For GOTHIC PEAK this costs almost nothing — Gothic's ordinary line goes up from the basin side and the extra mile to the lake buys no advantage — while for DEL CAMPO it does cost you, because Del Campo's southeast ridge is entered from the north side of Foggy Lake and camping short of it adds a mile and several hundred feet to summit day. Choose accordingly: this is the Gothic camp and the bad-weather camp, not the Del Campo one. Getting here means the Weden Creek trail, which is a mining-era path rather than a graded one — steep, direct, rocky, with slabby sections that are genuinely unpleasant when wet and a few spots where hands come out. It gains close to three thousand feet in under five miles after the flat mile of road walking. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to dig in, so waste comes out with you. Snow lies here well into July in an ordinary year and the timing moves by weeks between a heavy and a light winter. Old adits and workings are scattered through the basin and some are open holes in bad light; keep to the used ground.
bivy.water: Melt streams and the tarns run through the basin most of the season and thin out late in a hot August. TREAT THE PROVENANCE OF THIS WATER SERIOUSLY: the whole drainage is old mining ground and metals leached from tailings, arsenic in particular, are documented through this valley system. Filters, tablets and boiling deal with organisms and do nothing whatever about dissolved metals. Draw from snowmelt and small feeder runnels well above any workings rather than from anything draining a spoil heap, and if in doubt carry it in.
bivy.permit: National forest land OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no camping permit, no quota and no party-size limit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass to leave a vehicle. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED throughout the basin regardless of season, and there is nothing to burn anyway — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small parties spread wide. The ground is polished slab, boulder and thin heather with pockets of flat gravel rather than any built-up site, so it takes two or three tents comfortably and rewards walking another five minutes to find your own rather than crowding the first flat spot.

approach_variants.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 over Baldy and along the crest
approach_variants.notes:
There is no roadside access to this ridge; the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120, off FR-2870 / Lost Mountain Road, itself off Palo Alto Road south of US-101 near Sequim. Road-end parking at a dirt berm, about 3,300 ft, Northwest Forest Pass required.

Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the berm on an old roadbed and crosses Mueller Creek almost immediately — the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, so fill up. The trail narrows to single-track around 0.3 mile and then turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks, in places barely a boot-width across eroded crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale. It is a climber's path, not a graded trail.

At about 2.7 miles and 6,200 ft it tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring — the last dependable water on the route.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. North-facing gullies on the last stretch hold steep snow into July
hazards: Sudden fast-moving whiteouts and lightning on an open above-treeline ridge with miles of exposure
Loose shale and scree with occasional exposed steps along the crest
Lingering steep snowfields in north-facing gullies into July, warranting an ice axe
No reliable water once past the Baldy saddle spring
Long unmarked ridge navigation with route-finding around gendarmes and false summits
The Gray Wolf River bridge on the old Gray Wolf Trail route is out — do not plan to come in that way without a hazardous ford
Bear canister required within Olympic National Park
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIMB BEGINS WHERE THE TREAD ENDS, AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SADDLE BETWEEN TYLER PEAK AND BALDY. You know you are there because the trail stops going up in a line and the ground opens on both sides — navigation shifts from following tread to reading a ridge. There is also a signed Olympic National Park boundary marker in a saddle on this stretch and a spring path dropping off the crest. From here on you are on the crest and the crest is the route.

THE TEST THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS ON THIS ROUTE IS AT THE FAR END, AND IT IS A FALSE SUMMIT WITH A NAME AND A NUMBER: POINT 7076. From below, 7076 reads as the summit. It is not. The true summit of Gray Wolf is 7,218 ft and it lies FURTHER NORTH along the crest and is HIGHER. So the fog rule is simple: after Baldy you drop about 600 ft, climb back up over a prominent bump, and THAT BUMP IS NOT THE TOP. Keep going north over the last of the talus, detouring briefly round the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short Class 2-3 scramble on loose rock. If you turned round on the first big bump past Baldy, you turned round on 7076.

SECOND TEST, on the way to 7076 itself: the crest gets steeper and broken approaching it. The published avoidance is to TRAVERSE WEST at about 6,500 ft and then swing back to gain 7076 by its NORTHWEST aspect, and to stay in the basin below and RIGHT of the broken rock ridge until you can gain the saddle between the twin summits — 7076 has twin tops with snowfields between them. There is no trail at these decision points, which is why they are written down.

THIRD TEST, earlier: Point 6537 is a rocky gendarme and false summit below Baldy, normally SKIRTED ON ITS SOUTH SIDE rather than climbed over. If you are scrambling straight over a tower before you have reached Baldy, you have taken the crest too literally.
