HONEST LIMIT: long stretches of this crest are unmarked and off-trail and the whole thing is above treeline. Carry a map or GPS; the ridge is the handrail but the summit identification is not obvious by eye.

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and the east face, for a traverse rather than an out-and-back
approach_variants.notes:
The other end of the same ridge, and the reason to know it is that it turns this route into a traverse instead of a there-and-back over Baldy twice. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, the Royal Basin Trail leads to Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin. From the ridge, the east face drops roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail.

It is steep, loose and only lightly travelled: packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber looking for blazes and cairns. Some parties scree-ski the looser upper sections rather than rope up at all. It is not a bolted or standardised line — where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns.

Most commonly this is used as the EXIT after climbing from Maynard Burn, closing a loop out Royal Basin or back over the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Steep, loose, lightly travelled ground with no established line and improvised anchors if roped
Roughly 3,000 ft of descent or ascent on packed dirt and shattered shale
Brushy notches and timber navigation looking for blazes and cairns
Committing: once on the east face there is no easy return to the crest
Every ridge-crest hazard above, in a longer day
approach_variants.baseFinding: USED AS AN APPROACH, THE ARRIVAL TEST IS GAINING THE CREST — and this side has no marker sequence for doing it. Parties describe finding blazes and cairns through timber rather than following a line. Treat it as navigation, not route-following. THE SUMMIT TESTS ONCE ON THE CREST ARE THE SAME AND THEY ARE THE VALUABLE PART: POINT 7076 IS A FALSE SUMMIT. Coming from the Royal Basin side you meet the true 7,218 ft summit from the north-east rather than from the south, so the trap runs the other way — the bump you must not stop on lies SOUTH of the true summit on this approach. Fix which side of you 7076 should be before you commit to the crest in cloud. HONEST LIMIT AND A RECOMMENDATION: this variant is known as a descent far more than as an ascent, and there is no fixed, repeatable rappel count for the cliffy step — expect at most one or two short rappels well under 60 m if you choose to rope, and expect most parties to downclimb or scree-ski instead. Confirm current conditions before relying on it either way.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, straight up from the tracks
approach_variants.notes:
Leave US 2 at the Index turnoff, about 29 miles west of Stevens Pass, and drive into town. Take Avenue A west for roughly 0.6 miles to a small gravel parking area on the right, just before the road runs alongside the railway.

From the lot you cross the railway tracks — every approach at Index crosses them, and trains come through several times a day, so look both ways and expect to shout at your belayer.

Once over the tracks bear a little left and pick up the trail heading up toward the wall. The branch that turns RIGHT runs along the base of the Lower Wall to the harder ground; going STRAIGHT takes you to the Great Northern Slab. Two to five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day; the Lower Wall gets full sun when the sun is out
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach — active line, several trains daily
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking area
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Great Northern Slab is the low-angle left end of the Lower Town Wall, and the trail from the lot runs straight into it — do not turn left or right.

The start marker is a flat ledge carrying a 5.10c toprope problem. You want the CORNER just LEFT of that flat ledge.

The first pitch is 5.2 and it climbs rightward up a ramp and through some bushes, then straight up an easier ramp to two very large bolts — the old one-inch-diameter kind. Scrappy vegetated ground and a ramp that wanders right is CORRECT on pitch 1; it is not a sign you have started on the wrong feature. Steep clean crack climbing off the deck means you have walked too far right along the base.

approach_variants.name: Spur road end to Klinger Ridge
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail from the car. The line goes straight into thick huckleberry toward the talus above, but the mossy streambed running alongside that brush is far easier travel even though the rock underfoot is slick. Follow the drainage and its talus up into a rock basin around 4,300 ft, then make a rising traverse across talus into a gully and climb a heathered slope beneath a cliff band, which dodges a slide-alder tangle, onto the open meadow crest above 4,600 ft. Fog sits in the lower basin well past sunrise, and there are no markers to steer by.
approach_variants.season: July to October
hazards: Slick moss in the lower streambed
Standing dead timber and heavy regrowth across the burned south side of Klinger Ridge
Morning valley fog on ground with no trail to follow
Loose, exposed granite at the summit notch
A short near-vertical downclimb with loose rock at the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts at a notch just WEST of a prominent standing rock tower at about 5,300 ft, and the way to it is not the obvious one. Do not try to hold the literal east ridge crest — it cliffs out and does not go through as a route. From roughly 4,800 ft weave up through steep granite blocks and cross a final talus field to the notch, which is the gap immediately beside the one unmistakable tower on that stretch of crest. There is a decoy lower down: a single cairn near the meadow crest around 4,600 ft pulls parties off the direct line, and staying in the gully to about 4,800 ft is the straighter way. The move that confirms you are at the base is a DOWNclimb rather than a climb — a short, steep, near-vertical step drops off the south side of the notch, loose in places and the most exposed ground on the route, and only once you are through it does the gully below the summit block open up for the final class 3-4 scramble to the top.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek climbers' path — summer line
approach_variants.notes: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, do NOT take the maintained lake trail. Walk back down the access road about a quarter mile and pick up the old deactivated spur road — parties who know it often park at the spur's gated start instead of the main lot. Follow the old roadbed a hundred or two hundred yards to a FIRE-PIT CLEARING, turn right, and pick up the unmarked but well-trodden climbers' path. It drops to the creek and crosses on a log jam or by rock-hopping near the DOWNSTREAM TIP OF A SMALL MID-CHANNEL ISLAND; this crossing is the main early-season hazard. On the far bank the path swings west, then north, and starts climbing in earnest through sustained tight switchbacks in second-growth timber. Two decision points follow. Around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet the path forks near a BAND OF EXPOSED ROCK — stay RIGHT and do not scramble the outcrop straight ahead, which is a known trap; the correct line keeps traversing climber's-left beneath a cliff band. Then around forty-four hundred feet the summer line bends LEFT up a brushy weakness in the cliff band rather than continuing up the couloir, which holds snow late. Huckleberry and heather meadows lead to the saddle at about fifty-four hundred feet, the last reliable water.
approach_variants.season: June to September. Early June parties meet significant lingering snow and heavy brush; late July through August is typically the clearest.
hazards: Steep brush — alder, devil's club and salmonberry — on the lower approach
Log-jam crossing of the creek is slick and runs high in spring
The fork near the exposed rock band around thirty-six to thirty-eight hundred feet is a known route-finding trap; the outcrop ahead is not the way
Loose rock on the talus fan and at the ramp
No reliable water above the creek and the waterfall ravine in late summer
Cairns thin out badly above treeline and the boot path fades in the talus; route-finding rather than difficulty is the main hazard here
Multiple search-and-rescue incidents have occurred on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the saddle, drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt a cliff band and boulder-hop up the TALUS FAN toward the upper tree benches directly below the peak's south face. The base of the technical ground is the top of that fan — and the feature you are looking for CANNOT BE SEEN FROM BELOW. A ramp cuts up the face from the top of the talus and only appears once you are underneath it, which is exactly why parties overshoot by continuing up the rockslide. The unmistakable test is the single step at the ramp's foot: a boulder with TWO options off it, a left-hand line past a CHOCKSTONE that takes a steep low-fifth move, and a right-hand line, steeper and more exposed but on solid holds, which is what most parties take. If there is no boulder with a two-way step above it, you are not at the ramp. Negative marker: if you are still grinding up loose rockslide with no ramp cutting off to either side, you have gone past the entry — the ramp is entered FROM the talus, not from the top of it. Higher up, the next landmark is a keyhole notch through the ridge to the north side; if you have not passed the ramp step you will not reach it.

approach_variants.name: Tailgunner couloir — snow-season line
approach_variants.notes: The same start — the spur road, the fire-pit clearing, the creek crossing at the island, and the switchbacks up through the timber. The difference comes at about forty-four hundred feet: instead of bending left into the brushy weakness in the cliff band, the snow-season line continues directly up the couloir to the saddle. This same couloir is a documented WRONG TURN in summer and an avalanche path, so it is only reasonable when it is a continuous snow climb and conditions have been assessed.
approach_variants.season: Late spring, while the couloir holds continuous consolidated snow. Once it starts melting out it becomes the wrong answer and the summer line through the brushy weakness is correct.
hazards: Avalanche hazard — this couloir is an active path and holds snow late
Snow conditions vary hour to hour on it; assess before committing
Everything the summer line carries below the cliff band, including the brushy lower approach and the creek crossing at higher spring flow
The ramp above is harder to protect and downclimb when wet or holding snow, and it is the one place on this peak where parties commonly rappel
approach_variants.baseFinding: The couloir tops out at the same saddle as the summer line, so the base of the climbing is identical: drop about a hundred feet off the crest to skirt the cliff band, then boulder-hop up the talus fan to the upper tree benches below the south face. The ramp at the top of the fan is invisible until you are under it; identify it by the BOULDER at its foot with a two-way step above — a left-hand chockstone move at low fifth, or a steeper, more exposed line on good holds to the right. Negative marker: if you are still on snow when you expect to be on talus, you have carried on above the saddle into the wrong basin; the couloir delivers you to a saddle, and the talus fan starts on the far side of it.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Lake spur road to the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: There is no official trail. From a spur road near the Barclay Lake trailhead a faint climbers' path heads east into the forest and leads most of the way up. Cross Barclay Creek on logs, leave the old roadbed, and take steep zigzags through the southern slope to a headwall around 3,600 ft. The path then veers east beneath cliff bands and makes a short steep drop into a gully where water dribbles off the rock overhead — dry by late summer, a real flow in winter and spring. Above it cairns lead onto moderate ground, then meadows along the east side of Tailgunner's south ridge to a saddle near 5,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to October
hazards: Faint, unmarked climbers' path with sustained route-finding
Slick rock in the seasonal waterfall gully
Heavy slide alder and devil's club if you drift north out of the correct line
Loose rock and exposure on the summit block
Icy, avalanche-prone open slopes in winter and spring
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling starts where the traverse tops out on the east ridge at about 5,950 ft, and three separate identification problems stand between the car and it. At the bottom, an old fire pit on the spur road has been used as the marker for the path start and may no longer be there — look for the boot-worn line heading EAST into the forest rather than for the fire pit itself, and do not take the maintained lake trail. Above the waterfall gully, where cairns lead out onto moderate ground, the standard error is to head north into heavy slide alder and devil's club instead of continuing east beneath a buttress; if you are fighting devil's club you have gone the wrong way. Past the saddle below Tailgunner and Wing, bypass Point 5,760 by dropping roughly two hundred feet eastward around it rather than going over the top. From there a rising traverse above Gunn Lake through talus and heather brings you onto the crest near 5,950 ft. You are at the base when the traverse ends on the ridge and everything left is a short, exposed class 2-3 scramble on the summit block.

_raw.permit_type: Optional registration for alpine climbs; wilderness permit for overnight stays
_raw.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass ($5 day / $30 annual) or America the Beautiful Pass required for Downey Creek Trailhead
_raw.permit_pickup: Self-issued at trailhead; optional registration at ranger stations; access via Downey Creek Trailhead
_raw.special_hazards: Extremely difficult alpine ascent; Fred Beckey called it one of the most difficult summits to attain in the Cascades; exposed rock and ice
_raw.group_size_limit: Max 12 people in Glacier Peak Wilderness
_raw.seasonal_closures: Best June-October; winter/spring snow and avalanche hazards

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.permit: Optional registration for alpine climbs; wilderness permit for overnight stays
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Suiattle River Road (FR 26) is washed out and closed to vehicles at about milepost 4.5 after the December 2025 flood, under a closure order running to 1 January 2028 unless lifted sooner, so the Downey Creek Trailhead cannot be reached by car. The Downey Creek Trail itself is also closed through 31 December 2026 under a separate fire closure. Call the Darrington Ranger District, (360) 436-1155, before planning a trip.
access.seasonal: Mountain Loop Highway has a seasonal gate closure (Deer Creek–Bedal, ~14 mi), typically Nov–mid/late May. Suiattle River Road (FSR 26), the primary Glacier Peak access, has had storm-damage closures — check current conditions before a trip.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, jointly administered by Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass recommended

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register
overnight_permit.where: Sign the register at the trailhead. Camping on the North Cascades National Park side of Cache Col needs a park wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or Recreation.gov.

road.name: Downey Creek Trailhead via Suiattle River Road (FR 26)
road.status: Suiattle River Road (FR 26) suffered major flood/washout damage and is CLOSED to vehicles at approximately milepost 4.5 under a closure order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028. The Downey Creek Trail itself is also closed August 15 through December 31, 2026 under the Forest Service's Miner's Fire closure order. Vehicle access to the historic trailhead is not possible while the road order stands.
road.driveNote: Normally about 2.5-3 hours from Seattle via Darrington and the Suiattle River Road when fully open; while the road closure order (April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028) stands, it requires walking or biking the closed road from the MP 4.5 closure gate, adding several miles to the approach.

wa_gunsight_peak_standard.rappel_count_note: A four-station sequence of 50/50/50/20 m is sometimes attached to this route. It matches, figure for figure, a published trip report for NORTH Gunsight Peak's West Face — a 5.11+, 6-pitch, 600 ft rock route on a different summit — and does not belong to this Class 5.6 glacier route on the main spire. Nothing about those figures was measured here, so they are not carried. What is documented for this route is two double-rope rappels: "We belayed each other back down the exposed summit ridge, then made a double-rope rappel down the west face", and then "a diagonal double-rope rappel, putting in directional protection along the way, which allowed us to reach the snow finger in one shot." That party carried two 60 m ropes. No single-rope descent of this route is documented.

approach_variants.name: Chickamin Glacier to the snow finger between the main and south spires
approach_variants.notes: From the Chikamin-Dome col, a descending traverse of roughly ninety minutes drops onto the Chickamin Glacier and reaches a snow dome and rock outcrop at about 7,000 ft, closely below the peak; many parties move camp here or day-climb from the col. From that outcrop, boot up to the snow finger running between the main spire and the south spire. On the snow approach, take the FIRST col south of the south peak — the long-standing published advice to use the second col south of it has been corrected by parties who followed it, and the first is the right one. Descent reverses the line by rappel: from the top of the chimney, traverse to the notch, downclimb to a second station, rappel to the ledge above the glacier, then one more onto the snow.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Crevasse hazard on the Dome and Chickamin Glaciers — rope, and crevasse rescue gear
Loose rock in the basalt dike section
Wild exposure on the narrow summit ridge
A summit horn only one party member can stand on at a time
approach_variants.baseFinding: A REDDISH-BLACK BASALT DIKE IS THE LINE, AND IT IS SOFTER THAN EVERYTHING AROUND IT. From the 7,000 ft snow dome and rock outcrop, boot up the snow finger between the main and south spires; from a breach in that finger, a short wall leads to a broad ledge, then leftward to a steep dihedral of BLACK rock whose top fifteen feet is the exposed 5.6 crux on solid granite. Above it, traverse left on Class 3 granite into a distinctive dike of reddish-black basalt — this is the feature that carved the gunsight notch in the first place, eroding faster than the granite either side, so if the rock you are on is the same colour as its neighbours you are not in the dike. It scrambles easily, if loosely, to the high notch between the main and north spires. There a vertical headwall blocks a direct exit: DESCEND ABOUT TWENTY FEET and traverse right across steep, solid, well-broken rock into a shallow parallel gully. Short chimneys and cracks to 5.5 end at the crest beside a large horn slung with old rappel tat — that horn is not the summit; the summit is a separate horn about the size of a barstool further along the ridge.

watch_out: Rockfall danger is EXTREME and increasing due to November 2021 damage; route condition is marginal and getting worse
Traverse pitch now involves exposed 5.9-5.10 downclimbing with inadequate protection—many consider it not recommended
Loose rock and dirt throughout; expect to encounter unstable blocks and flakes requiring careful footwork
High consequence scrambling on approach and upper pitches
Afternoon wind, sun, and storm development rapid in July-September

pitch_detail.notes: Initial low to mid-5th class climbing through loose, crumbly rhyolite terrain; lots of holds but quality poor and exposed
Continuation of crumbly terrain leading toward Lunch Ledge; climbers should carefully test all holds
Final approach to Lunch Ledge (~300 ft from start); large comfortable belay ledge provides good rest point before upper pitches

The iconic Improbable Traverse pitch(es): traverse right on good foot ledges with several old fixed pitons for protection. CRITICAL: November 2021 rockfall destroyed ~30x40ft section; now requires downclimbing 5.9-5.10 from old pin with 30+ feet of unprotected traversing. Many now recommend this route is not safe.
Class 4 ramp climbing through alpine trees and rock slabs to summit ridge approach; short but exposed

approach_variants.name: Talus cone below the west face
approach_variants.notes:
The west face rises above the houses on the Alpental access road. Every road along it carrying a 'Strasse' name is private, and the Alpental Community Club has since 2021 prohibited both driving and walking on them; climbers report being confronted. The talus cone under the face therefore has to be reached by a line that does not cross private land, and there is no established or signed path to it — this is the part of the approach with no fixed answer.

Once on the talus, make a rising traverse up toward the far left (north) end of the west face's talus field. At the top end of the field there is a rocky stream bed, which may be dry depending on the season; that streambed marks the north end of the talus and is the last realistic water.

Wear a helmet on the talus. Climber-triggered rockfall here is a real hazard, from your own party as much as from anyone above.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct
hazards: no established approach to the talus - the direct approach crosses private roads that residents forbid, and climbers have been confronted
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus and on the mossy slabs
a couple of hundred feet of loose dirty slab scrambled unroped before the climbing starts
generally poor rock quality on the face
no reliable water past the streambed at the north end of the talus
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the top of the talus cone you scramble a couple of hundred feet of loose, mossy, dirty slab before any roped climbing. That dirty scrambling is part of the approach, not the route — the base of the climb is where it ends against the face proper.

The first pitch wanders about 100 ft of low fourth to low fifth class to a TREE belay. The tree is the confirmation. If you are 100 ft up and there is nothing to belay off, you are not on the line.

Negative marker: the rocky, usually dry streambed marks the far NORTH end of the talus field. If you are south of it and the wall above you is short and clean with bolts on it, you have drifted round to the sport climbing at the base of Guye's south wall and are on a different aspect of the mountain.

The rock on this face is generally poor and loose. Loose rock low down is normal here and is not evidence you are off route.

approach_variants.name: Cave Ridge saddle from Alpental
approach_variants.notes:
From the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead area (about 3,080-3,120 ft), take the unmarked climbers' boot path that leaves the pavement close to the Snow Lake trail sign — the one that serves Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, not the west-face talus approach. Follow it up to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, roughly a mile and a half in and reported around 4,500-4,600 ft.

From the saddle, turn right (north) and work toward Guye's north summit. Helmets are worth wearing from the point you leave the trail; climber-triggered rockfall is common on the talus and in the gully.

This peak is also reached from the northbound PCT trailhead through Commonwealth Basin, which is the east side of the mountain — a different approach to a different aspect.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct; also done as a winter scramble with axe and traction
hazards: moat against a large rock face around 4,840 ft if you take the right-hand line
steep snow traverse on the left-hand bypass
climber-triggered rockfall on the talus and in the gully
very steep gully - class 3 in summer, considerably more serious under snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Cave Ridge / Guye saddle is your fix. From it, Guye's north summit is directly to your right and north, and a scramble gully runs from the saddle area up to a point just north of the north peak. It is very steep but reported as class 3 in summer. If you are at a col and the ground to the north is walkable ridge rather than a steep gully, you are looking at the wrong side of the saddle.

The decision point is around 4,840 ft, where the gully runs into a large rock face. Going RIGHT there leads into a moat, and parties have found it very awkward and had to reverse. Going LEFT — a steep snow traverse in season — is the better option. If you are fighting a moat against rock, you took the right-hand option: back off and cross left.

Higher, near the north summit, the Hidden Ridge variation traverses right to an outcrop where a horn can be slung for a single rappel of about 30 ft into the notch between the north and middle summits. That rappel into a notch is the confirmation you found the variation; without it you are on the ordinary scramble.

approach_variants.name: Old Commonwealth Basin trail to a bearing of 290 degrees, then straight up
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Pacific Crest Trail North / Snoqualmie Pass North trailhead at about 47.4284, -121.4155, just off I-90 exit 52. Follow the old Commonwealth Basin trail north for roughly 1.4 miles, or the bootpack that stands in for it in winter.

When Guye lies directly west or northwest of you, leave the trail and go straight up the slope. The walking is short by Cascade standards; the difficulty is judging the snow on the slope between the trail and the gully, which is itself avalanche terrain on a loaded day.

About 2.25 km and 2,100 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Winter and early spring, roughly January to April, when the gully is filled and consolidated. The ideal is a cold night followed by a clear cold morning; by late spring the sunlit half turns to slush and the route becomes a wet-avalanche problem
hazards: Avalanche is the primary objective hazard — a confined gully below a summit ridge on a slope that loads readily
Sustained steep snow to about 70 degrees with essentially no protection; a fall in the upper section is unarrestable
Cornice formation at the exit onto the ridge between the true and false summits
Rapid sun-warming of the exposed half producing wet slides and rollerballs later in the day
Both descents — Cave Ridge west, Commonwealth east — cross avalanche terrain of their own, and the west bootpath is easily lost under snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TAKE A BEARING, BECAUSE THIS ONE CAN BE DONE BLIND. Walk the old Commonwealth Basin trail about 1.4 miles until the summit of Guye bears roughly 290 degrees — west-northwest — from you, then turn and go straight uphill. A published fix for the start of the route is about 47.4411, -121.4026. In cloud that pair of numbers settles it and nothing on the ground has to be seen.

WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO, IN ORDER, ONCE YOU COMMIT: the route starts by going 45 degrees straight up. Only then does the gully proper develop, turning NORTHWEST for about 40 m and steepening as it turns. After that it runs directly at the summit, which stays visible for much of the climb on a clear day. If the ground you are on stays uniformly angled and never turns northwest, you are on the open slope beside the gully rather than in it.

THE ANGLE IS THE OTHER TEST: this is the steepest of Guye's gully lines. About 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then progressively steeper, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. A gully that stays moderate all the way is one of the peak's other lines.

WHERE IT PUTS YOU: it finishes at the ridge between the TRUE and FALSE summits — not on a summit. If your line tops out on a summit block, it is not this one.

AND A CONDITIONS TEST THAT IS PART OF THE FINDING HERE: roughly half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which is what gives it solid snow under the surface. It also means the two halves can be in quite different condition on a warm day.

approach_variants.name: Cougar Divide Trail #601 and the open ridge south to Chowder Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east and turn onto Forest Service Road 33; follow about 11 miles of gravel — rough in sections, high-clearance recommended, sedans passable with care — to its end at the Cougar Divide trailhead, with room for eight to ten vehicles. The true trailhead may be roughly a kilometre past where online mapping routes you, so do not stop at the first turnaround that looks right.

Hike Cougar Divide Trail #601 along the ridge to its high point around 5,920 ft. That high point is where the trail tread ends and the route becomes cross-country: continue south along the open ridge, crossing near Dobbs Creek, to Chowder Ridge and the foot of Hadley's summit block.

This and the Skyline Divide route are two different walks to the SAME summit block; the beta below for the block is common to both.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Oct, once the ridge is out from under snow
hazards: Eleven miles of rough gravel road, and a trailhead that mapping apps place short of the real one
Cross-country ridge travel with no tread and no cairns once past the 5,920 ft high point
Loose scree below a short Class 3 step
Open ridge with no shelter and no water beyond the trailhead
In cloud, two different divides converge on this summit and neither exit is marked
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE RIDGE IS THE ROUTE AND ITS HIGH POINT IS THE HANDOFF. Trail #601 runs along the crest to a high point near 5,920 ft, and everything after that is open ridge. In cloud you do not need a view: stay on the crest, going south, with the ground falling away on both sides. The moment you are sidehilling with the drop on only one side, you have come off the divide.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING, and this is the test that matters: the summit block of Hadley is a SHORT CLASS 3 STEP above loose scree, roughly the last 100 ft of the day. Everything below it is walking. So the base is the point where the ridge stops being walkable and stands up in a single short step. If you are scrambling for hundreds of feet you are on the wrong feature; if you have not scrambled at all you are not at the summit.

THE APPROACH IS NOT A LOOP AND CHOWDER RIDGE IS THE CONFIRMATION. You should arrive at the block having travelled along Chowder Ridge. If you are dropping into a basin or crossing a glacier to reach a rock block, you are somewhere else on the north side of Baker.

WHICH DIVIDE DID YOU WALK IN ON? This is the one thing to be sure of before you commit to a descent line in poor visibility, because the two approaches to this summit leave in different directions and neither is signed. Cougar Divide comes in from the NORTH, straight down its own ridge; Skyline Divide comes in from the WEST, a parallel ridge about a mile and a half over across the Deadhorse Creek valley, and is the much longer walk. Note your entry point onto Chowder Ridge on the way up.

approach_variants.name: Skyline Divide Trail #678 and the long open ridge south to Chowder Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
ACCESS FIRST: from Glacier, WA drive SR-542 about a mile past the Glacier Public Service Center to Glacier Creek Road (FS-39), turn right, then immediately left onto Deadhorse Road (FS-37). FS-37 normally runs 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide trailhead. FS-37 has been closed to vehicles at mile 0.03 since June 1, 2026 while the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1 is repaired, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle. Confirm before planning around it.

When open, Skyline Divide Trail #678 climbs through old-growth switchbacks into meadows and reaches the ridge crest at about 2 miles and its high point near 6,563 ft at about 4.5 miles. From there the route is cross-country along the open ridge — roughly three miles of it — to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley's summit block.

The trail's high point on the crest near 6,563 ft is the landmark parties use to re-find the maintained trail on the way back.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Aug-Oct — this trailhead may not currently be reachable at all
hazards: FS-37 closed at mile 0.03 during washout repair — the trailhead is not drivable until the work ends
Three miles of cross-country open ridge with no tread and no cairns
A short Class 3 step above loose scree and talus
Two unmarked divides converging on one summit, with very different roads at the bottom
No water once past the meadows
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 6,600 FT VIEWPOINT IS THE GATE, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. It is where maintained trail ends and where you rejoin it. In cloud it is the only reliable waypoint on this approach, because everything beyond it is three miles of undifferentiated open ridge. Note it on the way out — parties who do not, spend the return walking a crest that all looks the same.

THE CREST IS THE HANDRAIL. From the viewpoint the route runs SOUTH along the ridge and then SOUTHEAST along Chowder Ridge, roughly three miles in all. Keep the crest under your feet with air on both sides; this ridge has heather benches falling away either side and it is easy to drift onto one and lose the line.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: the summit block is a SHORT CLASS 3 STEP above loose scree and talus — the last stretch of the day and the only scrambling on it. Walking stops, one short step of rock, summit. That is the whole climb, and it is the test: if you are scrambling for a long time, you are on a false feature; if you have not left your feet, you are not there.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH TO THIS SAME BLOCK: Cougar Divide arrives on Chowder Ridge from the NORTH-WEST after crossing near Dobbs Creek, and its trail high point is 5,920 ft. Skyline arrives from the WEST after roughly three miles of ridge from a 6,600 ft viewpoint. If you are descending in poor visibility, going down the wrong divide puts you 11 miles of gravel road away from your car on a road that may itself be washed out.

approach_variants.name: Bacon-Hagan saddle and the southwest couloir
approach_variants.notes: This is the line used by parties arriving on the traverse from the Watson and Bacon side: descend north off the glacier and past several tarns, then follow a heathered ridge to the saddle between Hagan Mountain and Bacon Peak, where a small tarn sits with reliable water. From the tarn, bushwhack north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands — the sustained route-finding crux of the whole approach — picking brushy ramps and weaknesses through each band to keep the ground climbable. Above them the timber breaks out onto open heather and grass on Hagan's south flank around 6,000 to 6,400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. Mark your line through the cliffbands with photos, cairns or a track before going higher: the weaknesses you threaded are hard to spot from above, and the descent is consistently slower and more error-prone than the climb.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Two cliffbands in steep timber with no marked line through them
Loose rock the whole length of the scree-and-talus couloir — helmets, and a tight party
Crevasses and moats on the Hagan Glacier ice apron even in summer
The descent reverses ground that reads very differently from above
approach_variants.baseFinding: A BROAD SCREE-AND-TALUS COULOIR, TOPPING OUT AT A COL AT THE SOUTHWEST END OF THE CRAGS. From the open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank, one broad couloir of loose scree and talus leads up to a col near the SOUTHWEST end of the line of Hagan summit crags, around 7,000 ft. That col is the base of the climbing, and the slabs above it on the south side go at Class 3 to the top. Hagan is a massif of several crags rather than a single peak, so which col you reach matters: if the notch you have gained sits in the middle of the crags with towers rising on both sides of you, it is not this one — keep working to the southwest end of the line. Note carefully where the couloir meets the heather benches before you leave them, because it is also the way down and it is far harder to identify from above.

approach_variants.name: Lower Blum Lake and the 6,831 ft pass
approach_variants.notes: The approach from the north, out of the Blum Lakes basin rather than off the Bacon side. From lower Blum Lake, traverse south and rope up for glacier travel to a pass at 6,831 ft that sits between the south and middle Hagan peaks. This is glacier ground and the rope goes on before the traverse, not at the pass. Parties reaching the Blum Lakes come up the climbers' path off the Baker River Trail near Blum Creek, a faint path in brush marked with flagging tape that climbs the ridge to about 4,000 ft before veering south and traversing toward the lakes.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard between lower Blum Lake and the pass
The Blum climbers' path is faint, brushy and marked only with flagging tape
Loose rock and exposure on the spur and summit ridge above the notch
Several named crags on one massif — easy to commit to the wrong summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE PASS SITS BETWEEN THE SOUTH AND MIDDLE PEAKS, AND IT IS THE SOUTH PEAK YOU CLIMB. Arriving at 6,831 ft, you should have a summit on either hand: this is a pass between two of Hagan's own peaks, not a col on the outside of the massif, and if only one side of you rises to rock you are in the wrong gap. The climbing then goes up the south peak's NORTH side to a notch on its UPPER EAST side — that notch is high on the peak, not at the pass, and it is on the east flank, so a notch you can walk into from the west is the wrong one. From the notch, traverse onto the south face and gain the summit ridge, work up a spur on the east, then bear around to the south, where slabs lead to the summit at Class 3. The finish is south-facing slab, not a gully: if you are grovelling up a loose gully at the top you have missed the traverse around to the south side.

bivy.name: South Hagan bench
bivy.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give the final scramble to the summit. It is also the natural stop for anyone continuing east toward Hidden Lake and Bacon. The bench is comfortable and the position is superb, but it is fully exposed and the water is seasonal, which is the reason most parties still base at the lakes and do Hagan in a long day.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small pools that shrink through the season; late summer parties should plan to carry water up from the Blum Lakes or from Hidden Lake below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This ground sits on the boundary between the Blum and Bacon Peak cross-country zones, so confirm which zone your permit is written for when you pick it up. Six-person party limit either way, no fires, no camping in meadow
bivy.capacity: Two tents on heather and gravel benches; informal, with no fixed site

bivy.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
bivy.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
bivy.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

bivy.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
bivy.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. IT IS NOT ON THE WAY TO BLUM OR HAGAN. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-valley to Sulphide takes you in the wrong direction. It is listed because it is the legal, comfortable option for a party that arrives late, wants a short first evening, or is waiting out weather at the bottom, and because low-elevation valley ground here is otherwise wet, brushy and off-limits. Elevation is valley-bottom, only a little above the trailhead.
bivy.water: Sulphide Creek and the Baker River, both close by. Treat the water; the river runs silty in high melt
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a designated camp, which is a different reservation than a cross-country zone — book it or ask for it at the permit office rather than assuming a zone permit covers it. No fires
bivy.capacity: Two established sites and a backcountry toilet; a small party each

approach_variants.name: Hairpin pullout and the scree gully to the notch north of Half Moon
approach_variants.notes: Park at the large pullout on the hairpin near milepost 163 and take the unsigned climbers' path south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — angling down toward the creek is the standard error here. Beyond the first mile the path crosses boulder fields and slab benches with occasional cairns and all but disappears on the slabs. About two miles from the car, before the path climbs to Kangaroo Pass, cross the last soggy meadow and look left: a talus and scree gully angles back to the deep notch immediately north of Half Moon, and the North Ridge starts in that notch.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: The avalanche path shedding off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak
Loose scree and rockfall in the gully to the notch with any party above
Cairns and tread vanish on the slab benches in fog or fresh snow
No water above the lower approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: HALF MOON IS A FIN, AND THAT IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE UNDER IT. It is a thin, crescent-shaped rock blade trending southwest to northeast, sitting between Wallaby Peak to the south and Big Kangaroo to the north; a broad blocky summit mass with a wide gully splitting it is Wallaby, not this. Aim for the deep notch immediately NORTH of the fin, reached by the scree gully that angles back from the meadow below Kangaroo Pass. The North Ridge starts in that notch, climbing the broad buttress directly above it toward the crest.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. The pass's elevation is uncertain, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

wa_helmet_butte_standard_route.approach: From Coles Corner on US-2 (about 20 miles east of Stevens Pass), take WA-207 north 4.4 miles, turn right onto Chiwawa Loop Road for 1.3 miles, then left onto Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200) and follow it roughly 23 miles to its end at the Trinity / Buck Creek Pass Trailhead (about 2,772-2,800 ft). IMPORTANT: as of May 20, 2026, FR 6200 is closed to vehicle traffic beyond Atkinson Flats Campground, cutting off drive-in access to Trinity indefinitely - confirm current road status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before relying on this approach. From the trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail #1513 (signed Buck Creek Pass Trail #789 on Forest Service pages), climbing steadily through forest and along Buck Creek roughly 8.8 miles to about 5,600 ft, where the standard line breaks off-trail to the right toward Pass No Pass.

road.name: Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200)
road.status: CLOSED beyond Atkinson Flats Campground to Trinity since May 20, 2026 due to storm damage, under Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11, which runs through December 31, 2027; the Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect from September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes the Chiwawa River Road and Buck Creek Trail #1513
road.driveNote: From Coles Corner take WA-207 N 4.4 mi, right onto Chiwawa Loop Road 1.3 mi, left onto Chiwawa River Road/FR 6200, then ~23 mi to the Trinity/Buck Creek Pass Trailhead
road.seasonalGate: Even when open, the road is a long gravel/paved Forest Service road not plowed in winter; verify current Forest Service alerts before any trip

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail to Pass No Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the highway junction take the state route north, then the loop road and the Chiwawa River Road (Forest Road 6200) to its end at the Trinity trailhead. Check current road status before committing to the drive: the road has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, which cuts off drive-in access entirely. From the trailhead hike the Buck Creek trail, climbing steadily through forest and along the creek to about 5,600 ft, where the standard line breaks off to the right. This is normally done as part of a backpacking trip to the pass rather than in a day, and the peak sits about half a mile northeast of that pass on the crest.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, once the high meadows melt out. The alternative grass-and-heather line is likely hazardous when wet.
hazards: A false trail lies just before the real cutoff, and on the way down the fork that crosses the creek into the woods is the wrong one
Road access to the trailhead has been closed below it at times, and fire closures have shut the trail — confirm before driving in
The boot path braids into several strands above about 5,800 ft
Exposed meadow crest with no shelter from afternoon weather
A false south summit stands beside the true summit block
A short scramble on the block itself, easy rock but genuinely a scramble
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE CUTOFF IS AFTER THE MAIN STREAM, AND THERE IS A FALSE TRAIL BEFORE IT. Well up the Buck Creek trail you cross a series of streams; the turn to the right for Pass No Pass comes after the main one, is unmarked, and is quite obvious once you are at it — but a false trail branches before that crossing and is the thing parties take by mistake. Coming back down, the fork that crosses the creek and heads into the woods is the false one; go left instead. A single established campsite sits just above the first stream and is a useful confirmation. From the turn a path runs north to a bare patch, then a fainter track aims north-northwest toward a grey stone block just above the edge of the trees, which gives the bearing. Above about 5,800 ft the path splits repeatedly — ignore the spurs, keep going uphill and north, and the strands consolidate at Pass No Pass, a saddle near 6,380 ft in a grove of mature conifers. At the pass or just short of it, make a sharp left and traverse uphill to the southwest; the summit block comes plainly into view as you gain height. Take it by the easy rock on its south, left-hand side, and do not settle for the false south summit standing beside it.

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Pass and the grass slopes
approach_variants.notes: The alternative stays on the trail past the off-trail turn and continues all the way to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes from the pass to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble to the top. It is the option for a party already camped at the pass on a backpacking trip, and it trades the braided boot path and the meadow traverse for a steeper direct climb.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn on dry ground only — this line is likely hazardous when the grass and heather are wet.
hazards: Steep grass and heather with poor runout, and likely hazardous when wet
No path on the climb from the pass
A false south summit stands beside the true summit block
The same short scramble on the block itself
Exposed to afternoon weather with no shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding: YOU IDENTIFY THIS LINE BY STAYING ON THE TRAIL PAST THE TURN. Where the off-trail path breaks right toward Pass No Pass around 5,600 ft, ignore it and carry on along the maintained tread to Buck Creek Pass itself. From the pass the peak stands about half a mile to the northeast on the crest, and the slopes rising toward it are steep grass and heather rather than the meadowy braided path of the other line. Climb them to reach the west side of the summit block. The test that you are on this variant and not the other is underfoot: continuous steep vegetation with no worn path, approached from the pass rather than traversed into from the southwest. Do not commit to it when the grass is wet, because that surface gives no purchase and the slope runs out badly. Whichever side you arrive on, the block itself is taken by the easy rock on its south side; the steeper aspects are not the route.

approach_variants.name: Rachel Lake Trail to the avalanche clearing, then the Hibox climbers' path over two cliff bands
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rachel Lake trailhead, Trail #1313, about 2,800 ft, at the end of Box Canyon Road / FR-4930. The trail climbs gently through forest along Box Canyon Creek, easy class 1 walking.

At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles and about 3,300 ft the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing. That clearing is the key landmark, because Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast from it.

Above the boot path the tread climbs steeply, mostly class 2 with fallen timber, about 500 vertical feet to a band of cliffs near 5,300 ft. Stay RIGHT of that first band, then work LEFT around a rock outcrop, continue through patchy timber to a SECOND, higher cliff band, and take the gully on the RIGHT through it. Above, a large sloping subalpine meadow funnels into loose talus and scree.

No reliable water past the lower forest. About 5.6 km and 3,900 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to October
hazards: An unsigned, easy-to-lose boot path through brushy avalanche clearings, especially confusing in fog and on descent
A deceptive gully on the southwest side of the summit block that cliffs out at class 4 — stay climbers' right of it
Loose talus and scree above about 4,600 ft with real rockfall risk onto parties below
An exposed class 3 notch and chimney on the summit block, whose downclimb is the part to think about before committing
Lingering snow and ice in the upper gully and basin into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLEARING IS THE FIRST TEST AND THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS ITS PROOF. At roughly 2 to 2.2 miles the maintained trail crosses a brushy avalanche clearing, and from it Hibox's summit block is visible on the ridge to the NORTHEAST. Just past that clearing — some parties say after the SECOND such clearing — watch the RIGHT, climbers'-right, side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path heading northeast and uphill into the forest. It is easy to walk past if you are not looking.

THE TWO CLIFF BANDS ARE A COUNTED SEQUENCE, WHICH IS WHAT YOU WANT IN FOG: first band, pass it on the RIGHT; then LEFT around a rock outcrop; second band, take the gully on the RIGHT. Two bands, right then left then right. If you have passed only one band you are not yet on the upper mountain.

AND HERE IS THE WRONG-TURN TRAP THAT MATTERS MOST, at the top: the talus tops out on the SOUTH side of the summit block, and the rock straight above you there is steeper and more broken than it looks. That is the spot where parties commit to the wrong line, and there is a deceptive gully on the SOUTHWEST side of the block that cliffs out at class 4. Do not climb what is above you.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL BASE FINDING: work RIGHT, staying along the south side of the rock and heading EAST, on loose talus over a sloping bed, until a reasonable gully opens on the EAST side of the block. That east gully is the route. It stays easy until the top, where a short NOTCH or narrow chimney gives a bit of genuine class 3 on good, solid holds to a small summit platform.

AND A DESCENT NOTE THAT BELONGS WITH THE FINDING: the boot path through the brushy avalanche clearings is easy to lose on the way down, especially in fog. Look back at the junction on the way up.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone arrow, Stump Hollow, the Barrier, and the Himmel-Otto col gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek Campground and trailhead on SR-20 just west of Newhalem at about 600 ft, follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the south side of Goodell Creek. It is flat and easy for roughly 4-4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn and stone marker, which climbers call the stone arrow, at the end of the roadbed. This marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. Steep, root-and-duff footing, brushy in spots, but reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher. No reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block. From there, rising-traverse on meadow, slab and early-season snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft, then cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: An icy, choss-and-moat gully to the col in late season
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass
Two Barrier crossings, both loose and exposed, with rockfall onto any party below
No reliable water between the Goodell roadbed and treeline
No bolted or fixed rappel stations anywhere on the route; all anchors are built
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A COL YOU REACH BY A NARROW GULLY, AND THE GULLY'S CHARACTER CHANGES COMPLETELY THROUGH THE SEASON. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the HIMMEL-OTTO COL. In early season that is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top. By late season it turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and AN OVERHANGING BOULDER NEAR THE COL OFTEN FORCES A LOOSE, EXPOSED CLASS 3-4 BYPASS ON THE LEFT, climber's left.

SO THE MARKER IS THE BOULDER, AND IT IS A COUNTABLE ONE: there is one overhanging boulder near the top of the gully, and getting past it on its left is the last obstacle before the col. If you have bypassed several such blocks, you are in the wrong gully.

ARRIVAL: you are at the col when the gully tops out into a gap with ground falling away on the far side. From there the standard route continues on easier ground, scrambling to low 5th class, onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit.

TWO CROSSINGS OF THE BARRIER EXIST AND BOTH ARE CORRECT: a LOWER crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a HIGHER crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mount Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour. Both are loose enough that a party above another is the real danger.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: descending north from the Himmel-Otto col rather than climbing from it. The north side is a different and harder proposition and leads onto the Mustard Glacier.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

approach_variants.name: From a high camp below the Chopping Block, up the snow slope and 600 ft of ramps to the grassy col at the base of the wall
approach_variants.notes:
The approach to camp is the standard Southern Pickets line: Goodell Creek trailhead, the old roadbed to the stone arrow at about 1,700 ft, the steep unmaintained climbers' path to treeline, Stump Hollow, and a crossing of the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin. This route's own camp is described as being BELOW THE CHOPPING BLOCK above Crescent Creek Basin rather than in the basin floor.

The first-ascent party left camp at 4 a.m. and was at the snow slope below the wall by 5 a.m. This is an eight-pitch line with a single published ascent, so treat the detail as one party's account rather than accumulated knowledge.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A single published ascent, so no accumulated route-finding knowledge
600 ft of easy but unprotected ramps and ledges simply to reach the rack-up point
Loose rock on the final pitch from the notch to the summit
The standard Southern Pickets approach: a relentlessly steep unmaintained path, no water, and a Barrier crossing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE RACK-UP POINT IS A GRASSY COL, AND IT SITS 600 FT ABOVE THE SNOW. From the snow slope below the wall, climb roughly 600 FT OF EASY ROCK RAMPS AND LEDGES to a GRASSY COL at the base of the wall. That col is where the first-ascent party racked up, and it is the base of the route.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS THREE THINGS AND YOU CAN COUNT THEM IN CLOUD: camp, then a snow slope, then 600 ft of easy ramps, then grass in a gap with the wall rising above it. Grass underfoot at the foot of a steep wall is the confirmation; a rock ledge is not, and neither is the top of the snow.

TIMING AS A CHECK, BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE MEASUREMENT THE FIRST ASCENT LEFT: about an hour from camp to the snow slope below the wall. If you have been walking for three, you are not below Stonehenge.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing past the wall toward the narrow gully that climbs to the Himmel-Otto col puts you on the peak's standard route, which is a different objective and a different side of the mountain.

WHY THERE IS SO LITTLE DETAIL ABOVE THE COL: the route has one recorded ascent and its published description stops at the grassy col. Nothing locates a particular crack or flake at the start, and inventing one would be inventing the fact a party in fog would rely on.

approach_variants.name: Libby Creek Trail #415 to Libby Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead follow Libby Creek Trail No. 415 southwest into the wilderness. The tread climbs gradually through mixed conifer and crosses several tributaries of Libby Creek on logs or hoppable rocks, and can be brushy and overgrown low down. A spring in the patchwork burn scar and then the ford of the North Fork of Libby Creek are the reliable water, with an established campsite on the far bank. At roughly four and a half miles a decaying old cabin stands in the middle of the trail, and that is where the climbing route leaves. Note that the standard line does not go to Libby Lake at all — the lake is the left-hand continuation and a fine camp, but the peak is reached from the cabin.
approach_variants.season: July into early October; especially popular in late September and early October when the basin and approach slopes fill with golden larch. Snow can hold in the ascent gully and on the upper ridge into June.
hazards: Brushy, lightly maintained tread and unbridged tributary crossings low down
The boot path fades in the clearing above the cabin and there are no cairns anywhere on the route
Choose-your-own-line boulder hopping to gain the ridge, with harder and easier ways and no defined route
Loose and unstable blocks on the summit ridge; test holds before weighting them
Lingering snow into June
Downloadable tracks for this peak are known to be wrong — do not follow one blindly
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE DECAYING CABIN IN THE MIDDLE OF THE TRAIL IS THE JUNCTION, AND YOU GO RIGHT OF IT. About four and a half miles in, an old collapsing cabin stands right in the trail. Continuing left or straight past it takes you up the final hill to Libby Lake; the peak is the faint boot path leaving to the RIGHT of the cabin, into open forest. That building is the whole of the marker — there is no sign and there are no cairns anywhere on this route. Follow the boot path to a large clearing, where it gives out; that is expected, because from the clearing the forest is open enough to see the peak's west ridge rising to the north, and you simply pick a line for it. Below the ridge is a boulder field, and gaining the crest from it is choose-your-own-adventure with harder and easier ways and nothing defined. Once on the ridge it is straightforward boulder hopping, with one thing to know: traverse climber's right of the summit spire and hook around it rather than trying to climb it head on. If you have arrived at a lake shore, you have walked past the cabin.

approach_variants.name: Sahale Arm, the secret gully, and the mining-equipment alcove
approach_variants.notes: From Sahale Glacier Camp traverse the boulder-and-heather plateau east, downclimb the steep snowfield, and gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge; follow a cairned climbers' trail down it, past one short 4th-class step, descending easterly to about 7,100 ft. Pick up the southeast rib that forms the west edge of Horseshoe Basin and follow it southeast to the top of the so-called secret gully at about 6,700 ft — full of snow some years, completely melted out and loose in others. Below it, traverse a wide ledge at 6,600 ft rising gradually to the base of a cliff at 6,800 ft where old mining workings sit, then contour loose scree until you are due south of the peak. Fill up at Doubtful Creek or Pelton Basin: the water in Horseshoe Basin is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Extended travel on loose talus, scree and slabs with real fall exposure
A snow crossing that wants an axe, and crampons in early season
Mine-tailings contamination of Horseshoe Basin water
Camping is prohibited in Horseshoe Basin itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: AN ALCOVE WITH OLD MINING EQUIPMENT STASHED IN IT IS THE UNMISTAKABLE MARKER. Dropping into Horseshoe Basin you use a narrow rock dike about eight feet wide that loses roughly a hundred feet: it starts Class 3, then a short downward Class 4 step lands you in that alcove with mining gear cached inside it, after which the dike stays Class 3 but loose and exposed. Nothing else on this ridge looks like it. Get the peak itself right before you commit: the crag climbers call Horseshoe is the HIGHEST point on Ripsaw Ridge, nearest Buckner, with the sharp Lick of Flame spire standing between the two. The twin-spired formation with a U-shaped notch in the MIDDLE of the ridge is the older, historical Horseshoe and is not the summit anyone bags — aiming at it puts you on the wrong tower. From the basin floor a snowfield at 30 to 45 degrees sits at the base of the peak and spills onto a large ledge about a hundred feet below the top; from there work leftward around a small buttress into the loose gully that leads to the notch just EAST of the summit, where the rope comes out for five feet of 5th class.

bivy.name: Buckner cross-country zone bivy
bivy.notes: The option for climbers who want to sleep on the route rather than at a valley camp — high bivies on moraine, slab or snow under Buckner's north side and the Ripsaw Ridge peaks. Zone rules are strict and worth reading before you go: camp at least a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight, and only on snow, rock or bare ground. No meadow camping, nothing within 100 ft of water, no fires. Because the permit is walk-up only, a trip built around a zone bivy is one you cannot lock in ahead of time — carry a fallback.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent — snowmelt and seasonal streams in the upper basin, dependable early, thin or gone by late season
bivy.permit: NPS cross-country zone permit required, WALK-UP ONLY. Buckner is not among the zones that take advance reservations, so it cannot be booked on Recreation.gov and must be picked up in person, generally no more than a day ahead.
bivy.capacity: 6 people per party, 6 parties per night in the zone

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: A set of hand-built rock-walled tent platforms at the toe of the glacier, at the top of Sahale Arm. It is high, exposed and above the last dependable water, so late-season parties should plan to melt snow or carry up from lower on the arm. For the Horseshoe Basin peaks it is a high camp rather than a basin camp — it serves approaches that cross Sahale Arm and drop toward Doubtful Lake and the head of the basin, and it puts you on the right side of the divide for Buckner's north aspect. Reported elevation varies slightly between sources.
bivy.water: Unreliable — snowmelt and glacier runoff only, and the seasonal trickles commonly dry up by late summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; one of the most contested designated camps in the park. Realistically needs the early-access lottery or the general on-sale window in late April.
bivy.capacity: 4 sites, 4 people per site

bivy.name: Pelton Basin Camp
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin sits about half a mile east of and below Cascade Pass, on the Stehekin side, which makes it the obvious first night for a party coming in over the pass rather than up from the lake. It puts Horseshoe Basin within a long day, though the basin itself is still several miles and a substantial descent-then-climb away. Snow lingers here well into summer and the trail across the basin can be hard to follow when it does, so early-season parties should expect to navigate rather than follow tread.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creek through the basin, though flow drops late in a dry summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp on the Recreation.gov system, and among the harder Cascade Pass sites to draw in midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp — the number of sites is not published, and it is few enough that it goes early on summer weekends. Assume it may be full and carry a plan that does not depend on it.

bivy.name: Basin Creek Camp
bivy.notes: The closest designated camp to the Horseshoe Basin trail junction, which sits at about 3,600 ft on the valley trail, so it is the practical base for anything up in the cirque. It has a separate cooking area, a bear box and its own privy. Capacity is tiny — three sites — so a party of four fills most of it and a weekend permit is not something to count on. From here the basin trail climbs roughly 1,300 ft in about 1.5 miles to the Black Warrior Mine and the waterfall headwall below Ripsaw Ridge and Buckner's north side.
bivy.water: Reliable — Basin Creek runs beside the camp all season
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required (North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA); designated camp reserved by site on Recreation.gov, with roughly 40% of inventory held for walk-up the day before at Marblemount or Golden West in Stehekin. Per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: 3 sites, 12 people total

bivy.name: Doubtful Lake Camp
bivy.notes: Doubtful Lake lies in a cirque below Sahale Arm, reached by a spur that drops off the arm trail. It is the natural middle camp on the Sahale Arm variation of the approach, breaking up a long crossing between Cascade Pass and the head of Horseshoe Basin. Water is the one thing never in question here, which matters if the alternative is Sahale Glacier Camp late in the season. The spur loses meaningful elevation off the arm, so factor the reclimb into the next day.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus its inlet and outlet streams
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camping at the lake, reserved or walked up like the other Cascade Pass-area sites.
bivy.capacity: A small designated camp at the lake, site count not published. Treat it as a handful of spots rather than a place a large party can count on.

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068, south-end saddle, southwest ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Lake Serene trailhead off Mount Index Road at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft to the north end of the lake, where the trail ends.

Traverse the WEST side of the lake over talus and huge boulders to the south end. In snow, stay lower, closer to the water — the slope is less steep near the shore. Expect massive avalanche debris on this stretch.

From the south end of the lake head EAST to the saddle, then take the ridge running SOUTHWEST from it. That forested ridge is the crux of the approach and the reason this is a spring route: roughly the next 1,000 ft is dense brush and intermittent cliffs, plus one airy ten-foot rock step usually climbed by grabbing roots.
