Snow cover makes the ridge dramatically easier; bare, it is a fight. Plan on 12+ hours car to car and over 6,000 ft of gain despite the peak being under 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Snow cover — roughly late winter through May; not recommended once melted out
hazards: Steep dense brush and intermittent cliffs on the forested southwest ridge
The airy ten-foot rock step on the ridge, usually climbed on roots
Avalanche debris and avalanche hazard around the lake and in the gully
The wet rock step in the constriction once the gully melts out
Very long day — 12 to 15 hours is normal
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the ridge until it runs into the cliffs of Index, then TRAVERSE UNDER the cliffs and take the FIRST WIDE gully on your RIGHT. That is the Hourglass. Its shape is the check: it is wide and easy where you enter, constricts high up, then opens again. A gully that is narrow at the point where you step into it is not the one — keep traversing. Once melted out, the constriction holds a large wet rock step; that step is the reason the route is climbed as a snow line rather than in summer, and passing it dry would be mid-to-high fifth on the right side via a short chimney and face, or harder on the left.

approach_variants.name: The short loop trail at the ranger station, then the west flank to the heather knoll
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,600 ft and pick up the short interpretive loop that begins there. Leave it eastward, cross Howlett Creek, and climb cross-country through moderately open forest on the mountain's western flank. There is no trail above the loop.

The forest goes reasonably on the way up and badly on the way down: parties consistently report dense brush and jackstraw deadfall as the time sink of the descent rather than of the ascent, so mark your line as you climb rather than trusting to memory.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the west flank is clear of snow
hazards: no trail above the interpretive loop, and a descent through jackstraw deadfall and brush that is far slower than the ascent
a creek crossing at Howlett Creek
route-finding on a uniform forested flank with no landmarks below the knoll
steep snowfields low on the route in early season
loose class 3 and 4 rock on the ridge above
reaching the ranger station at all depends on a boat or on a closed border gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL IS A CHANGE OF VEGETATION, NOT A CHANGE OF ANGLE. Climb the west flank until the timber gives out onto a HEATHERY KNOLL at about 5,900 ft. That knoll is where the north ridge is gained and where the route starts. IF YOU ARE STILL IN TIMBER, OR IN JACKSTRAW DEADFALL AND BRUSH, YOU ARE BELOW IT - the knoll is open ground and unmistakable when you reach it.

THE RIDGE ABOVE THE KNOLL IS THE ROUTE, AND IT SHOULD HAVE AIR ON BOTH SIDES. If you are climbing a face with the crest still above you and to one side, you have gained the flank rather than the ridge and should traverse to the crest before continuing.

CHECK WHICH SUMMIT YOU ARE UNDER. This is the NORTH peak, the higher and broader of the two main summits. THE OTHER SUMMIT SHOULD BE TO THE SOUTH OF YOU. If the higher ground lies north and you are looking up at a tower with a rotten connecting ridge running toward it, you are on the south peak's flank instead, and the ridge between them is not a way to correct that - it is a notoriously rotten traverse that parties deliberately avoid.

A CROSS-CHECK ON THE DESCENT: you must find the knoll again to get back into the correct drainage. From above, the flank is uniform timber in every direction, and the drainage you came up is only identifiable from the knoll's position. Fix it before you leave it.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Campground, north end of Ross Lake
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead for every route on the mountain and the only developed camping anywhere near it. It sits in deep forest on flat ground by the lake, with vault toilets, boat ramps and no trash service, so everything you bring comes out with you. There is no cell coverage and the nearest supplies are hours away in either country. The season runs roughly late May into October, bounded at the front by snow on the gravel road and at the back by the road being left unmaintained. The other way in is by water: a boat from the resort at the south end will run parties the length of the lake, taking up to six people with packs on a chartered trip that is booked and paid in advance. That is expensive and inflexible but it does not involve a border at all, which through several recent seasons has made it the only way anybody got here. In summer 2026 a lightning fire on the border grew to many thousands of acres immediately east of the mountain, crossed into Canada, and closed the entire Hozomeen area including the docks, the campground and the lake north of Silver Creek. Treat access to this peak as something to verify from scratch each season rather than as a fixed thing.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is provided while the campground is staffed. Outside that window, and any time the system is off, the lake and the creeks are the supply and need treating.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. THE BORDER IS THE COMPLICATION. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
bivy.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and parties often describe regretting that decision around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. THERE IS NO CAMP HERE — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
bivy.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.
bivy.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A SEASONAL CLOSURE APPLIES: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.

road.name: Silver-Skagit Road (Skagit Valley Road) from Hope, British Columbia
road.status: Unpaved for its full ~37 miles / 60 km. Maintained and graded periodically, but washboard and potholes are the norm and every source advises carrying a spare tire. Rebuilt after the 2021 B.C. flood washouts. As of 24 July 2026 DriveBC listed it CLOSED at km 6, past Silver Lake, because the Border 2 Fire - burning 2.4 km east of Hozomeen in Washington - had crossed the border into British Columbia.
road.driveNote: Trans-Canada Hwy 1 Exit 168 at Hope, then Flood-Hope Road to Silver-Skagit Road and south on gravel. About 1 to 1.5 hours to the far end. Skyline II trailhead is near km 55 (about 34 miles in); Hozomeen Campground and the Hozomeen Lake trailhead are at the very end. A passenger car handles it when freshly graded; ground clearance helps when it is not.
road.seasonalGate: B.C. closes Silver-Skagit Road for a seasonal winter shutdown, posted for 15 October 2025 to 14 April 2026. Separately and more importantly, the NPS gate at the international boundary at Hozomeen has been closed since 2020, with vehicle and foot traffic across the border there prohibited and no end date given on the park's fire-closure page updated 14 September 2026; the crossing has never been staffed and is camera-monitored.

approach_variants.name: The long way: the ridge trail from the north to a camp near the boundary high point
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this peak from the south. From the highway on the north side of the boundary, follow the valley road south on gravel through the provincial park to the trailhead - a slow drive of well over an hour. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning: the crossing at Hozomeen has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic.

From the trailhead, climb roughly four thousand feet on trail to the ridge junction, then turn south along the ridge over rolling ground to a camp near the boundary high point at about 6,345 ft. Take water from the three creeks in the forest below the ridge, because there is none again until you are well south of the boundary.
approach_variants.season: July through September; the gravel road governs the season at its own end
hazards: a boundary crossing that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services
no water south of the creeks below the ridge junction
an exposed ridge camp
a 545 ft descent from camp that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
loose rock on the buttress
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CAMP THE ROUTE STARTS BY LOSING HEIGHT - ABOUT 545 FT DOWN TO THE 5,800 FT SADDLE AT THE HEAD OF THE NORTH CIRQUE. ANY LINE THAT CLIMBS FROM THE CAMP IS THE WRONG WAY. The saddle is the low point at the head of a bowl, with the cirque falling away in front of you and the buttress rising on its far side.

RECOGNISE THE CIRQUE BY ITS SHAPE: it is an enclosed bowl beneath the north side of the peak, not an open flank. If the ground ahead of you drops away into a valley rather than into a bowl with walls around it, you have gone off the ridge too early or too late.

THE BUTTRESS IS ON THE NORTH-EAST SIDE, so from the saddle it should stand between you and the sun in the middle of the day rather than in it. A wall you approach in full afternoon sun is on the wrong aspect.

CHECK THE PEAK: this is the NORTH summit, the higher and broader of the two. The other main summit should lie to the south, connected by a rotten ridge that is not a usable link between them.

WATER IS THE OTHER FIXED POINT. The last of it is the creeks in the forest below the ridge junction, well before camp. If you have passed those without filling, the correct move is to go back for water rather than to press on to a dry camp above a dry cirque.

approach_variants.name: The short way: the border swath from the ranger station
approach_variants.notes: A much shorter start leaves from the ranger station at the head of the lake, follows the short interpretive loop, and then bushwhacks east up the overgrown boundary swath, past a swamp, gaining about three thousand feet to a col near 6,300 ft where it joins the ridge. It saves miles and costs hours - the swath is overgrown rather than cleared, and the ground is steep and brushy. Reaching the ranger station itself means either the water taxi up the lake or the gated road from the north.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and slower than its distance suggests
hazards: an overgrown boundary swath that is steep, brushy and slow
a swamp low on the line
three thousand feet of unrelenting bushwhacking with no tread
no water on the upper half
reaching the ranger station depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SWATH IS THE HANDRAIL - IT IS A CLEARED LINE THROUGH FOREST THAT RUNS EAST, AND IF YOU ARE NOT ON IT YOU ARE NOT ON THE APPROACH. It is overgrown, so it looks like brush rather than like a corridor from inside it; the tell is that it is straight, and it does not wander with the terrain the way a game trail does.

A SWAMP IS PASSED LOW DOWN. Reaching it confirms the line; never reaching it means you have drifted off the swath into ordinary forest.

THE JOIN IS A COL NEAR 6,300 FT, roughly three thousand feet above the start, where the swath's climbing ends against the ridge. From there the route is the same as the long approach: work along to the saddle at the head of the north cirque near 5,800 ft, WHICH MEANS LOSING HEIGHT AGAIN, and the buttress stands on the far side of the bowl.

IF YOU ARRIVE ON A RIDGE AND THE GROUND BEYOND IS AN OPEN VALLEY RATHER THAN AN ENCLOSED BOWL, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG COL. The cirque is walled; the valley is not.

approach_variants.name: Lightning Creek landing and the east-bank trail past Willow Lake
approach_variants.notes: Take the boat landing on the lake's east shore rather than continuing to the head of the lake, and pick up the east-bank trail there. Follow it north past Willow Lake, which is the last reliable water. Beyond the lake the trail is left behind and the travel becomes timber and avalanche debris, a ravine to cross, and then steep dirt and brush up to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Meadows near 5,000 ft mark the end of the worst of it. From the meadows the cliff bands are bypassed on their west side rather than forced, and the ground leads to a saddle at about 6,200 ft directly beneath the buttress. The first ascent party bivouacked there, roughly six hours from the landing, and there is no water on it.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: the longest walk-in of the massif's options
avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water above Willow Lake, and a dry bivouac at the saddle
friable rock on the buttress with scarce protection
a loose upper gully above the crux chimney
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WILLOW LAKE IS THE POINT OF DEPARTURE AND THE LAST WATER - FILL THERE, BECAUSE NOTHING ABOVE RUNS. Leave the trail just beyond it and turn east.

THE SEQUENCE UNDERFOOT IS THE NAVIGATION: timber and avalanche debris, then A RAVINE THAT MUST BE CROSSED, then steep dirt and brush. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A RAVINE, YOU HAVE NOT YET COMMITTED TO THE RIGHT LINE. Above the brush the timber opens onto a broad shoulder and then meadows near 5,000 ft.

THE CLIFF BANDS ARE PASSED ON THEIR WEST SIDE. Anything that wants a rope on this section means you have run into the band rather than round it.

THE BASE IS A DRY SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,200 FT WITH THE BUTTRESS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. Two confirmations: the buttress above you is DIVIDED rather than a single clean rib, and the way onto it starts with a steep chimney low down - a face with no chimney at its foot is not this buttress. If your saddle has running water on it you are somewhere else, because this one has none.

AND CHECK THE PEAK: this is the SOUTH peak, the lower of the two summits. The higher, broader summit should be to the north of you, not above you.

approach_variants.name: The lake-side trail from the campground, leaving it at the Hozomeen Lake outlet for the west basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the campground and trailhead at roughly 1,650 to 1,720 ft, a maintained trail runs toward Hozomeen Lake. Climbers leave it near the lake's outlet, cross Hozomeen Creek, and push east into the peak's west basin through heavy deadfall and devil's club - the brush here is the defining feature of the approach rather than an incidental one. The basin gives onto a rib and gully system that leads to a high camp or bivouac around 4,900 to 5,000 ft, and above that to a saddle reported near 6,800 ft below the final pitches.

Getting to the campground itself is the trip's first problem: either the resort water taxi up the lake, or the long gravel road down from the north side of the boundary, which has been closed to vehicles and walkers alike. Settle that before anything else.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the west basin has melted out
hazards: heavy deadfall and devil's club through the whole lower basin
a creek crossing to enter the basin
loose rock on the rib and gully system
an exposed high bivouac with limited flat ground
reaching the trailhead at all, which depends on a boat schedule or a closed border gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WEST BASIN IS ENTERED AT A CREEK CROSSING, NOT AT A VIEWPOINT. Leave the maintained trail near the outlet of Hozomeen Lake and cross Hozomeen Creek; if you are still on graded tread you have not left yet, and if you have not crossed water you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

THE BASIN ITSELF IS RECOGNISED BY WHAT STOPS: the deadfall and devil's club that define the lower push give out as the ground steepens into a rib and gully system. THAT RIB IS THE LINE - a gully with no rib beside it to escape onto is not the one, because the way up here uses both.

THE FIRST FIXED POINT IS THE BIVOUAC GROUND AT ABOUT 4,900 TO 5,000 FT, where the rib eases enough to lie down on. Above it the system continues to a saddle at roughly 6,800 ft, and that saddle is the base: the final pitches start from it.

CHECK THE PEAK ABOVE YOU BEFORE COMMITTING. This is a route on the SOUTH peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. IF THE SUMMIT ABOVE YOU IS THE HIGHER, BROADER ONE AND THE OTHER LIES TO THE SOUTH, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR NORTH AND ARE IN THE NORTH PEAK'S GROUND. The connecting ridge between the two is notoriously rotten and is not a way to correct the error from above; go back down and around.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the campground at the head of the lake
approach_variants.notes:
There is no public road to this end of the lake from the south. Drive to the trailhead near milepost 134, walk down to the resort, and take its water taxi north to the campground and ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,650 ft. Everything below is measured from there.

From the campground pick up the maintained lake-side trail, which climbs gently through open lush forest toward Hozomeen Lake. Reports differ on how far along it you should stay - anywhere from a mile and a half to four miles depending on where the party cut off - so budget for the longer figure. Leave the tread around 2,400 ft near the lake's outlet and start up cross-country, following the drainage east into the basin under the peak's south side. There is a genuinely bad brush section here: devil's club right at the creek crossing, and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft that reduces travel to a crawl. Fill water at the creek crossing or again in the basin near 5,000 ft, because everything above is dry.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the brush is passable and the upper gullies have melted out
hazards: a boat schedule that fixes both ends of the trip on a lake with no road out
devil's club at the creek crossing and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft
no water above the basin near 5,000 ft
a boulder-choked gully with chockstones to negotiate under a pack
loose, friable rock on the upper mountain
a tiny high camp that will not take a large party
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LADDER OF LANDMARKS ABOVE THE BASIN IS WHAT FIXES YOUR POSITION, AND THEY COME IN ORDER. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones - IF YOUR GULLY HAS NO CHOCKSTONE BOTTLENECK IN IT, YOU ARE IN THE WRONG DRAINAGE and should traverse rather than climb. Above the chockstones the ground turns to tedious red scree and heather. The next confirmation is a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, passed rather than climbed. Above it the angle steepens to a broad saddle and basin near 6,800 ft with small flat tent-sized sites - the standard high camp, good for one or two tents and no more.

FROM CAMP THE BASE OF THE ROUTE IS ANOTHER THOUSAND FEET OR SO ABOVE, GAINED ON SLABS AND CONNECTING GULLIES. You are looking for the point where the slabs run out against the face and the ridge proper takes over.

CHECK WHICH SUMMIT IS ABOVE YOU. This route is on the SOUTH peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. If the tower above you is the higher, broader one and the other summit lies to the SOUTH of you, you have drifted north into the wrong cirque and are under the north peak.

AND CHECK THAT YOU LEFT THE TRAIL AT ALL. The maintained tread is graded and obvious; the moment you are on it with easy walking under your feet, you are not on the approach any more. The departure is at a creek, at a lake outlet, not at a sign.

approach_variants.name: By road from the north to the ranger station, subject to the border gate
approach_variants.notes:
The campground and ranger station at the head of the lake can also be reached by driving a long gravel road south from the north side of the international boundary. That crossing has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic, so this variant may simply not exist in the season you are planning for - confirm the gate's status before building a trip on it, because there is no way to discover it is shut except by arriving.

If it is open, the walk from the campground is identical to the boat variant: the maintained lake-side trail toward Hozomeen Lake, then off-trail at the outlet near 2,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and only if the boundary is open
hazards: a border gate that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services at the end
the same devil's club, deadfall and dry upper slopes
loose rock and a small high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVAL CHANGES, THE APPROACH DOES NOT. From the campground at about 1,650 ft the sequence is the same: maintained trail to the vicinity of Hozomeen Lake's outlet near 2,400 ft, then cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east into the south basin.

THE MARKERS ARE THE SAME LADDER, IN THE SAME ORDER: a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones near 5,000 ft, red scree and heather above it, a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, and then a broad saddle and basin at about 6,800 ft with a few small flat tent sites. A drainage with no chockstone bottleneck is the wrong drainage.

THE SUMMIT TEST STILL APPLIES. This route is on the SOUTH peak, the lower of the two. If the higher, broader summit is directly above you and the other one lies south, you are under the north peak instead.

approach_variants.name: From the Lightning Creek landing on the lake's east shore, past Willow Lake
approach_variants.notes: A boat landing further down the east shore of the lake gives onto the east-bank trail system, which runs north past Willow Lake. Parties have used this to reach the south and south-east sides of the massif on foot rather than starting from the campground at the head of the lake. It is the longer walk of the two boat options and it approaches the peak from the south-east rather than from the west, so it suits parties heading for the south-east side of the south peak more than it suits the standard line.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: a much longer walk than the head-of-lake landing
timber, avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water between Willow Lake and the basin
cliff bands that must be bypassed in poor visibility
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEPARTURE FROM THE TRAIL IS JUST BEYOND WILLOW LAKE, AND THE LAKE IS THE MARKER. It is the last reliable water; everything above is dry until the basin, so this is where you fill.

FROM THERE THE GROUND IS THE TEST RATHER THAN ANY TREAD: timber and avalanche debris first, then a ravine to cross, then steep dirt and brush climbing to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Reaching MEADOWS near 5,000 ft is the sign the worst of the brush is behind you.

ABOVE THE MEADOWS THE CLIFF BANDS ARE BYPASSED, NOT CLIMBED. If you are forced onto rock that wants a rope, traverse and look for the way round rather than committing to it - the way through here is a walking line, not a climbing one.

THE ARRIVAL IS A SADDLE AT ABOUT 6,200 FT DIRECTLY BENEATH THE BUTTRESS on the peak's south-east side, with no water on it. IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED SOMEWHERE WITH RUNNING WATER, YOU ARE NOT THERE YET. From that saddle the standard south-east face and the south-east buttress lines are both above you, so identify which feature you are under before starting up.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and parties often describe regretting that decision around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. THERE IS NO CAMP HERE — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Campground, north end of Ross Lake
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead for every route on the mountain and the only developed camping anywhere near it. It sits in deep forest on flat ground by the lake, with vault toilets, boat ramps and no trash service, so everything you bring comes out with you. There is no cell coverage and the nearest supplies are hours away in either country. The season runs roughly late May into October, bounded at the front by snow on the gravel road and at the back by the road being left unmaintained. The other way in is by water: a boat from the resort at the south end will run parties the length of the lake, taking up to six people with packs on a chartered trip that is booked and paid in advance. That is expensive and inflexible but it does not involve a border at all, which through several recent seasons has made it the only way anybody got here. In summer 2026 a lightning fire on the border grew to many thousands of acres immediately east of the mountain, crossed into Canada, and closed the entire Hozomeen area including the docks, the campground and the lake north of Silver Creek. Treat access to this peak as something to verify from scratch each season rather than as a fixed thing.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is provided while the campground is staffed. Outside that window, and any time the system is off, the lake and the creeks are the supply and need treating.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. THE BORDER IS THE COMPLICATION. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
bivy.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
bivy.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.
bivy.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A SEASONAL CLOSURE APPLIES: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.

approach_variants.name: Ridge camp north of the peak, then the traverse down and across to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes:
Two stages, and the second is what stops people. The first is a long day of eleven miles and more under heavy loads from the road on the north side of the boundary to a camp just north of the peak - the same ridge and boundary-swath ground the north-side routes use. Confirm the boundary gate's status before planning any of it.

The second stage is the approach from that camp to the base of the wall, which the first ascent party found tedious and painstaking and which took them four and a half hours. Budget it as a half-day objective in its own right and do it in daylight; there is no version of this traverse that goes well in the dark.
approach_variants.season: Mid-summer, and the base approach should be done in daylight
hazards: a loose third-class gully downclimbed at the start of the day, and re-climbed at the end of it
several precipitous rock ribs on steep unstable ground
a base approach long enough to be its own objective
a west aspect that takes afternoon sun and afternoon rockfall
a boundary gate that has been closed to vehicles and walkers
a remote position with a heavy carry to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST MOVE OUT OF CAMP IS A DOWNCLIMB, NOT A CLIMB. A loose third-class gully drops from the ridge camp toward the west side, and the party who first did it called it dangerous but the lesser of two evils - meaning the alternatives were worse, not that the gully is good. IF YOU ARE GAINING HEIGHT ON LEAVING CAMP, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE RIDGE.

BELOW THE GULLY THE TRAVERSE IS THE ROUTE-FINDING: SEVERAL PRECIPITOUS ROCKY RIBS, CROSSED ONE AFTER ANOTHER, ON STEEP UNSTABLE GROUND. Counting ribs is the only progress measure you have. A traverse that stays on one continuous slope without crossing ribs is not this one - it means you have dropped too far and are below the line, on ground that leads away from the wall rather than across to it.

THE ARRIVAL IS A LAUNCH POINT BENEATH THE WALL, with the face rising directly above and no further traversing to do. THE WALL FACES WEST, so it takes the afternoon sun and stands in shadow in the morning - if the face above you is lit at dawn, you are on the wrong aspect and have crossed too far around the peak.

TIMING IS PART OF THE NAVIGATION HERE. Four and a half hours from camp to the base means a party that leaves at first light arrives late morning; a party that leaves late arrives with the wall in full sun and the loose ground behind them to reverse in the dark.

approach_variants.name: PCT past the Kendall Katwalk to a point due EAST of the summit, then straight up
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft, hike the PCT northbound past Kendall Pass and the Kendall Katwalk to Ridge Lake, then past Alaska Pass and around Alaska Mountain to Huckleberry Flats. The Commonwealth Basin shortcut rejoins the PCT and saves about a mile, and is the recommended line.

Walk on until you are essentially due EAST of Huckleberry's summit — roughly nine to ten miles in. That bearing is the trigger to leave the trail, not a named junction.

Many parties make this two or three days with a camp at Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake; a fit party has done it car to car in about eleven and a half hours.

About 17.4 km and 4,600 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to October
hazards: Stiff class 3 with class 4 moves on an exposed ridge — not a beginners' scramble
A loose block at the notch below the summit block
A crumbly class 2 ledge traverse above a big cliff
Rockfall in the alternative Beckey gully on the left, which has turned parties around
No simple walk-off: a 60 m rope is needed for the rappel off the summit block
A very long day, with parties commonly splitting it over two or three
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEAVE THE PCT WHEN THE SUMMIT IS DUE WEST OF YOU — A BEARING, NOT A LANDMARK, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT YOU WANT IN CLOUD. From that point head cross-country WEST up steep heather or talus.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS WHERE THE MELLOW TERRAIN ENDS AND THE GROUND TURNS ROCKY, at about 6,100 ft, marked by a ROCKY BUTTRESS. That change underfoot is the arrival, and it is felt rather than seen.

AND THEN COMES THE ONE DECISION THAT DECIDES WHICH ROUTE YOU CLIMB, WHICH IS THE MOST VALUABLE THING ON THIS PAGE. At the base of the rocks you have two options: LEFT takes you into a steep loose GULLY leading to a notch and the summit block — that is the older Beckey line, and it has turned parties around with rockfall. RIGHT takes you up the RIDGE on class 3+ terrain — that is the East Ridge, the historic first-ascent route, and it is what most parties now climb. If you are in a loose gully, you have gone left.

HOW TO FOLLOW IT ONCE COMMITTED, BECAUSE IT DOES NOT LOOK OBVIOUS FROM BELOW: the route goes up the RIGHT side of the east ridge, essentially linking CLUMPS OF TREES, tree patch to tree patch. Looking up at it, the line is genuinely hard to piece together by eye; once you start, the next move is usually clear. Staying towards the RIGHT is correct at the beginning.

CHECKPOINTS HIGHER UP: about halfway, maybe a little further, leave the ridge proper by heading LEFT on a short traverse to a BLOCKY RAMP, which you climb to a high point just before the summit block. Then descend about 20 ft to the NOTCH at the foot of the block — either straight down, or skiers' right and a class 3 traverse to a ramp leading down to the notch.

THE SUMMIT BLOCK ITSELF: go up the middle to an obvious SLABBY RAMP. From there either a short class 5 crack — one piece, a #1 Camalot at its start, is what the record describes — or follow the ramp climbers' LEFT to exposed class 3/4. Bring a 60 m rope: a 30 m is insufficient for the rappel off the block.

SCALE OF THE THING, SO NOBODY UNDERESTIMATES IT: there is no walk-up on this mountain, the scrambling is stiff class 3 with class 4 moves, and one of the 1915 first-ascent party wrote his will on his shirt cuff over doubts he would survive the descent.

approach_variants.name: Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road — the upper gravel section is gated and often does not open until late June or July — follow the well-graded Cascade Pass trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft. The last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low down, so fill up before the switchbacks.

At the pass leave the maintained tread for the climbers' path heading south-southeast, a rising traverse across snow or heather on Mixup Peak's flanks to the base of the CACHE GLACIER near 6,000 ft. Ascend moderate glacier and snow slopes to CACHE COL at about 6,900 ft. From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about a mile over loose rock and heather benches to KOOL-AID LAKE at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water in the basin.

From camp the peak is a side trip: up toward the south flank, across a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft, then broken granite slabs to the ridge. About a mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly an hour to an hour and a half for a fit party.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September; the Cache Col approach commonly holds firm snow into early July and wants an axe and crampons even after the peak itself is snow-free
hazards: Crevasses and snow bridges on the Cache Glacier approach to Cache Col
Icy, steep snow on the Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake descent, worse refrozen in the early morning or late in the day
A band of steep snow around 7,100 ft that wants an axe and crampons even mid-summer
Loose rock and multiple similar-looking gully lines on the granite benches — the main route-finding crux
Short but exposed moves along the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE IS KOOL-AID LAKE, and above it the climb is route-finding rather than following a line. ON THE WAY UP, THE STEEP SNOW BAND AROUND 7,100 FT IS THE POSITION CHECK: it sits between camp and the granite, it is there most of the summer, and it is why you carry an axe on a class 2-3 scramble. Beyond it, broken granite leads to a gully that gains the summit ridge. Several similar-looking gullies lead up; parties report that more than one of them goes, so pick the cleanest and keep checking that it tops out on the ridge. ON THE RIDGE YOU REACH A FALSE SUMMIT FIRST. The true top is a short way beyond it along the ridge, so do not turn around on the first high point. AND DO NOT CONFUSE THE BASIN WITH CACHE COL. Cache Col at about 6,900 ft is on the approach, between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak, and it is where you cross the glacier; Kool-Aid Lake is about a mile beyond it and a descent below it. The peak is also recorded under the names Ess Mountain and S Mountain, so a description of S Mountain is describing this same summit.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park. Stay on the trail roughly a mile and a half to two and a half miles, until you are almost past the wall.

A path descends through the woods to the log crossing on Snow Creek. On the far side climb boulders and talus to the bootpath, which gains about 500 ft to the base.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
hazards: The RPM start is a runout 5.10+ slab on dirty rock
Loose talus below the wall and the log crossing at high water
East-facing low-elevation rock, very hot midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Hyperspace runs up the LEFT side of the Shield, and its position on the wall is defined by its neighbours: it sits between Orbit on the left and Outer Space on the right.

It does not have a distinct independent ground start in common use. The two entries are RPM — a runout, dirty 5.10-plus slab — and, more usually, Remorse. Both begin where the climbers' trail arrives at the wall, at the high point of the base with the small scrub trees.

The base test is therefore the same one that catches everyone here: if your first move off the deck is a hard bolted friction slab, you are on RPM; Remorse is the easier, often vegetated gully about 30 ft to the RIGHT.

Higher up, a landmark confirms you: pitch 4 passes a large fresh rock scar, clearly visible from the belay when you look down.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead. Follow the trail roughly 1.5 to 2.5 miles until you are in the trees running parallel to the wall and the wall is directly opposite.

A path drops right through the woods to the log crossing on Snow Creek. Cross, then climb boulders and talus on the far side onto the bootpath that gains about 500 ft to the foot of the wall.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
hazards: Loose talus on the climbers' trail
The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water
Parties above you on the shared lower pitches
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Iconoclast starts from the ground, at the HIGH POINT of the wall's base — the same arrival point as RPM and Remorse.

Stand on the trail just to the LEFT of the small scrub trees that mark the highest part of the base. You want to be directly beneath the roofs that form the underside of Two Tree Ledge. The confirmation on the rock is a large flake wrapped in a lot of old slings, sitting about 20 ft below a small bush.

That flake is the marker. If you cannot see a heavily slung flake, or you have walked to where the base is dropping away downhill, you have gone left toward Orbit and too far.

Most parties do not climb Iconoclast's own opening — they use the first two pitches of Remorse or RPM and join it above. If you take that option, the same base test applies: the bolted slab straight ahead of you where the trail arrives is RPM at 5.10d, and Remorse is the easier vegetated gully roughly 30 ft to its right.

bivy.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
bivy.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
bivy.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, over Ruth Mountain, then the Icy Glacier's northwest slope to the west notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at road's end on FS Road 32, near 3,100 ft, hike Trail #674 roughly four miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft. Hannegan Camp about 3.5 miles in is the LAST reliable water on the route — fill up there, because there is nothing running past it.

From the pass go cross-country east and northeast up heather meadows and scattered timber onto Ruth's north side, with some third-class ground through trees, then rope up for the Ruth Glacier to Ruth's summit at 7,115 ft. Most parties treat trailhead-to-camp as a five to six hour day and camp on Ruth's summit plateau or in the saddle beyond.

From camp, descend Ruth's south and west side about 1,400 ft from the summit (about 900 ft from the notch camp) to the Ruth-Icy saddle near 5,700 ft, taking the heather slopes and game trail on climber's LEFT rather than the steep loose gully. From the saddle, traverse talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the Icy Glacier.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: No water source at all after Hannegan Camp
Crevasses on both the Ruth and the Icy Glaciers, and a bergschrund near the west notch in some seasons
Loose rock in the summit gully with the whole party funnelled through it — helmets are standard
The steep loose 'death gully' off Ruth, which is the natural fall line and the wrong option
Roughly 1,400 ft of regain from the Ruth-Icy saddle over Ruth on the way home
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ON THE ICY GLACIER, KEEP THE ROCK RIDGE ON YOUR LEFT AND THE CREVASSES ON YOUR RIGHT. That is the navigation instruction for the whole glacier and it works without seeing the summit: climb the northwest slope gradually southeast to about 6,500 ft with a rock ridge as your left-hand handrail. If the rock swings round to your right, you have crossed the glacier and are heading for the wrong side of the peak.

THE NOTCH IS THE BASE, AND IT IS WEST OF THE NORTHWEST SPIRE at roughly 6,500 ft. Traverse the upper glacier below Icy's west face, skirting the west notch — some seasons there is a bergschrund near the top of it — to reach the notch or saddle just west of the Northwest Spire.

THERE IS A LONG HORIZONTAL CREVASSE NEAR THE TOP OF THE GLACIER, right below the Icy towers, and it is a useful landmark rather than only a hazard: it runs across your line just where the glacier ends beneath the peak. Meeting it means you are at the top of the glacier.

THE CLIMBING STARTS AT THE FIRST PROMINENT GULLY. From the notch, about 500 ft of second and third class talus and snow up Icy's south side reaches the base of a LIGHT-COLOURED, roughly 100 FT FOURTH-CLASS GULLY on the LEFT, with solid jugs and ledges. There are rappel slings around a horn at its top, left by previous parties. Colour, length and the slings at the top are three independent confirmations, which is more than most gullies in the Cascades offer.

WHICH SUMMIT: the gully leads to the NORTHWEST summit, which holds the register. The true high point is a separate southeast tower about 11 ft higher, reached by more third and fourth class scrambling. Many parties only tag the northwest one — decide in advance rather than at the notch.

A FEW MOVES IN THE GULLY FEEL LOW FIFTH RATHER THAN FOURTH, depending on the exact line taken. That is not a sign you are off route; it is the route.

bivy.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
bivy.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
bivy.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Way Trail, Lake Ingalls and the North–East col gully
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead follow Ingalls Way Trail #1390 north beside the creek on an old mining-road grade. At the signed fork bear right onto #1390 where the Esmeralda Basin trail stays low and left, and at the second junction stay left where the Longs Pass trail branches east. Steady switchbacks through open larch lead to Ingalls Pass; cross it, drop slightly and follow cairns and boot track around the basin rather than giving up height, then climb a large steep boulder field to Lake Ingalls. Filter there — nothing above the lake holds water. A climbers' path skirts the east shore and heads up-basin toward the notch between the main summit and the horn-shaped East Peak.
approach_variants.season: July through September once the pass switchbacks melt out; microspikes and an axe are worth carrying into July in a heavy snow year.
hazards: The chossy central gully below the col is the main rockfall hazard on the approach — favour the clean slabs on the left
Several sub-gullies lead toward the notch and the largest, most direct one is the loosest and most dangerous
A great deal of loose rock on the route, so protection can end up run out on easy ground
Snow and ice on the upper trail switchbacks into July
The descent uses three rappel stations down the face — count them on the way up
No water above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE CHOCKSTONE IS THE PROOF FOR THIS ROUTE — AND IT IS THE ERROR SIGNAL FOR THE ONE NEXT DOOR, SO DO NOT TREAT IT AS A GENERIC MARKER. Follow the climbers' path along the lake's east shore and head up-basin toward the obvious notch between the main Ingalls summit and the horn-shaped East Peak, favouring the clean granite slabs on the left over the loose central gully. Climb the obvious snow gully; partway up a distinctly odd-looking band of rock crosses it, and fifteen feet left of that band is where the neighbouring East Ridge route starts. This route does not stop there — carry on to the notch itself, where a single chockstone is wedged in the gap, and the climbing begins about fifteen feet above it at a comfortable belay ledge. That jammed block is the confirmation. Several sub-gullies lead up here and the largest, most direct one is the loosest and the one to avoid. From the ledge, the first pitch takes slabs trending slightly left into a gully to a belay on route, and the second trends right onto the crest over a great deal of loose rock; three rappel stations take you back down the face.

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Designated sites just past Ingalls Pass, about half a mile before Lake Ingalls. Camping is not allowed at the lake itself, so this is the overnight option for parties who split the climb.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt; filter
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead
bivy.capacity: Designated sites only; several small groups

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda Basin trailhead, Ingalls Way over Ingalls Pass to Lake Ingalls
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead (about 4,240 ft) at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, FR 9737. A free self-issue Alpine Lakes wilderness permit is filled out at the register.

There are TWO forks and they are easily run together. The first comes at roughly a quarter to half a mile, where the old mine-road grade splits: bear RIGHT onto Ingalls Way #1390. Straight on is Esmeralda Basin #1394, a different valley. The second fork is higher, around 5,600 ft and roughly a mile and a half in: RIGHT climbs to Longs Pass, which is a viewpoint and the way toward Ingalls Creek and Stuart's south side, not a way to this climb. Stay LEFT.

From there the trail traverses steadily to Ingalls Pass at about 6,500 ft, where Mount Stuart and the Ingalls group come into view all at once. Continue about another mile to Lake Ingalls, roughly 6,400-6,480 ft and about 4 miles from the car. This is the last water.

From the lake, work up and climber's-left on Class 2-3 slabs, talus and boulders. Stay with the cairned line. Parties who leave it for a more direct-looking line get cliffed out; one party downclimbed past a waterfall to escape.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the slabs above the lake are clear; snow lingers below the notch into early summer
hazards: Cliffing out on the slabs above and beside the lake if you leave the cairned line for a direct one
Loose talus and scree in the approach gully with parties above
Afternoon thunderstorms on a wholly exposed ridge — start early
A 60 m rope does not reach on the descent rappels, roughly fifteen feet short; carry a 70 m or doubles
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is visible from the lakeshore: the cleft between the North and South peaks, with a single pointed spire sitting in it. That spire is the Dogtooth. Aim just left of it and let it draw you up the slabs.

At the Dogtooth, go RIGHT for the traditional approach gully. The last gully is scree. If the gully you are in is green and lush it is the wrong one and it will carry you too high — traverse right out of it onto clean scree.

Arrival is physical: a short section of Class 4 up a crack of roughly forty feet at the top of the gully lands you on a ledge. That ledge is where the rope comes out. Pitch one is the low-angle slab above it, taking the large crack system up the middle.

Touch test at the start: the rock here is green serpentine, an odd slick band quite unlike the surrounding granite, sitting just up from the Dogtooth crag. Large hexes work in it where cams skate. Confirmation higher up — the pitch-three ledge carries two big bolts and there are three more at the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and this is the one that matters. This route climbs the south ridge of the NORTH peak, and the North peak (7,662 ft) is the true summit. The South peak (7,640 ft) is a separate Class 3 scramble that starts from the SAME notch. If you reached the notch, dropped about fifty feet down its west side and scrambled easy gullies back to a top without ever roping up, you climbed the South peak. That is not this route and not the high point.

Second marker: finishing the technical pitches does not put you on the summit. There is a few hundred feet of walking left to tag the actual high point, so a summit that arrives the instant the climbing ends is the wrong one.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2 through Headlight Basin (the camping branch)
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Ingalls Pass. Just past the pass the trail splits and the right-hand branch is signed Ingalls Way Alternate #1390.2. It drops into Headlight Basin, crosses Headlight Creek, and holds the established campsites and the reliable water. The main #1390 stays high along the rim of the basin and is the more direct line to the lake.

The two rejoin at a signed junction less than a quarter mile below Lake Ingalls, so this costs you a descent and a re-ascent in exchange for a legal camp and running water. Parties climbing the same day generally take the high line; parties camping take the low one.
approach_variants.season: Same window; this is the branch to take if you are sleeping out, since camping at Lake Ingalls is prohibited
hazards: Headlight Creek crossing
Braided use paths through the basin camps — stay on durable ground, this is Alpine Lakes Wilderness
Extra descent and re-ascent on the way out with a full pack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This branch does not change where the climbing starts — it rejoins the standard line at the signed junction below the lake, and from there the Dogtooth, the scree gully and the forty-foot Class 4 crack onto the belay ledge are exactly as on the high route.

What it does change is your starting view. Coming up out of Headlight Basin you meet the lake from below rather than from the pass, so you will not have had the long look across at the peak that the high traverse gives you. Walk to the lake outlet and pick out the notch and the Dogtooth spire from there before starting up the slabs, rather than trying to identify them mid-scramble.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Way Trail to Lake Ingalls and the North–South col
approach_variants.notes: Follow Ingalls Way Trail #1390 from the road-end trailhead: bear right and uphill at the signed fork where the Esmeralda Basin trail drops away left, carry straight on where the Longs Pass trail branches right, and climb steady switchbacks through open larch to Ingalls Pass. From the crest the trail drops into the basin and contours to Lake Ingalls, giving back a few hundred feet. Two tracks cross the basin and rejoin; the more maintained of them avoids the Headlight Creek crossing. Fill and filter at the lake, because nothing higher holds water. Leave the maintained trail there and work up talus, slabs and boulders toward the saddle between the North and South Peaks.
approach_variants.season: July through September. Steep snow or verglas commonly lingers on the approach to the col into midsummer, so an axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying through July.
hazards: Unmarked route-finding on loose talus and boulders above the lake — the real crux of the day for most parties
Steep lingering snow just below the saddle into midsummer
Severe drop-offs on the west side of the ridge
Loose rock in the short west-side gullies, which land on anyone beneath — move one at a time
No water above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SMALL ROCK SPIRE IN THE SADDLE IS THE MARKER, AND THE DIKE IS THE HANDRAIL BELOW IT. Leaving the trail at the lake, work up talus, slabs and boulders toward the col between the North and South Peaks: an obvious dike runs up this ground and gives by far the easiest going, so fighting loose blocks with no continuous feature underfoot means you have drifted off it. A small rock spire stands in the notch itself and you aim to pass just left of it — that spire is how you know the col you have reached is the right one. From the col do not carry straight on up the crest. Drop about fifty feet onto the west side and pick one of several short gullies, roughly a hundred feet of loose rock, back up to the ridge; dropping less makes it steeper and dropping more makes it easier. If you are on the crest and the moves are turning hard, you have missed the drop. The summit block takes one short exposed move, and a crack between blocks lets you squeeze through and avoid the worst of the exposure.

pro_tips: Study the face from the walk-in and from the boulder camp in evening light; on this peak you will very likely be climbing in or under cloud and the ramp/dihedral/green-lichen-ledge features are hard to identify from close range.

After the first pitch the true Northwest Buttress goes LEFT onto the obvious ledge along the green-lichen face. Continuing straight up the crack system puts you on the 2021 Second Wind variation, which is significantly harder at 5.8+.
Base camp at the large boulders directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek, rather than at Home Lake — it cuts a meaningful chunk off summit day and gives you the view of the face.
Carry rappel material as a primary item, not an afterthought. With no fixed gear on the route, your retreat plan is entirely made of things you brought and are willing to leave.

The Upper Dungeness approach is the sane side of this mountain. The Dosewallips/Lake Constance side is shorter on paper but adds 6.5 miles of washed-out road plus a brutally steep scramble trail, and it deposits you in Avalanche Canyon on the wrong aspect for this route.

This is a rare route. Treat any description of it as a sketch, expect to make your own decisions on the ground, and be honest about whether the party is comfortable with poor rock and long runouts before committing.

pitch_detail.notes: From the boulder camp, up the scree field to an obvious ramp; follow the ramp around climbers' right of the prominent dihedral.

Turn LEFT onto the obvious ledge that runs along the green-lichen-covered face. This is the move that distinguishes the original buttress from the Second Wind variation, which instead continues into the crack system.
Steep Class 3/4 gully above the ledge system. Loose; keep the party close together or fully out of the fall line.
Final long, low-angle pitch to the summit proper — the pleasant part of the climb, on the more solid pillow basalt that caps the peak.
