road.name: Forest Service Road 2870 (Upper Dungeness), via FS 28 / FS 2880 from Palo Alto Road
road.status: Open, maintained gravel; passenger-car accessible to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead across the Dungeness River bridge
road.driveNote: From US 101 opposite Sequim Bay State Park take Louella Road, then Palo Alto Road (which becomes FS 28 at the forest boundary), right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then stay LEFT on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles. Large parking area with vault toilet, no potable water. Day-use fee $5/vehicle/day or $30/year; Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency and Digital passes honoured.
road.seasonalGate: No gate, but the road is snow-affected in winter and early spring; access is a summer/fall proposition

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake, then the Home Creek basin to the boulder camp
approach_variants.notes:
From US 101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn onto Louella Road, go about a mile to Palo Alto Road and turn left for roughly 1.1 miles to the forest boundary, where Palo Alto becomes Forest Service Road 28. Turn right on FS 2880, pass Dungeness Forks Campground, then stay left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead just across the Dungeness River bridge. Large parking area, vault toilet, no potable water, Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass required.

Hike Upper Dungeness Trail #833 up the river — easy, shaded, river-grade — to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at roughly 6.1-6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. Continue on the Constance Pass trail as it climbs out of the timber into rocky flowery terrain beneath Warrior Peak and Inner Constance, crossing into Olympic National Park, and climb to Home Lake at about 9.3 miles and roughly 5,308-5,330 ft, some 500 ft below Constance Pass.

From the lake, work up the Home Creek basin south-southwest toward the peak. Camp at the LARGE BOULDERS directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek. That boulder camp is the documented basecamp for this route and it is where the first-ascent party camped.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Rock quality described by climbers who have scouted it as among the worst in the Olympic Mountains, and as bad as anything in the range near the summit ridge
No fixed gear anywhere on the route — every rappel station on descent has to be built and left
Sparse protection with long runouts
The published description for this line is thin and climbers who know it advise ground-truthing it in person
A 9+ mile approach, and the same distance back out
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE TOP OF A SCREE FIELD WHERE AN OBVIOUS RAMP BEGINS, AND THE THING THAT IDENTIFIES THE RAMP IS THE BIGGEST CORNER ON THE FACE. From the boulder camp, climb the scree field to the base of the wall and pick up the obvious ramp. Follow it round CLIMBER'S RIGHT of the PROMINENT DIHEDRAL — the one large, unmistakable corner in that section of face — to a steep Class 3/4 gully. If the ramp you are on is taking you LEFT of the big corner, you are on the wrong side of it. THE SECOND TEST IS AT THE TOP OF PITCH ONE AND IT IS A COLOUR YOU CAN READ AT ARM'S LENGTH: after the first pitch this route turns CLIMBER'S LEFT onto an obvious ledge running along a GREEN-LICHEN-COVERED FACE. Green lichen on rock is visible in cloud in a way a skyline feature is not. If your first pitch does not end at a ledge beneath a lichen-green face, you are not on the Northwest Buttress — and specifically, if you have carried straight on up a crack system instead of stepping left, you are on Sean's Route / Second Wind, which shares this start and diverges exactly here. WHAT THE ROUTE'S OWN TEXT ALREADY TELLS YOU, AND IT IS THE HONEST LIMIT: the face is in full view from the boulder camp and from below, and that is described as the only reliable chance you get to pick out the ramp and the green-lichen ledge. Look at it, photograph it and fix the line in your head from camp. This is a route to identify in the evening and climb in the morning; there is no marker sequence that will find it for you if you walk up into the wall in cloud having never seen it.

bivy.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
bivy.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
bivy.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
bivy.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
bivy.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

road.name: Forest Service Road 2870 (Upper Dungeness), via FS 28 / FS 2880 from Palo Alto Road
road.status: Open, maintained gravel; passenger-car accessible to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead across the Dungeness River bridge
road.driveNote: US 101 opposite Sequim Bay State Park to Louella Road, then Palo Alto Road (becomes FS 28 at the forest boundary), right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then stay LEFT on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles. Large parking area, vault toilet, no potable water. Day use $5/vehicle/day or $30/year; Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency and Digital passes honoured.
road.seasonalGate: No gate; snow-affected in winter and early spring

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and the boulder camp — the same start as the Northwest Buttress
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Northwest Buttress: Upper Dungeness Trailhead at the end of FS 2870, Trail #833 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Camp at roughly 6.1-6.4 miles, then the Constance Pass trail over into Olympic National Park and down to Home Lake at about 9.3 miles. Basecamp is the large boulders directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek. The northwest face comes into view from below the lake.

This route and the Northwest Buttress share their approach, their camp, their scree field and their first pitch. They are one climb until the top of that pitch. The first-ascent party's round trip from camp — climb plus the descent into Avalanche Canyon and back round to the Home Lake cirque — ran about 12.5 hours.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Sparse, widely spaced protection — roughly one usable placement per 20 to 100 feet — so fall consequences are severe on the crux pitches
Persistent rockfall on typical loose Olympic basalt, and the first three pitches are explicitly rotten
The move out of the cave is exposed and committing, and retreat from it is not simple
No fixed gear; descent stations must be built
The descent is not the ascent line — it drops into Avalanche Canyon on loose sandy ledges and traverses back round to the Home Lake cirque
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS SHARED WITH THE NORTHWEST BUTTRESS AND SO IS THE TEST FOR IT: from the boulder camp, up the scree field to the OBVIOUS RAMP, and follow it round CLIMBER'S RIGHT of the PROMINENT DIHEDRAL to a steep Class 3/4 gully. Right of the big corner, not left.

THE TEST THAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE BUTTRESS COMES AT THE TOP OF PITCH ONE, AND IT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A LANDMARK — WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE GROUND. At that point the Northwest Buttress steps CLIMBER'S LEFT onto an obvious ledge along a green-lichen-covered face. Sean's Route does NOT. It stays with the crack system and follows it straight on up rotten loose rock for roughly three pitches in total.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS TACTILE, OVERHEAD AND UNMISTAKABLE IN ANY VISIBILITY: about three pitches up, the crack system ends at a CAVE BENEATH AN OVERHANGING ROOF. You cannot mistake being under a roof. That cave is the route's crux and its identity — you build an anchor in it and make a committing move out by underclinging the roof and traversing right about 10 to 15 feet onto the ramp leading to the slab above. If you have climbed three pitches and there is no roof over you, you are on the Buttress or on neither.

HONEST LIMIT: this is a shared base with a pitch-one divergence rather than a route with a base of its own, and it is recorded that way rather than dressed up. Above the roof it is a few pitches of Class 4 to low fifth to the southwest false summit, then it rejoins the Northwest Buttress for the last pitch to the true top. Protection averages one usable placement every 20 to 100 feet.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
approach_variants.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS CLIMB IS A FORK, AND THE FORK IS MARKED BY A ROCK FORMATION CALLED THE THUMB. Head up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb. That is where the South Chute (which belongs to MOUNT Constance) and the South Gully (which belongs to INNER Constance, this route) diverge. Two summits sit above one canyon and the Thumb is the thing that tells the two lines apart.

THE FOG TEST THAT DOES NOT NEED THE THUMB, AND IT IS THE BETTER ONE, IS THE SHAPE OF THE GULLY YOU END UP IN. From the broad couloir, veer RIGHT into a steeper secondary couloir, which narrows into a snow-filled DEFILE. That defile constricts to roughly a two-foot gap with moats five to ten feet deep opening on either side of the snow by mid-to-late season. Nothing else in this canyon does that. If your gully stays broad and open all the way up, you are in the Mount Constance South Chute and climbing the wrong peak.

SECOND TEST, higher: above the defile the snow finger goes discontinuous and you stem repeatedly between snow and rock to get round the moats, with short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep finger tops out at a notch on the East Ridge near 7,200 ft, gained by a short Class 3-4 rock step. If you are still on continuous snow with no stemming, you have not reached the defile yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS THE RECORDED WAY THIS ROUTE GOES WRONG: from the East Ridge the line pulls naturally toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which has no easy connection across to the true NORTHEAST high point. Follow the East Ridge crest on Class 2-3 pillow basalt to the northeast top; if the ridge you are on is running away southwest, you are heading for the wrong summit.

SAFETY NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE ROUTE-FINDING: snow blocks calve out of the defile constriction as the day warms — a refrigerator-sized block struck a climber there. Move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before weighting them.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CRYSTAL PASS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS DIRECTLY BELOW YOU RATHER THAN ABOVE YOU, WHICH IS THE ONE REAL ADVANTAGE OF THIS SIDE. Descend south into upper Avalanche Canyon on the intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, keeping to the RIGHT (north) side of the canyon, past the Thumb, and then contour and climb toward Inner Constance's northeast side.

THE TEST IS STILL THE THUMB AND THE DEFILE, and it still works from above: the fork you want is the one where the South Gully leaves the broad couloir and veers into a steeper secondary couloir that NARROWS to a two-foot gap with deep moats. Coming from Crystal Pass you can also take the northeast side directly — a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the RIGHT side of the north ridge crest, broken blocky Class 2-3 with occasional Class 4 and low fifth where the crest steepens.

THE FOG TEST FOR THAT NORTHEAST LINE IS WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST YOU ARE ON. Stay on the crest's RIGHT-hand side as you climb. If you have crossed over and are traversing on the other flank, you are off the line, and the rock over there is worse.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the same trap as the other variant — the mountain pulls toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which does not connect easily to the true northeast high point. Keep working toward the NORTHEAST top.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and early-season snow with real route-finding demands. A rope and axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass early in the year.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone-arrow boot path to Terror Basin, then the crevassed Terror Glacier to the bergschrund below the west end of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground just west of Newhalem off SR-20 and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail. The first roughly 4 miles follow an old streamside roadbed at easy grades from about 500 to 1,600 ft, crossing the creek and passing the LAST RELIABLE FLOWING WATER AROUND 1,600 FT. Fill up there; the trail is dry above.

A cairned stone-arrow junction, sometimes marked and sometimes not, sends climbers off the valley trail onto a steep, switchback-free boot path that claws straight up the forested hillside, gaining roughly 3,400-4,000 ft in about a mile and a half of unrelenting root-and-dirt tree climbing with no water and no easy grades. Parties widely describe this as the crux of the whole approach.

The boot path breaks out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft into meadows, slabs and often snow, and a rising traverse north-northeast leads to a broad saddle at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. Camp is typically just below it in Terror Creek Basin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing below the peak's south side; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
A bergschrund and a moat at the base that open through the season
Compact rock with scarce placements on the lower pitches
Loose blocks on the lower ledges
No water for the last 3,500 ft of the climb to camp
A rappel descent of 12-14 stations, with traversing raps that are rockfall-prone and stations that are hard to spot
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A BERGSCHRUND AND CLIMBS 300 FT OF GULLY TO THE TOE OF THE RIDGE, AND THAT IS AN EXACT INSTRUCTION. From camp, cross heather and snow slopes trending north-northwest, losing a little elevation to cross the outlet drainage from a small tarn just southeast of the McMillan Spires, then regain ground on slabs and snow up to the edge of the Terror Glacier. LEAVE THE GLACIER AT THE BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END OF THE PEAK and climb roughly 300 FT OF GULLY to reach the toe of the west ridge, where the roped climbing begins.

SO THE SCHRUND IS THE MARKER AND THE 300 FT IS THE MEASURE. The schrund and the moat where snow meets rock are the variable part; they open through the season and the crossing is easiest with continuous snow early. A party that has climbed a short gully and reached the toe of a ridge is at the base; a party still on ice has not started.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE SOUTH FACE, WHICH STARTS OFF THE SAME GLACIER AND IS THE COMMONEST CONFUSION HERE: the SOUTH FACE starts at the LOWER-LEFT CORNER of the south face WHERE A SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS MEETS THE GLACIER. This route starts at the WEST END of the peak, at a schrund, and goes UP A GULLY FIRST. If you are roping up at a buttress toe that touches the ice directly, with no gully above you, you are on the South Face.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: the first pitches work through corner systems and LICHEN-COVERED LEDGES on compact rock where placements are scarce. Above them the line gains the crest itself and the rock quality improves steadily, described as extremely good on the crest. Total climbing above the schrund is about 1,300 ft in 14 pitches. If the rock is good from the first pitch, you are not on the lower corners of this route.

A HOUSEKEEPING RULE FROM THE ROUTE'S OWN PRACTICE: loose blocks sit on the lower ledges and the standard practice is to clear them deliberately once the second is out of the fall line rather than leave them for a following party.

approach_variants.name: Summit road, down the grassy ledges under the powerlines
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Mount Erie summit road (Ray Auld Memorial Drive, off Heart Lake Road just past the Lake Erie Grocery) and park at the LAST parking area before the summit, at a sharp left-hand turn of more than 90 degrees. It holds about six cars; if it is full, park at the upper lot and walk down, under five minutes.

From the pullout, contour downward and westward along grassy ledges and short rock steps. A short section through woods and then under the powerlines brings you out on top of a cliff looking over Lake Erie and the strait.

A low third-class ramp then descends to the wall. Some parties rappel in from trees or scramble exposed ground to hang topropes; walking the ramp to the base and leading the well-bolted routes is the normal way.
approach_variants.season: Year-round; Mount Erie is open all year with no current raptor closure
hazards: Exposed contouring above a cliff top on the way in
Third-class ramp descent to the base
Small parking area — do not leave valuables in the car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At the bottom of the third-class ramp, turn LEFT for the lower tier of the wall.

Intimidator starts at the LOWEST POINT of the whole wall — that is the marker, and it is unambiguous underfoot: if the ground continues to drop away beside you, keep walking down.

The lower tier holds False Impressions, Lethal Weapon, Intimidator and Terminator. If you have scrambled up two distinct blocky fourth-class steps heading south you have gone up onto the upper tier, which is Tindall's Terror and Scarface.

approach_variants.name: Iron Cap Lake basin to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: However you reach it, the last of the walking is cross-country over open talus, heather benches and scree above the lake basin. Route-finding is the crux of the approach rather than any move on it: the ground is unmarked and lightly cairned, the footing is loose rock and dirt with occasional steep heather, and visibility-dependent cliff bands will stop a poorly chosen line. Water is scarce once you leave the valley floor, so tank up before the final push.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Loose dirt over rock on the upper slopes
Steep heather with poor runout
Cliff bands on the east side that will stop a badly chosen line
Snow lingering into early July on north-facing ground
No water above the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling begins on rock ledges above the outlet of Iron Cap Lake. Cross the outlet stream and start working upward to the SOUTHEAST on a series of ledges — the change from vegetated, dirt-over-rock ground to continuous clean ledges is the tell that you are on the route, and the rock here is genuinely solid, unlike everything below it. The line curves around the nose of the north ridge rather than attacking the summit block head-on. Higher, a short third-class downclimb drops into a notch, which reads as a dead end and is not one: beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, taking you across without sidehilling, and meets the broad north ridge. From there easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the true summit. Losing that ramp is the way parties end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands, so note the line as you go and retrace it exactly on the way down.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the railway. Cross the active tracks, bear left to the trail, take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Iron Horse sits in the tight cluster with Sagittarius and Numbah Ten and shares an anchor with Sagittarius.

The reliable marker is its neighbour: Numbah Ten is the BOLTED dihedral immediately LEFT of Iron Horse, and the obvious groove at the base of that dihedral belongs to Numbah Ten and Amandla, not to this. Step right off that groove.

Japanese Gardens is further right again, starting midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla.

wa_iron_peak_teanaway_scramble.approach: Start from the De Roux Creek Campground trailhead (~3,800 ft) at the end of Forest Road 9737 in the North Fork Teanaway drainage. Pick up the Iron Peak Trail, USFS Trail No. 1399, which climbs immediately and steeply alongside an unnamed creek on climbers-left — this creek is audible for roughly the first half of the hike and is your only reliable water source, since the trail rides a rib between two drainages that stay out of reach the rest of the way; tank up here, especially on hot summer days when this south-facing trail gets exposed and dry. The trail switchbacks up through forest, crosses the small creek at about 1/8 mile, then keeps climbing along the ridge toward Eldorado Creek and Eldorado Pass. Around the halfway point the trail crosses onto the ridge crest proper; tread gets rockier and uneven here, with some short, tight switchbacks. Continue to a broad saddle at roughly 6,100 ft (about 3 miles in, ~2,300-2,700 ft of gain from the trailhead), where the maintained trail fades and a well-worn boot/climbers' path takes over. From the saddle, leave the Eldorado Creek/Beverly Turnpike trail junctions behind and head south-southeast along the open ridge — this is Iron Peak's north ridge, so you climb it heading SOUTH (the higher summit a short distance north-northwest is Teanaway Peak) for about 0.7 mile of class 1-2 hiking/scrambling over a boot path with a few short rock patches near the top, gaining the last few hundred feet to the 6,510 ft summit. No technical climbing is required, but the upper ridge has some loose rock and mild exposure on the west (Teanaway River) side — stay on or east of the crest.

approach_variants.name: Iron Peak Trail #1399 to Eldorado Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead on the forest road just past the campground, Trail #1399 pitches up the moment it leaves the lot — there is no flat warm-up — with a creek audible through the trees on the left for the first few hundred yards. Cross that creek early and carry what water you need, because the trail then rides a rib between two drainages and the water goes out of reach and stays there. Switchbacks climb a south-facing forested slope, tightening and turning rocky as the trees thin, and bump over a minor ridge where the Eldorado Creek drainage becomes audible below to the east. The tread then works up the ridge above that drainage at a steady moderate grade to a broad open saddle where the maintained trail fades out.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October. Snow lies across the upper slopes into late June and can bury the tread on the last open stretch below the saddle.
hazards: The maintained trail carries on over the saddle and descends the far side — following tread instead of leaving it puts you in the wrong drainage
The only water is the creek in the first eighth of a mile; the rest is dry and the south-facing slope bakes in the afternoon
Lingering snow on the open crest into early summer, which hides the boot path
Loose rock and mild exposure on the west side of the upper crest
The scree slopes falling away west are steeper and looser than they appear from above
approach_variants.baseFinding: AT THE SADDLE THE PEAK IS TO THE SOUTH, AND THE HIGHER SUMMIT TO THE NORTH IS THE NEIGHBOUR. This is the one thing to get right here, because the ridge you walk is called the north ridge and the direction you walk it is south — the two are easy to conflate. Eldorado Pass is the broad open saddle where the maintained trail stops being useful; from it, this peak lies roughly half a mile south-southeast, and the noticeably higher summit a short distance north-northwest is Teanaway Peak. The terrain settles it even if the compass does not: the way to this summit is a simple open ridge walk on a climbers' trail, on low brush and rock with the whole line visible ahead. The neighbour's route immediately traverses around the east side and climbs gullies, so if you are sidehilling east into broken ground within a few minutes of leaving the saddle, you have turned the wrong way. The other failure is not turning at all — the maintained trail continues over the saddle and descends the far side toward the creek trail below, so a party following tread ends up in the valley rather than on either peak.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Trail, the PCT junction and the Old Snowy to Ives col
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Snowgrass trailhead, also called Berry Patch, at about 4,600 ft, reached by forest road off the highway west of Packwood. Follow Snowgrass Trail #96 south then east through dense forest; it drops slightly to cross Goat Creek on a plank crossing around the 2-mile mark, which is the only real water crossing and a reliable source. Climb through subalpine forest and meadow to Lower and then Upper Snowgrass Flat at roughly 6,400 ft, about 4 miles in — a broad wildflower meadow, closed to camping, with small creeks, the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue a further 0.3 to 0.5 mile to the PCT junction, follow the PCT north to about 6,700 ft, then leave it and head off-trail northeast, ascending talus and scree with no defined tread and only occasional cairns, toward the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak. The talus is unconsolidated and shifts underfoot. Snowfields linger on the approach slopes and in the col well into July — this basin can hold 25 to 40 ft of winter snowpack — so an axe is worth carrying for early and mid-season attempts.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul through mid-Sep, once the crest and shaded gullies have melted out
hazards: Loose, unconsolidated talus and scree with higher consequence on the descent
Chossy volcanic andesite on the summit south face
An exposed narrow ledge traverse below the summit, reached by downclimbing
Lingering snowfields and a moat crossing near the col into July
Off-trail route-finding with no maintained summit path
Exposure to afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN OLD SNOWY AND IVES IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU GET TO IT BY LEAVING A TRAIL, NOT BY FOLLOWING ONE.

Leave the PCT north of the Snowgrass Trail junction, at roughly 6,700 ft, and go off-trail NORTHEAST up talus. There is no tread. Occasional cairns are the only marks. If you are still on maintained trail you have not started the route.

YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE COL BECAUSE YOU ARE BETWEEN TWO PEAKS at about 7,250 ft — Old Snowy behind you, Ives ahead. A high point on one side only is not the col.

THE BUMP IS THE TRAP AND IT IS COUNTABLE: from the col the ridge crosses a ROUNDED INTERMEDIATE HIGH POINT before you reach the true summit block. THAT BUMP IS NOT THE SUMMIT. If you have not passed one rounded bump, you have not reached the summit block, whatever the ground in front of you looks like.

THE BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE IS A NOTCH BETWEEN TWO ROCK OUTCROPS, reached by a boot path up scree. And here is the test that settles it beyond doubt, because it is the opposite of what you expect at a summit block: ABOVE THE NOTCH IS A SHORT CLIFF BAND, AND THE ROUTE GOES DOWN FIRST. You downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face, then scramble about 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock to easy ground and the summit.

SO: IF THE LINE IN FRONT OF YOU ONLY GOES UP, YOU ARE AT THE WRONG NOTCH. Having to lose a little height at the notch is the confirmation.

DESCENT FINDING WORTH MAKING BEFORE YOU START: dropping straight southwest off the col into the basin is faster and is the loosest ground on the mountain. Traversing back over Old Snowy and down its established south-ridge path avoids the worst of it.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

bivy.name: Lower Snowgrass Flat / Lily Basin Trail (#86) junction

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene talus to the left side of the buttress
approach_variants.notes: Maintained trail to Lake Serene, then the short unofficial path around the right-hand (west) side of the lake, down granite slabs to the talus fan and up the talus to the wall. Fill water at the lake; there is none above it. In early summer the lakeside traverse crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow. With haul bags and a multi-day load this takes considerably longer than the mileage implies, and the last of it is steepening mossy slab and brush that parties commonly rope up for before they reach clean rock.
approach_variants.season: Late July to early September
hazards: Natural rockfall off North Index and out of the cleft between this buttress and Middle Index
Seasonal waterfalls running the lower pitches in spring and early summer
Loose and vegetated rock at the base and below the sixth pitch
Wet granite slabs on the lakeside traverse
A sustained overhanging wall with no walk-off
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is on the LEFT side of the buttress, about a hundred yards left of the Doorish line, in a crack system that runs continuously from the ground. That continuity is the tell — the neighbouring weaknesses on this side peter out within a couple of hundred feet, so if the crack you are looking at closes above you, you are not on it. Use the Doorish line as your reference and count leftward from it rather than trying to identify the start in isolation; from the talus the whole left flank looks alike. Do not sort gear at the foot of the wall: the base is a rockfall alley fed by North Index above and by the deep cleft between this buttress and Middle Index, so stay low near the lake to rack up and keep time directly beneath the face as short as you can. Below the clean granite is a band of steepening mossy slab and brush that is part of the approach rather than part of the route, and roping up for it is normal rather than timid.

approach_variants.name: Jerry Lakes and the bench below the east glacier
approach_variants.notes: The East Ridge is most often met as a descent, because parties who climb the North Ridge come over the summit and go down this way, but it is the better of the two to climb and it is reached from the opposite side of the mountain. Access is from the south: the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR 20 at about 1,900 ft, a ford of Canyon Creek, then the McMillan Park and Jackita Ridge trail gaining some 3,400 ft in four miles to the Crater Mountain trail, up past Crater Lake, and off-trail somewhere between 6,400 and 6,700 ft to a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, drop across the Jerry Glacier and down into the Jerry Lakes basin, where nearly everyone camps. Reckon on three days minimum, and note that the summit day begins by losing several hundred feet into the next basin north before any climbing starts. The ridge itself runs about 1,400 to 1,600 ft from its base up to roughly 8,600 ft, where it dies into the Southeast Ridge and a single common crest carries on to the top. Parties disagree sharply about the rock: the lower third is good blocky class three and four, the upper third is fractured and loose, and the published class four understates the ground — a recent party found three short pitches of fifth class, including a wildly exposed 5.0 step in the middle of the crest, and made one rappel lower down off existing tat. There is no other fixed gear, so carry slings and cord.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to mid-September
hazards: Fractured, loose rock on the upper third with almost nothing dependable to protect it
Sustained exposure along the whole crest, with a thousand feet of air below the middle section
The line strays off the crest to the north in the middle third, which is where parties lose it in descent
Only one existing anchor on the route, so every other rappel is one you build and leave
Collapsing snow fingers where the snowfield meets the toe of the east glacier
Long cross-country approach with no trail for the final miles, and 800 ft to regain on the way home
Very remote, with a difficult retreat from anywhere on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Jack's east and southeast ridges hold a small pocket glacier between them like a bay, and finding this route is entirely a matter of working out which side of that bay you are on. The Southeast Ridge is the bay's right-hand edge, the East Ridge its left, and the two merge at about 8,600 ft. From the Jerry Lakes camp the day starts by dropping several hundred feet into the basin to the north, then climbing the southeast arm to a level bench at roughly 7,000 to 7,200 ft. That bench is where the mountain's two commonly climbed routes part company, and the decision there is a single either-or. Traverse LEFT and west on scree under the south face and you are on the standard South Face route, whose landmarks are unmistakable once you start seeing them: a small snowfield, then a larger one likened to a fish or a lobster claw, a refrigerator-sized boulder with rope slung round its middle, a stream that only runs in the afternoon, and a short class four step into a hidden chimney. If you are hunting for a slung boulder, you are on the wrong route. Traverse RIGHT and north instead, onto the snowfield beneath the pocket glacier, and a few hundred feet of scrambling gains the crest proper. The confirmation is the view over the back. There is a notch at about 7,000 ft on this ridge, and from it the ground falls away onto a big broken glacier dropping north toward Devils Creek; if you can see that, you are on the East Ridge and not the Southeast. The second check is the rock, which low down is good blocky class three and four, where the South Face is loose almost from the start. One trap worth knowing: there are two cols at about 7,200 ft on this trip, the Crater Mountain saddle on the approach and this bench, and they lie four miles apart, so an altimeter alone will not tell you which one you are standing on.

approach_variants.name: East Bank Trail on foot from milepost 138, leaving it at May Creek
approach_variants.notes: Park at the East Bank Trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. The trail drops immediately to the bridge over Ruby Creek and then runs north along Ross Lake, mostly flat and fast, to the May Creek camp. This is the whole of the easy walking. At May Creek leave the trail and climb west to north-west, staying loosely between the creeks on the mountain's west side. Cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails rather than climbed; snow generally begins around 4,800 to 5,000 ft. Three miles or so of that work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice. Strong parties carry a second camp onto the upper glacier near 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably.
approach_variants.season: Late May through July while the headwall is still a snow climb; the highway gate closes the season at both ends
hazards: steep brushy timber with cliff bands from about 3,200 ft, far worse to reverse than to ascend
crevasses on the Nohokomeen Glacier, thinly bridged late in the season
sustained steep snow on the headwall itself, with a long runout onto the glacier below
rockfall and icefall off the wall once the sun reaches it
a two to four day commitment with no quick way off the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TIMBER BELT IS THE NAVIGATION, THE GLACIER TOE IS THE ARRIVAL. Leaving May Creek you are looking for weaknesses, not a line: the cliff bands from about 3,200 ft up are passed on boot and game trails that thread left and right, so a section that forces you to climb rock means you have pushed into the band rather than around it. The reliable signal that you are through is underfoot rather than overhead - continuous snow starting somewhere near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and above that the timber gives out onto open ground.

THE CAMP IS A FLAT BENCH, NOT A VIEWPOINT. Just over 5,200 ft the ground levels into a flat bench directly below the toe of the ice. If you are on sloping heather with the ice still out of sight above you, keep going; if you are already on the ice you have walked past the bench.

THE HEADWALL IS ABOVE THE GLACIER, NOT AT ITS TOE. From the bench the glacier runs up in front of you at an easy angle for a long way before anything steepens. The route's steep ground is the wall at the head of that ice, directly beneath the summit. IF YOU ARE ROPING UP AND SWINGING TOOLS WITHIN MINUTES OF LEAVING CAMP, YOU ARE ON A SERAC OR A CREVASSE WALL LOW ON THE GLACIER, NOT ON THE HEADWALL. The headwall is only reached after the whole gentle bowl has been crossed and the ground ahead of you rears up as one continuous face rather than a series of rolls.

A CROSS-CHECK AT THE TOP OF THE ICE: the summit should be directly above the headwall, not off to one side. If the wall in front of you tops out on a shoulder with more mountain visible beyond it, you have drifted around the bowl.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the eastern shore, cutting out most of the trail
approach_variants.notes: The resort at the south end of Ross Lake runs a water taxi that will drop parties on the eastern shore, which removes most of the flat trail miles and turns the approach into the off-trail climb alone. It has to be booked ahead and the schedule and drop points change, so confirm directly before building a trip around it. The trade is that you are committed to a pickup time on a lake with no road out, so build slack into the plan rather than into the summit day.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the trail approach, but only once the boat service is running for the year
hazards: fixed pickup times on a lake with no road out
the same steep brushy cliff-banded timber belt above the shore
arriving late enough that the timber belt is done in the dark
crevasses on the glacier above
no reliable communication once off the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LANDING THE FIRST TASK IS TO GET ONTO THE TRAIL AND FIND MAY CREEK - the East Bank Trail runs along this shore and the departure point is the creek, not a bearing. Once you leave the trail at May Creek every marker is identical to the walk-in variant: cliff bands from around 3,200 ft passed on game trails, continuous snow near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, and the flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the toe of the ice.

THE ONE THING THE BOAT CHANGES IS YOUR MARGIN, NOT YOUR ROUTE. Parties dropped late in the day have started the timber belt in fading light, which is where the cliff bands become genuinely dangerous, because the passages through them are found by eye. If you cannot reach open ground above the bands in daylight, camp low rather than commit to the belt.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SAME: if the ground ahead of you steepens into rock rather than easing onto snow, you are in a cliff band and should traverse to find the boot track rather than force it.

approach_variants.name: Before the highway opens: the gate at milepost 134
approach_variants.notes: The highway closes each winter between the gate west of the trailhead and a second gate far to the east, and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early summer depending on the year's damage and snowpack. Parties wanting the headwall in condition have started at the closed gate and covered the road on bikes or skis to the trailhead before starting the walk in. Everything above that is unchanged, except that the snow line is far lower and the timber belt may go faster on skis than it does on foot in summer.
approach_variants.season: Late winter and early spring, before the highway is cleared, when the headwall holds its best snow
hazards: avalanche terrain through the timber belt and on the glacier approach in early season
a long road section on bike or ski before the trip proper starts
short daylight and cold, with a committing position
cornices on the upper mountain
the road gate opening date moves year to year and can strand a plan
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROAD SECTION IS NAVIGATION-FREE; THE APPROACH STILL STARTS AT MAY CREEK. Ride or ski the closed highway to the trailhead near milepost 138 and pick up the East Bank Trail there. The departure from the trail is the creek, as in summer.

WHAT CHANGES IS WHERE THE SNOW STARTS. In this window continuous snow is likely to begin well below the 4,800 to 5,000 ft line that summer parties describe, which means the cliff bands between roughly 3,200 ft and there are being crossed on snow rather than on game trails. A band that would be walked around in August may be a loaded slope in April. IF THE PASSAGE YOU WOULD NORMALLY TAKE THROUGH A BAND IS A SMOOTH, WIND-LOADED RAMP RATHER THAN A BOOT TRACK, TREAT IT AS AVALANCHE TERRAIN AND NOT AS A ROUTE.

The flat bench just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe may be buried and unrecognisable as a bench; in that case the arrival marker is the change of angle where the ground stops climbing and the ice begins running away ahead of you toward the wall.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake to May Creek and the Nohokomeen Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A genuinely remote three-day outing on a mountain that sees almost no traffic, and the approach is the hard part of it. Parties reach May Creek Camp on the east shore of Ross Lake at about 1,600 ft either by walking seven or eight flat miles of the East Bank Trail from SR 20 or, far more often, by taking the resort water taxi, which removes nearly all of that. From the lake it is a few thousand feet of steep forest, and the trick is finding the open timber rather than fighting brush: parties who get it right leave the trail in open forest a couple of hundred yards from the junction, angle left of the fall line, and follow game trails through the rock bands between roughly 3,500 and 4,100 ft, where a short cliff step sometimes carries webbing left behind by earlier parties. Reaching the ridge crest around 5,000 ft, traverse to the top of the moraine, pass under the toe of the Nohokomeen Glacier and climb slabs on its left side to camp at about 6,700 ft. Some parties push on and camp higher on the glacier near 7,400 ft. The glacier above is usually straightforward and largely crack-free to its top at about 8,000 ft. Most parties climb this ridge and descend the East Ridge, which turns the trip into a traverse and puts the exit out to Jerry Lakes and the Crater Mountain trail rather than back down the timber.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to mid-September
hazards: Serac fall off the Nohokomeen Glacier onto the ground below its toe
Loose, fractured chert throughout, with little that will hold protection
Steep forest with cliff bands on the approach, far worse to descend than to climb
Wet slabs and a pitch of low fifth class where the glacier meets the ridge
Big exposure on the knife-edge crest and on the snow traverse below the summit tower
Crevasses low on the glacier, and a moat where snow meets rock late in the season
Very remote, several days from a road in any direction, with no realistic quick rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding: Nobody climbs this ridge from its toe; you meet it partway up off the Nohokomeen Glacier, and exactly where to leave the ice is unsettled, so treat the aiming points below as the frame and read the ground. Climb the glacier up its centre, passing just to the right of the large rock that stands out on the ice, and head for the crest to the LEFT of the summit tower rather than for the tower itself. The glacier runs out against rock at about 8,000 ft. The one unmistakable feature on the route is there: a hole clean through the rock, a keyhole big enough to squirm through, and that hole is how the crest is gained. Parties travelling in both directions have used it as their marker. Taken from the very top of the glacier the exit costs a pitch of wet, junky low fifth class and a scramble over greasy slabs, and the party who did it that way came away convinced an easier line onto the crest exists a little lower down, short of the glacier's top edge, so it is worth traversing under the rock and looking rather than forcing the highest weakness. Above the keyhole the confirmation is instant and unlike anything below it: a knife-edged crest of genuinely solid rock, which is rare on this mountain. If what is under your hands is fractured and rotten, you are not on the crest yet. One decoy matters. The north side's other line, the headwall, rises off the same glacier and tops out within minutes of the summit, so if the snow you are on runs straight to the top with no ridge left to travel, you are on the headwall and not this route. The North Ridge leaves the ice well below the summit and still has a long way to go: knife edge, then an exposed snow traverse south across and below the summit tower with occasional protection along the upper moat, and a final pitch of low fifth class up the East Ridge to the top at 9,066 ft.

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Canyon Creek Trailhead at about 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek and follow Trail #738 as it switchbacks hard through forest - three and a half to four thousand feet of climbing with no water on it, so fill up at the creek. Bear left at the Crater Lake trail junction and contour to the lake basin, then pick the trail back up above the lake for long, hot, exposed switchbacks with nothing to drink on them. Somewhere between 6,700 and 7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse to the gap between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak at about 7,200 ft. From that saddle the route goes downhill onto the Jerry Glacier: snow-covered and crevassed enough for a rope and crampons early, often patchy or bare late, when a slip runs further. Descend off the ice into the Jerry Lakes basin and fill water - it is the last of it before the face.

Check the Canyon Creek crossing before you commit: it has been described both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge gone, and it is the first obstacle of the trip.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Jerry Glacier crossing is reasonable and before fresh snow lands on the loose face
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the very start, which has washed out
long waterless switchbacks on both trail sections
crevasses and moats on the Jerry Glacier, worse as a bare-ice slip hazard late in the season
fire-damaged forest and unstable ground near Jerry Lakes
loose rock on the face where holds pull off freely - keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked
route-finding for the ramp and hidden chimney, which are hard to relocate on the descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FACE IS FOUND BY A SLUNG BOULDER AND A HIDDEN BREAK, NOT BY A BEARING. From the Jerry Lakes basin, traverse the heather shelf and go through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,000 to 7,200 ft. THIS SHOULDER IS THE DECISION POINT FOR THE WHOLE MOUNTAIN. For the South Face you now turn WEST and make a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, often moving in the shallow moat where old snow has pulled away from the rock.

THE POSITIVE MARKER IS A BOULDER WITH SLING MATERIAL ON IT, standing above the snow patches under the lower cliff band. The break in that band is a left-slanting ramp leading to a short class 4 step and then a hidden class 3 chimney, and IT STAYS INVISIBLE UNTIL YOU ARE ALMOST UNDERNEATH IT. Looking up from a distance and seeing no way through the band is the normal experience and is not evidence you are in the wrong place; looking up and seeing an obvious open gully is evidence that you are, because the break here is not obvious.

IF YOU ARE CLIMBING THE CREST OF THE RIDGE ITSELF RATHER THAN TRAVERSING BENEATH A FACE, YOU HAVE STAYED ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE AND ARE ON THE OTHER ROUTE. The South Face leaves the ridge at the shoulder and does not return to it until well above the cliff band, near 8,600 ft, where a band of scree beside a snow patch delivers you back onto the crest.

A CROSS-CHECK ABOVE THE BAND: 400 to 500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges linked by harder steps, then easier ground. Sustained hard climbing straight off the chimney means you have taken the wrong line through the band.

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.notes: The approach is identical as far as the Jerry Lakes basin and then forks on where you sleep. Camping at the lakes near 6,400 ft is the shorter day in and keeps water at the tent. Continuing over the notch just south of the lakes and dropping about six hundred feet into Crater Creek Basin puts camp in meadows near 6,000 ft north-west of Point 7,001 - a longer day in with a re-ascent at the end, but it starts summit day already on the right side of the notch and out of the wind.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows camp holds water later into the season than snow patches by the lakes
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of Crater Creek Basin if you camp low
no water above the lakes or the meadows
exposed camps with weather coming over the crest
loose ground on the traverse under the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER CAMP YOU USE, THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE SAME PLACE: THE LEVEL SHOULDER ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE NEAR 7,000 TO 7,200 FT. From the lakes you reach it by crossing the notch south of the lakes and climbing back out of Crater Creek Basin; from the meadows camp you climb straight to it.

THE SHOULDER IS RECOGNISED BY BEING LEVEL. The ridge relents here into a flat step before it rears up again, and the ground to the west opens into the scree traverse under the face. If you are still climbing steadily with no let-up, you are below it.

FROM THE SHOULDER THE SOUTH FACE GOES WEST AND DOWN-SLOPE OF THE CREST, ON SCREE AND DIRT, TOWARD SNOW PATCHES AND A SLUNG BOULDER UNDER A CONTINUOUS CLIFF BAND. If you find yourself scrambling directly up the crest above the shoulder you are on the Southeast Ridge line instead - a legitimate route, but not this one, and it has no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on it.

bivy.name: Crater Creek Meadows bench
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard staging point for the south face, on a heather bench above Crater Creek northwest of point 7001. Reached in roughly eight hours and eleven miles from the car, after the Jerry Glacier traverse and the drop into Crater Creek Basin. Parties choose it over Jerry Lakes specifically because it shortens the summit day onto the face. Terrain gives moderate wind shelter. Permit status is not confirmed for this basin — check the zone before you go.
bivy.water: Crater Creek, about 200 ft below camp
bivy.capacity: small — comfortable for a party of two

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, a grassy boulder-strewn bowl with several separate sites; the best of them sits by the small lake between the two large ones. Snow-free by mid-August. It is the more pleasant camp of the two and the obvious stop if you arrive late, but it leaves a longer traverse to the face on summit day. Open bowl, so afternoon wind. Fire-scarred forest on the approach into the basin. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: four alpine lakes
bivy.capacity: multiple parties across the basin

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes Peak south saddle
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp — on record only as an unplanned night out, sat through in a bivy sack and an emergency blanket with little wind protection and a cold, sleepless result. Worth knowing exists if a party is caught on the ridge between the lakes and the Crater Mountain saddle, and worth planning not to use.
bivy.water: none at the saddle

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes / Crater Creek Meadows camp

approach_variants.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, Crater Lake, and the traverse over the Jerry Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the South Face as far as camp. From the Canyon Creek Trailhead near 1,900 ft, cross Canyon Creek - reported both as a log-and-plank crossing and as a ford with the bridge destroyed, so look at it before you commit - and grind up Trail #738's switchbacks through forest to the Crater Lake trail junction. Carry water from the creek; the hillside above has none. Continue past Crater Lake and up long exposed switchbacks, then leave the tread between about 6,700 and 7,200 ft and traverse to the saddle between Crater Mountain's summit and its east peak near 7,200 ft. Descend steep snow and the crevassed Jerry Glacier, cross the saddle above Jerry Lakes, and camp at the lakes near 6,400 ft or in the Crater Creek meadows near 6,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, for dry rock on the crest and a crossable Jerry Glacier
hazards: the Canyon Creek crossing at the start
crevasses and steep neve on the Jerry Glacier both ways
loose blocks on the crest - the rock on this mountain pulls off freely
sustained exposure with rappels needed to reverse the steps
a long committing position with a multi-hour retreat to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS THE CREST, AND THE TEST IS THAT YOU NEVER LEAVE IT. From camp climb to the level step on the southeast ridge at about 7,000 to 7,200 ft. That step is the start: the ridge above it is the route, and everything you climb from there should have ground falling away on BOTH sides of you.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS HERE, BECAUSE THE WRONG TURN IS THE POPULAR ONE. From the same shoulder the South Face route turns WEST and makes a rising traverse on scree and dirt beneath the face, aiming for snow patches and a boulder with slings on it under a cliff band. IF YOU ARE WALKING SIDEWAYS ON SCREE WITH A WALL ABOVE YOU AND YOUR FEET IN A MOAT, YOU HAVE JOINED THE SOUTH FACE AND LEFT THIS ROUTE BEHIND. There is no slung boulder and no hidden chimney on the Direct.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THE SHAPE OF THE GROUND UNDER YOUR HANDS: the crest gives continuous scrambling with occasional steps rather than a traverse across a face, and the exposure is symmetrical. When the crest throws up a step you cannot scramble, the answer is a short pitch on the crest or a brief turn on its flank, not a traverse that takes you a rope length or more away from it.

A CROSS-CHECK HIGH ON THE ROUTE: near 8,600 ft the South Face rejoins the crest by way of a scree band beside a snow patch. If you are already on the crest well below that and stay on it, you and a South Face party will meet there having climbed two different mountains' worth of ground.

approach_variants.name: Two camps at the end of the same approach: Jerry Lakes or Crater Creek Meadows
approach_variants.notes: The fork is only about where you sleep. The lakes near 6,400 ft are the shorter day in with water at the tent. Crossing the notch just south of the lakes and dropping into Crater Creek Basin to camp in the meadows near 6,000 ft costs a descent and a re-ascent but starts summit day on the correct side of the notch, directly under the shoulder where the ridge is gained.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the meadows hold running water later than the snow patches above the lakes
hazards: a six hundred foot re-ascent out of the basin from the meadows camp
no water above the lakes or meadows
wind-exposed camps
loose ground on the climb back to the shoulder
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BOTH CAMPS FEED THE SAME STARTING POINT - THE LEVEL STEP ON THE SOUTHEAST RIDGE BETWEEN ABOUT 7,000 AND 7,200 FT. From the lakes, cross the notch to the south and climb out of Crater Creek Basin to it; from the meadows, climb straight up to it.

RECOGNISE THE STEP BY THE GROUND GOING FLAT. The ridge eases into a level shoulder before rearing up again, and that flat is where the climbing starts. If the angle has not relented, you are still below it.

FROM THERE, STAY ON THE CREST. The moment the ground under you becomes a sidehill traverse on scree rather than a ridge with air on both sides, you have drifted onto the South Face's line beneath the cliff band. Turn back to the crest rather than continuing, because the two routes do not rejoin until near 8,600 ft.

approach_variants.name: The old Little Jack trail, taken as the rightmost branch of the junction on the East Bank Trail
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Panther Creek and East Bank trailhead near milepost 138 at about 1,800 ft. Walk the East Bank Trail west for a little over two miles to a junction where several ways meet, and take the RIGHTMOST branch - this is the old Little Jack trail, cut a century ago to move pack animals up to the mountain's meadows, and it is neither signed nor maintained to the standard of the trail you have just left. It climbs steadily to Little Jack at about 6,745 ft, roughly four thousand eight hundred feet of gain from the junction. Water on the ridge is scarce and seasonal, so carry from low down rather than counting on the meadows.

This is the shortest line to the peak, and it is short in miles rather than in effort: the traverse from Little Jack to Jack is the part that takes the stamina.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the ridge is clear of snow and while the meadow water sources still run
hazards: an unmaintained century-old pack trail that is easy to lose in the meadows
very little water once you leave the lake shore, and none reliable on the crest
a long exposed traverse between Little Jack and Jack with no bail-out
loose rock on Jack's ridge, and holds that pull
the descent reverses the whole traverse, so turnaround discipline matters more than usual here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE BRANCHES AT THE JUNCTION - THAT IS THE ONE NAVIGATION DECISION THE APPROACH ASKS OF YOU. Several ways meet a little over two miles along the East Bank Trail, and the Little Jack trail is the rightmost of them. A branch that keeps running level along the lake shore is the East Bank Trail continuing; a branch that starts climbing hard and does not stop is the one you want. IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING FLAT GROUND HALF AN HOUR PAST THE JUNCTION, YOU TOOK THE WRONG BRANCH.

LITTLE JACK IS A SUMMIT AND IT IS NOT YOUR SUMMIT. The trail tops out on an open, meadowy high point at about 6,745 ft that was grazed rather than climbed - broad, grassy, and unmistakably the end of a graded pack trail. Reaching it means the trail's work is done, and everything beyond is cross-country on the crest.

FROM LITTLE JACK, FOLLOW THE CREST NORTH TO THE NOTCH, THEN TRAVERSE ACROSS TO THE FOOT OF JACK'S SOUTHWEST RIDGE. The base you are looking for is where that traverse ends against the mountain proper and the ridge above you rises unbroken toward the summit. IF THE GROUND AHEAD OF YOU IS STILL ROLLING CREST WITH KNOLLS ON IT, YOU ARE BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS AND NOT YET AT THE BASE; if you can see glacier ice below you on the far side, you have crossed too far around the mountain and are looking at the northern flank.

THE OTHER USEFUL CHECK IS UNDERFOOT: the pack trail is graded and evenly cut, the crest beyond Little Jack is not. If you are still on constructed tread, you have not yet left Little Jack behind.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, into town, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the railway. Cross the tracks — active line, several trains a day — bear left to the trail and then take the RIGHT branch running along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes from the car.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
Drifting right into Stern Farmer at the start
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Position it between two known things: this route starts roughly MIDWAY between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla. Godzilla is the corner system immediately right of the obvious City Park crack; Princely Ambitions starts straight off the trail.

The start itself is a short LEFT-facing dihedral with a 5.10a section, and the line then trends right and comes back left into a wide crack.

Negative marker that matters: from this same start you can trend right and stay right into Stern Farmer, a 5.12 corner. Drifting right and not coming back left puts you on a testpiece two number grades harder. Sagittarius is the line just LEFT of this one.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left onto the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same start as the full Japanese Gardens: roughly midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla, beginning in a short left-facing dihedral at about 5.10a, then trending right and back left into a wide crack, stopping at the first anchor.

The error to avoid is the same one: trending right out of the start and staying right leads into Stern Farmer, a 5.12 corner. Sagittarius is the neighbouring line to the LEFT.

approach_variants.name: Down into the avalanche moat before the couloir narrows, then the left-hand rib
approach_variants.notes:
A quick approach directly from the car, which is the only quick thing about this route. From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, descend to and cross the Cascade River, cross the terminal moraine, and gain the couloir apron.

The start is unusual and it is the route's signature: you DOWNCLIMB INTO AN AVALANCHE MOAT to gain the rock, around 4,400 ft, on sketchy lichen-covered dirty slabs.

What follows is honest about itself — initial fourth class into dense vertical tree-root climbing, a slabby horizontal gully traverse of about 60 ft at 5.5 with minimal protection, steep heather taken by finger-pressing rather than by holds, and then roughly 700 ft of genuinely good 5.6 rock leading toward a bivy site near the glacier, two pitches below the summit.

Two starts exist: the original 1951 line, faster but with a scary 5.7 pitch, and a 1957 variation that starts lower and adds about 500 ft on more logical terrain to avoid it.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late summer, July and August, once the rib is snow-free enough to climb but before it goes fully dry and looser
hazards: Extensive loose rock and lichen-slick slabs from the very first moves
Vegetation-dependent, largely unprotectable terrain — the climbing is real but the protection often is not
Icefall and rockfall from the hanging glaciers 5,000 ft above the route
Rockfall on the shared East Ridge and Sill Glacier descent
A descent whose steep heather section is repeatedly named as the most dangerous part of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU GO DOWN TO GET ON. That is the base finding and it is unlike anything else on this side of the mountain: from the moraine you DOWNCLIMB INTO AN AVALANCHE MOAT to reach the rock, at roughly 4,400 ft. If you are stepping up onto rock rather than down into a gap, you have not found the start.

THE COUNTING TEST IS THE COULOIR'S SHAPE, AND IT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE VARIATION THAT SHARES ITS NAME: LEAVE THE CASCADE-JOHANNESBURG COULOIR BEFORE IT NARROWS. The 1957 variation gains rock HIGHER, close to where the couloir visibly pinches down. IF YOU HAVE CLIMBED THE COULOIR UNTIL IT CONSTRICTS, YOU HAVE PASSED THIS ROUTE'S START.

THEN COUNT THE RIBS, BECAUSE THERE ARE TWO AND THEY ALMOST TOUCH DOWN LOW: two parallel ribs jut off the same buttress. THE 1951 ROUTE TAKES THE LEFT RIB. The 1957 route takes the more prominent RIGHT one. They nearly intersect at the bottom and only diverge as you gain height, which is exactly why the choice has to be made deliberately rather than by following the ground.

THE FIRST-MOVE TEST IS VEGETATION, AND HERE IT IS THE POSITIVE SIGN RATHER THAN THE WARNING: fourth-class ground leads straight into DENSE VERTICAL TREE-ROOT CLIMBING. If you are on clean rock from the start you are not on this rib — the 1963 Northeast Ridge, one line over, is explicitly the route with no bush climbing on it.

AND IF YOU ARE STILL IN SNOW AT THE TOP, you climbed the couloir itself — the 1938 original — which finishes at the Cascade-Johannesburg col and never touches either rib.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel from the top/Pitch 8 area down to its base, joining the established descent line.
rappel_detail.anchor: Established bolted/chain anchor at base of Pitch 8
hazards: One party who rappelled from the true top judged there were too many places for the rope to hang up to risk pulling it in one go from here
rappel_detail.station: Rappel the climbing line down to the point where the descent leaves it - the bottom of pitch 8 in the current 8-pitch numbering, also commonly called the bottom of pitch 6 (the same place; the count differs by whether the traverse pitches are numbered). A 70 m rope links the two rappels above it into one full-stretch 35 m shot and skips the semi-hanging belay; a 60 m needs both stations.

rappel_detail.notes: First of five further rappels to the ground; use every anchor station with a 60m rope.
hazards: Rappelling the fall line instead of traversing right lands you on the wrong ground; multiple parties report going too far left here and having to swing back
One party went so far wrong they considered simul-rappelling because the rock they were on looked very loose
rappel_detail.station: The rappel route leaves the climb here and this is the station people get wrong. From the anchor, go climber's RIGHT along the base of the wall, following a ramp and hugging the wall for about 30 m - not straight down. The published test is blunt: if your body is not touching the wall, you are not far right enough. The anchor is in a narrow gully on the far climber's right, under a small tree.

rappel_detail.notes: Continuing down; a 70m rope can link some of these into fewer, longer raps.
hazards: Having been told to go hard right on the rappel above, parties overcorrect and go too far right on this one
rappel_detail.station: This one is straight down the fall line, close to a full-length rappel. Look for the anchor to climber's LEFT as you come down.

rappel_detail.notes: Mid-sequence rappel.
hazards: This is the station named in the route description as somewhat hidden, and the tree anchor to its left is an active decoy that parties have rappelled to
A single 60 m rope reaches this station from the one above, but only if you land in the right gully; do not try to skip it
rappel_detail.station: The hidden anchor, and the one the route page itself flags. It is NOT straight down: go climber's right over a slight rib into the next gully. Look over the rocky spine for a blue-green gully; the station sits beneath a band of blue-green rock forming the gully wall. There is a big tree down and to the LEFT with a sling on it - that is the wrong gully and the wrong anchor.

rappel_detail.pull: The route description warns specifically to take care pulling ropes in the gully because of the volume of loose rock; stand out of the fall line and expect debris to come with the rope.
rappel_detail.notes: Mid-sequence rappel.
hazards: Parties report not seeing this anchor until they are on it, so do not assume you have missed it and keep going
The gully is loaded with loose rock and dirt - one party was showered with gravel while rappelling and pulling, and reported dodging larger blocks
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the gully. The final station sits on a rock directly below the end of the blue-green gully.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel to the ground.
hazards: A 60 m only just reaches on the last two rappels of this sequence
Loose rock in the gully above continues to be the hazard until you are out of the fall line
rappel_detail.station: The last station is at the end of the gully, on the climber's right. This rappel trends LEFT, following water-cleaned rock out of the gully to the ground, landing at a steep trail that returns to the start of the climb in a few minutes.

wa_junior_s_farm.rappel_count_note: Seven or more rappels on a 60 m rope (one fewer on a 70 m): first down the climbing line to where the descent diverges, then five on a dedicated rappel route to the ground. A single 60 m rope does the whole thing PROVIDED you use every anchor station - below the divergence you must not skip anchors or try to link rappels on a 60 or a 70, and parties confirm the last two are only just within reach of a 60. A 70 m buys exactly one thing: it links the top two rappels into a single rope-stretching 35 m shot and skips a semi-hanging belay. It does not let you skip anything lower. Note a numbering discrepancy that is not a disagreement about the route: the current numbering puts the divergence at the bottom of pitch 8 while an older numbering says the bottom of pitch 6 - the same spot, counted with and without the traverse pitches. A walk-off exists from the top of pitch 4 by way of a fixed line, but is not recommended in climbing shoes.

approach_variants.name: Denny Creek to Melakwa Lake and the south ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Denny Creek trailhead (about 2,280 ft) via Forest Road 58 off I-90 exit 47. Take Denny Creek Trail #1014 up the valley. At roughly 1.2-1.3 miles it crosses Denny Creek at the Slippery Slab — smooth cascading bedrock and pools, and the last easy reliable water before the climb steepens.

Beyond the slab the trail climbs through forest, crosses talus, and switchbacks to Hemlock Pass around 3.8 miles and 4,600 ft, where it meets the Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 junction. Bear toward Melakwa Lake and descend gently about half a mile to the lake at roughly 4,550 ft — good campsites, and the last dependable water before the summit push.
