From the lake, cross the outlet stream and pick up the well-defined but unmaintained climbers' bootpack on the ridge to the west (your left as you look up the lake). It climbs steeply through subalpine trees, heather and talus onto Kaleetan Knoll, Point 5,700.

The path then goes OVER that first prominence and drops several hundred feet down its west side into a rocky, west-facing talus bowl below the saddle separating Point 5,700 from Kaleetan's south ridge. Cairns mark that crossing. There is no continuous tread here, and the cairns are the first thing to disappear in cloud or early-season snow.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the northwest-facing finish holds snow into June or July
hazards: loose, exfoliating rock throughout the summit gully and upper ridge
snow lingering on the northwest-facing finish into June or July - trip reports carry axe and light traction
no continuous trail on the talus traverse below the saddle - cairn-following only, and useless in cloud
increasing exposure near the top
no dependable water above Melakwa Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
After the talus crossing you regain the ridge at the saddle and follow the boot path north, just below or along the crest, for a few hundred yards. The start of the actual scrambling is an obvious gully and ledge system splitting Kaleetan's south face — roughly 400-600 vertical feet of class 2-3 on loose, exfoliating rock, exiting onto a short summit ridge with one more brief scramble to the true summit at 6,259 ft.

The test at the foot of it: you should be able to look up the whole length of the gully and see it exit onto ridge crest, not run out into more face. A gully that closes down against the wall above is not the one.

Two negative markers. If you are still descending, or still crossing talus with the ridge above and to your right, you have not yet regained the saddle and are too early — the boot path drops before it climbs. And if you began scrambling before you dropped off the west side of Point 5,700, you are on the wrong prominence; the knoll is a bump to be crossed, not the peak.

In cloud, the sequence to hold onto is: lake outlet, up to the knoll, OVER it and DOWN its west side, across the talus on cairns, regain the ridge at the saddle, then north a few hundred yards to the gully.

wa_kangaroo_temple_north_face.comms: Cell service unreliable to absent at Washington Pass; expect no signal on approach and peak. Satellite communicator (Garmin InReach, SPOT) recommended for solo climbers or small parties.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout, the boulder-field path to Kangaroo Pass, then the traverse below Wallaby's slabs to the high notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start from the Hairpin turnout on SR-20 at about 5,150 ft, roughly a mile east of Washington Pass. From the large pullout, pick up the climber's trail that switchbacks up into the valley to the southeast; it is faint and boulder-hopping at first through talus and sandy gullies, with cairns, and the tread firms up after the first quarter mile, passing a small dried-up tarn. STAY ALONG THE RIGHT-HAND, WEST, EDGE OF THE TIMBER as you gain the valley headwall.

This path gains roughly 1,500 ft over about 1.5 miles to Kangaroo Pass, a broad view-filled saddle that is the key approach landmark; budget 1-1.5 hours from the car. No reliable water on this stretch. Car-to-base is typically 1.5-2.5 hours.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Route-finding where the boulder-field tread disappears and reappears repeatedly before the pass
Loose talus and scree underfoot throughout
Early-season snow or ice in the approach gully, warranting an ice axe
A 50 m rope barely reaches the second rappel station; the descent line goes over a sharp lip onto vertical face
Queues at the rap stations; this is a popular club route and weekend backups are common
No reliable water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT KANGAROO PASS, DO NOT DROP STRAIGHT DOWN THE FAR SIDE. THAT IS THE INSTRUCTION AND IT IS THE ONE PARTIES GET WRONG. Instead CONTOUR AND TRAVERSE SOUTH ALONG THE BASE OF THE SLABS DESCENDING FROM WALLABY PEAK, LOSING ABOUT 20 FT BELOW THE LEVEL OF THE PASS, to pick up a good, well-cairned climber's trail.

SO THE TEST IS TWENTY FEET, AND IT IS AN ALTIMETER-SCALE MEASUREMENT YOU CAN MAKE BY EYE: barely below the pass, not down into the valley beyond it. Follow that trail CLOSE BENEATH THE SLABS, STAYING BELOW ALL THE MAJOR SLAB BANDS, traversing toward Kangaroo Temple.

ARRIVAL: a GULLY SYSTEM LEADING UP TO THE HIGH NOTCH AT THE BASE OF THE NORTH FACE. Ascend that gully to the notch. THE NOTCH IS THE START OF THE ROUTE.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE NORTHWEST FACE, AND IT IS COUNTABLE IN FEET: ABOUT 200 FT BELOW THE NOTCH, AN OBVIOUS BENCH AND TRAIL SPLITS OFF RIGHT TOWARD THE NORTHWEST FACE. If you have taken a bench off to the right, you are on the Northwest Face approach. This route keeps going up the boulder-choked gully to the notch itself.

AND THE SOUTH FACE USES A COMPLETELY DIFFERENT LINE FROM THE SAME CAR, WHICH IS THE OTHER WAY TO END UP IN THE WRONG PLACE: it hikes southeast on the RIGHT side of the creek and NEVER CROSSES KANGAROO PASS AT ALL. If you have not been over Kangaroo Pass, you are not on the North Face approach.

CONFIRM ON THE DESCENT, WHICH IS COUNTABLE HARDWARE: three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from FIXED STATIONS (chains at some, slung cord on bolts at others), landing on downclimbable low-fifth and fourth-class terrain just above the high notch where the route began. A 50 M ROPE ONLY JUST BARELY REACHES THE SECOND STATION, so a 60 m is strongly preferred. The stations are fixed, though rigging varies; inspect each before loading.

approach_variants.name: Ragged Ridge Camp to the waterfall at 7,760 ft
approach_variants.notes: From the basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak, climb 200 to 600 ft to the saddle and bench on the ridge running down off Katsuk's west summit — tedious scree with a short 4th-class stretch near the top. From there hike a short way up the broad ridge, then veer left and make an ascending traverse below the cliffs. Past the waterfall the going crosses the basin on softer ground, then continues on a slight rising traverse following small marmot trails and rocky ledges through a run of ribs and gullies. A backcountry permit is required to camp at the basin.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: The gully is incredibly loose — every handhold needs testing
Continuous snow to 45 degrees in the gully before roughly July; axe, crampons and real snow technique
The final fifty feet to the summit sits above a long drop down the north face
Rockfall onto anyone below in the gully — do not stack up
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE WATERFALL AT 7,760 FT, THEN A MUSHROOM ABOVE THE GULLY. The ascending traverse below the cliffs ends at a small waterfall at roughly 7,760 ft, and that waterfall is the reference — the scrambling starts there. Bypass it up the LEFT (west) side of the stream, on fairly loose rock covered in kitty-litter scree. From that point the correct line is a single leftward-trending gully high on the peak, and what confirms it is what sits at its head: the gully ends right at the base of a summit block shaped like a mushroom, broader at the top than at its neck. If the gully you have entered tops out on a rib, a notch, or open scree with no mushroom-shaped block above it, you are in a neighbouring gully — this south side is a maze of them. The block itself is climbed on its west side by a series of blocks at class 3.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak

approach_variants.name: PCT then the old Commonwealth Creek trail, stopping short of the creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT North trailhead, follow the PCT and, at an early fork, break LEFT onto the old, overgrown Commonwealth Creek trail. Follow it until the trees open out into a clearing where the cliff and its ice come into view.

This is a short approach on trail or on whatever bootpack exists. There is no fixed hardware on the climb — descent is two rappels off ice-screw or V-thread anchors from cord and slings you carry in.
approach_variants.season: Winter into early spring, when the two ice pitches have formed. Assess the avalanche slide path between the pitches before committing
hazards: A slide path for snow between the two pitches — assess avalanche conditions before committing
No fixed anchors: descent is on ice screws or V-threads with cord you carry
A sustained, near-vertical first pitch on winter ice of variable formation
A north-facing cliff that stays cold and holds thin ice in lean winters
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE STOP SIGNAL IS A CREEK YOU MUST NOT CROSS. Follow the old Commonwealth Creek trail until the timber opens into a clearing with the cliff and the ice in front of you. DO NOT CROSS COMMONWEALTH CREEK. If you have crossed it, you have gone too far and the cliff is behind you. That is the cleanest fog test on this side of the pass, because a creek crossing is unmistakable underfoot even when you cannot see a cliff.

THE CLEARING IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE TEST: you are looking for the point where the trees end, not for a distance or a time. Overgrown trail, then open ground, then the ice. If you are still under timber you have not arrived.

WHAT THE CLIMB SHOULD BE, AS CONFIRMATION: two pitches. Pitch one is the harder, sustained and near-vertical. Pitch two eases off and is belayed from a SMALL CAVE that offers some shelter. A cave belay at the top of the second pitch is the confirming feature.

AND THE HAZARD THAT SITS INSIDE THE FINDING: there can be a snow slide path between the two pitches. Assess it before you commit to the first pitch, not from the belay above it.

approach_variants.name: PCT north to the stump at 5,200 ft, then the boot path east
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 52 the PCT northbound lot sits just off the ramp on a short dirt spur; a Northwest Forest Pass is required and the roughly 50-car lot fills early at weekends.

From about 3,000 ft, follow the PCT north through second growth: first switchback at 0.6 mile, a switchback pair at 1.5 miles, the wilderness boundary at 2.0 miles where the forest opens into talus. The trail eases slightly downhill to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction at 2.6 miles — stay RIGHT and straight on the PCT; the left-hand Commonwealth Basin trail is brushy and easy to mistake for the main tread. Two stream crossings near that junction are the last reliable water.

Beyond, the PCT climbs under Kendall Peak's west flank through open talus and heather — Kendall Gardens, around mile 5 — then switchbacks directly below the peak at about 5.5 to 6 miles and 5,100 to 5,200 ft.

About 7.4 km and 2,800 ft.
approach_variants.season: June to October; snow can linger in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse below Kendall Gardens into early summer
hazards: Steep, loose dirt and scree on the final boot path
Lingering snow in the boot-path gully and on the PCT traverse into early summer
The class 3-4 ridge alternative, more exposed and loose than the standard route, entered by accident if the stump is missed
No water above the Commonwealth Creek crossings
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MARKER IS A STUMP, AND IT IS IN YOUR WAY. At about 5,200 ft on the switchbacks below the peak, a large, distinctive stump partially blocks the LEFT side of the trail. Roughly 15 FEET BEYOND IT a boot path forks RIGHT (east) and climbs straight uphill. That stump-then-fifteen-feet pairing is the whole finding, and it works in cloud because you feel the stump on the trail rather than having to spot the peak.

WHAT FOLLOWS CONFIRMS IT: the final 400 to 500 vertical feet on that boot path are steep, loose dirt and scree with occasional hands-on class 2 moves, running to the NORTHERNMOST and highest summit. Steep loose dirt is right; if you are on rock and using your hands continuously, you are somewhere harder.

THE OVERSHOOT AND WHAT IT COSTS YOU, WHICH IS THE REASON TO CARE ABOUT THE STUMP: parties who miss it and carry on along the PCT to where it crosses the ridge on the east side can scramble the ridge crest south to the true summit instead. That line is class 3 to 4, has abundant loose rock, and is notably more exposed and dangerous. It is a real alternative, but it is not the standard route and you should choose it deliberately rather than by accident.

AND THE PROGRESS CHECK BEFORE THE STUMP: Kendall Gardens, the open talus and heather at about mile 5, is the last obvious landmark below the switchbacks. If you have crossed the Kendall Katwalk you have gone a long way past the turn.

approach_variants.name: Ragged Ridge Camp and the red ledge
approach_variants.notes: From the basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak, gain roughly 800 ft to a bench near 7,400 ft, then traverse west holding somewhere between 7,400 and 7,600 ft. The traverse is an endless maze of ribs and gullies and you will cross easily over a dozen of them. The hardest section is a rib about halfway along: drop to around 7,200 ft and look for two ledges that give passage, at the cost of some elevation to regain and a short stretch of class 4. Where a line looks like the easiest way through, it usually goes. There is no reliable water past the basin camp late in the season.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Sustained exposed traversing on loose ribs and gullies
The class 4 downclimb and narrow gully at the halfway rib
A cliffy cave section on the ledge around 7,800 ft
Route-finding failure in cloud — the ribs are indistinguishable from one another
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE RED LEDGE IS THE PROOF, AND IT IS OBVIOUS WHEN YOU ARE ON IT. Somewhere along the westward traverse the ground organises itself into one reddish ledge that cuts straight across every rib and gully — it runs almost like a trail, and it is the feature that makes this traverse reasonable instead of desperate. It crosses at the base of a couple of the Grotesque Gendarmes, the ragged towers standing on the crest above you, then carries on across roughly 7,800 ft through a cliffy cave section and delivers you to a couple of gullies that lead to the summit. If you are picking your way up and down individual ribs and gullies with no continuous ledge underfoot, you are above or below the line and should hunt for it rather than force the terrain. Take the broad, solid-granite gully to the ridge just WEST of the true summit; from its top a short class 3 scramble crosses a scree saddle east to the true top.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake to the West Face Wall — same base as the other two lines on the wall
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the approach for the other West Face Wall routes. From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below the West Ridge and on to the amphitheatre between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass. Camp at either pass.

This line is a direct start and direct finish grafted onto the existing routes: it climbs the first four pitches of the original line, steps left onto the middle pitches of the direct, and then breaks out onto its own two-pitch finish up an overhanging headwall splitter.

Because of that, none of the decisions on this climb are made at the bottom. The base is shared; what makes it this route is a pair of choices at the ledge system and again below the headwall.
approach_variants.season: Late summer into early September, before autumn storms; the headwall is the point of the route and it wants dry rock
hazards: Significant runouts between protection placements
Loose rock with hidden chockstones
Thirty-plus metres of overhanging exposure on the headwall pitch, with retreat from it awkward
Alpine weather on a west-facing wall late in the season
An unplanned bivy is a documented outcome on this route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SAME SPLITTER THE OTHER TWO ROUTES USE — a hand-and-finger crack starting on a small ledge 15 to 25 feet off the snow or talus, gained by a short scramble. There is no separate King Kong start to look for, and hunting for one is how parties waste an hour at first light.

SO THE REAL ARRIVAL TEST IS THE WALL, NOT THE ROUTE: you want the amphitheatre roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, with about 1,000 ft of rock rising straight out of the snow above you. Anywhere still on a pass, or anywhere the wall has petered out into talus, is wrong. And the aspect is WEST — this wall takes the afternoon sun, so if you are standing under a face that has been in shade all afternoon you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

WHERE THIS ROUTE ACTUALLY BECOMES ITSELF, which is what you have to know at the base because you cannot see it from there: four pitches up the original line, then LEFT onto the direct for two pitches, then the two-pitch finish. The connector out to the finish is a roof bulge and a stem-box on overhanging jugs; the headwall pitch above it is a splitter on a steeply overhanging wall with more than thirty metres of air under it and two fixed nuts at its top.

IF YOU REACH A LEDGE SYSTEM AND SIMPLY CONTINUE RIGHT, you are on the original line and will finish on it. Nothing will stop you or tell you. The decision is yours and it is made in the middle of the wall.

approach_variants.name: One col further: Klawatti Col to the Klawatti-Austera col, then the crest
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road to the Eldorado trailhead near 2,150 ft, then the standard Eldorado climbers' path: forest, boulder field, treeline, and camps in Eldorado Basin / Roush Creek around 6,000-6,300 ft. Climb the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge near 7,500 ft, then traverse roughly a mile and a half north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft.

Klawatti Col is NOT the start of this route. Continue past it, along a lobe of the McAllister Glacier under Klawatti Peak's WEST FACE, about 0.4 mile to the next break in the ridge — the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA COL at about 7,900 ft. The scramble takes about an hour from that col, up to two hours if you count from Klawatti Col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, when the crest and the connecting cols are snow-free enough to scramble
hazards: Crevasses on the Inspiration and the upper McAllister lobe
A moat at the Klawatti-Austera col that ranges from class 4 to class 5 depending on where you cross it
Exposure on narrow sections of the crest, where route-finding is what keeps the grade at third class
Loose rock on the ledge traverses around The Smokestack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE COLS: YOU WANT THE SECOND ONE. Klawatti Col at 7,800 ft is where the peak's other two routes start; this route starts at the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA col at about 7,900 ft, a further 0.4 mile north along the foot of Klawatti's west face and a hundred feet higher.

THE SECOND COL IDENTIFIES ITSELF BY BEING A PROBLEM, AND IT OFFERS A CHOICE OF TWO CROSSINGS — WHICH IS ITSELF THE CONFIRMATION. Receding snow leaves a moat here. The LOWEST notch is class 5 downclimbing; a crossing to the RIGHT (southeast) of the lowest notch is class 4. Parties have also found an old rappel anchor at this col and used it. A col you walked over without choosing between two ways down is Klawatti Col, one short.

GAIN THE LOWER RIDGE ON ITS EAST SIDE — the crest itself is harder than it needs to be low down, and the east flank is the easy way onto it.

THE SMOKESTACK IS THE CONFIRMING LANDMARK AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE. Class 3 scrambling up the crest brings you to a rock tower around 8,400 ft that the route is named around. YOU DO NOT CLIMB IT: go round it on its WEST side by a short gully and regain the crest above. A party that has climbed a tower on the ridge rather than walked around it has gone off route. A party that reached the summit without ever passing a tower was never on the North Ridge.

NEGATIVE TEST FOR THE OTHER DIRECTION: if the ground in front of you is a snow face rather than a ridge crest, you are below the south-facing snow line and one col too far south.

WHAT IS THIN HERE, SAID PLAINLY: this ridge is barely written up. The col elevations, the Smokestack and the east-side start come from the route's own record; the detail about the two crossings at the moat and the old anchor comes from accounts that could not be retrieved in full, so treat the crossing description as a warning to expect a choice rather than as a promise about which side is easier this year.

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

approach_variants.name: Klawatti Col and the south flank to the bergschrund below the face
approach_variants.notes:
Identical approach to the SW Buttress as far as the col: Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the Cascade River log crossing, the steep timbered climbers' path, the boulder field (stay climber's right — cairn lines trending left lead into cliffier ground), the basin at 5,500-5,800 ft, then Roush Creek and bivy sites at 6,100-6,400 ft at the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up there.

Climb the Eldorado Glacier, then make the long, mostly flat traverse east and north across the Inspiration Glacier to KLAWATTI COL at about 7,800 ft. Reckon roughly 7-8 miles and over 6,500 ft of gain one way from the car to the foot of the climb, normally split over two or three days.

From the col a short direct climb up the peak's south-facing flank reaches the base. Parties leave the col around 4 a.m. on purpose: this is a south-facing snow slope, icy in the pre-dawn shade and softening fast once the sun is on it, and it is roughly an hour and a half up and an hour down from the col.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Aug once the schrund bridges have consolidated; a separate Apr-Jun window exists for the face as a firm corn-snow line
hazards: A bergschrund, and later in the season a moat, guarding the base of the face
Several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow directly above the schrund, on ground where a slip does not stop
South aspect: icy before dawn, softening and wet-sliding by mid-morning
Whiteout on the Inspiration Glacier both ways — parties have been caught out right at the summit
A crumbly, elongated summit where the true high point is genuinely hard to identify
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BERGSCHRUND, AND THE SCHRUND IS THE ROUTE'S IDENTITY. From Klawatti Col you climb directly up the south flank until the snow pulls back from the rock. That gap — a schrund early, a moat late — is where the climbing starts, and the short 4th-to-easy-5th rock step that clears it is the technical crux of the whole route.

YOU MUST BE AT THE COL ITSELF: if you are not standing at the LOW POINT of the ridge dividing the Inspiration and McAllister glacier systems, you are not below this route.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHAT COMES AFTER THE STEP: SNOW, AND A LOT OF IT. Above the rock step the route is several hundred feet of 40 to 55 degree snow — through a constriction, steepening over a pseudo-cornice bulge on the upper southwest side — to the top of the face, then an easy walk along the southwest ridge. IF THE ROCK KEEPS GOING ABOVE THE STEP, a second and third pitch of it and no snow slope, YOU ARE ON THE SOUTHWEST BUTTRESS, which leaves from the same col. One of these wants a rack, the other wants a picket and possibly a second tool.

A SECOND CONFIRMATION THAT ALSO SERVES THE DESCENT: parties have found rappel slings on the EAST side of the constriction at the moat. A moat with old tat on its east side is the right one.

DO NOT WALK ON PAST THE COL. The North Ridge leaves from the Klawatti-Austera col about 0.4 mile further, and the ground there is a ridge crest, not a snow face. If you can see a rock tower standing up on the crest ahead of you, you have overshot by a col.

AT THE TOP THE SUMMIT IS THE HARD PART TO IDENTIFY, NOT THE BASE: the crest is crumbly and elongated, at least one party found no register and could not settle which bump was highest, and cairns mark a line back down the ridge toward the col. Note that line on the way up — it is the alternative to reversing the face.
