bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Eldorado ice-cap / Inspiration Glacier high camp

wa_klawatti_peak_sw_buttress.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From camp, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) climbing the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration ice cap, typically another 3-5 hours. Any overnight stay requires a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. IMPORTANT — this route is NOT on Eldorado Peak itself: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.

approach_variants.name: Eldorado ice cap to Klawatti Col, then the buttress that stands directly above camp
approach_variants.notes: The whole approach is the Eldorado one: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the river crossing, the steep unmaintained boot path through old growth to the boulder field, and up into Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek basin. Camp there or push on to the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,500-7,600 ft. From that camp the day is glacier travel, not a trail. Rope up, cross the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit, and continue north-northeast to KLAWATTI COL at about 7,800 ft, the saddle dividing the Klawatti and McAllister glaciers on Klawatti Peak's south side. This traverse is the navigational crux of the whole route — it is flat, featureless and whiteouts are routine, so carry a bearing or a track and be prepared to navigate blind. Parties commonly camp at the col itself. Three Klawatti routes leave from cols within half a mile of each other. A wilderness permit for the Klawatti zone comes from the Marblemount ranger station.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the Inspiration Glacier traverse and the moat at the foot of the buttress are reliably crossable
hazards: Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers, worst near Eldorado's east ridge
Whiteout navigation on a flat, featureless ice cap with no handrail
A moat at the foot of the buttress where the glacier has pulled back from the rock
Rock repeatedly described as lousy and loose — test every hold rather than trusting the grade
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BUTTRESS STANDS DIRECTLY ABOVE THE KLAWATTI CAMP AND IS MINUTES FROM IT — not a traverse away. That is the first thing that separates it from the peak's other two routes. If you have walked more than a few minutes from the saddle you have started the wrong climb.

THE DECIDING TEST IS WHAT IS ABOVE THE MOAT, AND IT IS A ONE-LOOK TEST. Cross the moat and the ground above is ROCK and keeps being rock: two or three short low-fifth pitches, then class 4, then scrambling. IF THERE ARE SEVERAL HUNDRED FEET OF 40-55 DEGREE SNOW ABOVE A SHORT ROCK STEP, YOU ARE ON THE SOUTH-FACING SNOW LINE KNOWN AS THE SOUTHEAST FACE, which starts from the same col and is a snow climb with one rock move rather than a rock climb. That difference decides whether you needed a rack or a second tool.

THE THIRD ROUTE IS AT A DIFFERENT COL ENTIRELY. The North Ridge starts from the KLAWATTI-AUSTERA col at about 7,900 ft, roughly 0.4 mile further along under Klawatti's west face — a separate notch a hundred feet higher, and one you have to solve rather than walk through. If you are walking a ridge crest north with a rock tower ahead of you, you have gone past this route to that one.

WHAT THE COL LOOKS LIKE: a broad saddle with usable bivy sites on the south side, and the LOW point between the Klawatti Glacier on one side and the McAllister on the other — so from it you can see down both. A spot where the ground only falls away one way is not the col.

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

approach_variants.name: Hairpin pullout, Kangaroo Pass and the Temple-Little Finger gully
approach_variants.notes: From the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass, walk south across the boulder field and pick up the faint, intermittently cairned climbers' path through forest and more talus to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour. From the pass an on-and-off trail traverses to the gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger, which leads up to the notch on the Temple's north side; the north, northwest and southwest face routes all start off this gully, roughly another hour. Koala Krack is the last short pitch on the summit block, so you reach it by finishing whichever line you have climbed rather than by a separate approach.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the gully between the Temple and Little Finger
The path across the slabs below Kangaroo Pass fades in fog or fresh snow
Fixed rappel anchors at the top of the pitch — inspect before loading
approach_variants.baseFinding: TWO TESTS: ONE IN THE APPROACH GULLY, ONE ON THE SUMMIT BLOCK. In the gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger, keep going up to the notch itself, where the North Face starts; the faint trail breaking off to the RIGHT roughly 200 ft below the notch leads to the Northwest Face instead. Either way, this pitch is only reached by finishing one of those lines. On the summit block itself, Koala Krack is the wide, LEFT-trending diagonal crack: start on the slab immediately to its right, traverse onto the crack, follow it up and left to a small sandy flat, then traverse left to a cairn marking the bolted rappel station. If the crack in front of you leans right instead of left, or there is no slab beneath it to start from, you are on a different feature of the block.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

what_to_bring: Water filter or treatment (no potable water at high camp)
GPS with a pre-loaded route track, or detailed map and compass
Satellite communicator (InReach/SPOT) - no cell coverage in the wilderness interior
Rain shell - weather changes quickly even in mid-summer

emergency.notes: No reliable cell coverage inside the Glacier Peak Wilderness - carry a satellite communicator (InReach/SPOT) and file a trip plan given the remote, multi-day, largely off-trail nature of this climb.
emergency.county: Straddles Snohomish County (west/North Fork Sauk approach) and Chelan County (east/White River approach)
emergency.rangerStation: Darrington Ranger District, (360) 436-1155 (west approach); Wenatchee River Ranger District, Leavenworth, (509) 548-2550 (east approach)
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Valley Hospital, Arlington WA (Level IV ED) via the west/Darrington approach; Central Washington Hospital, Wenatchee WA or Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth WA via the east/White River approach

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 to White Pass, then the Foam Basin traverse and the White Chuck Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Late summer opens the crevasses so you can see and weave them; early season covers them with bridges you cannot read, and puts Red Creek and Lightning Creek in flood
hazards: Open crevasses and a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice on the White River Glacier, worse late season
Red Creek and Lightning Creek run high and fast in snowmelt — the first is an ordinary ford at normal flow and a stopper at high water
Twelve-plus miles one way with the last several off any maintained trail, so a navigation error is measured in hours
Snow bridges over the White Chuck Glacier that are unreadable under early-season cover
Road closures on FR-49 and the Mountain Loop Highway that can shut the west approach entirely, turning this into a much longer trip from the east
approach_variants.baseFinding: THIS ROUTE HAS TWO ARRIVALS AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT KINDS OF THING. The first is where GLACIER TRAVEL starts, and the second is where the SCRAMBLING starts. Confusing them is how a party ends up unroped in the wrong place. GLACIER STARTS AT FOAM PASS. From camp climb to Foam Pass and step onto the White Chuck Glacier. Rope, axe and crampons go on here, not later — the crossing to Glacier Gap and then onto the White River Glacier is the whole of the day's crevasse exposure. SCRAMBLING STARTS AT THE 7,400 FT SADDLE, AND YOU GET THERE BY COUNTING RATHER THAN BY LOOKING. Off the glacier, gain the flat shoulder near 6,000 ft; follow the connecting ridge north-north-west over a bulge at 7,200 ft; cross the small basin below the east summit; then go WEST a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft. Shoulder, bulge, basin, saddle — four things in that order. If you have gone west without first crossing a basin, you are on the wrong side of the bulge. THE ARRIVAL TEST AT THE SADDLE: from it, one ridge runs away from you forming the EAST EDGE OF THE WHITE RIVER GLACIER CIRQUE. That ridge is the route. If the ground ahead does not have a glacier cirque falling away on one side of it, you are not on the saddle you want. WHAT TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing east instead of west from the 7,200 ft bulge takes you to the EAST summit rather than the summit ridge — and of the twin tops on the summit ridge the eastern one is the true high point by only 10-15 ft, so bag both. ONE THING TO EXPECT ON THE ICE RATHER THAN LOOK FOR: a roughly 200-yard band of exposed blue ice, a shallow icefall, on the White River Glacier. It is a crampon problem, not a navigation one, but it is the reason the descent takes longer than the map suggests.

bivy.name: White Chuck Glacier basin, under Kololo Peaks
bivy.notes: The climbing camp for KOLOLO PEAKS, and the reason Kololo is a three-day trip rather than a weekend scramble. It sits in the stark rock-and-snow basin on the edge of what remains of the White Chuck Glacier, reached from the North Fork Sauk road end by twelve or thirteen miles of walking — the long river approach, then the steep switchbacking climb to White Pass, then east on the crest trail and out along the Foam Basin path toward Foam Pass. Eight hours from the road to camp is a normal rather than a slow time for a party carrying overnight gear. From here the peaks themselves are straightforward, a walk on glacier remnant and snow followed by easy scrambling on rubbly volcanic rock, and moving from one summit to the next is simple. The glacier is the thing to understand: it has retreated further and faster than almost anything in the range and much of what maps show as ice is now bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds, with the surviving ice thin, hard and holed by open crevasses late in the season. That means crampons rather than a snow plod by September, and it means route descriptions written twenty years ago describe a surface that is gone. Lower camps on the same approach sit at the river bench, at White Pass and at the gap above this basin. Exposed ground with no shelter, confusing in fog, and a long way from help.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams and ponds through the basin, running all through the climbing season and often silty. Late in a hot summer the flow drops to a trickle off the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time. Everybody camped here drinks it, so site the toilet well away from it.
bivy.permit: GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit collected at the North Fork Sauk trailhead box, twelve-person party limit. No fires: this is bare rock, pumice and snow above treeline with nothing to burn and nothing that recovers. Human waste is carried out or buried properly well away from the meltwater. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
bivy.capacity: Open bare-ground bivouac sites scattered through the basin, with room for several parties and no crowding — this is a big, empty place. Rock-walled windbreaks left by previous parties are the nearest thing to a built site.

bivy.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
bivy.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. PAINTED MOUNTAIN, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a DAY OBJECTIVE with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
bivy.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
bivy.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

approach_variants.name: Blanca Lake Trail to Virgin Lake, then the south-ridge climbers' path
approach_variants.notes: From the Blanca Lake trailhead at the end of the North Fork road, follow the lake trail north into the wilderness. It climbs immediately in a long series of roughly thirty switchbacks, gaining most of the day's easy elevation over the first three miles to a ridge crest — muddy, rooty and icy in wet or early-season conditions. From the ridge the trail runs on through meadows to Virgin Lake, the trail's high point before it DROPS about six hundred feet to the big lake, and a good overnight camp and the last easy reliable water before the off-trail climbing. This is where the single most common navigation error happens.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Early season adds snow on the ridge and makes the glacier variant the safer of the two.
hazards: The unsigned turnoff at Virgin Lake is the commonest error on this peak
Route-finding on the faint ridge path, which is easy to lose in brush
Loose, crumbly rock on the summit block with real exposure
Dense blueberry brush and heather on the ridge, worse late in the season
A long single push with a likely after-dark return unless camped at the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: At Virgin Lake, do NOT continue downhill on the main tread — that goes to the big turquoise lake below and away from the peak. Instead pick up the faint, UNSIGNED climbers' path leaving the lake into the woods toward the ridge. It gains the peak's south ridge and follows it northeast, staying on the ridge's EAST side to get round minor gendarmes, levels out around fifty-three hundred feet, crosses to the WEST side around fifty-eight hundred, then climbs steep heather and scree working around cliff bands. The technical ground starts at a NOTCH beside a subsidiary point, reached across a boulder field — the notch is the first place the ridge is blocked by a rock step you cannot walk around, and above it the rock turns loose and pebbly for the scramble to the summit ridge. Negative markers: if you are on obvious maintained tread descending toward a turquoise, silty lake, you took the main trail at Virgin Lake and are heading away from the peak; if you are roped up on a glacier, you are on the alternative line rather than this one.

approach_variants.name: Columbia Glacier from the Blanca Lake basin
approach_variants.notes: The alternative line onto the upper mountain, and several parties pair it with the ridge path — one for the way up, one for the way down. From Virgin Lake, take the main tread down into the basin, cross or skirt the lake's south shore on logs and boulders (poles help), then work up the boulder field and heather slopes above the north shore to the glacier toe. Stay on the glacier's EAST side; the west-side ice is noticeably steeper.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Best when the glacier is snow-covered enough to bridge but firm enough to travel; midday summer slush makes it slow and sliding.
hazards: Crevasses on the Columbia Glacier — low-angle but real, especially where snow is soft
Soft, sliding midday slush in summer
Wading or log-crossing the lake outlet stream
Loose, crumbly rock on the lateral moraine and at the glacier exit
Camping is banned within half a mile of the big lake, so plan the overnight around Virgin Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the rock is the glacier's exit, and it is a specific and short one: about fifty feet of ledgy, somewhat loose third-class ground taking you off the ice onto rock, after which you traverse RIGHT toward the peak's southwest side and join the ridge line higher up. The test is the exit itself — a short ledgy step, not a long climb; if you are looking at hundreds of feet of rock rising straight off the ice, you are at the wrong point on the glacier's edge. Once on rock, the pebbly, loose 'kitty litter' ground and two narrow catwalks leading toward the summit block confirm you are on the standard line. Negative marker: if you are still gaining height on ice with cliffs above you and the summit off to the side, you have gone too far up the glacier past the exit.

approach_variants.name: Quartz Creek Trail over Curry Gap and the Pride Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is a different trailhead from the peak's scramble route — do not start at the Blanca Lake road end. Begin at the North Fork Sauk and Quartz Creek trailhead on the Darrington side and follow the Quartz Creek trail about four miles to Curry Gap, at the junction with the Bald Eagle Mountain trail. From the gap, head west and southwest along an up-and-down ridge toward the peak, leaving the ridge where the ground allows to cross the glacier west-northwest toward the cliffs below the neighbouring summit. The route-finding hazard on this leg is the cliff bands in the basin, not the glacier.
approach_variants.season: June to September; spring ski ascents and descents of this side are also recorded.
hazards: Crevasse-fall hazard on the glacier crossing
Cliff-band route-finding in the basin between the gap and the glacier
Rockfall on the third-class band above the glacier
The up-and-down ridge between the gap and the glacier is longer in practice than it looks on a map
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base of the climbing is where the GLACIER MEETS ROCK on the peak's northeast side, at about six thousand feet, and the physical test is which hand the ice is on. The line climbs third-class rock along the CLIMBER'S-LEFT EDGE of the glacier, so once you are on rock the ice should stay on your RIGHT the whole way up to the summit's southeast corner. If the ice is on your left, you have crossed to the wrong edge. The second confirmation is what you passed: the cliffs below the neighbouring summit are an AIMING MARK on the crossing, not the objective — you traverse beneath them and then turn up onto rock. Negative markers: if you are still on low-angle ice with cliffs directly overhead and the summit well off to one side, you are under the neighbouring peak rather than this one; if you have come up a faint climbers' path from a small lake with a subsidiary point beside you, you are on the south-ridge scramble from the other side of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Creek to the gap
approach_variants.notes: The first five miles of the Necklace Valley Trail are nearly flat along the river; save your legs, because everything above the log crossing of the East Fork Foss is steep. Roughly 2,400 ft of gain in three miles over large boulders and tree roots on rugged tread brings you to Jade Lake, then it is up-valley past Emerald toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes where the maintained trail effectively ends. From the Opal Lake camps pick up the crude path climbing beside La Bohn Creek — west-facing, unshaded and hot in the afternoon — to the lowest La Bohn Lake, then follow the shore and heather benches north to the upper lake.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Roughly 1,500 ft of piled boulders on the peak's flank, many of which wobble
Steep, unshaded and slick-when-wet boot path up the La Bohn Creek drainage
Foot-log crossing of the East Fork Foss at high snowmelt
Snow lingering on the upper slopes that masks the correct saddle
Cliffs above Lake Rowena on the ground east of the wrong gap
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identification problem here is the gap itself, and the map is against you: published mapping labels La Bohn Gap roughly two-thirds of a mile southeast of where it actually sits, and the slopes east of that false gap end in a precipitous drop toward Lake Rowena. Verify before you commit to any slope east of a saddle. The true gap is a broad, tarn-dotted saddle at about 5,900 ft, reached by a short talus-and-heather traverse EAST from the upper La Bohn Lake; it is genuinely broad and open, with Mount Hinman filling the view across it and La Bohn Peak's talus rising directly to the west. Lingering snow can hide the correct line into early summer, which is exactly when parties pick the wrong saddle. From the right gap the climbing is straightforward: head west up boulders and heather onto the east ridge and follow it to the top. The crest carries a false summit a short way short of the true top, with the final eighth of a mile a walk along the summit ridge.

bivy.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
bivy.notes: The main basecamp for LA BOHN PEAK, which stands directly at the head of this valley, and the first night of the standard west-side approach to MOUNT HINMAN. Drive the Foss River road off Highway 2 a short way east of Skykomish and turn into the Necklace Valley trailhead about four miles up. The trail is famously two-faced: the first five miles along the East Fork Foss gain only about 600 ft through regenerated second growth and go quickly, then the trail crosses the river and climbs roughly 2,400 ft in the next three miles to break out at Jade Lake around 4,600 ft. Emerald is a quarter mile further, Opal about 4,790 ft above that, with Ilswoot, Locket, Jewel and Cloudy scattered on either side. A weathered memorial cabin sits in the meadow just above Emerald; it is a landmark and a piece of the valley's mining history, not a shelter to plan on. From Opal or Emerald the route to La Bohn Gap climbs east under the cliffs, so Jade is fractionally further from the gap but Emerald and Opal put you closest to the day's work. Two honest caveats. The Foss River road has been under construction with weekday delays of about half an hour through the summer, and damage higher on the road has at times cut off the upper end, so allow slack and check before committing to a dawn start. And this valley is very popular for its own sake — a midweek trip is far more pleasant than a Saturday, and the steep middle section is genuinely unpleasant under a heavy climbing pack in the heat.
bivy.water: All four lakes, plus the creek linking them. Reliable the whole season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size limited to twelve including stock. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the range, which puts every lake in the valley under a fire ban — carry a stove and do not build rings.
bivy.capacity: Sites are spread across four separate lake basins rather than concentrated, so the valley absorbs a lot of parties — several groups at Jade, several more around Emerald and Opal, and quieter singles at Ilswoot, Locket and Jewel off to the sides. On a summer weekend the popular shorelines are full by mid-afternoon.

bivy.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
bivy.notes: The high camp for LA BOHN PEAK and the launching point for the west route on MOUNT HINMAN, and the single most useful piece of ground in this zone for a climber. La Bohn Gap is a broad boulder-covered saddle at roughly 6,000 ft on the crest between the Foss and Snoqualmie drainages, with the tarns of the La Bohn Lakes scattered on the benches around it and the Chain Lakes sitting lower at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak. From Necklace Valley the climb to the lakes goes either up to the gap itself or by a steeper line beside the waterfall; both are straightforward in summer and both hold snow into July. La Bohn Peak is a short class 2 walk west from the gap. For Hinman the ground continues east and then north, half a mile of easy going to gain the gap area and then a long open ascent to the summit — worth knowing that the Hinman Glacier shown on older maps has essentially gone, so what you will actually cross is a shrinking snowfield with the moat and loose-rock problems that come with that, and conditions vary enormously year to year. The gap is also the hinge of the whole area on foot: north drops into Necklace Valley, south drops toward Dutch Miller Gap and the upper Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and the view takes in Bald Eagle, Silver Eagle and Big Heart Lake off to the west. Camping here is committing. It is fully exposed, the weather arrives without warning, and a bad night in the gap is a real one — carry proper shelter or drop back to the Necklace lakes.
bivy.water: The La Bohn tarns and the Chain Lakes below the gap on the south side, plus lingering snowmelt into midsummer. Late in a dry season the smaller tarns can drop and turn silty; check rather than assume.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, picked up at whichever trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. Campfires prohibited outright — everything here is well above the 4,000 ft fire-ban line and there is no wood to burn anyway. Camp on rock or bare gravel, not on the heather, which takes decades to recover at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small, exposed pitches on granite benches and heather shelves between the tarns — realistically two or three tents in the good spots, more if you are willing to sleep on rock. There is no sheltered ground.

bivy.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
bivy.notes: The valley-bottom staging option for every Foss River objective, and worth a line of its own because of what the road has been doing. The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.
bivy.water: Piped or hand-pumped drinking water on site, with the South Fork Skykomish and the Miller River beside them. No treating required.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fees, and reservations for most sites. No wilderness permit needed at this elevation — pick that up at the trailhead the next morning. Campfires are allowed in the provided rings when there is no seasonal fire ban in force, which is the last time you will see one on any of these trips.
bivy.capacity: Money Creek has around twenty-five sites, a couple of them first-come; Miller River is a group camp of about fifteen sites with a gathering area. Both take vehicles and both fill on summer weekends, so reserve where you can.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three single-rope rappels down the south side toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.
hazards: Rope drag and route-finding after the slab traverse make this a confusing place to arrive; the anchor is above where most parties stop
The descent is repeatedly described as windy, which throws a tossed rope off line
rappel_detail.station: About 30 m down from where the route tops out and on the SKIER'S RIGHT, not on the summit itself. The top station is a bolted anchor - reached, from the West Face finish, by continuing about 50 ft above the top of that route's last pitch. It is worth noting where this anchor is on the way up: parties descending at dusk say knowing where the first anchors are is what makes a late descent reasonable. First of three single-rope rappels heading down toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.

rappel_detail.notes: Second single-rope rappel continuing toward the notch/gully.
hazards: This is the rappel reported as coming up about 5 ft short on a 60 m rope, finished with a short downclimb. Expect it rather than discovering it at the ends
The gully is loose and chossy, and snow-covered well into the season
rappel_detail.station: Second of the three single-rope rappels, down into the gully.

rappel_detail.notes: Third single-rope rappel reaching the notch.
hazards: The gully here is the one parties mistakenly ASCEND when route-finding up the chasm; on the way down it is loose and often snow-filled
Rockfall onto anyone still on the rappel above
rappel_detail.station: Third single-rope rappel, landing in the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire - often snow-covered. There is a tree at the notch that parties use as the landmark for the anchors here. A few minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing links this to the chockstone station.

rappel_detail.notes: Largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past the giant chockstone (~50 ft of air) from bolts on top of the chockstone.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor on top of the chockstone
hazards: Fully free-hanging with no way to reach rock once you are on it
You arrive at this station from above by scrambling loose gully ground, which is where material gets knocked onto anyone below
rappel_detail.station: The rappel this descent is known for. Below the notch, a short scramble leads to the giant chockstone in the gully; the station is a BOLTED rap anchor on top of the chockstone - not tat, and the same bolts parties belay from on the way up when climbing the Chockstone Route. The rappel goes off the chockstone and hangs completely free for around 50 ft, and is routinely described as the longest free-hanging rappel the party has done.

rappel_detail.notes: Final short (~30 ft) rappel, or downclimb/scramble alternative, back to the base.
hazards: Loose, steep gully walking either way
rappel_detail.station: A few more minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing below the chockstone, then a last short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree to the ground. Some parties downclimb this instead of rigging it.

wa_labor_pains.rappel_count_note: These five stations are the ORIGINAL chockstone/notch descent down the south side, and the count assumes a SINGLE rope for the three upper rappels plus TWO ropes for the chockstone rappel - accounts describe it as up to five rappels depending on conditions and the number of ropes carried, and parties with two ropes throughout combine some of the upper ones. The second gully rappel comes up about 5 ft short on a 60 m. IMPORTANT: many Labor Pains parties now use a different descent. A separate BOLTED rappel line was established down the West Face, running between the West Face route and Labor Pains itself, and it is that West Face line, rather than anything in this route's own gear list, that wants a 70 m rope; the list here is a 60 m. That line shares only the FIRST anchor with the chockstone descent - from it you head down the West Face instead of into the gully - and has nothing else in common with the stations listed here. It is currently six stations on bolts and chains ending a minute from the base of the routes, with one rappel that a 60 m does not make (parties report needing to block and extend a strand, or carry a 70), and a last anchor that is genuinely hard to find, on a rib below some shrubs and skier's left as you walk down loose dirt from the fifth station. Some parties still rappel from a nearby dead tree carrying no slings, which is not the anchor. Do not blend the two lines: the station list shown is the chockstone line.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Chockstone Route start, then up and LEFT to the ledge below the clean slab
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, the Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path lead into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group and past South Early Winters Spire to the west side of the two Early Winters Spires.

This route shares its start with the CHOCKSTONE ROUTE. From there, head up and LEFT toward a ledge below a clean slab to begin Labor Pains, which climbs the clean face between the Chockstone Route and The West Face. Five pitches, 5.11a, first climbed in September 1988.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start defined by its neighbours on both sides on a wall of closely spaced lines
5.11a over five pitches with a rappel descent down a different route
The approach passes South Early Winters Spire first; stopping there puts you on the wrong peak
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CHOCKSTONE ROUTE'S START IS THE ANCHOR POINT AND IT IS THE MOST UNMISTAKABLE FEATURE ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN: IT IS OBVIOUS, AT THE BASE OF THE MASSIVE CHASM SEPARATING NORTH AND SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRES. A chasm splitting two spires is not something you can be uncertain about, in any weather where you can see the rock at all.

FROM THERE THE INSTRUCTION IS TWO WORDS AND A FEATURE: UP AND LEFT, TO A LEDGE BELOW A CLEAN SLAB. Clean rock is the marker. This route takes the clean face; the ground either side of it does not read as clean.

SO THE ROUTE IS SANDWICHED, AND YOU CAN BOUND IT BOTH WAYS: THE CHOCKSTONE ROUTE IS TO ITS RIGHT, IN THE CHASM. THE WEST FACE IS TO ITS LEFT. If you are in the chasm you have not left the shared start; if you have traversed all the way left to the shared start with the Northwest Corner, you have gone past.

CONFIRM BY WHAT YOU ARE STANDING ON: A LEDGE, below a SLAB. Not a chimney, not a corner.

DESCENT, AND IT IS NOT A REVERSAL: rappel down the CHOCKSTONE ROUTE line, using the same bolted stations that route uses, rather than reversing the Labor Pains pitches. That means you finish where you started, back at the chasm.

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes or Narada Falls, Tatoosh Creek and the debris apron under the north face
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it is open, or at Narada Falls in winter and spring when the road is snow-gated — from Narada Falls a short steep climb of about 200 ft through open timber regains the road.

Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face.

From the basin, hike up and across a large TRIANGULAR APRON of avalanche and rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloirs. From the top of that debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft of couloir to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel point.

Roughly 2 to 2.5 miles one-way with about 2,000 ft of gain to the notch, and no water past Tatoosh Creek. The basin and lower couloir cross avalanche terrain, so this is a start-early, read-the-forecast approach.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Jun; most ascents are in winter and spring
hazards: Avalanche terrain in the basin and lower couloir, with both loose-dry and wet-loose problems documented on this aspect
Overhead hazard from other parties — this face is busy on good winter weekends and all three couloirs get climbed at once
Variable ice and mixed conditions in the steps season to season
A rappel that is longer than a single 60 m rope doubled, and rope-snag potential on rock features
Short winter days leaving little margin for retreat
Rockfall and spindrift funnelling into the couloir from above
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ON THIS FACE THE THREE COULOIRS ARE: LOVER'S LANE, THE ZIPPER, THE FLY. Learn that order before you leave the car. All three drop onto the same debris apron and on a busy weekend all three have parties on them at once, which means overhead hazard from other people as well as from the mountain.

THE ZIPPER IS THE MIDDLE ONE, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT LEANS LEFT AND SPLITS THE CENTRE OF THE FACE. From the top of the debris cone, angle CLIMBER'S LEFT. If you are working right, you are heading for the Fly.

THE STRONGEST TEST IS WIDTH, AND IT IS A THING YOU FEEL RATHER THAN SEE: THE ZIPPER NARROWS. About 40 ft wide at the base, closing to about 20 ft near the top. THE FLY IS BROAD — 40 to 50 ft — AND IT STAYS BROAD. If the walls are not closing in on you as you gain height, you are in the Fly, one couloir to your right, on easier ground than you came for.

THE SECOND TEST IS COUNTABLE AND IT IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES IT: THE ZIPPER HAS UP TO THREE SHORT STEPS — about 15 ft, then about 8 ft, then a 25 ft crux near the top. The Fly has none worth the name. IF YOU HAVE CLIMBED A THOUSAND FEET OF CONTINUOUS 45-DEGREE SNOW AND MET NO STEP AT ALL, YOU ARE NOT IN THE ZIPPER.

THE TOP-OUT IS AN OBJECT, WHICH IS THE BEST KIND OF CONFIRMATION: A DEAD TREE AT A NOTCH IN THE EAST RIDGE. That tree carries the fixed rappel slings. If you have topped out onto open ridge with no tree, you are on something else — Lover's Lane finishes on the ridge ABOVE this notch, and the Fly finishes at the west-ridge notch.

WHAT THE ANGLE SHOULD DO: build from about 40 degrees to about 45 near the top. It does not exceed that. Ground steeper than 45 sustained means Lover's Lane, which reaches about 60.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

approach_variants.name: Reflection Lakes or Narada Falls to the debris apron, then the rightmost couloir
approach_variants.notes:
Shared approach with the Zipper: from Reflection Lakes when the road is open, or from Narada Falls when it is gated, walk the road briefly and drop south into the basin toward Tatoosh Creek, then climb the debris triangle to the base of the couloir system. Roughly 2 miles with about 2,000 ft of gain; the approach usually takes 45 to 75 minutes from the road to the couloir base.

The Fly is a broad couloir about 40 to 50 ft wide, predominantly snow at around 45 degrees, and is the easiest objective on the north face with fewer technical sections than the Zipper. The most efficient line follows the obvious broad gully, trending slightly right as you gain height.

The runout zone at the base is avalanche-prone, so stable snow is essential.

From the top at the west-ridge notch, most parties continue round onto the South Face and descend the standard third and fourth class gully rather than reversing the couloir.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-Jun
hazards: An avalanche-prone runout zone at the base of the couloir
Overhead hazard from parties on the neighbouring couloirs and from rockfall out of the walls once the sun hits
Variable snow and ice conditions season to season
Short winter days
Wet-loose avalanche activity documented on the slopes below the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT: LOVER'S LANE, THE ZIPPER, THE FLY. THE FLY IS THE RIGHTMOST, AND IT IS THE BROADEST.

BREADTH IS THE TEST AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE YOU NEED AT THE BOTTOM: 40 to 50 ft wide, and IT STAYS THAT WIDE. IF THE COULOIR NARROWS TOWARD ABOUT 20 FT AND STARTS PUTTING SHORT ICE STEPS IN FRONT OF YOU, YOU ARE IN THE ZIPPER, ONE TO YOUR LEFT, ON HARDER GROUND THAN YOU CAME FOR.

THE SECOND TEST IS WHAT YOUR HANDS ARE DOING. This is the easiest line on the face — predominantly snow at about 45 degrees with no crux step. IF YOU ARE SWINGING TWO TOOLS INTO ICE, YOU ARE NOT ON THE FLY.

TREND SLIGHTLY RIGHT AS YOU GAIN HEIGHT. That is the route's own shape, and drifting left at the base is exactly how parties end up in the Zipper.

THE TOP-OUT NAMES THE COULOIR RETROSPECTIVELY, WHICH IS WORTH KNOWING IF YOU HAD ANY DOUBT ON THE WAY UP: the Fly finishes at the WEST-RIDGE NOTCH. The Zipper finishes at a notch in the EAST ridge, at a DEAD TREE carrying rappel slings. If you topped out at a tree, you climbed the Zipper.

A NEGATIVE THAT IS ABOUT PEOPLE RATHER THAN GROUND, AND IT IS SPECIFIC TO THIS FACE: on a good winter weekend all three couloirs carry parties at the same time, and a documented near-miss involved thirteen climbers and skiers spread across the three. Being able to see other parties is not confirmation you are in the right gully — it is a reason to watch what comes down.

WHAT THE ANGLE SHOULD DO: about 40 to 45 degrees for the main gully, easing to 30-35 in the last few hundred feet to the ridge. It does not steepen near the top.

approach_variants.name: Narada Falls, under Denman Peak, and the first steep avalanche funnel
approach_variants.notes:
Begin at the Narada Falls parking area, which is plowed and open year-round. Travel on skis or snowshoes along the closed Reflection Lakes road, then traverse steep hillsides under Denman Peak toward Lane Peak's base, turning sharply uphill at the first steep avalanche funnel to reach the base of the couloir.

The route is a north-facing couloir immediately climber's left of the Zipper, with two or three steeper ice and mixed sections needing screws or pickets, and an upper couloir that steepens to about 60 degrees before topping out on the ridge above the Zipper.

From the top, the standard move is a rappel of more than 100 ft — a double rope is recommended — down into the adjacent Zipper couloir, then climb the last few hundred feet of the Zipper and traverse to the summit; the way down is the standard South Face line and the Lane-Denman saddle.

The approach traverse is itself avalanche terrain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Dec-May
hazards: Avalanche exposure on the approach traverse beneath Denman Peak
Steep sustained ice and mixed ground that can be harder than rated depending on conditions
A rappel that transfers the party into the adjacent Zipper couloir, with rockfall and rope-pull consequences for anyone below
A rappel usually longer than a single 70 m rope doubled
Short winter days on a north aspect
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT: LOVER'S LANE, THE ZIPPER, THE FLY. THIS IS THE LEFTMOST — IMMEDIATELY CLIMBER'S LEFT OF THE ZIPPER.

THE APPROACH TEST IS A COUNT, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT WORKS ON A SKI TRACK IN THE DARK: traversing under DENMAN PEAK toward Lane's base, you turn sharply uphill AT THE FIRST STEEP AVALANCHE FUNNEL YOU MEET. FIRST, not second. IF YOU HAVE PASSED ONE FUNNEL AND CARRIED ON TO ANOTHER, YOU ARE AT THE ZIPPER.

THE CLIMBING TEST IS ANGLE, AND IT IS DECISIVE BECAUSE THIS ROUTE IS THE STEEPEST OF THE THREE: the upper couloir reaches about 60 degrees, with two or three steeper ice and mixed sections below it that want screws. IF NOTHING HAS EXCEEDED ABOUT 45 DEGREES, YOU ARE IN THE ZIPPER OR THE FLY.

THE TOP-OUT TEST IS THE DEFINITIVE ONE, AND IT IS UNIQUE TO THIS ROUTE: LOVER'S LANE FINISHES ON THE RIDGE ABOVE THE ZIPPER, AND THE STANDARD NEXT MOVE IS A RAPPEL OF MORE THAN 100 FT FROM THAT RIDGE INTO THE ZIPPER ITSELF, THEN UP ITS LAST FEW HUNDRED FEET TO THE SUMMIT. SO IF YOU CAN LOOK DOWN INTO A NEIGHBOURING COULOIR FROM WHERE YOU TOPPED OUT, YOU ARE ON LOVER'S LANE. If instead you topped out at a DEAD TREE IN A NOTCH with slings on it, you climbed the Zipper.

PLAN THE ROPE BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE CAR, BECAUSE THE TOP OF THIS ROUTE IS THE WRONG PLACE TO FIND OUT: the rappel is usually longer than 100 ft, so a single 70 m doubled will not reach cleanly in a normal year. Two ropes, or a very deliberate plan for downclimbing the first section.

AND THE THING THAT MAKES THIS ROUTE DIFFERENT FROM ITS NEIGHBOURS': you do not finish on your own line. You rappel into somebody else's, which is a good reason to know where parties on the Zipper are before you pull the rope.

bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass Road pullout
approach_variants.notes: East on the highway through Glacier for about thirteen miles, then the unpaved Hannegan Pass forest road on the LEFT just before the highway crosses the river near the milepost. A couple of minutes up the forest road there is a pullout, and the crag is the obvious cliff on the left a few feet from the road. The bolts on this line, like the rest of the wall's, are old and rusty, so the normal practice is to walk around to the top of the cliff and rig a top-rope from above rather than leading it — build that walk-around into the approach.
approach_variants.season: Spring to autumn for the rock grade while the road is open; also used as a cold-season dry-tooling line.
hazards: Aging, unreplaced bolts on this line and across the crag — top-rope rather than lead
The tricky, pumpy crux is right off the ground, so a fall there lands near the deck
Roadside setting with minimal but real traffic exposure while rigging
Any fixed line or anchor found in place is of unknown age
approach_variants.baseFinding: Find the wall's PROMINENT CRACK first — the one continuous, jammable crack line on this short wall, usually with a fixed static rope hanging down it — and then move IMMEDIATELY RIGHT. This route is the line just right of that crack. The physical test is the first ten feet: this start is technical and pumpy with no crack to jam and no easy way to stand up off the ground, and the crux of the whole route is in that opening sequence. If you can jam from the ground, you are on the wrong line. Negative markers: if a muddy ledge breaks the climbing partway up the line above you and the crack continues thinner to the top, you have stepped back left onto the crack route; if you have walked well past the crack and the wall has changed character, you have gone too far right.

approach_variants.name: Yang Yang Lakes, the secret stair, and the outcrop under the north face
approach_variants.notes: From camp between the Yang Yang Lakes, pass the southern tip of the southernmost lake, walk on about 900 ft, then turn sharply right onto a bearing of roughly 320 degrees. Two ways gain the ridgeline from here and neither is wrong on its own terms: a clear but very steep boot pack to the LEFT up a gully, and a mixed snow, dirt and talus ridge to the RIGHT. Take the gully when there is snow in it and the dirt ridge when there is not — using the gully dry, or the dirt ridge under snow, is the mistake. This is the most difficult and consequential piece of the whole leg. Above it the route follows the ridge south around forested ground and up talus.
approach_variants.season: Late Jul-Sep
hazards: Glacier travel with crevasse hazard just to reach the camp
The precipitous compacted-dirt path of the secret stair
Tedious loose talus on Peak 7004's east slope when the snow has gone
An exposed traverse of narrow, loose ledges near the top, on a summit with very little standing room
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE STAIR STARTS WHERE THE RIDGE RISES SHARPLY AND FALLS AWAY ON ITS NORTH SIDE. Climb the trail and talus up the forested ridge and watch the crest: at the point where it rears up and drops off on the RIGHT, or north, side, a precipitous path of compacted dirt and rock leads up through a small gully to a grassy ledge fifteen to twenty feet wide. Walk WEST along that ledge and make a full 180-degree turn at its far end to pick up the path to the top of the ridge — that reversal is what earns it the name, and if the ledge you are on runs out with no way to double back, it is not the stair. Follow the ridge to a rock outcropping immediately beneath Le Conte's north face; this is where parties drop their packs and it is the base of the climb proper. Peak 7004 is a hump on the ridge that is very hard to get around directly: bypass it on its EAST slope. Above, a loose rock gully gains a ridge on the north side and short steep snow near 7,200 ft leads to the east notch, then a quick, exposed traverse of a narrow ledge to the top.

bivy.name: Le Conte Pass
bivy.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
bivy.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: Reached by crossing Spider-Formidable Col and descending snow and scree. The standard camp for Le Conte, which is climbed from here in a day.
bivy.water: The lakes and a stream
bivy.permit: No permit required (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
bivy.capacity: Many established sites, the best at the south end of the south lake

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

wa_lemah_mountain_east_route.comms: Cell service is unreliable and spotty throughout the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Do not rely on cell phones for emergency communication. Satellite messengers (Garmin InReach, SPOT) are recommended. The area receives service from Kittitas County Sheriff's Search and Rescue; ensure someone knows your itinerary and expected return time.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT, leaving the trail at the Lemah Creek footbridge
approach_variants.notes: Walk the Cooper River trail #1323 about four flat miles to Pete Lake, then roughly another mile and a quarter past the lake staying left at every fork to meet the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn onto the PCT and follow it about a mile to Lemah Creek. The trail-leaving cue is sharp: LEAVE THE TRAIL BEFORE THE FOOTBRIDGE over Lemah Creek. There is a campsite at the bridge. If you have crossed the creek on a bridge you have gone past it. Note that it is unclear whether the Lemah junction is north or south along the PCT from Pete Lake, so navigate to the bridge itself rather than to a compass direction. A faint path climbs the creek side past waterfalls — Whinnimic Falls is the big one — and within about twenty minutes the ground opens onto rocky knobs. The valley floor above is flat and marshy at around 3,700 ft. Continue roughly a mile and more up the valley to the marshy basin under the long snow gully that starts on the north side of Lemah Five. Two lines lead from that basin up to the Lemah Glacier and neither is obvious from the marsh; one of them carries significant brush. Where the gully melts out at a waterfall, it is better to stay RIGHT and return to snow above than to scramble the left side. Leave the gully onto heather around 4,800 ft. One further note on names: Lemah has five summits and the MAIN one is the MIDDLE, Lemah Three. Lemah Two is a different top on the same ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; the chute below the summit is easier as snow than as loose rock, so earlier is often better
hazards: Cold, sometimes thigh-deep creek crossings in the Lemah valley early season
Brush and blowdown on an unmaintained, lightly-used path
The moat beside the rock step
Loose rock on the final hundred feet if you take the gully rather than the ridge
Very poor rock quality generally — this ridge is chossy even by Cascade standards
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival is a rock step, called a chute in published descriptions, and it sits below the main summit after you have crossed the glacier basin and traversed north under Lemah Two.

The touchable sequence at the step, from a party who did it: pass a small waterfall, climb a wet gully for about ten feet, then work RIGHT onto dry rock. Those ten feet are the fourth-class move and the landing beneath them is relatively safe. That waterfall-then-wet-gully-then-step-right is the thing to look for; it is the crux of the whole climb and it is where the approach ends.

There is a tempting alternative that does not work: a ramp far to the LEFT looks as though it would let you bypass the rock step entirely, but reaching it means an unpleasant moat crossing, and the party that looked at it came back down and took the step.

ABOVE the step, the recorded mistake is worth more than the recorded route. Between Lemah Two and Lemah Three there is a small snowfield. A published sketch puts the line just left of the summit rocks, and following that into a mostly snow-filled gully leads to a difficult top, a snow bridge onto loose rock, and about a hundred feet of loose third and fourth class. The party who did that found on the way down that the honest instruction is simply: gain the ridge where it looks easiest. It is.

One route people have taken and should not repeat: descending a gully from Lemah One to reach the glacier. It melts out into very unstable talus blocks.

The Spectacle Lake approach is documented but has been explicitly superseded — the slide area between the lake outlet and the shoulder has grown into ten- to twelve-foot slide alder on a thirty-degree slope, dense enough that you cannot see over it to aim at anything.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake, Upper Lena Lake and the way-trails to St. Peter's Gate
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at about 750 ft, the well-maintained Lena Lake Trail #810 runs about 3 miles through second- and old-growth forest along Lena Creek to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft. Beyond the lake the trail narrows to steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage, roughly 3.5 more miles and 2,700 ft to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft — 6.5 miles and about 4,000 ft from the road, the last reliable water and the last maintained-trail camp.

From Upper Lena Lake the traverse goes cross-country: the Scout Lake way-trail west across meadows and huckleberry-heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake, contour high round it into Scout Basin, then up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft overlooking Ullin's Bathtubs. From Ullin's Pass a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp angling across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending at a loose grungy moraine, then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft — roughly 2.2 miles and 2,200 ft above Upper Lena Lake.

No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Scout Pass and Ullin's Pass are largely clear; many parties still carry an axe
hazards: Extensive off-trail and way-trail route-finding over multiple ridges and passes
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate
A very long outing, up to about 16 miles and 9,000 ft of gain, with limited bail options partway through
Fog and whiteout navigation on Mount Stone's upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route
Exposed headwall sections with several-hundred-foot drops on the Putvin Trail below Lake of the Angels, some using a fixed handline or tree roots
Unbridged stream crossings requiring downclimbing to the bed and back out
The exit is at a different trailhead and needs a shuttle
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE SUMMIT CLIMB IS 300 FT BELOW ST. PETER'S GATE, AND THE FIRST MOVE IS DOWNHILL — WHICH IS THE WHOLE TEST. Reach the Gate (the traverse's high point at about 5,950 ft, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge). Then DESCEND ABOUT 300 FT to the BASE OF A BASALT CLIFF and cache your overnight packs there. The climber's path up the south-face gully starts at the foot of that cliff. A route that goes up from the Gate is not this one.

That is a good fog test precisely because it is counter-intuitive: standing in a notch with the summit above you, the instruction is to lose height first and pick the line up from underneath the cliff band.

SECOND TEST, in the gully: it is a vague climber's path up a Class 3-4 gully on Mount Stone's SOUTH face, and it leads into a ROCK BOWL below the summit block. The bowl is the confirmation — an enclosed basin of rock, not a ridge and not open slope. From it the line joins the standard west-ridge route for a final 100 ft or so of Class 2-3 scrambling on SOLID PILLOW BASALT to the true south summit. That last detail is worth trusting: the rock at the top of this peak is noticeably better than anything below it, so if the last hundred feet is still rubble you have not reached the summit ridge.

WHAT GOES WRONG HERE, AND IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN HYPOTHETICAL: fog is common on Mount Stone's upper mountain and multiple parties have lost the route and ended up in unplanned harder terrain, and in cloud the true south summit is confused with the Middle and North summits. Count your summits and do not accept the first one.

EXIT NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE PLAN, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the standard finish continues southwest half a mile to the Lake of the Angels basin and out the Putvin Trail — a DIFFERENT trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake. Arrange a shuttle or stash a bike before you start.

bivy.name: Upper Lena Lake
bivy.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway.
