Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
bivy.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
bivy.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A splits left. Cross Mountaineer Creek a second time on a log bridge, then climb steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to three hours depending on load.

Colchuck Lake is the LAST RELIABLE WATER; the basin and the wall are dry, though a spring at the base of the boulder field below the formation has been reported and should not be relied on.

The shorter of the two ways into the west basin: from the lake's north end, cross the outlet BELOW the small dam and follow a climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the wall — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the actual base.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
Loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final scramble to the wall
Loose basin talus
Long dry stretch above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: Let It Burn starts in the base gully on the wall's lower-LEFT section, and the last move of the approach is a scramble up a THIRD-CLASS RAMP out of the gully to the foot of the technical climbing. Ramp, not gully floor — belaying from the gully bed means you are below the start. A documented party took about three hours and 47 minutes from trailhead to base, which matches the three-and-a-half to four hour figure the route carries; substantially longer usually means the alder band or the wrong gully.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
approach_variants.notes:
The longer southern option, which avoids the outlet crossing. From Colchuck Lake follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, gaining talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds wet snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history.

Cut north / climber's-LEFT off the Aasgard trail through a band of dense slide alder and heather — genuinely a bushwhack, 15 to 20 minutes, with a cairned path through it if you can find it. Once past the alder, take the LEFT-MOST gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the west basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder band — a real bushwhack
Loose gully talus; snow lingering in the gully into early summer
Cairns stop at the base of the gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: There are a couple of cairns at the BASE of the correct gully and none above it, so do not expect to be led up. Leftmost is the discriminator: a gully further right will not top out into the basin. From the basin, Let It Burn starts on the wall's lower-left section, and the technical climbing begins above a third-class ramp out of the base gully rather than at the gully floor.

approach_variants.name: Summit road, down the grassy ledges under the powerlines
approach_variants.notes: Park at the last lot before the summit on the Mount Erie summit road, at a sharp left-hand bend. Contour downward and west along grassy ledges and short rock steps, through a short section of woods and under the powerlines, to the top of the cliff above Lake Erie. Descend the low third-class ramp to the wall.
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
hazards: Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent to the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Turn LEFT at the bottom of the ramp for the lower tier, which holds False Impressions, Lethal Weapon, Intimidator and Terminator.

Use Intimidator as the datum: it begins at the lowest point of the wall. Everything on this tier is located by walking the base from there.

Going south past the lower tier over two blocky fourth-class scrambles puts you on the upper tier with Tindall's Terror and Scarface — a different set of routes.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout, the steep forest path, and the treed ledge below the east face
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pond pullout on the south side of SR-20 about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass, a small dirt turnout marked by a roadside pond. The climbers' path starts just left, west, of the highway's east-side guardrail and immediately begins gaining elevation through forest.

It pops out of the trees onto an open scree-and-boulder slope that climbs directly toward the Liberty Bell group towers, with Lexington Tower's east face visible above. Figure 30-45 minutes, some parties closer to an hour, of steep hiking and scrambling from the pullout to the base, gaining several hundred feet over roughly a third of a mile. No water; carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Frequent rockfall in both gullies flanking the treed ledge
A 5.8 pitch as one of the two ways to gain the base
Snow lingering in the talus into early-mid summer
No water on the approach
A descent that finishes at the Blue Lake Trail, not at the pond pullout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A TREED LEDGE, AND THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO IT AND SNOW DECIDES WHICH. From the talus, either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge. Snow lingering in the talus and at the base of the wall into early-mid summer affects whether you gain the ledge from the left or the right.

SO THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A LEDGE WITH TREES ON IT, PART WAY UP THE WALL, NOT GROUND LEVEL. Trees underfoot on a bench beneath a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation, and it works without seeing the tower above.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE FROM THE SAME LEDGE, AND IT IS A LEFT-RIGHT TEST: TOOTH AND CLAW BEGINS NEAR THE LEFT SIDE OF THE TREED LEDGE AND ANGLES RIGHTWARD ACROSS SLABS TO ITS FIRST BOLT. If you are traversing right across slabs looking for a bolt, you are on Tooth and Claw, a 5.12a, not on the East Face.

HELMET UP BEFORE THE GULLIES, NOT AFTER: both gullies flanking the ledge see fairly frequent rockfall.

WHERE THE DAY ENDS, WHICH IS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE RIDGE: the standard descent is a walk-off from the NOTCH BELOW THE TRUE SUMMIT, not from the summit itself. Head west and downclimb a short gully on skier's left, about twenty feet of third class; old rap slings are present but most parties downclimb. From the base of that gully, traverse RIGHT, north, until you intersect the well-worn climbers' and cattle trail that also serves Liberty Bell, and follow it down to the Blue Lake Trail. Lower down, watch for a faint climbers' path that cuts back toward the highway and saves close to a mile of road walking.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch, then its FAR EASTERN edge
approach_variants.notes: Reach the Concord-Lexington notch via the standard Blue Lake Trailhead approach, trending toward the col between Concord and Lexington Towers rather than toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully. Higher in that gully a climbers' path appears along its left side and is better than the gully bed. Three pitches.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Two notches a few hundred feet apart on one ridge
A gully bed better avoided in favour of the path along its left side
Far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col, so fainter tread
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE'S FIRST BELAY STARTS FROM THE FAR EASTERN EDGE OF THE NOTCH. So there are two finds and they nest: the right notch, then the right end of it.

WHICH NOTCH: THE CONCORD-LEXINGTON NOTCH IS THE ONE WHERE CONCORD IS ON ONE SIDE OF YOU AND LEXINGTON ON THE OTHER, AND THE CONCORD WALL IN FRONT OF YOU GIVES ONTO LOW-ANGLE, GRAVELLY LEDGES RATHER THAN A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM. IF YOU ARE FACING A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM, YOU ARE AT THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH, ONE SADDLE BACK, AND LOOKING AT CONCORD'S NORTH FACE.

WHICH END OF IT: the FAR EASTERN edge. The notch is a gap with two ends; walk to the eastern one before racking up. Concord's south-face routes go the other way, up the wall on the notch's Concord side.

CONFIRM BY HARDWARE, BECAUSE THIS ROUTE HAS A DISTINCTIVE ONE: THERE IS A BOLTED SUMMIT ANCHOR. Parties either make one single-rope rappel to an intermediate bolted anchor partway down the face and continue down, or run a full double-rope rappel directly back to the Concord-Lexington notch. A bolted top and a bolted mid-face station on a three-pitch route is what this line offers.

FROM THE NOTCH THE APPROACH GULLY AND CLIMBERS' TRAIL LEAD BACK TO THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, which is the same car you started from. That is not true of Lexington's east-side routes, which start at the hairpin pond pullout on the other side of the ridge.

crowds.peakTraffic: Described by Climbing.com as "one of the more popular routes on the wall" on Liberty Bell's East Face — it shares the same popular approach/wall as the much-climbed Thin Red Line, boosting its relative traffic versus other harder East Face lines.
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Dozens per season among 5.12 free climbers (LOW-MEDIUM confidence estimate)

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then about 10 metres right of Thin Red Line
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as the other Liberty Crack-area routes: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the East Face talus.

Five pitches, about 200 m of climbing, established rope-solo in 2014. It shares some climbing with the old aid route Liberty Loop.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A ten-metre offset from a neighbouring route as the only positional marker
Several closely spaced starts on the same wall
Loose talus in the upper approach
Two ropes needed to rappel the route from its top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS ABOUT 10 METRES RIGHT OF THIN RED LINE, AND TEN METRES IS THE ENTIRE MARGIN FOR ERROR ON THIS WALL. That is a measured offset from a known line, which is the best that exists here, and it means you must locate Thin Red Line first.

HOW TO BOUND IT WITHOUT SEEING THE WHOLE FACE, USING THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft LEFT of Liberty Crack, then LIBERTY CRACK, then FREEDOM OR DEATH on a small leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, then THIN RED LINE, then THIS ROUTE 10 m right of it, then LIVE FREE OR DIE, then THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE at the far right or north edge under a red roof.

THE STRONGEST CONFIRMATION IS THE HARDWARE, AND IT IS COUNTABLE: EVERY STATION ON THIS LINE IS A TWO-BOLT ANCHOR WITH FIXED BINERS. If you top out a pitch and find no bolts and no biners, you are not on it. From the top of pitch 3 you can skip the pitch-2 anchor and rappel directly to the pitch-1 anchor, so two rappels get you back to the ground from P3.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: keep walking right and the next thing you meet is the ground Live Free or Die and the Independence Route use, at the far right end of the face. The Independence Route's own marker is unmistakable when visible: a red-coloured roof and alcove, the Baer Ceiling, about 85 m above its start.

AND WHERE IT GOES: at five pitches the route joins the top of pitch 7 on Thin Red Line, from which you either continue climbing or rappel this route's own anchors with two ropes back to the base.

wa_liberty_bell_beckey_route.rappel_count_note: Three rappels on a single 60 m rope, which is the rope this route recommends and the configuration these three stations describe. The count of two comes from the SAME station set rather than a different one: the first rappel, off the trees, is optional and replaces a downclimb of the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem, so a party that downclimbs that section starts at the second station and reaches the ground in two single-rope rappels. Accounts recording two and accounts recording three are describing the same anchors. Individual lengths are not published; the two lower rappels are reported at about 25 m each, and a single 60 m rope reaches the first ledge with room to spare. This is the standard descent line shared with the East Face and Northwest Face routes.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of SR-20, roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required and the lot is small enough that it fills on summer weekends.

Walk the maintained Blue Lake Trail for about a mile and a half. The turnoff is a signed junction — the sign points straight on for Blue Lake and left for Liberty Bell Trail #727, Climbing Access — and it sits just past a small stream in a meadow, with a large cairn beside it. That stream is the last water you can count on.

Trail #727 climbs hard through granite slabs, talus and heather benches toward the gully that drains the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. In the gully itself the loose ground is least bad if you keep to climber's left for the lower two thirds, then cross and hug climber's right for the rest. Where the boot path forks a couple of hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch; the right branch leads on toward Lexington and Concord's south side.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep (dry)
hazards: loose rock and party-induced rockfall in the notch gully — helmets on before entering, and avoid stacking up under other parties
steep 3rd-class steps on the climbers' path when wet
trailhead lot fills early on summer weekends; roadside parking on SR-20 is limited
approach_variants.baseFinding: Do not start climbing from the notch itself. The first pitch begins from a tree standing roughly 30 feet BELOW the crest of the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, on the Liberty Bell (north) side. From that tree a small ledge runs left; walk it and it delivers you to the foot of a blocky chimney, and that chimney is pitch one. If you are stood on the low point of the notch looking for a crack going straight up, you are too high and too far right — drop back down to the tree. Concord Tower's North Face starts from the top of the same notch, on the opposite (south) wall, so two parties can be at the same notch climbing in opposite directions; check which wall you are facing before you rack up.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow gully to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The same line as the summer approach, but the upper gully below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch commonly holds snow into late June and the boot path through the slabs and heather may be buried lower down. Parties carry an ice axe, and crampons if the snow has refrozen overnight.

SR-20 over Washington and Rainy Passes is gated every winter — it typically closes in late November or early December and reopens somewhere between mid-April and early May, with the exact dates set by snowpack and avalanche conditions rather than a calendar. Until the gate opens there is no drive-up access to the Blue Lake Trailhead at all.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening (typically mid-late Apr or early May) through late Jun
hazards: firm or refrozen snow in the gully — a slip runs a long way over rock
moat at the transition from snow to rock at the base of the first pitch
wet-loose and cornice debris in the gully during spring melt
SR-20 gated in winter — no vehicle access to the trailhead until the highway reopens
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow changes what the last hundred metres looks like. With the gully filled, the notch reads as a clean snow finish rather than a scree saddle, and the tree that marks the Beckey start — about 30 feet below the crest on the Liberty Bell side, with a small ledge running left to the blocky chimney — can be partly buried or standing above a moat. If you top out onto the notch crest and find no tree, you have gone above the start; downclimb the last stretch on the Liberty Bell side and look for it. Expect a moat where snow pulls away from the rock at the base of the chimney.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then the leftward-trending ramp just RIGHT of Liberty Crack
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. Roughly an hour, steep near the top, no water.

Four pitches, all belays bolted. The route can be rappelled with a 60 m rope from the top of pitch 3, or continued into the shared terrain of Liberty Crack toward the summit.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start only a few paces from Liberty Crack's, on a wall where several routes begin within a short distance
Loose talus in the upper approach
No water on the approach
Rappelling from the top of pitch 3 needs a 60 m rope
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS A SMALL LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP, AND BOLTS SHOULD BE VISIBLE ABOVE IT. That is the whole test, it is visual, and it works at arm's length in cloud where nothing else on this wall does: a ramp leaning LEFT, low down, with bolts on the face above it.

POSITION: JUST TO THE RIGHT OF LIBERTY CRACK. Not fifty yards right, just right. If you had to walk more than a few paces from the base of Liberty Crack, you have gone past it toward the Thin Red Line starts.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: LIBERTY CRACK IS REACHED BY TRAVERSING 40 FT LEFT ON 3RD AND 4TH CLASS LEDGES FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS. IF YOU ARE SCRAMBLING LEFT ON LEDGES, YOU HAVE OVERSHOT PAST THIS ROUTE IN THE WRONG DIRECTION.

A SECOND CONFIRMATION IF THE RAMP IS AMBIGUOUS: this is a four-pitch route with EVERY BELAY BOLTED. There is no gear anchor to hunt for at the top of pitch 1. If you finish a rope length and find no bolts, you are not on it.

AND THE ROUTE THAT SHARES THIS START, WHICH IS WHY GETTING IT RIGHT MATTERS TWICE: A Servant to Liberty climbs the first THREE pitches of this route before stepping right into Thin Red Line. Two parties standing at the same ramp may be going to two different places.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then LEFT along the base to the loose corner system
approach_variants.notes:
Standard East Face approach: park at the pond pullout near the hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile to the East Face talus.

Fourteen pitches. Although it is technically the easiest all-free route up the East Face, the route takes about one and a half times as much effort as Liberty Crack, on often poor rock and gear, and apart from where it intersects Liberty Crack there are no bolted belay stances.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Poor rock and poor gear over fourteen pitches
No bolted belays except where the line crosses Liberty Crack
Roughly one and a half times the effort of Liberty Crack for an easier grade
A descent that lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ONLY ROUTE ON THE EAST FACE THAT STARTS TO THE LEFT OF LIBERTY CRACK, AND THAT MAKES IT THE EASIEST START ON THE WALL TO CONFIRM BY ELIMINATION. It begins at a LOOSE CORNER SYSTEM ABOUT 100 FT LEFT OF LIBERTY CRACK.

SO THE TEST IS DIRECTIONAL AND COUNTABLE: from Liberty Crack, walk LEFT roughly 100 ft to a corner system. Every other line here is to the RIGHT of Liberty Crack. IF YOU ARE WALKING RIGHT ALONG THE BASE, YOU ARE WALKING AWAY FROM THIS ROUTE, and everything you meet in that direction belongs to something else: Freedom or Death, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All, Live Free or Die and the Independence Route in that order.

AND LIBERTY CRACK ITSELF IS FOUND BY TRAVERSING 40 FT LEFT ON THIRD AND FOURTH CLASS LEDGES FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS, so this route is roughly 140 ft of leftward travel from where the path meets the rock.

A HARDWARE TEST THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY FROM THE REST OF THIS FACE: there are NO BOLTED BELAY STANCES on this route except where it crosses Liberty Crack. Several of its neighbours are fully bolted. IF YOU REACH A BOLTED ANCHOR EARLY, YOU ARE PROBABLY NOT ON FREEDOM RIDER.

WHAT TO EXPECT SO YOU DO NOT SECOND-GUESS THE FIND: the corner system is described as loose, and the rock and gear on the route generally as often poor. Poor rock at the start is consistent with this line, not evidence you are off it.

DESCENT: the shared East Face rappel line into Beckey Gully, or downclimbing the sheltered Beckey Route slab in good conditions. Both put you on the west side of the mountain, away from the East Face pullout.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Beckey gully, stopping a couple of hundred feet BELOW the notch at the side gully with the large cave
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Beckey line: Blue Lake Trailhead, about 1.5 miles of maintained trail to the meadow and stream crossing, then the climbers' boot path up through slabs, talus and meadow into the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.

Three pitches. The route rejoins the Beckey Route line near its top, so the descent is the standard two single-rope rappels off chain and bolted anchors down to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start that is passed by every party heading for the notch
A cave feature shared with a neighbouring route
Rockfall in the main gully, which sits directly above the start
Early-season snow in the approach gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STOP SHORT OF THE NOTCH. A COUPLE OF HUNDRED VERTICAL FEET BELOW THE TOP OF THE LIBERTY-CONCORD NOTCH, LOCATE A SIDE GULLY ON CLIMBER'S LEFT WITH A LARGE CAVE IN IT. Walk partway up that side gully, then move RIGHT onto a TREED LEDGE to start.

SO THERE ARE THREE THINGS TO FIND AND ALL THREE ARE TACTILE RATHER THAN VISUAL: a SIDE GULLY on the left, a LARGE CAVE inside it, and a LEDGE WITH TREES on its right-hand side. Trees on a ledge are unmistakable underfoot.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE MOST USEFUL LINE HERE, BECAUSE THE ERROR IS ALWAYS THE SAME ONE: IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE NOTCH, YOU HAVE GONE ROUGHLY TWO HUNDRED FEET TOO FAR. This route leaves the main gully below its top. Everything at the notch itself belongs to the Beckey Route, Overexposure and the standard descent.

A SECOND ROUTE SHARES THE CAVE, SO THE LEDGE IS WHAT SEPARATES THEM: Sidewinder also scrambles to a major shelf or ramp BELOW the cave feature. This route goes PARTWAY UP the side gully and then steps RIGHT onto the treed ledge. Below the cave is Sidewinder's ground; up and right of it is this one.

WHERE IT GOES: three pitches rejoining the Beckey Route near its top, then the standard two single-rope rappels off chains to the notch and the gully back to the trail.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, then all the way RIGHT to the north edge of the face
approach_variants.notes: Park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face. TWELVE PITCHES, FIRST CLIMBED WALL-STYLE IN 1966 WITH 180 PITONS AND FIVE BOLTS OVER FOUR DAYS, and later freed. The line takes the profusely overhanging northeast corner of the East Face and joins Thin Red Line at M&M Ledge.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A profusely overhanging corner, first climbed over four days with 180 pitons
A cairned forest path that is hard to follow before dawn
Several closely spaced starts on the same wall
Loose talus in the upper approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
START ON THE FAR RIGHT, THE NORTH EDGE, OF THE EAST FACE, AND CONFIRM IT BY LOCATING THE RED-COLOURED ROOF AND ALCOVE OF THE BAER CEILING ABOUT 85 M ABOVE. That is the marker, it is coloured, it is high enough to be visible when the base is in cloud, and no other route on this wall has one.

SO THE TEST IS A COLOUR AND A HEIGHT: a red roof roughly 85 metres up, at the right-hand end of the face. If there is no red roof above you, keep walking right.

THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE, WHICH BOUNDS IT ON THE OTHER SIDE: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft LEFT of Liberty Crack, LIBERTY CRACK, FREEDOM OR DEATH on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, THIN RED LINE, LIBERTY AND INJUSTICE FOR ALL 10 m right of that, LIVE FREE OR DIE, and THIS ROUTE last. You cannot go further right and still be on the East Face; the ground beyond turns the corner onto the northeast aspect, where Dark Side of Liberty lives.

A SECOND CONFIRMATION FROM THE SHAPE OF THE ROCK: this is the PROFUSELY OVERHANGING northeast corner. If the wall above your start leans back rather than out, you have not reached the corner.

WHERE IT GOES, WHICH ALSO SETTLES THE DESCENT ARGUMENT: the route joins Thin Red Line at M&M Ledge, and fixed anchors let parties rappel from the top of pitch 8 back down the East Face to their packs on a single 70 m rope, rather than continuing to the true summit and finishing on the far side of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path toward Concord, then the ten-foot step onto the northwest plateau
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft on WA-20 roughly 1 mile WEST of Washington Pass, follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles through forest to a small meadow below Liberty Bell. THIS IS THE OPPOSITE TRAILHEAD FROM THE HAIRPIN POND PULLOUT USED BY THE EAST FACE ROUTES.

Leave the Blue Lake Trail on the well-beaten climbers' path that splits LEFT just past a small stream crossing, and follow it up through slabs, talus and heather benches toward Concord Tower. Roughly 2,000-plus ft of gain over 2-2.5 miles one-way; plan 1.5-2.5 hours. The gully below the plateau can hold snow into early summer and sheds rockfall as it melts, so helmet up through the talus and gully.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A rockfall-prone approach gully that holds snow into early summer
A ten-foot step that is easy to overshoot, leading parties onto harder ground
Queues at the popular Beckey rappels in busy weather; parties have reported stacking up several deep
One pitch of the descent can run slightly over 60 m, so a single-rope party may have to downclimb a short section
A loose gully downclimb from the notch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ENTIRE FIND IS A TEN-FOOT STEP, AND THE ROUTE'S OWN DESCRIPTION MAKES IT A NEGATIVE TEST: IF YOU ARE CLIMBING MORE THAN ABOUT TEN FEET OF EASY FOURTH OR LOW-FIFTH CLASS TO GAIN THE PLATEAU, YOU HAVE MISSED THE SPOT.

HOW YOU GET TO IT: rather than dropping into the main Beckey and Liberty Bell-Concord gully, STAY ON THE CLIMBERS' TRAIL AS IT CLIMBS TOWARD CONCORD FOR AS LONG AS IT REASONABLY CAN, then break LEFT onto that short, well-trodden step. The step gains the little-visited northwest plateau of Liberty Bell, a bench of LARCH GROVES below the northwest face proper.

SO THERE ARE TWO CONFIRMATIONS AND BOTH WORK WITHOUT SEEING THE SUMMIT: the step is TEN FEET AND WELL-TRODDEN, and above it you are standing on a BENCH WITH LARCH TREES ON IT. Larches on a bench, on the northwest side, below a wall, is the plateau.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTES OFF THIS PATH, WHICH IS WHERE PARTIES ACTUALLY GO WRONG: if you have dropped into the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord and are climbing scree toward a notch, you are on the Beckey Route and Overexposure approach, not this one. THIS ROUTE NEVER ENTERS THAT GULLY.

WHERE THE DAY ENDS UP, WHICH IS NOT WHERE IT STARTED: from the west summit you downclimb and scramble to the top of the Beckey Route line and descend that way rather than reversing the northwest face. Rappel about 20 ft down the upper Beckey pitch to a ledge, traverse left, east, to a TREE HUNG WITH RAP SLINGS, one single-rope 60 m rappel to a flatter stance, then a double-rope rappel from a bolted anchor to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft, and downclimb the loose gully back to the climbers' path.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Beckey gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then scramble ABOVE it
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey Route as far as the notch: Blue Lake Trailhead and Forest Trail #314, about 1.5 miles of maintained trail to the small meadow and stream crossing, then the climbers' boot path through slabs, talus and meadow to the fork below the notch, staying LEFT to the notch itself at about 7,300 ft. Roughly 2 miles and 2,100 ft of gain, 1.5-2.5 hours.

Expect the same early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Exposed opening moves off the notch, above the gully
Early-season snow in the approach gully requiring an axe
Rockfall in the approach gully as it melts out
Two notches on the same ridge that are easy to confuse
Congestion at the main descent line, which shares anchors with the Beckey Route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS RIGHT AT THE TOP OF THE NOTCH BETWEEN LIBERTY BELL AND CONCORD TOWER, AND SPECIFICALLY IT BEGINS ABOVE THE NOTCH RATHER THAN AT IT. That distinction is the whole find: Beckey Route parties stop at the notch and start climbing from it. This route asks for a little extra scrambling UP from the notch into the initial belay.

WHICH NOTCH, BECAUSE THERE ARE TWO ON THIS RIDGE AND THEY ARE ONLY A FEW HUNDRED FEET APART: the LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD notch, at about 7,300 ft, is the one this route uses. The CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch is further along and serves Concord's south face and Lexington's north face. The discriminating test at the top of the gully is what the wall in front of you offers: THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH FACES A CRACK SYSTEM. The Concord-Lexington notch gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges.

SO: CRACK SYSTEM IN FRONT OF YOU AT THE TOP OF THE GULLY MEANS YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT NOTCH FOR THIS ROUTE.

CONFIRM BY THE LENGTH OF THE CLIMB, WHICH IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: four pitches at Grade II 5.8, and THE SECOND PITCH TOPS OUT AT THE SAME BOLTED ANCHOR SYSTEM THAT STARTS THE STANDARD LIBERTY BELL DESCENT. Most parties either stop there or continue a few hundred feet of fourth and low-fifth scrambling to the true summit. If you have climbed four pitches and are nowhere near a bolted descent anchor, you are not on this route.

BUDGET EXTRA TIME AND CARE FOR THE SCRAMBLE INTO THE FIRST BELAY compared with Beckey Route parties, because it is exposed and it is where this route differs.

rappel_detail.notes: First of four double-rope rappels down the East Face, starting near M&M Ledge.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor, climber's-left of M&M Ledge
hazards: The M&M Ledge anchor is two pieces of old fixed gear, a pin and a wire. A large and reportedly bomber horn sits up and left of it that would make a much better station and nobody has rigged it - carry cord if you want to use it
Because the line trends left rather than dropping straight down, a rope end blown or thrown off line is awkward to recover
rappel_detail.station: The rappels begin at M&M Ledge. From it, work climber's LEFT to reach good bolts - the bolted stations are not directly beneath where the ledge drops you, and finding them is the only route-finding on this descent. If you rappel from the ledge's own anchor instead, that is a fixed piton and a fixed wire, and the rappel from it also trends climber's left.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the East Face line on double ropes.
hazards: Steep sustained face with nothing to stand on between stations - once on the rope you are committed to reaching the next anchor
rappel_detail.station: Second station on the bolted line down the East Face.

rappel_detail.notes: Continues down the East Face line on double ropes.
hazards: Anything knocked off a station here falls the full height of the wall
rappel_detail.station: Third station on the bolted line.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel, reaching the ground at the base of the East Face.
hazards: Talus and snow at the base of the face for much of the season
rappel_detail.station: Last rappel, essentially reaching the ground at the base of the East Face - the side you approached from, so this is where your pack is.

wa_liberty_bell_thin_red_line.rappel_count_note: Four rappels off bolts, reached by working climber's LEFT from M&M Ledge, and the description that gives that sequence assumes TWO ropes - four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground. Parties who first rappel from M&M Ledge's own fixed pin-and-wire anchor, which also trends climber's left, count five. No single-rope option is described for this line. The alternative descent, for parties who continue to the true summit rather than rappelling from the ledge, is the standard Liberty Bell notch route - a downclimb east to a two-bolt station and two rappels of about 25 m into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch - which is fewer rappels but lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face approach and from your pack. Per-station distances are not published; the figures given assume near-full-length double-rope rappels.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then RIGHT of Liberty Crack
approach_variants.notes: From the Highway 20 hairpin curve on the east side of Washington Pass, locate the small pond on the south side of the road; the pullout is on the north side of the highway. Follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond eastward into forest and up to the East Face talus. Note that this route's stored trailhead coordinate does not agree with the one every other East Face route on this peak carries. Use the pond and the hairpin, not a stored point.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start that has to be sighted from a distance rather than found along the base
Snow travel at the base into early summer
Several route starts within a short distance of each other on the same wall
A summit descent that strands you on the opposite side of the mountain from your car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS CLIMBER'S RIGHT OF LIBERTY CRACK, AND THE PUBLISHED METHOD FOR FINDING IT IS TO WORK DOWNWARD FROM THE FEATURES ABOVE RATHER THAN ALONG THE BASE. Look climber's right of Liberty Crack and connect the line down from the features higher on the wall. Some mellow snow travel is usually necessary to reach the base.

SO THIS IS THE ONE EAST FACE ROUTE WHOSE START IS HONESTLY DESCRIBED AS A SIGHTING PROBLEM, AND THAT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE THE CLOUD COMES DOWN. Fix the line from the talus while you can see the wall. If you cannot see the wall, you cannot locate this start by walking the base, and no description will change that.

WHAT YOU CAN DO WITHOUT A VIEW IS BOUND IT, BECAUSE THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE IS KNOWN. Left to right: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, LIBERTY CRACK, FREEDOM OR DEATH just right of it on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, THIN RED LINE, LIBERTY AND INJUSTICE FOR ALL about 10 m right of Thin Red Line, LIVE FREE OR DIE, and THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE at the far right or north edge of the face beneath a red roof and alcove called the Baer Ceiling about 85 m up.

SO: IF YOU ARE STANDING AT A LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP WITH BOLTS ABOVE IT, YOU ARE ONE ROUTE LEFT, ON FREEDOM OR DEATH. IF YOU CAN SEE A RED ROOF ABOUT 85 M ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE WALKED ALL THE WAY RIGHT TO THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE.

THE DESCENT DECIDES WHICH CAR YOU END AT, AND THIS ROUTE HAS BOTH OPTIONS: from the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face, returning to your pack and the East Face approach. If you instead continue to the true summit and take the standard Liberty Bell notch descent, you finish on the WEST side of the mountain and need a shuttle or a road walk back.

approach_variants.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and the Carbon Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Everyone walks in from White River Campground, and the walking is over quickly. The Glacier Basin Trail is maintained for about three and a half miles to the basin at roughly 5,900 ft, which holds the last running water you will see until the descent brings you down to Camp Schurman. Above the basin there is no trail: a boot track climbs snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, and from the far side of the pass you drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and stay roped for the rest of the trip. The counter-clockwise traverse under Mount Ruth and around the toe of Curtis Ridge is the part that decides the day, because it runs directly beneath Willis Wall and both walls shed rock and ice more freely once the sun is on them. Most parties split the approach with a bivy on lower Curtis Ridge somewhere between about 7,200 and 7,600 ft, right beside the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier, and it is the only place on the whole approach where you get a head-on look at the route to pick your line. Curtis Ridge is broad and deceptive in cloud and parties repeatedly think they have arrived when they have not; the rule everyone repeats is to stay low and, when in doubt, angle down and right. If what you are looking over is not a mellow fifty-foot talus slope, you are too high, and climbing further only cliffs you out. A climbing permit is required and this line carries its own briefing, so sort both before driving up rather than on the morning you want to leave.
approach_variants.season: Early May to mid-June
hazards: Rockfall and icefall off Willis Wall onto the Carbon Glacier traverse, worsening through the day
Serac collapse off the Liberty Cap Glacier onto the west side of the Carbon basin
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Winthrop and Carbon crossings
The moat between glacier and rock at the foot of the ridge, which turns parties around outright
Rockfall into Thumb Rock camp, which has been swept out by slides off the tower opposite
Sustained steep ice to around 60 degrees above the Black Pyramid
Altitude, and no retreat down the route once above Thumb Rock
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming off Curtis Ridge everything underfoot is glacier, so the ridge has to be picked out by shape and by what stands either side of it. Where Liberty Ridge meets the Carbon it is a rock NOSE, a prow of broken volcanic rock at roughly 8,450 to 8,600 ft rather than a snow slope, and often the place you can watch rocks peeling off. Memorise the compass check, because it holds everywhere on the climb. Facing uphill, Willis Wall is on your LEFT, to the east, and the Liberty Wall is on your RIGHT, to the west. If the big wall is on your right hand as you look up, you are on the wrong feature. Cross the Carbon up climber's right of the main icefall and aim for the nose. The real crux of the approach is the moat where the glacier pulls away from the rock, and parties are stopped here more often than anywhere else on the climb — not because the ridge is hard to see, but because there is no way across the gap that day. You can gain the crest from either flank or straight up the toe, at roughly 8,600 to 8,800 ft. The east flank is steeper and carries more rock bands, so most parties cross onto the west flank as soon as they are on the crest and stay there up to camp. Which side actually goes is decided by the moat and the crevasses rather than by preference, so scout instead of committing to the first weakness. In poor visibility the confirmation is not at the toe at all, it is above it: Thumb Rock, a 300 ft gendarme of broken volcanic rock at somewhere around 10,500 ft, with a second loose tower opposite it and barely room for two small tents in the saddle between. Parties fogged out at the base have started to retreat and turned around again only when Thumb Rock showed through a break in the cloud, so if you are unsure, wait for a window and look UP rather than along. You have gone too far west if the ground opens into the Carbon basin beneath the Liberty Wall's hanging ice; crevasses routinely push parties that way, and the next spine past that wall is Ptarmigan Ridge, a different climb off a different camp.

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the standard one — flat, partly wind-sheltered tent sites tucked behind the rock buttress, reached by moderate snow and loose rock bands. Reports place the platforms anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,700 ft depending on which bench and how much snow is in; the ground above the rock is more exposed and takes the full wind. There is no liquid water at any point. The approach ramps immediately below turn loose and unpleasant once they melt out, so late-season parties arrive slower than they plan.
bivy.water: none — melt snow or ice
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: a handful of existing snow platforms; can be crowded in season, and late parties dig their own

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier access bivy
bivy.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp, and the usual way to split what is otherwise a 7-10 hour push from the car to Thumb Rock. Established sites sit in the ramp that gains the Carbon at about 7,300 ft, with more ground on the ridge crest above. Parties camp here specifically so they can cross the exposed ground under Willis Wall early and cold. Do not pitch out on the open Carbon under the wall to shorten the morning — that is the fall line for serac collapse off the summit icecap.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a few small sites in the access gully and on the ridge

bivy.name: Glacier Basin camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED first camp for parties not pushing straight to Thumb Rock. Composting toilet, bear boxes. Last dependable running water on the route — from here it is snow and ice, and Thumb Rock has none.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: DESCENT camp. Liberty Ridge tops out near Liberty Cap and most parties come down the Emmons-Winthrop, so this is where a slow summit day ends rather than a forced night out high on the ice. Ranger hut and solar toilet, both potentially buried in snow — carry blue bags and pack them out. Reserve well ahead.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

bivy.name: Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and the Ptarmigan crest
approach_variants.notes: The prettier of the two ways in, and the one that puts you on the route's own ridge from the bottom. Mowich Lake sits at about 4,929 ft at the end of a road that has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed in April 2025 (before that it was often snowed shut into early or mid July), and that single fact decides whether this approach is available at all. From the lake it is three to four miles of trail up through Spray Park; at about 6,400 ft a beaten path breaks off right toward the permanent snow. Cross the Flett Glacier in the gap between Echo Rock, 7,870 ft, and Observation Rock, 8,364 ft, at somewhere around 7,500 ft, climb to the saddle immediately east of Observation Rock, and cross onto the Russell Glacier near 7,800 ft. From there the crest runs south, sometimes on rock but mostly on easy snow just left of the crest line, with the Russell falling away east. This stretch is uncrevassed and is genuinely a walk. The last few hundred yards to camp are not: the crest narrows to a knife edge with an overhanging rock step on it, and most parties bypass that by dropping about 200 ft onto 40 degree snow on the east side and traversing back. Well above the base, the exit gully through the rock buttress is the one identification climbers argue about — whether it is the first or the second break in the cliffs is genuinely unsettled, so climb to the fixed pin rather than to a count. The descent is the Emmons route out to White River, so coming in this way needs a car shuttle or a very long road walk.
approach_variants.season: June to early July
hazards: Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's ice cliffs onto the traverse between camp and the bergschrund
Bare rock at the crux chimney in lean years, which raises both the grade and the rockfall
Bergschrund and crevasses at the start of the technical ground, around 9,800 ft
Sustained 45 to 60 degree snow and ice, with a long exposed rising traverse
Rockfall off decomposing volcanic cliffs on everything below about 12,200 ft
Overhanging rock step on the knife edge into high camp
No road access to Mowich Lake since the April 2025 bridge closure, and a descent that finishes at a different trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding: The walking and the climbing are cleanly separated here and the boundary is a flat spot, but the climb does not start above camp — it starts several hundred feet BELOW it and on the far side of the ridge, and that is what parties get wrong. Follow the crest south from the saddle beside Observation Rock until the ridge stops rising and levels out at about 10,200 to 10,300 ft. You will know the place without being told, because four things sit together there and nowhere else: room for a couple of small tents on flat ground, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon Glacier immediately EAST of you, huge banded ice cliffs standing directly SOUTH above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and a clean view straight across at Liberty Ridge. From that camp the route drops WEST off the crest a few hundred feet onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, aiming for a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the middle of the face. Look that crossing over from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there and its condition changes year to year. The traverse down to it passes under the run-out of the ice cliffs and is usually walked across old avalanche debris and stray boulders sitting on the ice, so it is done in the dark and fast. Two ways to know you are wrong. If you have descended onto the Mowich Glacier and kept going west or south, you are wandering out onto Mowich Face ground rather than to the schrund. And if you cross a bergschrund with no ice cliffs above and to your left, stop: from the schrund the route rises back EAST, climber's left, toward those cliffs, not away from them. The route finishes on Liberty Cap; Columbia Crest is a separate trip across the summit plateau and is not part of this climb.

approach_variants.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and across the Carbon
approach_variants.notes: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May to early July
hazards: Hours of exposure to rockfall and icefall crossing beneath Willis Wall and the Liberty Wall
Ice avalanche off the Liberty Cap Glacier's cliffs onto the traverse into the route
Crevasses on the Winthrop and the Carbon, thin bridges early and open cracks late
Committing traverse with no quick exit once past Curtis Ridge
Sustained 45 to 60 degree ice and a rock or mixed crux around 12,000 ft
Very little traffic, so no established track above the Carbon and a slow rescue
Losing the faint Emmons descent to the well-trodden Disappointment Cleaver at the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: This is the approach on which Rainier's two Liberty Cap routes actually get confused, and the trap is a physical one: there is usually a bootpack running from St. Elmo Pass to the Carbon Glacier, and it was stamped in by parties going to LIBERTY Ridge. It is the right track as far as the Carbon and the wrong one after that. Working west you cross under Willis Wall and meet a narrow rock and snow ridge dropping straight to the glacier. That first spine is Liberty Ridge. Keep going. Past it the ground opens beneath a big pale cirque wall capped by hanging ice, and the next crest beyond that wall, roughly a mile and a half further west, is Ptarmigan Ridge. Put it the simple way and it is hard to get wrong: on Liberty Ridge the Liberty Wall is on your right, and on Ptarmigan Ridge it is on your left. Cross the Carbon below the seracs, gain the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge up to the flat high camp at 10,200 to 10,300 ft. That flat is the base of the climb, and four things fix it together: room for a couple of small tents, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon immediately east, banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and Liberty Ridge in full view straight across. From camp the route drops WEST off the crest onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, near a rock outcropping about the middle of the face — study that crossing from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there. Above the schrund the line rises back east, climber's left, toward the ice cliffs. If you have crossed a schrund with no ice cliff up and left of you, you are on the wrong part of the mountain.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout (east of Washington Pass)
waypoints.directions: Park in the pullout on the north side of SR-20 at the hairpin curve, roughly 0.3 to 0.5 mile past the Washington Pass Overlook turnoff and a short distance east of Washington Pass. SR-20 is gated for the winter and typically doesn't reopen until mid-to-late April or early May, so this approach isn't accessible until the highway opens for the season.

waypoints.name: Base of east face
waypoints.directions: Walk back west along the SR-20 shoulder toward the pass to the small pond on the south side of the highway, skirt the pond's east end, and pick up the cairned boot path heading north into the timber. It climbs steeply through forest for 15-20 minutes before breaking out onto talus directly beneath the East Face; the cairns are genuinely hard to follow before dawn, and there is no water between the car and the wall.

waypoints.name: Liberty Bell Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: From the talus, pick the line by the huge roof above you — the Lithuanian Lip — with Liberty Crack the continuous crack passing to its RIGHT; do not scramble straight up the fall line beneath it, which lands parties on the neighbouring East Face routes. The standard entry traverses in from the LEFT for roughly 40 feet on third- and fourth-class ledges to the ledges under the true first-pitch crack, and twelve pitches then lead to the bolted alcove near the summit shoulder.

approach_variants.name: East Face from the SR-20 hairpin pullout
approach_variants.notes:
This route is on the east side of the mountain and is NOT approached from the Blue Lake Trailhead. Drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20 a short way east of Washington Pass and park in the turnout there.

Walk back along the road toward the pass until you see the small pond on the south side of the highway. The boot path starts at the pond's east end and goes north into the timber; it is cairned, but the cairns are easy to lose in the dark on a pre-dawn start, so scout the first few minutes in daylight the evening before if you can.

The path climbs steeply through forest and then breaks out onto the talus directly under the East Face. Reported times run from about half an hour to an hour of steep walking. There is no water on this approach — carry it from the car.

One consequence worth planning for: if you continue to the true summit and take the standard notch descent, you come down on the WEST side of the mountain and will need a shuttle or a road walk back to the hairpin. Some parties instead rappel the East Face to return directly to their packs.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep (dry talus)
hazards: loose talus and boulders at the base of the wall
cairned forest path is genuinely hard to follow before dawn
no water between the car and the wall
rockfall from parties on the East Face routes above
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the talus, Liberty Crack is the obvious continuous vertical crack that passes to the RIGHT of the huge roof high on the wall — the roof is the Lithuanian Lip, and it is the single feature that identifies the line even in flat light. Do not scramble straight up beneath it. The standard entry traverses in from the LEFT for roughly 40 feet on third- and fourth-class ledges to reach the ledges directly under the true first-pitch crack; there is also a fourth-class alternative that goes up the right-hand side of the block at the base. Parties that head straight up the fall line from the talus end up on the neighbouring East Face lines rather than on Liberty Crack — the East Face here holds a whole cluster of routes within a few rope lengths of each other, so pick the line by the roof above you, not by whichever crack is nearest.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow and moat at the East Face base
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and same cairned path from the pond's east end, but early in the season the talus under the wall is buried in snow that firms up hard overnight. Parties have reported chipping steps in icy snow to reach the rock, and finding the snow lying steeply enough that a slip would carry you a long way down the slope.

Carry an axe and traction, and expect to be in boots for the walk in even when the wall itself is dry.
approach_variants.season: Late spring / early summer after the highway opens, while snow still covers the talus
hazards: deep moat between snow and rock at the base of the wall
hard refrozen snow over talus — a slip runs out badly
SR-20 is gated all winter, so this window only opens once the highway reopens (typically mid-late April to early May)
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identifier is still the big roof — Liberty Crack is the continuous crack running past the right side of the Lithuanian Lip. What changes is the last few metres: a deep moat opens where the snow pulls away from the base of the wall, and getting from snow into the rock can mean a committing step across or a short stemming move down and back up out of the gap. Scout along the base rather than dropping into the first moat you meet; parties have found the moat mellowing out within about thirty feet of where they first reached it.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the cairned East Face path, then 40 ft LEFT along the base
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to the hairpin turn on WA-20 just east of Washington Pass and park at the pullout on the curve. THIS IS A DIFFERENT TRAILHEAD FROM THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD used by the southwest and northwest face routes, and confusing the two costs an hour and a mountain.

Walk back toward the pass and find the small pond on the south side of the highway. A cairned climbers' path leaves the pond's EAST END and switchbacks up through forest for roughly a mile, breaking out into a talus field directly beneath Liberty Bell's East Face. The approach is short, about an hour, but steep in its upper section with loose talus underfoot near the top. No water; carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose talus in the upper approach
No water on the approach
A start that is only forty feet from a different route's start
A descent that lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face trailhead
Snow lingering in the base talus into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE BASE OF THE TALUS, TRAVERSE 40 FT LEFT ON THIRD AND FOURTH CLASS LEDGES. That is the instruction and it is a measured one: forty feet, climber's left, on ledges you scramble rather than climb, and then the crack system starts.

LIBERTY CRACK IS THE REFERENCE LINE FOR THE WHOLE FACE, WHICH MEANS EVERY OTHER ROUTE HERE IS DESCRIBED AS SO-MANY-FEET LEFT OR RIGHT OF IT. Get this one right and the rest of the wall becomes navigable. Left to right along the base the order is: FREEDOM RIDER about 100 ft LEFT of Liberty Crack, then LIBERTY CRACK, then FREEDOM OR DEATH just right of it, then THIN RED LINE, then LIBERTY AND INJUSTICE FOR ALL about 10 m right of that, then LIVE FREE OR DIE, then THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE at the far right or north edge.

SO THE POSITIVE TEST IS: you are on the crack system that runs continuously up the centre of the wall, reached by scrambling LEFT rather than right from where the path meets the talus.

THE NEGATIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS IN POOR LIGHT: IF YOU ARE LOOKING AT A SMALL LEFTWARD-TRENDING RAMP WITH BOLTS VISIBLE ABOVE IT, YOU ARE ON FREEDOM OR DEATH, ONE LINE TO THE RIGHT. And if you scrambled RIGHT from the talus instead of left, you are among the Thin Red Line and Independence starts, which are further right again.

WHERE THE ROUTE ENDS AND HOW YOU GET DOWN, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHICH CAR YOU WALK BACK TO: this line tops out at the same alcove and bolted anchor the original aid route uses. From there, ledges lead to a double-bolt rap anchor and two rappels drop into the BECKEY GULLY, the same rap line the standard Liberty Crack and Beckey Route descents use, landing near a tree anchor. That gully runs down to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch on the WEST side of the mountain, which is the opposite side from the East Face pullout you parked at.

approach_variants.name: Smithbrook Trail and the crest trail to Lake Valhalla
approach_variants.notes: From the Smithbrook Trailhead on the gravel spur off the highway, climb the signed Smithbrook Trail through nearly twenty short switchbacks to Union Gap, where it meets the crest trail; the summit is in view to the south for much of that stretch once the forest opens. Turn left and follow the crest trail south, contouring below the mountain's east flank through a mix of forest and open heather meadow and crossing Smith Brook, which is a reliable place to filter before leaving the trail. Where the trail bends away from Lake Valhalla, drop off it down a steep dirt path to the water and follow the rocky shoreline round to the lake's south tip.
approach_variants.season: Snow-free ground roughly July through October; the same slopes are skinned or snowshoed as a separate winter tour. The access road is unplowed in winter and typically melts out by early to mid summer.
hazards: There is no trail of any kind beyond the lake outlet — real tread only reappears on the summit ridge itself
More than one gully runs up this side of the mountain and only one of them is the route
The peak visible from the lake is a lower sub-summit, and parties have climbed it by mistake onto slick class 4 and 5 ground
Short cliff bands that force minor backtracking
Loose talus with rockfall onto anyone below
The gully often holds snow into early summer, so an axe and light traction are worth carrying outside peak summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: WHEN FACED WITH A CHOICE OF GULLIES, TAKE THE MIDDLE ONE — AND KNOW THAT THE PEAK YOU CAN SEE IS NOT THE SUMMIT. From the southeast area of the lake begin a slight ascent to the southeast, looking for the obvious rock-filled gully. Be careful here: there is more than one gully on this side of the mountain, and the middle of them is the route. Ascend it to where it terminates, then work around the first small cliff band to the LEFT, on its north side. Above that, climb right toward a gentle saddle; from the saddle a traverse northeast is the easier finish, while going northwest is the exposed option and is not the ordinary line. The wrong-place marker is the thing you have been looking at all along: from the lake the true summit is hidden, and what stands in front of it is a smaller unnamed peak that looks steep and sketchy. Parties have climbed toward it by mistake and turned back a few metres short on slick class 4 and 5 rock. There is no trail at all beyond the lake outlet, so finding none is expected; real tread reappears only on the summit ridge.

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

bivy.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
bivy.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
bivy.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
bivy.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

bivy.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
bivy.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
bivy.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
bivy.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge to the Kulshan Cabin site, then high and right on the Coleman beneath the icefall
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead on FS Road 39, Trail #677, near Glacier. Follow the trail roughly 2 miles through old growth and several avalanche-chute creek crossings to the flat former Kulshan Cabin site around 4,700 ft, which is the usual camp and staging area. From there climb the Hogsback moraine to the toe of the Coleman Glacier and rope up. Where the party heading for the southwest side of the mountain would cut away toward the Thunder Glacier cirque, this route stays HIGHER and further climber's RIGHT — east — on the Coleman, traversing beneath the Coleman icefall to reach the north-facing cirque wedged between Colfax Peak and Lincoln Peak. That traverse is longer and more exposed than the south-side approach: for a stretch you are directly beneath active serac bands on the upper icefall, so serac collapse is a real objective hazard and an early, cold start matters more here than it does on the other side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Winter to early spring. The only documented ascent was mid-March, in a lean cold winter — this is an ice objective and it needs the ice to exist
hazards: Traversing directly beneath active serac bands on the Coleman icefall
Crevasses on a long, exposed, high traverse of the Coleman
Roughly 2,000 ft of ice and mixed ground with conditions that vary enormously year to year
Loose rock reported on the face, which matters because the descent means building anchors on it
No documented independent descent — parties either reverse the face or traverse to the southwest gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A CIRQUE WITH A PEAK ON EACH SIDE OF IT, AND THAT IS THE TEST. Lincoln's north face sits in a north-facing cirque WEDGED BETWEEN COLFAX PEAK AND LINCOLN PEAK. You have arrived when the ground you are standing on is enclosed on two sides by rock rising to two separate summits, with the Coleman behind you. One peak above you is not enough; you need the cirque.

THE HANDRAIL IS THE ICEFALL, AND IT IS OVERHEAD RATHER THAN UNDERFOOT. From the Coleman's toe, stay HIGH and go RIGHT, traversing beneath the icefall. Icefall above you on your left is the confirmation you are on the correct traverse; it is also the reason to be there before the sun. If you find yourself descending toward a cirque with no icefall above you, you have cut left toward the Thunder Glacier side and are heading for the southwest face.

THE FACE ITSELF IS ABOUT 2,000 FT AND IT IS ICE. If the wall in front of you is a snow slope you could walk, it is not this route. The line is graded WI4/AI4+; rime, verglas and bare ice vary hugely by year, so what you find may be harder or easier than the grade but it will not be a scramble.

GO EARLY IN THE SEASON FOR TWO REASONS AT ONCE: the ice is better, and the crevasses on the traverse are better bridged. Those two arguments point the same way, which is unusual and worth using.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE: open snow basin, sun on your back, trees below you at 6,100 ft. That is the X Couloir approach from Rankin Creek and it is reached from a different road entirely.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.approach: The X Couloir is most directly approached from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38); the less direct alternative starts at Heliotrope Ridge and reaches the southwest face through the Thunder Glacier cirque. Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start hiking/bushwhacking the old decommissioned road around Pt. 4481 toward Rankin Creek — snow travel (often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch) leads past East Rankin Lake (~5,120 ft) and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, near the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. From camp, an alpine start gets the team into the southwest basin and across the bergschrund crux while it's still cold and firm, climbing roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40° snow and a steep serac step in the X Couloir to the 9,085 ft summit. Total approach is on the order of 7 miles and 3,350 ft of gain to the basin camp.
