IMPORTANT — access note: FR-38 (Middle Fork Nooksack River Road), damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026, and a separate seasonal gate at Wallace Creek (~mile 10) closes the road December 1-June 15 for elk calving; confirm current road status with the Mount Baker Ranger District (Glacier Public Service Center) before a trip, since the drivable road-end — and therefore the length of the approach — varies year to year.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
approach_variants.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the SOUTH via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached from Heliotrope Ridge through the Thunder Glacier cirque, a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

ACCESS: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
hazards: A bergschrund crossing that must be done cold and early
1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all of it above a long runout
FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec - 15 Jun
A gully that funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
A descent that is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGHEST TREES IN THE BASIN ARE THE CAMP, AND THE CAMP IS THE LAST THING YOU CAN NAVIGATE TO. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

DO NOT EXPECT ONE CLEAN COULOIR — THIS IS THE TRAP THE NAME SETS. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the HIGHEST notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

THE SERAC STEP IS THE CONFIRMATION. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

AND THE ASPECT SETTLES THE COARSE ERROR: this route faces SOUTHWEST and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Creek and Crystal Creek from the south
approach_variants.notes:
This is the back side of the mountain and has nothing to do with the Enchantments core approach. From Highway 97 south of the Y-junction, drive about 7.5 miles and turn onto Ingalls Creek Road to the trailhead.

The Ingalls Creek Trail is a gentle, well-maintained walk. Pass the Fall Creek trail junction at about 5.5 miles and continue roughly two more miles, to a point around 8 miles in where the Crystal Creek valley opens above you to the north.

Leave the trail on the right (north) at about 3,700 ft and climb moderate slopes, following cairns, into brushy ground up Crystal Creek. About 2,200 ft of gain brings you to a meadow-and-tarn basin near 6,000 ft, the usual camp.

Carry water. Parties have run out and become dehydrated on this approach, and the cairned path is easy to lose — descending parties routinely miss it and end up bushwhacking back to the Ingalls Creek trail.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: No reliable water once you leave Ingalls Creek — dehydration is on record here
Brush and route-finding up Crystal Creek; the cairned path is easily lost, especially on descent
Long walk out from a remote basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the tarn the route goes up a large talus-apron gully lying WEST of the tarn, toward a col at roughly 7,700-7,880 ft between Little Annapurna and the spires to its south. The technical climbing is on the south face above that, reached through the gully. The grade is the check: this face is around 5.5 to 5.6 over three pitches on solid rock. If you are on ground appreciably harder than that, you are not on the line. The strongest negative marker on this peak is the summit itself. Little Annapurna is reached from the Upper Enchantments by an essentially class 1 walk-up and is often called the easiest Bulger — so if the terrain above you never becomes technical, you have wandered onto the ordinary walking side of the mountain rather than the south face, and the day is a hike, not a climb. This approach is only weakly documented and no source consulted gives a per-pitch description of where the first pitch begins within the gully system; treat locating the exact first belay as work to be done on the ground.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's LEFT of the cliff bands. Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.
approach_variants.season: late Jul-early Oct
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain climber's right near the waterfalls, with fatalities on record
Misleading and duplicated cairns on the pass and on the peak itself
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above, on the pass and on the final slopes
No water past the Colchuck Lake outlet
Full sun and thunderstorm exposure on open talus above the pass — no shelter anywhere in the Core
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two separate 'find it' problems on this route and the first one is the trail junction, not the mountain.

Near the FAR END of the meadows, watch for an UNSIGNED path forking RIGHT (west) toward Little Annapurna. It is a use-path, not tread. The unambiguous overshoot marker is downstream of it: if you cross a small stream AND pass a sign for the toilet, you have gone too far and need to come back. That pair — stream then toilet sign — is the single most useful navigational fact on this route, because the junction itself has nothing to see.

From the pass at Aasgard, Little Annapurna lies to the SOUTHEAST and reads as a gently rolling hill rather than a peak, which is part of why people walk past the turn.

The second problem is the mountain itself, and the honest answer is that there is no single line. The 'route' is a scatter of well-worn boot paths over broad north-facing slabs and talus. Cairns are present, easy to lose, and mark more than one option. The working rule reported by everyone: take the path of least resistance up the peak's LEFT (east) side, switchbacking and scrambling, nothing harder than low 3rd class, to the summit at 8,485 ft.

If you find yourself on anything that feels like real climbing, you have drifted off the line — this is a walk-up with hands occasionally on rock, and any steepening means come back left and lower.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
approach_variants.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.
approach_variants.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges on the pass
Punchy afternoon snow over hidden ice
Patchy snow-to-slab transitions on the summit slopes
Uncontrolled glissade descending the pass — the classic afternoon incident here
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow covering the Core, the unsigned right-hand fork toward Little Annapurna and the stream-then-toilet-sign overshoot marker are all buried or unreliable, so navigate by the lakes instead: from the top of Aasgard, travel between Isolation Lake and Tranquil Lake and then head SOUTH toward the broad rolling summit mass that sits southeast of the pass.

On the peak, snow simplifies the problem — the braided boot paths and contradictory cairns that make the summer scramble confusing are gone, and the broad north-facing slopes go directly. Keep to the LEFT (east) side of the mountain and take the easiest angle available.

What to watch for instead: the transition from snow to bare slab, which happens patchily on a north-facing slope in early summer and is where an unroped slip becomes a slide.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
approach_variants.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
approach_variants.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, with variable soft, icy or moat-riddled conditions
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, on the ridge and on the face
No cell coverage, and a remote position that makes rescue difficult
The gap is a trail high point with several ways off it — confirm you are on the southwest side before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts DIRECTLY ABOVE THE GAP. From the low point of Dutch Miller Gap, turn onto the peak immediately southwest of it — the first ground above the trail that needs hands is the start, roughly five hundred feet of heather and rock steps rising onto the northeast ridge. The physical test is the sequence: heather steps give way to an OPEN BENCH, and above the bench you cross a SNOWFIELD into a cirque below the east face; if you have not crossed snow you have not reached the cirque, and the two short belayed pitches to the summit start from it. At the top of the first of those pitches, move climber's LEFT for the direct finish. Negative markers: if you left the trail at a small steel bridge well below the gap and dropped south into a side valley, you are heading for the long gully-and-crack route on the far side of the mountain; if you are looking up nine hundred feet of talus at a prominent left-trending gully, you are under that route and not this one.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above the gap
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming from the north you drop TO the gap rather than climbing to it, so the check is that you have finished descending and the peak is now above you on the left. The climbing begins at the first hands-on heather-and-rock steps above the gap, leading to an open bench and then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still descending and the ground ahead keeps dropping into a valley, you have passed the gap and are heading down the Middle Fork.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
approach_variants.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout
Remote with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, work into the peak's NORTHEAST BASIN. The route is guarded by a RIDGE NOTCH, and the notch is identified by a single feature: a LARGE VERTICAL CRACK forming a low-fifth-class step that most parties rope up for. If the notch you have reached can be walked through, it is not this one. Above the notch the ground eases and joins the snowfield and cirque used by the trail approach. Negative marker: if you are standing in a broad trail saddle with tread underfoot, you are at Dutch Miller Gap and on the standard line, where no such crack step exists.

approach_variants.name: Waptus River and Lake Ivanhoe from Salmon La Sac
approach_variants.notes: The long southeastern way in, usually spread over two or three days. From the Salmon La Sac road end north of Cle Elum, follow the Waptus River trail up its gentle valley to Waptus Lake, roughly nine miles. The old hiker bridge over the river below the lake is gone, so this is a real ford, about knee deep at normal summer flow. Past the lake the trail follows the southeast shore, which can hold steep snow into early summer, to a ford of Chief Creek near the head of the lake, about twelve miles from the car. From Chief Creek the Dutch Miller Gap trail switchbacks up the forested slope, passes Lake Ivanhoe and reaches the gap, roughly five more miles and about 2,000 ft higher. At the gap it meets the standard approach, and the climbing above is the same.
approach_variants.season: July to September. The river ford and the lakeshore snow are both much more serious during snowmelt.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford below the lake: cold and swift, and serious in snowmelt
Chief Creek ford near the head of Waptus Lake
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Very long approach far from help, with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming up from Lake Ivanhoe you climb to the gap from the east, so the check is that the trail has stopped climbing and starts to drop west toward the Middle Fork, with the peak above you on the left. The climbing starts at the first heather and rock steps above the gap and leads to an open bench, then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still beside Lake Ivanhoe or below it, you have not reached the gap yet.

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
bivy.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
bivy.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
bivy.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the Dutch Miller Gap trail climbs past Lake Ivanhoe to the gap, where the northeast face scramble starts. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
bivy.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
bivy.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

road.status: CLOSED at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given, as listed on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026 — this blocks vehicle access to the Elbow Lake Trailhead.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier straight to the foot of the wall, without going to the col
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Green Creek one: Elbow Lake Trailhead on FR-38, the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack crossing — the unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the marked ford is what most parties use — then off-trail to Green Creek, cross it, and ascend a rock buttress near 3,800 ft onto the Green Creek Glacier.

Where the Southeast Ridge continues to the Cinderella-Little Sister col at the glacier's head, this route stops at the face itself. It is graded around 5.4 and is the hardest of the peak's documented lines.

Descent is either rappelling the climber's-right side of the face on scattered fixed pin and tat anchors back to the glacier, or downclimbing the easier Southeast Ridge to the col and returning to the glacier from there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: No published line along the base of the face — the party chooses its own start
Scattered fixed pins and tat of unknown age as the rappel descent option
A north-facing wall that holds snow and ice at its base
A moat where the glacier meets the wall
The bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing shared by every route here
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE GLACIER RUNS INTO A WALL, AND THE WALL IS THE ROUTE. That is the arrival and it is the whole test: walk up the Green Creek Glacier until the ice ends against rock that goes up rather than along. There is no col, no notch and no ledge system to identify. THE COL IS THE OVERSHOOT MARKER AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL THING TO KNOW HERE. If you keep going and arrive at a low point on the ridge with Cinderella on the far side of it, you have walked past the north face and are at the base of the SOUTHEAST RIDGE — a different route, two grades easier, on a different aspect. Reaching a col means turn round. THE ASPECT IS THE CONFIRMATION. This face is NORTH. It is in shade, it holds snow and ice at its base later than anything else on the peak, and the rock is cold. If you are standing in sun at the foot of your intended line, you are somewhere else on the mountain. BE HONEST ABOUT WHAT IS PUBLISHED HERE: no source consulted gives a per-pitch start point along the base of this face. What is documented is the aspect, the grade, the approach glacier and the fact that the face is roughly a thousand feet high. A party arriving at the wall still has to choose its own line along the base, and should expect to. DESCENT DECIDES THE DAY AND MUST BE DECIDED ON TOP: the two options are rappelling the climber's-RIGHT side of the face on scattered fixed pin and tat anchors — old gear, unknown age, treat it as found rather than as fixed — or downclimbing the Southeast Ridge to the col and back to the glacier that way. The second is more walking and less trusting.

wa_little_sister_south_couloir.approach: From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road), the Elbow Lake Trail reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack River within a few minutes. THE BRIDGE IS GONE and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible during high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently in place. One group used a log crossing roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction; another used an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it, and treat the crossing as the crux of the day in terms of consequence. Once across, follow the Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old-growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback (near Hildebrand Creek), find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off and heading up the Green Creek drainage. It is marked with small blue diamond trail markers. Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, then up through the brush-filled Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. The Green Glacier approach is 5 miles one way with 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead over trail, climbers' trail, boulder fields, scree and slabs. For the South Couloir specifically, continue up the basin and climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of Little Sister, then traverse onto the south side and up into the gully. In deep winter one party found hard snow all the way to the col; snowshoes were left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.

road.name: Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road)
road.status: CLOSED at milepost 7 due to a washout, per a Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert dated 27 July 2026 — this blocks vehicle access to the Elbow Lake Trail 697 north trailhead and to Ridley Creek Trail 696. Verify current status on the forest's alerts page before driving. Separately, FR 12 (the southern approach to the Elbow Lake Trail via Pioneer Camp) was scheduled closed from Rocky Creek Bridge at MP 4.6 between 10-24 August 2026 for road repairs, remaining open to foot, bike and e-bike.
road.driveNote: From the Mt. Baker Ranger District office in Sedro-Woolley, drive north on Highway 9 to Acme. About 7.2-7.6 miles past the office, after crossing the South Fork Nooksack River, turn right on Mosquito Lake Road and follow it roughly 9 miles. After crossing the Middle Fork Nooksack River, turn right onto Forest Road 38 and drive about 11-12 miles to the Elbow Lake Trailhead on the right, with parking directly across the road. FR 38 is dirt and subject to washouts. Coming from Bellingham, reach Mosquito Lake Road via Highway 542 through Deming. Note that despite the 'Mt Baker Hwy' area label, SR 542 is not the access road for this peak.
road.seasonalGate: FR 38 is gated at Wallace Creek, 1.3 miles below the trailhead. Forest Service trail pages list the gate closure as Dec 1 - Jun 15; other Forest Service pages give Nov 1 - Jun 15. The southern access, FR 12, is gated Nov 1 - Jun 30 at Wanlick Pass.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of the summit, then round onto the south side
approach_variants.notes:
From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38, Elbow Lake Trail #697 reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack within a few minutes. THE BRIDGE IS GONE and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge to the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible at high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently there: one recorded party used a log roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction, another an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it and treat the crossing as the most consequential thing you do all day.

Once across, follow Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback near Hildebrand Creek, find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off up the Green Creek drainage, marked with small blue diamonds.

Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, up through the brush-filled valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with Class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. That is roughly five miles one way and 4,000 ft of gain from the trailhead.

In deep winter, snowshoes have been left at the snow line and crampons carried from there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jan-May. This is a snow line and a winter ascent of it is on record; in deep winter parties have found hard snow all the way to the col
hazards: A bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing that must be hunted for and is the day's biggest consequence
A south-facing snow gully — timing matters and it warms
A line with no recorded climbing first ascent and very little traffic
Two rappels on the descent, one from near the top and one below the col
Loose scree, boulder fields and Class 3 slabs to reach the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL SOUTHEAST OF THE SUMMIT, AT 6,240 FT OR A LITTLE ABOVE, IS THE HINGE OF THE WHOLE ROUTE — AND THE COULOIR IS ON THE FAR SIDE OF IT. From the basin, climb snow to that col. Then TRAVERSE ONTO THE SOUTH SIDE and up into the gully. Nothing on the Green Creek side of the col is this route; you have to go over.

SO THE TEST IS AN ASPECT FLIP, WHICH IS THE MOST RELIABLE KIND IN CLOUD. You approach on the NORTH-facing Green Creek side, in shade, on the glacier. You climb on the SOUTH side, out of the basin you walked in through. If you are still looking at the glacier you came up, you have not crossed the col.

CONFIRM THE COL BY ITS NUMBER AND ITS POSITION: 6,240+ ft, and SOUTHEAST of the summit. It is the col between Little Sister and Cinderella, the same one the Southeast Ridge starts from.

WINTER CHANGES WHERE THE APPROACH ENDS, NOT WHERE THE ROUTE STARTS. In deep winter, hard snow has run continuously to the col, which makes the walk simpler and the col no less the marker.

BE CLEAR ABOUT THE RECORD ON THIS LINE, because it affects what you should expect to find: no rock or ice first ascent is recorded. What is documented is a ski descent of the line during a traverse of the range, and a party in January 2015 reporting a suspected first winter ascent of the peak by this south-side ground. The winter party came down it with two rappels, one from near the top and one below the col. That is not a well-trodden route with a bootpack in it.

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Glacier on its looker's-left side to the Cinderella-Little Sister col
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Green Creek one shared by every route on this peak: Elbow Lake Trailhead on FR-38, the unbridged Middle Fork Nooksack crossing on whatever log is currently in place, then Elbow Lake Trail #697 and the blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path leaving it near a switchback around 2,600 ft.

Up the Green Creek drainage past the Wiseman Lake outlet, through brush, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with Class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier.

This route then differs from its neighbours in one instruction: travel the glacier staying on the LOOKER'S-LEFT — south — side, up to the Cinderella-Little Sister col, which is where the ridge starts.

The route is graded around 5.3 and runs about three pitches.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A moat at the glacier margin that grows through the season
A dangerously loose connecting ridge toward Cinderella that must not be used as a traverse
Fixed pins and tat of unknown age on the north-face descent option
The bridgeless Middle Fork Nooksack crossing shared by every route here
Loose scree, boulder fields and Class 3 slabs to gain the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A COL, AND THAT IS WHAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM EVERY OTHER LINE ON THE PEAK. The southeast ridge starts at the CINDERELLA-LITTLE SISTER COL, at the head of the Green Creek Glacier. You have arrived when you are standing in a low point on a ridge with a peak at each end of it — Cinderella one way, Little Sister the other — and glacier behind you.

THE GLACIER INSTRUCTION IS THE ONE THING TO GET RIGHT AND IT IS A SIDE: stay LOOKER'S-LEFT, the SOUTH side, on the way up. The other routes on this peak do not go to the col at all, so drifting right across the glacier puts you under the north face instead.

SO THE DISCRIMINATOR IS SIMPLY WHETHER YOU REACHED A COL. If you have walked until the glacier runs into a WALL, you are at the north face and you are on a different, harder route. If you have walked until the glacier runs into a NOTCH you can walk through, you are at the start of this one.

THE MOAT AT THE GLACIER MARGIN IS THE LAST OBSTACLE, and it is a season problem rather than a route problem: trivial in a heavy snow year, a real step late in the season, and the same in reverse coming down.

WHAT NOT TO DO FROM THE COL: do not continue along the connecting ridge toward Cinderella. At least one party describes that ridgeline as dangerously loose and recommends dropping back to the glacier instead. The col is a start point for two peaks and a through-route for neither.

DESCENT NOTE THAT DOUBLE-CHECKS THE START: most parties downclimb this same ridge back to the col. The alternative is to drop onto the NORTH FACE side and rappel scattered fixed pin and tat anchors back to the glacier — which is a different aspect and needs deciding on top, not in the moat.

approach_variants.name: Paradise and the Muir route to 8,600 ft, then east through the Cathedral Rocks notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route exits the upper Frying Pan Glacier's corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-May. This is the winter and early-spring line, used precisely when the White River road to Summerland is shut and the Fryingpan approach is unavailable
hazards: Serac fall and crevasse hazard across an extended Cowlitz and Ingraham traverse
A cliff and serac band immediately below the traverse line, which is why elevation must be held
Wind-slab avalanche potential on the ramp gaining the face in early season
Loose rock in the summit gully-chimney and on the final crest scramble
A long committing traverse with the same ground to reverse on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION IS AT 8,600 FT AND IT IS A LEAVING, NOT AN ARRIVING. You step off the Camp Muir track while still about 1,500 ft BELOW Camp Muir. IF YOU REACH CAMP MUIR YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR — by a vertical quarter of a mile, on the busiest bootpack on the mountain, which is exactly why it happens.

COUNT WHAT YOU CROSS: THREE GLACIERS AND ONE ROCK CLEAVER, in this order — Paradise, Cowlitz, then a NOTCH IN CATHEDRAL ROCKS, then the Ingraham. If you have crossed the Cowlitz and walked into rock without finding a notch, you are BELOW the notch and need to regain height. The traverse deliberately holds elevation to stay above a serac and cliff band; drifting down is the error that feels easy at the time.

THE BASE IS A RAMP, AND IT IS THE ONLY ramp: a snow or rock ramp at about 8,900 ft leading onto the south and east face. Arriving at the foot of a face with no ramp means you are round the wrong side of it.

THE NEGATIVE THAT SEPARATES THIS FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER ROUTE: the standard line on Little Tahoma comes from the FRYINGPAN side, over Whitman Notch, from the east. This one comes from PARADISE, from the southwest, and never goes near Summerland or Meany Crest. If you are looking for a notch between two glaciers with the Whitman below you, you are on the other route.

WHY THIS ROUTE EXISTS AND WHEN IT STOPS WORKING: it is the winter line, done before the Cowlitz and Ingraham become too broken to cross safely. Once those glaciers open up, the traverse is the hazard rather than the climb.

approach_variants.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
A bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, with about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHITMAN NOTCH AT ABOUT 9,100 FT IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU KNOW IT BY WHAT BECOMES VISIBLE RATHER THAN BY THE ALTIMETER: IT IS THE FIRST PLACE THE WHITMAN GLACIER COMES INTO VIEW. Until you can see a SECOND glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING PROPER IS HIGHER STILL, AND IT IS A CHANGE OF SURFACE: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a SHORT step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

THE ROUTE-FINDING TRAP IS LOW, NOT HIGH, AND IT IS THE ONE THING ON THIS CLIMB THAT REGULARLY COMMITS PARTIES TO BAD GROUND: between Summerland and Meany Crest, IF YOU FIND YOURSELF CONTOURING CLIMBER'S RIGHT INTO A BOWL UNDER ROCK BANDS, YOU ARE CLIFFED OUT AND OFF THE LINE. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

THE SUMMIT-CREST TEST IS A NEGATIVE AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

TIMING AS A FINDING: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout and the East Face path, to the ground between Thin Red Line and the Independence Route
approach_variants.notes:
Same East Face approach as Liberty Crack: park at the hairpin turn on WA-20 east of Washington Pass, walk back to the pond on the south side of the road, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile through forest to the talus below the East Face.

Eleven pitches, climbed in 2017. The route takes the East Face for eight pitches to M&M Ledge at roughly mid-height, then shares its final three or four pitches to the summit with the upper section of Thin Red Line.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: The route's identifying crack pitches sit roughly 700 ft up the wall, not at its base
A start defined only by the two routes on either side of it
A fixed pin and wire as the first rappel anchor off M&M Ledge
Two ropes needed to rappel from M&M Ledge
Loose talus in the upper approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS SANDWICHED, AND THE SANDWICH IS THE TEST: IT LIES TO THE LEFT OF THE INDEPENDENCE ROUTE AND TO THE RIGHT OF THIN RED LINE. Those two neighbours are the most identifiable lines at that end of the face, so bound the ground between them and the route is inside it.

THE RIGHT-HAND BOUND IS THE ONE YOU CAN SEE FROM FURTHEST AWAY: the Independence Route starts at the FAR RIGHT, or NORTH, EDGE of the East Face, and a RED-COLOURED ROOF AND ALCOVE, the Baer Ceiling, sits about 85 m above its start. If a red roof is above you, you have walked one route too far right.

THE LEFT-HAND BOUND: Thin Red Line is climber's right of Liberty Crack, and Liberty and Injustice for All sits about 10 m right of Thin Red Line on two-bolt anchors with fixed biners. If you are at a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners a rope length up, you started too far left.

AN HONEST WARNING FROM THE FIRST ASCENT, AND IT CHANGES HOW YOU READ THE WALL: the party recorded that the route's initial crack pitches WERE 700 FT UP THE WALL and seemed to have been reached by rappel from other routes, with no obvious way to reach them from below. So the visible feature that names this route is not at its base. Do not try to identify the line by the cracks; identify the ground between Thin Red Line and Independence and start there.

DESCENT FROM M&M LEDGE, FOR PARTIES WHO DO NOT TOP OUT, IS THIN RED LINE'S: from the ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber's-left to a set of bolted anchors and make four double-rope rappels back to the talus at the base of the East Face. Every station after the first is bolted; no natural or v-thread anchors are involved. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent on the west side instead.

approach_variants.name: From the north — Cascade Pass and the glacier corridor
approach_variants.notes: Lizard has no trailhead of its own and is normally met partway through the high traverse rather than approached. From the Cascade River Road end, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and then traverses meadow and talus to Cascade Pass, which is the last built tread of the trip. Leave it there and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow to the Cache Glacier and Cache Col, then drop the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. Beyond, the Red Ledge cuts the cliff band west of Art's Knoll, then the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the Spider-Formidable col and down to Yang Yang Lakes. From there the line climbs past Le Conte Mountain, crosses the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, and crosses the South Cascade Glacier to the col at its head before dropping into the White Rock Lakes basin. Lizard is the side trip from that camp: climb back out of the basin northeast to the broad notch on the peak's south ridge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the Cache Col snow has consolidated and the Red Ledge is clear of verglas; the whole corridor has to be in condition, not just the peak.
hazards: roped glacier travel on the Cache, Middle Cascade, Le Conte and South Cascade Glaciers, with crevasses opening through late season
steep heather above the Cache Col descent, where a slip runs out onto rock
the Red Ledge can hold an open moat, verglas or fresh snow well into summer
whiteout navigation at the Spider-Formidable col, with no bail once past Cache Col
loose blocks on the summit ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. The notch you want is the broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. Standing in it, White Rock Lakes should be below you to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice below you to the northeast; the ground rising off the col toward the high point is a single broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, and the top of it is visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep going up, you are at the wrong gap in the ridge. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling on loose blocks — if you meet a step that makes you want a rope, you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, where the rubble is worst. Stay near the crest and keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

approach_variants.name: From the south — Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek (road closed until January 2028)
approach_variants.notes: Not usable while the Suiattle River Road stays closed at milepost 4 under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 unless rescinded sooner; washouts cut off the Downey Creek Trailhead, and the Forest Service's Miner's Fire order (06-05-26-17) also closes the trailhead and the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails from August 15 through December 31, 2026. Before the closure this was the other end of the same corridor. From the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, Downey Creek Trail #768 enters wilderness within the first half mile and climbs gently through old growth, crossing tributary creeks that run high in early season, to the Bachelor Creek junction. The Bachelor Creek path is unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown, with an alder and slide-alder band around 3,800 to 4,400 ft that becomes a genuine bushwhack when snow has not flattened it. It fords Bachelor Creek itself, which runs fast and cold with snowmelt. Above treeline the tread breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake, reliable water and a common first camp. A steep, often snow-covered pitch gains Itswoot Ridge; from there the route climbs to Spire Col, descends the Dana Glacier to White Rock Lakes, and regains the col on Lizard's south ridge from the lakes.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September. The Bachelor Creek brush is worst before the snow has settled it and the Bachelor Creek ford is worst during peak melt.
hazards: road and trailhead cut off by washouts until at least January 2028
sustained blowdown and slide-alder bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
the Bachelor Creek ford during snowmelt
crevasse hazard on the Dana Glacier below Spire Col
multi-day evacuation distance with no cell coverage
loose blocks near the summit crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE COL IS THE REFERENCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN WHERE YOU CAN SEE BOTH BASINS AT ONCE. Climbing out of the White Rock Lakes basin you reach a broad pass in the south ridge at a little over 6,800 ft, roughly two thousand feet of horizontal distance west of the summit. From it, White Rock Lakes lie below to the southwest and South Cascade Glacier ice lies below to the northeast; the ground rising toward the high point is one broad, blocky, loose ridge of only about six hundred vertical feet, with its top visible from where you stand. If you cannot see both the lakes and the glacier from the notch, or if what rises above you is far more than six hundred feet, or if you have to step back onto glacier ice to keep gaining height, you are at the wrong gap. Nothing on the correct line is harder than hands-on scrambling — a step that makes you want a rope means you have drifted off the crest onto the flanks, which carry the worst of the rubble. Stay near the crest, and keep the party abreast rather than strung out directly below one another.

bivy.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
bivy.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

waypoints.name: FR-9070 / PCT (#2000) junction near Olallie Meadow, Snoqualmie Pass
waypoints.note: Where FR-9070 crosses the PCT: from I-90 exit 54, Hyak Drive NE becomes FR-9070 and runs 5.4 mi to this crossing. Past the junction, climbers take the LEFT fork of FR-9070 and drive or walk to a large turnaround just below Silver Basin, from which the crag base is a 20-30 min approach on foot. That turnaround has no published name or coordinate, so this junction is the closest fixed reference point rather than the exact parking spot.
waypoints.directions: Leave I-90 at Exit 54 (Hyak) and follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, staying on it past the end of the pavement for about 5.4 miles to the Ollallie Meadow junction where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and keep driving until the road ends in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin; that turnaround is where you park, and the pin here marks the PCT crossing rather than the road end itself. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from about July through November.

waypoints.name: The Obelisk (rock formation/crag), Silver Basin
waypoints.note: Elevation is an estimate from the surrounding terrain (Citidel base area is listed at 4,585 ft; The Obelisk sits further up-slope from the Sofa King Buttress sub-area) — no separate elevation figure is published for this formation.

approach_variants.name: Olney Pass, old road walk and the two cairns
approach_variants.notes:
US 2 to Sultan, left onto Sultan Basin Road at the last stoplight, paved for ten or eleven miles then gravel, about thirteen miles total to Olney Pass. Register at the kiosk.

Carry on to the fork, bear right around the south tip of the reservoir, and after roughly two miles cross a bridge and park in the first turnout on the left.

Walk the old eroded, overgrown road, crossing ravines where the culverts have gone. It stays largely level for 45-60 minutes. The first cairn appears just before a large, usually dry riverbed and marks the view up the bed toward the slabs and Static Peak. Cross the riverbed and look for the SECOND cairn, which sits on an old culvert and marks where the trail leaves the road.

From there the trail climbs beside the riverbed for 20-30 minutes to the base of the dome.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer days, daylight only — PUD access around Spada Reservoir is sun-up to sun-down with self-registration at the Olney Pass kiosk
hazards: PUD gate hours — sun-up to sun-down only
Washed-out culverts and ravines on the old road
Steep step with a short fixed line near the top of the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: The reference point on arrival is Online's first bolt — the first bolt visible from the ground, sitting almost exactly in the middle of the wall about 50 feet up over low-angle slab. Locate that, and you know where the middle of the wall is. Lost Charms is a separate five-pitch line on the same dome and the sources consulted do not describe its own ground marker, so identify it off the wall relative to Online's centre-of-wall bolt rather than from anything at your feet. Do not assume the first bolt you see is yours.

wa_lost_peak_pasayten_scramble.comms: No reliable cell coverage in this part of the Pasayten Wilderness backcountry; a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is recommended for the multi-day approach.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage in the Pasayten interior; this is genuine multi-day self-rescue country far from any road. Carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) and leave a detailed trip plan. Aero Methow Rescue Service (Winthrop-based) provides EMS/ambulance response for the Methow Valley, typically dispatched via Okanogan County 911.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA 98862 — (509) 996-4000 (permits, current trail/road conditions)
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster (509-689-2517) or Mid-Valley Hospital, Omak (509-826-1760) — both roughly an hour's drive from the Methow Valley
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies; Okanogan County Sheriff non-emergency/dispatch (509) 422-7232 opt. 4

bivy.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
bivy.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
bivy.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at Robinson Creek; Slate Pass and Monument Creek need none. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Robinson Creek; Slate Pass needs none. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

approach_variants.name: Railway tracks to The Country, Upper Town Wall trail, then climbed into
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lower Town Wall lot cross the railway tracks and follow them north past the Lower Wall to the clearing at The Country, cutting left near the huge tunnel door. Go to the far right of the clearing, near the start of GM and a possible notice board, and take the obvious path uphill.

About 30 minutes, short and very steep with cliffy drop-offs beside the trail.
approach_variants.season: Dry days
hazards: Steep climbers' trail with cliffy drop-offs
Railway crossing and track walking
Committing — you are three pitches up before this route begins
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Lovin' Arms is the standard continuation ABOVE Davis-Holland, not a ground start — the two together are the classic seven-pitch link-up of the Upper Town Wall.

So the base to find is Davis-Holland's: immediately LEFT of where the approach trail arrives at the wall, taking a corner left of a blank face. Climb the three Davis-Holland pitches and continue.

If you are casting around at the base of the Upper Wall for an independent start to this you will not find one.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30 annual day-use fee at White River Trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Pass, or Recreation.gov Digital Day Pass accepted
access.permit: Free self-issuing wilderness permit, available at the White River Trailhead — no quota or reservation required
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access. White River Road (FR 6400) itself is not on the Wenatchee River Ranger District's storm-damage closure order (06-17-07-2026-11), which keeps numerous other district roads closed through Dec 31, 2027 following the December 2025 storm event, though the Forest Service's road-conditions table (as of September 3, 2026) reports FR 6400 washed out in several places with sinkholes and exposed culverts; Stage 1 fire restrictions are common in late summer — check current Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest alerts before driving
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District, Leavenworth)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Pass and the sheepherder's traverse to the col west of Clark Mountain, then the upper Richardson Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft at the end of FR-6400, White River Trail #1507 runs almost level upstream through old growth for about four miles. The junction with Boulder Creek Trail #1562 sits roughly a quarter mile PAST the bridge over Boulder Creek — if you have crossed the creek and seen no sign, keep walking. Turn onto #1562 and climb gently through forest to the established camp at the creek crossing near 3,700 ft; whether that is a step-across or a genuine ford depends on the year. Above camp the trail switchbacks and climbs roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about three miles into the open basin below Boulder Pass. Snow lingers in that basin well into summer, and the pass is the last of the maintained, easy-to-follow trail. Above Boulder Pass the route becomes an unmaintained sheepherder's path that sidehills EAST across a series of cirques, losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining height near a 7,200 ft spur. That traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach: brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or under snow.
