This route also carries a set of waypoints describing a different line — over the pass, down to a ford of the Napeequa near 4,700 ft, and up to a high basin at 7,000 ft under the east face. Both are real ways to this mountain.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable. The Richardson has been reported thinning and breaking up in recent years, so a late-season party should expect it to be less straightforward than it used to be
hazards: Crevasses and moats on an upper Richardson Glacier that recent parties report thinning and breaking up
The sheepherder's traverse across the cirques — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in cloud or snow
A short low Class 4 step below the east ridge that can carry verglas and has no fixed anchor
Loose scree and rotten rock just below the summit block
A Thunder Creek exit that reads shorter on the map and is documented as slower, brushier and harder to follow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING IS A GLACIER, AND THE THING THAT GETS YOU TO IT IS A COL THAT BELONGS TO THE NEXT PEAK. From the 7,200 ft spur, make a RISING traverse across broad benches — often snow-covered well into summer — and easy Class 2 ledges to the roughly 7,600 ft COL WEST OF CLARK MOUNTAIN. You are navigating to a gap beside a different summit, which is what makes it findable: Clark is the big thing on your left.

FROM THAT COL, THE ROUTE IS ONE RISING TRAVERSE ACROSS THE UPPER RICHARDSON GLACIER TO LUAHNA'S EAST RIDGE. Rope up at the col. The glacier crossing is the route; the ridge above it is a scramble west to the summit.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT WHICH GLACIER YOU ARE ON, and this peak's own record has already been wrong about it once: THE PILZ AND BUTTERFLY GLACIERS ARE ON LUAHNA'S NORTH SLOPE AND BELONG TO A SEPARATE ROUTE APPROACHED FROM THE NAPEEQUA SIDE. This route uses the RICHARDSON, which lies to the SOUTH-EAST of the summit. If the glacier you have stepped onto is north of the peak, you are on the other mountain's business entirely.

THE SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER IS SIMPLER: if you never touched a glacier at all, you are on the south-west slopes and south-east ridge line, which is the other route on this peak and is deliberately glacier-free. Both finish on the same summit and neither is a variation of the other.

COMING DOWN, THE ONE PIECE OF TECHNICAL GROUND IS BELOW THE EAST RIDGE: a short, steep step reported as low Class 4 and sometimes verglassed in an adjacent gully. Strong parties downclimb it; a single 20-30 m rappel off a horn or block is common practice when it is wet or icy. There is no fixed anchor — carry webbing.

DO NOT TAKE THE THUNDER CREEK EXIT ON THE STRENGTH OF THE MAP. Dropping south into Thunder Creek looks shorter and is reported slower and rougher, with heavy blowdown, avalanche debris and a boot path that disappears near the creek crossing. Reversing the ascent line over Boulder Pass is the reliable way out.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass typically required at Forest Service trailheads in this area
access.permit: Free, self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access.
access.landManager: U.S. Forest Service — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Basin high camp and the sheepherder's trail through four cirques
approach_variants.notes: From the White River Trailhead near 2,300 ft, White River Trail #1507 and then Boulder Creek Trail #1562 lead to a ford and camp around 3,700 ft, and on up into Boulder Basin. High camp is a grassy knoll overlooking the basin at about 5,800 ft. From camp the route traverses a saddle into the White River drainage and then follows the old sheepherder's path across a chain of cirques. The path is fairly well defined but the FIRST cirque is where parties lose it and regain it repeatedly; the second, Clark Basin, is less brushy, more open and park-like with clear tread; the third, Luahna Basin, has good tread and is where parties describe camping as heaven on earth. There is a great deal of up-and-down and side-hilling on this traverse — the recorded elevation figure is far larger than for the peak's other route, which is what all that sidehill costs. This line is deliberately glacier-free, which is its whole reason to exist beside the other route on the peak.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep. A September ascent works but expect cold and the possibility of early snow on the traverse and the summit ledges
hazards: An exposed Class 3+ traverse on the NORTH side just beneath the summit, crossed with nothing to protect it
A long sidehilling traverse across four cirques with heavy elevation loss and regain, and a path that vanishes in the first one
Loose scree and rotten rock below the summit block
Lingering snow on the traverse and ledges early in the season
Remoteness measured in a day's walk from any road, with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU FIND THE BASE OF THIS ROUTE BY COUNTING BASINS, AND THE ANSWER IS FOUR. From the Boulder Basin camp the sheepherder's path crosses cirques in order: BOULDER, then CLARK, then LUAHNA, and the peak's base sits above the FOURTH — Chalangin Basin. Nothing about the ground tells you which cirque you are in, but the character does: the first is where the path keeps disappearing, the second is open and park-like, the third has good tread. Count them.

THE INTERMEDIATE MARKER IS A NUMBER ON THE RIDGE: make a rising traverse across Luahna Basin toward the roughly 7,500 ft RIDGE POINT, then follow a faint trail across scree and talus ABOVE the fourth cirque to the peak's base. Above Chalangin Basin, not in it.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS THE GRADE, AND IT IS EASIER THAN YOU EXPECT: the scramble begins on EASY CLASS 2 LEDGES on the SOUTH FACE, leading up to the right-hand skyline ridge. Class 2 ledges, south-facing, and a ridge on your right at the top of them. If your first ground is steep, or if you are on a glacier, or if the ledges lead left, you are not on it.

THE CONFIRMATION COMES HIGH AND IT IS ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN: just beneath the summit the route crosses an EXPOSED CLASS 3+ TRAVERSE ON THE NORTH SIDE before the final Class 3 scramble straight up. So the sequence is south-face ledges, gain the ridge, cross to the NORTH beneath the summit, then straight up. A route that never leaves the sunny side has not reached the summit block.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER ROUTE: the east slopes line crosses the upper RICHARDSON GLACIER from a col west of Clark Mountain and needs glacier gear. This route touches no glacier at all. If you are roping up for crevasses, you are on the other one, and it is a different day.

A NOTE ON WHAT IS PUBLISHED VERSUS WHAT PARTIES FIND: this is described as a second-class line, and most parties meet a short Class 3 or better traverse or step to bypass a gap in the ridge below the true summit. Expect it rather than treat it as evidence you are off route.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek into Luna Cirque, rather than the Luna Creek bushwhack
approach_variants.notes:
Reaching Luna Cirque is the crux of the trip. The historical line follows the Big Beaver Trail from Ross Lake, with a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort cutting about 6 miles off the hike, up to Luna Camp, then climbs steeply beside Luna Creek into the cirque. That bushwhack was described by the first-ascent party as the worst imaginable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows and alder.

Most contemporary parties instead approach via Access Creek, which branches off the same Big Beaver Trail rather than a separate trailhead. Continue on maintained trail past Luna Camp to the unmarked Access Creek and Big Beaver Creek confluence, then leave the trail and follow the Access Creek drainage, with an occasional bootpath, up into the cirque. Longer, and far less brutal.
approach_variants.season: Jun to early Aug. The hanging glacier is the crux of the route and can be impassable in late season, which is why the window is early
hazards: A hanging glacier that is the route's crux and can be impassable in late season
The Luna Creek approach, if chosen, is among the worst brush in the Cascades
Sparse protection on the slab pitches
Recrossing the glacier on the descent, on the same conditions that decided the ascent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS THE GLACIER IMMEDIATELY SOUTH OF THE PEAK, AND THE TEST IS THAT IT NARROWS. From the floor of Luna Cirque, get onto the hanging glacier that lies directly south of Phantom and follow it up to where it NARROWS AND STEEPENS as it flows down from higher on the mountain. That constriction is the route; there is nothing subtle about walking into a narrowing throat of ice with rock on both sides.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROCK, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL BASE OF THE CLIMBING: where the narrows END, turn NORTH and climb over a rock step to reach the highest snowfield on the peak. That turn is the transition from snow to rock and the point at which the party commits to the upper route. The whole climb above the cirque is only about 400 ft in four pitches, so if you have been climbing rock for more than a few rope lengths without reaching a summit block you are not on this line.

COUNTABLE CONFIRMATION: one rock step, two to three pitches of easy slab to the ridge, then a summit block of about 25 ft. Four pitches, 4th class with a move of easy 5th. Parties carry runners and a few pieces rather than a full rack, because placements on the slab are where the features allow rather than where you want them.

THE TURNAROUND TEST, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING ABOUT THIS ROUTE: the hanging glacier has to be recrossed to get home. A party that finds it in poor condition ON THE WAY UP should treat that as the turnaround decision rather than pressing on. Timing is the main decision this route asks of a party, and the answer is taken at the base, not at the top.

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes.comms: Cell/satellite communication absent in remote Picket Range. Satellite messengers (InReach, SPOT) strongly recommended for emergency use. Contact rangers before departure.

approach_variants.name: Access Creek basin, then the gap south of Point 6,730 and the 6,600 ft basin traverse to Luna Col
approach_variants.notes:
The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at about 2,050 ft, with parking right off the highway. About 0.8 mile of trail leads down to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft. The lake crossing is a logistical step rather than an afterthought, since the resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can reach the trailhead at all.

From the Big Beaver Trailhead, about 8 miles of well-graded trail through old-growth cedar along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek reach Luna Camp. Continue roughly 1.5 miles past it and watch on the left for a small, easy-to-miss boot path leaving the maintained trail just north of where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek at about 2,460 ft. Ford Big Beaver Creek there.

Around 3,700 ft the brush thickens; cross to the south bank of Access Creek, where intermittent cairns and a faint path use talus benches to dodge the worst of the slide alder and devil's club. This stretch is the approach crux. The path deposits you in the open basin at the Access Creek headwaters at about 4,400 ft, the common base camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Sustained bushwhacking, blowdown and route-finding in the Access Creek drainage, the approach crux
A ford of Big Beaver Creek that can run high with snowmelt
A narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest between the false and true summits, with cliffs on both sides
Loose talus and scree on the upper ridge with rockfall risk onto parties below
No reliable water above the Access Creek camp except lingering snowmelt
Losing the boot path in poor light on the way down, which several trip reports record
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE CONTOURS WHERE THE SOUTH RIDGE CLIMBS, AND THE DIFFERENCE STARTS ABOVE CAMP RATHER THAN AT THE COL. From the Access Creek basin, ascend broad talus gullies, snow-filled early season, southwest toward an OBVIOUS GAP IN THE RIDGE above. Once on the ridge, TRAVERSE SOUTH OF POINT 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's southeast side, then cross that basin AT ABOUT THE 6,600 FT LEVEL to Luna Col at 7,200 ft.

SO THE FOG TEST IS AN ALTIMETER TEST: the basin crossing is held at roughly 6,600 ft. Losing height into the basin or gaining it toward the crest both cost you, and both are what happens when you navigate by feel. Hold the contour and it delivers you to the col.

ARRIVAL: Luna Col at 7,200 ft is the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. You are there when the ground drops away on the far side.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB, AND THE COUNT IS SHORT: above the col the route is roughly 1,100 ft of class 2-3 talus and scree to the FALSE, SOUTHERN summit, then ONE short connecting ridge to the true summit. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left at the false summit.

THE ONE TECHNICAL SPOT, AND ITS TELL: drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit onto a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest with a snow-covered cliff falling several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff dropping the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the worst of it by dropping onto a ledge on the SOUTHEAST side and scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit. If you are on a crest with snow on your left and bare rock on your right, you are in the right place and there is one short section of it.

NO WATER ABOVE THE ACCESS CREEK BASIN. The summit push is done on what you carry.

approach_variants.name: Commonwealth Basin and Lundin Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT-North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead off the Alpental road (about 3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; within roughly half a mile bear left onto the Commonwealth Basin use trail, which climbs gently along Commonwealth Creek through old-growth for about 1.7 miles as the valley opens out.

Near 4,200 ft leave the main Red Pass tread and cut west, contouring into Lundin Basin below Red Mountain's south face. From there climb a broad couloir — snow in early season, scree and talus by late summer — up the steep south side of Lundin to gain the West Ridge at its notch.

This is much the better line while snow still covers the basin: it buries the brush and the boulders, and parties report a long glissade on the way out. Once melted out the lower basin is brushy with steep scree and talus, and that is the reason many parties switch to the Cave Ridge approach late in the season.

Commonwealth Creek is reliable water low down; nothing above is dependable, so fill up in the basin.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Jul on snow is the good window; brushy and slow once melted out
hazards: wet-slide and sluffing in the south-face couloir under afternoon sun - axe, crampons if firm, early season
heavy brush and steep loose scree in the basin once the snow is gone
no reliable water above Commonwealth Creek
the ridge is unsafe wet and unsafe without rock gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Both approaches converge at the low notch on the West Ridge, near 5,800 ft, and that notch is where the technical climbing starts — nothing below it needs a rope.

Coming up from the basin, aim for a depression in the face beneath the notch. Climb easy class 3 ground up to that depression, then the slabby depression itself is the crux of the entry, class 4 to low fifth, and you bear RIGHT at the top of it to arrive in the notch. If you are climbing slab and it does not lead to a col within a rope length or two, you picked the wrong depression.

Negative markers. If you gained the crest somewhere that walks easily on both sides, you are on the ridge but past the notch and the climbing above will not match any description. And if you find yourself scrambling straight at the summit block instead of setting out along a ridge, you came up the south face rather than to the west ridge notch.

The ridge involves class 4 to mid fifth moves and wants rock gear. Do not attempt it wet.

approach_variants.name: Cave Ridge traverse from Alpental
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Alpental day-use lot and find the unmarked, unmaintained Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail that starts about 50 ft south of the signed Snow Lake trailhead. It crosses below a small waterfall and climbs steeply through forest and slide alder.

At an unsigned split around 4,600 ft, paths fork toward Snoqualmie Mountain, Cave Ridge and Lundin. Take the Cave Ridge / Lundin fork, cross over Cave Ridge near its low notch, then follow an ascending climbers'-trail traverse below the ridge crest — staying on the Commonwealth Basin, north, side — to the West Ridge notch.

This skirts the brushy lower basin entirely, which is why parties prefer it once the snow has gone. There is no reliable water past the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct; the better late-season option
hazards: exposed and sometimes loose climbers'-trail traverse beneath Cave Ridge
early-season snow traverse on the crossing that can warrant an axe
unsigned trail split around 4,600 ft with three destinations
slide alder low down
no reliable water past the trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You arrive directly at the low notch on the West Ridge, around 5,800 ft, which is where the technical climbing begins. Arriving by this line you should be traversing beneath the crest on the north (Commonwealth) side and then step up into a col with the ridge rising to your right toward the summit.

If the traverse has you on the south side looking down into Lundin Basin, you have crossed the crest too early. If you top out on a walkable ridge with no notch, you have gone past.

As with the basin approach, the entry from below the notch goes class 3 to a slabby depression, then class 4 to low fifth up the depression, bearing right into the notch.

approach_variants.name: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier, then west across the glacier head to the face
approach_variants.notes:
This route and the Northeast Couloir come at the mountain from the OTHER side to everything else on it. From the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then cross the pass and descend east toward the Stehekin side. Pelton Basin Camp is about half a mile downhill and east of the pass.

From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the YAWNING GLACIER, which runs roughly 6,200 to 6,800 ft. Rope up. Follow the glacier southwest to the MAGIC-PELTON COL at 6,480 ft, between Magic Mountain and Pelton Peak.

From the col this route does not go straight up. It bears back and crosses the HEAD of the glacier westward to reach the north face, where about 600 ft of steep class 4 rock leads to a notch immediately northwest of the summit.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug; glacier cover and couloir conditions vary more year to year here than on the peak's south side
hazards: Crevasses on the Yawning Glacier — rope up rather than treating it as a snowfield
A steep couloir below the Magic-Pelton col that is exposed to rockfall
A schrund at the base of the rock that opens through the season and can be the crux by August
Broken, north-facing gneiss that is often wet or verglassed, with slung blocks for anchors and no fixed gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO ROUTES LEAVE THE MAGIC-PELTON COL AND THE TEST IS WHETHER YOU WALK OR TRAVERSE. At the col at 6,480 ft, THE NORTHEAST COULOIR GOES STRAIGHT UP FROM WHERE YOU STAND. THIS ROUTE FIRST BEARS BACK AND CROSSES THE HEAD OF THE GLACIER TO THE WEST. IF YOU STARTED CLIMBING AT THE COL, YOU ARE IN THE COULOIR.

THE SECOND TEST IS WHAT IS UNDER YOUR HANDS, AND IT SETTLES THE SAME PAIR FROM THE OTHER END: this route is ROCK — about 600 ft of steep class 4 above a schrund. The Northeast Couloir is SNOW, 40 to 50 degrees for 2,000 ft. IF YOU ARE PLACING PICKETS YOU ARE IN THE COULOIR; IF YOU ARE SLINGING BLOCKS YOU ARE ON THE FACE.

THE SCHRUND AT THE BASE OF THE ROCK IS THE BASE ITSELF, and it is the thing that changes most between June and August — by late summer it can be the hardest move of the day.

THE FINISH IS A NOTCH IMMEDIATELY NORTHWEST OF THE SUMMIT, AND THAT NOTCH IS SHARED WITH THE NORTHWEST RIDGE, which reaches it from the peak's southwest side by easy walking slopes and a chimney. So arriving at the notch does not confirm which route you climbed — but it does confirm you are 600 ft above the glacier on the correct face, and the summit is a short scramble from there.

AND YOU ARE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN ENTIRELY IF YOU CAME OVER CACHE COL: that is the Kool-Aid Lake approach, which serves the South Ridge, the West Ridge, the Northwest Ridge and the Southwest Cirque. This route and the Northeast Couloir come from Pelton Basin.

approach_variants.name: Pelton Basin and the Yawning Glacier to the col, then straight up the line
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft. Hike 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, cross it and descend east toward the Stehekin side; Pelton Basin Camp is about half a mile downhill and east of the pass, 4.9 miles and 1,800 ft from the trailhead including the camp spur.

From Pelton Basin, climb easy slopes and a steep couloir onto the YAWNING GLACIER, rope up, and follow the glacier southwest to the MAGIC-PELTON COL at 6,480 ft. Ski parties also reach this cirque from the Cascade Pass side across the Yawning Glacier without dropping to Pelton Basin.

Skiers know the northeast line as the Banana Couloir: roughly 2,000 ft winding down the shoulder, a lower half around 40-45 degrees, an upper section at 45-50, and a proper 50 at the very top.

Decide your descent BEFORE you leave the col. Reversing the couloir is direct but puts you in a sun-exposed funnel; walking off the South Ridge to the Magic-Hurry-up col and Kool-Aid Lake avoids it entirely but lands you on the opposite side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: April to late June or early July as a snow line, but the road is the constraint: Cascade River Road usually does not open to the Cascade Pass trailhead until the end of June, so a spring ascent means a long road walk or ski from the gate, commonly starting at the Eldorado parking area. In practice late June and early July is the sweet spot, when the road opens and the couloir is still full
hazards: Cliff faces on both sides funnel rockfall down the line — the lower section is potentially a bit of a garbage chute
Documented significant sluffing on spring snow, with large natural avalanches reported in the same zone later the same day
An upper couloir sustaining 45-50 degrees and reaching a proper 50 at the top, often a firm crust under a few inches of new snow
A crevassed Yawning Glacier on the approach and a sun-facing couloir below it, which shortens the descent window
Overhead hazard for the full length of the line
A cornice on the summit ridge in spring
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT THE MAGIC-PELTON COL AT 6,480 FT, THE COULOIR RISES DIRECTLY ABOVE YOU. THAT IS THE TEST: THE LINE STARTS AT THE COL, WITHOUT A TRAVERSE. If your next move after reaching the col is to bear back west across the head of the glacier, you are heading for the North Face — a rock route on the same mountain from the same col.

SO: PICKETS AND FRONT POINTS MEAN YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT PLACE. This is snow, 40-45 degrees low down and 45-50 above, for about 2,000 ft. If you are slinging blocks and climbing class 4 rock, you have traversed onto the North Face.

THE SHAPE OF THE LINE IS THE CONFIRMATION: consistently steep but WIDE, with rock faces on BOTH sides that shed into the gut. A narrow slot, or an open face with no walls beside it, is not this feature. Move through the lower section rather than resting in it — those walls are what make it a funnel.

BE AWARE THAT MORE THAN ONE NORTHEAST-FACING LINE IS DESCRIBED ON THIS MOUNTAIN AND IT IS NOT FULLY CLEAR WHICH IS WHICH. One is reached from a col on the northwest shoulder, one from a col named Alliteration Col, and one from the Magic-Pelton col — and two of these are sometimes treated as different lines. The col you stand at is what identifies your line, not the couloir seen from below, so record which col you crossed and how high it was.

AND THE SEASON IS A CHECK IN ITSELF: this is a snow route. The line can hold rock or snow depending on the year, but if you have arrived to find loose rock rather than a filled line, the couloir is out of condition and it is the same funnel with nothing holding it together.

approach_variants.name: Kool-Aid Lake side: easy slopes southwest of the peak to the chimney and the notch
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the South Ridge: Cascade River Road to the Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, 3.7 miles of switchbacks to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then leave the maintained trail for the Ptarmigan Traverse climbers' path — a rising traverse across Mixup Peak's flanks to the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft and over CACHE COL at about 6,900 ft, then down about 600 ft toward Kool-Aid Lake at roughly 6,200 ft.

From there, rather than dropping all the way to the lake and continuing to the Magic-Hurry-up col, continue onto the easy slopes on Magic Mountain's SOUTHWEST side and up to the base of the ridge and face.

The climbing is short: steep broken rock, then an easy chimney to a notch, then a traverse and a short finish on the northwest face.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Broken Magic Mountain gneiss with no fixed anchors — a retreat means leaving slings on blocks
A crevassed Cache Glacier on the approach, about 35 degrees, going to bare ice with open marginal moats late in the season
An aspect that dries late and stays greasy after rain; wet lichen on gneiss is treacherous on class 4 ground
Almost no traffic, so no bootpack, no cairns and no cleaned-off rock
No cell coverage on a rarely visited side of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IMMEDIATELY NORTHWEST OF THE SUMMIT IS SHARED WITH THE NORTH FACE ROUTE, SO THE NOTCH ALONE CANNOT TELL YOU WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ON. WHAT TELLS YOU IS HOW YOU GOT TO IT. This route reaches the notch from EASY WALKING SLOPES ON THE SOUTHWEST SIDE, off the Kool-Aid Lake basin, with no glacier involved. The North Face reaches the same notch from the Yawning Glacier on the far side of the mountain, with a schrund below it. IF YOU CROSSED A GLACIER TO GET WHERE YOU ARE STANDING, YOU ARE ON THE NORTH FACE.

THE SEQUENCE FROM THE BASE IS COUNTABLE AND IT ENDS IN A CHIMNEY: easy slopes to the base, then STEEP BROKEN ROCK, then an EASY CHIMNEY that leads to the notch. Rock first, chimney second, notch third. If you have not climbed a chimney, you have not reached the notch this route uses.

THE OTHER TEST IS WHAT YOU DID NOT CROSS. Two other routes leave from this same southwest side and both are identified by a feature this one lacks. THE WEST RIDGE CROSSES A BERGSCHRUND ON A POCKET GLACIER before it climbs anything — if you crossed a schrund, you are on the West Ridge. THE SOUTHWEST CIRQUE stays in the cirque and goes up HEATHER gullies — if you are on grass rather than rock, you are in the cirque. This route is dry walking, then rock, then a chimney.

AND IF YOU CONTINUED TO THE MAGIC-HURRY-UP COL YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR SOUTH: that col is the start of the South Ridge and of Hurry-Up Peak's own route, on the far side of this basin.

FINISH CHECK: from the notch the summit is a short traverse and climb on the NORTHWEST FACE. If the notch you reached puts the summit a long way off, it is not the right notch.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, Cache Col and Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cascade Pass trailhead at about 3,600 ft at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and roughly 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at about 5,400 ft. This stretch is well graded, well marked and by far the busiest — it is a popular day hike in its own right.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the climbers' path to climber's right, bearing south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse over snow or heather across the east flanks of Mixup Peak, crossing a spur ridge, to the base of the Cache Glacier at about 6,000 ft. The path is intermittent and in early season it is under snow, when route-finding matters more and the traverse has a bad runout.

Ascend moderate snow — up to about 35 degrees — to Cache Col at roughly 6,900-6,960 ft. The glacier here is small and generally reported free of significant crevasse hazard, but carry an axe and often crampons depending on firmness. Late season Cache Col itself can moat out and become awkward to cross.

From Cache Col make a descending traverse south-southeast, losing about 600 ft, to Kool-Aid Lake at about 6,120 ft — the standard camp for Magic Mountain and for the Ptarmigan Traverse, with reliable water. Most parties treat this as a two-day trip rather than a car-to-car push.

A Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking; overnight camping at Kool-Aid Lake needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, picked up in person at Marblemount for the Cascade River Road areas.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Snow-covered traverse below Mixup with a poor runout in early season
Cache Col moats out and becomes awkward late season
Loose rock on the summit tower ledges
The false summit — parties stop there or commit to the wrong side of it
No water on the upper ridge; last reliable source is Kool-Aid Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The South Ridge starts at the col between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, at about 7,100 ft. From Kool-Aid Lake it is roughly 1,000 ft of straightforward heather and scree straight up to that col — there is no gully to pick and no notch to confuse, which makes this the most forgiving base on this list to arrive at.

The route-finding problem is not the base but the top, and it is worth knowing before you set off. The first third of the ridge is an easy heather scramble, with possible snow, leading to a FALSE summit about 300 ft southeast of the true summit. That false summit is the landmark that tells you you are on route, and it is also where parties stop, believing they have topped out.

From the false summit the way on is counter-intuitive: find a dirty gully on the right and downclimb about 80 ft, then follow class 3-4 broken ledges that corkscrew around the east and northeast side of the summit tower. A hand line or a belay is worth having, and the descent goes back down the climbing route.

In poor visibility the two things to hold onto are that the col is the low point on the skyline between Magic and Hurry-Up, and that if you are standing on a high point with more rock still above you across a gap, you are on the false summit and need to lose height on the right before regaining it.

approach_variants.name: The pocket glacier under the west face, and the schrund that guards it
approach_variants.notes:
Approach by the general Cascade Pass and Ptarmigan Traverse access: Cascade Pass trailhead near 3,600 ft, the trail to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft, then the climbers' path across Mixup Peak's flanks, over the Cache Glacier and Cache Col near 6,900 ft, and down toward the Kool-Aid Lake basin.

From the basin, easy slopes on the west-southwest side lead to the small POCKET GLACIER under Magic Mountain's west face. That pocket glacier is the base area, and the bergschrund at its head is where the route begins.

Seven pitches: shelves to a blocky open book, the 5.6 open book, the slab taken on its easier left side, and an easy chimney on the left to gain the crest between the false and main summits.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, with the bergschrund crossing and the pocket-glacier conditions varying by snow year
hazards: A bergschrund below the west face whose difficulty varies by year and which can be the crux of the route by late summer
A crevassed Cache Glacier on the approach, about 35 degrees and bare ice late season
Broken gneiss with slung blocks for belays and no fixed gear
A thin slab pitch where protection is limited
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE ROUTE'S IDENTITY AND IT IS THE ONE-LOOK TEST AGAINST BOTH ITS NEIGHBOURS ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. THIS IS THE ONLY MAGIC MOUNTAIN ROUTE FROM THE KOOL-AID LAKE SIDE THAT CROSSES A SCHRUND. The Northwest Ridge walks up easy slopes to rock and a chimney; the Southwest Cirque goes up heather gullies. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED A GAP BETWEEN GLACIER AND ROCK, YOU ARE NOT ON THE WEST RIDGE.

THE POSITIVE LANDMARK ABOVE THE SCHRUND IS A NAMED SHAPE: shelves lead up to a BLOCKY OPEN BOOK — a dihedral corner. That open book is the 5.6 crux and the best-protected pitch on the route. IF YOU CROSS THE SCHRUND AND FIND NO OPEN-BOOK CORNER ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE CROSSED IT IN THE WRONG PLACE.

COUNT THE FOUR FEATURES IN ORDER, BECAUSE THEY ARE ALL DIFFERENT SHAPES: schrund, shelves, open book, slab. THE SLAB IS TAKEN ON ITS EASIER LEFT SIDE, not up the middle.

THE FINISH TELLS YOU WHICH SUMMIT YOU ARE UNDER: from below the ridge between the FALSE and MAIN summits, an easy chimney on the LEFT gains the crest. So the route deliberately arrives on the ridge BETWEEN the two tops — if the chimney you climbed put you straight onto a summit, you are on the false one and the ridge continues.

AND IF YOU HAVE TO RETREAT BELOW THE SUMMIT, THE SCHRUND HAS TO WORK IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: a retreat reverses the chimney and slab, downclimbs the open book and re-crosses the schrund. Look at it on the way up with that in mind, because there is no walk-off from this side of the mountain; the walk-off starts at the summit and goes down the South Ridge.

approach_variants.name: Holden Village to Holden Pass, then east up the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Access is by Lake Chelan ferry from Chelan or Field's Point Landing to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up eleven miles of gravel road and twelve switchbacks into the village. Both have been closed since the December 2025 flood; confirm they are running before anything else.

From the village, Railroad Creek Trail #1256 runs a mile up-valley to the fork, then the Holden Lake Trail climbs about four miles and 1,700 ft to Holden Lake at 5,278 ft. Above the lake the climbers' path gains a further 1,100 ft over heather benches and rocky terraces to Holden Pass near 6,400 ft. This is the same camp Bonanza's routes use, and it is effectively the last water.

The rock on this route is loose crumbly schist and marble all the way up, and parties route-find by cairn rather than by feature. There is a fixed rappel anchor near the top for the crux step.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, with August the most reliable
hazards: Loose, crumbly schist and marble across the entire route, on and off the crest
A short, exposed Class 4 step just below the summit — a fixed anchor is present but is not maintained by anyone
One gully looking exactly like the next on a route where cairns, not features, are the navigation
Sharing a camp with Bonanza parties and a pass with two mountains' worth of routes leaving it in opposite directions
Ferry and shuttle access to Holden Village, closed since the December 2025 flood
approach_variants.baseFinding:
HOLDEN PASS SERVES TWO MOUNTAINS AND THE DIRECTION YOU LEAVE IT IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM. The pass is the saddle BETWEEN Bonanza and Martin. Bonanza's routes go WEST from it, onto benches and the Mary Green Glacier. Martin's West Ridge goes EAST, straight up out of the pass. If you are traversing toward a glacier, you are on Bonanza's ground.

SO THE BASE IS THE PASS ITSELF: no approach across a glacier, no basin, no traverse. The ridge rises directly out of the saddle and the scrambling starts where the heather runs out.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST YOU ARE ON, AND IT REPEATS. Gain the ridge by a series of gullies and scramble on the RIGHT — the SOUTH — side of the crest, then repeat that pattern upward. Right side, gully, back toward the crest, right side again. A party on the north flank has left the route, and the north side of this crest is not the easier ground.

IN FOG, FOLLOW CAIRNS HERE RATHER THAN FEATURES. The rock is uniformly crumbly schist and beige marble and one gully looks like the next; on this particular route cairn-following is the documented method rather than a bad habit. That is the opposite of the advice for the scramble on Mount Pugh, where cairns lead to cliffs — do not carry one peak's rule to the other.

THE ARRIVAL AT THE CRUX IS AN ANCHOR, WHICH IS RARE ON THIS MOUNTAIN. About 100 ft below the summit a steep, exposed Class 4 gully is the route's hardest ground, with good holds, and a FIXED RAPPEL ANCHOR has been observed beside it. Finding fixed hardware on this peak means you are 100 ft from the top and on the standard line. Finding none, on ground much harder than Class 4, means you are not.

THE LOOSE BEIGE-MARBLE GULLY partway up is the other named feature and it is on the south side of the crest, so it doubles as a position check: you should meet it while traversing right, not while on the crest.

bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
bivy.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail, then the east-side gully
approach_variants.notes: Share the standard approach as far as the traverse: Sunrise Mine trailhead, two and a half miles of trail through the unbridged creek crossings to the LAST MAJOR SWITCHBACK before the pass zigzags, then the cairned northeast traverse across two talus fields. The difference comes at the end. Where the boot path for the other two routes carries on toward the open talus at the foot of the main west face, this one BRANCHES OFF into a gully on the RIGHT — the east side of the northern tower. The gully is steeper, more vegetated and slower than the open talus, and route-finding matters more on it than anywhere else on the approach.
approach_variants.season: June to September; spring snow lies low on the route and in the gully.
hazards: Loose blocks in the vegetated gully, particularly with parties above
Steeper and more route-finding-dependent final approach than the neighbouring routes
Loose rock on the belay ledges throughout the climb
Spring snow low on the route
Two unbridged creek crossings in the first mile of trail
approach_variants.baseFinding: Follow the gully on the east side of the tower up through CEDAR AND HEATHER — vegetation is the test, because the neighbouring routes' approach is bare talus and this one is not. The gully leads to a NOTCH ON THE SKYLINE RIDGE. From the notch, the last stretch is loose third-class with a few exposed fourth-class moves, landing on a GRASSY LEDGE that is the first belay. Confirm at the belay by looking up: the first bolt on this route is set notably HIGH above the stance and there are only about four bolts in the whole first rope length, so you scramble before you clip. Negative markers: if you are on open talus at the foot of the tower with two big boulders or a red gully in front of you, you never branched off and you are under the other tower's two routes; if you have found a single bolted belay on a narrow ledge past a lone fir, that is the arete route on the wrong tower.

approach_variants.name: As for Orbit, then one pitch up
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Orbit. Icicle Road 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead, Snow Creek trail about two to two and a half miles until the wall is opposite, right off the trail to the log crossing, then up boulders and talus and a bootpath gaining roughly 500 ft to the base.

From where the trail meets the wall, go left along the base for about 150 yards until the base and path start dropping steeply. Scramble up and left toward the large evergreen below the prominent dihedral, taking the gully on the looker's left of the tree.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
hazards: Exposed 5.6 scrambling to reach the Orbit ledge
A hanging belay at the end of the first pitch
The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route does not start from the ground, and that is the single fact that matters.

Mary Jane Dihedral begins from the nice flat ledge immediately ABOVE the Orbit chimney — climb Orbit's first pitch (the squeeze chimney) and the flat ledge you arrive on is the start. From there the first pitch goes straight up through some vegetation and a small overlap to a bolted hanging belay.

If you are standing on the ground craning up at the dihedral looking for a way onto it, you are one full pitch below the start. The dihedral itself is the most prominent feature above this end of the wall and is the landmark the Orbit approach scramble aims at — being able to see it clearly means you are in the right place, not that you are at the base of the route.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/interagency pass required to park at the Chiwawa-corridor trailheads (Trinity/Phelps Creek); $5/vehicle/day or $30 annual if you don't already hold a pass.
access.rules: Glacier Peak Wilderness caps group size at 12 people and stock combined; larger parties must split into separate groups with at least 1 mile of separation.
access.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead.
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) is closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground after December 2025 storm damage, under closure order 06-17-07-2026-11 in effect through 31 December 2027 unless lifted sooner, so the Trinity Trailhead cannot be reached by car. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes FR 6200 and the Chiwawa River Trail. Check with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before planning a trip.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the Trinity trailhead kiosk.

approach_variants.name: Chiwawa River Trail to the sheepherder's path and Massie Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the Chiwawa valley, fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit and follow the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 upstream through forest, watching the west side of the tread for the marker described below. Ford the river at that point — it can run thigh-deep and swift with early-season snowmelt, so cross in the morning when flows are lowest — and pick up the old sheep-drive path, which climbs steeply on a mix of axe and burn blazes and intermittent boot track to Massie Lake. There is essentially no reliable water between the ford and the lake. From the lake the faint sheep and game tread of the high route contours northwest toward the pass ahead; leave it and turn uphill onto the peak's broad west ridge.
approach_variants.season: The high country here is typically not fully snow-free until mid to late July; shaded sections of the high route and ridge hold snow and ice well into summer.
hazards: A false set of markers has existed roughly a mile short of the real junction and cost a party hours of bushwhacking
Unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River, thigh-deep and swift during snowmelt, with driftwood piles the only aid
Route-finding is the main hazard: the sheepherder path disappears in places and the whole line beyond the river trail is unsigned
Snow and ice on shaded sections of the high route and ridge into midsummer
No reliable water between the river and the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: TWO THINGS FACING EACH OTHER ACROSS THE TRAIL MARK IT: A LARGE BOULDER JUTTING IN FROM THE EAST, AND AN 'M' WITH AN ARROW CARVED INTO A TREE ON THE WEST. The boulder is what you actually see first. There is no sign and no trail number, and the path it marks is an old sheep-drive route that is easy to walk straight past. The river is forded immediately below the junction, with piled driftwood the only help across, so the ford and the carved letter go together. The serious trap here is a decoy: a false set of markers — a boulder in the bank and logs and arrows suggesting the lake — has existed roughly a mile short of the real junction, and a party that took it spent hours bushwhacking up the wrong hillside and came out on the ridge high above the lake. So do not settle for arrows alone; you want the boulder and the carved 'M' opposite one another, and cairns have since been built on both sides of the trail at the true crossing. Above the ford a steep, poorly-marked boot track climbs to the lake on axe and burn blazes that thin out with height. From the lake the faint high route contours away; leave it and turn uphill onto the broad west ridge, the only named feature near that decision being a shoulder around 6,420 ft.

bivy.name: Massie Lake basin
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Massie Peak and effectively the only one, because everything above it is dry and everything below it is a long way down. From the Trinity trailhead the Buck Creek trail runs a mile and a half to the junction, the Chiwawa River trail carries on up the valley and crosses the river on a bridge, and about three miles along it the Massie Lake trail turns off and climbs roughly two miles to the lake, at about 5,900 feet. THAT LAST STRETCH IS THE DIFFICULTY AND IT IS NOT A TRAIL IN ANY USEFUL SENSE. It is an unsigned and unmaintained old sheep driveway, steep, brushy and lost altogether in places, and the standard complaint about this lake is the amount of bushwhacking involved in reaching it. Expect to lose the line more than once and to be pushing through vegetation on the steepest part of the day. From camp the west route on Massie Peak goes on open slopes above the basin and is a scramble rather than a climb. The reward for the thrash is genuine solitude and good fishing; the register-level traffic here is a fraction of what the Buck Creek Pass side sees. Season is roughly mid-July into early October, later than a lake this height would suggest because the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable all season. This is the last certain water on the climb and the reason to camp here rather than higher: the slopes and benches above the basin run on snowmelt only and are dry by August in an ordinary year. Fill completely before going up. Treat it, though the shoreline sees very little use.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the Trinity trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book in advance. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at Trinity. Camp back from the shoreline and on existing bare ground; this is a small basin and it marks easily. Carry a stove — summer fire restrictions on this dry east side are routine and often total.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake for one or two parties. There is nothing developed, nothing signed and no toilet, and the basin is small — but it is also so little visited that competition for space is not a realistic worry.

bivy.name: Trinity trailhead roadhead
bivy.notes: The staging point, and it is recorded because the drive is the part of this trip that most often goes wrong. In a normal year the Chiwawa River road runs about twenty-two miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, with the last stretch rough gravel genuinely unsuited to low clearance, and arriving at the end of it late and tired is how parties end up starting the walk in badly. From the roadhead a short section of closed road leads onto the Buck Creek trail, and the junction where the Chiwawa River trail branches right for Massie is a mile and a half in. THE ROAD IS SHUT ABOVE ATKINSON FLAT under a storm-damage order running into 2027, with the 2026 fire closure sitting over the same corridor on top of it, and while that stands there is no legal way to drive to this roadhead at all. When the road is open again, expect it to remain the fragile part of any plan here: it has been damaged repeatedly, it carries no through traffic to justify quick repair, and the trailhead is far enough up it that a single washout removes the whole approach.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is close by and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap anywhere at this end of the road. Fill everything here, since the valley trail above is good for water and the climb to the lake is not.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is taken from the register here — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit including stock. Fire restrictions bite hard on this side from midsummer and commonly ban all open flame including in existing rings.
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the end of the public road with room to sleep in a vehicle. It is a roadhead, not a campground — no fee site, no tables, no toilet you should count on. The developed campgrounds strung along the Chiwawa River road below it are the proper drive-in option and are recorded in the Entiat and Holden file rather than repeated here.

bivy.name: The Chiwawa River trail camps above the bridge
bivy.notes: These are the first-night camps for a party that has driven a long way, or the last-night camps for one walking out, and on this approach both cases are common. The river bridge where the Buck Creek trail crosses is the usual spot and is the obvious place to stop, being flat, sheltered and on good water. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the Massie Lake turn is unsigned and the driveway above it is steep and vague — that is ground you want to meet in the morning with fresh legs and a full day, not at dusk. The valley walking below is gentle and fast, so a party that gets away from the road in the afternoon can be here comfortably. THE ROAD CLOSURE CHANGES THE ARITHMETIC ENTIRELY. With the Chiwawa River road shut above Atkinson Flat, Trinity is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns the walk to these camps into a long day on its own or a bike shuttle, and turns the trip as a whole from two nights into three or four.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is alongside for this whole stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is where the approach is generous with water, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Massie Lake is the steep, hot, brushy part and there is nothing dependable on it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit from the Trinity trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below the high country in existing rings outside a burn ban, but the Chiwawa valley is dry and bans are the norm from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the timber along the valley floor, including good ground where the trail crosses the river on the bridge. One or two parties each, nothing developed, and rarely anyone else there.

bivy.name: The benches above Massie Lake — no established camp
bivy.notes: Recorded honestly: Massie Peak is a day objective from the lake and there is no practical reason to sleep higher. The scramble from the basin is short enough that the only argument for going up is to be on the crest at first light, and the cost is carrying water two thousand feet and sleeping exposed with nothing to shelter behind. The one situation where these benches genuinely earn their place is the traverse northwest on the old sheepherder's line toward Pass No Pass and the Buck Creek Pass country, which runs two and a half to three miles on faint stock and game tracks that come and go, and which a party will not finish in the same day they climb the peak. If you are doing that, sleeping high on the way out makes sense. If you are climbing Massie and walking back down the driveway, it does not. Either way, do not plan on finding water and do not plan on finding a flat, cleared spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. By August there is usually nothing at all above the lake, and a party sleeping up here is carrying every drop from the basin below. This is the single most common way to get the trip wrong.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at Trinity. No fires this high — carry a stove. The ground is thin subalpine turf that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.capacity: None established. There is open ground on the benches and in the meadows above the lake where a small party could put down a tent, but nothing has been built, nothing is marked, and nobody camps here as a matter of course. That is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a site.

emergency.notes: No reliable cell coverage inside the Enchantments basin or on the McClellan approach/ridge; a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) is strongly recommended given the remote, permit-restricted zone.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, 600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA 98826, (509) 548-2550
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center (24-hr ED, Level V trauma), 817 Commercial St, Leavenworth, WA, (509) 548-5815; serious trauma is typically transferred/airlifted to a higher-level trauma center in Wenatchee.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff via RiverCom 911 (regional dispatch for Chelan/Douglas counties); emergency 911, non-emergency (509) 667-6851.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lakes to the core basin, then McClellan Ridge past the Prong
approach_variants.notes:
Snow Lakes Trailhead on Icicle Road about 4.2 miles from Leavenworth. Snow Lakes Trail #1553 climbs steadily through forest, passing Nada Lake at roughly 4 miles, then Lower and Upper Snow Lakes — the logjam between the two lakes is the known crossing hazard, especially at high water or on a pre-dawn start.

Above the Snow Lakes the tread coarsens into a climbers' path and switchbacks steeply into the core basin past Lake Viviane, then Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes. By this point most of the day's elevation is behind you.

Leave the trail at the flat, open ground around 7,000 ft between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes and head south-southeast for McClellan Ridge.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; late-season the slope below the ridge often goes icy
hazards: The logjam crossing between Lower and Upper Snow Lakes, worst at high water or in the dark
Steep snow below the ridge that turns firm and icy in late season — an axe or microspikes are worth carrying
Loose talus and scree gaining the ridge
No water above the basin lakes
Real route-finding with no trail on the upper half
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two features decide this route and both are recorded errors.

First, the Prong: a distinct rock tower standing on the ground above you. The line keeps WEST of it, climbing steep talus, scree or snow to gain the ridge crest. Parties who drift the other way, west into the jumbled cluster of towers called the Chessman, report dead-ending in impassable ground and having to traverse back north to find the correct line.

Second, and this is the one that costs people the summit: once you are on McClellan Ridge, do not start up the first thing above you. Scramble EAST along the SOUTH side of the ridge and keep going around until you are on the SOUTHEAST side of the summit block. From there it is an easy class 3 scramble that needs no thought.

The test is your first move. If it is a tricky slab followed by a chimney, you are on the SOUTHWEST side and have stopped short — a few more minutes around to the southeast turns the same summit into a walk-up. Parties have also gained the crest and had to drop about seventy vertical feet before wrapping round to the south side.

No reliable water past the lakes in the basin, and no water at all on the upper section.

approach_variants.name: High Bridge and the McGregor Mountain Trail
approach_variants.notes: There is no road to the bottom of this one — Stehekin is reached by boat, floatplane or the long trail in, and from Stehekin Landing the valley road runs eleven miles up to its end at High Bridge, walkable, bikeable or by shuttle. From High Bridge the tread heads north on the old wagon grade and the Pacific Crest Trail, climbs steadily to Howard Lake, and reaches the signed McGregor Mountain junction a short way past the lake, just before the crest trail tips over and starts back downhill. Howard Lake is reliable water and a useful confirmation you are on route; if you are losing elevation you have walked past the junction. Above the junction the trail winds behind the lake, commits to one long switchback across a hot, dusty open slope, and then settles into a relentless grind — close to a hundred switchbacks up an open southwest-facing shoulder with essentially no shade. A seasonal falls off a short scramble path near the first big viewpoint is worth the detour, because water is scarce from there on. The trail crosses a clear creek, reaches the lower of two glacial cirques on rocky, sandy moraine, and ends at Heaton Camp just above the terminal moraine among larches, where a snowmelt stream a short way below camp is the last dependable water. Above camp another set of tight switchbacks ends at a rocky outcropping and the maintained trail simply stops.
approach_variants.season: August into early September is the reliable window, once the talus and the shelf above the glacier have melted out. Carry an axe if snow still lies on either.
hazards: roughly a vertical mile of gain from the valley floor with almost no shade and no dependable water below Heaton Camp
loose gravel on slab directly above significant exposure on the summit ledges — the descent is the more dangerous half
route-finding, not climbing difficulty, is the real crux above the trail's end
a snowfield and talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier that can hold firm snow into midsummer
no road access to the trailhead itself, so an injured party is a long way from help
approach_variants.baseFinding: A PAINTED RED ARROW ON ONE LARGE BOULDER IS THE PROOF. Where the maintained tread ends at the rocky outcropping above Heaton Camp, talus leads on toward the summit block. Out in the middle of that boulder field, one large rock carries a big bright red arrow painted on it pointing uphill, and from that rock more arrows are visible above it in a chain running up the ledges. Find that first arrow before you commit to any line. The marked route loops right, then back left behind a lower sub-summit, crosses a snowfield and talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier, and finishes along a fairly level shoulder past an old radio installation to the true summit, where a park radio repeater now stands on the site of the old lookout. If you are working up talus and cannot see a painted arrow anywhere above you, you have not found the route yet — do not improvise a line, because the ground gets noticeably worse off the arrows and gravelly slab sits directly above serious drops. A second check: the marked line is scrambling on talus and ledges where hands come into play for balance and short steps, but it never turns into sustained, committing climbing. If you are making steep, committing rock moves, you are off the arrows.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

approach_variants.name: As for the West Ridge to the Terror Glacier, then all the way to the glacier's EAST end
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the West Ridge approach for its whole length: Goodell Creek trailhead, the climbers' path behind the large boulder, the blowdown-choked forest, the 6,200 ft notch and its loose north side, Terror Basin camp, the bench-and-slab traverse to the glacial lake outlet, and the slabs onto the Terror Glacier. This is a six-pitch 5.8- line and the route carries little detail of its own beyond where on the glacier to leave it.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: The same 400 ft of loose choss on the north side of the 6,200 ft notch
A short glacier crossing that can show bare ice by late summer
A descent by a different route than the one you climbed, which has to be found while tired
No published marker at the toe of the ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHOLE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THIS ROUTE AND THE STANDARD ONE IS WHICH END OF THE GLACIER YOU STOP AT, AND IT IS A DIRECTIONAL TEST YOU CAN MAKE IN FOG. From the Terror Glacier, CONTINUE TO ITS EAST END to reach the base of the southwest ridge, RATHER THAN taking the west-ridge gully that the standard route uses.

SO: IF YOU HAVE ROPED UP AT THE FOOT OF A SNOW GULLY LEADING UP TO A COL, YOU ARE ON THE WEST RIDGE, NOT THIS. The West Ridge gully climbs to the 7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan. This route does not go there at all; it leaves the ice further east, on the spire's own southwest flank.

WHAT CONFIRMS IT AFTERWARDS, AND IT IS AN ASYMMETRY WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: the descent from the summit is by the WEST RIDGE, not by reversing this ridge. Parties downclimb the West Ridge's 3rd-4th class scramble and its snow and ice gully back onto the Terror Glacier rather than rappelling the southwest ridge. So you will meet the other route's ground on the way down whether you looked for it or not; a party that cannot find the west-ridge gully on the way up will have to find it on the way down anyway.

THERE IS NO NAMED FLAKE OR CRACK AT THE TOE: nothing published locates one. The east end of the glacier is what is recorded, and it is a real, walkable, unmistakable limit rather than an invented marker.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek climbers' path to the 6,200 ft notch and Terror Basin, then the Terror Glacier to the Inspiration-McMillan col gully
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Upper Group Campground trailhead just east of Goodell Creek Campground off SR-20 near Newhalem, pick up the unsigned climbers' path that starts BEHIND A LARGE BOULDER near the campground.
