There is reliable running water along the roadbed and at a stream crossing just before the steep climb begins, and then none reliable again until Terror Basin.

The path first follows the old Goodell Creek roadbed up the valley for about 4 miles at a gentle grade and is notorious for blowdown; expect to climb over or duck under dozens of downed logs. At a cairned turnoff near 1,700 ft it turns uphill and switchbacks through forest along a spur ridge south of Terror Creek; around 3,200 ft it gains the crest of the forested ridge, and the whole climb from the turnoff is roughly 4,000 ft of gain in about 2 miles. Near 4,000 ft it crosses a small talus field, circles left, makes a rising traverse beneath a rock band at about 4,800 ft, then kicks up a final steep gully. Heather benches and open slabs then lead north for a couple of miles to a notch in the ridge crest at roughly 6,200-6,350 ft, the high point of the approach.

The north side of that notch is the crux of the approach, not of the climb: in late-season low-snow conditions it is steep, loose, chossy terrain for about 400 vertical feet, and you should STAY SKIER'S RIGHT rather than going straight down. Early season it holds a firmer snow finger with a short headwall reported up to about 80 degrees for the last 20-30 ft, which some parties rope up for. Below the notch, a small flat gravelly basin near 5,800 ft with running water is the standard Terror Basin camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Dozens of downed logs in the first couple of miles of the climbers' path
No reliable water between the foot of the steep climb and Terror Basin
400 ft of steep, loose choss on the north side of the 6,200 ft notch late season; stay skier's right
An early-season snow finger with a headwall reported to about 80 degrees at the notch
A moat at the top of the summit gully late season
Poor footing and rockfall onto a party strung out below on the scree ridge
Concentrated exposure in the last few moves between the false and true summits
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE FOOT OF A SNOW AND ROCK GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS THE ONLY ONE THAT LEADS TO A NAMED COL. From Terror Basin camp, a long traverse over benches and granite slabs, trending slightly downhill, reaches a GLACIAL LAKE OUTLET and then slabs below the Terror Glacier remnant. The glacier crossing is short and low-angle. This leads to the base of the snow and rock gully that climbs to the 7,200 FT COL BETWEEN INSPIRATION PEAK AND WEST MCMILLAN SPIRE, and that is where the technical climbing begins.

SO THE COUNTABLE HANDRAIL IS: camp, lake outlet, slabs, ice, gully. Three of those five are unmistakable underfoot in cloud. A lake outlet is running water leaving a lake; slabs are bare rock you can walk on; ice is ice.

WHAT DISCRIMINATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE OTHER LINE ON THE SAME SPIRE, AND IT IS THE END OF THE GLACIER YOU AIM FOR: this route takes the gully to the col between Inspiration and West McMillan. THE SOUTHWEST RIDGE ROUTE INSTEAD CONTINUES TO THE EAST END OF THE TERROR GLACIER. If you are walking east along the ice past the obvious gully, you are on the Southwest Ridge approach, not this one.

AND THE COL IS THE CONFIRMATION: axe and crampons get used in the gully even by parties who crossed the glacier unroped. Late in the season the gully loses its snow and the top of it can hold a moat where the snow has pulled back from the rock. Topping out of a steep snow gully into a gap between two peaks at about 7,200 ft is the start of the climbing.

ABOVE IT, THE ROUTE RELAXES, WHICH IS ITSELF A TEST: the ridge above the gully is a long, mellow 3rd to 4th class scramble on scree, heather and more scree, with no sustained difficulty. If the ground above the col is technical, you are not on the West Ridge.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Lake Trail to the Y-shaped drainage
approach_variants.notes: Start up the maintained Barclay Lake Trail through old-growth beside the creek — easy, well-graded walking. You leave it after a little over a mile, a few hundred feet past the log bridge over Barclay Creek and well before the lake, then pick through brush and talus toward the base of the south face to find the drainage. From there the drainage IS the route: boulder-hop and scramble straight up the creek bed past three waterfall steps into brush, forest and then upper heather meadows. Water runs in the gully most of the season; treat it before drinking.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: Loose, sandy granodiorite throughout the gully, worst at the crux waterfall
Rockfall from parties above in a narrow drainage
An exposed chockstone squeeze at the third waterfall
Wet snowfields and avalanche debris in the gully into June
High water in the creek bed after heavy rain
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two finds, and the first is the one parties miss. The drainage mouth is a Y-shaped side creek coming down off the peak — not the drainage nearer the lake — and it has grown in badly enough to walk straight past. The tell is a faint boot path of piled rocks running a hundred or two hundred feet into the trees to reach the creek bed proper; identify it against a track or a photograph rather than by feel, because it is the most commonly missed point on the route. Once in the bed you are on the climb. It is punctuated by three waterfall steps that mark your progress: the first is turned on climbers-left on an established boot path, the second by working right toward the cliff band and traversing over the top of the falls, and the third is the crux of the whole outing — large jammed boulders and chockstones blocking the gully completely, passed by a fifteen to twenty foot chimney squeeze on climbers-LEFT, small holds set in loose sandy rock with real exposure. A fixed rappel ring has been reported at the top of that third step; treat it as aged gear of unknown condition and back it up with a tree, log or boulder of your own if you use it. Put helmets on before you start up the bed.

emergency.notes: This is a remote, multi-hour cross-country evacuation off the Ragged Ridge crest with unreliable cell coverage; a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) is strongly advised. Serious trauma cases from this area are typically airlifted (Airlift Northwest or military SAR) directly to Harborview Medical Center, Seattle's Level I trauma center, rather than driven out.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount, WA 98267 (open mid-May to mid-October); (360) 854-7245.
emergency.nearestHospital: Skagit Valley Hospital (Level III trauma center), 300 Hospital Pkwy, Mount Vernon, WA — roughly 60-65 miles / 1.5+ hrs drive from the Easy Pass trailhead.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911; after-hours SAR coordination via Skagit County Sheriff (360) 336-9450, or NPS Communications Center after-hours (360) 873-4590 ext. 37.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, then the sidehill traverse to Mesahchie Col
approach_variants.notes: From the marked pullout on SR-20 near milepost 151 the Easy Pass Trail climbs steadily through forest and then open meadow and talus to the pass; streams are reliable low down and there is none at the pass, so fill up before the last switchbacks. Leave the trail just west of the pass, before it starts switchbacking down into Fisher Creek, and sidehill cross-country west-northwest across gullies, scree, talus, grass and blocky ground, well above the valley. Around 6,500 ft the line crosses a waterfall almost directly below the peak on an easy bench; the ground above and below that bench is much harder. Beyond it, climb to the basin below Mesahchie Col, the usual high camp, which has water. From the basin, work up the crest of the shoulder between Mesahchie and Katsuk, where a few Class 4 moves get you established, onto gentler but loose cairned terrain, then traverse slabs down to the col.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers in the approach gullies, on the traverse and in the basin into July.
hazards: genuinely rotten rock in the summit gullies — every hold needs testing and anything knocked loose funnels down the gully onto the party
the cliffy gully-and-rib maze on the summit pyramid, where parties repeatedly get cliffed out without a track or route photos
steep, loose Class 3/4 rock at the base of the west gully
the waterfall crossing below the peak, which goes easily only on the bench near 6,500 ft
a long, exposed ridge with few bail options and real exposure to afternoon thunderstorms
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts at MESAHCHIE COL, the col at the foot of Mesahchie's west ridge. From the basin, the shoulder crest leads up to cairned ground; follow the cairns to the base of the small peak between Mesahchie and Katsuk, turn right, and traverse slightly exposed slabs down to the col, which holds a well-built bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the FIRST obvious gully leading up the west ridge. The right gully is steep Class 3/4 at its base, then enters a broader, gentler gully past a string of cairns and tops out on the ridge crest; the crest is then followed east, exposed but moderate, to the summit. Negative marker: if you reached the peak along the crest from the east and are starting from a flat spot at the foot of the summit pyramid, you are on the East Ridge, not this route.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes:
Castle Rock sits right beside US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Around milepost 96.5 there is an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway; the rock is visible from the car.

Two different trails leave this one pullout and they go to different halves of the crag. For Upper Castle take the trail from the UPHILL, western end. It climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge, the wide bench that splits the formation in two. Ten to fifteen minutes puts you on the ledge and the first routes are five to ten minutes further.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons and early or late in the day — the wall faces southwest and takes a lot of sun
hazards: Heavily polished granite that climbs harder than the grade
Full southwest sun on the upper wall
Parties above you on a crowded classic
Descent is a climbers' trail off the back of the formation down to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Logger's Ledge is the test for every Upper Castle route: they all start FROM the bench, not from the ground. If you are at the foot of the rock with the highway noise still beside you, you are at Lower Castle and one full wall too low — that is the trail from the eastern end of the pullout.

On the ledge, Midway is found by the tower rather than by counting routes. It starts at Jello Tower, the pillar standing off the main wall, and the first pitch takes the corner and chimney on the tower's RIGHT side.

The adjacent feature is worth knowing so you do not confuse them: the wide crack and chimney separating the main wall from Jello Tower on the tower's WEST side is Damnation Crack, a much harder line at 5.9+ that starts hand-size and widens to offwidth and then chimney. If your first moves are strenuous wide climbing, you are on the wrong side of the tower.

Expect the rock to be heavily polished — this is a 1948 Beckey line and one of the most-climbed routes in the canyon, so 5.6 here does not feel like 5.6 elsewhere.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes: Oversized dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs and traverses east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Polished rock
Full southwest sun
Parties above you on the shared Midway terrain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
As for Midway: every Upper Castle route starts from Logger's Ledge, so if you are at the base of the rock at road level you are at Lower Castle, one wall too low.

The start is at Jello Tower — the pillar standing proud of the main wall — and the ordinary Midway line takes the corner and chimney on the tower's RIGHT side. The direct variation departs from that same feature rather than from a separate part of the ledge, so the tower is what you are looking for, not a second start.

Negative marker: the wide crack and chimney splitting the main wall from Jello Tower on its WEST side is Damnation Crack at 5.9+, and it climbs hands to offwidth to chimney. Strenuous wide climbing from the first moves means you are on the wrong side of the tower.

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail to the cairned talus traverse
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Sunrise Mine trailhead at the end of the forest road. The first mile crosses two unbridged creeks — a log, a root crossing and one more insistent ford — so expect wet feet and treat them seriously in early-season high water. The trail then climbs steadily through forest to the LAST MAJOR SWITCHBACK before it starts zigzagging steeply up toward the pass. That switchback is where you leave the trail; the pass is NOT. From there a cairned line traverses northeast across talus. Route-finding markers on the traverse, in order: pass just above a large FLAT-TOPPED BOULDER near the first stand of trees, thread a natural gap through those trees into a second open talus field, cross heather and more talus, cross a strip of trees near a rocky bluff. A seep just below the gully is the only reliable water and only runs mid-season.
approach_variants.season: June to September. Steep snow lies against the base and in the approach gully into June, and in a heavy year parties have found the base still buried in late May.
hazards: Two unbridged creek crossings in the first mile, serious in early-season high water
Loose talus on the cairned traverse, exposed in places
Steep lingering snow in the approach gully into June
Loose rock on the rubble ledges below the first belay — manage what you kick down onto anyone behind
The turnoff from the trail is unmarked and is at the switchback, not at the pass; parties without a track have overshot it
approach_variants.baseFinding: The traverse ends at the obvious RED GULLY on the right-hand side of the buttress. From the gully, scramble up and LEFT on rubble-strewn ledges to a LONE FIR TREE, then follow a narrow ledge about twenty feet to a SINGLE BOLTED BELAY — one bolt, on a ledge, past one tree. That belay is the start of the first pitch and there is nothing else like it on this tower. Negative markers: if you are standing on open talus under a dark grey face with TWO LARGE BOULDERS at its foot and a long line of bolts running away up a fifty-five-metre pitch, you are one line LEFT of here, on the west-face route that shares this tower's summit; if you left the traverse into a gully on the RIGHT-HAND (east) side of the tower and climbed cedar and heather to a notch on the skyline, you are on the neighbouring tower entirely and the route above you is a different climb.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the basin below the west face, then 20 ft DOWNHILL of the chockstone chimney
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the Northwest Face: Blue Lake Trailhead, Blue Lake Trail about 1-1.25 miles to the northwest-side clearing, then the climber's path up talus into the basin below the west face.

Nine pitches, 5.11b, first climbed in 2006. Pitches 7-9 are typically simul-climbed or pitched out onto the well-travelled Southwest Rib finish to the true summit.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Several lines starting within tens of feet of each other on the same wall
A finish that merges onto a different route's terrain
No water in the basin
Talus and heather with no maintained tread above the trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS AN OBVIOUS BOLTED FACE ABOUT 20 FT DOWNHILL FROM A LARGE CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY AND NOTCH, JUST LEFT OF PITCH 1 OF THE NORTHWEST FACE. THE CHOCKSTONE CHIMNEY IS THE KEY LANDMARK FOR LOCATING THE START AMONG SEVERAL CLOSELY SPACED LINES ON THIS WALL.

SO THE TEST IS: FIND THE CHIMNEY WITH CHOCKSTONES JAMMED IN IT, THEN GO 20 FT DOWNHILL, AND LOOK FOR BOLTS ON A FACE. Bolts off the deck are the distinguishing feature. The Northwest Face beside it starts by traversing into a steep CORNER with no bolts at the base.

THE OTHER NEIGHBOUR, AND THE DIRECTION SEPARATES THEM CLEANLY: FREE MOJO starts ROUGHLY 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT OF THE SAME CHIMNEY, ON A NONDESCRIPT CRACK. This route is 20 ft down and LEFT-ish of the chimney, on bolts. Down and right on a crack is the other route; down and left on bolts is this one.

CONFIRM BY WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU BAIL, WHICH IS A HARDWARE COUNT: to descend the route itself, rappel the FIRST THREE PITCHES with a single 60 m rope from BOLTED AND CHAIN ANCHORS back to the ground. A three-pitch fully bolted rappel line off the deck is what this route offers and its corner-system neighbour does not.

AND THE FULL-ROUTE FINISH ENDS SOMEWHERE ELSE: the top three pitches join the Southwest Rib to the true summit, from which the standard South Arete descent runs down to the RABBIT EARS and then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully.

approach_variants.name: Barlow Pass, the closed road and Glacier Basin
approach_variants.notes: Two clearly different stages before you leave maintained tread. From the gate at Barlow Pass the old Monte Cristo road runs four flat miles along the South Fork Sauk to the ghost town, crossing the river on cable and suspension bridges; the grade is easy and rideable in dry conditions, though road and bridge washouts mean most parties on bikes walk them through a short section or two. At the townsite, walk past the old cabins, cross the bridge over 76 Creek and follow the street through the settlement to pick up signed Glacier Basin Trail #719. The first half mile is an old mining road grade along Glacier Creek; then the tread turns steep, eroded and hands-on-rock, climbing past Glacier Falls on slick, root-braided rock steps that are considerably harder and more slip-prone descending than ascending. The trail crosses into wilderness, skirts the northeast edge of Mystery Hill and levels into Glacier Basin. Glacier Creek is reliable water the whole way but drains historic mine workings and carries elevated arsenic and heavy metals, worst low down near the townsite — treat it. The maintained trail ends at the basin; from there open talus and persistent steep snow, up to about forty-five degrees for a few hundred vertical feet, lead up the centre gully to the obvious col on the north ridge, with the Wilmans Peaks close overhead on the right.
approach_variants.season: June is the classic window: enough snow remains on the col talus to speed travel while the moat at the chimney's base is usually still closed. By late July the moat can open and block or seriously complicate access, and the talus turns loose and tedious once melted out.
hazards: a short but unavoidable roped rock chimney — this is not a Class 3 scramble move
steep firm snow to around forty-five degrees on the col approach, needing an axe and reliable self-arrest into midsummer
the moat at the base of the chimney, which can open by mid-to-late summer and add rock climbing or block access outright
loose red volcanic breccia above the chimney, worst in the final two hundred feet, with rockfall onto anyone below
washed-out river crossings on the closed road and no cell coverage in the basin
drifting onto neighbouring Cadet or Kyes terrain among the cluster of peaks
afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed upper mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: FIXED GEAR HANGING IN A SHORT CHIMNEY IS THE PROOF. From the col, step across the moat and contour south — climber's left — across snow or talus below the summit cliffs, scouting the rock band above you for the one obvious break. The correct break is a short chimney, on the order of thirty feet of actual climbing, and it is identified by what is hanging in it: old aid slings dangle from it, an old rusty piton is in it if you can spot it, and several much newer bolts have been added to it, so the line is protected where the rest of the wall is bare. If the break you are looking at holds no fixed gear at all — no slings, no piton, no bolts — keep contouring south, because that is not it. The moves through it go roughly at three short steps of moderate fifth class, and above them a bolted rappel anchor sits about twenty-five feet up. A second check on the far side: from the top of the chimney a steepish ramp leads left for around a hundred feet, and snow whales can slicken those slabs; above that it is loose scrambling on red volcanic breccia all the way, and that red rock is what the upper mountain is made of. If the ground above your chimney is clean grey slab rather than red rubble, you are not on the peak's standard line.

bivy.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
bivy.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
bivy.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Stillaguamish valley
approach_variants.notes: From the Sunrise Mine trailhead, follow the trail about half a mile. Just before it crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish, leave it for a faint path up the river's east side; it comes and goes and soon disappears into slide alder, brush and avalanche debris. Past a house-sized boulder near 3,000-3,100 ft, either cross the river and climb a ridge ramp southwest to the upper basin near 4,000 ft, or continue to the broad basin at about 3,700 ft and turn sharply up the steep gully directly east (or the slabs to its right). Snow-covered slabs then lead to the notch in the southeast ridge at about 5,600 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Earlier, snow on the slabs and in the gullies makes it a basic alpine climb, and an ice axe and crampons are standard until it has gone.
hazards: Thick brush, slide alder and hard avalanche debris along the east side of the river
Fording the river to dodge the brush is unsafe in high runoff
The snow-covered slabs below the notch are the route's main avalanche concern
The ~45° gully from the southeast basin to the south ridge is often icy when snow-filled
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route leaves the Sunrise Mine Trail about half a mile from the trailhead, just BEFORE the trail crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish: look for a narrow path staying on the east side of the river. If you have crossed the river and are climbing the switchbacks toward Headlee Pass, you have missed the turn; this route never goes to the pass. The scrambling proper starts at the notch in the southeast ridge (about 5,600 ft), where the summit comes into view: drop through trees into the southeast basin, traverse right below the cliffs to the first broad gully and climb it to the south ridge.

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
approach_variants.notes:
Killen Creek trailhead (~4,600 ft) is reached by Forest Roads 23, 21 and 2329 from either the Randle or the Trout Lake side. FR 2329 is gravel, runs north from Takhlakh Lake along the northwest edge of the wilderness, and is commonly still under snow into early summer — parties have had to park low and walk or bushwhack an extra mile or more of road to reach the trailhead. Call the Mount Adams Ranger District rather than assuming.

Killen Creek Trail #113 runs about 3.1 miles through lodgepole forest and wildflower meadow to the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 6,100 ft, in the area known as Adams Creek Meadows. Cross straight over the PCT onto High Camp Trail #10 and continue about 1.0 mile to its end at roughly 6,900 ft at the edge of the Adams Glacier's lateral moraine. Small cairns mark the upper section when it is under snow.

Camping: High Camp at about 7,000 ft has established flat dry sites; there are more between 7,000 and 7,600 ft; a glacial lake camp at about 7,650 ft gives the easiest glacier access; and some parties push to sheltered bivouacs around 7,100 ft in a shallow snow gully just left of the moraine.

Killen Creek, crossed low on the trail, is the last dependable running water — above camp, melt snow. The tread thins to a moraine and gully scramble above treeline and is easy to lose in the dark or under snow, so record landmarks or a track on the way up.

Permits: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, plus a Cascade Volcano Pass for travel above 7,000 ft in the summer season.
approach_variants.season: June into early July, while the icefall is still filled in
hazards: Serac collapse in the icefall between roughly 9,200 and 11,800 ft
Large crevasse near 10,800 ft that can force a long traverse to find a crossing
Losing the thin moraine tread above treeline in dark or whiteout
FR 2329 snow-blocked into early summer, adding road walking to the approach
No running water above Killen Creek
Very loose volcanic rock on the North Ridge descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the rare approach where the objective is in full view the whole way, and that is the strongest tool you have: as you walk up the High Camp Trail the Adams Glacier is directly in front of you, tumbling from the summit icecap, with the enormous crevasses of the main icefall facing you. If you cannot see a broken icefall ahead, you are not on the right side of the mountain.

The base is the toe of the glacier at roughly 7,000–7,300 ft, above camp. The test is underfoot: while you are still on rubble, moraine crest and scree you have not reached it. The toe is where continuous snow and ice begins and the scrambling stops — that is where you rope up.

Starting position matters. Begin on the RIGHT (climber's right, west) side of the glacier at its base and stay in the right third for most of the climb; the standard line then works left higher up to avoid crevasses.

The route above has its own confirmations. The angle steepens noticeably at about 8,500 ft. Around 9,500 ft you traverse toward a ramp beneath seracs. The real icefall — the crux, roughly 4,000 ft of tortured ice between about 9,200 and 11,800 ft — is where the maze of seracs begins and where screws and belays get used. Near 10,800 ft a large crevasse commonly forces an eastward traverse before a crossing appears. Above roughly 11,400 ft the ground relents to easy névé and you are on the summit plateau.

Negative marker for the descent: the North Ridge is the usual way down and it is very loose volcanic rock. If you are descending on ice with crevasses you are still on the Adams Glacier, not on the ridge.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek, the PCT and High Camp, then across the lava fields to the Lava Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Killen Creek trailhead on the forest road near Takhlakh Lake at about 4,600 ft, follow Killen Creek Trail #113 roughly 3.1 miles through open lodgepole forest, crossing East Fork Adams Creek near mile 2.5, to the PCT at about 6,100 ft. Cross the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, about 6,900 ft, on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine.

From High Camp this route is reached more directly than the Lyman: traverse off-trail east across the lava fields to the toe of the Lava Glacier, without needing to work around Lava Ridge.

The approach roads are gravel and seasonal, opening as snow clears.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun. This is a cold-season face: it turns icy and starts shedding rock as the snowpack recedes later in summer
hazards: Steep ice and snow with serac hazard on a face that must be climbed continuously
Rockfall increasing sharply as the headwall warms
Crevasse navigation on the Lava Glacier apron
A long descent of the North Ridge on loose volcanic scree with rockfall onto parties below
Seasonal gravel road access that opens late in a heavy year
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE RIDGES. THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, AND IT IS COUNTABLE IN CLOUD.

From High Camp the features run in this order as you work east: the ADAMS GLACIER, then the NORTH RIDGE (the North Cleaver), then the LAVA GLACIER, then LAVA RIDGE, then the LYMAN GLACIER. Three glaciers, two ridges between them, in that order.

THIS ROUTE'S BASE IS AT THE HEAD OF THE LAVA GLACIER — SO YOU CROSS ONE RIDGE PAST THE NORTH RIDGE AND STOP. IF YOU HAVE ROUNDED OR CROSSED A SECOND RIDGE, YOU ARE AT THE LYMAN GLACIER AND ON A DIFFERENT CLIMB.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A SHAPE, AND IT IS THE reason this route is worth doing: THE HEADWALL IS A TRIANGLE. It is the face closing between the North Ridge on one side and Lava Ridge on the other, the two of them converging above you. If the ground ahead is open glacier that does not narrow to a point, you are not under the headwall — you are on the glacier below it, and the apron will keep going for a while yet.

THE NEGATIVE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE IS THE NORTH RIDGE ITSELF, because it is the walk-off and it is right there: if you are climbing snow with a rocky cleaver on one hand and no closing headwall above, you are on the North Ridge, which is the descent for this route rather than the ascent.

CONFIRMATION ONCE COMMITTED: about 45-degree neve, climbed nearly continuously without belays because stopping under it is worse than moving. The first ascent went from 8,500 ft to the summit in around five and a half hours. If you are placing gear on every rope length you are not moving the way this face wants to be moved.

TIMING AS A FINDING: this face is graded for cold. Arriving at the triangle with the sun on it means going down, not looking for a better line.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek and High Camp, then east past Lava Ridge to the Lyman at 8,000 ft
approach_variants.notes:
From the Killen Creek trailhead, follow Trail #113 through open dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows — the last easy water before the high basin. The trees thin as the trail climbs rockier ground to the PCT at about 6,100 ft, roughly 3.1 miles in. Continue straight across onto High Camp Trail #10 for about a mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, near 6,900 ft.

From High Camp the maintained trail is done. Traverse east and southeast off-trail across lava fields, across the toe of the Lava Glacier and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, to the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This is glacier and talus travel with real route-finding, worst in a low-snow year; rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on ice.

Most of the route can be simul-climbed with a running belay on pickets. The standard descent is the North Ridge, not a reversal — long, loose volcanic scree, occasionally narrow, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul; climbed in late spring and early summer as moderate to steep snow and sometimes alpine ice
hazards: Crevasse and serac navigation on the Lyman, particularly on the south lobe's upper half
A short steep crux chute near 10,000 ft that varies from 45 to 65 degrees year to year
Long sustained high-altitude climbing with a late-season low-snow route-finding problem on the traverse
A descent down the North Ridge on loose rotten volcanic scree, with rockfall onto parties below
Seasonal gravel road access
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE RIDGES, AND FOR THIS ROUTE YOU MUST GET PAST TWO.

East of High Camp the order is: ADAMS GLACIER, NORTH RIDGE, LAVA GLACIER, LAVA RIDGE, LYMAN GLACIER. You cross the Lava Glacier and then go around or over the TOE OF LAVA RIDGE. Lava Ridge is the second ridge and it is the gate. If you have crossed only one ridge and stopped at a glacier, you are at the Lava Glacier Headwall — a different climb with a triangular face — not at the Lyman.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A FORK, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE ONCE YOU ARE ON IT: THE LYMAN SPLITS AROUND A NARROW ROCK OUTCROP into two lobes. The north lobe is the original line; the south lobe runs 40-degree unbroken neve on its lower half and is broken by crevasses and serac walls on its upper half. A glacier that forks around an island of rock is the confirmation you are where you meant to be.

THE CRUX CONFIRMS IT A SECOND TIME, HIGHER: both lobes lead to a chute near 10,000 ft that runs anywhere from 45 to 65 degrees over about 50 ft depending on the year. One short steep chute, then easier snow to the summit plateau. If you meet no constriction at all, you are on a neighbouring glacier.

THE BASE ELEVATION IS THE THIRD CHECK: about 8,000 ft. Arriving on ice much higher than that means you gained the glacier well above its toe and may have come onto it over the ridge rather than around it, which is fine but changes where the lobes sit relative to you.

WHAT THE DESCENT MEANS FOR THE APPROACH, AND IT IS WORTH DECIDING AT THE CAR: you do not come back this way. The walk-off is the North Ridge, back toward High Camp. So the ridge you counted past on the way in is not the ridge you come down.

approach_variants.name: Bird Creek Meadows and Sunrise Camp, on the Yakama Reservation side
approach_variants.notes:
This is the southeast side of the mountain and the approach crosses Yakama Nation land, which makes it an access problem before it is a climbing problem. A tribal-use permit for Tract D is required, bought at the fee station on entry at the Mirror Lake gate — it cannot be obtained in advance — and it is only available when the area is open to non-tribal use. Historically that window has run from about the start of July to the start of October for non-members. The area has also been closed outright in some years, so confirm with the Yakama Nation before building a trip around this approach; there is no alternative way in from this side.

From the Bird Creek Meadows parking area (about 5,576–5,700 ft), the trail is easy to follow to roughly 6,700 ft. Above that it is route-finding: any number of lines through moraine, scree and glacier remnants lead up to Sunrise Camp at about 8,300 ft. Carry a map — locating the camp is the part people get wrong. Trailhead to camp is about 3–4 hours.

Sunrise Camp sits at the base of the Mazama Glacier, tucked between the glacier and a small rock hill, with hand-built rock shelters. It is a fine fair-weather camp and a poor one otherwise: it is exposed to winds that can reach hurricane strength, and to rockfall off the glacier. The rock walls help, but only somewhat.

From camp to summit is about 5 hours.
approach_variants.season: Summer; non-tribal access to this side has historically been limited to a mid-summer to early-autumn window
hazards: Tribal-use permit required and only sold at the gate, in a limited seasonal window — no advance purchase, and the area has been closed in some years
Route-finding through moraine and scree above 6,700 ft to locate Sunrise Camp
Rockfall off the glacier onto Sunrise Camp
Extreme wind exposure at camp
Bergschrunds around 9,500 ft
Mistaking Piker's Peak, where the route tops out, for the true summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts directly above camp — the first ground you cross after leaving Sunrise Camp is the glacier itself, so the recognition problem here is finding CAMP, not finding the base.

Sunrise Camp: at roughly 8,300 ft, a flat with rock wind shelters, wedged between the toe of the Mazama Glacier on one side and a small rock hill on the other. If you are on open moraine with no rock hill beside you, you are short of it or off to one side; the terrain between 6,700 and 8,300 ft has many plausible lines and only some of them end at the camp.

Above camp the sequence is legible. Long stretches of glacier at about 40 degrees, then bear RIGHT onto the headwall proper, which runs about 45 degrees and is where pickets earn their place. Bergschrunds appear around 9,500 ft. The glacier narrows as it climbs.

The top is where the route makes you choose. Nearing Piker's Peak — the south summit at 11,644 ft — you can exit left onto easy 25–30 degree ground, or stay right for a short technical finish: roughly 40 ft of 60–70 degree snow and ice on the southeast corner, worth two or three screws.

Critical negative marker at the top: Piker's Peak is NOT the summit of Mount Adams. When the ground flattens out you have reached the south summit; the true summit is a further dome across the plateau to the north, with the geographic high point to the east. This route tops out on the false summit by design, so treat the flattening as a halfway signal rather than an arrival.

approach_variants.name: Killen Creek trailhead and High Camp
approach_variants.notes:
The same walk in as the Adams Glacier and the Northwest Ridge, and High Camp is the shared base for all three. Killen Creek Trail #113 from the trailhead (~4,600 ft) runs about 3.1 miles to the PCT junction at roughly 6,100 ft; cross straight over onto High Camp Trail #10 for another mile to its end at about 6,900 ft on the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine. Camping is spread between 7,000 and 7,600 ft, including a glacial lake camp near 7,650 ft.

Access is by FR 23, 21 and 2329; FR 2329 is gravel and holds snow into early summer. East Fork Adams Creek, crossed about 2.5 miles up the trail, is the last dependable water.

Permits: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, plus a Cascade Volcano Pass for travel above 7,000 ft in the summer season.

This is a longer and more committing day than the South Climb from a much quieter side of the mountain, and crevassed glacier lies on both flanks of the ridge and on the summit ice cap, so glacier skills are expected, unlike the South Spur.
approach_variants.season: June through September; a snow route early, a loose rock route once it melts out
hazards: Very loose volcanic rock the length of the ridge — helmets, and spacing between climbers
Crevassed glacier on both flanks if you leave the crest
Exposed snow travel between rock sections
Thin moraine tread above treeline, easy to lose in dark or whiteout
No running water above East Fork Adams Creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From High Camp the line is southeast, toward the foot of the ridge, and in clear weather you can see the whole thing from the approach — parties describe it as impossible to miss.

The recognition problem is entirely a poor-visibility one, and the test is what is under your boots. The North Ridge is the rubble-and-cinder rib that separates the Adams Glacier on its west from the Lava Glacier ground on its east. You should be on loose volcanic rock and scree, on a defined crest, with glacier falling away on BOTH sides. If you are on ice with crevasses, you have slid off the rib onto one glacier or the other, and which one tells you which way to correct.

A smooth, clean, snow-only ascent is the wrong sign on this route: it is a choss pile, and the loose rock is the confirmation rather than the complaint. Expect short easy scrambling steps low down.

The angle eases noticeably around 11,000 ft, which is the sign the ridge proper is behind you and the summit plateau ground is ahead.

waypoints.name: South Climb / Cold Springs Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-8040 north of Trout Lake, on the mountain's SOUTH side. This route's approach, its descent and its stored logistics all use this trailhead: the Wilson Glacier basin is reached by a long, mostly off-trail traverse east and then north around the mountain's eastern flank, not by a north-side approach.

approach_variants.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain Trail east around the mountain
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cold Springs and South Climb trailhead at about 5,600 ft at the end of the forest road north of Trout Lake, follow South Climb Trail #183 about a mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail.

Instead of continuing north toward the Lunch Counter, follow the Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below the Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson and Klickitat glacier basins. This is a long, mostly off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands.

The Wilson descends from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft, and it is split by a rock rib. Expect a full day to reach a camp near its toe before any summit attempt.

This is one of the least-visited and least-documented flanks of the mountain. The descent is not a reversal: parties top out and come down the standard South Climb to Cold Springs.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for the headwall itself; the surrounding east-side walls are rockfall-prone once warm
hazards: Persistent rockfall from the east-side cliff bands, directly over the contouring approach
A steep ice and snow headwall with serac hazard
Crevasse navigation on the Wilson
A long, mostly off-trail traverse with creek crossings and route-finding, and a full day just to reach camp
Rarely climbed, so conditions cannot be inferred from recent traffic and rescue would be slow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION HAPPENS ABOUT A MILE FROM THE CAR AND IT IS A TURNING, NOT AN ARRIVAL. At the junction of the South Climb Trail with the Round the Mountain Trail, the standard South Spur route goes NORTH toward the Lunch Counter; this route goes EAST. If you are climbing toward the Lunch Counter, you are on the standard South Climb and this route is already behind you.

THAT IS THE ONE ERROR WORTH GUARDING, BECAUSE IT IS RECOVERABLE ONLY BY WALKING BACK DOWN. Everything after it is a long contour.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS A GLACIER SPLIT BY A ROCK RIB. The Wilson runs from about 10,600 ft down to about 7,400 ft and a rock rib divides it. A headwall above a glacier that is bisected by a rib is the confirmation. An unbroken glacier with no rib in it is not the Wilson.

THE SECOND POSITIVE IS ASPECT AND IT IS THE COARSEST BUT MOST RELIABLE: you must be on the EAST side of the mountain. Going around the eastern flank is the whole approach. If the sun is rising behind the mountain rather than in front of you, you have not come far enough round.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS FOR SAFETY RATHER THAN NAVIGATION: the contour runs directly beneath cliff bands that shed rock. It is a place to keep moving. Persistent rockfall on these east-side headwalls is among the reasons most of them remain unrepeated, so a rope-length of comfortable ground is not evidence the ground above you is quiet.

WHAT BEING ON A NEIGHBOURING BASIN LOOKS LIKE: keep going round and you reach the Klickitat basin. The Wilson is the first of the two you meet coming from the south.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road about 8.5 miles to the road-end parking and leave the car there; the road beyond has been closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood, and the washout itself is about a mile farther on. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.
approach_variants.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
hazards: Crevasses on the upper Eel Glacier, including large ones on its eastern slopes
A bergschrund at the head of the Eel that is hardest to cross late in the season, with a short steep step above it
The Flypaper Pass snow finger at 40-45 degrees, firm or icy, steeper than older descriptions state
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off the cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly meta-sedimentary rock on the final summit scramble
Unbridged fords and heavy blowdown on the West Fork trail, plus roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS FLYPAPER PASS, AND THE TEST IS WHICH THINGS ARE ON WHICH SIDE OF IT. Flypaper Pass at about 6,500 ft is the notch between MOUNT ANDERSON on the east and ECHO ROCK (7,033 ft) on the west. Standing in the notch, Anderson is on your right and Echo Rock on your left when you are facing north through it. If both walls beside you are the same mountain, you are in a gully on a flank rather than in the pass.

THE APPROACH TEST, done before you can see the notch, is the tarn. From the camp saddle, traverse ABOVE the tarn — often still frozen — and take the single steep snow finger that runs up from the far side of it. There is one finger and it goes to one notch. If you are walking round the tarn at its level rather than above it, you have dropped too low and will meet cliffs.

SECOND TEST, and it is the one that says the pass is in the condition you planned for: the finger's steepest section now runs 40 degrees or more. Glacier recession has steepened it well beyond the older published figure of about 30 degrees over 300 vertical feet, so a party that finds it far steeper than the book has not gone the wrong way — those descriptions are old. If it has melted out to bare scree and ice, that is the season telling you to come back earlier, not a route-finding error.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: over the pass the ground drops onto the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund cuts across below the headwall, forcing an end-around to one side. If you are on glacier and looking for a way past a schrund, you are past the base and onto the climb.

approach_variants.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west
approach_variants.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a TRAIL the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.
approach_variants.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
hazards: Everything above the pass is the same: the 40-45 degree snow finger, the Eel Glacier crevasses and bergschrund, and loose summit rock
A long valley walk with river crossings and blowdown of its own
Arriving at the pass from the west means the shelter and the climbers' path are both below and behind you as you crest it
No cell coverage anywhere on either side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL TO THE DOSEWALLIPS VARIANT ABOVE, because both arrive at Anderson Pass and everything above the pass is shared: traverse above the tarn, take the one steep snow finger from its far side, and know you are at Flypaper Pass when MOUNT ANDERSON is on one side of the notch and ECHO ROCK on the other.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at the pass itself, because you arrive there from the opposite direction. Anderson Pass is a signed trail junction — the West Fork Dosewallips and East Fork Quinault trails meet there, with the Anderson Pass shelter (Camp Siberia) just below on the Dosewallips side at roughly 4,180 ft. The climbers' path leaves NORTH off the pass and up the moraine. If you have walked over the pass and begun descending the other valley, you have missed the turn; it is a boot path, not a signed one.

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the 4,900 ft saddle, then the boot path and cairns over Peak 5681
approach_variants.notes:
From the Austin Pass / Artist Point trailhead at the end of SR-542, follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600. It DROPS about 800 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up past Lake Ann — 4.1 miles one way to the lake area — to a saddle at 4,900 ft northwest of the lake.

From the saddle, leave the maintained trail for a boot path heading southwest then south along the ridge crest. Where the ridge steepens near 5,300 ft the path contours the EAST side before the crest re-forms; from there follow cairns over Peak 5681 and scramble roughly half a mile west along the summit ridge to Mount Ann.

About 10.5 miles round trip with roughly 4,000 ft of cumulative gain, part of which comes from the fact that the trail loses 800 ft at the start and you pay it back at the end.

NOTE ON THE NAME: this is the Lake Ann below Artist Point on SR-542, not the Lake Ann near Maple Pass. One route has already been recorded with the wrong Lake Ann's trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep snow-free; winter and spring ascents are done by experienced parties with mountaineering gear on a stable snowpack
hazards: Cairns as the only navigation above 5,300 ft, in both directions
Contouring low on the return, which cliffs out above the Swift Creek basin
An 800 ft descent at the start that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
Two Lake Anns in the North Cascades, and one of them has already been given the wrong trailhead
Lingering snow on the traverse in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 4,900 FT SADDLE NORTHWEST OF THE LAKE IS WHERE THE ROUTE STARTS, AND IT IS THE LAST PIECE OF MAINTAINED TRAIL. Below it, built tread. Above it, a boot path. If you are still on graded trail heading toward the Fisher Chimneys and Shuksan, you have walked past your turn — that is the same trail, continuing.

THE BEARING OUT OF THE SADDLE IS SOUTHWEST, THEN SOUTH, ALONG THE CREST. Two headings in sequence. In cloud, keep the crest under your feet.

THE ONE PLACE THE ROUTE LEAVES THE CREST IS NEAR 5,300 FT, AND IT GOES EAST. Where the ridge steepens the path contours the EAST side before the crest re-forms above. Contouring west here puts you on the wrong side of the ridge above the Swift Creek basin.

CAIRNS ARE THE HANDRAIL ABOVE 5,300 FT, and losing them is the main route-finding hazard in poor visibility, in both directions. Note them going up.

ARRIVAL: the scrambling ridge runs roughly half a mile WEST from Peak 5681 to Mount Ann's summit. Peak 5681 is not the top — if you are standing on a high point and there is more ridge running west, keep going.

AND THE RETURN TRAP, which is worth stating because it is a cliff problem rather than a navigation one: coming back, stay HIGH on the ridge rather than contouring low where the path is indistinct. Contouring low here cliffs out above the basin.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes
approach_variants.notes: There is no trail to this peak. From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20 the maintained trail climbs to Easy Pass, and from there you descend the west side into Fisher Creek Basin. Near the Fisher Camp junction a boot path heads up-valley but fades within about ten minutes at a pile of avalanche-downed trees; from there travel is cross-country up through meadows to the head of Fisher Creek, where an overlook camp works well as a base if you are short of time. From the head of the valley the headwall to Silent Lakes goes either by the obvious snow and ice couloir — steeper than it looks from below, and degrading into a loose rock gully by late season — or by the broken heather and cliff ramps to its left. An axe, and often crampons, are useful here into midsummer. From a camp at Upper Silent Lake, a roughly westerly traverse across heather leads to a saddle around 7,200 ft, then a rising traverse across a talus bowl gains the notch on the peak's south ridge where the scrambling starts.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September for the most reliable snow-free travel. An axe and often crampons are still worth carrying into July for the headwall couloir and the north side of Easy Pass. The highway itself is shut in winter.
hazards: extensive loose rock in the summit ridge's gullies and ledges, with rockfall onto anyone below
steep snow and ice in the headwall couloir to Silent Lakes — the real technical crux of the trip, not the summit scrambling
long off-trail route-finding through Fisher Creek Basin with no tread beyond the Fisher Camp junction
avalanche paths on the flanks near Easy Pass in early season
black bears through Fisher Creek Basin and the Easy Pass meadows
afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: AN ERODED BLACK DIKE SPLITS THE SUMMIT BLOCK, AND THAT SLOT IS THE ROUTE. The rising traverse across the talus bowl tops out at a pronounced notch in the south ridge at roughly 7,600 to 7,800 ft; from the notch, scramble up good rock along the crest until the summit block itself blocks the way. Look for a narrow defile cut into the block — a dark band that has weathered back into a slot, so the feature reads as a black stripe with a groove eroded along it. Climb the defile until you can traverse leftward on a sloping ramp that puts you back on the south ridge crest, then scramble the crest to the top. If the block above you is uniform pale rock with no dark band running through it, you are not at the defile: traverse and keep looking rather than forcing the face, because the ledges here are chossy and everything you dislodge falls on the party below. A second check: the correct line never asks for a rope. If you find yourself committed to moves you would want protected, you have gone up the face rather than through the slot.

bivy.name: Silent Lakes
bivy.notes: Alpine lakes between Mount Arriva and Fisher Peak, reached off-trail from upper Fisher Creek basin below Easy Pass. The upper lake sits near 7,000 ft and is the usual base for Arriva's south side.
bivy.water: Lakes
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites on heather and slab around the lakes

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs are not allowed at Easy Pass or anywhere beyond it, because the national park begins at the pass.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 to the moraine, then the lower Boulder Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the Boulder Ridge Trailhead at the end of FR-1131 off Baker Lake Road (about 2,700 ft — the lowest trailhead of any Baker route, which is where the 8,000+ ft of gain comes from), follow Boulder Ridge Trail #605. The first two miles are nearly flat through old clear-cut and timber and end at a boggy clearing at the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary; the maintained tread effectively stops there. Beyond it the route is a steep, unmaintained boot path up heather. Around 4,700 ft it crosses a Class 3 rock band, which parties have sometimes found protected by a fixed line left by an earlier team — treat any fixed line as unknown gear, not as trail furniture. Above the rock band the path gains the crest of a lateral moraine and follows it. Between the meadow and the basalt cliff, stay on or near the moraine crest north of Boulder Creek: the game trails here drop toward the creek and lead nowhere useful. Camp is on the ridge. Two elevations are published for it and they do not agree — so plan to camp where the ridge runs out into snow rather than at a number.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul. This is a short-season route: the Boulder shrinks and breaks up early, and by August the crevasse field that is walkable in June is a maze
hazards: A Class 3 rock band around 4,700 ft on an unmaintained boot path, sometimes with an unknown fixed line on it
Losing the moraine crest onto game trails that drop to Boulder Creek
A crevasse field that opens fast — this route has one of the shortest usable seasons on the mountain
Rockfall from the buttress near 9,300 ft on the upper mountain, on the way down as well as up
8,000 ft of gain from the lowest trailhead on the peak, so a late turnaround is a long descent in the dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MORAINE CREST IS THE HANDRAIL, AND THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE IT DIES. Everything from the rock band upward is a walk along a single narrow spine of moraine with the drop into Boulder Creek on one side. In cloud you do not need to see anything: keep the crest under your feet and keep the creek noise on the same side of you the whole way. If the ground under you goes flat and broad, or you are suddenly walking with the creek on the other side, you have come off the moraine and are on the game trails below it.

ARRIVAL: the ridge runs out into snow and ice near 6,300 ft, and that transition — trail-and-heather to glacier — is the base of the route. There is nothing subtle about it; the ground stops being walkable in boots.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE FROM THIS CAMP, and it matters because both start from the same spot: this route stays ON THE GLACIER. The Boulder-Park Cleaver route crosses the lower glacier northwest to the toe of a rock cleaver and gets onto rock. If you find yourself walking toward a rock rib and looking for a place to step off the ice, you are on the cleaver route, not this one. This route goes up the ice.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: contouring so far northwest that the Park Glacier headwall comes into view above you. That is the neighbouring aspect and its own set of routes.

approach_variants.name: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 to ridge camp, then across the lower Boulder Glacier to the toe of the cleaver
approach_variants.notes: The drive and the walk in are identical to the Boulder Glacier route: Baker Lake Road to FR-1130, then FR-1131 to the Boulder Ridge Trailhead near 2,700 ft, and Trail #605 for about two flat miles through clear-cut and timber to the boggy clearing at the wilderness boundary. Above that the user path climbs steep heather and takes a Class 3 rock step — the one parties have found with a fixed line on it — to a camp on the ridge where it meets snow and ice. A second, higher camp exists on a flat shelf sheltered by the cleaver itself around 7,500 ft, which shortens summit day considerably and is the reason some parties carry over. From camp the day begins with a glacier crossing rather than a glacier climb: cross the lower Boulder heading northwest to the toe of the cleaver, then follow the cleaver up to just below a large rock buttress near 9,300 ft, where several finishes are possible. This is Joe Morovits's 1894 line, and it is a different climb from the Boulder Glacier route despite sharing a trailhead, a camp and a name, and published first-ascent records for the two are muddled.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Aug — a longer usable window than the pure glacier line beside it, because the cleaver stays climbable after the ice below it has broken up
hazards: A Class 3 rock step on the approach with an unknown fixed line sometimes in place
Crevasse navigation on the short crossing of the lower Boulder to the toe, which changes year to year
Rockfall exposure near the 9,300 ft buttress, going up and coming down
The 7,500 ft high camp sits on the mountain with no bail-out short of reversing the cleaver
8,000 ft of cumulative gain — the biggest gain of any Baker route because the trailhead is the lowest
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A ROCK RIB THAT RISES OUT OF THE GLACIER, AND YOU FIND IT BY BEARING NORTHWEST OFF CAMP AND STOPPING WHEN THE ICE ENDS. That is the whole test and it works blind: from the ridge camp the crossing is a short one, the bearing is northwest, and the thing you are walking toward is the only rock rib coming down into the glacier on that side. Walk until the ice runs into rock. Do not look for a summit.

CONFIRM IT: at the toe you should be able to get off the ice and onto rock without climbing anything — the cleaver's foot is a walk-on, not a step. If you are standing under a wall you have to climb to get established, you are somewhere else on the glacier margin.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE ROUTE THAT SHARES THIS CAMP: the Boulder Glacier route never leaves the ice. If you are still roped up on glacier at 8,000 ft with no rock under you, you are on that route rather than this one. Conversely if you are on a rock spine with glacier falling away on BOTH sides, you are on the cleaver and you are right.

WHAT TOO HIGH LOOKS LIKE: the cleaver runs into a large rock buttress around 9,300 ft. That buttress is a decision point, not a base — it is where the finishes diverge, and if you have reached it you are about 2,500 ft above the toe of the cleaver.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at roughly 3,400 to 3,700 ft on Glacier Creek Road 39. The road washed out in December 2025 and reopened to vehicles in August 2026 after repairs; it has washed out before, so check its status before committing.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Camp
waypoints.directions: Trail 677 climbs through old-growth forest and flower-filled avalanche chutes, with a couple of unbridged creek crossings that are awkward early season or after rain. At about 2.25 miles the maintained trail forks; the left branch goes to the Coleman Glacier overlook, so take the RIGHT climbers' path that drops toward the moraine. Past the former Kulshan Cabin site near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, the last reliable running water, the path climbs steeply up the crest of the Hogsback lateral moraine to the usual camps between about 6,500 and 7,200 ft, roughly 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft above the car. Above camp there is no water except what you melt.

waypoints.name: Coleman Headwall Base
waypoints.directions: Rope up for glacier travel and cross the broken lower Coleman, generally trending up toward 8,000 ft to meet the North Ridge tracks before dropping back down and cutting under the Roman Nose to reach the base near 8,500 ft. This crossing is a real route-finding crux that changes year to year, with big crevasses to weave around, questionable snow bridges, and sometimes a committing, barely-reversible jump or a short vertical step to get established. Leave camp in the dark (starts between 11 p.m. and 4:30 a.m. are typical) so you are past the exposed crossing and the lower face before the sun brings rock and ice down off the headwall and the Black Buttes.

waypoints.name: Mount Baker Summit
waypoints.directions: Roughly a dozen pitches of sustained 45 to 50 degree neve and ice lead up the face: hard, dirty ice on leftward-trending traverses low down with rockfall exposure from a choss band above, then short steeper steps and an 800 ft band of brittle, plated 60 to 80 degree ice that takes screws well despite looking suspect. A bergschrund near 10,000 ft is the other crux and its lip often forces a short, occasionally overhanging step, sometimes belayed or lowered across off a screw or picket. Above it the angle relents to moderate snow and then an easy slope onto the summit plateau; 8 to 12 hours camp-to-summit is typical.
