approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge to a high Hogsback camp
approach_variants.notes:
Heliotrope Ridge trailhead via Glacier Creek Road. Trail 677 through old growth and avalanche chutes with a couple of unbridged creek crossings, then at about two and a quarter miles take the right-hand climbers' fork off the maintained trail onto the moraine. Past the old Kulshan Cabin site — the last running water — climb the Hogsback crest.

Parties on this route camp higher than the standard Coleman-Deming crowd, commonly around 6,700 ft and sometimes as high as 7,200, either on the ridge itself or on the flats toward the Black Buttes and the Roman Nose. Above camp everything is melted snow.

From camp the line goes up the centre of the broken Coleman. This is the real crux of the day: weaving round large crevasses, crossing bridges of uncertain quality, and occasionally a committing jump or a short vertical step to get established. It changes materially from season to season.

Starts are early — anything from late evening to half past four in the morning — specifically to be through the exposed glacier and onto the lower headwall before the sun loosens the wall and the Black Buttes above.

Glacier Creek Road has washed out more than once, most recently in the December 2025 floods, and it reopened to the trailhead in August 2026. When it is closed low it adds several miles on foot or bike before the kiosk, so check its status before a trip.
approach_variants.season: late Apr-Jun
hazards: the Coleman Glacier crossing itself — large crevasses, questionable bridges, occasionally a barely reversible move
rockfall and icefall off the headwall and the Black Buttes once the sun is on them
bergschrund at the base of the wall every season
no water above camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base sits at about 8,500 ft, immediately LEFT of the Roman Nose — the rock prow that bounds the headwall on its south side. Use the Roman Nose as the handrail: you want to be tucked under the face just past it, not out in the middle of the glacier.

The positive confirmation is that there is always a bergschrund here, and above it the slope kicks up into sustained forty-five to fifty degree ground that does not lie back again until around 10,200 ft. If the ground above you eases off within a couple of rope lengths, you are not on the headwall.

The negative marker matters because the two features are neighbours: the Coleman Headwall is a broad FACE, and the North Ridge is the defined arete bounding it. If you find yourself at the foot of a narrow crest with a double bergschrund rather than a wide slope, you have gone too far and you are at the North Ridge. Some parties deliberately trend up toward the North Ridge tracks around 8,000 ft to use the broken trail, then drop back down and cut under the Roman Nose — if you are following that plan, the drop back down is not optional.

approach_variants.name: Park Butte Trail 603 and the Railroad Grade to Sandy Camp
approach_variants.notes:
Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead at about 3,400 ft, at the end of the Sulphur Creek road. Cross Sulphur Creek near the start — bridged or on logs, but a genuine ford during peak snowmelt — then climb through the meadow and forest switchbacks.

At about two and a quarter miles a SIGNED junction sends you right onto the Railroad Grade Trail 603.2. Stone steps take you up onto the crest of the lateral moraine. There are three established camp areas along the way; Sandy Camp at about 5,900 ft is the usual one for climbing, roughly four miles in with 2,600 ft of gain.

Above Morovitz Meadows there is no reliable water other than melted snow.
approach_variants.season: May-Sep
hazards: Sulphur Creek crossing during peak melt
exposed, loose moraine crest in wind
crevasses on the broad Easton, worse late season
volcanic gas and unstable ground at Sherman Crater
no water above Morovitz Meadows
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the start when the moraine crest simply runs out. The Railroad Grade tapers off just before 6,000 ft into the sandy flats and rock-walled tent platforms of Sandy Camp; that is where the trail stops being a trail and where parties rope up for the glacier.

The simplest confirmation on the way up is which side the ice is on: walking the moraine crest toward the mountain, the Easton Glacier drops away on your RIGHT the entire way. If the glacier is on your left, or if there is no glacier beside you at all, you never took the signed junction and are still on the Park Butte trail heading for the lookout.

Higher, the feature that tells you the glacier is done is Sherman Crater — steaming, sulphurous ground at the head of the ice. The Roman Wall is the steep snow rising beyond it, and the true summit is a short traverse past the top of the wall. Smelling sulphur means you are at the TOP of the glacier and should be turning up onto the wall, not continuing toward the crater.

approach_variants.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman Glacier crossing
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to Coleman-Deming as far as camp: Glacier Creek Road to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two and a quarter miles, then the moraine crest to the Hogsback camps at around 6,000 ft — about three miles and 2,300 ft, four to five hours with a heavy pack. There are dry pitches at the top of the Hogsback.

From camp the two routes part company. The North Ridge crosses the Coleman toward the toe of the ridge, threading between hundred-foot seracs and large open crevasses. This crossing changes year to year and is genuine route-finding, not a bootpack — and because this route sees far less traffic than Coleman-Deming, there may be no track and no established bridges to follow.
approach_variants.season: May-Aug
hazards: double bergschrund with a reported hidden third crevasse between the two visible ones
serac and crevasse navigation crossing the Coleman with no established track
icefall and rockfall exposure near the ice cliff
the schrund can close the standard start out entirely by late summer
far less traffic than the standard route, so no broken trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The toe of the ridge is guarded by a DOUBLE bergschrund, and that pair of cracks is the thing to look for — it is the standard start and it is what tells you that you have arrived rather than stopped early on the glacier. Probe as you approach: parties have found a third, hidden crevasse tucked between the two obvious ones.

Above the schrunds the standard line goes up a broad snow gully of about forty degrees to gain the crest. Confirm before committing: the ground above should narrow into a defined snow-and-ice crest, and the enormous ice cliff that spans the north face should be overhead higher up. That ice cliff is the route's crux and its base is guarded by a big crevasse most parties turn on the left.

The usual error is being drawn onward by the boot track that keeps going up-glacier toward the Coleman-Deming col. If the ground ahead of you is broad open glacier trending toward a saddle, you have walked past the ridge. If the schrund is impassable or the snow is bottomless, parties have traversed hard toward the rock bands, on the reasoning that there are no crevasses in rock — but that is a fallback, not the route.

approach_variants.name: Artist Point, Ptarmigan Ridge and the Portals
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Mount Baker Highway to its end at Artist Point. Start on Chain Lakes Trail 682 for about a mile to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction, then follow Ptarmigan Ridge Trail 682.1 along the crest. Three miles from that junction the trail reaches the base of Coleman Pinnacle, and half a mile further is Camp Kiser — about five miles in from Artist Point. The snow on this stretch does not melt out until late in the season, so early parties face a long slog and steep snow chutes, while later parties get easier walking and much harder route-finding as the bootpaths multiply and diverge. Beyond Camp Kiser the graded tread ends and a bootpath threads the rocky ground of the Portals. From there the route drops onto the Rainbow Glacier, crosses onto the Park Glacier, and heads up toward the headwall with the Cockscomb above it. Most parties camp near the Portals. Note that the recorded elevation for Camp Kiser looks high; accounts describe it as a nondescript flat five miles in rather than a high camp on the mountain proper.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: long steep snow chutes on the approach early in the season
multiplying bootpaths through the Portals once the snow melts
crevasses on the Rainbow and Park Glaciers
Camp Kiser is unmarked and easily walked through
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Camp Kiser is almost impossible to identify if nobody is camped there — it is an unmarked flat spot, not a named feature you can see. Do not navigate by it. Navigate by Coleman Pinnacle, which the trail passes directly beneath half a mile earlier and which is a genuine landmark; Camp Kiser is the next flat ground after it.

The reliable test for whether you have left the trail system is underfoot: if you can still see graded tread, you have not reached the Portals. The Portals are rock formations and the ground through them is a braid of unofficial bootpaths going in several directions — that confusion IS the marker that you are in the right place, and the general direction is simply to keep gaining the ridge.

Beyond the Portals you must DROP onto the Rainbow Glacier before crossing to the Park. If you are still contouring at height with no glacier below you, you have not committed to the descent yet. The headwall itself is identified from the Park Glacier by the Cockscomb rising directly above it — the headwall is the wall beneath that formation, not any of the other steep ground on the glacier's rim.

Baker's Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers are on the opposite, west and north-west flanks and are never crossed on this approach; if you are on either of them you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Scott Paul Trail to Crag View
approach_variants.notes:
Same parking as the Easton route, at Schriebers Meadow. The Scott Paul Trail branches off within about a hundred feet of the trailhead and contours around the base of the mountain through forest, meadow and moraine.

After a few miles an UNMARKED junction sends the route north onto a steep climbers' path. That path leads to Crag View camp at about 6,500 ft, roughly three and a half miles in with 3,300 ft of gain. The Squak Glacier is gained near Point 6513, which some maps label Crag View.

This is the early-season choice on Baker's south side; later in the year a bergschrund develops on the route that is awkward to get past. Higher up the route merges with the Easton line near Sherman Crater.
approach_variants.season: best early season, May-Jul
hazards: unmarked trail junction at about 4,600 ft, easily walked past
exposed class 3 finish on the ridge to Crag View
bergschrund on the Squak that becomes difficult later in the season
volcanic gas near Sherman Crater where the route joins the Easton
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Two separate things to find, and the first one is the one people miss. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail at about 4,600 ft, very shortly after you reach the first open meadow with views out to Baker and Shuksan. There is no sign. If you are still walking graded tread that contours AROUND the mountain rather than climbing toward it, you have walked past the junction — the correct path goes up.

The second is the top of the ridge. Crag View is the end of the line for walking: the last hundred feet or so of the ridge narrow to a class 3 scramble with serious exposure in places, and the glacier is stepped onto near Point 6513 at the top of that. If the crest you are on still has a comfortable walking path, you are below Crag View — the change from path to scramble IS the marker.

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

approach_variants.name: Buck Creek Trail, Mount Cleator's east ridge and the alder tunnel to the twin gendarmes
approach_variants.notes:
From the Trinity / Buck Creek Trailhead, hike roughly six miles of Buck Creek Trail through an old burn recovering in fireweed, then drop through a meadow and ford Buck Creek — an easy crossing in normal summer flow.

Across the creek, climb to the crest of MOUNT CLEATOR'S east ridge through logged and burned forest with a great deal of downed timber. The forest opens considerably above about 4,800 ft, and around 5,500 ft a faint trail appears and contours LEFT.

That faint path leads to an ALDER TUNNEL at the base of some cliffs. Breaking out of it, traverse slippery heather and blueberry slopes across a basin beneath a waterfall, then climb steep goat trails to a grassy knoll beside a talus field.

The route is nearly 2,000 vertical feet of generally low-angle, low- to mid-fifth granite, broken by a distinct notch and a burly 5.8 chimney crux, then towers and gendarmes to the summit. Rock is consistently solid enough for fast simul-climbing except at the crux — which is what makes this the peak's one technical line.
approach_variants.season: Summer into autumn; carry an ice axe before August for lingering snow on the approach traverse
hazards: Extensive loose rock along the ridge, including trundle-prone blocks at the 5.8 chimney crux
A loose mid-fifth-class approach gully climbed by most parties unroped with overnight packs
Weather closing in fast on the exposed upper ridge, where the towers all look alike in poor visibility
A wet, brushy, muddy descent traverse that is materially worse after rain
Heavy downed timber in the burn on Cleator's east ridge, and an alder tunnel that has to be found rather than avoided
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO GENDARMES MARK THE START OF THE RIDGE, AND THE ROUTE GOES UP THE GULLY TO THEIR RIGHT — NOT BETWEEN THEM AND NOT TO THEIR LEFT. That is the whole identification, and it is a countable one: TWO towers side by side, and you take the weakness on the RIGHT-hand side of the pair.

WHAT THE GULLY LOOKS LIKE, SO YOU DO NOT REJECT IT: it is mangy. Loose, easy to mid-fifth-class scrambling, with the upper section the loosest — parties have gone up it in running shoes with full overnight packs. It is not attractive and it is correct. A clean-looking line beside it is not the route.

WHERE THE GULLY DELIVERS YOU, AND THIS IS WHERE THE CLIMBING PROPER STARTS: the NOTCH beside the twin gendarmes. Rope up there, not at the base of the gully.

THE APPROACH MARKER IMMEDIATELY BELOW IS A GRASSY KNOLL NEXT TO A TALUS FIELD, reached by steep goat trails out of the heather-and-blueberry basin under a waterfall. Grass, then talus, then two towers. If you are still in alder or on heather, you are below it.

THE ONE THING THAT WILL COST YOU THE MOST TIME LOWER DOWN is the contour at about 5,500 ft. The faint trail goes LEFT into an alder tunnel at the base of cliffs; the tunnel is the way through, not an obstacle to avoid. A party that stays on the ridge crest above it ends up cliffed against the same band the tunnel undercuts.

THE DESCENT DECISION IS MADE BEFORE YOU START: the recommended way back reverses the approach over the Berge-Cleator saddle, and the KEY IS A LEDGE TRAVERSE ABOVE THE LOWER SLABS which avoids losing and regaining height. Below that it is brushy, wet alder and steep heather back to the boot path. The alternative drops west via the High Pass trail, adds distance, and is really only worth it if you are also climbing Buck Mountain.

approach_variants.name: Little Giant Trail #1518 over the pass and down into the Napeequa
approach_variants.notes:
The Little Giant Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft roughly mile 19 of Chiwawa River Road, three miles down-valley of Trinity. The trail begins with an UNBRIDGED FORD OF THE CHIWAWA RIVER, right at the start — there is no way around it and it is the gate on the whole approach.

Trail #1518 then climbs steeply and badly-eroded to Little Giant Pass at 6,463 ft, with a small spring a few hundred feet below the pass at about 6,250 ft that is the last dependable water before the high basins. Maintained tread effectively ends at the pass.

From the pass the route drops toward the Louis Creek and Napeequa basin, then follows a climbers' path upstream to the end of tread at the creek draining Berge's south-west side. A steep, intermittent boot track climbs through timber to treeline and opens into the south-west basin. A narrow notch at about 7,840 ft in the ridge crest links the Louis Creek basin to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face, and gaining it is exposed scrambling.

All options to this peak are 15-plus miles round trip and are multi-day trips.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable. The Chiwawa ford at the very start of this trail is waist-deep and swift in early season and is only reliably safe in late-summer and autumn low water
hazards: An unbridged ford of the Chiwawa River at the very start of Little Giant Trail, waist-deep and swift outside late-season low water
Berge's north and west faces are cliffy and the direct line from High Pass does not go
A steep, badly eroded trail to Little Giant Pass and no maintained tread beyond it
An exposed gully of slanted slabs near 7,800 ft where a slip has serious consequences
A short fourth-class step to the true north summit, harder than the rest of the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A BROAD SADDLE ON THE SOUTH SIDE AT ABOUT 7,650 FT, AND THE WAY YOU GET TO IT IS A SNOW FINGER RATHER THAN A SLOPE. Near a snowfield around 7,000 ft the line uses a SNOW FINGER AND ITS MOAT, plus steep heather, to reach that saddle below the final summit block. Looking for a walkable slope will not find it; looking for the place where snow runs up into a narrowing tongue against rock will.

THE SADDLE IS WHERE THE ROUTE LEAVES THE BASIN. Below it you are traversing basins; above it you are climbing rock bands and steep heather toward the summit ridge. If you are still contouring, you are below it.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ON THIS PEAK AND IT IS ABOUT ASPECT: BERGE'S NORTH AND WEST FACES ARE CLIFFY. Parties must stay on the SOUTH-WEST side. Do not try to go straight up from High Pass — the direct line from the north does not go. If the ground above you is steepening into walls rather than rock bands and heather, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

THE ROUTE-FINDING RULE LOWER DOWN IS A DESCENDING TRAVERSE, WHICH FEELS WRONG AND IS RIGHT: near 5,400 ft the described line drops across into meadows, and it is from those meadows that several scrambling lines reach the top. Losing height on an approach to a summit is expected here.

THE LAST OBSTACLE HAS AN ELEVATION AND A CHARACTER: an exposed gully near 7,800 ft with SLANTED SLABS and real exposure near its top. Holds and ledges are solid and the passage is straightforward, and a slip there would be consequential — helmet.

THE SUMMIT IS NOT ONE POINT. The TRUE, NORTH summit needs a short FOURTH-CLASS step, harder than the third-class south summit. Standing on the easier top is not standing on the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Trinity and Buck Creek, or the High Pass high route from Buck Creek Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Two other ways reach the same mountain from the Trinity side.

The EAST approach: from Trinity, follow Chiwawa River Trail #1550 about two miles to the Buck Creek Trail #1513 junction, then Buck Creek Trail roughly four to five miles into the basin Berge shares with Mount Cleator and Buck Mountain on its east side.

The NORTH approach: continue past the Buck Creek junction to Buck Creek Pass, then take the climbers' path over High Pass and contour SOUTH under Berge's north side near Point 7839. This is the longest by mileage and has the least off-trail travel, which is the trade it offers.

Both involve unbridged or damaged creek crossings and both are multi-day. FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which affects the drive to Trinity.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, August most reliable
hazards: Berge's north face is cliffy — the direct line from High Pass does not go, and this approach puts you underneath it
Unbridged or damaged creek crossings on both the Buck Creek and Napeequa approaches
Brush and blowdown on unmaintained climbers' paths above the end of tread
An exposed 7,840 ft notch linking the two sides of the ridge
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat, affecting the drive to Trinity
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HIGH PASS APPROACH DELIVERS YOU TO THE WRONG SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN ON PURPOSE, AND THE RULE IS THAT YOU MUST KEEP GOING AROUND. Contouring south under Berge's north side puts a cliffy face above you. THE CLIMB IS ON THE SOUTH-WEST SIDE. Carry on around until the ground above you is rock bands and steep heather rather than wall, and only then start up.

THE ARRIVAL IS THE SAME PLACE FOR EVERY APPROACH TO THIS PEAK: the broad SADDLE ON BERGE'S SOUTH SIDE AT ABOUT 7,650 FT, where the south-west slopes route leaves the basin. Whichever valley you came up, that saddle is what you are walking to.

THE APPROACH-SPECIFIC MARKER ON THE HIGH PASS LINE is a numbered point rather than a shape: you contour beneath Point 7839. If you are still north of it you have not gone far enough around.

THE 7,840 FT NOTCH IS THE LINK BETWEEN THE TWO SIDES and it is worth knowing exists whichever way you came: a narrow notch in the ridge crest connects the Louis Creek basin on the Napeequa side to the Buck Creek and High Pass side beneath the south-west face. Gaining it is exposed scrambling, and it is the reason the two approaches meet at all.

AND THE SAME SUMMIT WARNING APPLIES: the true summit is the NORTH one and it takes a short fourth-class step. The south summit is third class and is not the top.

approach_variants.name: Eagle Lakes Trail #431 to Upper Eagle Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead at the top of the forest-road spur, fill out the self-issue wilderness permit and start up Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The tread crosses Crater Creek on a bridge early on — stay straight where the Crater Creek Trail splits — and climbs steadily, with an established camp roughly halfway. Past an overlook of the lower lake the trail reaches a junction: the left branch goes to the lower lake and the pass beyond, the right-hand spur climbs a half mile to Upper Eagle Lake. Take the spur. The upper lake sits in a cirque with established campsites and is the last reliable water and the staging point before the off-trail push, which starts from its northwest shore.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through October, once road and trail are snow-free. Snow lingers in the notch through the lower cliff band into summer and makes the route-finding harder.
hazards: Route-finding through the cliff bands is genuinely tricky, especially with snow still lying in the notch
Steep, loose scree and rock between the bands, with a loose path worn straight up it
Pushing too far climber's right onto the better rock cliffs you out at the end of the ridge
An eight-foot chimney below the summit block with poor handholds in small pebbles and sand — a slip there would be serious
The summit rises over 1,300 ft above the upper lake in about a third of a mile
No water above the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: GO UP THROUGH THE LARCHES AND VEER RIGHT TO THE NOTCH, THEN CUT LEFT UNDER THE NEXT BAND. From Upper Eagle Lake a path runs round the lake; above it the landmark is vegetation rather than rock. Climb up through the larch stand and veer right to a notch, then take easy slabby rock to get above the lower cliff band. Once above it, head LEFT, staying beneath the next band, and only when past that is it a straight push up steep scree and rock to just below the summit block. That alternation — right through the larches, then left under the upper band — is the shape of the route, and the error parties actually make is the opposite: the better, more stable rock lies further climber's right and tempts parties onto it, where they get cliffed out at the end of the ridge and have to downclimb. At the block itself, look for a notch with a chimney step of about eight feet and a sandy gully above it. The step is climbed upward and its top holds are poor, in small pebbles and sand; there is an easier scramble round to the LEFT at its base that rejoins the sandy gully just above the chimney, and taking it is the difference between a committing move and a walk.

approach_variants.name: Horsehead Pass and the west slopes
approach_variants.notes: The easier alternative stays on the main trail past the Upper Eagle Lake spur, continues to the lower lake and climbs to Horsehead Pass, then gains the peak's west slopes from the far side of the crest. It trades the exposed scrambling for distance and a long, loose walk-up, and is the sensible choice for a party that does not want the cliff-band route-finding or that finds snow still lying in the notch above the upper lake.
approach_variants.season: July through October. The west side melts out and stays passable later in the autumn than the shaded notch on the east side.
hazards: Long and described as annoyingly loose underfoot for its whole length
No water once you leave the lake basin
Exposed crest with no shelter from afternoon weather
approach_variants.baseFinding: THIS LINE IS IDENTIFIED BY WHAT IT DOES NOT HAVE: NO CLIFF BANDS AND NO SCRAMBLING. Carry on past the spur to the upper lake, stay on the main trail to the lower lake, and climb to Horsehead Pass on the crest. From the pass the peak's west slopes rise as continuous open scree and broken rock with a walkable line the whole way and nothing that needs hands. That is the confirmation you are on the right side of the mountain. If you find yourself traversing beneath a band of slabby rock, threading a notch, or looking at a short exposed step down into a sandy gully, you have ended up on the direct line from the upper lake instead and should reconsider whether the party is equipped for it. The west slopes are looser and longer than they look from the pass, so the trade is real: this variant removes the scrambling and adds a great deal of tedious ground.

waypoints.name: Crater Creek Trailhead (Eagle Lakes Trail #431)
waypoints.directions: From Twisp take SR 20 south two miles to the SR 153 junction, follow SR 153 south about twelve miles to County Road 1029 and on to CR 1034 (Gold Creek Road), which becomes FR 4340 after roughly five miles. Continue about 1.6 miles further, then turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it about 4.6 miles to the trailhead at 4,750 ft; the gravel is washboarded in places, so drive it slowly. From Carlton the equivalent is SR 153 south 3.5 miles, right on Gold Creek Loop Road for 1.6 miles, right on Gold Creek Road for five miles, 1.6 miles more, then left on FR 4340-300.

waypoints.name: Upper Eagle Lake — camp, last water, base-of-face scoping point
waypoints.directions: Take Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The first 0.7 mile climbs gently, rounds a bend into an opening with a view up the Eagle Creek valley, then drops slightly to the bridge over Crater Creek, after which the grade stays consistently easy through mature pine into subalpine fir and larch. At roughly five miles the trail reaches the Eagle Lakes area and forks: take the RIGHT fork for Upper Eagle Lake, about 6.2 trail miles and 2,350 to 2,430 ft of gain from the car, with many campsites, a large horse camp, and the last reliable water.

waypoints.name: Mount Bigelow summit
waypoints.directions: The East Face stands directly above the lake to the northwest; bear that way up talus and heather for roughly 0.4 to 0.5 mile and 900 to 1,000 ft to the base of the golden granite. Scope the line from the lakeshore before you go, because the crack systems are genuinely hard to read from below. Four pitches (an easy chimney and finger crack at 5.8, the fist-crack bulge and dihedral at 5.9, the balancy 5.10c 'S' crack crux, then a short stem between the face and a small tower) reach the summit ridge, where you unrope and walk north a short distance to the true 8,449 ft summit.

pro_tips: Scope the line from the shore of Upper Eagle Lake the evening before, ideally with binoculars — the FA party spent a long time from below and still could not reliably tell flaring offwidth from hand crack from seam until they were on the rock.

Bring a wire brush. The single most-repeated point in the first-ascent report is that cleaning lichen, sand and brittle edges by hand and foot is what made the climbing painfully slow, and that brushes would have been worth carrying.
Weight the rack toward hands and fists. The FA placed very little small gear, so leaving the micro-cams behind and doubling up 0.5" to 3" buys you more on the wide sections.
Ration wide gear on pitch 3. The FA leader ran out of pieces in the double fist-and-wider cracks above the crux and had to traverse out left on face holds to reach a stance.
Expect the face to be steeper than it looked from the lake — the first-ascensionists described it as pretty much plumb vertical, which is why the double rack mattered.
Camp at Upper Eagle Lake rather than trying it car-to-car. There are many established sites plus a large horse camp, it is the last water, and it puts you 900-1,000 ft under the base at first light.
Pull the pitch-3 crux with a plan to hang. The FA leader downclimbed to rest once before pulling it clean; treating one rest as normal rather than a failure saves a lot of flailing.
Take the RIGHT fork at the Eagle Lakes junction. The left fork goes past Lower Eagle Lake toward Horsehead Pass and the west side of the mountain, which is the scramble approach, not the East Face.
Test every hold before weighting it. Face and foot edges on this wall start as brittle flakes that break off — the FA party broke holds deliberately as they climbed.
Do not confuse this peak with the Mount Bigelow above Tucson, Arizona - a different mountain that shares the name.
wa_mount_bigelow_tribute_to_richard.approach: Drive to the Crater Creek Trailhead (4,750 ft, 48.2205 / -120.26801). From Twisp take SR 20 south 2 miles to the SR 153 junction, then SR 153 south about 12 miles to County Road 1029 and on to CR 1034 (Gold Creek Road). CR 1034 becomes Forest Road 4340 after roughly 5 miles; continue about 1.6 miles further on FR 4340, then turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it 4.6 miles to the trailhead. An alternate description of the same drive starts from Carlton: south on SR 153 for 3.5 miles, right on Gold Creek Loop Road 1.6 miles, right on Gold Creek Road 5.0 miles (becomes FR 4340), 1.6 miles more, then left on FR 4340-300 for 4.4 miles. The gravel is washboarded in places — drive it slowly. From the trailhead take Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The first 0.7 mile climbs gently, rounds a bend into an opening with a view up the Eagle Creek valley, then descends slightly to the bridge over Crater Creek. From there the trail climbs at a consistently gentle grade through mature pine into subalpine fir and larch. At roughly 5 miles the trail reaches the Eagle Lakes area and forks: take the RIGHT fork toward Upper Eagle Lake (7,115 ft, 48.213553 / -120.346815, about 6.2 trail miles and 2,350–2,430 ft of gain from the car). Upper Eagle Lake has many campsites and a large horse camp, and is the last reliable water. From the lake, the East Face of Bigelow is the wall directly above to the northwest — bear northwest up talus and heather to the base of the golden granite, roughly 0.4–0.5 mile and 900–1,000 ft above the lake. The FA party logged the whole thing as '8 miles more or less from TH, ~3500' to base' and called it a great, fast trail. Scout the line from the lake and from the base before racking up; the crack systems are genuinely hard to read from below.
wa_mount_bigelow_tribute_to_richard.descent_text: There is no rappel descent and no need for one. From the top of pitch 4 you are standing on the summit ridge; coil the ropes, stow the rack, and walk north a short distance to the true 8,449 ft summit. To get down, retrace the standard scramble line: from the summit, drop southeast and then east down the slopes and gullies that stay RIGHT (south) of the prominent rock wall you just climbed — do not try to downclimb into the top of the East Face. The scramble down is Class 2 with a couple of Class 3 moves and about 1,330 ft of loss to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,115 ft. Trend toward the lake basin rather than cutting straight down; the terrain immediately below the wall is broken and steep. Once at the lake, rejoin Eagle Lakes Trail #431 and follow it back down past the Eagle Lakes junction, over the Crater Creek bridge, and out to the Crater Creek Trailhead — roughly 6 miles of very good, fast trail. If you are benighted, Upper Eagle Lake has plentiful established campsites and water and is a far better place to sit out the dark than the loose ground under the face. In an early- or late-season attempt with snow on the slopes, the descent to the lake is the crux of the day rather than the climb — carry an axe.

approach_variants.name: The same Blum Creek path to the lakes, then past the northernmost lake and over the northwest shoulder into the glacial basin
approach_variants.notes:
Trailhead and approach are identical to the South Ridge as far as the Blum Lakes basin: Baker Lake Road to the Baker River Trailhead, the maintained trail to the suspension bridge, the unmarked climbers' path starting about 175 yards downstream of it on Blum Creek's north bank, and the steep climb up Blum Creek Ridge to the lakes.

What is different starts at the lakes. Carry glacier travel gear for this one; the South Ridge does not need it.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A glacial basin crossing requiring rope and crevasse-rescue gear
A false summit that can be mistaken for the top
The same faint, easily missed climbers' path start at the Baker River
Scrub pine and a broad loose gully on the standard exit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LAKES ARE A SEQUENCE AND THIS ROUTE USES THE LAST ONE. Continue to the NORTHERNMOST of the Blum Lakes, then cross the NORTHWEST SHOULDER into the glacial basin below the North Ridge. The count is the test: if you stop at the first or middle lake you are set up for the South Ridge, which is the other route from this basin.

ARRIVAL: you are in the right basin when you have crossed a shoulder and there is GLACIER below the ridge in front of you. The South Ridge side has a snow couloir; this side has a glacial basin. Rope and crevasse gear are needed for the crossing itself, which is a fair signal that you are where you meant to be.

WHAT THE DESCENT TELLS YOU ABOUT THE GROUND, AND IT IS WORTH READING BEFORE YOU GO UP: parties come down near the summit around the south or southwest side of a FALSE SUMMIT, following cairns past known bivy spots, down a snowfield, then skier's right into the top of a broad gully, then skier's right again through scrub pine to the creek and lakes basin. So there is a false summit on this peak, there are cairns and bivy spots on its south side, and the exit is a broad gully with scrub pine. Any of those seen on the way up are confirmation you are on the right mountain even if you are not on the ridge crest.

bivy.name: Middle Blum Lake
bivy.notes: A few hundred yards and a hundred feet of gain above the lower lake, and the more common choice for parties who want to shorten summit day on Blum. The ground is heather and slab, so tent sites are where the rock is, not where the flat grass is. It holds snow later than the lower lake and it catches more wind, which is a fair trade for mosquitoes in July. From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.
bivy.water: Lake water. Treat it
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake

bivy.name: Lower Blum Lake
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small outlet stream. Treat everything. This is the first reliable water since the river, four thousand feet below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required year-round for any overnight stay. The Blum cross-country zone is not one of the reservable zones, so it is walk-up only through the wilderness information center near Marblemount. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow, and keep a hundred feet back from the water. Human waste goes in a cathole or, on snow and glacier, in a blue bag carried out. Bear canisters are the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from, and can be borrowed in person at the permit office
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents on heather shelves and gravel near the outlet; the basin is tight and the park caps this cross-country zone at six people and two parties at a time

bivy.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
bivy.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMP ON THIS APPROACH, said plainly rather than recommending a place that does not exist. The 4,000 ft of steep forest between the Baker River and the Blum Lakes has no benches worth the name, no water on the crest and no clearings; parties who run out of daylight here flatten a spot among the trees and move on at first light. The right plan is to start early and reach the lakes in one push. Keep it in mind only as what you will actually do if the bushwhacking at the bottom eats more of the day than you expected, which it often does in wet conditions, or if somebody in the party is struggling with the load.
bivy.water: None dependable. Blum Creek is below the path and hard to reach from the ridge; carry what you need from the river or push on to the lakes
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit if you sleep here — the park boundary sits close to the river crossing, so assume the whole climb is inside the park and ask at the permit office where the line actually falls before you plan on it. No fires
bivy.capacity: One tent, found rather than chosen; the ridge is steep, timbered and littered with deadfall, and genuinely flat ground is rare

approach_variants.name: Baker River Trail to the suspension bridge, then the unmarked Blum Creek climbers' path to the Blum Lakes basin
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Baker Lake Road, Forest Road 11, 25.5 miles north from WA-20 at milepost 82 near Concrete, to its end at the Baker River Trailhead at 774 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required and there is a vault toilet on site.

Hike the maintained Baker River Trail #606 roughly half a mile, about ten minutes, to the Baker River suspension bridge. Cross it, then look for a faint, unmarked climbers' path beginning ABOUT 175 YARDS DOWNSTREAM OF THE BRIDGE, and about 25 yards UPSTREAM of a stringer bridge, following Blum Creek's north bank.

The path climbs steeply and indistinctly through dense forest and understory, becoming more defined higher as it follows Blum Creek Ridge; around 5,100 ft it contours the ridge's south side through huckleberry brush and talus into the Blum Lakes basin at roughly 5,000-5,700 ft. Figure 4-4.5 miles and 4,000-4,300 ft to the basin, about 5 hours for a fit party; the full round trip is about 9 miles and 7,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A faint, unmarked path start that is easy to walk past in either direction
Steep, indistinct climbing through dense forest and understory low down
Huckleberry brush and talus on the contour around 5,100 ft
A snow couloir below the south ridge saddle, wanting an axe when firm
7,000 ft of gain on a 9-mile round trip
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HARD FIND ON THIS ROUTE IS THE TRAILHEAD END OF IT, NOT THE MOUNTAIN END, AND IT IS COUNTABLE. Cross the suspension bridge and then measure: the climbers' path starts roughly 175 YARDS DOWNSTREAM of the bridge and roughly 25 YARDS UPSTREAM of a stringer bridge. Two bridges bracket the start. If you have walked past a second bridge you have overshot by about 25 yards; if you have gone more than a couple of hundred yards from the suspension bridge without finding tread, turn round.

HANDRAIL ABOVE THAT: the path follows BLUM CREEK'S NORTH BANK and then the crest of Blum Creek Ridge. Water on your right going up, the ridge under your feet higher. Around 5,100 ft it contours the ridge's SOUTH side. If you are contouring the north side you have crossed the crest.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP: the Blum Lakes basin. Lakes are the confirmation, and there is more than one of them; the middle lake is the usual camp.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: from the basin, the line goes up a SNOW COULOIR BELOW THE SOUTH RIDGE SADDLE. Snow in a confined gully leading to a gap in the ridge above is the start; open heather and talus is not. The route above the saddle is class 3.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing north past the northernmost of the Blum Lakes and over the northwest shoulder takes you into the glacial basin below the NORTH Ridge, which is the peak's other route and needs glacier travel gear this one does not.

From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.

bivy.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake
