bivy.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
bivy.notes: The highest practical ground on the Blum side, on the way from the main lakes toward the gullies and snow slopes leading to Blum's east ridge. It buys perhaps an hour on summit day and costs an extra 700 ft of carrying at the end of an already brutal approach day, so most parties leave it to those going on to Hagan or continuing the traverse east. Exposed to weather from every direction. In a low-snow year the tarn is dry and this stops being an option at all.
bivy.water: The tarn, when it is out; it is snow-covered well into summer and may be a snowpatch rather than water in early season. Carry from the lakes below if in doubt
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, Blum cross-country zone, walk-up only. No fires. Because this sits above the meadow line, expect to be camping on snow or bare rock, which is what the zone rules ask for anyway
bivy.capacity: One or two tents at most, on rock and gravel; there is no established site here, only ground that happens to work

wa_mount_buckindy_scramble.approach: From Darrington, drive north on SR 530 roughly 7-8 miles and turn right onto the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) just after crossing the Sauk River bridge. Follow FR 26 (pavement then gravel) about 20 miles, turn left onto FR 2680, and continue 6 miles to the Green Mountain Trailhead (~3,200 ft). Hike Green Mountain Trail #782 (about 4 miles, ~3,000 ft gain) through old growth and subalpine meadows to the lookout area, then go cross-country along the connecting ridge system east and southeast past the Horse Lake saddle, with slow sidehill travel toward Misch, to Buckindy's north slopes and glacier remnants. THIS WAY IN IS CUT: flood damage closed FR 26 to all motor vehicles at milepost 4 under a Forest Service order in effect since April 2, 2026, and the closure takes in the Green Mountain Road (FR 2680). The closure order runs until January 1, 2028 unless it is lifted sooner, which leaves the trailhead roughly twenty miles of closed road past the gate. Check with the Darrington Ranger District before counting on it. The way in that is open comes from the north. Drive Cascade River Road about 14 miles east of Marblemount to Kindy Creek Road (FR 1570), then about 2 miles up that rough spur to a small pullout near 1,850 ft. A climbers' trail climbs Kindy Ridge to a saddle near 4,800 ft south of Point 5116, the same start as for Snowking Mountain. From there, continue south through the Buckindy Range high country to the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages, where parties camp below Buckindy's north side. That ground is a second or third night out.

bivy.name: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
bivy.notes: THE GROUND THAT PUTS MOUNT BUCKINDY IN RANGE. Buckindy's standard route is a class 4 scramble on the north slopes, with glaciers on the north and east flanks, and the parties who climb it are camping either in the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or at the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages. Coming in from road 1570 this is a second or third night out, well beyond the Cyclone Lake ground. There is a second way in from the south, over Green Mountain and the Horse Lake saddle from the Suiattle side, with camps on the divide and in the basins on the way, but that country has its own long road problems and is not the approach this zone is built around. Nothing here is a site in any developed sense: it is remote, lightly visited ground where the answer to where you sleep is wherever the light runs out, and a party should carry the fuel to melt snow and the tolerance for a dry, windy night.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small basin streams, generally running through midsummer and thinning badly after that. There is ice on Buckindy's north and east flanks, so late in the season the water that is left is glacier outflow rather than clean snowmelt.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on durable ground, pack out human waste, no fires. There is no quota and no reservation anywhere in this zone, so the constraint on a trip here is the approach rather than the paperwork.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on snow, moraine or heather at the passes and in the basins beneath them. Nothing built, no toilet.

bivy.name: Horse Lake saddle camp
bivy.notes: First-night camp on the Green Mountain approach, past the south shoulder of Green Mountain. Beyond it the traverse toward Misch and Buckindy is slow sidehill travel.
bivy.water: Horse Lake and snowmelt nearby; treat it
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites just above the saddle

approach_variants.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
approach_variants.notes: READ THE NAME ON THIS ROUTE WITH CARE — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies WEST of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters. Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin, and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail beyond the basin
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August, over a buried climbers' path
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and along the ridge connecting the three summits
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Obstruction Point Road closes for most of the year and is not a route you can count on before July
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE IS CAMERON PASS AND THE TEST IS THE DIRECTION YOU TURN OUT OF IT: THE RIDGE YOU CLIMB RISES TO THE EAST. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest EAST and UP. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you. SECOND TEST, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST HERE: THE RIDGE IS A SEQUENCE OF FALSE SUMMITS. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going: the true top is still easy Class 1-2 ground, and steps of Class 3-4 mean you have passed it and are on the traverse. THIRD TEST, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route. HONEST LIMIT AND A LIVE DISAGREEMENT: this route's own summit waypoint calls the EAST Peak the true 7,190 ft high point, while traverse accounts reach the true summit FIRST from Cameron Pass and then go on to Middle and East. Those cannot both be right. Carry a map, count your summits, and do not treat either the route title or the waypoint name as settled.

approach_variants.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail
approach_variants.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — parties describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are universally recommended.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant, reached after a longer approach
Bear canister required; no reliable water above the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: IDENTICAL ONCE YOU ARE AT CAMERON PASS: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest EAST and UP, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground all the way to the top. The pass is WEST of the summit whatever the route title says. THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them. WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin
approach_variants.notes: Recorded because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and is not the recommended way in. From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach. If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Many extra miles including a long closed-road walk at each end
A multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant
approach_variants.baseFinding: IDENTICAL AT THE PASS: the ridge rises EAST out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, on Class 1-2 ground to the true top. THE TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS IS ABOUT WHICH VALLEY YOU ARE IN, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the route's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first. HONEST LIMIT: this approach is not the one the trailhead record names.

approach_variants.name: Sol Duc road end, High Divide and Cat Basin to the Catwalk
approach_variants.notes: Start at the road-end trailhead on the hot-springs road on the park's north side. Hike past the falls, on past the Deer Lake junction, and up to Heart Lake — the last reliable water. Climb to the High Divide crest and follow the primitive trail east from the junction above the lake toward Cat Basin, then take the unmaintained path over the exposed south side of the peak beyond it and across the CATWALK to the first camp on its far side. Do NOT plan an approach from Hurricane Ridge: it is a viewpoint separated from this range by miles of trailless glaciated terrain and there is no established route to this peak from it.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September, once the high traverse is clear of snow; an ice axe is still worth carrying for the summit basin.
hazards: The Catwalk — exposed, sharp, and a fall there could be fatal
Thin, crumbly ledges with major exposure on the south side of the peak just before the Catwalk
Steep, loose, unstable scree in the summit basin
Early-season snow in the basin, where an ice axe is advisable
No water between Heart Lake and the summit
Unmaintained and unsigned beyond the divide, requiring solid off-trail route-finding
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin camp, the line follows the peak's SOUTHWEST RIDGE — grassy and rocky walking at first — and the base of the real climbing is where that ridge stops being walkable crest and you have to CONTOUR OFF IT into a broad, steep, loose SOUTH-FACING SCREE BASIN at around sixty-five hundred feet. The test that you are in the right basin: it is loose, unstable scree in the sun, and the TRUE SUMMIT sits at its FAR RIGHT-HAND END, not at the high point directly above where you enter it. Finish on scree and snow. Negative markers: if you have roped up and are travelling on ice with crevasses, you are on the glacier variation on the northeast side of the peak; if you are still walking a grassy crest with no need to leave it, you have not reached the contour yet and are short of the basin.

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

access.fees: None beyond the Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking and the overnight wilderness permit fee, both stated above.
access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required ($5/day or $30/annual). No specific climbing permit.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (which includes most Picket Range approaches; 12 in on-trail corridors). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: No permit is required for a day climb. Every overnight stay in the North Cascades National Park complex needs a wilderness permit, which costs $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, youth 15 and under free.
access.closures: Graybeal, Graybeal Stock, and Whatcom Camps are CLOSED due to fire damage from the 2022 Chilliwack Complex. The trails themselves are open to hikers: Hannegan Pass/Chilliwack River and Brush Creek/Whatcom Pass.
access.landManager: N/A
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: N/A

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone), fee per person, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Hannegan-side permits can also be picked up at the Glacier Public Service Center on its limited summer days.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FS Road 32 (Ruth Creek Road) off WA-542, Trail #674 climbs a well-graded 2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass at about 5,100 ft. That pass is the last easy water and the point where the two approaches to Challenger split.

This one drops the far side, losing roughly 2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley at Boundary Camp, crosses the Chilliwack, and follows the Chilliwack River Trail past Copper Creek Camp to the Whatcom Pass backcountry camp. Log crossings of the Chilliwack are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack.

From Whatcom Pass you still have to get round Whatcom Peak. The direct North Ridge is loose, extremely exposed and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side. Treat that as glacier travel.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The Whatcom Glacier traverse is the season-limiting piece: in low-snow years it has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses
hazards: Unreliable log crossings of the Chilliwack River; parties have lost the crossing and been forced to bushwhack
The Whatcom Glacier traverse has been found down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years
About 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing, sometimes with a short rappel across a moat, just to get off Perfect Pass onto the glacier
A bergschrund on the Challenger Glacier and a moat below the summit rocks that can be impassable late season
No bailout worth the name once you are past Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PERFECT PASS IS THE ARRIVAL, AND YOU KNOW IT BECAUSE THE GROUND STOPS AND THE GLACIER STARTS. From the pass, getting down onto the Challenger Glacier at about 7,000-7,200 ft can involve roughly 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The exact entry point moves year to year with crevasse conditions, so do not look for a particular spot; look for the lowest place you can step from rock onto continuous ice.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME THING AS ARRIVAL AT THE GLACIER: the technical climbing on this route is 50 ft long and it is the last 50 ft. Above the bergschrund the glacier steepens into a snow arete, then a clean 3rd-class scramble runs out at the base of a short, well-protected 5.5-5.7 pitch. THAT PITCH IS THE ROUTE. If you are roping up anywhere lower than the foot of a single unbroken 50 ft wall with a rappel anchor visible at its top, you have roped up too early.

THE MOAT IS THE MARKER YOU WILL MEET FIRST, AND IN FOG IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Just below the summit rocks a moat has been reported up to about 5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to hunt a snow bridge. Reaching an uncrossable gap where the snow has pulled away from the summit rock means you are at the base, not lost.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing east along the crest away from the summit block puts you on the connecting ridge toward Poltergeist Pinnacle and Crooked Thumb, which is a different day entirely.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative from the same trailhead. From the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge and climb steeply onto the ridge, site of an old fire lookout. A faint climbers' path follows the crest past tarns and slabby sections, over Easy Peak, to a notch known as the Impasse, then continues cross-country toward Perfect Pass.

Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles, so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass or Perfect Pass, or both.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the Impasse notch can make the direct crossing either easier or impossible depending on the year
hazards: The Impasse: deep snow moats on both sides and wet down-sloping slabs, with an 800 ft drop-and-re-climb workaround on exposed class 4
Fords of the Chilliwack River
Whiteout navigation between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, where parties have mistaken Whatcom Peak's summit wall for the pass
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier and the moat below the summit rocks
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE IMPASSE IS THE CHECKPOINT, NOT THE BASE, AND CONFUSING THE TWO IS THE COMMON ERROR IN CLOUD. It is a notch in the ridge guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 step to regain the crest beyond.

BEYOND IT, THE TEST IS THE SAME AS ON THE OTHER APPROACH: Perfect Pass, then step onto ice, then keep going until the walking stops at a 50 ft rock wall. Nothing on this route is technical until that wall.

A NAMED WHITEOUT TRAP ON THIS LINE: on the snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass, parties in fog have headed for Whatcom Peak's summit wall instead of the pass. If the ground in front of you is steepening into a wall rather than levelling into a saddle, you are aimed at the wrong feature. Perfect Pass is a saddle with running water; Whatcom's wall has neither.

approach_variants.name: Illabot Creek Road, Arrow Creek switchback and the west slopes
approach_variants.notes: The trailhead is not a formal one — it is the point where the Illabot Creek Road reaches the Arrow Creek switchback, and you park on the road. A boot and fisherman's path leaves the road about twenty yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it is reasonably distinct with occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned. Follow it about a mile, then look for a crossing to the north side of the drainage near a significant side-creek confluence — an easy boulder hop by late summer, a genuine wet ford in early season, so check the flow before committing. Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder, which is the worst brush of the day, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000 to 4,300 ft. That band is the route-finding crux of the walk-in: intermittent cairns and flagging at best, and it is easy to end up in the wrong gully. Last dependable water is around 4,000 ft. Above, the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes and traverses and climbs east toward the summit block.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September. The road and the approach gullies typically do not clear of snow until July, and the peak sees almost no traffic outside that narrow window.
hazards: a pathless, committing approach through steep brushy old growth with stream crossings and sustained sidehilling
the cliff-and-gully band at 4,000 to 4,300 ft, where it is easy to commit to the wrong gully in either direction
snow-filled entrance gullies below the west face that can sluff or slide in warm or unstable conditions
exposed, moss- and heather-covered steps on the summit block ramp, worse descending than ascending
weak and unreliable water above 4,000 ft
frequent afternoon thunderstorms in the approach basins
approach_variants.baseFinding: YOU MUST CROSS TO THE NORTH SIDE OF THE RIDGE BEFORE THE RAMP EXISTS. From the open west slopes, climb northeast across the basin and up a steep gully to a pass in the ridge at about 5,920 ft, then cross over to the NORTH side of that ridge and traverse east until the west face of the summit block is in front of you. The line up that face is one large, obvious ramp, and its direction is the test: it climbs the face diagonally from LEFT to RIGHT to reach the summit ridge, where you turn LEFT and scramble to the top. If the ramp you are looking at runs right to left, or if you are still on the south side of the ridge, you have not reached the correct face. If you can see no single dominant ramp at all — just broken ground and heather steps — you are still short of the summit block and should keep traversing east. The rock on the ramp carries heather and moss rather than clean stone, so treat it as insecure, and note that the same ground is considerably harder facing outward on the way down.

bivy.name: Jug Lake
bivy.notes: THE BASE FOR MOUNT CHAVAL, which sits immediately southwest of Snowking and has three standard approaches and one longer non-standard one, none of them simple and all of them brushy. This is the most used of them. Park at the prominent switchback where Arrow Creek meets Illabot Creek Road at about 2,220 feet, roughly 16 miles up the road, and follow an old overgrown fishermen's path up the right bank of Arrow Creek to the lake; it is reasonably defined and flagged at the doubtful places. From the camps on the north shore the route climbs north-northeast to gain the ridge around 5,200 feet, traverses to the pass between the two points just over 6,350 feet, and then commits to a genuine cross-country bushwhack through cliffy ground into the Arrow Creek amphitheatre before steep hillsides and talus lead to the mountain. Reckon on about ten miles and 4,600 feet for the round trip from the road, and on the vegetation being the crux. No elevation is recorded for the lake because no confident figure was found.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable. Nothing dependable above it once you are on the ridge and in the Arrow Creek amphitheatre.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Parking is at the Arrow Creek switchback on Illabot Creek Road rather than at a developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass may not apply there in the way it does at Slide Lake; check with the district rather than assume either way. No fires at the lake, and pack out human waste.
bivy.capacity: Several good camps on the north side of the lake, roomy by the standards of this zone. Unimproved, no toilet.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
approach_variants.notes: Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge. From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 15.3-16.7 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
hazards: A loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col that has changed between seasons — treat published descriptions of it as provisional
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier with a moat at its top whose width varies year to year and by time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk, and refreezing snow in it on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
A thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Extreme remoteness — an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or a helicopter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM LOWER MARTINS PARK THERE IS ONE BROAD SNOW-AND-ROCK COULOIR AND IT RUNS SOUTH TOWARD THE PEAK. That is the whole arrival test and it is why parties consistently report finding it easily: you walk out of the lower meadows and over to the base of the snowfield. You are at the base when the meadow ends and continuous snow begins, with the couloir running away from you SOUTH — not west. If the drainage you are looking up runs any other direction, it is not this one.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS A NUMBER AND A DURATION: the couloir gains about 2,100 ft and tops out at a SADDLE ON THE NORTH RIDGE near 5,600 ft, and parties consistently report about three and a half hours for it. If you have climbed far more than 2,100 ft without reaching a saddle, you are in the wrong gully.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle, and it is the one that catches the real trap on this peak: from the saddle you DROP down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the CHRISTIE GLACIER. A route that only ever climbs is not this one. Rope up — reports describe few or no open crevasses but the angle is enough that parties treat it as glacier ground anyway. At the top of the glacier a MOAT forms where ice meets rock; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col. Check it before committing, because it is the thing that changes year to year.

WHAT WAITS AT THE COL, so it is not a surprise: the barrier above it is a chossy eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and it is the crux of the peak, not a formality. It has changed between recent seasons — one party found the expected weakness gone and had to force a line to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge on a tight rope. Expect dense krummholz above it before the rock improves and the Class 2-3 southeast ridge leads to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend
approach_variants.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the November 2017 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
hazards: Road closure at Olympic Hot Springs Road adds 6.2 miles each way and may change season to season
Everything above Low Divide is the same as the Quinault variant: the Class 4 step above the col, the Christie Glacier moat, and the entry couloir
A long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL TO THE QUINAULT VARIANT ONCE YOU ARE AT LOW DIVIDE, and that shared test is a good one: from LOWER Martins Park there is ONE broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs SOUTH toward the peak. Walk to where the meadow ends and the snow begins. Up it about 2,100 ft, roughly three and a half hours, to a saddle on the NORTH ridge near 5,600 ft; then DOWN loose gravel to the Christie Glacier; then the moat at the glacier's top and the high col east of the summit.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at Low Divide itself, because you arrive from the opposite direction. Low Divide is a trail junction and the site of the historic ranger station, and it is where the climbers' route LEAVES maintained trail for Martins Park. Coming up from the Elwha, that turn is on your right as you crest the divide and it is a rough fisherman's path, not a signed one. If you have started descending toward the Quinault, you have walked past it.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
From the Dosewallips River Road washout at roughly 550 ft, about 5 miles of road-walk or bike on the closed road, crossing Constance Creek on wooden footbridges near the start, to the unsigned, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,450 ft.

The trail gains roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in 1.8-2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — one of the steepest approaches in the Olympics. The first half-mile is brutal and eases only slightly into denser forest with exposed roots and rock steps needing hands. Expect scramble-grade tread with no switchbacks and cairn-and-flagging route-finding in places. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a full pack. Water at Constance Creek partway and at the lake outlet; treat everything.

The trail skirts the lake's east shore to established campsites at the north end, in a rocky bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon. Most parties camp there rather than going car to car. From camp, head north up scree into the canyon's lower basin, then bend east along a rib.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Residual snow in the South Chute makes it a far better climb than bare scree does
hazards: The Finger Traverse is a highly exposed, downsloping narrow ledge; footholds are marginal even with the crack in hand
Reversing it on descent goes round a blind corner and most parties find that harder than the way up
1,900 ft of loose scree in the South Chute, which sluffs rock onto parties below
The fixed pitons on the traverse are decades old — do not trust them without inspection
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics; the descent takes many parties nearly as long as the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS A TOWER CALLED THE CAT EARS, AND THE PUBLISHED INSTRUCTION IS A TRIGGER RATHER THAN A DESCRIPTION: BEGIN CLIMBING THE SOUTH CHUTE AS SOON AS THE CAT EARS ARE VISIBLE. Follow Avalanche Canyon north from the lake — roughly 0.6 mile — and watch east. The Cat Ears is the tower standing just LEFT of the notch you are aiming for at the top of the chute. The moment it comes into view, turn east and start up. Starting later means more scree; starting earlier puts you on the wrong ground.

IN CLOUD, WHEN THE CAT EARS CANNOT BE SEEN, THE FALLBACK IS THE CHUTE'S OWN SHAPE. The South Chute is a long gully that NARROWS as it climbs, gaining about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft at the notch in the south ridge. It is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake. If the gully you are in is widening rather than narrowing, or if you are still walking north up the canyon bed after well over half a mile, you have passed it and are heading for the North Chute and the Terrible Traverse instead.

SECOND TEST, and it is what confirms you were right about the chute: above the notch you cross a saddle, DROP about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge. A route that only ever goes up is not this one — the deliberate loss of height above the first notch is part of the line. From there the route threads gaps and ledges marked in places by faded WHITE PAINT DOTS. Painted dots are man-made, they do not move, and they are visible at arm's length in fog; if you are seeing them you are on the line.

THE FINGER TRAVERSE ITSELF IS A TACTILE TEST, WHICH IS THE BEST KIND HERE: a downsloping ledge above a large cliff with a HORIZONTAL CRACK running along its top edge, which you jam your fingers into for balance because the footholds are thin. A rusty decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along it. If there is no continuous crack at hand height above the ledge you are standing on, that is not the Finger Traverse.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail entirely. From the Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles, about 1.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off, to the old campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end. Take the Constance Pass Trail up through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft, then leave the trail and go cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and up to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif.

From Crystal Pass descend south into Avalanche Canyon on an intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, staying toward the north side of the canyon, and continue DOWN the canyon toward the lake until the South Chute opens on your left (east).

This is considerably longer than the lake approach and it exists because the lake trail is brutally steep, unmaintained and blowdown-choked. Most parties on it are on a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmarked cross-country travel between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass, on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass beyond transient snowmelt
Every hazard on the Finger Traverse itself, reached at the end of a longer day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ENTERING THE CANYON FROM CRYSTAL PASS PUTS THE CAT EARS TEST THE OTHER WAY UP: you must descend PAST the North Chute before the South Chute opens. The Cat Ears tower and the formation trip reports call the Thumb both sit in this stretch of canyon, and on this side you pass them going down rather than meeting them going up.

THE RELIABLE TEST ON THIS SIDE IS THE CHUTE'S TOP, NOT ITS BOTTOM. The South Chute tops out at a notch in the SOUTH ridge at roughly 6,600 ft, with the Cat Ears tower standing just left of that notch. Coming down the canyon from Crystal Pass you can pick your entry by which notch the gully above you leads to: the one with a tower just left of it is the South Chute. The chute that leads straight toward the Terrible Traverse without a tower beside its notch is the North Chute.

ABOVE THE CHUTE THE TESTS ARE IDENTICAL to the lake approach and they are the good ones: cross the saddle, LOSE about 150 ft, up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge, then gaps and ledges marked with faded WHITE PAINT DOTS, then a downsloping ledge with a continuous horizontal finger crack along its top edge and old fixed pitons in it.

HONEST LIMIT: the track fades near Crystal Pass and the drop into the canyon is unmarked. This variant is longer and navigationally harder; it is chosen for the trail it avoids, not for the ground it crosses.

bivy.notes: The base camp for essentially every ascent by the standard South Chute, reached by a savage climbers' path that gains roughly 3,300 to 3,400 ft in under two miles of hand-over-hand scrambling above the Dosewallips road. approach_variants.name: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.hours: 2.5-3.5 for the Lake Constance trail alone
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Dosewallips road washout around 600 ft, reached from US 101 at Brinnon on FR 2610. The road has been closed to vehicles since a washout in 2002, so the first 5 miles up the Dosewallips valley are on the old roadbed.

The Lake Constance climbers' path is signed but unmaintained and carries no Forest Service trail number — it is a boot path. It launches straight into root-and-branch pulling through old burn debris for the first 0.4 mile before the old growth closes in. At about 0.8 mile, Half Acre Rock is a large monolith with campsites beside Constance Creek and is the obvious rest and water stop; by late summer the creek and the canyon above it run dry, so treat it as the last reliable water below the lake.

Past 1.1 miles the brush opens onto steep exposed slopes, and by 1.3 miles the creek is forced through a defile and the path is pushed up and over a series of rock ledges and short cliff bands, using roots and a landmark Alaska cedar to gain the next ledge. Exposure increases with each one and a slip is serious.

All told it gains roughly 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles to Lake Constance at 4,680-4,800 ft, one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. Lake Constance is a reservable Olympic National Park backcountry site with reservations for the May 15-October 15 summer season; a wilderness permit is required for the overnight, and parties of seven or more must use the designated group sites.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; June snow makes the South Chute far pleasanter than late-summer scree
hazards: fatal-fall exposure on both the Terrible and Finger Traverses
steep firm snow on the Terrible Traverse - several pickets advised in early season
exposed rock ledges and short cliff bands on the Lake Constance trail above 1.3 miles
loose talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
no water above the lake in late summer, and Constance Creek itself runs dry
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the lake, follow the boot path around the shore, out onto a large scree cone, and north into Avalanche Canyon between Inner Constance and Mount Constance. A large rock called the Thumb sits on the canyon's left side; the South Chute lies on the south side of the Thumb, and due south of the Cat Ears.

The most useful rule on this mountain: START UP THE SOUTH CHUTE AS SOON AS THE CAT EARS COME INTO VIEW, not when the chute starts to look obvious. Entering low keeps you on firmer ground, where there is a path in places; parties who keep walking up the canyon and attack the chute higher get the worst of the loose scree. If the Cat Ears have been visible for a while and you are still walking north, you have overshot the entrance.

From the lake the chute line climbs roughly 1,900 ft of scree to a saddle near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears. Descend about 150 ft, then a second gully leads to a notch near 7,300 ft.

Above that is the exposed upper maze, and identifying which traverse you are on is the thing to get right. The Finger Traverse is a downsloping ledge above a cliff with old rusted pitons on it — the pitons are the identifier, and some parties clip them as a solo-belay anchor. The Terrible Traverse is a hard-snow traverse of roughly 45 degrees above a big cliff and a nasty drainage. Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4, ground leading to the base of the summit block. If you are on a traverse and the summit block is not visible above and ahead of you, you are on the wrong ledge.

The actual climbing is only the summit block, about 60 ft, with the North Chimney taking its north side at 3rd class — reported by plenty of people as feeling like easy 4th.

approach_variants.name: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
approach_variants.notes:
The roughly 5 miles of closed roadbed between the washout and the Lake Constance path is old road surface rather than trail, and mountain-biking it is a common way to cut the walk at both ends of the trip. The bike is left at the signed start of the climbers' path.

Everything above that point is identical to the walk-in variant: the same unmaintained boot path, the same 3,200-3,400 ft in under two miles, the same rock ledges and the same lake.

The same permit rules apply — a wilderness permit for the overnight at Lake Constance, reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season, with group sites required for parties of seven or more.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: old roadbed surface with washouts
everything above the bike drop is unchanged, including the exposed ledges on the Lake Constance path
approach_variants.baseFinding: Unchanged from the walk-in: around the lake, north into Avalanche Canyon, and up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears appear above you, with the Thumb on the canyon's left marking the chute's south side. The Cat Ears becoming visible is the trigger to start climbing, not a landmark to walk toward.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line where the South Chute's gully tops out, crosses the Finger Traverse (or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow), and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
hazards: Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes is called out explicitly for May-June conditions
A long, loose gully with rockfall onto anyone below
It leads to the same exposed upper crossings as the standard route: the Finger Traverse ledge, or the Terrible Traverse's steep snow above a cliff
Less traffic means less boot track and fewer people to ask
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM ON THIS ROUTE IS TELLING THIS CHUTE FROM THE OTHER ONE, AND THE TEST IS: KEEP WALKING UP THE CANYON PAST THE FIRST CHUTE. The published instruction for the South Chute is to start climbing east as soon as the CAT EARS tower is visible, and trip reports describing this line say plainly that you bypass the South Chute entrance and continue up loose talus to the MOUTH OF THE NORTH CHUTE further into Avalanche Canyon. So the discriminator is temporal, not visual: the first opportunity to leave the canyon eastward is the wrong one. IN CLOUD, where the Cat Ears cannot be seen at all, this is still workable because the test is about the canyon floor under your feet rather than about a skyline. From the lake, follow the canyon NORTH. Do not turn uphill at the first gully. Keep going on the talus until the canyon delivers you to a second, more northerly couloir, and take that. THE CONFIRMING TEST IS AT THE TOP OF THE CHUTE: it narrows and eases, and the summit block comes into sight to the north for the first time. Just above, a narrow exposed ledge trending left meets the point where the South Chute's loose gully comes in from below. From there the two routes are the same line: north through a notch, across a snowfield, then the Finger Traverse (a downsloping ledge with a horizontal finger crack and old pitons), or the lower Terrible Traverse, the steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, when conditions allow. HONEST LIMIT: this chute is documented mostly as a variation inside other parties' loops. It is long, loose and less travelled, and there is no marker sequence inside the gully itself.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes: The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass drop south into UPPER Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance routes, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmarked cross-country between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Avalanche and rockfall in the canyon and the chute
Commits to the exposed Finger or Terrible Traverse at the end of a long approach day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ONE APPROACH WHERE THE NORTH CHUTE IS THE EASY ONE TO FIND, BECAUSE YOU ARRIVE ABOVE IT. Dropping into Avalanche Canyon from Crystal Pass on the intermittent climbers' path, the FIRST couloir that offers a line up onto the Constance side is the North Chute. Take it. If you keep descending the canyon you will next pass the Cat Ears and the Thumb and eventually reach the South Chute entrance and then the lake — every one of which means you have gone below the route.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THE SAME AS ON THE LAKE APPROACH: near its top the chute narrows and eases, the summit block comes into sight to the north, and a narrow exposed ledge trending left meets the point where the South Chute's gully joins from below. Above that the line is shared with the standard route and crosses the Finger Traverse, or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow.

HONEST LIMIT: the climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass, so this variant's own approach is the navigationally hard part, not the chute.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail and Avalanche Canyon to the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
Road-walk or bike about 5 miles up the washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at roughly 1,450 ft. The trail is unmaintained and gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — steep from the first half-mile, exposed roots and rock steps needing hands, no real switchbacks. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a pack. Camp at the lake's north end.

From camp, head up into Avalanche Canyon on scree and talus. Firm snow, when it is there, makes this whole section faster and safer than bare scree. This route takes the same South Chute as the Finger Traverse, then a second gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft. From there the line loses a little height and traverses north on ledges to reach the Terrible Traverse itself at about 7,435 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Steep hard snow persists longer on the Terrible Traverse than on any other crux on this mountain, which is exactly the point of it
hazards: The Terrible Traverse crosses steep firm snow directly above a large cliff — an unprotected slip is very likely fatal
Hard, icy neve is common through June and early July; afternoon softening increases slip risk later in the day
Loose rock throughout the South Chute — classic Olympic choss, and rockfall from parties above is a real hazard
Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes, called out specifically for May-June conditions
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics, hard on the way down and slick when wet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS THE CAT EARS, AND IT IS A TRIGGER: START UP THE SOUTH CHUTE AS SOON AS THAT TOWER COMES INTO VIEW. Walk north up Avalanche Canyon from the lake past the Thumb and watch east. The Cat Ears is a rock tower standing just LEFT of the notch at the top of the South Chute; once you can see it, turn east and climb. If you are still walking up the canyon bed well after it appeared, you are heading for the North Chute instead.

In cloud, when the tower is hidden, use the chute's shape: the South Chute is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake, and it NARROWS as it climbs to the notch at about 6,600 ft.

SECOND TEST, above that notch: the line drops a little, climbs a second scree gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft, then loses height again and traverses NORTH on ledges. Here the two crossings part company. The Finger Traverse goes up and around a corner on a ledge with a horizontal finger crack along its top; the Terrible Traverse is reached over hard-packed scree to a cairned ledge heading north, and you meet the crossing itself at about 7,435 ft. It is unmistakable when you arrive: a steep exposed snow slope directly above a large cliff, or in late season a narrow rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above it. It is called the Terrible Traverse because a slip there does not stop.

WHAT THE SEASON CHANGES: early to mid summer this is hard steep snow wanting an axe, crampons and, for many parties, pickets. Late season it often melts back to that rock ledge, which most parties find more secure. Neither is the wrong condition; they are different climbs.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long way in, and the one parties choose to avoid the Lake Constance trail. From the same Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 1.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail, which climbs south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Published trail mileages differ by several miles depending on where the count starts, so none is quoted. The upper stretch is open meadow and scree with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail and travel cross-country west, dropping into the head of Crystal Basin and climbing to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass descend into UPPER Avalanche Canyon — which is where this variant differs usefully from the lake approach, because it puts you in the canyon ABOVE the lake rather than below it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow remnant below Crystal Pass is safe or gone
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and the descent into upper Avalanche Canyon is unmarked
Early-season snow remnant below Crystal Pass may want an axe and, for some parties, a rope
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt — carry it
All the Terrible Traverse hazards above, reached by a longer and more committing line
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COMING IN FROM CRYSTAL PASS YOU ENTER AVALANCHE CANYON FROM ABOVE, SO YOU MUST DESCEND PAST THE NORTH CHUTE BEFORE THE SOUTH CHUTE OPENS. Dropping south into the canyon, the first couloir you meet on the Constance side is the North Chute; keep going down the canyon toward the lake.

THE FIXED LANDMARKS on this stretch are the Cat Ears tower and the Thumb. The gully you want is the one whose top notch, at roughly 6,600 ft, has the Cat Ears tower standing just left of it: that is the South Chute. If you reach the lake you have gone below it.

ABOVE THE CHUTE THE TEST IS THE SAME AS THE LAKE APPROACH: a short drop and a second gully to the upper notch near 7,300 ft, then the route loses a little height and traverses NORTH on ledges to the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft — a steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, or a narrow rock ledge in late season.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and lingering snow with real route-finding. This variant trades a brutal trail for a navigation problem; in cloud it is the harder of the two.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to Crystal Pass
approach_variants.hours: 3-4 from the lake to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the standard route: the closed Dosewallips roadbed for roughly 5 miles, then the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail, which gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles with no switchbacks and hand-over-hand pulling in places. Figure 2.5-3.5 hours on that section. Camp at the established sites at the north end of the lake; a wilderness permit is required and the site is reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season.

From the lake, take the boot path around its eastern shore, come out onto a large scree cone, traverse north across the cone and into Avalanche Canyon. Do NOT turn off into the South Chute — that is the standard route. Instead keep going north up the canyon, past the Thumb, roughly 1.5 miles of steady uphill to Crystal Pass at the canyon's head.

The canyon is loose, poorly consolidated talus and scree when snow-free and much faster on firm early-season snow; carry an axe June into July. The final few hundred feet to the pass steepen, there is often a remnant of ice below the scree fan leading up to it, and softening snow by mid-morning is a good argument for an early start.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once Crystal Pass and the lower arete have shed snow; firm early-season snow in the canyon is faster and safer than bare talus
hazards: loose, poorly consolidated talus and scree the length of Avalanche Canyon when snow-free
steepening snow and an ice remnant below the scree fan at Crystal Pass
softening snow by mid-morning on the final slope to the pass
exposed rock ledges on the Lake Constance approach trail
cold wind at Crystal Pass
long committing approach with no water above the lake late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no ambiguity at the top: the West Arete is the prominent ridge rising DIRECTLY out of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon, and it runs straight up to Constance's summit ridge crest. If you are standing in a windy col with the canyon behind you and a ridge going up on your right toward the summit, you are at the start.

The negative marker is a turn made much lower down. If you found yourself climbing a scree chute out of the east side of the canyon with the Cat Ears above you, you are on the standard South Chute route and will end up in the upper maze and the traverses, not on the arete. The arete approach never leaves the canyon floor until the canyon itself ends.

On the arete, the climbing stays close to the crest on broken class 2 and 3 with the odd class 4 or low fifth step, so easy ground at the start is correct here and is not a sign you are off route.

bivy.name: Wild Lake
bivy.notes: Remote lake at the foot of the southwest flank, where the normal line up the peak begins. Reached only on multi-day traverses of the range.
bivy.water: Lake
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few tents

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

emergency.notes: Remote, largely trailless approach with no reliable cell coverage expected in the Sawtooth Ridge/Mount Skokomish Wilderness backcountry, typical of the southern Olympics.
emergency.rangerStation: Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District — consolidated office in Quilcene, WA (295142 US-101 S; 360-765-2200); the former Hoodsport ranger office closed in 2005. For the Flapjack Lakes/Staircase approach inside Olympic National Park, contact the park's Wilderness Information Center at 360-565-3100.
emergency.nearestHospital: Mason General Hospital (Mason Health), 901 Mountain View Dr, Shelton, WA — Level IV trauma center; roughly 40+ miles / about an hour's drive from the Staircase trailhead via Lake Cushman Rd and US-101.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies; Mason County Sheriff non-emergency line 360-426-4441. Technical/backcountry rescue is typically coordinated by Mason County Search & Rescue / SORT (Special Operations Rescue Team) with support from Olympic Mountain Rescue.

bivy.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
bivy.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

bivy.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
bivy.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
bivy.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

bivy.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
bivy.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
