The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side, Lake Ouzel and the Redoubt Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This one starts north of the border. From Chilliwack Lake Road, park at the large turnout shortly before the steel bridge over Depot Creek, where the unsigned dirt spur leaves; high-clearance vehicles can drive part of it, but it ends at a major washout where foot travel starts on the old logging-road grade. About two hundred yards of trail crosses the international boundary at the obelisk and register, and a wilderness permit is needed beyond it for overnight stays. The old roadbed runs under a mile before vanishing into forest, and for roughly three miles the route weaves through timber and brush with no consistent tread. At the valley headwall the trail parallels the falls on Depot Creek — expect a stream crossing at its base, wet slabs, and at least two fixed handlines on the exposed slab sections beside the water, which are a real fall hazard when wet or icy. Above the falls the path fades through talus and brush in the open basin before reaching Lake Ouzel, the standard base camp on flat sandy benches. From camp, scramble the large broken buttress southwest of the lake, cairned to help the return; partway up, traverse far climber's right, then continue to gain the Redoubt Glacier and cross or skirt it toward the peak.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September is most reliable — the crux gully and the upper basin snowfield usually melt out by early August. Earlier trips find firm or icy snow in both and want light crampons and an axe.
hazards: exceptionally loose, oxidized volcanic breccia throughout — a helmet is essential and no hold should be trusted
rockfall onto anyone below through the cliff band around 7,700 ft
steep, sometimes icy snow in the upper basin and the crux gully, especially early season
crevasse hazard on the Redoubt Glacier crossing
the fixed handlines beside Depot Creek Falls, which should not be attempted without them when the rock is wet
an approach that starts in another country with no cell coverage and a long carry-out
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE GAP YOU WANT IS TOO NARROW TO WALK THROUGH. From the glacier, work up to the obvious southwest basin at about 7,700 ft below the summit, then continue to the notch immediately SOUTH of the true summit at about 8,260 ft. The break through that notch is a short, vertical rock gully only six to eight feet wide, sometimes holding ice in its back, and pulling through it is the technical crux of the whole climb. That narrowness is the test: if the gap in front of you is wide enough to walk up, or you can gain the ridge without a vertical move, you are at a different notch and should keep traversing south along the base of the summit rocks. A second confirmation is the rock itself — this peak is built of rust-coloured, fractured volcanic breccia, and above the gully the south ridge to the summit is loose enough that parties have described the register entries about it in one word. If the rock above your gully is solid and takes weight cleanly, you are almost certainly not on this mountain's standard line. On the way down, the same gully is a downclimb or one short rappel off a natural boulder or horn — there is no fixed hardware here, so carry your own.

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass, the ledge traverse to Peggy's Pond, and the Southeast Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Cathedral Rock / Deception Pass trailhead at the end of FR-4330, about 3,400 ft, take the signed Deception Pass / Cathedral Pass trail. At about 1.8 miles a signed junction splits right to Squaw Lake — stay left. The trail climbs another two miles into subalpine meadow and switchbacks to Cathedral Pass at about 5,500 ft and 4.2 to 4.5 miles, at the PCT junction.

From the pass drop briefly toward Deep Lake on the PCT; a use path leaves at a switchback toward Peggy's Pond, or continue to the signed Peggy's Pond Trail #1375 junction. Either way the last half mile is a rough, primitive traverse across narrow ledges with real exposure to steep drop-offs. Go slowly with a pack; it feels harder than anything on the maintained trail.

Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft, five to five and a half miles in, is the last reliable water and the last established camp.

About 9 km and 2,700 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Snow can linger above the pond well into July and an axe is worth carrying then
hazards: An exposed, primitive ledge traverse into Peggy's Pond, harder than the trail that precedes it
An early creek crossing near the trailhead that can be a wet ford in high water
Loose talus and route-finding uncertainty below the East Summit
Real crevasses opening on the Daniel and Lynch glacier ice on the north side by late summer
Lingering snow into July that can require an axe on the slopes above the pond
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH HAS A HARD EDGE AND IT IS THE LEDGE TRAVERSE INTO PEGGY'S POND. That half-mile of narrow ledges with exposure is the last thing between trail and mountain, and it is the point at which a party knows it has left the walking behind. Peggy's Pond is the base camp and the last water.

FROM THE POND, THE FINDING IS AN ALTITUDE AND A SHAPE: braided boot paths head northwest then west across heather benches and talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft over about a mile, to the broad SOUTHEAST RIDGE at 6,800 to 7,000 ft. You are on the right ridge when it NARROWS WESTWARD with the HYAS CREEK GLACIER ON YOUR RIGHT and CIRCLE LAKE FAR BELOW ON YOUR LEFT. That pairing — glacier right, lake left — is the confirmation, and it does not need the summit to be visible.

THE NEXT CHECKPOINT IS A SADDLE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT between the East and Middle summits, reached by traversing climbers' trail and open scree BELOW the East Summit at 7,899 ft. The path is faint where it first leaves the ridge and well defined afterwards, so a faint start is not evidence you are off route.

WHERE THE GLACIER COMES IN: to use the Daniel Glacier proper, enter it just NORTH of a prominent spire on the Northeast Ridge and traverse west across it to the Middle Summit.

AND THE ONE THING NOT TO DO NEAR THE TOP: the true West Summit at 7,960 ft is reached over loose talus, lingering snowfields and the rocky margin of the Daniel Glacier remnant. Stay on the rock and scree spine. Wandering onto the glacier ice on the north side is where the crevasses are.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw
approach_variants.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do NOT follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse BELOW the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
hazards: Full-width crevasses opening late in the season across the Lynch Glacier
Loose, rotten rock on the ground used to gain and leave the ice — reported as the worst hazard on the route
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition that widens through the summer
Pea Soup Lake melting out and Lynch draw flooding from mid-July
Significant glacier recession, so old descriptions understate the rock and moat work
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A LAKE YOU WALK ACROSS. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to FROZEN PEA SOUP LAKE. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

WHAT TO DO WHEN THE LAKE HAS MELTED OUT, WHICH IS THE COMMON CASE FROM MID-JULY: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge SEPARATING the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the FIRST MINOR NOTCH at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' LEFT via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

GETTING ONTO THE ICE, IN EITHER SEASON: early, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT. Late, bypass on climbers' LEFT by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

AND THE TOP TELLS YOU WHICH SUMMIT IS WHICH: the glacier leads to the GAP BETWEEN THE TWO HIGHEST SUMMITS. From the notch, the WEST summit — on your RIGHT — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A SCOPE NOTE THAT MATTERS TO PEAK-LIST PARTIES: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.

approach_variants.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
approach_variants.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse WEST to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.
approach_variants.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
hazards: Crevasses across the full width of the glacier late in the season
The moat at the rock-to-ice transition
Loose rotten rock on the class 3 bypass
A long approach over Dip Top Gap with a descent to the lake that must be reversed on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AIMING FOR THE OUTLET OF PEA SOUP LAKE, AND THE SHOULDER ABOVE THE FOSS RIVER IS THE WAYPOINT THAT GETS YOU THERE. From Dip Top Gap the traverse is WEST until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. If you are looking down into a drainage that is not the Foss, you have not traversed far enough west.

FROM THE OUTLET THE FINDING IS THE SAME AS FROM PEGGY'S POND: get onto the ice ABOVE THE LOW ROCKS at the head of the lake. Early season, take the snow finger on climbers' RIGHT; late season, bypass by class 3 on climbers' LEFT and cross the moat. Then ascend the upper glacier toward the West Pyramid and the col between the Middle and True summits.

THE NEGATIVE TEST: this route is graded third class with only minor snow and ice difficulty. If you are on steep ice, you are not on the Lynch Glacier standard line.

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
bivy.notes: The base for MOUNT DANIEL and the eastern option for MOUNT HINMAN, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. THE CRITICAL 2026 CAVEAT: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.
bivy.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE MOST RESTRICTED CAMP IN THE ZONE AND THE RULES ARE THE POINT. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp ONLY on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
bivy.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.

bivy.name: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
bivy.notes: The low-effort basecamp on the Cle Elum side, less than two miles up the Deception Pass trail from the Tucquala Meadows road end on a gentle grade through meadow and forest, sitting at about 3,471 ft with Cathedral Rock and the Daniel massif standing over it. For MOUNT DANIEL it is the family-friendly alternative to Peggy's Pond and it is honest to say what that costs: camping here rather than at the pond adds roughly two thousand feet to summit day and puts the whole approach to the southeast ridge in front of you before the climbing starts. It earns its place for three reasons — it is the fallback when Peggy's Pond is full, which it often is; it is the sensible choice for a party larger than the pond's reduced limit allows; and it is by far the better place to sit out weather, being sheltered, wooded and low. The valley floor around Fish Lake and Tucquala Lake below the trailhead also holds dispersed and developed camping if you arrive late and want to walk in fresh. Two caveats. Mosquitoes here are serious from snowmelt through midsummer, worse than at the pond. And the same fire-area closure applies as at Peggy's Pond — the Cle Elum River road, the Deception Pass trail and the campgrounds along the road were all shut from mid-August to the end of October in 2026, so this entire approach depends on that closure having lifted.
bivy.water: The lakes and the Cle Elum River flowing through them. Reliable all season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Party size twelve. Camp at the established sites and keep back from the shoreline — a 200 ft setback applies at listed lakes on this side of the range. Check the current campfire order before lighting anything; at this elevation a fire may be legal when the district is not under a seasonal ban, but the sites nearest the water are heavily worn and a stove is the better choice regardless.
bivy.capacity: Plenty. Established sites and a privy along the shores of both lakes, spread out enough that even a busy weekend does not feel packed. This is the one place in the zone where a large party can settle without a problem.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin to Gilhooley Saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,500 ft, at the end of FR 2870; a Forest Service day-use pass is needed at the trailhead. Start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833.2), which climbs gently through old growth along the river. At around a mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right and south onto 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream.

The trail climbs gradually through forest, opens into rocky brushy ground above about 4,000 ft, and reaches Royal Lake at 5,100 ft roughly 6-7 miles in. That is the last easy reliable water and the usual overnight on a two- or three-day trip. Royal Lake runs on an Olympic National Park quota, so an overnight needs a wilderness permit arranged in advance.

From the lake, go around to its far end past Shelter Rock — a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter — then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet into Upper Royal Basin at 5,600-5,700 ft, about another mile and 500 ft. Good camping and snowmelt water there.

From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine, roughly a mile, then up a large snow slope — mud and scree once it melts out — on the west edge of Deception's northeast face, toward the Deception-Martin (Gilhooley) saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Helmets from the moraine up: the rock on the whole upper mountain is loose rotten pillow basalt, and parties above you will move it.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; before July is preferred while snow still covers the loosest ground
hazards: near-constant rockfall at Gilhooley Saddle, worst at its west end - do not loiter
rotten pillow basalt throughout the upper mountain, helmets mandatory from the moraine up
steep loose scree on the west side of the upper basin
rockfall triggered by parties above
steep, exposed and serious ground - early season before July is preferred while snow covers the loosest rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The saddle is your fix, and it is a place to move through rather than rest — rockfall there is close to constant, and worst at its west end. Do not stop and rack up in it.

From the saddle, descend about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant and traverse WEST, around Gilhooley Tower and the crags beside it. Do not try to climb over the tower; go around it.

The confirmation you got around correctly is the ground itself: once you are on the slopes SOUTH of Gilhooley Tower, everything remaining to the summit is a walk on class 2 slopes. Easy ground means you are right. If instead you are on steepening rotten rock, you did not go far enough west — reverse and continue around.

One route-finding trap worth naming: the alternative line through Surprise Basin avoids the steepest ground and is described by multiple trip reports as long, arduous and not worth taking. If your line has stopped feeling steep and has started feeling endless, check which basin you are in.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek log crossing, Stump Hollow to the Chopping Block camp, then the upper Barrier crossing
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Goodell Creek Trailhead at the Goodell Creek Group Camp, about 500-600 ft, off SR-20 just west of Newhalem. The first stretch follows an old logging-road grade and climbers' path along Goodell Creek for a little over a mile before narrowing to a boot-beaten track.

Roughly 4 miles in, near Terror Creek, watch for the unmarked junction where the Terror Creek climbers' path splits off, historically flagged only by a rock arrow, a post and a large cairn. Route-finding here is a genuine crux; the path is well-defined at first but dies out into creek-bottom brush and devil's club lower down.

Cross Terror Creek at about 2,000 ft. THE CUSTOMARY CROSSING IS A LARGE LOG ROUGHLY 500 FT UPSTREAM OF WHERE THE PATH HITS THE CREEK, but in high water that log is sometimes submerged and parties have had to scout alternates. From the creek the path grinds directly up the opposing hillside, gaining close to 4,000 ft in under two miles through forest and then open heather. It eventually merges into Stump Hollow and follows the narrow crest north to the basecamp area near Chopping Block Camp at about 6,000-6,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: An unmarked junction at Roost Creek that is a genuine route-finding crux
A Terror Creek log crossing that can be submerged in high water
Close to 4,000 ft of gain in under two miles on steep, loose ground; a torn calf muscle is on record here
The Barrier: loose, exposed, and consistently described as feeling far harder than its class-3 rating
The chossiest rock in the Southern Pickets, with running meltwater over slabby sections as a slip hazard
Old, weathered tat on the one summit-tower rappel anchor
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS THE NOTCH IMMEDIATELY SOUTH OF THE SUMMIT, AND THAT NOTCH IS ALSO THE UPPER BARRIER CROSSING. Those are the same feature, which is what makes it findable: it is a place hundreds of parties pass through for a different reason. From camp, traverse Stump Hollow to the roughly 6,400 ft saddle near the Chopping Block, descend about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin, then cross a snowfield and small glacier below Degenhardt's south side and CLAW UP DIRT AND BROKEN ROCK TO THE NOTCH IMMEDIATELY SOUTH OF THE PEAK, which is the top of the upper Barrier crossing.

TWO BARRIER CROSSINGS EXIST AND THIS ROUTE WANTS THE HIGHER ONE: a LOWER crossing over loose ledges at the base of the Terror Glacier, or a HIGHER crossing over moats and steep choss near the top of the glacier JUST BELOW DEGENHARDT. The higher one is the preferred option precisely when Degenhardt, Pyramid or Terror is the objective, because it puts you at the notch. If you took the low ledges you will have to climb back up.

HOW YOU KNOW THE NOTCH WHEN YOU ARE IN IT, IN CLOUD: it is the top of the worst rock on the route, and the route's own description says this ground marks THE END OF ANY GOOD CLIMBING IN THE AREA. Dirt and broken rock underfoot steepening into a gap in a rib, with the Terror Glacier behind you and the ridge running north above you, is the place.

FROM THERE THE COUNT IS SHORT AND THE ERROR IS ALWAYS THE SAME ONE: follow the ridge north over exposed but moderate ground. PARTIES REPORT TRAVERSING MUCH TOO LOW AND HAVING TO REGAIN HEIGHT. Stay near the crest. A SMALL TOWER guards the final notch and is TURNED rather than climbed direct, and the last moves onto the summit are short 4th class on poor rock.

Degenhardt is widely regarded as the chossiest peak in the Southern Pickets. Helmets and careful rope management matter more than the grade suggests.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

approach_variants.name: Thornton Lakes, Thornton Pass and Triumph Pass to the Despair Lakes basin
approach_variants.notes: A long, mostly off-trail crossing of two passes. From the Thornton Lakes Trailhead the trail runs nearly flat for a mile to a crossing of Thornton Creek, the last easy water before it goes fully cross-country. Leave the tread there and bushwhack upslope: small cliff bands force a leftward, northerly traverse through slide alder, then a ferny talus slope above a hanging meadow, then a steep push of about a thousand feet through cedar limbs and heavy brush to a rocky shoulder around 5,300 ft on Thornton Ridge. Budget most of a day for that stretch alone; it is the crux of the walk-in in effort and route-finding, not the climbing. From the shoulder, traverse north over rock and heather to flat benches near Thornton Pass, the standard camp. From camp, drop back to about 5,300 ft and cross shoulder-high brush to a cascading stream with open bedrock slabs, downclimb the slabs about two hundred feet, then drop through forest and steep duff to about 4,600 ft, traverse into the basin below Triumph Pass and climb to the pass. From there descend a north-facing snowfield, skirt Lake Regret on its west-side moraine, re-climb to about 5,300 ft, and traverse heather benches, slabs and shallow ravines to Upper Despair Lake.
approach_variants.season: Mid-summer through early fall, once the snow has consolidated and the brush is passable.
hazards: loose, moss-covered granite on the southeast face requiring careful hold-testing
dense slide alder and cedar-limb bushwhacking on the Thornton Creek approach
cliff bands above the Despair Lakes basin that are easy to wander into, especially at night
lingering steep snow on the southeast and south-facing slopes into July
a long, committing, largely trail-less crossing where poor visibility becomes a real navigation hazard
a full day out from camp, with parties routinely finishing the talus and brush in the dark
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE CLIFF BAND IS PASSED AT ITS FAR LEFT END, NOT WHERE YOU FIRST MEET IT. From Upper Despair Lake, climb the heathery ridge to the east of the lake, then talus and snow, until a continuous cliff band stops you directly beneath the southeast face. Do not attack it where you arrive. Traverse along its foot to its LEFT — southwest — end, where the band has an obvious weakness, and take that. Above the weakness the ground turns into the east ridge, which is a continuous, exposed but non-technical scramble the whole way to the summit block, and that continuity is the confirmation: if the ridge keeps going at a steady scrambling grade you are on the standard line. If instead you find yourself below a clean, steep dihedral and committing to fifth-class moves, you have started up the southeast face proper — a real line, but one that has to be rappelled to get back onto the ridge, and not the way most parties go. There are no fixed anchors on this peak, so any rope work is off natural horns and blocks you build yourself. Fix the line in your head on the way up; the same cliff band in reverse is where parties get cliffed out in the dark.

bivy.name: Upper Despair Lake
bivy.notes: NOT a documented camp — reports use it as a rest and water stop on the long traverse to the peak, and no established sites are described there. It is the last reliable water before the cliff band below the southeast face, and worth knowing about as an EMERGENCY stopping point if a party is benighted on the traverse rather than as a planned camp. Snow patches and steep chutes linger around the Despair Lakes into early summer.
bivy.water: the lake
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
bivy.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and a steep climb of about 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire: the park still lists the North Fork Skokomish and Home Sweet Home trails closed, with no reopening date, on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, and while they stay closed this is the direct way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

approach_variants.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
hazards: The southeast-facing chute is an avalanche funnel that becomes sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon — start early and check NWAC in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
A very popular and crowded trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on route
Fragile subalpine vegetation on the open upper slopes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION POINT ON THIS MOUNTAIN IS A SIGNED JUNCTION AT TIMBERLINE, ROUGHLY 4,500 FT, AND A SIGN IS THE BEST FOG MARKER THERE IS BECAUSE IT DOES NOT DEPEND ON VISIBILITY BEYOND ARM'S LENGTH. At that junction the WINTER CLIMBING ROUTE BREAKS RIGHT, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the MAINTAINED SUMMER TRAIL SWITCHBACKS LEFT across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the LEFT one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

SECOND TEST, higher: the summer trail threads a NARROW NOTCH and then crosses WEST-FACING slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS SEASONAL RATHER THAN NAVIGATIONAL: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.

approach_variants.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail
approach_variants.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
hazards: Same as the upper-trailhead variant, over a longer and gentler approach
The 3,900 ft merge is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
No water on the upper route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST TEST IS THE MERGE AT ABOUT 3,900 FT, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take DOWNHILL to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

THE DECISION POINT IS THE SAME SIGNED JUNCTION AT TIMBERLINE, ROUGHLY 4,500 FT, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the WINTER CLIMBING ROUTE BREAKS RIGHT up the chute, the SUMMER TRAIL SWITCHBACKS LEFT. Take the left.

AND THE SAME CONFIRMATIONS ABOVE IT: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.

approach_variants.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
approach_variants.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SIGNED TIMBERLINE JUNCTION AT ABOUT 4,500 FT AND THE RIGHT-HAND BRANCH OUT OF IT. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THAT THE GROUND STOPS SWITCHBACKING. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

THE TEST FOR WHETHER YOU SHOULD BE THERE AT ALL, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

bivy.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
bivy.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
bivy.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Deer Lake
bivy.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
bivy.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

access.fees: None — Phelps Creek Trailhead is a no-fee USFS site.
access.rules: Wilderness group-size limit of 12 people/stock combined applies (forest-wide rule for Okanogan-Wenatchee wildernesses other than Lake Chelan-Sawtooth and Pasayten).
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary (~2.6 mi up Phelps Creek Trail). No Northwest Forest Pass or trailhead fee is required at Phelps Creek Trailhead.
access.closures: IMPORTANT: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground, north to Trinity, since May 20, 2026, after a December 2025 storm/debris-flow damaged the roadbed. The Forest Service order (06-17-07-2026-11) runs through Dec 31, 2027 with no reopening estimate, and it blocks normal vehicle access to the Phelps Creek and Trinity trailheads. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes the Phelps Creek and Leroy Creek trails. Check current Okanogan-Wenatchee NF alerts before driving.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — administered by the Wenatchee River Ranger District (not the Chelan Ranger District, which covers the Stehekin/Lake Chelan side of the wilderness).

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the North Fork Entiat, Entiat River or Phelps Creek trailhead kiosk.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must DROP about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
hazards: A thousand feet of descent into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing
Icy forty-degree slopes near the top of the Gloomy Glacier, with crevasses below the usual line
Two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
The narrow exposed ledge traverse off the col, which is avoidable and should be avoided
Route-finding is the crux — this is regarded as the most complex of the three Entiat nine-thousanders
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FERNOW IS NOT VISIBLE FROM LEROY BASIN, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go UP THE WATERFALL, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

FIRST: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the RIGHT side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

SECOND, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, DO NOT go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at NINE THOUSAND on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.

wa_mount_ferry_standard.approach: There is no dedicated trailhead, road, or maintained path to Mount Ferry — reaching it means committing to 2-3 days of the Bailey Range Traverse, Olympic National Park's classic off-trail high route that links the Sol Duc River trailhead (via Sol Duc Falls Trail #630) in the north with the Elwha River/Whiskey Bend trailhead in the south, or with the North Fork Quinault trailhead via Dodwell-Rixon Pass on the longer loop variant. The most common approach starts at the Sol Duc Trailhead: maintained trail runs about 1 mile to Sol Duc Falls, then climbs steadily past Deer Lake and up the High Divide Trail toward Bogachiel Peak/Heart Lake — roughly 9-11 miles and ~3,300 ft of gain from the car, and the last reliable on-trail water and camp before travel goes off-trail. From High Divide near Cat Basin, the route leaves the maintained trail and follows the Bailey Range crest east: over Cat Peak's exposed 'Catwalk' (an airy class 3 knife-edge ridge, the first of two such sections on the traverse) and Stephen Peak, where steep heather benches with class 3-4 moves lead into a second, brushier catwalk with awkward gully crossings serious enough to warrant a blunt 'DON'T. FALL.' warning before dropping into Ferry Basin (~5,700 ft), the standard camp beneath Mount Ferry and roughly 2 days / 15-20 miles of travel in. Ferry Basin has dependable water — a small waterfall about 60 ft from the usual camp spot, plus a nearby tarn — and is often considered one of the nicer camps on the traverse. From camp, Ferry's summit is reached via a broad bench and scree/talus slope east of the true summit, loose 'dagger scree' (sharp, shifting shale-like rock) that demands careful footing but involves no technical climbing, just sustained off-trail scrambling. A less-common southern approach comes in via Dodwell-Rixon Pass and Queets Basin, up Ball Bearing Gully to the Scott-Ludden saddle, then along the Ferry-Ludden ridge to that same broad bench east of the summit. Either way, expect no signage, no bridges, unmarked creek fords, lingering snow/ice in gullies and on north-facing slopes even in August (ice axe and often crampons are standard kit), slide alder brush lower on the flanks, and serious route-finding responsibility — this is remote, high alpine terrain well beyond the maintained trail network.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the Ptarmigan Traverse to the Spider-Formidable col
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft at the end of the Cascade River Road. The maintained trail runs 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft — well graded, an hour and a half to two hours at a steady pace. Everything beyond is bootpath and it is the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse.

From the pass take the bootpath uphill to the south and traverse along Mix-Up Arm on heather, talus and snow, then up the mellow Cache Glacier to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft — corniced early in the season. From the col, a descending traverse south-south-east on more heather, talus and snow reaches Kool-Aid Lake at 6,100 ft, the standard base camp, roughly three hours and five to six miles from Cascade Pass.

South past Art's Knoll comes the Red Ledge: an exposed traverse over loose rock and lingering snow patches that many parties rope for, and by common consent the crux of the approach. It is noticeably worse when snow-covered.

Beyond it a rough path runs about a mile over meadow, snow, talus and small rock ribs toward the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall at around 6,500 ft. Rope up, ascend the glacier's left side weaving through crevasses, and reach the Spider-Formidable col at 7,320 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, best late Jul-Aug
hazards: the Red Ledge — loose rock, exposed, and materially worse when snow-covered
cornice at Cache Col early in the season
crevasses on the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall
steep snow and moat immediately below the Spider-Formidable notch
loose rock in the gullies on the south face
long, remote position with no maintained trail beyond Cascade Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the part that is easy to get wrong, and it is a counting exercise rather than a description.

From the col, go through the NARROW EASTERN notch and descend roughly 150 vertical feet of steep snow — or in the moat beside it — before it becomes feasible to start contouring right, to the west. Do not try to contour immediately from the notch; you have to lose that height first.

Continue west over slabs and snow, then heather and small rock outcrops. Leave the snow onto class 3 rock, climb up and then LEFT to a distinct ledge. From that ledge make a rising traverse to the north-west, scrambling ACROSS two gullies. Then cross a spur ridge to reach a THIRD gully — and it is the third gully that you climb.

So the test is: from the ledge, the first two gullies are crossed, not entered. If you start up the first gully you meet after the ledge you will be on steeper, looser ground short of the line. If you have crossed a spur ridge and are looking up a gully, that is the one.

Some trip reports also describe reaching the south-face snow alcove from a staging camp near a notch at about 7,050 ft below the col, by either a hidden gully on the left with fifth-class moves or, more commonly, a winding ledge on the right at class 3 with one harder step. The right-hand ledge is the usual choice; if you are pulling fifth-class moves you have taken the left option.

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; STAY LEFT at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the UPHILL fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
hazards: Extremely shattered rotten shale with real rockfall and ankle-turn hazard the whole way up
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes, with the steepest 500-600 ft immediately off the pass
Lingering steep snow on the Constance Pass to Deception Basin traverse into July, warranting an axe
Brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing near the ridge crest and col on the way out
A long, committing backcountry approach far from help
Boulder Shelter sits at the foot of an avalanche chute with snapped trees in the scar
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE COL BETWEEN FRICABA AND HAL FOSS, AND THE PUBLISHED TEST FOR IT IS THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS PEAK THAT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING: FROM DECEPTION BASIN, ASCEND EASTWARD AIMING FOR THE LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE CONNECTING FRICABA WITH HAL FOSS. Lowest point. Not the nearest gully, not the most obvious scree fan — the lowest saddle on that connecting ridge. In cloud you can still tell which way a skyline sags by walking toward the direction the ground stops climbing soonest.

SECOND TEST, once at the col: turn AWAY from Hal Foss and follow the ridge up to Fricaba. The North and SW ridges are the two most readily ascended and this is the SW one. The first 500 to 600 vertical feet off the pass is the STEEPEST part of the climb; after that it eases into a straightforward scree hike. So the shape of the effort is a check on the line: steep first, easy after. A route that stays uniformly moderate is not this one.

THIRD TEST, AND IT IS WHICH SUMMIT: FRICABA'S SW PEAK IS THE TRUE, HIGHER TOP. The NE peak lies about half a mile away along the NE ridge and is noticeably lower. If you have walked half a mile of ridge from the top you reached and are now standing somewhere higher, you were on the NE peak.

WHAT THE GROUND FEELS LIKE, so it does not read as a wrong turn: Fricaba is extremely shattered, rotten shale. Two steps up and one slide back is the normal experience, not evidence you are off route. Brief Class 2-3 scrambling appears near the ridge crest.

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and BEAR RIGHT onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the LEFT of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A 35-40 degree snowfield below the Royal-Deception notch, wanting an axe outside late season
Shattered shale and scree on Fricaba itself
Gendarmes on the approach ridge that must be skirted rather than climbed
Long approach with the last dependable water at Royal Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: SAME BASE, SAME TEST, APPROACHED ACROSS THE BASIN RATHER THAN DOWN INTO IT: from Deception Basin, ascend EASTWARD aiming for the LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE CONNECTING FRICABA WITH HAL FOSS. THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is the gendarmes on the way up: the usual line goes round them to the LEFT, then up steep scree. If you are scrambling over towers rather than skirting them, you have taken the crest instead of the scree. AND THE SAME SUMMIT TEST: THE SW PEAK IS THE TRUE TOP. The NE peak, half a mile off along the NE ridge, is lower. HONEST LIMIT: the scree route above the col is considered self-explanatory, which means there is no known marker for it. It is a walk-up on rubbish rock; the navigation problem is getting to the col, not what happens above it.

approach_variants.name: Luna Col, then the 6,300-6,600 ft traverse across the ribs to the 7,050 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
The line in is the standard one: SR-20 to the Ross Dam trailhead between mileposts 134 and 135, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the resort boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, then 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail through old-growth cedar past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, and another mile or so north.

Watch on the left for a small cairn or a scratched arrow on a split log marking the cut-off, and cross Big Beaver Creek on a log just north of where Access Creek enters it; some years you wade. Then the Access Creek bushwhack: valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the north side and climb directly upslope through huckleberry, then several hours of heavy forest, deadfall and slide alder. Near 3,800 ft cross back to the south bank where the brush pinches out between a tongue of forest and a tongue of talus, then follow cairns and a faint path up talus into Access Creek Basin at about 4,300 ft, a good first camp.

From the basin, up the long grungy scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft, then the notorious traverse on very steep heather, talus and slabs to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft, the standard high camp on glacially polished slabs. Some parties wear crampons for traction on the heather.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Route-finding across the ribs and gullies between Luna Col and the notch, in terrain with no path
Very steep heather on the Access Col to Luna Col traverse; some parties use crampons on it
Class 3-4 downclimbing on the east ridge, kept just south of the crest
Parties on this side of Fury routinely take six hours from the summit back to camp and finish in the dark
No shortcut off the peak; everything is a reversal
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS AT A NUMBERED NOTCH AND THE WHOLE APPROACH IS A CONTOUR TO REACH IT. From Luna Col drop a few hundred feet east, then traverse RIGHT at about the 6,600 ft level across ribs, gullies and small basins to the crest of a subsidiary ridge running southeast. Cross the large basin in front of you DROPPING NO LOWER THAN 6,300 FT, and from 6,300 ft in the middle of that basin start an ascending traverse northwest to the 7,050 FT NOTCH. That notch is where the route proper begins.

SO THE TEST IS AN ALTIMETER TEST, AND IT WORKS IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT NEEDS NO VIEW: the traverse is held between 6,300 and 6,600 ft, and then and only then does it climb. If you are below 6,300 ft you have dropped too far into the basin and will pay for it; if you never got below 6,600 ft you are still on the ribs and have not crossed the basin at all.

ARRIVAL: a notch is a gap you can stand in with ground falling away on both sides. From it the ridge runs west toward Fury and there is an exposed, level stretch the route's own account calls the sidewalk in the sky. Reaching an airy horizontal crest immediately above the notch confirms it.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing the ascending traverse past the notch, or contouring on around, puts you under the Southeast Glacier, which is the standard route's ground and a different climb.

COUNTABLE FEATURE ON THE ROUTE ITSELF: there is one 20 ft step on the east ridge that parties rappel on the way down off a medium cam or chock. One step, not several.

approach_variants.name: The backdoor: over the summit of East Fury and down into the Goodell Creek basin to the toe of the Southwest Buttress
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is identical to the standard East Peak route for its first 12-plus miles and then continues much farther. From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134, walk about a mile to the Ross Lake water taxi dock and cross to Big Beaver Landing, then follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail 11.5 miles up-valley, passing Luna Camp at roughly the 4.7-hour mark.
