About 29 minutes past Luna Camp, leave the trail at a large log crossing of Big Beaver Creek and turn up the Access Creek drainage: roughly a mile and 1,900 ft of gain through devil's club, a mid-height creek crossing near 3,800 ft, then huckleberry and talus into Access Basin. From the basin, a long grungy scree chute gains about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft.

From Access Col most Mongo Ridge parties do not stop at Luna Pass. They continue over the connecting terrain and up the Southeast Glacier route to the summit of East Fury, then descend into the upper Goodell Creek basin to the base of the Southwest Buttress to rack up. Most parties treat this as a multi-day expedition with a camp at Luna Pass or on the connecting ridge.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug
hazards: Roughly a dozen rappels along the crest, almost entirely off improvised anchors: loose blocks, horns and old tat
Retreat gets progressively harder the farther along the ridge a party commits
A rappel rope has been reported severed by rockfall mid-descent on this ridge
The Access Creek bushwhack and the loose scree chute to Access Col before any of it
A full ascent of East Fury simply to reach the start
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE AT THIS ROUTE FROM ABOVE, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE MODERN APPROACH. The buttress toe sits at the bottom of the Goodell Creek side, and the historically brutal, brush-choked Goodell approach is what the backdoor exists to avoid. So the sequence is: summit East Fury, then GO DOWN into the upper Goodell Creek basin to the base of the Southwest Buttress. If you are still gaining height after East Fury's summit, you have not started descending to the base yet.

WHY THAT MAKES THE BASE UNMISTAKABLE: there is exactly one summit between you and the start, and it is one you have to climb. A party that has not stood on East Fury has not reached the base of Mongo Ridge by this approach, whatever else it has found.

THE DECISION POINT, WHICH MATTERS MORE HERE THAN THE LANDMARK: the descent to the toe is time you will have to buy back, and the ridge above it holds roughly half a dozen major gendarmes and pinnacles including the tower nicknamed the Pole of Remoteness. Getting off each of them takes a rappel, roughly a dozen along the crest before you reach West Fury. Every one of them is irreversible once the ropes are pulled.

WHAT ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING LOOKS LIKE: rack up where the ridge stops descending and the first tower rises in front of you. Above that point the route is 25 pitches to Grade VI, 5.10.

bivy.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
bivy.notes: Open basin at the top of the Access Creek bushwhack above Luna Camp. The usual first night before climbing past Luna Col to East Fury.
bivy.water: Creek and snowmelt
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: Several tents on gravel and boulders

bivy.name: East Fury summit bivy
bivy.notes: Flat rock on the summit of East Fury used as the second night. The long descent to the base of the ridge starts here, and the bivy is often left in place for the return.
bivy.water: Snow only
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on flat rock

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

approach_variants.name: Luna Col, then over the back and 2,400 ft down into Luna Cirque to camp at Luna Lake
approach_variants.notes:
The modern approach mirrors the Luna Col line and then drops over the back: SR-20 to the Ross Dam trailhead, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, another mile to the marked cut-off, a log crossing of Big Beaver Creek just north of Access Creek, and the Access Creek bushwhack to Access Creek Basin at 4,300 ft.

From there the scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft and the steep heather traverse to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft. The whole approach is given as about 17 miles and 7,000 ft of gain from the water-taxi dock.

What is different begins at Luna Col: this route DESCENDS from it, north-northwest into Luna Cirque to Luna Lake at about 4,800 ft, then southwest to a camp on the cirque floor beneath the buttress. That descent costs 2,400 ft which has to be regained on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: 2,400 ft of descent into Luna Cirque that must be regained on the way out
The Access Creek bushwhack and the loose scree chute to Access Col
No descent down the buttress; the exit crosses the summit and the Southeast Glacier
Steep summit snow of about 300 ft, 40 degrees at the base to nearly 50 at the top, on the exit
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no realistic bailout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE 2,400 FT OF DESCENT IS THE TEST, AND IT IS THE ONLY ROUTE ON THIS PEAK THAT ASKS FOR IT. Every other line from Luna Col goes up or across. This one goes DOWN, and a long way down, into the cirque on the far side. If you have left Luna Col and are not losing height fast, you are on the wrong side of the ridge.

ARRIVAL AT CAMP: LUNA LAKE AT ABOUT 4,800 FT IS THE CONFIRMATION AND IT IS A WATER FEATURE, which is what makes it findable in bad visibility. Camp is on the cirque floor beyond it, beneath the buttress. Standing at a lake at the bottom of a cirque with walls on three sides, having descended roughly 2,400 ft from a col, is unambiguous.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: the buttress rises directly above that camp on the peak's north side. This is a 20-pitch line and the base is the toe of the buttress at the back of the cirque, not a feature part way along the wall.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing southwest along the cirque floor past the buttress toe brings you under the west side of the massif and the connecting ridge toward West Fury, which is a different objective and offers no way up here.

THE COMMITTING FACT THAT SHOULD SHAPE THE DECISION AT CAMP: the buttress is an ascent line only. The standard exit is over the top and down the Southeast Glacier on the other side of the mountain, and a party that camped in Luna Cirque still has to regain roughly 2,400 ft to Luna Col afterwards to retrieve gear and get out.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake water taxi, Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col and Luna Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134 at 2,150 ft, walk about a mile down to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock and cross to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, 11.5 miles of dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail up-valley takes roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp at about the 4.7-hour mark.

About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp a large log crossing of Big Beaver Creek, roughly 15 inches in diameter, marks the turnoff. Leave the trail there and head up Access Creek: a real bushwhack of about a mile gaining 1,900 ft, starting in valley-bottom devil's club, crossing to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then huckleberry and a final half-mile of talus into Access Basin.

From the basin a long, steep, loose scree chute gains about 1,800 ft to Access Col at 6,100 ft, 2-3 hours, and it can be brutally hot with no shade. From the col, 3-4 miles of notoriously steep heather and talus lead to Luna Pass, where most parties camp near lingering snow patches for water.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A mile of genuine bushwhacking up Access Creek through devil's club, deadfall and huckleberry with biting insects
A long loose scree chute to Access Col with no shade
Notoriously steep heather between Access Col and Luna Pass; an axe is worthwhile on the short steep sections
Crevasses on the Southeast Glacier and a bergschrund near 7,900 ft
A final snowfield to nearly 50 degrees, with crampon-balling reported on wet snow
Wet, mossy rock on the lower of the two rib ledges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROCKY RIB IS THE GATE, AND THE GLACIER STARTS ON THE FAR SIDE OF IT. From Luna Pass the day goes along the Northeast Ridge crest, then down a steep, narrow heather chute of about 500 ft into a talus basin around 6,500 ft, then contours southwest across talus, heather and polished slabs until a ROCKY RIB BLOCKS EASY PASSAGE. That rib is the landmark. It has two ledge options: take the LOWER one, exposed scrambling on wet mossy rock and steep heather, in preference to the looser and more exposed upper ledge.

ARRIVAL: immediately beyond the rib you rope up, because the Southeast Glacier starts there, between roughly 6,500 and 7,000 ft. Snow under your feet on the far side of the rib is the route.

COUNTABLE CONFIRMATION ON THE RIDGE: between Luna Pass and the heather chute the crest throws up one distinct rock step of about 25 ft with a climbable vertical crack, class 3. That step is the only rock climbing before the glacier. If you have done several such steps you are on the ridge crest too long and have missed the point where it drops away.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE: this route climbs the true right, i.e. climber's-right, side of the Southeast Glacier on moderate 20-40 degree snow and works around a bergschrund near 7,900 ft, usually passable on its left. If you are on the left-hand margin of the ice looking for a way onto rock, you are heading for the East Ridge, not this route.

AND THE ONE FEATURE THAT IS UNMISTAKABLE EVEN BLIND: the last of the route steepens from 30-40 degrees to nearly 50 degrees, firm enough to front-point but not always secure for flat-footing, then narrows to a short snow arete before the summit rocks. When the snow narrows to a crest with air on both sides, there is nothing above but the top.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail and Access Creek to Access Col, then the sidehill traverse around Luna Peak to the Fury-Luna connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR-20 at milepost 134, this is a multi-day approach and not a day hike. The standard option follows the Big Beaver Trail: hike, or take the seasonal water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, roughly 6 miles up the west shore of Ross Lake to the Big Beaver Creek trailhead, then the maintained trail up-valley through old-growth cedar past the Big Beaver and Luna camps to a point about 1.5 miles north of Luna Camp, roughly 10-11 trail miles in.

Leave the trail there, ford Big Beaver Creek and climb steep pathless forest and heather along the north side of Access Creek to break out into the open, meadow-floored Access Creek basin below Luna Peak, which is relatively brush-free compared with neighbouring drainages. Continue up-basin past a camping area near the headwaters, then climb a steep gully and heather system to a notch around 6,100 ft, Access Col, which gives the first view north into Luna Cirque and the Southern Pickets skyline.

From the col a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass and Luna Cirque, then gains the Fury-Luna connecting ridge.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug
hazards: Picking the wrong drainage off the Big Beaver Trail in poor visibility, a documented error here
Cliff-band route-finding on broken ledges where a wrong tier cliffs you out
Poor, vegetated rock that takes gear badly, and shockingly mobile large talus on the summit ridges of the massif
Gullies dropping into Access Creek involve cliffy downclimbing and occasionally short rappels
Water is abundant along Big Beaver and Access Creeks but scarce above Access Col
One of the most remote summits in the range, with no quick way off
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS ENTERED FROM A SMALL GLACIER, NOT FROM A RIDGE, AND THAT IS THE DISCRIMINATOR. The northwest side of West Fury is reached by a small glacier tucked beneath the peak, gained from the ridge system running toward Luna. Snow travel on it is reported as straightforward and kickable in good conditions. If you are scrambling rock to reach the start of this route you are in the wrong place; the start is where you step off snow onto dirty, ledge-broken ground on the northwest flank.

THE ROUTE-FINDING WARNING IS THE BASE FINDING, BECAUSE THE MISTAKE HAPPENS HERE: leaving the glacier, you work up broken ledge bands to gain the west ridge crest. The rock is poor and vegetated with few obvious anchors, and A WRONG TIER WILL CLIFF YOU OUT. Route-finding through the ledge bands is the real difficulty, not the climbing. Pick the tier that keeps going; if you have to make a hard move to stay on a ledge, you are on the wrong one.

CONFIRM HIGHER: from the crest, an ascending traverse east across loose rock leads into a chute that tops out slightly EAST of the summit. Topping out east of the top and having to walk back west is correct on this line, not an error.

WHAT DOES NOT BELONG HERE: this line is documented mainly as a DESCENT by parties traversing the Northern Pickets rather than as a commonly repeated ascent. Expect to be route-finding from first principles and treat any confident-sounding description of the ledges, including this one, as less precise than it sounds.

A NAMED NAVIGATION HAZARD LOWER DOWN, WHICH IS WHERE THE DAY IS ACTUALLY LOST: poor visibility has caused parties to pick the WRONG DRAINAGE off the Big Beaver Trail. Some parties cairn the correct creek crossing on the way in. Access Creek's basin is the open, meadow-floored, relatively brush-free one; if you are fighting continuous brush you are in a neighbouring drainage.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

approach_variants.name: Bridge Creek and the North Fork to the moat below the red ledges
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek / PCT trailhead off SR-20 near Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail southbound about ten miles, losing steadily along Bridge Creek, to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp. Turn up the North Fork Bridge Creek trail and head upstream; it gets brushier and less maintained the further you go, with a log crossing at Grizzly Creek.

Around mile 13-14 the maintained tread effectively ends. Ford the North Fork — cold and sometimes knee deep, and easiest a few steps upstream at a cairn — then work up scree and third-class slabs on CLIMBER'S RIGHT of the large waterfall draining toward the Goode Glacier, which is the way to avoid the worst brush. Look for the alder tunnel: a boot-path corridor through the slide alder that saves a great deal of thrashing.

Camp around the glacier toe at roughly 5,400-6,800 ft depending on how far you push. Plan on three to four days round trip.
approach_variants.season: Mid to late July through September. The moat crossing is easiest once the glacier has receded, around the third week of July, and gets harder again as the season goes on
hazards: A moat and bergschrund at the toe of the buttress with a steep step of about 50 degrees where the route steps off the Goode Glacier onto rock — worse as the season goes on, and reported by some parties as impassable late
Open crevasses and overhead serac hazard on the Goode Glacier
Loose and wet rock on the approach slabs beside the waterfall
Cornices on the approach in early season
A route that is difficult to retreat from once high on the buttress — commit only with a stable weather window
A descent by the Southwest Couloir that several parties report taking 8-10 hours from summit to car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LANDMARK IS A COLOUR: THE RED LEDGES AT THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS. Three independent accounts name them, and one quotes a published description doing so. You are looking for a band of RED ROCK where the Goode Glacier meets the foot of the buttress. If the rock in front of you is grey, keep looking along the toe.

THE BASE IS THE MOAT AT THOSE LEDGES, AND HOW YOU CROSS IT IS THE MEASURE OF THE SEASON: a collapsed or intact snow bridge, a jump, a downclimb, or a short rappel followed by re-climbing on the far side. Published elevations for this point range from about 6,400 to 7,800 ft across different years and different parties, which is a real disagreement rather than a single number — the glacier has retreated and the crossing point moves. NAVIGATE TO THE RED LEDGES, NOT TO AN ALTITUDE.

ABOVE THE MOAT, EXPECT ONE OR TWO PITCHES OF LOW FIFTH ON PRECARIOUS BLOCKS, TRENDING CLIMBER'S RIGHT to gain the buttress crest proper. If your first ground above the glacier is clean and solid, you are not on the toe.

TELL IT FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER LONG ROUTE BY WHETHER YOU EVER TOUCHED THE GLACIER: MEGALODON RIDGE IS GAINED FROM THE EAST WITHOUT CROSSING THE GOODE GLACIER AT ALL. If you crossed a moat off glacier ice, you are on the Northeast Buttress. If you never left brush and rock, you are on Megalodon.

CONFIRM AS YOU CLIMB: over 1,000 ft of 3rd and 4th class on the crest, often soloed or simul-climbed, then around 8,000 ft a short UNPROTECTABLE 5.7 SLAB on the crest that most parties deviate RIGHT to avoid, then roughly five pitches of 5.4-5.5 easing toward the summit. A route that is hard from the bottom is not this one.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass, the crest trail to Methow Pass, and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The long way, and the one that suits a two-day trip. From the large paved lot on the north side of SR-20 at Rainy Pass, follow the crest trail north as it climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek — fill up there, it is the last easy water before a long dry stretch of switchbacks — to Cutthroat Pass. From the pass the trail drops toward Granite Pass and a saddle beyond it, where a steep snowfield often lasts into August and has caused slide-for-life falls, so carry an axe if you are early in the season. Beyond, the trail contours across open, sparsely treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow, a common water and camp stop, with a short side trail west into the Snowy Lakes basin for a higher and more scenic bivy under Tower Mountain and Golden Horn. From the meadow, stay on the crest trail north to the open plateau at Methow Pass and leave it there: travel west and southwest off-trail through open heather and talus benches toward the peak's east ridge, gain the ridge, and follow moderate sand, scree and talus — loose in places, with real route-finding — up to the saddle between the true summit and its lower false summit.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, with July through September giving the driest scree. June ascents work but the final slopes and gully still hold snow and want an axe and crampons. The highway is shut for avalanche control through the winter, which closes both approaches outright.
hazards: loose scree, talus and blocky rock on the unmarked upper route, worst near the summit saddle and the final gully
a steep lingering snowfield just past Granite Pass that has caused slide-for-life falls into August
a long, mostly off-trail final leg with no marked line
afternoon thunderstorms and fast weather changes on exposed ridge crest and passes
wildfire smoke reducing visibility in late summer
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SADDLE YOU ARE AIMING FOR SITS BETWEEN THE TRUE SUMMIT AND A LOWER KNOB TO ITS EAST — DO NOT STOP ON THE KNOB. From Methow Pass, get up onto the east ridge as early as you can and keep close to its crest; the talus slopes below it are loose and slow, and parties who angle across them lose time. Moderate sand, scree and talus lead to the saddle between the summit and the eastern false summit. From the saddle, several hundred feet of blocky Class 2-3 scrambling on rock that takes hands reach the top. If the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance to the west, you are on the knob, and the saddle below it is where you cross to the true summit.

approach_variants.name: Swamp Creek pullout and the south ridge
approach_variants.notes: The short, steep alternative, and the way most day parties go. Start from the highway pullout at Swamp Creek and climb through brushy forest to the foot of the prominent ridge on the mountain's south side. Follow the ridge upward, staying on the crest where it lets you and moving climber's right to get around the cliff bands that block the crest around 5,200 ft — getting that traverse wrong is what turns parties back. Above the cliff bands the ridge opens out onto sand and scree and continues to the summit block. This side faces the sun and dries early, which is why it comes into condition before the crest-trail approach and why it turns into a loose, dusty grind by late summer; a snow finger on this flank can hold firm snow at a fairly steep angle into early summer, which speeds the ascent considerably for a party carrying an axe.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September once the snow finger has stabilised or melted, with July and August driest. Earlier in the season the finger is a snow climb rather than a scramble.
hazards: cliff bands around 5,200 ft where the crest is blocked and the bypass is on climber's right — the main route-finding failure on this side
a steep snow finger on this flank into early summer, with wet-slide and sluff potential
brushy forest on the lower ridge with no maintained tread
loose scree and blocky rock on the upper route and in the final gully
an exposed ridge crest with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
seasonal closure of the highway cutting off road access entirely
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE NOTCH IS ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE BLOCK FROM WHERE YOU ARRIVE, AND YOU HAVE TO TRAVERSE TO IT. At about 7,200 ft the ridge you have been following runs into the summit block; leave the crest there and scramble loose scree and granite blocks across the EAST side — climber's right — until you reach a notch tucked under the summit block. Cross the notch, and the way on is a short, SHALLOW gully leading up to the top. That gully is the marker: it is shallow and blocky rather than deep and cut, and it is the only break that goes at scrambling grade. If the block above you is unbroken wall, keep traversing right rather than starting up; if you have dropped far enough to be under steep cliff bands, you have gone too low and should regain height. The upper ground is several hundred feet of enjoyable blocky scrambling on rock that takes hands, and a lower false summit sits beside the true one — if the highest ground you can reach still has something higher a short distance away, you are on the false summit and the saddle between them is where you crossed.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

bivy.name: Methow Pass and the PCT meadow camps below Snowy Lakes
bivy.notes: Methow Pass is where the PCT crosses from the Granite Creek side into the head of the West Fork Methow, and the camps just beyond it are the sheltered alternative to Snowy Lakes for anyone who does not want a night in the open at six thousand seven hundred feet. They cost a little climbing back up on summit morning and are worth it in bad weather. This is also the departure point for Mount Hardy by the long approach: the PCT is left near the pass and a climbers' path leads up toward the peak, which stands directly to the west. Parties combining Hardy with Golden Horn and Tower usually base here or at the lakes and take Hardy on the way out, since the ridge rambling between the lakes and Hardy's south side connects the whole group. Camping on the established sites rather than in fresh meadow matters here more than most places, because the ground is soft and the trail is walked by a steady stream of long-distance hikers all summer.
bivy.water: Good here — this is the drainage side of the crest and the creeks running off toward the West Fork Methow are dependable. It is the reason to choose these camps over the lakes when the wind is up.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping at established sites, no permit and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A string of established sites in the meadows along the trail around a mile beyond Methow Pass, near where the boot path to the lakes leaves. Enough ground for several parties spread out, and lower and more sheltered than the lake basin.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
bivy.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

bivy.name: Granite Pass
bivy.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.
bivy.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.

approach_variants.name: Bagley Lakes and Chain Lakes Trail to the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then cross-country to the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Bagley Lakes Trailhead around 4,200 ft, at the south end of the upper Mount Baker Ski Area parking lot near the Heather Meadows Visitor Center. Follow Bagley Lakes Trail #684.1 south along the east shore of Bagley Lake — the only reliable water on the route, and it should still be treated.

At about three quarters of a mile the trail joins Chain Lakes Trail #682, which bends west and switchbacks up toward Herman Saddle at roughly 5,300 ft, about 1.5-2 miles and 1,100 ft above the lakes.

At the last switchback BELOW Herman Saddle, leave the maintained trail and climb open heather and a short band of scrub trees for a couple of hundred vertical feet to gain the connecting ridge between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman.

Then follow the crest generally EAST, staying mostly on the south and southwest side over heather benches and loose scree and talus, to the base of a short final east ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow lingers on the slope below Herman Saddle into July or August and the Forest Service flags it as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
hazards: An unmarked exit at the last switchback below the saddle, easy to miss in poor visibility
Lingering snow on the Chain Lakes switchbacks into July or August, flagged as avalanche terrain in winter and spring
Loose down-sloping scree and talus on the connecting ridge, easy to kick onto anyone below
Only one water source, at Bagley Lake, and it needs treating
Two summits on one ridge — Mazama Dome west, Herman east
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE EXIT IS BELOW THE SADDLE, NOT AT IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM. You leave Chain Lakes Trail #682 at the LAST SWITCHBACK BELOW Herman Saddle. The correct exit point is easy to miss in poor visibility and this is the route-finding crux of the day.

SO USE THE SADDLE AS A BACKSTOP RATHER THAN A TARGET. Herman Saddle is the LOW POINT on the ridge connecting Mazama Dome, to the west, and Mount Herman, to the east. If you crest the saddle and the ground starts falling away in front of you toward the Chain Lakes basin, you have gone past your exit — turn round and come back down to the last switchback. That is a reliable test in cloud precisely because a saddle announces itself underfoot.

WHAT YOU CLIMB TO REACH THE RIDGE: open heather slopes and a short band of SCRUB TREES, a couple of hundred vertical feet. Scrub trees at the top of a heather slope is the marker; if you are on scree with nothing growing, you are too high or too far east.

ARRIVAL: you are on the route when you are standing on the Mazama Dome-Herman connecting ridge with a peak at each end of it. From there the direction is EAST, on the south and southwest side of the crest.

THE CLIMBING ITSELF IS THE LAST SHORT EAST RIDGE. Everything before it is heather benches, loose scree and talus. If you have not left your feet by the time the ground runs out ahead of you, you are not at the summit yet; the true top takes a short scramble up that final ridge.

WHICH BUMP IS MAZAMA DOME? It is the WEST end of the same ridge. Turning west out of the saddle area climbs a different, lower feature.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley to La Bohn Gap and the lakes
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Necklace Valley trailhead at about 1,650 ft at the end of FR 68 and start up Necklace Valley Trail #1062. The first five miles are deceptively flat, gaining only about 600 ft along the East Fork Foss River, entering the wilderness at about 1.5 miles.

Around mile 5 the trail FORDS the East Fork Foss River — there is no bridge and it runs high and cold in early-season melt, so cross in the morning at low flow. Then it turns uphill in earnest, roughly 2,400 ft over three miles of steep, root-laced switchbacks. This is the real crux of the approach for tired legs.

The grade eases at Jade Lake at about 4,600 ft and eight to nine miles, then Emerald and Opal Lakes through the swampy Necklace Basin — good camping and reliable water, buggy in early summer.

From the head of Necklace Basin the maintained trail ends. Continue cross-country on an established, cairned climbers' path through meadow and boulder talus, up and east roughly a mile to a mile and a half and over 1,000 ft, to La Bohn Gap and the La Bohn Lakes. That is the standard high camp: about 10 to 11 miles one way with over 5,000 ft of cumulative gain.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Most parties make it a two or three day trip
hazards: An unbridged ford of the East Fork Foss River around mile 5, high and cold in early-season melt
2,400 ft of steep root-laced switchbacks with a multi-day pack
Crevasse and bergschrund hazard on the lingering glacier remnant, mostly early season
Loose rock on the final class 2 scramble
Mosquitoes in the lake basins in early and mid summer
A long walk out from a remote camp if anything goes wrong
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LA BOHN GAP AND ITS LAKES ARE THE ARRIVAL, AND THE HONEST FINDING IS THAT THERE IS NO LONGER MUCH OF A GLACIER TO FIND. Measured in August 2022, the Hinman Glacier had largely disappeared, leaving stranded patches of snow and ice. So do not stand at the gap looking for a glacier front to identify. What you are looking for is the basin above the gap: mostly bare rock and permanent snowfield in most recent seasons, with crevasse and bergschrund hazard only in early season or after a big snow year.

HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT LA BOHN GAP: it is where the cairned climbers' path out of the head of Necklace Basin tops out at over 5,500 ft, with the La Bohn Lakes in it. If you are still in swampy lake-studded basin on maintained tread, you have not left Necklace Valley.

WHICH WAY FROM THE GAP: the summit lies EAST-NORTHEAST of La Bohn Gap, and this route's own recorded positions make that unambiguous — the eastward travel is roughly three times the northward. The first move out of the gap is north-northeast into the basin; after that the line swings east-northeast. A party still heading due north well above the gap is drifting off the route. The objective is the snowfield basin immediately above the lakes, which is unmistakable once you are at the gap, and easy class 2 ridge and scree ground leads from it to the summit ridge.

THE FINAL TEST IS A DISTANCE ALONG A RIDGE: from where you gain the summit ridge, the true summit at 7,492 ft is about HALF A MILE along it. A party that tops out on the ridge and stops is half a mile short.

bivy.name: La Bohn Lakes, La Bohn Gap and the Chain Lakes benches
bivy.notes: The high camp for LA BOHN PEAK and the launching point for the west route on MOUNT HINMAN, and the single most useful piece of ground in this zone for a climber. La Bohn Gap is a broad boulder-covered saddle at roughly 6,000 ft on the crest between the Foss and Snoqualmie drainages, with the tarns of the La Bohn Lakes scattered on the benches around it and the Chain Lakes sitting lower at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak. From Necklace Valley the climb to the lakes goes either up to the gap itself or by a steeper line beside the waterfall; both are straightforward in summer and both hold snow into July. La Bohn Peak is a short class 2 walk west from the gap. For Hinman the ground continues east and then north, half a mile of easy going to gain the gap area and then a long open ascent to the summit — worth knowing that the Hinman Glacier shown on older maps has essentially gone, so what you will actually cross is a shrinking snowfield with the moat and loose-rock problems that come with that, and conditions vary enormously year to year. The gap is also the hinge of the whole area on foot: north drops into Necklace Valley, south drops toward Dutch Miller Gap and the upper Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and the view takes in Bald Eagle, Silver Eagle and Big Heart Lake off to the west. Camping here is committing. It is fully exposed, the weather arrives without warning, and a bad night in the gap is a real one — carry proper shelter or drop back to the Necklace lakes.
bivy.water: The La Bohn tarns and the Chain Lakes below the gap on the south side, plus lingering snowmelt into midsummer. Late in a dry season the smaller tarns can drop and turn silty; check rather than assume.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, picked up at whichever trailhead you start from. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size twelve. Campfires prohibited outright — everything here is well above the 4,000 ft fire-ban line and there is no wood to burn anyway. Camp on rock or bare gravel, not on the heather, which takes decades to recover at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small, exposed pitches on granite benches and heather shelves between the tarns — realistically two or three tents in the good spots, more if you are willing to sleep on rock. There is no sheltered ground.

bivy.name: Necklace Valley — Jade, Emerald and Opal Lakes
bivy.notes: The main basecamp for LA BOHN PEAK, which stands directly at the head of this valley, and the first night of the standard west-side approach to MOUNT HINMAN. Drive the Foss River road off Highway 2 a short way east of Skykomish and turn into the Necklace Valley trailhead about four miles up. The trail is famously two-faced: the first five miles along the East Fork Foss gain only about 600 ft through regenerated second growth and go quickly, then the trail crosses the river and climbs roughly 2,400 ft in the next three miles to break out at Jade Lake around 4,600 ft. Emerald is a quarter mile further, Opal about 4,790 ft above that, with Ilswoot, Locket, Jewel and Cloudy scattered on either side. A weathered memorial cabin sits in the meadow just above Emerald; it is a landmark and a piece of the valley's mining history, not a shelter to plan on. From Opal or Emerald the route to La Bohn Gap climbs east under the cliffs, so Jade is fractionally further from the gap but Emerald and Opal put you closest to the day's work. Two honest caveats. The Foss River road has been under construction with weekday delays of about half an hour through the summer, and damage higher on the road has at times cut off the upper end, so allow slack and check before committing to a dawn start. And this valley is very popular for its own sake — a midweek trip is far more pleasant than a Saturday, and the steep middle section is genuinely unpleasant under a heavy climbing pack in the heat.
bivy.water: All four lakes, plus the creek linking them. Reliable the whole season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Party size limited to twelve including stock. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the range, which puts every lake in the valley under a fire ban — carry a stove and do not build rings.
bivy.capacity: Sites are spread across four separate lake basins rather than concentrated, so the valley absorbs a lot of parties — several groups at Jade, several more around Emerald and Opal, and quieter singles at Ilswoot, Locket and Jewel off to the sides. On a summer weekend the popular shorelines are full by mid-afternoon.

bivy.name: Money Creek and Miller River campgrounds, Foss River roadhead
bivy.notes: The valley-bottom staging option for every Foss River objective, and worth a line of its own because of what the road has been doing. The Foss River road leaves Highway 2 just east of Skykomish and has been running weekday construction delays of about half an hour through the summer, with damage further up that has at times cut off the top of the road, while the West Fork Foss spur has been impassable to vehicles and adding a two-and-a-half-mile road walk. All of that argues for sleeping close to the highway the night before rather than driving out in the dark and discovering the situation at 5 a.m. Both campgrounds sit off the old highway just west of milepost 46 — one on the South Fork Skykomish in old growth, the other a mile or two up the Miller River road — and both are twenty minutes or so from either Foss trailhead. This is the practical first night for a party heading to Necklace Valley for LA BOHN PEAK or MOUNT HINMAN, or up the West Fork for BALD EAGLE PEAK. Open roughly late May through September; outside that, it is roadside pull-outs and your own judgement.
bivy.water: Piped or hand-pumped drinking water on site, with the South Fork Skykomish and the Miller River beside them. No treating required.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fees, and reservations for most sites. No wilderness permit needed at this elevation — pick that up at the trailhead the next morning. Campfires are allowed in the provided rings when there is no seasonal fire ban in force, which is the last time you will see one on any of these trips.
bivy.capacity: Money Creek has around twenty-five sites, a couple of them first-come; Miller River is a group camp of about fifteen sites with a gathering area. Both take vehicles and both fill on summer weekends, so reserve where you can.

access.fees: Olympic NP wilderness permit: $8 per adult (16+) per night plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee (free for 15 and under), or a $45/person Annual Wilderness Pass (reservation fee still applies). Duckabush Trailhead day-use parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/year) or Interagency/Digital Pass.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters are required for overnight food storage in this backcountry unit; campfires are prohibited above 3,500 ft; groups are capped at 12 people/8 stock animals within The Brothers Wilderness/Olympic NP on the Duckabush approach; dogs are not permitted once the route enters Olympic National Park.
access.permit: Overnight wilderness camping permit required year-round, reserved via recreation.gov; summer-season (May 15–Oct 15) reservations typically release in mid-April.
access.closures: The road is open, but the approach is not: the North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide and the Home Sweet Home Trail from First Divide down to the Duckabush River Trail junction have been CLOSED since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire (20,233 acres, contained 12 Nov 2025) while crews assess hazard trees and repair backcountry infrastructure, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page (updated September 14, 2026) or fire-conditions page (updated September 18, 2026). Flapjack Lakes, Six Ridge, Wagonwheel Lake and First Divide camp are closed as well, so neither the Staircase side nor the Duckabush side has an open trail to First Divide while the closure stands.
access.landManager: Olympic National Park (Daniel J. Evans Wilderness) for the peak and upper approach; the Staircase trailhead also lies inside Olympic National Park, while the Duckabush trailhead and lower valley trail are Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District.
access.land_manager: Olympic National Park (Daniel J. Evans Wilderness) for the peak and upper approach; the Staircase trailhead also lies inside Olympic National Park, while the Duckabush trailhead and lower valley trail are Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District.
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful / Olympic National Park pass at the Staircase entrance station

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, reserved in advance, per-night fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov before the trip; there are no same-day walk-up permits. Bear canisters are required at every wilderness camp in the park, and the Staircase trails are closed after the Bear Gulch Fire, so check status first.

bivy.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
bivy.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
bivy.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

approach_variants.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
approach_variants.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.
approach_variants.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
hazards: Several little bowls look like the peak's south face and one of them is the wrong drainage entirely
A well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north — that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring summit, not this one
No established route above Crescent Lake, and the descent is the crux of the day
Loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever gully you pick through the cliff band
Slippery grass and dense alder low on the face when descending
Water unreliable above Crescent Lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: MAKE SURE YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT DRAINAGE BEFORE YOU CLIMB — SEVERAL LITTLE BOWLS LOOK LIKE THIS FACE, AND THE ONE TO YOUR EAST IS ROYAL CREEK. That is the single mistake worth guarding against here, and it is made before you gain any height. From the northeast side of Crescent Lake, take the talus field at the head of the lake, directly below the obvious cliff band; a short thrash through woody brush leads to an upper talus field, and from there drift right to get around the cliff. Several gullies break the band and there is no single correct one — parties pick the easiest-looking line and find it loose, dirty Class 3 for about a hundred feet. That crux band is the confirmation you are on the face, not a sign to retreat, but it is unpleasant to reverse, so note your line. Above it the ground eases onto talus and dirt climbers' paths to the top. Note also that a well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north on the way in: that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring peak and not the way to this one.

approach_variants.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col
approach_variants.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks near 6,500 ft and descend roughly nine hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.
approach_variants.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
hazards: A substantial descent to Crescent Lake that must be reclimbed on the way out
Snow persisting on the col into late spring
Several little bowls look like the peak's south face — confirm the drainage before climbing
The same cliff band and loose, dirty Class 3 gullies above the lake
A long day made longer by the added distance and the col crossing
approach_variants.baseFinding: CRESCENT LAKE IS THE COMMON STARTING POINT, AND ON THIS SIDE YOU ARRIVE AT IT FROM ABOVE. Cross the col between the two peaks and descend several hundred feet on the far side to the lake; the tell that you are on this variant rather than the direct one is that you reach the water losing height rather than gaining it. From the lake the climb is identical, and so is the mistake to guard against: several little bowls in this basin look like the peak's south face, and being sure of the drainage before you start upward matters more than anything higher on the route. Take the talus field at the head of the lake directly below the obvious cliff band, push through the woody brush to an upper talus field, then drift right to get round the cliff. Several gullies break the band, none of them the single correct one; expect about a hundred feet of loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever you choose. Above it, talus and dirt climbers' paths lead to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the north side of North Peak
approach_variants.notes:
From US-2 at milepost 35.2 turn south on Mount Index Road and drive 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs roughly 3.6 to 4.1 miles and about 2,000 ft to the lake at around 2,600 ft, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur near mile 1.6. The maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

From there, traverse talus and very large boulders along the west and south side of the lake, near an old rockslide, toward the base of North Peak's wall. In early season this crossing goes over avalanche debris and snow and ice piled at the water's edge.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep, after several consecutive dry days
hazards: Wet moss on downsloping slabs — low-angle ground that is genuinely serious
Avalanche debris and lingering snow at the lake edge in early season
Vertical brush steps with no protection
Loose, vegetated rock throughout; slow retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing does not start on the clean wall you first walk under. The original line begins on the broken, BUSHY SPUR on the northeast, which rises out of the wooded ridge above the lake — you start on third and fourth class slabs and grass, not on clean rock. The confirmation is uncomfortable but reliable: the first few hundred feet are downsloping holds on generally solid slab, often sopping wet with moss, and that is what being on route feels like here. Dry, clean, positive rock at the start means you have wandered onto one of the harder faces.

The first fixed reference above the slabs is a VERTICAL WALL with a TWO-PITON ANCHOR — that is the normal point to rope up. Above it a ramp system passes as the 'hidden ledge', then a steep brush tunnel with vertical ten- to twenty-foot steps pulled on vegetation. Between roughly 3,000 and 3,600 ft the brush is at its worst. This face does not dry out at the rate other alpine rock does; several dry days beforehand are part of the route conditions, not a nicety.

bivy.name: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
bivy.notes: THE camp for both MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN, which stand less than a mile apart on either side of a small unnamed glacier directly above the basin. Both are scrambles rather than climbs — La Crosse at 6,417 ft goes at class 2 and was first climbed in 1928, White Mountain at 6,378 ft is class 2 as well — so from a camp here the two together are a single long day rather than an expedition. Lake LaCrosse sits at about 4,800 ft, roughly 400 ft higher and a mile and a half further than Marmot Lake, with Hart Lake in between; Marmot is covered in the Staircase file and is a perfectly good camp, but it is further from these two summits and it is the wrong side of the shelf. THE APPROACH IS THE ENTIRE DIFFICULTY AND THERE ARE THREE OF THEM, none short. From the Dosewallips you go up the West Fork and over LaCrosse Pass. From the East Fork Quinault you go through Enchanted Valley and over Anderson Pass. From the Duckabush you come up the river and over O'Neil Pass. Every one of those is two days in for most parties carrying gear, which is why these summits see so little traffic. July through September; the basin holds snow late and the passes either side of it later still.
bivy.water: Reliable — both lakes hold through the season and the outlet creeks run into autumn. This is the last dependable water before anything you climb from here; the slopes and the unnamed glacier between the two summits carry no running source once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. This basin is not itself one of the named quota areas, but the East Fork Quinault approach to it is, so which trailhead you walk in from changes what you have to book — check the whole itinerary rather than just the camp. An animal-resistant food container is required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the parkwide 3,500 ft line. Elk work this basin heavily and bears are regular visitors.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread between the two lakes, in and above open subalpine basin. Neither holds a crowd and the meadow ground is fragile, so use the established pads rather than making new ones.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

wa_mount_larrabee_south_ridge.approach: Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065 (the last 2 miles are rough, high-clearance terrain — many parties park lower and walk the road). From the trailhead, follow the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) briefly; at about 0.5 mile a signed junction splits left to Winchester Lookout and right onto the High Pass Trail (#676) — take the right fork. High Pass Trail #676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain (steep, exposed snowfields can linger here into August — an ice axe and snow-travel experience are recommended until the chute melts out), then continues up over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the old tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is reached roughly 2 miles / 1.5–2 hours from the trailhead and makes a scenic, if exposed, campsite. There is no reliable water past this point in late season, so treat/carry water from Twin Lakes or early snowmelt. Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends; an unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100–200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face (around 6,400 ft you pass a small cliff band). Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 ft. Here the route-finding crux: locate a gully system cut into the rock face — of two narrow parallel channels about 30 feet apart, take the RIGHT-hand one. Ascend the narrowing gully, which opens into broken rock, to gain the crest of the south ridge. Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit; a faint boot path and scattered cairns mark much of this stretch but both disappear for long sections, so be prepared to route-find. Total distance is roughly 8–10 miles round trip with on the order of 3,500–4,000 ft of cumulative elevation gain (the up-and-over via Low Pass and High Pass adds real gain beyond straight-line distance to the summit). The rock throughout — especially the gully and upper ridge — is notoriously loose and crumbly by Cascades standards; helmets are strongly recommended and parties should keep group size small (6 or fewer) and spread out to manage rockfall risk to those below.

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes, High Pass Trail #676 over Low Pass, then the basin to the southwest spur
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Twin Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS-3065; the last two miles are rough and many parties park lower and walk the road. From the trailhead follow Winchester Mountain Trail #685 briefly; at about half a mile a signed junction splits LEFT to the Winchester lookout and RIGHT onto High Pass Trail #676. Take the right fork.

#676 climbs through meadows and crosses an avalanche chute beneath Winchester Mountain, where steep exposed snowfields can linger into August, then goes over Low Pass and on to High Pass, passing the tailings and remains of the historic Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is roughly two miles and an hour and a half to two hours from the trailhead. There is no reliable water past this point late season.

Beyond High Pass the maintained trail ends. An unmarked climbers' path continues west, contouring and dropping 100-200 ft into the basin below Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, up to the southwest spur at about 6,900 ft.

Keep the party to six or fewer and spread out. The rock here is notoriously loose even by Cascades standards.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep at best; snow lingers in the gully into August and in the avalanche chute below Winchester
hazards: Two nearly identical parallel gullies thirty feet apart, only one of which is the route
Notoriously loose and crumbly rock in the gully and on the upper ridge — helmets, small parties, spread out
An avalanche chute below Winchester Mountain holding steep snow into August
A faint boot path and cairns that disappear for long sections above the gully
No reliable water past High Pass late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO NARROW PARALLEL CHANNELS ABOUT THIRTY FEET APART. TAKE THE RIGHT-HAND ONE. That is the route-finding crux of the whole climb, it is at the southwest spur around 6,900 ft, and it is the sentence to have memorised before you leave camp. Both channels are cut into the same rock face, both look plausible, and only one of them opens into broken rock and gains the south ridge cleanly.

FINDING THE SPUR ITSELF, in order and without needing a view: leave the maintained trail at High Pass. Contour WEST on the climbers' path and lose 100-200 ft into the basin. Pass a small cliff band around 6,400 ft. Cross boulder fields, then scree and dirt, and climb to about 6,900 ft. Losing height first is counterintuitive and correct; a party that only ever goes up from High Pass ends up on Larrabee's south arm ridge instead of in the basin under its face.

CONFIRM THE GULLY BY WHAT IT DOES: the right-hand channel NARROWS and then opens into broken rock that leads to the crest of the south ridge. A channel that stays uniform, or that cliffs out, is the other one.

ABOVE THE GULLY, FAVOUR THE WEST SIDE OF THE CREST. There is a faint boot path and scattered cairns, and both disappear for long stretches, so this is genuine route-finding rather than following.

WHAT THE NEIGHBOURING OBJECTIVE LOOKS LIKE: from the same High Pass the col in Larrabee's SOUTH ARM leads northeast to the Pleiades and the traverse under Larrabee's west flank leads to American Border Peak. Three separate objectives leave from one pass, so name yours before you set off.

climbing_route.label: Right-hand gully from the southwest spur
climbing_route.notes: From the southwest spur at approximately 6,900 ft, the route-finding crux: locate a gully system cut into the rock face and, of two narrow parallel channels about 30 feet apart, take the RIGHT-hand one. Ascend the narrowing gully, which opens into broken rock, to gain the crest of the south ridge. The rock here is notoriously loose and crumbly by Cascades standards; helmets are strongly recommended and parties should keep group size small (6 or fewer) and spread out to manage rockfall risk to those below.

climbing_route.label: South ridge crest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow the ridge crest, favoring the west side, to the summit. A faint boot path and scattered cairns mark much of this stretch but both disappear for long sections, so be prepared to route-find. The upper ridge rock is loose and crumbly.

bivy.name: Sixteen Mile Camp — the base directly under Mount Lawson
bivy.notes: This is the camp for MOUNT LAWSON and effectively the only one. The peak rises about 3,800 ft above the river in a mile and a third, straight out of the drainage the camp sits in, and the climb is a class 2 slog on steep forest and open slope rather than anything technical — the work is the approach, not the summit. The camp is roughly twelve miles up the valley from the North Fork trailhead, past Wolf Bar, Halfway House, Elip Creek and Trapper Shelter, and the walk is gentle until the last few miles where the valley narrows and the trail climbs and drops across steep sidehill. THE FORDS ARE THE WHOLE PLANNING PROBLEM. There are three of them — Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek and the North Fork itself right at this camp — and the river crossing here is regularly impassable during snowmelt or after heavy rain. Parties have been turned around at it having walked twelve miles. Go in late summer when the river is low, carry poles, and treat a high river as a trip-ending condition rather than something to force. Reach the trailhead by the North Shore Road; the South Shore Road has been washed out and a phone will still try to send you that way.
bivy.water: Reliable. The North Fork Quinault runs at the camp, which is also the reason the camp exists and the reason it can be unreachable; treat everything.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. The North Fork Quinault is not a quota area, so this is one of the easier permits in the park, but nothing here is held back as a same-day walk-up and camps this far in do not always surface in an online search — telephone the wilderness information centre if it will not show. An approved animal-resistant food container is mandatory throughout the park wilderness and free loaners are handed out with permits. This camp sits below the 3,500 ft fire line, so fires are legal in the established rings when no seasonal ban is running, and bans are usual by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Four established sites on the river flat, and it is rarely contested — almost everyone walking this valley is bound for Low Divide and passes straight through

bivy.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
bivy.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

bivy.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
bivy.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead.
