It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
bivy.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass at Forest trailheads; National Park fees if approaching via Staircase in Olympic National Park
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Follow wilderness regulations and Leave No Trace; bear canisters are required for food storage at Flapjack Lakes.
access.permit: Wilderness camping permits are limited and reservable year-round (early reservations recommended for the 6/15-9/30 season) if camping within Olympic National Park at Flapjack Lakes; self-issued wilderness registration on Forest land
access.closures: The Flapjack Lakes/North Fork Skokomish Trail and surrounding backcountry have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire (20,233 acres, 100% contained Nov 2025); the developed Staircase area itself reopened July 8, 2026, but the wilderness trails remain closed with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026 - confirm current status with Olympic National Park before attempting this route.
access.closureNote: As of the NPS trail-conditions update on 6/5/26, the Flapjack Lakes Trail and North Fork Skokomish River Trail are CLOSED due to the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date given — verify current status with Olympic National Park before this trip.
access.landManager: Olympic National Park (Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, trail/approach) and Mount Skokomish Wilderness, Olympic National Forest (summit block)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, trail/approach); the summit sits on the boundary with the USDA Forest Service's Olympic National Forest (Mount Skokomish Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: Olympic National Park entrance pass, or an America the Beautiful interagency pass, plus an NPS wilderness permit for overnight travel. No Northwest Forest Pass - Staircase is inside the national park.

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, reserved in advance, per-night fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov before the trip; there are no same-day walk-up permits. Bear canisters are required at Flapjack Lakes, and the Staircase trails are closed after the Bear Gulch Fire, so check status first.

approach_variants.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
approach_variants.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail north for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass. A southern alternative reaches the same pass from Stehekin: the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp — with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually NORTHWARD around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the FREMONT GLACIER SADDLE around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
approach_variants.season: July and August
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present — rope up
A bergschrund that opens below the summit ridge as the snow finger melts out late season, and a moat where the glacier meets the crest
Exposed, often unroped class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Footlog crossings over Thunder and Park creeks that are hazardous at night or in high water
No fixed anchors anywhere on the route — a rappel off the summit block has to be built from a horn, a chockstone or a picket
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE HOGSBACK — the snow spine at the UPPER edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a MOAT CROSSING to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

THEN COUNT THREE FEATURES IN ORDER, AND THE ORDER IS THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM: a class 3-4 ROCK PITCH gains a LEFT-SLANTING RAMP — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 LEDGES ON THE EAST SIDE of the ridge lead through a U-NOTCH between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST IS THE RAMP: IF YOU ARE TRYING TO CLIMB THE SUMMIT TOWER DIRECTLY FROM THE GLACIER, YOU HAVE MISSED IT. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants LEFT. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

THE U-NOTCH IS THE SECOND CONFIRMATION AND IT IS A SHAPE, NOT A HEIGHT: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's EAST flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

AND KNOW WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN YOU ARE ON BEFORE YOU START: this is the SOUTHEAST/SOUTHWEST approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the west; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable permit fee, mid-May through early October; free the rest of the year; free for youth 15 and under.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: NPS wilderness/backcountry permit required for all overnight stays; reserve on recreation.gov or get a walk-up permit at the Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA (SR 20 milepost 105.3).
access.closures: Easy Pass Trailhead (primary approach, SR 20 MP151) sits INSIDE SR 20's winter closure zone (gates at MP134-171) and is unreachable roughly December through mid-spring; exact open/close dates vary year to year (2026 reopened unusually late, June 14, due to storm-repair work) — check WSDOT before a trip. The alternate Thunder Creek/Colonial Creek Campground trailhead (~SR 20 MP130) sits outside the closure gates and is open year-round, but is a longer approach (~13 mi one-way vs. Easy Pass's ~10 mi one-way to the lake camp). Thunder Creek Fire: North Cascades National Park's fire-closure list (updated September 14, 2026; no end date given) closes the Thunder Creek Trail from the Fisher Creek Trail junction to Park Creek Pass, and Junction Camp (hiker and stock sites) at that junction. The Thunder Creek approach turns onto the Fisher Creek Trail at the junction, which the list does not close, but Junction Camp cannot be used while this stands. North Cascades National Park: (360) 854-7200.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (NPS) — Ross Lake National Recreation Area / North Cascades National Park
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — quota reservation or walk-up
overnight_permit.where: Reserve a night-by-night itinerary online via Recreation.gov during the early-access lottery, or get a walk-up permit in person (about 40% of sites) at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount up to 24 hours ahead.

approach_variants.name: Fisher Creek to the lake camp, over the ridge onto the Banded Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Two ways in, and which one you use depends on whether SR-20 is open. The always-open option is the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft for about nine miles to the Fisher Creek trail junction, then the Fisher Creek trail about three miles — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to a lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. Roughly thirteen miles one way. The shorter option is Easy Pass from SR-20 near milepost 151, over the pass at 6,500 ft and down into Fisher Basin, about ten miles, but the trailhead is gated by the highway's seasonal closure.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the BANDED GLACIER on the far side and ascend it to the BANDED-DOUGLAS COL.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
approach_variants.season: June and July
hazards: A major crevasse crossed on a narrow snow bridge on the Banded Glacier
Talus lying on top of bullet-hard glacier ice, described as a pile of marbles — treacherous in a whiteout descent
Cliff bands above the lake camp
Loose chossy rock on the summit ridge and rockfall in the approach gullies
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CRITICAL TRANSITION IS A NEGATIVE TEST: GAIN THE NORTHEAST RIDGE ON SOLID ROCK AT ABOUT 8,800 FT RATHER THAN ATTEMPTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK DIRECTLY FROM THE GLACIER. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

GETTING THERE IS A SEQUENCE OF TWO COLS AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT THINGS. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a LOW POINT ON THE RIDGE — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the BANDED-DOUGLAS COL, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to REACH ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

SO THE QUESTION THAT SETTLES YOUR POSITION IN FOG IS WHICH GLACIER IS UNDER YOU: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

AND ALL THREE LOGAN ROUTES END ON THE SAME 300 FT OF CLASS 3-4 SUMMIT BLOCK, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from FISHER CREEK and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

WATCH THE SCREE BELOW THE GLACIER ON THE WAY UP with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

approach_variants.name: Easy Pass, the Douglas Creek alder, then the west-side gully to the polished slabs
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Easy Pass trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 151, about 3,700 ft. Hike 3.5 miles and 2,800 ft to Easy Pass at 6,500 ft, then descend 1.5 miles through alpine meadows and forest into Fisher Basin and down to the Fisher Creek valley floor and the established campsites.

Cross Fisher Creek on a large fallen log and travel the east side of the Douglas Creek valley on a faint climbers' path. THIS IS WHERE THE ROUTE IS ACTUALLY DECIDED. The transition from forest to open terrain runs into a vast field of slide alder and brush over ten feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, cut by small rocky stream channels — progress measured in inches per minute. One 2022 party was turned back at 4,200 ft by this alone, having covered half a mile an hour for seven hours. The glacier travel is superb and the bushwhack miserable.

Above the brush, the way onto the glacier is a gully on the west side of the basin. Then it is glacier travel to the col and a short summit block.
approach_variants.season: June and July for the best glacier conditions
hazards: A slide-alder thicket over ten feet high that has defeated at least one party outright, with heavy mosquito and black-fly pressure
Cliff bands ringing the Fisher Basin cirque
Crevasses and glide cracks reported over 20 ft deep on the Douglas Glacier
A steep, exposed rock ramp of roughly 300 ft above camp that is hard to protect
Steep icy summit snow needing solid crampon and axe technique
Steep loose-rock switchbacks on the Easy Pass trail itself above mile 2.5
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE GULLY IS ON THE WEST SIDE OF THE BASIN AND IT IS IDENTIFIED BY WHAT IT DELIVERS YOU ONTO, NOT BY ITS ENTRANCE. It starts class 3, steepens quickly to class 4 or low fifth for a short section that is hard to protect, and TOPS OUT ON GLACIER-POLISHED SLABS. Polished slabs above a short steep step is the confirmation. From there it is about 1,500 vertical ft of scrambling on those slabs to the TOE OF THE DOUGLAS GLACIER. SO THE ORDER IS: BRUSH, GULLY, POLISHED SLABS, GLACIER. If you are on slabs without having climbed a short hard step, you have not been through the gully. THE ROUTE JOINS ITS NEIGHBOUR NEAR THE TOP AND THAT IS EXPECTED: ascend the Douglas Glacier — steep at its head — to the COL, then traverse to meet the BANDED GLACIER and finish up the same class 3-4 summit block, about 300 vertical ft. A summit block reached without crossing to a second glacier means you are still on the Douglas side of the col. THE APPROACH IS THE STRONGEST DISCRIMINATOR ON THIS MOUNTAIN, BECAUSE ALL THREE ROUTES END AT THE SAME SUMMIT BUT NONE OF THEM SHARE A VALLEY. This route comes from EASY PASS and the DOUGLAS CREEK drainage on the west. The Banded Glacier comes from Fisher Creek to a lake camp at 5,160 ft and crosses a col onto the Banded. The Fremont Glacier comes from Thunder Creek and PARK CREEK PASS on the southeast. If you passed Park Creek Pass this morning, you are not on the Douglas. AND THE HONEST GAP: no source publishes a countable marker for the gully entrance itself — it is described only as being on the west side of the basin. The polished slabs above it are the reliable confirmation, which means you find out you were right after the hard part.

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek and the Swamp Creek drainage to the west basin
approach_variants.notes: No road reaches this valley: take the passenger ferry or a floatplane up the lake, then the valley road or the shuttle to the bridge at the road end, and plan the trip around those timetables. Follow the crest trail south along Agnes Creek and work into the Swamp Creek drainage, which is a long way in — most parties camp en route rather than pushing through. From the drainage, climb through brush and open basin and then up scree and talus, with lingering snow possible, into the broad basin that sits below the peak on its west side. From that basin the climbing line turns south along the edge of a steep, larch-dotted scree slope and makes for the notch on the southwest ridge described below.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends. Snow can linger on the talus below the notch.
hazards: A long, committing approach with no maintained trail through the upper drainage
Lingering snow on the talus below the notch
The southwest ridge cliffs out if taken directly — the line has to drop and traverse round a buttress
Sloping slabs with loose small rock on the traverse below the overhang
The final stretch climbs through stacked, loose boulders
The jagged crest above is not the line and should not be followed
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE 7,300 FT NOTCH IS THE FIRST PROOF AND THE WHITE ROCK STRIP IS THE SECOND. From the broad basin below the peak, turn south along the edge of a steep scree slope dotted with larch and make a beeline through talus and snow for the notch on the southwest ridge at about 7,300 ft. That notch is the gateway; a gap without the scree-and-larch slope leading to it is the wrong one. From the notch, walking up the southwest ridge leads directly into cliffs — this is expected and is not a sign you are off route. The fix is to drop about a hundred feet on grass to get round a buttress, then traverse upward beneath a striking vertical strip of white rock, hugging the edge below an overhang and taking care on the small loose rock lying over sloping slabs. That white band is unmistakable and is the confirmation you are on the correct traverse. Above it, keep scrambling just below the ridgeline rather than following the jagged crest itself, and finish over stacked boulders to the summit block.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

approach_variants.name: Merritt Lake Trail and Nason Ridge Trail
approach_variants.notes: From the highway, turn north onto the signed spur for the rough forest road — high clearance is recommended — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Self-register at the kiosk. The maintained trail switchbacks up through old-growth forest to Merritt Lake, which has established campsites and a privy and is the last dependable water before the ridge. Continue past the lake junction onto the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it north; the unsigned climbers' path toward the peak's south slopes breaks off uphill about a mile along. Above treeline the path fades into open heather and loose talus with no maintained tread and no water at all, and the ridge crest becomes the only handrail to the broad flat summit.
approach_variants.season: July into October once the ridge melts out; commonly done as a long day and often paired with the neighbouring summit a mile west.
hazards: The route is entirely unmarked past Merritt Lake — navigation, not climbing difficulty, is the main challenge
Open heather and loose talus above treeline with no tread
Fog or whiteout makes relocating the descent path genuinely difficult
No water above Merritt Lake
One or two Class 3 moves around rock gendarmes on the crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: NOTHING MARKS THE TURN — THE TELL IS WHAT HAPPENS IF YOU CARRY STRAIGHT ON. Past Merritt Lake the maintained trail climbs to the ridge trail; a short way along it an unsigned junction sends the climbers' path uphill toward this peak's south slopes. There is no cairn, no post and no blaze, and parties carrying a track have still needed to hunt for it. The overshoot tell is the useful part: going straight on at that junction descends toward Lost Lake, so losing height toward water means you are past the turn and should come back. Higher, the route gives you the one genuinely visual landmark on the mountain — climb the ridge until the snow gives way to a rocky, jagged, narrow crest, which looks impassable at first glance. The line follows the moat between rock and snow just off to the left, stepping up onto the rock to cross ledges, then wraps a big rock tower on its RIGHT side, staying close in at its base, and scrambles dirt and ledges to a knoll and one last snowfield. The summit above is bare and flat rather than a point, and the register does not sit on the high point but off to the south of the flat area.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
approach_variants.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-four miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
approach_variants.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
hazards: Cornice at the top of the face — parties have had pieces release across their tracks
Four hundred feet of exposed descending traverse from the col on snow, ice and very loose Class 3
Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse
Leroy Creek crossing running high in early season
Very poor rock quality throughout this group of peaks
Descending a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS NOT THE ROUTE, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go DOWN about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

THE TEST IS VISUAL AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS: you have descended far enough when the face comes into FULL VIEW. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

WHAT NOT TO EXPECT: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the CORNICE at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay SOUTH and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

approach_variants.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
approach_variants.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side
A very long walk in on a trail that has burned in the past
Cornice at the top of the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base-finding here is one moment rather than a sequence: after the long grind up to Ice Lakes, you come over the crest and the face is right there in front of you. The first-ascent account says exactly that — the doubts about having picked the right way vanished on cresting the ridge.

Coming from this side you meet the face at its FOOT rather than partway up, which is the real difference from the col approach. That means descending steep snow slopes to a snowfield, then up to the glacier, and standing at the bergschrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above — around two thousand feet of it on the first ascent, averaging forty to forty-five degrees and over forty-five near the top.

So the test is which problem you are handed. If you are looking up at a schrund at the bottom of the whole face, you came from below. If you never saw one, you came across from the col.

wa_mount_maude_r2.rappels: None on the descent - the way off is the South Ridge on foot, which in good conditions takes only about 30 minutes from the summit back to the ridge and basin, far quicker than the ascent. Carry the rappel device and slings on this route's list for RETREAT rather than for the descent: bailing back over the icefall means building your own anchors, and the loose rock above it holds them poorly, so downclimbing carefully or waiting out conditions is usually the better option.

access.fees: None - the Forest Service lists the Phelps Creek Trailhead as a no-fee site, and the Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is free and self-issued
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Chiwawa River Road (FR 6200) is closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground after December 2025 storm damage, under closure order 06-17-07-2026-11 in effect through 31 December 2027 unless lifted sooner, so the Phelps Creek Trailhead cannot be reached by car. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes FR 6200, Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211) and the Phelps Creek and Leroy Creek trails. Check with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before planning a trip.

access.passRequired: None at the Phelps Creek Trailhead - the Forest Service lists it as a no-fee site, so no Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed to park. The Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is free and self-issued at the register.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk (Phelps Creek, Trinity, Entiat River, or the Holden trailheads). Holden Village and its access road are closed to hikers through at least summer 2026.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to a bivy at Icy Lake, then the notch onto the Entiat Glacier
approach_variants.notes: Approach as for the North Face: Phelps Creek trailhead, the Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the unmarked climbers' trail up the north side of Leroy Creek into the basin, and on up toward Ice Lakes. Sources spell it Icy Lake as often as Ice Lakes; it is the same water. Parties bivy on ledges above the south side of the lake, below the South Ridge. That is the sensible camp because the South Ridge is the descent — but be clear that it puts you on the WRONG SIDE of the mountain for this route, so the morning starts with a long traverse over a cliff band to reach the access notch. One party set themselves a turnaround rule of two hours from camp to the notch, on the grounds that any slower and there would not be time to finish. Cross the talus above the lake to the notch that lets you onto the Entiat Glacier. Rope up and descend to find a short crossing through the ablation zone of the receding glacier — this is harder than the old published photograph suggests. Skirt below the rock spur and head up toward the icefall.
approach_variants.season: Late summer for the ice, roughly Jul-Aug; the icefall has receded a long way and how much of it is climbable varies year to year
hazards: A decoy notch at about 6,900 ft that leads to a long scree detour
Crossing the ablation zone of a receding glacier, trickier than published photographs show
Big crevasses with vertical steps in the icefall
Crumbly rock with scarce protection on the nine hundred feet above the ice
A long traverse over a cliff band from the Icy Lake camp before the route even starts
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IS THE THING YOU CAN GET WRONG, and there is a documented decoy. The access notch is at about 7,200 ft. A climbers' path leads to a DIFFERENT notch at about 6,900 ft, and a party who took it for the right one paid for the error with a long detour in the wrong direction up an ugly scree bash. If the notch you have reached is around six-nine rather than seven-two, keep going.

Once through the correct notch and onto the glacier, the sequence is: descend, cross the ablation zone, pass under the rock spur, then work RIGHTWARD beneath the headwall. Arrival at the climbing is a change in the ice — you move from walking to big crevasses with short vertical steps, and above those the angle relaxes to about thirty-five degrees of ice running up to the base of the rock.

That base of rock is the second, unmistakable transition: roughly nine hundred feet of fourth and low fifth class above it, with several ramps to choose between. Take the line of least resistance trending slightly toward the ridge crest. The rock is crumbly and protection is scarce, so running belays are the usual method rather than pitching it. There is a distinctive step-across at the top of a couloir partway up.

A note on how much ice you will actually find: in a heavy snow year one party bypassed roughly two pitches of the icefall on steep snow slopes off to the side, and the whole icefall took them an hour of running belays where they had budgeted six. Do not plan the day around a pitch count from an older description.

Descent is the South Ridge, which took that party half an hour — which is exactly why the camp is where it is.

The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, also closes FR 6200, Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211) and the Phelps Creek and Leroy Creek trails. approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the west side of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
The lower approach is shared with the peak's north-side routes: Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft off FR-6211, Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to the Leroy Creek ford at roughly 3.5 miles, then the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route steeply up into Leroy Basin around 6,100-6,200 ft, where the established camps are. That climbers' trail gains about 1,200 ft per mile — it is short and steep and hot under an overnight pack.

Where this route parts company with its neighbours is at the basin: instead of heading for the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col or the Icy Lake notch, it continues onto the peak's WEST side to reach the couloir system near the standard West / South Slopes ground.

The climb is short — roughly 450 m of mostly slabby Class 3 with two brief Class 4 steps — and it pairs naturally with a descent of the South Shoulder to make a loop back into Leroy Basin rather than a there-and-back.
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep. This is explicitly a late-season line — it wants the snow gone and the rock dry
hazards: Loose rock among the summit-ridge towers on the traverse south
Brief exposed Class 4 moves that most parties climb without protection
Miscounting the gullies from the North Tower, which puts you on unrecorded ground on the same face
A steep unmaintained climbers' trail into Leroy Basin gaining roughly 1,200 ft per mile
A late-season route on an east-side peak, so afternoon thunderstorms and smoke are the normal conditions
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY IS FOUND BY COUNTING, AND THE THING YOU COUNT FROM IS THE NORTH TOWER. From the west side of the mountain the route is THE SECOND GULLY TO THE RIGHT OF THE NORTH TOWER. Not the first, not the third. That is the entire identification, and it works in poor light because a tower is a silhouette rather than a texture.

THE POSITIVE TEST ONCE YOU ARE IN IT: the line takes the SHALLOW RIGHT FORK up slabby Class 3 rock on clean stone. Shallow, right, slabby, clean. A gully that stays a single deep cleft with no fork, or one whose rock is rubble rather than slab, is the wrong count.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS A SIDEWAYS MOVE: after the first slabs the route steps RIGHT into ANOTHER couloir over a brief Class 4 step, then continues on sustained slabby Class 3 to the ridge crest. So the correct sequence is fork right, then move right again. If your gully runs straight to the crest with no lateral move and no short hard step, you are not on this line.

WHAT THE TOP OF THE ROUTE IS NOT: gaining the ridge crest is not the summit. From the crest the route TRAVERSES SOUTH toward the main summit, passing around towers on the WEST — the right — side, with occasional brief Class 4 moves. If you top out and start going north, you are walking away from the peak.

THE DISCRIMINATORS AGAINST THIS PEAK'S OTHER ROUTES, all three of which start from the same basin: the North Face route crosses the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col and then DESCENDS four hundred feet on the far side before it reaches anything; the ice-fall route goes through a notch at about 7,200 ft onto the Entiat Glacier. Both of those take you AWAY from the west side. If you have crossed a col or gone through a notch, you have left this route — it never leaves the peak's own west flank.

CARRY THE MEANS TO PROTECT ONE MOVE, OR NOTHING. Most parties solo this; the Class 4 steps are brief and unprotected in practice, and there is nothing on the route that a rope helps with except those.

approach_variants.name: Smithbrook Trail to Union Gap and the Lake Valhalla crest trail
approach_variants.notes: From the highway east of the pass, take the gravel forest road (closed to vehicles under a storm-damage order through December 31, 2027 unless lifted sooner) to the Smithbrook Trailhead and self-register for wilderness travel. Smithbrook Trail #1590 climbs through brush and an old boulder field and then old-growth forest, entering the wilderness within the first half mile, and tops out at Union Gap on the crest trail. Turn south onto a relatively flat, blueberry- and huckleberry-lined stretch with views toward the neighbouring peak and the ridge beyond. The trail runs through forest to an unnamed gap before it begins its drop toward Lake Valhalla, and it is at that gap that the climbers' path leaves it and turns north up the open slope.
approach_variants.season: July through October is the dependable window; the access road holds snow into early summer.
hazards: The turnoff carries no sign of any kind and the tread reads as a gully rather than a trail
The climbers' path braids into several social paths with no signage — pick the one that visibly heads for the summit
Lingering snow patches cross the path into early summer and can bury the tread
Steep and eroded going, with sections where you shimmy through foliage
The summit ridge carries a brief drop and reclimb before the true top, so the first crest is not it
approach_variants.baseFinding: A SINGLE WHITE ROCK MARKS IT, AND THE LAKE TELLS YOU IF YOU HAVE GONE PAST. Walking south on the crest trail from Union Gap, the climbers' path breaks off uphill to the right just north of the saddle between this peak and its neighbour — so you reach it before the saddle and before the lake, not after them. There is no sign and no cairn; the marker is one conspicuous white stone beside the tread, and the path itself looks more like a gully than a trail where it starts. The negative marker is unmistakable: the crest trail carries on through the saddle and begins descending, and Lake Valhalla comes into view through the trees almost immediately once you are past. If the lake is in sight or the trail is losing height, come back uphill and look for the white rock. Above it the path climbs steeply through huckleberry and heather, braiding into several social paths that go nowhere in particular — take whichever visibly heads for the summit. The crest flattens into an alpine garden, and the true top needs one brief drop to a saddle and a final climb to a rocky north-facing viewpoint.

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

bivy.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
bivy.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
bivy.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
bivy.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton

Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.

bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin, over the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead on FR-2870 — large parking area, vault toilet; an overnight stay needs an Olympic National Park wilderness permit booked in advance — take Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 about a mile. The trail forks just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge; BEAR RIGHT onto the Royal Basin Trail #832. The Maynard Burn Trail continues straight and is easy to mistake in early light.

Royal Creek Camp at about 3.4 miles is a common first night. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the main basecamp, with designated sites and a seasonal ranger post — the last dependable water before the dry climb. Many parties push on to camps around 5,800-6,200 ft in upper Royal Basin.

From upper Royal Basin, climb a moraine and a snowfield of roughly 35-40 degrees to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The notch below the divide holds 35-40 degree snow and an axe is worth carrying outside late season
hazards: Rotten, tilted pillow basalt that breaks away readily, with rockfall funnelled by the gullies above the col
A Class 4 step on poor rock over steep runout dirt that must be reversed on descent — one party graded a move on the downclimb at 5.8
A reported moat over 30 ft deep below the gully late in the season
Lingering steep snow on the approach gullies and Mystery Glacier into summer, and a 35-40 degree snow slope below the Royal-Deception notch
Remote terrain — a solo traveller died in a fall near the peak's south end in July 2022
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE LOWER LEFT CORNER OF THE MYSTERY GLACIER, AND THE THING THAT MARKS IT IS A LAKE YOU CANNOT MISTAKE FOR ANYTHING ELSE: A JADE-GREEN MORAINE-BOUNDED LAKE SITS AT THE GLACIER'S BASE. Drop off the benches into Deception Basin, cross a dark moraine, and the lake is at the foot of the ice. Get on the glacier at its LOWER LEFT corner. Colour is a fog-usable marker at short range and there is one such lake here.

THE TEST FOR THE GLACIER CROSSING IS A DIAGONAL: you enter at the lower LEFT and exit at the upper RIGHT, at a COL at about 6,700 ft on the peak's EAST side. The ice is stagnant and low-angle with a few small crevasses to step over — this is a walk with a rope on, not a serious glacier. If you are climbing straight up the fall line rather than trending right, you are not heading for the col.

SECOND TEST, above the col, and it is a specific distance and a specific side: from the col traverse mixed rock and snow to reach OPEN SNOW ABOUT 200 FT SOUTH OF THE COL, then climb those slopes STAYING SOUTH OF the blocky rock band immediately above. South of the rock band, not through it. Snow angles reach around 40 degrees and take pickets well. The gullies feeding this section are where the rockfall comes from, so move one at a time and keep the party to three or fewer.

THIRD TEST, and it is the commitment point: a short CLASS 4 STEP on poor rock, with steep runout dirt below it, gains a NOTCH NEAR 7,500 FT. Trend CLIMBER'S LEFT on the approach to it. This step has to be downclimbed on the way out, usually unroped, and one party rated a single move on the reverse at 5.8 — so it is worth being certain about before you commit. A moat over 30 ft deep has been reported below the gully late in the season, which changes how the section is entered and exited.

WHAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE THROUGH: beyond the notch a clean Class 3 gully leads to the summit block, and THE ROCK GETS MARKEDLY BETTER than anything below it. Good rock on this peak means you are nearly there.

approach_variants.name: Home Lake and Constance Pass, reaching Deception Basin from the south
approach_variants.notes:
The other side, and the one that suits a party already camped at Home Lake for Fricaba or Warrior. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, Trail #833.2 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Shelter at about 6.4 miles and 4,890 ft, then the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail to Home Lake at roughly 9.3 miles and 5,308-5,330 ft. From camp, climbers' paths lead up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, and from there the route traverses and descends west into upper Deception Basin.

This is the same basin the Royal Basin parties drop into, reached from the opposite end. It is the approach a high-route party is already on, and one detailed account describes exiting this way over Gunsight Pass toward Constance Pass and out the Dosewallips and Del Monte Ridge trail system with no rappels — a valid variant exit, distinct from reversing the ascent.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose scree traverses between Constance Pass and Deception Basin
All the summit-block hazards of the standard variant, including the reversible Class 4 step
Steep snow lingering on the Constance Pass and Deception Basin traverse into July
Long committing backcountry travel far from help
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL ONCE YOU ARE IN DECEPTION BASIN, and the shared test is the good one: the JADE-GREEN MORAINE-BOUNDED LAKE at the foot of the Mystery Glacier. Get on the ice at its LOWER LEFT corner and cross diagonally to the COL AT ABOUT 6,700 FT at its UPPER RIGHT, on the peak's EAST side.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at Constance Pass, because you arrive at Deception Basin along its length rather than dropping into its head. Leave the maintained trail at the pass and work WEST and DOWN into the upper basin. Loose scree on the descent is normal here. If you are contouring without losing height you have not committed to the basin; if you are climbing again you have crossed it and are heading for the Fricaba-Hal Foss ridge instead.

ABOVE THE COL THE TESTS ARE THE SAME: open snow about 200 ft SOUTH of the col, climbed staying SOUTH of the blocky rock band; then a short Class 4 step approached CLIMBER'S LEFT to a notch near 7,500 ft; then a clean Class 3 gully on markedly better rock to the summit.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Skokomish Trail #873 to Sundown Pass, then the Six Ridge crest and the Mount Olson Way
approach_variants.notes:
Mount Olson sees very few ascents and is normally reached as a side trip off the long Six Ridge traverse. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish Trailhead (Trail #873), reached via Skokomish Valley Road, FS-23 and FS-2361 from Shelton — FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April — the trail runs up the valley. There is an unbridged FORD of the South Fork at about 2.4 miles and 1,450 ft that is only ankle-deep and safely crossable in late summer or early autumn low water; at other times it is a serious hazard. The Olympic National Park boundary comes near 5.1 miles, after which tread grows fainter and an advance-reserved wilderness permit is required for overnight stays.

Sundown Pass, a forested saddle marked by a broken signpost, comes at about 7.2 miles and 4,125 ft — this is the junction with the Six Ridge Trail heading east along the crest. Lake Sundown is a short spur off the pass at about 7.6 miles and 3,810 ft and is a designated camp; small streams toward McGravey Lakes and a spring at Belview Camp further along the ridge also supply water.

Follow the Six Ridge Trail east along its sawtooth crest — a ridge either side with a gully in the middle, and brutal uphill for every downhill — past McGravey Lakes and Belview Camp to about 4,650 ft, where an unsigned, unofficial boot path known as the MOUNT OLSON WAY leaves the trail for the peak. It is faint and overgrown with blowdown and lingering snowfields into midsummer. A boulder-field tarn at about 5,100 ft below the summit block is the last water and a common bivy.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by two fords that are only reliably safe in late summer and early autumn low water
hazards: Two unbridged fords only safely crossable in late summer and early autumn low water
Route-finding on trail-less and boot-path terrain with an unsigned departure from Six Ridge
Dense brush and blowdown along the Six Ridge approach
A 55-60 degree grass and heather summit pitch that is loose and exposed, and worse descending
FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April
Afternoon weather on an exposed crest, and a multi-day return from a very lightly visited peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE PASS IMMEDIATELY EAST OF THE SUMMIT, AND THE TEST IS THAT THE CLIMBING STARTS THE MOMENT YOU STAND IN IT. From the pass, the final ascent to Olson's 5,289 ft top is a steep, unmarked scramble up a GRASSY AND HEATHER SLOPE pitched around 55-60 degrees in places — hands-on, solid Class 3 — directly above you. Grass and heather at that angle is a distinctive surface: it is neither talus nor rock, and you are either on it or you are not.

SECOND TEST, and it is what tells you the slope is easing correctly rather than that you have wandered: the pitch EASES AND CURVES ROUND THE NORTH SIDE of the peak onto a HEATHER BENCH, and then it is an easy stroll to the true summit. So the sequence is steep grass, then a bench that takes you leftward round the peak, then a walk. If the ground stays steep all the way to a top, or if you are on rock and scree rather than heather, you are on the wrong side.

THE APPROACH TEST BEFORE ANY OF THAT is the departure from Six Ridge, because it is the thing people miss: the Mount Olson Way leaves the Six Ridge Trail at the point on the sawtooth crest CLOSEST TO OLSON, at about 4,650 ft, and it is UNSIGNED. It is faint, overgrown and blowdown-choked. If you are still on obvious trail after passing the point where the crest is nearest the peak, you have walked past the turn.

HONEST LIMIT: there is no documented roped climbing route, rack or pitch-by-pitch description for this peak. It is recorded as a summit without a route write-up. This is a bushwhack and scramble objective for peak-baggers, and the markers above are the sum of what has been written down. Treat the notch and the upper summit meadow as the crux going both ways: both are loose and exposed and better handled with an axe or a pole for self-arrest, especially wet or under late snow.

bivy.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
bivy.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
bivy.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail, and has been since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026; that leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead, over Sundown Pass, as the way in.
bivy.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows
approach_variants.notes:
Hoh Rain Forest trailhead (about 578 ft) inside Olympic National Park. The Hoh River Trail runs east; the first ten and a half miles to Lewis Meadows are gentle old-growth walking beside the braided river, with water the whole way. Past the Olympus Guard Station the High Hoh Bridge crosses the gorge and the ground steepens. Elk Lake sits around mile 15 at 2,500 ft, and the trail then climbs in earnest to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about mile 17.2-17.5, which is the standard base camp.

About a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows the trail crosses a washout on a ladder of roughly 100 ft with a fixed rope beside it. For many parties that is the hardest part of the walk in.

In early season there are several steep, consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows that want an axe and crampons.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for every overnight stay in Olympic National Park, obtained in advance through Recreation.gov or a Wilderness Information Center, and the Hoh is one of the areas that runs on a daily quota. Camping is not permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: roughly 100 ft ladder plus fixed rope at the washout below Glacier Meadows
steep consequential snow slopes between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows in early season
narrow, loose lateral moraine crest with rockfall on the descent to the glacier toe
no camping permitted between Glacier Meadows and the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant ends at camp, not at climbing. The confirmation you are at Glacier Meadows rather than somewhere short of it is the washout ladder and fixed rope just below it — if you have not climbed a ladder, you are still below.

From the meadows a way trail runs about 0.8 mile up onto the crest of the lateral moraine, a narrow exposed catwalk with loose rock underfoot, then follows the crest roughly another 0.2 mile before dropping onto the toe of the Blue Glacier. The drop onto the ice is where you rope up; nothing before it is glacier travel.

approach_variants.name: Glacier Meadows to the summit block via Snow Dome and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Rope up at the toe of the Blue Glacier and travel up to Snow Dome around 6,600-6,800 ft. This is roped crevasse travel throughout. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is often passable only on a snow bridge, and that bridge has to be scouted afresh each season.

Olympic National Park points climbers at the Crystal Pass line as the standard: from Snow Dome over Crystal Pass, then traversing immediately south of and below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, and finally onto the true summit block of the West Peak. It is longer than the alternatives and generally regarded as the safer option through most of the season.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-mid Aug for straightforward glacier travel
hazards: crevasses throughout - a large crevasse near Crystal Pass often crossable only on a snow bridge that must be scouted each season
bergschrund or moat immediately below the summit block, variable through the season
loose deteriorating scree on the block and on the pinnacle east of it - rockfall onto your own party
the true summit is hidden from the north, so navigation is to a point you cannot see
the false summit is east of the true summit and catches parties out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The only technical climbing on this route is the summit block of the West Peak, and finding it is the crux of the day, because THE TRUE SUMMIT IS NOT VISIBLE from the north side. A party that keeps navigating toward the highest thing it can see from Snow Dome ends up at the five-fingered false summit, which is EAST of where it wants to be.

The rule that works: go south-southeast through one of the two gaps to the LEFT, or far left, of the five fingers, and come at the summit from the east or southeast — approaching an objective you cannot yet see.

Once through, a rising traverse leads to a loose rocky gully; you go up that, over, and down into a second rocky gully, then up a final steep snow slope that delivers you to the foot of the block.

You are there when you are standing under a discrete rock tower roughly 80 ft high. The standard finish is class 4 on loose rocky ramps; there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4. If you are under a snow slope with no rock tower above it, you have not arrived — keep going.

Expect a bergschrund or moat immediately below the block. Its state changes through the season and it can force a short detour or a stretch of short-roping; on the pinnacle just east of the West Peak parties have found a schrund below it and deteriorating scree above, and have grouped tightly or moved one at a time because of the rockfall.

wa_mount_olympus_west_ridge.rappels: If you descend the route: one rappel off the West Face on a single 50 m ROPE, with class 3 downclimbing below it, or two rappels off the North Face with a 60 m rope. The standard descent avoids rappelling the ridge at all. The 50 m is the rope, not the rappel - the summit block is about 100 ft and a 50 m doubled reaches 25 m, which is why the West Face option depends on the downclimb below it.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail and Blue Glacier to the West Ridge toe
approach_variants.notes:
The walk in is identical to the standard route: Hoh River Trail from the rain forest trailhead to Glacier Meadows at 4,200-4,300 ft, about 17.4-17.5 miles, including the ladder and fixed rope at the washout below the meadows. Then the way trail onto the lateral moraine crest and down onto the toe of the Blue Glacier, where you rope up.

Snow Dome at roughly 6,700-6,800 ft, about two miles of glacier travel above Glacier Meadows, is the recommended high camp for this route.

From Snow Dome, cross the Blue Glacier to the southwest WITHOUT gaining or losing much height, keeping Crystal Pass, Five Fingers Ridge and the West Peak in view as your three reference points.

A wilderness permit is required year-round for overnight stays in Olympic National Park and must be arranged in advance; the Hoh is a quota area.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Aug
hazards: moat at the ridge toe near 7,260 ft, condition varies through the season
crevasses on the southwest crossing of the Blue Glacier
runout protection on the ridge despite the moderate grade
snow bridges over the bergschrund below the direct summit line have collapsed as early as mid-July in some years
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ridge is gained at a MOAT at its lowest point, close to 7,260 ft. That moat is the confirmation — it is a specific place, not a stretch of ridge, and whether it can be crossed changes through the season, so plan to inspect rather than assume.

Above the moat there is roughly 600 ft of ridge and then about 100 ft of summit block.

The negative marker is easy to spot and easy to ignore: if you are GAINING height toward Crystal Pass, you have drifted onto the standard route and are heading for the summit block from the east instead of for the toe of the ridge. The crossing to the West Ridge is essentially level.

The ridge itself is never harder than 5.4 and never easier than class 3. It can be protected the whole way but is run out in places.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
