bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

bivy.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
bivy.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

bivy.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
bivy.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is GLACIER camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.
bivy.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities

bivy.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
bivy.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
bivy.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
bivy.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approach_variants.name: FR-62 road end to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes: From US-2 near Index take FR-62, bear left at the first junction around 1,600 ft, left again at the second near 2,380 ft, and drive the last increasingly rough mile to a small pullout at the road end around 2,800 ft. The road crosses private industrial timberland and its gate at the highway is locked at the owner's discretion with no warning, so be prepared to walk or ride an extra five miles and 2,500 ft of road. Above the pullout it is more boot path than trail — it vanishes intermittently in brush and is steep enough in places that you pull on trees.
approach_variants.season: June to October, or on winter snow
hazards: Dense brush and undergrowth that hide the boot path in several sections
Loose talus along the ridge traverse near Point 5017
A locked private-timberland gate that can add miles of road on short notice
Lingering snow and ice on the upper ridge and around the summit ponds into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: There is no sign, no cairn and no marked trailhead: the start is an unmarked, steep, well-trodden gully directly OPPOSITE the road-end pullout. Stand at the small parking area at the very end of the road and look across it — the line is the obvious trodden gully cutting straight up the hillside on the far side, not any of the spurs running off into the clearcut. It is steep from the first steps and stays that way; the first mile carries almost all of the day's 2,650-odd feet of gain, through young forest and clearcut into older cedar and Douglas fir. You know that section is behind you when the path levels out onto the ridge crest and begins crossing talus fields. From there the ridge runs east past Point 5017, dips about a hundred feet, and climbs past two small ponds to the true summit — so if you top out at a viewpoint and the ground drops away ahead of you, keep going.

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Lake Trail, Iodine Gulch and the Bathtub Lakes basin
approach_variants.notes: Do not use the standard Mount Pilchuck road — this is a different trailhead on the other side of the mountain. From the ranger station on the Mountain Loop, continue east about four and a half miles and turn onto the Schweitzer Creek forest road, signed for the lakes. Follow it under three miles to a junction, take the RIGHT fork, and continue a further mile and a half on rough road to the Pinnacle Lake trailhead at around twenty-seven hundred feet — a small lot of perhaps fifteen cars with no toilet. Hike the maintained trail to the lake. Beyond the lake there is no maintained trail at all, so this is genuine off-trail navigation from that point on.
approach_variants.season: August to October, best after snowmelt; spring travel needs an axe and traction, and snow and ice can persist in the gulch into early summer.
hazards: No maintained trail beyond the lake — real off-trail navigation, bushwhacking and scrambling through loose rock and brush
Two distinct steep sections within the gulch
Snow and ice persist in the gulch into early summer, needing an axe and traction
Many parties treat the small-lakes basin as the objective and turn round there; the summit scramble west of it is additional off-trail ground
approach_variants.baseFinding: The off-trail climbing starts at the SOUTHWEST SHORE OF THE LAKE, where the maintained tread ends and the creek enters. Walk round the lake to that corner and pick up the creek — the creek line IS the route from there, because there is nothing else. Follow it up through the gulch to its top; two distinct STEEP STEPS inside the gulch are the crux of the day and are the confirmation you are in the right drainage. At the top of the gulch, turn RIGHT and continue a short distance to the basin holding the small lakes, then scramble WEST to reach the summit. Negative markers: if you are still on continuous, obviously maintained trail, you have not left it yet — the trail does not go beyond the lake; and if you are crossing an open boulder field following ORANGE PAINTED BLAZES toward a fixed steel ladder, you have come up the peak's standard trail from the opposite side of the mountain.

bivy.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
bivy.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
bivy.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the FEDERAL pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed

approach_variants.name: Mount Pilchuck Road to the trailhead
approach_variants.notes: From Granite Falls take the highway east and then the Mountain Loop about ten or eleven miles to the ranger station. Continue about a mile past it, cross the river, and turn south onto the Mount Pilchuck road. Follow it roughly seven miles — a mix of paved and rough washboarded gravel that varies year to year with maintenance — to the trailhead parking area at around three thousand feet.
approach_variants.season: July to October. The trail is typically snow-covered into early or midsummer in some years, and traction is commonly needed through June.
hazards: Fatal falls have occurred on the exposed final scramble and lookout rocks, particularly in wet or icy conditions
Search and rescue is called to this peak several times a season, mostly for lost or injured parties on the boulder field and the old ski-slope ground
Snow obscures the trail and the painted boulder-field markers into early summer
The fixed ladder's rungs can spin underfoot
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling starts where the forest tread runs out at the OPEN TALUS AND BOULDER FIELD below the summit headwall, and the marker there is paint, not tread: the route across the boulders is carried by ORANGE BLAZES PAINTED ON THE ROCKS. If you are following blazes on boulders rather than a footpath, you are on route; if you are following a footpath, you have not reached the boulder field yet. The finish is unmistakable — twenty to thirty feet of hands-on boulder scrambling to a short FIXED STEEL LADDER whose rungs can spin underfoot, leading onto the lookout deck. Negative markers: if you find yourself descending an open brushy clearing to the WEST of the trail, you have wandered onto the old ski-area slope, which looks like a shortcut and has contributed to lost-hiker rescues; and if you are following a creek up a gulch from a small lake with no blazes anywhere, you are on the peak's other route, which comes from a completely different trailhead on the far side.

approach_variants.name: From the Heather Lake trailhead when the road is gated
approach_variants.notes: In years when the road is gated below the trailhead, the walk starts from the Heather Lake trailhead instead, adding roughly five miles and substantial gain each way. Everything above the normal trailhead is identical, so this is a road-walk variant rather than a different climb, but it changes a half-day into a long one and is worth confirming before driving out.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder season, when the forest road is closed below the trailhead — common in spring and autumn.
hazards: A much longer day than the standard start, with the same exposed finish at the end of it
Same fall and route-finding hazards on the boulder field and summit rocks
Snow more likely on the upper mountain in the shoulder seasons when this variant applies
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same starting point as the standard approach — the trailhead parking area at around three thousand feet — and from there the base of the scrambling is the same: the open talus and boulder field below the summit headwall, marked by ORANGE BLAZES PAINTED ON THE BOULDERS rather than by tread. The finish is the short fixed steel ladder onto the lookout deck. Negative marker: if you are still on road grade rather than trail, you have not reached the trailhead yet; the boulder field is well above it.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver valley to Thirtynine Mile Creek, then the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Ross Dam Trailhead the trail drops to the lake and follows the shoreline to the Big Beaver Trail junction; a water taxi to the Big Beaver landing removes that shoreline stretch and is what most parties use. The Big Beaver Trail then runs up the valley through old growth to Thirtynine Mile Creek and its camp, which has tent sites on the west bank and a stock camp on the east, and is the last reliable running water and the last legal campsite before you leave the trail. Leave the tread between the creek crossing and the camp marker post and climb north through a brushy gully and the rib beside it — this low section is a genuinely horrible bushwhack and it is where the bulk of the day's gain happens. Travel eases considerably once you break out on the ridge crest above, where open forest and then open walking carry you over the intermediate points to the saddle where the rib meets the south ridge proper. An informal saddle campsite there splits the climb into two days, but it has no running water, so carry up from the creek.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the cornices on the south ridge have melted out and the talus in the upper cirque is clear.
hazards: route-finding through forest and along the ridge crest, with no marked line anywhere above the trail
cornices on the south ridge in early and mid season
afternoon thunderstorms on an open crest
a brushy, steep departure from the valley trail that is easy to lose in either direction
no water above Thirtynine Mile Creek
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE HIGHEST POINT ON THE NORTH-SOUTH CREST IS NOT THE SUMMIT. Gain the south ridge at the saddle around 6,600 ft, where the brushy rib you climbed meets open crest. From there the travel is walking rather than climbing: follow the crest north over the first rounded point at about 6,690 ft, on to the rocky point at about 7,361 ft, and then to the point at about 7,547 ft. That last one is the false summit and it is the trap — it is the top of the north-south ridgeline and it looks final. The true summit is not on that line at all: from 7,547 turn WEST for a short distance, and the last few feet go at a short, steep scramble step with real but manageable exposure on both sides. So the test is directional. If you have topped out on the highest thing on the crest and there is still something higher a short way to the west, you are standing on the false summit and have not finished. If you are trying to climb something steep and sustained rather than walking a broad crest with two rocky steps, you have come up the wrong side of the ridge. The same short steps have to be downclimbed in reverse on the way out.

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

approach_variants.name: Mt. Pugh Trail #644 from FR-2095 to Stujack Pass
approach_variants.notes: From Darrington, follow the Mountain Loop Highway south for roughly 12.5 to 14 miles — the accounts differ — to a prominent Mount Pugh sign where FR-2095 branches left. It is narrow, one-lane and unpaved; the signed trailhead is on the right at the second switchback near 1,900 ft. Parking is a handful of cars, and the large pullout at the switchback below is the reliable overflow. Note that FR-2095 is gated 16 October to 1 June for wildlife, on top of any Mountain Loop Highway winter closure. Trail #644 climbs about 1.5 miles through old growth with several stream crossings to Lake Metan near 3,200 ft. That is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the route — everything above is dry and fully sun-exposed, so tank up there. Above the lake the trail rounds the north side and switchbacks hard up steep forest, breaking into an open boulder basin near 4,900 ft, and tops out at Stujack Pass at 5,700 ft after about 4.5 miles. This is one of the largest elevation gains of any maintained Washington trail that reaches a true summit, and the trail is an old fire-lookout line that is eroding and sloughing in places.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul-Sep, with October marginal. Before mid-July the permanent snowfield beside the upper ridge is the crux of the day and wants an axe; October is quiet and superb but the daylight runs short for a 5,300 ft climb
hazards: Stray cairns above Stujack Pass that lead to cliff bands and force unplanned Class 4 downclimbing
A knife-edge crest where the climbing is Class 2-3 and the consequence of a slip is not — two fatal falls are on record on this mountain
A small permanent snowfield beside the upper ridge that holds hard snow early and late in the day
An eroding, sloughing old lookout trail, worst on the meadow and talus switchbacks below the pass
No water above Lake Metan at 1.5 miles, on a fully sun-exposed 5,300 ft climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STUJACK PASS IS THE BASE, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE ON THIS MOUNTAIN YOU CANNOT MISTAKE IN CLOUD: it is where the MAINTAINED TRAIL STOPS. Up to there you have graded tread and switchbacks under your feet; above it you have a rough climbers' path on heather and then blasted ledges on a crest. If you are still walking on built trail, you have not reached the pass. It also marks the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.

WHAT HAPPENS IMMEDIATELY ABOVE IT, so you can confirm it from the other side: the path climbs LEFT out of the notch onto heather, contours the EAST side of the ridge, and crosses the head of a small permanent snowfield. Left, then east side, then snow. A path that stays on the crest straight out of the pass is not the route.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT CAIRNS, AND IT HAS HURT PEOPLE HERE. Multiple parties warn against following whatever cairn appears next: stray cairns on this mountain lead toward vertical cliff bands that then need unplanned Class 4 downclimbing to escape. Several boot paths braid the upper ridge and they are NOT all equal. Pick the line that keeps the crest or the blasted ledges under you; do not let a rock pile choose for you.

THE HANDRAIL ABOVE THE PASS IS THE CREST ITSELF — a razorback with drops on both sides, skirting the head of a small glacier. It is only Class 2-3, and the consequence of a slip is out of all proportion to that grade. There is an iron ring on the short chimney section; use it as a handhold, and downclimb that section facing in, because the exposure faces you on the way down and every account says it feels worse descending.

THE SUMMIT IS NOT THE FLAT GROUND. The plateau at the top has a roughly 10 ft boulder at its edge that has to be scrambled to tag the true high point. Standing on the flat is not standing on the summit.

bivy.name: Mount Pugh road end, Forest Road 2095
bivy.notes: The staging point for MOUNT PUGH, which most parties climb in a single long day from here — around five and a half miles and well over five thousand feet to the summit, with the character changing three times on the way. Forest and stream crossings to the lake at a mile and a half, then a steady climb to the pass, then a rough exposed ridge with a genuine scrambling section around the head of a small remnant glacier before it eases to the top. Sleeping at the car is the honest plan for that day: the spur is short enough that a party staying at any of the valley campgrounds can drive up in the dark, and the trail's first miles are straightforward walking that goes quickly by headtorch. The spur climbs steeply and is rough in places but is normally passable to an ordinary car driven with care. The road in from Darrington is the county-maintained section of the loop and stays open through the year to the seasonal gate further south, which puts this trailhead on the right side of the winter closure — but it is landslide ground and has been blocked outright by a slide within recent memory, so confirm before driving from any distance rather than assuming. Season for the peak is roughly July into October; the ridge above the pass with snow on it is a mountaineering proposition rather than a scramble.
bivy.water: None at the road end and none for the first mile and a half of trail. Everything gets carried up from the valley or drawn at the lake above.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, and the trailhead itself sits OUTSIDE designated wilderness — Glacier Peak Wilderness begins high on the mountain above Stujack Pass, not at the road. Reports differ on whether a fee pass is enforced at this particular trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass costs nothing extra to carry and settles the question. No self-issue permit at the road. Seasonal forest-wide fire restrictions apply and from midsummer normally mean no open flame.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only, and a thin one. Parking is a few turnouts along the last of the spur rather than a car park, with no sites, no tables and no toilet. Half a dozen vehicles fills it and there is nowhere to overflow to without blocking the road.

bivy.name: Lake Metan, Mount Pugh trail
bivy.notes: A mile and a half and about thirteen hundred feet up from the road end, on a short signed spur off the main trail, this is the only established camping on the Pugh approach and it turns a punishing day into a manageable one. Its real value is for a party that wants the ridge above Stujack Pass in the cool of the morning without a two-hour drive and a headtorch start, or for one that arrives too late in the day to sensibly begin. It buys about a third of the climbing but leaves the hardest two thirds — a further two and a half miles to the pass and then the ridge — for the summit day, so treat it as a soft first night rather than a high camp. The setting is wooded and enclosed, mosquito-heavy in early summer and cold in the shade well into the morning. Snow lingers around the lake into June in an ordinary year. Because it is the last water, an efficient party often does not sleep here at all but stops for twenty minutes to load up, and that is a perfectly good use of the place.
bivy.water: The lake, and this is the LAST WATER on the entire route. Nothing above it is dependable, and above the pass there is nothing at all except late-lying snow. Fill everything here going up and note it for the descent.
bivy.permit: National forest outside designated wilderness at this elevation, so no wilderness permit, no quota and no party-size limit for camping here. A Northwest Forest Pass covers the vehicle. Fires are subject to whatever seasonal restrictions are in force and are usually prohibited from midsummer; carry a stove regardless, because this is a small lake basin that takes heavy day-hiker traffic and does not need fire rings.
bivy.capacity: A few primitive spots in the trees on the short spur down to the lake — two or three tents on flat, well-used forest ground, with no built structures of any kind.

bivy.name: Stujack Pass and the benches just below it
bivy.notes: This is a high bivouac rather than a camp, and it exists for one purpose — putting a party on the exposed upper ridge of MOUNT PUGH at first light rather than in the afternoon, when the scrambling section around the head of the small glacier is more pleasant and the weather is more predictable. From the saddle the remaining mile and a half of ridge is rough, narrow in places and genuinely exposed, and it is much better done rested and early than at the end of a five-thousand-foot day from the car. The trade is severe and should be weighed honestly: you carry all your water up, you camp on ground with nothing to hide behind, and the pass funnels wind hard enough to make a marginal forecast miserable. Anyone who is not committed to the summit is better off at the lake. Snow holds on the north side of the pass and in the gullies below it long after the trail lower down is clear, and an early-season party will be kicking steps to reach it. In a thunderstorm this is the wrong place to be — the ridge above is the highest ground for some way and there is no descent that is quick. Camp on gravel or bare rock, not on the heather, which is thin and slow to come back.
bivy.water: NONE, and this is the defining constraint. There is no source at or near the pass. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted early in the season and are gone by August, after which every litre comes up from the lake nearly two and a half miles and two and a half thousand feet below.
bivy.permit: The pass itself is the boundary — camping in the saddle sits at the very edge of GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, and the ridge and summit above are inside it. Where wilderness applies, so does the twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together; no wilderness permit is needed. No fires: this is thin subalpine ground with no wood and nothing that recovers from a scar. Northwest Forest Pass at the road.
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a couple of tents at most on gravel and heather pockets in the saddle and on the shelves a little below it on the approach side. Nothing established, no flat platform, and no shelter of any kind from wind.

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side and the Lake Ouzel high camp
approach_variants.notes: The approach starts north of the border and crosses on foot, so carry a passport. From Chilliwack River Road, turn onto the narrow dirt Depot Creek spur and follow it to a rough turnout where the driving ends; high clearance helps on the upper part. The unmaintained trail climbs the valley, crossing the international boundary at an obelisk and register about two hundred yards in on foot, and a park backcountry permit is required to camp beyond. Near the head of the valley the path crosses the base of a very large waterfall on wet, misty, exposed slabs, including a slippery step that fixed handlines have been rigged for; that crossing is consequential when the rock is wet. Above it a boot track hugs the north edge of the valley and climbs to Lake Ouzel, a flat, sandy, treeless bench that is the shared high camp for this whole group of peaks. From camp, sidehill east and northeast across the bench above the Silver Lake basin toward the peak's south side, using snow coverage where it helps.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September. Earlier there is more snow underfoot, which buries the exposed arete but also hides crevasses on the glaciers used by parties linking this peak with its neighbours. Later the ice turns harder and crevasses open but become easier to see.
hazards: loose, chossy rock in the summit gullies
an exposed knife-edge snow arete partway up the correct gully
crevasse fall on the glaciers used when this peak is combined with its neighbours
the wet, slippery rock step near the falls on the approach
a long, committing cross-border approach with no cell coverage and a multi-day carry-out
approach_variants.baseFinding: THREE GULLIES DROP OFF THIS SUMMIT, AND THE FIRST ONE YOU MEET IS THE WRONG ONE. Coming across the bench toward the south side of the peak, a short band of loose rock guards the final slopes and three gullies come down through it from the summit. The one you reach first as you traverse is the hardest and steepest of the three; do not take it. Keep traversing and take one of the LEFTMOST gullies instead, which go at loose third and fourth class and are easier still when a snow finger is filling them. Two things confirm you are in the right one. Partway up, the correct line crosses an exposed knife-edge snow arete — a genuine, memorable feature, not a snow patch — and above that the ground gives way to a well-defined climbers' path that runs to the top. So: if you are grinding up steep loose fourth class with no arete underfoot and no boot track visible above, back off and move left. If you top out of a gully and find no trodden path, you are on the wrong side of the summit block. The summit itself is rubbly and unassuming and sits a very short distance south of the border. On the way down, reverse the same gully and the same arete rather than improvising a line.

approach_variants.name: White River, Glacier Basin, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop Glacier traverse
approach_variants.notes:
From White River Campground, hike the Glacier Basin Trail about 3.5 miles and 1,700 ft to Glacier Basin near 5,900 ft — a broad basin with the last reliable running water and a common camp. Continue on climbers' path up to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, another 1,500 ft over roughly a mile of steepening scree and snow.

At the pass, rope up. Drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and contour west and southwest between roughly 7,200 and 7,400 ft, threading crevasses, to reach the base of Curtis Ridge on its east side.

This is the same corridor Liberty Ridge parties use, so in season there is often a boot track and other parties on it. Above St Elmo Pass there is no water at all.

Rockfall on the traverse concentrates in three places: immediately after you drop onto the glacier, roughly halfway across, and at the far end. Move through those, do not rest in them.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun, in cold stable conditions when the rock is frozen in place
hazards: Serac-threatened sections below the Willis Wall icecap
Loose rock and mixed ground with complex route-finding
Rockfall concentrated at three points on the Winthrop traverse
Longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats running along the line of travel
Remote position with a long exit and no water above St Elmo Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH IS SHARED WITH LIBERTY RIDGE, SO THE ONLY QUESTION THAT MATTERS IS WHERE YOU STOP. Curtis Ridge is the FIRST ridge you meet after crossing the Winthrop. Liberty Ridge is beyond it, past the Carbon.

COUNT THE GLACIERS. Between St Elmo Pass and this base you cross ONE — the Winthrop. If you have dropped onto a SECOND glacier you are on the Carbon and you have walked past Curtis Ridge onto the Liberty Ridge approach.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THE VIEW, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE ONCE YOU HAVE IT: at about 7,200 ft the ridge gives you snow-free rock ground with the Carbon Glacier and the Willis Wall opening up on the far side. Standing on Curtis Ridge you are looking ACROSS at Willis Wall, not up at it. If the great capped wall is not in front of you, you are not on the ridge yet.

WHAT BEING SHORT LOOKS LIKE, AND IT HAPPENS IN THE DARK: if you walked INTO Glacier Basin and kept going up the valley, you missed the turn for St Elmo Pass. The pass is gained by leaving the basin, not by continuing through it.

WHAT BEING LOW LOOKS LIKE: the traverse holds 7,200 to 7,400 ft deliberately. Losing height on the Winthrop puts you into longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats that run the same way you are walking, which is the worst orientation to fall into one.

ONE MORE THING WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: this ridge is more confusing and more committing than either of its famous neighbours, with 4th-class scrambling through rock bands and at least one rappel on the way UP. If the ground is going smoothly you may be on the wrong feature.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park to the 9,600 ft divide, then across to the Edmunds Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Shared Mowich Face approach: Mowich Lake, the Wonderland Trail through Spray Park, then cross-country onto lower Ptarmigan Ridge and up to the bivouac at roughly 9,600 ft on the divide between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers. Rangers and climbing parties have both used that divide bivy as the base for this route.

From there, cross the glacier to the foot of the headwall. Parties commonly leave the bivy around 2 am and reach the base a few hours later; the crossing runs beneath the ice cliff run-out coming off the upper mountain, so it is a place to move rather than a place to sort gear.

The headwall itself is sustained steep snow and ice from roughly 9,900 to 13,400 ft, and its character swings between firm penitente neve and a considerably icier chute depending on the year. Above it the route traverses toward Liberty Cap on ground that can be heavily penitente-covered and slow.

Mowich Lake Road has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently in April 2025.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul; the headwall turns icier and starts shedding rock as summer goes on
hazards: Sustained steep snow and ice from about 9,900 to 13,400 ft
Rockfall and icefall down the headwall once it warms
Crevasses on the Edmunds and South Mowich approach
A glacier crossing beneath the upper-mountain ice cliff run-out
Penitente ground above the headwall that can make the exit far slower than the climb
Remote, committing position with no walk-off from the top of the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FOUR CLIMBS LEAVE THE SAME DIVIDE BIVY. THE SCHRUND IS WHAT TELLS THEM APART FOR THIS ONE.

THE POSITIVE TEST, AND IT IS A PAIR OF OBJECTS RATHER THAN A DESCRIPTION, WHICH IS WHY IT WORKS IN POOR LIGHT: the bergschrund bypass for the Edmunds Headwall is on CLIMBER'S LEFT, NEAR TWIN GENDARMES. Two rock towers, and you go left of the schrund beside them. No twin gendarmes means no Edmunds Headwall.

THE NEGATIVE AGAINST THE NEIGHBOUR ON ONE SIDE: the North Mowich Headwall opens with a 40 to 50 ft HOURGLASS of steep rock and ice within a rope length of the bivy. If your first ground is a tight mixed pinch rather than a schrund crossing beside gendarmes, you crossed the wrong glacier.

THE NEGATIVE AGAINST THE NEIGHBOUR ON THE OTHER SIDE: the Central Mowich Face's schrund is turned by a rock-band bypass on climber's left with no gendarmes at it, and its steep ground eases before 13,000 ft. This route is sustained a long way further — about 9,900 to 13,400 ft is the whole headwall.

THE CONDITION TEST TELLS YOU WHICH DAY YOU HAVE, AND IT IS WORTH MAKING AT THE SCHRUND RATHER THAN AT 12,000 FT: firm penitentes mean kicking and slow but secure progress; a bare icy chute means screws, and the same face is a different climb. Decide before you commit — there is no easy way off the middle of it.

THE TOP-OUT IS NOT THE MOUNTAIN'S SUMMIT. This route finishes at or below LIBERTY CAP, on the northwest rim, not at Columbia Crest. Standing on Liberty Cap and looking across at higher ground is correct, not a navigational error.

approach_variants.name: White River Campground, Glacier Basin, Inter Glacier and Camp Schurman
approach_variants.notes:
The Glacier Basin trailhead is in Loop D of White River Campground (about 4,300–4,400 ft), reached by the White River road off SR 410. That road and the campground are seasonal and open on the snowpack, not on a date.

The trail follows the Inter Fork of the White River on an old mining road grade, 3.5 miles to Glacier Basin Campground (~5,935 ft): six designated sites, a toilet and a bear-proof food cache. This is the last reliable water and the last forested camp.

Above Glacier Basin a climbers' path continues about a mile up the lateral moraine — conspicuously yellowish once it melts out — to the toe of the Inter Glacier at roughly 7,000 ft. The Inter Glacier is about 1,500 ft of moderate snow; it is the mildest glacier on the route but it opens real crevasses as the season goes on, and roped travel is standard. It leads to Camp Curtis on the rim at about 8,500–9,000 ft.

From Camp Curtis the route drops slightly and traverses onto the lower Emmons Glacier, rounding the southern side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (about 9,460 ft), where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers split around the Prow. There is an NPS ranger hut, an emergency radio on the front of it, toilets and a blue-bag barrel; tent platforms are dug into snow on the Emmons side.

Camp Schurman's nightly capacity is small — far smaller than Camp Muir's — so a permit here is worth reserving. The same Rainier permit structure applies: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, plus a wilderness permit for each overnight.
approach_variants.season: Late spring through August, once the White River road and campground are open and before summer melt opens the upper crevasse fields
hazards: Crevasses on the Inter Glacier, which open through the season despite its mild reputation
Loose, brittle volcanic rock on the direct scramble down the Prow into Camp Schurman
Rockfall onto the moraine path above Glacier Basin
Crevasse maze above 12,000 ft where the Corridor ends
Bergschrund near 13,000 ft, which can be impassable direct in late season
Creek crossings and old slide paths on the Glacier Basin trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Three recognition points, in order.

At 0.9 mile from the trailhead there is a signed junction where the Emmons Moraine Trail branches LEFT and crosses the Inter Fork on a seasonal footbridge. If you cross a bridge over the river this early, you have left the climbers' route. The way to Glacier Basin stays right, on the old mining road grade, and does not cross the river there.

The start of glacier travel is the toe of the Inter Glacier, roughly a mile past Glacier Basin and about 7,000 ft. You get there by following the moraine crest; the test is that the ground turns from rubble and moraine to continuous snow, and there is no more path. Rope up when it does.

Camp Schurman is the third. It sits at the foot of Steamboat Prow, on the saddle where the Emmons and Winthrop split, with a hut on it. If you have topped out on the Prow's rocky summit you are ABOVE camp — there is a short, steep, very loose scramble down the front of the Prow to the huts, and the more usual line drops from Camp Curtis onto the lower Emmons and comes at the camp along the Prow's southern side instead. Coming back down in cloud, the Prow is the handrail: keep it on your side and you will find the camp.

Above camp the climbing starts as soon as you step off the platform — the first thing under your boots is the Emmons. The feature to find is the Corridor: a smooth, wide ramp of about 30 degrees trending slightly east, running from camp up to roughly 12,000 ft. The test is smoothness. If the slope you are on is broken by parallel crevasse trains and you are already end-running, you have drifted out of the Corridor into the icefall on either side of it. Above 12,000 ft the smooth ground ends and the glacier does become a maze — that is expected, not a sign you are lost. The bergschrund is crossed near 13,000 ft, and late in the season it can force a long traverse onto the upper Winthrop toward Liberty Saddle.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, Glacier Vista and the Nisqually crossing to a Wilson Glacier camp
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise (5,400 ft) take the paved Skyline Trail about a mile to the Glacier Vista overlook (~6,300 ft). This is where the route leaves the tourist ground: a climbers' path drops several hundred feet west off the moraine onto the Nisqually Glacier, crossing at roughly 6,200 ft. Most parties rope up before stepping onto the ice — the crossing threads crevassed terrain under an icefall and is genuinely committing in poor visibility.

On the far side, a boulder-filled gully angles up and right onto the left-hand side of the Wilson Glacier. About 700 ft up that gully there is a sheltered rest point with bivy sites. The more usual choice is to continue onto the Wapowety Cleaver and follow its crest to a high camp at roughly 9,000–9,200 ft at the edge of the Wilson Glacier, where there are rock windbreaks and a large rock buttress for shelter.

Use the daylight from camp. The traverse of the Wilson Glacier under the Wilson Headwall to the foot of the couloir has real route-finding, and you will be doing it in the dark. Scope the line the evening before.

The route is climbed early in the day for one reason: the ground above the couloir catches sun very early, and the couloir is the drain for everything it loosens.
approach_variants.season: Spring, while the couloir is snow-filled and the rock above is still frozen
hazards: Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing at about 6,200 ft
Route-finding on the Wilson Glacier traverse, normally done in the dark
Rockfall funnelled down the couloir once the sun reaches the ground above it
Avalanche hazard in the couloir
Large crevasses on the upper slopes that can force long end-runs late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the mouth of the Fuhrer Finger, on the eastern side of the Wilson Headwall at around 9,500–10,000 ft, and the identification problem is that there is more than one gully there.

The Finger is the WIDE one, with an hourglass constriction partway up. The Fuhrer Thumb is the narrower gully immediately west of it — steeper, more constricted, and it can cliff out. If the gully you have entered pinches down immediately, walls closing on both sides, with no wide apron below the constriction, you are in the Thumb, not the Finger.

Positive test: from the base, you should be looking up roughly 2,000–3,000 ft of continuous snow at about 40 degrees, wide at the bottom, narrowing to an hourglass, and widening again. That is the Finger. It runs out onto the west side of the upper Nisqually Glacier and eventually joins the upper Kautz Glacier ground near 13,000 ft.

Negative marker on the approach itself: if you have crossed the Wilson and are directly beneath a broad steep ice face rather than beneath a gully system, you have gone too far and are under the Wilson Headwall proper.

The other test is time of day. If the sun is on the rock above the couloir and you are still in the lower half of it, you are in the fall line of the day's rockfall and the correct decision is to be out of it, not to keep climbing.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson Glacier to the narrow couloir
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise, drop southwest onto the Nisqually Moraine and onto the Nisqually Glacier, cross it westward, then work up the Wilson Gully, the Wilson Bench and the Wilson Chute on the west side of the glacier toward the camps near The Castle around 9,000-9,500 ft.

From camp, continue northwest to the foot of the couloir. Summit day from that camp is commonly 5 to 7 hours.

The couloir is about 50-degree snow and ice. It merges with the Fuhrer Finger on the west side of the Nisqually at roughly 11,500 ft, so above that point the two routes are one.

Most parties descend the Fuhrer Finger or the upper Kautz and the standard route back to Camp Muir and Paradise rather than reversing this line. There is no water above Paradise.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; a south-facing snow line that wants a hard overnight freeze and an early start
hazards: Rockfall funnelling through a steep, narrow couloir with no shelter in it
Icefall off the Kautz Ice Cliff onto the approach traverse
Wet-snow avalanche on this south aspect once it warms — an early start is the protection
Crevasses on the Nisqually and Wilson glaciers
The Finger and the Thumb merge high, so a misidentification cannot be detected above 11,500 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAND ON THE UPPER WILSON GLACIER AND LOOK UP. FROM LEFT TO RIGHT THE THREE FEATURES ARE: THE WILSON GLACIER HEADWALL, THE FUHRER THUMB, THE FUHRER FINGER. Learn that order before you leave the car — it is the only thing separating this route from its two neighbours in the dark, and all three start within a short distance of each other off the same bench of glacier.

THE THUMB IS THE MIDDLE ONE AND IT IS THE NARROW ONE. That is the whole test, and it is a shape test, which is what you want when you cannot see the mountain.

THE POSITIVE-NEGATIVE PAIR THAT SETTLES IT: THE FINGER IS WIDE AND FUNNELS THROUGH AN OBVIOUS HOURGLASS at around 10,000 ft on the eastern side of the headwall. THE THUMB IS THE NARROWER COULOIR IMMEDIATELY WEST OF IT. So if the gully in front of you is broad and necks down through a conspicuous hourglass, you are at the Finger and the Thumb is one gully to your LEFT as you face uphill. If you are looking at an open face rather than into a gully at all, you have gone one too far left and you are under the Wilson Glacier Headwall, which is a harder proposition than either couloir.

CONFIRMATION ON THE CLIMB: the two couloirs MERGE at about 11,500 ft on the west side of the Nisqually. So being one gully out becomes invisible above that height, which cuts both ways — it means a mistake is survivable, and it means you cannot use the upper mountain to work out which one you climbed. Settle it at the bottom.

WHAT BEING TOO EARLY IN THE APPROACH LOOKS LIKE: if you have not crossed the Nisqually Glacier westward, you have not started. Everything about this route is on the west side of that glacier, under The Castle and the Kautz Ice Cliff.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
hazards: Serac fall from the Kautz Ice Cliff onto Camp Hazard and the traverse beneath it
Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing
Avalanche, rockfall and steep snow in The Fan gully
Ice and rockfall raking the centre and east side of the Turtle snowfield
Thin or rotten ice in the chute late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts BELOW Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be LOSING height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: two steps of alpine ice separated by lower-angle snow. The first is the easier, anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of ice; the second is the crux, from a short pitch to more than 300 ft, steeper, and where a second tool earns its place. Both change a great deal from year to year. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

approach_variants.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.
approach_variants.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
hazards: Losing the moraine crest and the treeline trail junction on descent — carry a saved track
Steep unmaintained moraine travel above the end of maintained trail
Same serac and ice-cliff exposure above the Castle and at Camp Hazard
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant's finding problem is the reverse of most: the hard recognition is on the way down, not the way up. On the way up, the sequence is trail to a junction, more trail to the end of maintained tread, then a steep moraine crest — if you are still on graded tread above about 6,500 ft you have followed the wrong branch toward Van Trump Park's meadows rather than the climbers' line.

The merge point is the Upper Castle at about 9,400–9,500 ft, a rock rib with established camp sites and, from mid-June, running water. Once you are there the route ahead is the same as the Paradise approach: up the Turtle keeping to its western edge, to Camp Hazard, and then DOWN a short rappel into the gully beneath the ice cliff to reach the chute.

approach_variants.name: Paradise and Glacier Vista, across the Nisqually to the Turtle and Camp Hazard
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise at 5,400 ft, the common approach follows the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, then drops west onto the glacier. The route crosses the lower Nisqually, gains the Wilson Glacier and climbs to the Turtle Snowfield, with camps at The Castle around 9,200-9,500 ft and Camp Hazard at 10,800 ft at the top of the snowfield.

Roped travel and crevasse-rescue readiness are needed from the moment you leave the Nisqually. Water is available from snowmelt lower down on the Comet Falls and Van Trump side but not once you are on glacier ice.

Rockfall and icefall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall are the approach-zone hazards; move through the exposed ground early and efficiently.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-May to early Aug; the ice holds into summer but the approach and glacier conditions degrade quickly after the start of August
hazards: Two steep ice steps beneath serac and rockfall from the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall
Brittle or hard ice on the upper step, with screws the only protection
Genuinely complex crevassed glacier travel on the Kautz approach
A short rappel or fixed-line downclimb off the Camp Hazard bivy rock to reach the base
Descent rappels are on ice anchors you build yourself; old ascent-placed threads must not be reused
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HEADWALL AND THE STANDARD KAUTZ CHUTE ARE TWO DIFFERENT LINES OFF THE SAME CAMP, AND THE TEST IS HOW MANY STEEP STEPS YOU MEET.

COUNT TWO. This route presents as TWO ICE STEPS SEPARATED BY A BAND OF LOWER-ANGLE SNOW: the lower step around 35-40 degrees, the upper around 45-50. Step, bench, step. If you climb one sustained runnel and the angle then eases the whole way to the summit plateau, you were in the standard Kautz ice chute, not on the headwall.

THE UPPER STEP IS THE ONE THAT SETTLES IT — noticeably steeper and more sustained than the lower, needing two tools and screws in ice that is often harder or more brittle. The lower step is broad and stepped out and rarely steeper than about 35-40 degrees, and most parties get up it with a single tool and a couple of screws. If the harder ground came FIRST, you are not on this.

WHERE YOU ROPE UP IS PART OF THE FINDING: on the Turtle or Wilson Glacier BELOW the headwall, often after a short rappel or a fixed-line downclimb off the bivy rock at Camp Hazard. Descending off camp before you climb is correct and is a good sign you are on the right line rather than walking out along the chute.

THE APPROACH HAS TWO STARTS AND THEY LAND IN THE SAME PLACE, SO DO NOT LET THE DIFFERENCE UNSETTLE YOU: Paradise via Glacier Vista and the Nisqually Moraine, or the Comet Falls and Van Trump Park trail from a lower trailhead. Both cross the Nisqually onto the Wilson and climb the Turtle. If you find yourself on maintained trail beside a waterfall you are on the second of those, not lost.

WHAT BEING TOO LATE LOOKS LIKE: seracs and rockfall off the Wapowety Cleaver and the Kautz Icefall hang over the steep ground. The upper step must be climbed efficiently and early. The honest reading of arriving at it warm and in the sun is to go down.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass, Curtis Ridge and the Carbon Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Glacier Basin trailhead in White River Campground and follow the Glacier Basin trail. At about 6,700 ft leave the trail to the right and climb snow slopes to St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft). There are bivouac sites in this area.

From the pass, descend onto the lower Winthrop Glacier and traverse west across it, holding elevation, to the broad slopes of Curtis Ridge. Cross Curtis Ridge and aim for the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier at roughly 7,300 ft. Then ascend the Carbon southward toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, negotiating the crevasse fields on the way.

Access onto the ridge is somewhere between about 8,600 and 8,800 ft, and either flank can be used depending on conditions. Above that it is 30–40 degree snow with scree and rock traverses up to Thumb Rock at about 10,500 ft — the standard bivouac, with additional sites just above in the saddle. There are also bivouacs around 11,000 ft.

Most parties do not reverse this. The usual plan is a carry-over: finish at Liberty Cap and descend the Emmons–Winthrop to Camp Schurman and out to White River, which is why this route is often permitted as a multi-camp itinerary rather than an out-and-back.

Rainier permits apply: per-person climbing permit and a wilderness permit for each night.
approach_variants.season: May and June — after the winter storm cycle and before the ridge melts out to loose rock
hazards: Serac and icefall discharge from Willis Wall onto the traverse below it
Crevasse fields on the Carbon Glacier below the toe
Rockfall from the bands above Thumb Rock, worse as the season melts the ridge out
Committing terrain — retreat down the ridge is difficult, most parties carry over and descend the Emmons
Bergschrund and short vertical ice gaining the Liberty Cap Glacier near 13,500 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the toe of the ridge on the Carbon Glacier, and the whole approach is a sequence of things you must leave rather than things you arrive at — so the negative markers do the work.

Leave the Glacier Basin trail at about 6,700 ft. If you reach Glacier Basin Campground you have walked past the turn; the branch is a climbers' line up snow to the right, aiming at the notch of St Elmo Pass at 7,400 ft.

After St Elmo Pass you should be LOSING height onto the Winthrop Glacier and then traversing, not climbing. If you are gaining, you are heading up the Winthrop toward the Emmons ground and Camp Schurman — the wrong side of the mountain for this route.

The crossing under Willis Wall is the marker that you are close and the marker that you are exposed. Between Curtis Ridge and Liberty Ridge you pass beneath a huge dark face capped with ice cliffs. That is Willis Wall, it is not your route, and its summit seracs discharge onto the ground you are crossing. If you are still under that face, you have not reached the toe yet — and this is ground to cross without stopping, not ground to navigate on.

The positive test: Liberty Ridge is the rib that divides the Carbon Glacier from Willis Wall. When Willis Wall is behind and to your east and there is a defined rock-and-snow rib rising in front of you out of the Carbon, you are at the toe. Start looking for access between roughly 8,600 and 8,800 ft; take whichever flank is in condition rather than insisting on the crest.

Thumb Rock at 10,500 ft is the confirmation you got it right — the first real flat ground on the crest, with established bivouac platforms and a saddle just above.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake, Spray Park and Ptarmigan Ridge, then up the North Mowich Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Mowich Lake Road is unpaved and seasonal. In a normal year it opens well after the roads on the east and south sides of the park — commonly not until July — and closes with the first significant snow. Since April 2025, though, the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge that carried the only public road to it has been closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers, so Mowich Lake itself is now a long wilderness walk from another park entrance.

From Mowich Lake, follow the Wonderland Trail roughly 3-4 miles through Spray Park, passing Spray Falls. Where the Wonderland begins to descend toward the Carbon River, leave it and head cross-country southeast BETWEEN ECHO ROCK AND OBSERVATION ROCK, picking up a climbers' path onto the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge.

Near 8,300 ft you LEAVE the ridge and DROP about 1,000 ft of loose rock and snow to the North Mowich Glacier. Rope up there and climb the glacier, watching for fresh rockfall debris on the ice, to camps at roughly 9,600-10,200 ft below the face.

There is no water above Spray Park and no maintained trail for the upper two-thirds of this approach.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun for ice; the face bares out and starts shedding rock as it warms
hazards: Sustained steep ice and snow with multiple line options and no obvious separation between them
Serac and rockfall hazard on the face; the North Mowich crossing collects the debris
A bergschrund that is frequently impassable direct and must be turned
Roped glacier travel with crevasses under thin snow bridges on both the drop from camp and the return
No walk-off: topping out commits the party to a carryover and a car shuttle
Road access on this side has been closed since the April 2025 Fairfax Bridge closure
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO NAMED ROCKS ARE THE ONLY HARD MARKERS ON THE WHOLE CROSS-COUNTRY SECTION, AND THEY WORK IN CLOUD BECAUSE THEY ARE BIG AND THEY ARE A PAIR. You leave the Wonderland Trail and go BETWEEN ECHO ROCK AND OBSERVATION ROCK. Not past one of them — between the two. If you can only see one rock, you do not yet know which one it is.

THE SECOND THING IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IT IS WHERE PARTIES GO WRONG: AT ABOUT 8,300 FT YOU LEAVE THE RIDGE AND GO DOWN. The face is across the North Mowich Glacier from Ptarmigan Ridge. If you keep climbing the ridge past that point, you are on Ptarmigan Ridge, which is a different route to a different top-out. Losing height off the ridge is correct and is the single clearest signal that you are on this climb and not its neighbour.

THE BERGSCHRUND IS THE ARRIVAL AND IT IS FREQUENTLY NOT PASSABLE DIRECT. It has to be turned, so budget time for looking rather than treating the schrund as a formality. Reaching a schrund you cannot cross straight over means you are probably in the right place.

THIS IS THE UMBRELLA FACE, NOT A SINGLE LINE, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO CARRY IN. Four separate climbs share this wall and this camp — the North Mowich Headwall, the Central Mowich Face, the Edmunds Headwall, and Ptarmigan Ridge above and to the side of them. They are told apart by WHICH GLACIER you cross from camp and by WHAT THE FIRST GROUND ABOVE THE SCHRUND IS, not by the walk in, which is identical for all of them. Decide which one you are doing before you leave camp in the dark; there is roughly 4,000 ft of 40 to 55 degree ice and mixed ground above, and being one line out is not a thing you discover early.

WHAT RETREAT LOOKS LIKE, BECAUSE IT IS NOT THE WAY YOU CAME: there is no walk-off from the top of this face. Topping out commits you to a carryover down the far side of the mountain to Paradise or White River and a shuttle back. Backing off means reversing the North Mowich Glacier, climbing about 1,000 ft of scree and talus near Observation Rock, and walking out through Spray Park.

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge bivy above Observation Rock
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the most sheltered ground on this side of the mountain: old stacked rock windbreaks sit here and parties describe it as the best bivy shelter in the area. The catch is position, not comfort — from here you still have to descend loose scree onto the North Mowich Glacier, and parties who camped here have called that descent the inefficient part of their trip. Cross-country zone; permit required.
bivy.water: none reliable — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a couple of tents on hand-built platforms

bivy.name: Edmunds/North Mowich glacier divide camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED alternative used by parties who cross the North Mowich above Needle Rock rather than staying high on Ptarmigan Ridge. Puts you on the correct side of the glacier for the face, at the cost of more elevation to regain in the morning.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: one to two tents

bivy.name: High camp below the North Mowich headwall
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp closest to the base of the face, and the most exposed of the three. Parties who have used it wore helmets in camp because of rockfall and icefall shedding off the deteriorating headwall above; there is no fully sheltered ground up here. Worth it only when conditions are cold and you intend to start on the face within a few hours. Search around 9,200 ft first if the higher ground looks loaded — flat sites there are limited but out from under the wall.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents; flat ground is scarce and has to be dug

bivy.name: Liberty Cap saddle
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY bivy only, on the broad saddle between Liberty Cap and the summit, used by at least one party benighted after topping out. It is more sheltered than the true summit and less wind-hammered than climbers expect, but it is an unplanned option to know about, not a camp to aim for — going there means you are spending a night above 13,000 ft with whatever you carried up the face.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: improvised, no prepared ground

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Skyline Trail and the Nisqually Glacier to the lower bergschrund
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise at about 5,400 ft, follow the Skyline Trail up past Glacier Vista and Pan Point, then leave it and drop west onto the Nisqually Glacier. This is the same access point the Wapowety Cleaver lines use. Rope up before you step onto ice; there is no maintained trail from here on and no reliable water once you leave Paradise, so plan on melting snow.

Ascend the Nisqually alongside the Wapowety Cleaver, gaining steadily to about 9,900 ft where the lower bergschrund marks the start of the technical ground — typically 40 to 50 ft of steep ice or snow to gain the icefall itself.

Above that the route threads broken, crevassed terrain in the upper Nisqually basin toward the top of the Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft. That basin is the most time-consuming and the most dangerous section of the whole climb: it sits directly under active icefall and rockfall, and the correct tactic is to move through it without stopping to regroup. The seracs rearrange themselves every season, so expect to find your own way rather than follow anyone's line.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun. This is an early-season line: the icefall wants to be frozen, and hazard rises steeply through the summer as the glacier warms
hazards: Active icefall with collapsing seracs directly above the upper basin
Complex crevasse and serac navigation that changes every season
Hazard rises rapidly with warming through the day, so the upper basin must be crossed early
Documented history of large slide activity in the icefall
No reliable water above Paradise
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIMBING STARTS AT THE LOWER BERGSCHRUND AT ABOUT 9,900 FT. Everything below that is glacier walking, and the whole recognition problem is not confusing that walking with progress.

FIRST TEST, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE DAY: which way you go at Glacier Vista. This route drops WEST off the Skyline Trail onto the Nisqually. If you are still walking uphill on maintained trail toward Pebble Creek and the Muir Snowfield, you are on the Camp Muir approach and the icefall is behind your left shoulder. Parties have made that mistake in the dark because the first mile is identical.

SECOND TEST, AND IT WORKS IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT IS A SIDE, NOT A LANDMARK: the Wapowety Cleaver — the rock cleaver dividing the Nisqually from the Kautz — must stay on your LEFT the whole way up. If it has ended up on your right you have crossed onto the Kautz side of it and you are on the Kautz Glacier route.

THIRD TEST, POSITIVE: the schrund is the first steep ground on the route. If you have walked moderate glacier for hours and met nothing steeper than a crevasse crossing, you have not arrived — keep going, do not start climbing something because it is steep.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE MOST USEFUL ONE HERE, AND IT INVERTS THE USUAL INSTINCT: a boot track is EVIDENCE YOU ARE WRONG.
