This route is circuitous enough and dangerous enough that it is rarely climbed in any given season. A trench underfoot on the Nisqually almost certainly belongs to parties walking to Camp Muir, not to anyone on this line.

WHAT BEING TOO HIGH LOOKS LIKE: if you are in the upper basin with seracs above you and have not crossed a bergschrund, you have wandered into the icefall from the side rather than climbing into it, which is exactly the ground you least want to be standing still in.

approach_variants.name: Mowich Lake and Spray Park
approach_variants.notes:
From Mowich Lake, follow the trail roughly 3 miles to Spray Park, then climb the lower slopes of Ptarmigan Ridge. The ridge narrows above Observation Rock; continue along it until you find bivouac sites. High camp is normally somewhere between about 9,500 and 10,300 ft, at the point where Ptarmigan Ridge runs into the main cone below the Liberty Cap icefall. Higher camps are worth the extra carry because they let you look at the bergschrund and pick a line the evening before.

This is the shorter of the two approaches, and it is the one most parties would choose if the road cooperated. Since April 2025 the Mowich Lake road has had no public access, because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; this start is unavailable until that changes. Even before that, the summer-only road usually opened after the route came into condition.

The approach to high camp is normally split over two days.
approach_variants.season: May-Jul; the road to Mowich Lake has had no public access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed permanently on April 22, 2025, so this start cannot be reached by car
hazards: Bergschrund crossing off the Mowich Glacier, conditions-dependent
Loose rock descending from high camp onto the glacier
Icefall exposure below the Liberty Cap icefall near high camp
Verglassed rock and water ice on the upper mixed ground
Committing position with a descent by a different route — plan the carry-over
approach_variants.baseFinding:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you DESCEND, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Follow the Glacier Basin trail from White River Campground and leave it for St Elmo Pass (7,400 ft), about 4 miles in. Descend onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west toward Curtis Ridge, holding elevation. Cross Curtis Ridge, cross the Carbon Glacier, then climb moderate snow slopes onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point, where there are good bivouac sites.

This is the long way around the north side of the mountain and it shares its first half with the Liberty Ridge approach. It usually implies a car shuttle or, more often, a carry-over with descent by the Emmons–Winthrop back to White River — which conveniently is also the standard descent from the route itself.
approach_variants.season: Available earlier in the season than the Mowich Lake road, at the cost of a much longer approach
hazards: Serac discharge from Willis Wall on the traverse between Curtis Ridge and the Carbon
Crevasse fields on the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers
Long committing traverse with no quick exit
Same bergschrund and upper mixed-ground hazards as the Mowich approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Up to the Carbon Glacier this is the Liberty Ridge approach, and the same negative markers apply: leave the Glacier Basin trail rather than walking into Glacier Basin, lose height off St Elmo Pass rather than gaining it, and treat the ground under Willis Wall as a crossing rather than a place to stand.

Where it diverges: instead of turning up the Carbon toward the toe of Liberty Ridge, you continue west across the Carbon and climb snow onto Ptarmigan Ridge below its 10,200 ft high point. If you find yourself gaining a defined rib immediately above the Carbon with Willis Wall right behind you, you have stopped at Liberty Ridge — Ptarmigan is further round to the west.

Once camped on Ptarmigan Ridge the start of the climbing is the same as from the Mowich side: down off the ridge onto the Mowich Glacier, then the bergschrund, then 40–45 degree snow to the base of the rock cliffs.

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one the route is built around. Comfortable bivy ground on the ridge crest, deliberately sited just outside the serac fall line off the Liberty Wall — that icefall is the single largest objective hazard on the climb, so the exact spot matters more than the comfort. Fully exposed to wind. Parties who want an acceptable risk margin wait for an overnight freezing level at or below about 12,000 ft.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on dug snow platforms

bivy.name: Glacier Basin camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the last established campground on the White River approach. Composting toilet a short walk away and bear boxes on site. Melts out early and is the last dependable running water before the route goes onto snow and ice for good — most parties fill here rather than carry from the car.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required (reserve or self-register); designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED first-night option when the traverse from White River is split over two days; the park's own route notes list it as the standard intermediate camp before Ptarmigan high camp. Sits on the crest between the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers, which is the point — you hear serac collapse off Willis Wall all night but the crest keeps you out of the runout. Do not drop and camp on the open Carbon below the wall to save an hour.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: small parties; scattered flat ground on the ridge crest, no established platforms

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: DESCENT camp, not an ascent camp — most parties come off Ptarmigan Ridge down the Emmons-Winthrop and use this. Has a ranger hut and a solar toilet, but both can be buried in snow well into the season, so plan to be self-sufficient and pack out waste. Reserve early; this is one of the first camps on the mountain to fill.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

approach_variants.name: Westside Road, Round Pass, St Andrews Park and the Puyallup Cleaver
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Westside Road gate near 2,900 ft, about a mile past the Nisqually entrance. The road is gravel and open to vehicles only for the first few miles; beyond that it is foot or bike travel, and has been that way for years because of flood damage in the Tahoma Creek drainage. Treat the walk as part of the route rather than as an inconvenience that might be lifted.

Walk the road roughly 3.5 miles to Round Pass, then take the South Puyallup River Trail to the Wonderland Trail and on to St Andrews Park. Leave the trail there and climb north through alpine meadows onto the Puyallup Cleaver, passing Tokaloo Spire.

Leave the cleaver at about 8,500 ft and traverse the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers into the Sunset Amphitheater. Camps are used on Colonnade Ridge, on the Puyallup Cleaver near 9,000 ft, in the open near 9,600 ft, and at the bergschrund in the amphitheater itself.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jun, best frozen; typically out of condition by July
hazards: Serac and icefall hazard above the Sunset Amphitheater
Rockfall in the amphitheater headwall
A long crevassed traverse of the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers just to reach the base
Rotten volcanic rock on the knife-edge ridge between the gendarmes
Remote west-side position with a road walk at both ends of a very long day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION IS A LEAVING, NOT AN ARRIVING, AND IT HAPPENS AT ABOUT 8,500 FT ON THE PUYALLUP CLEAVER. Up to there you are simply walking a ridge. At 8,500 ft you step off it onto glacier and traverse. If you keep climbing the cleaver you will end up over on the Tahoma Glacier side and this route is gone.

PASSING TOKALOO SPIRE IS THE CONFIRMATION THAT YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT CLEAVER. It is the named rock feature on the way up from St Andrews Park. No spire, no cleaver — you left the trail in the wrong place.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE IS THAT THE GROUND CLOSES AROUND YOU. The Sunset Amphitheater is a bowl shut off by a headwall, with the serac band above it. If you are traversing open glacier that does not close into a bowl, you are still contouring and have not arrived — or you have dropped too low and are heading out across the South Mowich toward the Mowich Face, which is a different climb reached from a different trailhead on the far side of the mountain.

THE CLIMB'S OWN SIGNATURE IS TWO GENDARMES, AND IT CONFIRMS THE ROUTE RATHER THAN THE BASE. Above the steep ground the ridge runs as a knife edge BETWEEN TWO PROMINENT GENDARMES on notably loose, rotten volcanic rock. If the ridge above you has no pair of towers on it, you are on a neighbouring feature.

WHAT THE CRUX LOOKS LIKE, SO YOU KNOW YOU ARE ON IT: roughly 1,000–1,300 ft of 55- to 60-degree neve or ice, and it is the only sustained steep ground on the route. Anything shorter and you have not started; anything that keeps going far past that and you are on the amphitheater headwall rather than the ridge.

approach_variants.name: Westside Road and Tahoma Creek to St Andrews Rock, then the Sickle
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Westside Road gate at the Dry Creek trailhead near 2,900 ft. The road is gated to vehicles a few miles in because of repeated Tahoma Creek flooding and debris flows; the remainder is walked or biked, and has been for years. Plan the road as part of the climb.

From the gate, take the Tahoma Creek Trail up to the Wonderland Trail near 5,600 ft, then onto the southern side of the Tahoma Glacier. Camps are used near Emerald Ridge lower down and around 9,800-10,400 ft near St Andrews Rock.

The glacier is climbed with a series of diagonal traverses: zigzag the south side to about 7,200 ft, then traverse back and forth around 9,000-10,000 ft to get through crevasse bands, then into the Sickle and out onto the plateau near 12,600 ft.

Car-to-car this is a very long outing — a documented itinerary from the road closure ran about 21.5 miles.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Jul, best in June; a west aspect that holds firmer snow later into the morning than the south-side routes
hazards: Complex crevasse navigation with several bands that have to be traversed around
Serac and icefall hazard in and below the Sickle, with unavoidable run-out exposure on the traverse
A long road walk at both ends and a very long car-to-car day
Route-finding on a committing west-side approach with no maintained trail above 5,600 ft
Thin late-season snow bridges over the upper glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ST ANDREWS ROCK IS THE RECOGNITION POINT, AND THE THING THAT CONFIRMS IT IS THAT YOU GO DOWN.

You climb to a ridge just short of 10,000 ft BELOW ST ANDREWS ROCK, and then you DROP several hundred feet on a ramp onto the Tahoma Glacier proper at around 9,600 ft. Losing that height is correct. It is the clearest single signal that you are on this route: a party that never gives height back has stayed on the Puyallup Cleaver and is heading for Sunset Ridge, one drainage north.

THE SICKLE IS THE SECOND MARKER AND IT IS A SHAPE, NOT A PLACE. At about 11,200 ft the route enters a NARROW CHUTE THAT CURVES LEFT AROUND A CLIFF — the reason it is called the Sickle. If you are climbing straight up open glacier with no constriction and no cliff to curve around, you are still below it, whatever the altimeter says.

CLIMB THE SICKLE ON ITS NORTH SIDE, KEEPING LEFT OF THE ICY RIDGES, to the plateau at about 12,600 ft. Topping the Sickle is the point at which you are out of the icefall run-out, and that is the honest marker for 'the dangerous part is behind you'.

THE NEGATIVE THAT MATTERS FOR TIMING RATHER THAN NAVIGATION: the traverse below the Sickle runs under its run-out zone, which funnels ice debris. There is no line through that avoids it. Being there in the dark and frozen is the only protection, so if you arrive at the base of the Sickle in the sun, the finding is that you should not be there, not that you should look for a better line.

WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG SIDE LOOKS LIKE LOW DOWN: the route works the SOUTHERN side of the glacier from the Wonderland Trail at 5,600 ft. Drifting north early puts you into the crevasse bands the diagonal traverses exist to avoid.

approach_variants.name: White River, St Elmo Pass and the Winthrop-to-Carbon traverse under Curtis Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
The traditional approach was the Carbon River road to Ipsut Creek and up the Carbon Glacier. Carbon River access ended in April 2025, when the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge, the only public road in, was closed permanently to cars, bikes and walkers; the Carbon side is now a very long wilderness walk rather than a drive-in.

The approach most parties now use starts at White River Campground: Glacier Basin Trail to Glacier Basin, climbers' path to St Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, then rope up, drop onto the Winthrop and traverse west and around beneath Curtis Ridge onto the Carbon Glacier at about 7,300 ft.

From the Carbon, walk up under the wall. Bivy sites exist in the Curtis Ridge access gully and on Curtis Ridge itself.

This is one of the most objectively dangerous pieces of ground in the range. The whole wall is capped by the summit icecap and swept by what comes off it. Nothing in the rack protects you from that; being there in the cold hours does.
approach_variants.season: Cold, hard-frozen conditions only — a narrow and unpredictable late-spring window, and the route is more often not in condition than in it
hazards: Extreme objective hazard from the hanging summit icecap seracs, along the entire wall
Continuous rockfall down the face
No easy retreat once committed; a long, serious approach on both sides
Crevassed glacier travel on the Winthrop and Carbon, and again on the summit icecap above
Carbon River road access has been closed since April 2025, which makes that side a multi-day walk
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE TEST IS WHAT IS ABOVE YOU, NOT WHAT IS IN FRONT OF YOU. Willis Wall is capped along its entire top by the hanging summit ice cliff, and all three of its ribs rise from the base of the wall directly above the Carbon Glacier, underneath that cliff. If you are standing beneath a face that is NOT capped by a continuous ice cliff, you are not under Willis Wall. THE TWO WAYS TO BE WRONG ARE ON OPPOSITE SIDES, AND THE RIDGES NAME THEM. Willis Wall is bounded by CURTIS RIDGE on one side and LIBERTY RIDGE on the other. Facing the wall from the Carbon Glacier, Curtis Ridge is the rib you came around to get here and Liberty Ridge is the rib beyond the far edge of the wall. If you have walked past Liberty Ridge you are under Liberty Wall, which is a different wall with a different reputation. COUNT THE GLACIERS: TWO. Winthrop, then Carbon. One means you stopped at Curtis Ridge. THE ROUTE DOES NOT NAME A RIB, AND THAT IS THE FACT TO CARRY IN. This wall carries three distinct ribs, climbed in different years by different parties and of materially different character. Which one you are under is a decision to be made at the base, from photographs taken before you left, and not something the approach settles for you. Do not treat 'the base of Willis Wall' as though it were one start. WHAT BEING TOO LATE LOOKS LIKE: nothing visual. The wall does not change. Time of day is the variable that kills here, so the honest base finding is that arriving under it after the sun has been on the icecap means turning round, not looking harder for the rib.

approach_variants.name: Gem Lake's west shore to the southeast gully
approach_variants.notes: Snow Lake Trail from the Alpental lot to Snow Lake, then the climbers' path along the north shore and on to Gem Lake — the last reliable water before committing to the ridge. An unmaintained boot path leaves Gem Lake's west shore and climbs a steep westward-trending ridge toward Roosevelt's north sub-summit; it is easy to lose in fog or fresh snow. Weekend traffic and parking congestion on the shared lower trail are heavy enough to be worth planning around.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Loose dirt over rock in the gully
Snow persisting in the summit gully well into summer in heavy years
Brushy, poorly marked boot path above Gem Lake
An exposed, essentially unprotectable final step
No water on the upper ridge or in the gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is the foot of the southeast gully, and the cairned traverse that reaches it is the crux of the route-finding rather than the crux of the climbing. From the ridge crest above Gem Lake the boot path skirts LEFT (east) of a band of buttresses; near 5,400 ft it tops out, and a short scree slope and rising traverse — roughly two hundred feet of gain, cairn-marked — lead west into a small snow-and-talus basin beneath the two summit humps. The gully rising out of that basin is the peak's only non-technical line: loose rock, heather and dirt that turns north and steepens, dangerously slick when wet or under a skiff of snow, and essentially impossible to protect. Above it a short, semi-exposed ramp leads to a final step of about twenty feet at class 2-3. The decoy on this mountain is at the top rather than the bottom — Roosevelt has two summit humps, and the lower NORTH one has turned parties around thinking they had finished. The true summit is the higher, more southerly hump.

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/year day-use fee at White River Trailhead
access.rules: Standard Glacier Peak Wilderness rules apply: campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft elevation (covers essentially this entire route above the lower trail), so plan on a stove only; practice Leave No Trace and pack out all waste.
access.permit: Free self-issuing Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, available at the White River Trailhead kiosk
access.closures: White River Road (FS-6400) is CLOSED under Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner; the order closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, the only access to this route. The road has separately seen storm-damage closures and washouts in past seasons — check current Wenatchee River Ranger District road and trail conditions before driving out.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA; (509) 548-2550)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at the White River Trailhead — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency (America the Beautiful) pass; alternatively pay $5/vehicle/day or $30/year on-site (Recreation.gov Scan & Pay accepted) — vault toilet at trailhead, no potable water

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead register at the end of the White River road.

road.name: White River Road / Forest Service Road 6400
road.status: Paved from SR-207 for several miles, then gravel Forest Service road to the trailhead; generally passable in summer but subject to washout closures. CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is the only access to this route.
road.driveNote: From Leavenworth: US-2 west 15 mi to Coles Corner, right onto SR-207 (Lake Wenatchee Hwy) 10.5 mi, then FS-6400/White River Road 10 mi to the White River (Indian Creek) Trailhead.

approach_variants.name: Indian Creek Trail and the Airplane Creek bushwhack to Airplane Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the road-end trailhead above Lake Wenatchee, the Indian Creek Trail crosses the White River on a footbridge — which has washed out in past years, forcing a ford — and runs up the valley through old growth and sections of burned, dead forest. Somewhere near Airplane Creek you leave the maintained tread; nothing marks the departure and it is easy to lose in brush or fog. The bushwhack from there to the lake is the hard part of the day: roughly two thousand feet of gain through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, made worse by the standing dead timber. Favouring the drainage about a quarter mile downstream of Airplane Creek reportedly avoids the worst of the brush. Snow cover typically begins around 4,000 ft and becomes continuous near 4,700 ft in early season, so step-kicking on firm snow is normal here into July. Airplane Lake is the last reliable water and the only sensible flat camp. Time the White River and Indian Creek crossings for the morning, when the water is lower.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September is the reliable window. In July expect snow from around 4,000 ft and continuous cover above 4,700 ft, which makes the upper slopes a snow climb and calls for an axe.
hazards: off-trail bushwhacking through devil's club, vine maple and blowdown, worsened by burned standing timber
White River and Indian Creek crossings that get harder through the afternoon as snowmelt rises
hidden cliff bands north of Airplane Lake that can cliff out a party working toward the northeast ridge
lingering snow on the upper east slopes into July
loose rock and steep talus on some summit variations
a sheer northwest face that is not a descent or a bail option
approach_variants.baseFinding: GO EAST-FACING AND CLEAN, NOT NORTH AND BROKEN. From Airplane Lake the summit push starts at the foot of the upper east face at roughly 6,200 ft, where three distinct lines diverge and you have to pick one. The one to aim for is the direct ascent of the clean upper east-face slabs — recognisable because the rock is continuous and relatively clean rather than piled and broken, and because it faces the morning sun squarely. The other two are a steep, looser talus variation and the northeast ridge. The northeast ridge is the one to be careful of, and it carries its own negative marker: gaining it means working around a cliff band north of the lake that is not visible until you are on it and that has cliffed parties out. So if you find yourself traversing north of the lake into broken ground and then meeting a wall you did not expect, you are on the northeast-ridge variation, not the direct line. Snow coverage should decide the choice; on a snowy year the direct slabs may be a snow climb wanting an axe. The summit itself is broad with jagged rocks at the top, and the register sits west of the highest point among rocks about fifteen feet below it — worth knowing, because the true high point is not where the register is.

bivy.name: Airplane Lake
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Mount Saul and effectively the only one, and camping here is what turns a brutal outing into a reasonable two days. Done in a single push from the road the standard route runs about sixteen miles round trip with five thousand three hundred feet of gain, which is a long day by any measure and a very long one on ground this rough. The lake sits roughly two thousand two hundred feet above Indian Creek, in a large depression under the upper east slopes, with the summit still some two thousand feet above it — so a party sleeping here has the worst of the climbing behind them and a clean morning on the east slope and east face. THE APPROACH PATH IS THE HARD PART. It leaves the Indian Creek trail at about four and a half miles, immediately before a valley campsite, marked only by a sign stating that marking of routes is prohibited; there is no other signage and the track is faint. It climbs steeply through the 2016 burn, which means loose footing, no shade, blowdown that changes with every windstorm and standing dead timber overhead. Recent volunteer work has had the trail in good condition in places, but that is a season-by-season matter rather than a promise. Season is roughly mid-July into early October; the east side melts out reasonably early but the upper slopes hold snow and an axe is worth carrying in the first half of the summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the climbing season along with snowmelt into the inlet early on. This is the last certain water on the mountain: the two thousand feet of slope between the lake and the summit carry nothing once the snow has gone. Fill everything here for the climb and for the night, and treat it.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the White River trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at the trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground; the basin is small. Carry a stove — the district runs summer fire restrictions on this dry east side as a matter of course and they are often total bans.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on benches around the lake for one or two parties. Nothing developed, nothing signed, no toilet — and almost certainly nobody else there. This is a genuinely lightly visited basin and solitude is the main thing it offers.

bivy.name: White River road end trailhead
bivy.notes: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. THE ROAD IS THE FRAGILE PART, AND IT IS CLOSED RIGHT NOW. Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead. It is not named in the Wenatchee River District storm-damage road order (06-17-07-2026-11, 20 May 2026 through 31 December 2027), which closes seventeen other roads. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.
bivy.water: The White River is at the trailhead and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill here, and fill again from Indian Creek on the way up, because everything above the valley is dry.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit comes from the register here rather than being arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit. Fire restrictions on this side are near-permanent through summer and commonly ban open flame entirely.
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the road end with room to sleep in a vehicle, and no campground facilities. This is a roadhead recorded because a party arriving from the west side in the evening needs somewhere to be before starting an approach this long.

bivy.name: The Indian Creek valley camps and the Airplane Lake junction site
bivy.notes: The junction camp is the useful one and it is the landmark as much as the site: the climbers' path for Airplane Lake turns off immediately before it, so a party that reaches an obvious valley campsite and has seen no turning has just walked past the only one there is. Sleeping here rather than at the lake trades a shorter, easier first day for a much harder second one, and most parties would rather push to the lake. Where it earns its place is on the way out, and for a party that has been slowed by the road or the burn and does not want to start the two-thousand-foot climbers' path in the evening. The valley trail itself runs about ten and a half miles in total to the Pacific Crest Trail at Indian Pass, crossing the White River on a bridge right at the trailhead and then climbing very gently; it is brushy and boggy in places, which is a nuisance rather than an obstacle. Expect burn for long stretches, and treat the dead timber overhead as a real reason not to pitch under it in wind.
bivy.water: Indian Creek runs beside the trail for the whole of this stretch and water is abundant; parts of the valley trail are boggy in early season for the same reason. Every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous half of the approach and it ends the moment you start climbing.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal in existing rings at this elevation outside a burn ban, but bans are usual here from midsummer and much of the surrounding forest is fire-killed, so use a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the Indian Creek trail, one or two tents each, including the established spot immediately past the unsigned turn for Airplane Lake. Nothing developed and no facilities.

bivy.name: The east slope above Airplane Lake — no established camp
bivy.notes: The honest answer for this peak is that Airplane Lake is the camp and there is nothing above it worth having. The lake already puts the summit within a straightforward morning on the east slope and east face, so climbing higher with a pack buys almost nothing and costs the water, the shelter and the flat ground all at once. The northwest face is sheer and is not the way anyone goes; the east side is open scrambling terrain and the difficulty of this mountain lies in the approach rather than in the climbing. Where a high bivouac has any argument at all is for a party linking Saul with the ridge country toward Indian Head and the crest, which is a different and much longer trip, and even then the sensible pattern is to sleep at water and move over the tops in the day. Treat anything above the lake as emergency ground.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. From roughly August onward there is nothing at all above the lake, and anyone sleeping here carries every drop up two thousand feet. This is the mistake to avoid rather than a plan to make.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the White River trailhead. No fires at this elevation and nothing to burn. The ground is thin alpine turf and scree that scars for years — camp on rock or gravel if you camp at all.
bivy.capacity: None established. There is broken ground and the occasional flat spot on the slope between the lake and the summit rocks where a small party could put a tent down, but nothing has been built and nobody camps here as a matter of course. Recorded so the absence is stated rather than filled in with an invented site.

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Seattle Meadows
bivy.notes: High camp in Upper Seattle Basin above Seattle Creek, below the summit's west side. The closest camp to the peak.
bivy.water: Streams in the upper basin
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required
bivy.capacity: A few tent sites in meadow

bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season

approach_variants.name: Leave the Ruth Creek trail near 3,450 ft, drop southwest across the creek and take talus to the couloir
approach_variants.notes:
Same road access as the Southeast Ridge route: SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) and Ruth Creek Road toward Hannegan Campground. This variant then goes further up the valley before leaving the trail.

From the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft, leave the trail, drop SOUTHWEST to cross Ruth Creek, and cross talus to the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.

One documented attempt turned around near 4,300 ft on rock the party judged unmanageable — mossy, muddy and soaked. That is a real and repeatable outcome rather than an anomaly, and it is the main reason to want this line under snow.
approach_variants.season: Best when the couloir holds continuous snow. Parties have been turned around on wet, mossy, muddy rock in the lower couloir — this line wants snow cover, not bare rock
hazards: An unbridged Ruth Creek crossing with no established log
A documented turnaround on wet, mossy, muddy rock in the lower couloir
Avalanche-prone gully terrain on Sefrit's north side
Loose rock and a shattered summit block on the peak generally
No maintained tread from the moment you leave the Ruth Creek trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS FOUND BY ELEVATION AND BEARING, NOT BY LOOKING FOR A FEATURE, AND THE TWO NUMBERS ARE 3,450 AND 4,000. You leave the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft and you meet the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft on the far side of the creek. Between them the instruction is a single word: SOUTHWEST. Drop to the creek, cross it, and go up the talus on the other side. Five hundred and fifty feet of gain from trail to base.

THE CONFIRMATION IS UNDERFOOT AND IT IS A WARNING AS WELL AS A MARKER. If the ground at 4,000 ft is bare, mossy, muddy and wet rather than snow, you have found the couloir in the condition that has already turned a party around. Being in the right place does not mean the route is in.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST WALL STREET, which is the same peak's other north-side gully and less than two miles away: Wall Street is entered from the pullout near MILEPOST 3 at about 2,950 ft, after a creek crossing and 45 minutes of alder, and it is a 50-ft-wide corridor with steep walls on both sides holding a uniform 30-35 degrees for 1,500 ft. Bloody Head is entered from the TRAIL at 3,450 ft, higher up the valley. If you walked up the valley on a trail before dropping to the creek, you are heading for Bloody Head. If you crossed the creek straight out of a pullout and thrashed alder, you are heading for Wall Street.

AND THE COARSE CHECK: both of these are on Sefrit's NORTH side and are reached from Ruth Creek. The Southwest Ridge is reached from the Nooksack Cirque trailhead on a different forest road and faces the other way.

approach_variants.name: Ruth Creek crossing near milepost 3, then the Wall Street couloir to the Northwest Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Drive SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to the pullout near milepost 3, just past where a creek flows over a concrete weir, at about 2,950 ft. This is NOT the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of the road.

Cross Ruth Creek. There is no bridge; parties cross on whatever logs are in place, and a three-log cluster has been used. Then about 45 minutes of thrashing through slide alder and devil's club to the avalanche debris at the foot of the snow gully.

The couloir runs roughly 1,500 vertical feet and opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft; from there the route crosses the glacier to a saddle near 6,500 ft and scrambles the southeast ridge to the summit.

Timing is the whole trade: earlier means more snow and more avalanche risk, later means thicker brush and discontinuous snow.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep for the scramble; the couloir has also been climbed and skied in winter, when it is an avalanche path rather than a walk
hazards: An unbridged crossing of Ruth Creek on logs that change year to year
45 minutes of slide alder and devil's club with no tread
A 1,500 ft avalanche path — the debris at its foot is the evidence
Crossing the Northwest Glacier above the couloir
Shattered summit rock on the southeast ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WALL STREET IS A CORRIDOR WITH WALLS ON BOTH SIDES, AND THAT IS THE TEST. Once you are in it, the gully holds a remarkably UNIFORM GRADIENT of 30-35 degrees and a UNIFORM WIDTH of about 50 feet, with very steep rock walls on BOTH sides, for roughly 1,500 vertical feet. Nothing else on this side of the valley does that. In cloud you do not need to see the top: if you can touch rock on your left and rock on your right and the angle is not changing, you are in Wall Street. If your gully fans out, or has a wall on only one side, it is not.

GETTING TO IT: the marker at the bottom is AVALANCHE DEBRIS. After the creek crossing and roughly 45 minutes of alder and devil's club, the brush ends at the debris pile at the foot of the snow gully. Debris is what tells you the gully above you actually runs — and it is also the reason to be there early and cold.

THE ARRIVAL AT THE TOP OF THE COULOIR IS THE GLACIER. The corridor opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft. Walls end, glacier starts.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER TWO ROUTES, and it is decided in the car park rather than on the mountain. THREE routes on Sefrit start from three different places: this one from the Ruth Creek pullout near MILEPOST 3 on Ruth Creek Road; the Bloody Head Couloir from the Ruth Creek TRAIL higher up the valley near 3,450 ft; and the Southwest Ridge from the NOOKSACK CIRQUE trailhead at the end of FR-34, a different road entirely. If you drove to the end of FR-34 you cannot reach this route today.

approach_variants.name: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead at the end of FR-34, then an ascending traverse through the cliff band
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, drive SR-542 east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR-34), and follow FR-34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead. This is a DIFFERENT trailhead from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR-32, and from the milepost-3 pullout the Wall Street route uses.

Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge.

Follow the old roadbed and Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west and southwest ridge, passing through or around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system.

A separate, lower-angle line on the north side — Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier, finishing on the southeast ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed Class 3 traverse and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak. The two are easily confused in planning and impossible to confuse on the ground, because they start on different roads.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Early summer high water can make the Ruth Creek ford at the trailhead difficult or unsafe
hazards: An unbridged ford of Ruth Creek at the trailhead, difficult or unsafe at early-summer high water
A cliff band to be negotiated on an unmarked ascending traverse
Several similar-looking forks in the summit gully, only one of which is the easy line
Loose rock near the summit ridge
Fixed slings of unknown age at the crux step
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIFF BAND IS THE GATE, AND THE GULLY YOU WANT IS ABOVE IT. Fifty minutes up Trail #750 you leave the trail and traverse upward, passing through or around a cliff band. Everything below the band is approach; the summit gully system starts above it. If you are still under continuous rock, you have not got through the band yet.

THE GULLY SPLITS, AND THE ANSWER IS LEFTMOST. Above the cliff band the summit gully divides into several forks. Take the LEFTMOST fork — or, put the other way round, the one immediately WEST of a snow couloir lying to its right. Those two descriptions are the same instruction from two sides and together they are checkable in poor visibility: find the snow couloir, then take the rock fork on its left.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS A CONFIRMATION. On this line the rock is generally solid low down and gets looser near the summit ridge. If your fork is loose from the first moves, you are probably in one of the other forks.

WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN AM I ON? This is the coarse test and it is settled by the drive: this route starts on FR-34 at the NOOKSACK CIRQUE trailhead and works up the peak's WEST and SOUTHWEST side. Sefrit's other two routes are both reached from Ruth Creek on the NORTH side and neither of them can be reached from here without going back to the car.

DESCENT NOTE THAT CROSS-CHECKS THE START: parties reverse this line, and some rappel the short crux step off pre-existing slings rather than downclimb it. Slings on a short step above a cliff band is the same feature seen from above.

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann Trail #600 from SR 542
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Lake Ann trailhead on the east side of the Mount Baker Highway, roughly a mile below Artist Point. The trail goes DOWN first — several hundred feet over its first mile and a half — before climbing back to the broad saddle above Lake Ann at roughly four miles.

Just past the saddle there is an unsigned fork. The right branch drops to the lake, the campsites and the outlet, which is the last easy water. The left branch is the climbers' boot path, and it is distinct and well trodden — a very obvious break heading east toward the mountain.

That path sidehills north beneath Shuksan's lower moraines, switchbacking and crossing two gullies over talus and lingering snow tongues, and becomes vague right where you need it most: just short of the first chimney. Parties typically reckon around six hours from the car to the high camp on or above the chimneys, and expect the snow tongues to be firm enough for microspikes and an axe in the early morning well into July.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: rockfall inside the chimneys, especially with parties above
firm or icy snow tongues on the talus traverse before the sun hits
the route-finding itself — the boot path deliberately goes obscure right at the chimney entrance
several dead-end side paths ending at cliff edges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the crux of the whole approach and it is regularly got wrong. Where the boot path fades, stop and look EAST at the cliff band. You want a small snowfield pushed up against the base of the cliff, with a right-slanting ramp of slope at its foot and, almost straight across from you, a deep green gully. Drop about fifty feet and cross straight over the talus and snow — usually there is an obvious boot pack — until you are at the cliffs.

The test that settles it: the correct gully has a beaten dirt TRAIL running up it and rock scoured clean by thousands of boots, and at its foot there is a rappel station slung around a tangle of dead tree roots. Look for the trail, not for a plausible line of weakness.

The negative markers are unambiguous. If you are looking up a gully whose rock is furred with moss or lichen, it is the wrong one. If you are climbing on heather with no path underfoot at any point on this route, you are off it. And there are tempting side paths that lead out to cliff-edge viewpoints and stop — if the ground ahead simply ends at a drop, reverse and find the trail again rather than pressing on. The chimneys are a braided ledge-and-step system, so it is also easy to overshoot the entrance entirely and end up traversing along the base of the cliff band past it; if the cliff on your right has become continuous with no green break in it, you have gone too far.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Creek from the old lodge site, up the White Salmon Glacier to the dividing shoulder
approach_variants.notes: Get the backcountry permit at the Glacier Public Service Center on the way in — it is required, not advisory. Then continue up the Mount Baker Highway to the pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge site, walk round the gate, and follow the old roadbed roughly a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. From the road-end, with adequate snow cover, drop northeast off-trail to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Roped travel usually begins at the toe, and the crevasse hazard grows through the season. Ascend glacier and moraine to a bivy below the first rock and ice barrier. Published bivy elevations for this route disagree by around a thousand feet — so the honest instruction is to camp at the rock outcrops on the eastern edge of the White Salmon, where the ridge meets the face, rather than at a number. The Hanging Glacier and North Face approach is in the White Salmon Creek drainage, one valley east of Price Lake — not on the Nooksack and Ruth Creek side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug. Earlier the valley is snow-covered and simpler but the true North Face above you sheds avalanches; later the crevasses on the White Salmon are open and the lower valley is alder
hazards: Frequent avalanches off the true North Face onto the traverse, worst in early season
Serac fall from the hanging glacier itself, which is described as very active
Open crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier that grow through the season
Brush and alder in the lower White Salmon valley once the snowline recedes
A traverse with no easy retreat once committed, and a bivy on the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
PRICE LAKE MUST STAY BELOW YOU AND TO YOUR WEST, AND THAT IS THE TEST. From the bivy the day is a traverse climber's LEFT, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier. In cloud you will not see the summit and you do not need to: the lake is the reference and it belongs on your left-hand side, downhill.

ARRIVAL: you are at the base of the technical climbing when you reach the SHOULDER — the snow-and-ice rib that divides the White Salmon cirque from the Price Glacier cirque. It is the only place on this traverse where the ground stops being a sidehill and becomes a defined rib with a cirque falling away on each side. Stand on it and you should be able to look down into two separate basins.

THE ERROR THAT KILLS PEOPLE HERE IS DRIFTING LEFT, and it is worth stating as a hard rule: stay RIGHT during the traverse. Going further left puts you onto the true North Face, which sheds avalanches frequently, especially early season. Left feels like progress toward the mountain and is the wrong direction.

AFTER 500 FT OF TRAVERSE the line goes UP, on a firn-and-ice finger west of the upper hanging glacier. If you are still traversing horizontally after a long way, you have gone past the finger and are running out under the face.

approach_variants.name: Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide, then down the White Salmon Glacier to the base
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative used by parties who would rather start from the standard trailhead than from the White Salmon roadbed: from the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, climb the Fisher Chimneys and Winnie's Slide to a bivy near the Upper Curtis Glacier, then descend about 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier and traverse the northwest rib to reach the foot of the Hanging Glacier.

It is longer in vertical terms because it climbs to a camp and then gives back a thousand feet, and it commits you to regaining that thousand feet on the way out if you return the same way. Its advantage is a maintained trail to a known camp instead of a valley bushwhack, and it does not require the White Salmon roadbed to be walkable.

No trailhead-to-base time is given for this variant; published figures for it vary too much to quote one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug, once the Lake Ann trail is out from under snow
hazards: A 1,000 ft descent that must be re-climbed on the return if you reverse this variant
Winnie's Slide, which is sometimes rappelled rather than downclimbed when icy
Crevasses on both the Lower Curtis and the White Salmon
Avalanche exposure from the true North Face during the traverse
Committing to a route whose descent normally exits a different valley from the one you started in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE FROM ABOVE, SO THE TEST IS INVERTED — YOU ARE LOOKING FOR THE BOTTOM OF A DESCENT, NOT THE TOP OF A CLIMB. From the Upper Curtis bivy you drop roughly 1,000 ft down the White Salmon Glacier. Stop descending when the ground lets you traverse northeast onto the northwest rib; if you keep going down the White Salmon you end up in the valley the other variant walked up, and you will have thrown away the whole approach.

THE RIB IS THE MARKER. The northwest rib is a defined feature between the White Salmon and the Hanging Glacier, and once you are on it the foot of the Hanging Glacier is the next thing you meet.

CONFIRM WITH THE SAME TEST THE OTHER VARIANT USES: from the base of the climbing, Price Lake should be below you and to the west, and you should be standing on the shoulder that separates the White Salmon cirque from the Price cirque, with a basin on each side of you.

AND THE SAME HARD RULE APPLIES: do not drift left onto the true North Face. It avalanches, and arriving from this side does not change that.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Lodge road (standard)
approach_variants.notes:
Pull off at the old White Salmon lodge site on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate, and follow the old road past the lodge for about a mile to where it finishes in an old clearcut.

What you do next depends entirely on snow cover, and getting this wrong is the single biggest time sink on the approach. With GOOD cover, drop northeast off the clearcut down to White Salmon Creek and walk the valley toward the toe of the White Salmon Glacier — pleasant going. WITHOUT good cover, do not descend into the valley at all: hold your elevation as you enter the clearcut and contour around instead, giving up height only where a rock band or a stream crossing forces it. The valley bottom without snow is slide alder and devil's club.

From the glacier area, the route continues up toward the shoulder at the foot of the face.
approach_variants.season: spring to early summer; needs snow cover
hazards: avalanches off the Hanging Glacier, which is very active and sweeps the approach terrain
slide alder and devil's club in the White Salmon valley once the snow has gone
unbridged stream crossings when contouring the low-snow variation
crevasses on the White Salmon Glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the shoulder at about 5,500 ft on the divide between the White Salmon Glacier and the Price cirque, and it is confirmed by what you can see BEHIND and BELOW you rather than above: from the shoulder you look down onto Price Lake. If Price Lake is not below you, you have not gained the shoulder — you are still on the glacier or on its moraine, and the face above you is foreshortened enough that it will look like the start.

The shoulder has good bivy sites, which is the second confirmation: flat ground here is scarce, so a usable bivy platform at this height on this ridge is the place.

From there the face itself is entered by a gully angling up and to the LEFT onto the North Face. Some parties instead continue up the glacier past the shoulder; if you have passed the bivy ground and are still on continuous glacier, you have gone by the entrance.

approach_variants.name: Mount Baker Ski Area (Chair 8) traverse
approach_variants.notes: An alternative used mainly by ski parties: start at the base of Chair 8 in the ski area and make a downhill traverse into the bottom of the White Salmon Creek valley, then climb over four thousand feet up the glacier. It removes the clearcut and the road walk at the cost of a long climb from the valley floor and a committing descent to start the day.
approach_variants.season: winter/spring, on skis
hazards: avalanche exposure from the Hanging Glacier across the whole basin
the initial descent commits you to regaining that height on the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same shoulder at roughly 5,500 ft with Price Lake visible below to the north-west. Coming up from the valley floor rather than contouring in, the trap is stopping at the first flat ground on the glacier's margin — keep going until you are on the divide itself and the ground on the far side falls away toward Price Lake.

approach_variants.name: White Salmon Creek roadbed, then the ridgecrest opposite the ski area
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR-542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. This first stretch is common to both options.

The direct option then drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest DIRECTLY OPPOSITE THE SKI AREA, then follows that crest to the base of the mountain's north side.

This is a long Cascade adventure route rather than a line with a bootpack: bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel, all in one day.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. This is the more direct of the two options and it is a bushwhack, so it wants the ground clear rather than snow-covered
hazards: Bushwhacking with no tread, where a wrong drainage costs a day
Runout climbing on loose rock high on the arête
Moderate alpine ice and extensive glacier travel on the same outing as the rock
A very long day, with no good bivy on the crest
A descent that exits down the upper and lower White Salmon Glacier rather than reversing the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SKI AREA IS THE ONE THING YOU CAN SEE FROM ANYWHERE, AND IT IS THE AIMING MARK. The crest you want is the one directly opposite the ski area across White Salmon Creek. Cross the creek, climb, and stop when you are on a crest with the ski area behind you and level with you. In flat light that back-bearing is more reliable than anything ahead of you, because the ski area's cut runs and lift lines are the only man-made shape in the drainage.

ARRIVAL AT THE ROUTE ITSELF: the crest is a ramp, not the climb. Follow it until it runs into the mountain's north side, and the arête proper is the pillar the crest delivers you to. It is roughly 1,300 ft of climbing above that point.

DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE ROUTES EITHER SIDE OF IT: this is a ROCK PILLAR, not a glacier and not a snow face. If the ground in front of you at the base is a glacier you are looking at the White Salmon; if it is a broad snow-and-ice face you are looking at the North Face. The northwest arête is the pillar between them, and the first ground you touch on it is rock.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the valley past the point where the opposite crest is climbable puts you on the other variant — up the valley to the lower White Salmon Glacier. That is a legitimate approach, but it is a different one, and mixing the two mid-way leaves you sidehilling.

approach_variants.name: Up the White Salmon valley to the lower glacier, then onto the crest
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative from the same parking: continue up the road as far as it goes, then travel off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier, and gain the crest of the arête from there.

It trades the creek crossing and the direct climb to the crest for more valley travel and a glacier approach. Parties choosing between the two are choosing between bushwhack-then-ridge and valley-then-glacier; both are documented and neither is a shortcut.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Extensive glacier travel with crevasse hazard on the lower White Salmon
Off-trail valley travel with no tread and brush low down
Loose rock and runout climbing on the arête above
Complex route-finding, one of the route's defining features
No quick retreat: the descent is a separate glacier descent, not a reverse of the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GLACIER IS THE HANDRAIL, AND YOU LEAVE IT WHEN THE ROCK STARTS. Stay in the valley until the slopes open enough to walk onto the lower White Salmon Glacier, then work up the glacier with the arête's rock on your side and step onto it where the two meet.

THE TEST THAT SETTLES IT is the same one the direct variant uses, from the other direction: at the base of this route you are on ROCK, with the White Salmon Glacier on one side of the pillar and the North Face ground on the other. If you can still see glacier on both sides of you, you have not stepped onto the arête yet.

WHAT DROPPING TOO LOW LOOKS LIKE: if the valley narrows and you are still in trees and brush with no open slope, you have not gone far enough up-valley to reach the glacier access, and pushing sideways onto the mountain from there puts you on steep vegetated ground below the pillar rather than at its foot.

AND THE ORIENTATION CHECK: the descent for this route comes down the upper and then the lower White Salmon Glacier and deposits you back in this drainage. If your intended base is somewhere you could not plausibly walk back to down a glacier on this side, you are on the wrong side of the mountain.

approach_variants.name: Nooksack Cirque Trail #750 via Hannegan Pass Road
approach_variants.notes:
Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32) off the Mount Baker Highway, then Nooksack Cirque Road (FS-34) to its end. There is no bridge over Ruth Creek at the trailhead — the crossing is on a large logjam a little downstream, and in high water or after rain it has turned parties around before they started.

Beyond the crossing the old roadbed runs about two miles through old growth to the original trailhead, then it is river-bottom travel along the North Fork Nooksack: gravel bars when the water is low, riparian brush when it is not. You pass the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary at roughly three miles and the national park boundary at about four.

Rather than continuing into the cirque, leave the tread and watch ACROSS the valley for the steep drainage of Price Creek. Cross the Nooksack on a log and climb the forested hillside toward Price Lake — steep, open forest with old flagging, about an hour and a half from the river to the lake basin at roughly 4,700 ft. Budget the better part of a day for the approach; most parties treat the whole climb as two to three days.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun; a heavy snowpack is preferred
hazards: unbridged Ruth Creek log crossing, sometimes impassable
brush and vague route-finding along the river flats
steep, loose, unofficial climbers' path to Price Lake
rockfall and icefall down the gully between Nooksack Tower and the glacier's main lobe — large blocks reported
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two candidate stopping points and they are not the same place. From the moraine below Price Lake, work up through the cliff bands onto the heathery ridge on the lake's SOUTH side, then ascend the rock slabs up and to the RIGHT. The first bivy sites are flat granite just below the ridge crest at the glacier's margin, around 6,000-6,500 ft — that is a camp, not the start of the route.

The start of the climbing is the exposed snow saddle beneath Nooksack Tower, roughly an hour further along the glacier. You get there by gaining the glacier at the ridge crest and traversing climber's right. You will know you are there because Nooksack Tower's mass is directly above you and the gully between the tower and the main lobe of the Price is the thing you are trying to get past — it is the rockfall funnel, and it has delivered blocks the size of a television down onto the traverse.

If you are still on heather and slabs above Price Lake with no glacier underfoot, you are below the start. If you are on flat granite with a view down to the lake, you are at the bivy, not the saddle.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the Mildred Lakes trailhead; no pass or fee is needed to park at the Putvin trailhead. Entering via Staircase/Olympic NP requires the $30 park entrance fee (7-day private-vehicle pass; $15 for a walk-in/bike individual pass) or an interagency pass, plus an $8 per person per night backcountry camping fee (booked via Recreation.gov) for Flapjack Lakes.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness regulations apply (no bikes/motorized use, max group size limits, camp 200 ft from water). Mountain goats are frequently encountered around the peak's base and Lake of the Angels basin — do not approach or feed them; give them a wide berth as they can be aggressive toward hikers seeking salt.
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required for day trips on Olympic National Forest land (Mildred Lakes, Putvin Trail). Camping at Lake of the Angels, which lies inside Olympic National Park, requires an Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit. If approaching via Flapjack Lakes inside Olympic National Park, an overnight wilderness camping permit is required, reservable on Recreation.gov for the Flapjack Lakes zone (bookable mid-April, camping dates mid-June through mid-October); contact the Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100.
access.closures: UPDATED (as of July 8, 2026): the Mildred Lakes Trail (#822) and Mildred Lakes Trailhead on FS-25 — along with the Mt. Rose Trail/Trailhead, Dry Creek East Trailhead, and the Staircase developed area (campground, ranger station, Rapids Loop Trail) — REOPENED on July 8, 2026 per a joint Olympic National Forest/Olympic National Park press release, ending the closure tied to the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire. Still CLOSED pending hazard-tree removal and infrastructure repair: wilderness trails beyond the developed Staircase area, including the North Fork Skokomish River Trail (from the Staircase Rapids Loop to Home Sweet Home) and the Flapjack Lakes Trail, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, plus FS-2451 and the Copper Creek Trail (Olympic National Forest alert updated July 8, 2026). The Putvin Trail/Lake of the Angels approach, on a different drainage further north off Hamma Hamma River Road, was never part of this closure and remains the standard approach to Mount Skokomish. Always check the Olympic National Forest alerts page and NPS Olympic fire-conditions page before a trip, as backcountry trail status keeps changing as repair work continues through summer 2026.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest (Hood Canal Ranger District) for the Mildred Lakes and Putvin trailheads; Olympic National Park (Wilderness Information Center) for the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish/Flapjack Lakes side.
access.land_manager: Olympic National Forest (Hood Canal Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: None for day use; NPS wilderness permit for overnight camping.

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit
overnight_permit.where: Get it in advance on Recreation.gov, by phone, or in person at a park Wilderness Information Center.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
approach_variants.notes: THIS IS THE STANDARD APPROACH AND THE ROUTE'S WAYPOINT LIST DESCRIBES A DIFFERENT ONE. Published and trip-report accounts are consistent that Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels. The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAND AT LAKE OF THE ANGELS AND THE CIRQUE ITSELF TELLS YOU WHICH WAY TO GO: MOUNT STONE IS ON YOUR RIGHT, ANOTHER PEAK IS ON YOUR LEFT, AND MOUNT SKOKOMISH IS STRAIGHT AHEAD. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

THE TURN IS AROUND THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE LAKE, on a way trail heading WEST to the ridge. Then take a broad gully SOUTHWEST and up toward the SADDLE JUST NORTH OF POINT 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud, which is why it is quoted here rather than a description of the terrain.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours SOUTH and SOUTHWEST across scree, grass and rock benches around the EAST and SOUTH flanks of the peak, PASSING A LARGE TARN. The tarn is the confirmation. TURN RIGHT AND START CLIMBING WHEN YOU ARE ABOVE THE LARGE TARN — that is the published trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

THIRD TEST, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around LEFT to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has THREE SUMMIT HORNS and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

EXPLICIT WARNING FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is directional: contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut WEST over the ridge instead.

approach_variants.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
approach_variants.notes: RECORDED BECAUSE THE ROUTE'S OWN WAYPOINTS DESCRIBE THIS APPROACH, not because it is the standard one. It is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln. From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford HUCKLEBERRY CREEK at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot ROOT AND ROCK LADDERS, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail.
