Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — in the Bear Gulch Fire closure area
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE ON THIS SIDE IS THE OPEN BASIN AND SADDLE BENEATH THE SOUTH PEAK AT ABOUT 5,500 FT, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS UNDERFOOT: THE FOOTING TURNS TO LOOSE, ROTTEN ROCK FROM THERE UP. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything. THE TEST FOR THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE ROOT LADDER, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then DESCENDS off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one. HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS VARIANT IS SECOND: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. Published and trip-report accounts put the standard route on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin camp
approach_variants.notes: Book a water taxi for the long run up Ross Lake and get dropped at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft; above that the route is cross-country with occasional blazes, across slide alder and forest slopes, to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft. This is the shorter side for this particular route and it keeps the whole trip inside the United States, at the cost of depending on a boat.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the old cabin
crevasses on the glacier above the col
a wide gully that collects anything falling from the slopes above it
a high camp with a long committing retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A COL, NOT ON A FACE, AND THE COL IS BETWEEN TWO PEAKS. From the lake basin camp, gain the WIDE GULLY ON THE NORTH SIDE OF THE SADDLE and climb it to the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. The glacier route begins there.

RECOGNISE THE COL BY WHAT IS ON BOTH SIDES OF IT. You should be standing in a gap with a summit rising to either hand and ground falling away in front and behind. IF THE MOUNTAIN IS ABOVE YOU AND THERE IS NOTHING BEHIND YOU BUT THE SLOPE YOU CAME UP, YOU ARE ON A SHOULDER RATHER THAN THE COL.

THE GULLY IS THE POSITIVE MARKER ON THE WAY UP - a wide one, on the NORTH side of the saddle. A narrow gully, or one on the south side, is a different line.

AND THE NEGATIVE MARKER THAT MATTERS MOST: THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE ON THIS PEAK STARTS AT THE TOE OF A DIFFERENT GLACIER ON THE OTHER FLANK, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border, over the col between the two peaks
approach_variants.notes: The other way in starts on the Canadian side: a rough spur off the lake road to a washout at about 2,600 ft, an overgrown roadbed to the boundary obelisk and register, and then the climbers' path up the creek through old growth to the falls, whose wet slabs and old fixed hand-line are the crux of the walk-in. Above them the path leads to the lake camp at about 5,700 ft. From that camp the way to this route climbs toward and over the col between the two peaks rather than onto the south-west side.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, and only with passports
hazards: an international border crossing on foot
wet slabs and an old fixed hand-line at the falls
an overgrown approach road that washes out
crevasses on the ice above the col
two routes leaving one camp, with the wrong turn costing a day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE DEPOT CREEK CAMP YOU ARE APPROACHING THE COL FROM THE OPPOSITE SIDE, so descriptions written from the other camp will have the gully and the col in the wrong relative positions - read the ground rather than the page.

THE FIXED POINT IS THE SAME: THE COL AT ABOUT 7,380 FT BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS NEIGHBOUR TO THE NORTH-WEST. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully on the col's north side is the connection to the basin on the far side.

THE TEST THAT YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT GAP is that BOTH summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

DO NOT CONFUSE THIS START WITH THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME CAMP. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. IF YOU HAVE NOT GAINED A COL, YOU ARE NOT ON THIS ROUTE.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, for a crossable glacier and a passable creek
hazards: an international border crossing on foot, with a register at the obelisk
a road that washes out and lengthens the walk without warning
wet slick boulders and slabs at the base of the falls, with an old fixed hand-line of unknown condition
crevasses on the south-west glacier and one marginal snow bridge on the standard line
a short steep loose gully at the head of the glacier
thirty-five to forty degree snow near the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CRITICAL INSTRUCTION IS THAT YOU LEAVE THE DRAINAGE BEFORE THE PASS, NOT AT IT. From camp, ascend the broad talus couloir and stream drainage north to north-east toward the saddle at roughly 7,200 ft - but WELL BEFORE reaching that saddle, cut RIGHT around the toe of a steep rocky buttress into open heather and moraine basins.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS EXACT AND EASY TO USE: IF YOU HAVE ARRIVED AT THE SADDLE AND ARE LOOKING DOWN INTO THE CIRQUE ON THE FAR SIDE, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR. Go back down and find the buttress toe.

THE BUTTRESS TOE IS THE FEATURE - a steep rock nose that the couloir runs past on its left. Turning its foot puts you into open heather and moraine, which is different ground from the couloir you have been climbing, and that change underfoot is the confirmation.

THE BASE IS THE TOE OF THE SOUTH-WEST GLACIER, reached by traversing those basins. Rope up and put crampons on there rather than part-way across. THE LINE UP THE ICE IS ITS CLIMBER'S-RIGHT MARGIN, which holds hard snow and ice at thirty to forty degrees and relatively few crevasses; about half-way up, one poor-looking crevasse has to be crossed on a marginal bridge, so probe it and expect it to be worse late in the season.

CONFIRM AT THE TOP OF THE ICE: a short steep loose rock gully at the glacier's head tops out on a low col on the south-west ridge, above the cirque. That col is where the summit scramble starts. If the ice runs you out onto a broad snow shoulder with no gully and no col, you have taken the glacier's centre or its left side instead of its right margin.

approach_variants.name: From Ross Lake by boat and up Silver Creek to the lake basin
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the mountain is reached without leaving the United States. A booked water taxi runs a long way up Ross Lake to a drop at the mouth of Silver Creek at about 1,600 ft. A trail climbs the north side of the creek for roughly two and a half miles to an old cabin at about 2,900 ft, above which the way is cross-country with occasional blazes across slide alder and forest slopes to the camp in the Silver Lake basin at about 6,763 ft.

This puts you on the opposite side of the peak from the Depot Creek camp, so it changes which col you reach and in what order - plan the climb from this camp rather than translating a description written from the other one.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the boat is running and the cross-country is clear of snow
hazards: a booked boat on a lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
slide alder and unmarked cross-country above the cabin
a long carry to a high camp
crevasses on the glaciers either side of the divide
a camp position that makes descriptions written from the other approach misleading
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE OLD CABIN AT ABOUT 2,900 FT IS THE PROOF YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE CREEK. The trail climbs the NORTH side; if you have not passed a cabin by the time the trail gives out, you are on the wrong bank and should cross before the cross-country starts, not after.

ABOVE THE CABIN THE MARKERS ARE OCCASIONAL BLAZES ON TREES rather than tread. Blazes that stop appearing mean you have drifted; the slide alder will let you keep going anyway, which is why this is worth checking rather than assuming.

THE CAMP IS THE LAKE BASIN AT ABOUT 6,763 FT, and from it the route to this peak's south-west side goes up and over toward the col between it and its neighbour to the north-west.

BE CLEAR WHICH ROUTE YOU ARE ON WHEN YOU ARRIVE. From this side the natural line gains the col at about 7,380 ft between the two peaks, which is where the glacier route on the north side starts. THE SOUTH-WEST ROUTE INSTEAD WANTS THE TOE OF THE SOUTH-WEST GLACIER, WHICH IS REACHED BY TRAVERSING INTO OPEN HEATHER AND MORAINE BASINS ROUND THE TOE OF A ROCK BUTTRESS, NOT BY GAINING A COL. If you find yourself standing in a saddle between two summits, you are on the other route's start.

approach_variants.name: Climbers Bivouac and the Ptarmigan Trail to the marked ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Climbers Bivouac trailhead at about 3,700 ft — the highest vehicle access on this side of the mountain — start on the signed Ptarmigan Trail #216A through open forest. It climbs a moderate 1,100 ft over about 2.25 miles to timberline near 4,800 ft. That is the last shade and the last practical water; a couple of small seasonal creeklets cross the lower trail and nothing is reliable above, so most parties carry everything from the car.

At timberline the trail ends and the route moves onto the open volcanic slopes of Monitor Ridge itself: a broad rib of old lava flows flanked by loose pumice and ash.

A permit is required above 4,800 ft year-round and is checked at or near the trailhead.

There is no technical climbing here. It is a long, steep hike and scramble, and the difficulty is navigation and footing rather than terrain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct for the summer route; full winter conditions with ice axe and crampons can apply well into late spring
hazards: Losing the wooden posts in fog or whiteout, which puts parties onto steep loose off-route ground
Unstable cornices and fall-through risk at the crater rim
Deep loose pumice and ash above 7,000 ft with poor footing in both directions
No water above the lower trail
Full winter conditions and avalanche terrain on the upper slopes well into late spring
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE POSTS ARE THE ROUTE, AND KNOWING WHERE THEY END IS THE WHOLE FINDING.

FROM TIMBERLINE AT ABOUT 4,800 FT TO ABOUT 7,000 FT THE LINE IS MARKED BY LARGE WOODEN POSTS. They end at the monitoring equipment near 7,000 ft. Above that, the last roughly 1,300 ft to the crater rim is unmarked ash, pumice and scattered rock.

SO THE TEST IN FOG IS A NEGATIVE AND IT IS EXACT: IF THE POSTS HAVE STOPPED AND YOU HAVE NOT PASSED THE MONITORING EQUIPMENT, YOU HAVE DRIFTED OFF THE LINE — you have not finished the marked section. Stop and go back to the last post you saw rather than continuing on a bearing. Losing the posts is the single biggest route-finding hazard on this climb, and a small drift puts you on steep loose off-route ground.

THE SURFACE TEST TELLS YOU WHETHER YOU ARE ON THE RIB OR BESIDE IT: the route climbs the ROCK RIBS of old lava. If you are sliding two steps back for every step up in loose ash, you are in the gullies beside the rib. Move onto the rock — it is both faster and a signal you have found the line again.

THE TOP IS NOT WHERE YOU THINK: the crater rim at about 8,363 ft is the top of the climbing, and the true high point is a walk along the rim from where you arrive. Do not treat first sight of the crater as the summit.

AND THE RIM ITSELF IS A NEGATIVE, NOT A MARKER: it is corniced and unstable with a history of fall-throughs. Do not walk to the edge to work out where you are.

bivy.name: Climbers Bivouac
bivy.notes: The summer roadhead for Monitor Ridge, and effectively the only place to sleep close to that route, since the mountain above 4,800 feet is closed to camping. It is a rough clearing in second-growth timber at the end of a Forest Service road, with tent pads and fire rings but nothing else, and the sites are small and packed in. The value is purely positional: the summit trail leaves from here and a night at the trailhead turns a long day into a manageable one. Plan the permit before the campsite, because the permit is the real constraint — the quota tightens sharply in mid-May, and the whole summer sells on release day. Arrive with your blue bag and use it; there is a composting toilet where the trail meets the tree line, and above that there is nothing at all.
bivy.water: None. There is no water at the trailhead, so carry everything you need for the night and for the climb. Pit toilets are provided
bivy.permit: Camping itself is free, but the parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass, or a small day fee. SEPARATELY AND UNAVOIDABLY, a climbing permit is required year round for anyone going above 4,800 feet on the mountain, and camping above 4,800 feet is prohibited outright. From April 1 to October 31 that permit carries a daily quota and a per-climber fee of about twenty dollars: 350 climbers a day from April 1 to May 14, then only 110 a day from May 15 through October 31. Permits are sold first come, first served with no lottery, released a month at a time on the first day of the preceding month at seven in the morning Pacific time, and the summer dates sell out within minutes of release. From November 1 to March 31 the permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead with no quota. Blue bags are mandatory for all human waste above the tree line and are stocked at the trailhead kiosk.
bivy.capacity: Around fourteen small primitive tent sites, close together, first come and first served only; motorhomes and trailers are directed elsewhere

approach_variants.name: Marble Mountain Sno-Park and the Swift Creek Trail to Worm Flow Ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Marble Mountain Sno-Park at about 2,700-2,800 ft, follow the Swift Creek Trail #244 north into forest, marked in winter by blue diamond blazes on the trees. It climbs steadily through timber for roughly 2 miles to about 3,700-3,750 ft, breaking out of the trees near Chocolate Falls on Swift Creek.

Just above the falls, cross to the WEST side of Swift Creek. This ford can be swollen with meltwater in spring or after a warm spell, and the crossing point and its sign are often buried in winter snowpack.

Above treeline the route enters the open barren Worm Flows lava and mudflow terrain. Wooden posts mark the line from about 3,700 to roughly 4,800 ft; above that the posts thin out and occasional cairns, plus wands placed by parties, mark broad ridges and open slopes. The route follows Worm Flow Ridge past an old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft, then up snow and scree to merge with the summer Monitor Ridge line at about 7,400 ft, and roughly 850 ft more to the crater rim.

A Sno-Park permit is required to park in the winter months. This is the standard winter and spring access because the summer trailhead on the far side is snow-gated.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, with the best conditions typically Feb-Apr when the snowpack is deep enough to bury the loose ash and consolidated enough to climb and glissade
hazards: Whiteout descents into the wrong drainage — the documented failure mode on this route
Avalanche terrain on loaded slopes and in gully bottoms after new snow or wind loading
Cornice collapse and unstable footing at the crater rim
A Swift Creek ford that can run fast with meltwater and whose crossing point is buried in winter
High wind exposure across the open upper mountain
No reliable water above Chocolate Falls
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THREE HARD MARKERS, IN ORDER, AND THEY WORK BECAUSE THEY ARE OBJECTS RATHER THAN DESCRIPTIONS OF SLOPE — which matters here, since snow buries everything else.

ONE: CHOCOLATE FALLS, at about 3,700-3,750 ft, where the trail breaks out of the trees. You cross to the west side of Swift Creek JUST ABOVE THE FALLS. In winter the crossing point and its sign are usually under snow, so treat the falls themselves as the marker and never a sign.

TWO: WOODEN POSTS, from about 3,700 to about 4,800 ft. Above 4,800 they thin to cairns and wands.

THREE: THE OLD SEISMIC MONITORING STATION near 6,200 ft on Worm Flow Ridge. This is the last hard object on the whole route and the best single confirmation you are on the ridge and not on one of the broad open slopes beside it.

THE NEGATIVE THAT CATCHES PARTIES LOW: if you have crossed Swift Creek and are STILL IN TREES, you crossed too low — below the falls. Regain the east bank and keep climbing to the treeline break.

THE MERGE AT ABOUT 7,400 FT IS THE LAST CHECK: from there you are on the summer Monitor Ridge line and it is roughly 850 ft to the rim.

THE MOST IMPORTANT FINDING ON THIS ROUTE IS ABOUT COMING DOWN, NOT GOING UP. Whiteout wrong-drainage descents are the documented failure here. From the rim the correct line is back down WORM FLOW RIDGE — a ridge, not a gully. Do not descend into a gully because it is going downhill; and record your bearings on the way up while you can still see the ridge you are on.

bivy.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
bivy.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
bivy.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

bivy.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
bivy.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
bivy.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

bivy.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
bivy.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
bivy.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
bivy.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

bivy.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
bivy.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire: the park still lists the North Fork Skokomish and Home Sweet Home trails closed, with no reopening date, on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, and while they stay closed this is the direct way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

approach_variants.name: Olney Creek Road gate, the closed logging road and One Acre Lake
approach_variants.notes: The drive ends at the gate where Olney Creek Road leaves the Sultan Basin Road, and the day starts on foot up the closed roadbed. Walk the road uphill for a little over two miles, past a first switchback and on to a second one where the grade noticeably eases around 3,700 ft — that second switchback is the key junction and there is nothing signed about it. Mapped road alignments in this area are known to be wrong, so trust the switchback you can see on the ground over the line drawn on a map. Leave the road there and pick up an unsigned but well-established boot path on the right, north side, which climbs onto a forest ridge crest and follows it. The path fades out somewhere around 4,050 to 4,200 ft; from there leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge and cross open slopes into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake. Pass the lake on its east side, follow the drainage above it to a cluster of small tarns, and then work up and around toward the bowl directly beneath the summit block. This mid-mountain sequence — road to ridge path to cross-country bench — is the crux of the walk-in and is easy to lose in fog or on a first visit.
approach_variants.season: July through September once the gully has melted out and the lower brush has died back. The gully holds snow and ice into June, and it refreezes with the first fall storms. It is also climbed as a snow route in winter and spring, when parties rope up for the final pitch and manage cornice and avalanche hazard.
hazards: a short, steep, exposed fourth-class gully near the summit — loose, often wet and muddy, and the real crux
at least one avalanche-prone slope below the summit bowl in winter and spring
cornices along the summit ridge that can look like solid ground
dense slide alder and devil's club on the lower off-trail sections
an unreliable gate status on the access road that can add unplanned miles
mapped road alignments that do not match the road on the ground
approach_variants.baseFinding: TAKE THE GULLY ON THE RIGHT, THE ONE THAT TOPS OUT JUST WEST OF THE SUMMIT. From the rocky basin and boulder field beneath the summit block, more than one weakness leads toward the crest. The correct one is the gully to the RIGHT, immediately west of the summit hump, and it runs to the notch just under the summit ridge. Its condition is the second identifier and it is not a pleasant one: this gully is characteristically wet, muddy and loose, easy fourth class on dirt and rock rather than clean stone, and it becomes noticeably harder once the snow that fills it in winter and spring has melted out. Near the top of it are natural anchor options — slings around trees and rock horns, including one built around a mountain hemlock — because parties who dislike downclimbing it rappel roughly fifty to sixty feet past the steepest section. If the gully you are in tops out anywhere other than the crest immediately west of the summit hump, it is the wrong one. Above the notch, the ridge runs east across a small plateau and then a short, genuinely airy section to the final rock hump; stay climbers' right through the difficult bits and rig a hand line if anyone is uneasy, since cornices along this crest look solid and are not.

bivy.name: One Acre Lake, under Mount Stickney
bivy.notes: The one place worth camping on Mount Stickney, and the reason the peak is doable at all now that the road is gated low. The route leaves the Sultan Basin road onto the old Olney Creek logging road, which used to let a high-clearance vehicle grind up to around 2,100 feet and is now closed at its very beginning, so the road walk is five to six miles before any climbing starts. Where the road levels near 3,700 feet a trail cuts off to the right along a ridge; leave that around 4,050 feet and traverse southeast to the lake. From camp the route continues southeast past a set of tarns near 4,500 feet, up to about 4,800, and then traverses into the boulder basin below the summit, taking a gully just west of the top to gain the crest. THIS IS A WINTER AND EARLY SPRING PEAK by preference, not a summer one: the low western start means it comes into condition when everything else is buried, and deep snow covers a boulder field that is loose, awkward and slow when bare. The trade is that the same snow brings real avalanche exposure on the traverses above the lake, and early-season parties have found route-finding and slope assessment to be the hard part rather than the climbing. Expect a long day either way, and expect the road walk to feel longer on the way out.
bivy.water: The lake, and snowmelt in the drainages above it well into July. Treat everything; the basin is shallow and the water warms.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is outside the Wild Sky boundary on a mix of state and federal land. No pass at the gated roadhead. Fires are a poor idea in a basin this small and are restricted through most summers.
bivy.capacity: A few flat spots on the benches around a small tarn, informal and unimproved. Two or three tents.

bivy.name: Sultan Basin road pullouts and the Olney Creek gate
bivy.notes: A pure staging pullout for Mount Stickney, included because the road walk is now long enough that starting it at first light matters. From US 2 in Sultan, the Sultan Basin road runs north for roughly eleven and a half miles before the Olney Creek road turns off on the right, and the gate is at the very start of that turn. Sleeping at the gate saves an hour of driving in the dark and puts the five-to-six mile approach march in the coolest part of the morning. The Sultan Basin road is paved for its lower miles and gravel above; it is generally drivable in a normal car to the gate, but conditions after a wet winter are worth checking. This is working forest and watershed land rather than recreation land, so expect industrial traffic, expect gates to move, and do not count on a pullout being available where it was last year. There is no established camping anywhere between here and One Acre Lake.
bivy.water: Olney Creek, a short way along the closed road, where a spur drops to a bridge and a gravel bar. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Mixed state and municipal watershed land, with day-use restrictions posted in places and gates that change. Read the signs at the gate rather than assuming dispersed camping is permitted where you have parked. Fire restrictions here are usually stricter than on national forest and are enforced.
bivy.capacity: Gravel pullouts and a turnaround at the gate. Room to sleep in or beside a vehicle, nothing more. No toilet, no table, no fire ring you should trust.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
approach_variants.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the basin above the lake well into summer
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, genuinely exposed when wet, and worse descending on tired legs
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block with rockfall onto parties below
An ambiguous Class 3/4 crux near the summit
Fog is common here and multiple parties have lost the route on the upper mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS A NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S WEST RIDGE, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS A TURN YOU MAKE BEFORE A GATE. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward ST. PETER'S GATE — the obvious notch above the basin. JUST BEFORE THE GATE, TURN SHARPLY LEFT (SOUTH) and traverse along the BASE OF THE CLIFFS to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through. That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill. SECOND TEST, at the notch: turn RIGHT and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short LOW CLASS 3 CHIMNEY to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line. THIRD TEST, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a GROOVE on the LEFT side that BENDS RIGHT, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it. WHAT THE ROUTE'S OWN TIMING SAYS: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate. FOG WARNING SPECIFIC TO THIS MOUNTAIN: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
hazards: Extensive off-trail way-trail route-finding over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes on the final ramp
Fog on the upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route here and ended up in harder terrain
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
A very long approach with limited bail options partway through
approach_variants.baseFinding: COMING FROM THE EAST YOU ARRIVE AT ST. PETER'S GATE ITSELF, WHICH IS THE HIGH POINT OF THE TRAVERSE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT AND AN OBVIOUS ROCKY NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S SOUTHEAST RIDGE. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side. FROM THE GATE THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO THE PEAK AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT CLIMBS. The one this route describes is the west-ridge notch: go THROUGH the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the WEST ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse route's line, not this one. SO THE FOG TEST FOR THIS VARIANT IS WHICH SIDE OF THE GATE YOU END UP ON: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder. ABOVE THE NOTCH THE TESTS ARE IDENTICAL to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 CHIMNEY to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a GROOVE on the LEFT that BENDS RIGHT to the true south summit.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail #813 to Lake of the Angels, then the traverse under the cliff band
approach_variants.notes: this route and the Lake of the Angels route appear to be the same climb entered twice. The variants here are written for the ground the route itself describes. Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813) at about 1,565 ft on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25). A slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles; check Forest Service status. The trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek a few hundred feet, then starts a long unrelenting climbing traverse west, gaining nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles without easing. Around 1.3 miles it crosses an OLD LOGGING ROAD, and the tread is easy to lose there — look for the continuation slightly DOWNHILL. Around 4,200 ft comes the short headwall with an old hand-line or a large exposed tree root as the handhold, the crux of the trail and a common turnaround point when wet. Maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles at about 4,500 ft, and a rougher way-trail continues up steep rocky ground to Lake of the Angels at about 4,900 ft near 4 miles.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Consolidated snow has been reported from about 4,500 ft up well into summer in the north-facing basin above the lake
hazards: Exposed scramble moves near the summit block and a 15-20 ft Class 4 crack step with no fixed anchor
Lingering steep snow in the north-facing basin above the lake into early-mid summer
Route-finding above Lake of the Angels is loose and nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow
The 4,200 ft headwall on the trail is greasy when wet and the hand-line is not maintained
The tread is easy to lose where it crosses the old logging road at about 1.3 miles
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE CLIMB STARTS WHERE THE TRAIL ENDS, AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A CLIFF BAND, NOT A SUMMIT VIEW. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail: a boot path climbs a couple of hundred feet toward ST. PETER'S GATE, and SHORT OF THE GATE you turn LEFT along the BASE OF THE LONG CLIFF BAND. Rock wall at your shoulder on one side and scree dropping away on the other is a check you can make in cloud without seeing anything further. SECOND TEST: along the cliff base, Class 2-3 ground and a couple of narrow chutes lead up toward a NOTCH ON MOUNT STONE'S WEST RIDGE, BELOW the feature called ST. PETER'S GATE. Below, not through. St. Peter's Gate is the notch in the SOUTHEAST ridge and it belongs to the traverse from Lena Lake; the notch you want is on the WEST ridge and sits lower and to the south of it. If you have walked up to a notch that opens onto an entirely different basin to the east, that is the Gate and you are past your turn. THIRD TEST, on the summit block: the final 150 to 200 ft is mostly Class 3 but contains one well-documented 15 to 20 ft CLASS 4 STEP up a SHALLOW CRACK, often marked by a CAIRN. A cairn is man-made and does not move. If you have reached the top without meeting a short crack step, you are on a sub-summit — this mountain has three, and parties confuse them in fog. WHAT THE ROUTE'S OWN TIMING SAYS: Mountaineers reports for this line log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car to car. CAUTION FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is route-finding advice rather than a hazard note: at least one party took a steep mossy waterfall gully as a descent shortcut and found it far worse than reversing the ascent. Reverse the cliff-base traverse; do not improvise a line down the south side.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the St. Peter's traverse, arriving at the Gate from the east
approach_variants.notes:
The long way to the same mountain, kept here because it is a genuinely different approach rather than a variation of the Putvin walk. Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft and 6.5 miles. From there, off-trail west past Lena Tarn and Scout Lake to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake and round into Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above Ullin's Bathtubs, then a rising traverse to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending on loose moraine, and finally exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

Most parties then continue southwest about half a mile into the Lake of the Angels basin, which is where this approach rejoins the Putvin ground, and exit down the Putvin Trail — a different trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake, so plan a shuttle or a stashed bike.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Extensive off-trail route-finding across Scout Pass, Scout Basin and Ullin's Pass on faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt slopes below St. Peter's Gate
Requires a car shuttle or stashed bike between two trailheads about 4 road miles apart
Fog on the upper mountain, where parties have repeatedly lost the route
Unbridged stream crossings on the way-trail sections
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ARRIVAL TEST IS ST. PETER'S GATE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT: the traverse's high point, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's SOUTHEAST ridge, reached up a steep snow-and-dirt ramp over loose moraine. Ground stops rising, notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens beyond. THE TEST THAT PUTS YOU ON THIS ROUTE'S LINE RATHER THAN THE GULLY LINE: from the Gate, continue southwest into the Lake of the Angels basin and pick the route up from there — the traverse left along the base of the cliff band, and Class 2-3 ground to the notch on the WEST ridge below the Gate. The alternative from the Gate is to drop about 300 ft directly to the base of a basalt cliff and take the south-face gully; that is the Lena Lake traverse route, a Class 3-4 gully, and a different climb. ABOVE THE WEST-RIDGE NOTCH THE TEST IS THE SAME: a short Class 4 step up a shallow crack, often cairned, in the last 150 to 200 ft, on a mountain with three summits. HONEST LIMIT: coming from the east adds a day and several passes of unmarked way-trail. It is chosen for the country, not for the climb.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
approach_variants.notes: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference. Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach. From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft. Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (east) about a mile to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir. This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus
hazards: Sun-exposed hillside to Longs Pass with no water and no shade
Ingalls Creek can run high in early-season melt; find the summer log rather than fording blind
The couloir is loose top to bottom — sand, scree and unstable blocks; serious rockfall risk from parties above
Upper couloir braids into a maze of use-paths and cairns; genuinely confusing in cloud or at dawn/dusk
The 8,800 ft snowfield must be passed on the climber's left
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Look at the mountain from Longs Pass and settle the line there. It is the only point on the approach where the entire south face is laid out in front of you, and once you have dropped to the valley floor at 4,800 ft the couloir's mouth is one of several timbered gully mouths that all look alike from below and from inside the trees.

What you are aiming for: the couloir bottoms out in the meadow at roughly 4,800 ft, upvalley (east) of where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, and a beaten climbers' path leaves the meadow directly into it. It is a wide, sandy, scree-floored trough rather than a narrow cleft, and it runs unbroken for about 4,000 ft.

The confirmation that you are in the right gully comes about two thirds of the way up: a permanent snowfield around 8,800 ft, just south of the false summit. The established talus path passes it on the CLIMBER'S LEFT. Parties who take the right-hand side of that snowfield end up on much harder ground and have found old rappel-station remnants there — that is the tell that you have gone wrong, not a sign you are on route.

The couloir does not top out on the summit. It delivers you to the false summit at about 9,200 ft; the true summit at 9,415 ft is a class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge from there, and this is the second place parties in cloud go wrong — stopping at the false summit, or dropping off it in the wrong direction on the way down.

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
approach_variants.notes:
The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.
approach_variants.season: May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier
hazards: FR 9737 unmaintained in winter/spring — verify access before driving out
Avalanche exposure on the Longs Pass hillside and in the couloir itself
South-facing: wet-slide and rockfall risk build through the day, so an early turnaround is not optional
Firm/icy snow at dawn on the north side of Longs Pass
Uncontrolled glissade on descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow cover the couloir reads far more clearly from the valley than it does in summer — it is the continuous white ribbon running the full height of the south face, and the timbered gully mouths that confuse people in August are buried. Still take the look from Longs Pass, because the valley-floor approach is in trees.

The 8,800 ft snowfield that is a landmark in summer is not a distinct feature when everything is snow, so the useful marker on the way up is the false summit at about 9,200 ft where the couloir ends. Do not treat topping out as summiting; the true summit is a scramble further east along the ridge.

On the descent in these conditions the risk inverts: the couloir is a glissade or boot-ski for most of its length and parties overrun themselves. Keep the axe in hand.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

approach_variants.name: Ice Cliff Glacier to the top of the ice, then four easy pitches to the pillar
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the Ice Cliff Glacier's approach, and everything said about that line applies here: from the Stuart Lake trailhead follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake junction, leave it where it turns uphill for Stuart Lake, cross Mountaineer Creek and follow the climbers' path in the valley bottom to the hanging basin under the glaciers. Moraine camps sit around 6,800-7,000 ft; the flat basin below at about 5,400 ft is the more common bivy.

From camp the route ropes up and climbs the Ice Cliff Glacier itself. That glacier is the objective hazard of the day, not the pillar: icefall, spindrift and crevasses. Parties keep left to stay out from under the falling ice and swing wide right around the biggest crevasses.

At the top of the glacier is the ice cliff step, anywhere from ten to well over a hundred feet of 50-70 degree snow and ice.

There is no water above the moraine — carry it or melt.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. The ice cliff step is shorter and more amenable early and gets steeper and barer as the season runs on, so the rock and the ice want opposite conditions
hazards: Icefall and serac collapse on the Ice Cliff Glacier — the route's principal danger
Crevasses and spindrift on the glacier
A steep ice cliff step whose height and hardness vary through the season
Large loose blocks near the top of the pillar
No retreat: reversing the route through the icefall is more dangerous than continuing over the summit
No water above the moraine camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT THE PITCHES ABOVE THE ICE, BECAUSE THE PILLAR IS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE GLACIER. From the top of the ice cliff step it is FOUR easy pitches to the base of the pillar, at roughly 8,200-8,400 ft. If you have done one or two and are already looking at hard cracks, you are on the face rather than on the pillar.

WHAT THE PILLAR IS: a discrete steep feature on the northeast face above the icefall, and the thing that identifies it is that the climbing changes character completely. Four moderate pitches of ordinary alpine ground end, and the next pitch is an immediately steep hand crack that jogs right at its top and ends on a poor, small ledge. That handcrack is the entrance. If the ground above you keeps rambling at the same angle, you have not reached it.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE CONFIRMS IT, and is worth carrying in your head because the first belay is a bad one and you will want to know you are committing to the right thing: steep hands, then a pitch that shuffles about ten feet LEFT off the belay to a thin crack and finger-jams through the crux out RIGHT, then perfect hands on steep dirty rock to the top of the pillar. Three pitches, no more.

AND THE HARD RULE ABOUT BEING HERE AT ALL: there is no reasonable way to reverse this. Downclimbing or rappelling back into the icefall is worse than finishing, so arriving at the base of the pillar is a commitment to going over the top. Make that decision at the bottom of the glacier, not here.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake trailhead and the Mountaineer Creek valley to the 5,400 ft basin
approach_variants.notes: Start at the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, about 3,400 ft. Follow the main trail to the first fork, roughly two and a half to three miles in near 4,600 ft, and stay RIGHT for Stuart Lake. Left is Colchuck Lake, a different basin on the other side of the ridge. About a mile to a mile and a half past that junction, the Stuart Lake trail turns uphill and swings right, away from the water, and begins switchbacking. That turn is your cue. Leave the trail there and stay flat in the valley bottom with Mountaineer Creek. The test is simple and works in poor visibility: if you are gaining elevation on switchbacks you are walking to Stuart Lake and you have missed it. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs. There is no single canonical log and parties describe several sporty crossings that shift with the snowpack; early season, snowbanks make dropping onto a log awkward. On the far side, pick up the climbers' path along the creek. It is unmaintained, full of blowdown and re-routes, and the cairns are not to be trusted: they invite you up and right into a boulder slope around 4,675 ft. Two parties independently say stay LOW beside the creek instead, with the creek on your left — the path is unpleasant but the better line. Some parties do use the boulder field deliberately to avoid the creek crossings, so treat it as a genuine choice rather than a mistake. After about a mile and a half the valley steepens. Turn right and west and climb talus and forest into a hanging flat basin at about 5,400 ft, under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers. That right-turn-and-climb out of a steepening valley into flat ground is the arrival cue for the bivy.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jun; the ice cliff and the couloir exit get harder and more broken as the season runs on
hazards: Serac fall from the hanging ice cliff you traverse beneath — a party watched a large piece break away and shatter on the ledge below them
Rockfall and avalanche in the couloir
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the lower glacier
A cornice at the couloir exit, which becomes the crux when large
An unmaintained climbers' trail with blowdown and misleading cairns
Sporty log crossings of Mountaineer Creek, worse under early-season snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NORTH RIDGE ROCK RIB IS THE DISCRIMINATOR, not the look of the ice. Standing in the 5,400 ft basin facing the mountain, in order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, then the Stuart Glacier beyond it.

So: if that rib is on your RIGHT, you are on the Ice Cliff. If you have walked around the rib and it is now on your LEFT, you are on the Stuart Glacier and have gone too far west. If there is no hanging ice anywhere above you and the slope is a uniform moderate angle, you are on the Sherpa and have gone too far east.

The name is the second test. Ice Cliff is the only one of the three carrying a hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. Sherpa has none.

The move itself: walk the moraine up to the FOOT of the North Ridge, then cut hard LEFT and traverse east under the ice cliff at about 6,600 ft. You are aiming under the cliff, not up the rib.

TOUCH TEST at the base, and it is unmistakable in cloud: the ground is not clean snow. It is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen chunks of glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of snow and ice. Standing on that is direct evidence you are underneath the ice cliff.

Both the far left and the far right side of the icefall are used, and which one goes is a conditions question rather than a route question. The same is true of the bergschrund: one published description passes it on the climber's right, another on the left. Do not treat either as fixed, and look before committing.

Exit: surmounting the cornice puts you on the south-facing ridge just BELOW the false summit near 8,600 ft. Standard descent is the Sherpa Glacier, immediately east of the couloir exit, starting around 8,200 ft and dropping back into the same basin — so a party reversing the Ice Cliff is doing something unusual.

approach_variants.name: Early-season approach with the Eightmile road gated
approach_variants.notes:
When Eightmile Road is snowed or gated below the trailhead, add roughly two and a half miles of road before the trail proper. Parties walk that stretch and then put skis on, skinning the Stuart Lake trail, before continuing on foot.

This is a genuinely different day rather than a longer walk: the valley is snow-covered, the log crossings may be buried or may be harder to reach off a snowbank, and the boulder-field-versus-creek question largely disappears under snow. Postholing on the cross-country section is the common complaint.

No reliable published trailhead-to-bivy time exists for either version, so plan from your own pace rather than from a number.
approach_variants.season: Spring, roughly Apr-May, when the route is in as snow and ice
hazards: Avalanche on the approach slopes and in the couloir
Buried or unreachable log crossings
Deep postholing once off skis
Extra road mileage each way when the gate is down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identification is the same and the North Ridge rib is still the thing to steer by — Sherpa left, Ice Cliff centre, the rib on your right, Stuart Glacier beyond it.

What changes in spring is that the frozen-debris touch test at the base may be buried or covered by fresh avalanche deposit, so it is less useful. Fall back on the geometry: you want to be under the ice cliff with the North Ridge rib immediately to your right, having cut left off the moraine at the foot of the rib rather than continuing up alongside it.

approach_variants.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
approach_variants.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin — poor footing, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Committing: standard descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or a very long walk-around is required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are climbing the COMPLETE North Ridge, which begins at about 6,600 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to NOT mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.

approach_variants.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and Goat Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.
