The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through the summer
~2,000 ft of descent on the way in, all of which must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass
Approach consistently underestimated; parties arrive at the toe late and tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the WEST, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,600 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer LEFT to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues WEST, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.
approach_variants.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier below the couloir
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
The steep steps turning to bare ice or dry-tooling ground later in the season
Six pitches of mixed climbing above the notch, on the far side of the mountain from camp
An unmarked, often snow-covered off-trail turn out of the Mountaineer Creek valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE NORTH RIDGE ROCK RIB DECIDES IT, AND THE SIDE IT IS ON IS THE ANSWER. From the basin you are looking at four things in a row: the Sherpa Glacier, the Ice Cliff Glacier, the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, and beyond it the Stuart Glacier. You want to be past the rib. So: if the North Ridge rib is on your LEFT (east) you are on the Stuart Glacier and correct. If it is still on your RIGHT you have not gone far enough west and are on the Ice Cliff side. That is the same test the Ice Cliff Glacier route uses, read in the opposite direction, and it is the reliable one in cloud because it does not depend on seeing the summit. SECOND TEST — WHAT THE COULOIR LEADS TO. This couloir does not go to the summit. It goes to a notch in the WEST RIDGE, which is on the far side of the mountain from where you camped. If the line you are looking up appears to head for the top of the peak, you are looking at the wrong feature. THIRD, THE SHAPE. Entry is at about 7,800 ft and the couloir NARROWS above you before it widens again — moderate snow, then a short steep step, then a second shorter one, then an open snowfield. A line that is uniformly wide with no steps is not this one. And the negative test: no hanging ice cliff or serac band should be above you anywhere. If there is one, you are back on the Ice Cliff Glacier, on the wrong side of the rib.

approach_variants.name: Reached only by climbing the North Ridge — the base is a point on the route, not a place you walk to
approach_variants.notes:
There is no independent approach to this feature. The Great Gendarme is a tower high on Mount Stuart's North Ridge and you arrive at its base having already climbed either the complete ridge from the toe near 6,600 ft or the upper ridge from the notch above the Stuart Glacier. Reckon on roughly eight or nine pitches of ridge above the notch, and considerably more from the toe.

What matters at the Gendarme is the decision made at its base, because the Gendarme is the one place on the ridge where there is a real choice and where a party that has not decided in advance loses time at 9,000 ft.

Both options are established. The tower goes in two pitches — a lieback, then the offwidth — and it can also be turned on ledges to the west, which is what the original 1956 ascent did and what most parties still do. The bypass is not an escape hatch invented by tired climbers; it is the older line.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, as for whichever North Ridge line you are on
hazards: Arriving at the tower late in the day with the summit still above and no quick way off the ridge
1,000+ ft of exposure on both sides of the crest
Rockfall from parties above on a popular ridge
Cold wind, and an unplanned bivy if the choice at the base costs too long
Retreat from above the Gendarme is awkward in either direction
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AT THE BASE WHEN THE RIDGE STOPS BEING SCRAMBLING AND STANDS UP IN FRONT OF YOU. Everything below is fourth to mid-fifth class on excellent granite that you have been moving together on. The Gendarme is where that ends: a steep tower blocking the crest, roughly 500 ft below the summit, and there is nothing else on the ridge it can be confused with.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS WHETHER YOU CAN WALK ROUND IT. If a line of ledges leads off left (west) and lets you keep moving without roping up properly, you are at the bypass — the same place, and the decision point. If you are looking straight up at a clean lieback flake with an offwidth above it, you are at the climb.

SO THE TEST IN FOG IS A NEGATIVE ONE, and it is worth stating because parties do get this wrong on the way to the summit: if you are still on the ridge and have not yet had to make that choice, the Gendarme is ahead of you and the summit is not. If you have made it and are back on blocky fourth and low-fifth ground, the Gendarme is behind you and the summit is close.

A useful sanity check on the two pitches themselves: the second one has a reputation far worse than the climbing, and parties consistently report it going on good holds and jams with fixed gear in it. If the offwidth you are in feels desperate and unprotectable, look again at where you are — you may have entered the wrong crack on the tower.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass to upper Ingalls Creek
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail and, at the junction about half a mile in, stay right for Longs Pass rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin. Switchback up open slopes to the pass, which gives the first clear view of Stuart's west side.

Descend the steep dusty north side of the pass, losing close to 1,000 ft, and cross Ingalls Creek in the timber below. In normal summer flow this is a rock-hop; it is also the last reliable water before the ridge, so fill up.

Pick up the climbers' path heading east up the valley toward Stuart Pass. You leave it well SHORT of Stuart Pass, in the upper meadows at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft, and traverse climber's-left (north) across talus and heather benches to the foot of the ridge. There is no tread on this traverse and it is the part of the day people get wrong.

Some parties break the approach by camping near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep for dry rock; snow lingers on the Longs Pass north side into early summer
hazards: No maintained tread on the talus/heather traverse from the Stuart Pass trail to the ridge — several minor gullies look alike
Steep loose descent off the north side of Longs Pass; icy at dawn in early summer
Loose talus below the ridge with rockfall exposure from parties above
No water past the Ingalls Creek crossing
Descent is the Cascadian Couloir, and 'not staying right' near the top of it is a documented route-finding error
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is identified by counting gullies, not by elevation. Three roughly parallel gullies come down the lower west ridge; the route takes the MIDDLE one, and it is deeper than its neighbours. The confirming feature is at its foot: a single enormous block, described by everyone who has been there as the size of a house, sitting at the base of that gully. If there is no house-sized boulder, you are one gully over.

From the boulder you push up through scrub into the gully and climb up and rightward inside it. The gully ends at a notch — scramble through the notch and Long John Tower is directly in front of you, a distinct pinnacle on the crest. That sighting is the second confirmation that you took the right gully; if you top out of a gully and there is no tower, you are not on the West Ridge.

The climbing past Long John Tower goes up a chimney on the tower's LEFT — about three quarters of a pitch, with a chockstone near the bottom. (An alternative works a short dihedral with a fixed piton, or a layback further along the ledge, before regaining the crest.) Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse beyond it are the two places parties most often stall for route-finding.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

approach_variants.name: Standard trail to the falls junction, then the unofficial boot track
approach_variants.notes: Start from the same paved trailhead as the standard route — the Teneriffe lot, three miles past the neighbouring peak's trailhead, not that one. Take the graded trail up the access path and along the old logging-road grade to the SIGNED FALLS JUNCTION at about two and a half to three miles. Everything to here is shared. From near the falls the unofficial track leaves and climbs the forested southwest flank directly, and it is steep, rocky and eroded rather than graded.
approach_variants.season: May to October. Snow lingers near the ridge crest into early summer, and the track is markedly more slip-prone when wet.
hazards: The unofficial track is steep, root- and rock-covered and prone to erosion, and is worse on descent than on ascent
Wet or mossy rock on the ridge raises slip risk sharply compared with the standard trail
Route-finding on the boot track is less obvious than on the signed trail, especially in poor visibility
Loose rock and minor exposure on the ridge crest, with lingering snow near the crest into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: At the signed falls junction, leave the maintained trail. The boot track BYPASSES THE FALLS ON CLIMBER'S RIGHT — that is the physical test, because the falls themselves are the landmark and the track goes round them on one specific side. Above the bypass the tread changes character completely: it stops switchbacking and climbs the FALL LINE on roots and rock, gaining a SADDLE on the southwest ridge. From the saddle the route is a direct, largely switchback-free push up the open ridge crest through meadow and a rock band, with a short scramble move at the true summit. Negative markers: if the trail underfoot is still graded, signed and switchbacking with the falls spur behind you, you missed the turnoff and are on the maintained trail; and if you are dipping to a saddle after a viewpoint over the valley, having never left graded tread, that is the standard trail's saddle, not this ridge.

approach_variants.name: Mount Teneriffe Trail from the paved trailhead
approach_variants.notes: From the freeway exit into North Bend, continue through town and turn north onto the road running below the peaks. Carry on about three miles PAST the neighbouring peak's trailhead to the paved seventy-car lot — this is the Teneriffe trailhead, not the Si one, and the two are easy to confuse. A short access path switchbacks up to an old logging-road grade, which climbs gently for a mile and a half through young forest and meadow. The trailhead gate closes seasonally about an hour before dusk; vehicles left past closing risk being locked in.
approach_variants.season: March to November, best from June to October. Snow lingers on the upper mountain and ridge crest into June and makes an otherwise easy trail steep and icy.
hazards: Seasonal snow on the upper mountain and ridge crest into June, creating steep icy sections on otherwise easy trail
No reliable water beyond the falls — carry what you need for the round trip
The trailhead gate closes seasonally about an hour before dusk
approach_variants.baseFinding: The checkpoint is the SIGNED SPUR down to the falls at about two and a half to three miles — everything before it is old road grade, everything after it is narrower trail on switchbacks. Stay on the graded, signed trail there. Continue through the switchbacks, past a viewpoint over the valley to the north, and on to a SADDLE at around forty-two hundred feet where the trail dips before the final stretch. The base of the only hands-on ground on this route is above that saddle: a short rocky step at the true summit, about a mile further on, needing sure footing but nothing more. Negative marker: if you have left the graded tread at the falls junction onto a steep boot track of roots and rock climbing the fall line beside the falls, you are on the unofficial ridge line and are committed to a much steeper day.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the Terror Basin boot path, then over the Barrier to Crescent Creek Basin and the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek Group Camp trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the unpaved Goodell Creek Road that turns north off Highway 20 directly across from Newhalem Campground, follow the old abandoned roadbed and boot path northeast along Goodell Creek for roughly 4-4.5 miles of gentle grade to a stone-cairn and arrow junction near 1,700 ft.

DO NOT CONTINUE STRAIGHT PAST THE CAIRN. That fainter track follows Terror Creek toward Crescent Creek Basin and is a separate, notoriously brushier approach. Instead take the HARD RIGHT and start up the steep, well-beaten Terror Basin boot path, which climbs directly through old-growth forest, roughly 3,000-plus ft of gain in about 1.5 miles, before breaking out above treeline around 5,000-5,200 ft.

Above the trees a rising traverse across heather benches, slabs and early-season snowfields leads to a broad saddle near 6,200 ft; the standard high camp is in a gravelly, wildflower basin about 400 ft below and beyond the saddle, around 5,800 ft, fed by several small streams.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Committing to the wrong rib on a 2,000 ft face with limited options to reverse
A heavily crevassed, mostly unbridged Mustard Glacier below the face by mid-season
Steep, extremely loose rock near the top; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a block that had appeared solid
A narrow, rockfall-prone descent gully with an undercut melted-out moat by mid to late season
Stuck ropes in the confined descent gully, and a loose, marginal final 100 ft
Retreat from high on the route is genuinely difficult
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWFIELD AT THE BOTTOM OF THE FACE, AFTER THE WALL IS ACCESSED FROM ITS WEST SIDE. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp the technical start is reached by crossing the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descending the Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque, then rounding into position under Terror's wall. Cross the glacier remnant beneath the face, then start JUST LEFT OF THE SNOWPATCH at the bottom.

THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK AT THE BASE IS THE USUAL OBSTACLE, AND IT IS ALSO THE MARKER: you are at the base when you are standing at the gap between the snowpatch and the wall, on its left.

THE DECISION THAT DEFINES THIS ROUTE, AND IT IS MADE BEFORE THE HARD CLIMBING RATHER THAN DURING IT: THE FACE IS SPLIT BY TWO RIBS, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE RIGHT, OR WESTERN, ONE. The main risk on the lower face is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib. Long, mostly third-class pitches climb above the snowfield while TRAVERSING STEADILY RIGHTWARD; the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse. If your traverse is taking you left, you are on the wrong half of the wall.

TWO CONFIRMATIONS HIGHER, BOTH VISUAL AND BOTH USABLE IN THIN CLOUD: aim for the right or western crest of the buttress about TWO THIRDS OF THE WAY UP THE LOWER FACE, IDENTIFIABLE BY THE ROCK DARKENING. And A SHARP PROW marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Darkening rock and a sharp prow are features of this rib and not of its neighbour.

WHAT THE UPPER FACE GIVES YOU: a LONG SNOW FINGER forming a ramp that carries the route a good distance, then scrambling on a wildly exposed crest, a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits, an exposed easy-fifth hand traverse over the false summit, a downclimb, and the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top.

On the approach, when crossing from Stump Hollow into Crescent Creek Basin: DO NOT DROP INTO THE LOW NOTCH NORTH OF THE CHOPPING BLOCK. The correct line into Crescent Creek Basin is ABOUT 100 YARDS NORTH OF THAT NOTCH, AT A FLAT, BIVY-SITE SHELF ON THE RIDGE.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and Terror Basin, over the Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin, then slabs and talus on the east side to the Terror-Degenhardt saddle
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead off SR-20 near Newhalem, follow the old roadbed and Terror Basin climbers' path, about 4 miles then a steep cairned side trail, to the 5,800 ft Terror Basin camp, then continue over the roughly 6,400 ft Chopping Block col into Crescent Creek Basin.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A descent by a different route than the one climbed, off a large chockstone in a loose gully
The Chopping Block col and Crescent Creek Basin traverse before any climbing
Loose rock throughout, in a range where that is the defining characteristic
The full Goodell Creek approach with roughly 6,000 ft of gain to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE SADDLE BETWEEN TERROR AND DEGENHARDT, AND YOU REACH IT FROM THE BASIN BY ITS EAST SIDE ON SLABS AND TALUS. That saddle is a gap between two named summits, which is what makes it findable without a view: ground rising on both sides of you, falling away ahead. THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S OTHER LINES, AND IT IS A SIDE-OF-THE-MOUNTAIN TEST: the NORTH FACE and Stoddard Buttress are reached by going OVER the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col or through McMillan Cirque and down onto the north side, and they start at a snowpatch at the foot of a 2,000 ft wall. The WEST RIDGE tops out at the notch between Terror's true and false summits, marked by a large chockstone. This route starts from the Terror-Degenhardt saddle on the EAST. If you are on the north side of the mountain, or at a chockstone, you are not here. ARRIVAL AT THE SADDLE: from Crescent Creek Basin the ground to it is slabs and talus, taken on the saddle's east side. Four pitches at Grade III-IV 5.6 follow. If you are on sustained harder ground, or on more than a handful of pitches, you are not on the East Ridge. WHAT YOU DO NOT DO ON THE WAY DOWN, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING THE ROUTE RECORDS: the standard descent is NOT a reversal of this ridge. It is the WEST RIDGE GULLY back into Crescent Creek Basin, with multiple rappels off a large chockstone. So the day is a traverse of the peak, up one side and down the other, and the chockstone at the top of the west gully is the feature to identify from the summit.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
