bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Terror Creek crossing and the flagged climber's track into Crescent Creek Basin, then the west gully to the chockstone notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead, follow the old roadbed about 4.5 miles, cross Terror Creek, and climb a steep climber's track marked with pink flagging past moss-covered cliffs to reach Crescent Creek Basin. Total approach gain to basecamp is nearly 6,000 ft.

This is the standard descent route for every north-side line on the peak, so it sees traffic in both directions and its features are described mostly from above.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully with little shelter
An undercut, melted-out snow moat in the gully by mid to late season
A loose and marginal final 100 ft of the gully
Stuck ropes in the confined terrain
Dropping into Crescent Creek Basin from the wrong notch north of the Chopping Block
Early-season snow and ice in the choss gully
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOP OF THIS ROUTE'S GULLY IS MARKED BY A LARGE CHOCKSTONE, AND THAT CHOCKSTONE IS THE SINGLE BEST FEATURE ON THE PEAK FOR ORIENTING IN CLOUD. From Crescent Creek Basin, the west gully system climbs to the low notch between Terror and The Rake, and a large wedged chockstone sits near the head of it. Everything on this side is described relative to that block.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS COUNTABLE FROM BELOW: climb a narrow, loose, rockfall-prone gully out of Crescent Creek Basin and keep going until a chockstone blocks it near the crest. That is the notch. Above it the route is a short summit tower.

ON THE APPROACH, THE DROP INTO CRESCENT CREEK BASIN IS THE THING PARTIES GET WRONG: DO NOT USE THE LOW NOTCH NORTH OF THE SUB-PEAK KNOWN AS THE CHOPPING BLOCK. The correct line from the Chopping Block ridge down into Crescent Creek Basin is ABOUT 100 YARDS NORTH OF THAT NOTCH, AT A FLAT, BIVY-SITE SHELF ON THE RIDGE. A flat shelf big enough to sleep on, 100 yards north of the obvious low notch, is the marker.

WHAT THE GULLY IS LIKE, SO YOU KNOW YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT ONE: narrow, with little shelter from rockfall, frequently holding an undercut melted-out snow moat by mid to late season, and with a loose and marginal final stretch. Two or three rappels in the gully, plus one or two above the notch, get parties down, on a mix of pre-existing slings and natural chockstone and horn anchors.

AT THE TOP: the summit tower is downclimbed or a short section rappelled back to the notch off existing sling anchors.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the basin, then the lowest notch on the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the PCT North / Commonwealth Basin trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass, about 3,000 ft: cross under I-90, take the first right, lot on the right. Follow the PCT northbound through timber on long switchbacks for roughly 5.5 to 6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk at about 5,400 ft, a narrow ledge blasted into the rock of Kendall Peak's south side — solid underfoot, very exposed, and worth care if icy or windy.

Continue north about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake at about 5,260 ft, the last reliable water and a common camp; roughly two to two and a half hours and about seven miles from the car.

About 0.4 to 0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching LEFT (west) off the PCT. It climbs a steep 200 ft to Bumblebee Pass at about 5,400 ft, above Alaska Lake. Drop off the far side into Bumblebee Basin, then contour and climb northwest across talus and scree toward the ridge.

About 8 to 8.5 miles and 2,900 to 3,000 ft to the base, typically four to five hours for a fit party.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: The Kendall Katwalk, exposed and dangerous when icy or windy
Loose and eroded tread on both sides of the Bumblebee Pass boot path
Talus and scree in the basin below the ridge
A descent by the East Ridge, meaning a route-finding descent on unfamiliar ground at the end of a long day
A long day: many parties climb it car to car
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AIM FOR THE LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE, AND KNOW IN ADVANCE THAT IT IS FURTHER LEFT THAN IT LOOKS. From Bumblebee Basin, scrambling up scree, the beginning of the ridge that you can see from below is NOT where you want to be. The notch you want is LEFT of it, at the ridge's lowest point, around 5,960 ft. That single correction is the most useful thing on this approach, because the eye pulls you right every time.

THE NOTCH IS SMALL, AND ITS SIZE IS THE CONFIRMATION: it holds about three people at most. If you have topped out on a broad, comfortable saddle, you are not at the start of the West Ridge.

EXPECT SHORT FOURTH-CLASS SCRAMBLING AROUND GENDARMES to reach it. Once you top out on the ridge you scramble over a small gendarme, traversing rightward toward the crest, to gain the notch itself.

THE FIRST MOVE SETTLES IT ABSOLUTELY: pitch one begins with a STEP LEFT INTO A WELL-FEATURED CHIMNEY. That step-left-into-a-chimney is the signature of this route and is probably the crux of the whole climb. If your first pitch is a face or a slab, you are not in the right notch. The first two leads run up a series of chimneys in solid rock.

AND THE OTHER ROUTE ON THIS PEAK IS ON THE OPPOSITE SIDE: the East Ridge is class 3-4 and is gained from a notch at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side, from the same basin. If you are on easy scrambling ground the whole way, you are on the East Ridge and you have circled to the wrong end of the mountain.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

bivy.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
bivy.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

rappel_detail.notes: West Ridge toward the Notch.
hazards: The crest anchors are slings over natural features, not fixed hardware - inspect and back up rather than clipping and going
rappel_detail.station: The traverse finishes by descending Forbidden, so this is Forbidden's own descent. From the summit ridge, the first rappels are off in-situ slings on horns and blocks along the West Ridge crest, with simul-downclimbing between them, heading for the West Ridge notch where most parties left a cache.

rappel_detail.notes: West Ridge toward the Notch.
hazards: Rappelling the fall line here takes you past the station
rappel_detail.station: The second station of the descent is the one that is offset: it sits at climber's LEFT. Every other station on the sequence is either straight below the last one or at climber's right, so if you are hunting left further down you are looking in the wrong place.

rappel_detail.notes: West Ridge toward the Notch.
hazards: This is where parties regroup and where rockfall from anyone still on the ridge above concentrates
rappel_detail.station: Last of the ridge-crest rappels, landing at the West Ridge notch. From here the descent switches to the gully system back toward Boston Basin.

rappel_detail.notes: Upper Cat Scratch Gullies.
hazards: All of the gullies here are full of loose rock and party-induced rockfall is the single biggest danger on this descent
rappel_detail.station: First station below the notch. The rappel line follows the fixed anchors on the small arete bordering the gully rather than the gully's own fall line, which is what keeps you out of the rockfall channel.

rappel_detail.notes: Cat Scratch Gullies.
hazards: Anchors of mixed age and quality; carry webbing and rings to rebuild
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the arete beside the gully. Stations are numerous - this is the standard way off Forbidden and off the traverse - so expect several options and pick the one that keeps you out of the channel.

rappel_detail.notes: Cat Scratch Gullies.
hazards: Wet, loose rock in the gully bed grits up a rope and makes pulls stiff
rappel_detail.station: Mid-gully. Stations are visible from roughly a rope length away once you know to look at the arete rather than the gully bed.

rappel_detail.notes: Cat Scratch Gullies.
hazards: Rope ends thrown into the gully bed snag on loose blocks
rappel_detail.station: Continues down; downclimbing between stations is normal and is how the count varies between parties.

rappel_detail.notes: Cat Scratch Gullies.
hazards: Anchor quality does not improve toward the bottom - the lowest slung-boulder anchor has been found stripped by a previous descending party
rappel_detail.station: Lower gully, approaching the last cliff band above the snow.

rappel_detail.notes: Cat Scratch Gullies.
hazards: Going over the last cliff on the wrong line leaves you above the moat with no anchor within reach
rappel_detail.station: Second-to-last station. Before you commit to rappelling the last cliff onto the snow, look for the station off to the LEFT rather than going straight over the edge.

rappel_detail.pull: Pull before anyone commits to the moat crossing - a stuck rope with the party split across a moat is the worst place on the descent to be.
rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel onto the snowfield/glacier remnant below Forbidden’s South Face. Its exact length is not recorded. Treat the moat and the glacier edge below with general caution.
rappel_detail.anchor: fixed/in-situ anchor (best available near glacier remnant)
hazards: The landing crosses the moat between rock and snow and this can be genuinely difficult - the first person down should carry a picket, ice axe and crampons so they can climb out of the moat if needed
Rope up again immediately below: the ground below is glacier remnant, and the waterfall slabs further down toward Boston Basin have killed people (that hazard is on the walk out, not on this rappel)
rappel_detail.station: The final rappel down the last cliff band onto the snowfield at the base of the cat scratch gully.

approach_variants.name: Thornton Lakes Trail, the middle lake and the gully to the bivy col
approach_variants.notes: From the highway near milepost 117, the Thornton Lakes spur road runs about five miles, rough and unpaved, to the trailhead; high clearance is worth having. The trail follows an old logging-road grade for the first couple of miles, then climbs more steeply to the ridge above the lakes before dropping to the lake outlet. Traverse the brushy, sometimes faint climbers' path around the east and south side of the middle lake, following the right bank of the stream, then make a high rising traverse and climb a long, loose scree and talus gully — on the order of twelve hundred feet of gain — northwest to a col at roughly 5,750 to 5,840 ft. That col is the standard bivy and the last place with reliable water; there is a second bivy two pitches up the ridge with room for about five people and no water at all, which saves time on the climbing day if you are willing to carry water to it. From the col, the ridge is gained by crossing the small pocket glacier remnant on the peak's eastern flank, which can be easy snow, or rock slabs and a bit of ice, depending on the season and the year.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the approach gully and the glacier remnant have melted out enough to reduce snow and icefall hazard. The gneiss on this ridge is considered unsafe wet or rimed, which keeps the route to a short dry-rock window.
hazards: rockfall and icefall from beneath the small receding glaciers on the north and east faces
loose gneiss, especially on the upper ridge and the final summit scramble
crevasse and moat hazard crossing the glacier remnant, worse early season
a long, complex multi-rappel descent on loose, exposed rock, which is where most epics on this route happen
old fixed slings and rings at most rappel stations on rock loose enough that anchors need backing up or replacing
approach_variants.baseFinding: AIM FOR THE LOW NOTCH IN THE RIDGE, AND GAIN IT BY THE RAMP ON ITS RIGHT. From the col camp you do not climb straight up. Descend snow and traverse the glacier remnant across the peak's eastern flank toward a prominent LOW notch in the northeast ridge — the notch is the lowest obvious gap in the crest between you and the peak, and it is the only feature on that skyline you should be walking toward. Gain it by an easy ramp on its RIGHT-hand side rather than by attacking the crest below it; that ramp is short and unmistakable once you are under the notch. Two confirmations: the first few pitches above the notch are very nice, easy face and crack climbing rather than anything desperate, and the ridge only sharpens and narrows afterwards. So if the first pitch off your start is hard, or if you are trying to climb the crest from its very toe rather than entering it partway up at a notch, you are in the wrong place and should traverse further. Fix the traverse in your mind on the way in — the descent reverses this ridge with a long string of rappels and downclimbs back to the same col, and losing the notch on the way down is the standard way this route goes wrong.

approach_variants.name: FR-2419 up the Big Creek drainage to the road-end trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Northwest Forest Pass to park; no wilderness permit is needed.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, best Jul-Sep. Spring and early summer put avalanche-capable snow in the gully
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the entry gullies and on the talus — spread the group out rather than stacking above and below
Sustained exposure on the Dog Walk Ledge / Catwalk, where the tread is one boot wide with drops on both sides
Steep avalanche-prone snow in the gullies and on the saddle in spring and early season
The scree field below the false summit is greasy and slick when wet
Significant elevation loss on descent, hard on knees and ankles, and slower than the climb
Route-finding through the forested lower section, meadows and talus in poor visibility
Little shade above treeline; the route gets hot
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF THREE TERRAIN CHANGES AND EACH ONE IS A CHECK YOU CAN MAKE WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING. First: forest gives way to OPEN MEADOW BENCHES around 3,800 ft — that is where the ridgeline and neighbouring Mount Ellinor come into view on a clear day, and where the ground briefly eases. Second: above the meadows you enter SCREE AND TALUS and the rule is to stay primarily on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of a large loose rocky gully. Left side of the gully, all the way. Third: the path winds above the gully until it GAINS THE SOUTHERN RIDGELINE, and from there the ground drops away on BOTH sides.

THE ARRIVAL TEST FOR THE REAL CLIMBING IS THE SOUTH SADDLE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT, AND IT HAS TWO MARKERS: it is a KNOWN BIVY SITE, and it is the FIRST POINT ON THE ROUTE WHERE THE TRUE SUMMIT BECOMES VISIBLE. Flat ground you could sleep on, high on a ridge, is a thing you can identify by standing on it.

SECOND TEST, above the saddle: a STONE WIND SHELTER sits on the ridge. A built structure is unambiguous in any weather. From the wind shelter a final short Class 3-4 scramble gains the true 6,255 ft summit. If you have topped out without passing a stone shelter, you are on the false summit below it.

THE SECTION IN BETWEEN IS THE ONE PEOPLE REMEMBER: the ridge-crest traverse called the Dog Walk Ledge or the Catwalk, where in several spots the tread narrows to barely one boot-width with real exposure on both sides. Class 3 with a couple of Class 3+/4 moves. If the crest you are on is comfortably wide the whole way, you have not reached it yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: a trip report warns specifically that contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Stay left of the drop-off on the north side.

approach_variants.name: From Mount Ellinor, across the connecting ridge or the west-side basin
approach_variants.notes: Recorded as an approach because parties do reach Washington from Ellinor rather than from Big Creek, usually as half of a traverse. Ellinor is reached by Trail #812 from its Upper or Lower Trailhead, both on the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor, and from Ellinor's summit the connecting ridge runs northeast toward Washington. It is not a walk. The crest is fractured, weathered pillow basalt with sustained Class 4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes, and it carries a loose 50 ft downclimb that most parties call the least enjoyable part of the day. The alternative that several parties prefer is the west-side basin traverse: drop into the basin below the crest and cross it, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line rather than fighting the ridge. Used as an approach to Washington this is a long way round for a peak with a 3.2 km trail of its own, and it is here for traverse parties.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Fractured, weathered pillow basalt on the connecting ridge with a crux gendarme downclimb of notably poor rock and severe exposure
Sustained Class 4 scrambling past gendarmes with a loose 50 ft downclimb
Committing terrain between two summits with no quick exit
All the Washington summit-ridge hazards at the end of it
approach_variants.baseFinding: COMING FROM ELLINOR THE ARRIVAL TEST FOR WASHINGTON'S SUMMIT GROUND IS THE SAME STONE WIND SHELTER on the ridge, with the final short Class 3-4 scramble above it to the 6,255 ft top. THE TEST ON THE CONNECTING RIDGE ITSELF, WHICH IS WHERE THE DAY IS DECIDED: hidden ledges keep the difficulty at Class 4 or below on most of the gendarmes, so if you are pulling harder than that you have taken the crest where a ledge existed. Look below the obvious line before committing to it. Where the ridge gets too difficult or exposed to continue unroped, the usual answer is to DROP INTO THE BASIN BELOW and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a snow finger. HONEST LIMIT: the usual advice on the crux gendarme downclimb is to avoid it — the rock is notably poor and the exposure severe, and several parties recommend the west-side basin instead of the direct ridge. That is a recommendation to change route, not a marker, and this variant is written down mainly so a party knows the option exists before they are standing on it.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

approach_variants.name: Watson Lakes Trailhead, Trail #611 and the east gully to the saddle
approach_variants.notes: Park at the end of the forest road above Baker Lake and follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail into the woods. At about a mile, stay right or straight where the Anderson Butte Trail climbs left toward the old lookout site. Around 4,700 ft a second junction splits: the right fork drops to lower Anderson Lake, the left fork climbs a short way to a small saddle at the wilderness boundary before dropping to the Watson Lakes. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and are the last reliable water, since nothing higher on the mountain runs dependably — treat before filling. The maintained trail ends there; from the basin the route becomes an open, cairned climbers' line up talus and, well into summer, snow. Established bivy sites on open slopes around 5,400 ft shorten the summit day considerably. Route-finding across the unmarked basin and ridge in flat light is the main difficulty of the approach, since there is no tread to follow.
approach_variants.season: July through September is most reliable, though snow often lingers in the summit gully and on the saddle traverse into early July. Many parties prefer August for drier ground and fewer mosquitoes. An axe is worth carrying even in mid-summer.
hazards: a moat and unstable snow bridge that develop in the west-side gully late season
lingering snow in the summit gully and on the saddle traverse into July
an airy summit ridge with drop-offs on both sides near the top
off-trail route-finding through talus and heather above the lakes, with nothing marked
loose talus and scree in the gully below the saddle on the descent
heavy mosquito pressure at the lakes through summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: TWO GULLIES LEAD TO THE SADDLE AND ONLY THE EASTERN ONE IS SAFE, AND THE SUMMIT GULLY IS THE ONE CHOKED WITH TREES. Getting to the ridge first: from the basin, take the WIDEST gully EAST of the peak up to the saddle at about 5,900 ft. The western gully looks like an alternative and is not — it develops a large moat and an unstable snow bridge late in the season and parties have been forced to reroute out of it. From the saddle, head west and scramble the ridge on its SOUTH side, over easy heather and treed slopes, into the basin below the true summit; cross that basin, crossing one more small snowfield, to a heather-and-dirt gully immediately on the SOUTH side of the summit block. That gully has an unmistakable signature: partway up it squeezes tight through a clump of trees, tight enough that packs have to come off and be passed through by hand. If the gully you are in is clean rock with nothing growing in it, it is not this one. Above the squeeze, the final block is a short scramble on rock that takes hands, and then a narrow ridge of around thirty feet with real drop on both sides — a hand line is commonly carried for that section and is the sensible call in either direction.

bivy.name: Watson Lakes designated camps
bivy.notes: The substance of this zone and the best camping anywhere near these three peaks. It is a genuinely short walk — about two miles from the road end, through forest to a meadow junction, over a saddle at around 4,700 ft and down to the pair of lakes at 4,400 ft — which makes it the rare alpine camp in the North Cascades that costs a heavy pack almost nothing. Mount Watson rises straight above: from the lakes the line works up the north side, traverses to the large col near 5,900 ft between the East Peak and the jumbled western summits, then takes heather and treed slopes west to the basin under the true summit, a heather and dirt gully on the south side of the summit block, and a short exposed class two to three ridge to the top where many parties want a fixed line. For Bacon Peak this is the staging night rather than the base, since the summit is a long way east across the massif. The lakes are notoriously buggy through midsummer and hold snow into early season. Everything here is heavily used and the designation exists because it was being trampled.
bivy.water: The lakes and a nearby stream, reliable through the season. There is no potable water on the road or the trail, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, which the trail enters at the saddle before dropping to the lakes. No overnight permit is required or issued. A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. CAMPING IS ALLOWED ONLY IN THE DESIGNATED SITES and campfires are prohibited outright — carry a stove. Standard wilderness rules otherwise: keep the party small, camp on rock or bare ground rather than in the heather, pack out everything, and secure food overnight since there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites at the two lakes, first come first served with no reservations, plus a backcountry toilet. Flat ground is mostly rock outcrop along the shoreline; the upper lake takes the larger share of parties.

bivy.name: Camp on slopes below Mount Watson (~5,400 ft)
Anderson Creek road end, Watson Lakes trailhead
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this side of the massif the road decides what the trip is. It is a rare thing in this range — a driveable gravel road that delivers you to 4,200 ft, within two miles of an alpine lake basin — and it is why the Anderson and Watson Lakes are the substance of this zone rather than a footnote. THE ROAD IS THE PROBLEM: FS 1107 has been closed at a washout at milepost 3.8, well below the road end, since July 8, 2026, and the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert, still posted on September 26, 2026, gives no end date; the closure cuts off the trailhead and the Anderson Creek Sno-Park. While it is in force the whole approach becomes four or five miles of road walking with 1,500 ft of gain before the trail even starts, which turns a comfortable overnight on Mount Watson into a serious two-day trip and puts Bacon Peak out of reach for most parties from this side. Confirm the road with the ranger district before driving out, and if it is open, sleeping in the lot the night before is a normal and sensible way to save the morning. The road holds snow late and is not usually driveable to the end until well into the season.
bivy.water: None at the road end. Carry what you need for the evening; the first water is at the lakes, which are close enough that most parties simply walk in.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass required, and a state Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. This is national forest outside the wilderness boundary, so a night in the lot or a pullout is generally tolerated, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a turning place. The wilderness rules start at the saddle above.
bivy.capacity: A modest gravel lot at the road end with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and a few flat spots to sleep beside them; no facilities, and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lower Anderson Lake
bivy.notes: Half a mile down from the second trail junction and a hundred feet above the Watson Lakes, and the more useful of the two basins for anyone climbing rather than hiking, because BACON PEAK'S APPROACH RUNS DIRECTLY ABOVE IT. From the saddle about 1.4 miles up the Watson Lakes trail a boot path climbs south onto the ridge high above this lake and opens into the meadows that lead east across the massif toward the Bacon summits, so a party camped here is on the line rather than beside it. It also solves the problem the designated sites create — when the four-and-four at the Watson Lakes are taken there is nowhere legal to squeeze in, and this basin is the fallback. Anderson Butte, a former lookout site with a long view over Baker Lake and across to Baker and Shuksan, is a short spur off the same trail junction and is worth the twenty minutes on an evening you are not going anywhere. Bugs are as bad here as at the lakes over the saddle.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Dependable all season.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. This lake sits on the trail before it crosses into the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness, so the strict designated-site rule that governs the lakes beyond the saddle does not apply in the same way here — but the campfire ban, the small-party expectation and the pack-it-all-out rule should be treated as applying regardless, because the ground is identical and equally fragile. Recreation pass at the trailhead; Sno-Park permit instead from December through April. No permit is issued for an overnight and none is needed.
bivy.capacity: A small number of informal sites at the lake with a backcountry privy; quieter than the sister lakes over the saddle and usually the one with space left

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. From the LOWER, eastern end walk about fifty yards downhill to the climbers' trail, which climbs steeply to the base of the Lower Wall.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished rock
Roofs overhead at the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The two trails out of this one pullout go to different halves of the crag, and taking the western one puts you on Logger's Ledge at Upper Castle — a full wall above where this route starts.

Mr. Clean is on the Lower Wall along with Brass Balls and the west-to-east run of The Fault, Catapult, The Vertebrae and The Bone. The Fault is the fixed reference: the short trail from the right of the parking area leads straight to it.

The Lower Wall announces itself by the many roofs overhead and by Logger's Ledge running above you. Older lines here are on gear; the NEWER routes on the RIGHT side of the wall carry more bolts, so an unexpectedly bolted line means you have drifted east of where you meant to be.

bivy.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
bivy.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
bivy.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

approach_variants.name: Cutthroat Creek Trailhead and the forest traverse to the wall's right side
approach_variants.notes: Turn off the highway a little over four miles east of Washington Pass, following signs for the Cutthroat Creek trail, and drive about a mile to the trailhead lot, which has restrooms. Do not confuse this with the Cutthroat Peak approach, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout well west of here and serves a different objective entirely. Start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail, then leave it a short way along and walk up through the woods toward the wall — the ground gains elevation quickly at first, then the line traverses leftward through open forest and across slabby benches. There is no maintained tread on this section; parties report cairns and an intermittent climbers' path, but treat it as open-forest navigation rather than a trail. The traverse ends on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side, which is where the climbing starts. Allow the better part of a couple of hours from the car to the base.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, matching the neighbouring crags on the same approach. Early-season parties should expect bushier, dirtier cracks, since this wall sees very little traffic and the cracks have not been cleaned by use.
hazards: vegetated and dirty cracks, especially on the less-travelled lower pitches
runout terrain on the middle pitches
loose rock, given how rarely the wall is climbed
open-forest and slab navigation with no maintained trail to the base
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SHOULDER AT THE RIGHT-HAND END OF THE WALL IS THE ARRIVAL POINT, AND THE ROUTE STARTS ON LOW-ANGLE GROUND, NOT STEEP GROUND. The traverse through the forest and across the slabby benches deposits you on a shoulder at the base of the wall's RIGHT-hand side; that shoulder, rather than any point along the middle of the cliff, is where you should be standing. From it, the start of this route is clean, LOW-ANGLE crack systems running up a big ramp that trends LEFT as it rises. Low angle and left-trending together are the test. This wall holds only two known lines and the other one is several grades harder and sustained, so if what is above you is steep, continuous crack climbing with no ramp under it, you have walked past the start and are beneath the hard line. Likewise, if you are still in trees and have not come out onto a distinct shoulder with the right edge of the wall above you, you have not finished the traverse. Expect the cracks on the lower pitches to be bushy and dirty rather than clean — that is normal here and is another sign you are on the right, less-travelled line. The upper pitches merge into the harder route's corner and finish on its final blocky pitch, and the descent rappels that line.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.notes: Squire Creek Road from Darrington to the washout gate, old roadbed on foot past the flagged landslide crossing, then right at the two cut logs with old logging cable onto the boot track. Ford the creek, climb steeply through old growth into open grassland, and reach the grassy saddle bivy at about three hours.
approach_variants.season: Summer
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep dirty forest below the grassland
Exposed apron crossing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the grassy saddle bivy, cross the granite apron, passing the start of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer, and carry on to two-bolt ring anchors on the OPPOSITE wall. Those ring anchors are the start.

The two discriminators are direction and hardware: you walk across the apron rather than up ramps, and you are looking for ring anchors rather than a bolt or a dirt ledge. Going up class 4 ramps from the saddle instead puts you on Primal Scream or Miracle Ramps.

The route's own payoff feature — the soaring hand crack above the apron — is visible from the apron, so sight it before committing.

approach_variants.name: Stafford Creek Trail #1359 to Navaho Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the small road-end lot, Trail #1359 leaves at an easy grade through dry ponderosa and lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek; a short rerouted section of steeper switchbacks near the half-mile mark bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread. The creek crossing in the meadows is the last easy water and worth topping off at. Stay on #1359 at the signed Standup Creek Trail junction, and the trail opens into a large marshy subalpine meadow with a feeder stream and established campsites — the usual overnight base. Above the meadow the tread leaves the trees and switchbacks up open, rocky, sparsely vegetated slope for the last stretch to the pass.
approach_variants.season: July into October. Snow patches linger on the upper ridge into July, when poles and light traction are worthwhile.
hazards: No water and essentially no shade above the meadows, on ground that bakes on a warm afternoon
Loose scree over dirt on the climbers' path onto the ridge, steepening quickly and easy to push down onto a party below
Lingering snow patches into July
Slopes on either flank of the summit ridge are looser and steeper than they look from above
Several miles of the trail run through the 2025 burn: dead and burned trees can fall, especially in wind
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SUMMIT PATH IS NOW MORE WORN THAN THE TRAIL IT LEAVES, AND THE WRONG TURN HAS A NAME. Navaho Pass is unmistakable ground — small, rocky, sparsely vegetated and wind-exposed, with the Stuart Range filling the view — and it is where the trail meets the old crest trail along the county line. Head EAST out of the pass, paralleling the range. The old boot-path junction that descriptions still mention has effectively vanished: the beaten track now IS the summit path, more worn than the crest trail beside it, so the thing to look for is the most-used tread rather than a faint branch. If instead you follow the connecting ridge LEFT from the pass, you are heading for Wrong Turn Peak, which is what it is called and why. Two more confusions worth knowing: the prominent peak straight ahead on the walk in is Little Navaho, not this one, and the final ridge throws up several false tops before the true summit, which is small — barely higher than a rocky outcrop just east of it. On the way down, do not follow the southeast ridge all the way toward Little Navaho; there are cliffs below it.

approach_variants.name: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Park at Tiffany Springs Campground at about 6,760 ft. Three long gravel drives reach it — from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek road, which is the roughest and where high clearance is worth having; from the Methow Valley; or the longer South Fork line over Baldy Pass, which is the gentlest on a low car. All are an hour or more of gravel. A trailhead further along the ridge system also serves the area.

From the campground, trail #373 runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft in roughly forty-five minutes of easy walking. That pass is the hinge of the whole approach.

The roads are snowbound most of the year and typically open around late June, which is awkward here: this route wants snow and the road wants none. The overlap is narrow and it is the reason this line gets climbed so rarely.
approach_variants.season: June into early July while the snow is still continuous; by mid-summer it degrades to scree and dirt
hazards: Avalanche and wet-snow release in the only window when the route is in condition
The narrow upper section is the crux and steepens to around fifty-five degrees
Road access and route condition barely overlap; too early and you cannot drive in, too late and the snow is gone
The unmaintained descent trail above the lower lake is faint and easy to lose
Long gravel drives from every direction and no quick way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Honeymoon Pass, leave the trail and traverse south along the open grassy east slope below the ridge crest into the small cirque at the foot of the north face, at roughly 7,360 ft. The face rises about six hundred and fifty feet above that cirque and it is split into two halves by a rock tower.

THE FACE HAS TWO KINDS OF LINE AND THEY ARE ON OPPOSITE SIDES. Snow gullies on the LEFT, a rock tower and its ridge on the RIGHT. This route is on the left. If you are standing under a tower of rock with an arete running up to it, you have walked too far right and you are under the two rock routes.

Among the gullies on the left, take the LONGEST, MOST CONTINUOUS AND MOST DIRECT one — the chute that runs unbroken from the cirque floor to the summit ridge without stepping out onto rock. The others are shorter and more broken. Sighting up the line from the cirque floor is the test: you should be able to follow one connected ribbon of snow all the way to the skyline.

CONDITION IS PART OF THE IDENTIFICATION HERE, not a separate question. The gully averages about forty degrees with steeper sections to fifty-five, and the crux is where it NARROWS high up. If the narrow section is bare scree and dirt rather than snow, the route is out — this line does not work as a rock climb, and by late summer that is its normal state.

NEGATIVE MARKER on the descent, which is not a reversal: from the top of the couloir on the summit ridge, walk off by the north-west ridge, then drop to the old unmaintained trail above the smaller lake to the north-east and follow it back down to trail #373 near Honeymoon Pass. Downclimbing the couloir in afternoon conditions is the mistake this descent exists to avoid.

approach_variants.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp, then the grassy south-east slope onto the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Reach Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by any of the long trails — Andrews Creek #504 is the shortest drive, the Cathedral Driveway #510A the shortest walk, Thirtymile via the Chewuch #510 the middle option. All are multi-day and all put you in the same basin.

From the Boundary Trail below the peak, this route does not go into the Cathedral–Monk gully at all. Scramble up the grassy south-east slope directly from the main trail to gain the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Continuing north along the ridge toward The Pope and the Canadian border
Loose rock on a long broken ridge
Very long walk out from a remote basin if anything goes wrong
A no-fall step-across on the standard walk-off descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is CORRECT here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a DIKE, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

NEGATIVE MARKER for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the WEST, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Andrews Pass
bivy.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
bivy.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
bivy.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

approach_variants.name: Agnes Creek crest trail to Swamp Creek Camp and the ridge
approach_variants.notes: No road reaches this valley: take the passenger ferry or a floatplane up the lake to the landing, then the valley road or the shuttle up to the bridge at the road end, and plan the whole trip around those timetables. Walk a few hundred yards up the road to pick up the crest trail heading south, then follow well-graded tread through old-growth forest into the Agnes Creek valley past the first creekside camp, and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork — the standard overnight base. The peak shows itself up-valley along that stretch. From camp pick up the unmaintained trail up the Swamp Creek drainage, with blowdown, eroded tread, heavy brush and a crossing of Swamp Creek on a large downed log, and leave it near 3,200 ft below the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, and tied to the boat and shuttle timetable at both ends. Snow lingers on the upper talus even in summer.
hazards: The Swamp Creek path is unmaintained and heavily overgrown, with wasps a recurring nuisance in the brush
About 1,800 ft of trackless steep brushy climbing on vegetation, dirt and small rock steps
A slick polished slab at the head of the gully near 5,000 ft, bypassed with a rope and a tree belay
Serious exposure above the talus field and loose, wobbly blocks near the notch and on the summit ridge
No water on the ridge — it has to be carried up from below
The crest overhangs near the top and the last stretch drops into a narrow gully that has to be reversed or rappelled
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE POLISHED SLAB LOW DOWN AND THE BUTTRESS BETWEEN TWO GULLIES HIGHER UP ARE THE TWO PROOFS. Leave the unmaintained drainage path near 3,200 ft, below the ridge, and climb straight up steep brushy hillside with no tread at all — vegetation, dirt and small steps of rock. Around 5,000 ft the ground funnels into a gully whose head is a slick, polished slab; that slab is where the route stops being a walk and is how you know you are in the right drainage. Do not force it. The line escapes west through the taller band of rock, with a tree belay for a couple of hundred feet to regain the top of the gully, so carry a rope for this leg. Above it the angle eases and the first clear view of the peak comes at about 5,400 ft off a mild grass slope. Higher, below the sheer north face, two gullies are separated by a buttress: take the WEST one, or better the rib immediately west of it where the krummholz gives better holds. The east gully looks less steep and is the trap — it goes over cliffs, and its crux is crossing the cliff tops. The two lines merge in the upper basin about 600 ft higher.
