approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead at about 1,150 ft on the highway, the maintained trail runs a little over two miles and fifteen hundred feet to the lake, where camping is prohibited. Continue on the rougher climbers' path along the lake's west side, which climbs steeply and directly - and with no water beyond this point - through talus and brush onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge and treeline camps near 5,400 ft. From there continue south to the terminal moraine of the Colonial Glacier, or to the col beyond it between about 6,000 and 6,800 ft, which is the usual base camp. The approach rather than the climbing is the crux of this route.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September
hazards: a steep brushy climbers' path with no water above the lake
loose rock and short route-finding steps on the Pyramid east ridge crest
crevasses on the Colonial and Neve glaciers
a featureless crossing where the exit point must be identified by the gully rather than by position
one exposed rib crossing in the entry gully
an exposed notch traverse near the summit, reversed on the way down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WEST RIDGE IS GAINED FROM THE GLACIER BY A GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS THE POSITIVE MARKER. From camp, climb the Colonial Glacier to the broad col near 6,840 ft - it carries a stream, so a dry saddle is the wrong one - then drop 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve and cross it roped.

LEAVE THE ICE ON THE PEAK'S NORTH-WEST SIDE, near the prominent rock feature there around 7,700 ft. THE ENTRY IS A CLASS 3 GULLY WITH ONE EXPOSED RIB CROSSING IN IT, and it tops out on the ridge three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ON A GLACIER WITH NO LANDMARKS: IF YOU STEP OFF THE ICE ONTO ROCK THAT RISES STRAIGHT INTO THE SUMMIT PYRAMID WITH NO GULLY BESIDE IT, YOU HAVE CROSSED TOO FAR AND ARE UNDER THE FACE. Traverse back rather than committing upward - the face and the ridge are different propositions and the ridge is the easier ground.

THE SECOND CHECK IS THAT THE RIDGE HAS AIR ON BOTH SIDES. Once out of the gully you should be on a crest, not on a flank. A line that keeps a wall on one hand the whole way is not the ridge.

Above that the finish is common to both lines: a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, a short exposed traverse onto the south side, and blocky scrambling with one move that can feel low class 4. That notch is downclimbed on the exit, so read it on the way past.

approach_variants.name: Alpental groomer lot, the Phantom Slide, and the NW shoulder notch into Thunder Creek cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the groomer lot about 200 ft past the main Alpental day lot. Walk up the open south-facing hillside toward the Alpental waterfalls. At the foot of the falls, cut LEFT into the trees for roughly 100 ft and climb through two steep, usually snowed-up cliff bands. After about 300 ft of gain, move back RIGHT onto the Phantom Slide.

The Phantom Slide is a broad avalanche path that slides regularly, including on people on the upper apron. Check the NWAC forecast and time the crossing rather than lingering on it.

Climb the slide to about 4,900 ft, then trend up and left through more open ground to a notch on the northwest shoulder near 5,200 ft. Reckon roughly one and a half to three hours car to base, and much of that depends on whether a skin track already exists — most of the approach is through thick trees.

No water on this approach in winter; melt snow.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to March. A sustained cold snap usually gives the fattest ice; warm or dry winters leave it thin and force dry-tooling
hazards: The Phantom Slide is an active avalanche path and the approach crosses and climbs it
Five closely spaced lines on one face — racking up below the wrong one is the routine error
Loose, chossy rock on pitch two and through the box gully
Thin or absent ice most winters; be ready to dry-tool rather than swing
A cold, shaded northwest aspect with winter temperatures at the belays even on clear days
Alpental ski patrol conducts explosive avalanche control nearby
The descent finishes down the Southwest Slopes scramble, itself 3,100 ft of steep loose ground, or back down the Phantom Slide
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE NOTCH, DOWNCLIMB ABOUT 200 VERTICAL FEET AND TRAVERSE TO THE FIRST OBVIOUS GULLY. That is the published test and it is the one that works in cloud, because it is counted rather than seen: you are not identifying a gully by its shape from a distance, you are walking beneath the face from a fixed point and taking the first one you meet.

WHY THAT MATTERS HERE MORE THAN ANYWHERE ELSE ON THIS PAGE: this face carries FIVE closely spaced ice and mixed lines — Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully and LA Express — and they are near enough together that racking up under the wrong one is the normal failure. Count from the notch, do not pick by appearance.

THE PITCH-ONE CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS A GOOD ONE: ascend roughly 200 ft up the gully and then take an OBVIOUS RAMP OUT TO THE LEFT, belaying from a quasi-cave. Gully, then a left-trending ramp, then a cave belay. If your first rope length does not offer a left ramp at about 200 ft, you are in a neighbouring line.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS HIGHER AND UNAMBIGUOUS: the route runs up obvious weaknesses to a SMALL HEADWALL split by a 5.8 CRACK, historically aided and now freed. That crack is the route's signature. A line with no headwall crack is not New York Gully.

AND A HONEST WARNING ABOUT THE APPROACH ITSELF: most of it is through thick timber and the published advice is to go with somebody who knows it or follow an existing skin track. Without a track, expect it to be slow and to be the part of the day where you lose time.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then north along the base of the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Nearly all the routes on North Early Winters Spire are on its west side, so the Blue Lake Trailhead is the right side of the mountain to start from — the hairpin pullout on the east serves the East Buttress and couloir lines, not this one.

From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,200 ft) on SR-20 about a mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail for roughly a mile and a half to the signed Liberty Bell Trail #727 climbing-access junction, which sits just past a small stream and is marked with a large cairn. That stream is your last reliable water.

Trail #727 switchbacks up slabs, talus and heather into the basin under the west faces. Approach as if for South Early Winters Spire and then traverse LEFT (north) along the base of the formations, scrambling, until you are under North Early Winters Spire. Most parties report one to two hours from the car.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: lingering snow and avalanche debris in the basin and approach gully into June
braided climbers' paths through the upper talus make it easy to drift onto the wrong formation
no water past the stream at the Trail #727 junction
poorly protected chimney section low on the first pitch
approach_variants.baseFinding: Keep traversing north along the base. The Northwest Corner begins at a distinct corner-and-crack system whose first pitch — around 45 metres of 5.8, including a short chimney section with sparse gear — runs up to a broad ledge covered in trees. That treed ledge is the landmark: it is visible from below and from across the basin, it is the top of pitch one, and the route continues up and left off its left-hand edge. If you are under blank slab with no corner leading to a treed ledge, you have not gone far enough north yet. The corner start is shared with the West Face route, so being at the right corner puts you at the right place for either — the two diverge above the ledge, not below it.

approach_variants.name: Ruth Creek washout, Nooksack Cirque, Price Lake moraine and the ridge to the 5,900 ft slab bivy
approach_variants.notes: From the Mount Baker Highway, turn left onto Nooksack River Road (FS-32) immediately before the Nooksack River bridge, about 13 miles past Glacier. Stay left at 0.5 miles, right at 1.4 miles, and park at the washout at 2.3 miles from the highway, by Ruth Creek at about 2,156 ft. Walk the abandoned road beyond the washout for two miles to the original Nooksack Cirque trailhead at 2,550 ft. Ford the Nooksack. There is a recorded log crossing near N48.87097 W121.61267 — new logs get swept away every year, so treat the coordinate as where to start looking rather than as a bridge. Go up the forested mountainside east of the creek, starting on the west bank of Price Creek until a good log turns up. Continue to the moraine above Price Lake at 3,911 ft, then follow the ridgeline BETWEEN the Price and East Nooksack Glaciers up to a rock slab bivouac around 5,900 ft. From the bivy, get onto the glacier, traverse climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, then drop down and work onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. This route belongs to Nooksack Tower and not to Mount Shuksan — it was merged from a duplicate Shuksan entry, and the Price Glacier route on Shuksan is a different climb sharing much of the same ground.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier the river is high and the couloir is safer; later the river drops but the couloir bakes and sheds rock
hazards: Fording the Nooksack on logs that are swept away and replaced yearly
Rockfall down the couloir, recorded on the first ascent and in every account since
A hollow bergschrund that has forced parties to swing wide left
A descent of roughly ten 60 m rappels off gear you build yourself — fixed anchors here should not be trusted
Parties routinely still on the couloir or the lower approach after dark; one team took 21 hours from camp back to camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BERGSCHRUND AT ROUGHLY 6,500 FT IS THE BASE, AND THE COULOIR ABOVE IT IS THE ONLY ONE. Beckey and Schmidtke's own account of the first ascent puts them at the bergschrund at the foot of the final north face at 6,500 ft, with 800 ft of 50-degree ice couloir above. That is the arrival: a schrund, then a single steep couloir that guards the Tower.

THE RIDGE BETWEEN THE TWO GLACIERS IS THE HANDRAIL. From the Price Lake moraine you climb a rib with the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. In cloud you do not need the Tower: keep a glacier on each side of you and go up. If you only have ice on one side, you have come off the rib.

THE SADDLE IS THE HINGE, AND IT IS COUNTERINTUITIVE. From the bivy the traverse is climber's RIGHT to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, and then you DROP DOWN onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. Losing height here feels wrong and is correct. A party that refuses to descend off the saddle stays high on the wrong side and never reaches the couloir.

CONFIRM AT THE SCHRUND: the couloir starts around 50 degrees and steepens to about 60 at the top, with a single 70-degree step where it hits rock. If your line eases off rather than steepens, it is not the couloir. Parties have found the schrund hollow and swung WIDE LEFT to avoid it entirely — that is a known variation, not a sign you are lost.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the Price Glacier past the Tower's couloir puts you on the Price Glacier route on SHUKSAN, which is a different mountain's climb reached from the same basin. Nooksack Tower is the freestanding tower below and north of Shuksan's summit; if the ground above your couloir keeps going for thousands of feet rather than ending on a tower in about 1,200 ft of fourth class, you are on Shuksan.

bivy.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.
bivy.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
bivy.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

bivy.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
bivy.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.
bivy.water: The river and its tributaries are everywhere and never fail, but the North Fork is heavily glacier-fed and runs opaque with rock flour. Filter from a clear side stream rather than the main channel where you can.
bivy.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
bivy.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.

approach_variants.name: The Beckey approach as far as the Price Lake moraine, then the East Nooksack Glacier instead of the Price
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Beckey-Schmidtke route as far as the moraine above Price Lake: Ruth Creek washout, two miles of abandoned road to the Nooksack Cirque trailhead, the Nooksack ford, the forested slope east of the creek, and the moraine at 3,911 ft.

The two routes then part company at the top of the rib. Instead of continuing toward the Price Glacier, traverse onto the EAST NOOKSACK Glacier and climb to the base of the south face, somewhere between about 6,500 and 7,000 ft, where the wall rises directly out of the glacier.

Several variations exist depending on snow and ice conditions, and the climb starts on the RIGHT side of the face. It was first climbed in July 2001 and it is a much longer rock route than the Beckey line — twelve pitches against ten.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug
hazards: Choosing the wrong glacier at the top of the Price Lake rib, which is unrecoverable that day
Twelve pitches on a rarely repeated face with variations that depend on conditions
A descent by a different route on the opposite side of the tower
The same Nooksack ford and log-crossing problem as the Beckey route
Crevasses on the East Nooksack Glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM IS WHICH GLACIER YOU END UP ON, AND THE ANSWER IS THE EAST ONE. The rib above Price Lake has the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. The Beckey route commits to the Price. This route commits to the East Nooksack. That single decision, made at the top of the rib, is the difference between a north-face ice couloir and a south-face rock climb, and once you are on the wrong glacier nothing further down the day will correct it.

THE ASPECT SETTLES IT IN FOG, WITH NO VISIBILITY AT ALL. This route faces SOUTH. If the wall in front of you is in shade all morning and holds ice, you are under the north face and on the Beckey route's ground. If the wall catches the sun and is dry rock, you are where you meant to be.

ARRIVAL: the south face rises DIRECTLY ABOVE THE GLACIER — there is no intervening basin, moraine or approach slope. You walk on ice until the ice ends at the wall. That directness is the marker; a wall you reach after scrambling up talus is not this one.

AND THE START IS ON THE RIGHT. Having reached the foot of the face, the climb begins on its RIGHT side. A party that starts up the middle or the left of a twelve-pitch face on a rarely climbed tower has committed to unknown ground with a technical descent waiting for them.

DESCENT NOTE THAT DOUBLE-CHECKS THE START: the first-ascent party did not reverse this face. They descended the standard north-face route on the front of the tower, i.e. over the top and down the other side. If you are planning to rappel your line of ascent, you are planning something nobody has recorded.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the Concord-Lexington gully
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 just under a mile west of Washington Pass. Follow the maintained Blue Lake Trail until the terrain opens up — around a mile and a half to two miles — and pick up the well-established climbers' path branching left at a large cairn.

From there, trend LEFT of the line most parties take toward the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, and work up into the gully that separates Lexington Tower from Concord Tower. As you gain height in that gully a decent boot path shows up along its left side; use it. It brings you to the Concord-Lexington col.

Carry water from the trailhead. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin dry up by mid-summer.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in the Concord-Lexington gully
lingering firm snow or névé in the upper gully into early summer — axe or traction useful
the descent uses slung horns rather than fixed anchors, so carry spare webbing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route does not start from the high point of the col. From the crest, move slightly WEST and drop a couple of feet: the first pitch begins at an obvious slanting, right-leaning crack in the Lexington side of the notch, and the 5.7 crux is the very first thing you climb — awkward moves straight off the ground. Follow the leaning crack for about 15 to 20 feet and it eases into stemming up a chimney at around 5.6. If your first moves are easy you are probably on the Concord wall opposite, which is the South Face of Concord and starts by walking gravelly ledges rather than pulling on a crack. A hard start on a right-leaning crack, just below and west of the col, is the confirmation.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow to the Concord-Lexington col
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach, but the upper gully to the col commonly holds firm snow into early summer, which buries the boot path along its left side and turns the last stretch into a snow climb. Carry an axe, and crampons if it is refrozen.

SR-20 is gated across Washington Pass through the winter — typically closing in late November or early December and reopening between mid-April and early May — so there is no drive-up access until the highway reopens.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through late Jun
hazards: firm snow in the gully below the col
moat where snow meets the Lexington wall
SR-20 closed in winter — no vehicle access until reopening
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow in the col the slanting crack that starts the route can be partly buried, and the couple of feet of drop west from the high point may instead be a step down into a moat. The feature to hold onto is that the start is on the LEXINGTON side, slightly west of and just below the crest, at a right-leaning crack, and the hardest climbing of the first pitch is immediately off the deck. If snow has filled the crack's base, expect to start higher up it than the summer start and to be dealing with wet rock for the first body length.

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
approach_variants.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
hazards: At least four unmarked lines on one wall, two of them starting close together on the same buttress
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the climbing
Roughly half the pitches are at the upper end of the grade, with the crux on a corner low down
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger, not by reversing the climb
Multi-day approach and a retreat measured in days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

FIRST, PLACE THE CENTRAL BUTTRESS. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is NOT on it. This route takes the LEFT MARGIN of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

SECOND, FIND THE GULLY OR CHIMNEY AT THE BUTTRESS'S LEFT EDGE. The start is in the BLOCKY LINE OF FACE HOLDS JUST LEFT OF IT. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

THIRD, AND THIS IS THE CONFIRMATION HIGHER UP THAT NOTHING ELSE ON THE FACE GIVES YOU: this route follows a DISTINCTIVE YELLOW QUARTZ DYKE up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock.

NEGATIVE MARKERS, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE LEGAL POINT FIRST. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it follows the marked trail from Lightning Lake up the Frosty Mountain area to a pass near 8,000 ft, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south over the boundary, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Several unmarked routes on one face, two of them on the same buttress
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger rather than the way you came up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come DOWN toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the LEFT MARGIN of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a GULLY OR CHIMNEY at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the BLOCKY LINE OF FACE HOLDS JUST LEFT OF IT. The confirmation above is a YELLOW QUARTZ DYKE, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

NEGATIVE MARKERS. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the gully to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch
approach_variants.notes: From the signed Blue Lake trailhead on the highway a short distance west of Washington Pass, follow the Blue Lake Trail about a mile and a half to a small meadow, then take the climbers' boot path that breaks off just past a small stream. That path climbs through slabs, talus and meadow toward the gully descending from between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. Where the path splits, bear left and continue up the gully to the notch at its top. The gully commonly holds snow and ice into late June and is a known rockfall channel, particularly during spring and early-summer snowmelt, so move through it efficiently and keep helmets on. The notch at the top of the gully is where the route starts. Access work on the lower path has reduced the time spent in the loose ground, but the gully itself is still the part of the day worth hurrying through.
approach_variants.season: July through September. The approach gully commonly holds snow into late June, and the face itself stays wet after rain and freezes early and late in the season.
hazards: rockfall in the approach gully, especially during spring and early-summer snowmelt
sustained, steeper climbing than the standard line with correspondingly less margin
a long, wandering second pitch prone to serious rope drag
a small, exposed summit shared with parties on the neighbouring routes
north-facing rock that stays wet after rain
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE HUECO WALL IS WHERE THE TWO ROUTES PART, AND THIS ONE GOES RIGHT. The base is the top of the notch between Concord Tower and Liberty Bell, reached by the gully — if you scrambled LEFT out of the gully a couple of hundred feet below the notch onto a broad sloping bench, you are on Liberty Bell's west side and on a different mountain's route entirely. From the notch, the first pitch follows a crack system to a large ledge with some small trees growing on it; that ledge with trees is the confirmation you are on the North Face and not somewhere else on the tower. The second pitch is the one that matters here. Move right on easy ground, then straight up on rock that sounds hollow and flaky, to a section of ten to fifteen feet of unprotectable blank wall covered in huge huecos with excellent holds. At the top of that hueco wall is the decision: the standard line steps LEFT, and this variation continues RIGHT, up steeper crack and corner terrain to a prominent vertical crack, then traverses back left across the face to a large boulder. If you stepped left above the huecos, you are on the standard route at an easier grade, not on this variation. Expect severe rope drag on that long right-then-left pitch; extend everything.

approach_variants.name: From the west: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack River Trail and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes:
About 16-17 miles one-way. Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, at about 3,100 ft, and follow Trail #674 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass, then descend the far side to Boundary Camp in the Chilliwack River valley.

Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, unmaintained and rough in sections with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris, past Copper Creek Camp, then turn up at the Brush Creek Trail junction and climb through US Cabin Camp, Graybeal Camp and Whatcom Camp to Whatcom Pass. A cable-car crossing of the Chilliwack exists near U.S. Cabin Camp as an alternative to fording. Typically split over two days with a valley-bottom camp.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class choss in the final several hundred feet below the summit
Downclimbing that ground with an overnight pack, which reports rate as the riskier option
An unmaintained Chilliwack River Trail with stretches obliterated by avalanche debris
No fixed anchors anywhere on the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE BROAD TOE OF THE RIDGE, AND YOU FIND IT BY WALKING SOUTH OFF THE PASS UNTIL THE PATH DIES. From Whatcom Pass a faint, informal climbers' trail leaves the maintained trail and heads DIRECTLY SOUTH, gaining the broad toe of Whatcom Peak's north ridge. The path quickly gives way to snow patches and broken rock, and from there the route-finding rule is STAY ON THE CREST rather than follow any marked line.

SO THE FOG TEST IS A HANDRAIL TEST, AND IT IS THE BEST KIND: once you are on the crest, keep it under your feet. Any time you find yourself sidehilling with the crest above you, you have come off it. There is nothing to identify on this ridge except the ridge.

ARRIVAL AT THE START: you are on the route as soon as the informal path stops being a path and the ground becomes broken rock rising to a crest. That transition happens within a few hundred feet of the pass; this is not a route with a long walk to its base.

WHAT THE UPPER RIDGE IS LIKE, BECAUSE IT DECIDES WHETHER YOU COME BACK THIS WAY: the final several hundred feet below the summit are described bluntly by climber reports as a chossy nightmare of loose, exposed 3rd to low-4th-class terrain, and downclimbing it with a heavy overnight pack is considered the harder, riskier option even though it is shorter. Many parties instead go over the summit and down the South Spur side.

AND THE OTHER THING THIS RIDGE IS: it is the direct line from Whatcom Pass to Perfect Pass that Challenger parties are told NOT to take. It is loose, extremely exposed and called a formidable obstacle. If you are on it as a shortcut rather than as your objective, you have chosen the wrong tool.

approach_variants.name: From the east: Ross Lake water taxi to Little Beaver, then 16 miles up-valley to Whatcom Pass
approach_variants.notes: Comparable in mileage to the western line. Hire a water taxi from Ross Lake Resort, near Diablo off SR-20, to the Little Beaver Creek trailhead at about 1,600 ft on Ross Lake, then follow the Little Beaver Trail roughly 16 miles up-valley, passing Perry Creek Camp at 4.6 miles and Twin Rocks Camp around mile 8, then the Big Beaver Trail junction at 10.5 miles, before the final steep switchback climb through big-fir forest up to Whatcom Pass.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A 16-mile valley walk that depends on a water-taxi booking at both ends
The same loose upper ridge as the western approach
Returning over the summit strands you on the wrong side of the peak from this trailhead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER WAY YOU ARRIVE AT WHATCOM PASS, THE BASE TEST IS IDENTICAL: leave the maintained trail, head DIRECTLY SOUTH on the faint climbers' path, and stay on the crest once the path dies. The two approaches differ only in how you get to the pass.

THE ONE THING THIS SIDE CHANGES, AND IT IS A LOGISTICS FACT RATHER THAN A NAVIGATION ONE: your car is at Ross Lake, not at Hannegan. That rules out the common descent option of crossing the summit and coming down the South Spur side to Perfect Pass, unless you are prepared to loop back around the peak's east side or across the Whatcom Glacier to regain Whatcom Pass.

HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE AT THE PASS AND NOT AT A CAMP BELOW IT: the last stretch from the Big Beaver junction is a steep switchbacking climb through big fir. The pass is where that climb stops.

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. Whatcom Camp and both Graybeal camps have been closed because of fire damage from 2022, and the park's fire-closures page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists them closed until further notice, so there is no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

approach_variants.name: The SR-20 South Buttress pullout, then bear RIGHT into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch
approach_variants.notes:
The standard approach uses the same SR-20 pullout as the South Buttress, on the north side of the highway about 1.5 miles WEST of Washington Pass. Follow the South Buttress approach: creek crossing, brushy climbers' path into the meadow, up into the boulder field.

Eight pitches at 5.7. It sees far less traffic than the South Buttress, the peak's classic line.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch with marginal protection simply to reach the base of the ridge
A descent that leaves the ridge at the notch and continues down a different route's rappel line
Loose rock and brush on the lower approach
A more direct West Ridge descent from higher on the North Ridge exists but is considered worse for rockfall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT THE BOULDER FIELD, BEAR RIGHT AND NORTH INTO THE BASIN BENEATH THE NORTH RIDGE NOTCH, RATHER THAN LEFT TOWARD THE SOUTH BUTTRESS GULLY. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

THE ROUTE'S REAL BASE IS THE NOTCH, AND GETTING TO IT IS ITSELF A PITCH: from the basin, A LOOSE, RUNOUT 5.7 PG13 PITCH GAINS THE NORTH RIDGE NOTCH. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, AND THIS PITCH SHOULD BE TREATED AS THE TECHNICAL AND PSYCHOLOGICAL CRUX OF THE APPROACH, NOT OF THE RIDGE ABOVE IT.

SO THE TEST IS BLUNT: IF THE HARDEST, SCARIEST THING YOU HAVE DONE IS THE PITCH THAT GOT YOU TO THE NOTCH, YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT ROUTE. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

ARRIVAL: a NOTCH, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

THE NORTHERN ALTERNATIVE, WHICH ARRIVES AT THE SAME NOTCH FROM THE OTHER SIDE: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the PORCUPINE CREEK drainage, then climb TWO OR THREE SHORT PITCHES OF LOW FIFTH CLASS to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

DESCENT DOES NOT REVERSE THE APPROACH PITCH ALL THE WAY: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of BOLTED CHAIN RAPPEL ANCHORS and continuing down the same FOUR-RAPPEL West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.

approach_variants.name: Round to the unnamed glacier north of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
This is a genuinely obscure line and every recorded approach to it is a variation on getting round to the mountain's NORTH side, which no other Primus route visits.

The first recorded ascent reached it from the Klawatti side: descend a couloir where the NORTH KLAWATTI GLACIER meets Primus's WEST RIDGE, then traverse an unnamed glacier north of Primus to the foot of the crest. The first-ascent account says in as many words that it was unlikely this approach had been used before.

Other parties have come from the Thunder Creek side instead — the same trailhead, ford and Lucky Ridge climb as the East Slope, to a bivy near 6,000 ft at the toe of the Borealis Glacier — and then reached the ridge by circling the glacial lake at the glacier's terminus and crossing a short section of glacier to the base, rather than climbing the glacier toward Lucky Pass. One party took that line specifically because conditions at the standard Primus-Tricouni saddle were hazardous that day.

The ridge itself is about 1,000 ft and took the first-ascent party roughly an hour.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August; a documented late-September attempt found the crux notch glazed with bullet ice and the loose rock unbonded, which made the route markedly harder and more dangerous
hazards: Very loose, serrated rock along the entire crest — blocks and towers described as good but somewhat loose
A 5.6 crux notch with no fixed protection: natural gear and slung blocks only
Verglas glazing the notch in cool or wet weather, which is what defeated a late-September attempt
Committing retreat once above the crux — the recommended descent is the East Ridge to Lucky Pass, not this ridge
Glacier travel on an unnamed, rarely visited glacier with no established line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS WHICH SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN YOU ARE ON, AND IT IS DECIDED BY WHETHER YOU HAD TO GO DOWN TO GET THERE. Every approach to this ridge involves LOSING height onto a glacier NORTH of Primus — down a couloir from the North Klawatti Glacier where it meets Primus's west ridge, or down and around the glacial lake at the Borealis Glacier's terminus. If your day has been a continuous climb, you have not reached this route.

THE NEGATIVE TEST IS UNAMBIGUOUS AND IT IS THE ONE TO CARRY: LUCKY PASS IS NOT THIS ROUTE. If you are standing at a col at about 7,200 ft at the head of the Borealis Glacier, with Tricouni Peak's route splitting off east, you are at the start of the East Slope — a class 3 walk. The North Ridge is reached by turning away from that pass, not through it.

WHAT THE BASE ITSELF LOOKS LIKE: the foot of a 1,000 ft crest of blocks and towers, met from a glacier rather than from a notch. There is no published cairn, marker or fixed anchor at the start; the ridge is very rarely repeated and nothing on it should be assumed to be in place.

CONFIRM ON THE GROUND YOU CLIMB, NOT ON THE APPROACH: the lower ridge is 3rd and 4th class blocks and towers; the upper ridge is BANDED ROCK at low fifth, and that banding is what the first-ascent party singled out. A ridge that stays third class to the summit is not this one — and a ridge that never carried you above a glacier on the peak's north side never was.

bivy.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
bivy.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
bivy.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

bivy.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
bivy.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
bivy.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

bivy.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin toward the Cat Scratch gullies, then the notch right of the ridge
approach_variants.hours: Half a day from Boston Basin camp
approach_variants.notes:
The Aiguille is a small formation, not a peak of its own: it is the cockscomb dividing the high Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on its west side and an unnamed glacier on its east, sitting just south of the Torment-Forbidden traverse line. It is named for its resemblance to the Chamonix aiguille of the same shape — a deliberate echo, and a coincidence worth being clear about rather than a mistake.

Approach exactly as for Forbidden Peak: Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles to the small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg, the old Diamond Mine roadbed, then the steep unmaintained climbers' path with several stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the Boston Basin camps at about 5,300 and 6,400 ft.

From camp, head up toward the Forbidden Gully / Cat Scratch gullies area and traverse to the notch. It is a half-day objective from camp, which is most of its appeal.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; July and August are the most settled, and snow can linger around camp into July
hazards: Rockfall off the ridge and the tower is the primary hazard
Weather that builds fast, with afternoon thunderstorms usual
A very small, exposed tower top that many parties choose not to stand on
Approach terrain shared with Forbidden's West Ridge descent, so parties may be above you in the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FORMATION IS THE EASY PART: THE AIGUILLE IS CONSPICUOUS ON ENTERING BOSTON BASIN and reads as the letter it is named for. Use it to orient the whole basin. The route is the harder part.

THE BASE IS THE NOTCH TO THE RIGHT OF THE NORTH RIDGE — you traverse to it from the Cat Scratch / Forbidden Gully side; you do not start at the toe of the ridge. A start at the very bottom of the crest is not this route.

COUNT THE PITCHES, BECAUSE THE COUNT IS THE ROUTE: THREE TO FOUR PITCHES OF FOURTH-CLASS SCRAMBLING TO THE BASE OF A TOWER, AND THEN ONE 40-FT PITCH TO ITS TOP. That is the whole climb. If you have run out four pitches and there is no tower standing in front of you, you are on the wrong side of the formation.

THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW ABOUT THE TOP IS THAT IT IS NOT THE TOP. The route finishes on a subsidiary tower; the true high point of the Aiguille looks as though it is about to topple over and most parties deliberately stop short of it. So a summit that feels wrong is not evidence you are off route — on this formation it is the expected outcome, and it is the reason the descent is a single 40-ft rappel from where you stand.

TELL IT FROM THE SOUTH RIDGE BY WHICH SIDE YOU WALKED ROUND. The two routes differ only in which flank of the same small formation is climbed from the same camp; the South Ridge is the longer, harder and much less documented of the two, and its start is not published — so if you are unsure which side you are on, the four-pitch scramble to a tower is the one that can be confirmed.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Lyman Lakes and Cloudy Pass
bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. From the west it is roughly two miles and 1,700 ft above Spider Meadow over Spider Gap, crossing the permanent snowfield below the gap and dropping onto the Lyman Glacier, which puts an ice axe and traction on the packing list even in August. From the east it is a long valley walk up Railroad Creek from Holden, with intermediate camps at Hart Lake and at Rebel Camp about a mile beyond it that break the approach in two. North Star and Cloudy are scrambles off the Cloudy Pass trail from here; Chiwawa is reached by traversing the Lyman Glacier to its east ridge, which is a roped glacier objective rather than a walk. Cloudy Pass itself is scenic and thoroughly exposed to wind and lightning. With the Holden road closed and the Chiwawa road under its own closures, both ends of this corridor have been unreachable at times through 2026.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lakes, the Lyman Glacier outflow and creeks all through the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. Camping and campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of Lyman Lake's shoreline, so pitch back from the water; carry a stove rather than planning on a fire. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

bivy.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
bivy.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
bivy.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

bivy.notes: This basin is the reason North Star Mountain, Cloudy Peak and Chiwawa Mountain sit in the same zone as Bonanza — it is reachable from both sides and belongs to neither. Reached from the west, no recreation pass is needed at the Phelps Creek trailhead, which the Forest Service lists as a no-fee site; reached from the east it needs the ferry and bus booking instead.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at Lower Lyman Lake, more scattered ground toward the upper lakes, and a small number of exposed camps at Cloudy Pass; a popular corridor, so plan on sharing

Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

bivy.name: Phelps Creek Campground and the Chiwawa River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: These are staging camps, not climbing camps: the point of them is that the drive up the Chiwawa River road is around twenty-three miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, the last twelve are rough gravel and dirt genuinely unsuited to low clearance vehicles, and doing that at the end of a long drive from the west side is how parties end up starting the walk in tired and late. Phelps Creek Campground sits near the confluence of Phelps Creek and the Chiwawa a short distance below the Phelps Creek trailhead, and the Trinity trailhead at about 2,800 ft — the start of the Buck Creek trail toward Buck Creek Pass and Fortress Mountain — is a mile or so away, so one night here stages either objective. The road is the fragile part of this whole side of the zone. Storm damage has closed it above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year order, and a 2026 fire closure covered the Chiwawa River road and the Phelps Creek spur on top of that, so check whether you can drive to the trailhead at all before planning around it. When the road is shut above Atkinson Flat the lower campgrounds are still a reasonable base but the trailhead becomes a long walk or ride further on.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is right there but these are primitive campgrounds — treat water and expect no potable supply or trash service
bivy.permit: Small nightly fee at the developed sites, first come first served with no reservations, so arrive early on a summer Friday. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers trailhead parking the next morning, and the free self-issue wilderness permit is picked up at the trailhead itself. Fire restrictions bite here in late summer and often ban all open flame including in the fire rings.
bivy.capacity: Phelps Creek Campground has roughly seven tent sites plus half a dozen equestrian sites; Atkinson Flat, Schaefer Creek, Rock Creek and the other small forest campgrounds strung along the road below it each hold a handful more

bivy.name: Spider Meadow and Phelps Basin
bivy.notes: About five and a half miles and 1,250 ft from the Phelps Creek trailhead at roughly 3,500 ft, this is the standard first night for almost everything on the Chiwawa side. It stages the Spider Gap crossing to Lyman Lakes and so serves North Star, Cloudy and Chiwawa; Phelps Basin half a mile above the head of the meadow is the base for Dumbell Mountain, whose route climbs northwest out of the upper basin, steepens around 6,100 ft and works up talus and a weakness to the notch west of the summit. Higher bivouac ground exists at Larch Knob, about 1,600 ft above the meadow on the switchbacks toward Spider Gap, with a few platforms partly sheltered from the wind pouring through the gap. The same trailhead also serves the Carne Mountain trail, whose basin at about 6,100 ft holds several camps with good water and is the link to the saddle above Ice Lakes and across to Leroy — those saddle camps have no water other than snowmelt. Road access is the weak point here: the Chiwawa River road is long, the final twelve miles are rough gravel unfriendly to low clearance, and the last two miles of the Phelps Creek spur are rougher still.
bivy.water: Reliable — Phelps Creek runs the length of the meadow and the basin above holds snowmelt streams well into the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead, which is entered about two and a half miles up. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at Phelps Creek. Camp on established bare sites rather than in the meadow itself, and expect fire restrictions from midsummer onward on top of the usual high-elevation limits.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites through a mile-long meadow, plus quieter ground in Phelps Basin above it — the meadow absorbs a lot of parties but is genuinely busy on summer weekends

approach_variants.name: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass, then the east slope traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Tiffany Springs Campground sits at about 6,760 ft and is reached by long gravel drives from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek road, from the Methow Valley, or over Baldy Pass on the South Fork. The Conconully line is the roughest of the three. Expect an hour or more on gravel whichever you choose.

Trail #373 leaves the campground east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft, about forty-five minutes of easy walking. From the pass, traverse south on the grassy east slope below the crest into the small cirque at the base of the north face, at roughly 7,360 ft, then climb the boulder field to the foot of the climbing at about 7,600 ft.

Compared with anything else in this corner of the state the approach is short and easy, which is most of this face's appeal. Roads are snowbound for much of the year and generally open around late June.
approach_variants.season: June through early September, once snow has cleared the lower rock
hazards: Shares its entire lower half with the easier arete beside it; the split is at the tower, not at the base
The flaring chimney and offwidth crux takes awkward and sparse gear
Loose rock and teetering blocks on the ridge and near the tower
The old descent trail above the lower lake is faint and easily lost
Long gravel access from every direction with no quick exit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the cirque, read the face as two halves: SNOW GULLIES ON THE LEFT, and a distinct ROCK TOWER with a ridge running up to it ON THE RIGHT. Both rock routes are on the right half. If you are looking up a continuous snow chute, you are on the wrong side of the face.

Both rock routes gain the same ridge and finish over the same tower, so the base is genuinely shared and the split happens on the climb. Start up the lower rock on the right side of the face, two pitches of fourth-class ground, and follow the ridge scramble to the FOOT OF THE TOWER. Everything to that point is common.

HERE IS THE TEST, AND IT IS A PHYSICAL ONE. At the tower this route goes STRAIGHT UP IT. The pitch is about seventy-five feet of good climbing that turns into a WIDE FLARING CHIMNEY with an offwidth section, and the gear placements in it are awkward. That chimney is the crux of the route and it is the single thing that identifies this line rather than its neighbour.

SO: if you are standing under a steep tower wall looking at a flaring chimney and reaching for your widest pieces, you are on this route. If instead your line traverses LEFT to avoid a vertical step and stays at fourth class, you have taken the easier arete beside it — same tower, same summit, no technical crux, and you should know that is what happened rather than believing you climbed this.

Above the chimney it is fourth class to the top of the tower and then third-class walking along the crest to Tiffany's main summit slope.

NEGATIVE MARKER on the descent: it is not a reversal. Take the north-west ridge down to about eight thousand feet, contour north-east toward the smaller lake, and pick up the faint old ridge trail that returns to Honeymoon Pass.

bivy.name: Tiffany Springs Campground
bivy.notes: This is the base for the north face and the trailhead in one, which is unusual and is what makes the face approachable at all: the walk to the bottom of the routes is under an hour, so a party can sleep at the car and still be climbing at first light without a bivouac. Trail 373 begins across the road from the campground and runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at around 7,150 ft, from where the face is below you. THE DRIVE IS THE COMMITMENT. Three ways reach it and they are not equivalent: a narrow four-wheel-drive road over Lone Frank Pass from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek, about twenty miles; a longer gravel road over Baldy Pass suited to two-wheel drive, about thirty; and a good two-wheel-drive gravel line from the Methow, north out of Winthrop on the Chewuch River road and then east and north on the 37 and 39, about twenty-six miles. Road 39 itself has not been graded in some time and is not recommended for low-clearance passenger cars. At this elevation the road holds snow late into the spring and can shut with the first serious autumn storm, so the usable window is short and both ends of it are worth checking rather than assuming.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AND NO TAP — this is the single most important practical fact about the place, and its name is misleading. There is no piped supply, no water service and no rubbish service. Bring everything you need for drinking, cooking and washing, or plan to treat from Tiffany Lake, which is a short walk east on the trail and is the nearest dependable open water. In late summer this whole plateau is dry and what looks like a creek on a map may be nothing at all.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside designated wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery — the opposite of the permit expectation a few miles west in the Pasayten. There is a small nightly fee at the campground and sites are first come, first served. Fire restrictions on this dry high plateau run through most of the summer and are commonly total bans, which given what has burned here recently should be treated as the default rather than the exception. Party size and stay limits are the usual forest ones.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive forest campground with a handful of sites, taking tents and modest vehicles. Trailers are not appropriate given the road. It is rarely full and it is the only organised camping anywhere near this face.

bivy.name: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
bivy.notes: Under a mile from the campground and directly on the approach, this is the camp for a party who would rather sleep on water than at a car, or who has arrived to find the campground full or closed. It is the last certain water before the face. The trail continues around the shore and climbs about six hundred feet to Honeymoon Pass, which is the gateway to the north side; parties leaving a second vehicle at the Freezeout Ridge roadhead can carry on over Whistler Pass at around 7,600 ft to the summit and descend the Freezeout trail, an open loop of some eleven miles that is the standard way to combine the walk-up with a look at the face. THE BURN IS PART OF THE LANDSCAPE HERE. This trail travels through old fire scars that have opened the views and filled the ground with wildflower meadow, and the 2026 fire has added to that directly on this mountain — expect standing dead timber, no shade, and blowdown that changes with each windstorm. Do not pitch under dead trees in wind.
bivy.water: The lakes, and they are the dependable supply for the whole north side of this mountain — everything above them on the pass and the face runs on snowmelt and is dry once that has gone. Access to the water is easy from the trail. Treat it; these are shallow, warm, well-used lakes rather than cold alpine tarns.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness. No permit, no quota, no reservation, and no fee to camp at the lakes. A pass is not required to park at the campground trailhead across the road. Fire restrictions apply through the summer and are usually total bans; carry a stove. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground, and note that this trail is open to horses and mountain bikes as well as walkers, so pitch clear of it.
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal spots around the shores, with the established ground at the north-west end of Little Tiffany Lake. Room for a party or two. Nothing developed and no toilet, and it sees family day-hiking traffic rather than climbers.

bivy.name: Honeymoon Pass
bivy.notes: The pass is where the trail crosses onto the north side and the face comes into view, and it is the tactical camp rather than the comfortable one. Its argument is a dawn start: from here the base of the routes is a short drop and a scramble rather than a walk from the road, which matters for the north-east couloir where the snow wants climbing early and matters much less for the rock, since the campground is under an hour away regardless. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WIND, in that order, and on a face this short the trade is rarely worth it — most parties are better off sleeping at the campground or the lake and walking in. Where it does earn its keep is for a party spending two days on the face, or one continuing over Whistler Pass to the summit and out by Freezeout Ridge. Nights are cold at this elevation from late August onward and there is no shelter at all if weather comes across the plateau.
bivy.water: None dependable. Snowmelt early in the season and nothing at all once it has gone. Everything is carried up from Tiffany Lake, six hundred feet and half a mile below, and the party that forgets this ends up walking back down for it in the evening. In the ice season it is a snow camp and you melt.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation, no fee. Fire restrictions run through the summer and there is nothing to burn at this height in any case. The turf here is thin and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass for a small party on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and nothing to shelter behind. Windswept is the word most often used about this crest and it is accurate.

bivy.name: The talus and benches below the north face
bivy.notes: The routes start here and, on a face six hundred and fifty feet high forty-five minutes from a campground, essentially nobody sleeps here. It is written down because a party reading a list of camps should not be left to assume there is a bivouac at the base — there is not, and the answer to a late arrival is the campground, not the wall. THE FACE ITSELF is broken by several couloirs, aretes and vertical granite cliffs; the north-east couloir is the longest and most direct of the snow lines, on the left, and the tower at the right-hand end carries the rock routes, with the ridge line giving a vertical crack, a wide flaring chimney and long stretches of easy fourth-class scrambling on generally excellent rock.
