Because the snow goes soon after the roads become passable, the ice and couloir lines are a shoulder-season or winter objective and are reached by ski or snowmobile in that season rather than by driving to the campground. Treat the rock routes as the summer proposition and the couloirs as a separate trip requiring a separate approach.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the couloirs early, and nothing whatsoever once that has gone. Given how early the snow leaves here after the roads open, that window is short. Carry water from the lakes; there is no source at the base of the face you should plan on.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation. No fires: this is bare rock and talus with nothing to burn and fragile alpine ground around it. Standard leave-no-trace applies and human waste has to be carried out from the base of a face this small and this close to a road.
bivy.capacity: No established camping. There are boulder-field benches and scraps of flat ground at the foot of the wall where one or two people could put down a bag, and nothing more — this is a place to leave packs and gear up rather than a site, and it is recorded to say so rather than to invent one.

wa_north_twin_sister_scramble.approach: Drive Road 38 west from Mosquito Lake Road, cross Clearwater Creek at about 4.5 miles, and take the right fork down to the gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack. From the gate, the approach is entirely on old logging roads and then ridge/brush for roughly 7 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car-to-summit, one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble — most parties mountain-bike the road portion to save time and legs. Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and ascend the well-graded logging road for about 2.5 miles; at the first major fork stay right (the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry). About 0.2 miles later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the left branch here. Around the 5-mile mark, near a dirt mound and a cairn, leave the logging road proper and pick up an old, overgrown road spur that switchbacks up through a clearcut; this is the point where route-finding gets harder and the brush thickens noticeably (expect to get soaked in wet weather — the clearcut brush is notorious for saturating pants and boots even without rain). By about 6.4 miles you pass an old fire-ring in the clearcut and enter a final band of brush before reaching timber at the base of the west ridge; from there, follow the timbered ridge itself up to where it opens onto rock and the class 3 scrambling begins. There is no reliable water source once you leave the river at the trailhead, so carry what you need for the day. In low cloud/fog, which is common on the Twin Sisters, the clearcut and lower-ridge sections lack obvious cairns or a defined tread and route-finding can be genuinely difficult; parties should be comfortable navigating by map/GPS through brushy, featureless clearcut terrain. On the ridge proper, cairns mark a Class 3 line — the lower ridge goes on or just right (south) of the crest, but from the small headwall below the false summits stay LEFT (climber's left); drifting right up there leads toward false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 terrain on loose, exposed rock.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack bridge gate, the logging roads to the cairn at mile 5, then the clearcut spur to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
This is a Twin Sisters approach, so start with the range check: the Twin Sisters here are the olivine peaks west of Mount Baker, reached off Mosquito Lake Road and the Middle Fork Nooksack. Every road name below belongs to that range and to no other Twin Sisters.

Drive Road 38 west from Mosquito Lake Road, cross Clearwater Creek, and take the right fork down to the gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack. From the gate it is roughly 7 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car to summit, almost all of it on old logging road and then ridge — one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble, and most parties mountain-bike the road.

Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and climb the well-graded logging road about 2.5 miles. At the first major fork stay RIGHT; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the LEFT branch.

Around mile 5 the road walking ends. From there an old overgrown spur switchbacks up through a clearcut, and by about mile 6.4 you pass an old fire ring and enter a final band of brush before timber at the base of the west ridge.

The roads are on private timberland; access status changes, so confirm before the trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the scramble. In May and June parties still get up it but the north-slope snowfield is in play
hazards: Route-finding through a featureless clearcut with no cairns and no tread, in the cloud that is normal here
Brush that saturates clothing and boots without rain
Drifting right near the false summits into unintended Class 4-5 on loose, exposed rock
Private timberland access that changes year to year
No water after the river at the gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DIRT MOUND AND CAIRN AT ABOUT MILE 5 IS THE MOST IMPORTANT MARKER ON THIS APPROACH, BECAUSE IT IS WHERE THE NAVIGATION GETS HARD. Up to there you are on graded logging road and the only decisions are two forks — RIGHT at the first major fork about 2.5 miles in, then LEFT at the next fork 0.2 mile past the second bridge. At the mound and cairn near mile 5, leave the road for an old overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut.

THE FIRE RING AT ABOUT MILE 6.4 IS THE SECOND MARKER, and it confirms you took the right spur. Past it is a final band of brush and then timber at the base of the west ridge.

IN LOW CLOUD, WHICH IS NORMAL HERE, THE CLEARCUT IS THE HARDEST GROUND ON THE ROUTE AND IT IS NOT THE MOUNTAIN. There are no cairns and no defined tread through the clearcut and lower ridge, and the terrain is genuinely featureless. Parties should be prepared to navigate this section by map and GPS. The brush will also soak you to the waist without any rain falling.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING: follow the timbered ridge up until it opens onto rock. Trees stop, rock starts, Class 3 begins. There is no bergschrund, no notch and no col to look for — the transition is vegetative.

THE FOG TEST FOR THE RIDGE ITSELF: LOW ON THE RIDGE THE LINE RUNS ON OR JUST RIGHT OF THE CREST; FROM THE SMALL HEADWALL BELOW THE FALSE SUMMITS, STAY LEFT — CLIMBER'S LEFT. Cairns mark a Class 3 line that way. Drifting RIGHT up there leads to false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 ground on loose, exposed rock. If the climbing has got harder than Class 3 and the rock has got worse, you have drifted right; traverse back left rather than pushing on.

THE ROCK ITSELF IS A CONFIRMATION YOU ARE IN THE RIGHT RANGE. The Twin Sisters are dunite — olivine-rich ultramafic rock, exceptionally grippy, commonly compared to coarse sandpaper. If the rock under your hands is ordinary Cascade granite or volcanic rubble, you are not on the Sisters.

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate at the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, then the Dailey Prairie roads to the West Ridge path
approach_variants.notes:
The same gate and ridge, described by road names with the Dailey Prairie road-end as the marker: via Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38. Park at the gate near 1,200 ft and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads — commonly by mountain bike — to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.

Several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie make GPS or a GPX track genuinely useful here; wrong turns on this network are common and expensive.

The gate situation on this network changes year to year. Treat the drivable road-end as unverified until confirmed for your trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network around Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
Private-timberland gates whose status changes year to year
The same drift-right-into-Class-5 trap near the false summits
Brushy, wet climbers' path with no maintained tread
Long approach with no water above the road network
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROAD NETWORK IS THE CRUX AND THE MOUNTAIN IS NOT. Around Dailey Prairie the logging roads fork repeatedly with no signage, every branch looks like the main line, and a wrong turn costs miles. Carry a track. THE END OF RIDEABLE ROAD IS THE MARKER, and on this network it is commonly identified by a LARGE CULVERT PIPE at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes there and continue on foot. THE CLIMBERS' PATH IS BRUSHY AND WET AND NOT HARD TO FOLLOW — that combination is itself the confirmation. It climbs through timber onto the ridge crest. ARRIVAL: the same as the other variant, because it is the same ridge. Timber gives way to rock and Class 3 scrambling starts. Low on the ridge the line runs on or just right of the crest; from the headwall below the false summits STAY CLIMBER'S LEFT, because drifting right there puts you on false summits and unintended Class 4-5 ground. WHICH SISTER AM I ON? This matters because the same road network serves North Twin, South Twin, Little Sister, Cinderella and Skookum, and the peaks look alike. NORTH TWIN's west ridge tops out at 6,644 ft and is reached from the road network north of the range. SOUTH TWIN's west ridge is gained at an obvious NOTCH in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft above Orsino Creek Basin, and its summit is 7,004 ft. If your ridge started at a defined notch, you are on South Twin.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the glacier's true-right margin to the lowest point of the buttress
approach_variants.notes:
As for the Colchuck Glacier route: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed fork, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,200 ft, and the last reliable water on the route.

Follow the east-shore boot path to the inlet at the south end, then climb talus and snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft. Instead of continuing toward the col, angle up and across the glacier's true-right margin toward the peak's northeast side.

Cross the moat where snow meets rock — a snow bridge or a wedged block in a good year, and the technical crux of the approach in a lean one. Parties do rope for this.

Given fourteen-plus pitches and a multi-stage approach, most parties either start well before dawn from the car or camp at Colchuck Lake and climb from there. There is no water above the lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the rock; the moat crossing is easiest early and hardest in a lean year late
hazards: A moat crossing that can be the technical crux of the day in a lean snow year
Two established starts that do not converge until around pitch five
Inconsistent rock — clean crack pitches interspersed with loose, mossy and lichened ground
Loose debris on the long rising ledge traverse, onto anyone below
No water above Colchuck Lake
A long walk-off down the Colchuck Glacier after a fourteen-pitch day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BUTTRESS IS THE ROCK JUST SOUTH OF THE COULOIR, AND THE COULOIR IS THE THING YOU LOOK FOR FIRST. It is easier to identify a deep slot in a face than a rib on it, so use the Northeast Couloir as your marker and then step south onto the rock beside it. If you are in a narrow snow slot, you are one feature too far north.

ARRIVAL IS THE LOWEST POINT OF THE ROCK. The commonly climbed start gains the buttress at its lowest point and heads for wide, broken cracks at about 5.8. Standing at the right place there is nothing lower to climb — the rock runs down into the glacier and the moat, and you had to cross that moat to reach it.

TWO STARTS EXIST, AND MIXING THEM IS THE ROUTINE ERROR HERE. There is the more travelled version described above and an older, separate start; they do not meet until around the fifth pitch. So a party that steps onto rock wherever the moat happened to be crossable can find itself on neither, on unfamiliar ground, with no way to tell. Cross the moat where it puts you at the LOWEST rock, not where it is most convenient.

CONFIRMATION IN THE FIRST TWO PITCHES: wide, broken cracks on generally solid rock leading to the crest below a large headwall, then a downclimb of about fifteen feet off the crest before ramps take you up and right. A start with no downclimb in the first few pitches is not this line.

AND THE BAIL-OUT WARNING: this route has a real reputation for parties retreating because they cannot find the crux dihedral higher up. If the base was ambiguous, the rest of the day will be worse.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass, the traverse corridor to the Red Ledge, and the Formidable Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A deep objective reached along the same corridor as its neighbours, and the walk-in is a full day or more of committing glaciated terrain rather than a hike. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, take the maintained trail to the pass, then leave it and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow bands, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake, climb out of the basin toward the cliff band running west off the knoll above; the Red Ledge cuts through it, usually entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin and a few feet of easy rock, and it is broad and walkable unless it is holding snow or verglas. Roughly a quarter mile past the ledge, descend several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between the two large icefall sections, cross that bench, and continue to the foot of the Formidable Glacier. Note that this is a different objective from the peak's ordinary walk-up on the south side, which is the descent line rather than the approach.
approach_variants.season: Early to mid summer suits it best: early enough that the couloir still holds firm snow or ice rather than bare, rockfall-prone rock, but late enough that the moat at the top of the glacier has opened enough to allow access to the face.
hazards: large blocks have come down on this route
the approach crosses above a heavily crevassed glacier
the standard descent on the south side has difficult route-finding, constant exposure and loose rock, and has been the scene of a fatality
a snow couloir that steepens past sixty-five degrees with overhanging chockstones at its top
sparse protection on the crux, with one long pitch reported as protected by a single piece
approach_variants.baseFinding: GO RIGHT ON THE GLACIER, AND THE MOAT IS THE GATE. Ascend the Formidable Glacier by traversing RIGHT, to its northern end, and climbing the easier, safer section there — the direct line up the middle weaves through many large cracks and is not the way. At the top of the glacier, stop and hunt along the margin for a place to cross the large moat, because that crossing, not the climbing, decides whether the route goes at all on a given day. Above the moat, the route begins in a rubble-covered fourth-class gully, and the rubble is the identifier: this is broken, dirty ground rather than clean rock, and it feeds directly into a snow couloir hidden from below. If what rises above your moat crossing is clean, steep rock with no rubble gully and no couloir behind it, you are too far along the face and should traverse back toward the glacier's northern end. Once in the couloir it steepens past sixty-five degrees in a couple of spots, with good cracks for rock protection on its right side and overhanging chockstones to pull through at the top, landing on a large ledge. The crux above that is two pitches around a loose thirty-foot granite tower split by a three-foot crack — if you have not passed a tower like that, the crux is still ahead of you.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: About one mile and 700 ft below Cache Col on a boot path. The usual first camp south of Cascade Pass and the base for Spider, Formidable and the south side of Magic.
bivy.water: The lake and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required; the lake is outside the national park
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites on rock and heather benches around the lake

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

approach_variants.name: Straight off the road end: the C-J couloir to the hanging glacier, then the leftmost rib
approach_variants.notes:
This is one of the shortest approaches in the range and one of the least forgiving. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road near 3,600 ft, walk a short way back down the road, descend a dirt embankment, ford or cross the infant Cascade River, and cross the terminal moraine and snowfield. Serious ground starts around 3,500 ft — you are on the route within an hour of the car.

Climb PARTWAY up the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir to the hanging glacier on the RIGHT, then take the leftmost rib to the summit. Twelve pitches, about 4,000 ft.

The descent is a separate expedition: the East Ridge's loose 3rd and 4th class gendarme ledges to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, then either the couloir or 'Doug's Direct' — beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehilling steep heather, across Mixup Peak's north ridge and down to the Cache Glacier. Parties have taken four and a half to nine hours from the col.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, once the road is open and the lower couloir approach holds consolidated snow
hazards: Hanging glaciers above the route — the Sill Glacier among them — that release ice and rock; parties describe rocks and ice bouncing for three or four seconds at a time
The mountain's standing reputation for rockfall, with loose rock reported across trip reports and a documented near-miss on a 2020 descent
Steep 45-60 degree snow on approach and descent with real fall consequence — one party found the heather descent the most dangerous part of the trip
A Cascade River ford at the very start, which rises through the day
A routefinding-intensive descent with suspect rappel anchors, and a history of parties returning a day or two late
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST FOR THIS ROUTE IS WHETHER YOU ARE TOUCHING VEGETATION, AND IT IS THE CLEANEST DISCRIMINATOR ON THE WHOLE FACE. This side of Johannesburg carries at least five named lines within a few hundred metres of each other, and most of them start with hundreds of feet of vertical bushwhacking — alder, turf, tree roots, tunnelling through near-vertical pines. THIS ROUTE DOES NOT. Its own published description ends with the words no bush climbing. IF YOU ARE PULLING ON TREES OR HEATHER TO MAKE UPWARD PROGRESS, YOU ARE ON THE NORTHEAST RIB OR THE NORTHEAST BUTTRESS, NOT ON THIS.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS: STAY IN THE COULOIR. Do not break out onto rock low down. Climb the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir until a HANGING GLACIER appears on your RIGHT — that glacier is the landmark, and it is what you leave the couloir for. The Northeast Rib lines leave the couloir far lower, before it narrows.

FROM THE HANGING GLACIER, TAKE THE LEFTMOST RIB. That is the whole route-finding instruction and the word that matters is leftmost. Several rib features present themselves at that shelf; the correct one is the far left of them.

ORIENT YOURSELF ON THE FACE AS A WHOLE BEFORE YOU START, BECAUSE IT IS CROWDED: running WEST to EAST across it the order is the Northeast Rib lines, then a route in a vertical cleft with a waterfall, then the Northeast Buttress. The Cascade-Johannesburg couloir is the broad snow line that separates Johannesburg from Cascade Peak, and this route uses it as a stairway rather than climbing it to the col.

AND KNOW WHAT THE COULOIR ITSELF IS: it is the original 1938 line and the most popular one, finishing at the col rather than on any rib. If you are still in the snow at the top, you never left for the rib.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake TH cross-country up Mountaineer Creek to the north basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail and go STRAIGHT PAST the Colchuck Lake turnoff. Continue to about 4,700 ft, where a faint path leaves the trail for Mountaineer Creek. Follow it over and down to the creek, then up the creek to roughly 4,780 ft, and bushwhack up to a boulder field below Argonaut at about 4,925 ft.

Traverse the boulders following cairns south-southwest and cut through slide alder — this brush is the notorious part of the day, and staying on talus to climber's right where you can avoids the worst of it. Then head up in or beside the trees, through boulders, talus, scree and dry creek beds, past waterfall slabs, into the north basin below Argonaut at about 6,700 ft. Roughly four hours car-to-basin for an efficient party.

Expect to lose the boot path in the boulder field. Most of this approach is navigated by feel; there is no marked trail. Wet, mossy logs over Mountaineer Creek are a nuisance in both directions.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; parties report significant snow and slush still hampering things into late June
hazards: Dense slide alder in the Mountaineer Creek drainage
Wet, mossy log crossings of Mountaineer Creek
Boot path disappears in the boulder field — sustained off-trail navigation
Firm or icy snow finger to the col late season
Waterfall slabs on the approach
Descent route-finding is genuinely tricky and is not a place to be in poor visibility
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the north basin at about 6,700 ft, a SNOW FINGER runs up to the southwest. Climbing it — late in the season with some loose, dirty rock where the snow has pulled back — brings you to a small COL / NOTCH at the very foot of the Northwest Arete. That col is the start of the roped climbing.

So the sequence in poor visibility is: basin floor, single obvious snow tongue heading southwest, top of the tongue, notch. The snow finger can be firm or icy late in the season and looks more intimidating than the grade suggests — carry an axe and consider crampons even though this is a rock route.

Above the col the arete gives six to eight pitches of blocky, generally solid Class 4 to 5.6 with route-finding that is described as straightforward. If the climbing above your notch is immediately hard or featureless, you are not on the arete.

Do not plan to reverse the arete: the descent traverses off east to the Argonaut-Colchuck col with roughly four rappels, so you finish on the other side of the mountain from your packs and your approach.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek to the West Face meadows
approach_variants.notes:
FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft; Bedal Creek Trail #705 along the creek through old growth until the maintained tread gives out at a washout below the West Face basin, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in.

Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path — it leaves LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft and is usually flagged pink — then climb steeply through forest to about 4,900 ft, cross talus and a meadow bench, and reach the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft. Water here or at the streams just below.

From the saddle stay in the meadows below the broad West Face. Do not continue southeast toward the glacier toe.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Brushy, blowdown-choked washout where the maintained trail ends
Route-finding through the forest band above the washout
Loose rock in the meadow-to-face transition
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Northwest Buttress is reached on foot with no glacier travel at all, and that is the test: if you are putting crampons on, you have walked past it onto the standard Corkscrew line. From the meadows, the route starts at the lowest and left-most point of the face, on a corner of noticeably DARKER rock than the wall either side of it. Rock you can walk up to dry-shod, with grass and meadow underfoot rather than ice, is the correct base.

bivy.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
bivy.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river
bivy.permit: Developed fee campground on national forest land; the per-night fee covers it and no pass or permit is needed to occupy a site. Nothing here is inside wilderness.
bivy.capacity: Around 20 developed sites with tables, tent pads, fire rings and vault toilets; fee campground, typically open late spring to fall

bivy.name: Bivy at the base of Sloan's southwest face
bivy.notes: On the Bedal Creek approach below the west and southwest faces. Parties who do not climb in a single long day sleep near the base of the face.
bivy.water: Running water near the base of the routes through midsummer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead
bivy.capacity: A few small tent or bivy sites

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout and Kangaroo Pass, then break off the gully about 200 ft BELOW the notch
approach_variants.notes:
The Temple is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass, the same parking used for the neighbouring Hairpin Crags and Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus, faint and intermittently cairned, up to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour.

From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Expect about 11 hours car to car.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A 200 ft window in which to leave the gully, above and below which you are on a different route
Loose talus and a boulder-choked gully
Rope-stuck issues on the descent, which is why some parties break it into three shorter rappels
Early-season snow or ice in the approach gully
No reliable water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NORTHWEST FACE BREAKS OFF ONTO A CLIMBER'S TRAIL ABOUT 200 FT BELOW THE NOTCH, INSTEAD OF CONTINUING INTO THE BOULDER-CHOKED GULLY. That is the whole find and it is a measured one: two hundred feet short of the top of the gully, an obvious bench and trail splits off RIGHT.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS: IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE NOTCH, YOU HAVE GONE ROUGHLY 200 FT TOO FAR AND YOU ARE AT THE START OF THE NORTH FACE. And if you are fighting up a boulder-choked gully bed rather than walking a bench, you have missed the split.

GETTING TO THE GULLY IN THE FIRST PLACE: from Kangaroo Pass, traverse left to the GULLY BETWEEN KANGAROO TEMPLE AND LITTLE FINGER, then ascend toward the notch. Do not drop straight down the far side of the pass; contour south below the slabs descending from Wallaby Peak, losing about 20 ft below the pass, on a good well-cairned trail beneath the slab bands.

WHAT THE OTHER TWO ROUTES DO FROM THE SAME PLACE, SO THE THREE ARE SEPARABLE: the NORTH FACE goes all the way up the gully to the high notch. THIS ROUTE takes the bench 200 ft below it. THE SOUTH FACE crosses the same pass but then drops below it and traverses across to the far side of the formation, and its face is not even visible from the highway.

DESCENT: from the summit, downclimb or scramble to the fixed rappel anchors on the NORTH side of the formation. Accounts differ slightly, with some parties making two full-length rappels of about 30 m and others three shorter single-rope rappels, roughly 150-160-plus ft in total, to avoid rope-stuck issues, landing at or near the North Ridge notch. From the notch, the standard descent gully leads back down to Kangaroo Pass.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie, then cross-country into Summit Chief Valley
approach_variants.notes: Do NOT walk the trail to Dutch Miller Gap. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, head up the valley on the trail until you reach a SMALL STEEL BRIDGE, well short of the gap — that bridge is the turnoff. Leave the trail there and travel cross-country in a southerly direction into the mouth of Summit Chief Valley, then up the valley to a camp at around the level where the timber thins. From camp the peak is on the EAST SIDE OF THE VALLEY: look across and up, not back at the trail.
approach_variants.season: August to September for the documented ascents; snow can linger in the approach gully system earlier in the summer.
hazards: Loose rock on the approach talus and on the lower pitches
Exposed, unprotected final ridge pitch to the summit
Residual snow and ice on the pocket glacier and the polished slabs used on the descent, into midsummer
The turnoff is a small bridge on a long valley trail with no sign — miss it and you commit to a very long day getting back
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the valley camp, the base is at the TOP OF A TALUS FIELD roughly nine hundred feet above you, and the marker at its top is a PROMINENT LEFT-TRENDING GULLY. That gully is the start: the first several rope lengths climb it at fourth and low-fifth class and can be moved together. The physical test is the direction of the gully — it leans LEFT as it rises, and it is the dominant weakness on this side of the peak; a gully that runs straight up or leans right is not it. Above the gully system the climbing becomes continuous crack and groove work on sound rock, so if you are still on broken talus-strewn ground after nine hundred feet of gully you have not reached the route proper. Negative markers: if you have tread underfoot and are standing in a saddle with a trail crossing it, you walked past the steel bridge and are at Dutch Miller Gap on the other route; if you are climbing heather and rock steps directly out of a saddle toward an open bench and a snowfield, that is the gap route too.

bivy.name: Summit Chief Valley gravel flats
bivy.notes: Leave the Middle Fork trail at the small steel bridge and go cross-country south into Summit Chief Valley to a flat gravel wash below the face. The descent returns here.
bivy.water: Creek
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few low-impact sites on a gravel wash

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the northwest clearing, then the basin below the west face and the steep corner system
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1-1.25 miles, roughly an hour, to the clearing and meadow on the spire's northwest side. Leave the trail on the well-worn climber's path and ascend talus and heather into the basin directly below the northwest face.

THIS IS THE SAME BASIN USED TO ACCESS THE SOUTHWEST RIB, MOJO RISING AND FREE MOJO, so route-finding to the base is shared and only the last few dozen feet along the wall separate the lines.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Several closely spaced starts on one wall, separated by tens of feet
Committing 5.10 moves on the first pitch before any belay
No documented rappel-the-face option; bailing mid-route means natural gear anchors
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS IDENTIFIABLE BY A STEEP CORNER SYSTEM, AND THE FIRST PITCH TRAVERSES INTO IT. That is the positive test: a steep CORNER, not a face and not a chimney, entered by traversing rather than climbing straight up. The first pitch makes committing moves at about 5.10 up to a prominent ledge, where some parties belay while others continue to a tree-anchored stance.

THE LANDMARK EVERY LINE ON THIS WALL IS MEASURED FROM, AND THE ONE TO FIND FIRST: A LARGE CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY AND NOTCH between the two spire formations. Get to that and the wall becomes readable.

RELATIVE TO IT, THE ORDER IS COUNTABLE AND IN FEET: MOJO RISING starts on an obvious bolted face ABOUT 20 FT DOWNHILL of the chockstone chimney, just LEFT of this route's first pitch. FREE MOJO starts ROUGHLY 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT of the same chimney, on a nondescript crack leading to a two-piece fixed anchor on a pedestal.

SO THE THREE-WAY DISCRIMINATOR IS: BOLTED FACE 20 FT DOWNHILL OF THE CHIMNEY MEANS MOJO RISING. NONDESCRIPT CRACK 40 FT DOWN AND RIGHT MEANS FREE MOJO. STEEP CORNER ENTERED BY A TRAVERSE MEANS THIS ROUTE. If you are clipping bolts off the ground you are not on the Boving-Pollock.

SIX PITCHES, WHICH MAKES IT THE SHORTEST OF THE WEST-SIDE LINES ON THIS SPIRE, and parties typically continue to the true summit rather than rappel it, then take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete, third and fourth class with a short fifth-class step, to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek, Lake Ouzel and the Redoubt Glacier traverse
approach_variants.notes: The approach starts in Canada and crosses the border on foot. Drive the Chilliwack River Road and turn onto the narrow Depot Creek spur, where high-clearance helps for the last stretch; park where the road becomes impassable. An old logging road runs a couple of miles to the state line and the official start of the trail, which climbs steeply for the last half mile through forest to Depot Creek Falls. A climbers' path scrambles past the waterfall assisted by fixed ropes, then continues to Lake Ouzel, the standard camp. From the lake, scramble the steep broken buttress southwest of the water to gain the Redoubt Glacier, then traverse the glacier for roughly two miles, working west-southwest and climbing to a flat area around 7,300 ft before contouring southeast toward the saddle below the col between the two spires at about 7,200 ft. That saddle is the high camp and the last flat ground before the climbing.
approach_variants.season: Mid-summer through early fall for stable conditions on the glacier and the least wet rock on the headwall.
hazards: loose rock throughout, with lichen and water seepage making holds unreliable — test everything
a very remote and committing position with a complex rappel descent
the roped waterfall crossing on the approach
crevasse hazard across roughly two miles of glacier travel
wet slabs on the crux, where the manteling is the hardest climbing on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE HEADWALL IS AT THE EASTERN EDGE OF THE GLACIER AND IT IS GREY AND WET-LOOKING, NOT CLEAN. After the long traverse of the Redoubt Glacier, the base of the climbing is at the glacier's EASTERN edge, directly beneath the northeast ridge of the lower, northwestern spire. What confronts you there is a headwall that reads as steep, grey and foreboding, scattered with patches of slippery wet slab rather than dry clean granite; that wet grey character is the identifier, and it is why the crux here is manteling damp slab rather than pulling on cracks. Two pitches of committing low fifth class gain the ridge crest above it. The negative markers are simple: if you can walk or scramble onto the ridge crest without roping up, you are not at the base of this route; and if you are still on open glacier ice with the wall well away to one side, keep contouring southeast toward the saddle below the col between the two spires, which is the reference point at around 7,200 ft. Above the headwall the ridge eases to third and fourth class with occasional low fifth-class moves to the summit, so if the difficulty is not dropping off after two pitches you are off the crest. Lichen and seepage make every hold suspect; nothing here should be weighted untested.

bivy.name: Ouzel Lake basin, head of Depot Creek
bivy.notes: For Redoubt and Spickard this is the standard high camp and the reason both peaks are usually done together: the sandy, largely treeless benches near the lake sit within reach of the glacier approaches to each. Getting there involves a steep, brushy climb beside a large waterfall on ground that has at times had fixed line in place, and the condition of that section is variable and should not be counted on. Some parties push higher and bivy nearer the Depot Glacier for an earlier start, trading comfort for time. NOT reachable from the Hannegan Pass trailhead — it must never be treated as an alternative camp on that approach.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams are dependable through the season, fed from the glaciers above
bivy.permit: THIS ONE IS DIFFERENT. The approach starts in BRITISH COLUMBIA — up Chilliwack Lake Road and onto the rough Depot Creek spur — and walks south across the international boundary on foot into Washington. There is no port of entry on this route, so the trip raises a genuine customs question in both directions that none of the Hannegan-side approaches do; sort out reporting obligations with the relevant border authorities before going, and carry passports. Once across, the camp is inside North Cascades National Park and a park backcountry permit applies, which is awkward given Marblemount is a long drive away on the other side of the range.
bivy.capacity: Open flat benches with room for several tents; informal, with no built sites, toilet or bear hardware

approach_variants.name: Inspiration to McAllister, then the small col at the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes:
Shared Eldorado approach: from the large trailhead parking area on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, about 20 miles from Marblemount, backtrack a short way downstream to a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path on the far bank. The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft, before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. Cairns and flagging lead up and right into a broad basin around 5,500-5,800 ft with scattered camps near 6,100 ft. Most parties push on to an Inspiration Glacier high camp near 7,400-7,600 ft — roughly 5.3 miles and 5,300 ft, five to six hours car to camp.

From high camp, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, pass through or near the TEPEH TOWERS saddle, and drop onto the McAllister Glacier, favouring its left (south) side to dodge a large crevasse that opens on the right later in the season.

Ascend the McAllister's steep upper apron, about 30 degrees, trending northwest to its top. This is the easiest established route on the peak and is commonly used as the descent for the harder ones.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, depending on glacier and moat conditions
hazards: Crevasses on the McAllister Glacier, variable by year and generally avoidable
A large moat where the route gains the ridge, which deteriorates significantly by late summer
Aging and degraded rappel webbing left by past parties — one party reported an anchor block dislodging during a rappel here
Fractured rock with loose flakes prone to catching or dislodging the rope on the way down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A SMALL COL AT THE TOE OF THE RIDGE, AT THE TOP OF THE McALLISTER GLACIER'S 30-DEGREE APRON, AND THE THING DIRECTLY ABOVE IT IS A LINE OF GENDARMES ON THE CREST. Gendarmes on the skyline above a small col at the top of the apron is the confirmation.

CROSS THE MOAT AT THE COL, NOT AT THE SNOW GULLY. There is an alternative snow gully nearby that parties sometimes use to gain the ridge, and it is guarded by a LARGE MOAT that usually still needs a short rappel to bypass. The route's own start is easy fifth-class rock straight off the small col at the toe. If you are eyeing a snow gully with a big gap at its head, you are looking at the alternative, not the route.

THE LENGTH TEST IS DECISIVE ON THIS PEAK BECAUSE THE FOUR ROUTES ARE WILDLY DIFFERENT LENGTHS: this one is THREE pitches, each WELL UNDER 25 m. If you are running full rope lengths, or if you are still climbing after three, you are on the Southwest Buttress (nine pitches from the other side) or the East Ridge (a long day off a different col).

A FIXED-GEAR CONFIRMATION, AND A WARNING WITH IT: the crest carries a lot of OLD FIXED SLINGS ON ROCK HORNS left by earlier parties, and higher up a PITON marks a slabby section leading to a V-SLOT GULLY. Plenty of tat on horns is a sign you are on the trade line — but it is aging tat, an anchor block has failed here before, and it should be backed up rather than trusted.

AND KNOW WHICH SIDE OF THE NEEDLE YOU ARE ON: this route is reached by climbing the McAllister's apron NORTHWEST. The Southwest Buttress lines are reached by continuing to the MARBLE CREEK-McALLISTER PASS and dropping about 700 vertical ft to a snow gully below it. The East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle. Three different cols; check which one you crossed.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left onto the trail and follow the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes from the car.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Numbah Ten is the BOLTED DIHEDRAL, and it sits LEFT of both Sagittarius and Iron Horse.

Bolts in a corner are the discriminator here — almost everything around it on this part of the wall is gear-protected. The obvious groove at the base, left of Iron Horse, is the start; Amandla shares that start before diverging.

If you are under a line that shares its anchor with Sagittarius you are on Iron Horse, one line right.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, the gully split, and the west-side bench
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the parent route, since this is a single-pitch variation on it. From the Blue Lake trailhead, follow the Blue Lake Trail about a mile and a half to a small meadow and take the climbers' path that breaks off to the left just past a small stream. The path climbs through slabs, talus and meadow to below the gully that descends from between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. Where the path splits, bear left and head up toward the notch — but you are not going to the notch. Watch the gully for a prominent split in it, roughly two hundred feet below the notch, and leave the gully there. That gully has a history of looseness and rockfall, though trail work on the approach has cut down the time spent exposed to it. Above the split, scramble left and up over a short low-fifth-class step to gain the broad sloping bench on Liberty Bell's west side, and walk the bench toward its far end.
approach_variants.season: June through September.
hazards: the variation's crux is a runout flared groove and slab above only two bolts, and has been described as unsuitable for most parties compared with the standard third pitch
looseness and rockfall history in the approach gully below the peak
the descent rappel line backs up badly on busy days, with queues of several parties adding exposure time after the climbing is done
a short low-fifth-class step to gain the bench, which has to be reversed or bypassed if you retreat from the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: A BUSH GROWING OUT OF A LEFT-LEANING GROOVE IS THE PROOF, AND THE NOTCH IS THE OVERSHOOT. Getting onto the face: leave the approach gully at the prominent split about two hundred feet below the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and scramble left and up onto the broad sloping bench on the west side. Walk the bench to its far end. About eighty feet before the bench runs out, traverse left at the base of the slabs and up through thin timber to a LEFT-LEANING CRACK AND GROOVE WITH A BUSH SPROUTING OUT OF IT HALFWAY UP. That bush in that groove is the start. If you have continued up the gully all the way to the notch, you have gone too far and are at the start of the neighbouring tower's routes instead. Then the variation itself: it does not diverge until the third pitch, so climb the first two as for the parent route to a belay ledge. From that ledge the standard line moves RIGHT up flakes. This one goes straight up the clean-looking crack directly above the ledge, trending slightly left, well protected at around moderate fifth class for the first forty feet or so. Place a final solid piece where the crack narrows, because the last stretch takes no gear: it turns into a flared groove protected only by two bolts and finishes on tricky slab at the belay ledge. If you are on flakes trending right, you are on the standard pitch.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake east shore to the Jabberwocky Tower notch
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road). Colchuck Lake Trail #1599 for 4 miles and 2,280 ft — Mountaineer Creek log bridge at 1.5 miles, stay RIGHT at the Lake Stuart Trail junction — to Colchuck Lake in about two and a half to three hours. Last water.

This route is NOT approached through the west basin. Work around the EASTERN shoreline and talus instead. One documented ascent recorded roughly 4,760 ft of total gain and a twelve-hour car-to-car day.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock in the gully below the notch
Rope-up terrain in the upper gully
No water above Colchuck Lake
Long day — twelve hours car to car is documented
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The marker is a piece of rock, not a path: JABBERWOCKY TOWER, the granite spire standing between Colchuck Lake and Colchuck Balanced Rock. From the east shore, find the obvious gully that splits toward the NOTCH ABOVE that spire and ascend it — loose in places, with rope-up terrain in its upper section — to the notch. From the notch you step onto class 3 ground on the NW Ridge proper, and the climbing starts there.

Negative marker: the cairned climbers' path that leads left off the Aasgard trail through slide alder into the west basin goes to the West Face, The Scoop and the rest of the wall routes, and it leads AWAY from this one. If you are bushwhacking through alder you are on the west-side approach and on the wrong side of the formation.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to the right side of Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout; it climbs east onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Full southwest sun
Polished granite
Walk-off down the back of the formation to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.baseFinding: One of the classic trad lines on the southwest-facing upper wall, on the RIGHT side of Logger's Ledge along with Canary, Saber, Cat Burglar, Century and Crack of Doom. The anchor landmarks for that end of the bench are Saber — far right, large low roof with a left-angling ramp to its right — and Canary, roughly 100 ft to Saber's left. The standing check for this whole wall: every route here starts from the bench, not the ground. Being at road level means you are on Lower Castle and took the wrong trail out of the pullout. No source consulted gives a start marker specific to this route; place it against a topo from the Saber roof.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass and the traverse corridor to the LeConte Glacier
approach_variants.notes: This is a side trip off a multi-day high traverse, not a day climb. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, the maintained trail switchbacks up a forested rib and eases into a long ascending traverse through meadow and talus to the pass, where the tread ends. Leave the trail there and head south and east, traversing and climbing across the Mixup arm on boot path, talus and snow bands, then onto the Cache Glacier and up it to Cache Col; the step onto the glacier is short but steep and can be corniced, and an axe and crampons are normal here into midsummer. Descend the steep snowfield on the far side to the bench holding Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. From there the Red Ledge bypasses the cliff band west of the knoll above, entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin. Past the ledge, the corridor crosses the Middle Cascade Glacier, climbs to the Spider-Formidable col and drops to the Yang Yang Lakes basin, after which a ledge system leads up onto the LeConte snowfield and glacier. Camp near the col between LeConte and Sentinel, or at White Rock Lakes, and climb the peak from there.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August is most reliable, since the route depends on the whole corridor being passable rather than on local conditions. Early trips face larger cornices at Cache Col and a more consequential Red Ledge; a low-snow autumn exposes more bare glacier ice.
hazards: roped glacier travel with crevasses on the LeConte Glacier, and a bergschrund or moat at the foot of the snow ramp late season
loose rock on the upper scramble
remoteness with no easy bail once past Cache Col
steep early-season snow on the col approaches and on the ramp itself
the ramp softens to punchy postholing by afternoon, with the runout back onto the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding: ONE SNOW RAMP RISES OFF THE GLACIER TO THE SUMMIT RIDGE, AND THE MOAT AT ITS FOOT IS THE GATE. From the LeConte Glacier the peak shows a single moderate, gradually-angled snow finger running up to the summit rocks; that ramp is the route, and getting onto it — finding the spot where the moat or bergschrund at its base allows a step across — is usually the awkward move of the day. It is a few hundred feet of steep snow, best taken early while it is firm, because by afternoon it turns to punchy postholing and the runout is straight back onto the glacier. Above it, the finish is a short scramble of a few hundred feet on blocky, high-friction gabbro that takes hands and stays straightforward. Two negative markers. Sentinel Peak is the adjacent summit immediately WEST of this one and is a few feet lower than this one — if the peak you are under is the western of the pair, you are below Sentinel. And if the rock above the top of your snow ramp turns into two pitches of mid-fifth-class climbing rather than a hands-on scramble, you are on this peak's east ridge, which is a real route but not this one. Stash the axe and crampons somewhere you will find them; the descent reverses the same ramp.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the northwest ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old bypass trail — stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 6,400 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Continue past the two trail junctions to the PCT at roughly 7,100 ft and turn right, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill on Old Snowy's west flank.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul through Sep, most reliable in August
hazards: An unmarked, easily missed turn off the PCT — the route's one real navigation problem
A persistent snowfield on the PCT traverse below the summit, firm and icy in early morning
Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
High wind and lightning exposure on an open crest, with common afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once off the PCT
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the wilderness
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TURN OFF THE PCT IS UNMARKED, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING ON THIS ROUTE YOU CAN GET WRONG.

THE TEST THAT WORKS IN FOG IS ABOUT MOTION, NOT LANDMARKS: the PCT here is SIDEHILLING — traversing across the slope. The climbers' path is THE FIRST THING THAT TURNS UPHILL AND STOPS CONTOURING, branching right, east, toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge. Take the first thing that climbs.

THE NEGATIVE IS EQUALLY MECHANICAL: IF THE PCT STARTS DESCENDING ON THE FAR SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN, YOU HAVE WALKED PAST THE TURN. Go back; do not climb straight up from where you noticed.

DISTANCE CROSS-CHECK: about 1.8 miles north of the Trail 96 junction at 7,100 ft, and the path switchbacks steeply for about half a mile from where you leave the trail.

SECOND MARKER, AND IT SITS BEFORE THE TURN RATHER THAN AFTER IT: a persistent SNOWFIELD on the PCT below the summit lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot on the exposed sidehill traverse. Meeting it means the turn is still ahead of you. It is firmest and safest crossed in the morning.

A SOFT CONFIRMATION AT THE SADDLE, WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT IS VISIBLE FROM A DISTANCE: many parties stash trekking poles there for the scramble. A cache of poles on a rocky saddle is a good sign you are at the right one.

BASE OF THE SCRAMBLE: the last few hundred feet to the summit is Class 2-3 hands-and-feet on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rock knocked down by parties above is the hazard, so do not stack directly below other climbers.

AND A NEGATIVE THAT IS ABOUT VISIBILITY RATHER THAN GROUND: once you leave the PCT there is no maintained tread. Poor visibility is the recorded route-finding difficulty on this peak, and the honest response is to turn round at the PCT rather than to search for the spur.

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Goat Lake basin
bivy.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.
bivy.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
bivy.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

bivy.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
bivy.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
bivy.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center (about 578 ft) the Hoh River Trail runs east up the valley for roughly 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at about 4,300 ft, past Five Mile Island, the Olympus Guard Station near mile 9, Lewis Meadow near mile 11 (the usual overnight if you split the walk in), the High Hoh Bridge near mile 13, and Elk Lake near mile 15. A washed-out cliffside stretch about a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows is crossed on a fixed ladder; rungs have been reported missing in recent seasons, so look at it before you commit weight. Water is frequent the whole way.
