From Glacier Meadows a way path climbs about 0.8 mile to the crest of the Blue Glacier's lateral moraine and follows it roughly 0.2 mile before dropping onto the ice. That drop is loose and rockfall-prone; some parties fix a short line. Rope up on the ice. Cross the flat lower glacier and climb moderate snow, threading the rock islands to the right of the main icefall before swinging back left below the massif, to the crest of Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft. Snow Dome is the standard high camp, a thousand feet below the summit.

From Snow Dome the standard line goes up to and over Crystal Pass, then traverses just south of and below Five Fingers Ridge and over a false summit to the summit pyramid. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is usually bridged through midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier and the trail above Elk Lake is steep snow; later and the moat at the base of the summit rock opens and the ramps go from snow-covered to loose
hazards: Crevasses on the Blue Glacier and a large one near Crystal Pass, usually snow-bridged and not always
Rockfall on the moraine descent onto the ice, and a fixed-ladder washout around mile 16 of the trail
Loose rock on the east-face ramps and rockfall from parties above on them
A developing moat at the base of the summit rock in warm or late-season conditions, forcing a committing step onto rock
Whiteout on Snow Dome — the crevassed plateau is where the 1993 fatal unroped fall happened
A 17-mile walk out with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A FLAT TOP AT THE FOOT OF AN 80 FT TOWER, AND IT WORKS IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT IS UNDERFOOT, NOT ON THE HORIZON. Off the false summit you drop into a sharp saddle, then climb a short steep snow slope with a clean runout. That slope ENDS FLAT. The moment the ground stops rising and you are standing on a small flat platform of snow with an 80 ft rock tower directly above you, you are at the base of the summit block, on its NORTHEAST side. There is nothing else on this mountain that is a flat snow top under an 80 ft tower. SECOND TEST, and it is the one that separates this finish from the two other routes on this same block: from that platform the East Face Ramps line goes RIGHT, around the corner onto the east face, and climbs a series of ramps angling up and across it before joining the last Class 4 / 5.4 step. If you are climbing straight up the face directly above the platform you are on the North Face Direct, and if you have walked round to the far side you are on the Northwest Edge. All three finish on the same 80 ft tower and all three start from this platform; the only thing that tells them apart is which way you turn. WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: if you are still gaining height on snow with no rock tower over you, you are on the five-fingered false summit east of the true one and have not yet dropped into the saddle. If you can see the Blue Glacier below you on your right the whole way, you are still on the traverse and have not reached Crystal Pass. HONEST LIMIT: the ramps themselves are loose and the correct one is chosen by eye. A fog test can get you to the foot of the block; it cannot pick the ramp for you.

approach_variants.name: From the Bailey Range: Queets Basin, Blizzard Pass and the Humes Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach of parties already on the Bailey Range Traverse rather than a way anyone drives to. It comes at Olympus from the SOUTH instead of the north: from the High Divide out of Sol Duc, along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, then down into Queets Basin, and up over Blizzard Pass onto the Humes Glacier. From the Humes the summit massif is gained from the south side and the summit block is reached from the opposite direction to the Snow Dome line.

It is longer by days and it exists in the record because traverse parties use it, not because it is easier. A party carrying glacier gear can also run it the other way and exit down the Blue Glacier to the Hoh, which is how most traverses finish.

Nothing about the approach shortens the climb: the last five hundred feet, the false summit, the saddle and the summit block are the same ground the Hoh parties cross.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Bailey Range crest is walkable and the Humes is not avalanching
hazards: Multi-day committing wilderness travel with no bail options once on the Bailey crest
Crevasses and icefall on the Humes Glacier
Blizzard Pass holds steep snow and is named for what happens there
Route-finding on the Bailey crest in cloud, where the ridge is the only handrail
No resupply and no reliable rescue access; NPS has reported multiple helicopter rescues per season among permitted Bailey parties
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SAME FLAT SNOW TOP UNDER THE 80 FT TOWER — the block does not care which side of the mountain you walked in from. What changes coming from the south is which way you meet the false summit: from the Humes side you are working up toward the summit ridge from below rather than dropping onto it from Crystal Pass, so the sharp saddle between the false summit and the true one is reached from the opposite end.

The test that you have not overshot on this side is Five Fingers Ridge. The standard line runs just SOUTH of and BELOW it. If Five Fingers Ridge is below you rather than above you, you are on the crest itself and too high; drop back under it and keep the ridge on your uphill side until the false summit is passed and the saddle opens.

HONEST LIMIT: this approach is thinly documented as an approach — it is described in traverse accounts, which are about the traverse. Treat the Hoh variant as the one with detail and this one as the one that gets a traverse party to the same platform.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, QUOTA-LIMITED, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

bivy.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
bivy.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

bivy.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
bivy.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is GLACIER camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.
bivy.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
approach_variants.notes: Identical to the standard approach for every route on this peak: Hoh River Trail from the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at roughly 4,300 ft, the moraine way path and the drop onto the Blue Glacier, roped glacier travel across the flat lower ice and up through the rock islands right of the icefall to Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft, then Crystal Pass, the traverse below Five Fingers Ridge, the false summit, and the sharp saddle beneath the true summit pyramid. The only thing this route changes is what you do once you are standing at the foot of the tower.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug; early or late season this face can carry ice, which changes it from a 5.4 pitch into something else
hazards: Fixed tat at the top of the pitch is old and unmaintained — inspect and back it up
The face is steeper and more exposed than either other summit-block finish, and holds ice early and late in the season
The descent rappel is roughly 80-100 ft, which late in the season can take nearly all of a 60 m rope doubled
Everything on the approach: Blue Glacier crevasses, the Crystal Pass crevasse, moraine rockfall, whiteout on Snow Dome
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHARED ARRIVAL TEST IS THE FLAT SNOW TOP AT THE FOOT OF THE 80 FT TOWER, on its northeast side, where the steep snow slope out of the saddle stops rising.

THE TEST THAT YOU ARE ON THIS FINISH AND NOT ONE OF THE OTHER TWO IS ROPE, NOT ROCK, AND IT IS THE BEST FOG MARKER ON THIS MOUNTAIN. Enough parties end up on this exact line that a semi-permanent rappel station has built up at the TOP of it — a boulder or horn wrapped in slings with a rap ring and a quick link. From the platform, look straight up the face above you. If there is tat hanging down the line you are about to climb, that is the North Face Direct and you are in the right place. If there is no tat above you, you are looking at the east-face ramps (round the corner to the right) or the northwest edge (round to the left), and you have not found this finish.

The fixed gear is not agency-maintained and slings weather fast, so back it up and do not lower onto it unexamined — but as a piece of route-finding evidence in cloud it is unambiguous, because it is the only fixed anchor on the block and it hangs down THIS face.

SECOND TEST: the pitch is about 80-100 ft on generally solid rock at 5.4, steeper and more exposed than the ramps. If your first fifty feet is a wandering scramble across ledges rather than a face, you have drifted onto the ramp system.

wa_olympus_summit_block_west_edge.rappels: 1 rappel of 25-30 m down the northwest edge to a belay ledge, then scramble and downclimb to rejoin the standard East Face ramps descent. Check the rope before you commit: a 25-30 m rappel needs a 60 m rope doubled. A 30 m rope is enough to CLIMB the single pitch but reaches only 15 m doubled, and a 50 m reaches 25 m with nothing spare.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
approach_variants.notes: The approach is the standard one and is identical to the point where you are standing on snow at the foot of the summit tower: Hoh River Trail about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows, the moraine and the Blue Glacier, Snow Dome at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft, Crystal Pass, the traverse below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, down into the sharp saddle, and up the short steep snow slope to the platform. It is the same as the Blue Glacier / East Face route until the summit block base, approach time identical. The variants here exist to say what to do with your eyes once you are there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, on the same window as every other line on this block
hazards: Significant exposure on the edge, with more air under you than on either other finish
Traversing the base of the block on snow to reach it, above the drop back into the saddle
A moat at the rock-snow junction late in the season
Everything on the approach: Blue Glacier crevasses, the Crystal Pass crevasse, moraine rockfall, whiteout on Snow Dome
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHARED ARRIVAL TEST IS THE FLAT SNOW TOP AT THE FOOT OF THE 80 FT TOWER. You reach it on the tower's NORTHEAST side, which matters, because this finish is on the far side from where you arrive.

THE TEST FOR THIS FINISH IS THAT YOU HAVE TO WALK ROUND THE TOWER TO FIND IT. From the platform, the east-face ramps leave to your right and the north face rises directly above you with its rappel tat hanging down it. The Northwest Edge is neither: it is the arete on the opposite side, and reaching it means traversing round the base of the block anticlockwise until the face you are under is no longer the one with the tat on it and the ground has swung round to the northwest.

SECOND TEST, and it is a feel test rather than a sight test, which is what you want in cloud: the rock on this edge is noticeably MORE SOLID than the east-face ramps. The ramps are loose, gravelly and rockfall-prone; the northwest edge is described consistently as clean rock, steeper and more exposed, with several 5.3-5.4 moves. If the first moves off the snow are on rubble-covered ledges you are on the ramps; if they are on positive holds on an exposed edge you are on this line.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: keep traversing anticlockwise past the northwest edge and the ground under the block drops away steeply on the west side with no reasonable line above it. If you are downclimbing to keep going round, stop and come back.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome — the traverse begins on the West Peak
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Olympus approach and nothing else: Hoh River Trail from the visitor center about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at roughly 4,300 ft, with Lewis Meadow near mile 11 the usual overnight; the moraine way path and the loose drop onto the Blue Glacier; roped glacier travel across the lower ice and up through the rock islands to Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft; then Crystal Pass, the traverse under Five Fingers Ridge, the false summit and the saddle to the West Peak.

What the traverse adds is everything after that: West Peak (7,980 ft) to Middle Peak (7,929 ft) to East Peak (7,762 ft), all of it off-trail glacier and ridge ground, with crevasse and icefall exposure the whole way and a full rescue kit needed for the entire outing rather than just for the West Peak block. Standard exit is toward Glacier Pass and back down to Glacier Meadows.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. The Middle Peak's east-side moat is the thing that decides whether this goes at all, and it runs deep in some seasons
hazards: 14-16+ hours of climbing from Glacier Meadows, so cumulative fatigue is itself a hazard
Sustained crevasse and icefall exposure across the whole traverse, not just on the approach
The Middle Peak east-side moat can be impassable and force a different exit
Route-finding between the peaks is poor in flat light and there is no easy retreat mid-traverse
A conditions-dependent short rappel or careful downclimb off the Middle Peak's loose upper rock in some seasons
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE'S BASE IS A SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE ONE PIECE OF GOOD NEWS IN IT. The traverse starts on the WEST PEAK, and you know you are on the West Peak because you have just climbed an 80 ft rock tower off a flat snow platform — no other high point on this massif is gained that way. If you have not climbed a rock tower, you are on the five-fingered false summit east of the true one and the traverse has not started.

THE TEST THAT DECIDES WHETHER THE TRAVERSE GOES IS A MOAT, AND IT IS AT THE OTHER END. Between West and Middle Peaks the descent to the saddle is careful downclimbing on non-technical ground, but the Middle Peak's EAST side carries a snow moat that in some seasons is too deep to pass. That is the go / no-go, and it is checked by walking to it rather than by looking at it from the West Peak. Parties that find it impassable have exited via Glacier Pass instead, which carries its own icefall hazard — decide that at the moat, not after committing past it.

SECOND TEST, for the icefall: the traverse line has to work around a heavily crevassed section of the upper Blue Glacier. Stay RIGHT of the icefall on the way across and swing back LEFT below the massif. If you are threading crevasses rather than skirting them, you are in the icefall and should back out to the right.

HONEST LIMIT: route-finding between the three peaks is explicitly described as not straightforward, and there is no marker sequence for it. In poor visibility this is a route to turn round on, not to navigate.

approach_variants.name: Cutthroat Creek trail #483 from the Cutthroat Lake trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
This is not the Cutthroat Peak approach. That one leaves an unmarked highway pullout west of the pass with no maintained trail. This wall starts at the signed Cutthroat Lake trailhead at about 4,500 ft, a mile up a spur road off the highway east of the pass — kiosk, vault toilet, large gravel lot, no water.

Walk the maintained Cutthroat Creek trail for the first few minutes, on the old roadbed running parallel to it, then turn uphill on the climbers' left into the forest. From there, a climbers' path through brush, trees and talus trends climbers' right toward the buttress and reaches a flat area beneath the cliff.

Cairns exist along the way and not all of them mean anything. Navigate on the wall rather than on the rock piles. Because of the approach, parties usually have this wall to themselves.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September; access is gone entirely while the highway is gated for winter
hazards: Its start is uphill and left of the obvious base; parties rack up at the patio by mistake
Loose rock on the second pitch, including stacked blocks at the top of the corner
Cairns on the approach are not all route markers
Shares an area name with a peak reached from a different trailhead
If you take the shared walk-off instead of rappelling, the obvious gully below the notch is the wrong one
approach_variants.baseFinding:
DO NOT STOP AT THE OBVIOUS BASE. The first thing you reach under this wall is a GRANITE PATIO where two other routes start about fifty feet apart. This route is not there. It is about a HUNDRED AND FIFTY FEET CLIMBERS' LEFT OF AND ABOVE that patio, so from the patio you keep walking left and gaining height rather than racking up.

The marker is vegetation, and it is specific: a SMALL OUTCROPPING OF TREES uphill of the left-hand patio route's start. Find that patch of trees. The route begins in the ROCK-SCARRED OPEN BOOK JUST LEFT OF IT. Scarred rock and an open book, immediately left of a small stand of trees, uphill and left of the patio — that is the whole identification, and it is the only start on this wall with a plant landmark.

CONFIRM BY THE FEATURE ABOVE: this line takes the obvious LEFT-FACING BROKEN CORNER SYSTEM in the centre of the buttress, left of the blockier ground that carries the two patio routes. If the corner above you faces right rather than left, you are on the wrong side of the wall.

NEGATIVE MARKERS. If you are standing on a flat slab platform with a second route start visible fifty feet away, you are still at the patio and have not walked far enough. If your line is wandering through featured ground past big gnarled trees and later a distinctly SPIRAL TREE, you are on the 5.9 that starts right of the patio.

This route is also the one on the wall whose descent is different, and knowing that is worth a lot at the top: parties find it faster to RAPPEL THE ROUTE — three full sixty-metre rappels reach the ground, starting from a tree slightly up and left of the belay at the top of pitch five — rather than take the shared notch descent. Watch for stacked blocks near the top of the second pitch's corner.

approach_variants.name: Olney Pass, old road walk and the two cairns
approach_variants.notes:
From US 2 at Sultan, turn onto Sultan Basin Road at the last stoplight. It is paved for around ten to eleven miles and then becomes well-graded gravel; carry on to Olney Pass and the Spada Reservoir area, about thirteen miles in.

Stop at the kiosk at Olney Pass and register your vehicle — the basin is Snohomish County PUD land with sun-up to sun-down access, and this is a standing rule rather than a temporary notice.

Continue to the fork and bear right around the southern tip of the reservoir. After about two miles cross a bridge and park in the first turnout on the left.

Walk the old road, which is eroded and overgrown and crosses numerous ravines where culverts have washed out. It is largely level for 45-60 minutes. The two markers are cairns and they do different jobs: the FIRST cairn, just before a large and usually dry riverbed, marks the point where you get a view up the bed to the slabs and Static Peak. Cross the riverbed and find a SECOND cairn sitting on an old culvert — that one marks where the trail leaves the road and goes uphill.

Follow it uphill alongside the riverbed for 20-30 minutes to the base of the dome. A short fixed line protects the last steep step before the Online sector, and it deposits you on a thin sandy ledge.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer days only, and DAYLIGHT ONLY — the PUD roads around Spada Reservoir are open sun-up to sun-down and you must register at the self-check kiosk on the way in
hazards: PUD gate hours — being caught inside after sun-down
Washed-out culverts and ravines on the old road
Short fixed line on the final steep step to the sector
Runout below the first bolt
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the sandy arrival ledge, look up and find the first bolt you can see anywhere on the wall. That bolt is Online's, and it sits almost exactly in the MIDDLE of the wall.

It is roughly 50 feet up, and the slab below it is low-angle — about 5.5. So a long, easy, unprotected-feeling run to the first bolt is CORRECT here and is not a sign you are below the wrong line.

This is not a sport crag: the bolts were placed between expected gear placements, so wide spacing between bolts on a 5.10 is normal. Corners over on the LEFT side of the wall belong to Epitaph, a shorter 5.9, not to this.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the rightmost line on the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Identical approach to the peak's other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, the maintained trail about a mile and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake, the last water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded rise; work up and right into the talus and dirt gully on the northwest side, where a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to Unicorn Col, then follow the traversing use trail below the cliffs on the south side to the base of the horn.

This route takes the right-hand end of the south face rather than the face direct, and it is the easiest of the three summit-block lines — a step down from the Classic Route and well below The Roof.

Roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft of gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Wide-crack climbing that is awkward and poorly protected without large cams
Loose rock in the gully and chimney terrain around the summit tower
Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out
An exposed step near the top of the horn with real air below on the east side
A 30 m rope that may not reach on one of the two rappel lines
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ALONG THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. OPEN BOOK IS THE RIGHTMOST AND THE EASIEST.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS UNMISTAKABLE AND IT IS A COUNT: TWO WIDE, LEFT-LEANING CRACKS, ABOUT 50 FT RIGHT OF THE CLASSIC ROUTE'S BASE. Two of them, wide, leaning left. From there the line climbs up and LEFT toward the anchor shared with the other routes.

THE NEGATIVE IS ABOUT CRACK WIDTH AND YOU FEEL IT IN THE FIRST FEW MOVES, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHEN YOU WANT TO KNOW: IF THE CRACK TAKES YOUR FINGERS AND HANDS COMFORTABLY, YOU ARE ON THE CLASSIC ROUTE, 50 FT TO YOUR LEFT, AT 5.4. Open Book's cracks are wide and awkward and want large cams — that awkwardness is the route, not a sign you are off it.

THE SECOND NEGATIVE IS OVERHEAD: IF THERE IS A ROOF ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE WALKED THE ENTIRE WIDTH OF THE BLOCK AND YOU ARE ON THE ROOF AT 5.6 — the hardest of the three and the far left end of the list.

ORIENTATION TEST: this line is at the RIGHT-HAND END of the SOUTH face. The Classic Route goes straight up the MIDDLE of the same face. If you are directly beneath the south face looking up at blocky ground with a piton visible at half height, you are one line to the left of here.

DESCENT: the same shared anchor as the other two — the large rock horn on the south side, about 40-50 ft above the notch. AVOID THE OLD DEAD SNAG some older reports mention; it is no longer trustworthy. A 30 m rope has been found marginal or short depending on which of the two rappel lines you take off the horn, so 40 m removes the doubt. Downclimbing this line is viable given the grade, but it is still exposed near the top.

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing, then 150 yards left along the base
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles from the west end of Leavenworth to the Snow Creek trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass to park.

Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill roughly two to two and a half miles, about an hour, until the wall is directly across the drainage. Branch right at an early opening, scramble down to the flat ground by Snow Creek and cross on the log. Up through boulders and talus on the far bank to a bootpath that gains about 500 ft to the base.

From where the trail meets the wall — roughly under the Shield — walk LEFT along the foot of the wall for about 150 yards, until the base and the path start dropping steeply downhill. That drop is the signal to stop. Rack up and stash packs there.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall; midsummer is hot on this east-facing wall
hazards: Exposed 5.6 scrambling on the approach to the first ledge, unroped by most parties
The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water
Loose talus below the wall
Mountain goats habituated to climbers at the base
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Scramble up and left over easy ground toward a large evergreen sitting below the prominent Mary Jane dihedral, which is the biggest feature overhead here and the thing to navigate on.

The published description of a 'hanging tree with many slings' actively misleads people and is worth knowing about in advance: the tree is not hanging — it is roughly horizontal — and it carries no slings at all. The slings are on the ROCK beside it. Do not stand about looking for a slung tree; you have probably already found the tree.

Use the gully on the LOOKER'S LEFT of that tree for the easiest way up. The last moves onto the ledge are about 5.6 and feel exposed, and some parties rope up for this scrambling.

You are on the right ledge when there is an obvious squeeze chimney directly above you — that is pitch one. If you have scrambled to a ledge and there is no chimney above it, you are on the wrong ledge; and if you are still walking on level ground at the foot of the wall, you have not gone the full 150 yards.

approach_variants.name: Slate Pass, the Middle Fork Pasayten, and Fred's Lake to Lake Doris
approach_variants.notes: Drive FR 5400 from Mazama to Harts Pass, at roughly 6,181 to 6,204 ft. Trailers are prohibited past the 5400000/5400060 junction because the road is narrow and steep with few turnouts, and whether an ordinary car should attempt it is genuinely disputed, so judge it on the day. From Harts Pass turn right at the guard station onto FR 5400-600. The Pacific Crest Trail trailhead is at the first switchback and SLATE PASS at the second, at about 6,900 ft. Early in the season you walk the last half mile or so. From Slate Pass take the Buckskin Ridge trail #498, and at about half a mile a cut-off drops to the Robinson Creek / Middle Fork trail #478. Follow the Middle Fork of the Pasayten — an unbridged crossing, reported anywhere from ankle deep to needing boots and trousers off — for roughly nine miles to the Fred's Lake turn-off. The tread through here is in good condition with essentially no brush. Then over the pass to Lake Doris at about 6,975 ft, reported at just under six hours from the car. A naming caution before you cross-reference maps: this water is usually called Lake Doris and sometimes Lake Dorothy. Do not assume they are separate. Despite the route name, the ordinary way up this peak works the SOUTH or SOUTH-WEST slope, not a west one.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the pass above Fred's Lake holds snow on its north side and softens through the day
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork Pasayten crossing of very variable depth
Blowdown that worsens beyond Fred's Lake, in places hundreds of logs through burn zones
Lingering snow on the north side of the pass above Fred's Lake, soft late in the day
Wet lichen making the talus slippery
Fourteen hundred feet of loose scree with no shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEAVE THE TRAIL AT THE STREAM CROSSING JUST BEFORE THE LAKE, not at the lake. Two independent accounts do exactly that: cross the stream, head north-east up into open forest, and break out of the trees onto talus.

The arrival test is the ground itself. The talus is CONTINUOUS and endless — no benches, no trees, no interruption — running roughly fourteen hundred feet straight to the top. There is no elegant line on it; you put your head down and climb. If you are still weaving between trees and heather benches you have not reached the slope proper.

NEGATIVE MARKER for leaving too early: one climber went up toward what he took to be the south-west ridge, found it was not, and had to work up and down to reach the real one, where bits of use trail run through the least-bad talus. Use-trail fragments are a sign you are on the right slope.

SUMMIT TEST: the top is ringed by cliffs on every side EXCEPT the scree slope you came up. If you are on a summit with more than one walkable side, it is not this one.

HOW TO KNOW IT IS OSCEOLA AND NOT CARRU: Mount Carru is about a mile EAST and it is HIGHER — 8,595 ft against Osceola's 8,587. From the top of Osceola you look east across a deep notch at a higher peak. The ground between the two is described by one climber as somewhere between awful and impassable, so that notch is a wall, not a link. Osceola, Carru and Lago all keep their steep and cliffy ground on the NORTH, which gives a broader check: a peak in this group whose easy ground is on the north side is none of the three.

Nothing published reports a false summit on Osceola.

wa_ottohorn_southeast_route.descent_text: Descend the Southeast Route by reversing the east ridge back down to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col — a few pitches of low-5th-class downclimbing/scrambling to the notch. From the col, the standard return for this route is down the SOUTH side, back into Crescent Creek Basin: this is the easier, non-technical line (snow early season, loose class 3-4 talus/scree scrambling once late-season melt strips the snow) and does not require rappelling under normal conditions. If coverage is thin and a section of the loose downclimb feels too exposed, some parties back it off with a single short rappel off a sling on a natural anchor (block/horn) rather than downclimb it, but this is not the norm. Note that the NORTH side of the col is a different, and harder, proposition and is not part of this route's own descent — parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn/Mustard Glacier descend that side via one single-rope rappel from an established rap station about 150 ft below the col onto the Mustard Glacier (or, when well filled-in, a steep snow couloir); don't confuse that crossing with the Southeast Route's own walk-off. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: traverse back to the base of The Barrier, regain the ~250 ft to the 6,200 ft notch, then descend the steep gully/talus/heather line back down to the Goodell Creek trail and out to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully below the Barrier notch and for creek crossings running high on hot afternoons. To continue on to Frenzel Spitz, descend roughly 500 ft from Ottohorn's north side, per the original 1961 first-ascent account.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek, the Barrier notch and Stump Hollow, then the Crescent Creek Basin traverse to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col
approach_variants.notes:
From the Goodell Creek trailhead at about 600 ft, reached via the gravel road that forks off Hwy 20 across from Newhalem and dead-ends at a gravel pit with parking but no trailhead sign, follow the old logging roadbed along the east bank of Goodell Creek. The first 1.5 miles thread through dozens of downed trees and washouts before a faint trail emerges in the timber; the tread then levels around 1,100 ft for roughly a mile.

Around mile 3.5, at about 1,700 ft, the trail crosses a stream, the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, near a small campsite and a cairn marking the unsigned climbers' path up the Barrier. Fill bottles there.

From the cairn the path steepens hard: a traverse around 3,200 ft, a talus field near 4,000 ft, a rock band around 4,800 ft, then a steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees, to a rocky streambed near 5,200 ft. Heather benches and slabs then lead to the crest of the Barrier, a roughly 6,200 ft notch that is the high point of the approach and a common bivy. From the notch, descend about 250 ft into Stump Hollow, then contour on a long rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin holding roughly the 5,800 ft level to a camp near Mount Terror and Himmelhorn.

A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the Crescent Creek Basin zone is required.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A steep brush-choked gully with early-season snow or ice to about 35 degrees on the Barrier climb
An overhanging boulder near the col forcing a loose exposed bypass
A moat at the col that can become an overhanging pit by August
A fresh rockfall scar reported about 30 ft below the summit ridge
The north side of the col takes multiple rappels off improvised anchors; do not descend it by mistake
Steep grassy ledges on the Barrier that are considerably worse downhill-facing and tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE BEGINS AT THE OTTOHORN-HIMMELHORN COL AND YOU CRAMPON THE LAST OF THE WAY THERE. From camp, continue the rising traverse across Crescent Creek Basin toward the col, and crampon up the final snow and scree pitch to the col itself. Once melted out late season that last pitch turns to loose, chossy class 3-4 scrambling, with AN OVERHANGING BOULDER NEAR THE TOP sometimes forcing a chossy class 3 or 4 bypass on the LEFT.

SO THE OVERHANGING BOULDER IS THE ARRIVAL MARKER: one block near the top of the gully, passed on its left, and then the col. The route text stops at the col because the col is the start.

THE NEGATIVE TEST, AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT LINE HERE: FROM THE COL, THIS ROUTE GOES UP THE EAST RIDGE AND ITS WALK-OFF RETURNS DOWN THE SOUTH SIDE, BACK INTO CRESCENT CREEK BASIN. THE NORTH SIDE OF THE COL IS A DIFFERENT AND HARDER PROPOSITION. Parties continuing a traverse toward Himmelhorn and the Mustard Glacier descend that side by a single-rope rappel from an established station about 150 ft below the col, or a steep snow couloir when well filled in. If you are looking down at a glacier and rigging a rappel, you are on the wrong side of the col for this route.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB, AND THE MEASUREMENTS ARE SMALL: from the col the summit is reported as easy scrambling, class 3, and parties have done it from the col in roughly an hour round trip, some without taking rope or rack out of camp. It is one of the few Southern Picket summits that is not fifth class. If you are on sustained fifth class you are not on the standard line.

ONE CONDITIONS-DEPENDENT COMPLICATION, RECORDED BECAUSE IT CHANGED A PARTY'S DAY: at least one party found the easy line broke into a FRESH ROCKFALL SCAR about 30 ft below the summit ridge and backed off rather than cross it, returning with a rope for about two pitches of juggy 5.7. Do not commit to the last 100 ft until you can see it.

THE MOAT AT THE COL IS THE THING TO SCOUT ON THE WAY UP: where the snow meets the rock it is a non-event when snow-filled early season and can be an overhanging pit by August. Note where you crossed it; you will want that on the way down.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
From the Icicle Road junction at the west end of Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Walk the Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill for roughly two to two and a half miles — about an hour — until the wall stands directly opposite you across the drainage. The trail never touches the rock, so what you are watching for is the wall coming abeam, not a junction or a sign.

At one of the first easy openings, branch right off the trail and scramble down into the flat ground beside Snow Creek to find the log crossing. On the far bank, climb up through boulders and talus until a bootpath forms; it gains about 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall.

Weekends are busy and this is the most popular route in Leavenworth — a queue at the base is normal.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall; the wall is low and faces east, so midsummer bakes
hazards: The log crossing of Snow Creek — high water in spring
Loose talus on the 500 ft climbers' trail below the wall
East-facing, low-elevation rock that gets very hot in summer
Annual raptor monitoring in this drainage; check for a current nesting closure before going
Crowds and parties above you on the most popular route in the area
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Find the route by its top, not its bottom. Outer Space is the long, well-cleaned crack splitting the upper headwall — the Shield — and it is the most obvious single feature on the wall. Trace that crack downward to where it ends at a ledge with several bushes on it.

The route's own original start is the ledge-and-dihedral system about 80 ft RIGHT of that point and 100 ft DOWN from it.

In practice most parties never use that start: they climb the first pitches of Remorse instead, which begins essentially where the climbers' trail arrives at the wall. That arrival point is the highest part of the wall's base, with a few small scrub trees on it. Standing there, the clean bolted slab straight in front of you is RPM's first pitch at 5.10d; Remorse's much easier line is the often-vegetated gully about 30 ft to the RIGHT of it.

So the single most useful test at the base: if your first move off the ground is a hard, blank, bolted friction slab, you are on RPM, not on the Remorse start to Outer Space. Step right into the scruffy gully.

approach_variants.name: Dingford Creek, bike the closed road, then ford the Middle Fork under the big cliff
approach_variants.notes: From I-90 exit 34 go north, then right onto SE Middle Fork Road, FR 56, and follow it about twelve miles to the Taylor River junction. Bear right onto FR 5620 and continue to the Dingford Creek trailhead at roughly 1,500 ft. FR 56 is notorious for potholes and ruts and high clearance is genuinely useful; the stretch beyond the gate is reported to be in better shape than the public road. FR 5620 is decommissioned beyond Dingford Creek. The closed stretch to the old Dutch Miller Gap trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp is given as seven, eight or ten miles, so do not plan on a precise number. A bike is universally recommended and cuts hours off both ends. Beyond the road, parties use three genuinely different lines, none of them confirmed by another, so read all three before choosing. The most specific of them fords the Middle Fork on a visual cue rather than a mileage: walk roughly four miles of trail until you can SEE the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the foot of Overcoat. Push through about ten minutes of alder, ford there, and you land on the talus field at the base of those cliffs. Further north-east the alder gets much thicker. A second line crosses about a mile before the Dutch Miller Gap trail proper and climbs steep forest to camp at Overcoat Lake. A third crosses the river on rocks, climbs steep brushy ground into a two-mile rocky corridor sometimes called the Valley of the Chiefs, meets continuous snow around 4,600 ft, and goes over a pass at about 6,140 ft. On the traverse toward camp, one party's correction: they climbed to the ridge and then realised the line stays LOWER, and had to drop back to find the sloping rock crux and downclimb to the snow. A durable warning about the road rather than the mountain: the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road has a long-standing reputation for unsavoury activity, including gunfire, and at least one regular visitor reports it on every trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The river ford is the timing constraint — thigh deep in the morning has been recorded as waist deep on the same day by evening
hazards: A real ford of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, thigh to waist deep and colder in the afternoon than the morning
Dense slide alder on both banks, worse to the north-east of the standard crossing
Moats around the margin of the Overcoat Glacier
Crevasses part way up the snow finger
Poor protection and loose rock on the summit pyramid
A long decommissioned road walk or ride at both ends of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The snow finger is not visible until you are underneath it, so do not try to identify it from camp or from the glacier below.

The sequence that works: reach the Overcoat Glacier, make a long rising traverse of five hundred feet or so to the top of the mild glacier, and only then does the steep snow finger show itself, with dark towers standing above it.

THE DARK TOWERS ARE THE TRANSITION. You leave snow for rock at their foot, then round the corner EAST and the glacier reappears below you. From there it is steep gully climbing on solid holds with a few exposed steps over tall blocks to the summit.

The consistent fact across every published account, and the one to steer by: the summit pyramid is gained on its EAST or NORTH-EAST side. Nobody describes climbing it from the south-east. If you are working around to the south side of the block looking for a way up, you have gone the wrong way round.

Grade opinions on that finish run from Class 3 to low fifth, and parties have pitched it out in two short pitches with a few small cams and nuts, with one rappel and some downclimbing to get back to the top of the snow finger. Expect thin protection and poor rock rather than a scramble.

Moats around the glacier margin and crevasses part way up the snow finger are the two things that most often force a detour here, and both were reported as more awkward than expected by parties who had read otherwise.

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

approach_variants.name: Sloan Creek Road, the lookout trail, and the southwest ridge
approach_variants.notes: Park at the campground and trailhead at the end of the road up the North Fork Sauk. The signed trail there is the valley trail, but this route splits off almost immediately: look for the signed lookout trail branching left about a hundred yards in. It is low-key enough to walk straight past — if you have been on the main trail more than a couple of minutes you have missed it. The lookout trail switchbacks steadily through old growth for about a mile, gaining roughly seven hundred to a thousand feet, and ends on a flat bench where the fire lookout once stood, with views into the basin below. That is the last easy-to-follow section of the day and where most hikers turn around. Above it the path keeps climbing steeply and a cliff band appears within a few hundred vertical feet. Beyond the cliff band, an intermittent boot track marked with old pink flagging follows the crest and southwest side of the ridge through open meadows. There is no reliable water past the lower creek crossings, and the upper half is dry, south-facing and sun-exposed, so carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September is the reliable window. Snow can linger on the ledges and the ridge boot path into July in heavy-snow years, hiding the flagging and icing the ledges. The scramble is far safer and easier to navigate dry.
hazards: an exposed ledge scramble of about seventy vertical feet just above the end of the maintained trail — loose dirt on rock, slick when wet, and harder facing outward on descent
a faint, unmaintained boot path above the ledges marked only by intermittent pink flagging, easy to lose in fog
loose scree and talus on the upper southwest ridge and summit slopes
lingering snow that can hide the flagged path into July
an open, exposed ridge with no shelter from afternoon thunderstorms
no reliable water above the lower creek crossings
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SCRAMBLE STARTS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TREAD DIES AT THE OLD LOOKOUT BENCH, AND THE LEDGES SWITCHBACK RATHER THAN GO STRAIGHT. Walk the lookout trail to the flat bench around 2,800 ft where the fire lookout once stood; that bench is the reference point and the maintained tread effectively ends there. Keep climbing steeply and a cliff band appears within a few hundred vertical feet. The route takes about seventy vertical feet through it on a series of ledges, and the shape of the line is the test: it SWITCHBACKS up the ledges rather than climbing the rock directly. The ledges themselves are steep rock covered in dirt and moss rather than clean stone, so they feel insecure, and that is normal here. If you are forcing a direct line up clean rock, you are off the route. Above the band, the confirmation is pink ribbon flagging on an intermittent boot track along the crest and southwest side of the ridge. Two more checkpoints higher: the visible path effectively ends around 5,800 ft at an overlook above the small tarn in the basin, and there is a last band of stunted trees near 6,700 ft, also flagged, above which there is no ground cover at all. Note where you leave the timber, because that spot is not obvious from above on the way down. The summit above is a broad massif of red-stained rock and loose scree.

bivy.name: Sloan Creek Campground and the North Fork Sauk road end
bivy.notes: The staging point for the eastern half of this zone and the drive-in night before two very different trips. PAINTED MOUNTAIN, which older maps and signs call Red Mountain, goes from right here as a DAY OBJECTIVE with no established camp anywhere on it: a mile of maintained trail to about 3,100 ft, then a short steep step of dirty ledges that is real scrambling, then a faint intermittent path along the southwest ridge past the site of a long-gone lookout, then scree to a summit just under seven thousand feet — roughly eight miles round trip for nearly five thousand feet of gain, which is a full day from the car and the reason this campground matters. KOLOLO PEAKS is the opposite kind of trip and starts from the same place: twelve to thirteen miles up the North Fork Sauk trail to White Pass and beyond, with its camps already recorded in the Glacier Peak file. The access road is the honest caveat here. It is rough, with washout sections around the first and sixth miles where high clearance is strongly wanted, and it has a recent history of closures — a landslide on the main loop road cut off the junction entirely through one winter, and a lightning-caused fire in the drainage closed the road, this campground and both trailheads for two months of one autumn. That fire stayed small and its closure has lapsed, but burnt ground above a trail means deadfall and loose footing for years afterwards. Confirm the road with the district before the drive; this is not a place to discover a gate.
bivy.water: No potable supply. Sloan Creek and the North Fork Sauk both run close by and filter fine; this is clean valley water with none of the old-mine metals problem that spoils the drainages further west.
bivy.permit: The campground and the road end sit just outside GLACIER PEAK WILDERNESS, which the trails enter shortly above. Free self-issue wilderness permit from the box at the trailhead for anything going up, twelve-person party limit counting people and stock together. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass for the vehicle. Fires in the existing rings only, and forest-wide summer restrictions routinely close even those from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive campground of a handful of sites in the trees beside the trailhead, with a vault toilet and little else — no hookups, no host, no reservations. Being the road end for several long trips, the parking beside it fills before the sites do.

_raw.approach: Box Creek Meadows area; Class 2 route to summit via Ice Creek Ridge
_raw.land_manager: USFS Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District)
_raw.special_features: North face has steep cliffs and glacier remnants; ideal season late Sept-Oct
_raw.fire_restrictions: No fires within 1/2 mile of Ice Lakes, 1/4 mile of Image Lake, or above 4,000 feet on Lime Ridge
_raw.seasonal_closures: NOTE: April 2026 - extreme access limitations due to December 2025 storm damage
_raw.camping_restrictions: No camping within 1/4 mile of Image Lake or 200 feet of Holden/Lyman Lakes
_raw.parking_pass_required: Recreation Pass at trailhead (if developed recreation site)

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: None required for day climbing
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: No pass reported for the roadside hairpin pullout (unlike the Blue Lake/Cutthroat Lake/Rainy Pass trailheads on the west side of the pass, which require a Northwest Forest Pass or Recreation.gov day pass).

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then across the east side to the Pernod–Chianti notch
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout on SR-20 about 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, directly across the highway from the Wine Spires, a boot and climbers' trail drops off the shoulder, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs or a rock-hop, and climbs a timbered rib on the climber's-left side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. The creek can run high and require a wet ford in early-season snowmelt. The trail gains steeply and steadily, on the order of 2,000 ft over the first 1.5-2 miles, to a broad flat bench at roughly 6,400-6,600 ft that holds established camps. THIS BENCH IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER: small tarns and a creek trickle that can run dry by late summer. Above it the trail climbs steep talus and scree to Burgundy Col, the usual camp for this climb. From the col the route crosses to the east side of the spires and traverses south below their east walls to reach the notch between Chianti and Pernod.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the climb to Burgundy Col
Snow and névé at the edge of the Silver Star Glacier basin on the east side, with moats along the rock late in the season
Roughly three pitches of mostly 4th and 5th class to reach the notch
A rappel descent back down the east side, followed by a re-ascent to Burgundy Col
Old first-ascent bolts on the summit block; carry cord to back up or replace old slings
The bench is the last reliable water and can run dry by late summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS LINE IS CLIMBED FROM THE EAST, NOT FROM THE WEST FACE GULLY. Stay on the main climbers' trail past the bench all the way to Burgundy Col; the gully that contours right off the bench leads to the base of the west face, which is the start of a different and much harder route.

FROM THE COL, CROSS TO THE EAST SIDE AND GO SOUTH. Traverse below the east walls of Chianti and then Pernod, on snow and talus at the edge of the glacier basin. Pernod is the highest of the four spires and sits just south of Chianti.

THE KEY FEATURE IS THE NOTCH BETWEEN CHIANTI AND PERNOD. From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to that notch; the ground is mostly 4th and 5th class, roughly three pitches. Going south from the col you pass below Chianti first, and the notch you want is the one immediately south of it. The next notch beyond Pernod separates Pernod from Chablis and is the wrong one.

FROM THE NOTCH THE ROUTE GOES UP THE NORTHEAST CORNER to the small summit block, which carries old first-ascent bolts that are worth backing up.

FOR PARTIES WHO CAMP HIGH: Burgundy Col holds three or four bivy sites, one large enough for a two-person tent, with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing. Those shelters are a positive identification of the col.

DESCENT IS BY RAPPEL: back to the notch, then long rappels down the east side to the snow at the edge of the glacier basin. From there climb back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' trail.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Whatcom Pass and Perfect Pass to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine
approach_variants.notes: The northern option, favoured by several recent parties. From the Hannegan Trailhead at 3,100 ft, the Hannegan Pass Trail leads over the pass to the Chilliwack River Trail, which includes a cable-car crossing, then up the Brush Creek Trail to Whatcom Pass. From there the route leaves trail and goes off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. Expect 2-3 days of travel each way.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: A bergschrund on the summit snow finger, crossed via a slabby rock step
Somewhat rotten rock on the summit tower and gully section, with natural anchors only
Rockfall off the buttress walls onto the snow finger
A 1,000 ft descending traverse that has to be regained on the return
The Chilliwack cable-car crossing and the Whatcom Glacier traverse on the way in
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS A SADDLE INSIDE THE BUTTRESS, AT ABOUT 6,100 FT, AND YOU GET THERE BY LOSING HEIGHT FIRST. From the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp, the way to Phantom is a roughly 1,000 FT DESCENDING TRAVERSE EAST across snow and talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft WITHIN the buttress. That saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing.

SO THE TEST IN CLOUD IS THE SHAPE OF THE GROUND, NOT THE VIEW: you go DOWN and EAST for a thousand feet, then UP a snowfield, and you stop when the snowfield delivers you into a gap in a rock rib rather than onto open mountainside. A saddle inside a buttress has rock rising on both sides of you; open snow does not.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing the descending traverse east past the buttress toe drops you toward Luna Cirque and the ground the peak's other route uses, which is a different climb from a different camp.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: above the saddle the route takes a pocket glacier and snowfield to a bergschrund crossed by a slabby rock step, then a snow finger, then broken class 2-3 rock to a false summit and a short exposed step to the true summit. One bergschrund, one snow finger, one false summit. If you have crossed two schrunds you are not on this line.

approach_variants.name: Big Beaver Trail to Luna Camp, then the Luna Creek bushwhack up Phantom's south side
approach_variants.notes: The line the recorded distance reflects. From Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake, roughly $35 and saving about 6 miles, to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it is about 9 to 10 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage through old-growth cedar and past beaver ponds to Luna Camp, an established backcountry site where a wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends. Climbers leave the tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom's south side, gaining roughly 4,000 ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Modern parties report huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder dense enough that half a mile an hour is a good pace, with heavy insect pressure.
approach_variants.season: Late Jun-Aug
hazards: Some of the worst brush in the Cascades, at roughly half a mile an hour, with devil's club and slide alder
Fords of Luna Creek that get harder the lower you are
High risk of falling into a hole hidden by brush, and of separating from a partner
Heavy mosquito and fly pressure in summer
No trail, no cairns and real disorientation on the way back down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IN THIS DRAINAGE THE NAVIGATION RULE IS ABOUT HEIGHT, NOT DIRECTION, AND IT IS THE ONE THING THAT MAKES THE DAY WORK. The creek must be forded in places, and FORDS GET HARDER THE LOWER AND FARTHER DOWNSTREAM YOU ARE. Gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as you can rather than fighting the brush along the creek. If you are still beside running water after a couple of hours, you are on the losing line.

ARRIVAL, WHICH IS UNAMBIGUOUS EVEN WITH NO VISIBILITY: above the brush line the drainage OPENS into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. The brush stopping is the signal. Nothing else in this valley changes character that completely.

FROM THERE THE BASE TEST IS THE SAME ONE THE NORTHERN APPROACH USES: find the snowfield that leads up into a saddle at about 6,100 ft within the southwest buttress. That gap is where the technical climbing starts.

A REAL RISK PECULIAR TO THIS APPROACH, RECORDED BECAUSE IT HAS HAPPENED: in brush this thick, parties have become separated from each other. Agree a regrouping rule before entering it, not during.

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
