bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine high camp
Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. Whatcom Camp and both Graybeal camps have been closed because of fire damage from 2022, and the park's fire-closures page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists them closed until further notice, so there is no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass, then over the Challenger Glacier to a bivy under Ghost Peak
approach_variants.notes:
An involved two-day approach. Roughly 10 miles on trail up and over Hannegan Pass, wading the Chilliwack River, then the scenic 5-mile traverse of Easy Ridge, soloing exposed 4th-class terrain across the Imperfect Impasse, climbing through Perfect Pass and over the Challenger Glacier, then descending and traversing steep snow, talus and more glacier to a bivy site.

The route was first climbed in July 2021 and is documented in a single first-ascent account, so treat everything about it as sparsely reported.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug
hazards: The Imperfect Impasse, soloed as exposed 4th class on the way in
Crevasses on the Challenger Glacier
A rockfall-exposed snowfield crossing on the descent, worse later in the season
A single published ascent, so no accumulated route-finding knowledge to fall back on
Wading the Chilliwack River
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BIVY IS THE VIEWPOINT AND THAT IS THE POINT OF IT: the camp sits UNDER GHOST PEAK, Phantom's neighbour immediately to the NORTH, and the first-ascent party chose it because THE FULL WEST RIDGE COMES INTO VIEW FROM THERE. So the test is not a feature at the base of the climb but a named peak overhead: if the summit above your camp is not Ghost Peak, and Phantom is not the next summit SOUTH of you, you are camped in the wrong place.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN USUAL HERE: this ridge has one published ascent. Nobody has recorded a marker at its toe, and inventing one would be inventing the only fact that matters. What is recorded is the vantage point, so use it: from camp, with the ridge in view, pick the line and note it BEFORE the cloud comes in. This is a route to reconnoitre the evening before rather than to find in the morning.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, ON THE APPROACH: past Perfect Pass, the Challenger Glacier is crossed and then LEFT again on the far side. If you are still gaining height on ice you have not started the descent toward the Ghost Peak bivy.

ON THE DESCENT, AND WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU START: the way off is the southeast face, including a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall. The first-ascent party noted that crossing would be more straightforward earlier in the season with more snow cover.

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
bivy.notes: Moraine camp at the southern edge of the Crooked Thumb Glacier, below Ghost Peak, reached from Perfect Pass across the Challenger Glacier. The bivy for the west ridge, which starts from a 6,100 ft saddle below. Fully exposed to weather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier melt only
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few tents on a narrow moraine

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

wa_philadelphia_mountain_scramble.approach: Park at the Lake Serene Trailhead (from Hwy 2 ~21 mi east of Monroe, turn onto FR 6020, then FR 6020-109; Northwest Forest Pass required, two outhouses at the lot) and start up Lake Serene Trail #1068, a well-graded, heavily-used maintained trail through second-growth forest. At roughly 1.6 miles a signed junction splits off a short spur to Bridal Veil Falls — stay right/uphill for Lake Serene. Shortly after, the trail crosses Bridal Veil Creek on a long footbridge (last easy, reliable water before the lake) and begins a sustained set of switchbacks, gaining about 1,900 ft over the next two miles. Around 3.5 miles and ~1,920 ft of gain (roughly 2-2.5 hrs at a moderate pace) the trail levels out at Lake Serene's outlet, marked by a toilet/outhouse sign — this is where the maintained tread ends and the scramble begins. There is no established bootpath up Philadelphia: most parties backtrack a couple hundred feet down the trail, then cut uphill into a brushy boulder field on the south side of the lake (the first ~50 ft is the worst of it) to gain the ridge above the lake's south shore. Follow that ridge crest southeast, trending close to the cliff edge above the lake (exposed, view-heavy but with real fall potential) before the angle eases through forest thick with slide alder, blowdown, and moss-slick rock. At about 3,200 ft the ridge bends east and merges into the broader west ridge of Philadelphia Mountain — a mostly timbered, Class 2 walk with a few small meadow openings — which climbs the final ~1,000 ft over roughly a mile of undulating, multi-false-summit terrain to the flat, viewless top (4,258 ft). Hazards: no path or cairns to follow (route-finding is entirely on the party), dense brush and downed timber low on the ridge, mossy rock that's slick when wet, and lingering snow into late spring — many parties intentionally time this climb for a continuous snowpack specifically to bury the brush, which trades bushwhacking for steeper, more exposed snow travel above the lake and minor avalanche/cornice considerations on that slope. Partway up the west ridge, work around a cliff band by trending left (north) rather than pushing straight through it — the cliffs are on the SOUTH side of this upper ridge, and this is the spot parties most often get stuck. Note that the handedness flips at the bend: lower down, the drop is on the north, into the lake.

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene outlet to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes: Shares the busiest day-hike in the valley for its first three and a half miles: gently graded tread to the Bridal Veil Falls spur junction, then the long footbridge over Bridal Veil Creek — the last easy water — and a sustained set of switchbacks gaining most of the day's trail elevation over the next two miles. The maintained tread ends abruptly at the lake outlet by the toilet sign, and there is no established boot path onto the peak beyond it. Under continuous snowpack the whole line is markedly easier, which is why many parties save it for winter.
approach_variants.season: June to October, or under snow
hazards: Slide alder and heavy blowdown on the off-trail ridge
Moss-covered boulders that are slick even when dry
A cliff band on the upper west ridge, turned on the north (left) side — the cliffs are south here
Real fall potential where the crest runs along the drop above the lake
No cairned line to follow in fog, and several convincing false tops
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scramble starts in a brushy boulder field above the lake's south shore and nothing marks it. From the outlet at the toilet sign, backtrack a couple of hundred feet DOWN the trail before cutting uphill off the tread — leaving from the outlet itself puts you into worse ground. The first fifty feet or so of bushwhacking is the worst of the entire route, and once through it the boulder field gives onto the crest of the ridge above the lake's south shore. That crest, followed southeast with the drop to the water immediately below, is the route; blowdown rather than steepness is what makes it slow, and the faint track comes and goes between the logs. Around 3,200 ft the ridge bends east and merges into the broader west ridge, and from there it is a timbered class 2 walk over a series of bumps and flats. Partway up, a cliff band has to be worked around rather than pushed straight through, and it is the spot parties most often get stuck. Turn it on the LEFT, the north side: the cliffs here are on the south flank of the upper ridge, and the north side is also where the breaks in the trees give the views out to the Monte Cristo group, Gunn and Merchant. Note that this is the opposite hand from the section below the bend, where the drop is on the north into the lake — a party carrying the lower ridge's habit up onto the west ridge is walking toward the edge rather than away from it.

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle and the south gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Pinnacle Peak trailhead — a signed unnumbered trail directly across Stevens Canyon Road from the Reflection Lakes pullouts at about 4,860 ft — the maintained trail climbs at a steady, fairly steep grade through sparse subalpine forest. Around half a mile you get the first partial view of Rainier through the trees, then the trail switchbacks up through meadow. At about 1.25-1.3 miles and roughly 1,000-1,050 ft you top out at Pinnacle Saddle near 5,900-5,920 ft, where the maintained trail ends and the view opens south. Carry water from the car; there is no reliable source on the trail or in the gully except lingering snowmelt early in the season. Past the saddle the route becomes an unmaintained climbers' path. The rock is old, variable-quality lava flow — solid in places and rotten in others — so test holds and watch for loose blocks with parties above or below. This is a fully exposed ridge with quick-building afternoon thunderstorms in summer; plan to be off the summit by early afternoon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; snow or verglas can linger in the gully into July in a cold year
hazards: Loose, unstable rock through the south-facing summit gully
Steep dropoffs and exposure on sections of the maintained trail itself, not only above the saddle
Snow lingering in the summit gully into early or mid summer after the trail has melted out
Rockfall onto parties below on a heavily travelled line
Sudden afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed south Cascades ridge
No water anywhere on the trail or the scramble
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PINNACLE SADDLE, THE PEAK IS EAST. Pinnacle is the peak east of the saddle and Plummer is the peak west of it, and the boot paths fork there. GOING WEST FROM THE SADDLE PUTS YOU ON PLUMMER — a different summit, and a party can climb it believing it is this one.

SO: CONTOUR OR SCRAMBLE EAST into the gully system on the south and southeast face.

THE SEQUENCE INSIDE THE GULLY IS WHAT TELLS YOU IT IS THE RIGHT ONE, AND ONE ITEM IN IT IS UNEXPECTED ENOUGH TO BE A REAL TEST: it starts as class 2 scree and blocky steps, steepens into sustained class 3 with real exposure over its upper third, THEN WORKS THROUGH A BAND OF TREES, then a final short scramble to the summit block. TREES HIGH IN THE GULLY ARE THE CONFIRMATION. A gully with no tree band in it is not this one.

MULTIPLE GULLY LINES EXIST HERE, AND THE CORRECT ONE IS THE MOST TRAVELLED. The negative is tactile: if you are dislodging blocks with every step, you are off the beaten line. Loose rock is worst away from it.

THE EARLY-SEASON NEGATIVE IS A TURN-AROUND, NOT A ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM, AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: snow or verglas in this gully turns easy scrambling into a slip you cannot stop, on ground with no protection. That is the condition to go home on rather than to push through with an axe you are not going to be able to use in a chimney.

ONE MORE THING AT THE SADDLE THAT IS NOT A NAVIGATION MARKER BUT WILL BE THE FIRST THING YOU MEET: mountain goats here are habituated and come for the salt. They are not a sign you are on route.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side
approach_variants.notes:
THE APPROACH THAT MATTERS HERE IS THE SOUTHERN ONE, AND IT IS NOT THE SPIRES TRAIL. The climbers' path from the unsigned pullout further west serves the spires and the col on the other side of the crest. It does not put you under this face.

For the south face, walk the Cedar Creek trail from its own trailhead off the highway. After roughly five miles, turn off to the RIGHT below the old burn, where a rough path follows the RIGHT-HAND side of the creek that drains the south side of the formation.

There are good meadows for camping at about 6,200 ft. This is a rarely visited corner and there is no established climbers' camp, no fixed gear on the approach and very little traffic — expect to see nobody.

A parking pass or day fee covers the trailhead. This is national forest, so there is no permit system and no quota, and the general dispersed-camping rules apply.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-June through late September; July and August are the driest and most reliable
hazards: The Wine Spires pullout and its climbers' trail lead to the far side of the crest, not to this face
Rarely climbed, so there is no traffic, no chalk and essentially no current conditions information
Rappel anchors on the descent are sparse and some must be built; carry extra webbing
Two long routes share this face and its summit
Remote enough that a retreat from high on the face is slow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is CLEAN WHITE GRANITE, which is the first confirmation and a good one — it is visibly paler than the rock either side and it is why the formation gets climbed at all. Follow the creek up to the meadows and then to the foot of that white wall. Two long routes share it and they share a summit, so the identification has to be done at the ground and re-checked on the climb.

THE START IS A FLAKE, AND IT IS A BIG ONE. This route begins with a LAYBACK OFF A LARGE CLEAN FLAKE that leads into a LONG LEFT-FACING CORNER SYSTEM carrying finger cracks. Large detached flake at the bottom, left-facing corner above it: that pairing is the whole identification and there is nothing else on this face like it.

CONFIRM WITH THE ROOFS, IN ORDER. Above the corner system the route crosses RIGHT beneath a ROOF into a SPLITTER CRACK that reaches a ledge partway up the face. Higher, a SECOND ROOF leads to a hand crack and then stemming corners with a hard exit. Two roofs, the first crossed rightward and the second climbed through, is the sequence.

THE SUMMIT PITCH IS THE CLEANEST TEST OF ALL, and it is worth knowing before you leave the ledge: this route tops out THROUGH A DEEP SUMMIT CHIMNEY. You finish inside the chimney. The other long route on this face finishes on blocky ground JUST RIGHT OF that chimney and never enters it. If you are stemming a deep slot to the top, you are on this route; if you are scrambling blocks beside one, you are on the neighbour.

NEGATIVE MARKER at the start to match it: if you began on the RIGHT-HAND side of the face on flakes, corners and splitters and arrived at a BROAD LEDGE running most of the way across the face at about half height, you are on the neighbouring line. This route has no such crossing ledge low down; its mid-height ledge is reached from a splitter after a rightward move under a roof.

Protection throughout is cams and nuts to about three inches. Descent is a series of rappels down the south-east side; a seventy-metre rope is the standard, fixed anchors are sparse, and you should expect to build some — carry extra webbing.

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle, the tarn shelf and the north slopes
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road. The signed Pinnacle Peak Trail leaves the south side of the road, directly across from the largest of the lakes.

The trail climbs moderately through mountain hemlock and Alaska yellow cedar for the first half-mile; around 0.5 mile you get a first partial view of Rainier, and at about 0.6 mile you cross a seasonal cascading creek — the only reliable water on the hike, and dry by late summer in a low-snow year. By 0.7 mile it breaks into open talus and heather below Pinnacle's cliffs and steepens noticeably. Lingering snow on these shaded north-facing switchbacks is the trail's main hazard, since a slip on hard morning snow above the talus can slide a hiker into rock. Around 0.9-1.0 mile the trail passes beneath the cliff bands on Pinnacle's north face, then switchbacks up a short exposed final pitch to Pinnacle Saddle at about 1.25-1.3 miles and roughly 5,920-5,960 ft.

The saddle is the trail's official end and the junction where unmaintained paths fork east toward Pinnacle and The Castle and west toward Plummer and Denman.

Stevens Canyon Road is open roughly late May through late October and the small trailhead lot commonly fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct; a snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July
hazards: Lingering snowfield on the steep shaded switchbacks below the saddle, icy in early morning — the most common problem spot
Steep, eroded, loose tread and exposed traverse sections on the upper approach trail
Afternoon thunderstorms and lightning on an exposed ridge and saddle with no shelter above treeline
Loose rock and thin tread on the final scramble, which feels more exposed descending
Winter avalanche terrain on the peak's slopes
No water past the seasonal creek low on the trail
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PINNACLE SADDLE, PLUMMER IS WEST — the opposite direction from Pinnacle, and the paths fork right there.

BUT THE SADDLE IS NOT THE DECISION POINT. THE TARN IS. Here is the sequence, and the middle item is the whole route-finding problem:
1. Continue a short distance PAST the saddle and look for a climbers' path branching RIGHT, west.
2. It crosses a FLAT ROCKY SHELF HOLDING A SEASONAL TARN. The tarn is the marker.
3. AT THAT SHELF A FORK CONTINUES STRAIGHT TOWARD DENMAN PEAK. DO NOT TAKE IT. BEAR LEFT, south and uphill, onto the boot path climbing Plummer's open rocky north slopes.

SO THE ENTIRE PROBLEM REDUCES TO ONE SENTENCE: AT THE TARN, STRAIGHT IS DENMAN AND LEFT IS PLUMMER.

THE NEGATIVE IS A MOTION TEST AND IT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING: IF YOU ARE STILL WALKING LEVEL, OR LOSING HEIGHT, YOU ARE ON THE DENMAN FORK. Plummer's path climbs from the tarn.

THE BASE OF THE HANDS-ON GROUND: the last few hundred feet is class 2-3 with a couple of short hands-on steps, and A FEW WELL-PLACED TREES AID THE FINAL MOVES. Trees on a summit slope at this height are unusual enough to be a confirmation.

THE SUMMIT IS SMALL AND THAT IS THE LAST CHECK — roughly 50 by 15 ft. If you are standing on a broad top, you are on the shoulder below it.

EARLY-SEASON DETAIL THAT IS A REAL FORK RATHER THAN A CAUTION: a snowfield often crosses the boot path near the saddle into July. Either kick steps straight up it or skirt LEFT onto the rockier tread. Both rejoin near the top, so neither choice loses the route.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

waypoints.name: Westside Road / Dry Creek (Tahoma Creek) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of driveable Westside Road (3.2 mi from the Nisqually-Longmire Rd junction), gated at Dry Creek. CHECK THIS BEFORE YOU DRIVE: the National Park Service's only two listed accesses to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground — the next waypoint on this route — are Kautz Creek (11.5 mi round trip) and Longmire (13 mi round trip). The Westside Road and Tahoma Creek corridor is not among them, and route beta for Success Cleaver reports the Tahoma Creek Trail closed for flood hazard, leaving Longmire via the Wonderland Trail as the standard approach. The mileages recorded on this route's waypoints are measured from this Dry Creek gate, so they describe the older corridor rather than a Longmire or Kautz Creek start — treat them as approximate if you approach from either of those, and confirm current trail status with a wilderness information centre.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 706 to the Nisqually Entrance in the park's south-west corner; the road is paved and open essentially year round, conditions permitting. Westside Road leaves the Nisqually to Longmire road and is driveable about three miles to the gate at Dry Creek, where a standing, non-seasonal closure caused by repeated Tahoma Creek washouts stops vehicles; past the gate it is open to foot and bike traffic only. Longmire, where the nearest wilderness information centre is and where you register in and out, lies about 3.5 miles further along the main road.

waypoints.name: Indian Henry's Hunting Ground (patrol cabin)
waypoints.note: Historic 1915 patrol cabin marks where the route leaves the maintained Wonderland Trail for cross-country travel toward the Mirror Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Mirror Lakes
waypoints.note: Small tarns about a mile off the Wonderland Trail; last dependable water before contouring dry southwest/west slopes of Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained Wonderland Trail at the patrol cabin and take the Mirror Lakes spur west, crossing marshy meadow on a series of plank walkways. Maintained tread ends part way along and the path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft, in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak, roughly a mile off the Wonderland. These tarns are the last dependable water before the dry south-west and west slopes of Pyramid Peak.

waypoints.name: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
waypoints.note: Flat campsites just north of this 6,631 ft high point give broad views of Success Cleaver; position is estimated, not surveyed — interpolated along the contour around Pyramid Peak.
waypoints.directions: From the tarns it is cross-country travel. Head north-east out of the basin and contour the south-west then west slopes of Pyramid Peak, staying roughly between 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. There is no boot-pack and only sparse cairning through here, so carry a map or GPS track and expect to find your own line; snowmelt water is often available around the point into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak near 6,300 ft is a common first night.

waypoints.name: 6,400 ft saddle below Success Cleaver
waypoints.note: Short descent NNE from Point 6631 to this saddle; typical high camp before scrambling onto the lower cleaver at first light.
waypoints.directions: Drop north-north-east from Point 6631 a short way to the saddle at about 6,400 ft, which is the start of Success Cleaver proper. It is a scree and loose-boulder col and it looks unpleasant, which is how you know it is the right place. There is an easier way down into it than the obvious line, and parties record missing it and taking the worst ground, so pick the descent out before you commit and note it for the return.

waypoints.name: Lower Success Cleaver gendarmes
waypoints.note: Loose rock towers force weaving route-finding on the lower rib; rockfall risk climbs if other parties are above; bivy options around 8,100-8,300 ft.
waypoints.directions: From the col the cleaver rises straight ahead and does not let up: loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, no track and no cairned line, weaving among rock towers on ground you route-find yourself. Use what is on either side as the test. The South Tahoma Glacier should fall away to climber's left and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to climber's right; if you find yourself on a glacier, or if the going out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you have drifted off the cleaver and are contouring around Pyramid Peak instead. Rockfall risk rises sharply with any party above you, the rock firms up above roughly 7,000 ft, and there are bivy sites around 8,100 to 8,300 ft.

waypoints.name: Rockfall chutes to Kautz Cleaver headwall
waypoints.note: Angle across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall and gain the Kautz Cleaver near 12,600 ft; helmet mandatory, best crossed before sun loosens rock.
waypoints.directions: Follow the cleaver crest up through class 3 and short class 4 rock bands and steep chutes, past bivy benches near 9,400 ft and the small col at about 10,700 ft. Higher, the crest holds a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow has melted off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies and across three loose, rockfall-swept chutes to the headwall, joining the Kautz Cleaver between roughly 12,200 and 12,600 ft. Cross those chutes early, before the sun starts releasing rock and ice; helmets on.

waypoints.name: Point Success
waypoints.directions: From the Kautz Cleaver climb steepening snow and ice, generally around 45 degrees, to the headwall below the summit. A cliff band bars the way and is passed either by a short low fifth class rock step, exposed and sometimes wet or icy, or by an isolated snow and ice pitch of about 15 ft at up to 55 degrees, depending on the season. Above it the angle eases onto the summit plateau at Point Success, 14,158 ft.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge, Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier
approach_variants.notes: A multi-day expedition into one of the range's most remote corners with essentially no bail options once committed. From the trailhead at the end of the forest road, the trail climbs steadily through forest to Hannegan Pass, where the maintained tread ends. Drop east into the Chilliwack River valley — the last reliable water for a while — then regain height onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the remains of an old lookout on the ridge high point. From Easy Ridge, contour toward the east flank of the neighbouring peak to the notorious moat-and-cliff notch that cuts the ridge; it often still holds snow well into summer and typically needs a short stretch of low fifth-class downclimbing, or a scramble around or under a snow tunnel, to cross. Beyond it, climb snowfields to Perfect Pass, the standard base camp; whiteout here is a genuine hazard, and parties have set off toward the wrong wall. From Perfect Pass, rope up and traverse east around the Challenger Arm and cross several miles of upper glacier toward the cirque below the south side of the subsidiary summits. In lower-snow years a broken icefall blocks the direct line and most parties detour high above the first crevasse band, or drop back toward the arm for a lower line.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through early September, once the glacier has consolidated enough to cross and before autumn storms return. The first week of August is statistically the driest stretch here. Early-season attempts find more snow on the glacier and on the connecting ridge.
hazards: a severely runout crux pitch with roughly forty feet of essentially unprotectable climbing and groundfall potential
crevassed glacier travel for several miles each way, worse late season and in low-snow years
loose rock and exposed downclimbing at the moat-and-cliff notch on Easy Ridge
icefall hazard near the Challenger Arm and the cirque below
extreme remoteness, with no realistic prospect of quick outside help
approach_variants.baseFinding: A HUGE SHIELD STREAKED WITH DIKES LIKE BOLTS OF LIGHTNING IS THE PROOF, AND YOU CAN SEE IT FROM OUT ON THE GLACIER. This is the SOUTHERNMOST of the prominent subsummits on the ridge between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb, and it is identified by one feature rather than by its shape: the base of the tower carries an enormous shield of dark granite crisscrossed by hundreds of pale dikes running across it like bolts of lightning. That streaking is unmistakable and visible from well out on the glacier, so pick the tower off before you commit to a line across the ice. The climbing starts in a clean dihedral just LEFT of the dike-streaked shield, roughly twenty feet above the snow, and the bergschrund or moat at the foot of it is the first thing to assess, because it decides whether that start is reachable at all on the day. If the wall in front of you is uniform dark granite with no lightning-streak dikes, you are beneath the wrong subsummit and should continue south along the base. Once on it, the first pitch tiptoes rightward across parallel dikes for about forty feet to the very edge of the face; that stretch takes essentially no protection and a fall on it is long, with cracks only appearing higher up.

bivy.name: Challenger Arm camp
bivy.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
bivy.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
bivy.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Beaver Pass Camp
bivy.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
bivy.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
bivy.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

bivy.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge, Perfect Pass and the Challenger Glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead at the end of the forest road, the trail climbs steadily through forest for about four miles to Hannegan Pass, where the maintained tread ends. Descend the climbers' path east toward the Chilliwack River and Boundary Camp area, the last reliable water for a while, then regain height onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the old lookout foundation and antenna remains on the ridge high point. From Easy Ridge, contour toward the east flank of the neighbouring peak to the moat-and-cliff notch that cuts the ridge; it often holds snow into summer and usually needs a short stretch of low fifth-class downclimbing or a scramble around or under a snow tunnel, and it is the cross-country crux of the approach and a common turnaround point in poor conditions. Beyond it, climb snowfields to Perfect Pass, the standard base camp; fog here is a real hazard and parties have mistakenly set off toward the wrong wall. On the second day, rope up at the Challenger Arm and cross roughly three miles of upper glacier into the cirque below the south side of the subsidiary summits, detouring high above the first crevasse band in low-snow years when the icefall blocks the direct line.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through early September, once the glacier crevasses are more consolidated and the pass approach is snow-free enough to travel. Earlier attempts find more snow on the glacier, on the route and on the connecting ridge.
hazards: sparse protection on the crux pitch, with roughly forty feet of essentially unprotectable dike climbing off the bergschrund
crevasses on several miles of glacier approach each way
extreme remoteness with no quick outside help
the moat-and-cliff notch on Easy Ridge, wet and slippery above a deep gorge
a descent that is not back down the face — it continues over the connecting ridge and off the neighbouring summit's glacier, so glacier gear has to be carried over the top
approach_variants.baseFinding: A HUGE SHIELD STREAKED WITH DIKES LIKE BOLTS OF LIGHTNING IS THE PROOF, AND YOU CAN SEE IT FROM OUT ON THE GLACIER. This is the SOUTHERNMOST of the prominent subsummits on the ridge between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb, and it is identified by one feature rather than by its outline: the base of the tower carries an enormous shield of dark granite crisscrossed by hundreds of pale dikes running across it like bolts of lightning. That streaking is unmistakable and visible from well out on the glacier, so pick the tower off before committing to a line across the ice. Leave the glacier at the tower's foot. The climbing starts in a clean dihedral just LEFT of the dike-streaked shield, roughly twenty feet above the snow, and the bergschrund or moat at the base is the first thing to assess, because it decides whether that start is reachable at all. If the wall in front of you is uniform dark granite with no lightning-streak dikes, you are beneath the wrong subsummit and should keep going south along the base. Once established, the first pitch tiptoes rightward across parallel dikes for about forty feet to the very edge of the face and takes essentially no gear for that whole stretch; cracks appear higher and the pitch runs the better part of a full rope length.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

approach_variants.name: Rainy Creek climbers' path to the ridge above Rainy Lake
approach_variants.notes: From the Middle Fork lot, cross the river on the footbridge and follow the Pratt Connector west for roughly half a mile of easy, well-graded tread. The unofficial Rainy Creek climbers' path branches off near the Rainy Creek crossing and climbs steadily and steeply beside the creek, crossing a couple of seasonal drainages around 3,100 ft before angling south into steepening forest. It is boot-trodden, muddy and brushy with occasional blowdown, and it largely disappears under snow through late spring. Rainy Lake is the last reliable water. This is a long day — around 5,000 ft of gain — and most parties leave the lot before dawn.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to October, or on snow
hazards: Unsigned, unmaintained boot path that is easy to lose, especially descending
A short rock band near 3,700 ft with real exposure, worse to downclimb
Mossy slab that is slick when wet
Cliff bands between roughly 4,200 and 4,800 ft above the lake
Cornices building along the summit ridge in winter and spring
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts at Rainy Lake, but the harder find is the path that gets you there. Watch for the unsigned climbers' path branching off the Pratt Connector near the Rainy Creek crossing — it is not an official trail, it is not marked, and it is easy to walk straight past. Around 3,700 ft a short rock band forces roughly a hundred feet of scrambling before you can side-hill in to the lake; that band is the one spot on the approach with real exposure and it is your confirmation you are on the right line. At the lake the path ends entirely. Leave it at the outlet and climb the ridge that rises east and then curves south above the lake's east shore, staying on the LAKE side — the right or west side of the crest — to skirt the cliff bands between about 4,200 and 4,800 ft. The ground is brushy at first, opens into slabby mossy terrain, and turns to open slopes above roughly 4,800 ft, ending on a flat bench holding a small unnamed tarn near 5,200 ft. Several braided boot paths exist through the brush low down, so do not assume the one you are on is the one you want.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Squire Creek Road from Darrington to the washout gate, then the old roadbed on foot past the flagged landslide crossing.

The South Face turn-off is marked by two cut logs lying either side of the road with old logging cable visible. Turn right there onto a well-beaten boot track, ford the creek, and climb steeply through old growth — steep and dirty near the top — until it opens into grassland and the grassy saddle bivy. About three hours from the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Summer; saddle bivy is a high-summer camp
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep, dirty forest on the upper boot track
Class 4 ramp scrambling to reach the start
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the grassy saddle bivy, cross class 4 ramps to a shallow dihedral with a small tree in it, then continue to a dirt ledge at the base of a short wall. That dirt ledge is the start.

The small tree in the shallow dihedral is the discriminator. Miracle Ramps uses the same class 4 ramps but leads to a dihedral and then a starting wall ledge that it shares with this route's upper start, and the two only diverge higher; Nature's Way goes the other way, crossing the apron past Concerto's start to two-bolt ring anchors on the opposite wall.

This is an old-school ridge ramble: lichened overlaps and dirt-filled cracks low down are CORRECT here, not evidence of being off route. The crux does not arrive until pitch 9.

approach_variants.name: The far end of the Eldorado ice cap: five glaciers and a notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col
approach_variants.notes:
This is the way to Primus's south side, and it comes from the opposite side of the mountain to the Thunder Creek approach. From the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road near 2,100 ft, cross the Cascade River, climb the steep root-laced boot path through timber, cross the boulder field around 4,000 ft following cairns on the right side of the talus, and reach the meadows of Eldorado Basin. Continue to the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and rope up — it is broken and thinly bridged in a normal-to-low snow year.

From the upper Eldorado Glacier, traverse north below Eldorado's east ridge and continue on the Inspiration Glacier toward Klawatti Col near 7,800 ft. Parties describe crossing the Inspiration's crevasse fields with zero visibility, so plan for it.

Summit day from a Klawatti Col camp: downclimb or make a short rappel of about 50 ft through the notch at the McAllister-Klawatti col onto the Klawatti Glacier, rope up, and traverse below the south side of Austera's east ridge, rounding its end near 6,800 ft onto the North Klawatti Glacier — probing, because this stretch has caught parties by surprise even in good visibility — to the foot of Primus's south side. Then unrope and walk.

The route crosses the Eldorado, Inspiration, McAllister, Klawatti and North Klawatti glaciers in sequence; Austera Towers is passed and bypassed on a short scree ramp along the glacier's eastern edge.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August, when the glacier bridges are most consolidated and whiteout risk is lowest
hazards: A heavily crevassed North Klawatti and McAllister glacier system, especially late season
Thin, unreliable snow bridges by August and September — probe before committing weight
Complex glacier route-finding around Klawatti Col in poor visibility
A short technical step at the McAllister-Klawatti notch that has to be reversed at the end of the day
Extreme remoteness: a multi-day approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ONE FINDABLE FEATURE ON THIS ROUTE IS THE NOTCH AT THE McALLISTER-KLAWATTI COL, AND IT IS FINDABLE BECAUSE IT IS THE ONLY PLACE ALL DAY YOU NEED A ROPE FOR ROCK. It is a step of roughly 50 ft: downclimbed, hand-lined, or rappelled off a sling on a horn or block — there is no fixed hardware. If you have crossed a col without a technical step, you are not through it yet. AFTER THE NOTCH, THE TEST IS WHAT YOU ARE STANDING ON RATHER THAN WHAT YOU CAN SEE. You drop onto the KLAWATTI GLACIER, traverse below Austera's east ridge and round its end onto the NORTH KLAWATTI GLACIER. The climbing begins where you take the rope OFF: snow-covered talus, class 2-3, straight to the 8,508 ft summit. There is no notch, no rib and no marked start above the glacier — the honest answer is that this route has no rock landmark at its base, and the col behind you is what tells you where you are. THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE STRONG ONE AND IT SETTLES THE WHOLE PEAK: THE OTHER STANDARD LINE ON PRIMUS IS REACHED FROM THUNDER CREEK, AND IT STARTS AT LUCKY PASS — a notch at the head of the Borealis Glacier where the route to Tricouni Peak splits off east. IF YOU ARE AT A PASS WITH A SECOND PEAK'S ROUTE LEAVING IT, YOU ARE ON THE EAST SLOPE AND YOU CAME UP THE WRONG VALLEY FOR THIS ROUTE. The two lines are on opposite sides of the mountain and share no ground below the summit. AND WATCH THE FALSE SUMMIT WHATEVER SIDE YOU CAME FROM: a false top stands around 8,270 ft and is passed on climber's-left. A high point reached without traversing round anything is not the summit.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek and the Borealis Glacier: the east ridge from Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The other way onto Primus comes from the north, and it finishes on a different line: the east ridge, not this route's south side. From Colonial Creek Campground on the North Cascades Highway, walk the Thunder Creek Trail about six miles to McAllister Camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek there has washed out, so expect to ford cold, fast water or hunt for a log crossing.

Across the creek, a faint, steep boot path climbs the long, brushy lower north ridge of Tricouni Peak to the toe of the Borealis Glacier near 6,000 ft, where there is good camping. From camp, climb the glacier along its eastern edge, keeping clear of the icefall in its middle, to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni near 7,200 ft, and follow the east ridge to the summit on class 3 ground.

The brush on the ridge above Thunder Creek is slow going in either direction, and worse carrying skis or a long pack.
hazards: An unbridged ford of Thunder Creek at McAllister Camp
A steep, brushy boot path that is easy to lose on the ridge above Thunder Creek
An icefall in the middle of the Borealis Glacier that has to be skirted
Class 3 ground on the east ridge above Lucky Pass

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, fifty feet left of the standard south-face line
approach_variants.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining about 2,000 ft of steep loose scree and dirt, the physical crux of the approach, with a hidden creek and moat under lingering snow into early July.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. Parties commonly bivy at the tarn, about twenty minutes from the base. There is no maintained trail for the last stretch.

The Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative when Aasgard or the trailhead is closed: past Nada and Snow Lakes to Lake Viviane, then up and right toward Temple Lake and up climbers' paths through boulders to the base of the south face.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the route is a hard rock climb and wants dry, warm granite
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree with a hidden creek and moat under early-season snow, and a fatal history
A 5.11+ crux on the first pitch, so retreat decisions come early
A loose block in the finishing chimney
Mixed rappel anchors on the north side — one bolted station near the top, gear and slung naturals below
Unmarked cross-country approach over slabs and talus
Core Zone camping needs a permit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FIFTY FEET LEFT OF THE STANDARD SOUTH FACE ROUTE. That is the published position and it is a pace count, not a description — find the classic line at the middle of the base of the face, then walk left about fifty feet.

THE FIRST PITCH IS THE CHECK, AND IT IS A BRUTAL ONE. This route's opening pitch is 5.11+. The line fifty feet to your right opens at 5.6 or 5.7 in a chimney. There is no ambiguity between those two pieces of climbing: if you are cruising your first pitch, you are on the wrong route, and if you are fighting a tipsy crux entering a stembox, you are on this one.

WHAT THE FIRST PITCH LOOKS LIKE FROM THE GROUND, so you can commit before you leave the deck: an easy, unappealing LEFT-SLANTING crack system leading up to a stance below an obvious stembox. The unremarkable start is deceptive and is exactly why the fifty-foot offset matters — the interesting rock is not visible from the base.

BELAY CONFIRMATION: pitch one ends at a TWO-BOLT ANCHOR after liebacking and stemming up the right of twin cracks. Most of this face is natural gear; arriving at bolts is strong evidence you are on this line rather than on a neighbour.

AND THE NAMED PITCH HIGHER UP: an undercling flake pitch that parties call the money pitch, then a committing corner where the route switches cracks. If you never leave one crack for another, you have wandered onto adjoining ground.

DESCENT NOTE THAT AFFECTS THE APPROACH DECISION: this one rappels the north side in five, then needs one more rappel from the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge to get back down to your packs.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the left flank of the south face
approach_variants.notes:
As for the rest of the face: Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,600 ft, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction, right and across Mountaineer Creek — a rock-hop or log crossing, and the last easy water for a while — then 1.6 miles of switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then Aasgard Pass: 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose dirt and scree, cairned when snow-free. In early season, and often into July, snow bridges a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; people have been badly hurt and killed there postholing or glissading into it.

From the pass at 7,841 ft, drop into the upper Core past Isolation and Tranquil Lake and continue cross-country a mile or so north over slabs and heather benches toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn. The start is fifteen to twenty minutes from a Gnome Tarn camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Loose rock past the chimney at mid-height
Natural, non-bolted rappel anchors on the north side shared with several routes; inspect and back up old tat
Cross-country navigation over slabs with no tread for the last mile
Core Zone camping requires a permit that most parties do not have
approach_variants.baseFinding:
GO TO THE OUTSIDE CORNER AND START JUST RIGHT OF IT. The left flank of the south face ends in an outside corner — the arête where the south face turns the corner onto the west side — and this route begins just to the RIGHT of it, on a right-leaning crack system leading to a stembox.

THAT CORNER IS THE ANCHOR FOR THE WHOLE LEFT END OF THE FACE, and the three routes here are placed off it:
  - Left of the corner, on the west face proper: a line with a large roof at its base, sometimes called the Elephant Ear.
  - Just right of the corner: this route.
  - About 100 ft further right: another four-pitch line to the West Ridge.
So if you are under a roof, you have gone one route too far left; if you have walked a hundred feet right of the corner, one too far right.

THE HONEST WARNING ABOUT WHERE THIS ROUTE ENDS, because it is the best single check that you are on the left flank at all: this line and its immediate neighbours top out on the WEST RIDGE, not on the summit. Only the classic line at the middle of the face reaches the true summit. If you have come for the summit and started here, you have an extra scramble at the top and you started on the wrong route.

SEQUENCE CHECK: right-leaning cracks to a stembox, then a roof and hand-crack pitch, then slabby and wide ground past a chimney with loose rock, then a final splitter corner. Five pitches, about 450 ft. A seven-pitch line with two big V-features low down is Beckey-Davis, well to your right.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's LEFT of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain to climber's right, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Rappel descent on the north side is shared by several south-face routes and backs up when busy
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse NORTHEAST to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of DEEP CHIMNEYS on the face. The route starts to the LEFT of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep WHITE granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just BELOW SOME SHRUBBY PINES. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay CLIMBER'S LEFT (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east and south through the Core's tarns and slabs to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.
approach_variants.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
hazards: Aasgard Pass: veering climber's right into the cliffed waterfall terrain has killed people
Loose talus and rockfall the full length of Aasgard, worse in the afternoon heat
Misleading and multiplying cairns on the pass and in the Core
No water between Colchuck Lake and the Core tarns
Very long day; parties routinely finish the descent of Aasgard in the dark
Descent from Prusik is rappels, not a walk-off — do not arrive without the gear
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the highest point of Prusik Pass, do NOT go over the first bump in front of you — go AROUND it. Parties who climb straight over it lose time and, more importantly, lose the path.

Past the bump the climbing line drops out of sight. Keep scrambling easy blocky class 2 ground and it reappears. The landmark you are heading for first is a huge BALANCED, DISH-SHAPED ROCK — that is the right place to stash packs and put on shoes, and it is not yet the start of the climbing.

One more knob of scrambling past that brings you to the actual base: an OVERHANGING ROCK at the foot of the route, which is the natural sheltered spot to leave big bags.

The first pitch is the final confirmation and it is unmistakable even in cloud: a long pitch up a WIDE CRACK, about 5.6, in a conspicuously WHITE section of rock. The white band is the marker — the surrounding stone is not that colour. A distinct crack of roughly 5.6 leading up through blocky ground to the ridge is what you want; if you are staring at clean, hard, featureless granite you are on one of the south-face routes instead.

Belay at a slingable block; the 5.7 slab crux with an old piton comes above that.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.
approach_variants.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Hidden creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges
Punchy afternoon snow concealing ice
Uncontrolled slide on the pass, ascending or descending
Snow on Prusik's north side lengthens and complicates the rappel descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Prusik Pass landmarks survive the snow, because they are large rock features: go AROUND the first bump rather than over it, find the huge balanced dish-shaped rock to gear up at, then one more knob to the overhanging rock at the base.

The first pitch's white rock band and wide 5.6 crack still identify the start. What changes early season is the ground below the base — snow can cover the scrambling approach entirely, so the sequence of bump, dish rock, knob, overhang is what you navigate by rather than any boot path.

approach_variants.name: Cascade Pass to Cache Col
approach_variants.notes: Drive Cascade River Road out of Marblemount to its end and take the maintained Cascade Pass Trail up its open switchbacks to the pass. That trail is the last graded tread on the whole traverse and the pass is the last easy water; everything south of it is unmarked cross-country travel over glaciers and talus. Most parties set a car shuttle to the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle side, or reverse the trip out over the pass when the southern road is washed out.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September, once the Cache Glacier snow has consolidated and the cornice on the far lip of Cache Col has dropped
