hazards: The north lip of Cache Col is commonly corniced into mid-summer and is a hazard on the way out as much as the way in
Permanent, steep snow on the Cache Glacier — axe and crampons rather than optional
No tread, no markers and no signage anywhere past the pass
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cascade Pass itself is the reference, and the test is which way you leave it. The maintained trail arrives at a broad saddle and then continues EAST, dropping in switchbacks toward Pelton Basin and the Stehekin side; if you are losing height on good graded tread with a valley opening ahead of you, you have walked past the start of the traverse. The traverse leaves the pass on the opposite bearing: turn SOUTH, step off the tread onto heather and talus, and aim for the obvious apron of permanent snow hanging under the ridge above you. That snow is the Cache Glacier and the notch at its head is Cache Col. The proof is underfoot within a few minutes — no cut trail at all, only boot-scuffed talus and occasional cairns — and overhead, with the snow directly above you rather than across a valley. If you are still walking on benched trail ten minutes after the pass, you are on the wrong side of it.

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake climbers' path
approach_variants.notes: From the small pullout on the north shoulder of the highway near milepost 126.8, cross the road to the signed trailhead at the foot of Pyramid Creek's cascades. The maintained tread climbs steadily through second-growth and remnant old-growth, fords the creek beside a stand of old cedars — the last reliable water of the day, so treat it there — and switchbacks to Pyramid Lake, where it ends. Above the lake it is a cairned boot path the whole way, intermittent and easy to lose, and the route-finding rather than the climbing is the crux.
approach_variants.season: July to early October; east-facing snowfields and the notch below the summit ridge hold snow well into summer, so an axe is worth carrying even in mid-season
hazards: Boot path fades completely under early-season snow or in cloud
The traverse below the peak's east-side cliffs is prone to sliding
No reliable water above the cedar ford; the timberline tarns are dry by late summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: Pyramid Lake's outlet is the reference and the end of the maintained trail is the proof. The graded, Park-built tread stops dead at the water and there is no maintained continuation anywhere around the lake, so if you are still walking on cut, benched trail you have not reached the start. At the outlet bear RIGHT, to the west, cross a small rock knob and a brief dip, and pick up cairns — the climbers' path turns uphill almost at once and climbs the ridge directly and steeply on roots, brush and dirt. Two features confirm the line: the knob at the outlet, and far above it a boulder field sitting directly beneath a steep rock knob. Do not cross those blocks. The cairns route AROUND them on a brushy path along the field's SOUTH side, and this is the single place parties most often go off-route. If you are scrambling over the open boulders, or contouring the lake's east shore, you are off the line.

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) leaves the Mountain Loop Highway roughly 27-28 miles east of Granite Falls; about 2.3-2.5 miles of gravel end at the Sunrise Mine trailhead, around 2,400 ft, with a pit toilet and a Northwest Forest Pass requirement.

Trail #707 starts in second-growth and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs — a genuine obstacle in high runoff. It then climbs through Wirtz Basin and out onto open cairned talus to Headlee Pass, about 4,720 ft at 2.7 miles: a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Beyond the pass the trail drops through trees and crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, following it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft and 3.5 miles. That is the last dependable running water.

The north-face routes are NOT approached from the lake basin. Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing NORTH across the slabs. Allow three hours or more from the car to the base.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the ledge traverse holds snow into mid-summer
hazards: Rockfall from parties above in the Headlee Pass couloir
Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish in high runoff
Steep exposed heather on the ledge traverse — treacherous when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into mid-to-late summer; axe worth carrying early season
approach_variants.baseFinding: The confirmation that you are in the right place to start traversing is TWO LARGE CAIRNS on a saddle at about 5,700 ft, near 48.01375 -121.51451, with Copper Lake visible below to the northwest. Do not drop into the saddle. The heather-covered ledge system starts about 30 ft ABOVE the cairns on third-class slabs and runs east across the north face for roughly 800 ft, with a goat trail worn through it; there is one exposed step down off the saddle before it widens. Sources name this saddle inconsistently — the mapped approach calls it the Vesper-Wolf saddle, several route write-ups call it the Vesper-Sperry col. The two cairns and the view of Copper Lake are the reliable test, not the name. At the far end of the traverse, where the ledge runs out, the ORIGINAL start goes up and then right on about 60 ft of low fifth to third-class slabs and an obvious flaky gully. The cleaner and now more common variation is reached by backtracking slightly and making an exposed third-class traverse down and around the toe of a buttress to a clean 5.6 LAYBACK FLAKE. Negative marker: Ragged Edge jogs hard RIGHT within the first pitch or two. A first pitch that runs straight up the face and stays there is True Grit, not this route.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

approach_variants.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib, then the ledge system below the col
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain rather than for the spires, and the climbers' path itself is unmarked.

Go down the talus and into the forest, cross Early Winters Creek on a log, and climb the steep timbered rib on the LEFT, the north side, of the creek draining the col. About two hours brings you to the basin bench at roughly 6,500 ft, where there is a spring — the last reliable water.

From the bench another three-quarters of an hour or so gains the col at about 7,720 ft. Unlike its neighbour on the same pinnacle, this route wants you high, so keep going up.

The pullout is where most parties sleep. It is undeveloped and the highway is audible all night.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access ends with the highway closure
hazards: A very loose slope is crossed to gain the approach ledge, above the col trail
The route starts at the far right end of the ledge, not where you step onto it
Precariously stacked blocks and flakes on the scramble toward the neighbouring spire
Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS REACHED FROM HIGH, NOT FROM LOW, and that single sentence separates it from the other line on this pinnacle.

There are two ways onto its ledge, described from opposite directions and they meet in the same place. Either cut RIGHT off the col trail before topping out, crossing a VERY LOOSE SLOPE to gain the LEFT END of an obvious LEDGE SYSTEM; or go all the way to the col and DESCEND ABOUT THREE HUNDRED FEET along the pinnacle's flank to the same ledge. Both are quick.

THEN WALK THE LEDGE RIGHTWARD TO ITS FAR END. This is the step people skip. The ledge is third class and it goes further than you expect; the route does not start where you step onto it. Keep going until the ledge runs out.

AT THE FAR RIGHT END OF THE LEDGE, A STEEP CLEAN CORNER RISES STRAIGHT OFF IT. That corner is the route. It is a big obvious corner system on the right side of the pinnacle's main face, and the climbing in it is continuous, clean and steep — the physical test is that the rock quality is conspicuously better than the loose slope you crossed to get there.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB. Pitch one is moderate with a chimney-behind-a-block move. Pitch two is the standout: a steep continuous corner to a TRIANGULAR ROOF, passed on finger locks. Pitch three is the hardest, off a DETACHED FLAKE into steep flaring finger and hand jams on the left wall. Pitch four is corner climbing into an offwidth section. A triangular roof on the second pitch and a detached flake on the third are the two features that settle it.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if you left the trail down at the BENCH around 6,600 ft, contoured right past a spring in a dry sandy gully, and found a CHOCKSTONE at the toe of a ridge, you are at the other route on this pinnacle — several number grades easier and a different day. A chockstone at a ridge toe is not this climb; a corner at the far right end of a ledge is.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER: the neighbouring spire's routes start from the col itself and are the usual link-up partner. Standing at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are here; you still have to lose height.

At the top, either scramble third-class ground north-east toward the neighbouring spire's north face to continue a link-up, downclimbing over precariously stacked blocks and flakes, or make two thirty-metre rappels down the gully back to the col.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path, then RIGHT at the gully fork to the Beckey Route start
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the meadow, then take the climbers' path left past the small stream up through slabs and talus toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully.

Four pitches at 5.8. The route shares its FIRST PITCH with the Beckey Route, so the approach is the standard Beckey approach to the same base.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A gully fork where left and right lead to entirely different routes
Early-season snow and rockfall in the approach gully
A 5.6 boulder problem downclimbed on the descent
Queues at the shared Beckey descent rappels on busy days
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FORK IN THE GULLY IS THE DECISION, AND THIS ROUTE TAKES THE RIGHT-HAND BRANCH. Follow the standard Beckey approach and STAY RIGHT AT THE GULLY FORK to reach the same base the Beckey Route uses. This route's first pitch IS the Beckey Route's first pitch, so if you are on Beckey's first pitch you are on route.

THE NEGATIVE TEST, AND IT COVERS THE TWO WAYS PARTIES LEAVE THIS APPROACH: STAY LEFT AT THE FORK and you are heading for Serpentine Crack and the Independence-style ledges across the west face. NEVER DROP INTO THE GULLY AT ALL, staying instead on the climbers' trail toward Concord and breaking left onto a ten-foot step, and you are on the Northwest Face approach to the larch-covered northwest plateau. Both are different routes on the same mountain from the same trailhead.

HOW YOU GET DOWN: after the scramble and short 5.6 slab to the ridge, you downclimb the ridge and a 5.6 boulder problem into a gully to the first set of rappel bolts, and two single-rope rappels reach the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. That is the same descent the Beckey Route uses, and it lands close to where you started.

approach_variants.name: Gold Creek and the Crater Creek spur to the lake, then the south-east ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From Twisp, run south on the highway to the Gold Creek loop and continue onto the Gold Creek road, which becomes forest road 4340 after several miles. Turn onto the Crater Creek spur and follow it a little under five miles to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft; a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs just under four miles and roughly two thousand two hundred feet to the lake. From the lake the route leaves the trail and follows the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft and on to the summit.

Be careful with names when planning this one: the lake and creek names in this part of the range repeat across neighbouring drainages, and there is an unrelated lake and mountain of the same name in a different part of the state entirely. Navigate by the road numbers you turned onto and the trailhead elevation you actually parked at.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the upper ridge is out of snow
hazards: no water and no tread above the lake
loose talus and boulder-hopping along the crest
flanking gullies with very poor rock that will draw a party off the ridge
a long forest road drive on a fee trailhead
several false summits between the col and the true high point
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE LEAVES THE TRAIL AT THE LAKE - THERE IS NO TREAD BEYOND IT. From the lake basin the south-east ridge rises to the north-west toward a col at about 8,000 ft. THE RIDGE IS THE ROUTE AND THE TEST IS SYMMETRY: once established you should have ground falling away on both sides of you.

IF THE GROUND CLOSES IN AND YOU ARE CLIMBING A CONFINED, EXTREMELY LOOSE CHUTE, YOU HAVE SLIPPED OFF THE CREST ONTO A FLANKING GULLY. Those gullies are the other route's ground, gained from the next drainage north, and they are notably worse rock than the crest.

AT THE COL NEAR 8,000 FT THE SUMMIT IS ALONG THE CREST, NOT DIRECTLY ABOVE. A SMALL SEPARATE PEAK STANDS WEST OF THE RIDGE SADDLE AND IS ROUTINELY MISTAKEN FOR THE TOP; the true high point is the EASTERN one and reaching it is a tedious traverse over talus and large boulders past several intervening bumps.

SO THE CONFIRMATION IS EFFORT, NOT ELEVATION: if you arrived at a summit within a few minutes of gaining the crest and did not cross bouldery bumps to get there, you are on the wrong high point and should look east along the ridge.

approach_variants.name: From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415, gaining the crest by the gully above the lake
approach_variants.notes:
The other drainage reaches the same crest. From the Libby Creek road system - a turn onto the main forest road, a left, a right onto a spur and a left onto a second spur - park at the small roadside trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft, with no toilet and no water. Trail #415 leads to the lake, past a dilapidated cabin used by some parties as a camp, with root holes and burn damage underfoot in the lower and middle miles.

This approach is shorter to the crest and pays for it with a single very loose gully, which is the crux of that side of the mountain.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the gully is free of snow
hazards: a very loose gully as the only way from the lake to the crest
rockfall onto a party strung out in a confined chute
burn damage and root holes on the lower trail
no water or facilities at the trailhead
the lower peak west of the saddle, which is easiest to mistake for the summit from this side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE LAKE THE CREST IS GAINED BY A LOOSE GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS UNPLEASANT ENOUGH THAT ITS QUALITY IS THE CONFIRMATION. Parties commonly exit it about half-way up onto the parallel rib, which holds more solid rock, and return to it higher; the rib is a refuge beside the gully rather than a separate line, so keep the gully in sight.

IF THE CHUTE YOU ARE IN IS SOLID AND ENJOYABLE, IT IS PROBABLY NOT THE ONE - several chutes rise out of this basin and the route's own is notorious.

AT THE TOP THE SADDLE IS ON THE CREST, AND THE SUMMIT IS EAST OF IT. A SMALL PEAK STANDS JUST WEST OF THE SADDLE; a summit reached in a few minutes by turning left out of the gully is that lower point, not the top.

THE TRUE HIGH POINT COSTS A TRAVERSE over talus and large boulders past intervening bumps. Arriving without that traverse means you are in the wrong place. Coming from this side the ridge is joined further west than the south-east ridge joins it, which is exactly why this mistake is easier to make on this approach than on the other one.

approach_variants.name: Libby Creek road and Trail #415 to Libby Lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the highway south-east of Twisp, turn up the Libby Creek road and follow the forest road system - a turn onto the main forest road, then a left, then a right onto a spur, then a left onto a second spur - to the small trailhead between about 4,400 and 4,430 ft. Roadside parking takes roughly ten vehicles and there is no toilet and no water.

Trail #415 climbs from there to Libby Lake. Watch for root holes and trail damage through the burned section in the lower and middle miles, which is uneven underfoot rather than hard to follow. A dilapidated cabin sits beside the trail high up and is used by some parties as a base camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, after the snow has left the gully and before it returns to it
hazards: an extremely loose gully that is the defining hazard of the route
rockfall from parties above in a confined chute
burned-out trail with root holes underfoot in the lower miles
no water or facilities at the trailhead
loose talus and large boulders on the ridge traverse
a lower summit west of the saddle that is easily mistaken for the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY ABOVE THE LAKE IS THE ROUTE AND IT IS THE WORST GROUND OF THE DAY - that is how you know you are on it. From the lake basin, the line ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge crest. Parties routinely exit the gully about half-way up onto the RIB THAT PARALLELS IT, because the rib holds more solid rock; the rib is an escape from the gully rather than an alternative to it, so if you cannot see the gully from the rib you have wandered.

IF THE GROUND YOU ARE CLIMBING IS PLEASANT, YOU ARE NOT IN THE RIGHT GULLY. Several chutes rise out of this basin; the one that is the route is the one that leads to the saddle on the crest.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS ON THE RIDGE, NOT ON THE APPROACH: A SMALL PEAK STANDS JUST WEST OF THE SADDLE, AND IT IS NOT THE SUMMIT. Once on the crest the true high point is reached by an easy scramble EASTWARD along the ridge. IF YOU TOPPED OUT OF THE GULLY AND WENT LEFT TO A SUMMIT WITHIN A FEW MINUTES, YOU ARE ON THE LOWER POINT WEST OF THE SADDLE.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE TOP IS THE WALK. The true summit is a ridge scramble away over talus and large boulders, with intervening bumps, rather than an immediate high point above the gully. Ground you can traverse in minutes is the wrong answer here.

Also note the name trap in the roads and lakes on this side of the range: the drainage this variant uses and the one the south-east ridge uses have similarly named creeks and lakes on the same forest road system, so navigate by the road numbers and the trailhead you actually parked at rather than by the name of a lake.

approach_variants.name: From the Crater Creek road and the lake basin, gaining the crest from the south-east
approach_variants.notes:
The same summit is reached from the next drainage south. From the highway, take the Gold Creek road system on to forest road 4340 and then the Crater Creek spur to the trailhead at about 4,750 ft, where a day-use fee or an interagency pass is required. The maintained trail climbs a little under four miles to the lake, and from there the route continues off-trail up the south-east ridge to a col near 8,000 ft.

This avoids the loose gully entirely at the price of more off-trail ridge travel, so it is the better option for a party unhappy with a confined chute and the worse one for a party short of time.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September
hazards: a long off-trail ridge with no tread and no water above the lake
loose talus and large boulders on the crest
flanking gullies that will pull a party off the ridge into very loose ground
a day-use fee area with a long forest road drive
intervening high points that hide the true summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START OF THE CLIMBING IS WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL ENDS AT THE LAKE AND THE RIDGE ABOVE IT BEGINS. The south-east ridge rises from the lake basin toward a col at about 8,000 ft - the ridge is the handrail and it should have ground falling away on both sides once you are established on it.

IF YOU FIND YOURSELF IN A CONFINED, VERY LOOSE CHUTE, YOU HAVE DROPPED OFF THE CREST INTO ONE OF THE GULLIES ON ITS FLANK. That is the other route's ground, approached from the other drainage, and it is not where this line goes.

AT THE COL, THE SUMMIT IS THE HIGH POINT ALONG THE CREST AND IT IS NOT THE FIRST BUMP. The ridge here carries several intervening high points, and a small peak stands west of the ridge saddle that is regularly mistaken for the top. THE TRUE SUMMIT IS THE EASTERN HIGH POINT; if you have gone west from a saddle and arrived quickly, you are on the wrong one.

The practical cross-check is talus. Reaching the true summit involves a tedious out-and-back over talus and large boulders rather than a quick step up from wherever you gained the crest.

approach_variants.name: PCT and Commonwealth Creek trail to the cairn by the tarn, then the west-slope boot path
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass West, I-90 exit 52. Follow the rerouted PCT north roughly 2 to 2.5 miles of well-graded trail through old growth. At the signed junction, turn LEFT (west) onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, and follow it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek, the one reliable water on the approach — fill up there, because the scramble slopes above are dry.

An older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin trail leaves about 20 yards up from the parking lot and switchbacks directly into the basin, rejoining near the same split. It is shorter, harder to follow, and not recommended in poor visibility.

About 12.9 km round trip and 2,900 ft.
approach_variants.season: July to October. Snow lingers in Commonwealth Basin and on the upper slope into early-to-mid July, and the fractured rock is genuinely unsafe wet, so late July to September is the sweet spot
hazards: Rockfall on loose, heavily fractured red rock, with documented close calls near the summit
Slick, dangerous rock when wet — an easy class 2 slope becomes unsafe in rain
Route-finding above the basin tarn where maintained trail becomes a cairned boot path
Lingering snow and postholing into early summer
Cliffed-out class 3-4 ground if a party tries to shortcut east toward the Kendall Katwalk
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TAKEOFF IS MARKED BY A CAIRN PLANTED IN THE MIDDLE OF THE PATH, AND THAT IS THE ARRIVAL TEST. As the trail levels out near a small tarn below Red Mountain's west slope, a cairn sits in the middle of the tread. That is where the scramble leaves the maintained trail. A cairn off to one side is not it; this one is in the way, deliberately.

FROM THE CAIRN, WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO: a boot path climbs the west slope. It is intermittent and easy to lose on scree. THE RULE WHEN YOU LOSE IT IS TO STAY CLOSE TO THE RIDGE CREST ON CLIMBERS' RIGHT — the south side. That single rule replaces route-finding for the whole upper slope, and it also keeps you off the loose gut of the scree where you would be kicking rock onto people.

WHAT THE LAST 900 FT SHOULD FEEL LIKE: a 30 to 40 degree slope of fractured, iron-stained RED rock, loose scree, heather and scattered alpine trees, alternating class 2 and low class 3, with no real exposure. Hands needed intermittently. If you are on genuinely exposed ground with real fall consequence, you have drifted off the line.

AND THE MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE, WHICH IS ABOUT THE DESCENT BUT BELONGS HERE: do NOT traverse east or south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Katwalk as a shortcut. That terrain becomes class 3 and 4 and cliffs out without a rope.

HONEST NOTE ON THE ROCK: helmets are for the whole party, not just a leader. Red Mountain's rock is notoriously fractured and there are documented close calls with softball- and grapefruit-sized rock near the summit.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trailhead, back down the road to the driveway
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Snow Creek trailhead on Icicle Road; the crag is a few hundred feet above the houses just downstream of the lot.

Walk back along the road about 0.1 mile to a driveway signed to the effect that hikers and climbers enter at their own risk. Follow it to a retaining wall, then take the trail rising to the RIGHT toward the crags; a sign marking the boundary onto public land appears shortly after leaving the driveway. The path continues up past smaller outcrops — about 30 minutes in total.

The lower ground is private. Start near the parking lot and traverse above the residences rather than cutting through them.
approach_variants.season: Early season — south-facing with little shade and no relief in high summer
hazards: Private land on the lower approach
South-facing, little shade, hot
A thin crux crack right off the deck on pitch one
Ledge tiers that make it easy to mistake which level you are on
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Regular Route takes the prominent DIHEDRALS running up the middle of the BIGGEST rock face on the crag, aiming straight at a large lone tree. Those are three independent things you can check from below: biggest face, obvious corner system, single conspicuous tree at the top of the line.

The first-pitch test is the thin crack right at the start — that is the crux of the whole route, and it is protected by BOLTS above the thin section. So a hard, thin opening followed by bolts confirms it; if your first pitch is easy or the corners are clean and moderate from the ground, you are on one of the upper tiers or a neighbouring route.

Everything above the first pitch is easier: clean, enjoyable dihedrals on gear from about half an inch to two inches, with small nuts and TCUs on the last pitch.

If you are at the LEFT edge of the rock rather than in the middle of the big face, you are at Careno Corners and Bale/Kramar.

There is an obvious walk-off after pitch three, though the route carries on for a fourth.

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail to the North Buttress, then traverse from Silent Running
approach_variants.notes: FR 2060 off the Mountain Loop Highway southeast of Darrington, RIGHT at the mile-5 fork, park at the Eightmile Creek trailhead, and walk the built trail for 30-40 minutes through second growth and old timber until it steps onto the talus and runs into the North Buttress slab.
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
hazards: Traversing terrain to reach the start — rope management on the leftward traverse
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Revolver's five independent pitches are reached by traversing LEFT from Silent Running — it is not a line you walk up to on the ground and start.

So the base to find first is Silent Running's: the low point of the North Buttress slab where the trail touches rock, with a single bolt about 20 feet above a right-facing dihedral. From there the traverse leftward across the north slab gains this route.

If you are looking for an obvious independent ground start on the north slab and cannot see one, that is because there is not one.

approach_variants.name: Tieton Road spring and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes: From the highway west of Naches, carry on past the Rimrock Lake dam and turn south onto the reservoir road. Drive a couple of miles down it and park in one of the pullouts a short way past a SPRING marked by a SPLIT-RAIL FENCE — the fence is the landmark, not a sign or a sign-board. Walk back to the spring and pick up the steep climbers' trail that leaves from the right-hand side of it. The trail is short but steep and gains the base directly. Rattlesnakes are documented on both the approach and at the cliff base, so watch where you put hands and feet in the scrub.
approach_variants.season: May to October — the area melts out early and stays climbable late, but it bakes in midsummer.
hazards: Loose material sits on the slopes above the cliff and comes down — helmets on from the base
Rattlesnakes documented on the approach trail and at the cliff base
A past rockfall event closed part of this area for over a month; rockfall exposure here is recurring rather than theoretical
Steep, loose climbers' trail with poor footing when dry and dusty
Loose rock increases with height on this route, and a hanging boulder field sits above the top pitches
approach_variants.baseFinding: The trail itself is the marker for this route: it climbs from the spring and TERMINATES at the base of this climb. Where the boot track stops gaining height and you are standing under rock with no path continuing upward, you are there. Confirm by looking up — the opening pitches run up a face directly below a PROMINENT ROOF, and the first four or five belay stations are BOLTED, which is unusual on this cliff and does not carry through to the upper pitches. Count them if in doubt: bolted anchors low, natural gear higher. Negative markers: if you have carried on past the end of the trail and are TRAVERSING LEFT along the foot of the cliff, you are walking toward the other documented line and will end up under a low-angle mossy slab rather than a roof; if the first thing above you is easy moss-and-face climbing to a TREE belay, you have gone too far left.

approach_variants.name: Climb East Fury first; the traverse starts on its summit
approach_variants.notes:
This route has no approach of its own in the ordinary sense. It is the connecting ridge between the two summits of Mount Fury, and the only way to arrive at its start is to have climbed East Fury, which is reached from the Ross Dam Trailhead by water taxi to Big Beaver Landing, the Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col, Luna Col and the Southeast Glacier.

Budget the East Fury ascent as a full day in its own right before this one begins, and note that the traverse is about half a kilometre of ridge, which says nothing useful about how long it takes.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, with each rappel making retreat harder
A committing position on a ridge between two of the most remote summits in the range
Loose class 2-3 talus on the descent of East Fury's east side
The whole outing sits behind a full day's climb of East Fury and a multi-day approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS ROUTE IS A SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE ONE THING ON A MOUNTAIN YOU CANNOT WALK PAST. You are at the start when you are standing on the top of East Fury with the ridge running west toward the West Peak. There is no gully to find, no bench to identify and no chance of starting the wrong line: if you are not on East Fury's summit, you have not started.

WHAT THAT MEANS IN PRACTICE, AND IT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A LANDMARK: the commitment happens at the first rappel, not at the summit. Getting off each tower on the traverse means rappelling off poor-quality anchors on chossy rock, and EACH RAPPEL DOWN MAKES RETREAT PROGRESSIVELY HARDER. The place to decide whether the weather and the hour justify the traverse is on East Fury's summit, before the first pull.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, ON THE OTHER END: once off the traverse, the way home is back over East Fury and down its east side to the saddle on loose class 2-3 talus, then down the Southeast Glacier to Luna Col. Descending anywhere off the north side of the connecting ridge drops you into Luna Cirque, 2,400 ft below the col you camped at.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Park Creek Camp, at the valley road
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE CAMP THE PARK ITSELF POINTS OVERNIGHT PARTIES TO NOW THAT FLAT CREEK IS SHUT, and that closure is the single most important planning fact for this peak. The camp at the Flat Creek trailhead, which would otherwise be the obvious base, has its access trail closed for hazard trees and has dropped out of both the park's camp list and its booking system; no reopening date has been given anywhere. Park Creek sits lower down the same road, so using it lengthens an approach that is already long — you are walking further to the trailhead each morning rather than sleeping at it. Note this is the camp on the VALLEY ROAD where the Park Creek trail leaves it, not the stock camp several miles up that trail toward the pass. The four-person cap is worth checking against your party before you plan around it.
bivy.water: Park Creek at the camp, reliable all season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, arranged by email before you travel as above. A TOTAL CAMPFIRE BAN has been in force across the entire Stehekin valley since the end of June, covering anything that produces ash including propane fire pits, with no end date announced — so the ring here is out of use regardless of what the camp table says about fires. Gas and propane STOVES are still allowed, with clearance around them and a working shut-off valve. Confirm the ban's status when you get the permit.
bivy.capacity: Two sites, each capped at four people, so this is a small-party camp only. No stock. It has a fire ring, which is not the same as permission to use it right now.

bivy.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
bivy.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It forms the southern rim of the upper Flat Creek valley — everything falling off its far side goes into the West Fork of Agnes Creek instead — and it looks across at the glaciated back of the crest that the classic traverse walks along. Accounts of that traverse do not mention it, because climbers up there are facing the other way, and no ascent account of it was found at all. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail of about four miles that gains only a few hundred feet through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. The trail ends well short of the head of the valley and the summit is beyond where it ends. Budget four days minimum for something that would be an afternoon if a road came near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window; the valley walk is snow-free long before the head of it is.
bivy.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
bivy.permit: THE AGENCY CHANGES ON THIS TRAIL, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the national forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. Checked against the boundary rather than assumed: the summit itself lies inside that wilderness. It takes a free self-issue permit filled in at the trailhead rather than a park permit, with no reservation and no fee, and a party limit of TWELVE counting people and pack animals together — larger than the park's limit down in the valley, and a rare case where walking further gets you a looser rule. Groups over twelve must split and stay a mile apart. Your park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is NO park cross-country zone for Flat Creek; that is not a gap in the record, the zone system simply does not reach here because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice otherwise: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury, and no fires.
bivy.capacity: No established camping and no site count. THERE IS NOTHING UP HERE. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.

bivy.name: Tumwater Camp, Stehekin valley road
bivy.notes: The first camp of consequence above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge, and its job on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day and the last shuttle up the valley goes in the late afternoon, so nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on day one — you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way up the old road, and sleep in flat riverside forest with no view and no alpine character at all. It has a history of high-water damage and was closed after a bad flood, though it stands in the park's current camp table; confirm it is genuinely open when you arrange the permit rather than assuming, because there are not many camps up here and losing one reshapes the whole itinerary.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River is right there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river carrying silt and everything else off the drainage.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park. THERE IS NO PERMIT DESK IN STEHEKIN — the visitor centre at the landing does not issue them and is closed. For a trip starting in the valley the permit is arranged by EMAIL with the park's wilderness office, sent early on the morning BEFORE your start date, with a short mandatory video to watch and a signed copy to print and carry. There is no cell service in Stehekin, so all of that has to happen before you get on the boat. Food lockers are provided at these valley camps and no bear canister is required.
bivy.capacity: Two sites, each taking up to six people, so six is the party ceiling. No stock. Assigned by night on the permit.

bivy.name: Shady Camp, Stehekin valley road
bivy.notes: Further up the old road than Tumwater and the only camp on this stretch that is held back from the booking system entirely, which is exactly why it is worth knowing about. A party whose permit request comes back with a hole in the middle of the itinerary can often fill it here. It is another flat forested river camp with nothing to look at, used purely for position. Note that the road above the washout is closed to BICYCLES as well as vehicles — the upper section is decommissioned or maintained as a non-motorized, non-mechanized trail, so the obvious idea of riding the old roadbed to save a day is not permitted. It is walking or stock, and that is what makes this approach as long as it is.
bivy.water: River water beside the camp, dependable through the season and needing treatment.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, arranged the same way as the rest of the valley — by email to the wilderness office the morning before you start, since nothing can be issued in Stehekin itself. Because the site is walk-up rather than reservable, it cannot be locked in months ahead; ask for it in that same email.
bivy.capacity: A single site taking up to eight people. No stock. WALK-UP ONLY — this one takes no reservations at all, which makes it the useful fallback when everything else on the road is booked out.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From Highway 530 in Darrington turn south on Madison Ave, follow it to a T, turn right on Darrington Street, which becomes Squire Creek Road, and follow it to where a washout gates it off.

Walk the old roadbed. A landslide crossing comes about five minutes in and is flagged. The original road end is about 30-40 minutes from the car. Carry on along the old trail for another 20-30 minutes.

The turn-off is a landmark, not a sign: a large dry streambed roughly 50 feet wide and full of white boulders. This is the LAST turnoff before the Squire Creek trail swings south out of the valley toward Squire Creek Pass — if the trail starts climbing away southward, you walked past it.

Drop about 200 feet down the streambed, trending left into alders, where an informal path becomes visible. Follow that upvalley for roughly 30 minutes to a ford of Squire Creek. Past a small creek channel the trail fades; keep following the underground creek bed and it opens into the basin, about two hours from the car.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford is low; the Roan Wall base commonly holds residual avalanche snow well into the climbing season
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek — difficult in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
Residual avalanche snow at the base for much of the season
Faint informal path through alder; the trail fades entirely in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
In the basin, keep following the creek bed until a thin, boulder-filled watercourse comes down directly out of the wall above you. That watercourse is obvious once it appears, and scrambling up it puts you at the base of Roan Wall — the big red slab split by a prominent corner system.

The overhung boulder called Martha's Place, which carries sport routes on its underside, sits near the base and is the bivy; if you can see it you are in the right place.

Critical: the first two pitches are approach pitches, not the route. An obvious bolted 80-foot 5.8 slab, then a low-fifth 150-foot groove, come BEFORE the climbing proper. Easy bolted slab at the bottom of a 5.11 route is correct here, not evidence you are on the wrong line. Center Stage takes the middle of the wall; the harder crux slab pitch is high (P7), not low.

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

approach_variants.name: Robinson Creek #478 to the Beauty Creek trail #579, then the tarn basin
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 west from Winthrop about fifteen miles, right onto Lost River Road, a half mile then left to stay on it, seven and a half paved miles and another mile and a quarter of gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek trailhead on the right. The trailhead sits at 2,500 to 2,600 ft. Ballard Campground is a minute or two away and is the standard car-camp.

Walk the Robinson Creek trail #478 — an easy valley walk through big timber — about two and a half miles to the Beauty Creek junction near 3,560 to 3,600 ft. Mileages for it range from two to two and eight tenths, so use the ELEVATION and the landmark rather than a mile count.

The landmark is the SECOND bridge, the one over Beauty Creek, with Beauty Creek Falls cascading beside it. The junction is thirty to a hundred feet PAST that bridge, on the uphill side, and it is unmarked. Two parties independently warn that it is far less obvious than you would expect, one describing it as covered in bushes and nearly walked past. If you get thirty feet beyond the bridge and have not seen it, stop, go back, and look up on climber's right.

Beauty Creek #579 — not #479, which is a different trail entirely — is unmaintained and does not appear on maps. It STAYS ON THE WEST AND NORTH-WEST SIDE OF THE CREEK the whole way. One party notes their topo showed it on the east side and the topo was wrong; that is a usable check. Blowdown is the recurring nuisance, typically five to nine logs.

Total for the peak is fourteen to fifteen miles with somewhere between 6,200 and 6,900 ft of gain, and four separate parties report ten to fourteen hours car to car as a single day.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep on rock. Earlier, with snow on the upper scree, is genuinely easier — the scree is the worst thing about this climb and snow removes it
hazards: An unmarked, bushy junction thirty to a hundred feet past the Beauty Creek bridge
Blowdown on an unmaintained trail that is not on maps
No water above the 6,700 ft tarn
A universally loathed scree slope with recorded party-inflicted rockfall — helmet
Fifty to sixty feet of exposed Class 3 just below the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE SECOND TRANSITION IS AN UNBRIDGED CREEK, at about 5,200 to 5,260 ft. That creek is the outflow of the tarn you are heading for. Just a few feet past it the ground opens into meadow. Turn LEFT, north-west, and go up. The boot path there is easy to miss — one climber walked past it thinking it was where a few goats had gone up the hill. About a hundred feet above the creek it turns into a well-worn track. If you cannot find it, do not hunt: several parties simply climbed north-west through the open meadow and reached the tarn anyway. NEGATIVE MARKER: if the Beauty Creek trail starts a gradual TRAVERSE below Robinson into the Beauty Creek headwaters, you have gone past the crossing. ARRIVAL is a small heart-shaped tarn in a rocky basin at about 6,700 to 6,750 ft, sitting between two spur ridges, reached in fifteen hundred feet or so of climbing in well under a mile. This is the standard high camp and it is the LAST WATER — there is none above it. Above the tarn the ridge is gained somewhere between 7,400 and 7,600 ft depending on where you take it, up a scree slope that parties universally complain about. Carry patience and a helmet; there has been a near-miss from party-inflicted rockfall here. THE FALSE SUMMIT IS POINT 8,280. It sits north-west of the tarn, it looks exactly like the top, and the real summit is another HALF MILE beyond it. The test is simple: if you top out and there is more ridge, more gendarmes and a higher point about half a mile to the north-west, you are on the 8,280 south-east peak. It can be sidehilled rather than climbed. The true crux comes just before the summit: a notch below the last false top, then about fifty to sixty feet of exposed Class 2-3 ridge. Two parties independently say the first five or six feet are the worst of it. Parties carry rock protection and do not place it. One disambiguation: Robinson PEAK, above Harts Pass, is a different mountain a mile or so down the ridge from Robinson MOUNTAIN. Harts Pass is not an approach to this climb.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.notes: As for the rest of Waterfall Basin: Squire Creek Road from Darrington to the washout gate, the old roadbed past a flagged landslide crossing, original road end at 30-40 minutes, then 20-30 minutes to a wide dry streambed full of white boulders. Down the bed about 200 feet, left into alders onto an informal path, 30 minutes upvalley, ford Squire Creek, then along the fading trail into the basin at roughly two hours.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the ford is low
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is a short sport route in the basin rather than a wall route, and the reference point is Martha's Place — the enormously overhung boulder near the base of Roan Wall which carries the basin's sport climbing on its underside.

So you are looking DOWN at a boulder, not up at a thousand-foot slab. If you have scrambled the boulder-filled watercourse and are racking a rack for a wall you are on the wrong objective; this is at the bivy.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth near milepost 96.5.

Take the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot and climb the steep hill to Logger's Ledge. Do not stop there: traverse the ledge EAST and then keep climbing a long, steep hillside above it. Reckon on roughly 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from Logger's Ledge to the rock.

This crag closes annually. Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock are seasonally closed for peregrine falcon nesting from 1 April until roughly 31 July, or until the young fledge or the Forest Service determines nesting will not occur. That is a repeating yearly pattern, not a one-off notice — plan around it.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — the crag is closed for peregrine nesting for most of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
The route cannot be reached without first leading another pitch to the mid-height ledge
Northwest aspect — cold and shaded in the morning early and late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You reach the LEFT side of Midnight Rock first, coming up and right from Logger's Ledge. Midnight is the tall face — around 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging, seamed with parallel-sided cracks — and it faces northwest, so it is in shade through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime is the neighbouring formation and is barely developed; if the wall in front of you has almost nothing on it, you have gone past Midnight.

For ROTC specifically, the crucial fact is that it does NOT start on the ground. It begins from an enormous ledge that cuts across the middle of the CENTRE part of Midnight Rock, and that ledge is reached by first climbing Stevens Pass Motel, The Sting, or Wasp.

So if you are standing on the deck scanning the wall for a splitter to start up, you are a pitch too low. From the ledge, ROTC is the dead-vertical splitter running from fingers through thin hands to perfect hands, taking gear the whole way to two inches. A line that wanders or changes angle is not it — this crack is straight and plumb.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Road about 4.25 miles from the west end of Leavenworth to the Snow Creek trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass is required.

Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill about two to two and a half miles — roughly an hour — until the wall is directly across the drainage. The trail never touches the rock, so you are watching for the wall to come abeam.

Branch right at the first easy break, scramble down to the flat ground beside Snow Creek and cross on the log. Climb boulders and talus on the far bank until a bootpath forms, gaining about 500 ft to the base.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
hazards: A sparsely bolted, dirty 5.10d slab as the very first pitch
A rope-stretching pitch over 60 m — a 70 m rope is assumed
The log crossing at high water and loose talus below the wall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
RPM is what you are standing under when the climbers' trail runs out. That is the cleanest base-finding fact on this wall: the path tops out at the highest point of the base, marked by a few small scrub trees, and the slab directly in front of you there is RPM's first pitch — a short, dirty, sparsely bolted 5.10d.

So the test is inverted from the usual one. If your first move looks HARD, you are in the right place. Parties who want to avoid that slab step about 30 ft RIGHT into the often-vegetated gully, which is Remorse at around 5.0, and scramble up to rejoin.

Pitch two is the one to confirm on: a dihedral climbed by jamming and laybacking to a three-foot roof at about 35 metres, then easier ground through a V-slot and an easy offwidth to Two Tree Ledge. That pitch is over 60 metres despite looking compact, so a 70 m rope is the working assumption.

Most parties do not climb RPM to the top — they continue up Outer Space after pitch two.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes: Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park. Snow Creek trail uphill roughly two to two and a half miles until the wall is directly opposite, then right off the trail, down to the log crossing on Snow Creek, and up boulders and talus onto the bootpath — about 500 vertical feet to the base.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall
hazards: The 5.10d bolted slab if you lead the direct start
A long pitch two, over 60 m — carry a 70 m rope
The log crossing at high water and loose talus below the wall
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Identical start to RPM, and the arrival point does the identifying for you: where the climbers' trail runs out at the wall you are at the highest part of the base, beside a few small scrub trees, with RPM's bolted 5.10d slab directly in front of you.

If you would rather not lead that slab, the standard workaround is the often-vegetated gully about 30 ft to the RIGHT, which is Remorse at around 5.0 and lets you scramble up to the same place.

The early exit is a decision made on the route rather than at the base: pitch two's crux is a three-foot roof about 35 metres up, and the escape is taken after that rather than continuing RPM's harder line. So at the base there is nothing different to find — if you are hunting for a separate, easier start on the ground, there is not one.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass and Ruth Mountain first, then down to the Ruth-Icy saddle and across to the Icy Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the Ruth Glacier route: Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead up Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then the faint climbers' path east and south past the pond, around the cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft.

The traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another 800 ft or so — about 1,600 ft in total off Ruth's summit — to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft.

From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and follow talus and boot path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper.

The re-ascent of Ruth on the way home is the sting in the tail and cannot be avoided on the standard car-to-car version.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A steep loose 'death gully' that is the natural fall line off Ruth and the wrong line
A long horizontal crevasse near the top of the Icy Glacier below the towers
A bergschrund near the west notch in some seasons
Loose rock funnelled through a single summit gully with the whole party in it
Roughly 1,600-2,000 ft of re-ascent over Ruth on the way home, at the end of a twelve-hour day
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION THAT MATTERS IS WHICH LINE YOU TAKE OFF RUTH, AND IT IS NOT THE OBVIOUS ONE. There are two ways down the 1,600 ft to the Ruth-Icy saddle: a steeper, more direct gully that parties call the death gully, and cairned heather slopes and game trails to CLIMBER'S LEFT holding second and third class ground. Take the HEATHER, on the left. The direct gully is the one you will drift into if you simply point downhill, which is what makes this worth stating rather than assuming.

ARRIVAL AT THE SADDLE: it is the LOW POINT between the two peaks, around 5,700-5,800 ft, and there are trees in it. Trees are the confirmation — you have dropped below the alpine on both sides. If you are still on open snow or talus with nothing growing, you have not reached the saddle.

THE NOTCH WEST OF THE NORTHWEST SPIRE IS THE BASE OF THE CLIMBING, at about 6,500 ft. From the saddle, cross the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier and aim for a notch or saddle just WEST of Icy's Northwest Spire. Watch for a long horizontal crevasse near the top of the glacier below the Icy towers, and for a bergschrund near the notch in some seasons.

THE SUMMIT GULLY IS THE FINAL TEST AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS. From the notch, about 500 ft of second and third class up an obvious LEFT-HAND, LIGHT-COLOURED gully system reaches the base of the summit block. The climbing is a single 100 ft fourth-class gully with solid jugs and ledges, real exposure, and rappel slings around a horn at its top. Take the FIRST PROMINENT GULLY. Sling anchors at the top of a 100 ft gully are the arrival marker; if there is nothing at the top and the gully keeps going, you are in the wrong one.

AND THE ONE THAT CATCHES PEOPLE AT THE VERY END: the true high point is the SOUTHEAST point, about 11 ft higher than the peak most maps label as the top. The register is on the northwest summit. Decide before you leave the notch which one you are going to.

bivy.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
bivy.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
bivy.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 and the climbers' path past the pond to the toe of the Ruth Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
