READ THE NAME CAREFULLY. This route is filed under a name that encodes the direction you WALK, not the side you climb: the line goes over Hannegan Pass and up the NORTH-side Ruth Glacier. Its aspect is N. A party expecting south-facing slopes will be looking for the wrong mountain-side all day.

From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of FR-32, about 5.3 miles off SR-542, follow Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley. The first 2-2.5 miles climb gently through old growth with Ruth Creek alongside and views north to Mount Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge. Around mile 3, Hannegan Camp is a designated backcountry camp and the last reliably running water on the standard line; above it the trail switchbacks through meadows to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, about mile 4 and roughly 2,000 ft of gain.

At the pass, leave the maintained trail for a climbers' path heading east then south. Most parties camp on the far side of the notch northwest of Ruth's summit, on snow, to keep impact down.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: A faint climbers' path at Hannegan Pass that parties routinely lose in flat light
A glacier that looks like a snow walk and has produced a crevasse fall
No reliable running water above Hannegan Camp in a typical snow year
Route-finding around a cliff band on a shoulder with no cairns
A long valley walk out after a summit day, commonly finished tired
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE POND IS THE SINGLE HARDEST THING TO FIND AND THE ROUTE TURNS ON IT. At Hannegan Pass you leave maintained tread for a faint climbers' path that goes east then south, staying on the SOUTH SIDE OF A SMALL POND. The tread here is faint and partly hidden in trees, and this is the easiest place on the entire route to lose the line — flat light and early morning are when it happens. Find the pond, put it on your left, keep going south.

SECOND MARKER, AND IT IS TACTILE: after the pond the path goes up and LEFT AROUND THE BASE OF A CLIFF BAND onto a shoulder. A cliff band you have to walk around is a physical thing you cannot miss in cloud. If you are climbing straight up into rock, you have not gone far enough left.

ARRIVAL: from the shoulder, traverse SOUTH across heather and talus to gain the broad ridge feeding the toe of the Ruth Glacier's north slope at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. That is where you rope up, and it is the base of the climb. The transition is obvious underfoot — heather and talus give way to permanent snow.

TREAT IT AS A GLACIER FROM THE FIRST STEP, AND THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING ON THIS ROUTE. The lower Ruth is a moderate, welcoming-looking snow slope and it looks like a walk. It has produced at least one documented crevasse fall in years with thin or soft cover. The pleasant appearance is exactly the hazard.

WHAT TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up and climber's-left brings you to the broad notch just northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft. That is the camp and the start of the traverse toward Icy Peak, not the base of this route.

bivy.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

bivy.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
bivy.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
bivy.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge, then far right
approach_variants.notes: Large dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout — it climbs east across the formation onto Logger's Ledge in ten to fifteen minutes. Then walk the ledge to its far right end.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Very polished granite on the first pitch
Full southwest sun
Sandbagged for the grade because of the polish
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Saber begins from the FAR RIGHT end of Logger's Ledge, and the feature that names the spot is a large, low ROOF. The route starts on a left-angling ramp immediately to the RIGHT of that roof.

Follow the ramp up until it reaches the base of a left-facing dihedral. That dihedral is the confirmation — and the rock in it is conspicuously polished, which is itself a marker that you are on the right, heavily-travelled line.

The useful cross-check is Canary, which starts about 100 ft to the LEFT of Saber and also on the right-hand portion of the ledge. If you have walked past a start roughly a hundred feet before this one, you passed Canary and are correctly placed.

Both routes finish on Saber Ledge, which is the reference point for the upper pitches. Note that Saber is a 1950 line rated anywhere from 5.4 to 5.6, and the polish makes it climb harder than either number suggests — do not treat it as a soft lead.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge, then far right
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. Trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout, east onto Logger's Ledge, ten to fifteen minutes. Walk the ledge to its far right end.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Very polished rock
Full southwest sun
Harder than the ordinary Saber line off the same start
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Same start area as Saber, at the FAR RIGHT end of Logger's Ledge. The landmark is the large low roof, with the left-angling ramp immediately to its RIGHT and a left-facing dihedral at the ramp's top; the polish on that dihedral is the giveaway.

The direct is a harder variation on the same feature rather than a separate ground start, so what you are locating is Saber, and the divergence happens on the pitch.

If you are about 100 ft further left along the ledge you are at Canary, not here.

approach_variants.name: Copper Creek roadbed, three waterfalls and the tunnel
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Dreamer approach. FR 2060 from the Mountain Loop Highway, RIGHT at the fork, past the Eightmile Creek trailhead, and on until the road quits about 1.5 miles later.

Walk the old road extension half a mile until it drops to an older mining road, cross a side fork of Copper Creek, bear slightly left, follow the main fork to three waterfalls, and then take the sharp RIGHT into the brushy rocky tunnel. Do not keep going up beside the waterfalls, and do not trust flagging you find near them. Through the tunnel a small gully leads up and right into the maples and opens into a larger gritty gully that runs to the base.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
hazards: Missing the tunnel at the waterfalls
Non-climber flagging near the waterfalls
Creek crossings on Copper Creek
Runout slab climbing from the first pitch onward
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Arrive at the staging area a few hundred feet below the steeper rock — recognisable only by a handful of small cedars standing upright where the vegetation above is bushier.

Safe Sex shares this staging with Dreamer: scramble up and rightward, then continue past the dihedral to the right and up the apron beneath the buttress proper. Parties record easy, enjoyable scrambling to reach the first real pitch, followed by a 5.7 slab pitch with spaced protection — so a long scrambly warm-up before the rope comes out is CORRECT.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, into town, Avenue A west 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the road runs beside the railway. Cross the tracks, bear left to the trail, take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Sagittarius sits just LEFT of Japanese Gardens, which itself starts about midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla.

The useful cluster to hold in your head: from left to right you have Numbah Ten — the bolted dihedral — then Iron Horse and Sagittarius, which share an anchor, then Japanese Gardens.

So if the feature in front of you is a bolted dihedral you are one or two lines too far left; if it is a short left-facing dihedral at about 5.10a you have stepped right onto Japanese Gardens.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
approach_variants.notes: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead near 3,880-3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water. Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. That junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it. From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail WEST and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day. This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
approach_variants.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall throughout the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge
Cliff bands below the south-west face that have caught descending parties in icy or snow-covered conditions
A narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest that has to be avoided rather than followed
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July in heavy years
Heavy blowdown and washed-out sections on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past wildfires and storm damage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE COL AND THE DIRECTION OFF IT IS WEST. From the basin camp, about 600 ft of gain on talus, scree or lingering snow reaches the EMERALD-SASKA COL at roughly 7,700 ft — a notch on the south ridge with a peak on either side. From the col, HEAD WEST toward Saska. Emerald is the other way. If you leave the col climbing east you are on the neighbouring peak's ground.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS THAT YOU DO NOT STAY ON THE CREST. The connecting ridge is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line DROPS SLIGHTLY ONTO ITS WEST FLANK to pick up an OBVIOUS SCREE-AND-ROCK GULLY, then follows a CAIRNED RISING TRAVERSE back toward the crest. West flank, gully, cairned rising traverse. A party grimly balancing along the crest itself has missed the line rather than found the hard way.

THE FINISH IS COUNTED IN FEET, NOT FEATURES: roughly 300 ft of final Class 3 on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold — nothing here is fixed and no rope is standard, although the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them.

THE DESCENT MARKER IS A WARNING WITH A DOCUMENTED CONSEQUENCE: CLIFF BANDS SIT BELOW THE SOUTH-WEST FACE. Stay well clear of them when the ground is snow-covered or icy. A winter party misjudging that descent line in icy conditions lost a ski over those cliffs. In early-to-mid season the continuous snow below the col gives a glissade or boot-ski; by August and September the same ground is loose scree and dirt that has to be walked slowly.

LOOSE ROCK IS THE THEME OF THE WHOLE CIRQUE. Helmet, and do not stack the party directly above one another, from the moment you leave the basin.

approach_variants.name: Longmire, the Nisqually suspension bridge and the Eagle Peak Trail to the saddle
approach_variants.notes:
The Eagle Peak trailhead is about 300 ft past the suspension bridge on the east side of the Nisqually River at Longmire, which is normally reachable year-round.

The maintained trail — about 7.2 miles round trip and nearly 3,000 ft of gain — climbs steeply through old-growth forest for roughly two miles to a stream crossing, continues about a mile to a meadow, then steepens over rocky ground for a final half mile to Eagle Peak Saddle at about 5,700-5,720 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

The saddle is exposed, with cliff edges that hold cornices into early summer. Everything above it is scrambling on a climbers' path.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the saddle can be corniced with lingering snow into June
hazards: Exposed terrain at the saddle with cliff edges and cornices into June — falls here are fatal
Loose holds on the class 4 rock step, which most parties should bypass
The crux step is harder to descend than to climb, with a blind foothold
Rockfall between parties on a narrow ridge
Steep meadow avalanche terrain in winter
Wet rock materially increases the scrambling difficulty
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MAINTAINED TRAIL ENDS AT THE SADDLE, AND THE SADDLE IS NOT THE SUMMIT. Eagle Peak Saddle is about 5,700 ft; the summit is 5,958 ft, roughly a quarter mile east along the ridge. The trail ending is the start of the route, not the end of it.

THE BASE OF THE TECHNICAL GROUND IS A ROCK STEP WITH LOOSE HOLDS, reached by following the path EAST from the saddle. That step is class 4 and it is harder coming down than going up.

THE MOST USEFUL FINDING HERE IS ABOUT THE BYPASS, BECAUSE MOST PARTIES WANT IT AND IT IS BEHIND THEM BY THE TIME THEY NEED IT: GO LEFT 100 TO 200 FEET INTO A SHORT CLASS 3 GULLY, climb it to a ledge, and rejoin the main line at the TOP of the rock step. SO IF YOU ARE STANDING UNDER A LOOSE CLASS 4 STEP WONDERING WHETHER IT IS HARDER THAN ADVERTISED, YOU WALKED PAST THE BYPASS ONE TO TWO HUNDRED FEET BACK ON YOUR LEFT.

THE FALSE SUMMIT IS ON YOUR LEFT AND THE RULE IS SIMPLE: STAY RIGHT. If the high ground ahead of you is off to the left, that is the false summit, not the top.

THE RIDGE IS EXPOSED ON BOTH SIDES for the whole stretch above the saddle, on uneven ground. Ground that only falls away on one side means you are still on the approach path, not on the crest.

AND ONE THING WORTH FIXING IN YOUR HEAD BEFORE YOU COMMIT, BECAUSE IT IS THE DESCENT THAT CATCHES PEOPLE: the crux step is harder downwards, with a blind foothold. Face outward, pivot right to face into the rock, then step down. Deciding that at the top of it in the rain is too late.

approach_variants.name: FR-2419 past the second Big Creek crossing, the way trail to the Shield Wall
approach_variants.notes:
From US 101 at Hoodsport take North Lake Cushman Road (SR-119) about 9 miles to the T, go right on FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left on Forest Road 2419 up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to the road-end parking the standard route also uses. Park there and continue on foot: this route's way trail leaves the old roadbed roughly 1,000 ft BEYOND the standard route's trail entrance, just past the crossing of Big Creek at about 3,100 ft, so do not take the first trail you come to.

Follow an old roadbed across Big Creek and a climbers' trail up a rock rib, gaining roughly 1,600 ft toward the bowl below the Shield Wall. A small way trail leads to the base of the large rock section of the southeast ridge at about 3,700 ft; bear RIGHT (east) around those rocks and follow the ridgeline until you are forced RIGHT (north) by prominent gendarmes. A gully then ascends up and left to a notch at the wall's LEFT corner at about 4,850 ft, where the technical climbing begins.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Generally poor rock for much of the route, with only one to five placements available on many pitches
Retreat from partway up is reported as difficult and potentially dangerous — commit only in good weather with a competent party
Loose blocks on the parapets of the upper SE ridge above the Shield Wall proper
Few opportunities to sling horns or blocks despite what older published descriptions suggest
Three rappels interleaved with climbing high on the route, on loose ground
The descent is an exposed Class 3-4 scramble at the end of thirteen pitches
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A NOTCH AT THE LEFT-HAND CORNER OF THE WALL AT ABOUT 4,850 FT, AND THE THING THAT PROVES IT BEYOND ARGUMENT IS BOLTS. This route's first pitch carries TWO FIXED BOLTS mid-pitch and a BOLTED BELAY STATION at its top. That is the only fixed hardware on the lower mountain and it is on this pitch. So: if you have climbed a rope length and there is no bolt anywhere on it, you are not on the Shield Wall — go back down and find the notch. Bolts are man-made, they do not move with the season, and you can find them by hand.

THE SEQUENCE THAT GETS YOU THERE IS THREE FORCED TURNS AND EACH IS A CHECK: (1) the base of the large rock section of the SE ridge at about 3,700 ft — bear RIGHT, east, AROUND the rocks rather than up them; (2) follow the ridgeline until PROMINENT GENDARMES FORCE YOU RIGHT (north) — you are not choosing to go right, the terrain makes you; (3) the gully then goes UP AND LEFT to the notch. Right, right, then left. If you have made only rightward moves, you have not found the gully.

WHAT WRONG LOOKS LIKE AT THE START: taking the standard route's trail entrance instead of the one a thousand feet further along the old roadbed puts you on the walk-up scramble, which is the DESCENT for this climb. That is not a disaster — it is the way down — but it will not deliver you to the Shield Wall.

WHAT CONFIRMS THE ROUTE ABOVE PITCH ONE: the Shield Wall proper is seven pitches of low fifth to 5.7, and the crux is a WELL-PROTECTED FINGER CRACK passing the second tower ON THE RIGHT. On a route where most pitches take only one to five pieces, a pitch that protects well is itself a marker. Above the wall the ridge continues through rock parapets and gendarmes with three 30 m rappels interleaved with about six more pitches of third class to 5.7 to the summit.

DESCENT NOTE THAT BEARS ON THE APPROACH: you come down Mount Washington's standard Class 3-4 scramble to the same FR-2419 trailhead area, so the two trail entrances are a thousand feet apart at the road and you will use both in one day.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

approach_variants.name: Le Conte-Sentinel col from Yang Yang Lakes
approach_variants.notes: This peak is reached from a camp on the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than from a road end. From Cascade Pass go over Cache Col to Kool-Aid Lake, take the Red Ledge beneath Art's Knoll through the cliff band, cross to Yang Yang Lakes, then climb the broad Le Conte Glacier to the notch north of the peak. The notch carries dry bivy platforms and most parties leave overnight gear there and climb on light packs.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September, and climbed in the morning — the basin snow takes crampons cleanly at dawn and goes soft by afternoon
hazards: The Le Conte Glacier is actively crevassed — rope up and carry a rescue kit
The Red Ledge is genuinely serious when banked with snow, which is common into early July
Snow in the west basin reaches 35-40 degrees near its top and softens through the day
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Le Conte-Sentinel col is the reference: a flat notch at the top of the glacier carrying dry gravel bivy platforms, the only level dry ground for a long way in any direction. From the notch the peak's west side presents one continuous basin of snow running up to a rock face, and that snow is the route. Its top is the only place on the face where a broad, walkable LEDGE cuts leftward, to the north, beneath a short cliff band. Those two features together are the proof: continuous snow steepening as it rises, and an obvious ledge running left off the top of it. If the snow you have chosen tops out against blank rock with no ledge leading off it, you are too far south in the basin. If you are on bare rock with no snow beneath you at all, you have wandered onto the east side, which degrades into rotten rock and steep snow — that is the side parties get wrong on the descent, and it is not the route.

bivy.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col
bivy.notes: The two saddles either side of Sentinel Peak, crossed one after the other on the way from the Le Conte Glacier to the South Cascade Glacier. These are the highest useful sleeping spots on this part of the crest and the direct bases for Sentinel Peak and for Lizard Mountain, which stands just east of the col that carries the route across to the far side. accounts disagree on the elevations of both saddles by several hundred feet, with Lizard quoted anywhere from the high 6,000s to the mid 7,000s, so no numbers are recorded. A camp here is a fair-weather decision and nothing else: there is no shelter, no water, and the ground on both sides is glaciated, so retreating in cloud means downclimbing snow you only saw once in daylight. Most parties cross both in a day and sleep at a lake; the ones who stop are the ones who came to climb the peaks rather than pass them.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow, or carry from the lakes below on whichever side you came from. In a late, thin season the snow at the saddles can be gone and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The camp at the south end of the high traverse, under the Dana and Chickamin glaciers. Sentinel and Old Guard are climbed from here or from the col above.
bivy.water: The lakes and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
bivy.capacity: Several sites on slabs and heather near the lakes

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

bivy.name: Le Conte Pass
bivy.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
bivy.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers
bivy.notes: SAY IT PLAINLY: THESE ARE NOT SITES, THEY ARE WHEREVER A PARTY GETS TO. Elephant Head is the southernmost peak, standing on the divide above the lakes at the south end of the crest with big cliffs dropping east into the head of the west fork of Agnes Creek, between the ice on either side. It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. The same is true of anyone caught out on the South Cascade side by weather or by a slower day than planned. The season is short and matters more here than anywhere else: July into August has the glaciers covered and the bivouac snow usable, while September brings open crevasses, bare ice and no water at all. Anyone planning a night on this ground should carry the fuel to melt snow and treat the whole thing as an unplanned shelter that happens to be foreseeable.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable after midsummer. The last certain water on this stretch is the lakes below, and everything east of the divide is snow, ice and bare rock.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek to Leroy Basin, then the couloir toward the Maude col
approach_variants.notes: From the Phelps Creek trailhead at about 3,500 ft, walk the Phelps Creek trail roughly three and a half miles to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft. It is occasionally given as two and a half miles, but three and a half is the usual figure. Immediately after the crossing, turn right onto the unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek. It gains roughly two thousand feet in about a mile and a half of steep, sometimes brushy boot tread and is the hardest sustained work of the day. It levels into the flat Leroy Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, which is the standard camp, with reliable water. Round trip for the peak is commonly given as about thirteen miles with 5,600 ft of gain, a figure two independent parties record.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; a snow gully out of the basin may want an ice axe early in the season
hazards: Uniformly loose rock and scree on the whole upper mountain — this group has a bad reputation and deserves it
Party-inflicted rockfall in the couloir out of the basin; small parties are strongly preferable
A lingering snow gully in the entry couloir early season
No shelter above the basin and no defined trail, so poor visibility makes the spires-and-ravine sequence much harder
Steep, brushy climbers' trail gaining two thousand feet out of the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the basin the terrain opens and the way up is genuinely apparent — this is one of the rare peaks in the group where the route reveals itself. Take the obvious couloir leaving the basin eastward, toward the saddle between Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude.

The sequence of touchable landmarks above that, in order: climb to the BASE OF CLIFFS at about 7,200 ft, then cut RIGHT to a BENCH at about 7,800 ft — you can reach the same bench more safely by coming at it from further south. From the bench, traverse steep scree northward staying BELOW the summit spires. Keep following the base of the spires until, near the top, you reach a DEEP NARROW RAVINE. Cross that ravine at its TOP, not lower down, and a climbers' trail from there takes you to the summit.

There is a second, more direct line out of the basin some parties use: a boulder field and a west-facing gully to the south shoulder at about 8,000 ft.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS AT THE TOP AND IT IS EXCELLENT: the true summit is the NORTHERN-most crag, which from the basin side reads as the LEFT-most hump. A climber in a whiteout climbed what looked like the highest thing, found it was not the summit, climbed the next crag north, found that was not either, and only the third was. Here is the test — the true summit crag is Class 2-3, and the two false crags to the SOUTH of it are HARDER, at Class 3. So if the crag you just climbed felt like the most difficult thing you had done all day, you are on a false summit and the real one is further north.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

wa_sheep_gap_mountain_scramble.rope_note: Mostly Class 3/4 rock and brush; one short pitch requires a rope belay going up, and the same section is rappelled off a tree anchor on descent. A 150 ft (45 m) rope covers both: 30 m is long enough to LEAD the short step but not to rappel it, since doubled through the tree anchor it reaches only about 49 ft.

approach_variants.name: Park Butte Trail and the Railroad Grade moraine to Sandy Camp, then the Easton Glacier to the crater rim
approach_variants.notes:
From the Park Butte Trailhead at the end of FR-13 near 3,360 ft, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. Within the first 0.3-0.4 mile the trail fords Sulfur Creek — braided, silty glacial melt that runs high and fast on warm afternoons, usually rock-hoppable or bridged by a seasonal plank early in the summer.

Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche terrain, crosses more meltwater streams, and switchbacks into Morovitz Meadows about two miles in. At the upper meadow bear RIGHT at the signed Scott Paul Trail #603.1 junction to stay on Park Butte, then take the NEXT RIGHT onto Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass. Straight ahead at that second fork goes to the Park Butte lookout instead — a pleasant hike and the wrong one.

Railroad Grade #603.2 climbs onto the crest of the lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a uniformly graded ridge, hence the name, with steep drops on both sides in places. Designated camps sit at 2.25-2.75 miles; High Camp is around 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp near 5,900 ft is where maintained tread ends.

There is no potable water at the trailhead. Treat from Sulfur or Rocky Creek near the start, or melt at camp.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: A braided glacial ford of Sulfur Creek that runs high on warm afternoons
Exposed drops on both sides of the Railroad Grade moraine crest, worse in wind or on frosty mornings
A crevasse field that is the technical crux of the approach and moves season to season
Baker's characteristic cloud cap and whiteouts on the south side, above the last natural handrail
Active fumaroles and acid-degraded rock at the Sherman Crater rim
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MORAINE CREST IS A HANDRAIL YOU CAN FOLLOW BLIND, AND SANDY CAMP IS WHERE IT ENDS. Railroad Grade is exactly what its name says: a narrow, uniformly graded spine with the drop on both sides. In whiteout — which is the normal condition on Baker's south side, where a cloud cap forms on otherwise clear days — you do not navigate on this stretch, you follow the spine. When the maintained tread stops at Sandy Camp near 5,900 ft, you are at the end of the handrail and the start of the route.

FROM THERE THE ROUTE IS CROSS-COUNTRY over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier. Rope up somewhere around 6,800-7,200 ft depending on conditions. The glacier heading is NORTH, angling slightly WEST toward Sherman Peak, and the standard line stays EAST — climber's right — of the glacier's major crevasse bands.

WAND IT. This is not a hedge; it is standard practice on this route precisely because the crater rim and the moraine crest offer no natural handrail above Sandy Camp and the cloud cap arrives without warning. Route-finding through the crevasse field is the technical crux of the whole approach and it shifts season to season, so your own wands going up are the only reliable line coming down.

ARRIVAL AT SHERMAN PEAK ITSELF: above roughly 9,600-9,800 ft you reach the rim of Sherman Crater, and you will smell it before you see it — active fumaroles vent sulphurous steam, and the rock near them is acid-degraded. That smell is the confirmation that you are at the crater rim and not on the Roman Wall heading for Baker's true summit, which is the other thing this glacier leads to. Stay on the established boot path here and keep gear off the degraded rock.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing up past the crater rim onto the steep sustained snow of the Roman Wall means you have left Sherman Peak below you and are climbing Mount Baker.

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake Trail, the first switchback and Mountaineer Creek
approach_variants.notes: A short technical route with a rough approach in front of it. From the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, take trail 1599 to the fork at about 4,500 ft and keep right for Stuart Lake. Carry on through the beaver meadows and leave the trail at the first switchback, where it quits the flats and starts climbing to the lake; how far past the fork that is depends on who you ask, anywhere from half a mile to a mile and a half, so navigate by the swamp and the switchback rather than by the odometer. Cross the Stuart Lake outlet on logs and work south up the Mountaineer Creek drainage with the creek on your left. The path has not been maintained in a very long time: blowdown, re-routes, slide alder, boulder fields and cairns that lead somewhere else. Follow the drainage up to a flat area around 5,800 ft in the basin between Sherpa and Argonaut, which is where nearly everyone camps. The climb above is snow or ice to about 50 degrees, taken with pickets and the odd screw on a running belay, then a scramble to the summit. Most parties reverse the couloir, which is slow and slushy work in the afternoon; the alternative is to drop the far side of the ridge and come back around the rock ribs to the low pass between Sherpa and Argonaut. Carry two tools, a small rack to three inches, and expect the descent to take longer than the climb.
approach_variants.season: Late April to June, snow-dependent
hazards: Rockfall funnelled down a scoured chute in the middle of the couloir, worse as the face warms
Snow and ice conditions that vary enormously year to year and even day to day
Runout snow averaging 45 degrees with steeper steps, where a slip is not stoppable
A thin mixed section low in the couloir when it is lean
Unmaintained approach with heavy blowdown, slide alder and boulder fields
Creek crossings on logs, considerably worse during runoff
Exposed ledges and a short low fifth-class pitch above the couloir, often in mountaineering boots
approach_variants.baseFinding: The decisive mistake on this route is made low down, at a fork in Mountaineer Creek, and by the time you can see a couloir you have already made it. Work up the drainage and take the SOUTH, climber's-left branch into the basin between Sherpa and Argonaut, camping on the flat around 5,800 ft. The other branch leads north-west to a basin near 5,400 ft under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers, which is Mount Stuart's north face, and the big obvious couloir up there tops out at a col at about 8,600 ft on Stuart's east ridge — a fine climb, on the wrong mountain. At least one party has gone up the wrong branch and had to cross a buttress to correct it, and accounts differ on whether there are two branches or three, so count carefully and ignore the cairns, which lead toward Stuart. From the correct basin the northeast face carries several gullies and no verbal description separates them cleanly. What identifies this one is the approach to it and what it opens onto. The couloir is entered after about 1,000 ft of scree, rock and gravel up an obvious avalanche path, it runs roughly 1,000 ft at an average of 45 degrees, and it usually has a scoured channel cut down its middle that rockfall follows, which is both the confirmation and the thing to stay out of. It tops out in a NOTCH on Sherpa's east ridge at about 8,000 ft, and from that notch the balanced rock is in plain view along the ridge. That is the check: notch with the balanced rock in sight, not a col with Mount Stuart rising beyond it. Above the notch, head up and right on easy third-class ledges and ramps to one short pitch of low fifth-class rock (about 5.0), then a brief scramble to the top. The true summit is the west block; the free-standing pillar across the notch beside it is about two feet lower and much harder, needing a shoulder stand and an old bolt, so you do not have to climb it.

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and Table Rock
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda / Longs Pass trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take Longs Pass Trail #1229 through open pine and sage switchbacks about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft.

Drop off the north side on the steep eroded boot path, losing 1,400-1,600 ft over about a mile to Ingalls Creek at roughly 4,800 ft. Ford the creek — a rock-hop in low water, a real wet crossing in snowmelt — and follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike junction at about 4,700 ft. That junction is the last dependable water before the alpine basin.

A climbers' boot path switchbacks up through forest and talus from there; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide between two gullies and drop into the EASTERN one, which leads toward Sherpa. Class 2 slopes above it reach Table Rock, a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and the usual high bivy.

Carry all your water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction; the upper basin is dry.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the gully system above Ingalls Creek is dry
hazards: A steep, loose descent off Longs Pass in both directions
An Ingalls Creek ford that is a genuine crossing in early-season snowmelt
Loose rockfall-prone gully and basin terrain — helmets strongly advised
A dry upper basin: no water above the Beverly-Turnpike junction
An exposed Class 3-4 crest traverse to reach the pillar
A single ageing bolt as the rappel anchor off the top
The unroped downclimb back to camp can take as long as the technical pitch itself
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A FREE-STANDING PILLAR, NOT A FACE, AND THAT IS WHY THIS ONE CANNOT BE MISTAKEN ONCE YOU ARE CLOSE. From Table Rock a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch just WEST of Sherpa's summit on the range divide, putting you on the crest EAST of the balanced rock. Follow the crest west over blocks and sandy exposed benches at Class 3-4 until you are standing at the foot of a detached granite pillar. That pillar is the route.

THE MOVE AT THE BASE IS THE PROOF: you cannot simply start climbing. Gaining the pedestal at the bottom needs a shoulder-stand off a partner, or a rope thrown or lassoed over the point of the pedestal. If you have found a start you can climb unaided, you are on the peak's ordinary ridge scrambling and not on this feature.

SECOND CONFIRMATION, AND IT IS UNUSUAL FOR THE RANGE: above the pedestal the climbing is BOLT-PROTECTED FRICTION at about 5.7 to a flat top, with a single ageing bolt up there used to rappel back down. Bolts on Sherpa are rare enough that finding them is strong positive evidence.

DIRECTION CHECK IN CLOUD: you arrive at the crest EAST of the pillar and walk WEST to it. If you are heading east along the crest you are walking toward Sherpa's true summit and away from the rock.

AND A SCOPE WARNING WORTH READING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: this is not a route up the mountain. It is the technical feature near the summit, and most parties combine it with the Class 3-4 ridge traverse to Sherpa's main summit. If your objective was the peak, the pillar is an add-on rather than the way up.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek south fork to the basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, follow the Lake Stuart / Colchuck Lake trail past the fork and leave the maintained tread near the meadow at about 4,500 ft, heading southwest and following the south fork of Mountaineer Creek upstream.

After a couple of miles a steep talus and boulder slope leads into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak. This is the standard camp for the whole north side, and the flat ground itself is the arrival cue.

The glacier has three parts and it is worth knowing them before you set off in the dark: a lower snowfield, the glacier proper, and a steeper couloir in its northwest corner. Parties rope for the short glacier section and take the rope off above it.

This is a compact two-day outing, and it is the line most parties descend after climbing the Ice Cliff Glacier — so if you meet people coming down it at midday they are probably finishing a different climb.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Jul while the glacier still carries continuous snow; it is also the standard early-season DESCENT off the north side, which is when most parties are on it
hazards: Crevasses in the middle section of the glacier and an icefall at its toe
Wet-snow avalanche and rockfall onto the glacier as the day warms
Straying right into the Ice Cliff Glacier's serac fall zone in poor visibility
A steep, unmaintained talus climb into the hanging valley with no trail
Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that move with the snowpack
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHERPA IS THE ONE WITH NO ICE ABOVE IT, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE TEST. Standing in the basin facing the mountain, the three features run in this order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the huge rock rib of the North Ridge.

So the Sherpa is the LEFTMOST — the easternmost — of the two glaciers, and it is the one with nothing hanging over it. The Ice Cliff, immediately to its right, carries an obvious hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. If there is a serac above you, you are one glacier too far right.

TOUCH TEST, and it is the one that works when you cannot see: the ground under the Ice Cliff is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of ice. The Sherpa's toe is ordinary snow over ordinary moraine. Standing on rubble made of ice is direct evidence you have drifted right.

WHERE IT TAKES YOU, as a confirmation rather than a route description: the Sherpa tops out at a notch on Mount Stuart's upper NORTH RIDGE at roughly 7,600 ft, followed by a short scramble. It does not lead to the West Ridge — that is the Stuart Glacier Couloir, on the other side of the rock rib.

And the steep part is in the glacier's NORTHWEST corner, not up its middle. If the steepest ground you can see is straight above the centre of the snowfield, look again at which feature you are under.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass, then east to the 8,000 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
The approach shares everything with the West Ridge as far as the basin: Longs Pass Trail from the Esmeralda trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft, down to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft, ford, east on the Ingalls Creek Trail to the Beverly-Turnpike junction, then off-trail up the rib and into the basin beneath Sherpa.

From the basin the two routes diverge. Instead of heading for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's LEFT — east — traversing a grassy slope and then climbing a talus and scree gully toward the notch east of the summit.

This is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge line, and picking the right gully is the main problem. There is another level of basin higher and southwest of the summit; ending up in it means you have gone the wrong way. Carry a 50m rope from the notch, since the route above uses fixed slings at several obstacles.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the north-facing approach gully holds snow into early July
hazards: Loose talus and scree in the approach gully
Route-finding: the higher basin southwest of the summit is the overshoot trap
Snow lingering in the north-facing gully into early July
Ingalls Creek ford and the long brushy off-trail section, same as the West Ridge
Fixed slings on the route and on the descent are weathered — carry replacement cord
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is a notch at roughly 8,000 ft, EAST of the true summit and about 600 vertical feet below it. Gaining the ridge crest itself happens about 100 ft ABOVE (east of) that notch, on class 2 ground — so the notch is a waypoint, and the crest is gained just past it, not in it.

From the basin the gully leading to it is the obvious one heading up toward that saddle east of the summit, and trip reports confirm that the gully that looks right from below IS the right one. The failure mode is overshooting rather than picking the wrong-looking line: parties climb too far and end up in the higher basin to the southwest of the summit.

The orientation check: at the notch the summit should be UP and to your WEST, roughly 600 ft above you. If the summit is above and east, or if you are level with the summit, you are in the wrong saddle.

Sherpa's Balanced Rock sits on the summit ridge and is visible from below — it is the West Ridge's landmark, not this route's start, but it tells you where the summit ridge runs and therefore which way to count from.

Most parties do not reverse this ridge. The accepted descent finishes near the summit, traverses to the top of the West Ridge, and uses that route's rappel line — so plan to end the day on the other side of the peak from where you started climbing.

bivy.name: Sherpa south basin camp
bivy.notes: Sitting a couple of thousand feet above the Ingalls Creek trail in the cirque south of Sherpa, this is where a party wanting a reasonable summit day on the East or West Ridge sleeps. Getting here means leaving the valley trail and grinding up open slopes and gullies with no path to speak of, so the climb from the creek is the crux of the day rather than the ridge. The payoff is that the East Ridge start is an easy morning from here instead of a pre-dawn thrash. It is also the natural base for the Northeast Couloir on Sherpa Balanced Rock, which is reached by continuing up the basin to the notch east of the balanced block. Ground is a mix of scree and low heather and level spots take some hunting; the basin is open and catches wind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams draining the basin are reliable into midsummer and thin out by September; late-season parties should fill on the way up from Ingalls Creek rather than assume
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, Alpine Lakes Wilderness, outside the Enchantment Permit Area. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, no lottery, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda. No campfires at this elevation, and pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than on the meadow.
bivy.capacity: A small number of established spots on gravel and heather benches; two parties is comfortable, three is crowded

bivy.name: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
bivy.notes: A large flat block high in the basin below Sherpa's south side, used by parties who want the East Ridge to start within minutes of waking rather than an hour and a half above camp. From here the route climbs a broad gully trending north-northeast to gain the crest east of the balanced rock, then follows blocks and sandy benches west past the block to the summit. It is exposed, windy and cold compared with the basin camp a thousand feet lower, and whether the extra height is worth carrying water up for is a real judgement call rather than an obvious yes. Anyone attempting Sherpa Balanced Rock's Northeast Couloir gets the most from this position, since the couloir tops out close by. Leave no trace of a platform; the rock is bare and the ground around it is fragile.
bivy.water: None dependable. Snow patches persist into midsummer and can be melted, but treat it as a dry bivy and carry water up from the basin below.
bivy.permit: Cle Elum Ranger District, free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, no Enchantment lottery involved. Northwest Forest Pass at Esmeralda if you came over Longs Pass. No fires, and nothing here to build one with.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat rock; this is a perch rather than a campsite, and there is nothing else level nearby

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin, then talus west-northwest to the lower notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead on Eightmile Road, follow the Stuart Lake Trail along Mountaineer Creek for roughly three and a half to four miles. Before the lakes, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path and cairns climbing talus benches on the slope west of the creek — staying a couple of hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the water — aiming for the Sherpa-Argonaut basin.

Do not follow cairns out into the boulder field: parties specifically warn that the cairned line invites you off the better path. Stay with the creek.

Around 5,800 ft the ground steepens into sustained loose talus. The usual bivy is at the top of a talus field in the basin, and from there it is another hour and a half to two hours of talus-hopping to the toe of the ridge.

A southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek exists but is a longer, less direct way to this particular route.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep once the talus is clear; the basin holds snow into early summer
hazards: Sustained loose talus above 5,800 ft, more tedious than technical but a long way
Misleading cairns that pull you off the creek into the boulder field
Blowdown on the unmaintained climbers' path
Straying onto the crest and adding unprotectable 5.6-5.8 ground
Large detached blocks making protection difficult on the upper pitches
A descent that is not a reversal of the route and is considered its trickiest part
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AIM FOR THE DOUBLE V AND CAMP JUST INSIDE THE LOWER ONE. Approaching the Sherpa-Argonaut col from the basin, the skyline reads as two V-shaped notches. The bivy sits at the top of a talus field just inside the LOWER V, and that pairing — two Vs, camp inside the lower — is the most reliable landmark on this approach because it is a skyline shape rather than a feature you have to be close to.

FROM THE BASIN, THE MOVE IS WEST-NORTHWEST AND UP A DEEP GULLY. Ascend talus west-northwest to a deep gully that runs to a NOTCH on the ridge at about 7,000 ft. That gully is the way onto the route; contour up and climber's RIGHT out of the basin to reach the base of that lower notch.

ARRIVAL: at the notch there are easy slabs that can be scrambled before you rope up. Easy slabs at a notch at roughly 7,000 ft, reached by a gully, with about 1,500 ft of ridge above you — that is the start.

WHAT GETTING IT WRONG LOOKS LIKE, and it is expensive here: the ridge is largely Class 2-4 and you want to stay JUST ON THE EAST SIDE OF THE CREST. Straying onto the crest itself at the wrong point adds unavoidable 5.6-5.8 pitches on a route that is already long. So a party that gains the ridge somewhere other than the notch will find the climbing immediately harder than advertised — that is the signal to downclimb and traverse rather than to press on.

CONFIRMATION LOW ON THE ROUTE: the first section ends with a roughly 25 m rappel from slings into a notch. If you have climbed a long way with no rappel, you are not on the ridge proper.

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and up from Ingalls Creek
approach_variants.notes:
Esmeralda Basin / Longs Pass Trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road (FS-9737), about 4,300 ft. Longs Pass Trail (FST 1391) for roughly 2.3 miles and 2,300 ft to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft.

Drop the north side, losing 1,300-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft — early season there are snow fingers here that glissade well. Ford or rock-hop the creek, join the Ingalls Creek Trail and follow it RIGHT (east) about a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at about 4,700 ft.

Leave the maintained trail there. Ascend rightward across the meadow to where the slope steepens at about 5,000 ft, cross the stream, and climb the rib staying LEFT of its crest. At around 5,800 ft traverse right, cross over the rib, and contour into the basin below Sherpa.

There is a flat table-rock shelf at about 7,400 ft that parties use as a bivy or gear-up spot. Around 6,000 ft the climbers' path enters a spot where the gully narrows; from there some parties gain a few hundred feet east to the divide separating that gully from the one leading more directly toward Sherpa, then drop grudgingly into the correct gully and take class 2 slopes up to the table rock.

Six to seven hours one way is typical. Water at Ingalls Creek and from snowmelt in the upper basin in season.
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; snow lingers on the approach benches and north-facing ground into early July
hazards: Steep loose drop off the north side of Longs Pass
Ingalls Creek ford runs high in early-season melt
Brushy bushwhack between the Ingalls Creek Trail and the open basin
Long boulder and talus field beneath Sherpa — a stamina and route-finding crux both
Picking the correct gully out of the basin: the obvious narrowing at ~6,000 ft is a decision point, not the line
Descent is rappels off mixed fixed slings, some reported as poor — carry cord
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark that settles this route is Sherpa's BALANCED ROCK — a distinctive perched block on the summit ridge, and it is visible from the basin below. Use it.
