From the basin at about 7,000 ft, climb a broad gully trending NORTH-NORTHEAST to gain the ridge crest just EAST of the balanced rock. That is the correct point on the crest. From there the line runs WESTWARD over blocks and sandy benches, passing the balanced rock, to the summit — class 3-4.

So the check in cloud is: pick the crest, find the balanced block, and make sure it is to your WEST when you arrive. If the block is behind you to the east, you gained the crest too far along and are between the balanced rock and the summit rather than below it.

The flat table-rock at about 7,400 ft is the intermediate confirmation on the way up — it is a distinct flat platform in otherwise broken ground and it sits on the correct line. Do not confuse the table rock (7,400 ft, a bivy shelf) with the balanced rock (on the summit ridge, a perched block); they are different features doing different jobs.

The descent uses a rappel line back to a notch west of the technical climbing, so know where the notch is before you go up.

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail to the North Buttress
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington take the Mountain Loop Highway southeast about 3 miles and turn right onto Forest Road 2060, the Clear Creek logging road, opposite the campground.

Drive roughly 6 miles up 2060. At about 5 miles the road forks and this is the decision that matters: bear RIGHT on the main fork for the Eightmile Creek trailhead. The LEFT fork is the Exfoliation Dome / Witch Doctor side of the same road system, several miles of driving away from anything on Three O'Clock Rock. Parking is on the left.

The trail climbs steeply through second growth, then levels into big old timber with some large cedars. After roughly 30-40 minutes it leaves the forest and starts across an old, partly overgrown talus slope. The path here is well built rather than a thrash — if you are fighting brush on the way in you are not on the Eightmile Creek trail.
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct; west-side granite slab needs several rainless days before it is worth walking in for
hazards: Talus slope crossing part-way along the trail — loose blocks under brush
Wrong fork at mile 5 on FR 2060 puts you on the Exfoliation Dome road instead
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Stay on the main trail all the way across the talus. It runs straight into the rock, and where it touches the cliff is the low point of the North Buttress slab; the trail then continues along the base.

Standing at that contact point, look for a right-facing dihedral low on the slab with a single bolt roughly 20 feet above it. That bolt is the first piece of Silent Running. This is the central line up the shield of the North Buttress.

Negative marker: partway across the talus, about 100 feet before the trail reaches rock, a climbers' path branches up and LEFT into the slide maples. That branch is the South Buttress access (Great Arch, Big Tree). If you found yourself pushing uphill through maple brush you took it — come back down and keep going straight to where the trail hits the slab.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col and the glacier, in a day
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about four miles east of Washington Pass. Drop the embankment — around 150 to 200 feet down loose ground — to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log; the logjam moves year to year, so scout, and be ready to ford in early-season high water.

On the far side pick up the well-defined climbers' path up the timbered rib on the west side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. It climbs steeply and almost without switchbacks. Treat the creek as your last reliable water.

Around 6,000 to 6,400 ft the grade eases at the bench, an open larch and heather shelf with established campsites. Above it, continue toward Burgundy Col — roughly 3,500 ft of gain from the highway to the col.

Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col: it is loose and exposed. Stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above the camp area, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col at about 7,770 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet or washed out, ford is cold and fast in early season
steep eroding brushy tread in the timber, easy to lose
loose ball-bearing rock on the final gully and traverse into the col
crevasses on the upper glacier, more open late season
the return traverse drops BELOW the elevation of Burgundy Col, so the descent includes a couple of hundred feet of reclimbing steep snow back up to the notch — parties are caught out by this
descending the loose ground below the col has taken parties three hours or more
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the FAR side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy RAMP about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.

approach_variants.name: Camp at the bench, summit the second day
approach_variants.notes:
The same line from the milepost 166 pullout, broken at the open bench at roughly 6,000 to 6,400 ft where the climbers' path first eases. There are several established sites there, usually with a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby, and it is the standard overnight for this peak.

Camping here means you cross the glacier on firm morning snow and are back over the col before the afternoon softening, which matters given the reclimb to the col on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: the direct gully to the col is the wrong line — loose and exposed
no water above the bench once the seasonal trickle dries
crevasses on the upper glacier
the reclimb back up to Burgundy Col at the end of the day
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the bench, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp — not the obvious direct gully toward the col, which is loose and exposed — and near its head traverse rightward under the cliffs on heather slabs into Burgundy Col. Then drop about 200 feet of steep snow off the east side of the col onto the Silver Star Glacier and rope up at the glacier's edge. The col has Burgundy Spire on one side and Paisano Pinnacle on the other, and a glacier behind it; if there is no glacier on the far side, it is not the col.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your LAST RELIABLE WATER until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the WEST (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing — log can be wet, mossy or washed out; ford in high water
Steep eroding brushy tread that is easy to lose in the timber
Loose microwave-sized blocks in the gully bed above the bench
Loose kitty-litter slabs on the final traverse into the col
No water between the creek and the bench
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The unmistakable break on this approach is THE BENCH, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. THAT GULLY IS THE WRONG ONE — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay LEFT and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's LEFT of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the RIGHT, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
approach_variants.notes:
The walk-in is the standard route's: Trail #768 six and a half miles to the camp at about 2,440 ft, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path, a ford to the south side near 3,700 ft, the old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber, a pass near 5,900 ft, a lake at about 5,338 ft, and a high camp on the ridge above between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft.

From camp the difference begins: continue over the col between the two glaciers at about 8,500 ft and descend onto the larger northern icefield, then traverse beneath the peak's north side to reach the foot of the face.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September for the approach; the face itself favours a firm, cold night
hazards: the same ford, avalanche-debris zone and brushy climbers' path as the standard approach
a descent onto a large crevassed icefield with the return climb still to come
a long traverse beneath a face, exposed to anything coming off it
a bergschrund at the base of the face
a shaded north aspect that holds hard ice and cold, with a committing position
an approach that reaches its base by losing height, so retreat means re-climbing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DEFINING INSTRUCTION IS THAT YOU DO NOT TURN UPHILL AT THE COL THE STANDARD ROUTE USES. From the glacier col, descend onto the big icefield and KEEP TRAVERSING EAST BENEATH THE PEAK. The base of this route is out on that ice, under the face, not at any saddle.

IF YOU HAVE CLIMBED TO A COL WITH A BERGSCHRUND ON IT AND ARE LOOKING AT AN EASY SNOWFIELD CONTOURING ROUND TO A SUNNY SIDE, YOU HAVE ARRIVED AT THE STANDARD ROUTE'S ENTRY AT ABOUT 7,640 FT AND GONE PAST YOUR OWN. Drop back onto the ice and continue east under the wall.

THE ASPECT IS THE OTHER TEST AND IT IS UNAMBIGUOUS. This face is the SHADED side. If the wall above you is in morning or afternoon sun while the icefield behind you is bright, you are round on the southern flank and looking at the wrong ground. The face should be holding shadow when the rest of the basin is not.

AND CHECK THE MOUNTAIN, NOT JUST THE FACE. This summit sits just under a mile EAST of its larger and better-known neighbour along the connecting crest, and the same icefield runs beneath both. A north face reached quickly after crossing the first col is the neighbour's; keep traversing until the summit above you is the eastern one.

Watch the bergschrund at the foot of the face, which is a separate feature from the one on the standard route's col and behaves differently through the season.

approach_variants.name: From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
approach_variants.notes: The first ascent came at the face from the other direction, from the col to the west, traversing the northern icefield across to the peak. That is the natural line for a party already high in this range on a multi-peak traverse rather than for a party walking in for this route alone; it involves no new trailhead but a great deal more glacier travel, and it should be planned as one leg of a bigger trip.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn, and only as part of a larger traverse of the range
hazards: long committed glacier travel with no camp of its own
crevasses across the whole traverse
exposure beneath a face for the length of the approach
a bergschrund at the foot of the wall
a plan that only makes sense inside a larger traverse, so a retreat is a multi-day proposition
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ARRIVING FROM THE WEST, THE ICEFIELD IS THE HIGHWAY AND THE PEAK IS PICKED OFF IT. Traverse east along the ice beneath the crest until the summit above you is the EASTERN of the two on this section of ridge - the larger, better-known peak lies just under a mile to the west, so the first big north face you pass is not yours.

THE FACE IS THE SHADED ONE. If the wall you are approaching takes direct sun while the ice around you is in shadow, you are on the wrong aspect or the wrong peak.

THE BASE IS ON THE ICE ITSELF, BENEATH THE WALL, with a bergschrund at the junction. THERE IS NO COL INVOLVED - if you have climbed to a saddle to reach your start, you have joined the standard route's entry on the far side of the crest instead.

Because this arrival involves no fixed camp of its own, fix a retreat plan before crossing beneath the face: the ground you traverse in to reach it is the ground you must reverse to leave, and it is all crevassed.

road.name: Suiattle River Road (Forest Road 26)
road.status: CLOSED to motorized vehicles at approximately milepost 4.5 due to washout damage from a December 2025 atmospheric-river flood; USFS closure order in effect from April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 (subject to change)
road.driveNote: Previously: paved then gravel FR 26 for about 20.6 miles east from Hwy 530 near Darrington to the Downey Creek Trailhead just past the Downey Creek bridge. With the current closure, climbers must walk or bike the closed road from the MP 4.5 gate, adding roughly 16 extra round-trip miles before even starting the Downey Creek Trail.
road.seasonalGate: A hard multi-year closure (not a seasonal gate) under a Forest Service order in effect April 2, 2026 through January 1, 2028 — check the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts page before planning a trip.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at about 1,450 ft on the river road, Trail #768 runs six and a half miles - easy, well graded, mostly flat forest walking with a suspension bridge crossing - to a camp at about 2,440 ft. The maintained trail ends there.

Continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first and fording to the south side around 3,700 ft; treat that as a real crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large old avalanche-debris zone, and this stretch is slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber even in good conditions. Above the debris the path climbs to a pass near 5,900 ft, then drops about five hundred feet to a lake at about 5,338 ft. Most parties push on from there onto the ridge above at roughly 6,400 to 6,900 ft for high camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the overgrown section is passable and the creek has dropped
hazards: a real creek ford at about 3,700 ft, dangerous in high water
an old avalanche-debris zone near 4,500 ft where the tread disappears into slide alder and downed timber
crevasses on both glaciers, with rope and rescue gear required
a bergschrund at the col that has needed a short rappel late in the season
very loose rock in the gully to the west ridge
a multi-day committing position with a long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE ROUTE IS ENTERED AT A COL, AND THERE ARE TWO COLS IN A ROW - GETTING THE ORDER RIGHT IS THE NAVIGATION. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the first glacier. Rope up before stepping onto the snow. Cross OVER the first col, then DESCEND the second, larger glacier to about 7,200 ft, then TRAVERSE RIGHT - eastward - across it. THE COL YOU WANT IS AT ABOUT 7,640 FT AND IT SITS BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS LARGER NEIGHBOUR TO THE WEST. A BERGSCHRUND GUARDS IT and can be hard to cross late in the season, sometimes needing a short rappel to get down onto or across it. THE SCHRUND IS THE CONFIRMATION AS MUCH AS THE OBSTACLE: a col reached without one is likely the first col, not the second. THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE COL IS WHERE YOU GO NEXT: CONTOUR ON AN EASY SNOWFIELD ROUND TO THE PEAK'S SOUTH SIDE and climb a loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge. IF YOU ARE STILL ON THE NORTH OR SHADED SIDE OF THE CREST WITH THE FACE ABOVE YOU, YOU HAVE NOT CONTOURED FAR ENOUGH ROUND. THE MOST IMPORTANT NEGATIVE MARKER IS ABOUT WHICH MOUNTAIN YOU ARE ON. THE SUMMIT LIES JUST UNDER A MILE EAST OF ITS BETTER-KNOWN NEIGHBOUR ALONG THE CONNECTING RIDGE. If you have topped out on the summit block immediately above the first col you crossed, you are on the neighbour, not on this peak. Keep going east. There is also a direct alternative from the col: an exposed class 3+ ridge taken straight from the saddle instead of the gully. Both finish on the same crest; the gully is the standard and the loose rock in it is the main hazard on the climb.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
approach_variants.notes:
The lake at about 5,338 ft is reached by dropping five hundred feet off the pass and has reliable water and good camping. The ridge above it, between roughly 6,400 and 6,900 ft, is the higher camp most parties use, with open views across to the peaks and a much shorter summit day. The trade is exposure and a further climb at the end of an already long day in.

The drop from the pass into the lake basin holds snow into midsummer, and on snow it is normally the crux navigation of the approach day.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the ridge camp is exposed to weather in a way the lake is not
hazards: a five-hundred-foot descent into the lake basin, on snow into midsummer
an exposed ridge camp
crevassed glaciers between camp and the col
a bergschrund guarding the col
no easy retreat once past the first col
approach_variants.baseFinding:
EITHER CAMP FEEDS THE SAME LINE: TRAVERSE THE UPPER BASINS NEAR 7,000 FT TO GAIN THE FIRST GLACIER, CROSS ITS COL, DESCEND THE SECOND GLACIER TO ABOUT 7,200 FT, AND TRAVERSE EAST TO THE 7,640 FT COL BETWEEN THIS PEAK AND ITS NEIGHBOUR.

COUNT THE COLS. The first is crossed and the second is the destination, with a bergschrund on it. Standing at a col with a large icefield behind you and the summit block immediately above is the FIRST col and the neighbouring peak, not this one.

FROM THE CORRECT COL, CONTOUR ROUND ON EASY SNOW TO THE PEAK'S SOUTH SIDE AND FIND THE LOOSE GULLY. A route that climbs directly out of the col on exposed class 3+ crest is the direct variant rather than the standard, so choose it deliberately rather than by accident.

If you camped at the lake, budget the extra height gain into the morning; if you camped on the ridge, budget the wind into the night.

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek washout to the west saddle
approach_variants.notes: Drive Squire Creek Road out of Darrington until the washout blocks it and park at the gate. Follow the old roadbed past the landslide crossing, watching for two cut logs on either side of the road with old logging cable visible, where a well-established boot track drops right toward the creek. Ford Squire Creek at its shallowest point, follow the climbers' track upstream across a tributary, then climb through two gullies on steep, muddy tread until the ground opens at the grassy saddle below the wall.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer into early autumn, once the Squire Creek ford has dropped; the wall itself faces south-southwest and takes direct sun only through the middle of the day
hazards: The Squire Creek ford is difficult in early season
Faint, flagged approach track through alder and streambed with several places to lose it
The bolts on the first pitch are old and hard to see against the pale stone
approach_variants.baseFinding: The grassy saddle where the climbers' path tops out is NOT the start of this route — that is where the other lines on this wall begin, and stopping there is the commonest mistake. From the saddle keep going LEFT, west, along the base of the wall for five to ten minutes to a second and smaller saddle, then scramble up grass into a minor gully. The proof is the first pitch itself: it climbs a narrow whale's back of stone, a rounded rib of clean grey-white granite standing proud between two facing corners of much more broken rock, with a line of bolts up it. Those bolts are old and hard to pick out against the pale stone, so identify the rib shape first and the hardware second. If you are on broken, cornered rock rather than a smooth rounded rib, you are in one of the flanking corners and not on the route. If the main grassy saddle is still below and to your right, you have not walked far enough west.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
bivy.permit: None
bivy.capacity: Small ledges, one party

approach_variants.name: Green Creek Cirque and the ridge from South Twin
approach_variants.notes: From the north trailhead of the Elbow Lake Trail, follow the maintained trail across the Middle Fork and up to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where the unmaintained, sparsely blue-blazed Green Creek climbers' path leaves it — it is easy to walk past. The path climbs into the Green Creek Cirque; treat the creek at the cirque mouth as the last reliable water. Loose third and fourth class scrambling out of the cirque gains the ridge crest just south of South Twin, and the route then follows the connecting ridge south. The road and the river crossing at the trailhead have both been damaged by flooding, so confirm access before driving in.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, once the cirque slabs are dry
hazards: Unbridged Middle Fork crossing at the trailhead, unfordable at high flow
Loose third and fourth class ground gaining the ridge out of the cirque
Immense exposure on the knife-edge sections of the ridge itself
approach_variants.baseFinding: Skookum sits on the ridge running SOUTH from South Twin, and the tower immediately north of it is Jaws' Tooth — a slender detached spire that reads as a tooth rather than a summit and is the single best identifier on this stretch of crest. The base of Skookum's north ridge is the notch on the far, southern side of that tooth, and it is normally reached by rappelling off the tooth rather than by walking to it; that rappel is the proof, because the crest between South Twin and Skookum does not simply go on foot. The rock is the second confirmation: the whole ridge here is reddish-orange olivine, coarse and startlingly grippy, and the ridge above the notch climbs on small positive edges with big air on both sides. If you are still down in the green, stream-fed Green Creek Cirque looking up at slabs, you have not gained the crest. If the summit in front of you is the high point of the whole range with everything else below it, that is South Twin, not Skookum.

approach_variants.name: Skyline Lake and the boulder garden
approach_variants.notes: The start is unsigned: walk to the far east end of the Stevens Pass north lot, beside the small grey utility building, and take the gravel service road on its left beneath the powerlines. A steeper, faster boot path splits off directly across from that building and skips the road switchbacks. Stay left, then bear right shortly after; a vehicle gate blocks the road about a quarter mile up. Roughly 1.2 miles of steady climbing through forest and talus reaches Skyline Lake, which is the last water — carry what you need from there.
approach_variants.season: July to October
hazards: Loose, blocky talus in the boulder garden and along the ridge crest
Faint boot path beyond the lake, easy to lose in fog or at dusk
Steep heather and talus traverse below the true summit with real runout on a slip
Known avalanche terrain on the exposed south-facing slopes in winter
Little shade and no water past the lake
approach_variants.baseFinding: Pass Skyline Lake on its SOUTH side and keep going until the ground steepens; immediately before the first rocky scrambling you run into a garden of car- to house-sized blocks. That boulder field is the marker for the start of the climb and the main route-finding wrinkle on the whole approach — angle southwest through and around it to regain forest on the far side rather than committing to a line straight up the middle, and expect it to be slow and ankle-twisting when wet or snow-covered. Beyond it, gain the gap in the crest just northwest of the lake and follow the undulating ridge west, traversing beneath a band of rocky outcrops with the ridge repeatedly regaining elevation. The decoy sits at the far end rather than the near one: the ridge tops out at a lower, rockier sub-summit that most day-hikers take for the summit and turn around on. The true high point needs a steep traverse across the SOUTH side of that outcrop and a short final climb beyond it.

bivy.name: Skyline Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
bivy.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
bivy.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
bivy.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

approach_variants.name: Up and left off the Main Wall trail
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the gravel pullout with the information kiosk on the east side of Heart Lake Road, about 0.2 miles north of the Lake Erie Grocery. Take trail 248 into the woods on the RIGHT of the gate, follow it 5-10 minutes to the T junction with trail 247, and turn right.

The Skyline Arete cliffs sit WEST of the Main Wall, and the way in is by trails that lead up and LEFT off the Main Wall trail (off 247), with some scrambling. This is a complex series of cliffs bordered by steep brush and gullies, so expect to be picking a line rather than following a built path.

Approaching from above, near the Powerline and Orange areas, involves rappels and is not recommended for this crag.
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
hazards: Steep brush and gullies between the cliffs — this is the most complex ground at Mount Erie
Scrambling on the approach trails off 247
Approaching from above requires rappels and is discouraged
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Skyline Arete starts at the FAR LEFT END of Black Lichen Slab — so the slab is the feature to identify first, and then you walk to its left-hand extremity.

The first climbing takes airy moves through the LEFT side of the prominent roof, then follows the RIGHT side of the arete above.

If you are heading through the right side of the roof, or are on a slab with no arete above it, you are on a neighbouring line. At 5.5 this is one of the easiest routes on the mountain — if the moves off the ground feel hard you are not on it.

approach_variants.name: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the forest road east of Skykomish, the Tunnel Creek trail climbs about eleven hundred and seventy feet in under a mile and a half from roughly 3,100 ft to a small lake on the crest, where it meets the long-distance crest trail. Turn south and follow that trail several miles to the pass at roughly 5,800 ft.

This is the option with the least climbing and the easiest tread. It is a little longer along the crest than the other trailhead, and the walking is straightforward the whole way, which makes it the better choice with heavy loads or a late start.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the crest trail is clear
hazards: an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass with no signage
a long enough round trip that many parties camp, so a day attempt commits to a late finish
loose rock on the tower and on the ridge approach to it
a two-pitch face that still needs a rope, a rack and a plan to get back down
no water on the ridge between the pass and the tower
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE PASS IS THE GATE AND THE CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES DIRECTLY FROM THE TOP OF IT. Do not look for it below the pass or beyond it: an unmaintained path runs SOUTH along the ridge from the pass itself. IF YOU ARE CASTING ABOUT ON THE TRAIL BELOW THE PASS FOR A JUNCTION, YOU HAVE NOT GOT HIGH ENOUGH.

THE TOWER IS A DISTINCT ROCK TOWER ON THAT CREST AND IT IS THE FIRST ONE. The face you want looks back toward the pass on the NORTH-EAST side, so from the path it presents itself as you approach rather than after you have passed it.

THE CRITICAL NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE MOUNTAIN FURTHER ALONG THE SAME RIDGE. If you have walked past the tower and are looking at a broad peak with a lake basin below it, YOU HAVE CONTINUED TO THE MOUNTAIN AND GONE PAST THE TOWER. Turn round; the tower is a slender formation and the mountain is not.

THE ROUTE CONFIRMS ITSELF ON THE SECOND PITCH: two pitches of easy fifth class, with the upper one DIAGONALLING LEFT INTO A GULLY AND FINISHING AT A LARGE BOULDER NEAR THE TOP. A line that runs straight up with no leftward gully, or that takes more than a couple of pitches, is not this face.

One more caution about names: there are several mountains called Thunder in this state and more than one formation of this sort on crest trails. The identifying combination here is a pass on the long-distance crest trail with an unmaintained path leaving its top southward, and a tower standing before the mountain on the same ridge.

approach_variants.name: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
approach_variants.notes:
The other trailhead climbs the Surprise Creek trail past the first lake at about 4,500 ft and its neighbour, then switchbacks up to the same pass. It is roughly a mile shorter to the pass than the crest-trail option and costs several hundred feet more climbing, and it is in the trees for essentially the whole way, so it gives less to look at and less warning of the weather ahead.

Both trailheads meet at the pass and nothing above it differs.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: more climbing than the other trailhead for a slightly shorter distance
forested trail the whole way, with little view of conditions ahead
an unmaintained ridge path beyond the pass
loose rock on the tower
no water on the ridge beyond the pass
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE PASS THE APPROACH IS IDENTICAL TO THE OTHER TRAILHEAD'S: AN UNMAINTAINED CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES THE TOP OF THE PASS AND RUNS SOUTH ALONG THE RIDGE.

THE TOWER IS THE FIRST DISTINCT ROCK FORMATION ON THAT CREST, AND ITS NORTH-EAST FACE LOOKS BACK TOWARD THE PASS. Because this approach arrives at the pass from below and in trees, take a moment on the pass itself to pick the tower out along the crest before starting the path - it is much harder to identify from underneath.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SAME AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS: THE MOUNTAIN LIES FURTHER ALONG THE SAME RIDGE, ABOVE A LAKE BASIN. A broad peak with lakes below it is not the tower. If you are walking under a mountainside rather than under a slender formation, you have gone too far.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB ITSELF: two pitches of easy fifth class with the second diagonalling LEFT into a gully to a large boulder near the top. If your first pitch is hard or your route runs straight up a face for several rope lengths, you are not on it.

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the LEFT near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the forest band below 4,900 ft is clear of snow
hazards: Losing the 3,500 ft climbers'-path junction and ending in the brushy washout
Firm early-morning snow on the open slopes above 5,800 ft
Crevasses on the Sloan Glacier, normally bridged but open in lean years
Rough, narrow FR 4096 access spur
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Corkscrew does not begin at the glacier — it begins after you are off it. Cross the Sloan Glacier and keep going until you are standing on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block, around 7,300 ft; that bare-rock arrival is where parties cache rope, axe and crampons, and it is the single most reliable confirmation on the route. From there a boot track runs along heather ledges for ten to fifteen minutes. Watch to your RIGHT for a gully of pale, near-white rock and take that. Two negatives to check yourself against: if you are still on snow or ice you have not reached the start, and if you have walked the heather for much more than a quarter hour with no white-rock gully on the right, you are contouring too low — climb.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
approach_variants.notes:
The start is an UNSIGNED climbers' pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk. It is not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649 — that is a different trailhead a short distance back along the road, and taking it is the common mistake.

The path runs flat and brushy through stinging nettle and then devil's club for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the river. The river must be forded or crossed on a log jam; jams are usually adequate around half a mile in but shift from year to year and are a poor bet in high water. The path then crosses river braids two or three times over the next mile before turning up Cougar Creek on a faint, intermittently cairned and flagged track through sandy streambed and forest.

Around 3,000-3,200 ft the path crosses Cougar Creek itself; lower crossings can be impassable, so hold out for the 3.2K-ish one. Steep forest switchbacks follow, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft — roughly two to two and a half hours from the car and the last reliable water before the basin. Above the falls the track leaves the trees onto scree and slabs and angles up to the 5,800 ft basin on Sloan's northeast side, where there is a small stream and the standard bivy. This line converges with the Bedal Creek approach around 5,000-5,500 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug, after the North Fork Sauk drops from snowmelt flow
hazards: Fording or log-crossing the North Fork Sauk — deep, cold and fast in early season
Log jams that move year to year and cannot be relied on
Devil's club and nettle on the lower path
Faint, easily lost tread up the Cougar Creek streambed
approach_variants.baseFinding: Same as the Bedal line: from the basin, ledges and slabs lead to the toe of the Sloan Glacier — rope and gear up there, not earlier. The climbing begins only once you are back on bare rock at the southeast edge of the summit block near 7,300 ft, and the entry is the gully of pale rock on your RIGHT, ten to fifteen minutes along the heather ledges from where you leave the ice.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, then climbed into from below
approach_variants.notes: Index turnoff from US 2, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot on the right before the railway. Cross the active tracks, bear left to the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes to the base of the wall.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
Two pitches of climbing before you reach the start — committing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This pitch does NOT start from the ground. Looking for a ground-level start is the error.

The normal way in is to climb Godzilla — the corner system immediately right of the obvious City Park crack — and then the second pitch of City Park, which deposits you at the base of this pitch.

Once there, the start is a flake in a left-facing corner: you either traverse into it or step straight onto it, place a small cam around 0.4, and make a hard move into finger locks in a right-facing corner. If you are stood on the deck at a left-facing corner you are somewhere else entirely.

approach_variants.name: North Exfo approach to lower Salami Slab
approach_variants.notes:
Salami Slabs are the west-facing slabs below the north end of Exfoliation Dome, reached from the same FS 2060 (Clear Creek / Frog Creek Road) system as the rest of the dome — south from Darrington, and the LEFT fork at about 5 miles rather than the right fork that leads to Three O'Clock Rock.

The approach to lower Salami is an unmarked climbers' path and is described by locals as neither hard nor trivial; there is no maintained trail and no signage. The useful sighting aid is that the whole slab is plainly visible from Three O'Clock Rock across the valley, so pick the feature out from over there before you commit to the walk in.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn; these are west-facing friction slabs
hazards: Unmarked, unmaintained climbers' path with no signage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Snagglepuss starts exactly where the approach path reaches lower Salami Slab — arriving at the rock and finding yourself at the start of the route is the confirmation, not a coincidence.

It takes the heart of the slab: the first three pitches link slabby corridors to get over the prominent overlap and reach Salami Ledge. If the line above you does not run at the obvious overlap you are off to one side.

Negative marker: a long clean friction slab with almost no knobs, off to the RIGHT of where the path lands, is Chehalis, not this.

approach_variants.name: Old logging grade and creek to Witch Doctor Wall (east face)
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington head south onto FS 2060 (Clear Creek / Frog Creek Road), drive about 5 miles and take the LEFT fork. Roughly half a mile after the fork, just after crossing the bridge, there is a small pullout — that is the Witch Doctor access.

From the pullout walk a few metres along the road to where an overgrown old logging grade cuts back north-east into the forest on the left. Follow that old road for about a quarter mile to a switchback at a creek.

Leave the road there, enter the forest and pick up a faint climbers' path that handrails the creek. Keep the creek beside you for about 30 minutes until the boulder field and the wall come into view. Traverse the boulder field below the north side of the dome, then follow the wall southward.

Budget two hours, and closer to three if you lose the path — losing it here is common and is why the creek handrail matters more than any flagging.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer; the wall is steep and east-facing, so it gets morning sun and dries earlier in the day than the slabs
hazards: Faint unmarked climbers' path — easy to lose, and route-finding failure is the normal way this approach goes wrong
Boulder field traverse below the north side of the dome
Creek crossing at the logging-road switchback
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are working south along the base of an east-facing wall that is unusually steep for Darrington. The base of the route sits just BEFORE a major gully, and that gully is on the left of the route as you face it.

The start itself is the obvious left-arching crack/flake. If you have walked into or past the major gully you have gone too far south; the arching flake is behind you.

Steep, non-slabby rock is CORRECT here. Witch Doctor Wall is the exception to the Darrington friction-slab character, so steepness is not evidence you are on the wrong formation.

approach_variants.name: The unsigned boot path 50 ft below the Snow Lake trailhead sign
approach_variants.notes: Park in the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road; a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the kiosk. Walk toward the signed Snow Lake trailhead but do not take that trail. About 50 ft DOWNHILL (south) of the Snow Lake sign, an unsigned boot path and old roadbed drops into a band of slide alder. That is the shared start for both Guye Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain. The path steepens at once and follows the Source Creek drainage through roots, talus and brush. At roughly a mile and 1,000 ft of gain a junction splits — the RIGHT fork goes to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge, and the Snoqualmie route continues left and straight. A third of a mile past that the path fords the creek by a 50 ft waterfall, the main water on route. A quarter mile beyond the crossing it breaks out of the trees onto the open west-facing slope below Cave Ridge and switchbacks up it for the final mile. About 3.8 miles round trip with 3,100 ft of gain, though accounts differ on where the mileage is measured from.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September for a snow-free scramble; the upper gully commonly holds snow into July. Also climbed as a winter and spring snow route by parties competent to assess avalanche danger
hazards: A steep, loose, unmaintained climbers' path — easy to kick rock onto a party below
Snow lingering in the upper gully and switchbacks into July; an axe and the skill to use it may be needed
An exposed fourth-class step to reach the true east summit
Avalanche terrain on the approach slopes in winter and spring, with ski patrol control work nearby
The descent is looser and harder to control than the ascent; the gully funnels into trees and rock lower down, which matters if you glissade
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH IS THE ROUTE HERE, SO THE FINDING IS ABOUT THREE JUNCTIONS RATHER THAN A CLIFF, AND EACH ONE HAS A PHYSICAL MARKER.

FIRST, THE START: 50 ft DOWNHILL of the Snow Lake trailhead sign, into slide alder. It is an old roadbed, not a trail, and it is easy to walk straight past. If you are on wide, well-graded tread you are on the Snow Lake trail and you are on the wrong path from the first step.

SECOND, THE FORK AT ABOUT A MILE AND 1,000 FT: right goes to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge, left and straight is Snoqualmie. Getting this wrong puts you on a different mountain, and it is the junction where parties most often go astray.

THIRD, THE WATERFALL: about a third of a mile past that fork the path fords the creek beside a roughly 50 ft waterfall. Crossing beside a waterfall is confirmation you are still on the Snoqualmie line, and it is the last reliable water.

AND THE SUMMIT ITSELF HAS A TRAP WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU GET THERE: the trail-accessible summit is not the true one. A rugged pinnacle roughly 550 horizontal feet EAST was resurveyed in 2023 as about 3 ft higher, and reaching it needs an exposed fourth-class step. A party that walks to the top and stops has stopped 3 ft short, deliberately or not.

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the signed gravel pullout on the north side of the highway near milepost 126.8 at about 1,150 ft, the maintained trail climbs steadily through old growth. Rock-hop the creek at roughly a mile - that crossing and the lake are the last easy water for several hours. At the lake, camping is prohibited, so it is a water stop only.

Leave the maintained trail on the lake's south, right-hand side and pick up the unmaintained climbers' path. It is steep and brushy from the first steps and gains roughly two thousand feet in switchbacks onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge, then follows a narrow knolly crest with loose rock and short route-finding steps. Short of Pyramid Peak itself, do not climb it: drop slightly and traverse, often on lingering snow, to the terminal moraine and meltwater tarn at the foot of the Colonial Glacier. The moraine benches are the standard first camp and the tarn is the water. An overnight in the park needs a wilderness permit picked up on the way through.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September, once the climbers' path is clear of snow and the glacier bridges are still sound
hazards: a steep brushy unmaintained climbers' path with loose rock on the ridge crest
no water between the lake and the moraine tarn
crevasses on both glaciers, with bridges softening through the afternoon
a long crossing with almost no visual reference points, and whiteout navigation as the standing problem
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the west ridge
verglas or rime on the upper rock early in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CAMP IS FOUND BY REFUSING A SUMMIT. The climbers' path leads toward Pyramid Peak and the correct move is to drop slightly BEFORE it and traverse across scree and boulders to the moraine. IF YOU HAVE SCRAMBLED TO A SUMMIT, YOU HAVE CLIMBED THE WRONG PEAK AND GONE PAST THE TRAVERSE. The arrival marker is a meltwater tarn sitting against a terminal moraine with the ice above it.

FROM CAMP THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF THREE PIECES OF GROUND AND THEY MUST COME IN ORDER. First, rope up before leaving camp and climb the Colonial Glacier south past a rock feature on its east flank, on snow up to about thirty degrees, working around the moraine lake to a broad col near 6,840 ft. A STREAM RUNS AT THAT COL - a saddle with no water on it is not the right one.

Second, from the col you DROP roughly 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped. IF YOU ARE STILL GAINING HEIGHT AFTER THE COL, YOU HAVE NOT FOUND THE CROSSING. This is the stretch with no reference points, so track your line for the return; whiteout navigation here is the standing problem of the route.

Third, leave the glacier on the peak's NORTH-WEST side near a prominent rock feature around 7,700 ft and gain the west ridge by a class 3 gully with one exposed rib crossing. That puts you three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit. IF YOU ARE STILL ON ICE WITH THE SUMMIT PYRAMID RISING STRAIGHT ABOVE YOU AND NO GULLY BESIDE IT, YOU HAVE CROSSED TOO FAR AND ARE UNDER THE FACE RATHER THAN THE RIDGE.

The finish is a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, then a short exposed traverse onto the south side and blocky scrambling. You downclimb that notch on the way out, so read it as you pass.

approach_variants.name: Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Instead of stopping at the moraine, some parties carry over the Colonial Glacier and camp at the broad col near 6,840 ft, where a stream supplies water. It costs a roped carry with overnight loads and puts the tent on an exposed saddle, and it buys a much shorter summit day: the Neve crossing begins immediately from camp rather than after a glacier climb.

The judgement is about weather rather than fitness. The col camp is committing in poor visibility, because the crossing beyond it has no landmarks; the moraine camp keeps you below the ice with an easy retreat.
approach_variants.season: Same window; only worth the extra carry once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed saddle camp with weather funnelling through it
a roped carry with overnight loads over crevassed ice
a featureless crossing that is committing in poor visibility from a high camp
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
one exposed rib crossing in the gully onto the ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL IS IDENTIFIED BY THREE THINGS AT ONCE: it is broad, it has a stream on it, and the ground beyond it DROPS onto a second, much larger glacier. A saddle that is dry, or one with nothing but rock beyond it, is not this col.

FROM CAMP THE FIRST MOVE IS DOWNHILL - 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve - and then a roped crossing on which the cleanest line runs through the centre of the crevasse field. Bridges are usually sound by midsummer and need active route-finding around open slots. MARK YOUR OUTBOUND LINE. Coming back to a col you cannot see, across ground with no features, is the part of this route that goes wrong.

LEAVE THE ICE ON THE PEAK'S NORTH-WEST SIDE around 7,700 ft, near the prominent rock feature there, and take the class 3 gully with its single exposed rib crossing onto the west ridge, three to four hundred feet below the summit. IF THERE IS NO GULLY WHERE YOU STEP OFF THE ICE, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR ACROSS.

approach_variants.name: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
approach_variants.notes:
From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.
approach_variants.season: June through September
hazards: an unsigned path leaving the roadbed that is easy to miss on the descent, especially in fog
two large washouts on the road walk, awkward in high snowmelt
no water between the road and the boggy bench near 4,800 ft
a faint ridge tread through grass and boulders that is routinely lost
crevasses and exposed blue ice on the glacier by mid to late summer
softening snow bridges on the afternoon return
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HARDEST THING TO FIND ON THIS APPROACH IS THE PATH ITSELF, AND IT IS FOUND AT A FIREPIT. Walk the closed roadbed uphill through windfall and encroaching brush, crossing two large washouts, until the road ENDS at a small clearing with an old firepit. THE CLIMBERS' PATH LEAVES ON THE LEFT NEAR THAT CLEARING, unsigned and steep from its first step. FIX THE SPOT IN YOUR MIND ON THE WAY IN - from above, in fog, it is much harder to find, and parties overshoot it on the descent.

THE SECOND DECISION IS A CAIRNED FORK NEAR 5,200 FT. A fainter fisherman's trail drops away toward a lake; STAY RIGHT AND UPHILL ON THE CLIMBERS' PATH. IF YOU ARE LOSING HEIGHT TOWARD WATER, YOU HAVE TAKEN THE FISHERMAN'S TRAIL.

EXPECT TO LOSE THE TREAD ON THE RIDGE AND NOT TO PANIC ABOUT IT. Through grass and boulders the path is faint and parties routinely lose it and pick it up again a few hundred feet higher. WHEN IN DOUBT, STAY ON THE CREST.

THE CLIMB PROPER STARTS ABOVE THE LAKE MEADOWS. Work round the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A ROCK WALL LINES THE EAST SIDE OF THAT OUTLET; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the END of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall itself. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west onto slabs and benches, past small tarns, then traverse rocky slopes to a notch and take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier.

ROPE UP BEFORE STEPPING ONTO THE SNOW, NOT PART-WAY ACROSS. IF YOU ARE TRYING TO CLIMB A ROCK WALL BESIDE THE OUTLET STREAM, YOU HAVE MISSED THE TURN AROUND ITS END.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
approach_variants.notes: The meadows by the lake are the most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites. The rock and snow benches above, around 6,200 ft, shorten summit day but are exposed and take the wind, with limited flat ground for tents. Parties splitting the approach over two days also use the boggy bench near 4,800 ft as a low camp, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher benches are wind-exposed with limited flat ground
hazards: wind-exposed benches with limited flat ground
seasonal water at the low bench that can dry to puddles
cliff bands on the buttress that must be turned rather than climbed
a crevassed stretch of glacier below the notch
timing the return before the afternoon softens the bridges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
WHICHEVER CAMP YOU USE, THE CLIMB STARTS AT THE HEAD OF THE LAKE'S OUTLET STREAM. Work counterclockwise round the lake to the outlet. A ROCK WALL RUNS ALONG THE EAST SIDE OF IT - the move is to drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the END of that wall with a single class 3 step. FORCING THE WALL DIRECTLY IS THE WRONG ANSWER AND IS HOW PARTIES GET STOPPED HERE.

Above the wall, climb the gentle granite buttress to the south-west, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto slabs and benches. Past the small tarns, traverse rocky slopes toward the notch and take the short drop into the gap onto the glacier.

THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE NOTCH, NOT THE ANGLE. You should step DOWN into a gap to reach the ice. If you have walked onto snow without dropping through a notch, you are on a different bench and should keep traversing.

Cross the glacier to the south-west aiming straight at the peak and leave the snow for rock on the LEFT, where a faint scree path picks up. Sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks finishes it from the south-east ridge or the south slope.

bivy.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
bivy.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
bivy.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Climb the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, traverse the ledge EAST, and keep climbing the long steep hillside above — roughly 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge to the rock.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock are closed annually for peregrine falcon nesting, about 1 April to 31 July, or until the young fledge.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
40-45 minutes of sustained steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep coarse granite with scarce moderates
Northwest aspect — cold mornings
approach_variants.baseFinding: You arrive at the LEFT side of Midnight Rock first, coming up and right off Logger's Ledge — that is the fixed point. Midnight is the tall one: around 300 ft of vertical to slightly overhanging coarse granite, mostly parallel-sided cracks, northwest-facing and therefore shaded through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime is the adjacent formation and holds very few routes; a nearly bare wall means you overshot. The crag-wide trap: several of Midnight's best-known lines start from an enormous ledge across the middle of the CENTRE of the wall, not from the ground, and that ledge is gained by leading Stevens Pass Motel, The Sting or Wasp first. Check whether the line you want is a ground start before concluding you cannot find it. No source consulted here documents this route's own position along the base; place it against a topo from the left end.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the southwest toe of the spire
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: wet or snow-covered granite slabs low on the climbers' path
braided path and loss of definition on the upper talus
old snow persisting in shaded gullies into early summer
queueing at rappel stations on busy weekends, since this is also the descent line for other routes
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the southwest corner — the toe where the south ridge of South Early Winters Spire runs down and ends, which is the right-hand (southernmost) of the two spires, reached before the saddle between them. The arete itself is broad and broken rather than a knife edge, and it separates the Southwest Couloir on its left from the steep East Face on its right; standing at the base you should have the couloir up to one side and steep unclimbable-looking wall to the other. The first pitch begins with a short steep crack; above it you either go right and up across a slab at 5.5 to a small tree, or left across a short friction slab at 5.5. If you are stood at the bottom of a broad snow or scree gully with nothing to climb, you have drifted into the Southwest Couloir and need to move right onto the ridge toe. If you are under steep continuous rock, you have gone too far right onto the east side.

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in the basin
approach_variants.notes:
The same line in from Blue Lake, but with the basin under snow the climbers' path through the slabs and talus is buried and you are navigating by terrain rather than by boot track. Firm morning snow makes the ascent quicker than summer talus; softening afternoon snow makes the descent slower.

SR-20 across Washington Pass is gated every winter, typically from late November or early December until mid-April to early May, so the season begins when the highway does.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through Jun
hazards: moat at the base where snow pulls off the rock
firm snow in the couloir requiring axe and possibly crampons
buried climbers' path — navigate by the couloir and ridge toe, not by cairns
SR-20 gated in winter
approach_variants.baseFinding: With snow filling the basin the Southwest Couloir is a clean white line and the arete is the rock rib on its right-hand side — that contrast actually makes the toe EASIER to identify than in summer, when couloir and ridge are both grey. Walk up the snow of the couloir's edge and step right onto the rock at the ridge toe, where the short steep crack of the first pitch starts. Expect a moat at the snow-rock junction. Take an axe: the alternative descent down the couloir holds firm snow well into summer.

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the dirt pullout on the obvious hairpin turn on SR-20, directly beneath the east faces of the two Early Winters Spires. Do not use the Blue Lake Trailhead — that is the west-side approach and it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain.

Walk up the obvious gully, which is the easy way through the first band of cliffs above the road. Above that cliff band a faint climbers' path leaves the gully on a gently rising line to the RIGHT, crossing easy slabs and vegetated dirt. Roughly three quarters of an hour out you come to some fourth-class slabs.

The classic sequence of landmarks, and the one to hold in your head: up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last big tree in the middle of the gully; from that tree traverse right across talus; that brings you under the gully that runs up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires; then traverse left to the foot of the buttress.

The whole line is visible from the road, so look up and read it before you start walking.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully, with parties above
fourth-class slabs partway up the approach — a fall there is consequential and unroped
vegetated dirt slopes that are greasy when wet
no water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: The buttress toe is the LOW POINT of the prow, sitting immediately LEFT of the gully that separates North from South Early Winters Spire — so you find it by first locating that dividing gully and then stepping left out of it, rather than by heading straight up from the talus.
