The first pitch is rambling 5.6 with moss, dirt and some loose rock; a scruffy easy pitch is the correct start here, and if your first pitch is clean and steep you are too high on the buttress or on one of the harder east-side lines. The last large tree in the centre of Spire Gully is the checkpoint before this: if you are still climbing the gully and have passed no such tree, you have not reached the traverse point yet.

approach_variants.name: Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
approach_variants.notes: Same line from the hairpin, but with snow in Spire Gully the traverse right from the last big tree is done on snow rather than talus. Crampons and an axe are worth carrying; sources on this approach say so explicitly for the early season. SR-20 is gated over Washington Pass through the winter, typically from late November or early December to mid-April or early May, so this window opens with the highway.
approach_variants.season: Highway opening through Jun
hazards: snow traverse above a runout
moat at the base of the buttress
wet-loose slides off the east faces on a sunny spring day
SR-20 gated in winter
approach_variants.baseFinding: Snow does not move the buttress toe — it is still the low point of the prow just left of the North/South Early Winters dividing gully. What it changes is the traverse: on snow the rightward traverse from the last large tree in the gully is a straightforward but exposed snow crossing rather than a talus scramble, and the transition back onto rock at the base of the buttress will likely involve a moat. Fix the dividing gully visually from the highway before you start — from inside a snowy Spire Gully in flat light the individual features all read the same.

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin
approach_variants.notes:
The east-side approach, shared with the other East Buttress lines. Park at the dirt pullout at the hairpin turn on SR-20 beneath the east faces of the Early Winters Spires — not at the Blue Lake Trailhead, which serves the west side.

Go up Spire Gully, which breaches the first cliff band above the road, following occasional cairns. Continue to the last large tree standing in the centre of the gully. From there traverse right across talus, which brings you below the gully leading up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires, then traverse back left to the foot of the buttress.

Early season the traverse is on snow rather than talus and an axe and crampons are worth having.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully
exposed traverse across talus or, early season, snow
no water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: The reference feature is the gully dividing North from South Early Winters Spire. The buttress toe is the low point of the prow immediately LEFT of that gully — locate the gully first, then step left. The last big tree in the middle of Spire Gully is the checkpoint that tells you where to leave the gully and start traversing right; reaching it is what confirms you are far enough up.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the South Arete base, then down and right about ten minutes to the fir tree and double cracks
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead, the climber's trail reaches the South Arete base in about an hour. Seven pitches at 5.11d, first climbed in October 1991.

The traverse to the start eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain, so expect to lose height rather than contour.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Two routes starting about 100 ft apart on the same traverse
Loss of height along the base to skirt steeper terrain, which has to be regained
5.11d over seven pitches with no route-specific rappel line
No water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE SOUTH ARETE BASE, HEAD DOWN AND RIGHT ALONG THE BASE OF THE WALL FOR ABOUT TEN MINUTES TO A START AT DOUBLE CRACKS BESIDE A FIR TREE. A tree at the foot of a pair of cracks is the marker, and a tree is something you can walk into in cloud.

SO THE TWO CHECKS ARE A DURATION AND A TREE: TEN MINUTES OF SCRAMBLING AND TRAVERSING FROM THE SOUTH ARETE, AND A FIR. Not thirty seconds and not half an hour.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST ITS NEIGHBOUR, AND IT IS SHORT AND COUNTABLE: THE HITCHHIKER BEGINS ROUGHLY 100 FT FURTHER ALONG THE SAME TRAVERSE, AT A SMALL LEFT-FACING DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS. IF YOU ARE STANDING AT A DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS IN IT, YOU HAVE GONE 100 FT TOO FAR.

AND IF YOU HAVE NOT LOST HEIGHT, YOU HAVE NOT ARRIVED: the traverse eventually drops away to skirt steeper terrain. Contouring level along the wall keeps you on South Arete ground.

WHERE IT ENDS: the route is not commonly rappelled top to bottom. Parties top out and use the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete, third and fourth class with one short more exposed step, to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base, and out via the climber's trail to the Blue Lake Trail.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail into the west basin (snow)
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the main trail roughly a mile and a half to the well-worn climbers' trail and take it up into the basin on the west side of the Liberty Bell group. Early in the season the trailhead lot itself may still be snowed in.

On a cold morning parties approach in boots and crampons without flotation; later in the day the same snow softens badly. Start early and plan to be off the couloir before the afternoon.

This is the quickest line to the summit of the south spire, and it exists only for a short window: it comes into condition once the highway opens and deteriorates as the snow goes. Late in the season the couloir empties out into loose rock and is not worth climbing.
approach_variants.season: A few weeks to a couple of months after SR-20 reopens — roughly May-Jun
hazards: avalanche and wet-slide hazard on a sun-affected slope, worsening through the day
snow and occasional ice to around 50 degrees in the upper narrows
late season the couloir fills with loose rock and becomes a rockfall trap — not recommended once melted out
route depends entirely on SR-20 reopening, typically mid-April to early May
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin, the couloir is the snow gully rising on the southwest side of South Early Winters Spire, immediately left of the South Arete rib as you look up. It broadens low down at a modest 25 to 30 degrees, and the identifying feature is the FORK higher up where the gully splits — the right-hand branch is the route, and it steepens to 40 to 50 degrees and narrows above the split. If you are in a gully that never forks, you are in the wrong drainage. Because the whole thing is a snow feature there is no rock start to find; the transition is simply from basin snow into the gully bed, so the navigational work is choosing the correct gully from the basin, in daylight, before the ground steepens.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Creek rib to Burgundy Col
approach_variants.notes: From the unsigned roadside pullout, find the faint boot path dropping east through loose talus into the trees past a trail register, then cross Early Winters Creek on a log. The path climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply, to a basin bench around 6,400 to 6,500 ft where there is good camping and a late-season spring, then continues up scree and snow to Burgundy Col.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn. This face takes sun through the day, so it comes into condition earlier and holds later than the shaded sides of the group
hazards: Loose talus and scree on the climb to the col
Early Winters Creek log crossing can be awkward at high flow
Nothing on the approach is signed or marked
approach_variants.baseFinding: Burgundy Col is the reference and the tower's position at the col is the test. Coming up the timbered rib and scree from Burgundy Creek, Vasiliki Tower is the formation standing on your LEFT as you arrive at the col; the Wine Spires proper are the group on the right, and the crest running away beyond the tower on the left is Vasiliki Ridge. The route starts from the col itself: scramble up broken ground to a system of dihedrals that trend RIGHTWARDS across the face above you. Those right-trending corners are the proof — the ordinary line simply follows them, and the harder direct variation on this face is the one that steps left out of them onto cracks. If the corners above you lean the other way, or the wall you are under is in shade for most of the day, you are on the wrong side of the tower: this is the sunny side, which is why it is climbed early and late in the season.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
approach_variants.notes:
The drive is the easy part — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft. The walk is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state.

Trail #504 climbs the drainage for roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, crossing an old burn for much of that: hot, rocky, buggy, and no shade. From the pass the trail drops into the next drainage before the Cathedral Lakes side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft, below the peak's south-west side.

Treat this as a two-to-four day backpack with a summit push from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass. There is no cell coverage anywhere on this trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Three separate routes share this face and the lower ground accepts almost any line
The tower in front of the wall carries its own routes under a colliding name
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above on a wall this size
Walk-off descent to the west whose crux is a no-fall step across a gap
No cell coverage and a multi-day walk out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and then climb scree and talus to the foot of the main wall. Thirty to sixty minutes.

FIRST, RULE OUT THE TOWER. A semi-detached tower leans against the lower right side of the wall, and a deep gully separates it from the mountain. If that tower is between you and the rock, you are under the buttress route, which climbs the ridge behind it. This route is on the OPEN WALL, and specifically on its CENTRE. Nothing should be standing in front of you.

Start low and central, near the bottom of the wall rather than off to one side. The line then confirms itself by a run of features in a fixed order, and this is the identification that actually works, because the lower face accepts many lines:

Low down there is a boxed-in feature the first ascent called a confession box. At mid-height there is a SPECTACULAR CURVING CHIMNEY — this is the single best confirmation on the route and it is visible from the ground if you look for it. High up you cross a pulpit ledge and then a belfry ledge before easier ground runs to the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it matters because the two lines converge: if instead of a curving chimney you find yourself pushed rightward along a long ramp toward a steep thin crack in a headwall, you have drifted onto the harder line that takes the right-hand third of the face. That one is several number grades above this and it takes very thin protection. Come back left and look for the chimney.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER: the tower in front of the wall has its own small south face carrying several short routes. Beta written about the tower will also be headed South Face. The tower's routes are two to five pitches; this wall is about a thousand feet.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach_variants.notes:
The high trailhead above Loomis, reached by Toats Coulee Road and the forest roads beyond it, sits at about 5,570 ft. This is a trail and not a four-wheel-drive road, whatever you may have read; the high-clearance warning in circulation belongs to a different spur.

The trail drops from the trailhead to meet the valley trail lower down, then follows the valley up to the Cathedral Lakes basin. It is the shortest walk and the least total climbing of the ways in.

Both ends carry a penalty. The drive is about two hours longer than from Winthrop, and because the trailhead is high and the trail loses height to reach the valley, the trip finishes with roughly 1,300 ft of climbing on the way out.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: 1,300 ft of climbing at the very end of the trip on the way out
A trailhead published under several different names
The wall foreshortens badly from directly below, so the mid-height chimney is hard to relocate at the base
Same walk-off descent with a no-fall gap crossing near the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is the same and reached the same way from camp. What changes is where you first see the wall, and on a face this size that is worth more than any description.

Coming up the valley you enter the basin from below rather than over the pass, so the whole south side stands up in front of you at once. Stop at the lake and sort out three things before walking up: the small detached TOWER at the lower right of the wall; the deep GULLY between that tower and the mountain; and the OPEN CENTRE of the wall to the left of both. This route is the open centre.

While you are looking, find the CURVING CHIMNEY at mid-height in that centre panel. It is the feature that proves the line and it is far easier to pick out from across the water than from underneath, where the wall foreshortens and everything reads as featured granite. Fix it against the skyline above it so you can re-find it at the base.

NEGATIVE MARKER from the lake: if the panel you are looking at has a long ramp cutting rightward across it toward a steep headwall crack, that is the right-hand line, not this one. And if the wall you are looking at is only a few pitches tall and stands clear of the mountain, you are looking at the tower.

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: FREE self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at the Andrews Creek trailhead. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or a day fee to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

bivy.name: Andrews Pass
bivy.notes: The natural first-night stop if you leave the trailhead in the afternoon, roughly twelve miles up the drainage and about the halfway mark to the Cathedral basin. Everything below here is BURN — the lower Andrews Creek drainage has been through repeated fire and the trail was closed for years after it, so expect open, hot walking with little shade and standing dead timber that comes down in wind. Blowdown volume in the burn varies a lot year to year and is worth asking the Methow Valley district about before committing to a schedule. Breaking the walk here rather than pushing to the lakes makes a big difference to how the second day goes.
bivy.water: Streams on both sides of the pass, and the trail below it runs genuinely boggy in places early in the season. This is the last stretch of the approach where water is easy; reliability drops off through August and September.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Andrews Creek.
bivy.capacity: A pleasant site just off the trail at the pass plus dispersed spots on the bluff to the east; several parties can spread out without stacking up

bivy.name: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
bivy.notes: Useful mainly as a high, quick bivy if you arrive late or want to be moving before dawn, since it saves the drop into the lake basin and puts you already at the crest. The ground is rock and thin turf, so pick a slab and leave the vegetation alone. Wind is the real cost — the pass funnels it and there is nothing to hide behind. Most parties are better off dropping to the lake and accepting the extra few hundred feet of regain.
bivy.water: A small tarn and lingering snowmelt only, and both are unreliable. By late summer the pass area can be dry and the trail east toward Tungsten is reported dry for its whole length, so treat this as a place you carry water TO, not one you collect at.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue trailhead permit; no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on flat rock; there is no established site and no shelter from wind

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike and Fourth Creek Pass to an Ingalls Creek camp, then straight up the south side
approach_variants.notes:
From the Beverly Turnpike trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112 off the North Fork Teanaway Road, at about 0.5 mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391. Taking the Bean Creek fork here is a commonly reported mistake, so read the sign.

At about 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1, the Fourth Creek Trail; at about 3.6 miles you crest Fourth Creek Pass with the first open views of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to roughly 6 miles and 4,200 ft, ford Ingalls Creek, and camp at the Fourth Creek confluence. Day one is about 6 miles and 2,000 ft.

From camp, follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west about half a mile, then cut sharply left and north and climb straight upslope. Expect roughly 300 vertical feet of tangled forest and then close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above that — progress can drop to a few hundred feet an hour.

At about 5,200 ft the brush relents. Climb the LEFT side of a large drainage gully to about 6,600 ft, then the gully itself.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The brush is the reason: it is impassably wet in early season and the gully may hold snow in the shoulders
hazards: Close to 1,000 ft of dense slide alder above 300 ft of jackstraw forest — the defining feature of the day
An Ingalls Creek ford that can be cold and swift early, and ice-covered in the shoulders
Loose blocks low on the route
Possible snow in the gully in the shoulder seasons — carry axe and crampons if in doubt
The descent rappels a chockstone gully where ropes are reported to hang up on the chockstone
A heavily worn sling anchor above that chockstone: inspect and back it up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO TESTS, ONE AT THE GULLY FORK AND ONE AT THE WALL, AND YOU NEED BOTH.

FIRST, THE FORK AT ABOUT 7,100 FT. The gully you have been climbing splits. The standard line is the LEFT branch. The right branch also reaches the mountain but is far less travelled, so a party that drifts right will find progressively less sign of passage — that absence is the signal to come back down and cross over.

SECOND, THE WALL ITSELF, and this is the one that matters in fog because the gully fork can be ambiguous under snow. At the base of the south face there are TWO SHORT LEFT-FACING CORNERS side by side. The route starts in the RIGHTMOST AND LARGER of the two. Not a corner — two corners, and you take the bigger, right-hand one. If there is only one corner in front of you, you are not at the start.

WHAT THE CLIMBING SHOULD FEEL LIKE, as a check on all of the above: blocky, generally solid rock, three pitches, graded 5.6 — but an old-school 5.6 that parties consistently report climbing like modern 5.9 or harder. So sustained-feeling climbing is NOT evidence you are off route here. Watch for a few loose blocks low down.

A SEPARATE FEATURE WORTH NOT CONFUSING WITH THE START: high on the mountain there is a 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top, Class 4, taken by stepping right at the overhang, which tops out on the east ridge a short way from the summit. That is the finish of the ordinary scramble line, and the approach description on this route describes it as though it were the route. It is not the base of the 5.6 face climb, and a party navigating to it will end up on the scramble.

bivy.name: Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence camp
Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

approach_variants.name: Burgundy Col, then the loose fourth-class traverse round the east side below Chianti to the Pernod-Chablis notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166, the climbers' trail drops off the highway, crosses Early Winters Creek almost immediately at around 4,080 ft via logs, and climbs steeply, gaining nearly 2,400 ft, to the bench camp at roughly 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard staging area for all the Wine Spires. From there the trail works up scree gullies to Burgundy Col at 7,770 ft.

Two pitches at 5.9 A0, Grade II. Carry a rope for the final approach moves and expect loose rock underfoot the whole way in.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose fourth-class traverse around the east side of the ridge below Chianti
A two-piton summit anchor equalized with cord, and a mix of one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger on the short summit aid block
A single 60 m rope can leave a party several metres short of the notch on the descent
Rope-eating cracks a few feet below a slung-horn rap station; build that anchor as high as practical
Loose rock underfoot for the whole approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE NOTCH BETWEEN PERNOD AND CHABLIS, AND THERE ARE TWO WAYS TO IT THAT ARRIVE FROM OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. Both are worth knowing before you leave camp, because the choice is made at the col and not at the base.

OPTION ONE, FROM BURGUNDY COL: rather than dropping straight to Pernod's south side, most parties continue traversing and scrambling around the EAST, Silver Star Creek, side of the ridge BELOW CHIANTI, aiming for the Pernod-Chablis notch. Expect LOOSE FOURTH-CLASS TERRAIN on this stretch, which is itself the confirmation: if the ground you are on is walkable, you have not started the traverse.

OPTION TWO, AND IT IS THE COMMON ONE BECAUSE THE ROUTE IS SHORT: climb CHABLIS SPIRE'S EAST FACE first, then downclimb or make a short rappel across loose rock to reach the base of Pernod's south face. That approach arrives from above rather than along.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS ABOUT WHICH SPIRE IS ABOVE YOU: this route sits TUCKED BETWEEN PERNOD'S BIGGER WEST FACE AND CHABLIS. If the wall above you is the tallest in the group, you are under Pernod's west face and on the Direct West Face ground, not here. That route is reached from the BENCH, not from the col.

AND THE NOTCH IS A NAMED GAP BETWEEN TWO NAMED SPIRES, which is the most reliable kind of feature in this basin: Pernod on one side, Chablis on the other.

DESCENT IS BY RAPPEL AND IT LINKS BACK ONTO CHABLIS: rappel the south face to the notch on two 60 m ropes. A single 70 m can just barely work, but a single 60 m can leave you several metres short of the notch. From the notch a short fourth-class scramble regains the East Face rappel line on Chablis, and two double-rope rappels down it reach the base rather than re-climbing back over to Burgundy Col.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch
approach_variants.notes:
The South Face is reached from the notch between Concord and Lexington, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord notch that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass) follow the maintained trail until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left marked by a large cairn.

Instead of trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers. Higher in that gully a reasonable climbers' path appears along its LEFT side; take it rather than fighting up the gully bed. It leads to the Concord-Lexington notch.

This notch is the quieter of the two — it sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose ground in the Concord-Lexington gully
easy to end up in the Liberty Bell-Concord gully instead — check which two towers flank your notch
no reliable water above the stream near the climbers'-path junction
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You want the Concord-Lexington notch, meaning the saddle with Concord Tower on one side and Lexington Tower on the other. From it, the South Face is on the Concord (north) side, and it begins gently: a class-2 walk across gravelly, slightly down-sloping ledges gets you to the first belay, so if your first move is a hard pull you are on the wrong line. Higher, a roped scramble along the crest brings you to a sandy stance under a thin blade of rock that climbers call the shark fin, and the last pitch goes over that fin onto the summit block, belaying from bolts. The shark fin is the confirming feature — it is unmistakable and there is nothing like it on the North Face side.

The common error is arriving at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch instead. That col has Liberty Bell on its far side, not Lexington, and from there the Concord wall in front of you is the North Face crack system, not walkable ledges.

wa_south_face_4.approach: The Temple (Kangaroo Temple, on Kangaroo Ridge) is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass — the same parking area used for the neighboring Hairpin Crags/Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus (faint, intermittently cairned) up to Kangaroo Pass, about 1 hour. From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face, or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. IMPORTANT — this route shares the approach to Kangaroo Pass with Temple's North/Northwest Face routes but finishes differently: rather than climbing toward the notch, drop some elevation below the pass and traverse across to the base of the South Face, roughly 2-4 hours from the car in all. The face isn't visible from the highway.

approach_variants.name: The Hairpin turnout and Kangaroo Pass, then drop below the pass and traverse to the South Face
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the same hairpin pullout on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass that the Temple's other routes use, and follow the same climbers' trail over Kangaroo Pass, about an hour.

Beyond the pass the routes part company: instead of heading up toward the notch between the Temple and Little Finger, lose some height below the pass and traverse across to the base of the South Face. Allow roughly 2.5 to 4 hours from the car in all.

Seven pitches at 5.8, first climbed in summer 1965.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A route with no view of its own face from the road, so the objective cannot be assessed before committing
Longer than the approach to the peak's north-side routes
Slide and boulder areas low on the trail
A shared trail as far as Kangaroo Pass with the north-side routes, so the split beyond the pass is easy to miss
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SOUTH FACE SHARES THE KANGAROO PASS APPROACH AND SPLITS FROM THE OTHER ROUTES ONLY BEYOND THE PASS.

From the hairpin, follow the climbers' trail through the boulder fields and forest up to Kangaroo Pass, about an hour. The North and Northwest Face routes then traverse to the gully below the notch between the Temple and Little Finger and go UP it. THIS ROUTE DOES NOT CLIMB TOWARD THE NOTCH: drop some height below the pass and traverse across to the base of the South Face, on the far side of the formation.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS: IF YOU ARE ASCENDING THE GULLY TOWARD THE NOTCH, YOU ARE ON THE WAY TO THE NORTH-SIDE ROUTES, NOT THIS ONE.

THE SOUTH FACE IS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE HIGHWAY, so you cannot pick your line from the car; read the wall when you arrive under it. Expect the walk to the base to take roughly 2.5 to 4 hours, longer than the approach to the north-side routes.

Returning to the base after the climb is awkward, so carry everything up the route with you; poles can be left at the pass and collected on the way out.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek to the Glee Peak saddle camp, then through the Terror Glacier icefall to the buttress at the lower-left corner of the face
approach_variants.notes: Park at the small pullout just before Goodell Creek Campground at about 600 ft and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail heading north from the Highway 20 corridor. The first 3.75-4 miles follow an old, gently graded forest roadbed along Goodell Creek, brushy with some downed logs in the first mile, and crossing TWO BOULDER-STREWN WASHOUT SECTIONS where the tread disappears into the creek's flood debris and you pick a line across large boulders. That is the trickiest route-finding of the lower approach. ABOUT 200 YARDS PAST THE SECOND WASHOUT, AT AN OBVIOUS CAMPSITE WITH A FIRE RING, an unsigned climbers' boot path breaks right off the roadbed, historically marked by a stone arrow on the ground at roughly 1,700 ft. That is the turn for Terror Basin; missing it means continuing pointlessly up the McMillan Spire approach. From the turnoff the boot path climbs steeply and directly through forest, hand-over-hand in places on roots and branches, and breaks out of the trees around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above treeline a rising traverse across meadow, slab and early-season snow reaches a saddle or notch at about 6,200 ft near Glee Peak; the standard camp sits about 400 ft below the saddle at roughly 5,800 ft. A seasonal trickle down a rock outcrop a few hundred feet below camp is the early-season water source; by late summer parties melt snow.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; the first ascent was made in mid-June in a low-snow year
hazards: Two boulder-strewn washouts where the tread vanishes, the lower approach's route-finding crux
A broken Terror Glacier icefall with open crevasses that worsens through the season
A camp water source that dries out by late summer
A sustained multi-rappel descent down the West Ridge and then the South Face, with no bolts anywhere on the peak and fixed pin stations of variable quality
Loose rock in the descent gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on traversing rappels
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AIM FOR THE LOWER-LEFT CORNER OF THE SOUTH FACE WHERE A SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS MEETS THE GLACIER. THAT BUTTRESS IS THE START OF THE ROUTE. It is a place where rock touches ice directly, with no intervening gully, and that is what tells it apart from the peak's other lines.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE WEST RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME GLACIER: the West Ridge leaves at a BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END of the peak and then climbs ABOUT 300 FT OF GULLY before any ridge. If there is a gully above you, you have gone past this route's corner and are set up for the West Ridge.

GETTING THERE IS THE ICEFALL PROBLEM, NOT A NAVIGATION ONE: from camp, rope up and cross the Terror Glacier. THE ICEFALL IN ITS MIDDLE IS BROKEN AND OFTEN HAS OPEN CREVASSES; parties commonly work a LEFT-TRENDING SNOW RAMP OR ICE BRIDGE ABOVE A LARGE CREVASSE to get through it onto gentler slopes beyond. That crossing gets more serious as the season progresses.

SO THE HANDRAIL THROUGH THE ICEFALL IS THE LARGE CREVASSE ITSELF: the way through is above it, trending left. If you are dropping below the big crevasse looking for a bridge, you are on the wrong side of the feature parties use.

A COUNTABLE APPROACH MARKER LOWER DOWN THAT SAVES THE WHOLE DAY: TWO WASHOUTS, then 200 yards, then a fire ring. That is how you find the turn in poor light. A stone arrow may or may not still be there; the second washout and the fire ring are ground features that do not move.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

approach_variants.name: PCT and Commonwealth Creek trail, then a heather traverse to the red gully
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT trailhead at I-90 exit 52, hike the Pacific Crest Trail north to the Commonwealth Creek trail junction, then follow that trail for about two miles until Red Mountain comes into view.

Leave the trail and traverse on heather across the base of the mountain. The trail will often carry you too far WEST before you notice the peak, so expect to traverse back over the ridge and possibly downslope to reach the start.

Most parties climb the whole thing unroped and rope up only if they want to.
approach_variants.season: June to October, once the heather bands and rock are dry and snow-free
hazards: Rockfall onto parties below where the route funnels through gullies
Loose rock typical of Red Mountain, though the south ramp is the most solid ground on the peak
A steep and roofy direct finish on the summit block that needs a rope
Route-finding on the traverse in, where the trail tends to carry you west past the start
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROCK IS THE MARKER AND IT IS BRIGHT RED. You are looking for a low-angle gully or ramp of SOLID, BRIGHT RED rock at the base of the mountain — solid is the operative word, because it is the most solid rock on a peak otherwise famous for being fractured. The colour and the low angle together identify it; nothing else on this flank looks like it.

AND THE OVERSHOOT TEST IS THE ONE TO REMEMBER, BECAUSE IT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING: IF YOU REACH RED MOUNTAIN POND, YOU HAVE GONE TOO FAR. Popping out of the trees on the flank of Red commonly puts a party too far west; the pond tells you so unambiguously. Turn back east and traverse on heather until the red gully appears.

WHAT THE FIRST GROUND SHOULD FEEL LIKE: class 3, no gear required, two pitches of it. If you are pulling on anything hard from the ground you are not in the ramp.

WHERE IT LEADS, SO YOU CAN CHECK YOURSELF LATER: you pop over a small ridge into the MAIN GULLY below the summit. Keep going up that until the summit block above you turns steep and roofy. That roofy steepening is the signal to move LEFT onto the class 2 hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge — or, if you want it, to continue directly up the block at class 4 or low 5 with a rope.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead off I-90 exit 52, about 3,000-3,040 ft. Follow the PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles through second-growth, climbing gently, to the signed junction with the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033).

Follow #1033 into Commonwealth Basin. Not far past the junction it crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last reliable water on the approach, and a tricky ford in early season at high snowmelt.

Immediately beyond the crossing, leave the maintained tread. There is no trail from here. Climb cross-country to the northwest, first through open timber and then boulder and talus, into the open cirque at the headwaters of Commonwealth Creek beneath Lundin's south face.

An equivalent description used by many parties: stay on the Commonwealth Creek trail until soon after the stream crossing, where it starts moving up onto the flank of Red Mountain, then leave it and head northwest into the basin. Many climbers deliberately come early in the season, when snow covers the brush and boulders and the cross-country leg is quick.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; early season on snow is preferred
hazards: Commonwealth Creek ford in early season high flow
no trail from the creek crossing onward - open timber then boulder and talus
lingering snow patches in the upper basin into early summer
route-finding across talus to locate the true toe of the face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The south face rises straight out of the head of the basin, and the route begins at the LOW POINT of the face, directly beneath the summit.

The way to get this right is to line yourself up by eye before you walk in: pick out the summit from the basin floor, drop that line to where it meets the bottom of the face, and walk to that point. Parties who instead head for the first inviting rock they reach end up starting left or right of the low point, and the climbing above does not match — the route runs several low-fifth pitches to a slab, with the final pitch steeper.

If the ground at the foot of your line rises noticeably before it meets rock, you are off to one side; the true start is where the face is lowest.

In poor visibility this is a hard place to be sure of yourself, because the basin is featureless talus and the face is continuous. The summit-to-toe line is the only test that works, so take the bearing while you can still see the top.

wa_south_face_center.approach:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), about 30 miles west of Winthrop and about a mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass is required and the small lot fills early. Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left, marked by a large cairn.

The South Face routes are reached from the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord col that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. Rather than trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers; higher up, a reasonable climbers' path appears along its left side and is better than fighting up the gully bed. It sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.

You are at the right saddle when Concord is on one side of you and Lexington on the other, and the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges rather than a steep crack system. If you are facing a crack system, you are at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and looking at the North Face.

There is no approach detail specific to South Face Center beyond this shared approach.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail, then up and LEFT into the Concord-Lexington gully rather than the Liberty Bell-Concord one
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft, roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop and about a mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook. A day-use fee or Northwest Forest or Interagency pass is required and the small lot fills early. Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the LEFT, marked by a large cairn.

The South Face routes are reached from the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which is a DIFFERENT SADDLE from the Liberty Bell-Concord col that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. Rather than trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers; higher up, a reasonable climbers' path appears along its LEFT side and is better than fighting up the gully bed. It sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Two notches a few hundred feet apart on one ridge, reached by the same path
A gully bed that is better avoided in favour of the path along its left side
Far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col, so less obvious tread
A small trailhead lot that fills early
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARE AT THE RIGHT SADDLE WHEN CONCORD IS ON ONE SIDE OF YOU AND LEXINGTON IS ON THE OTHER, AND THE CONCORD WALL IN FRONT OF YOU GIVES ONTO LOW-ANGLE, GRAVELLY LEDGES RATHER THAN A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM. IF YOU ARE FACING A CRACK SYSTEM, YOU ARE AT THE LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD NOTCH AND LOOKING AT THE NORTH FACE.

That is the notch test, and it is the one that matters, because the two saddles are a few hundred feet apart on the same ridge and both are reached from the same trailhead by the same path.

ARRIVAL AT THIS PARTICULAR ROUTE, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM ARRIVAL AT THE NOTCH: LOOKING FROM THE NOTCH, START UP THE OBVIOUS CRACK IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WALL. This route takes the centre of Concord's south face, climbs through a bulge, and continues trending LEFT. Two right-facing corners put you at a TREE right below the summit block.

SO THE COUNT IS: one crack in the middle, one bulge, two right-facing corners, one tree. If your line runs up the edge of the wall rather than its centre, you are on the tower's other south-face route.

WHY THE NOTCH TEST AND THE ROUTE TEST BOTH MENTION CRACKS WITHOUT CONTRADICTING EACH OTHER: at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch a STEEP crack system rises directly in front of you, which is the North Face. At the Concord-Lexington notch the wall reads as low-angle and gravelly overall, and this route's crack is the obvious feature UP THE MIDDLE of that easier-angled wall. Judge the wall first, then the line.

DESCENT: downclimb or make one full double-rope rappel from the summit back to the notch; with a single rope, use two shorter rappels off intermediate anchor stations.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
approach_variants.notes:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far LEFT until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, once the gully has filled and consolidated — that is also exactly when the avalanche problem is live, so the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is a mandatory read
hazards: Avalanche: a confined south-facing gully below cliffs, adjacent to controlled ski terrain
Ski-area avalanche blasting on neighbouring slopes in season
Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite with a documented fatal history from rockfall and breaking holds
Poor, deep slush and hidden moats at snow-to-rock transitions on the South Spur
Large overhanging cornices along the summit ridge and above the north summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIFFS ARE THE MARKER, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS TO OVERSHOOT THEM BY 100 FT. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further LEFT past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

WHAT CONFIRMS IT ONCE YOU ARE IN: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the FIRST CHOCKSTONE, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A SECOND chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

THE EXIT TEST FOR LATER: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn LEFT before the gully ends — look for TWO LARGE TREES and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

AND ONE DESCENT WARNING THAT PARTIES GET WRONG: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the MIDDLE summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.

approach_variants.name: Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
approach_variants.notes:
From I-90 exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area. Guye Peak's rock rises directly above the parking area, so there is essentially no approach walk to the south-side routes. Respect the posted no-parking signs on the private sections of road; access on foot through the Alpental Community Club's private ground has been closed to climbers, so plan a line from public ground.

Once below the peak, find the obvious gully on the south side and scramble it.

The summer version of this line is not well loved: discontinuous rock, vegetation, deep pine needles and general gully looseness are what a dry ascent actually delivers.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to October as an easy-fifth-class rock scramble — a completely different and lower-consequence outing from the winter climb
hazards: Highly fractured, crumbly rhyolite; climber-triggered rockfall is very likely and the peak has a documented history of fatalities from rockfall and breaking holds
Rockfall multiplies with parties stacked in the gully — helmet on from the talus upward
Wet or mossy chockstone sections in shoulder-season conditions
Discontinuous rock, deep pine needles and vegetation make the dry version loose and unpleasant rather than technical
Access: private property on the walking approach, closed to climbers
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE GULLY IS THE OBVIOUS ONE ON THE SOUTH SIDE, AND THE TEST IS THAT IT FORCES YOU OUT LEFT. Walk round the south side until you are under the single obvious gully cleaving it. That is the whole identification at ground level; there is no second candidate on this aspect.

THE CONFIRMATION IS THE CHOCKSTONE, AND IT COMES EARLY. Scramble the gully until one or two chockstones jammed in it stop you and force you climbers' LEFT out onto the adjacent face for a short section before you regain the gully and follow the South Spur. If you can walk the gully to its top without ever being pushed onto the face, you are not in the right one.

WHAT THE ROCK SHOULD FEEL LIKE: easy fifth class at most, protected by a small rack and slung trees, with parties sometimes rigging a hand line over the exposed ground above the chockstones. Anything sustained or steep is not this route.

AND THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST ITS NEIGHBOURS: the big WEST face and the South Rib are separate features on other aspects. If you are looking at a large clean wall rather than into a vegetated cleft, you are round on the west side.

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go WEST along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, with July the usual month; late season the loose ground below the headwall gets worse rather than better
hazards: Frequent rockfall in the cirque and on the headwall, made worse by other parties
Sustained loose scree and choss on the ascent to the cirque, with no trail
A steep eroded descent path off Longs Pass, hard on the knees in both directions
An Ingalls Creek crossing that is a genuine ford in early-season snowmelt
Early-season snow and ice in the cirque
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above the clearing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CIRQUE IS THE ARRIVAL, AND IT IS UNMISTAKABLE EVEN IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT CLOSES AROUND YOU. You climb loose ground for a long time and then the walls come up on three sides — very steep cliffs at about 8,700 ft with the summit directly above. That enclosure is the cue. Scree that keeps going with open ground on both sides means you are still below it.

WHICH CLEARING, WHICH IS THE ACTUAL PROBLEM: from the Ingalls Creek trail, count west from where the Longs Pass trail came down to the creek. The correct line is the FIRST MAJOR CLEARING WEST of Ulrich's Couloir. Ulrich's is the big obvious gully; if you are ascending a defined gully rather than an open clearing, you are in Ulrich's itself and on a different route entirely. And if the clearing you picked is EAST of that point, you are heading for the Cascadian Couloir — the standard walk-up and the usual descent — which is easier ground and will not put you under a headwall.

CONFIRMATION AT THE BASE: the technical pitches start up the CENTRE of the headwall, and they top out very close to the true summit. Nothing on this route is harder than 5.7. If the ground in front of you looks harder than that, you have drifted to one side of the centre.

PREVIEW IT FROM LONGS PASS. This is the rare approach where the whole objective is visible from a trail junction two thirds of the way through the day, and a party that identifies the headwall and the correct clearing from the pass essentially cannot get this wrong afterwards.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

approach_variants.name: Sahale ski track and the south-side talus fans
approach_variants.notes:
Park somewhere along Alpental Road. Parking on the road near the Sahale Ski Club is sometimes possible, but it often is not and you may have to leave the car further away and walk. Respect the posted no-parking on the private sections.

From there head up the Sahale ski track toward Guye for roughly three quarters of a mile to a mile. Where the track starts to peter out, climb through the boulder field and a short band of slide alder to reach the base of the cliff.

Then traverse EAST along the base of the wall. You will pass Blood Sport on the way. Keep going until you reach a taller talus fan, and go up that fan to the cliff.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Oct as rock; also done in winter
hazards: rockfall on the talus and in the gullies
slide alder between the boulder field and the base of the cliff
limited and partly private parking on Alpental Road
the ski track fades rather than ending at a definite point, so the turn-off uphill is judged not signed
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The taller talus fan east of Blood Sport is the marker, and it is a comparative one rather than a described one: it reaches noticeably higher up the wall than any of the talus you passed getting there. When the ground under you starts climbing the face rather than just banking against it, that is the fan you want.

Blood Sport itself is the negative marker. It is a bolted line at the base of the south wall — arriving at it tells you that you are on the right side of the mountain but have not traversed far enough east. Do not start up there.

If you are still on the ski track with the wall above and to your left, you have not yet reached the point where the track fades and you are below the traverse entirely.

wa_south_ridge.descent: Do not reverse the ridge. From the summit a rappel of roughly 35 m drops north off the top, and a second rappel takes you east onto the Blue Glacier, which drains the peak's east side. Expect a moat where rock meets ice — parties here have repeatedly found a deep gap at the base, and at least one rappel on this side hung free over it, so plan to land beyond the lip and carry enough cord to leave an anchor. Heading back toward the Chickamin Glacier and the Ptarmigan Traverse camps, cross the south ridge at the FIRST col south of the South Peak; the second col is a common mistake, and one party describes losing time and backtracking after heading there.

_raw.notes: Glacier Peak Wilderness, approached from the Downey Creek Trailhead on the Suiattle River Road
_raw.permit_type: Self-issue wilderness permit (sign the trailhead register)
_raw.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
_raw.group_size_limit: Maximum 12 per party (people and stock combined)
_raw.parking_pass_required: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass
_raw.permit_pickup_location: Self-issue at the Downey Creek Trailhead register

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit: sign the register at the Downey Creek Trailhead
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Suiattle River Road (FR 26) is washed out and closed to vehicles at about milepost 4.5 after the December 2025 flood, under a closure order running to 1 January 2028 unless lifted sooner, so the Downey Creek Trailhead cannot be reached by car. The Downey Creek Trail itself is also closed through 31 December 2026 under a separate fire closure. Call the Darrington Ranger District, (360) 436-1155, before planning a trip.
access.seasonal: Suiattle River Road (FS 26) is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4.5 after flood washouts, under an order running to January 1, 2028 unless lifted sooner — check current conditions before a trip.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, jointly administered by Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass required at the Downey Creek Trailhead — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register
overnight_permit.where: Sign the register at the trailhead. Camping on the North Cascades National Park side of Cache Col needs a park wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or Recreation.gov.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
approach_variants.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, work through the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor over Itswoot Ridge and Cub Lake and up Bachelor Creek. Off-trail, brushy, and with glacier travel before you reach the peaks; a full day or two of approach is normal. Once in the basin, this route is reached from the lake side rather than from the glacier under the east faces.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the approach is out of snow.
hazards: Long, committing off-trail approach with glacier travel
The cannonhole gap on the traverse pitch is exposed and the feature is relatively young rock
Weather-window dependent — this is a remote crest with no quick way off
Both start dihedrals look alike; picking the wrong one is harmless, picking the wrong FACE is not
approach_variants.baseFinding: Do not start under the summit — walk SOUTH along the foot of the ridge past it. The start is a PAIR of clean dihedrals side by side on the ridge's WEST flank, and the pair is the test: two obvious corners, either of which will take you to the crest, with nothing else of the kind nearby. Both give about a rope length of climbing on chickenheads and good face features once you step right out of the corner. The second confirmation is overhead and unmistakable: look along the ridge crest above you for the CANNONHOLE, a gap punched clean through the ridge, which the route traverses on its second pitch. If you cannot see a hole through the crest from where you are standing, you are not below this line. Negative markers: if you are under a single chimney tucked into the left side of a face directly beneath the summit, you have stopped short and are at the west face route; if you are on glacier ice with a moat between you and the rock, you have gone round to the east side entirely.

approach_variants.name: Access Creek to Access Col and Luna Pass, then straight up the broad south ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Lake Trailhead off Hwy 20 near Ross Dam, most parties take the seasonal water taxi across the reservoir to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft, skipping roughly 7 rolling lakeshore miles. From there the maintained Big Beaver Trail runs about 8 miles to Luna Camp, the standard permit basecamp, then roughly another 1.5 miles north.

Watch on the left, the west, for a boot path near where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek, and cross Big Beaver Creek there. A log crossing is sometimes usable, otherwise wade. That is where maintained trail ends.

Follow a surprisingly well-defined boot path along the north bank of Access Creek through semi-open forest. NEAR 3,700 FT THE BRUSH TURNS THICK WITH SLIDE ALDER, SO CROSS TO THE SOUTH BANK AROUND 3,800 FT; several trip reports warn specifically that skipping this crossing leads to a miserable bushwhack. From the south bank, cairns and a fainter path link talus benches into the open upper basin at the Access Creek headwaters, the usual basecamp, with reliable water.

From camp, the Access Couloir gains roughly 1,500-2,000 ft of steep loose scree and talus, with a notably loose upper section of dirt and heather clumps, to Access Col at about 6,300 ft. From the col a faint path traverses west across heather and talus to Luna Pass, the Luna-McMillan col at about 7,200 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Swift, sometimes swollen crossings of Big Beaver and Access Creek
Heavy slide-alder bushwhacking and genuine route-finding difficulty in Access Creek; multiple parties report following the wrong drainage
Loose rock in the Access Couloir and on the south ridge, with real rockfall risk onto climbers below
Lingering snow and possible avalanche exposure on the couloir and southeast snowfields in early season
No water above the Access Creek basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
AT LUNA PASS THE TWO ROUTES ON THIS PEAK PART COMPANY, AND THE TEST IS SIMPLE: THIS ONE GOES STRAIGHT UP. From the pass, turn directly up the broad south ridge on class 2 talus, roughly 1,000-1,100 ft of gain, straight to Luna's false, southern summit. There is no traverse and no contour. If you are sidehilling across snowfields on Luna's southeast flank you are on the Southeast Slopes route, which is the other line from this same pass.

ARRIVAL AT THE PASS ITSELF, WHICH IS THE HARDER FIND: Luna Pass is the col between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left, at about 7,200 ft, reached by a faint traverse west from Access Col. It is a gap on a crest, not a shoulder. If the ground ahead of you keeps rising instead of dropping away on the far side, you have not reached it.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, ON THE RIDGE: this route as scoped tops out at the FALSE, SOUTHERN summit. Continuing past it toward Luna's true summit means a separate exposed class 3-4 ledge traverse across the notch between the two summits, where some parties use a rope and running belays. That is beyond this route, and the notch is where you decide whether to take it on.

A NAMED APPROACH ERROR, BECAUSE MULTIPLE PARTIES HAVE MADE IT: several report initially following the WRONG DRAINAGE out of Big Beaver. Access Creek is the one with the boot path on its north bank and the 3,800 ft bank change; if there is no boot path, you are in the wrong creek.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then the unmarked path past Lewis Lake to Wing Lake
approach_variants.notes:
