Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area and Lake Ann trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 157.5 at about 4,850 ft, a 40-car lot with a privy. THIS IS THE RAINY PASS LAKE ANN, NOT THE LAKE ANN BELOW MOUNT SHUKSAN ON THE MOUNT BAKER HIGHWAY; the two are about 80 km apart and share a name.

Follow the Lake Ann and Maple Pass Trail #740 about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and TAKE THE RIGHT FORK TOWARD HEATHER PASS; the left continues on the Lake Ann and Maple Pass loop. Climb through meadows to Heather Pass at about 2.6 miles and 6,100 ft, WHERE THE MAINTAINED TRAIL ENDS.

From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading NORTH, crossing two talus and boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake at about 3.5-4 miles and 5,700 ft, with timbered campsites on the north side and water. THIS OFF-TRAIL STRETCH IS THE MAIN ROUTE-FINDING CHALLENGE OF THE APPROACH, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake at about 5 miles and 6,900 ft, the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake.
approach_variants.season: May-Oct, best Jun-Sep
hazards: An unmarked off-trail stretch between Heather Pass and Lewis Lake, the approach's main route-finding challenge, worse with cairns buried by snow
Cliff bands directly below the south col if you climb the gully straight up rather than angling right
An exposed cairned ledge traverse below the summit block
A short class 4 step at the summit
Two lakes in Washington named Lake Ann; this route uses the Rainy Pass one
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TWO LAKES IN SEQUENCE ARE THE APPROACH'S SPINE, AND THEY ARE WATER FEATURES, WHICH IS WHY THIS APPROACH IS SURVIVABLE WHEN THE CAIRNS ARE BURIED. LEWIS LAKE FIRST, THEN ABOUT TWELVE HUNDRED FEET OF CLIMBING, THEN WING LAKE. If you have reached only one lake you are not at camp.

FROM WING LAKE, GO AROUND THE RIGHT, NORTH, SIDE OF THE LAKE AND AIM FOR THE OBVIOUS TALUS AND SNOW GULLY LEADING INTO THE COULOIR JUST SOUTH OF THE SUMMIT. Climb that gully, then ANGLE CLIMBER'S-RIGHT OUT OF IT TO AVOID CLIFF BANDS DIRECTLY BELOW THE COL, topping out at THE SOUTH COL ON THE CREST OF THE SOUTH RIDGE. THE SOUTH COL IS THE TRUE START OF THE CLIMBING.

SO THE ONE INSTRUCTION THAT KEEPS YOU OUT OF TROUBLE IS THE EXIT FROM THE GULLY: ANGLE RIGHT NEAR THE TOP. Going straight up puts you under cliff bands below the col.

ARRIVAL AT THE COL: a gap on a ridge crest with the summit pyramid to the north of you. Above it the route is cairned class 3 along the ridge to the summit pyramid, then a CAIRNED CLASS 2 LEDGE SYSTEM traversing below the summit block, exposed near its end, and finally A SHORT CLASS 4 STEP OF ABOUT 15 FT to the true summit.

SO THE COUNT ABOVE THE COL IS: cairned ridge, one ledge system, one 15 ft step. There is no other technical ground on this route. A BOULDER IS SLUNG AT THAT STEP for an optional short rappel or hand line; a 30 m rope is more than enough, and many parties skip the rope and downclimb it facing in.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE PEAK'S NORTHEAST RIDGE, WHICH LEAVES THE SAME CAMP: that route ascends snow toward the LOW POINT IN THE NORTHEAST RIDGE, following the HOGSBACK MORAINE WIDE RIGHT and then traversing back left to the notch. Both routes cross moraine above the lake, so that alone tells you nothing; a notch on the northeast side instead of the south col means you are on the other route.

approach_variants.name: Glacier flank traverse from the east ridge camp
approach_variants.notes: From the parking area on Cascade River Road, backtrack along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River, then take the steep unmaintained climbers' boot path up through old-growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine basin above. Camp on the rocks by the broad flat of the glacier — the standard camp for the ordinary east-ridge line — and traverse from there. Overnight stays need a free backcountry permit.
approach_variants.season: July to September, once the glacier flank snow has consolidated but before the ground above the notch melts out to loose scree
hazards: The traverse to the base is steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier — crampons are mandatory
Ground above the ridge is broad and turns to loose scree when melted out
Glacier travel with crevasse-rescue gear is required to reach camp at all
approach_variants.baseFinding: Seen from the glacier on the standard camp approach, this route is the LEFT-hand skyline. The right-hand one is the ordinary way up — a broad snow crest leading to the summit arete — so the first check is simply which of the two skylines you are under. Pick the LOWEST point on the left skyline and traverse the flank of the glacier to it; that traverse is steep, exposed snow and crampons are not optional. The base is then proved by a single feature you can see from the snow before committing: an obvious crack running up the face directly above you to a U-shaped notch cut into the ridge crest. The crack and the U-notch are one thing and either alone is not enough. If there is no U-notch above the crack you have picked, you are too high or too far along the ridge, and the ground there rolls back into loose scree. If you are walking on broad snow with nothing but a snow crest above you, you are on the ordinary route and not on this climb at all.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

approach_variants.name: Boston Basin high camp
approach_variants.notes: From the small pullout on Cascade River Road, take the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the old mine roadbed, across several streams and out above treeline to the Boston Basin camps. The formation is visible and easily picked out from the basin, and the climb is a half-day outing on light packs from camp. Overnight parties need a wilderness permit for the basin.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, from an established camp in the basin
hazards: Route-finding here is markedly less obvious than on the other side of the formation — scout the line from the basin before committing
Exposed ridge with short fifth-class steps between fourth-class scrambling
Glacier and snow travel to reach the foot of the crest
approach_variants.baseFinding: The formation is the cockscomb standing on the divide between the upper Forbidden basin and the Torment basin with its glacier — a small, sharply notched crest that reads as an M from below, which is where its name comes from, and it is unmistakable once you are up out of the basin. Two skylines run down off it and the whole question is which one you are under. The RIGHT-hand skyline is the other route on the formation; the LEFT-hand one is this climb. The negative marker is exact and easy to check on the ground: the right-hand route is entered from a notch on the RIGHT of that skyline, and from that notch it gives three or four pitches of fourth class to the foot of a tower and then one short pitch to its top. If you are standing in a notch on the right-hand side of the formation looking at a tower, you are on the other route. This ridge is gained round the far end of the crest, is the longer and less obvious of the two, and parties consistently find the route-finding on it the harder part of the day.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack ford and Easy Ridge over the Imperfect Impasse to Perfect Pass
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of Hannegan Pass Road, FS-32, off SR-542 at about 3,100 ft, Trail #674 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to Hannegan Pass at roughly 5,050-5,100 ft. The trail then switchbacks down the far side into the Chilliwack River valley to Boundary Camp and continues down-valley to the Chilliwack River crossing.

That ford is the approach's main hazard: it can be thigh-deep and swift at mid-summer flow, and is harder earlier in the season or after rain. From the ford, leave the maintained trail system and pick up the old, unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' trail, which climbs steeply out of the valley to Easy Saddle at about 5,200 ft, a common camp, roughly 5.5 to 8.5 hours and 8-9 miles in depending on pace and the ford.

From Easy Saddle the route follows the crest over or around Easy Peak at 6,613 ft to the Imperfect Impasse, then continues to Perfect Pass at about 6,200 ft, the standard high camp, about 16 miles in, commonly the end of a second day, though fast parties reach it in one. There is no reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season; fill at Easy Saddle or from snowmelt.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A thigh-deep, swift ford of the Chilliwack River at mid-summer flow
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs, and an 800 ft descent to an exposed class 4 step as the workaround
Moats where the south snowfield meets the summit rock, worse late season
A short but very exposed summit crest on poor rock with limited protection
No reliable water at Perfect Pass in late season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS WHERE THE CAMP ENDS: FROM PERFECT PASS, HEAD NORTH AND UP ONTO THE BROAD SOUTH SNOWFIELD. That snowfield is the lower margin of the Whatcom Glacier, the angle is moderate, and the line aims at a CONSPICUOUS COL IN THE SUMMIT RIDGE above. Reports describe it as long but straightforward, roughly an hour from the pass.

SO THE AIMING POINT IS A NOTCH IN A SKYLINE, AND IN CLOUD THE SUBSTITUTE FOR IT IS THIS: keep climbing snow at a moderate angle until the snow RUNS OUT AGAINST ROCK. The snowfield is left at the col. Where snow meets rock is where a moat or a lip of hard snow is most likely to be awkward, and it is worse late in the season, which is exactly why you will notice it.

CONFIRM ABOVE: the final stretch along the crest is SHORT, on the order of a hundred feet, but very exposed with drops on both sides, on poor rock with limited protection. Many parties belay it even though the moves are only third to fourth class. If you are on a long ridge rather than a hundred-foot one, you are not on this route.

THE VARIATION THAT IS NOT AN ERROR: some parties break out onto ramps and ledges to the NORTHEAST of the col and rejoin the crest higher. Both reach the same place.

THE IMPASSE, WHICH IS THE OTHER THING YOU HAVE TO FIND ON THIS APPROACH: it is a notch guarded by deep snow moats on both sides and down-sloping, often wet slabs. In many seasons the direct crossing is unsafe or impassable; the established workaround drops roughly 800 ft to about 4,400 ft and re-climbs an exposed class 4 rock step, which many parties belay, to regain the ridge on the far side. Dropping 800 ft to get past a notch feels wrong and is correct.

approach_variants.name: The low-orbit traverse from Whatcom Pass, skipping Easy Ridge and the Impasse entirely
approach_variants.notes: An alternative that avoids the Impasse. From Whatcom Pass, reached via the Chilliwack River and Brush Creek trails or via the Little Beaver Creek Trail from Ross Lake, a low-orbit traverse around Whatcom Peak's east side on scree and snow reaches the same south-side snowfields.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; treat as glacier travel in early season
hazards: Moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the Whatcom Glacier; treat as glacier travel in early season
Scree and snow sidehilling with no path
The same summit crest exposure as the Easy Ridge variant
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS VARIANT IS DEFINED BY WHAT IT AVOIDS, AND THAT IS THE TEST: IF YOU HAVE CROSSED THE IMPASSE, YOU ARE NOT ON IT. The low orbit contours around the peak's east side instead of over the ridge crest, and delivers you onto the same south-side snowfields the Easy Ridge line reaches from Perfect Pass.

ARRIVAL IS THE SAME ARRIVAL: broad moderate snow below a conspicuous col in the summit ridge, and the route is where the snow runs out against rock.

WHAT YOU TRADE FOR IT, AND WHY THE CHOICE IS A CONDITIONS CALL RATHER THAN A PREFERENCE: the low orbit exposes you to the moats and possible crevasses at the edge of the WHATCOM GLACIER, so it should be treated as glacier travel with a rope and crevasse-rescue gear in early season. The Impasse is a rock problem; this is a glacier problem. Pick the one your party is equipped for.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. Whatcom Camp and both Graybeal camps have been closed because of fire damage from 2022, and the park's fire-closures page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists them closed until further notice, so there is no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

approach_variants.name: Dailey Prairie roads and Orsino Creek Basin, then higher and left to the 5,800 ft saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Access is via the Dailey Prairie logging-road network from the Middle Fork Nooksack River bridge near 1,200 ft on the north side of the range. The DNR and private gate situation changes year to year, so treat the drive-in as unverified until confirmed.

From wherever the gate stops you, most parties bike roughly 6-7 miles of climbing and quarry road, stashing bikes near the old pipe barrier at the end of road, at the base of the western cirque between North Twin and South Twin.

From there a climbers' path — brushy, overgrown and wet but not hard to follow — drops into timber and works southeast, fading into a red talus slope. Traverse RIGHT, south, across the talus, cross a timbered rib, and pass the ruins of an old log cabin. Orsino Creek along this stretch is the last reliable water for the climb and the camp.

Beyond the creek the path becomes a steep grind of dirt, scree and talus into the open basin below the North Twin / South Twin cirque, often holding snow into midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Earlier gives firmer snow bridges on the Sisters Glacier and more crevasse-fall risk; later opens the crevasses and widens the moat
hazards: Glacier travel on the Sisters Glacier with a moat at the rock margin that widens all season
A basin headwall with multiple plausible lines and none of them obvious
The last 400 ft on the crest, steeper and more exposed than anything below and possibly low fifth class
A documented cliffing-out trap for parties drifting right below the summit
The North Ridge is not reversed on descent — the standard way down is the West Ridge, a different line
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A SADDLE BETWEEN TWO PEAKS AT ABOUT 5,800 FT, AND THE MISTAKE THAT COSTS YOU THE ROUTE IS STOPPING SIX HUNDRED FEET LOWER. This approach is identical to the West Ridge's as far as Orsino Creek Basin. The West Ridge gains the crest at an OBVIOUS NOTCH around 5,200 ft. This route deliberately does not: it continues HIGHER and further CLIMBER'S LEFT — north — up basin snow or talus to the saddle between NORTH TWIN's southeast ridge and SOUTH TWIN's north ridge.

SO THE TEST IS: CAN YOU SEE, OR FEEL, GROUND RISING ON BOTH SIDES OF YOU TO TWO SEPARATE PEAKS? A notch in one ridge is the West Ridge. A col with a mountain at each end is the North Ridge. That distinction survives cloud because it is about the shape of the ground you are standing on.

EXPECT THE ROUTE-FINDING TO BE THE CRUX OF THE APPROACH RATHER THAN OF THE CLIMB. Multiple plausible lines run up the basin headwall depending on snow coverage, and parties consistently report the basin slog and the final gain to the notch as the most tedious and least obvious part of the day.

ABOVE THE SADDLE THE FIRST GROUND IS GLACIER, NOT ROCK. The crest is gained by way of the Sisters Glacier and the snow on the north side of the ridge. In early summer coverage is good and bridges are reported solid, but treat it as glacier travel. THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK IS THE RECURRING OBSTACLE and it widens through the season — late in the year parties are stopped by the moat rather than by the crevasses.

THE HIGH NOTCH AT ROUGHLY 6,600 FT IS THE DECISION POINT ON THE ROUTE, not the base. Above it the character changes, and it is where you choose between the steep exposed final crest and the south-side gully bypass. If you have reached a distinct notch at 6,600 ft you are 800 ft above the start of the climbing.

AND THE DOCUMENTED ROUTE-FINDING TRAP IS NEAR THE TOP: parties that drift too high and too far RIGHT below the summit get cliffed out and have had to rappel to get back on line.

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate, bike the Dailey Prairie roads, then Orsino Creek Basin to the 5,200 ft notch
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River near 1,200 ft at the end of FR-38, reached via Mosquito Lake Road off WA-542. From the gate most parties mountain-bike the old quarry and logging road system for roughly 6-7 miles and well over 2,000 ft of gain, threading several forks near Dailey Prairie, until the road becomes too rough or overgrown to ride — usually marked by a large culvert pipe at the timber-road terminus. GPS or a GPX track is genuinely recommended on this network.

Stash bikes and pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot: brushy, wet, occasionally overgrown, but not hard to follow. It drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and fades out at a red talus slope which often holds snow well into summer.

From the talus, traverse RIGHTWARD — south — up and across, over a timbered rib, past the ruins of an old miner's log cabin, then up into Orsino Creek Basin. Orsino Creek is the last reliable water before the climb.

About four miles of foot travel from the bike cache to the summit, four to five hours one way for most parties, with combined bike and foot gain around 6,100 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly May-Oct, with snow-free scrambling typically Jul-Sep. Earlier or later trips want an ice axe for lingering snow near 6,500 ft
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network near Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
A red talus slope holding snow into summer, and lingering snow near 6,500 ft
A steep loose dirt gully to gain the notch
Low fifth-class steps on the upper crest that force an improvised rappel if the bypass is missed
Orsino Creek is the last water for the whole climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE RUINS OF AN OLD LOG CABIN ARE THE ONE MAN-MADE THING ON THIS APPROACH AND THEY ARE THE CHECKPOINT. From the red talus slope where the climbers' path fades, traverse RIGHT — south — up and across, cross a timbered rib, and pass the cabin ruins. If you have not passed a collapsed cabin, you have not made the traverse and you are still below the basin.

ORSINO CREEK IS THE LAST WATER AND THE ENTRY TO THE BASIN. Fill up. There is nothing above it.

THE BASE IS AN OBVIOUS NOTCH IN THE RIDGE CREST AT ABOUT 5,200 FT, AND YOU GET TO IT UP A STEEP LOOSE DIRT GULLY. That combination — an unpleasant slog up steep dirt, scree and talus, then a defined notch in a crest — is the arrival, and it works in cloud because a notch is a thing you stand in with air on the far side. This is the standard start and it is where the West Ridge is gained down low.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER ROUTE OUT OF THIS BASIN, AND IT IS A SINGLE NUMBER: the NORTH RIDGE route continues HIGHER and further CLIMBER'S LEFT — north — up basin snow or talus to a saddle around 5,800 ft between North Twin's southeast ridge and South Twin's north ridge. So 5,200 ft and the obvious notch is the West Ridge; 5,800 ft and a saddle between two peaks is the North Ridge. Six hundred feet and a bearing separate two routes that share every step of the approach up to the basin.

THE ROCK CONFIRMS THE RANGE: dunite, olivine-rich, exceptionally grippy, like coarse sandpaper. It is why parties choose to gain the ridge low rather than high — to maximise time on it.

HIGHER UP, THE FALSE-SUMMIT BYPASS IS WORTH CARRYING BEFORE YOU NEED IT: leave the crest to the RIGHT — south — traverse ledges, and regain the crest about 200 yards short of the false summit, roughly 500 ft above where you left it. Staying exactly on the crest through that step is what forces parties into an improvised rappel.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Turnout at old Diamond Mine Rd fork off Cascade River Rd; climbers trail to Boston Basin, Quien Sabe Glacier approach to Sharkfin Tower. SAFETY NOTE: a 2005 accident occurred here from parties entering the wrong approach gully, resulting in fatalities.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small, unsigned Boston Basin pulloff at about 3,200-3,300 feet. It's a rough, sometimes rutted gravel road, so a bit of ground clearance helps. Park at the pulloff alongside the road. A Boston Basin wilderness permit is required for the trip.

waypoints.name: Sharkfin Tower summit
waypoints.note: This is Sharkfin Tower's summit, not Mount Torment's — a different, neighboring Boston Basin peak. The coordinate matches the summit waypoint already on this peak's sibling Southeast Ridge route.

watch_out: SIGNIFICANT ROCKFALL HAZARD from above and within approach gully—signs of rockfall damage visible; gully floor contains numerous 10-50 pound rocks precariously balanced in fine sand; traverse quickly and watch continuously for falling rocks

Critical route-finding to identify correct approach gully—documented cases of parties entering wrong gully, leading to complex traverses and tragic accidents (2005 incident with 3 fatalities); study photos and topos carefully; may want to hire guide for first ascent

Exposed 5.10 alpine rock climbing with limited protection in some sections—high run-out potential on compact slab pitches; requires confident climbing and solid judgment on when to place protection vs. accept exposure
Rappel anchor quality variable—fixed slings/bolts wear over time and may have reduced holding power; always back up rappel anchors or build new ones; inspect carefully before committing full weight
Gully system loose and unstable—rockfall debris accumulation indicates ongoing hazard; potential for rockfall triggered by climbing party or weather changes; stay aware of partner locations

Weather exposure on open face—afternoon clouds common; thunderstorm potential in summer; electric storms with rock climbing exposure is extremely dangerous; start early and retreat if weather deteriorates

Descending gully in darkness—route-finding becomes difficult without daylight; headlamps not fully sufficient for gully route-finding; strongly consider camping at base if climb extends past early afternoon
Altitude and sustained climbing (5000+ vertical from trailhead)—technical grade combined with elevation can cause dehydration and altitude effects; start well-hydrated and maintain energy intake

approach_variants.name: The correct gully off the Quien Sabe, then two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and a rappel to reach the face
approach_variants.notes:
Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small unsigned Boston Basin pulloff near 3,200-3,300 ft. The old mining road runs about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, then an unmaintained but well-travelled boot path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams — top off bottles there — to treeline around 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches at 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on the knoll above the green meadows at 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up and traverse EAST along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully below the tower. If a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left give an alternate entry and rejoin the couloir about 100 ft up.

There is no separate approach to the Southeast FACE. You reach it by climbing the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and rappelling.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, the same window as the Southeast Ridge; being steeper rock it sheds snow a little faster after an early-season storm
hazards: Getting into the wrong gully: on 10 July 2005 a six-person party climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here, a climber was struck by rockfall during the roped traverse back toward the standard line, and minutes later a natural boulder anchor failed during the retreat rappel, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth
Loose rock and rockfall in the approach gully, worsening as the season progresses
Crevasse hazard on the upper Quien Sabe Glacier
The two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains and no rap rings, and there is no anchor at all at the very base of pitch 1
Frequent bear activity at Boston Basin camps; food canisters required
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS FACE IS NOT WALKED TO. IT IS RAPPELLED INTO — and that is the cleanest test on the whole tower. A party standing at its start has already climbed the first two pitches of the SOUTHEAST RIDGE and made two rappels of about 75 ft each from the fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2. A party that WALKED to where it is standing is at the Southeast Ridge notch, one route to the side.

YOU CAN SEE THE FACE FROM THAT NOTCH, WHICH IS WHY THE MIX-UP HAPPENS: the clean southeast face is visible from the base of the Southeast Ridge and looks approachable. It is not, from there.

IDENTIFY THE RIDGE NOTCH BY ITS ANCHOR, NOT BY ITS SHAPE: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 carries NO chains and NO rap rings. That absence is a positive identification, and it is also a planning fact — you will be leaving a biner, a ring or a short cord to get down.

BEFORE ANY OF THAT, GET THE APPROACH GULLY RIGHT, BECAUSE THIS IS WHERE PEOPLE HAVE DIED. Traverse east along the TOP of the Quien Sabe several hundred feet; the correct gully leads to a SNOW PATCH DIRECTLY AT THE TOWER'S BASE and then a short gully to the notch. A similar-looking gully nearby does not. If your gully does not deliver you to a snow patch at the foot of the tower, stop and re-check rather than continuing or traversing across — the 2005 accident happened during exactly that correction, not during the mistake.

CONFIRM ON THE FIRST MOVES OF THE FACE ITSELF: pitch 1 steps onto a DETACHED BLOCK and then follows a widening finger-to-ring-lock seam that zig-zags just LEFT of the arete to a bolted anchor in a notch. If you are not standing on a detached block, you are not on this pitch.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
approach_variants.notes:
From the parking on the abandoned logging spur off the lake road on the Canadian side at roughly 2,350 ft, walk the old roadway grade uphill, taking the left-hand fork, about a mile to the boundary marker, where you cross into the park and should sign in at the kiosk. Carry a passport.

From there the way is an unmaintained, unmarked climbers' path through old growth for roughly three miles to the base of the falls - one of the tallest in the state - where the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along their left edge. A fixed handline is present at the crux scramble and this is the approach's main technical hazard: exposed greasy rock, far worse in the wet and worse again in the dark, and several parties have lost the tread here at night.

Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain and reaches treeline, where most parties change into mountaineering boots. Class 3 tread gains roughly eight hundred feet into the glacier basin, where the lake is the usual first camp.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, when the talus is out and the glacier is still bridged
hazards: an international border crossing on foot with a register at the boundary
steep wet slabs beside the falls with a fixed handline of unknown condition, and a tread that parties lose in the dark
crevasses on the glacier, usually minor and avoidable in normal late-season conditions
a thousand feet of unstable sandy talus below the col, which is the dominant hazard of the upper approach
exposed class 4 ground on loose rock above the col that many parties belay
no water above camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS IS THE WHOLE NAVIGATION, AND THE TRAP IS THAT THERE ARE TWO SUMMITS. From high camp, traverse east across snow and glacier beneath the southern side of the western summit toward the saddle between the two peaks, finishing with a steep thousand-foot climb over notoriously unstable sandy talus - helmets on well before the col.

AT THE COL, CHECK WHICH TOWER YOU ARE UNDER. THIS ROUTE IS ON THE EASTERN SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE HARDER AND HIGHER OF THE PAIR. IF THE PEAK ABOVE YOU IS THE ONE YOU TRAVERSED BENEATH ON THE WAY IN, YOU ARE FACING THE WESTERN SUMMIT AND HAVE TURNED THE WRONG WAY OUT OF THE SADDLE.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE THE COL IS A LADDER OF SPECIFIC SHAPES, IN ORDER, AND IT IS HOW YOU KNOW YOU ARE RIGHT: a ramp leading RIGHT past a snow patch into a gully; then class 4 scrambling up and right, exposed enough that many parties belay it, toward a notch in a ridge of gendarmes; then a short sequence of ledges that zig-zag right, left, right through that notch; then a brief DESCENT to a small flat area. THE FLAT SPOT AFTER A DOWNCLIMB IS THE CONFIRMATION - a line that only ever goes up has missed the notch.

FROM THAT FLAT AREA, LOCATE THE CORRECT GULLY LEADING TO A HIGH NOTCH ON THE WEST RIDGE. That notch is where the roped climbing starts: two pitches of fifth class to the summit tower, then a short exposed scramble, kept roped, to the top. IF YOU ARE UNCOILING A ROPE AT THE COL ITSELF, YOU ARE HUNDREDS OF FEET TOO LOW.

Carry water from camp. The glacier and the lake supply it below; the upper ridge does not.

approach_variants.name: Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
approach_variants.notes: The lake in the glacier basin is the common first camp and has water. Most parties then move camp three or four hours further up onto the glacier saddle at about 7,150 ft, which is flat glacier travel with minor and usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions, and which puts the party far closer to the peaks for summit day. The trade is an exposed camp on ice with weather and visibility to consider, and a second carry.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the higher camp is only worth it once the glacier is reasonable
hazards: an exposed camp on the glacier edge with poor visibility common
a second carry to move camp
crevassed travel between the two camps
the same loose talus and exposed class 4 above the col
no water above the lake basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM EITHER CAMP THE ROUTE MEETS AT THE SAME PLACE: THE SADDLE BETWEEN THE TWO MOX SUMMITS, gained by traversing east beneath the western peak's southern side and then climbing a steep thousand feet of loose sandy talus.

THE HIGH CAMP'S OWN MARKER IS THAT IT SITS ON ROCK OUTCROPS AT THE GLACIER'S EDGE at the top of a broken buttress, rather than on open ice. Rope up there for the crevassed travel beyond; visibility on this ground is often poor, and the saddle is not visible from camp.

AT THE SADDLE, THE SUMMIT YOU WANT IS THE EASTERN ONE - the higher and harder of the pair. The western summit is the one you traversed beneath on the way in, so if the tower above you is on the side you came from, you have turned the wrong way.

THE CONFIRMATION SEQUENCE IS THE SAME LADDER: ramp right past a snow patch into a gully, class 4 up and right to a notch in the gendarme ridge, ledges zig-zagging right-left-right through it, then a short DOWNCLIMB to a small flat area, and only then the gully to the high notch on the west ridge where the rope comes out.

approach_variants.name: Shannon Ridge and the Sulphide Glacier to the notch on the southeast ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Shannon Ridge Trailhead, climb east-northeast up Shannon Ridge and onto the Sulphide Glacier — the standard Shuksan approach, and the same one the Sulphide Glacier route uses. Most parties camp on the large flat plateau around 6,400 ft, which is the usual staging point for summit day.

The snow between roughly 5,400 and 6,400 ft is where visibility bites: it is featureless open ground and parties report it as the tricky stretch in reduced visibility. Above camp the upper Sulphide is mellow, with a few small crevasses that are generally stepped over.

This route then leaves the standard finish. Where the Sulphide Glacier route walks to the foot of the summit pyramid and takes its Class 3-4 gully, this one gains the ridge at a notch further east and climbs about six pitches of well-featured 5.3 rock to the top.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Sulphide is walkable and the rock is out from under snow
hazards: Featureless snow between 5,400 and 6,400 ft that is genuinely hard to navigate in reduced visibility
Limited protection on well-featured but sparsely protectable 5.3 rock
Severe exposure on both sides of the crest on the final steps
Crevasses on the Sulphide, small but present
A descent that rappels a gully shared with the standard route, so parties above you are a rockfall source
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IS THE ROUTE, AND YOU CAN FEEL IT RATHER THAN SEE IT. Gaining the southeast ridge happens at a PROMINENT NOTCH at the top of the upper Sulphide. In cloud, work up the glacier until the snow stops rising and you can step onto rock at a low point in the ridgeline with ground falling away on the far side. A notch you can stand in with air behind you is the arrival; a rock wall in front of you with snow still under your feet is not.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE STANDARD ROUTE, and it is the mistake to avoid: the Sulphide Glacier route's finish is a FOURTH-CLASS GULLY up the summit pyramid, and it is the line almost everyone on the mountain is walking toward. If you find yourself queueing at the bottom of a gully with a bootpack into it, you are at the standard finish, not at this route's start. This route gains a ridge crest, not a gully.

SECOND TEST, ON THE ROPE: the climbing here is six pitches of extremely well-featured rock that parties describe as easy in boots, with limited protection and severe exposure on BOTH sides of the crest. If your first pitch is a gully with walls either side of you rather than a crest with air either side of you, you have started in the wrong place. Exposure on both sides is the confirmation.

WHAT WALKING PAST IT LOOKS LIKE: continuing up the Sulphide beyond the notch brings you under the summit pyramid's south side, where the standard gully is. That is the descent for this route — the same gully is rappelled on the way down — so recognising it does not mean you are lost, but it does mean you have gone past the start.

bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier camp
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the most straightforward route on Shuksan and the best launching point for the summit pyramid. The plateau is flat, spacious and well positioned, and a privy has been maintained on the ridgeline here in recent seasons, which is unusual at this elevation. The permit is the binding constraint on the whole trip rather than the terrain, so plan the paperwork before the climb. Snow covers the site into early summer, and late in the season the approach turns to loose ground and heather that is harder work than the mileage suggests.
bivy.water: Usually available — running water is often audible and reachable over the rocks near camp — but this is a snowmelt supply that varies with the year and the week. Bring the means to melt snow and treat found water as likely rather than certain.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry (wilderness) permit required — this is a DIFFERENT authority from the Mt Baker side, and a Forest Service pass does not cover it. Permits come through Recreation.gov, with a spring early-access lottery followed by a general on-sale, and a share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Reservation and per-person nightly fees apply — these permits are no longer free. The zone carries a small daily party quota.
bivy.capacity: A broad flat plateau on the ridgeline with room for several parties, though the daily permit quota caps how many can legitimately be there

bivy.name: Shannon Ridge crest camps, below the park boundary
bivy.notes: The fallback for parties who could not get a North Cascades backcountry permit, and honestly worse than the camp above — lower, drier, and leaving a much longer summit day. The trade is administrative rather than scenic, so decide before you drive out whether you would rather chase a walk-up permit at a ranger station. FS Road 1152 and its spur are low elevation and generally open early in the season with no need for high clearance, which makes this the most road-reliable approach to either mountain. Check where the boundary actually falls on your map before pitching a tent, because the ridge does not advertise it clearly.
bivy.water: Poor. There is essentially nothing between the trailhead streams and the Sulphide Glacier itself, and what does exist on the ridge is gone by late June in most years. Carry water up from the bottom.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE the national park boundary — no backcountry permit needed here, which is the entire reason parties use these sites. A recreation pass is required at the Shannon Ridge trailhead. The park boundary is roughly half a mile further up the ridge, and everything beyond it needs a National Park Service permit.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites along the open ridge; adequate but cramped compared to the Sulphide camp above

bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier high camp
bivy.notes: Some parties carry above the main plateau to shorten summit day to the pyramid, camping on the glacier around 7,500 ft. It is fully exposed, on snow, and above any water, so it only makes sense for a party comfortable with a glacier bivy and a settled forecast. The gain over the lower camp is modest for most people, which is why the 6,400 ft plateau remains the norm. If weather is uncertain, the lower camp is the better place to be.
bivy.water: None dependable — melt snow. Anything running at this elevation is a hot-afternoon accident rather than a supply.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, same as the 6,400 ft camp — through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with fees. Confirm that your permit covers camping this high in the zone rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms only, for one or two parties; no established sites

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pullout and Spire Gully to the last large tree, then right across the talus toward the inter-spire notch
approach_variants.notes:
Same as the Direct East Buttress: park at the hairpin pullout on Highway 20 east of Washington Pass. THIS IS THE EAST-SIDE TRAILHEAD, NOT THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD used by the spire's west-side routes.

Nine pitches. The route shares the East Buttress's first pitches, then splits off around halfway up to climb the south-facing headwall on the upper south side of the peak for its final five pitches.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Vague, unfixed belays on the upper headwall, so bailing means building natural anchors
A shared start with a much more travelled route, with the split made mid-height
Talus and snow on the traverse below the inter-spire notch
Two trailheads on opposite sides of the pass serving this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
HIKE SPIRE GULLY, WHICH IS CAIRNED, TO THE LAST LARGE TREE. THAT TREE IS THE TURN. From it, traverse RIGHT across talus and snow to the gully leading to THE NOTCH BETWEEN NORTH AND SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE, then traverse LEFT to the base of the east buttress.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS THREE MOVES AND A TREE: UP the cairned gully to the LAST LARGE TREE, RIGHT across talus, then LEFT to the buttress base. The tree is the only thing in that sequence you can put a hand on, which is why it is the marker rather than the gully.

WHY THE NOTCH MATTERS EVEN THOUGH YOU DO NOT GO TO IT: the gully you aim at is the one running to the gap between the two spires, the same continuous cleft that on the west side is the chockstone-filled chimney. It is the biggest feature on this side of the group. Aim at it, then step left before reaching it.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS: IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE NOTCH ITSELF YOU HAVE GONE UP TOO FAR, and if you are on the far side of the cleft you are on NORTH Early Winters Spire, where Flycatcher Buttress starts from a flat ledge.

WHAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE EAST BUTTRESS IT SHARES A START WITH, AND IT IS A DECISION MADE HALFWAY UP RATHER THAN AT THE BASE: Southern Man splits off around mid-height onto the SOUTH-FACING HEADWALL. Its own belays are described as vague and not yet fixed, which is itself a tell: DO NOT EXPECT A FULLY BOLTED RAP LINE if you need to bail from the upper headwall. Natural anchors would be required there.

DESCENT: from the summit, the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete with a short more exposed fifth-class section to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.

approach_variants.name: Marble Creek-McAllister pass, then 700 ft down to the snow gully at the toe
approach_variants.notes:
The hike in matches the East Ridge of Eldorado exactly: from the Eldorado trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the river near the parking area (backtrack downstream for a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest — no water on this stretch — to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback past 6,000 ft, and drop through a short class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin at 6,100-6,400 ft, which has reliable water and is a good lower camp or bail-out point.

From the basin, ascend 20-30 degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier around 7,500 ft — rope up from here on — and camp on rock or moraine near the glacier shoulder.

Where this route diverges is the final glacier traverse: cross the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister, heading for the MARBLE CREEK-McALLISTER PASS, generally crossing on the pass's east side. The base is then reached by a prominent gully, often snow-filled year round, that begins roughly 700 VERTICAL FEET BELOW THAT PASS and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
approach_variants.season: Late July through August; the approach gully often holds firm snow into August, which helps the glacier travel but wants crampons on the gully
hazards: A steep, often snow-filled approach gully to about 35 degrees
A moat guarding the base of the climb that can present an exposed, deep gap
Crevasses on the Eldorado, Inspiration and McAllister glaciers en route
Loose blocks in places on the upper buttress and unreliable holds described as traps
A large boulder balanced on an overhang ledge near the route
An exposed knife-edge summit ridge at the top
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE TOE OF THE BUTTRESS AT THE FOOT OF A PROMINENT, OFTEN YEAR-ROUND SNOW GULLY, AND THE GULLY IS LOCATED BY DESCENDING — IT STARTS ABOUT 700 VERTICAL FEET BELOW THE MARBLE CREEK-McALLISTER PASS. If you have not lost roughly 700 ft from the pass, you are not at the gully yet.

AT THE TOP OF THAT GULLY THERE IS A FORK, AND IT IS THE ONE THING ON THIS PEAK MOST WORTH GETTING RIGHT. THIS ROUTE GOES AROUND TO THE RIGHT. The Direct Southwest Buttress instead goes STRAIGHT UP from the same point to three vertical cracks. Same gully, two routes, one turn.

THE STRONGEST NEGATIVE TEST IS PUBLISHED AS A WARNING AND IT IS WORTH CARRYING VERBATIM: DO NOT CLIMB DIRECTLY BELOW THE RIDGE CREST AT THE START. That variation leads into unwanted 5.10 OVERHANGING TERRAIN ON LOOSE ROCK. If the ground turns overhanging at 5.10 low on the route, you are on the wrong side of the crest and should reverse rather than push on — this route's own crux is 5.8 in a corner and it comes at pitch five, not at the start.

CONFIRM ON PITCH ONE: it is a FULL rope length, 55 to 57 m, up a corner and then slightly RIGHT, mostly 5.6 with one committing 5.7 or 5.8 move near the top, and the anchor is on cams to three inches in a crack. A short first pitch is not this route.

AND CONFIRM BY WHICH COL YOU CROSSED: this line is reached over the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The Northwest Ridge starts from a small col at the top of the McAllister's apron on the other side of the Needle and is only three short pitches; the East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a DIFFERENT cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

approach_variants.name: Standard Tooth approach, but break off north of the Pineapple Pass gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, follow the Snow Lake trail about a mile and a half, fork toward Source Lake, cross the talus and start up toward Pineapple Pass on the standard line. The difference is at the top. Do NOT finish the gully to the pass. Break off to the NORTH of it and climb the open books on the face above instead. This is the route parties take when the South Face is backed up, and it is deliberately the path of least resistance between The Tooth Fairy and the South Face. About 4.8 km and 2,500 ft from the car.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to September, once the approach snow has gone; heavy weekend traffic in that window
hazards: Loose blocks on the open-book corner pitches
The route sits directly above the busy South Face — rockfall onto parties below is the documented concern here, not just a generic one
Rockfall risk to and from routes sharing the approach gully and the summit area
Descent route-finding: the broken west and north side offers several plausible gullies, and the loose east-side gully should not be rappelled
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A THING YOU DO NOT DO: DO NOT GO UP TO PINEAPPLE PASS. Hike the stable talus toward the pass and then leave it, heading NORTH of the gully that finishes at the pass. If you have stood in the notch at Pineapple Pass, you have overshot the start of this route and you are at the start of the South Face.

WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR ON THE ROCK: OPEN BOOKS. Pitches one and two climb open-book corners that begin north of the Pineapple Pass gully, and they lead to a LEFT-FACING SLAB. Corner, corner, then slab facing left. That sequence is the confirmation, and none of it requires seeing the summit.

AND A THIRD-PITCH CHECK IF YOU ARE STILL UNSURE: pitch three finds THREE CRACKS running up to an overhang, and the route face-climbs to the LEFT of those three cracks. Three cracks under a roof, and you go left of them. If you are climbing the cracks themselves you have drifted right.

HOW IT DIFFERS FROM ITS TWO NEIGHBOURS: The Tooth Fairy is further left again and goes at 5.9; the South Face starts from the notch at the top of the pass at 5.4. This route sits between them, both physically and in difficulty, at 5.5. If your first pitch feels like 5.9, you have gone too far left.

A WARNING THAT BELONGS WITH THE FINDING: this face is loose, and it sits above the popular routes. Being on the correct start also means being above other people.

approach_variants.name: Pinnacle Saddle, then east to the chute beside the western prominence
approach_variants.notes:
From the signed Pinnacle Saddle trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, across from the Reflection Lakes parking area, follow the maintained trail south. It switchbacks up through subalpine forest and meadow, passes beneath cliffs around 0.9 mile, and gains about 1,000-1,050 ft over 1.3 miles to the saddle at 5,920 ft between Pinnacle and Plummer.

At the saddle, leave the maintained tread and follow the unmaintained boot path roughly a quarter mile toward the western side of Pinnacle's south face, to the base of the obvious ascent chute.

From there, hike and scramble a mix of scree and loose rock along or below the ridge on the most-travelled line to a chute east of the western prominence. The chute climbs on increasingly steep, exposed but better-cleaned rock to top out near the summit.

Stevens Canyon Road is gated in winter and spring, typically opening around late May and closing at the first significant snowfall.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose rock and choss on the scree approach and lower chute
No fixed protection on the class 4 section; only natural horns and trees near the top
Increasing exposure in the upper chute as the rock steepens
Loose rock is more dangerous descending than ascending
Afternoon thunderstorms on a fully exposed south face
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PINNACLE SADDLE YOU GO EAST. PLUMMER PEAK IS WEST, AND THE BOOT PATHS FORK AT THE SADDLE, SO THIS IS A DECISION AND NOT A DEFAULT.

THE BASE IS DEFINED BY TWO OBJECTS AND THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THEM: A WESTERN PROMINENCE, AND AN OBVIOUS CHUTE IMMEDIATELY EAST OF IT. About a quarter mile of boot path from the saddle. If you cannot identify a prominence, you cannot identify the chute — go on until you can see one, rather than starting up the first weakness.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH CARRYING: THE CORRECT CHUTE GETS BETTER AS IT GETS STEEPER. The lower approach is scree and choss; the chute itself is progressively steeper AND progressively better-cleaned rock. SO IF THE ROCK IS GETTING LOOSER AS YOU CLIMB, YOU ARE IN THE WRONG GULLY. That is the reverse of what most loose volcanic scrambles do, and it is the most reliable signal on this route.

STAY ON THE MOST-TRAVELLED LINE ON THE APPROACH SCREE. There are multiple possible lines; the worst loose rock is off the beaten one.

A CLEAN NEGATIVE ABOUT HARDWARE: THERE IS NO FIXED PROTECTION ANYWHERE ON THIS ROUTE. Only natural options exist — a few horns and trees near the top that can be slung. IF YOU FIND BOLTS, A PITON, OR A FIXED STATION, YOU ARE ON ONE OF THE PEAK'S ROPED LINES, NOT ON THE SCRAMBLE. The East Ridge, in particular, has an old piton and a fixed rappel anchor.

DOWNCLIMB PLANNING AS PART OF THE FINDING: the class 4 section is more hazardous in descent than ascent because the rock is loose. Parties who intend to back off do it with an improvised sling on a horn or a tree near the top — worth spotting one on the way up.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp
bivy.notes: The base people reach for when Stevens Canyon Road is gated and Lane Peak or Pinnacle is the objective, since it puts you at the top of the road walk rather than the bottom. In practice most parties skip it: the Zipper and Lover's Lane, and Pinnacle and The Castle in winter dress, are routinely done car-to-car from the Narada Falls lot, and the honest variable on those routes is the approach and the snow stability, not where you slept. The reason to camp is the gate — the road above Longmire is closed overnight and reopens on a morning schedule, so a dawn start from a car is not available the way it is elsewhere. Habituated foxes here have a long record of working over unattended food.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow
bivy.permit: Winter wilderness permit, obtained IN PERSON at Longmire rather than online. Camping on snow is broadly allowed once the pack is deep enough, which the park sets at roughly two feet for the Reflection Lakes and Mazama Ridge side and five feet at Paradise itself. Blue bags for waste; food hung or in a hard-sided container.
bivy.capacity: Parties up to 12; anything larger is directed to the designated Paradise group area

access.fees: Lady of the Lake ferry fare (Chelan or Field's Point Landing to Lucerne) plus the Holden Village bus; Northwest Forest Pass at the Railroad Creek trailhead.
access.rules: Glacier Peak Wilderness regulations: Leave No Trace, group size limits, no motorized/mechanized travel. CURRENT CLOSURE: FR 8301 (Lucerne-Holden) and Holden Village are closed to hikers for the 2026 season following a Dec 2025 flood/landslide (Okanogan-Wenatchee NF order through Dec 31, 2027) — verify access is restored before planning this route.
access.permit: Self-issued wilderness permit; respect Holden Village access arrangements.
access.closures: Holden Village/FSR 8301 closed and boat shuttle suspended under USFS order #06-17-05-26-04, in effect 28 January 2026 through 31 December 2027.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District)
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at some trailheads (fee day-use sites) — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk (Phelps Creek, Trinity, Entiat River, or the Holden trailheads). Holden Village and its access road are closed to hikers through at least summer 2026.

road.name: Lake Chelan boat access to Lucerne, then Holden Village bus (no road to trailhead)
road.status: CLOSED for the 2026 season — FR 8301 between Lucerne Landing and Holden Village, and Holden Village itself, are closed to hikers following a December 10-11, 2025 flood/landslide; the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest closure order runs through December 31, 2027. Confirm current status with the Chelan Ranger District before planning this trip.
road.driveNote: Drive to Chelan or Field's Point Landing, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (~4 hr) to Lucerne, then a Forest Service/Holden Village bus to Holden Village; hike in via the Railroad Creek Trail to Hart Lake. No drivable road reaches the peak. NOTE: as of the Dec 2025 flood/landslide, FR 8301 and Holden Village are closed under USFS order #06-17-05-26-04, in effect 28 January 2026 through 31 December 2027 — this normal approach is not currently usable; check Chelan Ranger District status before relying on it.

weather.typical: N/A during the actual climbing window (late Aug-Sept, no snowpack on the buttress); only a shoulder-season attempt (June/Oct) would carry real avalanche/wet-slide exposure on approach snowfields, though the route is not practically climbed then anyway
weather.probability: Weather deterioration high on the face has essentially no good escape option per the FA team's own account

seasonal_hazards.exposure: HIGH — 2,300 ft of sustained, mostly gear-protected climbing on notably loose reddish rock bands ('if it's red, watch your head' per repeat parties); descent (a long, multi-hour gendarmed ridge traverse with rappels) is where benightment risk concentrates — getting caught there after dark is the single biggest tactical hazard

avalanche.zone: NWAC East Slopes North (nominal — Bonanza sits deep in wilderness well outside NWAC's typical field-observation network; treat as a rough regional proxy, not site-specific)

approach_variants.name: Railroad Creek Trail to Hart Lake, then the terraces to the North Star-Bonanza col
approach_variants.notes: From Holden Village follow Railroad Creek Trail #1256 WEST up the valley about 3.5 miles to Hart Lake at about 3,956 ft. The Holden Lake Trail branches off partway along and is NOT your turn — stay on the main valley trail the whole way. Hart Lake is the last easy water and the last straightforward walking. Leave the maintained trail at the lake and fill up, because the ground above holds very little water. Climb out of the lake basin onto the rock-and-heather terraces on the true left (west) side of the drainage, staying LEFT of the waterfalls and cliff bands that come down off the west-facing buttress. Open forest gives way to heather benches and then blocky, loose ground — roughly 3,000 ft of gain, two and a half to three hours, and genuinely routefinding-heavy. There is no trail above Hart Lake. Camp is the flat ground near the 7,100 ft col between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak, with snowmelt and tarns for water. The wall above this camp is one of the largest in the Cascades and carries THREE routes.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Aug into Sep, when the rock is driest
hazards: Rockfall from loose reddish rock bands, worst below the summit headwall
Almost no weather escape high on the route on a wall this size
A long descent traverse over a gendarmed ridge followed by two 200 ft rappels off anchors that are not fixed
Route-finding on the terraces above Hart Lake, which has no trail and is loose and brushy enough to be a crux of its own
Extreme remoteness and very few repeat ascents, so nothing about conditions can be inferred from recent traffic
