approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE SOVIET IS A CHIMNEY, AND IT IS NOT AT THE LOWEST POINT OF THE BUTTRESS. From camp cross the talus basin to the foot of the buttress — a little under an hour of walking on loose blocks with no trail. The climb starts about 60 FT ABOVE THE LOWEST POINT OF THE TOE, where a narrow chimney takes the first pitch at 5.7. Narrow chimney, 5.7, roughly a rope length: that is the confirmation. If your first pitch is a face, or if it is harder than 5.7, you are not on it.

LEFT TO RIGHT ACROSS THIS WALL, FACING IT FROM THE WEST, THE THREE ROUTES ARE: OREGONIAN, SOVIET, CASCADIAN. Learn that before you leave camp. The Soviet is the MIDDLE one, and the two neighbours identify themselves at the base by things you can see in poor light.

HOW TO KNOW YOU HAVE NOT GONE TOO FAR LEFT: the Oregonian is reached by walking PAST this buttress to the north and crossing the toe of a small POCKET GLACIER. If you have put crampons on, or stepped onto snow to reach rock, you have walked past the Soviet.

HOW TO KNOW YOU HAVE NOT GONE TOO FAR RIGHT: the Cascadian starts on WHITE SLABS beside a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and its opening pitch is an easy 5.4 scramble leading to an obvious large open book. Easy slabby ground and a big corner above means you are one route right of here.

THE ROUTE-FINDING KEY IS HIGH, NOT LOW, AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING FROM THE GROUND: around half height a SLOPING RAMP cuts diagonally across the buttress crest from east to west. That ramp is the whole line — it bypasses two headwalls that block anything direct. Below it there is a cave-like alcove used as a belay by both the first-ascent party and later parties, which is the one comfortable stance on the climb and a reliable position check.

WHAT THE ROCK TELLS YOU: it is meta-granitic and mostly good, with bands of loose RED rock. Below the summit headwall the rock turns visibly redder and looser. Favour solid grey stone where the line allows — where you are on red rock, you are where the route is at its worst, not where you are off it.

THE DESCENT IS NOT A REVERSE. From the Southwest Peak you traverse the north-east ridge to the West Peak over gendarmes with one short rappel, then make two roughly 200 ft rappels down slabs on the north-west side. Anchors there have historically been improvised — a nut and a piton on one recorded descent — so carry cord and rack for them and a rope long enough for 200 ft raps.

bivy.name: High camp near North Star-Bonanza pass (~7,100 ft)
Holden Village
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is CLOSED to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin over Leroy and Freezer passes to the Ice Lakes basin
approach_variants.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Phelps Creek Trail #1511 climbs the east side of the valley at roughly 275 ft per mile, crossing into the wilderness at 2.6 miles and reaching the Leroy Creek ford at about 3.5. Immediately across the ford the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route branches steeply north-east and climbs about 1.5 miles into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft, where the camps are. That half is hot and exposed under a pack.

From camp pick up the Carne Mountain high trail — an old sheepherder track — south-east; it gives up a little height to cross the south fork of Leroy Creek before climbing to Leroy Pass at 6,850 ft. Cairns mark the way but several paths braid apart in the basin: stay on the LOWER and better-trodden line where they diverge.

Continue east on faint footpaths through heather, then talus and scree, gaining about 750 ft over roughly a mile to Freezer Pass at 7,600 ft. There is no maintained tread here and the boot paths come and go, so TRACK YOUR OWN LINE FOR THE RETURN.

Drop north-east off the pass into the Ice Lakes basin, losing about 1,000 ft past the north end of Upper Ice Lake and down the dry stream bed to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake. Both lakes are reliable water.
approach_variants.season: Aug is the reliable month. Early-to-mid July can still hold snow and high water on the Freezer Pass traverse and at the washed-out stream bed; late September adds larch colour and takes away daylight
hazards: A washed-out gully crossing at 6,600 ft where dropping too low cliffs you out
Sustained loose rock and talus on the ridge and the scree ramp, with real rockfall risk onto anyone below
The north side of the south-west ridge is cliffy and must not be entered when the crags force you off the crest
No reliable water beyond the washout crossing — carry four to five litres in summer heat
Cairns that blend into the surrounding rock across the Ice Lakes traverse and on the descent from the summit block
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS AN OPEN BASIN FLOOR BETWEEN TWO SUMMITS AND THAT IS WHY IT IS FINDABLE IN CLOUD — you are not looking for a feature on a face, you are walking into a gap between the two Buttes at about 6,800 ft. The traverse eases into it. If the ground is still side-hilling and everything moves under your feet, you have not arrived.

GETTING THERE, THE ONE PLACE PEOPLE GET HURT: from Lower Ice Lake the old Ice Lakes Trail fades and you SIDEHILL EAST AT ABOUT 6,600 FT on slippery scrub and loose rock with no tread. Keep the party STRUNG OUT IN A LINE rather than stacked one above another — almost everything here moves. About a third of a mile brings the lip of a WASHED-OUT GULLY. Downclimb the loose clay and scree into it and climb the far side back to ABOUT THE SAME ELEVATION.

THAT ELEVATION RULE IS THE NEGATIVE MARKER AND IT HAS A STATED CONSEQUENCE: DROPPING TOO LOW IN THE WASHOUT LEAVES YOU CLIFFED OUT. Cross at 6,600, not below it. This is also the last reliable water before the summit, so fill there.

THE CLIMBING STARTS AT A RAMP: from the basin floor, a SCREE-AND-TALUS RAMP of about 400 ft gains the crest of the south-west ridge. Ramp first, ridge second. If you are on the crest without having walked up 400 ft of scree, you got onto the ridge somewhere else.

THE SIDE RULE ON THE RIDGE, AND IT IS ABSOLUTE: broken crags and short cliff bands repeatedly force the route OFF the crest onto ledges on the SOUTH side. THE NORTH SIDE OF THE RIDGE IS CLIFFY AND SHOULD NOT BE ENTERED. If you have been pushed off the crest and the ground below you drops away in a way that feels wrong, check which side you stepped onto before you commit.

THE CRUX HAS AN ELEVATION: around 7,700 ft a spire forces a short chossy chute, a traverse on down-sloping rock, and a Class 3 dike. Some parties call it low Class 4. That is the hardest ground and it is a single passage, not a section.

CAIRNS HERE BLEND INTO THE ROCK. On the way up that costs time; on the way down it costs a great deal more, because from the summit block you have to find the crest again at about 8,100 ft. Pick the line up deliberately rather than drifting down the first ledge system that goes.

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Challenger Col
approach_variants.notes: This is one of the longest approaches in the range and takes two or more travel days each way. From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead follow the maintained trail to the pass, then descend the far side into the Chilliwack valley, past the Copper Ridge branch, to the river ford below Easy Ridge — that low point is the bottom of the whole trip. Switchback back up onto Easy Ridge and follow the open, dry crest over Easy Peak to the bivy beyond it. Day two crosses the Imperfect Impasse, regains Challenger Col, and traverses the southern Challenger cirque to the west ridge of Phantom Peak, the usual second camp. From there it is cross-country across the western slopes to the foot of the ridge.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn; Easy Ridge is hot, dry and shadeless and would be brutal late in the season or in a dry year, so time it for when water is still running on the crest
hazards: Cold, thigh-deep Chilliwack ford in early season — cross before the afternoon melt
A bergschrund opens near the top of Challenger Col by mid to late season
The Imperfect Impasse must be downclimbed and re-ascended and is consistently slower than it looks
Sustained loose and shattered rock on the ridge, including a gendarme that needs a rappel into the gap
approach_variants.baseFinding: The ridge rises straight out of Pickle Pass, the gap immediately below the peak's serrated crest of hoodoos, and that pass is what you are aiming for on the traverse in from Phantom Peak; it holds snow well into the season and is sometimes skirted rather than crossed. Do not start in the entry notch itself. The line begins on the ground just to the RIGHT of that notch: roughly 100 ft of fourth class leads into blocky fifth-class rock, then easier low-fifth ground to a large ledge dotted with small trees, from which you traverse LEFT onto the crest proper. That tree-dotted ledge is the proof — it is the only vegetated terrace low on this side and it is the thing that puts you on the ridge. If you started in the notch and are fighting up a mossy gully, you are left of the line; the mossy gully is a feature the route deliberately keeps on its right higher up, not a place to begin.

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

approach_variants.name: Headlee Pass and Lake Elan
approach_variants.notes: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead the trail makes an awkward, sometimes roped crossing of the South Fork about half a mile in, climbs through forest to Wirtz Basin, then steepens sharply into a narrow, loose chute switchbacking to Headlee Pass. Beyond the pass the trail contours the peak's south and east flank and drops into the upper basin at Lake Elan. Leave the maintained trail at the lake outlet. Water is available at the river crossing and the lake and essentially nowhere above it, so fill before leaving.
approach_variants.season: July to early October, once the Headlee Pass chute is clear of snow
hazards: The South Fork crossing can be dangerous after heavy rain or in early-season melt
The Headlee Pass chute is notorious for rockfall from parties above and is an avalanche path in shoulder-season snow
Loose, often wet dirt and heather with class 3 steps on the upper third of the peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: The saddle between Vesper and Sperry, around 5,300 ft, is the base, and Lake Elan below it is the handrail. Follow the lake's EAST shore from the outlet and scramble the slabs above it directly to the saddle; there is very little path in the saddle itself, which is normal rather than a sign you are off route. From the saddle turn onto the south-west slope and pick up intermittent boot tread. The feature that tells you where the real route-finding begins is a down-sloping bench of talus and heather running across the face, separating a lower band of cliffs from an upper one. Below that bench the ground is easy and the tread is obvious; above it the line stops being obvious, the exposure comes on, and it becomes loose dirt, heather, short class 3 rock steps and a few tree-assisted moves to the summit block. If you are on continuous walkable heather with no cliff band above you, you are still below the bench. If you are contouring away from the saddle around the peak's south side, you are heading back toward Headlee Pass rather than up.

bivy.name: Sunrise Mine road end — the Sperry and Vesper Creek staging point
bivy.notes: This is the working start for SPERRY PEAK, and Sperry is honestly a day objective with no camp of its own — parties leave from here in the dark, ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, grind up through the talus of Wirtz Basin under Morning Star, take the switchbacked chute to Headlee Pass and traverse under Sperry's south side before scrambling the summit blocks. The only established camp on that line lies beyond the pass in the upper Vesper Creek basin, which the earlier upper-loop file already carries, so the realistic choice here is a long day from the car or a night in that basin. Sleeping at the road end is what most parties do and it works: the spur is short, and a pre-dawn start gets you through the chute before the day's rockfall gets going. Three things decide whether the trip happens at all. The FORD half a mile in is the real gate and it is not a formality — it runs hard in snowmelt and log crossings that worked one season are gone the next. The CHUTE below Headlee Pass is loose, narrow and known for rock coming down it, so parties should not stack up in it and helmets belong on well before the base. And SNOW holds in that chute and on the pass long after the valley is bare, which regularly turns a June or early-July attempt around. The spur itself is rough with potholes and encroaching brush; a low car can usually manage it slowly but scrapes are common. There is no cell coverage from the moment you leave the main loop road.
bivy.water: None at the road end. The creek crossings begin half a mile in and the first of them is the difficult one, so load every litre down in the valley rather than planning to draw here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass to leave a vehicle, and nothing else. This is national forest but NOT designated wilderness, so there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no party-size cap. Overnight parking is allowed. Fires at the road end are governed by whatever seasonal forest-wide restrictions are running, which from midsummer usually means no open flame at all.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only. A small gravel turnaround at the end of the spur with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and no sites, tables or pads. It overflows onto the road shoulder on summer weekends and the last cars in walk a fair way back to the trail start.

bivy.name: Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Sunrise Mine road, about ten miles below it on the paved section of the loop, and therefore the sensible base for SPERRY when you want a real night rather than a car bivy at a crowded road end. It is markedly closer to the Sunrise Mine spur than the larger campgrounds down at Verlot and much quieter, at the cost of fewer sites and no drinking water. Being on the paved lower loop it stays reachable all year and is entirely unaffected by whether the gravel section beyond Barlow Pass has opened for the season, which matters more here than it looks: that gravel stretch between Barlow Pass and the Bedal gate shuts each winter and typically does not open until somewhere in the second half of May. Barlow Pass itself is reached from this paved western side and normally opens earlier, but a slide anywhere below it closes everything above at a stroke and has done so recently, in which case basing low here and driving in each morning is the way to keep the trip. Sixteen sites go quickly on a fine Friday and none of them are reservable, so arrive early or have a fallback. Two group-only campgrounds sit within a couple of miles further up the same stretch, both reservation-only, and both are worth knowing about for a club climb that needs one site for a large party rather than several small ones. No cell coverage.
bivy.water: No potable supply on site. The South Fork Stillaguamish runs alongside and filters fine here — this is a different drainage from the mineralised Sauk-side ground above Barlow Pass, so the metals problem that dogs Gothic Basin does not apply.
bivy.permit: A developed fee campground on national forest land — the per-night fee is all that is needed and no pass or permit applies to the site itself. Nothing here is inside wilderness. Fires are allowed in the rings when seasonal restrictions permit, and those restrictions routinely shut them from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Around sixteen developed sites on the river bar, taking tents and small vehicles, with tables, fire rings and vault toilets. Fee campground, first come first served, open roughly late spring through early autumn.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: About one mile and 700 ft below Cache Col on a boot path. The usual first camp south of Cascade Pass and the base for Spider, Formidable and the south side of Magic.
bivy.water: The lake and snowmelt
bivy.permit: No permit required; the lake is outside the national park
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites on rock and heather benches around the lake

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: THE WORKING BASE CAMP FOR BOTH SPIDER MOUNTAIN AND MOUNT FORMIDABLE, and the reason to know about it is that a party climbing either peak stops here while a party walking the traverse does not. The twin notches of the col divide the two mountains, and it is reached by crossing the upper Middle Cascade Glacier almost due south from the Red Ledge. Spider Mountain is climbed from here by its south gully, stepping onto the buttress to the east and finishing along a corniced east ridge, about nineteen miles round trip from the Cascade Pass trailhead. Formidable is the other direction, and its south scramble is only class 3 but is long, loose, exposed and hard to route-find, with a fatality on record; the same ground is the only practical descent. Estimates of the col's height run from roughly 6,600 to 7,400 feet. The descent off the south side toward Yang Yang can be very steep snow and parties have resorted to a hand line anchored on buried pickets.
bivy.water: Water trickles off the slabs beside the col through most of the climbing season, which is unusual for ground this high and is the main reason the col gets used as a base rather than just crossed. It is meltwater, so it weakens through August and can stop entirely in a light snow year, and there is nothing else until the lakes well below on either side.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from. Camp on snow, rock or bare slab rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere south of Cache Col. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: A small number of party-sized spots split between the west notch of the col and the ground above the east pass, on glacial slabs and snow. Two parties is comfortable, three is crowded, and there is no toilet.

approach_variants.name: Spider-Formidable col to the south face
approach_variants.notes: From Cascade Pass follow the climbers' path across talus to Cache Col, drop the steep snowfields on its far side into the Kool-Aid Lake basin, then cross talus and scree east toward the peak's south side. A steep, narrow sidehill traverse reaches the fringe of the Middle Cascade Glacier, which is crossed roped to the Spider-Formidable col — an alternate and higher camp than the lake. The col has two notches; the left, eastern one is narrow and is the one that gives access to the far side.
approach_variants.season: Late July to mid-September
hazards: Crevasses on the Middle Cascade Glacier — rope up
The gully is choked with loose rock and holds parties above you
The rock throughout is schist and notoriously rotten
The summit arete is corniced; stay on its south side
approach_variants.baseFinding: One feature settles this: a prominent rock buttress bisects the peak's south face, and the gully you want is the one immediately to its RIGHT, to the east. Get there by dropping off the south side of the col — slither down the shallow moat beside the steep snow finger rather than fighting the snow itself — then traverse eastward across a broad slope of dirt, scree and talus cut by erosion runnels, angling up toward the face. The proof at the gully's foot is a deep, ugly erosion runnel spewing out of its mouth. Rather than crossing that runnel head-on, take the talus ramp beside it that leads up and into the gully. Inside, the gully is very narrow, quite steep and completely choked with loose rock: if the gully you are in is broad, clean or comfortable, it is the wrong one. If the big central buttress is on your RIGHT rather than your left, you have gone one gully too far west.

approach_variants.name: North Fork Skykomish riverside to the northwest saddle
approach_variants.notes: Everything above the valley is off-trail. Leave the riverside near the road and head directly up the steep, blowdown-choked slope — the first several hundred feet are the worst of it — onto a well-defined hogsback that runs from about 2,700 ft to roughly 3,300 ft. Above the hogsback the slope steepens toward cliff bands, and there is no tread anywhere on the mountain. Carry water from the river; there is none once you leave it, and there is no usable cell coverage anywhere on route.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Entirely off-trail with sustained blowdown and brush low down
Cliff bands on the north side between roughly 4,200 and 4,400 ft that need careful route-finding to turn
A moat or bergschrund forming at the saddle depending on snow cover
Permanent snow and ice on north and east aspects near the summit even in late summer
A short exposed class 5 step considerably harder than the route's overall grade suggests
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling starts at a saddle around 5,940 ft northwest of the summit, and you identify it by what you crossed to reach it. Large cliff bands block the north end of the peak between roughly 4,200 and 4,400 ft; the way past is a traverse SOUTHEAST beneath them onto the mountain's west and northwest side, and that traverse ends by rising onto a distinct notch on the ridge rather than onto any summit. Depending on the season a moat or bergschrund forms right at the saddle and is the last obstacle before you get on rock. Spire has three summits and the crest above the saddle is airy: mostly class 3, but with a short exposed mantle step of roughly ten feet at about 6,100 ft where many parties put a rope on, harder than the peak's overall billing prepares you for. Do not stray north or east off the crest — that ground steepens quickly into permanent snow and cliffs — and note the traverse line carefully, because reversing it through the cliff bands with no tread to follow is slow work.

bivy.name: San Juan Campground, Index-Galena road
bivy.notes: The nearest developed camp to the Spire Mountain roadhead, sitting on the Index-Galena road a few miles below where the climb starts. It spent close to two decades unreachable by vehicle after flood damage took out the road, and access has been restored and lost again more than once since; treat its availability as a question to answer before you drive rather than an assumption. When the road is cut at the North Fork bridge it is unreachable from the Beckler River side entirely. Even when it is open it is a low, damp, mosquito-heavy site in early summer, and its value is convenience rather than pleasure — it puts a party within twenty minutes of the start of the Spire approach, which is worth a great deal on a climb that wants a pre-dawn departure. Beckler River Campground and Troublesome Creek Campground serve the same road system and are covered in the neighbouring zone, so check those first if this one is closed.
bivy.water: River water only, treated. There is no potable supply.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee when it is operating. No wilderness permit is involved at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A small forest campground of a dozen or so sites in second-growth beside the North Fork Skykomish, with vault toilets and no water system.

bivy.name: Spire Mountain — the saddle northwest of the summit
bivy.notes: Spire Mountain has no established camping of any kind and most parties climb it in a single very long day, which is the honest answer. The route is entirely off-trail: leave the Index-Galena road at the snowplow turnaround just past the bridge, drop south into old forest, and fight through six hundred feet of steep ground choked with fallen timber before the slope becomes merely steep. Cliffs on the north end of the mountain are turned between about 4,200 and 4,400 feet, then a rising traverse southeast reaches open ground around 5,400 feet below the summit spire. The saddle above that, northwest of the true summit, is the only ground on the route flat enough to lie down on, and a party that has misjudged the day will end up there whether they planned to or not. From it the last three hundred feet are technical enough that most rope up for short exposed sections. ROAD STATUS IS THE LIMITING FACTOR: the Index-Galena road has repeatedly been cut by flood damage and bridge failure on the North Fork Skykomish, and when the bridge is out the road is simply not drivable from the Beckler River road, which adds many miles of walking to an approach that is already brutal. Confirm the road is open before committing to this peak. Best season is late July to early October, once the timber is dry and before the first storms make the traverse slabs greasy.
bivy.water: None. There is no water anywhere on this route once you leave the North Fork Skykomish at the road, and the saddle holds nothing but lingering snow patches into July. Carry everything, or melt snow early season.
bivy.permit: Wild Sky Wilderness, no permit required. Parking is a roadside pullout, so no forest pass is needed there.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties at most, on whatever flat ground the ridge crest offers. There is no established site here and nothing has been built.

approach_variants.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, the fixed-rope climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
Drive east over Washington Pass and park in the turnout about two miles beyond it, near milepost 165, at roughly 4,900 ft. This is a highway pullout, not a trailhead — nothing is signed.

The climbers' path leaves the WEST or south-west end of the turnout and drops steeply through loose dirt and rock into the trees. It is well worn but unmarked apart from intermittent cairns. It crosses Early Winters Creek on logs and resumes on the far side, then climbs into an open rocky drainage and talus below the formation.

Higher up the old line uses TWO OR THREE FIXED LINES on an avalanche path before topping out on a flat area. A newer variation bears RIGHT just before the fixed lines are reached and needs only a small amount of scrambling; most parties now prefer it. Reckon roughly an hour and a half.

Do not treat the fixed ropes as maintained equipment. They are informal, weathered, and nobody replaces them on a schedule.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the creek crossing and the approach snowfield have melted out
hazards: Weathered informal fixed ropes on the old approach line; the newer right-bearing variation avoids them
Early Winters Creek is crossed on logs and is worse in high water
Long unroped scrambling between pitches on a route people rack up for as a 5.7
Rappelling the line is slow and ropes snag on flakes, sometimes needing re-ascent to free them
The alternative descent gully is loose and sits above the approach path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MARKER AT THE BASE IS DEAD TREES. As the ground steepens toward the formation and BEFORE the gully, look on your LEFT for TREE SNAGS — standing dead timber against the rock. The first pitch climbs cracks up from a snag. That is the start, and it is the only start on this formation with a landmark you can walk up and touch.

If you have entered the gully itself, you have gone too far right. The gully parallels this route and is used both as a descent and as a fast way to reach the bolted line beside it — it is not this climb.

CONFIRM ON PITCH TWO, which is the strongest check the route gives you: it TRAVERSES UNDER A ROOF. If your second pitch runs sideways beneath an overhang rather than straight up, you are on line. Above that expect steepening ground with cracks and a good layback, then a wide ten-inch crack with finger and hand sections, then a corner crack to lieback, and a headwall finish.

Expect long SCRAMBLING SECTIONS BETWEEN THE PITCHES. That is this route's defining character and the main complaint about it — it is the reason a 5.7 with seven pitches takes a full day. Continuous roped climbing with no walking between would mean you are somewhere else.

NEGATIVE MARKERS for the two neighbours. If you have traversed a long way rightward from the base on third and fourth-class ledges toward the middle of the face before starting, you are heading for the hard line that finishes on this route's last pitches. And if your first pitch is protected by BOLTS, you are on the partly bolted line — this route takes natural gear throughout.

Descent is most often a rappel of the line itself, and parties report it is slow and that ropes snag on flakes. The alternative is the third-class gully to climbers' right, faster but loose; stay high and skier's-right to limit what is above you.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, then the gully paralleling the arete
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the highway turnout about two miles east of Washington Pass, near milepost 165. The climbers' trail starts at the FAR WEST END of the pullout, drops steeply through loose dirt and rock, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs, then traverses an avalanche path — the old line has two or three informal fixed rope sections here — toward the base of the formation. Around an hour and a half.

A newer variation of the path bears RIGHT just before the fixed lines and needs only a small amount of scrambling, which most parties now prefer.

There are two ways to reach this route once you are under the formation, and they are genuinely different days. The faster one takes the GULLY THAT PARALLELS the arete beside it. The other climbs the first three pitches of that arete and then cuts across the gully, which is how parties who wanted a longer outing get here.
approach_variants.season: July through September; snow and debris linger on the avalanche-path approach into early summer
hazards: Positioned only in relation to its neighbour and a gully; the bolts are the only absolute identifier
The gully approach sits below the climbing and takes anything the parties above knock off
Snow and debris linger on the avalanche-path section of the approach into early summer
Weathered informal fixed ropes on the old approach line
Early Winters Creek is crossed on logs and is worse in high water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECIDING TEST IS BOLTS, AND IT IS ABSOLUTE. This is the only partly bolted line on the formation; both neighbours are natural gear from bottom to top. If you cannot see a bolt from the ground, you are not at the start of this route.

Work out first which side of the gully you are on. The arete route starts by the TREE SNAGS on the left before the gully. This route lies BESIDE that gully on the lower buttress, and the fast way to it is up the gully itself rather than up the arete.

The start is found by a shape and then confirmed by hardware: look for a LEFT-TRENDING OVERLAP low on the rock, and the FIRST BOLT sits just above it. Overlap below, bolt above — that is the start. Pitch one then runs over three bolts on face climbing.

CONFIRM ON PITCH TWO, because it is the only place a wrong line would still look plausible: you climb past TWO BOLTS to a crack, and then at the THIRD BOLT you TRAVERSE RIGHT onto easier cracks to the anchor. A rightward traverse at a bolt on the second pitch is this route. Pitch three is effectively a sport pitch with a hard start that eases after the first twenty feet; pitch four is fun moderate cracks to the top.

NEGATIVE MARKERS. If you are climbing cracks up from a dead tree snag with no fixed gear anywhere, you are on the arete. If you got here by traversing hundreds of yards rightward across the face on ledges and started up a long easy chimney, you are on the hard line that finishes on the arete's top pitches. Neither of those has a bolt in it.

The count matters too: FOUR pitches. Descend by rappelling the route on a single seventy-metre rope. Parties finishing higher on the formation can instead come down the arete's rappel line to reach the gully near this route.

bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core Enchantments to the middle of the south face
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then climb Aasgard Pass — about 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose scree, the physical crux of the approach. Into early July, snow can bridge a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; that hazard has caused serious injuries and at least one death.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, drop gently into the upper Core basin and travel cross-country north over slabs and heather past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, the usual bivy. The base of the south face is roughly fifteen to twenty minutes from there.

Overnight camping in the Core Zone needs a permit, so many parties do the whole thing in one long day instead.

When Aasgard or this trailhead is closed, the Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative, reaching the same face past Lake Viviane.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is clear of the snow that bridges the creek beneath it
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the last stretch, with no tread
A flaring squeeze chimney at mid-height that is awkward with a pack
A shared north-side rappel descent that gets congested when several parties are on the face
Snafflehounds at the base and at bivy sites will chew boots and gear left out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ROUTE IN THE MIDDLE, AND THAT IS THE FIRST AND MOST USEFUL FACT. Walking along the foot of the south face, the start sits at about the MIDDLE of the base. The lines on the left flank of the face all top out on the West Ridge; this one is the classic that goes to the actual summit.

THE FEATURE TEST: you are looking for a chimney system on steep white granite. Pitch one takes either a 5.6/5.7 chimney or a wide crack immediately LEFT of that chimney, and lands on low fifth-class ground with trees on it. Trees at the top of your first pitch is a good confirmation.

HOW TO TELL IT FROM ITS TWO NEIGHBOURS, which is the actual problem on this face because three routes start within a hundred feet of each other:
  - If you can see TWO PROMINENT V-SHAPES on the face and you are at a chimney to the LEFT of them, you are at Beckey-Davis — one route too far RIGHT.
  - If you are about fifty feet LEFT of where you think the standard line is, you are at Der Sportsman, and its first pitch is 5.11+ rather than 5.7. A first pitch that feels desperate is the loudest possible signal you are on the wrong route.

STARTING COORDINATE, published for pitch one: roughly 47.48681, -120.78457. In fog with a GPS that is decisive; on a clear day the shape of the face is better.

AND THE ARRIVAL CONFIRMATION HIGHER UP: pitch five squeezes between a chockstone into a flaring chimney, and pitch six is a left-facing corner to the SUMMIT. If your route runs out on the West Ridge instead of the summit, you are on one of the left-flank lines.

approach_variants.name: Lower Town Wall lot, right along the base to the Main Wall
approach_variants.notes: US 2 to the Index turnoff, Avenue A west about 0.6 miles to the small gravel lot before the railway, cross the active tracks, bear left onto the trail and take the RIGHT branch along the base of the Lower Wall to the Main Wall. Five minutes.
approach_variants.season: Any dry day
hazards: Railway crossing on the approach
Car break-ins are frequent at the Lower Wall parking
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Start as for Japanese Gardens — roughly midway between Princely Ambitions and Godzilla, in the short left-facing dihedral — and then trend RIGHT into the corner instead of coming back left.

So the ground marker is not this route's own; it is Japanese Gardens'. The divergence happens above the start, and getting it wrong in the other direction is how Japanese Gardens parties accidentally end up on a 5.12 corner.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, then traverse the ledge EAST and climb the long steep hillside above — about 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close annually for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep approach hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep, coarse granite; the moderates here are scarce
Northwest aspect — shaded and cold in the morning
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up and right from Logger's Ledge you meet the LEFT side of Midnight Rock first. Midnight is the tall, vertical-to-overhanging face of about 300 ft, full of parallel-sided cracks and facing northwest; Noontime alongside it is barely developed, so a near-empty wall means you have walked too far. This route matters as an access line as much as a climb: Stevens Pass Motel is one of the three routes — with The Sting and Wasp — used to reach the enormous ledge that runs across the middle of the CENTRE section of Midnight Rock. ROTC and other lines start from that ledge rather than the ground. So the confirmation that you are in the right part of the wall is what is above you: a large mid-height ledge system cutting the centre of the face. If there is no such ledge overhead, you are at the wrong end of the crag. No source consulted for this pass gives this route's own start marker at ground level; confirm against a topo.

approach_variants.name: The shared Goode approach to 7,400 ft, then the talus cirque and the right-most notch
approach_variants.notes:
Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek and is one of the range's most remote summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Goode's south side.

The most common is Thunder Creek: from Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, the Thunder Creek trail roughly 13 miles with little gain to the McAllister Creek confluence, past Junction, Skagit Queen and Thunder Basin camps, then the Park Creek Pass trail junction and the switchbacks to PARK CREEK PASS. Alternatives are McAlester Pass and Rainbow Creek from SR-20, or a boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp then the Park Creek trail from the south. From Stehekin the boot path starts on the north side of a large whitish-rock washout about two miles above the Two Mile camp, near 4,100 ft, five minutes further into the woods.

Every approach joins that trail: from Thunder Creek, cross Park Creek Pass and descend its south side to the washout. Leave the trail at the small cairn, climb the burned ridge beside the washout ravine, trend climber's left through heather and game trails, and follow cairns above about 6,500 ft to the basin below Goode at about 7,400 ft. From there, traverse snow and talus, favouring climber's left, roughly a mile to the cirque below Storm King's east and west towers. A rib camp around 7,450 ft with nearby water is the usual base.

From the cirque, a long and very loose talus and scree slope leads up toward the southwest gully system. Helmet on and space out — that slope is the approach's main hazard.
approach_variants.season: Late July through September; snow often lingers in the basin above about 7,400 ft into early August, so carry an axe and consider crampons even for a nominally dry climb
hazards: Loose blocky rock on the talus approach and the summit ridge, with rockfall onto parties below
Lingering snow and ice in the basin and the summit gully into early August, and bullet-hard patches
An exposed class 4 ledge traverse just below the summit with real fall consequences
In-situ slings at the crux that are aging tat and need backing up before they are weighted
Extreme remoteness — assume a multi-day evacuation or a helicopter for any serious injury
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW ABOUT THIS APPROACH IS THAT BELOW 7,400 FT IT IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM GOODE MOUNTAIN'S. The same trail, the same basin, the same cairned climber's path. A party in fog below that elevation cannot tell from the ground which peak's route it is on. The split happens above it, where this route trends toward the towers while Goode's continue toward the glacier or Black Tooth Notch.

THE COUNTING TEST IS THE NOTCH, AND THE WORD IS RIGHT-MOST. There are several notches in the summit rocks; the route crosses at the RIGHT-MOST one. Most of the way up to it is loose scree and talus, which is what makes the notch worth confirming rather than guessing.

CROSS TO THE NORTH SIDE OF THAT NOTCH AND THE GROUND CHANGES CHARACTER COMPLETELY: a fun ledge traverse on the BACKSIDE of the tower, roughly 70 ft, with two or three class 4 moves and full exposure. IF YOU HAVE NOT CROSSED TO THE NORTH SIDE, YOU HAVE NOT FOUND THE LEDGE TRAVERSE, and there is no version of this route that goes up the front.

CONFIRM ON THE LEDGE: it includes a SQUEEZE UNDER A SLIGHT OVERHANG, and there are IN-SITU SLINGS at the crux left by earlier parties. A squeeze move plus old tat is the strongest positive confirmation on the climb — though the tat is aging and is not to be trusted with body weight without backup.

THE LAST MOVE IS A CHOICE, NOT A CRUX: a 15-ft solid class 4 face crack, or a wrap around its LEFT side on class 3 blocks. Both reach the register and the rappel slings.

AND KNOW WHICH TOP YOU WANT: two 8,520-ft-plus points sit east of a triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit, and the EASTERNMOST is the true high point.

bivy.name: Rib camp below Storm King/Goode basin
bivy.notes: Flat, grassy camp on a small NE/SW-trending rib just south of Storm King, with a nearby water source. It is reached by a mostly level traverse from the basin below Goode.

bivy.name: Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

bivy.name: Junction Camp
bivy.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fisher Basin and Easy Pass leaves from here, so it also works as a hinge for loop itineraries. The climb up gains roughly a thousand feet in a bit over two miles and is the first real work of the approach.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is the source and is dependable, but the camp sits on a bench well above it, so water means a descent and a climb back with full bottles. Arrive with enough to cook on if you get in late.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the rest of the corridor. Fire rings and a privy are present here, unlike the cross-country zones higher up — but confirm current fire restrictions on the permit rather than assuming the rings mean fires are legal.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, one tucked away and more private than the others. A separate stock camp sits nearby. The quota is small enough that a weekend party without a reservation should have a fallback in mind.

bivy.name: Skagit Queen Camp
bivy.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but high water in the side creeks earlier in the season is still worth asking about at the permit desk.
bivy.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. The quota applies to the specific camp and night, so an itinerary that slips a day needs the permit amended rather than ignored.
bivy.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

bivy.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
bivy.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
bivy.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED AT PARK CREEK PASS ITSELF, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
bivy.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley in spring, river braids and a camp below the face
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road, NF-56, to its plowed or drivable end, then bike or hike the remaining distance — about a mile in the first-ascent party's case — into the valley.

Continue on foot through snowy forest along the valley trail, crossing MULTIPLE BRAIDS of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie. Those crossings are the crux of the approach in high water and are unprotected. Then climb to a camp below the north face. The first-ascent party took about six and a half hours from vehicle to camp.
approach_variants.season: A narrow spring window, roughly March to April, while the ice and snowfields are in. This line forms only briefly and has almost no repeat trip-report history
hazards: A rarely-climbed alpine ice route with essentially no repeat beta
Difficult, unprotected crossings of multiple river braids on the approach
Avalanche and wet-slide hazard on the spring approach and the snowfields
Near-constant spindrift funnelling down the runnels during and after storm; spindrift avalanches swept the face during the first ascent party's descent
Scarce rock protection between ice sections
A descent by an unfamiliar side of the peak at the end of a committing route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST AND MOST IMPORTANT FINDING IS WHETHER THERE IS ANYTHING TO FIND. This face is condition-only. The single published account is the first ascent, and it describes roughly 2,000 vertical feet linking runnels and couloirs, with the defining section being a RAMP HOLDING ABOUT 600 VERTICAL FEET OF WATER ICE at WI2 to WI3. If that ramp is not iced, there is no route at the base and no amount of searching will produce one. Look for the ramp from the valley before committing to the walk in.

THE ARRIVAL ITSELF IS A CAMP, NOT A NOTCH: you are aiming for camp below the face, and the base of the climb is the lowest runnel beneath the ice ramp. There is no published discriminating feature at ground level beyond the ramp, and there is nothing else to look for.

THE SEQUENCE ABOVE, SO YOU CAN CHECK YOURSELF ONCE COMMITTED: about 600 ft of WI2-3 water ice on the ramp, then a first snowfield, then a second snowfield, then an AI2 exit step near the summit. Two distinct snowfields separated by easier ground is the confirmation you are on the line the first ascent took.

A PROTECTION WARNING THAT BELONGS WITH THE FINDING BECAUSE IT COMES FROM THE ONLY PARTY WHO HAS BEEN THERE: they carried only two titanium ice screws and found that badly short for the ice actually encountered, supplementing with knifeblade pitons in compact rock between ice sections. Rock protection on the ice section is scarce. Carry a real screw rack.

AND PLAN THE DESCENT BEFORE YOU START, BECAUSE RETREAT FROM HIGH ON THE FACE IS NOT SIMPLE: the first ascent did not reverse the route. They descended the SOUTHWEST side, downclimbing neve and making two 30 m rappels down a snow gully to a col west of the peak.

READ EVERYTHING ABOVE AS ONE PARTY'S CONDITIONS, NOT AS AN ANNUAL EXPECTATION.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and the PCT switchbacks to the Vista Lakes tarns
approach_variants.notes:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying BELOW the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, but see the moat note — the gate at 7,000 ft can shut by mid-July, earlier in a thin snow year
hazards: A moat around 7,000 ft that can close the route outright after mid-July
Icy gully beyond the notch in the morning — crampons are worth carrying for it
Steep dirt and very loose rock on the final five hundred feet
Rockfall from parties above on the hardpan and talus below the notch
No water at all above the Vista Lakes
Sloping slabs on the traverse from camp, avoidable by dropping to the scree around 6,000 ft
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is a specific chain of features here and it ends at a piece of ground that is unmistakable once you know to look for it.

From the upper basin, find a small NOTCH in the skyline ridge to the west. To reach it, head north-west toward a MINOR ROCK RIDGE that runs west-south-west to east-north-east across the base of the summit. That minor ridge IS the base of the climb — arriving at it is arriving.

Gain it by the snow in the gap at its RIGHT, LOWER end, then walk along the top of the ridge to the notch at its WEST end. On the far side of the notch is a steep gully, usually icy in the morning, and beyond that a loose-rock gully; the exit is the gully on the right just below the summit.

NEGATIVE MARKER, learned the hard way and independently corroborated: from the snowfield below the south-east face, the FIRST and LEFT-MOST snow finger leading to the south ridge is a dead end. It runs into a deep notch and the party that took it had to retreat. Go instead to the UPPER RIGHT corner of the snowfield, exit onto steep dirt and scree, and pick up a left-slanting ramp to a higher notch. Two separate accounts arrive at the same instruction from opposite directions.

THE MOAT IS THE GATE and it has a date on it. Where the mountain rises in earnest at about 7,000 ft a moat forms, and it may be impassable after mid-July, perhaps earlier in a low-snow year. If it stops you, there may be Class 3 rock in the middle of the basin as an alternative, but plan the trip around the calendar rather than hoping.

Do not trust a single photograph for the crossing point on the south ridge; parties report the pictures circulating online do not match the ground.

The top five hundred feet is steep dirt and thoroughly untrustworthy rock — one climber said it had earned honorary Olympic Mountains status. That looseness is normal for this summit and is not a sign you have wandered onto harder ground.

approach_variants.name: Lemah Meadow shortcut, cutting the PCT switchbacks
approach_variants.notes: A recorded variant that saves about three miles. After gaining roughly a thousand feet on the tight PCT switchbacks, leave the trail at the corner around 4,000 ft and head north, climbing about six hundred feet to the crest. The party who did it found plenty of windfall and pockets of vine maple, and called it irritating rather than difficult. It is a single-source variant, so treat the line as a hint rather than a route.
approach_variants.season: Same window; the bypass is brushier and is a trade of distance for thrashing
hazards: Windfall and vine maple on the bypass
No tread and no cairns
Same moat and loose-rock hazards above
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The shortcut rejoins the standard line on the crest above and does not change where the climbing starts. Everything from the upper basin onward is as for the standard approach: the skyline notch to the west, the minor rock ridge running west-south-west across the base of the summit, the snow gap at its lower right end, and the moat around 7,000 ft as the real gate.

What you lose by taking it is the view of the peak that the PCT switchbacks give you on the way up, so identify the minor ridge and the notch from the basin rather than expecting to have already picked them out.

approach_variants.name: Bedal Creek on skis to the 5,000 ft meadow, then the right-hand line on the west face
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bedal Creek Trailhead on FR-4096 the approach is normally skinned — the road is not plowed, so in a normal winter the skinning starts below the trailhead. Four to five hours gets you into the Bedal Creek valley and the meadow beneath the west face around 5,000 ft. Parties commonly carry on up the spur ridge west of the peak to about 5,700 ft and leave skis there before the technical ground.

The climb is about 1,000 ft: an approach pitch of rambly ice, a solid near-vertical curtain of roughly 25 ft at WI4, then close to 60 m of fat WI3 in the main gully, 100 m and more of easier ground with ice smears through an easy chimney, and a short WI3 step before the upper snowfields.

It was first climbed to the snowfields rather than to the top; the continuation to the summit was done later. Above the ice there are several hundred feet of snowfield left before you are anywhere.
approach_variants.season: Late Nov to mid-Mar, most reliably Jan-Feb when a settled cold spell has let the ice form
hazards: Wet loose avalanche on the steep upper snowfields becoming likely by midday
Rockfall and spindrift increasing through the afternoon as the west face warms
A descent choice that must be made in advance — V-threads down the line, or up and over to the standard descent
Unplowed road access, so a slow day ends with a long ski out in the dark
Ice that forms only in settled cold; a warm week can leave the whole feature unclimbable
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE OBVIOUS LINE ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF THE FACE, AND "OBVIOUS" IS THE TEST RATHER THAN A FIGURE OF SPEECH. Standing in the meadow beneath the west face, the steep weakness on the RIGHT is the one that reads as a line from a distance. Every other winter route on this face is to its LEFT and none of them look as continuous. If you have walked left of centre looking for something better, you have left this route.

START HEIGHT: about 5,700 ft, gained by climbing the spur ridge west of the peak out of the 5,000 ft meadow. That 700 ft of rise between the meadow and the start is the reason parties leave skis at the top of it — it is where walking stops.

THE POSITIVE TEST AT THE BASE: there are several flows in the bottom of the feature and any of them will get you started; they all lead into ONE ice gully proper. So do not stand and choose. Climb the easiest flow you can reach and expect the ground to funnel — if it does not funnel into a single gully within a rope length or two, you are not on it.

THE CONFIRMATION IS A CURTAIN, AND IT COMES SECOND. The first real difficulty is a solid, roughly 25 ft near-vertical curtain at WI4 above the rambly start, and above that close to a full rope length of fat WI3. Rambly first, curtain second. If your FIRST ground above the snow is steep and hard, you are on one of the harder lines to the left.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER THAT MATTERS MOST: the central weakness left of this route carries lines with a hanging dagger and an overhanging mixed crux on fixed pitons. If you find yourself under a dagger, or looking at fixed pins in overhanging rock, you are on a route two grades harder than the one you came for.

WHERE IT ENDS IS NOT THE TOP. The ice runs out into upper snowfields several hundred feet below the summit. Finishing the ice is not finishing the mountain, and by then the west face has been in the sun.

approach_variants.name: Lake Ann, then right onto the Lower Curtis Glacier to its upper southeast corner
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR-542, about a mile below Artist Point at roughly 4,770 ft, take Lake Ann Trail #600 to the lake and on toward the Fisher Chimneys.

Before the Chimneys, traverse RIGHT — east — onto the Lower Curtis Glacier and follow it up to the upper southeast corner of the glacier basin. This is where the technical climbing starts, at the foot of the icefall.

The descent for this route goes back via the Hourglass and the Upper Curtis to the Shuksan Arm — the Fisher Chimneys descent — so the day is a loop rather than a reverse, and the whole thing is commonly cited at around eight hours round trip from Lake Ann.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Aug
hazards: A large transverse crevasse across the line in the first 100 ft
Icefall exposure at the foot of the upper southeast corner
About 1,000 ft of easy fifth-class buttress climbing with alpine protection
A descent by a different line (Hourglass and Upper Curtis to the Shuksan Arm), so the way home is not the way up
Crevasses on the Lower Curtis on the approach traverse
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FISHER CHIMNEYS ARE THE JUNCTION, AND THE INSTRUCTION IS ONE WORD: RIGHT. Everyone else on this trail is going up the Chimneys. You go right, east, onto the Lower Curtis. If you are climbing a chimney system, you have missed the turn.

ARRIVAL: keep going up the glacier until you are in the UPPER SOUTHEAST CORNER of the basin — the deepest, highest inside corner of the cirque, where the glacier runs out against the mountain. The base is at the foot of the ICEFALL. In cloud, the corner is found by feel: keep the rock on your right and climb until the glacier stops going anywhere.

THE FIRST HUNDRED FEET CONFIRMS IT, and this is the strongest test on the route. The climbing opens with about 100 ft of steep snow leading to a LARGE TRANSVERSE CREVASSE running across the line. That crevasse is unmistakable, it is at the start rather than in the middle, and it is the thing that tells you you are in the right corner. Above it is roughly 300 ft of steep ice and snow to the base of the headwall.

WHAT BEING IN THE WRONG CORNER LOOKS LIKE: if the first 100 ft of snow leads to open glacier rather than to a crevasse spanning your line, you are still out in the basin. If the ground above the first steep snow is a rock wall you cannot get above in 300 ft, you are too far east against the headwall proper.

AND THE SEQUENCE ABOVE, worth carrying because it double-checks the start: at the base of the headwall the route traverses LEFT to a weakness, 100 ft of fourth class to a ledge, then left again around a corner onto a buttress. A route that never traverses left is not this one.

approach_variants.name: The northern line: Access Creek and Luna Col, then the high traverse over Luna, East Fury and West Fury to the Swiss-Fury saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Dam Trailhead at milepost 134 on WA-20, about a mile of trail and service road drops to Ross Lake, crossed by the resort water taxi or by paddling or walking round. Pick up the Big Beaver Trail north along the lake and follow it roughly 10 miles to Luna Camp, then about 1.5 miles further to the Access Creek drainage.

Leave the trail and climb the brushy, moderately steep Access Creek valley, staying on its north side, to the open basin east of Luna Peak at about 4,300 ft. This is described as the easiest and least brushy approach on the east side of the Pickets. From there, gain Access Col and traverse cross-country and glaciated terrain over Luna Peak, East Fury and West Fury to reach the Swiss-Fury saddle.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A full traverse of both Fury summits simply to reach the saddle
Glaciated terrain between Luna Col and the Fury summits
One of the most remote positions in the range, with no independent descent
Very little published route detail, and the peak itself is imprecisely located
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE IS A SADDLE BETWEEN TWO NAMED SUMMITS AND YOU REACH IT BY HAVING CROSSED BOTH SUMMITS OF FURY. That is a hard test to fail and a hard one to pass: there is no way to arrive at the Swiss-Fury saddle by this line without having traversed West Fury, so if you have not climbed Fury, you are not there. ARRIVAL: a saddle is the low point between two rises. From it, this route climbs the southwest face, and the descent runs back down near the NORTHWEST ridge toward the same saddle. If the ground above you steepens into a face rather than a ridge, that is the route. WHY THERE IS SO LITTLE HERE, SAID PLAINLY: Swiss Peak has one described route and no first-ascent record, the peak itself is not precisely located, and nothing published locates a feature at the foot of the southwest face. What is locatable is the saddle and the ridge. Do not expect a cairn, a gully or a flake to confirm you; expect the shape of the col.
