WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: continuing northwest along the crest past Swiss takes you toward the ground the Northern Pickets traverse uses, with no easier way down on that side.

approach_variants.name: The southern line: Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly and Mystery Ridges, Jasper Pass and Crowder's northeast ridge to Pickell Pass
approach_variants.notes:
The alternate, and the shorter of the two in spirit if not in effort. It reaches Swiss from the south via Bacon Creek Road, Porkbelly Ridge, Mystery Ridge, Jasper Pass, Pioneer Ridge and Mount Crowder's northeast ridge, down to a camp at Pickell Pass.

This line is off-trail for most of its length and is described only in outline, so treat the ridge sequence as the route rather than any particular tread.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A long off-trail ridge sequence with no maintained tread
No independent descent; exiting the range means committing to one of the long approach drainages
Very little published detail for either approach to this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM PICKELL PASS THE SOUTH SIDE OF SWISS IS CLIMBED DIRECTLY, AND THE TEST IS THAT YOU ARE GOING UP RATHER THAN ALONG. Camp is a heather bench at the pass; the climbing starts on the class 3 south side immediately above it. Parties on this line downclimb the same class 3 south side back to the bench, so the ascent and descent are the same ground, and a party that has to traverse to find its line has left the route.

HOW TO KNOW YOU ARE AT PICKELL PASS RATHER THAN ANOTHER SADDLE ON THE SAME RIDGE SYSTEM: it is reached by descending Mount Crowder's NORTHEAST ridge. The last named summit before the pass is Crowder. If you have not been on Crowder, you have not arrived by this line.

WHY THIS SIDE MAY BE THE BETTER CHOICE, AS A PLANNING FACT RATHER THAN A LANDMARK: the northern line requires traversing Luna, East Fury and West Fury. This one does not require crossing Fury at all. The cost is a long ridge sequence with no trail and no bailout.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

approach_variants.name: Table Mountain Trail #681 from the Artist Point lot, up the southeast-face switchbacks
approach_variants.notes:
From the Artist Point trailhead at about 5,100 ft, at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, walk to the NORTHWEST CORNER of the large paved parking lot. Table Mountain Trail #681 starts OPPOSITE THE VAULT TOILETS, on the side of the lot away from the highway.

The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path and reaches its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there it climbs a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — a narrow, exposed catwalk with drops of 400-800 ft toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek.

After roughly 400 ft of gain, about 0.4-0.5 mile from the car, the switchbacks top out on the broad flat summit plateau. Follow the tread west-northwest along the south rim; braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.3 miles two small tarns frame Mount Shuksan and mark the usual high point.

There is no water: the tarns are shallow and silty. Carry everything from the car.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it is the road and the snow in the cliff band that decide it rather than the calendar
hazards: An exposed catwalk cut into a cliff band with 400-800 ft drops and loose gravel underfoot
Snow or verglas in the cliff band into July, which is the usual reason parties turn back
Braided use-trails on a flat plateau, the classic place to lose direction in cloud
No water — the summit tarns are shallow and silty
Beyond the tarns the tread degrades into an unmaintained scramble toward the glacier
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ONE THING PEOPLE GET WRONG HERE IS THE TRAILHEAD, AND IT IS IN A CAR PARK. The Artist Point lot is large and paved and has several trails leaving it. Table Mountain Trail #681 starts at the NORTHWEST CORNER, OPPOSITE THE VAULT TOILETS, on the side AWAY from the highway. Three independent descriptors for one gate — corner, toilets, away from the road — which is what you want when the lot is in cloud.

THE CLIMBING, SUCH AS IT IS, STARTS AT THE FIRST SWITCHBACK, a few hundred feet in. From there the route is a catwalk cut into the cliff band, and the tread is loose rock and gravel over hard pack with a 400-800 ft drop on the outside.

THE CLIFF BAND IS THE CRUX AND ALSO THE TURNAROUND POINT FOR MOST EARLY-SEASON PARTIES. Snow or verglas lingers in this section into July, and many parties turn back here without traction devices. That is the honest statement of what this route is: 400 ft of exposed switchback, then a walk.

ARRIVAL ON THE TABLE: after roughly 400 ft of gain the switchbacks top out on a broad, relatively flat plateau. Flat ground is the confirmation you are through the cliff band.

ON THE PLATEAU, HUG THE SOUTH RIM. Numerous braided use-trails cross the tabletop, and in cloud a plateau with braided paths is the easiest place on this route to end up walking in the wrong direction. The south rim looks straight down onto the Chain Lakes Trail and is the handrail.

WHERE TO STOP: the two small tarns at about 1.3 miles are the last easily identified landmark. Beyond them the trail degrades into an unmaintained scramble path descending toward the Table Mountain Glacier. If the path starts going DOWN and gets rough, you have passed the point most parties turn around at.

access.fees: $5/vehicle day-use (or $30 annual) Northwest Forest Pass, Digital Day Pass, or Interagency Pass at the White River Trailhead
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register, required for Glacier Peak Wilderness travel
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access. White River Road (FS 6400) has experienced storm-damage closures in past winters — check current Okanogan-Wenatchee NF road-condition alerts before driving out.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest / Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest / Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency Recreation Pass

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach_variants.name: Over the col west of Tenpeak and down the Honeycomb Glacier to the couloir's base
approach_variants.notes: There is no short way to this side of the mountain. Parties reach it either from the White River Trailhead by way of the PCT and the upper White Chuck and Suiattle basins, or by dropping onto the Honeycomb from a high camp out on the Kololo Peaks — which is why it is most often climbed as one leg of a multi-day traverse rather than as an objective on its own. Either way the ground you cover on the day is the same: reach the col that sits immediately WEST of Tenpeak, cross onto the Honeycomb Glacier there, and lose height across the glacier before traversing in beneath the north side. The couloir itself is roughly 1,200 ft of snow up to about 35 degrees — a boot-and-axe climb rather than a technical one — finishing on the north-west ridge, where a single short rock pitch of about 5.4 leads to the summit. That last pitch is the reason to carry a rope on a route that otherwise does not obviously need one. This is the thinnest-documented line here. What is written here comes from a small number of accounts and this route's own record; treat the couloir's condition as unknown until you can see it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Apr-Jul. This is a spring line: it wants continuous firm snow, and it has been climbed and skied as early as mid-April and as late as mid-July. By mid-summer the apron melts out and the couloir bakes to bare ice and scree
hazards: A committing position — once in the couloir the bailout is back down 1,200 ft of snow onto a glacier, hours from anywhere
Rockfall out of the cliff bands flanking the couloir, worse as the day warms
Crevasses on the Honeycomb and the upper Suiattle basins, crossed on the way in and again on the way out
A short rock pitch at the very top that a party carrying no rope cannot protect
Lightning exposure on wholly open upper-mountain terrain with no shelter for miles
approach_variants.baseFinding:
YOU ARRIVE AT THIS ROUTE BY GOING DOWN, AND THAT IS THE TEST THAT SEPARATES IT FROM EVERY OTHER LINE ON THE PEAK. Cross the col WEST of Tenpeak onto the Honeycomb Glacier and then LOSE over a thousand feet down the glacier. If you crossed the col and immediately started climbing again, you are on the wrong side of the mountain and probably on the standard south-east line's ground.

THE HANDRAIL IS THE GLACIER AND THE MARKER IS A KNOLL. After the descent, climb to a small knoll and traverse from it into the foot of the couloir. The traverse is easy ground; the knoll is the point you leave the glacier proper. In cloud, the sequence is col, then descent, then one short rise, then a level traverse — four changes of direction, in that order.

WHAT THE BASE LOOKS LIKE, AND THE SEASONAL TRAP THAT COMES WITH IT: early in the season the couloir runs out into a continuous snow apron and you simply walk onto it. By mid-July that apron has melted and the snow starts higher, above bare ground — so a late party finds a gap between the glacier and the climb that an April party never sees. Do not read a missing apron as being in the wrong place.

THE CONFIRMATION ONCE YOU ARE ON IT: about 1,200 ft of sustained snow at up to roughly 35 degrees, no steeper. If the ground stands up beyond that, or if you are on ice and rock rather than snow, you are either in the wrong gully or you are here too late in the year.

THE TOP-OUT IS NOT THE SUMMIT. The couloir finishes on the north-west ridge and there is still one short rock pitch, about 5.4, above it. A party that tops out and starts walking has stopped one pitch short.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful interagency pass) required to park at either the White River or North Fork Sauk trailhead.
access.rules: Standard Glacier Peak Wilderness rules: maximum group size 12 people/stock combined, camp at least 200 ft from water and trails where possible, no wheeled or mechanized equipment, pack out all trash and waste.
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead register for all Glacier Peak Wilderness travel (day and overnight).
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access. White River Road (FR 6400) has a history of flash-flood and winter-storm washout closures (e.g., a 2023 flash flood closed it, and winter-storm damage has repeatedly required repairs); check the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest current-conditions page before driving in. The sheep-trail approach beyond the White River Trail is not an official, maintained trail and is frequently choked with brush and blowdown after heavy-snow winters.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (White River side, Chelan County); Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (North Fork Sauk/Suiattle side, Snohomish County) — the summit sits on the shared boundary within the Glacier Peak Wilderness.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry it with you.

approach_variants.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
approach_variants.notes: From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing. Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the WEST side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread up to about 5,000 ft. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak. The route carries three different elevations for that camp. Camp on the slabs by the tarns rather than at a number. A far longer alternative comes in from the west — North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, while the snow between camp and the col is still continuous enough to walk and the summit rock is dry
hazards: Loose, rotten rock in the summit gully and the broken chimney above it, directly over anyone belaying below
Dense slide alder choking the old sheep path to about 5,000 ft — the slowest half-mile of the approach by a wide margin
Crevasses on the small hanging glaciers crossed on the northern approach variations
Cornices and wind-loaded slopes on the approach ridgelines into early summer
White River Road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so the drive is the first thing to verify
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COL EAST OF THE SUMMIT BLOCK IS THE BASE, AND THE THING THAT CONFIRMS IT IS THE WIND. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

GETTING THERE IS A SINGLE BEARING FROM CAMP: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits EAST of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

THE POSITIVE TEST FOR THE START OF THE CLIMBING: from the col the route takes a LOOSE GULLY ON THE LEFT for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

THE SECOND CONFIRMATION IS A CRACK. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

WHAT IT IS NOT: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

RACK AND ROCK: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.

approach_variants.name: Forty-five minutes north-northwest off the Eldorado ice cap
approach_variants.notes: Everything below the ice cap is the standard Eldorado approach: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 at about 2,100 ft, backtrack a short way along the road to a safe crossing of the Cascade River (a large log or a braided ford, and it shifts year to year), then the steep unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,000-3,500 ft through old growth to a boulder field, across Eldorado Creek, and into the alpine meadows of Eldorado Creek basin — commonly five to six hours from the car. Push on to the Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,600 ft. From that camp it is roughly a 45-minute roped glacier walk north-northwest to where the towers rise out of the icecap. The towers sit at the saddle you cross anyway to get from the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister — so most parties pass beneath them on the way to Klawatti, Austera or Dorado Needle and climb one as a side objective. Round trip from camp is well under two hours.
approach_variants.season: Once the Inspiration Glacier moat below the tower has opened enough to cross safely but before it becomes too wide late in the season — usually July or August, most often as part of an Eldorado/Klawatti/Austera traverse
hazards: Hidden crevasses on the Inspiration Glacier approach — roped travel and crevasse rescue gear, not an unroped stroll
The moat where the glacier rests against the rock, which is the whole gate on this climb
Loose rock near the summit
Softening snow bridges on the return, which is the real time constraint on such a short objective
approach_variants.baseFinding: TEPEH TOWERS IS AN ARÊTE OF MANY SPIRES, NOT ONE TOWER — that is the first thing to understand, and it is why the base finding here has to be about the moat rather than about the skyline. The formation is a rock arête poking out of the icecap northwest of the Inspiration Glacier, with Eldorado to the west and Klawatti to the northeast, and it carries a great many small spires. SO THE PROCEDURE IS: CLIMB HIGH ON THE GLACIER UNTIL THE ICE IS RESTING AGAINST THE ROCK, AND CROSS THE MOAT THERE. You are looking for the point where the snow meets the rock cleanly enough to step across; that point, not a particular spire seen from a distance, is what you navigate to. THE POSITIVE CONFIRMATION IS FIXED GEAR, AND IT IS THE ONLY DISCRIMINATOR PUBLISHED FOR THIS FORMATION: THE TOWER PARTIES CLIMB HAS RAPPEL ANCHORS DIRECTLY BELOW ITS SUMMIT. If you top out and there is no anchor below you, you have climbed a neighbouring spire — which is not dangerous here, but it is not the recorded line either. THE LENGTH TEST IS SHORT AND UNAMBIGUOUS: ONE short low-fifth pitch above the moat, then scrambling to the top. If you are running out a second and third rope length, you are on something else on the same arête. WHAT IS HONESTLY NOT KNOWN: no published account names which of the spires is the climbed one or gives a way to tell it from its neighbours at a distance. That gap is stated here rather than filled — treat the anchor below the summit as the confirmation and the moat as the navigation.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A BEAR CANISTER is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail, then the South Buttress branch
approach_variants.notes:
Drive as for the North Buttress: Mountain Loop Highway southeast of Darrington, right onto FR 2060 (Clear Creek), about 6 miles up the road staying RIGHT at the fork near mile 5, park at the Eightmile Creek trailhead.

Walk the Eightmile Creek trail through second growth and then old timber, roughly 30-40 minutes, until it steps out of the forest onto the old talus slope.

The branch you want is easy to walk past. Once you are out of the woods, look LEFT within about the first 100 feet for a climbers' trail heading up and left into the slide maples. It is a boot path, not a built trail, and it is brushy from the start — that is normal here, not a sign you are wrong.
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
hazards: Unmarked, brushy climbers' path through slide maple
Talus slope with loose blocks hidden under vegetation
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The South Buttress path pushes up through maple and hits rock at a prominent zig-zagging crack. That crack is the start of The Big Tree; you are on the South Buttress, home of the Great Arch.

Negative marker: if the trail took you all the way across the talus and ran into a clean slab with a single bolt above a right-facing dihedral, you are about 100 feet too far along — that is Silent Running on the North Buttress, a different formation face and a much harder day.

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. From the LOWER, eastern end of the pullout walk about fifty yards downhill to find the climbers' trail up to the Lower Wall.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished granite
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Confirm the trail first: the path from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout goes to Logger's Ledge and Upper Castle. Gaining a wide bench means you are one wall too high.

West to east, the Lower Wall's selected routes run The Fault, Catapult, The Vertebrae, The Bone — so this is the furthest east of that group. The Fault is the fixed point, reached directly by the short trail from the right of the parking area.

The wall is recognised by its many roofs, sitting directly beneath Logger's Ledge. Two pitches from here reach that ledge and a trail leads from the ledge back to the car.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
approach_variants.notes:
Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25, around 700 ft. About 3 miles and 1,100 ft of gain on maintained trail through second- and old-growth, crossing several creek drainages, to Lena Lake at roughly 1,800 ft — a busy backpacking destination with a ranger station, and the last easy reliable water and camping before the climbers' route.

Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden Brothers boot path, which follows the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth known as the Valley of the Silent Men for roughly 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp around 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring. Most parties use this as high camp for a two-day ascent.

Route-finding gets hardest immediately after leaving camp for the summit push, where the boot path repeatedly appears to vanish. Follow a climbers' path upstream and west along the west fork for about a mile. It crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs — some with hand-lines or steps cut into them — hide the line, and creek fords may be needed. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs toward the couloir.

Water is reliable at the lake and up Lena Creek to high camp. Above camp there is nothing dependable once you are on scree and snow.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; by late August the couloir is often scrambling rather than snow
hazards: avalanche debris field of slide alder and downed logs between high camp and the couloir, with possible creek fords
moat opening at the base of the Hourglass as the snow recedes
thin snow bridge through the Hourglass constriction in spring
misleading cairns on the upper route
class 4 with real exposure on the last 200 ft
no reliable water above high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the base of the actual climb when the climbers' path fades out in a large meandering gully at the bottom of a broad debris and deposition fan, with the couloir narrowing above it — roughly 4,000-4,300 ft. The path ending is the marker; there is no cairn or sign.

Above that, two features tell you the route is going right.

The Hourglass, near 5,800 ft, is a narrow rock and snow constriction and the crux of getting to the summit block: a couple of exposed 3rd-to-4th class moves in summer, or a steep 35-45 degree snow neck in spring which can be a thin snow bridge and which opens a moat at its base as it melts.

Higher, at the top of the snow, there is a notch with a large rock in it. Climb AROUND that rock to the RIGHT to reach the scree gully beyond. The general rule reported by parties who lose the thread here is: when in doubt, go right.

Cairns exist most of the way, but several of them are misleading. Treat a cairn as a hint and the terrain as the authority. The final roughly 200 vertical feet to the true south summit is class 4 with real exposure.

approach_variants.name: Early-season snow ascent
approach_variants.notes:
The classic time for this route is early season, roughly April into May, because the gullies fill in with dense brush later and the snow-covered version is much faster.

The approach is the same — Lena Lake, the Brothers boot path up the East Fork, the climbers' camp near 2,900 ft — but the avalanche debris field between camp and the couloir is easier under snow, and the couloir itself becomes a snow climb requiring an axe and reliable self-arrest rather than a scree slog.

Snow also buries the boot path, so the route-finding difficulty immediately above camp is worse, not better: there is no tread to find at all.
approach_variants.season: Apr-May, snow
hazards: avalanche hazard in the couloir and on the approach slopes
thin or collapsing snow bridge at the Hourglass
steep 35-45 degree snow requiring axe and solid self-arrest
no boot path visible under snow above high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The deposition fan at the foot of the couloir is still the mark, but under snow the fan and the couloir merge visually. Read it by width: the base is where the open fan narrows into a defined couloir line, several hundred feet of which you then climb before exiting onto its west side and continuing up toward the spur.

The Hourglass around 5,800 ft is the feature to inspect from below. In spring it is a steep snow neck at 35-45 degrees and is sometimes a thin snow bridge — a moat at its base is the sign it is going.

The notch with the large rock at the top of the snow is still passed on the RIGHT.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake Trail and the Valley of the Silent Men to the climbers' camp, then the North Peak side
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FR-25 (Hamma Hamma Road) at roughly 685-750 ft, take Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft. Past the lake the trail runs up a remote forested canyon known as the Valley of the Silent Men to the climbers' camp roughly 6 miles from the trailhead. Most parties camp at Lena Lake or at the climbers' camp rather than trying it in a day.

From camp this route splits away from the ordinary South Couloir line: cross the creek westward, cross a slide meadow and old burn scar, and climb a wide gully north to about 5,500 ft to gain the North Peak side of the mountain. The traverse is recommended north to south, so the North Peak is the start and the South Brother is the finish.
approach_variants.season: June is the usual recommendation, with consolidated snow in the Great Basin; conditions vary a lot year to year
hazards: The 6,200 ft notch drops onto a 200 ft cliff — a documented dead end that costs time and exposes a party on retreat ledges
Steep snow descent into the Great Basin
Exposed fourth-class scrambling to the notch
A sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side of the ridge
Moat belays on the mixed sections, which move with the season
A long committing day with no easy bail once across the Great Basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A STEP IN THE RIDGE CREST AT ABOUT 6,100 FT, AND THE WAY YOU KNOW IT IS THE RIGHT ONE IS THE THING THAT HAPPENS IF YOU GO 100 FT HIGHER. Working up and rightward from camp on scree, heather and lumpy basalt, crossing many small ribs and gullies, you meet the crest. There are two places you can meet it. The higher one, at about 6,200 ft, is a small notch whose FAR SIDE IS A 200-FOOT CLIFF — a party that tops out there has to back off and traverse out on exposed ledges with Class 3-4 slots between them. The one you want is the small STEP in the crest at about 6,100 ft, from which the ground drops steeply but climbably into the snow-filled Great Basin.

SO THE FOG TEST IS: TOP OUT, THEN LOOK DOWN. If the far side goes, you are at the step and on route. If the far side is a cliff, you are a hundred feet too high — do not try to force it, come back down and traverse.

SECOND TEST, once in the Great Basin: from it you climb a moderately steep snow couloir angling toward the North Brother, narrowing to a snow finger that reaches the summit ridge. If your couloir is running away from the north summit rather than toward it, you crossed the basin in the wrong direction.

WHAT THE TRAVERSE ITSELF FEELS LIKE, so nobody mistakes the connecting ridge for a mistake: the crest between the two Brothers is giant boulders forming a jagged run of horns and pinnacles, and traversing it is slow. Slow is correct here. The route is roughly seven roped pitches — fourth class to the notch, steep snow into the Great Basin, moderate snow on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed ground with moat belays, and a final steep couloir to the South Brother.

bivy.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
bivy.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
bivy.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
bivy.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, then DROP 50 feet down the north side
approach_variants.notes:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft, roughly 30 miles west of Winthrop and about a mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest or Interagency pass is required.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climbers' boot path breaking off just past a small stream, climbing through slabs, talus and meadow to the gully between LIBERTY BELL AND CONCORD TOWER. That gully is often snow-filled and icy into late June and carries high rockfall risk after snowmelt.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: An approach gully that is often snow-filled and icy into late June
High rockfall risk in the gully after snowmelt
A 5.8 R grade, so a fall on the wrong ground is consequential
Two notches on one ridge reached by the same path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE NOTCH, DROP ABOUT 50 FEET DOWN THE GULLY ON THE NORTH SIDE OF CONCORD TOWER TO THE START OF THE TWO DIAGONAL CRACKS THAT MARK THE ROUTE. That is a measured descent and a countable feature: fifty feet down, then TWO cracks running diagonally.

SO THE TEST IS THAT YOU GO DOWN, NOT UP. Every other line off this notch starts at the notch or above it. If you have arrived at the notch and started climbing straight away, you are on the standard North Face or one of its variations, not on this route.

WHICH NOTCH, BECAUSE THE PEAK HAS TWO AND THEY ARE REACHED THE SAME WAY: this is the LIBERTY BELL-CONCORD notch, and the test at the top of the gully is that A STEEP CRACK SYSTEM RISES IN FRONT OF YOU. If instead the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges, you are at the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which serves the tower's south face, and you are on the wrong side of Concord.

COUNTABLE ON THE ROUTE: three pitches at 5.8 R. If you are more than three pitches up and still climbing, you have linked into something else.

DESCENT: the same as the standard North Face. Rappel chains at the summit allow a doubled-rope rappel toward the notch, or downclimb and scramble back to it.

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side
approach_variants.notes:
THE SPIRES TRAIL IS THE WRONG APPROACH FOR THIS FACE. The unsigned pullout further west and the col above it serve the spires on the other side of the crest, not the southern wall this route is on.

Take the Cedar Creek trail from its own trailhead off the highway. At roughly five miles, turn off to the RIGHT below the old burn; a rough path then follows the RIGHT-HAND side of the creek draining the south side of the formation. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping.

This is a quiet corner by the standards of this highway. There is no established climbers' camp, no fixed approach gear and effectively no traffic.

A parking pass or day fee covers the trailhead; there is no permit system and no quota on national forest ground here.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-June through late September; July and August are typically driest
hazards: The Wine Spires pullout and its climbers' trail lead to the far side of the crest, not to this face
Its own descent is not separately documented; the shared rappel line is an inference from the shared summit
Rappel anchors are sparse and some must be built; carry extra webbing
Rarely climbed, so there is no chalk, no traffic and no current conditions information
Two long routes on one face that share a mid-height ledge and a summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The wall is CLEAN WHITE GRANITE and it is visibly paler than what surrounds it, which is the first check that you are under the right formation. Follow the creek to the meadows and then up to the foot of it.

THIS ROUTE IS THE RIGHT-HAND LINE. Start on the RIGHT SIDE of the south face, on flakes, corners and splitters. Its neighbour begins with a layback off a LARGE CLEAN FLAKE into a long LEFT-FACING corner system; if that is what is above you, walk right.

THE DEFINING FEATURE IS A BROAD LEDGE AT HALF HEIGHT, and it is the strongest thing this route has. Roughly halfway up the face the climbing arrives at a wide ledge that runs across the wall. That ledge is the route's hinge: from it you WALK LEFTWARD before starting the upper half. A route that reaches a broad crossing ledge and then requires you to walk left along it is this one.

CONFIRM ON THE UPPER FACE. The first pitch above the ledge heads for the LEFT SIDE OF THE MOST PROMINENT ARETE OR PILLAR in the middle of the upper wall. That arete is the biggest feature up there and being on its left is the check. Two more pitches, then the line trends RIGHTWARD to the summit.

THE SUMMIT PITCH SEPARATES THE TWO ROUTES ABSOLUTELY. This one finishes on BLOCKY GROUND JUST RIGHT OF A PROMINENT CHIMNEY. It does not go into the chimney. The neighbouring route tops out THROUGH a deep summit chimney. So: blocky ground beside a slot means this route; stemming up inside the slot means you have crossed onto the other line.

NEGATIVE MARKER lower down, since the two lines are close: if there was no broad crossing ledge and instead you moved rightward under a roof into a splitter to reach a smaller ledge, you are on the neighbour.

Descent is not separately documented for this line. Because it shares the summit and the mid-face ledge with its neighbour, parties use that route's rappels down the south-east side: a seventy-metre rope, sparse fixed anchors, and enough webbing to build your own. Treat that as an inference rather than a described descent and go up prepared to make anchors.

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake to the Little Beaver landing, then the Perry Creek drainage
approach_variants.notes:
Access starts on the water. From the trailhead near milepost 134 walk down to the resort and take its water taxi, or paddle, a long way up the lake to the dock at its northern end. From the dock follow the maintained but lightly travelled valley trail west, through cedar and fir with several brushy meadows and creek crossings, to a camp with a three-sided log shelter - the effective end of maintained tread for climbers headed toward this massif.

Beyond the shelter there is no trail. This is a genuinely serious approach and not a formality: the first ascent party spent two days and roughly fourteen hours of actual travel in the rain covering under two miles from the lake to the base, and described it as one of the worst approaches in the range. Expect cold fords, soaked gear, and skin torn by devil's club and slide alder - the plant the route is named for. Water is everywhere and should be treated.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn; the creek travel is the governing factor rather than the climbing
hazards: a water taxi or a paddle up a long lake with no road out, fixing both ends of the trip
cold creek fords and continuously wet travel
devil's club and slide alder dense enough to stop progress on the wrong bank
avalanche paths on the north side of the drainage
moats between snowfield and rock at the toe of the face
a base days from any road with a very long retreat
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHELTER IS THE LAST FIXED OBJECT YOU WILL SEE - a three-sided log structure at the camp. Everything after it is read off the creek.

STAY IN OR BESIDE THE CREEKBED ITSELF AS LONG AS IT LETS YOU. Rock-hopping and easy scrambling in the bed is the fastest travel available and it holds to about 3,600 ft, where dense slide alder chokes the channel and forces you up a bank.

THE ONE DECISION OF THE APPROACH IS WHICH BANK, AND IT HAS A RIGHT ANSWER: TAKE THE SOUTH, TRUE-LEFT SIDE. It holds older, more open forest and fewer avalanche paths. THE NORTH SIDE IS A NEARLY IMPENETRABLE SLIDE-ALDER THICKET - so if you are swimming through continuous alder with no let-up and no open timber, YOU ARE ON THE WRONG BANK and the fix is to cross rather than to keep pushing.

THE CONFIRMATION THAT YOU CHOSE RIGHT COMES AS A CHANGE OF VEGETATION: above the alder band the forest opens into blueberry meadows and sparser timber, and travel speed roughly triples. If your speed has not changed, you have not cleared the band.

THE BASE IS THE CIRQUE AT THE HEAD OF THE DRAINAGE, beneath the connecting ridge that runs to the summit, with talus and season-dependent snowfields and moats guarding the toe of the face. THE FACE ITSELF IS THE FEATURE - a continuous wall of well over two thousand feet rising straight out of the cirque. IF THE GROUND ABOVE YOU IS BROKEN INTO LEDGES AND GULLIES RATHER THAN A SINGLE SUSTAINED FACE, YOU ARE UNDER THE FLANKING GROUND AND NOT UNDER THE ROUTE.

WATCH THE MOAT WHERE SNOW MEETS ROCK AT THE TOE; how bad it is depends entirely on the season and it decides where the first pitch can start.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the hanging valley, then straight to the toe of the ridge
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road (about 3,400 ft), follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake fork and keep going. Roughly a mile beyond that fork the maintained trail turns uphill and switchbacks away to the right for Stuart Lake. Leave it there and stay flat in the valley with Mountaineer Creek. Cross the creek on logs — there is no canonical log and the crossing moves with the snowpack — then follow the south fork upstream. After a couple of miles the valley steepens; turn up a steep talus and boulder slope into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak, where the bivy sites are. That flat ground under the glaciers is the arrival cue for camp. From the hanging valley the last leg is a faint climbers' path through trees and talus to the moraine, then up the edge of the moraine to rock. The Direct start is the same climb as the Complete North Ridge with a lower-ridge variation on its first pitches; if you are looking at an entry on this app for 'North Ridge (Complete)' as well, treat the approach as identical.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul; best early, while the Sherpa Glacier still gives a straightforward descent back to this side
hazards: Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that shift year to year and are worse under early-season snow
Rockfall and icefall off the Ice Cliff Glacier while traversing the moraine beneath it
An open moat between snow and rock at the toe late in the season
Loose rock and crumbly black lichen on the lower pitches
A committing 20-pitch route with the Great Gendarme high on it and no easy retreat once above the lower ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
KEEP THE ICE CLIFF GLACIER ON YOUR LEFT AND WALK UNTIL THE ROCK STOPS YOU. That single sentence is the whole test, and it works in cloud because it is about which side the ice is on rather than about seeing the summit. Climbing out of the hanging valley towards the mountain, the Ice Cliff Glacier must stay on your left the whole way. If it swings round to your right you have walked past the toe and out onto the Stuart Glacier side.

The toe itself is the lowest rock of the ridge, at roughly 6,600 ft, where the moraine runs into the buttress. You are at the correct place when there is nothing lower to climb — the ridge above you rises unbroken and the ground on either side falls away into a glacier.

SECOND TEST, and it is what tells the Direct start from a wander onto the flank: the first belay is off a BIG LEDGE about 150 ft above the base of the toe, with a small tree on it. If you have not passed a big ledge with a tree inside the first rope length, you are not on the line. The three opening pitches are the hardest on the whole route — an awkward squeeze slot and then a long, sustained lieback crack on the left. If your first pitches feel easy, you have started too high and joined the ordinary ridge.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the ridge you are standing under gains a deep notch with flat bivy ground in it. That notch is where the Upper North Ridge starts, and reaching it on foot means you have skipped the 1,200 ft this route exists for.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass, traversing east below the Stuart Glacier to the toe
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then pick up the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass, about 7,600 ft — the col between Point 7893 and the West Ridge.

This is now the common way parties reach the ridge, and its advantage is that it puts you on the SOUTH side of the range where the descent also finishes, rather than committing you to a north-side camp you then have to walk back around to.

From Goat Pass, do not drop onto the glacier and go up. Traverse EAST below the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe.

Bivy sites exist at Goat Pass and at Stuart Pass. Published trailhead-to-base times for this variant vary widely enough that no figure is given here.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Ingalls Way trail is clear and the Stuart Glacier traverse is walkable
hazards: Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the Stuart Glacier traverse
Loose moraine and talus on the traverse below the glacier
Route-finding error at Goat Pass in cloud, where dropping onto the glacier feels natural and is wrong
A long committing route with the Great Gendarme high on it
No water between the last melt stream and the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAY ABOVE THE MORAINE MOUND AND KEEP TRAVERSING. Coming from Goat Pass the mistake is vertical, not horizontal: the ground invites you to drop down onto the glacier or to climb up onto the ridge crest early, and both put you on the route above its start.

The line is a rising traverse east, above the large moraine mound below the Stuart Glacier, all the way to the toe. If you find yourself walking DOWN onto flat glacier ice you have dropped too low. If you find yourself scrambling onto ridge crest before you have gone round the end of the rock, you are on the west flank and above the toe.

ARRIVAL: the toe is the point where the buttress runs out into the moraine and there is nothing below it to climb, at roughly 6,600 ft. Confirm it the same way the north-side party does — from the toe, the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far (east) side of the ridge and the Stuart Glacier is behind you to the west. If both glaciers are on the same side of you, you are not at the toe.

And the same first-pitch check applies: the opening belay is a big ledge with a small tree roughly 150 ft up, and the first three pitches are the hardest of the route. Easy first pitches mean you started too high.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the LOWER ledge
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout near milepost 166, head straight uphill to the north into the talus below the gully, take the short forced dogleg out left, and rejoin the gully. This route is the one climb here that does NOT need the full walk-in — stop at the first ledge system rather than continuing to the upper one. Everything above you is a different, much longer route, so it is worth being certain you are low before you rack up.
approach_variants.season: June to September; the highway over the pass is gated closed for the winter and the approach is unreachable by car until it reopens.
hazards: Loose talus in the approach gully
Rockfall from parties on the long routes above the lower ledge
South-facing exposure — the apron bakes in full summer sun with no shade
The single ground-level bolt is the only marker; there is no cairn or path along the lower ledge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Stop at the LOWER of the wall's two ledge systems — the first one you reach, before the talus steepens for the last stretch. This line climbs the apron BELOW the wall's long routes, not the wall proper. Walk the lower ledge and look for a SINGLE BELAY BOLT on a small ledge: it is the only piece of fixed gear at ground level here, and it marks the start. Confirm it from the rock immediately above: the first pitch is easy, taking small wires in cracks as well as bolts, so if the wall above your head is steep, clean and blank you are in the wrong place. Sight upward for the second confirmation — the start of the right-hand cave route is directly above you, and the tennis-court-sized cave that names the wall is higher still, not overhead. Negative marker: if you are standing on a broad ledge with several routes' worth of bolted anchors along it and the cave dominates the view above, you have carried on to the UPPER ledge and are roughly ten minutes above this climb; drop back down the gully.

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes:
Oversized dirt pullout on the north side of US-2 at about milepost 96.5, two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth — the crag is visible from the road.

For the Lower Wall, walk from the LOWER, eastern end of the pullout about fifty yards downhill to pick up the climbers' trail, which then climbs steeply to the base. There is also a short trail from the right of the parking area that leads directly to The Fault.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished rock
Highway noise and proximity — the crag is right beside US-2
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The first thing to get right is which trail you are on. Two paths leave the same pullout: the one from the UPHILL, western end traverses east onto Logger's Ledge and serves Upper Castle. If your path is climbing away east onto a big bench, you are heading for the wrong half of the crag.

The Fault is the leftmost of the Lower Wall's selected routes as they run west to east — The Fault, then Catapult, The Vertebrae, The Bone — and it is the route the short trail from the right of the parking area leads to directly.

The Lower Wall as a whole is recognised by its ROOFS: this half of the formation is described as identified by many roofs, and it sits directly beneath Logger's Ledge. So if there is a wide bench above you and roofs overhead, you are in the right half; if you are standing on that bench, you have gone one wall too high.

Two pitches from here reach Logger's Ledge, and a trail leads from the ledge back down to the parking area.

bivy.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
bivy.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

bivy.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
bivy.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
bivy.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail to the South Arete base, then PAST the Passenger's fir tree another hundred feet to the four-bolt dihedral
approach_variants.notes:
Approach as for the Passenger: Blue Lake Trailhead climber's trail, about an hour, to the South Arete base, then traverse down and right along the base of the wall.

Nine pitches on the steep southeast face, first climbed in 2007. A long day, up to eight hours, of sustained face climbing with about twenty bolts but still requiring a full trad rack.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A start 100 ft beyond a similar start on the same traverse
Up to eight hours of sustained face climbing at 5.11-
About twenty bolts over nine pitches, so a full trad rack is still mandatory
No water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE START IS A SMALL LEFT-FACING DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS IN IT, ROUGHLY 100 FT PAST THE PASSENGER'S START ALONG THE SAME TRAVERSE. FOUR BOLTS IS A COUNT, AND COUNTING IS WHAT YOU CAN STILL DO WHEN YOU CANNOT SEE THE TOP OF THE WALL.

SO THE SEQUENCE IS: South Arete base, then down and right about ten minutes to a FIR TREE WITH DOUBLE CRACKS, which is the Passenger. THAT IS NOT THIS ROUTE. Keep going roughly 100 FT FURTHER to a SMALL LEFT-FACING DIHEDRAL WITH FOUR BOLTS.

THE NEGATIVE TEST BOTH WAYS: A FIR TREE AND TWO CRACKS MEANS YOU STOPPED SHORT, ON THE PASSENGER. Nothing beyond the four-bolt dihedral is documented along this traverse, so if the wall is running out and you have found no bolts, you have passed it.

A HARDWARE CHECK THAT KEEPS WORKING ABOVE THE GROUND: this route carries about twenty bolts over nine pitches, which is enough that you should keep meeting them, but not enough to climb without a full trad rack. Meeting no bolts at all after a rope length is a sign you are off the line.

DESCENT: the route tops out at the summit rather than being rappelled. Take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete with a short more exposed step to the RABBIT EARS, then three single-rope rappels on a 60 m rope, which matches the rope length in the route's own protection notes, from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.

road.name: SR-119 (North Lake Cushman Road) to Forest Road 24, to the Staircase trailhead
road.status: OPEN (trailhead/road only — approach trail beyond closed)
road.driveNote: FS-24 and the Staircase developed area (campground, ranger station, trailhead) reopened July 8, 2026, after being closed since the July 2025 Bear Gulch Fire. However, the North Fork Skokomish Trail beyond the Staircase Rapids Loop — including the Flapjack Lakes Trail and campsite, the only approach to The Horn — remains closed while NPS crews complete hazard assessments and repair fire-damaged infrastructure, with no end date given as of the Olympic National Park fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026. Check current NPS alerts before planning a climb.

emergency.notes: Remote, off-trail terrain — cell coverage is unreliable in the North Fork Skokomish drainage; carry a satellite communicator/PLB.
emergency.rangerStation: Staircase Ranger Station (360-877-5569, seasonal) / Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center (360-565-3100)
emergency.nearestHospital: Mason General Hospital, Shelton, WA — Level IV trauma center, 24/7 ED, roughly 1–1.5 hr drive from Staircase
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Mason County Sheriff's Office; technical high-angle rescue in this drainage is typically handled by the Sheriff's SORT (Special Operations Rescue Team) with Mason County Search & Rescue and Olympic Mountain Rescue

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the shared treed-ledge start
approach_variants.notes: Same walk-in as the wall's other long routes: from the pullout near milepost 166 go straight uphill north into the talus below the gully, out left where it forces you, back into the gully, past the lower ledge, and on to the upper ledge. Allow more time than the distance suggests — the ground is talus, loose, and steepens near the top.
approach_variants.season: June to September, once the gully is clear; no access while the highway over the pass is gated for winter.
hazards: Loose talus in the approach gully and rockfall from parties above
Old fixed pitons from the original aid ascent remain in place and must not be trusted
Very few repeat ascents, so expect route-finding uncertainty from the first pitch onward
The cave traverse higher up holds loose rock and stays cold and damp
approach_variants.baseFinding: The start is the treed ledge in the middle of the wall, and it is NOT unique to this route — the eleven-pitch centre line begins from the same place. What identifies this climb is the first rope length. Stay in the left-facing corner and run it well past the point where a short pitch would end: this line's first belay is a PIN-AND-GEAR ANCHOR set beneath a roof, more than twice the length of the neighbouring route's first pitch, and there is no bolted station at the short-pitch height on this line. Above, the giveaway is the fixed gear: old pitons left from the original aid ascent stud the line and appear on no other route on the wall — treat every one of them as decoration, not protection. Negative markers: if you clip into a bolted anchor about twenty-five metres up, you have taken the centre line's first belay; if you started from a broad ledge on the wall's right-hand side beneath the big cave with twin left-slanting cracks above, you are on the cave route entirely.
