approach_variants.name: Andrews Creek trail #504 to Upper Cathedral Lake, then the Cathedral-Monk gully
approach_variants.notes:
Paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek trailhead at about 3,050 ft, then one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state on foot. Trail #504 climbs roughly twelve miles to Andrews Pass above 6,680 ft, mostly through an old burn with no shade, then drops into the next drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft.

Most parties treat this as a two-to-four day backpack and climb from camp in the basin. A free self-issue wilderness permit is taken at the trailhead along with a parking pass.

The alternatives are the valley trail from the Thirtymile trailhead, and the high trail from Loomis, which walks least, drives longest, and leaves 1,300 ft of climbing for the way out.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July through the first snow of October
hazards: Five routes share this one small tower and none of the starts is marked
Beta headed South Face may describe the mountain's thousand-foot wall rather than the tower
Rappel anchors in the north-east descent gully are not documented as fixed; carry webbing and rings
Loose rock in the gully separating the tower from the mountain
Remote basin; any injury is a multi-day walk out with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOWER IS THE POINT. This route is not on the mountain's big wall; it is on the small semi-detached tower leaning against the wall's lower right side, separated from it by a deep gully. From camp, cross meadows and talus toward that gully, then work onto the tower's own south-facing rock on the RIGHT-hand side of the gully. If you are climbing the left wall of the gully, you are on the mountain and you are on the buttress route, which is a much bigger day.

On the tower, this line starts at the LOWEST POINT of the south face and climbs straight up the middle of it. Walk the base until the ground stops dropping and starts rising again — that low point is the start. Nothing is fixed and nothing is marked.

CONFIRMATION IS A ROOF, AND ITS SIDE. At mid-face there is a prominent roof. This route passes it on the LEFT. That single decision is the defining move of the climb and it is what tells you the line was right; if the roof is nowhere above you, you are not on this line at all.

NEGATIVE MARKERS, and there are three because there are four other routes on this tower. If you started in a chimney or gully feature LEFT of centre and topped out in three pitches on a splitter jam crack, you are on the neighbouring crack line, a grade harder and two pitches shorter. approach_variants.baseFinding:
The objective is the small semi-detached TOWER at the lower right of the mountain's south wall, not the wall itself. Walk from camp toward the deep gully between the two and get onto the tower's own rock on the RIGHT side of that gully.

This line is the RIGHT-HAND one on the tower's south face, and it has the only start on this face you can actually stand on and name: a LARGE LEDGE low down, near the right side of the lowest part of the rock. Walk the base rightward until you can step up onto a ledge big enough to organise a rack on. That is the start. If you are standing on broken talus at the very bottom of the face with no ledge under you, keep walking right.

The route then confirms itself by BEHAVIOUR rather than by a landmark: it ZIGZAGS. Five pitches that keep cutting back and forth across the right side of the face, which is why long slings are not optional here — rope drag is the thing people complain about, and drag is itself evidence you are on the correct line.

If your first two pitches were a chimney or gully left of centre, you are on the three-pitch crack line further left. If you started at a PAIR of parallel cracks on the lower left and were off after two pitches, you are on the short cracks.

It comes off the tower by the north-east gully in three rappels of about seventy-five feet, each covered by a doubled sixty-metre rope. If somebody has told you to walk west off the summit, they were describing the mountain, not the tower.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
START WITH THE NAME, BECAUSE THE NAME IS MISLEADING. These are called the West Cracks and they are on the LOWER LEFT OF THE TOWER'S SOUTH FACE. Do not go looking for a west-facing wall; you will not find these there.

The objective is the small semi-detached TOWER at the lower right of the mountain's big south wall, reached from camp by crossing toward the deep gully that separates the two and getting onto the tower's own rock on the RIGHT side of that gully.

Walk the base of the tower's south face LEFTWARD, past the lowest point of the rock, until you find A PAIR OF PARALLEL CRACKS running up the lower left of the face. Two cracks, side by side, close enough that you will see them as a pair rather than as two separate features. That pair is the whole landmark. If you can only see one crack, you have not found them yet.

The right-hand crack of the pair has no chimney crux; its hard climbing is face and crack higher up, and it goes a full grade easier.

SO: if you are wedged in a chimney on pitch two and wishing you had brought the big cam, you are on the correct line. If pitch two is open crack climbing and feels easy for the grade, you are one crack to the right.

If you are still going on the third, you have linked into the upper formation, and the descent changes with it: most parties simply rappel this route on gear from the top of pitch two, whereas topping out on the tower commits you to the north-east gully in three rappels of about seventy-five feet each.

approach_variants.name: Colonial Glacier col to the Neve rim
approach_variants.notes: Take the maintained trail to Pyramid Lake, then the unmaintained climbers' path around the lake's east side up steep root-laced forest into heather and boulders, along a narrowing ridge and across a scree traverse to the toe of the Colonial Glacier. Camp on the flat bench below the glacier. From camp, rope up, climb south to the col at around 6,900 ft, drop a couple of hundred feet onto the Neve icecap and work west along its rim.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, while the snow arete is still continuous and the bergschrund can be turned
hazards: Open crevasses scattered across the east side of the Neve Glacier
The bergschrund at the foot of the snow arete has to be turned or bridged and moves through the season
Sustained class 3 with full exposure on the ridge, on loose rock
A knife-edge section immediately below the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: Work west along the RIM of the icecap rather than out into its middle, passing Horseman's Pack and then The Horseman. Once The Horseman is behind you, turn NORTH and keep following the ice edge until a snow arete runs up out of the glacier to a rock ridge. That arete is the base of the route and there is nothing else like it along this rim — everywhere else the ice edge simply meets broken ground. The bergschrund at its foot is the proof and also the thing to inspect on arrival, because it has to be turned or bridged to get onto the arete and how far along you must walk to do that changes through the season. Above it the ridge runs north and then west around a corner into sustained class 3. If you are still south of The Horseman, or you have drifted into the middle of the icecap toward the bigger peak, you have not reached the turn. If the ground above you rolls back at an easy angle instead of narrowing to a crest, you are on the glacier rim and not on the spire.

approach_variants.name: Cutthroat Creek trail #483 from the Cutthroat Lake trailhead
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that matters is the one you do NOT take: the neighbouring peak of the same name is reached from an unmarked highway pullout west of the pass with no maintained trail. This wall is reached from the signed Cutthroat Lake trailhead at about 4,500 ft, a mile up a spur road off the highway east of the pass.

From the kiosk, walk the maintained Cutthroat Creek trail a short way, still on the old roadbed that parallels it, then turn uphill on the climbers' left into the forest. A climbers' path then trends climbers' right through brush, trees and talus to a flat area beneath the cliff.

There are cairns and they are unreliable; steer by the buttress. Reckon the better part of an hour to two, and expect to have the wall to yourself.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September, once snow has cleared the upper pitches and approach slabs
hazards: Two starts about fifty feet apart on one slab platform
Deliberate variations at several pitches make being off-line hard to detect
Lichen and loose rock; no bolts and very little fixed gear
The rappel runs over a chockstone tunnel that snags ropes on the pull
The obvious descent gully below the notch is the wrong one and is loose
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base landmark is a GRANITE PATIO, a flat slab platform under the wall where two routes begin about fifty feet apart. THIS ROUTE IS THE RIGHT-HAND ONE. The left-hand start heads up and left into a corner and is the harder line; this one is right of it.

The first pitch has an UNDERCUT START leading into an open book, with several ways through — featured face, a crack and arete, or the corner — all arriving at the same quality crack and a cam anchor. Several lines through one short piece of steep undercut rock is the correct experience here, not a sign you are lost.

CONFIRMATION IS TREES, IN TWO STAGES, and it is the most reliable thing this route offers. Pitch two ends on a LEDGE WITH TWO BIG GNARLED TREES that make solid anchors. Above that, an easy ramble right of those trees reaches a minor bowl with a good tree anchor below a distinctive SPIRAL TREE. If you have passed two gnarled trees on a ledge and then a spiral tree, you are on this route and no other line on this wall gives you that sequence.

Be ready for the route's own character: the described line has parallel options at several pitches, so a variation is normal rather than an error. Rock is generally solid but still lichen-covered and loose in places, there are no bolts and very little fixed gear, and some anchors are tree slings.

NEGATIVE MARKERS. If you started LEFT of the patio and the highlight is a long right-facing corner near the top, you are on the neighbouring line. If you walked uphill and left of the patio to a small stand of trees and started in a scarred open book, you are on the third route, a full grade harder.

The descent is the day's real crux and must be studied on the ground: from the topout walk a hundred to two hundred feet along the ridge to a minor notch between the westernmost and the higher central buttress, marked by a slung horn or tree. One rappel on a single seventy-metre rope over a chockstone tunnel, which snags ropes on the pull, drops to a dirty ramp with a small cave. Then take the UPWARD-trending gully or ledge system on skier's LEFT back around to the base. The obvious gully directly below the notch is loose and is the wrong way.

approach_variants.name: Twin Lakes and High Pass, then the col in Larrabee's south arm and the gully to the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east about 12 miles to the WSDOT Shuksan maintenance facility and turn onto Twin Lakes Road (FS-3065). The first 4.5 miles to the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead are passenger-car friendly; beyond that the road narrows and is not maintained for passenger vehicles, and high-clearance is recommended for the final two miles to Twin Lakes. If the upper road is out, park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and add roughly four miles round trip and 1,500 ft of gain.

From the isthmus between the Twin Lakes take the High Pass Trail — about two miles, LOSING roughly 300 ft as it skirts below Winchester Mountain before climbing to the pass.

From High Pass, ascend the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's SOUTH ARM; there is a trail here in summer. From the col descend slightly and traverse the basin.

The Pleiades are a series of jagged spires on Larrabee's east ridge, so this is not one summit but several.
approach_variants.season: Roughly late Jul-Sep
hazards: Loose sandy rock where downclimbing is as hazardous as ascending
A rough final two miles of FS-3065 that may add four miles and 1,500 ft to the day
Three separate objectives leaving from High Pass, easy to confuse in the basin
The first (west) Pleiad is far more serious than the second and looks similar from the notch
No water past High Pass
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE CLIMB STARTS AT A GULLY LEADING TO THE NOTCH BETWEEN THE FIRST AND SECOND PLEIADES, AND FINDING IT IS A THREE-STEP SEQUENCE FROM HIGH PASS. Up the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's south arm. DOWN slightly from the col. ACROSS the basin. Then UP the gully to the notch. The descent in the middle is the step people skip, and skipping it puts you on Larrabee's south ridge instead. THE NOTCH IS BETWEEN TWO SPIRES AND THAT IS THE CONFIRMATION. You are not aiming for a summit, you are aiming for the gap between the first and second towers of a jagged row. Arriving somewhere with rock on both sides of you and the basin below is the arrival. FROM THE NOTCH THE TWO PEAKS ARE VERY DIFFERENT, AND THE CHOICE MATTERS. The SECOND peak, to the EAST, is an easy scramble. The FIRST peak, to the WEST, is third class in summer and has been reported as a snowy knife-edge with slabby, high-consequence exposure in winter conditions. Going the wrong way out of the notch is the difference between a walk and a serious ridge. WHAT BEING ON THE WRONG OBJECTIVE LOOKS LIKE: Larrabee's own South Ridge route leaves the same basin and its base is TWO PARALLEL CHANNELS about 30 ft apart on a southwest spur at 6,900 ft — take the right-hand one for Larrabee. American Border Peak's route contours much further north around Larrabee's west flank to a col at 6,200-6,300 ft. All three leave High Pass. Only this one crosses the basin under Larrabee's EAST-side spires. THE ROCK IS LOOSE AND SANDY throughout, which makes downclimbing as hazardous as the climb up. Keep the party close so nobody is under a falling stone.

approach_variants.name: Terror Basin, the upper Barrier crossing and the Degenhardt col
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead the climbers' path parallels the creek on easy old roadbed before a punishing push to treeline in Terror Basin — faint tread, dense brush, and class 3 root-pull sections through cliff bands. Most parties reach the basin in one long day. From the basin cross the Barrier at its UPPER notch, near 6,200 ft, by way of heather benches and loose rock and moats, into Crescent Creek Basin below the peaks. A direct line into Crescent Creek Basin exists but is buggier and less consistent.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September, once the Crescent and Terror Creek approach is snow-free enough to be reliably passable
hazards: Broken, loose ground working across to the notch
Rock quality flips repeatedly between clean gneiss and dirt-covered choss
A few low fifth-class moves off the ridge crest with no easy retreat
The lower Stump Hollow Barrier crossing leads to a different objective and is the wrong one here
approach_variants.baseFinding: The col between this peak and Degenhardt is the base, and the climbing starts by dropping a few low fifth-class moves OFF the crest at the col onto the peak's western side — you do not start below the col and climb up to it. The proof once you are on that side is a gully or couloir system leading up and right toward the summit with a band of clearly OVERHANGING rock capping it directly above. The line stays LEFT inside the gully and avoids that overhang entirely; parties who take the roof head-on have found the hard and unnecessary way. Two negative markers. If you crossed the Barrier at the lower Stump Hollow notch rather than the upper one near 6,200 ft, you are set up under a different peak entirely. And a stretch of rubbish, dirt-covered rock is not on its own evidence you are off route here, because this peak's rock alternates between surprisingly solid gneiss and choss on the same face.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail, South Buttress branch, then up to the terrace
approach_variants.notes: Drive and walk exactly as for the Great Arch: FR 2060 off the Mountain Loop Highway, RIGHT at the mile-5 fork, Eightmile Creek trailhead, then the Eightmile Creek trail for 30-40 minutes to the talus slope, and the climbers' branch up and LEFT into the slide maples within about 100 feet of leaving the woods.
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
hazards: Unmarked brushy climbers' path through slide maple
Scrambling onto the terrace above the Great Arch
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route does NOT start where the approach path meets the rock. It starts from a terrace that sits between the Great Arch area and the start of The Big Tree, and the easiest way onto that terrace is from the Great Arch side.

So the sequence is: reach the Great Arch, then gain the terrace and walk along it toward the Big Tree side. If you are standing on the ground at the zig-zag crack you are at The Big Tree, not this route; if you are at the large left-facing flake with a bolt on it you are at Under the Bored Walk.

Having to scramble up onto a terrace before racking up is CORRECT here.

approach_variants.name: Crescent Creek Basin to the Terror col
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead follow the climbers' path up the old roadbed, crossing two branches of the creek, then take the steep cairned ascent into the Terror Creek drainage. Either climb the Terror Basin line — faint tread, dense brush and a class 3 root-pull section at a cliff band — or the more direct but notoriously brushy Crescent Creek Basin line, to a high camp beneath the peak. There is no maintained trail anywhere on this approach and it is a long day or more of unmarked bushwhacking.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September, once the basins are melted out enough to camp and travel
hazards: Rubble-choked entry gully with continuous rockfall potential
Very steep rock immediately off the notch, with old fixed pins rather than modern anchors
About half a mile of serrated alpine ridge above, with committing terrain and no easy escape
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is the low notch between Mount Terror and this peak, and the way in is a single deep, rubble-choked gully running up to it. Climb that gully staying RIGHT, on slightly harder but far more solid class 3 rock, rather than wading up the debris in its bed. From the notch the ridge starts immediately above on very steep, vertical to overhanging rock, taken directly precisely in order to avoid the loose gully below and to the side of it; the first ascent drove pitons here, so old fixed pins are what you may find rather than bolts. The proof is that the hard climbing begins at once, off the notch, with no walking terrain in between — if you are standing on easy ground hunting for a start, you are in the wrong place. Beyond it the climb becomes roughly half a mile of serrated ridge, which is where the peak's name comes from. Check your orientation in the notch: Terror's bulk should be on your EAST and the saw-toothed crest you are climbing on your west.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake and Unicorn Col to the leftmost line on the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Same approach as the other summit-block lines: from the Snow Lake trailhead, the maintained trail about a mile and roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake for the last reliable water. Past the lake the tread fades over a wooded hump; contour up and right into the obvious northwest talus and dirt gully, where a heather-bench climbers' path reappears near the top and drops you into the basin under the peak. Climb the moraine beside the small basin snowfield to Unicorn Col, then follow the traversing use trail below the summit cliffs on the south side to the base of the horn — roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way and about 2,400 ft of gain.

This is the hardest and most exposed of the three summit-block lines, following a steeper and more sustained line than either neighbour, with an old piton at about half height.

Carry a double-length runner or a cordelette. The top anchor for this line sits set back from the edge, so the rappel power-point has to be extended out to the lip to keep the rope running cleanly over the roof feature.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose rock reported in the gully and chimney section
The steepest and most exposed of the three summit-block lines, and awkward to reverse
A top anchor set back from the edge, which drags the rope over the roof unless extended
An old piton at half height that should not be treated as protection
A 30 m rope that may not reach on one of the two rappel lines
approach_variants.baseFinding:
LEFT TO RIGHT ALONG THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. THE ROOF IS THE LEFTMOST AND THE HARDEST.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS A JUNCTION RATHER THAN A CRACK, WHICH IS WHY IT IS EASY TO FIND IN POOR LIGHT: IT STARTS ABOUT 20 FT LEFT OF THE CLASSIC ROUTE, AT THE POINT WHERE THE RIDGELINE MEETS THE SUMMIT BLOCK. Ridge into block — that meeting point is the marker.

THE FEATURE ITSELF IS THE SECOND CONFIRMATION AND IT IS OVERHEAD: A WIDE GULLY OR CHIMNEY RUNNING BENEATH A ROOF. You climb the gully, then STEP RIGHT UNDER THE ROOF onto a ledge, then up to the belay. IF THERE IS NO ROOF ABOVE YOU, YOU ARE NOT ON THIS ROUTE. There is an old piton at about half height.

THE TWO NEGATIVES, BOTH TO YOUR RIGHT:
  — 20 FT RIGHT, blocky climbing straight up the open south face with a piton mid-pitch, and no roof: that is the CLASSIC ROUTE at 5.4.
  — 70 FT RIGHT, two wide left-leaning cracks: that is OPEN BOOK at easy fifth.
So every way of being wrong here makes the climbing EASIER, not harder — which is the safer direction, but it also means nothing about the ground will warn you that you missed the route you came for.

GRADE AS A CHECK: 5.6, noticeably burlier than the Classic Route's corner and well above Open Book. If it feels like the easiest thing on the block, you are not on it.

AND THE ONE PIECE OF DESCENT PLANNING THAT HAS TO HAPPEN BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE GROUND: the top anchor for this line is SET BACK FROM THE EDGE. Extend it with a cordelette or long sling so the rope runs over the lip rather than dragging on the roof. Most parties rappel this line even if they downclimbed elsewhere on the peak, because reversing it is considerably more exposed than reversing its neighbours. A single-rope rappel of roughly 40-50 ft; 30 m has been reported marginal depending on which of the two lines off the horn you use, so 40 m removes the guesswork. Use the rock horn, not the retired snag.

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake outlet into the west cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; Northwest Forest Pass). Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.25 miles with a Mountaineer Creek log bridge near 1.5 miles, to the junction where Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A branches left; a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing, then steepening rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, roughly one and three-quarter to two hours for a fit party.

The shorter line into the west basin: cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside straight into the cirque — about an hour from the lake, plus 15 to 25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the wall. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water; carry what you need for a long day.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Slick or partly submerged log bridges over Mountaineer Creek early season
Loose talus in the basin and the final scramble
No water above Colchuck Lake
Snow lingering in the basin into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding: In the basin, The Scoop starts to the RIGHT of the West Face and the Tempest and to the LEFT of Rikki Tikki Tavi. The confirmation is not at the ground but three pitches up: the first three pitches, to about 5.10a, lead to LAUNCH LEDGE, the platform sitting directly below the namesake Scoop corner. If the ledge you reach after three pitches has no large corner system rising above it, you are not on The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble to the wall.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, leftmost gully
approach_variants.notes: Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, gaining talus and heather about 400 ft above the lake, then cut north through the slide-alder band — cairned, but a genuine bushwhack of 15 to 20 minutes. Take the LEFT-MOST gully and climb it about 1,000 ft to its top, then contour east on an easy path into the basin. One and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line but no ford.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; ice axe useful before mid-July
hazards: Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder
Loose gully talus; late snow in the gully
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cairns mark the base of the correct gully and stop there. Leftmost is the test. From the basin, The Scoop is right of the West Face and Tempest and left of Rikki Tikki Tavi; Launch Ledge, three pitches up with the Scoop corner above it, is what confirms the line.

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Take the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot to Logger's Ledge, traverse the ledge EAST and climb the long steep hillside above — 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close annually for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July, or until the young fledge.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
40-45 minutes of steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep, coarse granite
Northwest aspect — cold mornings
approach_variants.baseFinding: You reach the LEFT side of Midnight Rock first off Logger's Ledge. Midnight is the tall face of around 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging, seamed with parallel-sided cracks and facing northwest, so it is shaded through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime beside it is nearly undeveloped. The Sting is one of the three lines — with Stevens Pass Motel and Wasp — that get you to the enormous ledge crossing the middle of the CENTRE section of the wall, from which ROTC and others start. So the feature confirming you are in the right sector is that mid-height ledge system directly overhead. No ledge above you means you are at the wrong part of the crag. No source consulted here documents this route's exact position along the base; use a topo from the left end of the wall.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard-side lakeshore, slide alder, base gully
approach_variants.notes: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, about 8.5 miles from Leavenworth). Colchuck Lake Trail #1599: the first 1.5 miles climb gently through forest along Mountaineer Creek to a log-bridge crossing; about a mile past that, stay RIGHT at the signed junction with the Lake Stuart Trail. The final push switchbacks up a boulder moraine to the Colchuck Lake outlet — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft, two and a half to three hours at a steady pace. Fill water here; it is the last reliable source. Work around toward the lake's south/east side and pick up the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, following it up steep talus and heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake in 30 to 40 minutes. That slope holds snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history. Break off climber's-LEFT through the band of dense slide alder and heather — the brushy crux of the walk in, 15 to 20 minutes — to the base of the gully system below the main wall.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Slick log bridges over Mountaineer Creek in high early-season flow
Wet snow on the Aasgard slope into July
Dense slide alder band
Loose 3rd/4th class ground in the final scramble to the wall
approach_variants.baseFinding: The Tempest begins at the CENTRE of the face, below the long bulge and roof, roughly mid-way along the base of the wall — a little RIGHT of where the West Face starts out of the gully. The overhanging bulge above is the feature to sight on: if there is no roof over your head, you are either left at the West Face's gully start or right toward The Scoop. Expect loose 3rd/4th class rock in the final approach scramble; many parties rope up for it. Three and a half to four hours trailhead to base.

approach_variants.name: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
approach_variants.notes: From the roadside pullout near milepost 166, go directly uphill to the north through talus and forest toward the gully below the wall, taking the forced dogleg out left and back in. Pass the lower ledge and keep going to the upper ledge. There is an exposed easy-fifth step in the gully on the way, so this is not a walk with your hands in your pockets. Rockfall in the gully is worse when another party is above you and worse again after rain.
approach_variants.season: July to September; the highway over the pass is gated shut through winter and into spring, so the wall is car-inaccessible for roughly half the year.
hazards: Loose talus and an exposed easy-fifth step in the approach gully
Rockfall in the gully, particularly with parties above or after rain
South-facing aspect gives full-day sun and real heat in summer
Two routes leave the same treed ledge — confirm which anchor you are heading for before you commit to a rope length
approach_variants.baseFinding: On the upper ledge, work to the CENTRE of the wall — this line is neither the right-hand cave line nor the apron below. The start is a treed ledge, and it is shared: two routes leave from the same spot, so identify it by the ledge and the trees, then identify the ROUTE by where you stop. The first pitch here is short — a slabby left-facing corner, about twenty-five metres, ending at a belay well below the first roof. Negative markers: if you run the same corner out to more than sixty metres and finish at a pin-and-gear anchor tucked under a roof, you are on the free variation of the old aid line, which shares this ground; if the corner you started up is forty metres long and leads to a stance under twin left-slanting cracks, you are on the right-hand cave line; and if you are on a narrow ledge below the whole wall with a single bolt beside you, you stopped one ledge too low.

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, the Aasgard trail, then left through the brush to the base gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead on FR 7601, take the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599 — four miles and 2,280 ft, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at about 1.5 miles, right at the Lake Stuart junction, then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet in about two and a half to three hours. Fill water here; it is the last source. Head round toward the lake's south and east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and gain talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake, thirty to forty minutes. Then leave it: break climber's LEFT through a dense band of slide alder and heather, fifteen to twenty minutes of real bushwhacking, to the obvious gully leading up to Colchuck Balanced Rock. The final scramble to the wall is loose third and fourth class; rope up if in doubt. Reckon three and a half to four hours car to base.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse above the lake holds wet snow into July and has produced serious slips
hazards: A wet-snow traverse above Colchuck Lake into July with a history of serious slips
Fifteen to twenty minutes of dense slide alder and heather to reach the gully
Loose third and fourth class scrambling in the base gully with parties above
No water above Colchuck Lake
Above the fourth-pitch anchor there is no rappel retreat — the route must be finished
A long walk-off round the peak after topping out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE MARKER IS A BOLT WITH A BLACK HANGER ABOUT EIGHT FEET UP A LEFT-FACING CORNER, AND IT IS THE ONLY UNAMBIGUOUS THING AT THE BASE OF THIS WALL. Get to it in three steps.

STEP ONE — THE SANDY LEDGE. Scramble the base gully as for the wall's ordinary line until you reach the sandy ledge that every route here starts from. If you have not found a sandy ledge, you are still in the approach gully.

STEP TWO — TEN FEET AND STEP LEFT. From the sandy ledge, climb about ten feet of easy ground and step LEFT onto a small ledge. There is a TREE on it. A small ledge with a tree, one short step left of the sandy ledge, is the belay.

STEP THREE — LOOK UP. Above that ledge is a LEFT-FACING CORNER with a bolt roughly eight feet off the deck carrying a BLACK HANGER. That bolt is the confirmation, and it is why this route is worth a base finding while its neighbours are not: it is a fixed, findable object rather than a relative position.

WHERE THIS SITS ON THE WALL: to the LEFT of both the ordinary west face line and the harder line beside it. So if you never stepped left off the sandy ledge, you are on one of those two instead.

GRADE CHECK ON THE FIRST MOVES: getting off the ground is thoughtful 5.11 with a second punchy section midway. The wall's ordinary line starts far easier. If the first moves are casual, you are not on this route.

AND A RETREAT FACT WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE GROUND: the anchor at the top of the fourth pitch is the last point from which a rope reaches back down — two 40 m rappels return you to the base gully from there, with an intermediate anchor if your rope is short. Above it you are committed to finishing over the top.

approach_variants.name: Alpental to Pineapple Pass, then west along the base past The Tooth Fairy
approach_variants.notes: Take the Snow Lake trail from Alpental, fork toward Source Lake, cross the talus and climb the steep gully to Pineapple Pass — the standard approach every route on this side of The Tooth shares. From the pass, keep going LEFT (west), past the foot of The Tooth Fairy, and continue along the base of the cliff. The route is a bolted line, so the walk is over ground the other routes here have already made obvious. About 4.8 km and 2,700 ft to the summit.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June to September on dry rock; the approach gully to Pineapple Pass holds snow into early summer and an axe is worth carrying then
hazards: About 100 m of unprotected third and fourth class scrambling on the North Ridge above the last bolt to reach the true summit
An all-bolt sport line on an alpine peak, with alpine weather and no quick escape
Parties on the South Face and Tooth Fairy above and beside you sharing one descent
The approach gully to Pineapple Pass holds snow into early summer
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COUNT OFF FROM THE TOOTH FAIRY AND FIND THE GULLY. This route starts roughly 500 ft climbers' LEFT of The Tooth Fairy, and the feature that fixes it is a LARGE GULLY THAT SPLITS THE CLIFF. The route takes the LEFT-HAND SIDE of that gully. So: Tooth Fairy behind you on the right, big cleaving gully in front of you, start on its left wall.

THE HARDWARE TEST, which works in any visibility: this is an all-bolt line. Quickdraws and nothing else. If you are pulling out cams to protect the first moves, you are on one of the peak's trad routes, not on this one.

THE FIRST-PITCH GRADE TEST: pitch one goes at 5.9 to 5.10a, with an easier 5.8 alternative start bolted to the RIGHT. If the first pitch is going at 5.4 you are round on the South Face; if it feels like broken fourth-class scrambling you have not left Pineapple Pass.

AND A CONFIRMATION HIGHER UP FOR A PARTY THAT WANTS ONE: the third pitch CROSSES THE GULLY on a large chockstone, and the fourth pitch takes a V-slot at 5.10b. Crossing that gully mid-route on a chockstone is the signature of this line.

FINALLY, WHERE IT PUTS YOU: the last bolted anchor is not the summit. One more bolt above it leads onto the North Ridge and about 100 m of unprotected scrambling to the true top. A route whose bolts run out at the summit is not this one.

approach_variants.name: Alpental valley to the northeast basin (winter)
approach_variants.notes: From the Alpental upper lot (about 3,100 ft), go up the valley on the left side of the creek toward Source Lake, following the Source Lake line and whatever ski or boot track exists. In winter this means the valley bottom rather than the summer switchbacks, which cross the valley's avalanche chutes. Beyond Source Lake, climb the snow finger into the basin on the Tooth's northeast side, then continue up the snow slope beneath the face. Skis are normally cached at the bottom of that slope. Route-finding above the talus is cairn and boot-track only — there is no maintained tread — so fresh snow or a whiteout removes the only navigational aid you have.
approach_variants.season: Dec-Mar, and into spring on firm snow
hazards: Source Lake basin and the slopes below the Tooth have a documented avalanche accident history and are rated challenging avalanche terrain
the summer path is not a safe line once snow is present
thin, poorly protectable ice on the second pitch with long runouts
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high flow
no maintained tread above the talus - navigation is by cairn and boot track only
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at the foot of a distinct gully at the top of the snow slope on the northeast aspect. Pitch one climbs that gully; pitch two continues to the ridge crest above it; pitch three begins from a TREE anchor on the ridge.

That tree is the confirmation. If the ground above your gully leads onto a bare rock rib with no trees on it, you have gone up the wrong feature — drop back to the snow and traverse. Likewise, if you are still on open snow with nothing gully-shaped above, you are short of the base; the slope continues.

The second pitch is the one to think about before committing: parties report thin ice, long runouts, and balancy mixed slab where screws and pickets are hard to place. Deciding at the base whether it is in condition is the real judgement call.

rappel_detail.pull: Decide which side you are pulling from before the last climber leaves, and keep both strands clear of the clefts.
rappel_detail.notes: Topmost station reversing the South Face.
rappel_detail.anchor: 3 rap rings, backed by sling around tree/horn
hazards: Large clefts flank the line that look purpose-built to catch a rope - feed the rope down rather than throwing it
Trip reports repeatedly record the rope sticking on this descent and needing tugging to free
rappel_detail.station: A small step down from the summit leads to the notch where the easy version of pitch 4 ends, and the tree growing there is the top anchor. As of a 2021 inventory it carries three rap rings plus a quantity of slings and cord. About 25 m back down to the pitch-3 ledge.

rappel_detail.notes: Second rappel down the face.
hazards: A 60 m rope doubled comes up just slightly short of the tree at the top of pitch 2, so the last few metres are an unroped downscramble. An added pitch-3 anchor exists specifically to cut that exposure out on a 60 m
rappel_detail.station: The station on the pitch-3 ledge, where the first rappel lands. Currently an 8 mm cordelette doubled around the anchor with two quicklinks.

rappel_detail.pull: The tree sits back from the lip, so the rope saws across the flat top of the ledge and this pull is stiff. Pull from immediately beside the slung rock horn at the top of pitch 1 - moving any further out before pulling is what jams it.
rappel_detail.notes: Third rappel, well-equipped fixed station.
hazards: The tree has taken most of the traffic on this peak for years and its long-term health is a stated concern - use the rock anchor beside it where it is in place
The lower rappels are lichen-covered and slippery when wet
rappel_detail.station: The ledge at the top of pitch 2: the anchor is the large, straight tree on the skier's-LEFT side. Two trees here each carry a few slings, and by August 2024 a rock-based anchor had been added alongside them.

rappel_detail.notes: Lowest station, reaching Pineapple Pass.
rappel_detail.anchor: several slings + 3 rap rings around a block
hazards: A slung block rather than fixed hardware: load it in line with the pull rather than shifting it

A second, partly hidden set of bolts sits off to the side of pitches 1 and 2 so descending parties do not have to share ground with climbers. It is a different line, and it needs a small swing climber's-right at the bottom to put your feet on the ground; continuing along the ramp there creates rope drag that makes the pull difficult
rappel_detail.station: Atop pitch 1, a block and horn carrying several slings and three rap rings - the same spot you pull the previous rope from. About 30 m returns you to exactly where you first roped up.

wa_the_tooth_south_face.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on a SINGLE 60 m rope used doubled, each under 30 m, reversing the four pitches back to Pineapple Pass - this is what almost every party does and how the stations are spaced. Two 60 m ropes let you link them into fewer, longer rappels. One 60 m rappel in the sequence comes up just short of the next tree, leaving a short unroped downscramble, which an added pitch-3 anchor now avoids. A separate, partly hidden bolted line beside pitches 1 and 2 exists so that ascending and descending parties are not in the same place; it is a different set of anchors, not a variation. Below Pineapple Pass the east gully holds two more bolted chain stations for two further rappels on a 60 m - optional, and many parties scramble out instead; there is meaningful rockfall hazard in that gully. Do not scramble directly up to Pineapple Pass on the way in: that ground is the rappel route.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake Trail to Great Scott Bowl and Pineapple Pass
approach_variants.notes: Upper Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Road (about 3,100 ft), I-90 exit 52. Take the Snow Lake Trail (#1013) north; a cat track runs up the valley from the end of the lot, just left of the stream, before the tread narrows to normal trail. At roughly 1.5-1.6 miles a small signed junction splits Source Lake from Snow Lake — bear left toward Source Lake. Cross the Source Lake basin contouring near 4,000 ft, then at about 4,400 ft you crest a lip and drop into Great Scott Bowl (also called Pineapple Basin). Work up the bowl on talus, or on snow if any remains, toward Pineapple Pass at the head of it, passing beneath the Fang — the pinnacle on the bowl's west side that carries the Edge of Time route. The common error is here, not lower down: a boot path running around the back of the Fang leads into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth. Parties who take it have to backtrack several hundred feet through trees and rock fields to get back onto the right ground. The second error is going straight up to Pineapple Pass itself — that col is the rappel line down, not the way up.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep (snow-free)
hazards: loose talus underfoot the whole length of Great Scott Bowl
steep sustained snow slope below Pineapple Pass in early season - axe, sometimes crampons
moat, and in some years a cornice, where the bowl's snow meets rock at the pass
rockfall from parties above on a face that is often busy
no reliable water past the Source Lake outlet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Great Scott Bowl, scramble to the notch just SOUTH of Pineapple Pass, then contour clockwise around the Tooth's south side. The last part of that contour is short class 3-4 and is not exposed; if it feels serious you are on the wrong ground.

You are at the start when you are standing under a broad, blocky face roughly 400 ft high with an obvious big vertical crack system splitting it. The first moves are easy ramps that angle LEFT to a large rectangular block, then back right into that crack system. About 100 ft up, the first belay is a slung rock horn with a balanced, flat-topped block sitting on it — that block is the confirmation you are on the standard line.

Two negative markers. If you are looking up a steep, narrow gully rather than an open face, you are in the gully between the Fang and the Tooth, one formation short — go back down and continue around. And if you scrambled straight up into a notch with rappel slings hanging above you, you are standing at Pineapple Pass on the descent route; downclimb and take the next notch south, then contour.

In early season a steeper gully runs up toward the base of the face. Do not use it unless it is filled with snow.

approach_variants.name: Winter and spring, snow-covered Alpental valley
approach_variants.notes: Once there is meaningful snow the summer tread is not the route. The talus slopes the summer trail crosses are the Alpental valley's avalanche chutes — seventeen of them are counted along its length — and the winter line instead climbs the valley on the south side of the South Fork Snoqualmie toward Source Lake rather than following the summer switchbacks across those paths. From below Source Lake, traverse up into Great Scott Bowl, typically on an upward-traversing line on the west side of the bowl passing beneath the Fang, and join whatever track leads to Pineapple Pass. Most parties cache skis or snowshoes in the bowl before the final slope. The entire trip through the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins is avalanche terrain; this is a stability decision, not a route-finding one.
approach_variants.season: winter to early summer, snow
hazards: avalanche terrain the full length of the Alpental valley - roughly seventeen chutes cross the summer trail line
the summer boot path is not a safe winter line once snow is present
cornices at Pineapple Pass
moat between the snow and the rock at the top of the bowl
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high early-season flow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The finish is the same: the notch just south of Pineapple Pass, then a clockwise contour. Under snow the thing that decides where you can actually reach rock is the moat at the top of the bowl's snow. Probe it, and be ready to work around its edge on rock rather than force the direct step across.

With the base buried, the 'easy ramps left to a large rectangular block' start can be under snow. If you cannot find that block, you are probably below the true start — keep contouring around rather than climbing the first weakness above you, which is what puts parties into the gully between the Fang and the Tooth.

approach_variants.name: Sibley Creek Pass and the north-side glacier
approach_variants.notes: From the Hidden Lake Trailhead hike the maintained trail through forest and wildflower meadows to about 5,400 ft, where it begins a long traverse; leave it there and climb steep meadow and heather to Sibley Creek Pass. From the pass a boot path follows a grassy ridge crest before dropping onto the small glacier on the peaks' north side, which is crossed past all three summits — often on rock-hard ice under a thin skin of snow — to the col at the east end. This is a full approach day and is normally done with a high camp near the pass or on the glacier apron.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September, gated by the gravel road in and by snow on the ridge and glacier edge
hazards: Hard ice under thin snow on the glacier crossing — crampons
A steep, loose gully of dirt and rock lying on top of steeper rock and heather drops to the base
Sparse protection on the short exposed pinnacle pitch to the true summit
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cross the small unnamed glacier on the north side and then find the descent, because the base of this ridge is BELOW you, not above. The way down is a steep, loose gully of dirt and rock sitting on top of even steeper rock and heather — unpleasant enough that parties who have done it have given it a name — and it drops from the glacier edge to the foot of the ridge between the east summit and the main one. From the bottom, the climbing starts on ramps and a slabby section trending up and RIGHT toward the ridge crest. The proof you have picked the right line is an old rappel anchor on the crest, which marks where the ground eases above it; the committing fourth-class move used to pull onto the ridge from the ledge system below is the hardest thing on the route and it comes BEFORE that anchor, not after. If you are standing on the glacier looking for a way up, or you have not lost height since leaving the ice, you have not reached the base.

approach_variants.name: East end of the pullout, downhill to the Lower Wall
approach_variants.notes: Pullout on the north side of US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. From the LOWER, eastern end walk about fifty yards downhill to the climbers' trail, which climbs steeply to the Lower Wall base.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Steep climbers' trail from the road
Full southwest sun and polished rock
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Take the trail from the eastern end of the pullout, not the western one — the western trail traverses onto Logger's Ledge and serves Upper Castle, a full wall higher.

Running west to east along the Lower Wall's selected routes, the order is The Fault, Catapult, The Vertebrae, The Bone, so this is the third along. The Fault is the one the short trail from the right of the parking area reaches directly, which makes it the easiest fixed point to count from.

The wall itself is identified by its many roofs and by sitting directly under Logger's Ledge. Newer routes on the RIGHT side of this wall carry more bolts than the older ones, so an unusually well-protected line here means you have drifted east.

approach_variants.name: Blue Lake Trail into the basin, PAST South Early Winters Spire, then left along the base
approach_variants.notes:
From the Blue Lake Trailhead at about 5,400 ft on WA-20 west of Washington Pass, follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, PASS SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE, and traverse LEFT along the base to the shared start with the Northwest Corner. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base.

Six pitches, 5.11-, first climbed in 1965 and freed in 1985.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Two spires in a row on the same approach, with the near one carrying its own routes
A free-hanging rappel over a chockstone on the original descent line
Sustained 5.11- climbing over six pitches
No water in the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TWO SPIRES ARE PASSED IN ORDER AND THIS ROUTE IS ON THE SECOND ONE, WHICH IS THE WHOLE NAVIGATION PROBLEM ON THIS SIDE. Coming up the climbers' path into the basin, SOUTH Early Winters Spire comes first. YOU MUST WALK PAST IT. NORTH Early Winters Spire is beyond, and this route is on its west face, reached by traversing LEFT along the base.

SO THE NEGATIVE TEST IS: IF YOU HAVE STOPPED AT THE FIRST WALL YOU REACHED, YOU ARE UNDER SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRE, WHICH CARRIES ITS OWN CLUSTER OF WEST-SIDE ROUTES AND IS A DIFFERENT PEAK.

THE FEATURE THAT SEPARATES THE TWO SPIRES, AND IT IS THE BEST LANDMARK IN THIS BASIN: A MASSIVE CHASM, A CHOCKSTONE-FILLED CHIMNEY, SPLITS NORTH AND SOUTH EARLY WINTERS SPIRES. It is the Chockstone Route's line. You must have that chasm behind you or beside you before you are under North Early Winters Spire's west face.

ARRIVAL: this route shares its start with the Northwest Corner, reached by traversing LEFT along the base after passing the chasm. It also sits immediately RIGHT of Labor Pains, which climbs the clean face between the Chockstone Route and this one. So the order across this wall, from the chasm outward, is: CHOCKSTONE ROUTE in the chasm, LABOR PAINS on the clean face beyond it, then THE WEST FACE.

DESCENT, WHICH GIVES YOU A THIRD CONFIRMATION IF YOU TOP OUT UNSURE: two options exist. The original drops down the left side through a notch with THREE single-rope rappels, including ONE FREE-HANGING RAPPEL OVER A CHOCKSTONE, and finishes with scrambling back to the base. The bolted alternative is SIX BOLTED RAP STATIONS STARTING ABOUT 15 FEET RIGHT OF WHERE PITCH 6 TOPS OUT, and is generally faster and less committing.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to 7,300 ft, then right across scree
approach_variants.notes: Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail junction at 2.6 miles, then on to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft. From the lake's south side pick up the Aasgard Pass climbers' path and climb roughly 85 percent of the pass, to about 7,250 ft. Keep to the climber's LEFT throughout the pass — at the larch grove and again at the cliff band with the waterfall near 6,400 ft — and do not follow side paths toward the waterfall. At about 7,250 ft the main path crosses the largest braid of the creek that drains the pass. This is the pass's main water source and can thin out by late summer. Continue five to ten minutes past that crossing, then leave the path somewhere between 7,300 and 7,400 ft and make a rising traverse RIGHT across loose scree toward the toe of Dragontail.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Loose, unstable scree on the exposed rising traverse to the base
Aasgard Pass rockfall, and cliff-out ground right of the trees near the waterfall band
The creek braid at ~7,250 ft is the only water and can dry up late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base sits about 300 ft BELOW the point where the top of Aasgard Pass meets the toe of Dragontail — so you are aiming under the junction of pass and mountain, not at it. Overshooting up the pass and then coming down is the common error.

The start is described as being in the middle of the protruding tower. On the ground the marker is above your head rather than at your feet: the first belay ledge is roughly 190 ft up and carries two bushes, and the route starts directly below the RIGHT-HAND side of the right bush.

The first pitch also identifies itself by how it climbs. Fifty feet of easy ground leads to about ten feet of face moves around the RIGHT side of a recessed pod, and then back into the main crack system. If your first fifty feet is hard, or if there is no recessed pod to skirt, you are not on it.

The scree traverse in is the crux hazard of the approach — loose, exposed, and consequential given what is below.

approach_variants.name: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.notes: Note the access before anything else: the road up to the historic trailhead has a permanent washout, so the day starts with a long bike or walk past the vehicle gate before the trail proper begins. From the trailhead, the trail climbs through forest to the small lake at about two and a half miles — last easy water, and no fires or camping within two hundred feet of it. Continue up into the open meadows of the flats at about four and a half miles, the best camping on the route, then a further couple of miles to the GAP at roughly six miles, where the maintained tread ends and most parties bivy. The gap gives the first real view of the three summits and of the glacier below them.
approach_variants.season: July to September. Crevasses open on the glacier by midsummer and bare ice with a moat appears late in the season; an axe is a year-round item on this peak.
hazards: Glacier travel with real crevasse risk crossing to the col
A moat between rock and ice that widens through the season, with bare ice by late summer
Loose rock in the chimney and ramp system
No established trail or cairned route above the gap — route-finding is entirely on you
The descent is a committing series of rappels, and some stations are fixed slings of unknown age
Fog on the glacier traverse has triggered multiple multi-hour rescues on this mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the gap, drop about four hundred feet off-trail down snow and talus onto the glacier, cross it, and CLIMB BACK UP roughly a thousand feet on the far side to the COL BETWEEN THE MIDDLE AND NORTH TOWERS. That col is the base of the climbing, and the thousand-foot re-ascent is the discriminator: this is the only one of the three summits whose route requires you to gain a col before you touch its rock. From the col the line is a RAMP that leads LEFT and then angles RIGHT into a SHALLOW CHIMNEY — the chimney is the check, being the one chimney breaching the block from this col, and it is fourth class with a move or two of low fifth. Above it an exposed fourth-class ridge leads to a grassy ramp and the summit. Negative markers: if you are standing under THREE STACKED WOODEN LADDERS bolted into the rock, you are at the lookout summit at the southern end of the ridge, two towers away; if you have climbed a short face straight off the glacier with no col gained, you are on the middle tower's south face.

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.
bivy.water: Reliable through most of the season from the tarns and small streams in the meadows, though the standing water is shallow and warms up late in summer. Treat everything. Later in a dry year the tarns shrink and the better water is the running melt above the flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
bivy.capacity: The main camping area on this approach — several established pockets spread through the meadows and around the tarns. It absorbs a fair number of parties but is genuinely crowded on summer and autumn weekends, and it is the overflow when the lookout is full.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap high camp
bivy.notes: The last flat ground before the glacier, roughly a mile short of the lookout, and the correct camp for a party that wants the summit block early and cold rather than soft. The maintained trail effectively ends here, so everything above is a bootpath, snow and the ladders. Its value is that it puts the glacier crossing and the ladders in the first hour of the day, when the snow is still firm — a real advantage over starting from the meadows two miles back. The cost is exposure: it is a gap, it catches weather, and there is nothing sheltering about it. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin vegetation, and take a hard look at whether the crossing above is in condition before committing to a camp that only makes sense if you go up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only for most of the season, and nothing at all once the snow around the gap has gone. Assume you are melting or carrying from Goat Flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit required. Federal recreation pass to park. Campfires prohibited on this whole stretch of trail; there is no fuel here regardless.
bivy.capacity: A few small pitches on rock and snow at and just below the gap; one or two parties, not a group site

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.
bivy.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation

approach_variants.name: Trail #641 to Tin Can Gap, then a glacier-side camp
approach_variants.notes: Identical approach to the other two summits as far as the glacier: the long bike or walk past the permanent road washout to the trailhead, then the trail to the small lake at about two and a half miles, the open meadows at about four and a half, and the GAP at roughly six to seven miles where the maintained tread ends. From the gap drop about four hundred feet off-trail onto the glacier and cross it. Most parties bivy on or near the glacier below the peaks rather than trying all three summits in a push, and this route in particular is normally done from such a camp rather than from the gap.
approach_variants.season: Summer. The moat and any open crevasses drive the timing more than the rock does.
hazards: Loose, suspect rock in the upper part of the scramble, with rockfall onto anyone below
Glacier travel and crevasse risk on the shared approach
A moat between rock and ice that widens through the season
Very little published route detail for this summit — treat it as a lightly documented alpine objective and be prepared to route-find
Fog on the glacier has triggered multiple multi-hour rescues on this mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the glacier-side camp, this summit's SOUTH FACE is reached by a short climb and traverse straight to the foot of the peak — and the discriminator against its northern neighbour is the absence of a col: you do NOT gain a saddle first and you do not climb a thousand feet on the far side of the glacier before touching rock. If you have gained a col, you are on the wrong tower. The face is BROADER than it looks from the ice, so pick the line from the glacier before you start up; the lower rock is solid third and fourth class and it turns looser and more broken higher, which is the confirmation you are on the described line rather than a cleaner variation. Negative markers: if you are following a ramp leftward into a shallow chimney out of a saddle, you are on the northern tower's route; if you are under three stacked wooden ladders pinned into the rock, you are at the lookout summit at the far southern end of the ridge.
