approach_variants.name: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
approach_variants.notes:
Trail #641 from the Tupso Pass trailhead at the end of FR 41. Forest to Saddle Lake at about two and a half miles — the last easy water, with no fires and no camping within two hundred feet of the shore beyond this point — then up through meadows to Goat Flats at roughly four and a half miles, which has the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound.

From Goat Flats the trail climbs about two more miles to Tin Can Gap at roughly six miles, banking most of the day's gain. That is the effective end of the maintained trail and where most walkers turn back.

The trail has been maintained by volunteers in recent years, with large numbers of logs cleared; note that a big fallen log above Saddle Lake has rerouted the tread, and there is a rough connector going straight up and down to the next switchback.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: moat between glacier and rock that widens through the season and is hard to enter in poor visibility
crevasses on the Queest-Alb once it opens up
exposure on the ladders, particularly between the second and third
unverified fixed hand-line on the rock step past Tin Can Gap
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the MOAT between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the SOUTH peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.

approach_variants.name: Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
approach_variants.notes:
FR 41 has washed out repeatedly and the closure point has moved. Reported blockages have been around five miles up from the Mountain Loop Highway, and at other times past the Canyon Creek bridge, leaving roughly nine miles of road between the closure and the trailhead. Vehicles are barred past the barrier but foot and bike traffic are allowed, and biking the road is the common tactic.

Treat this as a standing possibility rather than a one-off: check with the Darrington Ranger District or the Verlot Public Service Center before committing, because the difference is a day hike versus an overnight. There is now a sign at the road marking the old trailhead.
approach_variants.season: whenever the road is closed at the washout
hazards: several miles of road walking or biking each way with the resulting late finish
all the hazards of the standard variation once on trail
approach_variants.baseFinding: Once you reach Tupso Pass the route is identical, and the same markers apply: cross to the north side of the ridge past Tin Can Gap to meet the top of the Queest-Alb, find the moat entrance rather than stepping onto open ice, and finish on the three stacked ladders on the SOUTH peak.

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek Trail, then off-trail through the vine maple to the south-side talus
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead at about 2,400 ft, cross the Kachess River ford, follow 1.7 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek crossing, then about a mile further through vine maple brush to the base of the long talus slope on Middle Peak's south side.

This shares the trailhead and initial trail with the East / Main Peak standard route, and the divergence is where you leave the trail into the brush.

About 4.3 km beyond the road and 4,600 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: June to September
hazards: An unbridged Kachess River ford at the trailhead
Off-trail travel through vine maple brush to reach the talus
Long loose talus below the notch
A class 4 chimney and a broad exposed ledge traverse
Rockfall onto anyone in the notch below the chimney
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH YOU WANT IS MARKED BY A CHOCKSTONE, AND THAT IS THE ONE UNAMBIGUOUS OBJECT ON THIS SIDE OF THE MOUNTAIN. The long south-side talus steepens toward the notch between the MAIN and MIDDLE peaks, and a chockstone sits in that notch. Chockstone in the gap between two summits: that is your arrival, and it is a thing rather than a description.

FROM THE NOTCH THE LINE IS A LEDGE, NOT A RIDGE. Traverse a BROAD SOUTH-FACING LEDGE to a rock gable roughly 150 ft below the summit. If you are on a crest rather than on a wide ledge, you have taken the ridge instead of the traverse.

AND THE CLIMBING ITSELF CONFIRMS IT: a solid, enjoyable CLASS 4 CHIMNEY runs directly from the gable to the top. Solid rock is worth noting because so little on this peak is. If the ground above the gable is loose scrambling rather than a defined chimney, you are not at the gable.

THE DESCENT IS THE MIRROR AND IT IS SHORT: two 60 ft rappels down the South Chimney regain the ledge system, then reverse the talus and the trail.

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE PEAK'S OTHER LINES: the standard scramble goes to the East / Main Peak and the West Peak is reached from Spectacle Point on a multi-day approach. If you have walked past the Main-Middle notch and are heading for a different summit, you are on a different route.

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin
bivy.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.
bivy.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other

approach_variants.name: Mineral Creek Trail to the break in the timber west of the waterfall gully
approach_variants.notes:
From the Mineral Creek trailhead, Trail #1331, at roughly 2,360 to 2,400 ft via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass, the trail promptly crosses the Kachess River — look for logs, and wade if they are not there. It climbs gently north through second growth and brushy old avalanche paths, muddy in places with occasional blowdown.

At about 1.6 to 1.7 miles it crosses Mineral Creek itself, which carries enough current in early season that parties often lay a log rather than ford. The ruins of an old mine and mill sit just off-trail here — a landmark and the last good water.

Continue upstream through brushy trail roughly another mile, to about the 2.7-mile mark.

About 8.85 km, with 1,400 to 1,700 ft of off-trail gain above the trail.
approach_variants.season: July to September
hazards: An unbridged Kachess River crossing at the trailhead and a Mineral Creek crossing with real current in early season
A brushy, easy-to-miss trail departure between two similar drainages
Loose rock and rockfall through the upper talus and choss gullies — helmets, and keep the group tight
A snow ramp around 5,200 ft persisting into midsummer
Brief but genuine class 3 with shifting blocks on the final 400 ft, harder than the published grade suggests
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE TAKEOFF IS A BREAK IN THE TIMBER ON THE RIGHT, AND THE WAY TO GET IT RIGHT IS TO KNOW WHICH DRAINAGE IT IS NOT. At about 2.7 miles, between roughly 3,300 and 3,500 ft, watch on the RIGHT (west) for a break in the timber where an obvious boot and social path leaves the maintained trail and cuts west through 100 to 200 ft of vine maple brush to the base of the south-face talus. THE DISCRIMINATOR: leave the trail WEST OF THE BROAD WATERFALL GULLY that drains the south face — NOT at the drainage directly above the Mineral Creek crossing. Trip reports flag exactly this junction as easy to get wrong in the brush, and the two drainages are the reason. Old mine ruins at the creek crossing, then roughly another mile, then the break past the waterfall gully. WHAT THE GROUND SHOULD DO ONCE YOU ARE OFF TRAIL, in order, so you can check yourself without seeing the peak: the lower 1,000 ft is moderately angled, largely stable LARGE talus. Above that the rock turns smaller and looser and funnels into choss gullies, class 2 with short class 3 steps. A snow ramp is commonly met around 5,200 ft and can persist into midsummer, so carry an axe early in the season. THE FINAL 400 FT IS THE MOST EXPOSED GROUND ON THE ROUTE, with brief but genuine class 3 and blocks that shift underfoot. Published descriptions calling this section class 3 are considered generous by parties who found it heads-up throughout. NOT TO BE CONFUSED WITH THE PARK LAKES LINE: a longer two-day route from a camp at Upper Park Lake climbs the north side to the Main-Middle notch and crosses a ledge system on the north face. It is a separate route on the other side of the mountain, and none of the markers above appear on it.

access.fees: Standard Okanogan-Wenatchee NF trailhead/parking fee policies apply in addition to the wilderness permit.
access.notes: Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit required (May 15-Oct 31; self-issue at trailhead, no fee). Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Pass required. CLOSED by the Three Queens Fire closure: Order 06-17-03-2026-44, effective September 18 through October 31, 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes the Mineral Creek Trailhead, the Mineral Creek Trail and the Spectacle Lake Trail. Cle Elum Ranger District: (509) 852-1100. No campfires above 5,000 ft elevation.
access.permit: Self-issue, free wilderness permit at the trailhead.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Cle Elum Ranger District (Alpine Lakes Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry your copy.

bivy.name: Spectacle Point high camp
bivy.notes: High camp on the ridge above Park Lakes, used as the base for the West Peak.
bivy.water: Uncertain late in the season; carry water up from Park Lakes
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: Small; a few tent sites on the ridge

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Thunder Mountain Lakes
bivy.notes: Lake basin under the granite of Slippery Slab Tower and Thunder Mountain, reached by the unofficial trail south from Trap Pass. The closest camp to the north face. Fragile ground; camp only on rock or bare sites.
bivy.water: The lakes
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
bivy.capacity: A few small sites on durable ground

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

approach_variants.name: Summit road, powerlines, then south to the upper tier
approach_variants.notes: Park at the last parking area before the Mount Erie summit, at the sharp left-hand bend on the summit road. Contour down and west along grassy ledges and short rock steps, through a short belt of woods and under the powerlines, to the cliff top above Lake Erie, then descend the low third-class ramp.
approach_variants.season: Year-round; no current raptor closure at Mount Erie
hazards: Two fourth-class scrambles at the base with exposure below
Exposed contouring above the cliff top
Third-class ramp descent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the bottom of the ramp, go LEFT and then keep heading SOUTH past the lower-tier routes (False Impressions, Lethal Weapon, Intimidator, Terminator). Intimidator, at the wall's lowest point, is the marker you pass.

The confirmation is two distinct blocky FOURTH-CLASS scrambles: you have to do both to reach the upper tier. Having to scramble twice is correct here and is not evidence you have wandered off the approach.

Tindall's Terror and Scarface are the upper-tier routes. If you never scrambled, you are still on the lower tier.

approach_variants.name: Yellow Aster Butte Trail, then the Tomyhoi Arm ridge to the moat below the false summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead, around 3,600-3,700 ft, on Twin Lakes Road (FR-3065), start on Yellow Aster Butte Trail #686. It climbs through forest switchbacks with a couple of seasonal creek crossings in the first mile.

At roughly 1.5 miles the signed Tomyhoi Lake Trail splits off RIGHT toward Gold Run Pass near 5,400 ft. Stay left, then contour into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns at about 5,200-5,600 ft — roughly two hours and four miles from the car, and the last dependable water.

From the basin leave maintained trail: head north-northwest over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm.

As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the NORTH — right — side rather than staying on the crest. The path fades into scree and talus near the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. The moat below the false summit opens as the season goes on and is the crux either way
hazards: A rock-and-ice moat at the notch that is the crux of the outing and widens through the season
Glacier-polished slick rock at the snow margin
Minor crevasse hazard traversing the top edge of the Tomyhoi Glacier
Loose, exposed, non-obvious route-finding on scree and rock benches approaching the notch
The descent through the V-slot is the most exposed step of the day and is where parties rope up
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS A MOAT, NOT A LEDGE — THE CLIMBING STARTS WHERE THE GLACIER MEETS THE ROCK AT ABOUT 7,200-7,250 FT, AT A NOTCH IN THE JAGGED RIDGE BELOW THE FALSE SUMMIT. Traverse along the TOP EDGE of the Tomyhoi Glacier to avoid several rock pinnacles, and aim for that notch. Getting into it means a traverse on hard snow around a small moat, and in many years that shallow rock-and-ice moat is the crux of the entire outing.

THE ROCK BY THE GLACIER IS GLACIER-POLISHED AND SLICK, and that is a tactile confirmation you are in the right place as well as a warning. Smooth, scoured rock at the snow margin means you are at the moat.

THERE IS A DOCUMENTED ALTERNATIVE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU COMMIT: drop 100 to 200 ft LOWER and climb a rock finger to reach the same notch. A party that arrives at an open moat it does not like has a published option other than retreat.

GEAR IS GENUINELY DISPUTED HERE and the honest statement is that reports differ: some parties manage the moat traverse with an ice axe alone on firm snow, others want crampons. It opens as the season goes on. Carry for the worse case.

ABOVE THE NOTCH, THE SEQUENCE IS THE CHECK: an exposed traverse around a rib gains the climbable side of the summit block, then roughly 160 ft along the LEFT edge of the ridge, then a ledge crossed WEST to a wide corner where the crux is a short V-shaped SLOT. Third class throughout with that one slot harder. The block looks far worse from the false summit than it climbs — repeatedly, in every account — so an intimidating view from the false summit is not evidence you are off route.

OLD RING PITONS ON THE ROUTE are a reminder this is not a maintained line, not a sign you are on the right one.

bivy.name: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)
bivy.notes: The standard camp for the southeast ridge of Tomyhoi Peak, and the reason Tomyhoi is a comfortable overnight rather than a very long day. From the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead at about 3,700 ft the trail climbs towards Gold Run Pass, forks left onto the meadows trail and reaches the scatter of tarns at roughly 5,580 ft in about four miles. From camp the route drops northwest over a hump to a col near 6,266 ft and follows the ridge over benches and a small glacier remnant to the false summit and the class 3 summit block. This is one of the most heavily impacted alpine basins in the district and the rules exist because the meadow was being destroyed; a single careless night on heather leaves a scar that lasts years. Mountain goats frequent the basin, are habituated, and will come to camp for the salt in urine, so pee on rock well away from the tents. Snow covers the basin into July and the tarns can still be part frozen at the start of the season.
bivy.water: The tarns themselves. They are shallow, warm late in the season and shared with a great many campers, so filter and draw well away from where people wash.
bivy.permit: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail EXCEPT at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. Party size twelve, and food must be canistered, in a protective sack or hung well clear of the ground and trunk. Recreation pass at the trailhead, free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.
bivy.capacity: Perhaps eight to ten small sites among the tarns, all of them well used; expect company, and expect to take whichever pad is left rather than the one you wanted

bivy.name: Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this approach the road is the variable that decides what the trip is. The first four and a half miles to the Tomyhoi Lake and Yellow Aster Butte trailhead are rough gravel that an ordinary car can manage with patience; the straight section below the switchbacks is the worst of it, with loose rock and deep potholes. The final two miles to Twin Lakes are narrow, unmaintained for passenger cars, short of pullouts, and genuinely want high clearance. Parties turned back at the lower lot are looking at an extra two miles and roughly 1,500 ft of road walking each way before the climb even starts, which turns a comfortable day on Winchester or a two-day Larrabee trip into something much longer, and is a good reason to plan on sleeping out. The road is snowbound well into the season most years and is often not drivable to the upper end until July. Call the ranger station before committing, and if you park low, camping in a pullout the night before is a common and reasonable way to save the morning.
bivy.water: Creeks cross the road in places but there is nothing reliable at the lot itself; carry water up from the valley or plan to filter higher
bivy.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and the state parks pass is not accepted here. Fill in the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register where one is provided. Dispersed roadside camping on national forest land outside the wilderness boundary is generally allowed, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a pullout.
bivy.capacity: A dozen or so vehicles in the trailhead lot, plus scattered pullouts along the road; it fills on summer weekends and there is nowhere to turn around if you keep going and change your mind

rappel_detail.pull: On two 70s this is close to a full-length rappel, so set the knot well clear of the lip and knot the ends.
rappel_detail.notes: Top anchor allowing a rappel from the very top of the route with double 70m ropes.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted station ~20-30 ft above the old P6 slung-block anchor
hazards: Rope choice is decided at this station and the margin is not discretionary: from the top anchor two 70 m ropes reach the bolted anchor atop pitch 5, and doubled 60 m ropes DO NOT reach between them
The older slung-block anchor below the bolts is still the more obvious thing to see; it is not the current station
rappel_detail.station: The top station is a BOLTED anchor sitting roughly 20-30 ft above the old slung-block anchor at the top of pitch 6 - the old block is the landmark, the bolts are above it. Parties on doubled 60 m ropes cannot reach the pitch-5 anchor from here and must stop at the fixed nut-and-sling anchor about halfway down pitch 6.

rappel_detail.notes: Described generically as an 'obvious, good-quality anchor'.
hazards: Slab above and below with little to stand on, so arrive at the anchor rather than near it - there is nothing to grab if you end up off line
rappel_detail.station: The bolted anchor at the top of pitch 5, immediately above the route's very thin slab crux. This is the station the first rappel is measured to, and the reason two 70 m ropes are the published requirement.

rappel_detail.notes: Same as above; individual rappel lengths aren't known.
Continuing down the route on double ropes.
Continuing down the route on double ropes.
Final rappel to the ground.
rappel_detail.anchor: Bolted or tree anchor near base
hazards: Pitch 1 is described as sustained, heady and delicate with alpine crumbliness - the loosest ground on the route, and both strands run over it
rappel_detail.station: Last rappel, down pitch 1 to the base of the wall.

approach_variants.name: The hairpin pond pullout to the treed ledge, then its LEFT side and rightward across slabs to the first bolt
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as the East Face: from SR-20, park at the informal pullout on the north shoulder of the highway a short walk east of the small pond, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass. No permit needed.

A well-beaten climbers' trail leaves the east end of the pond and climbs steeply through timber; in roughly 30 minutes it breaks out at the edge of the large boulder and talus field that lines the eastern base of the Liberty Bell group, meaning Liberty Bell, Minuteman, Concord and Lexington Towers. From there, work up and LEFT across the talus toward Lexington Tower's east side, 30-45 minutes total from the car for most parties. No reliable water; the roadside pond is not worth using.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: Frequent rockfall in both gullies flanking the treed ledge
Doubled 60 m ropes do not reach the first rappel station from the top of the route
Surviving original 1989 bolts and an aging fixed-nut anchor despite rebolting
The walk-off traverse borders on unprotected fifth-class slab; many parties stay roped
No water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding:
TOOTH AND CLAW BEGINS NEAR THE LEFT SIDE OF THE TREED LEDGE AND ANGLES RIGHTWARD ACROSS SLABS TO THE FIRST BOLT. Those are three checkable things in sequence: the LEFT end of a ledge with trees on it, a rightward line across SLABS, and a BOLT.

GETTING ONTO THE LEDGE IS THE FIRST PROBLEM AND SNOW DECIDES IT: either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge. Snow in the talus and at the base into early-mid summer determines whether you gain it from the left or the right. Helmet up well before committing to either gully; both see fairly frequent rockfall.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE ROUTE THAT SHARES THIS LEDGE: the EAST FACE, 5.9-plus and ten pitches, is the other line here. This one is 5.12a and it is the one that traverses RIGHT off the left end of the ledge to a bolt. If you are starting up cracks from the middle of the ledge without traversing, you are on the East Face.

HARDWARE AS A CHECK, AND IT IS A MIXED SIGNAL WORTH READING CAREFULLY: the descent stations lower on the route are described as obvious, good-quality anchors on trees or bolts, but SOME ORIGINAL 1989 QUARTER-INCH-CLASS BOLTS REMAIN DESPITE A POST-2016 REBOLTING PUSH, and at least one older fixed-nut and sling anchor is noted as aging. New-looking bolts are not proof of a modern line here.

DESCENT, AND THE ROPE LENGTH IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: from the top, the first anchor is a bolted station roughly 20-30 ft ABOVE the old pitch-6 slung-block anchor. WITH DOUBLE 70 M ROPES you can rappel from the very top; DOUBLED 60 M ROPES WILL NOT REACH THAT FIRST STATION. Most parties instead take the walk-off from the East Shoulder: an exposed, somewhat sketchy fourth-class traverse west, bordering on unprotected fifth-class slab in spots, to gain the same descent gully the East Face uses.

approach_variants.name: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass, then the east slope traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Drive to Tiffany Springs Campground at about 6,760 ft on the forest road system, reached either from Conconully to the south or from Winthrop to the north by the East Chewuch road. Both are long gravel drives of an hour or more; a third, gentler line comes over Baldy Pass on the South Fork.

From the campground, walk trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft, roughly forty-five minutes of easy trail. Leave the trail there and traverse south across open grassy slopes into the small cirque at the base of the north face, about 7,360 ft.

The face rises around six hundred and fifty feet above the cirque and is split by couloirs and a rock tower. The whole approach is short and easy by the standards of this corner of the state, which is the point of coming here.
approach_variants.season: June through early September, once snow has cleared the lower sections
hazards: Indistinguishable from the harder tower route until the vertical step, which is three pitches up
Loose rock and boulders throughout; the arete is exposed on both sides
The old descent trail is faint and easy to lose above the lower lake
No technical crux means parties move unroped where a slip is consequential
Long gravel drives from every direction
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the cirque, split the face in half: SNOW GULLIES LEFT, ROCK TOWER AND ITS RIDGE RIGHT. This route is on the right. A continuous snow chute above you means you are under the couloir line instead.

This route shares its start with the harder line on the same tower, and there is no way to separate them at the bottom, so do not try. Climb the rocky ridge from the cirque — roughly a hundred feet of fourth-class ground to gain the arete — and then take low-angled ridge travel along the crest with real exposure on both sides.

THE SPLIT IS AT THE VERTICAL STEP, AND IT IS THE ONLY TEST THAT WORKS. Where the ridge steepens into a vertical section, this route BYPASSES IT ON THE LEFT and stays at fourth class. The other line goes straight up the tower into a wide flaring chimney and offwidth at 5.7 to 5.8. So: if you are looking at a chimney and reaching for wide gear, you have taken the harder line by accident. If you are moving left onto easier ground and never pull a hard move, you are on this route as intended.

CONFIRM BY DIFFICULTY, WHICH IS UNUSUAL BUT HONEST HERE: five pitches, all of them fourth class or third, no technical crux anywhere. A pitch that feels like real rock climbing is evidence you are somewhere else. The route finishes with a short approach to the top of the tower and then a crest traverse of walking to Tiffany's main summit slope.

NEGATIVE MARKER on the descent: it is not reversed. From the top, descend the north-west ridge on mostly third-class ground to roughly 7,950 ft, contour north-east and find the old ridge trail — it may be faint — and follow it down to rejoin the main trail at Honeymoon Pass.

bivy.name: Tiffany Springs Campground
bivy.notes: This is the base for the north face and the trailhead in one, which is unusual and is what makes the face approachable at all: the walk to the bottom of the routes is under an hour, so a party can sleep at the car and still be climbing at first light without a bivouac. Trail 373 begins across the road from the campground and runs east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at around 7,150 ft, from where the face is below you. THE DRIVE IS THE COMMITMENT. Three ways reach it and they are not equivalent: a narrow four-wheel-drive road over Lone Frank Pass from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek, about twenty miles; a longer gravel road over Baldy Pass suited to two-wheel drive, about thirty; and a good two-wheel-drive gravel line from the Methow, north out of Winthrop on the Chewuch River road and then east and north on the 37 and 39, about twenty-six miles. Road 39 itself has not been graded in some time and is not recommended for low-clearance passenger cars. At this elevation the road holds snow late into the spring and can shut with the first serious autumn storm, so the usable window is short and both ends of it are worth checking rather than assuming.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AND NO TAP — this is the single most important practical fact about the place, and its name is misleading. There is no piped supply, no water service and no rubbish service. Bring everything you need for drinking, cooking and washing, or plan to treat from Tiffany Lake, which is a short walk east on the trail and is the nearest dependable open water. In late summer this whole plateau is dry and what looks like a creek on a map may be nothing at all.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside designated wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery — the opposite of the permit expectation a few miles west in the Pasayten. There is a small nightly fee at the campground and sites are first come, first served. Fire restrictions on this dry high plateau run through most of the summer and are commonly total bans, which given what has burned here recently should be treated as the default rather than the exception. Party size and stay limits are the usual forest ones.
bivy.capacity: A small primitive forest campground with a handful of sites, taking tents and modest vehicles. Trailers are not appropriate given the road. It is rarely full and it is the only organised camping anywhere near this face.

bivy.name: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
bivy.notes: Under a mile from the campground and directly on the approach, this is the camp for a party who would rather sleep on water than at a car, or who has arrived to find the campground full or closed. It is the last certain water before the face. The trail continues around the shore and climbs about six hundred feet to Honeymoon Pass, which is the gateway to the north side; parties leaving a second vehicle at the Freezeout Ridge roadhead can carry on over Whistler Pass at around 7,600 ft to the summit and descend the Freezeout trail, an open loop of some eleven miles that is the standard way to combine the walk-up with a look at the face. THE BURN IS PART OF THE LANDSCAPE HERE. This trail travels through old fire scars that have opened the views and filled the ground with wildflower meadow, and the 2026 fire has added to that directly on this mountain — expect standing dead timber, no shade, and blowdown that changes with each windstorm. Do not pitch under dead trees in wind.
bivy.water: The lakes, and they are the dependable supply for the whole north side of this mountain — everything above them on the pass and the face runs on snowmelt and is dry once that has gone. Access to the water is easy from the trail. Treat it; these are shallow, warm, well-used lakes rather than cold alpine tarns.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness. No permit, no quota, no reservation, and no fee to camp at the lakes. A pass is not required to park at the campground trailhead across the road. Fire restrictions apply through the summer and are usually total bans; carry a stove. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground, and note that this trail is open to horses and mountain bikes as well as walkers, so pitch clear of it.
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal spots around the shores, with the established ground at the north-west end of Little Tiffany Lake. Room for a party or two. Nothing developed and no toilet, and it sees family day-hiking traffic rather than climbers.

bivy.name: Honeymoon Pass
bivy.notes: The pass is where the trail crosses onto the north side and the face comes into view, and it is the tactical camp rather than the comfortable one. Its argument is a dawn start: from here the base of the routes is a short drop and a scramble rather than a walk from the road, which matters for the north-east couloir where the snow wants climbing early and matters much less for the rock, since the campground is under an hour away regardless. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WIND, in that order, and on a face this short the trade is rarely worth it — most parties are better off sleeping at the campground or the lake and walking in. Where it does earn its keep is for a party spending two days on the face, or one continuing over Whistler Pass to the summit and out by Freezeout Ridge. Nights are cold at this elevation from late August onward and there is no shelter at all if weather comes across the plateau.
bivy.water: None dependable. Snowmelt early in the season and nothing at all once it has gone. Everything is carried up from Tiffany Lake, six hundred feet and half a mile below, and the party that forgets this ends up walking back down for it in the evening. In the ice season it is a snow camp and you melt.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation, no fee. Fire restrictions run through the summer and there is nothing to burn at this height in any case. The turf here is thin and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass for a small party on gravel and thin turf. No established sites, no facilities and nothing to shelter behind. Windswept is the word most often used about this crest and it is accurate.

bivy.name: The talus and benches below the north face
bivy.notes: The routes start here and, on a face six hundred and fifty feet high forty-five minutes from a campground, essentially nobody sleeps here. It is written down because a party reading a list of camps should not be left to assume there is a bivouac at the base — there is not, and the answer to a late arrival is the campground, not the wall. THE FACE ITSELF is broken by several couloirs, aretes and vertical granite cliffs; the north-east couloir is the longest and most direct of the snow lines, on the left, and the tower at the right-hand end carries the rock routes, with the ridge line giving a vertical crack, a wide flaring chimney and long stretches of easy fourth-class scrambling on generally excellent rock. Because the snow goes soon after the roads become passable, the ice and couloir lines are a shoulder-season or winter objective and are reached by ski or snowmobile in that season rather than by driving to the campground. Treat the rock routes as the summer proposition and the couloirs as a separate trip requiring a separate approach.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the couloirs early, and nothing whatsoever once that has gone. Given how early the snow leaves here after the roads open, that window is short. Carry water from the lakes; there is no source at the base of the face you should plan on.
bivy.permit: National forest, non-wilderness — no permit, no quota, no reservation. No fires: this is bare rock and talus with nothing to burn and fragile alpine ground around it. Standard leave-no-trace applies and human waste has to be carried out from the base of a face this small and this close to a road.
bivy.capacity: No established camping. There are boulder-field benches and scraps of flat ground at the foot of the wall where one or two people could put down a bag, and nothing more — this is a place to leave packs and gear up rather than a site, and it is recorded to say so rather than to invent one.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT over Cutthroat and Granite Passes to Snowy Lakes, then the reddish boulder and the cave
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead at about 4,875 ft on SR-20, 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass at about 6,800 ft, roughly 4.9 miles. THIS STRETCH HAS ONLY INTERMITTENT SMALL STREAMS, SO FILL UP AT THE LAST STREAM BELOW THE PASS, WHICH IS ITSELF DRY; there is little reliable water again until Snowy Lakes.

From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass at about 6,300 ft, roughly 6.5-7 miles in. Granite Pass holds snow into July or August and when snow-covered is steep and exposed enough to warrant an ice axe. Beyond it the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut blasted-out section, loses a little elevation into a meadowed basin.

Roughly 9.5-10 miles in, about a mile before Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers' use path branches RIGHT, east, off the PCT and climbs about half a mile and 400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin, the standard base camp with reliable water and good tent sites.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: A notoriously loose and rockfall-prone summit gully; climb one at a time through constrictions
Granite Pass holds snow into July or August and is steep and exposed when covered; carry an axe
Little reliable water between Cutthroat Pass and Snowy Lakes
A cliff-cut, blasted-out section of trail between Granite and Methow Passes
Roughly 10-11 miles one-way to camp before any climbing
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH FROM CAMP HAS THREE MARKERS AND ALL THREE ARE OBJECTS YOU CAN PUT A HAND ON, WHICH IS RARE AND IS WHY THIS ROUTE IS UNUSUALLY FINDABLE IN CLOUD.

FIRST: from camp near Lower Snowy Lake, head cross-country SOUTH toward Tower Mountain on a climbers' path, then make a short but strenuous traverse across a TALUS FIELD, AIMING FOR A DISTINCTIVE LARGE REDDISH BOULDER PARTWAY ACROSS. A single big red block in a talus field.

SECOND: BEYOND THE BOULDER, A RAMP ON THE LEFT SIDE OF A LARGE CAVE. THE CAVE CUTS ABOUT 25 YARDS INTO THE MOUNTAINSIDE and makes a good wind-sheltered rest stop. A cave you can walk twenty-five yards into is not something you can mistake for anything else.

THIRD: that ramp leads UP TO THE BASE OF THE MAIN SUMMIT GULLY. That gully is the route.

SO THE ORDER IS: TALUS, RED BOULDER, CAVE, RAMP ON ITS LEFT, GULLY. If you have crossed the talus and found no red boulder, you are off the traverse line. If you have found the boulder but no cave, keep going.

FROM THE BASE OF THE GULLY the route follows LEDGES ON THE GULLY'S RIGHT SIDE, zigzagging back toward the gully-notch in the ridge and up broken rock to the summit. Right-hand ledges, not the gully bed.

THE GULLY IS THE MAIN HAZARD OF THE WHOLE OUTING AND THE RULE IS ABOUT SPACING RATHER THAN TECHNIQUE: the rock is notoriously loose and rockfall-prone, so helmets on and CLIMB ONE AT A TIME THROUGH THE NARROWEST SECTIONS, staying right and moving efficiently.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass PCT north trailhead
bivy.notes: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.
bivy.water: None at the lot, and this matters more here than it looks. The crest north of the pass is dry, so what you carry out of the car is what you have until well down the far side.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit, no quota and nothing to reserve anywhere in this zone — this is national forest, and the park permit system that governs the country west of here does not apply.
bivy.capacity: A large paved lot on the north-east side of the highway at the pass, shared between climbers, larch-season day hikers and long-distance walkers. It fills early on weekends from late summer onward and there is no overflow.

bivy.name: Snowy Lakes basin
bivy.notes: This is THE climbers' camp for both Golden Horn and Tower Mountain and the whole point of walking the PCT north. From Rainy Pass it is roughly twenty miles round trip over Cutthroat and Granite Passes, with the trail contouring past Tower Mountain and dropping to about six thousand three hundred feet before a signed spur climbs half a mile of well-graded switchbacks to the lakes. Lower Snowy Lake comes first, Upper is a short way above. From camp, Golden Horn is taken by gullies on its south side, mostly loose class 3 scrambling, ending at a summit block where the last twenty feet of mantling above a big ledge is the one move that stops parties; Tower Mountain's west and south sides are a choice of class 3 gully systems on generally sound rock buried under loose surface debris, while its east face is a sheer wall and no business of a scrambling party. Both can be done from this camp in one long day. August and September are the season; snow on the traverse and the north-facing slopes governs anything earlier.
bivy.water: Both lakes, and they are reliable all season. After the dry crest behind you this is where the water problem ends, which is why parties push through to it rather than stopping short.
bivy.permit: None. This is national forest — no backcountry permit, no quota, nothing to book. Use the established sites rather than making new ones; the meadow here is thin, slow-growing and visibly worn where people have spread out. Campfires are a bad idea on principle at this elevation and are usually banned outright by mid summer under a forest-wide order.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites at and between the two lakes, mostly one or two tents each, plus more on the meadow benches along the PCT below the turn-off. Popular enough that a summer weekend will see several parties, and heavily so once the larches turn.

bivy.name: Cutthroat Pass, PCT crest camps
bivy.notes: Cutthroat Pass is about five miles north of Rainy Pass by a steadily graded trail and is the first natural stop for anyone heading for Golden Horn or Tower Mountain, though a fit party carrying enough water will push straight past it toward Granite Pass or the lakes. It is not a climbers' camp for any peak — nothing is climbed directly from it — but it is the obvious bad-weather or late-start stop, and it is where a party discovers whether it brought enough water. The larch stands here are the reason the pass is crowded from the third week of September. This is also the point where the Cutthroat Creek trail comes up from the east, so a party can leave one car at each trailhead and walk through.
bivy.water: NONE AT THE PASS, and this is the planning problem of the whole approach. The last certain water is on the climb up, roughly three miles from the trailhead, and there is little to nothing again until close to the lakes far ahead. Carry enough for the evening, the night and the next morning's walk, which for two people is more than most parties expect to shoulder.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit and no reservation. Camp on durable ground rather than in the meadow, and note that the quarter-mile camping closure around Cutthroat Lake, well below and to the east, does not reach up here. Forest-wide campfire bans are normal from mid summer; there is nothing worth burning at this elevation anyway.
bivy.capacity: No established or numbered sites, but a scatter of well-used flat patches on the shoulders and in the larch benches either side of the pass. Several parties can spread out. It is one of the most popular overnight spots on this stretch of trail in larch season, so a Friday arrival in late September will not have it to itself.

bivy.name: Granite Pass
bivy.notes: Granite Pass sits a couple of miles beyond Cutthroat Pass as the trail swings north-west and begins the long traverse under Tower Mountain. Its value is position rather than comfort: it breaks the walk from Rainy Pass to Snowy Lakes into two manageable halves and it puts a party on the right side of the exposed traverse ahead. That traverse is the reason to think about timing — beyond Granite Pass the trail is cut and blasted into the cliffs, and while it is a walk in dry conditions, it is genuinely dangerous under snow. Snowfields cross the trail here into August in a normal year and an axe belongs in the pack until they have gone. Most parties passing through are heading for the lakes and stop here only when the day has run out.
bivy.water: Seasonal at best. There is nothing dependable at the pass and the trail either side of it is dry. Treat this as a dry camp and plan accordingly.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park back at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: One small site at the pass, room for a party or two at most. It is a stopgap rather than a destination and will not absorb a group.

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
approach_variants.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.
approach_variants.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
hazards: a corniced pass early in the season, with an alternative col that carries its own hazards
a descent east from the pass that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
avalanche terrain in the couloir and the basin below it in spring
wet-snow release and rockfall out of the couloir once the sun reaches the face
a remote basin with a long retreat and no trail on the eastern side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE COULOIR IS VISIBLE FROM THE LAKE AND THAT IS THE POINT OF APPROACHING FROM THIS SIDE. From the water, look south-west at the peak: THE ROUTE IS THE OBVIOUS NORTH-FACING SNOW LINE THAT SPLITS THE SUMMIT BLOCK ITSELF. Pick it out before you start moving, because from underneath the flanking gullies all look alike.

THE POSITIVE TEST IS WHERE THE LINE ENDS. IT MUST TOP OUT ON THE SUMMIT BLOCK, NOT ON THE RIDGE BESIDE IT. A couloir that finishes at a notch with more mountain above it and to one side is one of the flanking gullies and not the route.

THE SECOND TEST IS ASPECT. This is the NORTH side: it should be the shaded flank, holding firmer snow than anything around it in the morning and going soft late. IF THE SNOW YOU ARE STANDING ON IS IN EARLY SUN, YOU HAVE COME ROUND ONTO AN EASTERN OR WESTERN FLANK.

THE THIRD TEST IS CONTINUITY. The route is a single continuous line from the basin to the top of the block. If the snow you are following breaks into disconnected patches with rock steps between them, you are either too late in the season for it or on a different feature.

AND CHECK THE MOUNTAIN. There is a similarly named peak elsewhere in the range that is reached from an entirely different valley and has nothing to do with this one. The confirmation here is that the lake lies immediately north-east of your peak and the summit stands directly across it from you.

approach_variants.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
approach_variants.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
hazards: an approach that depends on boat or floatplane schedules to reach the valley at all
an unmarked, steep off-trail push into the basin with no tread to follow out
conflicting written descriptions of which drainage is used, so navigate from maps rather than prose
avalanche terrain in the couloir in spring
a long committing distance from any road
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIXED POINT ON THIS SIDE IS THE LAKE, AND EVERYTHING ABOVE IT IS READ OFF THE PEAK ITSELF. The lake sits immediately NORTH-EAST of the summit, so from the water the mountain stands to the south-west and the route faces you.

THE ROUTE IS THE CONTINUOUS NORTH-FACING SNOW LINE CLEAVING THE SUMMIT BLOCK. It must finish ON the block. A gully that tops out on the ridge to either side of the summit is a flanking line, not the route.

USE SHADE AS THE CONFIRMATION: the north side holds shadow while the basin around it is lit, and the snow in it stays firm longest in the morning.

BECAUSE THE APPROACH FROM THIS SIDE IS UNMARKED, FIX YOUR LINE INTO THE BASIN ON THE WAY IN. There is no tread to follow back out, and the basin has no obvious exit when seen from above.

approach_variants.name: Up the valley from the landing, then off-trail into the lake basin
approach_variants.notes:
There is no road to this side of the peak. Reach the valley by ferry or floatplane, then take the valley road or the park shuttle to a campground and pick up the valley trail from there. The lake below the peak is reached by leaving that trail and pushing off-trail and unmarked into the basin - a steep, poorly marked fisherman's path at best, and map-and-compass travel above it. Figure a full day of travel each way and plan on two or three days with a camp at or below the lake.

One caution about the paperwork rather than the ground: the written descriptions of this approach and the recorded waypoints for it name different drainages for that off-trail section, and the recorded distances do not match the recorded positions. Plan the departure point from current maps and imagery rather than from any single written description.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer through early autumn, once the basin is walkable and the valley road and trail are open
hazards: reaching the valley at all depends on a ferry or floatplane and a shuttle
an unmarked off-trail push into the basin with no reliable path
loose unconsolidated talus and steep heather benches with unstable footing
no tread to follow on the descent, on ground where every slope looks the same
an exposed class 3 finish off the ridge
conflicting records of the approach drainage, so the departure point must be planned from maps
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE LAKE IS THE ANCHOR AND THE ROUTE IS READ FROM IT. The lake sits immediately NORTH-EAST of the summit, so from the water the peak is to the south-west.

LEAVE THE LAKE BASIN AND GAIN THE BROAD BASIN AND SLOPES DIRECTLY ABOVE IT ON THE SOUTH SIDE, aiming for the LOW POINT ON THE SUMMIT RIDGE rather than for the summit itself. There are no cairns and no path here; the terrain is the navigation.

THE GROUND CONFIRMS ITSELF AS YOU GAIN HEIGHT: loose unconsolidated talus interspersed with heather benches on a steep grade, with unstable footing and no established tread. NOTE YOUR ASCENT LINE, because on the descent one talus-and-heather slope looks exactly like the next and there is nothing to follow.

THE FINISH IS THE TEST THAT YOU CHOSE THE RIGHT SIDE. From the ridge the last stretch to the top is a short EXPOSED CLASS 3 SCRAMBLE. IF THE GROUND ABOVE YOU IS A STEEP CONTINUOUS SNOW LINE SPLITTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK, YOU HAVE COME ROUND ONTO THE NORTH SIDE AND ARE UNDER THE COULOIR ROUTE, which is a different proposition entirely and wants an axe, crampons and a season this route does not.

Also confirm the peak: a similarly named summit elsewhere in the range is approached from a completely different valley. The lake immediately north-east of your summit is what identifies this one.

approach_variants.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road and down to the lake from the west
approach_variants.notes:
The lake can also be reached from the other side of the range, by climbing to the pass at about 5,392 ft at the head of the river road - or the nearby col used when the pass is corniced - and then travelling east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond to the lake at about 4,170 ft.

This avoids the ferry and the unmarked valley push entirely, at the cost of a pass crossing in each direction and a descent that has to be re-climbed at the end of the trip.
approach_variants.season: Late spring into summer, while the pass is straightforward and the basin beyond is still simple travel
hazards: a corniced pass in early season
a descent from the pass that must be re-climbed on the way out
loose talus and heather with unstable footing and no tread
an exposed class 3 finish
a basin with no path and no obvious exit seen from above
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM THE PASS THE TRAVEL IS EAST AND DOWNHILL TO THE LAKE, so the arrival marker is water at about 4,170 ft with the peak standing to the SOUTH-WEST of it.

FROM THE LAKE, THE SOUTH SLOPES ARE GAINED BY GOING ROUND THE PEAK, NOT UP THE SIDE FACING YOU. The face you can see from the lake is the northern one. THE ROUTE IS ON THE OPPOSITE FLANK - the broad basin and slopes above the lake basin on the south side, taken toward the low point on the summit ridge.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS THE SNOW LINE. IF YOU ARE LOOKING UP AT A CONTINUOUS COULOIR SPLITTING THE SUMMIT BLOCK AND ARE TEMPTED BY IT, THAT IS THE NORTH COULOIR ROUTE AND NOT THIS ONE. It is a snow climb with a different season and different equipment.

THE POSITIVE MARKERS ON THE ROUTE ARE UNDERFOOT: loose talus and heather benches on a steep grade, with no cairns, followed by an exposed class 3 scramble off the ridge to the top. Note your ascent line for the descent, because nothing here is marked.

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway to the basin, at the end of what used to be the upper Stehekin Valley road. It has a privy, fire rings, picnic table and bear boxes, though the boxes are set well back from the cooking area. ACCESS IS THE THING TO PLAN AROUND: the road washed out for the last time in 2003 and the Stehekin shuttle now turns around at High Bridge, so reaching Cottonwood from the boat means an extra day of walking the old roadbed rather than the bus ride older descriptions assume. Check the current shuttle schedule before committing — upper-valley service has varied year to year.
bivy.water: Reliable — creek water a short walk below the camp
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp, same Recreation.gov reservation and walk-up system as the rest of the complex.
bivy.capacity: Several sites, including one that takes a larger group and a few small secluded ones

approach_variants.name: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the North Peak north face
approach_variants.notes:
US-2 at milepost 35.2, south on Mount Index Road 0.3 miles to the Lake Serene trailhead at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4 miles and 2,000 ft to the lake basin; the maintained trail ends at the lake's north end.

Traverse the WEST side of the lake over talus and very large boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system toward the base of North Peak's north face. That gully carries snow into early summer.

Budget headlamps in the morning to reach the lake so the technical section starts at first light: parties commonly need 12 to 15 hours or more, and many bivy.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Aug for dry rock across all three summits
hazards: Wet mossy slabs on the lower face
Steep brush with vertical steps and no protection
Rotten rock and sparse protection on the ridge between summits
Notches on the traverse needing careful downclimbing or short rappels
Very long committing day with poor escape options
approach_variants.baseFinding: The traverse begins by climbing the North Face route on North Peak, and its start is a broken, bushy spur rather than a clean wall — third and fourth class slabs and grass, frequently wet, with downsloping holds. That wetness and vegetation is the confirmation, not a sign you are off route. A vertical wall with a two-piton anchor above the initial slabs is the normal rope-up point. Between about 3,000 and 3,600 ft the brush is thickest; it forms a tunnel with vertical ten- to twenty-foot steps. Clean, dry, steep rock at the start means you have drifted onto a harder line.

approach_variants.name: Green Ridge and Charlie Brown Lake
approach_variants.notes: The trailhead is an unsigned climbers' and fishermen's path on the north shoulder of the Middle Fork road, roughly 1.1 miles before the Dingford Creek trailhead at about 1,350 ft — no sign, no formal parking, and easy to drive straight past. Climb Green Ridge steeply, staying left where a fork drops northeast to Green Ridge Lake, over the ridge high point near 4,840 ft, past a small tarn, then DOWN about 800 ft into the Upper Garfield lake basin and north through steep forest to Charlie Brown Lake. That mid-route descent has to be re-climbed on the way out, so it costs far more than the raw mileage suggests.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September
hazards: Unsigned roadside start that is easy to miss
Broken cliff bands and loose duff on the slopes above the lake
800 ft of elevation loss and regain in the middle of the route
A steep gully walled by rock that holds snow and ice into summer
A corniced summit ridge on the north side
approach_variants.baseFinding: Charlie Brown Lake at about 4,390 ft is where the walking stops and the scramble begins, and it is the right place to stop because the whole remaining route is visible from its shore. From the outlet, work onto the peak's southeast slopes and thread up through broken cliff bands and duff to a broad talus field at roughly 4,850 ft — that talus field is the marker that you are on the correct line rather than one of the several plausible-looking weaknesses below it. From the top of the talus, angle LEFT into an obvious gully with grassy slopes at its head. The gully is walled by rock on both sides and tops out near 5,400 ft at a notch beside a protruding rock on the south ridge, and it shoots you straight out onto the more south-facing slopes of the mountain. If you are traversing across the face rather than gaining height in a defined gully, you have gone past it. Above the notch the last few hundred feet are easy but steep heather to the summit ridge. Carry an axe and traction if snow is still sitting in that gully.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek, Borealis Lake and Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes: From the large lot above the boat ramp at Colonial Creek, follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south to McAllister Camp; the old bridge near mile 6.6 is gone and the crossing is now a log felled downstream of the old site. At the camp leave the maintained trail and pick up the unmaintained boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and blowdown up the north ridge past a viewpoint that gives the first look at the peaks. Continue through forest and heather to the flat bench at Borealis Lake, the base camp. From camp rope up and follow the west edge of the Borealis Glacier, which has retreated into an upper and a lower tier separated by slabs and cliffs, to the col.
approach_variants.season: July and August are best; earlier ascents need ice technique, and the south-facing snow above the col softens dangerously through the day
hazards: Crevasses on the Borealis Glacier, worse late in the season
Brushy, poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp
Afternoon softening of the south-facing snow finger — start early
Class 3-4 rock ramps and ledges above the snow
approach_variants.baseFinding: Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and this peak, is the base, and which way you turn on it is the whole test. Standing on the col, Primus is the peak to the EAST and this one is to the WEST; the route turns west. Above the pass on that side a single steep snow finger runs up roughly 200 ft. It is unmistakable from the col and there is no second candidate, and it is the entry to the climb. Above the snow the ground becomes rock ramps and ledges, class 3 to 4, following the west ridge to a bouldery summit. If you have left the col heading east onto a broad class 2-3 ridge, you are climbing Primus instead. If you are still threading crevasses on slabby, tiered ice below the col, you have not reached the pass at all — the glacier here is split into two tiers by slabs and cliffs and it is the upper tier that runs to the col.

bivy.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
bivy.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
bivy.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

bivy.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
bivy.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
bivy.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

bivy.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

bivy.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
bivy.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether it is usable at all depends on snow: early season gives flat platforms, late season leaves broken rock. Treat it as an emergency or opportunistic bivy and carry the means to melt water.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
bivy.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.notes:
Sunrise Mine trailhead off the Mountain Loop Highway via Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065). Trail #707 crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish on a log almost immediately — a real obstacle in high runoff — then climbs through Wirtz Basin, breaks into cairned talus and boulder fields, and reaches Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles. The pass is a narrow rocky notch with loose footing where rockfall from above is a genuine hazard.

Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek and follows it up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan) at about 4,950 ft, 3.5 miles and 2,700 ft from the car — last reliable water.

Stay on the ordinary Vesper summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then leave it and swing north across the slabs. Three hours or more car to base.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier needs axe and crampons for the ledge traverse
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Steep exposed heather benches, slick when wet
Snow on the ledge traverse into early-to-mid summer
Loose rock on the face — treat as alpine despite the bolted belays
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Aim for the two large cairns on the saddle at about 5,700 ft (near 48.01375 -121.51451), with Copper Lake below to the northwest; the heather ledge system starts about 30 ft ABOVE the cairns on third-class slabs, not from the saddle floor. Traverse east on the goat trail through the heather.

True Grit itself is identified by its first anchor, not by its first moves. Pitch 1 is about 200 ft of easy, clean granite and finishes by stepping LEFT to a BOLTED belay sitting directly beneath an obvious NARROW CHIMNEY. If there is no chimney above the anchor you have reached, you are not on True Grit. It is the more direct of the two lines here — Ragged Edge jogs sharply right in its first pitch or two, so a line that keeps going straight up is this one.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

approach_variants.name: Skyline Lake and the ridge gap drop-in
approach_variants.notes: Start from the large day-use lot on the north side of the highway at the pass, beside the ski area's substation and utility building, on the gated service road. Around a mile in, an easy-to-miss cairn-marked left fork leaves the road for Skyline Lake and the ridge — staying right on the road takes you to a cell tower instead. Past the lake the route crosses the low point in Skyline Ridge, drops into a creek drainage on the ridge's back side, and climbs back out to gain the Tye Ridge crest. There is no maintained trail; snow-free this is a stiff bushwhack, which is why most ascents are made on continuous snow.
approach_variants.season: Late June to October, or on snow
hazards: A roughly 150-ft slope near fifty degrees on the back side of the ridge gap, which can cornice in winter
Mossy, loose rock and brush on that drop-in when snow-free
Dense brush low on the route once the snow melts out
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes
Wind-exposed summit ridge and no water above the creek drainage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The route's crux is at its start, and the start goes DOWN rather than up. From Skyline Lake climb northwest through timber to the low point in the crest of Skyline Ridge at about 5,200 ft. The far side is not a walk-through: it is a drop of roughly 150 feet at close to fifty degrees, mossy loose rock and brush when snow-free and liable to cornice in winter. That drop-in is the confirmation you are in the right gap — a gap you can simply stroll over is the wrong one, and there are several plausible low points along that crest. It bottoms out at the head of a small creek near 4,800 ft, an early-season water source and the last one. From there a steep wooded slope opens into gentle meadows around 4,900 ft and thins through timber to the crest of Tye Ridge near 5,000 ft, which is where the brush finally clears and the going turns to open heather benches. Follow the crest north to the saddle between Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, then climb the ridgeline directly, staying on the highest ground to avoid cornices in winter and loose talus in summer.

bivy.name: Skyline Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
bivy.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
