bivy.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
bivy.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

rappel_detail.pull: The constriction above the wide crack is the documented rope-eater on this face. Watch where the ends land and keep both strands out of it.
rappel_detail.notes: Drops down the middle of the upper face to a bolted ledge anchor.
hazards: A single 60 m rope comes up about 10 ft short of the bolts and the last of it is an unroped downclimb on easy 5th class; a 70 m single reaches
A party rappelling here got a rope end wedged in a constriction above a wide crack and had to lead 5.8 to recover it
rappel_detail.station: The slung summit boulder, dropping down the upper north face to the only bolted anchor anywhere on this rappel route. Below it every station is slung natural gear, so this is the single anchor you can positively identify.

rappel_detail.notes: Down lichen-covered rock to a large ledge near a rock arch; traverse the ledge to a constriction with slings.
hazards: The rappel line diverges from the climb, so the terrain below you is ground you have not seen
rappel_detail.station: Down toward the main ledge system, rappelling climber's-LEFT of the climbing line rather than straight down it.

rappel_detail.notes: Drops to a horn slung with blue webbing.
hazards: Loose material accumulates on these ledges and sits directly above whoever is next on the rope
rappel_detail.station: One rappel from the ledge system down to the ledge at the bottom of the third pitch.

rappel_detail.notes: Down to broad scree ledges.
hazards: Not visible from where the previous rappel lands - you have to walk under the block to find it
Traversing with ropes deployed is where they hang up here
rappel_detail.station: Cut climber's LEFT from the ledge; the station is just past the point where you walk back underneath the large block. Accounts also describe a station at the top of pitch 4 reached by traversing the ledge - navigate by the ledge and the block, not by looking straight down.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel back to Burgundy Col.
hazards: Below the col the descent is loose gullies on foot rather than more rappelling
rappel_detail.station: The remaining rappels run down through the sandy terraces to Burgundy Col; from the last stance the line is a straight shot down through the obvious notch in the rock below to the ground.

wa_ultramega_ok.rappel_count_note: Five stations is the DOUBLE-ROPE count. Ultramega OK has no rappel line of its own - it is a Northeast Buttress route that merges into upper North Face terrain, and parties take the North Face descent. The same ground is 9-10 rappels for a party doing many shorter ones on a single rope, and a two-60 party describes it as a doubled first rappel, one single rappel to the ledge at the bottom of pitch 3, then three more double rappels to Burgundy Col - all three counts describe one descent under different rope setups. Rope opinion is genuinely split rather than settled: two ropes are quicker, but a first-hand account calls double ropes here annoying and prone to sticking and prefers a single 70 m, and a single 60 m does not reach the only bolted anchor on the route. Per-station distances are not published in any available account.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then further around the north face to the twin cracks with loose blocks
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the long highway pullout on SR-20 at about 4,310 ft near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 miles east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain. A boot path drops east through loose talus into forest; look for a REGISTRATION BOX a few minutes in.

The path fords Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft, a swift wade in early season. From the creek it climbs steadily east through forest and open slopes for roughly 2,200 ft to a broad flat bench and campsite around 6,460 ft, the approach's natural midpoint and a good high camp or bail point. Above the bench the boot path traverses loose scree gullies below Burgundy's northwest side and finishes up a final stretch of unstable, cairn-marked ball-bearing scree over slab to Burgundy Col at about 7,770-7,800 ft, the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle. About 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Unstable ball-bearing scree over slab below the col, with rockfall onto party members below
Lingering snow on the traverse around the north face, wanting an axe into July
No independent rappel line; the descent merges into another route's terrain
A single 70 m rope leaves the descent tight, with downclimbing between stances
A swift wade of Early Winters Creek in early season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE STARTS JUST SHORT OF ACTION POTENTIAL ALONG THE BASE, AND THE MARKER IS COUNTABLE: A TWIN-CRACK SYSTEM WITH OBVIOUS LOOSE BLOCKS ABOUT 60 FT UP. Two cracks, and blocks visible sixty feet above you.

SO THE INSTRUCTION IS: FROM THE COL, SCRAMBLE LOOSE ROCK, OR KICK STEPS IN LINGERING SNOW WITH AN AXE INTO JULY, DOWN AND AROUND THE BASE OF BURGUNDY'S NORTH FACE, AND KEEP GOING. THIS START IS CLIMBER'S-LEFT OF THE NORTH FACE, AND ONLY ABOUT 15 FT CLIMBER'S-RIGHT OF ACTION POTENTIAL.

THE ORDER ALONG THE BASE, GOING AWAY FROM THE COL: FIRST THE NORTH FACE'S START, SCRAMBLING STRAIGHT UP FROM THE COL, then THIS ROUTE'S TWIN CRACKS about 5-10 minutes along, then ACTION POTENTIAL'S CLEAN SPLITTER FLAKE roughly 15 FT FURTHER. IF YOU HAVE STOPPED AT A SINGLE CLEAN SPLITTER, YOU HAVE GONE ONE ROUTE TOO FAR.

AND THE NEGATIVE TEST FROM THE OTHER DIRECTION: if you are still at the col below the North Face's start you are short of this start, and a single clean splitter with no loose blocks above it means you have walked about 15 ft past it.

ARRIVAL AT THE COL, WHICH IS THE OTHER FIND ON THIS DAY: Burgundy Col is the NOTCH BETWEEN BURGUNDY SPIRE AND PAISANO PINNACLE, at about 7,770-7,800 ft, and it is reached by the last stretch of cairned ball-bearing scree over slab. Rock towers on both sides, the ground dropping away ahead, at the top of the worst scree of the day.

DESCENT, AND THE ROPE MATH IS TIGHTER HERE THAN ON THE NORTH FACE: this route has no independent rappel line and most parties merge into upper North Face terrain near Burgundy Ledge, then take the North Face's five-rappel descent. DOUBLE 60 M ROPES MAKE THAT CLEAN. Parties with a single 70 m have got down with some downclimbing between stances, but it is tighter on this line than on the standard North Face.

bivy.name: Burgundy Col high camp — WEST side, the Wine Spires
bivy.notes: The narrow saddle between Burgundy Spire and the ridge, and the standard high camp for the Wine Spires and for the Silver Star Glacier approached from the highway side. Published elevations disagree by a couple of hundred feet, with figures from roughly 7,720 to 7,950 in circulation, so treat any single number as approximate. It is exposed to wind from both sides and several parties have dropped back down the west slope to sleep after a rough night. Camping here removes about 1,500 ft of the scree from summit day, which is most of the argument for carrying overnight gear up it.
bivy.water: No spring or stream. Parties melt snow from the lingering patches on the glacier side of the col, which normally hold into late summer but can be rock-hard in the morning or gone entirely in a dry, late season. Many simply haul all their water up the scree, which is the single heaviest decision on this approach.
bivy.permit: None. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any designated wilderness — no quota, no reservation and no self-issue permit, unlike the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Two to four rock-ringed bivy platforms; roughly one is level enough for a two-person tent, so a large party should expect to sleep scattered or send some members back down

bivy.name: Burgundy Creek bench camp — WEST side
bivy.notes: The flat, sheltered alternative to sleeping at the col, in trees before the timbered rib gives way to open scree. Reports consistently call it the more pleasant camp of the two, at the cost of extra vertical on summit morning. Elevation is quoted anywhere from about 6,400 to 6,500 ft depending on which flat spot a party used. Its value is almost entirely the spring: if that has failed, the bench loses most of its advantage over the col.
bivy.water: The most dependable water on this approach, but NOT from the obvious place. The creek shown on maps immediately east of the bench is frequently dry, while a spring roughly ten minutes north of camp keeps running well into September in most years. Confirm it before committing, and expect insects around it.
bivy.permit: None required. Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, non-wilderness, so no permit or reservation applies.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots on a wooded bench, with a large boulder and an old fire ring as the usual landmark; comfortably three or four tents

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

bivy.name: Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — WEST side
bivy.notes: Not an established campsite so much as a fallback for a party that has run out of daylight or water partway up the talus. The main reason to know about them is that the water situation on this hillside is patchy rather than uniform, so a dry creek at the wooded bench does not necessarily mean a dry mountainside above it. Anyone counting on this should carry a stove and be prepared to find nothing.
bivy.water: Genuinely unreliable and conditions-dependent. At least one party found a trickle running here in a season when the bench camp creek below was dry, which makes it worth checking on the way up, but nothing about it is dependable enough to plan a camp around.
bivy.permit: None. Non-wilderness National Forest land; no permit, quota or registration.
bivy.capacity: Improvised, one or two small parties at most; flat ground has to be found or built rather than chosen

approach_variants.name: Eightmile Creek trail, South Buttress branch to the Great Arch
approach_variants.notes:
As for The Big Tree — FR 2060 from the Mountain Loop Highway, right at the mile-5 fork, Eightmile Creek trailhead, then the Eightmile Creek trail for about 30-40 minutes to where it breaks out of the forest onto the talus.

Take the climbers' branch up and LEFT into the slide maples within roughly 100 feet of leaving the woods, and follow it to the South Buttress.
approach_variants.season: Dry spells roughly May-Oct
hazards: Unmarked brushy climbers' path through slide maple
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the first climb the South Buttress path brings you to, on the right-hand side of the Great Arch area — so if you have walked past several route starts you have gone too far.

The marker is a large left-facing flake with the first bolt on it. You can start on the flake itself or step onto it from just below. Above the flake the ground is low-angle slab past two more bolts to a two-bolt chain anchor, then three more bolts to anchors sitting below the roofs of the Great Arch.

Easy, low-angle friction off the deck is CORRECT here — this is the area's warm-up. If your first moves are steep or technical you are on one of the harder lines further along the Great Arch.

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake, the northwest gully and Unicorn Col to the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lake trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes. The lot holds only about 15-20 cars and fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.

Follow the maintained Snow Lake Trail through subalpine forest and meadow, past the Bench Lake junction, to Snow Lake at about 1-1.25 miles — the last reliable water. Skirt the lake's west and north shore, then leave the maintained tread where a climbers' path breaks off and climbs a steep drainage about half a mile into the large open bowl on Unicorn's northwest side, shared with Foss and West Unicorn.

The basin is loose talus and scree; through much of July the gully above the lake can still hold firm snow, so carry an axe and, in early season, crampons.

From the basin, climb to the saddle on the peak's west side, then traverse and scramble east and around to approach the summit pinnacle from its south side — sustained class 2-3 on talus and blocky rock. About 2.4 miles one-way and 2,397 ft of gain to the base of the summit block, where the roped climbing starts.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; the approach gully holds firm snow through much of July
hazards: Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out, usually mid-to-late July
Wet-slide and cornice hazard in the northwest gully and bowl in late spring, with documented slide paths off the cliffs above Snow Lake
An exposed step near the top of the summit horn with real air below on the east side
Climber-built rappel anchors of uncertain age, including a tree reported as no longer sound
Afternoon thunderstorms in summer and unreliable cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE HORN IS THE POINT AND THE COL IS NOT. Unicorn Col, the saddle just west of the summit at about 6,400 ft, is where the route-finding stops feeling hard — but the summit is still a traverse away, EAST, and around onto the SOUTH side.

THE TEST AT THE COL IS A SHAPE: the summit block is a FREE-STANDING 50 TO 70 FT HORN, the thing the peak is named for. IF NOTHING IN FRONT OF YOU LOOKS LIKE A DETACHED TOWER, YOU HAVE NOT COME FAR ENOUGH EAST.

THE APPROACH NEGATIVE IS IN THE GULLY AND IT IS THE ONE THAT PUTS PARTIES ON BAD GROUND: aim for the MAIN gully out of the basin above Snow Lake, and AVOID THE STEEP HEADWALLS TO ITS LEFT. If the ground ahead gets steep and rocky rather than staying a talus or snow chute, you have drifted left. Go back down and across rather than pressing up.

THE TRAVERSE NEGATIVE IS ABOUT HEIGHT, NOT DIRECTION: the correct use trail traverses BELOW the cliffs on the south side, and it is easier travel than the loose scree above and below it. If you are scrambling up onto the ridge crest instead of contouring underneath it, you are above the path and on worse rock.

AND THE THING THAT MATTERS MOST AT THE FOOT OF THE HORN: THREE SEPARATE LINES START WITHIN ABOUT 70 FT OF EACH OTHER THERE, and they run from easy fifth class to 5.6. LEFT TO RIGHT THEY ARE: THE ROOF, THE CLASSIC ROUTE, OPEN BOOK. All three finish at the same slung block, so the only place to get this right is at the bottom. Know which one you came for before you rope up.

DESCENT FINDING, DECIDED BEFORE YOU START UP: most parties rappel the horn rather than downclimb it — a single-rope rappel of about 50 ft down the south side. The traditional anchor is an aging tree at the top of the block; many parties instead sling the rock horn on the south side, which carries slings and rings left by others. Both are climber-built and neither is maintained: inspect and back up before weighting anything. There are two rappel lines off that horn and they land in different places, so confirm which you are on.

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. TWO SITES IS A HARD CEILING, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes:
Castle Rock stands beside US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. There is an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway at around milepost 96.5.

Take the trail from the UPHILL, western end of the pullout. It climbs and traverses east across the broad bench that splits the formation — Logger's Ledge — and reaches the first routes in five to ten minutes, the ledge itself in ten to fifteen.

There is no water at the crag and no named trail number.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Full southwest sun; the formation faces predominantly southwest
Polished granite from very heavy traffic
No water at the crag
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identifying feature for everything in this area is Logger's Ledge: a wide bench running across the middle of the formation, reached by an obvious trail from the west end of the parking area. Upper Castle routes are set up FROM that bench.

If you are at the base of the rock at road level you took the other trail — the one leaving the LOWER, eastern end of the same pullout, about fifty yards downhill — and you are at Lower Castle, a full wall too low.

Descent from anything topping out is a good climbers' trail off the back of the formation, returning to Logger's Ledge, and a trail from the ledge leads back to the parking area.

approach_variants.name: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder under Stuart's West Ridge and northwest to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft.

From Goat Pass, traverse ONTO and ACROSS the Stuart Glacier rather than along beneath it, aiming for a fourth-class gully that runs up to the obvious notch in the North Ridge. This is the difference between this route and the complete ridge in one sentence: the complete-ridge party traverses east BELOW the glacier to the toe, this party crosses the glacier and goes UP.

The notch is a bivy: there are two good sites in it, which is why parties who intend to climb the upper ridge in a day from a high camp use it.

Published descriptions of this route are frank that the last of the navigation is yours — one of them says outright to take a topographic map and work it out. Treat that as a real warning rather than as rhetoric.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the gully to the notch holds snow and the glacier crossing is simpler, later it is bare and looser
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier crossing
Loose rock in the fourth-class gully, with parties above you in it
Knife-edge exposure on the ridge above the notch
The Great Gendarme's offwidth high on the route, with retreat from there awkward
Cold wind on an exposed crest; parties routinely carry bivy kit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE NOTCH IS A PLACE YOU CAN SIT DOWN, AND THAT IS THE TEST. There are two good bivy sites in it. If you have arrived somewhere on the crest with no flat ground, you are not at the notch — you have gained the ridge somewhere else along its length.

The approach to it is a fourth-class GULLY off the Stuart Glacier, not a scramble up the ridge flank. If the ground you are climbing is open face rather than a defined gully, you are not in the right line.

ORIENTATION AT THE NOTCH, which settles it: standing in the notch, the whole lower ridge falls away below you to the north and the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far side of it. Everything above you is the upper ridge, and the Great Gendarme is roughly eight or nine pitches up from here. If the big tower is already below you, you have joined the crest above the notch and above two of the route's three named features.

WHAT YOU HAVE DELIBERATELY GIVEN UP: about 1,200 ft of climbing, including the sustained lieback crack that is the hardest pitch on the complete ridge. So the notch is not a shortcut to be found by accident — a party that meant to climb the complete ridge and ends up here has walked past its own route. Confirm which climb you are on before you start up.

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

approach_variants.name: Copper Creek roadbed, three waterfalls and the tunnel
approach_variants.notes:
As for the rest of Green Giant Buttress. FR 2060 off the Mountain Loop Highway for five or six miles, RIGHT at the fork, past the Eightmile Creek trailhead, then on until the road stops being driveable roughly 1.5 miles later.

On foot: old road extension for half a mile, drop onto the older mining road, cross a side fork of Copper Creek, bear slightly left, follow the main fork to three waterfalls, then sharp RIGHT into the brushy rocky tunnel and up the gritty slab gully to the rock. Continuing up alongside the waterfalls instead of taking the tunnel is the classic mistake.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer and early autumn
hazards: Missing the tunnel at the waterfalls
Creek crossings on Copper Creek
Long unmaintained road; no cell service
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Reach the same staging area used by the whole buttress — a few hundred feet below the steeper rock, marked only by small upright cedars against bushier growth above.

Urban Bypass is a short bolted variation on the buttress rather than a separate approach; it is climbed off the same right-side start as the Dreamer lines, so find the staging area first and pick the line off the apron from there. It is the only sport-bolted option here, so a line of bolts is the discriminator against the trad lines beside it.

wa_vanishing_point.rappels: Rappel anchors have been updated to stainless steel, and the approach can be reversed with a single 70 m rope where the updated anchors allow it. Most parties do not rappel the route — they top out and walk off via the BASE-jumper trail.
wa_vanishing_point.descent: Walk off via the heather descent to a BASE jumper trail system, then follow well-worn switchbacks through forested ridge system back to the Barclay Lake trailhead parking area. Approximately 3 hours car-to-car from summit.
wa_vanishing_point.descent_text: From the summit, descend via the established BASE jumper trail system (marked on climbing area maps). The descent is non-technical but lengthy. Follow the forested ridge and switchback trail through old-growth forest back down to the Barclay Lake trailhead. The descent can be muddy and root-strewn; allow 3 hours total for descent and return to parking.

pitch_detail.notes: Starts just left of the prominent arete dividing Dolomite Tower; the first two bolts are visible from the ground. Pull left under a small overhang straight off the ground, then follow bolts up and left and back right around the arete. Graded 5.10 to 5.10c. Often linked with pitch 2.

Straight up, then trend left on bolts, turn the corner and pull back onto the arete to a bolted stance on a pedestal. Optional finger-sized gear, or a hand crack to the right at 5.10a. A 60 m rope barely links pitches 1 and 2.

Scramble up a ledge, clip a bolt and traverse right onto a pedestal of stacked blocks, then climb the corner on three bolts and gear. Before the 2020 bolt additions this pitch was runout and loose. Ends on a good ledge.

Steep finger and thin-hand crack in the corner beside a crystalline face, with the hardest moves just above the anchor. The main gear pitch. Belay on a ledge out left about 25 ft below the roof; do not climb past it.

Up steep blocks and left onto a face with three bolts, then jog right on two more; do not head out to the arete. A large part of the original roof has fallen away. Parties who climbed the older line felt it far harder than its 5.11c grade.

Step down and right off the belay, then follow roughly 10–12 bolts through a band of poor rock, with a 5.11c section near the top on the arete. Test holds; the bolting is close enough that a broken hold is not a disaster.
Steep arete climbing just left of the prow, with a thin, hard sequence close to the belay and tricky moves above. A small piece protects the final moves. Some parties rate the key move 5.12+.

Three bolts of 5.11 on the arete, then veer left into a slabby, shallow dihedral with a bolt on the arete. The most serious pitch on the route: the upper section has runouts of about 25 ft on 5.7–5.9 ground. Bring small and medium nuts.
One of the two best pitches: a crimpy boulder problem on the arete, a rest at deep pockets, then a second hard boulder. Bring every draw.
Past four bolts in lichen-covered rock to the old death-flake anchor, then clip the bolt above the roof and traverse right on jugs. The 2020 reroute avoids the loose death flake entirely.
Pull back left out the roof on big jugs to a hard boulder problem on the vertical headwall, just out of sight from the belay. Short, all bolts, and the likely crux of the route (5.12b).
Pockets and crimps up steep ground, then back right to the arete and a belay perched on the prow. All bolts. It can be linked with pitch 11 to avoid the poor intermediate belay.
Straight up past a bolt onto ledgy climbing, with gear and one or two more bolts, to chains on a slab.

Two bolts up a dirty slab to a juggy hand crack, over a bolted roof, then slab to a two-bolt anchor right at the lip and the edge of the woods. Scramble down heather to pick up the BASE-jumper descent trail.

approach_variants.name: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish). Walk the pleasant, level main Barclay Creek trail for about 20 minutes and roughly a mile to a bridge crossing a large creek — often dry by mid-to-late summer.

DO NOT CROSS THE BRIDGE. Just before it, break RIGHT into the forest around a LARGE BOULDER. Bushwhack through relatively open forest, or walk the creek bed, until you reach an open boulder field. Cross the boulder field to large trees and an open wash.

The wash leads to a steep, chossy, dirty waterfall; climb around its RIGHT side, staying out of the bushes — this stretch is exposed. Above that a ramp with hand lines, then a 60-70 degree forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, including a low-fifth step in a gully protected by a fixed line, and a small rock face with a bolt. Then roughly 800 ft of mostly roped slab in 35-50 m pitches on bolts and natural gear. Competent parties with good beta take two and a half to four hours; the approach is technical and hard to get right even with information.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Exposed scrambling around the right side of the chossy waterfall
Fixed lines of unknown age and condition
60-70 degree forested rib — a fall here is not survivable ground
Loose rock and brush throughout
Route-finding: the correct line is not obvious even with beta
approach_variants.baseFinding: The end of the fixed and roped section is where you unrope and scramble UP AND LEFT to the base of the tower. The test the first-ascent party wrote down is a negative one and it is the most useful thing on this approach: IF WHAT YOU ARE DOING FEELS SKETCHY, YOU ARE OFF THE LINE. The approach is unpleasant but it is protected the whole way — fixed lines, hand lines, bolts — so unprotected, committing ground means you have lost the route, not that the route has got harder. The base of the tower is the foot of a nearly 1,500 ft overhanging prow; there is no mistaking it once you are under it.

approach_variants.name: The Wine Spires pullout to the Bench, then NORTH along the ridge crest to Ares Tower
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the unsigned Wine Spires pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass, roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff near milepost 166, at about 4,300 ft. A boot path drops down loose scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft.

The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700-plus ft to Burgundy Col at about 7,800 ft. A flat bench campsite, the Bench, at about 6,460 ft sits about halfway up AND IS THE MORE COMMON CAMP FOR THIS OBJECTIVE than the col itself.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep
hazards: A class 4 ridge traverse with real exposure to reach the tower
Loose scree-covered talus on the initial drop from the highway
A log crossing of Early Winters Creek
The whole approach shares a trail with the Wine Spires objectives and then deliberately departs from it
approach_variants.baseFinding:
VASILIKI RIDGE AND ARES TOWER RISE DIRECTLY NORTH OF BURGUNDY COL AND THE WINE SPIRES CAMP AREA. SO THE TEST IS DIRECTIONAL AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF EVERY OTHER ROUTE FROM THIS TRAILHEAD: FROM THE BENCH OR THE COL, GO NORTH.

Every Wine Spires objective, Burgundy, Chianti, Pernod, Chablis, is reached by going to Burgundy Col and then SOUTH or EAST from it. Ares Tower is the one you reach by contouring and scrambling NORTH along the ridge crest. IF YOU HAVE DROPPED ONTO SNOW BENEATH AN EAST-FACING WALL, YOU HAVE GONE SOUTH AND YOU ARE UNDER THE WINE SPIRES.

ARRIVAL: Ares Tower is the HIGH POINT of Vasiliki Ridge at about 8,190 ft. Following the crest north, you are at the base when the ridge stops being scrambleable and rises into a tower. The climbing is a 4th-class scramble to a notch, then one short low-5th-class step to the true summit; Grade II-III.

CONFIRM BY THE HARDWARE, AND ON THIS ridge IT IS THE ONE PIECE OF FIXED GEAR WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: THERE IS A FIXED ANCHOR AT THE ARES TOWER SUMMIT, and the standard descent is a single rappel from it down to the notch to retrieve stashed gear, then a reversal of the fourth-class ridge scramble.

SO THE PATTERN OF THE DAY IS: stash gear at a notch below the tower, climb the short summit step, rappel back to your gear. If there is nowhere sensible to leave a pack, you are not at the tower yet.

CAMP CHOICE AS A PLANNING FACT: the Bench at about 6,460 ft is the more common camp for this objective than Burgundy Col, which is 1,300 ft higher and in the wrong direction.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From Granite Falls drive the Mountain Loop Highway about 27-28 miles, turn onto Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) and follow roughly 2.3-2.5 miles of gravel to the Sunrise Mine trailhead at about 2,400 ft. Northwest Forest Pass; pit toilet on site.

Sunrise Mine Trail #707 runs about 2.7-3 miles and 2,600 ft to Headlee Pass at 4,720 ft, crossing the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs low down and passing through Wirtz Basin onto cairned talus. Past the pass the trail continues around Sperry Peak's south flank into the Vesper Creek and lake basin, then the main summit trail climbs talus and slabs to about 5,600-5,700 ft. Leave the trail there and head north/northwest across the slabs.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; expect steep snow on the ledge traverse in June
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Steep snow on the ledge traverse in June — ice axe and crampons
Wet heather on the traverse
Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two large cairns mark the saddle at roughly 5,700 ft, near 48.01375 -121.51451, with Copper Lake in view to the northwest — that is the marker, and it is what you look for in cloud. Third-class slabs about 30 ft ABOVE the cairns lead onto the heather-covered ledges of the north face. Traverse those ledges roughly 800 ft eastward to reach the original start near 48.01376 -121.51736, gained by fourth-class moves on an up-then-right arch. An alternative start uses a small notch overlooking the remnant Vesper Glacier. If you have dropped into the saddle rather than climbing 30 ft above it, you are below the ledge system and it will not go.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

approach_variants.name: Witch Doctor approach continued to the far east end
approach_variants.notes:
Same start as Snake Charmer: FS 2060 south from Darrington, LEFT fork at about 5 miles, small pullout roughly half a mile past the fork just after the bridge, then the overgrown logging grade heading north-east into the forest, a switchback at a creek, and a faint path handrailing the creek to the boulder field beneath the dome.

Recorded times from the pullout are around 45 minutes to the first landmark and about an hour and a half of walking in total, carrying big loads.
approach_variants.season: Dry summer
hazards: Faint unmarked climbers' path
Boulder field beneath the wall
This is the aid-climbing end of the formation — loose blocks on the approach ledges
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This line sits on the FAR EAST end of the Witch Doctor Wall, on the section the first-ascent party called the Solar Wall — so you keep going past the ground below the arching flake of Snake Charmer.

The confirmation on arrival is two bivouac boulders sitting below the base of the wall, with a stream running behind that camp. If you are not standing near two obvious bivy rocks you have stopped short.

The climbing starts from Bombardier Ledge rather than from the deck.

approach_variants.name: Kangaroo Pass from the highway hairpin
approach_variants.notes: Park in the large paved turnout at the first hairpin turn about a mile east of the pass summit. Nothing is signed; the boot path starts on the uphill side of the pullout into timber and boulders. Head south and south-east toward the foot of the large talus slope below the big tower to the north, pick up the path skirting the bottom of the talus, and follow cairns carefully — this lower boulder band is the trickiest route-finding of the approach and is much worse under snow. Above it the tread firms into a distinct cairned trail through the upper basin to the pass. A small tarn just below the pass is the only water anywhere on the route, and it can be dry by late summer or fall.
approach_variants.season: July to early October, and the ridge is at its best when the larches turn; the highway is gated through winter and lingering snow reaches the pass into early summer
hazards: A corniced snow arete between the access notch and about 7,400 ft into late spring
The summit gully is loose scree and rock and parties above will kick debris onto those below
The slabs just below the summit block are committing when wet or snow-covered, even in midsummer
approach_variants.baseFinding: Kangaroo Pass is the base and the big tower is the marker: it stands immediately NORTH of the pass, so at the pass you turn away from it, north-east onto the south-west ridge. A faint climbers' trail runs a short way off the pass and then dies on rock, which is normal. Stay on or very near the crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree and grassy benches. The feature to find is an access notch near 7,200 ft where the crest narrows; the short stretch between that notch and about 7,400 ft is the technical crux and is where a corniced snow arete lingers into late spring. At about 7,400 ft step OFF the crest onto the south flank into the summit gully, a moderately steep runnel of loose rock and scree with cleaner class 3 rock on its margins. If you are still on the crest above 7,400 ft with the ground steepening into real climbing, you have missed the swing onto the south side. If you are descending west from the pass, you are back on the approach path to the road.

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
bivy.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail, Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter to the southeast cirque
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn on Louella Road for a mile, then Palo Alto Road for 1.1 miles to the forest boundary, where Palo Alto becomes FS Road 28. Right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required at the kiosk.

Trail #833.2 is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike 3.2-3.4 miles and about 600 ft to Camp Handy at roughly 3,100 ft, a riverfront meadow with a cedar-shingle shelter, then take the uphill fork and continue about 3 miles and 1,850 ft to Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at 6.3-6.4 miles and roughly 4,890-4,950 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the approach.

From Boulder Shelter hike SOUTH about 2 miles on the Dungeness / Constance Pass trail, crossing several creeks, toward Home Lake.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the summit couloir into early season is an improvement on the scree that replaces it
hazards: Loose, poor-quality rock on the final headwall above the 7,000 ft saddle — a recurring theme in every account
Rockfall in the couloir between the twin summits, worst with parties above or after freeze-thaw
Glissade and uncontrolled-slide risk descending the snow chute if the runout is not fully visible — one party described nearly going over a cliff band on nearby terrain
Faint use-trail-only route-finding above the trail through forest, meadow and talus
Fast-moving Pacific frontal systems and late-summer afternoon thunderstorms
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST TEST IS A CREEK YOU MUST NOT CROSS. Leave the trail BEFORE crossing the major stream that drains the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque. That stream is the last and largest of the several you meet going south from Boulder Shelter. Then climb EAST — steep forest, then steep open meadow, then talus — STAYING NORTH OF THE STREAMBED the whole way. The streambed is the handrail and it stays on your right. If you have crossed it and it is now on your left, you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE CIRQUE AT ABOUT 5,900 FT, and it is unambiguous because it is a closed basin: the ground stops rising in front of you and the headwall closes round. From there, head NORTH to the obvious COULOIR BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS. Warrior has twin summits and the couloir runs up between them to a saddle at about 7,000 ft. There is one gully in that headwall with a summit on each side of it. If the gully you are in has a summit on only one side, it is not the one.

THE TEST AT THE TOP OF THE COULOIR IS WHICH WAY TO TURN, AND IT IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE FOR THIS PEAK IN FOG: AT THE SADDLE, THE HIGHER PEAK IS ON YOUR RIGHT. The southeast summit is the true top; the northwest summit at roughly 7,285 ft is the lower one. Coming up the couloir from the cirque, the true summit is to the RIGHT. Turn left and you will climb the wrong peak on ground just as loose.

SECOND TEST, on the summit block: above the saddle there is 20 to 50 feet of exposed, poor-quality rock rated Class 4 to low fifth on the block's NORTHWEST side, often gained over steep snow or a snow moat, and many parties fix a hand line on it. If your last obstacle before the top is a walk rather than a short difficult rock step, you are on the wrong summit.

WHAT THE SEASON CHANGES: the couloir is steep but straightforward when snow-filled, common early season; melted out it is a brutal scree slog to the same saddle. Both are the route.

approach_variants.name: Home Lake basecamp, from either the Dungeness or the Dosewallips side
approach_variants.notes:
Home Lake at about 5,308-5,330 ft, walled in by Mount Constance and Warrior Peak just below Constance Pass, is the standard basecamp for this climb and it is reachable from two directions: north up the Upper Dungeness / Constance Pass trail at roughly 9.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, or south from the Dosewallips road end over Constance Pass. An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required.

Camping at Home Lake rather than pushing from Boulder Shelter turns this into a comfortable two-day trip and puts you a mile from the cirque. It is also the camp shared with Mount Fricaba, Mount Mystery and Mount Deception parties, so it is well-used ground with an established site.

From the lake, leave the basin and climb EAST into the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque through meadow and talus.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Same as the Boulder Shelter variant: loose summit rock, couloir rockfall, glissade runout, faint route-finding
Home Lake sits below Constance Pass, so an exit north regains meaningful height before the long descent
Wilderness permit required and the site is popular with parties climbing four different peaks
approach_variants.baseFinding: FROM HOME LAKE THE TEST IS THE SAME STREAMBED, WORKED FROM THE OTHER END: leave the lake basin heading EAST into the cirque, STAYING NORTH OF THE STREAM that drains it. The stream is the handrail either way — approaching from Boulder Shelter you must not cross it, and approaching from the lake you must keep it below and to your right as you climb. THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SAME CLOSED CIRQUE AT ABOUT 5,900 FT, and then the obvious COULOIR BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS running north to the saddle at about 7,000 ft — the one gully with a summit on each side of it. AND THE SAME TURN AT THE TOP: AT THE SADDLE THE HIGHER, TRUE SUMMIT IS ON YOUR RIGHT (southeast). The 20 to 50 ft Class 4 / low fifth step on the block's northwest side is the last obstacle; if there is no step, you are on the northwest summit. HONEST LIMIT: this variant differs from the one above only in where you sleep and which direction you walk in. It is recorded separately because the route is titled for the Home Lake approach and a reader should not have to reconcile that with an approach description that starts from Boulder Shelter.

bivy.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
bivy.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
bivy.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
bivy.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
bivy.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

approach_variants.name: Climb Mount Washington first from FR-2419 — the traverse starts on its summit
approach_variants.notes:
This route has no trailhead and no approach of its own. It begins on Mount Washington's summit and runs southwest along the connecting ridge to Mount Ellinor, rather than descending Washington's standard route.

So the approach is Washington's standard south route: FS Road 24 off North Lake Cushman Road for about 1.5 miles, left onto FS Road 2419 and up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to the road-end trailhead at about 3,026 ft; steep boot path through forest to the meadow benches; scree and talus staying climber's-left of the large loose gully; the southern ridgeline and the exposed Dog Walk Ledge; the scree field below the false summit and the goat trail up its climber's-right edge to the stone wind shelter; and a final short Class 3-4 scramble to the 6,255 ft summit.

Most parties finish at Ellinor and walk out its standard trail from the upper trailhead, which is a different parking area on the same road corridor — plan the shuttle. Reversing the traverse back over Washington is possible but nobody recommends it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
hazards: Fractured, weathered pillow basalt the whole length of the crest
A crux gendarme downclimb with notably poor rock and severe exposure that guides often advise bypassing entirely
Sustained Class 4 with hidden ledges — the difficulty depends on finding them
A loose 50 ft downclimb
Committing ground between two summits with no quick exit
The exit is at a different trailhead from the start; plan a shuttle
approach_variants.baseFinding: THE BASE OF THIS ROUTE IS A SUMMIT, AND THE TEST THAT YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT ONE IS A BUILDING: you passed a STONE WIND SHELTER on the ridge just below and then made a short Class 3-4 scramble to a top with a summit register on it. If you have not passed a stone shelter, you are on Washington's false summit and the traverse has not started. THE TEST THAT YOU ARE ON THE TRAVERSE AND NOT ON A DESCENT IS THE FIRST FEATURE, AND IT IS THE BEST SECTION OF THE ROUTE RATHER THAN THE WORST: from the summit, follow the narrow crest of fractured pillow basalt SOUTHWEST. The first thing you meet is THE WEDGE, about 150 ft of POSITIVE low-fifth / Class 4 climbing on good holds. Positive holds on this mountain are unusual enough to be diagnostic. If the first 150 ft off the summit feels loose and unpleasant and you are losing height fast, you have dropped off the crest into the standard descent gully instead of onto the ridge. SECOND TEST, further along: past the Wedge the ridge continues as sustained Class 4 past a series of gendarmes, and HIDDEN LEDGES usually keep the difficulty at Class 4 or below. So if a gendarme is presenting you with fifth-class moves, look below the obvious line before you commit — the ledge is probably there and you have not found it. One loose 50 ft downclimb is the section everybody dislikes; it is part of the route, not a sign you are off it. THE DECISION POINT: where the crest becomes too hard or too exposed to continue unroped, the usual answer is to DROP INTO THE BASIN BELOW and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a SNOW FINGER, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line to that summit. Several parties recommend taking the west-side basin traverse into Ellinor's northeast couloir over the direct ridge from the start, specifically because the crux gendarme downclimb has poor rock and severe exposure.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington, Madison Ave south to the T, right on Darrington Street into Squire Creek Road, drive to the washout gate.

Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing (about five minutes), reach the original road end in 30-40 minutes, then continue 20-30 minutes on the old trail to a large dry streambed about 50 feet wide and full of white boulders — the Waterfall Basin turn-off, and the last turn-off before the trail leaves the valley southward.

Down the bed about 200 feet, left into alder to find the informal path, roughly 30 minutes upvalley to the ford of Squire Creek, then along the fading trail and the underground creek bed into the open basin at about two hours.
approach_variants.season: Summer; east-facing, so morning sun and afternoon shade, but the base is often buried in leftover avalanche snow
hazards: Residual avalanche snow at the base for much of the climbing season
Debris and meltwater shed off the slab above
Ford of Squire Creek in high flow
Landslide crossing on the old roadbed
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the prominent rib sitting ABOVE the Martha's Place bivy boulder, immediately left of Roan Wall's big slab and its major waterfall streak. Standing at Martha's Place and looking up at a defined rib rather than a broad red slab is the confirmation.

The rib's position left of the waterfall is what gives it some shelter from snow and debris coming off the slab above — so if you are stood under the wet streak itself you are on Roan Wall, not this.

The base is commonly buried under leftover avalanche snow for much of the season, so expect to be starting off snow rather than dirt.

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

overnight_permit.what: No overnight permit required in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register
overnight_permit.where: Sign the register at the trailhead. Camping on the North Cascades National Park side of Cache Col needs a park wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or Recreation.gov.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek and the southern Ptarmigan corridor
approach_variants.notes: The standard way in: Downey Creek trailhead off the Suiattle River Road, then the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor over Itswoot Ridge and Cub Lake and up Bachelor Creek, with bushwhacking and glacier travel and a full day or two of approach before the rock. The route carries almost nothing else — no descent, no gear list, no hazards — so treat everything above the base as needing your own assessment on the day.
approach_variants.season: July to September.
hazards: Long committing off-trail approach with glacier travel
The route carries no hazard, gear or descent information of its own — plan the way off before you leave the base
Remote crest with no quick exit if weather closes in
Three routes on three aspects of one small summit; confirm which side of the peak you are on before racking up
approach_variants.baseFinding: Stay on the WEST side of the peak and stop DIRECTLY BENEATH THE SUMMIT — do not carry on south along the foot of the ridge. The start is a CHIMNEY on the left-hand side of the face, and 'chimney' is the physical test: a body-width slot you climb inside, not a corner you lieback. From it the route runs four roughly equal rope lengths, traversing right onto the open face at the top of the first, so the second confirmation is that the ground above the chimney opens out rather than continuing as a crack. Negative markers: if you are looking at TWO clean dihedrals side by side and you can see a hole punched through the ridge crest above, you have walked too far south and are under the ridge route; if the rock above you rises straight out of glacier ice with a moat at its foot, you have crossed to the east face.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.permit: N/A

The Downey Creek Trail itself is also closed through 31 December 2026 under a separate fire closure. Call the Darrington Ranger District, (360) 436-1155, before planning a trip.

overnight_permit.where: Sign the register at the trailhead. Camping on the North Cascades National Park side of Cache Col needs a park wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or Recreation.gov.

wa_west_face_2.rappel_count_note: Four rappels, and they are DOUBLE-rope rappels: the published descent is roughly 50 m, 50 m, 50 m and a short 20 m, so two 60 m ropes are needed and one rope will not complete it. Two independent accounts describe the descent as double-rope throughout. The stations are the north-ridge line down to the packs at the base of the route.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek, Itswoot Ridge and the Dome-Chikamin col
approach_variants.notes: This is a two-day approach each way and there is no short way in. From the Downey Creek Trailhead follow the valley trail to the Bachelor Creek crossing, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path through heavy brush to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge for the first camp. From there continue over the ridge and glacier ground to the Dome-Chikamin col and make a high camp. On the climbing day, cross the Chikamin Glacier from the col to the foot of the wall.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn; the glacier crossing opens up as the season goes on and later parties have reached the ice by the rock rib coming down off the neighbouring summit instead
hazards: Big crevasses on the Chikamin Glacier; the bergschrund is crossed on a snow bridge and is a place to move quickly
Heavy bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
Sustained hard free climbing on a very steep face, two days from the car in either direction
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cross the glacier from the col to the foot of the face and then stop looking at the wall — the start is not reached from the ice. Get onto the RAMP that runs beneath the LEFT side of the face and scramble along it. The ramp SPLITS, and the route starts just past that split, with a small cairn on the ground marking it. Those two things together, the split in the ramp and the cairn beside it, are the proof; either on its own is not enough on a face this size. From there the first climbing goes up a shallow corner on thin cracks, flakes and occasional knobs on clean white granite, and the objective is the centre of the wall. If you are still on the glacier below a uniformly steep face with no ramp beneath you, you have not gained the access ledge. If the ramp is running on unbroken with no branch in it, keep going — you are short of the start.

approach_variants.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib to the bench, then the contour right
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain above rather than for the spires, and nothing marks the climbers' path.

The path drops down the talus and into the forest, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log, and then climbs steeply up the timbered rib on the LEFT — the north side — of the creek that drains the col above. Two hours or so of steep walking puts you on the basin bench at about 6,500 ft. There is a spring near the bench camp and it is the last reliable water.

From the bench the trail continues another three-quarters of an hour to the col at about 7,720 ft, which is the hub for the whole cluster. This route does not need to go that far.

The pullout doubles as the overnight for most parties. Nothing there is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
approach_variants.season: Roughly June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access disappears when the highway closes
hazards: Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path with no trail signs anywhere
The start is a single jammed block; the lower ridge offers several plausible wrong starts
The final pitch is runout exposed face climbing with marginal protection
Rope drag on the long crest pitch if slings are not managed
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE STARTS LOWER THAN EVERYTHING ELSE IN THE CLUSTER, and that is the fact to hold onto. The spires above the col get climbed from the col; this one does not.

Leave the col trail at the BENCH, around 6,600 ft, and CONTOUR RIGHT — south — around the bench toward the pinnacle's lower section. You are aiming for the toe of the ridge rather than for anything above you. There is a DRY SANDY GULLY on this contour with a SPRING in it, which is a useful confirmation that you are on the right ground and the last water before the climb.

The start itself is marked by a CHOCKSTONE — a jammed block at the foot of the ridge.
