That chockstone is the identification, and it is the reason accounts of this route keep saying to pay attention to the topo: without it, the lower ridge offers several plausible ways on and parties have burned an hour sorting it out.

If you come at it from the col instead, drop about two hundred feet of mostly fourth-class rock to sandy ledges just left of the pinnacle's top and work down and along; that reaches the same ground from above.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB. Seven or eight pitches of sustained mid-fifth-class hand and finger cracks along the ridge crest, with big comfortable belay ledges. The technical crux is about halfway up, on the fourth pitch, on a short section of steep TWIN FINGER CRACKS. The last pitch is exposed, runout face climbing that most parties call the real crux for reasons that have nothing to do with the grade.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if you walked all the way to the col, then dropped a few hundred feet along the pinnacle's flank onto a third-class LEDGE SYSTEM and walked it rightward to a steep clean corner, you are at the other route on this pinnacle, several number grades harder. A ledge system leading to a corner is not this climb; a chockstone at the toe of a ridge is.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER: the neighbouring spire's north face is the usual link-up partner and its routes start from the col itself. Being at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are at this route.

Descent is a few hundred feet of downclimbing, then two rappels of about thirty and twenty metres into the gully beneath the col, downclimbing between the anchors, then the trail back past the bench.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Klipchuck and Early Winters have drinking water in season, shut off outside it. Lone Fir has none, but sits on Early Winters Creek, which needs filtering.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

approach_variants.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp to the Eye Col gully
approach_variants.notes: From the Goodell Creek trailhead follow the climbers' path up the old overgrown logging-road corridor; beyond the fork where the maintained tread ends it becomes a boot path through talus with sparse flagging, so follow cairns. Cross Terror Creek at the cairned ford — a rock-hop late in the season and a genuine wet crossing in early summer — then climb the steep brushy rib known as the Barrier, which is the route-finding crux of the walk in. The path tops out and drops a couple of hundred feet into Crescent Creek Basin, then traverses north across scree to the standard camp fed by two streams off the slabs above. Water is scarce above about 5,400 ft, so treat the last of it below the Barrier as your fill-up.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September, once the basin and the gully system are melted out
hazards: Loose rock throughout the gullies
Sustained route-finding through brush and scree with an easy-to-lose boot path on the Barrier
Unreliable water above the Barrier
Chockstone pitches at the col on low fifth-class rock, including one narrow crack normally belayed
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin camp, the peak's south side shows TWO gullies separated by a dividing buttress, and picking the wrong one is the failure here. The right-hand gully is the trap: it cliffs out in a closed chimney and does not go. The line takes the minor rib on the climber's LEFT of that rightmost gully. Get there by dropping about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek and making a rising traverse beneath the gully system, past the adjacent buttress. The proof higher up is the chockstones: the gully leading to the notch at about 7,400 ft is blocked by large jammed blocks, and pitching past them, including one narrow crack normally taken on a belay, is the crux of reaching the notch. If the gully you are in runs clean with no chockstones and narrows into a closed chimney above, back off — that is the right-hand gully. Above the notch, easy slabs and scrambling lead to the summit.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp (below Mt. Terror)
Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: Crescent Creek Basin sits on the north side of the crest and is what you cross the Barrier for, reached over the roughly 6,400 ft saddle northeast of the Chopping Block. It is the working base for East and West McMillan Spire, Inspiration, the Twin Needles, and for the Ottohorn and Himmelhorn by way of the col between them; Frenzel Spitz sits off the main chain near the Ottohorn's north side. Parties camp at several benches at different heights.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and pools fed by the basin's snowfields, reliable early and mid season and unreliable late once the snow has pulled back. Plan on melting snow in a lean year.
bivy.permit: This is the SEPARATE Crescent Creek cross-country zone, not Terror Basin — a trip camping in both needs both zones written onto the same permit, night by night. Like Terror Basin it is walk-up only at Marblemount rather than bookable in advance.
bivy.capacity: A few parties on gravel, slab and snow; the zone is capped at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Stump Hollow bench
bivy.notes: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only. Trickles and small pools are dependable through early summer while snow lingers, and can dry up or retreat entirely by late season; late-summer parties should expect to search or carry.
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone permit from the Wilderness Information Center. This bench sits close to the divide between the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones, so ask which zone the rangers are writing you into rather than assuming — the answer decides what the rest of your itinerary can say.
bivy.capacity: Small — a couple of parties on heather benches and slabs, and it is easy to end up spread out

bivy.name: High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
bivy.notes: The western summits — the Twin Needles, Ottohorn, Himmelhorn and Frenzel Spitz — are far enough along the crest that a party working from a basin camp faces a very long day, so some take a bivouac high on the traverse instead. These are improvised spots rather than established sites, and quality varies from a decent gravel bench to a night sitting on a ledge. There is no shelter and no water, so this only makes sense with a settled forecast and a party willing to move fast the next morning.
bivy.water: No dependable source. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs: carry water up or melt snow, and expect nothing at all once the summer snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Still inside a cross-country zone and still requires a wilderness permit with the night assigned to the correct zone. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, keep 100 ft from water, no fires, and carry waste out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: One party, and often only a ledge or a gravel patch for two people

approach_variants.name: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From Darrington take Squire Creek Road to the washout that gates it, then walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing.

The South Face turn-off is two cut logs, one either side of the road, with old logging cable visible — turn right there onto the well-beaten boot track. It drops to a ford of the creek, then climbs steeply through old growth, steep and dirty near the top, into open grassland. The main grassy saddle bivy is about three hours from the trailhead, with a second smaller saddle roughly ten minutes further west along the wall.
approach_variants.season: Summer
hazards: Ford of Squire Creek
Steep dirty forest on the upper boot track
Hand-drilled bolts of unknown age on the face sections
approach_variants.baseFinding: Get to the right saddle first. The main grassy saddle sits at the start of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer and is the reference every South Face line is described from; the smaller saddle ten minutes west is a different camp. From the saddle the grey granite apron of the South Face is in front of you and the individual lines are picked off it. This route takes a dihedral with a lieback/stemming crux on pitch 2 and a delicate smearing finger traverse on pitch 3, sandwiched between easier friction above and below — so easy friction on pitch 1 is CORRECT here, not a sign you are on the wrong line. Protection is a mix of hand-drilled bolts on the faces and gear in the dihedral and cracks; a face with no gear placements at all is not this route. The sources consulted do not give a ground-level marker specific to this line beyond the wall and the saddle reference — confirm against the wall topo before committing.

bivy.name: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
bivy.notes: Sits in old-growth timber near where Squire Creek meets the North Fork Stillaguamish, a few miles west of Darrington on SR 530 — not on the Mountain Loop Highway, and not up the Squire Creek road itself. It is the most comfortable base for a weekend on the Darrington granite, with flush toilets and a swimmable creek, at the cost of a drive back into town each morning. Because it is county-run rather than Forest Service, the fee schedule, season and reservation window are set separately from the national forest campgrounds and should be checked on their own.
bivy.water: Piped drinking water via spigots through the campground; reliable in season
bivy.permit: None — this is a COUNTY park, not Forest Service. Nightly fee, reservations through the Snohomish County Parks system. A Northwest Forest Pass does nothing here.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 30 non-hookup sites, tents and RVs, reservable

bivy.name: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
bivy.notes: The Squire Creek road out of the west end of old Darrington has been cut by a washout well short of its historic end for many years, so the drivable road end is A MOVING TARGET and the walk in to Squire Creek Wall is longer than older descriptions suggest. Parties sleeping in the car or under a tarp at the closure are doing so to get an early start on that extra walking, not because there is anything established there. Confirm the current closure point before committing — how far you can drive has changed repeatedly between seasons, and it is the single biggest variable in a Squire Creek Wall day.
bivy.water: Squire Creek runs close by and is dependable, but needs treating
bivy.permit: None for dispersed camping on forest land; the usual 14-day and setback rules apply.
bivy.capacity: A few parties, informal

bivy.name: Squire Creek Wall on-route ledges
bivy.notes: The long routes on Squire Creek Wall have a couple of usable ledges high on the face, the better-known ones roughly a third and two-thirds of the way up, and parties moving slowly on the full-length lines have used them to split the climb. This is genuine bivouac ground rather than camping — a ledge, a rope, and whatever you hauled. Most parties climbing here do not need it, and it should be treated as a planned option for the biggest routes or as an emergency out, rather than as a reason to carry overnight gear by default.
bivy.water: A rock pocket at the lower ledge holds water through much of the season, but it is a puddle, not a source — assume it may be dry and carry what you need
bivy.permit: None
bivy.capacity: Small ledges, one party

approach_variants.name: Hannegan Pass, the Chilliwack cable car and Brush Creek to Whatcom Pass, then onto the Whatcom Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,100 ft at the end of Ruth Creek Road, FR-32, off the Mt. Baker Highway, Trail #674 runs 4.2-4.6 miles and about 2,000 ft alongside Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, the last easy reliable water before dropping into the national park.

From the pass, descend the Chilliwack River Trail through long viewless switchbacks, losing roughly 2,800 ft, past Boundary and Copper Creek camps. THE RIVER IS CROSSED VIA A HAND-PULLED CABLE CAR NEAR US CABIN CAMP RATHER THAN A FORD, which is the practical difference between this and the Easy Ridge approach.

Continue up-valley on the Brush Creek Trail toward Graybeal Camp, roughly 14 trail miles and a cumulative 4,400 ft of gain from the trailhead. The small creek near Graybeal is unreliable and can run dry by late summer, so fill earlier at the Chilliwack or US Cabin Camp. Past Graybeal the maintained tread gives way to a steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path gaining roughly 2,000 ft over the final 3 miles to Whatcom Pass at 5,206 ft, passing Whatcom Camp and the first real views of the Challenger Glacier.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Crevasses and moats on the Whatcom Glacier, deteriorating to bare ice with gaping moats later in the season
A steep, brushy, root-and-timber climbers' path above Graybeal Camp
The creek near Graybeal can run dry by late summer
An exposed class 3 summit ridge on poor rock
A glacier that is more open on the descent than on the ascent
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE'S OWN GROUND IS THE GLACIER, AND YOU ARE ON IT AS SOON AS YOU LEAVE WHATCOM PASS. From the pass, leave the trail and climb and contour SOUTH AND EAST to gain the Whatcom Glacier at roughly 5,200-5,500 ft, then rope up and travel toward Perfect Pass, the notch and saddle south of the peak.

SO THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE OTHER TWO ROUTES ON THIS PEAK IS THE FIRST MOVE OUT OF WHATCOM PASS, AND IT IS THREE-WAY: SOUTH and up the crest is the North Ridge. SOUTH AND EAST onto ice at 5,200-5,500 ft is this route. Nothing from Whatcom Pass is the South Spur, which is approached from Easy Ridge on the other side.

ARRIVAL AT THE CLIMBING PROPER: from the glacier's high point near Perfect Pass, the route ascends the broad SOUTH-FACING snowfield below the summit and finishes on an exposed but moderate class 3 scramble along the south ridge crest. The snowfield is the same one the South Spur uses. The two routes share their last hour and differ entirely in everything before it.

WHAT THE GLACIER DOES THROUGH THE SEASON, WHICH IS THE REAL VARIABLE: crevasses and moats open as the year goes on and the surface can go from soft neve early to bare, polished ice with exposed water channels by mid to late summer. On the descent they are typically MORE open than on the way up as the afternoon sun softens the snowpack, so budget time for careful navigation rather than a quick glissade.

AN ALTERNATE EXIT WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU NEED IT: if the summit notch is badly melted out and choss-prone, a descent drops about 200 ft north of Peak 7347 to reach the Wiley Glacier instead of reversing through the notch.

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. Whatcom Camp and both Graybeal camps have been closed because of fire damage from 2022, and the park's fire-closures page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists them closed until further notice, so there is no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. LEAVE THE PCT ALMOST IMMEDIATELY and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is WHISTLER MOUNTAIN ABOVE RAINY PASS in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; route-finding the whole way
Downed logs in the lower forest
Loose talus and scree in the gullies, with class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Downsloping slabs and loose gravel in the summit gully
No reliable water above the lower forest
Early-season snow lingering in the forest and basin, firming the gullies
approach_variants.baseFinding:
CLIMB UNTIL THE FOREST OPENS. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A MEADOW BASIN BELOW THE WEST RIDGE AND GULLY COMPLEX, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

FROM THE BASIN, TREND SOUTH AND SOUTHEAST ON A RISING TRAVERSE TO GAIN THE COL AND BASIN BETWEEN WHISTLER AND THE SOUTHWEST PEAK OF CUTTHROAT. THAT COL IS THE AIMING POINT, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the BROAD WEST RIDGE, or the SHALLOW GULLY JUST NORTH OF IT, to the summit shoulder.

THE LAST SECTION IS THE ONE THAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE ON THE SUMMIT LINE RATHER THAN A NEIGHBOURING GULLY: A ROCK GULLY WITH A VISIBLE RAMP ALONG THE HEADWALL, OVER DOWNSLOPING SLABS AND LOOSE GRAVEL. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

approach_variants.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
approach_variants.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile BEFORE the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the WEST EDGE OF A STAND OF TREES.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Oct
hazards: An unmarked trailhead identified only by its distance from the Blue Lake trailhead
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
No reliable water on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TRAILHEAD IS UNMARKED AND THE PATH START IS A TREE-LINE EDGE, SO THE FIND IS AT THE ROAD RATHER THAN ON THE MOUNTAIN. The pullout is 0.7 MILE BEFORE THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD coming from Rainy Pass. IF YOU HAVE REACHED THE BLUE LAKE TRAILHEAD, YOU HAVE DRIVEN 0.7 MILE TOO FAR. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a STAND OF TREES begins, and the boot path leaves from its WEST EDGE.

FOLLOW THE BOOT PATH UP THROUGH A MEADOW, THEN RISING-TRAVERSE TO INTERSECT THE LEVEL PORTION OF WHISTLER'S SOUTH RIDGE AT ABOUT 6,180 FT. A LEVEL SECTION OF RIDGE IS THE ARRIVAL, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

FROM THERE, SCRAMBLE UP THE RIDGE AND CONNECTING GULLIES TO THE SUMMIT. THE ALTERNATIVE, WHICH IS ALSO CORRECT: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies LEFT, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

SO THE DECISION AT 6,800 FT IS A REAL FORK AND BOTH BRANCHES WORK: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

THE NEGATIVE TEST AGAINST THE OTHER APPROACH, WHICH MATTERS BECAUSE BOTH START WITHIN THREE MILES OF EACH OTHER ON THE SAME HIGHWAY: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a MEADOW BASIN at 6,100 ft below the WEST ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the SOUTH ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

bivy.name: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
bivy.notes: THE camp for both MOUNT LA CROSSE and WHITE MOUNTAIN, which stand less than a mile apart on either side of a small unnamed glacier directly above the basin. Both are scrambles rather than climbs — La Crosse at 6,417 ft goes at class 2 and was first climbed in 1928, White Mountain at 6,378 ft is class 2 as well — so from a camp here the two together are a single long day rather than an expedition. Lake LaCrosse sits at about 4,800 ft, roughly 400 ft higher and a mile and a half further than Marmot Lake, with Hart Lake in between; Marmot is covered in the Staircase file and is a perfectly good camp, but it is further from these two summits and it is the wrong side of the shelf. THE APPROACH IS THE ENTIRE DIFFICULTY AND THERE ARE THREE OF THEM, none short. From the Dosewallips you go up the West Fork and over LaCrosse Pass. From the East Fork Quinault you go through Enchanted Valley and over Anderson Pass. From the Duckabush you come up the river and over O'Neil Pass. Every one of those is two days in for most parties carrying gear, which is why these summits see so little traffic. July through September; the basin holds snow late and the passes either side of it later still.
bivy.water: Reliable — both lakes hold through the season and the outlet creeks run into autumn. This is the last dependable water before anything you climb from here; the slopes and the unnamed glacier between the two summits carry no running source once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site. This basin is not itself one of the named quota areas, but the East Fork Quinault approach to it is, so which trailhead you walk in from changes what you have to book — check the whole itinerary rather than just the camp. An animal-resistant food container is required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the parkwide 3,500 ft line. Elk work this basin heavily and bears are regular visitors.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread between the two lakes, in and above open subalpine basin. Neither holds a crowd and the meadow ground is fragile, so use the established pads rather than making new ones.

approach_variants.name: Snow Creek trail, log crossing and the climbers' trail
approach_variants.notes:
From the Icicle Road junction at the west end of Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead lot; a Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Walk the Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill roughly two to two and a half miles, about an hour, until Snow Creek Wall stands directly opposite you across the drainage. The trail stays in trees and never touches the rock.

Branch right at an early opening, scramble down into the flat ground beside Snow Creek, and cross on the log. On the far bank climb up through boulders and talus until a bootpath forms; it gains about 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall.
approach_variants.season: Spring and fall; the wall is low and east-facing and bakes in summer
hazards: The log crossing of Snow Creek at high water
Loose talus on the 500 ft climbers' trail
Annual raptor monitoring in this drainage — check for a nesting closure before going
approach_variants.baseFinding: The one fixed reference on this wall is where the climbers' trail arrives: that is the HIGH POINT of the base, marked by a few small scrub trees, directly under the roofs forming the underside of Two Tree Ledge, with a large slung flake about 20 ft below a small bush. RPM's bolted slab is straight ahead of you there and Remorse's easier vegetated gully is about 30 ft to its right. Everything else on the wall is located by walking left or right from that spot — Orbit is about 150 yards left, until the base starts dropping steeply downhill. Where White Slabs itself starts relative to that arrival point is unknown. Identify it on the ground against a current topo rather than assuming it shares the Remorse start.

approach_variants.name: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Niederprum trailhead at the end of Old Mine Road above Darrington. The Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded for years, so parties park at the gate, get past the barricade on foot and walk the road roughly a mile and a quarter to the real trailhead — extra distance and gain that older published figures do not include.

Trail #653 switchbacks through forest into the Boulder River Wilderness and reaches 'the flat' at about 3,200 ft, a level clearing on the site of an old mining cabin and the natural rest or camp spot. Beyond it the maintained tread ends and a boot path threads thinning, brushy forest with deadfall.

Above that the route traverses south through moderately dense forest between roughly 4,500 and 4,700 ft to reach a broad snow couloir, which is climbed to Lone Tree Pass at about 5,000 ft. From the pass, traverse east along the ridge and then drop several hundred feet southeast to a small lake and flat meadow — a sheltered bivy. A long rising traverse east below cliff bands then leads to a broad gully up to High Pass at about 6,100 ft, and over it onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier.
approach_variants.season: late Apr-Jun for snow cover; the line goes later but on more rock
hazards: barricaded Moose Creek bridge at the start
avalanche terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass
vague, brushy route-finding with deadfall above 'the flat'
crevasses on the Whitehorse Glacier from roughly July onward
summit bergschrund and moat, often a fifth-class or roped step by midsummer
no reliable water once you are on snow
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Lone Tree Pass CANNOT be picked out from directly beneath it, and that is the single most useful thing to know about this approach. Look at the mountain from the valley before you start — from the highway at Darrington — and fix where the pass sits relative to the shoulder, because once you are traversing inside the forest between 4,500 and 4,700 ft there is nothing to aim at. The confirmation from inside the trees is the ground itself: you are traversing, not climbing, and the correct entry is where that traversing forest opens into a BROAD snow couloir. A narrow gully or a steep timbered rib is not it.

For the upper half, the landmark is White Benchmark, Point 6357 — a blocky tower that works as a lighthouse for the whole rising traverse to High Pass. Keep it in view and aim at it; the broad gully up to the pass is right there. If you have run out of the rising traverse without a blocky tower above you, you are low and short of the pass.

The climbing itself starts at High Pass, where you cross onto the glacier. Snow travel of up to about thirty-five degrees leads to the summit snow ridge. The final marker is at the very top: by midsummer the bergschrund and moat below the summit rock often force a short section of fifth-class rock or a delicate roped step across a snow bridge, so the route does not simply walk out on snow.

approach_variants.name: Snow Gulch direct (deep snow only)
approach_variants.notes: A more direct line used by some early-season and ski parties. From the Niederprum trailhead area, follow the old forest-road grade toward Snow Gulch, then ascend the creek drainage. The section between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft is a steep bushwhack through slide alder or up the adjacent slabs, and it only makes sense once deep snow has buried the brush. Parties commonly stash skis or boards around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
approach_variants.season: early season, deep snow burying the brush
hazards: slide alder and slabs between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft when snow cover is thin
avalanche hazard in the gulch and on the glacier headwall in the early-season window
approach_variants.baseFinding: This variation rejoins the same upper ground, so the markers are unchanged: White Benchmark (Point 6357) for the traverse to High Pass, and High Pass itself as the step onto the glacier. The specific trap here is timing rather than terrain — if you are fighting slide alder rather than walking on snow, the line is out of condition and the standard Niederprum trail is the better choice that day.

approach_variants.name: Lone Tree Pass and High Pass, early season
approach_variants.notes: Park at the steel gate and boulder barricade where the road is closed at the washed-out creek bridge and walk the old mining-road grade south. The standard line climbs to the sloping bench by the old mine workings, marked by a large broken silvered snag, then makes a rising leftward traverse to Lone Tree Pass, with the broad snow platform just beyond it serving as the high camp. From there traverse to High Pass at the top of the broad snow couloir below the prominent point to its north, and step onto the glacier. Climbed early in the season some parties instead take the more direct Snow Gulch line up the creek drainage, which only makes sense once deep snow has buried the slide alder; skis are commonly stashed around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
approach_variants.season: Roughly April to June, while the couloirs, glacier basin and connecting slopes are still continuous corn or neve rather than open crevasse and bare ice
hazards: The whole uptrack sits in a large avalanche-prone zone — go on a consolidating freeze-thaw cycle, not a loading one
Crevasses, seracs and rockfall from the subpeaks above the glacier
A steep, firm summit block that can be neve or bare ice, often rappelled rather than skied on the way down
Firm early-morning snow demands a timed start
approach_variants.baseFinding: High Pass is the entry to the glacier and the summit block above it is the base of the climbing proper. Come over Lone Tree Pass, make the long rising traverse to High Pass at the top of the broad snow couloir beneath the prominent point north of it, and step onto the glacier there. Climbed at this time of year the whole basin is continuous snow, so the marker is not a rock feature: the proof that you are at the foot of the final pitch is a large bergschrund running right around the PERIMETER of the summit block, visible from well down the glacier. Above it the ground steepens to roughly 50 degrees and can be firm neve or bare ice, and it is where parties stash skis and go to crampons. If you are still on low-angle, skinnable glacier with no schrund across your line, you are below the summit block. If you are threading open crevasses and bare ice rather than moving on continuous snow, you are here too late in the year for this variation and should be on the melted-out rock-and-snow line instead.

bivy.name: Whitehorse high camp, benches near Lone Tree Pass
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for the Northwest Shoulder, and most parties who do not intend a twelve-to-sixteen hour car-to-car day use it. The route is around 6,000 to 7,000 feet of gain from a low trailhead and the lower trail is notoriously steep and brushy, so splitting it at the pass converts a punishing single day into two reasonable ones and puts the glacier and the exposed summit scrambling in the morning. The sheltered meadow just beyond the pass is the pick — trees break the wind and it looks straight at the summit. Everything about this approach depends on the Mine Road out of the highway west of Darrington: it is rough, narrow, overgrown enough to scratch a vehicle, and has had bridge and washout closures that push the start well down the hill and add road walking. Confirm how far you can drive before you plan the day. Early season with snow cover over the brush is much the better time; by late summer the glacier above develops crevasses and a large bergschrund and the brush below is at its worst.
bivy.water: Snowmelt in season and the small tarn below the pass on the traverse east; both are seasonal. By late summer this side dries out and there may be nothing, so carry up or plan to melt. There is no water on the trail below.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no permit to camp, no quota, no self-issue box. No fee at the trailhead, which is unusual for this area and reflects how minimal the parking is. Fires are a bad idea on this ground and are commonly banned outright in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a flat sheltered meadow just past the pass takes a couple of tents, with smaller pockets on benches nearby and more ground on the traverse east toward the small lake below the pass. One or two parties.

bivy.name: Whitehorse Community Park campground, Darrington
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in base to the Mine Road, sitting just outside Darrington with the mountain itself directly in view, which makes it a useful place to look at conditions on the northwest side the evening before. Its real role is staging: the Niederprum trailhead has room for only a handful of vehicles and nothing else, so sleeping in town and driving up in the small hours is the usual pattern rather than camping at the road end. Because it is county-run its season and fees are set separately from the forest campgrounds and change independently of them. The winter closure is the catch — the best window for the Northwest Shoulder is spring, and the campground may not be open yet.
bivy.water: Developed park water in season; confirm before relying on it outside summer
bivy.permit: COUNTY park, not national forest — a nightly fee applies and no federal or state pass does anything here. Seasonal: closed and winterized through the winter months, roughly mid-autumn to mid-spring, which rules it out for the spring snow season when Whitehorse is actually in condition.
bivy.capacity: A developed county campground with tent and equestrian sites on a large park property; nightly fee

approach_variants.name: Road walk from the pullout to the foot of the wall
approach_variants.notes: From Randle, head south and follow the main forest road roughly nineteen miles, then turn off at the signed meadows turning and follow the next road under three miles before turning again onto the last one. That final road is rough and wants high clearance; follow it about two miles until the rock appears, then carry on to the large pullout where the climbers' trail is obvious. From the pullout, simply walk up the road toward the wall and onto its base. There is no cell service on the approach or at the crag.
approach_variants.season: June to October.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia studded with cobbles and knobs that can pop loose without warning
Rough gravel approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service on the approach or at the crag
The formation's base wraps a long way; the toe is a specific point, not a general area
approach_variants.baseFinding: Go to the LOWEST TOE of the West Face — the point where the wall's base comes down closest to the road, rather than anywhere along its higher flanks. The start is a short PROW, and the test is bolts you can count: TWO of them, low, on the prow, within reach from the ground. Confirm from the pitches above — the first climbs a short face onto clean ramps to a ledge belay, and the second traverses across a SADDLE to a CHAIN ANCHOR, which is a distinctive shape for a second pitch and not something a neighbouring line does. Negative marker: if you are under a long face with no bolts within reach of the ground and the only protection on offer is slinging the embedded cobbles and knobs, you are on one of the older knob-slinging lines rather than this bolted one.

approach_variants.name: Around the East Face and through the Gap
approach_variants.notes: The other way onto this side of the formation, and the one to use if you are coming from routes on the far side. From the same pullout, take the climbers' trail around the EAST face of the rock — this trail traverses the whole formation — and pass through the deep gully that splits it, then drop down to the LEFT onto the West Face's base. It is longer than walking up the road but it links the two sides without returning to the car.
approach_variants.season: June to October.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia with loose cobbles and knobs
The traverse round the formation is on climbers' trail with loose ground below the walls
Rough approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service anywhere on the approach or at the crag
approach_variants.baseFinding: Having dropped down and left out of the walk-through gully, keep descending along the base until you reach the LOWEST TOE of the West Face — the far low point of the wall, not the first rock you meet after the gap. The start is a short PROW carrying TWO bolts within reach of the ground. Confirm above: a short face to clean ramps and a ledge belay, then a traverse across a saddle to a chain anchor. Negative markers: if the deep walk-through gully is still behind and ABOVE you and you have not dropped down and left, you are on the flank rather than at the foot of the face; if you are looking at a long unbolted face where knobs are the only protection, you are on an older line.

approach_variants.name: Monte Cristo and Glacier Basin
approach_variants.notes: From Barlow Pass walk the gated road to the old townsite; the road is bike-friendly and the river crossing near the first mile is a large log or a ford, with no bridge. Surface water near the townsite can carry arsenic and metals from old tailings, so treat or carry it. Past the townsite the Glacier Basin trail turns very steep and climbs wet, slick bedrock beside the falls — poor footing, worst on the descent — to the campsites on the timbered knoll where the maintained trail effectively ends. Leave the trail there and climb steep, very loose talus, or snow early in the season, to the col on the dividing ridge.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn, once the basin talus is snow-free
hazards: Slick wet bedrock beside the falls, especially descending
Steep, very loose talus gaining the col
A short exposed class 3-4 step on the summit block that is not a walk-up
Contaminated surface water near the old townsite
approach_variants.baseFinding: The identification that matters happens at the col on the dividing ridge, because parties from this trailhead routinely commit to the wrong summit. The SPIRES lie along the crest and are slender, detached towers; their routes are all fifth class and roped, and the nearest of them has a famously tiny summit reached by a separate climb. The peak this route goes to is the broad, bulky mass carrying the tall north face, and the line gains it by the NORTH-WEST ridge from the col. Stand at the col and settle which of the two you are beneath before starting up — a tower with a pointed, detached profile is the wrong answer. The second check is at the top: the final summit block is a short, exposed class 3-4 step on volcanic breccia, so if you have arrived at what you think is the top on pure walking ground with no scrambling move at all, you are on a shoulder and not on the summit.

bivy.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
bivy.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
bivy.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

approach_variants.name: Winchester Mountain Trail #685 from Twin Lakes to the 1935 lookout
approach_variants.notes:
From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft — the parking area between the two lakes, with a vault toilet — pick up Winchester Mountain Trail #685 heading north-northwest. It starts as a moderately steep, well-graded tread through blueberry and heather.

At roughly a quarter to half a mile there is a signed junction with High Pass Trail #676, which goes on toward the Gargett Mine and Mount Larrabee. Stay LEFT or straight to remain on #685.

Beyond the junction the trail leaves the last trees onto open, treeless southeast-facing slopes and climbs by tight switchbacks. Around 0.9 mile an unmarked climbers' path splits off offering a more direct, rougher scramble line up snow and scree; the standard trail continues by switchbacks and is the preferred line.

At about 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just west and south of the summit; a short final push along the open ridge reaches the 1935 fire lookout at 6,521 ft. About 3.4-3.5 miles round trip with 1,300 ft of gain.

There is no water on route or at the lookout.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct, and the limiting factor is the last two and a half miles of FS-3065 rather than the trail
hazards: The last two and a half miles of FS-3065, rough and one-lane in places, high-clearance recommended
Hard lingering snow on the upper switchbacks into August in heavy-snow years, over consequential runout
A signed junction at 0.25-0.5 mile that serves five much larger objectives
An unmarked climbers' path at 0.9 mile up snow and scree
No water on route or at the lookout
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THERE IS NO CLIMBING ON THIS ROUTE AND SAYING SO IS THE HONEST ANSWER — WHAT THERE IS, IS ONE JUNCTION YOU CAN GET WRONG AND ONE SLOPE THAT CAN HURT YOU. The route is a maintained trail from the car to the lookout, so 'the base' is the trailhead between the two lakes.

THE JUNCTION AT A QUARTER TO HALF A MILE IS THE ONLY REAL DECISION. #685 for Winchester goes LEFT or straight; #676 for High Pass, the Gargett Mine, Mount Larrabee, American Border Peak and the Pleiades goes RIGHT. It is signed, but it is the branch point for five different objectives in this basin and taking it by accident sends you toward a very much bigger day. If you find yourself contouring around the WEST side of Winchester Mountain and losing height toward a pass, you are on #676.

THE SECOND ONE IS UNMARKED, at about 0.9 mile: a climbers' path splits off up snow and scree as a direct alternative to the switchbacks. It is rougher and it is not the standard line. In cloud, a path that stops switchbacking and goes straight up is the wrong one.

ARRIVAL AT THE RIDGE: at roughly 1.3 miles the trail crests the ridge just WEST and SOUTH of the summit, with only a few hundred feet of open ridge left. Cresting a ridge with the lookout to your northeast is the confirmation.

THE REAL HAZARD IS THE UPPER SWITCHBACKS, and it is worth reading as a base finding of a different kind: steep snow lingers on the upper switchbacks and the southeast slopes into August in heavy-snow years, it hardens overnight, and the runout below is consequential. An ice axe is a reasonable thing to be carrying on a lookout trail in early season.

bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.notes: This is the camp for WINDY PEAK and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. EXPECT BURN. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass, then past Brynhild Lake and around to the south side of the tower
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at about 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail south along Mountaineer Creek; at about 2.5 miles bear left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail. Cross Mountaineer Creek on logs and boulders — an awkward wet ford in early-season high water — and climb through forest and a boulder field to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, roughly four miles in. Last reliable water.

Take the climbers' path along the lake's east and south shore through talus to the foot of Aasgard Pass, then up the eroded boot track: roughly 2,200 ft in well under a mile of loose scree and blocks, holding snow and ice into July.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, work south to southwest across talus — initially as though heading for the snow route on Dragontail's east side — toward the tower, then up beside the west shore of Brynhild Lake (snow early in the season) and around behind the tower to its south base.

Figure six and a half to seven miles one way with something like 4,700-4,900 ft of gain.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; earlier the traverse from the pass is a snow crossing and the slopes below the tower want an axe
hazards: Aasgard Pass: 2,200 ft of loose eroded scree with rockfall from parties above, holding snow into July
Serious exposure on the ledge traverse onto the east side of the tower
A four-foot slot that must be jumped to reach the true summit, with real consequence
Fast-building afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter in the Upper Enchantments
The downclimb off the south face is the crux for most parties
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TOWER ITSELF IS THE LANDMARK — a distinct rock pinnacle standing alone at the west end of the Enchantments, dividing the upper basin between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It is a pinnacle, not a summit on a ridge, so once you are close enough to see anything at all it is unambiguous.

WHICH SIDE OF IT YOU WANT: the SOUTH side. From Aasgard Pass go up beside the west shore of Brynhild Lake (on snow early in the season) and swing around behind the tower to its south base. The scramble starts there: head up toward the band of white rock, pick up the ledge that leads around onto the east side, then climb the large black blocks to the top.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: this line does not go to the col southwest of the tower, and it never needs a rope. If the ground ahead of you calls for one, you have left the scramble for one of the tower's roped lines.

ARRIVAL CONFIRMED BY THE SUMMIT ITSELF: the top of this tower is guarded by a four-foot slot you have to jump. If you have scrambled to a high point and there was no slot, you are on a subsidiary block and not on the tower.

GRADE CHECK: nothing on this line is harder than Class 3. The ledge is easy but airy; take it slowly when it is wet or holds snow.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the same southwest col, taking the corner rather than the face traverse
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the south face approach as far as the col: Stuart Lake trailhead to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path round the lake's east and south shore, Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft, then south across talus toward the tower and up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of it.

Published figures for the day put it at roughly six to eight hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this point, which is a wide enough spread that it should be treated as a range rather than a plan.

From the col the climbing is short: about 100 ft up the sharp ridge, a few feet right onto the south face at Class 4, a 5.5 step-up, a short face, and a scramble to the summit slot.

What separates this route from the south face one is not where you stand but what you do from there, so the useful content is in the base finding rather than in the walk.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, snow into July
Exposure on the sharp ridge above the col
Hard-to-find protection on the 5.5 crux
A four-foot summit slot that must be jumped
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter
Downclimbing the south face back to the col is the usual descent and is Class 2-3 with one harder step
approach_variants.baseFinding:
SAME COL, DIFFERENT FIRST MOVE — AND YOU SHOULD KNOW WHICH YOU ARE DOING BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE COL. From the col southwest of the tower, this line goes straight up the SHARP RIDGE ABOVE THE COL for about 100 ft. That ridge crest is the route. The south face line uses the same ground and then commits to the traverse right; both converge at the same Class 4 step and 5.5 move.

SO THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE COL, and it has three parts:
  1. You reached it by ascending SNOW or CLASS 2 ROCK from the basin — not by crossing a steep snowfield, which is the west-side approach, and not by traversing across light rock under Dragontail's south ridge, which is the east face.
  2. Above you the ground rises as a defined, narrow crest rather than as an open face.
  3. The tower's summit block is directly above that crest, with the four-foot summit slot the last obstacle.

IF THE CREST FEELS WRONG: the ridge is sharp and exposed, and the recorded warning about this line is that placements on the crux are tricky to find. That is a route-finding statement as much as a protection one — a leader who cannot find gear may be a few feet off the correct line, on ground with fewer features.

AND THE COMMON MISTAKE: parties heading for the tower from Aasgard Pass drift too far EAST, toward Dragontail. If Dragontail's bulk is directly ahead of you rather than off to your right, you have gone past the tower.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the col, then a steep snowfield crossing onto the west side
approach_variants.notes:
As for the other routes on the tower: Stuart Lake trailhead, the Colchuck Lake Trail to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path round the lake, and Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft. Then south across the basin to the col behind the tower.

What is different here is the last few hundred feet. From the col a STEEP SNOWFIELD has to be crossed to reach the base of the buttress on the west side. An ice axe is the standard recommendation, and parties downclimb it in self-arrest position on the way out, which tells you the angle.

The climbing above is mostly Class 4 on solid granite with good holds, a short Class 5 chimney partway up, and a friction section to finish. Two pitches.

The descent combines rappelling and downclimbing, including an exposed ledge traverse, back to the col — so the snowfield gets crossed twice.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The snowfield is the point of this variant and it is present through most of the usable season — carry an axe regardless of the date
hazards: A steep snowfield crossing to reach the base, and again in descent — ice axe essential
Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, snow into July
An exposed ledge traverse on the descent
A short Class 5 chimney mid-route with a pack
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter and a snow crossing between you and the way out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SNOWFIELD IS THE ROUTE MARKER, AND IT IS THE CLEANEST ONE ON THE WHOLE TOWER. Of the tower's routes, this is the only one where the base is reached by crossing steep snow after the col. So: if you left the col and immediately started climbing rock, you are on one of the other lines. If you left the col, crossed a steep snowfield, and are now standing under rock on the WEST side, you are here.

CARRY THAT AS A DECISION, NOT AN OBSERVATION. Arriving at the col without an axe means this route is off the table for the day, and that is a judgement to make at Colchuck Lake rather than at 8,400 ft.

CONFIRMATION FROM THE ROCK: the buttress here is solid granite with good natural hand and footholds and it goes mostly at Class 4, with one short Class 5 CHIMNEY partway up and a friction face to finish. The other routes on the tower are characterised by a sharp ridge above the col and a traverse onto the south face; neither has a chimney. A chimney at mid-height is positive evidence you are on the west buttress.

ORIENTATION CHECK IN CLOUD: from the base you are on the far side of the tower from the Upper Enchantment lakes basin you walked in through. If the lakes are still below and behind you, you have not crossed to the west side.

AND THE DESCENT MATTERS TO THE ARRIVAL DECISION: the way down involves an exposed ledge traverse and rappels back to the col, then the snowfield again in self-arrest position. This is the tower's most committing line and the base is where you commit.

bivy.name: The Tungsten Creek trail camps below the Boundary Trail junction
bivy.notes: This is where a party climbing Wolframite from the Chewuch actually sleeps on the second night, and it matters because the arithmetic of the approach is punishing without it. The Tungsten Creek trail breaks off the Chewuch trail a little past eight miles and climbs steadily for about six more, with the creek on the left and the bulk of Wolframite ahead — so a party that has walked in from Thirtymile is looking at a long day before the climbing even begins. Breaking the climb here rather than pushing to the Boundary Trail junction puts you on running water, in shelter, and with the steep work done in the cool of the morning. It is also the sensible fallback when the ground at the junction is occupied by a horse party, which happens more often than the remoteness suggests. Expect burned forest in stretches, little shade, and blowdown that changes with every windstorm. Late July through September is the working season; snow holds on the north sides of the passes above into July.
bivy.water: Tungsten Creek runs alongside for the whole climb and is the dependable supply on this approach, holding into the autumn. THIS IS WHERE YOU FILL FOR THE SUMMIT, because the Boundary Trail crest above the junction runs on tarns and snowmelt and is unreliable by August, and the peak itself carries nothing. Old iron pipe from the mining days is scattered along the trail, which tells you where the workings took their water and not that any of it is usable now. Treat everything.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the easy one: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation and nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Thirtymile. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight — this is heavily used horse country. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer in this dry drainage and the wood is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the climb beside the creek, most taking one or two tents, with the better ground in the lower half where the timber is still standing. Nothing developed and no facilities, and you are unlikely to meet anyone.

bivy.name: Tungsten Mine Camp / Boundary Trail #533 junction

approach_variants.name: Castle Rock lot, Logger's Ledge, then the long hill east
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the main Castle Rock pullout on US-2 near milepost 96.5, west of Leavenworth. Take the Upper Castle trail from the uphill, western end of the lot up to Logger's Ledge, then traverse the ledge EAST and keep climbing the long steep hillside above — about 40 to 45 minutes of sustained uphill from the ledge.

Midnight Rock and Noontime Rock close every year for peregrine falcon nesting, roughly 1 April to 31 July, or until the young fledge or the Forest Service determines no nesting will occur.
approach_variants.season: August to autumn — closed for peregrine nesting for much of the first half of the year
hazards: Annual peregrine falcon closure, roughly 1 April to 31 July
A sustained 40-45 minute steep hillside above Logger's Ledge
Steep, coarse granite with few moderate lines
Northwest aspect — shaded and cold in the morning
approach_variants.baseFinding: Coming up and to the right from Logger's Ledge you arrive at the LEFT side of Midnight Rock first — so the left end of the wall is the fixed point to work from, not the centre. Midnight is the taller of the pair: roughly 300 ft, vertical to slightly overhanging coarse granite, mostly parallel-sided crack lines, facing northwest so it holds shade through the morning and early afternoon. Noontime sits alongside and is barely developed; if you have walked to a wall with only a handful of routes on it, you have gone past Midnight. Note the general trap at this crag: several of the best-known lines here, ROTC among them, begin from an enormous ledge halfway up the CENTRE of the wall rather than from the ground, and that ledge is reached by climbing another route first. Before assuming a line is unreachable, check whether it is a ground-up start at all. No source consulted for this pass records where Yellow Bird itself starts along the base; identify it against a topo from the left end of the wall.

approach_variants.name: Heart Lake Road kiosk pullout, trail 248 to 247
approach_variants.notes:
From I-5 take SR 20 west toward Anacortes and Deception Pass, trend right onto Campbell Lake Road, then right at the Lake Erie Grocery onto Heart Lake Road.

About an eighth of a mile (roughly 0.2 miles) north of the grocery there is a gravel pullout on the east side of Heart Lake Road with an information kiosk. That is the Main Wall parking.

Take trail 248, which enters the woods on the RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE GATE. Follow it 5-10 minutes to a T junction with trail 247. Turn RIGHT — this is the junction that decides your day, because turning LEFT here takes you along mostly flat ground past a bench to Shady Hollow and the New Millennium Wall instead.

After the right turn, walk 2-5 minutes watching for a less-travelled UNMARKED trail on the LEFT. Take it uphill into the woods. It climbs short rock steps and then enters a clearing that gives a clear view of the Headwall and Snag Buttress routes. Keep going uphill and stay RIGHT at the final fork — the left branch leads to Ramp Wall. Fifteen to twenty minutes total.
approach_variants.season: Year-round; Mount Erie is open all year and no raptor closure was listed on the city's Community Forest Lands page as of September 26, 2026
hazards: Unmarked junction — the left turn off trail 247 is easy to walk past
Short rock steps on the approach path
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The trail meets the cliff at a prominent RIGHT-FACING CORNER, and that corner is the first pitch of Zig Zag. Where the path stops being a path is the route.

That corner is also the anchor point for the rest of Main Wall West — everything else here is found by walking along the base from it.

If you came out at a clearing looking across at a buttress rather than standing under a corner, you are still below the wall: carry on uphill and stay right at the fork.

watch_out: CRITICAL AVALANCHE TERRAIN: Slope angle of 35-45 degrees with extensive vertical relief and frequent terrain traps—couloir is prime avalanche slope with multiple fatal accidents (3 deaths in Feb 2023); only climb in ideal snow conditions with confirmed low/minimal avalanche hazard
Entry and exit of steep couloir can be technical with snow or ice up to 60 degrees—difficult down-climbing if route-finding error occurs; requires excellent snow/ice judgment
Rock and ice fall from walls above couloir—stay alert and compact party; position out of direct fall line; watch for ice/rock loosening due to solar warming
Bergschrund crossing at glacier base—may be significant obstacle early/mid-season with potential fall hazard; probe and belay crossing if uncertain
Late-season glacier becomes bare ice (July+)—surface becomes extremely difficult and icy; crampons and ice tools essential; increased rockfall risk from warming
Crevasses in upper Colchuck Glacier approach (though fewer than on other glacier routes)—travel roped; probe continuously
Limited escape options once committed to upper couloir—retreat can be hazardous in poor conditions; plan to turn back early if conditions deteriorate
Navigation difficulty in whiteout conditions—few visual landmarks; GPS/map essential; descending in low visibility is particularly risky
